- Contract scope: convert a 2,500-foot 1970s tunnel between 116th and 125th into a station box, bore an 8,400-foot tunnel to Malcolm X Boulevard, mine the 125th Street station cavern, dig ancillary shafts.
- 1.5 million-pound German-made variable-density TBM; delivery expected early 2027; reduces crew 40%, saving an estimated $100 million in labor.
- Phase 2 about 10% cheaper than Phase 1; changes saved an estimated $1.3 billion; four of six cross passages eliminated; 32 "value engineering" proposals.
- Jamie Torres-Springer: "Phase One opened in 2017, but the residents of East Harlem have been left without subway service". Next contracts: 106th Street station box (procurement) and station fit-out (design).

wikis.title: MTA project page: Second Avenue Subway Phase 2
wikis.summary: MTA page describing Phase 2 extension of the Q line into East Harlem, with timeline, contracts, benefits and community outreach.
wikis.body:
- Updated Sep 15, 2026. Phase 2 extends Q service north from 96 Street to 125 Street with three new ADA-accessible stations at 106, 116 and 125 streets; 125 Street connects to the 4/5/6, Metro-North and M60 SBS.
- Timeline: April 2004 FEIS; November 2018 SEA/FONSI; January 2022 enters Engineering phase of the CIG program; November 2023 full funding grant agreement with $3.4 billion federal funding; January 2024 C.A.C. Industries selected for utility relocation (Contract 1); August 2025 Contract 2 to Connect Plus Partners (tunnel boring 116 St to 125 St); 2026 civil construction on new tunnel begins; June 2026 Contract 3 to Skanska-Walsh-Traylor JV for the 106 St station; 2027 tunnel boring from 120 St and 2 Av to 125 St and just beyond Lenox Av begins with 116 St station construction.
- Three of four contracts awarded. Benefits: about 300,000 riders daily on Phases 1 and 2 combined; commute savings "as much as 20 minutes" for some.
- East Harlem "has been a subway desert ever since the Second Avenue El stopped service above 57 Street in 1940". Community Information Center at 69 East 125 Street.

wikis.title: California High-Speed Rail: overview and background
wikis.summary: First part of the Wikipedia article on California High-Speed Rail, covering the system, phases, costs, funding status and legislative history.
wikis.body:
- Publicly funded high-speed rail under construction by the California High-Speed Rail Authority; authorized by a 2008 ballot (Prop 1A, $9 billion bonds, about 53% of the vote).
- Phase 1 about 494 miles (795 km) linking the Bay Area and Greater Los Angeles; must provide a non-stop San Francisco-Los Angeles trip in two hours 40 minutes. Phase 2 extends to Sacramento and San Diego; full system 776 miles. Top speed 220 mph (350 km/h).
- Initial Operating Segment Merced to Bakersfield (171 miles, 35% of Phase 1) cost $36.7 billion; revenue service "projected to commence in 2032" (infobox: operation 2031-2033). Construction began in the Central Valley in 2015; as of August 2025, $13.8 billion spent.
- Full Phase 1 not yet funded; estimated $89-$128 billion. Interim goal as of August 2025: connect the Bay Area to the IOS via Gilroy to Bakersfield or Palmdale by 2038; San Francisco-Bakersfield estimated $54 billion, San Francisco-Palmdale $84 billion.
- Project politically controversial; delays and cost overruns from management issues, legal challenges, permitting and utility relocation. Chief executive Ian Choudri; operator DB E.C.O. North America Inc.
- Background: first proposed 1979 by Governor Jerry Brown; High-Speed Rail Authority formed by 1996 Act.

wikis.title: California high-speed rail faces $6.5B shortfall, possible federal investigation
wikis.summary: Construction Dive article (Feb. 10, 2025) on a state Inspector General report of a $6.5 billion funding gap for the Merced-Bakersfield segment.
wikis.body:
- Published Feb. 10, 2025 (Dan Zukowski). Per a Feb. 3 California Office of the Inspector General report, the Authority faces a $6.5 billion funding gap for the initial 171-mile Bakersfield-Merced segment; finishing by the 2033 target is "increasingly unlikely".
- President Donald Trump said he would begin a federal investigation: "the worst-managed project I think I've ever seen".
- Project began with 2008 voter approval of a bond measure. Authority: "Of approximately $13 billion spent on the project, $10.5 billion have been funded exclusively by the State of California."
- 2024 business plan estimated $28.5 billion to $35.3 billion for the 171 miles; service committed between 2030 and 2033. Schedule changes "have already used a third of the excess time".
- Authority sought $8 billion from the 2021 infrastructure law but was awarded $3.3 billion. In 2019 the Trump administration canceled a $929 million grant and sought about $2.5 billion back.
- Authority response on X, Feb. 4: "Ignore the noise. We're busy building."

wikis.title: Al Maktoum International Airport (Dubai World Central)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on Dubai's Al Maktoum International Airport: history, operations and the 2024 expansion plan.
wikis.body:
- IATA DWC, ICAO OMDW; also Dubai World Central; in Jebel Ali, 37 km southwest of Dubai; owned/operated by Dubai Airports Company; hub for Emirates SkyCargo. Runways 12/30 (4,500 m) and 13/31 (1,838 m).
- Opened 27 June 2010 (text also says 24 June) with one runway and cargo flights only; first flight 20 June 2010 an Emirates SkyCargo Boeing 777F from Hong Kong. Passenger flights officially began 26 October 2013 with Flynas and Wizz Air.
- Planned as the main part of Dubai South; full completion "not before 2035"; 36,000 acres; projected 12 million tonnes freight and 160 to 260 million passengers annually. Government estimated total cost US$82 billion. Runway completed 2007; originally expected fully operational by 2017, delayed by the 2008 financial crisis to 2027.
- Passenger numbers first half 2016: 410,278 (209,989 in first half 2015). Low usage led to it being described as a "white elephant". As of 2021 only a handful of airlines flew passengers.
- 28 April 2024: Emirates announced Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid al-Maktoum approved a new 128 billion AED (US$34.85 billion) passenger terminal; five parallel runways, 400 gates, capacity up to 260 million passengers, about five times Dubai International. Emirates plans to use it as its only hub, with Dubai International to close.

wikis.title: Al Maktoum International Airport development milestones (Dubai Media Office, June 2026)
wikis.summary: Dubai government press release of June 15, 2026 saying phase one of the new Al Maktoum International Airport is on course to begin operations in 2032.
wikis.body:
- Monday, June 15, 2026. Dubai Government affirmed phase one is proceeding in line with approved timelines; "on course to commence operations in 2032".
- Milestones: enabling works, runway infrastructure, initial structural foundations for passenger terminals and gates; second runway completed in preparation for rehabilitating the existing runway.
- Contracts valued at AED13 billion under execution; preparations to award strategic packages worth more than AED55 billion by year-end: Western Passenger Terminal substructure and superstructure, fourth concourse building, Automated People Mover, Baggage Handling System, first three concourses, long-span frameworks (about 1.5 million sq m), southern airfield, power generation and district cooling. Facade and roofing packages also planned this year.
- Works: more than 17,000 concrete piles, over 45 million cubic metres excavation, about 4.5 million cubic metres concrete in core infrastructure; over 10 million work hours in 15 months; workforce about 9,000, expected to rise to about 120,000 at peak.
- Statements by Sheikh Hamdan bin Mohammed (Crown Prince), Sheikh Ahmed bin Saeed Al Maktoum (Chairman of Dubai Airports), Suzanne Al Anani (CEO Dubai Aviation Engineering Projects), Khalifa Al Zaffin (Dubai Aviation City Corporation); project linked to the Dubai Economic Agenda D33; transition of operations from Dubai International to be "smooth and carefully managed".

wikis.title: Dubai's Al Maktoum airport expansion on track for 2032 launch
wikis.summary: Gulf News report (June 15, 2026) on progress of the new Al Maktoum International Airport and its planned 2032 phase 1 opening.
wikis.body:
- Last updated June 15, 2026 (Nivetha Dayanand). Phase 1 scheduled to begin operations in 2032.
- Once the final phase is complete: annual capacity of more than 260 million passengers and 12 million tonnes of air cargo; five parallel runways, two passenger terminals, seven concourses, more than 430 aircraft stands, an Automated People Mover and rail/road links.
- Contracts of Dh13 billion under execution; strategic contracts exceeding Dh55 billion to be awarded next (Western Passenger Terminal, fourth concourse, People Mover, baggage handling, power and district cooling and more).
- More than 10 million work hours over 15 months; 17,000+ concrete piles; 45 million cubic metres excavation; about 9,000 workers now, about 120,000 at peak; second runway completed.
- Wider upgrades: Dh16 billion budget for aviation infrastructure projects at Dubai International and Dubai World Central, over Dh7.5 billion already awarded; terminal expansion at DWC for flydubai including Boeing 787 introduction.
- Sheikh Hamdan quoted on the Dubai Economic Agenda D33.

wikis.title: Gateway Development Commission: Hudson Tunnel Project (Gateway Program home page)
wikis.summary: Gateway Program homepage describing the Hudson Tunnel Project, its ten construction packages, jobs and target opening dates.
wikis.body:
- Gateway Development Commission (GDC) is building the Hudson Tunnel Project: nine miles of new passenger rail track between New York and New Jersey, including nearly five miles of tunnel boring for a new two-tube tunnel under the Hudson River, and rehabilitation of the North River Tunnel (in service since 1910).
- "The new train tunnel will open for service in 2035 and the rehabilitation of the North River Tunnel will be completed in 2038."
- Ten distinct construction packages; seven in progress or completed: Tonnelle Avenue Bridge and Utility Relocation (North Bergen, 400 jobs), Hudson Yards Concrete Casing Section 3 (4,800 jobs), Hudson River Ground Stabilization (2,300), Palisades Tunnel Project (first boring; 5,500), New Jersey Surface Alignment (about 1.5 miles), Manhattan Tunnel Project (7,200), Hudson River Tunnel Section.
- Figures: 95,000 total jobs; $19.6 billion economic activity; $87 million monthly purchases; 200,000 daily passengers; could prevent a tunnel shutdown costing $16 billion.
- Hudson Tunnel Project is the cornerstone of the Gateway Program on the 10-mile Northeast Corridor stretch between Newark and New York Penn Station.

wikis.title: Hudson Tunnel Project on track to be completed by 2035 (Mass Transit)
wikis.summary: Mass Transit magazine article (Feb. 18, 2025) on scope, contracts, timeline and $16.3 billion funding of the Hudson Tunnel Project.
wikis.body:
- Feb. 18, 2025, Brandon Lewis. Construction began November 2023; three components: two-track Hudson River tunnel between Bergen Palisades and New York Penn Station, the final Hudson Yards Concrete Casing segment, and rehabilitation of the North River Tunnel (damaged in Superstorm Sandy, 2012). Two new tubes under the river "for the first time in 115 years".
- GDC created in 2019 by New York and New Jersey; seven-member board including Amtrak. Ten mini-projects; three under construction at the time.
- Tonnelle Avenue Bridge and Utility Relocation expected to conclude fall 2025; Hudson Yards Concrete Casing Section 3 expected 2026; Hudson River Ground Stabilization (Weeks Marine, heavy construction from summer 2024; no work January-June due to a sturgeon "fish window").
- February 2025: $1.18 billion Manhattan Tunnel Project contract to Frontier-Kemper-Tutor-Perini JV, expected complete by 2029. Palisades Tunnel Project (Schiavone Dragados Lane JV): two tunnels each about 5,100 feet, 25 feet 2 inches inside diameter, expected complete by 2027.
- Funding: GDC secured the entire $16.3 billion: $6.9bn FTA CIG, $3.8bn FRA, $2.7bn Port Authority, $1.3bn New York, $1bn Amtrak, $308m New Jersey, $292m MEGA grant, $25m RAISE.

wikis.title: Notre-Dame de Paris: overview and key dates
wikis.summary: First part of the Wikipedia article on Notre-Dame de Paris cathedral: description, key dates from 1163, the 2019 fire and the December 2024 reopening.
wikis.body:
- Medieval Catholic cathedral and basilica on the Île de la Cité, 4th arrondissement, Paris; French Gothic (rib vault, flying buttress, rose windows). Length 128 m, width 48 m. Founded 1163 (cornerstone), construction began under Bishop Maurice de Sully, "largely completed by 1260"; infobox years built 1163-1345. Archbishop Laurent Ulrich; rector Olivier Ribadeau Dumas.
- Key dates: 1790s revolutionary desecration; 2 December 1804 Napoleon crowns himself Emperor; 1844-1864 restoration by Lassus and Viollet-le-Duc; 26 August 1944 Liberation Mass; 1963 facade cleaning; 1991-2000 restoration.
- 15 April 2019 fire destroyed much of the roof and the flèche (spire); reconstruction began 2021 and lasted 3 years; reopening ceremonies 7-8 December 2024.
- About 12 million visitors annually in the early 21st century, the most visited monument in Paris. Owned by the French government since 1905. Holds relics including the crown of thorns and a sliver and nail from the True Cross. UNESCO World Heritage (Paris, Banks of the Seine, 1991).

wikis.title: Reopening of Notre-Dame de Paris (7-8 December 2024)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the 7 December 2024 reopening ceremony and inaugural mass at Notre-Dame after the 2019 fire.
wikis.body:
- Reopened 7 December 2024, five years after the 15 April 2019 fire; ceremony presided by Archbishop Laurent Ulrich with President Emmanuel Macron and other dignitaries. Inaugural mass on 8 December consecrated a new altar (relics of five saints placed inside).
- Background: fire began just before 18:20 CEST on 15 April 2019; Macron set a five-year deadline on 17 April 2019; by September 2021 donors had given over €840 million. Macron toured the cathedral 29 November 2024 with chief architect Philippe Villeneuve.
- 7 December: ceremony began just after 19:00 CET with the bells and the doors; Ulrich struck the door three times with a crosier made from a surviving roof beam; choir sang Psalm 122 and Totus Tuus; 160 firefighters and artisans applauded; Macron gave a speech; a message from Pope Francis (who did not attend) was read. The restored organ was blessed and heard for the first time since 2019. Vestments by Jean-Charles de Castelbajac. A recorded concert with Lang Lang, Yo-Yo Ma, Pharrell Williams and others aired after the service because of Storm Darragh.
- 8 December: about 170 bishops attended; first public mass at 18:30. Octave of special services 8-15 December including return of the crown of thorns on 13 December; public admitted from 15:30 on 9 December; normal hours from 16 December with reservations.

wikis.title: Notre-Dame de Paris reopens after accelerated but incomplete reconstruction (Architectural Record)
wikis.summary: Architectural Record report (December 9, 2024) on the reopened cathedral, its restoration choices, controversies, costs and organization.
wikis.body:
- By Andrew Ayers, December 9, 2024. Notre-Dame reopened "five years and not quite eight months after the blaze", but work "won't finally complete until 2028 at the earliest" (scaffolding still on much of the exterior). Almost $900 million donated.
- Conservationists won early: restored to last-known state; Viollet-le-Duc's 1859 lead-and-oak spire recreated; medieval roof ("forest", from over 1,000 oaks) rebuilt in oak; 7,952-pipe main organ taken apart and reassembled; new fire-detection system in the roof.
- Controversy: clergy replaced six of Viollet-le-Duc's south-aisle chapel windows with contemporary designs (competition; artists Daniel Buren, Philippe Parreno, Yan Pei-Ming submitted designs); grisailles to be shown in a future Musée de l'Œuvre Notre-Dame.
- New elements: Guillaume Bardet's bronze altar and lectern, Ionna Vautrin's 1,500 oak chairs, Jean-Charles de Castelbajac vestments, Patrick Rimoux lighting (1,400 programmable LED units).
- Cross placed atop the spire December 2023; 39-foot chevet cross lifted in May; north belfry's eight bells replaced in September.
- Organisation: special body under retired general Jean-Louis Georgelin (died 2023; succeeded by Philippe Jost); 250 contractors. $740 million spent, $148 million left for exterior work such as the east-end flyers.

wikis.title: Tesla Cybercab
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on Tesla's two-passenger autonomous Cybercab robotaxi: unveiling, production, launch, regulatory scrutiny and design.
wikis.body:
- Two-passenger battery-electric robotaxi from Tesla for its Robotaxi service; no steering wheel, pedals, side mirrors or rear window; camera-only autonomy (unlike Waymo and Zoox lidar/radar). Front-motor 219 hp, 47.6 kWh (page also says 48 kWh), range about 293 mi, curb weight 3,113 lb; assembled at Gigafactory Texas, Austin; designer Franz von Holzhausen. Target operating cost under $0.30 per mile.
- Unveiled 10 October 2024 at the "We, Robot" event, Warner Bros. Studios Burbank; Musk then said production before 2027. On the 23 October 2024 call: volume production in 2026, aiming for at least 2 million a year.
- November 2025 shareholder meeting: production to begin second quarter 2026. First production vehicle February 2026; formal production April 2026.
- 3 September 2026 invitation-only launch event in Austin (Musk absent, no livestream); paid Cybercab rides in Austin started the next day (Robotaxi service operating since June 2025 with Model Y). About 45 Cybercabs registered as of August 2026. Asia road show from 9 September 2026 (Hong Kong, planned Japan and China).
- September 2026: NHTSA audit of Tesla's self-certification of compliance with federal standards written for human-driven vehicles.
- Design: unboxed process, gold body panels via reaction injection molding, drag coefficient under 0.20, 165 Wh per mile, designed life 500,000 miles, Starlink v5 antenna, braille buttons.

wikis.title: Tesla Cybercab production starts Q2 2026, Musk confirms (Teslarati)
wikis.summary: Teslarati article (November 7, 2025) on Elon Musk saying at the 2025 shareholder meeting that Cybercab production starts April 2026.
wikis.body:
- Published November 7, 2025 (Simon Alvarez). Musk at Tesla's 2025 Annual Shareholder Meeting: Cybercab production "will begin in April 2026", at Giga Texas.
- Described as a clean-slate design with no steering wheel, pedals or side mirrors, "optimized for the lowest cost per mile in an autonomous mode"; the first Tesla designed specifically for unsupervised self-driving.
- Manufacturing "closer to a high volume consumer electronics device than it is a car manufacturing line"; Musk expects "ultimately, less than a 10-second cycle time, basically a unit every 10 seconds"; Model Y line is 34 seconds (per a posted claim). Could mean 2 or 3 million a year, theoretically 5 million at a 5-second cycle time.

wikis.title: Electrek: Tesla rolls first Cybercab unit off the line
wikis.summary: Electrek article (Feb 17 2026) on Tesla's first production Cybercab at Giga Texas, critical of Tesla's unproven autonomy.
wikis.body:
- Fred Lambert, Feb 17 2026: Tesla said the first Cybercab production unit rolled off the line at Gigafactory Texas; no steering wheel and no pedals. "Continuous production is not expected to start until April."
- Electrek's claims: Tesla's Austin Robotaxi pilot (Model Y) had roughly 14 crashes over an estimated 800,000 cumulative miles (one per 57,000 miles vs Tesla's benchmark of one per 229,000 for humans); 19% availability over a 48-hour period; about 200 vehicles across Austin and San Francisco; "unsupervised" rides were followed by trailing cars with safety monitors.
- Musk said in January Tesla needs roughly 10 billion miles of data for safe unsupervised self-driving (projected around July 2026); AI5 chip delayed to mid-2027 so Cybercab launches on AI4.
- Electrek's description: two-passenger, butterfly doors, 35 kWh battery with 200 miles range and inductive charging, target cost under $30,000, cycle time target one unit every 10 seconds. The "Cybercab" trademark was not yet secured. (This is the outlet's own account and opinion; other sources give different battery/range figures.)

wikis.title: Artemis III: planned crewed Earth-orbit demonstration mission
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on Artemis III, now a low Earth orbit test of Orion docking with commercial lander test vehicles, planned for no earlier than June 2027.
wikis.body:
- Upcoming crewed NASA Artemis mission; "Planned for 2027", a demonstration flight in low Earth orbit rather than a lunar landing; launch NET June 2027 from Kennedy LC-39B on SLS; duration about two weeks; splashdown planned in the Pacific off San Diego. Prior to February 2026 the mission was the first landing mission (Artemis IV now planned as the first crewed lunar landing).
- Profile: Orion docks with a Blue Origin lander test vehicle (about 2 days; "Blue Moon Mark 1.5") and a SpaceX Starship v3 test article (about 1 day); crew tests AxEMU spacesuit interfaces. Orbit about 230 nmi (430 km), 33 degrees inclination. Three launches in total. SLS flies with a non-propulsive spacer instead of the ICPS (announced May 2026), preserving the ICPS for Artemis IV.
- Crew announced June 9, 2026: Randy Bresnik (commander), Luca Parmitano (ESA, pilot), Frank Rubio and Andre Douglas (mission specialists); backup Bob Hines. No women; NASA administrator Jared Isaacman acknowledged "reactions ranging from disappointment to outrage".
- Hardware: core stage upper section delivered April 28 2026; RS-25 engines refurbished; ESM-3 delivered September 2024; Orion internal readiness date January 2028 as of early 2026. As of April 2026 neither lander test vehicle had completed human-rating certification.
- Originally Exploration Mission-3 and the first crewed lunar landing since Apollo 17 (1972).

wikis.title: Solar eclipse of August 2, 2027
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the total solar eclipse of August 2, 2027, nicknamed the Eclipse of the Century, with path, duration and local times.
wikis.body:
- Total solar eclipse on Monday, August 2, 2027; magnitude 1.079, gamma 0.1421; greatest eclipse 10:07:50 UTC at 25.5N 33.2E; maximum duration 6 min 23 s (text also 6 min 22 s near Luxor); path width 258 km. Saros 136. Nicknamed the "Eclipse of the Century".
- Path: eastern Atlantic, Strait of Gibraltar, North Africa and Middle East. Totality cities: Cadiz, Malaga, Gibraltar, Ceuta, Tangier, Oran, Sfax, Benghazi, Luxor, Jeddah, Mecca, Sana'a, northeast Somalia, British Indian Ocean Territory islands.
- Second longest total eclipse of the 21st century (after July 22, 2009, 6 min 39.5 s); "the longest total solar eclipse on easily accessible land in the 21st century; a longer one will not occur until June 3, 2114".
- Partial visibility: eastern Maine, Atlantic Canada, Greenland, Iceland, Ireland, Great Britain, nearly all Europe, most of Africa, Middle East, South and Southeast Asia. First of three total eclipses over Tunisia this century; second total eclipse in Spain within a year (after August 2026).
- Local totality times: Cadiz 2:56 duration, Sfax 5:41, Benghazi 6:11, Luxor 6:22 (max in Luxor 13:05:26 local), Jeddah 5:53, Mecca 5:10. Partial: London 41.92%, Paris 51.31%, Madrid 86.38%, Cairo 94.79%.

wikis.title: NASA catalog of long total solar eclipses, 2001 to 3000
wikis.summary: NASA GSFC catalog listing total solar eclipses longer than 6 minutes 0 seconds between 2001 and 3000, including the August 2, 2027 eclipse.
wikis.body:
- Between 2001 and 3000 Earth will experience 2,388 solar eclipses: 847 partial, 834 annular, 650 total, 57 hybrid.
- Longest central eclipses: total 2186 Jul 16 (07m29s); annular 2010 Jan 15 (11m08s); hybrid 2013 Nov 03 (01m40s).
- Catalog rows for totals over 06m00s include: 2009 Jul 22 (06m39s); 2027 Aug 02, greatest eclipse 10:07:50 TD, Saros 136, gamma 0.1421, magnitude 1.0790, 25.5N 33.2E, path 258 km, duration 06m23s; 2045 Aug 12 (06m06s); 2096 May 22 (06m07s); 2114 Jun 03 (06m32s); 2132 Jun 13 (06m55s); 2150 Jun 25 (07m14s); 2168 Jul 05 (07m26s); 2186 Jul 16 (07m29s); 2204 Jul 27 (07m22s); 2222 Aug 08 (07m06s); 2237 Apr 25 (06m05s).
- Data based in part on the Five Millennium Canon of Solar Eclipses.

wikis.title: NSO map of the August 2, 2027 total solar eclipse
wikis.summary: National Solar Observatory page giving an overview and interactive map of the August 2, 2027 total eclipse across Europe, Africa and the Middle East.
wikis.body:
- The August 2, 2027 total solar eclipse will cross Spain, Gibraltar, Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, Libya, Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Yemen and Somalia, plus the Atlantic and Indian oceans; cities under totality include Cadiz, Tangier, Gibraltar, Benghazi, Luxor and Jeddah.
- Maximum totality near Luxor, Egypt: 6 minutes 22 seconds, "the second longest solar eclipse of the 21st century" (the longest was in 2009).
- Safety: looking at the Sun is unsafe except during totality; use eclipse glasses or solar viewers; homemade filters and ordinary sunglasses are not safe.
- Map is for general display; does not account for atmospheric refraction or the Moon's irregular edge. Total eclipses occur about every 18 months; partial eclipses every few months.

wikis.title: NASA awards launch services contract for Dragonfly mission
wikis.summary: NASA release (Nov 25, 2024) selecting SpaceX Falcon Heavy to launch the Dragonfly rotorcraft mission to Saturn's moon Titan in July 2028.
wikis.body:
- Contract release C24-042, Nov 25, 2024 (Abbey A. Donaldson). NASA selected SpaceX to provide launch services for Dragonfly, a rotorcraft lander mission under the New Frontiers Program to explore Titan.
- Firm-fixed-price contract value approximately $256.6 million, including launch services and other mission-related costs.
- Targeted launch period July 5, 2028 to July 25, 2028, on a SpaceX Falcon Heavy from Launch Complex 39A at Kennedy Space Center.
- Rotorcraft-lander will travel between and sample diverse sites on Titan; payload will characterize habitability, investigate prebiotic chemistry, and search for chemical indications of whether water-based or hydrocarbon-based life once existed.
- Managed at Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory; fourth mission in the New Frontiers Program (managed by Marshall Space Flight Center); launch service managed by NASA's Launch Services Program.

wikis.title: NASA authorizes Dragonfly to proceed with estimated 2028 launch readiness
wikis.summary: JHU APL news (Nov 28, 2023): NASA approved Dragonfly's Phase C with a revised July 2028 launch readiness date.
wikis.body:
- November 28, 2023. NASA authorized Dragonfly to proceed to Phase C (final design and fabrication) toward a July 2028 launch; earlier in 2023 it passed its Preliminary Design Review; the team replanned to fiscal year 2024 budget levels. NASA to assess the launch readiness date in mid-2024 at the Agency Program Management Council.
- Dragonfly is a car-sized, nuclear-powered rotorcraft to fly over and land on Titan's organic-rich sands; "NASA's only mission to the surface of another ocean world".
- Progress: guidance, navigation and control tests over California deserts; flight-system tests in Langley wind tunnels; full-scale lander model in APL's new 3,000-cubic-foot Titan Chamber.
- Quotes: Nicola Fox (NASA SMD), Elizabeth "Zibi" Turtle (principal investigator), Bobby Braun (APL).
- Partners include Goddard, Lockheed Martin, Sikorsky, Ames, Langley, Penn State, Malin Space Science Systems, Honeybee Robotics, JPL, CNES, DLR and JAXA. Fourth New Frontiers mission.

wikis.title: Solar eclipse of July 22, 2028 (Great Australasian Eclipse)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the total solar eclipse of July 22, 2028 crossing Australia and New Zealand, including Sydney.
wikis.body:
- Total eclipse Saturday, July 22, 2028, "also called the Great Australasian Eclipse by some media outlets"; magnitude 1.056; gamma -0.6056; greatest eclipse 2:56:40 UTC at 15.6S 126.7E; maximum duration 5 min 10 s (310 s); path width 230 km; Saros 146.
- Path: Kimberley region of north-west Australia south-east through Western Australia, Northern Territory, south-west Queensland and New South Wales near Wyndham, Kununurra, Tennant Creek, Birdsville, Bourke and Dubbo, through the centre of Sydney (over three minutes), then Queenstown and Dunedin in New Zealand; also Christmas Island and the Cocos (Keeling) Islands.
- Sydney's first total eclipse since March 26, 1857 and the last until June 3, 2858. First total eclipse anywhere in New Zealand since 1965; first for Dunedin since 1163.
- Local totality durations: Christmas Island 3:53, Doon Doon near Kununurra 5:10, Tennant Creek 3:26, Bourke 4:05, Dubbo 3:51.
- Paths of the November 2030, July 2037 and December 2038 total eclipses intersect this path within 10 years.
- Impact: by August 2026 one Dunedin hotel was booked out for its "solar eclipse package", 35,000 visitors predicted; a winter night-sky festival planned from Matariki to the eclipse ten days later.

wikis.title: NASA interactive eclipse path map: total solar eclipse of 2028 July 22
wikis.summary: NASA GSFC page hosting an interactive path map for the total solar eclipse of 2028 July 22, with method notes and no event narrative.
wikis.body:
- Interactive MapLibre map of the path of the 2028 July 22 total solar eclipse; northern and southern limits blue, central line red; clicking calculates local eclipse times.
- Implementation based on Xavier Jubier's Five Millennium Canon of Solar Eclipses Web Tool; OpenFreeMap tiles.
- Predictions generated for the Moon's center of mass using VSOP87/ELP2000-82 ephemerides and ΔT = 76.6 s; credit "Eclipse Predictions by Fred Espenak (NASA's GSFC)". Page dated 2026 Aug 14.

wikis.title: 99942 Apophis: discovery, naming, physical characteristics and orbit
wikis.summary: First part of the Wikipedia article on asteroid 99942 Apophis, a potentially hazardous near-Earth asteroid, covering discovery, name, size, rotation and close approaches including 13 April 2029.
wikis.body:
- Potentially hazardous Aten near-Earth asteroid; discovered 19 June 2004 by Roy A. Tucker, David J. Tholen and Fabrizio Bernardi at Kitt Peak (provisional designation 2004 MN4; precovery from 15 March 2004). Numbered 99942 on 24 June 2005; named Apophis on 19 July 2005 after the Greek name of the Egyptian serpent Apep. Tholen denied reports it was named after the Stargate SG-1 villain, calling the connection coincidental.
- Size: diameter initially estimated 450 m, later 350 m; NASA impact risk page as of 2013 listed 330 m; radar suggests an elongated, possibly bilobed 450 x 170 m object. Rotation about 30.4 hours; a tumbler.
- Orbit: inclination 3.3 degrees, between 0.746 AU and 1.099 AU. Will pass Earth on 2029-04-13 at 0.000254 AU (38,015 km, uncertainty ±3.3 km); it will change from an Aten to an Apollo-type asteroid after the 2029 encounter.
- Later approaches: 2036-03-27 at 0.3097 AU; 2051-04-20 at 0.04149 AU; 2066-09-16; 11 September 2102 close encounter; April 2116 about 0.02 AU (could be 0.001 to 0.1 AU).
- After the 2029 impact possibility was ruled out, a small chance of a keyhole passage leading to a 13 April 2036 impact kept it at Torino Level 1 until August 2006, when the probability was determined negligible and it was lowered to Level 0.

wikis.title: Asteroid Apophis (NASA Science overview)
wikis.summary: NASA Science's overview page on near-Earth asteroid Apophis, its April 13, 2029 close pass and the spacecraft observing it.
wikis.body:
- NASA says it is confident Apophis poses no impact risk to Earth for at least 100 years.
- Discovered June 19, 2004 by astronomers Roy Tucker, David Tholen and Fabrizio Bernardi at Kitt Peak National Observatory in Tucson, Arizona; at first it appeared it could potentially impact Earth in coming decades.
- Described as a potentially hazardous near-Earth asteroid that "will safely pass close to Earth on April 13, 2029", about 20,000 miles (32,000 km) from Earth's surface, closer than many geosynchronous satellites (about 22,236 miles / 36,000 km altitude).
- Radar images were recorded in March 2021 by the Deep Space Network's Goldstone complex (California) and the Green Bank Telescope (West Virginia) when the asteroid was 10.6 million miles (17 million km) away.
- NASA has redirected a spacecraft (OSIRIS-APEX) to study Apophis at its April 2029 closest approach; Earth-based telescopes will also observe it. OSIRIS-APEX "may use its thrusters to stir up rocks and dust on the surface" so scientists can see just below.
- A 3D model data set based on ground-based radar images is offered.

wikis.title: NASA analysis: Earth is safe from asteroid Apophis for 100-plus years
wikis.summary: JPL's March 25, 2021 news item saying new radar and orbit work rule out any Apophis impact risk, including in 2068, for at least a century.
wikis.body:
- Asteroid 99942 Apophis, discovered 2004, is estimated at about 1,100 feet (340 m) across. An impact risk in 2029 was ruled out earlier, then the risk in 2036; until March 2021 a small chance of impact in 2068 remained.
- Around March 5, 2021 Apophis made a distant flyby (about 10.6 million miles / 17 million km, about 44 times the Earth-Moon distance); radar observations refined its orbit, ruling out 2068 and "our calculations don't show any impact risk for at least the next 100 years" (Davide Farnocchia, NASA's CNEOS, managed by JPL).
- Orbit uncertainty "collapsed from hundreds of kilometers to just a handful of kilometers when projected to 2029"; Apophis can be removed from the Sentry Impact Risk Table.
- Radar campaign led by JPL scientist Marina Brozovic used the 70-m Goldstone antenna, with the 100-m Green Bank Telescope receiving (a "bistatic" experiment that doubled received signal strength). Distance accurate to about 150 m (490 ft); image resolution 38.75 m (127 ft) per pixel.
- Earlier radar suggested a "bilobed", peanut-like shape (at least one in six near-Earth asteroids over 660 ft / 200 m have two lobes). Scientists are studying its spin state; the 2029 encounter could change it and even cause "asteroid quakes".
- April 13, 2029: passes less than 20,000 miles (32,000 km) from Earth's surface, closer than geosynchronous satellites, visible to the naked eye for observers in the Eastern Hemisphere.

wikis.title: Extremely Large Telescope (ELT), ESO
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on ESO's Extremely Large Telescope under construction on Cerro Armazones, Chile: history, cost, optics, dome, instruments and schedule.
wikis.body:
## Overview
- Under construction; "when completed, it will be the world's largest optical and mid-infrared" telescope. Part of the European Southern Observatory (ESO), on Cerro Armazones, Atacama Desert, Chile, 23 km from Paranal Observatory. Renamed from E-ELT in 2017.
- 39.3 m segmented primary mirror, 4.25 m secondary, adaptive optics and six laser guide star units. Gathers about 250 times the light-gathering area of Hubble and, per specifications, images 15 times sharper than Hubble.
- Dome 93 m diameter, 80 m height (largest dome ever built for a telescope).

## History and schedule
- Site chosen 26 April 2010 (Cerro Armazones). Design cut in 2011 from a 42 m to about 39 m primary, reducing projected cost from 1.275 billion to 1.055 billion euros. Council approved civil works 11 June 2012; construction on site began June 2014; ESO authorised construction December 2014 with over 90% funding; about 1 billion euros for the first phase. First stone laid 26 May 2017; 2017 construction cost estimate 1.15 billion euros incl. first-generation instruments.
- Originally planned to take 2014-2025; halfway point passed July 2023. Technical first light planned March 2029; first scientific observations December 2030. Dome complete as of April 2025, doors being installed.

## Optics
- Five mirrors: M1-M3 curved (three-mirror anastigmat, 10-arcminute field), M4 flat adaptive (2.4 m, 2 mm thick, up to 5,000 actuators, adjusted 1,000 times/s, six petals), M5 tip-tilt (2.7 x 2.2 m).
- M1: 798 hexagonal segments (~1.45 m across, 50 mm thick), plus 133 maintenance segments; Schott AG casts Zerodur blanks, Safran Reosc polishes about one segment per day to 7.5 nm rms; two segments to be recoated and replaced each working day. 4608 edge sensors from FAMES consortium (Fogale, Micro-Epsilon); 2394 actuators. Support units by CESA and VDL.
- M2: 4.25 m, 3.5 tonnes, largest secondary and largest convex mirror ever produced, polished by Safran Reosc to 15 nm; close to final accuracy by early 2024. M3: 4.0 m concave, cast and being polished as of July 2023. As of July 2023 over 70% of segment blanks and supports were manufactured; tens of segments polished by early 2024.
- Main structure: 20,000-tonne seismic mass pier, rotating mass about 3,700 tonnes.

## Science goals
Exoplanets (including attempts to image Earth-like ones), protoplanetary disks, first galaxies, black holes, direct measurement of the universe's expansion acceleration, and variation in fundamental constants. First-generation instruments: MICADO, HARMONI, METIS and adaptive optics system MORFEO.

wikis.title: Europa Clipper: history, design, instruments and launch (Wikipedia)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on NASA's Europa Clipper: mission history and funding, objectives, spacecraft design, nine instruments and the October 14, 2024 Falcon Heavy launch.
wikis.body:
## Overview
- Mission by NASA (JPL with Johns Hopkins APL), previously the Europa Multiple Flyby Mission. Launched by Falcon Heavy on October 14, 2024 (16:06 UTC, 12:06 p.m. EDT); planned to enter Jupiter orbit April 2030 and conduct flybys of Europa from March 2031. "Largest interplanetary spacecraft ever launched by NASA." Mars gravity assist March 2025 (closest approach March 1, 2025), Earth assist December 2026.
- Launch mass 6,065 kg incl. 2,750 kg propellant; dry mass 3,241 kg; payload 352 kg; 5 m tall, solar panel span 30.5 m; 600 W from solar panels.
- 49 close flybys of Europa (later text also says 45) at altitudes 25 to 2,700 km over a 3.5-year mission, using gravity assists from Ganymede, Europa and Callisto; ends 2034 or later by deliberate crash, likely into Ganymede, to prevent contamination of Europa. Name refers to fast 19th-century clipper ships.

## History and cost
- Cost estimate rose from about US$2 billion in 2013 to US$4.25 billion in 2020. National Research Council recommended a Europa mission in 2013; March 2013 US$75 million authorised; May 2014 House bill raised FY2014 funding from US$15M to US$100M.
- May 2015: nine instruments chosen (about US$110 million over three years); June 2015 concept approved; a lander added January 2016 was cancelled in 2017 as too risky. Phase B February 2017; Phase C August 19, 2019; Phase D March 3, 2022; main body completed June 7, 2022; all instruments installed by January 30, 2024; arrived at Kennedy May 2024.
- June 2024: components found less radiation-hardened than believed; re-testing found transistors likely to "self-heal". Launch stood down October 6, 2024 for Hurricane Milton; launched October 14.
- Launch vehicle: Congress had mandated SLS; NASA directed a commercial vehicle January 25, 2021; Falcon Heavy in fully expendable configuration chosen July 2021 (cost about $178 million). Trajectory announced February 10, 2021: 5.5-year route via Mars and Earth (SLS would have been under three years direct).

## Design
- Radiation: expected total dose 2.8 megarads; 150 kg vault with 9.2 mm aluminum-alloy walls. Solar power chosen over MMRTG (decided September 2013, announced October 3, 2014); panels by Airbus Defence and Space, 18 m2 each, 150 W each at Jupiter.
- Propulsion module (built at Goddard, delivered by APL): nearly 2,700 kg monomethyl hydrazine and dinitrogen tetroxide, 50-60% for the 6-8 hour Jupiter orbit insertion burn; 24 engines. 3.1 m high-gain antenna (X-band and Ka-band; up to about 500 kbit/s Ka).

## Science goals and instruments
- Goals: ice shell and ocean, composition, geology; assess habitability and help pick a landing site for the proposed Europa Lander.
- Nine instruments (82 kg): E-THEMIS (PI Philip Christensen), MISE (Diana Blaney), EIS cameras (Elizabeth Turtle; NAC to 0.5 m/pixel from 50 km), Europa-UVS (Kurt Retherford), REASON ice-penetrating radar 9 and 60 MHz (Donald Blankenship), ECM magnetometer on 8.5 m boom (Margaret Kivelson; replaced ICEMAG cancelled for cost overruns), PIMS (Joseph Westlake), MASPEX (Jim Burch), SUDA dust analyzer (Sascha Kempf); plus gravity/radio science.

wikis.title: Europa Clipper mission timeline (NASA)
wikis.summary: NASA's timeline of the Europa Clipper mission from concept selection in 2015 through launch, the Jupiter tour and possible end of mission in September 2034.
wikis.body:
- Launched Oct. 14, 2024 to survey Jupiter's moon Europa for places below the surface that could support life; arrives at Jupiter in 2030, then nearly 50 flybys of Europa.
- Concept: a flyby mission orbiting Jupiter in resonance with Europa, chosen over an orbiter or lander for strong science, lower cost and risk, and reduced radiation exposure.
- May 2015: multiple-flyby concept and nine science instruments selected (Phase A) incl. cameras, spectrometers, particle detectors, ice-penetrating radar, magnetometer.
- February 2017: design phase (Phase B). March 2017: officially named Europa Clipper, after 19th-century clipper ships.
- August 2019: fabrication begins (Phase C). March 2022: assembly and testing begins at JPL (Phase D); spacecraft larger than an SUV, solar arrays spanning a basketball court. Main body built and delivered by Johns Hopkins APL.
- Spring 2024: shipped to Kennedy Space Center (unloaded May 23, 2024); high-gain antenna (nearly 10 ft / 3 m) installed June 17, 2024; then integration with rocket.
- Science: repeated flybys of Europa's anti-Jovian side first (closest approach as low as about 16 miles / 25 km), then a second campaign over the sub-Jovian hemisphere.
- September 2034: possible end of mission, with the current plan to deorbit into Ganymede's surface.

wikis.title: Europa Clipper mission overview (JPL press kit)
wikis.summary: JPL press-kit overview of Europa Clipper's launch on Falcon Heavy, cruise with Mars and Earth gravity assists, Jupiter arrival on April 11, 2030 and tour.
wikis.body:
- Launch targeted for October 2024 from Launch Complex 39A, Kennedy Space Center, on a SpaceX Falcon Heavy procured by NASA's Launch Services Program. Launch period opens Oct. 10, 2024 through Oct. 30, with contingency dates in early November; instantaneous daily window around midday EDT.
- Rocket fully expendable except recoverable fairing; reuses side boosters from the 2023 Psyche launch. Separation a little over an hour after liftoff (about 1 h 1 min to 1 h 10 min); solar arrays take about 10 minutes to unfold.
- Journey to Jupiter takes 5 1/2 years via gravity assists: Mars flyby Feb. 28-March 4, 2025 (about 304-646 miles / 490-1,040 km altitude), Earth flyby Dec. 2-7, 2026 (about 1,951-2,144 miles / 3,140-3,450 km). Cruise lasts about five years and three months.
- Arrival fixed for April 11, 2030 for all launch dates; a Ganymede flyby about 12 hours before Jupiter orbit insertion (within about 120 miles / 200 km) slows it, then an engine burn of about six hours.
- Prime mission a little over four years, 2030 to 2034, with flybys of Europa, Ganymede and Callisto. Orbits designed to limit time in Jupiter's intense radiation; Galileo (1995-1997 primary, extended mission to 2003) is cited as a previous mission with less time in the hazardous zones.

wikis.title: Europa Clipper is ready to launch (JPL, Oct. 13, 2024)
wikis.summary: JPL's pre-launch article describing the Oct. 14, 2024 Falcon Heavy launch sequence, the journey to Jupiter and Europa Clipper's science goals.
wikis.body:
- Launch set for 12:06 p.m. EDT Monday, Oct. 14, 2024 from Launch Complex 39A, Kennedy Space Center, with additional instantaneous opportunities through Nov 6. Plans to launch Oct. 10 were delayed by Hurricane Milton.
- Spacecraft will fly by Europa 49 times, as close as 16 miles (25 km), and is the largest spacecraft NASA has built for a planetary mission; arrays span 100 feet (30.5 m). Journey 1.8 billion miles (2.9 billion km) via Mars then Earth gravity assists. Orbits Jupiter from April 2030; the 49 flybys start in 2031.
- Payload: nine science instruments plus a gravity science investigation; loaded with over 6,060 pounds (2,750 kg) of propellant; encapsulated in fairings Oct. 2.
- Sequence: side boosters separate, core stage expended in the Atlantic; fairing separates about 50 minutes after launch and is recovered and reused; spacecraft separates about an hour after launch; stable communication expected about 19 minutes after separation; solar arrays deploy one at a time about three hours after launch; three months of initial checkout and commissioning follow.
- Not a life-detection mission but will tell whether Europa is promising. Europa may have "twice as much liquid water as all of Earth's oceans combined". Objectives: ice shell thickness and ocean interactions, composition, geology.
- JPL (managed by Caltech) leads with Johns Hopkins APL, which designed the main spacecraft body.

wikis.title: Jupiter Icy Moons Explorer (Juice): mission, spacecraft and launch (Wikipedia)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on ESA's Juice mission to Ganymede, Callisto and Europa: selection, spacecraft design, payload, April 2023 launch and 2024 Moon-Earth flyby.
wikis.body:
- ESA interplanetary spacecraft to study Ganymede, Callisto and Europa; first spacecraft to the outer planets not launched by the US and first intended to orbit a moon other than Earth's.
- Launched 14 April 2023 (12:14:36 UTC) on an Ariane 5 from Guiana Space Centre after a weather postponement from 13 April; Airbus Defence and Space is main contractor (selected July 2015, assembled in Toulouse). Cost estimated by 2023 at 1.5 billion euros ($1.6 billion). Selected as ESA's first L-class mission on 2 May 2012.
- Expected to reach Jupiter in July 2031 after four gravity assists and eight years; enters orbit around Ganymede in December 2034; operations overlap with NASA's Europa Clipper.
- Design: about 3,000 kg chemical propellant, delta-V about 2,700 m/s, more than 25 gravity assists and two Europa flybys; 2.5 m high-gain antenna; 425 N main engine.
- Payload 280 kg: JANUS, MAJIS, UVS, RIME, GALA, SWI, J-MAG, PEP, RPWI, 3GM, PRIDE, RADEM. RIME antenna failed to deploy after launch and was freed on 12 May 2023.
- August 2024: first gravity assist using the Moon then Earth (Moon closest approach 21:15 UTC 19 August, +0.9 km/s relative to the Sun); all 10 instruments active at the Moon and eight at Earth.

wikis.title: Juice's journey and Jupiter system tour (ESA video)
wikis.summary: ESA video page describing Juice's planned eight-year cruise, gravity assists, Jupiter tour, Ganymede orbit and end-of-mission impact.
wikis.body:
- Juice set to launch April 2023 (launch window 5-25 April 2023) on an Ariane 5 from Europe's Spaceport in Kourou, the final Ariane 5 launch.
- Gravity assists: Earth-Moon (August 2024, a world-first Lunar-Earth gravity assist, Moon then Earth 1.5 days later), Venus (August 2025), Earth (September 2026, January 2029). Arrival at Jupiter July 2031; science begins about six months before.
- Two Europa flybys in July 2032; Callisto flybys 2032-2034 change orbit angle to view Jupiter's polar regions; Ganymede orbit insertion December 2034, first spacecraft to orbit another planet's moon (initial elliptical, then 5000 km circular, then 500 km circular orbit).
- Four years of observing Jupiter, Ganymede, Callisto and Europa. Ganymede is the only moon with a magnetosphere. Orbit decays and Juice makes a grazing impact on Ganymede in late 2035.

wikis.title: Juice mission calendar (ESA Cosmos)
wikis.summary: ESA Cosmos page listing key flight-activity dates for Juice, edited last April 2025, with cruise events and payload checkouts.
wikis.body:
- Page says it was last edited in April 2025 and draws on the JUICE Mission Calendar (Report 1.6).
- Baseline trajectory "150lb": launched with Ariane 5 on 14/04/2023; planned arrival at Jupiter 21/07/2031.
- Covers cruise eclipses and oppositions, the hot inner cruise expected to constrain spacecraft operations, and periodic payload checkouts (indicative dates, may be revised), including pointing campaigns #1 to #5, checkouts near the last Earth gravity assist and near superior conjunctions.

wikis.title: International Space Station: overview, origins and research (Wikipedia, part 1)
wikis.summary: First part of Wikipedia's ISS article: key figures, partners, how the station was conceived from Freedom and Mir-2, and its scientific research uses.
wikis.body:
- ISS: space station in low Earth orbit operated by NASA, Roscosmos, ESA, JAXA and CSA; first module launched 20 November 1998; continuous human presence since 2 November 2000. Current expedition listed as 75.
- Orbit about 400 km, inclination 51.64 degrees, 7.67 km/s, about every 93 minutes (15.5 times a day). 109 m by 73 m, pressurised volume 1,005 m3, 43 modules and elements, 16 major pressurized modules, eight docking/berthing ports. Russian Orbital Segment and US Orbital Segment.
- As of August 2025, 290 individuals from 26 countries had visited.
- Plans: at least one more module (Payload Power Thermal Module by Axiom Space); expected operational until the end of 2030, then de-orbit via the US Deorbit Vehicle; critique of the plan and a higher-orbit parking proposal has congressional support as of 2026.
- Origins: 1975 Apollo-Soyuz; NASA's Freedom (ESA invited 1984, Columbus approved by 1987, Japan's Kibo announced 1985) plus Soviet Mir-2 combined; September 1993 Al Gore and Viktor Chernomyrdin announced the new station.
- Research: microgravity science in astrobiology, astronomy, materials, space weather, human research; Alpha Magnetic Spectrometer (AMS) aimed at dark matter.

wikis.title: NASA selects SpaceX to build the ISS US Deorbit Vehicle
wikis.summary: NASA release of June 26, 2024 announcing SpaceX as developer of the U.S. Deorbit Vehicle for the International Space Station, under a contract worth up to $843 million.
wikis.body:
- NASA (release 24-090, Jun 26, 2024) selected SpaceX to develop and deliver the U.S. Deorbit Vehicle to deorbit the ISS in a controlled manner after the end of its operational life in 2030 and avoid risk to populated areas.
- Single-award contract with a total potential value of $843 million; the launch service is a future procurement. SpaceX develops the vehicle; NASA takes ownership after development and operates it. The vehicle and station are expected to break up destructively during re-entry.
- Quote from Ken Bowersox (NASA Space Operations): the decision helps ensure "a safe and responsible transition in low Earth orbit" and supports future commercial destinations.
- Context: five agencies (CSA, ESA, JAXA, NASA, Roscosmos) have operated the ISS since 1998; the US, Japan, Canada and ESA participating countries committed to operate through 2030. In its 24th year of continuous crewed operations, more than 3,300 experiments conducted.

wikis.title: SpaceX to build ISS Deorbit Vehicle (Spaceflight Now, July 18, 2024)
wikis.summary: Spaceflight Now report on SpaceX's custom Dragon-derived Deorbit Vehicle that will push the ISS to a controlled re-entry around 2030.
wikis.body:
- SpaceX is building a souped-up cargo Dragon to drive the ISS out of orbit for a controlled re-entry over an uninhabited stretch of ocean when retired in the 2030 timeframe. NASA awarded the contract in late June (up to $843 million); the launch rocket is not yet selected; NASA Administrator Bill Nelson asked Congress for about $1.5 billion for the deorbit operation.
- Station: long axis 218 feet, truss 310 feet, mass 925,000 pounds, about 17,100 mph. Vehicle carries about 35,000 pounds of propellant for 46 Draco engines (30 in an extended trunk). SpaceX's Sarah Walker: it needs six times the usable propellant and three to four times the power generation and storage of today's Dragon, and must operate with the station for about 18 months.
- Plan (Dana Weigel, ISS program manager): launch the DV about one and a half years before the final re-entry burn; dock to the forward port; final crew stays until altitude falls to about 205 miles, about six months before final re-entry; at about 140 miles the DV performs burns, with a final burn some days later. Debris pieces as large as a small car may survive along a narrow 1,200-mile footprint; a remote South Pacific zone is likely, target not specified.
- Why: drag at 260 miles; earlier plan to use three Progress cargo ships was dropped because the Russian segment could not control three at once. Two companies bid: SpaceX and Northrop Grumman.

wikis.title: ITER fusion project: overview, goals, cost and schedule (Wikipedia, part 1)
wikis.summary: First part of Wikipedia's ITER article covering the international tokamak fusion project's purpose, members, cost growth, delayed schedule and fusion-gain goals.
wikis.body:
- ITER: international nuclear fusion research project under construction near the Cadarache research center, southern France; under construction since 2013; assembly of the tokamak began 2020. Expected first plasma in 2033-2034 (2024 schedule: deuterium-deuterium operations from 2035), when it will be the world's largest fusion reactor. Formation 24 October 2007; partners formally agreed to fund it on 21 November 2006.
- Purpose is research and technology demonstration, not electricity generation. Goals: Q = 10 momentarily and Q = 5 at steady state; burning plasma; tritium breeding tests; superconducting magnets, cryogenics, remote handling. Uses deuterium-tritium fuel; uses over 300 MW of electrical power to heat plasma.
- Members: China, EU, India, Japan, Russia, South Korea, US. UK participated via F4E until September 2023; Switzerland via Euratom/F4E until 2021, poised to rejoin in 2026.
- Cost: originally about EUR 5-6 billion; projected total EUR 18 to 22 billion; other estimates $45 to $65 billion (disputed by ITER). Original plan had first plasma in 2020 and full fusion by 2023.
- Best tokamak Q is 0.67 (JET); best fusion result overall Q = 4.13 at NIF in April 2025; NIF reached burning plasma on 8 August 2021. Successor DEMO (EUROfusion) is to produce electricity experimentally.

wikis.title: Implications of the new ITER schedule (IPP commentary)
wikis.summary: Max Planck Institute for Plasma Physics scientific director Sibylle Guenter comments on ITER's 2024 new baseline, with research operation starting in 2034.
wikis.body:
- ITER Director-General Pietro Barabaschi announced a new baseline: research activities start in 2034; deuterium-deuterium plasmas and full magnetic energy in 2036 (three years later than the original plan); deuterium-tritium operation scheduled from 2039 (four years' delay). Original schedule had first plasma as early as 2025.
- Barabaschi cites the COVID-19 pandemic, quality issues and too-optimistic planning for a "first of a kind" project.
- Guenter (IPP): plan "re-prioritised and reorganised" work rather than just postponing; tungsten replaces beryllium for the first wall (enabled by ASDEX Upgrade research); much stronger plasma heating than originally planned. Delay "less than we feared"; the 2025 facility would have been slimmed down anyway.
- ITER still needed: nothing else will analyse Q=10 power balance and tritium breeding in the wall. Smaller devices such as ASDEX Upgrade and JT-60SA should be used for preparation. Says more than thirty private fusion companies have made headlines; the announcement is "no cause for celebration".

wikis.title: Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on DUNE, the Fermilab-to-South Dakota long-baseline neutrino experiment: goals, beam, detectors, cost increases and international collaboration.
wikis.body:
- Under construction: near detector at Fermilab (Illinois), far detector at Sanford Underground Research Facility (SURF), South Dakota, 1,300 km away and 1,490 m deep; more than 1,000 collaborators, scientists from over 30 countries as of 2022.
- Goals: neutrino oscillations and CP violation, neutrino mass ordering, supernova neutrinos, proton decay search. P5 ranked it in 2014 as "the highest priority project in its timeframe". Competitor: Hyper-Kamiokande (Japan), scheduled to begin data-taking in 2027.
- Beam (LBNF): 2.4 MW proton beam design from the Main Injector; PIP-II (approved to begin construction April 2022, expected complete by 2028, cost $1.28B as of 2022) provides 1.2 MW. Far detector: 70 kilotons of liquid argon in four LArTPC modules. Prototypes at CERN (ProtoDUNE first tracks September 2018). Near detector about 600 m from production.
- Cost rose from under $2B to over $3B (Phase I combined costs exceed $4B); described as "troubled" by Science and Scientific American. Foreign contribution to the $3B project $570M (about 20%); UK STFC announced GBP 65M in 2017. In August 2024 first neutrinos were detected with a DUNE prototype detector at Fermilab.
- Began as US-only LBNE; CD-1 approval December 2012 for $850M budget.

wikis.title: Fermilab marks 70 years of neutrino science and DUNE
wikis.summary: Fermilab news item on 70 years since the neutrino's discovery, Fermilab's neutrino experiment history and delivering a neutrino beam to DUNE by 2031.
wikis.body:
- Fermilab's top institutional priority is delivering a neutrino beam to DUNE at LBNF by 2031. DUNE "is the largest science project in our laboratory's history" (Director Norbert Holtkamp).
- PIP-II linear accelerator will produce the world's most intense neutrino beam, sent from Illinois to Lead, South Dakota, 800 miles away; DUNE will increase travel distance from NOvA's 500 miles to 800.
- History: Fermilab founded 1967; tau neutrino discovered by DONUT in 2000; NuTeV in the late 1990s; Main Injector completed 1999 with NuMI beam leading to MINOS, MINERvA (data 2010-2019) and NOvA (near detector at Fermilab, far in Ash River, Minnesota; the only operating US long-baseline experiment). Booster Neutrino Beam: MiniBooNE, then SBND, MicroBooNE (stopped 2021) and ICARUS, investigating a possible sterile neutrino.
- DUNE could also drive innovation in detector design, cryogenics, medical imaging and high-performance computing.

wikis.title: High Luminosity Large Hadron Collider (HL-LHC)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on CERN's HL-LHC upgrade: luminosity targets, physics goals, timeline to Run 4 in mid 2030 and key machine upgrades.
wikis.body:
- Upgrade of CERN's LHC (French-Swiss border near Geneva); led by Lucio Rossi 2011-2020, Oliver Bruning from 2020. Design study began 2010, FP7 grant 2011, CERN Council approval 2016. Physics data-taking expected at the earliest in 2030.
- Delivers 14 TeV proton-proton collisions with integrated luminosity 3 ab^-1 for ATLAS and CMS (50 fb^-1 LHCb, 5 fb^-1 ALICE). Peak luminosity expected 5 x 10^34 cm^-2 s^-1 (LHC nominal 1 x 10^34); collisions per bunch crossing up from 60 to 140.
- Goals: Standard Model measurements, beyond-Standard-Model searches, flavour physics, Higgs boson properties, QCD matter.
- Timeline: 2018-2020 prototypes tested, final TDR published; 2022 underground civil engineering terminated; 2023 surface buildings handed over; 2025 inner triplet quadrupole magnet production ongoing; replacement at end of nominal LHC running, projected mid 2026; 2026-2030 installation of magnets, crab cavities, cryo lines, absorbers, collimators, superconducting links. Run 4 from mid 2030 to end of 2033; Long Shutdown 4; Run 5 from mid 2036, approved through end of 2041.
- Quadrupole magnets of 11.3 tesla vs 8.6 tesla in the LHC.

wikis.title: HL-LHC Technical Design Report (CERN Yellow Reports, 2020)
wikis.summary: CERN Yellow Reports listing for Vol. 10 (2020), the High-Luminosity LHC technical design report, with editors and chapter authors.
wikis.body:
- Vol. 10 (2020), CERN Yellow Reports: Monographs. Editors: I. Bejar Alonso, O. Bruning, P. Fessia, M. Lamont, L. Rossi, L. Tavian, M. Zerlauth. ISBN 978-92-9083-586-8 (paperback), 978-92-9083-587-5 (PDF).
- Abstract: the LHC, opened energy frontier exploration in 2010, serves about 9000 scientists; it "will need a major upgrade in the 2020s" to raise instantaneous luminosity by a factor of five beyond the original design value. The document describes technologies and components as "the basis for the detailed engineering design of the HL-LHC".
- Lists chapters with authors, e.g. Chapter 6 circuit layout, powering and protection; 6A cold powering; 6B warm powering; cryogenics; Chapter 10 energy deposition and radiation to electronics.

wikis.title: LHC operation and the HL-LHC upgrade project (arXiv 2505.03535)
wikis.summary: arXiv abstract page for a Bruning and Zerlauth paper on the main concepts and performance goals of the LHC and HL-LHC.
wikis.body:
- Authors: Oliver Bruning and Markus Zerlauth. Abstract: "describes the main concepts and performance goals for the LHC and HL-LHC projects. It summarizes the main technical challenges and highlights the key technologies that have been developed for both projects."
- 18 pages, contribution to the CAS - CERN Accelerator School: Advanced Accelerator Physics, 10-22 November 2024, Spa, Belgium. Submitted as arXiv:2505.03535v1 [physics.acc-ph].

wikis.title: Square Kilometre Array (SKA) radio telescope project
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the SKA: sites in Australia and South Africa, history since 1991, SKAO founding in 2019, phases and schedule.
wikis.body:
- Intergovernmental radio telescope project: SKA-Low (low-frequency) at the Murchison Radio-astronomy Observatory, Western Australia, and SKA-Mid (mid-frequency) in Meerkat National Park, South Africa. SKAO headquarters at Jodrell Bank Observatory, UK (chosen April 2015, officially opened July 2019). Name refers to a notional collecting area of about one square kilometre.
- Timeline: conceived 1991, working group 1993, first Memorandum of Agreement 2000; PrepSKA began 2008, full design 2012; SKA Organisation formed November 2011; SKAO founded in Rome on 12 March 2019 by seven countries (Australia, China, Italy, Netherlands, Portugal, South Africa, UK); 14 members as of 2021; New Zealand withdrew July 2019. China's rival KARST proposal is mentioned.
- Construction began 5 December 2022 in ceremonies in Australia and South Africa (per page); construction of telescopes to take 8 years from July 2021, first SKA-Low antennas in 2024, first SKA-Mid receiver in 2025. First phase SKA1 scheduled as of 2025 for science operation in 2032; a possible larger SKA2 later.
- Precursors operating as of November 2020: MeerKAT, HERA, ASKAP, MWA and LOFAR.

wikis.title: SKA-Low's first image of the Universe (SKAO)
wikis.summary: SKAO news item on the first image from an early working version of SKA-Low in Western Australia, made with 1,024 of 131,072 planned antennas.
wikis.body:
- First image from SKA-Low (under construction on Wajarri Yamaji Country, Western Australia), released using data from the first four connected stations: 1,024 antennas, under one percent of the full telescope and spread over less than 6 km. Page dated 17 March 2025.
- Image covers about 25 square degrees (about 100 full Moons) and shows around 85 of the brightest known galaxies, each with a supermassive black hole. When complete the same frame is expected to show more than 600,000 galaxies.
- Planned total: 131,072 antennas. Dr George Heald (Lead Commissioning Scientist): quality "beyond what we hoped". Dr Sarah Pearce (SKA-Low Telescope Director) also quoted.

wikis.title: SKAO construction journey
wikis.summary: SKAO page timeline of SKA-Low and SKA-Mid construction milestones from 2024 to early 2026 and the staged array-assembly plan.
wikis.body:
- January 2026: SKA-Mid achieved "first fringes" combining the astronomical signal from two dishes. End of 2025: seven dishes standing on the SKA-Mid site and 15,000 antennas assembled at SKA-Low.
- August 2025: SKA-Low completed verification testing of the first four stations (1,024 antennas), which produced an early image in March. July 2025: first receiver (Band 2, 950-1700 MHz) installed on an SKA-Mid dish, measuring first astronomical signal (galactic neutral hydrogen).
- 2024: first SKA-Mid dish structure (9.5 m pedestal, 15 m reflector) arrived in Cape Town early 2024 after a journey of over 16,000 km from China; 'big lift' July; first four SKA-Low stations each had 256 antennas by July 2024; first SKA-Low antennas (made in Italy) installed, first of 131,072.
- Construction takes eight years (including 18 months contingency), begun July 2021. Staged array assemblies from AA0.5 (2024-2025). Baseline design (AA4): 197 SKA-Mid dishes and 512 SKA-Low stations; initial focus on a preliminary array AA* of 144 dishes in South Africa (rest of sentence not given in source).
- Recent news: France awarded first SKAO construction contract (Eviden, science data processor hardware); Germany reaffirmed commitment.

wikis.title: 2028 Summer Olympics, Los Angeles (Wikipedia, part 1)
wikis.summary: First part of Wikipedia's LA28 article: dates, host selection, sports programme and transport plans.
wikis.body:
- Games of the XXXIV Olympiad, Los Angeles, July 14 to 30, 2028, with events across Greater Los Angeles and two subsites in Oklahoma City.
- Bidding: LA bid for 2024; after Budapest, Hamburg and Rome withdrew, the IOC approved awarding 2024 and 2028 concurrently (Extraordinary Session July 11, 2017). July 31, 2017: LA sole candidate for 2028 with $1.8 billion additional IOC funding; formally awarded at the 131st IOC Session in Lima on September 13, 2017.
- Programme: skateboarding, sport climbing and surfing move to the core programme; flag football and squash debut as optional sports; baseball/softball, cricket (first since 1900) and lacrosse (first medal event since 1908) return.
- Transport: "car-free" plan and Twenty-eight by '28 initiative (by then-Mayor Eric Garcetti); by March 2024 11 of 28 projects revised; late 2024 concern only 5.2% of LA Metro's $3.3 billion Olympic list was funded. D Line extension phase 1 completed May 2026, second phase to Century City by late 2026, third to VA Medical Center by 2027. Buses primary mode: an additional 2,700 buses estimated, doubling Metro fleet of 2,320.

wikis.title: LA28 unveils Olympic and Paralympic ceremony venues (May 8, 2025)
wikis.summary: LA28 announcement that the LA Memorial Coliseum and the Stadium in Inglewood will host the 2028 Opening and Closing Ceremonies.
wikis.body:
- Los Angeles, May 8, 2025: LA28 confirmed the Coliseum and the Stadium in Inglewood as ceremony venues, largely consistent with the 2017 bid plan; the Paralympic Closing Ceremony location was revised.
- Olympic Opening Ceremony July 14, 2028, shared between the two venues (dual-venue). Olympic Closing Ceremony July 30, 2028 at the Coliseum. Paralympic Opening August 15, 2028 at the Stadium in Inglewood; Paralympic Closing August 27, 2028 at the Coliseum.
- The Coliseum will be the first venue in history to host events for three Olympic Games; the Inglewood stadium's Olympic debut. Quotes from Casey Wasserman (LA28 chairperson), Mayor Karen Bass, Mayor James T. Butts Jr., USC President Carol Folt and Rams owner E. Stanley Kroenke.
- LA28 is Los Angeles' third Olympic Games (after 1932 and 1984). Updated Paralympic venue plan to follow.

wikis.title: ESPN: Coliseum and SoFi set as LA 2028 Olympic opening and closing venues
wikis.summary: ESPN report (May 8, 2025) that the LA Coliseum and SoFi Stadium in Inglewood will host the 2028 Olympic and Paralympic opening and closing ceremonies.
wikis.body:
- LA28 announced on Thursday that the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum and SoFi Stadium in Inglewood will be the venues for the opening and closing ceremonies of the 2028 Olympic and Paralympic Games.
- Olympic opening ceremony July 14, shared between the Coliseum (first venue to host events for three Olympic Games) and SoFi in an "unprecedented dual-venue celebration". Paralympic closing ceremony August 27 at the Coliseum, home of USC's Trojans football team (SoFi is home of the Chargers per the page).
- LA hosted Olympics in 1932 and 1984; 2028 is its first Paralympics. The announcement was "little surprise" since the venues were floated in the 2017 bid plan. Casey Wasserman (LA28 chair) quoted.
- LA28 the month before unveiled other venue plans: beach volleyball at Alamitos Beach in Long Beach and squash on the Universal Studios lot.

wikis.title: UEFA Euro 2028 (Wikipedia, part 1)
wikis.summary: First part of Wikipedia's Euro 2028 article: hosts, bidding, qualification format, stadiums and schedule.
wikis.body:
- 18th UEFA European Championship, 9 June to 9 July 2028, co-hosted by England, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland. Spain are defending champions (2024 final vs England).
- Bidding: UEFA received three proposals on 23 March 2022 (Russia, Turkey, joint UK and Ireland bid); Russia's bids declared ineligible May 2022; Turkey withdrew early October 2023 to bid for Euro 2032 with Italy; UK-Ireland bid selected unanimously on 10 October 2023 in Nyon.
- Northern Ireland's Casement Park in Belfast was dropped by late 2024, so Northern Ireland hosts no games. Nine stadiums. Anfield ineligible (pitch 4 m short); Old Trafford ruled out.
- Qualification: all four hosts enter qualifying, with two automatic spots held in reserve. Twelve groups of four or five; winners plus eight best runners-up qualify; remaining runners-up enter playoffs with Nations League teams.
- Schedule announced 12 November 2025; opening match at Millennium Stadium, Cardiff on 9 June 2028; kick-offs 14:00, 17:00 and 20:00 local; round of 16 in all venues except Wembley; each host country stages a quarter-final.

wikis.title: UEFA Euro 2028: all you need to know (UEFA.com)
wikis.summary: UEFA.com explainer on Euro 2028 in the UK and Ireland: hosts, nine stadiums, dates, format and qualifying schedule.
wikis.body:
- Hosted by the UK and Republic of Ireland; joint bid appointed by the UEFA Executive Committee on 10 October 2023. Nine stadiums incl. Wembley, Hampden Park, Dublin Arena and the National Stadium of Wales; around three million tickets.
- 9 June to 9 July 2028; first game at National Stadium of Wales, Cardiff; final and both semi-finals at Wembley. Kick-offs 15:00, 18:00 and 21:00 CEST; final 18:00 CEST / 17:00 local. Format: 24 teams, six groups, top two plus four best third-placed teams into round of 16, then knockout.
- Qualifying: 12 groups of four or five, home and away; group stage March 2027 to November 2027; playoffs March 2028. Qualifying draw in Belfast on Sunday 6 December 2026. Spain won Euro 2024.

wikis.title: UEFA Euro 2028 match schedule revealed (England Football, Nov 2025)
wikis.summary: England Football article on the Euro 2028 schedule: England's group venues, nine host cities, 51 matches and knockout venues.
wikis.body:
- Tournament 9 June to 9 July 2028; kick-off in Cardiff Friday 9 June (per page), final at Wembley Sunday 9 July 2028. Qualifying draw in Belfast on 6 December 2026.
- If England qualify directly, opening game at the City of Manchester Stadium; other two group games at Wembley; Ireland, Scotland and Wales play in Dublin, Glasgow and Cardiff.
- 51 matches, 24 teams, 31 days, biggest men's Euro to date; host cities: Birmingham, Cardiff, Dublin, Glasgow, Liverpool, London, Manchester, Newcastle (page says nine). Round of 16 in each host city except Wembley; quarter-finals at Dublin Arena, Cardiff, Hampden Park and Wembley. Kick-offs 2pm, 5pm and 8pm (GMT); full details after the final draw in early 2027.

wikis.title: 2030 Winter Olympics (Alpes 2030), French Alps (Wikipedia)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the 2030 Winter Olympics in the French Alps: bid process, financial guarantees, clusters and venue disputes in 2026.
wikis.body:
- Scheduled 1 to 17 February 2030 in the French Alps (Lyon metropolis, Savoie, Haute-Savoie, Hautes-Alpes); speed skating planned in Heerenveen, Netherlands. First Games officially hosted by a region rather than a city; France's fourth Winter and seventh overall Games.
- Nominated as preferred candidate on 29 November 2023; conditionally ratified at the 142nd IOC Session in Paris on 24 July 2024, conditional on financial guarantees by October 2024 (delayed by the French political crisis; Prime Minister Michel Barnier sent a confirming letter to IOC president Thomas Bach in October 2024). Introduced at the close of the 2026 Winter Olympics in Verona.
- Venue clusters: Lyon, Briancon, Haute-Savoie, Savoie; five Olympic villages planned. Dispute over Nice: March 2026 report of threat by Renaud Muselier to move events to Lyon; 28 April 2026 organisers moved ice hockey away from Nice (Allianz Riviera plan too costly); 29 May 2026 Lyon called "the best solution" for ice events; June 2026 tentative Lyon plan with LDLC Arena and Eurexpo for ice hockey and Halle Tony Garnier for figure skating.

wikis.title: IOC invites French Alps (2030) and Salt Lake City-Utah (2034) to Targeted Dialogues
wikis.summary: IOC Executive Board press release inviting the French Alps and Salt Lake City-Utah into targeted dialogue for the 2030 and 2034 Winter Games, with Switzerland 203x in privileged dialogue for 2038.
wikis.body:
- The IOC Executive Board, on the Future Host Commission's recommendation, invited the CNOSF (French Alps, 2030) and the USOPC (Salt Lake City-Utah, 2034) into Targeted Dialogues, and gave Switzerland 203x "Privileged Dialogue" for 2038. (The page text gives no date.)
- A possible double allocation of 2030 and 2034 was approved by the 141st IOC Session in Mumbai in October (to bring security in climate-reliable regions).
- French Alps reasons: sustainable winter tourism vision, existing venues, four clusters, experience (FIS Alpine World Ski Championships in Courchevel and Meribel in February that year), Paris 2024 structures, private-sector and government support, regional governments guaranteeing the budget.
- Salt Lake City-Utah reasons: building on the 2002 legacy and the Games Legacy Fund to extend venue and programme lifecycles.

wikis.title: 2030 FIFA World Cup (Wikipedia)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the 2030 World Cup hosted by Morocco, Portugal and Spain with centenary matches in Uruguay, Argentina and Paraguay: bid, hosts, stadiums and qualifying.
wikis.body:
- 24th World Cup, jointly hosted by Morocco, Portugal and Spain; centenary celebration at Estadio Centenario in Montevideo plus one match each in Uruguay, Argentina and Paraguay. First World Cup across more than one confederation, first in Africa since 2010 and first in North Africa. Six hosts qualify automatically; Spain first defending champions to host, after winning in 2026 per the page.
- Possible one-off 64-team expansion: CONMEBOL proposed March 2025; on 20 July 2026 CONMEBOL president Alejandro Dominguez announced 64 teams (not confirmed by FIFA per the page).
- Bidding launched 2022; Portugal-Spain intent 7 October 2020; Morocco joined 14 March 2023 (sixth Moroccan bid). Awarded on 11 December 2024 (virtual extraordinary FIFA Congress) alongside 2034 to Saudi Arabia.
- Venues: twenty stadiums in seventeen cities (six in Morocco, three in Portugal, eleven in Spain at bid). Malaga withdrew 12 July 2025; A Coruna withdrew 15 March 2026; Valencia and Vigo submitted as replacements late March 2026. CONCACAF qualifying format announced 6 February 2026.

wikis.title: CBS Sports: Morocco, Spain and Portugal named 2030 World Cup hosts (Oct 4, 2023)
wikis.summary: CBS Sports report on FIFA's October 4, 2023 announcement that Morocco, Portugal and Spain host the 2030 World Cup with centenary opening games in Uruguay, Argentina and Paraguay.
wikis.body:
- FIFA announced that the Morocco-Portugal-Spain joint bid is the sole candidate for 2030, hosting and qualifying automatically, in a tournament uniting "three continents and six countries".
- The three opening games go to Uruguay, Argentina and Paraguay (one match each), the first at Estadio Centenario in Montevideo, site of the 1930 final; a centenary celebration ceremony in Montevideo. 1930 winner Uruguay beat Argentina in the final.
- Bidding for 2030 and 2034 to run concurrently under confederation rotation. Gianni Infantino: "In a divided world, FIFA and football are uniting."

wikis.title: Expo 2030, Riyadh (Wikipedia)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on World Expo 2030 in Riyadh: dates, theme, and the candidate cities that led to Riyadh's selection on 28 November 2023.
wikis.body:
- Expo 2030 (BIE-sanctioned) in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia: opens 1 October 2030, closes 31 March 2031 (181 days). Second Middle Eastern host after Dubai 2020. Theme "Foresight for Tomorrow"; sub-themes "Transformational Technology", "Sustainable Solutions", "Prosperous People".
- Bidding: Russia (Moscow) first bid 29 April 2021; five bids confirmed by BIE 29 October 2021: Busan (South Korea, entered 23 June 2021), Riyadh (29 October 2021), Rome (28 September 2021), Moscow, Odesa (15 October 2021). Moscow and Odesa withdrew in May 2022 following the Russian invasion of Ukraine.
- Riyadh elected host in the final vote on 28 November 2023.

wikis.title: Riyadh chosen to host World Expo 2030
wikis.summary: Arab News report that Riyadh won the vote to host World Expo 2030, succeeding Osaka 2025, beating South Korea and Italy.
wikis.body:
- Riyadh will host World Expo 2030 after defeating challenges from South Korea and Italy, picked by a majority of 119 out of 165 votes by member states of the Paris-based Bureau International des Expositions (BIE). Secret electronic ballot; dated November 28, 2023 (page updated 23 October 2025).
- Riyadh is "confirmed as the successor host to Osaka in 2025". The event is expected to represent the culmination of Vision 2030 and showcase the Kingdom's achievements, focused on hospitality, tourism and culture.
- Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan thanked 130 countries that had announced support, and said the Kingdom will "provide facilities packages of $348 million to a pool of 100 eligible countries."
- Themes: sustainable solutions for cities of tomorrow, clean mobility, renewable energy, the Green Riyadh Program (raise green coverage from 1.5 percent to 9.1 percent).
- Infrastructure: 70,000 new hotel rooms; a new metro linking Expo City to a reconstructed King Salman Airport (57 million sq. meters); Riyadh Air flights to 100 countries by 2025.
- Riyadh Expo 2030 team member Ghida Al-Shibl: "By Feb 2028, participant parcel and expo village will be open." A participant lab launches in 2025 and runs through 2030 as a 24/7 concierge service.
- A color-coded map with planned pavilions, performance venues, support facilities and an exhibition village was unveiled at a Paris symposium in November.

wikis.title: Expo 2030 Riyadh official site
wikis.summary: Official Expo 2030 Riyadh homepage giving dates and headline expected figures.
wikis.body:
- Dates: 1 October 2030 - 31 March 2031 (countdown to 1 October 2030).
- Described as "a platform for nations to collaborate, showcase innovation, and translate foresight into action."
- Headline figures: 42M+ visits expected; 197 participating nations; 230+ pavilions; ~6M sqm total Expo site.
- Ways to get involved: partners and vendors, international participants, volunteers.

wikis.title: Riyadh Expo 2030 key details (BIE visit, site and themes)
