wikis.summary: Argaam overview of Riyadh's Expo 2030 bid: dates, site size and layout, themes and expected participants, published 21/03/2023.
wikis.body:
- BIE delegation recently concluded its visit to Riyadh, discussing the bid to host World Expo 2030.
- Scheduled Oct. 1, 2030 to April 1, 2031 on a six million sqm site in north Riyadh, a five-to-10-minute drive from King Khalid International Airport and close to King Abdullah Petroleum Studies and Research Center.
- Site per the Riyadh Expo 2030 report: 3.38 million sqm of pilot space in a gated area, nearly 432,000 sqm for national pavilions, 2.62 million sqm for facilities support (logistics, transportation/parking). Designed as a futuristic city around an old valley, combining oasis and garden concepts.
- Main theme "Together for a Foresighted Tomorrow"; sub-themes "A Different Tomorrow," "Climate Action" and "Prosperity for All".
- Site to feature recreational, cultural and sporting activities: public parks, gaming spaces, mega theatres.
- 226 participants expected (international pavilions, global organizations, informal participants).
- 170 member states will vote during the 171st general assembly of BIE at the end of November 2023.

wikis.title: 2032 Summer Olympics (Brisbane): selection, venues and stadium saga
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the planned Brisbane 2032 Games, covering the bid, organisation, venue and stadium changes, infrastructure and proposed sports.
wikis.body:
- Officially Games of the XXXV Olympiad, "Brisbane 2032"; scheduled 23 July to 8 August 2032 in Brisbane, Australia, with venues across Queensland. Third Olympics in Australia (after Melbourne 1956, Sydney 2000); held in Brisbane's winter.
- Selection: IOC Future Host Commission named Brisbane preferred candidate on 24 February 2021; awarded at the 138th IOC Session in Tokyo on 21 July 2021 (72 Yes, 5 No, 3 abstentions). 11 years and 2 days ahead, described as the most time a host city has had.
- Organising committee established by the Queensland Government in 2021, board led by Andrew Liveris AO.
- Costs: a 2019 feasibility study put net cost at $900 million excluding agency costs and IOC/private contributions; 68% of required venues already existed or could be upgraded. In 2023 the Commonwealth pledged $2.5 billion for the Brisbane Live arena and $1 billion for other infrastructure.
- Venues: Brisbane, Gold Coast, Sunshine Coast, Cairns, Townsville; Melbourne and Sydney host football preliminaries.
- Stadium history: Gabba rebuild (50,000 seats) rose from $1 billion to $2.7 billion by February 2023; Lord Mayor Adrian Schrinner withdrew support in December 2023; on 18 March 2024 Premier Steven Miles scrapped it (Lang Park and QSAC to host ceremonies and athletics). After the October 2024 election, Premier David Crisafulli ordered a 100-day review; on 25 March 2025 he announced a 63,000-seat stadium at Victoria Park, estimated by the review at AU$3.8 billion (not publicly confirmed). The Gabba is to be demolished for residential redevelopment after the Games.
- Brisbane Live arena scrapped in favour of a 25,000-seat aquatics centre at Centenary Pool Complex (reduced to 8,000 after the Games); the arena continues as a "market-led" project without federal funding.
- Infrastructure: Cross River Rail (over A$17 billion, due by 2029), Brisbane Metro, Maroochydore railway line (expected by 2032). Main Athletes' Village at Bowen Hills; satellite villages at Royal Pines, Maroochydore, Rockhampton, Hervey Bay. In December 2025 Unite32 (Aecom and Laing O'Rourke) was appointed delivery partner.
- Sports: initial programme to be determined in 2026; baseball/softball, rugby league nines and cricket bids are mentioned.

wikis.title: Brisbane 2032 (Australian Olympic Committee page)
wikis.summary: Short Australian Olympic Committee page giving the host nation and dates of the Brisbane 2032 Games.
wikis.body:
- Games: Brisbane 2032; host nation Australia.
- Dates: Friday 23 July to Sunday 8 August 2032.
- Page links to a video, "Brisbane 2032 - a new way to elect hosts for the Olympic and Paralympic Games", and older news items (Green and Gold Runway launch, National Reconciliation Week).

wikis.title: Brisbane City Council: Brisbane 2032 Games preparations and benefits
wikis.summary: Brisbane City Council page on how it is preparing for the 2032 Olympic and Paralympic Games and the legacy benefits it expects.
wikis.body:
- Brisbane will be Host City of the 2032 Olympic and Paralympic Games; described as a chance to showcase South East Queensland and stimulate infrastructure and connections.
- Legacy plan "Brisbane Beyond the Games" (shaped by the "Brisbane Making our Mark" city-wide conversation) commits to work with business, industry, community and governments.
- Team Brisbane AAF Athlete Scholarship Program, in partnership with the Aussie Athlete Fund.
- Stated benefits: new pedestrian and cycling bridges and safe paths; aligned national/state/regional/city plans to ease congestion; a cooler, shadier city (Towards 2032 Planting Program along transport corridors and near venues); energy-efficient lighting, solar panels, electric vehicles and recycling to minimise Games-related emissions; more tourism, trade, investment and jobs.
- Brisbane 2032 Procurement Program is live for local businesses to submit expressions of interest to the Brisbane 2032 Organising Committee.

wikis.title: Halley's Comet: overview, orbit calculation, orbit and origin, structure (part 1)
wikis.summary: First part of the Wikipedia article on Halley's Comet: key orbital data, how Halley recognised its periodicity, its retrograde orbit and origin, and the nucleus and coma.
wikis.body:
- Halley's Comet (1P/Halley) is "the only known short-period comet that is consistently visible to the naked eye from Earth", appearing roughly every 74-79 years. Last perihelion 8 February 1986; next perihelion 28 July 2061 (then approx. 27 March 2134).
- Observed and recorded since at least 240 BC; in 1705 Edmond Halley recognised the returns as the same comet, using 1531 (Apianus), 1607 (Kepler) and 1682 comets, and predicted a return in 1758.
- Return first seen 25 December 1758 by Johann Georg Palitzsch; perihelion on 13 March 1759, delayed 618 days by Jupiter and Saturn (computed beforehand by Clairaut, Lalande and Lepaute). First time anything other than planets was shown to orbit the Sun; named for Halley by Lacaille in 1759. Jamaican astronomer Francis Williams also independently recognised the return.
- 1986: first comet observed in detail by a spacecraft (ESA's Giotto, 14 March 1986 nucleus image); Vega 1 and 2 passed on 6 and 9 March, as close as 8,890 km and 8,030 km.
- Orbit: eccentricity 0.967; perihelion 0.59 au (between Mercury and Venus); aphelion 35 au (about Pluto's distance); retrograde, inclined 162 degrees; period varied between 74 and 80 years since 240 BC. Associated meteor showers: Eta Aquariids (early May) and Orionids (late October).
- Origin: a Halley-type comet, probably from the Oort cloud; likely in its current orbit 16,000-200,000 years; chaotic long-term dynamics, dynamical lifetime about 10 million years; expected to evaporate or split within tens of thousands of years, or be ejected within a few hundred thousand years.
- Nucleus: about 15 km x 8 km x 8 km, mean diameter 11 km, "dirty snowball" of ices and dust, dark surface; coma up to 230,000 km; tail may extend more than 100 million km.

wikis.title: NASA Science: 1P/Halley facts and history
wikis.summary: NASA page on Halley's Comet covering its history, 1986 spacecraft encounters, size, orbit, lifetime and naming.
wikis.body:
- Last seen in Earth's skies in 1986; "will return in 2061 on its regular 76-year journey around the Sun."
- History: until Edmond Halley (1656-1742), comets were believed to make one pass. In 1705 Halley used Newton's theories to compute orbits, linked comets of 1531, 1607 and 1682, and correctly predicted a 1758 return. Linked to observations back more than 2,000 years; featured in the Bayeux tapestry (Battle of Hastings, 1066).
- 1986 fleet: Japan's Suisei and Sakigake, Soviet Vega 1 and 2, ISEE-3 (ICE), ESA's Giotto (imaged the nucleus), plus NASA's Pioneer 7 and Pioneer 12.
- Meteor showers: Eta Aquarids (May) and Orionids (October).
- Size about 15 km by 8 km (9.3 by 5 miles); albedo 0.03 (reflects 3% of light); diameter 11 km; day length 2.2 Earth days.
- Orbit: retrograde, tilted 18 degrees; average period 76 years (shortest 74.42 years 1835-1910, longest 79.25 years 451-530); aphelion beyond Neptune. Closest approach to Earth 837 (0.033 AU on April 10, 837, magnitude about -3.5); 1986 nearest approach 0.42 AU. Perihelion Feb. 9, 1986 at 0.5871 AU, moving 54.55 km/s; aphelion 1948 at 35.25 AU.
- Lifetime: loses an estimated 1 to 3 meters of surface per orbit; average periodic comet completes about 1,000 trips; in present orbit at least 16,000 years.
- Named for Halley because he made the first such return prediction; "P" means periodic (under 200 years).

wikis.title: Halley's Comet reaches aphelion and heads back toward 2061 perihelion
wikis.summary: Space.com column (Joe Rao, 8 December 2023) saying Halley's Comet reaches aphelion on Dec. 8, 2023 and previewing its inbound path and 2061 apparition.
wikis.body:
- Aphelion at 8 p.m. Eastern Time on Friday, Dec. 8, 2023 (0100 GMT Dec. 9): 3.27 billion miles (5.26 billion km) from the sun, 472.2 million miles beyond Neptune's orbit. Last at this point in April 1948. Orbital velocity then 0.565 miles (0.909 km) per second, versus 33.77 miles (54.52 km) per second at perihelion on Feb. 9, 1986.
- Planet-orbit crossings inbound: Neptune (30.6 AU) May 7, 2041; Uranus May 1, 2053; Saturn Dec. 7, 2058; Jupiter June 25, 2060; Mars May 16, 2061; Earth June 19, 2061; Venus July 9, 2061. Perihelion July 28, 2061.
- 2061 apparition: morning sky from mid-June (June 18 near the Pleiades, about magnitude +5.6, 167 million miles from Earth); July 1 about +4.3; July 10 about +3.5, 93 million miles away; July 23 perhaps first magnitude; July 25-28 visible in both morning and evening as about magnitude zero. From August exclusively an evening object; Aug. 4-8 "might well be the pinnacle" with a tail perhaps 10 or 15 degrees; Dec. 24 within a degree of Venus at about magnitude 3.3.
- 2061 is described as a mirror image of 1986; the comet should appear at least 10 times brighter than in 1986.
- Author warns light pollution could obliterate the view; anyone born after 1982 has a better than 50-50 chance to see it given about 79-year US life expectancy.

wikis.title: Mumbai-Ahmedabad high-speed rail: overview, history, design and cost (part 1)
wikis.summary: First part of the Wikipedia article on India's under-construction Mumbai-Ahmedabad bullet-train line, covering its specifications, planning history, environmental clearances, design, cost and JICA financing.
wikis.body:
- Under construction; owner/operator NHSRCL; connects Mumbai (Maharashtra) and Ahmedabad (Gujarat), 12 stations; India's first high-speed line. Shinkansen technology from Japan (rolling stock E10 Series Shinkansen / B28 "Vande Bullet"), with technology transfer for Make in India.
- Specs: line length 508.18 km; standard gauge; 25 kV AC; operating speed 320 km/h (design speed 350 km/h); ETCS Level 2; a 353 km viaduct.
- Planned opening: 15 August 2027 (Surat to Bilimora), 2029 (entire line). Construction commenced February 2021 after COVID-19 delays.
- History: revived for feasibility study in the 2009-2010 Rail Budget; MoU with SNCF on 14 February 2013; Pune-Mumbai section dropped March 2013; India-Japan feasibility MoU September 2013 (study cost ¥500 million); approved by Modi in May 2014; NHSRCL SPV registered January 2016; tripartite consultancy agreement December 2016; detailed design study began March 2017; groundbreaking with the Indian and Japanese prime ministers in Ahmedabad in 2017.
- Fastest current train: Ahmedabad-Mumbai Vande Bharat Express, 5 hours 40 minutes at max 130 km/h; bullet trains expected to cover the distance in two hours.
- Environment: National Board for Wildlife clearance January 2019; conditional clearance on 18 March 2019 to cut 53,467 mangrove trees; June 2019 design change of Thane station saved 21,000, leaving 32,044 affected.
- Design (508.09 km): 460.3 km viaduct (90.6%), 25.87 km tunnels (5.1%), 12.9 km cut and fill, 9.22 km bridges; a 21 km Thane-Virar tunnel of which 7 km undersea; starts at underground Bandra-Kurla Complex station.
- Cost: estimated ₹1.1 lakh crore (US$16.4 billion in 2017 dollars); JICA agreed in 2017 to fund 81% through a 50-year, ¥1.5 trillion loan at 0.1% interest with a 15-year moratorium; elevated design added about ₹10,000 crore. Spent ₹28,442 crore by July 2022 (analysis suggested 48% escalation to ₹1.6 lakh crore); as of October 2024, ₹67,486 crore spent and 47% of civil works completed. JICA loan tranches total ¥1,150 billion.

wikis.title: India's first bullet train to start operations on August 15, 2027
wikis.summary: Deccan Herald teaser: Railway Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw says India's first bullet train will begin operations on Independence Day, 15 August 2027.
wikis.body:
- Headline: India's first bullet train to commence operations on August 15, 2027.
- Quote from Vaishnaw: "On Independence Day 2027, people will be able to buy a ticket for India's first bullet train," underlining the symbolic importance of the launch date.
- Page by Ajith Athrady, published 01 January 2026. Only this teaser text was available.

wikis.title: Brightline West: history, funding, construction and route (part 1)
wikis.summary: First part of the Wikipedia article on Brightline West, the privately run Las Vegas to Rancho Cucamonga high-speed rail line under construction, covering context, funding, construction status and route.
wikis.body:
- Privately run high-speed line under construction in California and Nevada linking the Las Vegas Valley and Rancho Cucamonga via Interstate 15; 218 miles (351 km); average journey about 2h 10m; stops at Victor Valley and Hesperia; max speed TBC 180 or 200 mph; 25 kV 60 Hz overhead electrification. Connects to Metrolink's San Bernardino Line. Revenue service planned by late 2029.
- Developed from 2005 as DesertXpress; acquired by Fortress Investment Group (owner of Florida Brightline) in September 2018 (XpressWest); rebranded Brightline West in September 2020.
- Context: about 50 million people travel between Los Angeles and Las Vegas annually, 85% by car; driving over four hours; Las Vegas lost its last passenger train (Amtrak Desert Wind) in 1997.
- Funding: US DOT awarded a $3 billion grant in December 2023 (signed September 2024); $2.5 billion of private activity bonds in January 2024 plus $1 billion in 2020; remainder (about $12 billion as of April 2024) to be privately financed. Because of rising labour and material costs the company requested a $6 billion loan; costs now estimated at $21.5 billion (January 2026 disclosure). Wes Edens estimated $8 billion in 2020.
- Construction: groundbreaking April 22, 2024 at the Las Vegas station site; peak jobs about 18,000; heavy construction originally early 2025, as of October 2025 major construction expected April 2026. Originally aimed for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics; as of April 2025 officials anticipate service September 2029. Michael Reininger moved to Managing Director role in January 2026. PCM Railone plans a US $20 million concrete-tie facility in North Las Vegas.
- Route: mostly the I-15 median, initially mostly single-track with passing sidings; 49-mile Rancho Cucamonga segment up to 180 mph; maintenance facility moved to a 246-acre parcel in Sloan, Nevada; Las Vegas station south of the Strip on Las Vegas Boulevard in Enterprise (110-acre site). A 50-mile extension to Palmdale is under consideration; later phases may reach Phoenix, Salt Lake City or Denver.

wikis.title: Brightline West completion date pushed to late 2029
wikis.summary: Newsweek (15 January 2026) reports Brightline West's Las Vegas to Southern California line is now scheduled for completion by late 2029, missing the 2028 Olympics target.
wikis.body:
- 218-mile project; the company told FOX5 it is "now scheduled for completion by late 2029." Currently in the "civil construction" phase; estimated price tag "at least $12 billion".
- Earlier optimism to be ready for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics; Biden said in 2023 it was "on track to be completed by the 2028 Olympics".
- Route runs mainly in the I-15 median; work is active at the future Las Vegas station site; track-laying start not announced; fieldwork and land preparation ongoing through 2026.
- Background: Brightline acquired XpressWest in 2018; California approved the Las Vegas-Victorville line in 2020 and Caltrans agreed an I-15 median lease; COVID-19 caused a 2021 postponement. Newsom promised a third I-15 lane on the California side, not yet delivered.
- Correction 1/16/26: the article notes Brightline West is a private company, separate from California High Speed Rail.

wikis.title: Francis Scott Key Bridge (Baltimore): history, 2024 collapse and replacement
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the Baltimore Key Bridge, opened 1977, destroyed by the MV Dali on March 26, 2024, and its replacement plans and cost.
wikis.body:
- Steel continuous through truss bridge carrying four lanes of I-695 across the Patapsco River; opened March 23, 1977; total length 8,636 feet, main span 1,200 feet; about 34,000 daily traffic; maintained by the Maryland Transportation Authority. Originally the Outer Harbor Crossing, renamed in 1976 for Francis Scott Key. Original cost $141 million.
- Origins: a planned Outer Harbor Tunnel ($220 million bond issue, October 1968) drew bids well above estimate in July 1970, so a four-lane bridge was chosen; approved by the General Assembly April 1971; designed by J. E. Greiner Company.
- Collapse: on March 26, 2024, at 01:28 EDT the main spans collapsed after the Singapore-registered container ship MV Dali lost power and hit the southwest support pier. Six maintenance workers were killed; two rescued. A mayday call let police halt traffic, likely saving many lives. NTSB noted the bridge predated redundant support structures. Shipping to the Port of Baltimore was almost entirely halted; initial losses estimated at $15 million per day; three temporary channels by April 20 allowed about 15% of pre-collapse shipping.
- Replacement: on May 2, 2024 officials planned late 2028 at $1.7 billion to $1.9 billion. On November 17, 2025 Maryland announced the projected cost rose to $4.3 billion to $5.2 billion and opening was delayed to late 2030 (the article says completion is scheduled December 2030).
- Progressive design-build contract awarded to Kiewit in August 2024; $350 million insurance payout from Chubb; October 2024 DOJ settlement of $101.98 million with Dali's owner and manager; December 2024 law set the federal Emergency Relief share at 100 percent. Pre-construction was scheduled to begin January 7, 2025.

wikis.title: Kiewit awarded Key Bridge replacement design-build contract
wikis.summary: South Baltimore news release (September 4, 2024) relaying the MDTA's August 29 award of the Francis Scott Key Bridge replacement to Kiewit, with opening expected Fall 2028.
wikis.body:
- MDTA Board approved a $73 million Phase 1 contract naming Kiewit Infrastructure Co. Progressive Design-Builder for complete design and construction of the I-695 Francis Scott Key Bridge replacement. Rebuild slated to begin in 2025; replacement "expected to open in Fall 2028".
- Two-phase progressive design-build: after Phase 1, Kiewit has exclusive negotiating rights for Phase 2 (final design/engineering and construction); if no guaranteed maximum price is agreed, MDTA will deliver the work under a separate mechanism.
- MDTA also approved temporary suspension of toll collection on the I-695/Exit 44 turnaround until the rebuild is complete (pilot began in May).
- In July the FHWA issued a Categorical Exclusion/NEPA approval because the bridge stays within the former right-of-way with the same four travel lanes.
- A General Engineering Consultant RFP was released in July; MDTA expects to award the $75 million contract in January 2025.

wikis.title: New Key Bridge could be rebuilt by fall 2028 at $1.7-1.9 billion
wikis.summary: CBS Baltimore (May 3, 2024) reporting Maryland officials' estimate of $1.7 billion to $1.9 billion and fall 2028 for a new Francis Scott Key Bridge, plus salvage updates.
wikis.body:
- Maryland transportation officials: new bridge would cost between $1.7 billion and $1.9 billion and would not be completed until fall of 2028.
- Bridge collapsed the early morning of March 26 when the Dali hit it, knocking eight construction workers into the water; two rescued, six killed.
- Biden committed federal funding: "We're gonna move Heaven and Earth to rebuild this bridge as rapidly as humanly possible." Chubb, the insurer, is preparing to pay $350 million to the state (per the Wall Street Journal).
- Former Gov. Larry Hogan called the timeline "unacceptable".
- Crews hoped to refloat Dali by May 10; 182 containers removed, enough to refloat; steel atop the ship still to be removed. A fifth worker's body was recovered (Miguel Angel Luna Gonzalez, 49); Jose Mynor Lopez remained missing.

wikis.title: Strait of Messina Bridge: history, approvals and status
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the proposed Sicily-Calabria suspension bridge, its centuries of proposals, repeated cancellations and revivals, and the 2025-2026 approval and Court of Audit setback.
wikis.body:
- Proposed 3.6 km suspension bridge from Torre Faro (Sicily) to Villa San Giovanni (Calabria); total length 3,666 m, longest span 3,300 m, pylons 399 m; six road lanes plus emergency lanes and two rail tracks; would be the longest suspension bridge in the world. Construction start/end listed as TBD.
- Strait: about 3 km at narrowest, up to 16 km wide; strong tidal currents and significant seismic activity.
- Early history: Romans (Pliny the Elder mentions a boat bridge), Charlemagne, Robert Guiscard, Roger II; 1852 Alphonse Oudry proposal; 1953 David B. Steinman plan.
- Modern attempts: first detailed plan in the 1990s. Consortium led by Impregilo (now Webuild, 45%) selected in 2005; contract March 2006; estimated cost EUR 3.9 billion over six years. Cancelled 12 October 2006 when parliament voted 272 to 232 against; revived by Berlusconi (March 2009: EUR 1.3 billion pledged toward an estimated EUR 6.1 billion, completion claimed by 2016; preparatory rail diversion at Cannitello December 2009); cancelled February 2013 by Monti.
- Meloni government: decree approved 16 March 2023; Webuild's Pietro Salini said work should begin by 2024 and finish in 2032; Decreto Ponte approved 31 March 2023. Final government approval August 2025 (CIPESS Resolution No. 41 on 6 August 2025), with the bridge to be treated as a defence-related expense toward the NATO target, which the US called "creative accounting".
- On 29/30 October 2025 Italy's Court of Audit declined to validate/rejected the resolution, delaying a possible November 2025 start. Its concerns: IROPI update, a new opinion from the Superior Council of Public Works, assessment of the financial plan, and an alleged 50% increase in contract value.
- February 2026: Salvini said a decree would keep cost at EUR 13.5 billion and work should begin in 2026. Stretto di Messina CEO Pietro Ciucci said a new CIPESS resolution was expected by September 2026.
- Concerns: earthquakes, currents, bird migration, possible mafia infiltration (Cosa Nostra and 'Ndrangheta). A belvedere at 374 m on the towers is in the designer's report (March 2024).

wikis.title: Messina Bridge construction to start end-April, finish end 2032 (Webuild CEO)
wikis.summary: ANSA English (14 March 2025): Webuild CEO Pietro Salini says Messina Bridge construction begins at the end of April and completes by 2032, at an estimated EUR 13.5 billion.
wikis.body:
- Salini said Friday construction "will begin at the end of April" and the bridge will be completed by 2032: "I hope to be there and to be able to cross it together with the whole team by the end of 2032."
- Investment currently estimated at 13.5 billion euros for the bridge, 40 km of road and rail links, three new train stations and a business center in Calabria.
- Transport Minister Matteo Salvini said it would create more than 100,000 jobs per company estimates and be "the largest anti-mafia operation"; project delayed by cost, environmental concerns and fears of 'Ndrangheta and Cosa Nostra infiltration.
- Bridge span over 3.2 km; would surpass the 1915 Canakkale Bridge in Turkey (2,023 m span). Design recently tweaked to raise its height so cruise ships can pass.

wikis.title: Italy approves EUR 13.5 billion Strait of Messina bridge
wikis.summary: Euronews (6 August 2025) reporting Italy's final approval of the Messina suspension bridge, with concerns over security classification, environment, mafia and earthquakes.
wikis.body:
- An inter-ministerial committee approved the EUR 13.5 billion project on Wednesday (6 August 2025), per the Transport Ministry; Salvini called it "an accelerator for development" in southern Italy. Preliminary work could begin later in summer.
- Bridge nearly 3.7 km long, suspended span 3.3 km, surpassing Turkey's Canakkale Bridge; four lanes plus a double-track railway; capacity 6,000 cars an hour and 200 trains a day. Approved and cancelled multiple times since Italy first solicited proposals in 1969; revived by Meloni's government in 2023.
- Meloni: "a strategic infrastructure for the development of Southern Italy and the entire country".
- Security: the government would classify the bridge as defence-related to help meet NATO's 1.5% security component of a 5%-of-GDP target; over 600 professors and researchers signed a letter opposing it; opponents say it could become a target.
- Environmental groups complained to the EU (migratory birds); President Mattarella insisted the project stay under general anti-mafia legislation.
- Awarded to a consortium led by WeBuild (won in 2006, cancelled 2013). WeBuild says suspension bridges are less vulnerable to seismic forces, citing the 1908 Messina-fault quake concerns; Salini: "a game-changer for Italy."

wikis.title: Chacao Channel Bridge (Chile): history, design, construction and controversy
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the Chiloe suspension bridge under construction across the Chacao Channel, from 1960s proposals through the 2017 design, delays and planned second-half 2028 opening.
wikis.body:
- Suspension bridge under construction linking Chiloe Island with mainland Chile (Pargua-Chacao, Los Lagos Region); largest suspension bridge in South and Latin America once complete; total length 2,634 m in the infobox (2,750 m per the 2017 design text). Builder Hyundai Engineering & Construction; construction start 2017 (site work officially February 2018); opening planned for the second half of 2028.
- History: first proposed in the mid-1960s by congressman Felix Garay (US$80 million); shelved after the 1973 coup. Revived in the 1990s; 2001 estimate US$300 million; concession awarded January 2005 to a Vinci/Hochtief/American Bridge/Besalco/Tecsa consortium at US$527 million. Cancelled July 2006 by Bachelet's government after the cost rose to US$930 million (ceiling US$605-607 million); US$2 million indemnity; "Plan Chiloe" offered instead.
- Revival: Pinera confirmed in May 2012; bidding opened May 2013; December 2013 approval of the sole bid (OAS, Hyundai, SYSTRA, Aas-Jakobsen; 360.134 billion pesos, ceiling US$740 million); Comptroller approval February 2014, then expected 79 months and a 2019 opening; Hyundai won the contract in 2014.
- Design (2017): crosses the narrowest point, 2.5 km, between Punta San Gallan and Punta Coronel; four lanes; central tower 179 m on Roca Remolino, towers of 199 m and 157 m; designed for gusts up to 200 km/h; crossing about three minutes at 80 km/h. Final design delivered June 2017, approved December 2018; the consortium sought an extra US$200 million in August 2018 and delivery moved to 2023. OAS (49%) withdrew (finalised 2019), leaving Hyundai.
- Construction: 36 piles complete by September 2019; Hyundai halted work 23 December 2019 over about 218 billion pesos of extra costs; resumed by May 2020 after February 2020 agreement. April 2024 halfway point (north tower 120 of 200 m, south 112 of 157 m, central 67 of 165 m). Two months later the ministry confirmed delivery pushed to the second half of 2028.
- Criticism: 2015 survey of 425 residents, 86 percent felt funds could have gone to more urgent needs; concerns over cultural identity, Huilliche opposition, lack of indigenous consultation and transparency; 2019 inquiry into whether OAS was favoured.

wikis.title: Chacao Bridge delivery: minister says October 2028, successor says up to 2030
wikis.summary: BioBioChile (24 February 2026): outgoing Public Works minister Jessica Lopez says the Chacao Bridge will be delivered in October 2028, while incoming minister Martin Arrau says opening could slip to 2029 or 2030.
wikis.body:
- Minister of Public Works Jessica Lopez announced in Chiloe that the Chacao Channel bridge would be delivered in October 2028, "within the established deadlines", after meeting mayors at the Chacao Municipal Delegation.
- Incoming minister Martin Arrau, in Puerto Montt, said the inauguration could come only in 2029 or even 2030, since after construction the project must go through technical verification and certification before operating.
- Tolls: a single toll under a free-flow system, expected to be similar to the current ferry cost; the amount was not given. The minister also addressed the future of the existing ferry (barge) system.
- Lopez visited the viaduct works, which the article says show 63% progress; the crossing will take about three minutes.
- Article dated Tuesday 24 February 2026 (Paula Villasenor, reporting by Hans Burrows). Text is in Spanish.

wikis.title: Chacao Bridge 58% complete, delivery set for October 2028
wikis.summary: BNamericas press release (published Monday, October 13, 2025, machine-translated) from the Infrastructure Policy Council: the US$760 million Chacao Bridge is 58% complete and due October 2028.
wikis.body:
- A delegation of 30 council members, directors and executives of the Infrastructure Policy Council (CPI), led by president Eduardo Frei, visited the site; construction is 58% complete; investment US$760 million.
- Bridge about 2,750 m long, the longest suspension structure in Latin America; extends Route 5 from Arica to Quellon; cuts the crossing from 30-40 minutes by barge to 3 minutes.
- Undersecretary of Public Works Danilo Nunez: "We're 58% complete, and everything indicates that we will continue to move forward on the schedule we've already defined for the second half of 2028, October 2028."
- Three reinforced concrete piers, one on Whirlpool Rock (Roca Remolino) in the canal; tallest almost 200 m. Project manager Carlos Contreras: southern pier two meters from max height (before year end); northern pier 10 meters away (also this year); central pier at max height by mid next year; then cable and deck installation. Deck sections originally 20 m long, made in Korea, will likely arrive in 60 m lengths.
- Contractor is Hyundai; the highway toward Quellon is also being built.

wikis.title: Sizewell C nuclear power station: history, financing and status
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the Sizewell C two-EPR plant under construction in Suffolk, covering ownership, the July 2025 final investment decision, GBP 38 billion cost and opposition.
wikis.body:
- Two EPR reactors (2 x 1,630 MWe planned; about 3,200 MWe combined) at Sizewell, Suffolk, next to Sizewell B; operator NNB Generation Company; reactor supplier Framatome; sea-water cooling. Expected to meet up to 7% of UK electricity demand; 60-year service life; construction takes nine to twelve years depending on Hinkley Point C.
- History: 2008 policy for new nuclear on existing sites; 2012 EDF proposals; October 2015 EDF/CGN partnership (80%/20%); application submitted 24 June 2020; Development Consent Order issued 20 July 2022; UK government bought CGN out for just over GBP 100 million in late 2022 (50% stake for GBP 679 million announced November 2022); groundworks/construction formally began 15 January 2024.
- Final investment decision signed 22 July 2025: UK Government 44.9%, La Caisse 20%, Centrica 15%, EDF 12.5%, Amber Infrastructure 7.6%. Proposed GBP 5 billion Bpifrance Assurance Export debt guarantee; National Wealth Fund supports majority of debt. Regulated Asset Base model under the Nuclear Energy (Financing) Act 2022: bills rise by GBP 1 a month during the ten construction years. Financing deal agreed November 2025.
- Cost: expected GBP 38 billion as of July 2025 (a 20% saving over Hinkley Point C, per government); earlier GBP 20-30 billion; January 2025 reports of close to GBP 40 billion, disputed by EDF and government. 2025 spending review allocated GBP 14.2 billion capital investment for 2026-2030; Treasury expects 10,000 jobs and power for six million homes; GBP 2 billion a year system savings claimed.
- Opposition: Together Against Sizewell C (TASC), Stop Sizewell C; RSPB concern over four acres of woodland and adjacent RSPB Minsmere.

wikis.title: Sizewell C reports project progress to parliament
wikis.summary: World Nuclear News (31 January 2025): Sizewell C's first annual progress update to MPs says the project is on time and on budget, with GBP 1 billion of savings from replicating Hinkley Point C.
wikis.body:
- Update delivered to MPs by Sizewell C (majority owned by the UK government) at the start of Nuclear Week: project "on time and on budget" and "the best prepared nuclear project in modern nuclear history" (from independent due diligence by Enco for HSBC).
- Two EPRs producing 3.2 GW, around six million homes for at least 60 years; design similar to Hinkley Point C.
- GBP 1 billion of cost savings identified through innovation and replication; contracts worth GBP 2.5 billion agreed with 290 UK suppliers; will support over 70,000 jobs and over 2,000 UK suppliers; 1,000 people employed on site.
- GBP 2.92 of economic value per GBP 1 invested during construction; over GBP 100 billion of value across the lifecycle.
- Received an additional GBP 2.7 billion in the 2024 Budget; Final Investment Decision due in the upcoming Spending Review. Quote from Pyke and Cann: "Sizewell C is on time and on budget and has a stable cost base."

wikis.title: Will Sizewell C lower energy bills? Cost, timeline and opposition
wikis.summary: Yahoo News UK (updated 22 July 2025) explainer on the Sizewell C final investment decision: stakeholders, GBP 38bn cost, mid-2030s timeline and effect on bills.
wikis.body:
- Government gave the final investment decision the green light, described as the UK's biggest investment in nuclear energy in 50 years; enough power for six million homes.
- Stakes: government 44.9%, La Caisse 20%, Centrica 15%, EDF 12.5% (lower than its previously stated 16.2%), Amber Infrastructure initially 7.6%. Chancellor Rachel Reeves: reduces reliance on "foreign dictators" via "publicly owned clean power".
- Location: near Sizewell on the Suffolk coast between Aldeburgh and Southwold, next to Sizewell B (began operating 1995). First earmarked in 2010.
- Cost: target construction cost GBP 38bn, with total investment above that as an overrun buffer; National Wealth Fund providing majority of debt with a loan of up to GBP 36.6bn; nearly double EDF's forecast of about GBP 20bn five years earlier. Stop Sizewell C previously estimated about GBP 40bn; campaigners call it "HS2 mark 2". Government says 10,000 jobs including 1,500 apprenticeships; GBP 330m contracts already signed with local firms.
- Timeline: Miliband: "Around a decade... mid-2034 is the date" (article: mid-2030s); EDF said in 2023 the earliest one reactor could operate would be end of 2033; company lawyer Hereward Phillpot: both reactors operational by mid-2034. Dale Vince notes Hinkley Point C was meant for 2017 and is now expected from 2031.
- Bills: average GBP 1 a month added to household bills from autumn during construction; up to GBP 2bn a year system savings once running; household savings not confirmed.
- Opposition: Together Against Sizewell C (Jenny Kirtley) cites wildlife impact and housing pressure.

wikis.title: Snowy 2.0 pumped hydro project: history, delays and design
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on Snowy 2.0, the under-construction pumped-hydro battery in New South Wales, covering its history, cost blowouts, tunnelling delays and design.
wikis.body:
- Pumped-hydro project in Kosciuszko National Park expanding the Snowy Mountains Scheme; owner/operator Snowy Hydro; 2,000 MW nameplate (text: 2.2 GW capacity and about 350 GWh storage; up to 175 hours); connects Tantangara (top) and Talbingo (bottom) reservoirs (700 m height difference) via 27 km of tunnels and an underground power station 800 m down. Construction began 2019; cost AUD 12 billion; largest renewable energy project under construction in Australia.
- History: plans discussed in 1966, studies 1980 and 1990; current project originated in Malcolm Turnbull's 2017 climate policy at about $2 billion; 2017 feasibility study (released 21 December 2017) put cost at $3.8-4.5 billion. Originally expected complete by 2024 (other sources 2021).
- Delays and cost: COVID-19, supply chain, complex design and geology. Confirmed $12bn cost blowout (RenewEconomy, 31 August 2023); AU$4.3 billion spent by 2023. Currently expected fully operational by end of 2028; in October 2025 reported 67% complete and not completable within A$12 billion.
- Tunnelling: three tunnel boring machines (a fourth needed); TBM Florence stuck for 19 months in soft rock near Tantangara, sinkhole December 2022, stuck again in hard rock May 2024, cleared by 11 July with ultra-high-pressure water jetting; tunnelling halted early 2025 over safety concerns. Main cavern excavated June 2023 to January 2024.
- Design: Webuild builds it; power station 22 m wide, 50 m high, 250 m long with six reversible Francis pump-turbine units (three variable speed) of 333 MW each, supplied by Voith; inclined pressure shaft 10 m diameter, 1.6 km long, 25-degree incline; HumeLink transmission line (opposed by community groups); operational footprint under 0.01% of the park.

wikis.title: Snowy 2.0 pushed back to late 2029, costs to blow out again
wikis.summary: RenewEconomy (3 May 2023): Snowy Hydro says Snowy 2.0 is delayed a further 12-24 months, possibly to December 2029, with more cost blowouts to come.
wikis.body:
- Snowy Hydro said full commercial operation may not be reached until December 2029: "delayed by a further 12-24 months from the current publicly released dates." More detail on budget implications expected around July 2023; latest official cost number was $5.9 billion; critics fear it could reach $10 billion excluding transmission.
- Causes named: covid, supply chain issues, design changes due to complexity, and tunnel boring machines stuck in soft soil.
- Energy minister Chris Bowen: "Obviously when a project takes longer, it will cost more"; he said earlier delays had been hidden from the market operator and public by the board and then energy minister Angus Taylor; he welcomed new management's "honesty". Contractors reportedly already put in claims for another two years.
- CEO Dennis Barnes wants a "safe, efficient and realistically achievable timeframe".
- AEMO said the announcement does not materially affect forecast reliability outcomes because of NSW transmission limits. Article notes Snowy 2.0 was not expected to fill capacity lost from Eraring's 2025 closure but could affect coal closure dates such as Vales Point (2029).

wikis.title: Snowy 2.0 faces another two-year delay
wikis.summary: pv magazine Australia (3 May 2023): Snowy Hydro confirms up to two more years of delay to Snowy 2.0, pushing full commercial operation to December 2029 with added costs.
wikis.body:
- Federal government-owned Snowy Hydro confirmed a delay of "a further 12-24 months" beyond current dates, i.e. December 2029, with likely "cost impacts beyond the contingency allowed."
- Project: expansion of the existing 4.1 GW Snowy scheme, originally forecast to provide 2 GW on-demand generation and 350 GWh storage; announced 2017; links Tantangara and Talbingo dams via 27 km of tunnels; originally due 2021 at about $2 billion; previously expected online in 2027; last estimates close to $6 billion, some say $10 billion-plus.
- CEO Dennis Barnes: "it's pretty clear that the schedule will go out by between one and two years"; a reset of timeline and budget is under way with principal contractor Future Generation (Webuild and Lane Construction JV).
- Causes: COVID-19, global supply chain disruptions, inflation, design changes, geological issues. TBM Florence, one of three machines, was at a standstill for four months in soft ground, having dug about 150 metres of a 15 km tunnel since November.

wikis.title: Dogger Bank Wind Farm: phases, ownership and construction status
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the Dogger Bank offshore wind cluster (Dogger Bank A, B, C, Sofia, South and proposed D) in the North Sea off Yorkshire, with 2026 construction updates.
wikis.body:
- Group of offshore wind farms 130-200 km off Yorkshire's east coast, considered the world's largest offshore wind farm; 8.1 GW expected as of 2024. First electricity 10 October 2023. All four farms won 2019 CfD auctions.
- History: Forewind consortium (SSE, RWE, Statoil, Statkraft) formed November 2008, developer from January 2010; plans scaled from 9 GW to 7.2 GW (2014) and 4.8 GW (2015). August 2017: SSE and Equinor each 50% of Creyke Beck A, B and Teesside A; Innogy (RWE) took Teesside B, now Sofia Offshore Wind Farm. Eni acquired 20% in December 2020. RWE and Masdar to fund with an 11 billion pound investment agreed at COP28 (1 December 2023).
- Dogger Bank A and B: up to 1.2 GW each, 131 km offshore (515 and 599 sq km); 190 GE Haliade-X 13 MW turbines total (95 each), about 1.235 GW per site; planning consent for up to 400 turbines on 17 February 2015; 15-year PPAs November 2020; cable laying April 2022; first unmanned HVDC substation April 2023; a 107 m blade failed during commissioning at A. Per 16 February 2026 SSE notice all 95 turbines installed at A; B expected complete in 2027, with 33 of 95 turbines installed as of 27 July 2026.
- Dogger Bank C: GE Haliade 14 MW turbines; 15-year PPA November 2021; as of 27 July 2026 all 87 foundation/transition pieces and 58 of 87 inter-array cables installed.
- Sofia: 100 Siemens Gamesa 14 MW turbines; all foundations, turbines and cables installed as of 22 June 2026; started generating electricity on 16 August 2026.
- Dogger Bank South (RWE): two 1.5 GW farms; RWE and Masdar won a CfD auction in January 2026 for 3 GW to be delivered in 2030/2031; planning permission May 2026. Dogger Bank D (SSE and Equinor, 1.5 GW): consultation launched June 2026.
- As of 2026 A, B, C and Sofia expected to produce 5 GW, plus 3 GW at South. Also mentioned: North Sea Wind Power Hub concept (TenneT study: up to 110 GW).

wikis.title: SSE Renewables: Dogger Bank Offshore Wind Farm
wikis.summary: SSE Renewables project page describing the 3.6 GW Dogger Bank Wind Farm under construction in three 1.2 GW phases.
wikis.body:
- 3.6 GW farm more than 130 km off England's North East coast; joint venture SSE (40%), Equinor (40%), Vaargronn (20%); built in phases A, B and C of 1.2 GW each; when complete, capable of powering up to 6 million UK homes annually. SSE leads construction; Equinor will operate for a lifetime of up to 35 years. Potential fourth phase Dogger Bank D being progressed.
- Consent as a Nationally Significant Infrastructure Project in 2015; 15-year CfDs for 3.6 GW in the 2019 auction. A and B reached financial close November 2020, C in December 2021 (described as the largest offshore wind project financing globally).
- Turbines: GE Haliade-X up to 14 MW; first began generating in October 2023; one rotation can power a UK home for more than two days. Installation vessel: Voltaire (Jan De Nul), 3,000-tonne lifting capacity.
- First UK offshore wind HVDC connection; power comes ashore in the East Riding and Teesside. Dogger Bank A about 515 sq km and B 599 sq km, both 131 km from shore at closest.
- Jobs: more than 2,000 UK roles created or supported; over 400 long-term local roles.

wikis.title: Dogger Bank Wind Farm official site
wikis.summary: Official Dogger Bank project site describing the three-phase 3.6 GW offshore wind farm, its partners, community fund and planning documents.
wikis.body:
- Developed in three phases (A, B, C), 130-190 km from the North East coast of England; each phase 1.2 GW; combined 3,600 MW, the world's largest offshore wind farm; the UK's largest single source of renewable energy.
- Joint venture: SSE (40%), Equinor (40%), Vaargronn (20%); SSE leads development and construction; Equinor operates on completion for around 35 years. Uses one of the world's most powerful turbines (GE Haliade-X) and the largest installation vessel.
- Each turbine can power 16,000 British households; one rotation can power a UK household for two days. Homes figure based on 2,700 kWh per household, 55% load factor.
- Community: fund supports STEM careers and grants up to 1,000 pounds; STEM programme has supported more than 10,000 South Tyneside youngsters over five years (7 July 2026 news). 12 August 2026: up to 180 new offshore wind jobs at Port of Nigg, Scotland.
- Planning: DCO achieved by Forewind; Dogger Bank C draft Decommissioning Programme consultation (to 7 January 2022); Dogger Bank C and Sofia planning application for a construction access at Wilton International (10 September 2020).

wikis.title: King Salman International Airport (Riyadh)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia stub on the planned King Salman International Airport at Riyadh, its origin in December 2022, design team and capacity goals.
wikis.body:
- International airport under construction serving Riyadh, to succeed King Khalid International Airport and be built around it; designed by Foster + Partners with engineering consultancy Jacobs.
- History: in December 2022 Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman proposed a new airport to boost tourism, as part of Vision 2030.
- Facilities: six passenger terminals, an iconic terminal, a private aviation terminal and six runways; area 57 sq km; aims to handle 100 million passengers per year by 2030 and 185 million by 2050, and 3.5 million tonnes of cargo per year by 2050. Plans to rely on renewable energy and seek LEED Platinum certification; single concourse with a loop connecting terminals; a 4.2 sq mi area reserved for retail and office space. Aims to be among the world's largest airports.

wikis.title: King Salman International Airport scheduled to open by 2030
wikis.summary: AeroTime (4 March 2024) on Riyadh's planned King Salman International Airport: runways, passenger targets, contractors and expected opening by 2030.
wikis.body:
- Six parallel runways; expected 120 million passengers per year, which would make it the largest by passenger numbers; no IATA code yet; expected to open by 2030.
- Per the Saudi Infrastructure Expo, it would lift Saudi passenger traffic from 29 million to 120 million by 2030 and 185 million by 2050; aircraft traffic from 211,000 to more than 1 million flights per year; 150,000 jobs expected.
- Contractor bidding for the 57 km project began November 2023. On 29 February 2024 MEED reported UK firm Mace Group won the delivery partner role (project management, design management, cost consulting, procurement advice). Foster + Partners won the master plan; Jacobs will plot infrastructure.
- Largest airport by size currently: King Fahd International Airport (DMM).

wikis.title: King Salman International Airport, Saudi Arabia: project overview
wikis.summary: Airport Technology project profile (8 December 2025) of the $30bn King Salman International Airport at Riyadh, expected to open in 2030, with design, capacity and contractors.
wikis.body:
- Developer King Salman International Airport Development Company (KSIADC), a Public Investment Fund company; new airport type; estimated investment $30bn; construction started September 2025 (per the page); expected opening 2030; annual passenger capacity 185 million.
- Master plan unveiled by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman in November 2022; part of Vision 2030. Aims for LEED Platinum certification.
- Targets: up to 120 million travellers by 2030; up to 185 million passengers and 3.5 million tonnes of cargo by 2050; contributes SR27bn ($7.2bn) annually to non-oil GDP; about 103,000 direct and indirect jobs; aircraft traffic from 211,000 to more than one million flights annually by 2050.
- Location: north of Riyadh next to King Khalid International Airport; site about 57 km2 (45 km2 airport area, about 12 km2 support, residential, recreational and logistics real estate), six parallel runways and nine terminals (royal, commercial airline, private aviation, Terminal 6 for low-cost-carrier cargo) plus existing King Khalid terminals; Wadi Loop green corridor.
- Contractors: Foster + Partners (master plan won November 2022; next design phase agreement August 2024); Jacobs (master plan validation, runway design); Bechtel (executive partnership May 2025 for three terminals); Parsons (two four-year delivery partner contracts for airside infrastructure, May 2025); Mace (monitoring planning and construction); Nera (airspace design); Saudi Icon Company; a JV of Nesma and Partners, AlAyunik Limak and Samsung C&T formed February 2025. July 2025 MoU with Biofuel Company for B100 biodiesel during construction.

wikis.title: The Line (Neom, Saudi Arabia) - Wikipedia overview
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on The Line, the planned 170 km linear city in Neom, Tabuk Province, its design, cost estimates, criticism and reported scaling back or suspension.
wikis.body:
- The Line is a planned linear settlement in Neom, Tabuk Province, Saudi Arabia, to be housed in a single very long arcology. Announced in 2021, envisioned as a smart city with no cars, streets or carbon emissions; conceived by Saudi ruler Mohammed bin Salman. "By 2025, the megaproject had been substantially scaled down or suspended."
- Initial plan: 170 km long, 500 m high, 200 m wide, capacity 9 million people (25% of Saudi Arabia's 2022 population of 35.5 million), glass mirror exterior, all basic services within a five-minute walk. Powered entirely by renewable energy; three layers (pedestrian surface, underground infrastructure, underground transport); AI monitoring.
- Cost: estimated US$100-200 billion (some estimates as high as $1 trillion). In 2022 the crown prince said the first phase would cost SAR 1.2 trillion (US$320 billion), with the Public Investment Fund providing half. Government claimed 460,000 jobs and SAR 180 billion (US$48 billion) to GDP by 2030.
- Criticism: unrealistic costs and timelines, impractical shape, environmental harm, human rights violations; thousands forcibly moved and villages razed. An architect said the design relied on "a lot of technology that we don't have today".
- April 2024: reported "scaled back". Wall Street Journal (2025) reported an internal audit finding "evidence of deliberate manipulation" and that the first phase would only be 2.4 km long; Saudi officials denied this. After $50 billion spent, the aim had become to complete the first half-mile section in 2034. WSJ said a 2023 draft board presentation estimated completion in 2080 at a cost of $8.8 trillion.
- By end of 2025 the project appeared suspended with no construction work; in May 2026 Semafor reported construction delayed until at least after 2030.

wikis.title: Saudi Arabia plans 100-mile-long mirrored skyscraper megacity (The Guardian)
wikis.summary: Guardian report of 27 July 2022 on Saudi Arabia's unveiling of The Line, a 200 m wide, 500 m high mirrored linear city at Neom, and doubts about its feasibility.
wikis.body:
- The Line is described as a linear city 200 metres wide made of two long mirror-encased skyscrapers stretching more than 100 miles from the Red Sea, a future home for 9 million people; centrepiece of Neom near the Gulf of Aqaba.
- Crown prince Mohammed bin Salman outlined it; officials claim it will be the world's most liveable city "by far". Economists, architects and analysts are "not quite sure" it can be realised, even those working on it.
- Design: 500 m high, 200 m wide, car-free, carbon neutral, AI central to life, temperate regulated microclimate; "all daily needs" within a five-minute walk, outdoor skiing facilities and "high-speed rail with an end-to-end transit of 20 minutes".
- Funding: the "first phase", lasting until 2030, would cost 1.2tn Saudi riyals (about £265bn); sources include government subsidies, the private sector and a Neom IPO expected in 2024.
- Neom first announced in 2017; expected to house 1.2 million people by 2030 (as stated by the prince). Environmentalists are sceptical of Saudi net zero by 2060 pledge. A consultant said "only eight years left before residents are meant to move in, it's a lot to take on trust".

wikis.title: Neom uses one fifth of the world's steel (AGBI)
wikis.summary: AGBI report that Neom's chief investment officer said the giga-project consumes about 20% of global steel and will be the world's largest construction-materials customer for decades.
wikis.body:
- Neom is currently using one fifth of all steel produced in the world, said Manar Al Moneef, Neom's chief investment officer, at the Global Logistics Forum in Riyadh (reported on a Monday in October 2024).
- She called it a $500 billion project; Neom demand equals 5 percent of the global logistics market; "we are 20 percent of the global steel market"; also large demand for elevators and cement.
- Saudi projects are valued at more than $1.25 trillion, but some have slowed as the Public Investment Fund faces funding pressure from lower oil prices and priorities in Riyadh before World Expo 2030 and the 2034 World Cup.
- The Line: horizontal city due for final completion at 170 km in 2045; a 5 km central section targets 2030. Neom also includes Trojena winter resort, 12 luxury resorts called Magna, Sindalah island resort and industrial city Oxagon.
- The project "has been plagued by reports of mismanagement, overspending and construction delays".

wikis.title: City Rail Link (Auckland) - Wikipedia overview
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on Auckland's City Rail Link, a pair of 3.45 km tunnels linking Waitemata Station to Maungawhau, with its history, construction and opening.
wikis.body:
- The City Rail Link (CRL) is a pair of 3.45-kilometre (2.14 mi) tunnels under Auckland's city centre, extending the North Island Main Trunk from Waitemata Station (formerly Britomart) to a junction with the North Auckland Line at Maungawhau Station.
- Planned since 2013, construction began in 2018 (per the article) and included two underground stations, Te Waihorotiu near Aotea Square and Karanga-a-Hape near Karangahape Road. Waitemata became a through station; Mount Eden station was replaced by Maungawhau, with four platforms as an interchange with the Western Line.
- History: proposals date to the 1920s (New Lynn Town Board tunnel to Morningside in 1918; planning 1924, abandoned 1930); 1969 plan for a $12m loop; 1970s Dove-Myer Robinson scheme rejected in 1976 by the Muldoon government as too costly; 2004 Auckland City Council plans for three new stations. Renewed interest after Britomart opened in 2003; the 2012 Auckland Spatial Plan called it the most important transport investment for Auckland.
- The article states the link opened to the public on 13 September 2026.

wikis.title: CRL opening morning: passenger boom on first day (Stuff)
wikis.summary: Stuff report on the first public passenger service through Auckland's City Rail Link on Sunday 13 September, with more than double the usual Sunday passengers.
wikis.body:
- First passenger service left Otahuhu Station (South City Line) at 4.57am on the opening Sunday; more than 150 people queued, some since 4:10am. Passengers chanted "tunnel, tunnel, tunnel" and cheered at Karanga-a-Hape. Transport Minister Chris Bishop, MPs and former deputy mayor Penny Hulse were aboard, as was AT chief executive Stacey van der Putten.
- By midday AT estimated about 14,300 people had travelled versus 6800 at the same time the previous Sunday (more than double).
- First time the public could travel through the tunnels connecting Waitemata (formerly Britomart) with refurbished Maungawhau (formerly Mt Eden). Announced date was September 13.
- Background: costing $5.4 billion, two new 3.5 km tunnels and two new CBD stations (near Karangahape Road and Aotea Square); the source says construction began in 2015 and the idea was first proposed in the 1920s by Railways Minister Gordon Coates; Len Brown put it in his 2010 mayoral platform. KiwiRail network upgrades raise peak train capacity by at least 50%. Council says it will double the number of people able to reach the city centre by public transport within 30 minutes.

wikis.title: City Rail Link handed over as opening day moves closer (1News)
wikis.summary: 1News report of 30 June 2026 that the CRL was handed to KiwiRail and Auckland Transport and would open on a Sunday, with candidate dates from August 16 to September 20.
wikis.body:
- Auckland Transport confirmed the CRL will open on a Sunday, after more than $5 billion of spending. Ownership passed from the Link Alliance construction consortium to KiwiRail and AT on 30 June 2026.
- Opening set to fall at least six-to-eight weeks after handover (rail staff roster notice). Earliest possible date August 16; other contenders August 23, August 30, September 6, September 13 and September 20. Mayor Wayne Brown expected opening around this period.
- Rail network closes over Matariki weekend from July 9 for a network-wide "dress rehearsal" of the new timetable. Opening Sunday to have extra services, no large formal ceremony; first trains early in the morning.
- Remaining "paper project": safety assurance with rail regulator NZTA and code-of-compliance certification for three new station buildings; compared with Sydney Metro's 2024 delay. Bledisloe Cup test at Eden Park on October 10 and the election campaign were factors. AT said opening "will be in the second half of this year".

wikis.title: Panama Metro (with Line 3 monorail) - Wikipedia overview
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the Panama Metro, covering Lines 1 and 2 in service and the Line 3 monorail under construction, its financing, cost growth and trains.
wikis.body:
- Panama Metro serves Panama City. Line 1 opened April 6, 2014 (18.1 km, 15 stations). Line 2 opened to regular service April 25, 2019 (24 km, 18 stations; airport branch to Tocumen opened 2023). San Miguelito is the interchange. Annual ridership listed as 116,088,070.
- Line 3: a 24.5 km monorail with 11 stations under construction, linking Ciudad del Futuro (Arraijan) with Albrook station where it connects to Line 1; expected daily demand 160,000 passengers, 37 minute travel time. Financed by Japanese loans via JICA; first Japanese-technology monorail in Latin America, rolling stock by Hitachi Rail.
- Costs rose from an initial US$2.6 billion estimate to more than US$4 billion, attributed to design modifications, nationwide protests in 2023, delays to a nearby highway, and higher materials costs (COVID-19, war in Ukraine). Three planned stations were removed and the fleet cut from 28 to 26 six-car trains. "The final cost of Line 3 remains undetermined."
- Trains: 26 six-car Hitachi straddle-type monorails, about 1,000 passengers each; first trainsets arrived in Panama in early 2024; dynamic testing on the elevated viaduct had begun by 2026.
- Master plan: ten-line network planned by 2035-2040 (four rapid transit, three tram, two monorail, one aerial lift).

wikis.title: Panama Metro Line 3: first phase 2027, second phase 2028 (La Prensa)
wikis.summary: La Prensa Panama report on the sixth addendum ($765 million) that splits Metro Line 3 into two phases, raising cost to $3,989 million and giving 2027 and 2028 delivery dates.
wikis.body:
- With the sixth addendum, costing $765 million, Metro de Panama and the Korean group (Hyundai Engineering & Construction and Posco E&C, HPH Joint Venture) agreed to split Line 3 into two phases (elevated and underground segments). The Contraloria endorsed it on December 4, 2024; it was signed November 20.
- Original 2020 contract: $2,844 million. The underground section (6 km tunnel between Balboa and Panama Pacifico station) was not in it, after the Cortizo administration decided the monorail would not use the fourth bridge over the Canal. Current cost $3,989 million, an increase of $1,145 million.
- Construction originally 54 months; phase 1 now estimated at 74 months, due to the tunnel and delays not attributable to the contractor (pandemic, the Roberto F. Chiari highway, protests against the mining contract). Claims exceeding $8 million.
- Stations reduced to 12 of 14 originally planned over the 24.5 km route. Phase 1 in 2027, phase 2 in 2028 (per the headline). Contractor has 180 days after substantial acceptance to finish pending works. The article notes a recent three-day Suntracs strike may affect cost and schedule.
- The fourth bridge (3.6 km cable-stayed, six lanes) was 18% complete, expected to finish in 2028 (China Communications Construction Company).

wikis.title: Metro de Panama Line 3: when will it be operational? (Telemetro)
wikis.summary: Telemetro piece saying Line 3 could be operational in 2027 from Ciudad del Futuro to Panama Pacifico, plus details of the tunnel under the Canal.
wikis.body:
- Line 3 will benefit residents of Arraijan and La Chorrera in Panama Oeste; it "could be operational in 2027" from Ciudad del Futuro station to Panama Pacifico.
- The tunnel crossing the Canal will be excavated at a depth of 65 metres by the "Tuneladora Panama", with work scheduled to start between late September and early October 2024 at the underground section at Panama Pacifico; excavation to last 22 months.
- Route: a section after Panama Pacifico station, a traditional 300 m tunnel, then a 100 m launch shaft at Farfan; 3 km under the Canal navigation channel to a second shaft at Balboa; finishing at Albrook station, completing a 4.5 km connection to Line 1.
- The TBM has special compartments for workers for up to 72 hours in case of an incident.

wikis.title: Bogota Metro - Wikipedia overview
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the elevated Bogota Metro Line 1 under construction, projected to operate in 2028, with a long history of proposals since the 1940s.
wikis.body:
- Bogota Metro is a rapid transit project under construction in Bogota, Colombia, projected to operate in 2028 (infobox: March 2028); construction started October 2020. Line 1 is elevated, standard gauge (1,435 mm), from Gibraltar to Calle 72, operator Metro Linea 1 S.A.S.; headway 3 min.
- Bogota currently has no rail service and relies on the TransMilenio bus rapid transit system.
- History: debated since the 1940s; 1955 city chose buses; 1981 Fedesarrollo studies (92 km main line, average US$797 million); projects shelved; 1990 agreements; Sener-TMB won 2009 study contract; Aug 2009 four routes; mayor Samuel Moreno announced possible operation by 2016; Carrusel de la Contratacion scandal paralysed the project; May 5, 2013 mayor Petro's "final agreement"; October 7, 2014 final studies for an underground metro (cost about COP $15 billion), estimated inauguration 2021.
- Later mayors (Penalosa from 2016) redirected the project (text beyond this excerpt not read).

wikis.title: Bogota Metro gets a launch date (ColombiaOne)
wikis.summary: ColombiaOne report of 2 September 2026 that Mayor Carlos Fernando Galan set March 15, 2028 for first passengers on Metro Line 1, now more than 80% complete.
wikis.body:
- Mayor Carlos Fernando Galan confirmed first passengers can ride Line 1 on March 15, 2028; the project is "more than 80% complete".
- Line 1 is approximately 24 km with 16 stations, elevated, connecting the southwest with central and northeastern Bogota.
- Schedule: railway track installation completed in January next year; construction expected complete September 2027, when a trial operation period begins to test trains and systems.
- Trains use GOA 4 automatic operation (no driver), six cars each, capacity nearly 1,800 passengers; stations have platform screen doors.
- History: Mayor Carlos Sanz de Santamaria first raised the need in 1942; attempts in the 1950s (Rojas Pinilla), 1966 (Jorge Gaitan Caracas Avenue), 1981 studies (23 km line, about US$797 million).

wikis.title: Bogota Metro viaduct phase begins, completion set for 2028 (Bogota.gov.co)
wikis.summary: City of Bogota release on Mayor Claudia Lopez signing the act starting viaduct construction of Metro Line 1, with a 42% progress figure and March 2028 commercial operation target.
wikis.body:
- Mayor Claudia Lopez, Metro Company manager Leonidas Narvaez and Metro Line 1 legal representative Wen Ding signed the act starting the construction phase of the 24 km viaduct at the workshop yard in Bosa.
- Six new work fronts begin, for nine simultaneous, four using a pile driver ("a technology never before used in Colombia"). Bidding for the Septima Green Corridor to open "next Monday, July 31st".
- Progress cited 24.23% (workshop yard, 72nd Ave/Caracas interchange, Primero de Mayo/Carrera 68 bridge); trains being built in China. One passage cites approx. 42% (context not fully read).
- Narvaez: first train must arrive August 2025 for testing; by September 2027, 4,000 linear metres of viaduct needed so testing starts, with commercial operation in March 2028.
- Transaction Contract No. 1 settled a non-compliance process started May 9, 2023: consortium pays a fine of 1,885,000,000 pesos for missing the March 30, 2023 detailed-designs deadline. Cost of Line 1 stated at 22.3 trillion pesos (2017 value).

wikis.title: Paris Metro Line 17 (Grand Paris Express) - Wikipedia overview
wikis.summary: Wikipedia stub on Paris Metro Line 17, an automated Grand Paris Express line to Charles de Gaulle Airport planned to open in phases from 2027 to 2030.
wikis.body:
- Line 17 is one of four Grand Paris Express lines, "planned to open in phases from 2027 through 2030", with above-ground sections including Parc des Expositions station.
- Infobox: planned opening late-2027 (Saint-Denis-Pleyel to Le Bourget-Aeroport); 2028 (Le Bourget-Aeroport to Parc des Expositions); 2030 (full line); after 2030 for a Saint-Denis-Pleyel to Nanterre-La Folie extension (under study). Text says mid-2027 for the first stage.
- Delays: first stage originally planned for 2024 to coincide with the Summer Olympics; delayed in 2022 to 2026; in February 2025 a further delay to mid-2027 was announced because of delays on line 15, which shares its automated driving system with lines 16 and 17.
- May 2023: Keolis to operate, RATP manages infrastructure. A station at the planned Terminal 4 of Charles-de-Gaulle was dropped after the terminal was cancelled in 2021 (announced October 2024).
- Route connects the Plaine Commune employment area to Charles de Gaulle Airport (connection with line 14 at Saint-Denis-Pleyel); passes Le Bourget, Gonesse, Triangle de Gonesse, Parc des Expositions (RER B), CDG Terminal 2 and ends at Le Mesnil-Amelot.
- Trains: Alstom selected July 2018 for 183 trains (EUR 1.3bn) across the project; March 2019 order of 23 three-car trains shared with line 16; 54 m long, 1500 V DC via pantograph.

wikis.title: Skyline (Honolulu) - overview and early planning history (Wikipedia, part 1)
wikis.summary: First third of the Wikipedia article on Honolulu's Skyline light metro: opening dates of segments, and the planning, environmental review and early cost history up to about 2021.
wikis.body:
- Skyline is a light metro in Honolulu on Oahu. Segment 1 (East Kapolei to Aloha Stadium) opened June 30, 2023; Segment 2 (to Pearl Harbor, the airport and Middle Street) opened October 16, 2025; Segment 3 (across Urban Honolulu to Downtown) "is due to open in 2031". The 18.9-mile (30.4 km) automated line was built by HART; Hitachi Rail built the railcars and operates it for the Honolulu Department of Transportation Services. "The largest public works project in Hawaii's history."
- History: mayor Neal Blaisdell suggested rail in 1966; Frank Fasi began planning in 1977; cancelled 1981, restarted 1986, stopped by a 1992 council vote against a tax increase; Harris pursued bus rapid transit; Mufi Hannemann began the Honolulu High-Capacity Transit Corridor Project.
- Milestones: Alternatives Analysis Report November 1, 2006; Draft EIS cleared October 29, 2008 (released two days before the 2008 election, criticised); Final EIS approved June 14, 2010; record of decision January 18, 2011. Burial Council refused programmatic agreement on October 21, 2009 over likely burials on Halekauwila Street.
- Construction, originally due December 2009, was delayed. A December 2, 2010 state study projected a $1.7 billion overrun above the $5.3 billion projected cost. HART's first CEO Dan Grabauskas was hired March 2012. Interim service on the first ten miles was scheduled for October 2020, pushed back three months by COVID-19, then to late 2021 due to testing-equipment delays (per November 2020).

wikis.title: Honolulu's Skyline opens for service (Mass Transit)
wikis.summary: Mass Transit report that Skyline's 11-mile first phase opened June 30 (2023) between Kualaka'i (East Kapolei) and Halawa (Aloha Stadium) stations.
wikis.body:
- Skyline, a mostly elevated autonomous rail system, opened June 30; first phase is an 11-mile segment with nine stations between Kualaka'i (East Kapolei) and Halawa (Aloha Stadium).
- Ceremony with local, state and federal officials; Mayor Rick Blangiardi: "you cannot overstate the word historic". Fares waived on all transit through July 4; a HOLO card is needed.
- The project "took years of planning, 12 years of construction, incurred delays, cost overruns and leadership turnover and the threat of losing federal funding before a project recovery plan was developed".
- HART oversaw construction and handed control to the City and County of Honolulu in early June 2023. Next phases: Airport Extension (planned 2025, four stations to Middle Street-Kalihi Transit Center) and City Center Extension (2031, six stations to Civic Center).
- Hitachi Rail built railcars, tested and commissioned the system and will operate and maintain core systems; billed as the first true mass transit GoA4 system in the U.S.; up to 40,000 fewer car journeys a day once complete, per Hitachi's Alistair Dormer. HART CEO: Lori Kahikina.

wikis.title: HART: Honolulu's full rail line expected done in 2031 (Civil Beat)
wikis.summary: Civil Beat report that HART's new estimate puts completion of the full 20-mile, 21-station line to Ala Moana Center in 2031, with a cost of around $11 billion.
wikis.body:
- HART's latest estimates: about 10 more years to build the 20-mile, 21-station line to Ala Moana Center; new 2031 completion date to be presented at the March 18 board meeting by Nathaniel Meddings, director for project controls, with an official new "estimate at completion" cost. Unofficial estimates the previous fall put the cost at around $11 billion.
- In November, city leaders outside HART had said it could take until 2033; HART said that was "not an official HART number" and that it could deliver in late 2027 or 2028. The full line was originally due January 2020.
- HART still aims to have the first half, to Aloha Stadium, ready by the end of this year; unclear when the city might start service.
- Executive director Lori Kahikina. (Year of the article is not stated in the text read.)

wikis.title: North East Link (Melbourne) - Wikipedia overview
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on North East Link, Victoria's most expensive road project, a freeway and tunnel completing Melbourne's Metropolitan Ring Road between Greensborough and the Eastern Freeway.
wikis.body:
- North East Link runs from Greensborough (M80 Ring Road) south to a Y-interchange with the Eastern Freeway (M3); interchanges at Grimshaw Street, Greensborough Road, Lower Plenty Road, Manningham Road and Thompsons Road. Infobox: "Late 2028 (scheduled)".
- It "would complete Melbourne's Metropolitan Ring Road project" and is estimated to carry around 100,000 vehicles a day, easing freight movement between Dandenong, Campbellfield and the Donnybrook freight hub, and reducing reliance on Fitzsimons Lane, Heidelberg Road and Rosanna Road.
- Cost: "the most expensive road project ever constructed in Victoria", with cost blowouts from an originally planned $10bn to $26bn. A March 2020 announcement created a state-owned "North East Link State Tolling Corporation" to collect tolls.
- Criticism: a shift of around 25,000 commuters per day from public transport to road expected (PTUA's Tony Morton criticised it); several community groups and councils (including Yarra City Council) opposed the tollway. Related: Eastern Busway to be built with the project.

wikis.title: Dig done: tunnelling complete on North East Link (Premier of Victoria)
wikis.summary: Victorian Premier's media release that TBM Gillian broke through at Bulleen, completing excavation of both 6.5 km North East Link tunnels, with opening set for 2028.
wikis.body:
- Tunnelling is complete on North East Link: TBM Gillian broke through at Bulleen, finishing the southbound tunnel; the northbound excavation finished in May "this year" (year not stated).
- "Set to open to traffic in 2028"; twin 6.5-kilometre tunnels, creating more than 12,000 jobs, taking up to 15,000 trucks a day off local roads and cutting up to 35 minutes off trips between Melbourne's north and east; Victoria's biggest road project and largest road tunnel.
- The TBMs removed 2.5 million tonnes of rock and dirt and installed nearly 43,000 pre-cast tunnel segments, on schedule. Above-ground works continue (interchange ramps, motorway control centre, Greensborough Road boulevard) plus Eastern Freeway and M80 upgrades.
- Jointly funded by the Australian and Victorian governments; quotes from ministers Catherine King and Gabrielle Williams and local MPs.

wikis.title: New Administrative Capital (Egypt) - Wikipedia overview
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on Egypt's New Administrative Capital east of Cairo: announcement, financing through ACUD, landmarks and the 2024 inauguration as seat of government.
wikis.body:
- The New Capital is a new urban community and de facto capital of Egypt east of New Cairo. As of May 2023, 14 ministries and government entities had relocated. On 2 April 2024 President al-Sisi took the oath for a third term there, "officially inaugurating the new capital city as the seat of Egyptian government".
- Announced by housing minister Mostafa Madbouly on 13 March 2015 (Egypt Vision 2030). Planned area figures in the infobox: 5.6 km2 city centre, 714 km2 urban. Naming proposals include "Wedian", "Masr", "Kemet", "Al Mustaqbal", "Al Salam" but no official result.
- Cost to move the government: expected over US$100 million; full cost and timeline not revealed.
- Builders: Emirati Capital City Partners (Mohamed Alabbar) MoU cancelled September 2015; China State Construction Engineering Corporation MoU, later limited to the CBD (2017). Administrative Capital Urban Development Company (ACUD) set up 21 April 2016: Ministry of Defense 51% (land), NUCA 49% (EGP 20bn capital injection; authorised capital EGP 204bn).
- Landmarks: Octagon (Ministry of Defense HQ); Green River Park 35 km planned (first 10 km under construction); mosque and cathedral inaugurated January 2019 (Grand Mosque largest in Africa; Nativity of Christ cathedral 8,000+); over 30 skyscrapers under construction incl. the Iconic Tower; planned Oblisco Capitale 1,000 m for 2030; Capital International Airport opened 2019.

wikis.title: Egypt aims to house 6 million in the New Administrative Capital (Egypt Independent)
wikis.summary: Egypt Independent report that the capital's spokesperson said the finished three-phase city will house six million, at a cost of about LE380 billion.
wikis.body:
- Spokesperson Khaled al-Husseini said on Tuesday that once the three phases are complete six million citizens will be housed; the city is twice the size of Cairo and currently in its first phase.
- Key projects: Cultural Arts District, commercial towers, government district, commercial centres and residential areas.
- Cost approximately LE380 billion; will be Egypt's administrative and financial capital with dozens of embassies. Aims to relieve congestion in Cairo (over 20 million people).
- State employees to be moved in stages; employees scheduled to be transferred within six months before work is piloted from the new ministry headquarters.
- Statements made at the third Conference of Egyptian Entities Abroad (346 participants, 45 entities, 38 countries).

wikis.title: Tallest skyscraper in Africa topped out in Egypt's new capital (Daily News Egypt)
wikis.summary: Report that the 385 m Iconic Tower, built by China State Construction in Egypt's new capital, held its topping-out ceremony on Thursday (June 2021).
wikis.body:
- Topping-out ceremony for the 385-metre Iconic Tower, "the tallest building in Africa upon completion", in the CBD of the new administrative capital about 50 km east of Cairo.
- Construction started May 2, 2018; 78 floors above ground, two underground, total area 65,000 m2; office, hotel, business and sightseeing functions. Core tube started April 2019, built at one floor every four days.
- The CBD project by CSCEC has about 505,000 m2 and 20 high-rises. Housing minister Essam el-Gazzar called it "the most important building in modern Egypt".
- Egypt expects the new capital, with inauguration expected "at the end of this year", to create around 2 million jobs. Madbouly said the tower would be a landmark on a par with the pyramids.

wikis.title: Building Egypt's $58bn new city in the sand (The B1M)
wikis.summary: The B1M video page on Egypt's USD 58bn new capital 45 km east of Cairo: masterplan, phases, funding problems and criticism.
wikis.body:
- Egypt is investing US$58 billion in a new capital; Cairo grew from 2.5 million (1950) to over 20 million and, as of September 2019, has three metro lines. A 2010 World Bank study found congestion losses above 4% of GDP.
- The city, 45 km east of Cairo, over 700 km2, master-planned by SOM, for about 6.5 million inhabitants when complete in 2050; 100 residential neighbourhoods, over 1200 mosques and churches, 553 hospitals and clinics, 40,000 hotel rooms, a theme park, a central park twice the length of New York's, a 90 km2 solar farm.
- First phase 168 km2: business district with an 85-storey tower to be Africa's tallest, 20 more skyscrapers, a government quarter for 34 ministries, and the country's largest mosque and church. High-speed rail link to Cairo set to complete in late 2020.
- Problems: phases two and three delayed after Chinese investor Fortune Land Development pulled out; critics say it targets wealthy citizens and diverts funds from Cairo's congestion.

wikis.title: Thirty Meter Telescope - Wikipedia overview (Mauna Kea)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the proposed Thirty Meter Telescope on Mauna Kea: design, site selection, funding partners and the opposition that halted construction.
wikis.body:
- TMT is a proposed extremely large telescope on Mauna Kea, Hawaii island.
