- Two steel columns collapsed/buckled on July 7 in the 37-story tower at 235 East 42nd Street (Midtown, the former Pfizer Building), causing floors above to sag and the city to evacuate surrounding blocks (a "blocks-wide evacuation") for fear of catastrophic collapse.
- Engineers interviewed by Gothamist said the columns did not appear to have the reinforcing plates called for in the project plans. GACE Consulting Engineers had called for added steel plates along the length of the two columns to support the 15 residential floors above.
- GACE Principal Engineer Chris Behan blamed the failure to install the reinforcement on three floors, including the 21st where the collapse occurred: "The reinforcement from the 19th floor to the top of the 21st floor, which would have significantly increased the columns' strength, was never installed... The structure was not reinforced as GACE's design required."
- The reinforcement would have turned the I-shaped columns into solid steel boxes. Chris Cerino (past president, Structural Engineers Association of New York): "It looked to me that it wasn't there." Joe DiPompeo (former president, Structural Engineering Institute at ASCE) said photos clearly do not show the boxed reinforcement in the drawings.
- The Department of Buildings has not determined the cause and declined to comment on whether the steel was installed. On the day of the failure it declared the building structurally sound after emergency work shored up each floor.
- Developer MetroLoft did not immediately respond; MetroLoft principal Nathan Berman told The Real Deal on the day it was possible the columns weren't properly reinforced. It is unclear why the work was not done or why inspectors did not catch it.
- MetroLoft's conversion is the city's largest office-to-home conversion: expanding 10 stories above the collapsed columns and adding four floors to the original 33-story tower.
- This week the city sent building safety inspectors across five boroughs to review unidentified construction sites; New York City investigators opened a preliminary criminal inquiry whose scope and target are unclear.

wikis.title: Heathrow board greenlights third runway planning application work
wikis.summary: Heathrow's 15 January 2026 press release says its Board approved investment to start a third-runway planning application while key 2026 regulatory and policy decisions will determine whether expansion proceeds.
wikis.body:
- Dated 15 January, 2026. Heathrow confirmed it approved new investment to begin work on a planning application for a third runway, described as the UK's most important growth project and the Government's flagship infrastructure project.
- Government has set the timetable to secure planning permission by 2029 and bring a third runway into operation "in a decade".
- Shareholders strongly support expansion; the project "will only proceed once the necessary regulatory and policy frameworks are firmly in place".
- 2026 milestones: spring 2026 - clarity needed from the Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) on how early costs can be recovered; over the summer - DfT to publish the draft Airports National Policy Statement (ANPS) and the CAA to decide the long-term regulatory model determining whether private investment will be forthcoming; autumn - Parliament asked to decide the final ANPS, setting the planning framework and putting the UK on course for first flights in a decade.
- CEO Thomas Woldbye: the Board greenlights starting work on the planning application; "we are on track to secure planning permission by 2029"; vital 2026 milestones are essential to the next phase.
- Related stories listed: expansion set to unlock over 100,000 jobs nationwide; local community majority support.

wikis.title: Electron-Ion Collider achieves DOE Critical Decision 1 approval
wikis.summary: DOE's 6 July 2021 announcement that the Electron-Ion Collider at Brookhaven National Laboratory received CD-1, starting the project execution phase with preliminary design.
wikis.body:
- Office of Science, July 6, 2021 (Upton, NY and Newport News, VA). DOE granted Critical Decision 1 (CD-1) for the Electron-Ion Collider (EIC), to be built at Brookhaven National Laboratory on Long Island, after approving mission need (CD-0) in December 2019. CD-1 completes the definition phase/conceptual design and authorizes the execution phase, starting with preliminary design; next is establishing a performance baseline to guide construction.
- Total project cost expected to range from $1.7-2.8 billion, funded primarily through the DOE Office of Science. About $100 million in New York State funding will support new infrastructure (buildings, roads) at Brookhaven.
- Thomas Jefferson National Accelerator Facility (Jefferson Lab), Newport News, Virginia, is a major partner.
- Facility: a 2.4-mile-circumference collider, "the first of its kind in the world", colliding high-energy polarized electrons with polarized protons and atomic nuclei for precision 3-D snapshots of their internal structure. Design includes a new electron storage ring and electron accelerator components working with existing infrastructure of the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC), operating since 2000.
- Physics goals: study the strong nuclear force, where the proton gets its spin and mass.
- EIC User Group: 251 member institutions from 33 countries, 88 US institutions representing 27 states, Puerto Rico and Washington, D.C.
- "Construction of the EIC is expected to begin in 2024, with the facility beginning operations early in the next decade."
- Quotes from Kathleen Hogan (DOE Acting Under Secretary for Science and Energy), Doon Gibbs (Brookhaven), Stuart Henderson (Jefferson Lab), Eric Gertler (Empire State Development), Bernd Surrow (EIC Users group chair).

wikis.title: EIC steps towards construction: DOE approves Critical Decision 3A
wikis.summary: CERN Courier (3 May 2024) reports that in April DOE approved CD-3A for the Electron-Ion Collider, allowing long-lead procurements.
wikis.body:
- CERN Courier, 3 May 2024. The Electron-Ion Collider (EIC) at Brookhaven National Laboratory, built in partnership with Jefferson Lab, moved closer to construction: in April the US DOE approved "Critical Decision 3A", the formal go-ahead to purchase long-lead procurements.
- The EIC collides polarised high-energy electrons with polarised protons, polarised light ions or heavy ions, aiming at 3D "nuclear femtography" of nucleon structure (spin and mass).
- It reuses infrastructure of the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider; costed at $1.7 to 2.8 billion; "scheduled to enter construction in 2026 and to begin operations in the first half of the next decade".
- Items that can now be ordered: superconducting wire and materials, cryogenic equipment, experimental solenoid, lead-tungstate crystals and scintillating fibres, electrical substations, support buildings.
- Project director Jim Yeck: the project can now execute contracts with industrial partners that "will significantly reduce project technical and schedule risk".
- User group: more than 1500 physicists from nearly 300 laboratories and institutes. DOE and CNRS signed a statement of interest on French contributions; the UK announced it will invest £58.8 million in detector and accelerator technologies.

wikis.title: 520 Fifth Avenue, Manhattan supertall (Wikipedia)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the 1,001-foot, 76-story mixed-use supertall at Fifth Avenue and 43rd Street, its site history, development by Mickey Rabina, design by KPF, and construction timeline.
wikis.body:
- Mixed-use supertall at Fifth Avenue and 43rd Street, Midtown Manhattan; 1,001 ft (305 m), 76 floors; architect Kohn Pedersen Fox (also architect of record); developer Mickey Rabina; interior design Charles & Co. (Vicky Charles). Construction started March 1, 2022; estimated completion June 1, 2026 (as of 2025).
- Site history: formerly 516 and 518 Fifth Avenue and an office building at 520. Aby Rosen/RFR and Tahl-Propp tried to redevelop in the 2000s; Thor Equities (bought 2011-2012) filed in December 2014 for a 71-story, 920-foot tower by Handel Architects, then sold to Ceruzzi Properties and SMI USA for $325 million in 2015; they defaulted on a Mack loan in 2018.
- Rabina bought the site in 2019 for $205 million, with a $110 million Bank OZK mortgage; KPF plans filed early 2021 (896 ft, about 100 residences, terracotta facade); $540 million construction financing from Bank OZK and Carlyle in March 2022; foundation work later in 2022.
- Sales began April 2024 (cheapest apartments $1.7 million); topped out October 2024 with three-fifths of apartments sold; steelwork done end of December 2024; 85% of units sold by February 2025; first office tenants leased July 2025 (including JAB Holding Company and Texas Capital); refinanced December 2025 with a $640 million Carlyle loan; penthouse sold May 2026 for $12 million.
- Design: about 100 residences (1-4 bedrooms; five full-floor penthouses) on upper floors, about 200,000 sq ft of office on floors 9-34 with operable windows, restaurants on the first three stories, private club Moss (Babette restaurant, Turkish baths, pickleball court). Air rights bought from neighbouring buildings allowed about 200,000 sq ft extra. Pencil tower with 15:1 height-width ratio, setbacks with terraces, terracotta lower facade and painted aluminum upper facade, about 5,500 curtain wall panels, 500-short-ton tuned mass damper in the top five stories, foundation 48 ft below ground.

wikis.title: Fraport inaugurates Terminal 3 at Frankfurt Airport
wikis.summary: Fraport's 22 April 2026 press release on the official opening of Terminal 3, completed on schedule and budget, with first flights on April 23.
wikis.body:
- Press release dated 2026-04-22. Fraport AG officially opened Terminal 3 with more than 400 invited guests, marking completion of the largest infrastructure project the MDAX-listed company has undertaken. Guests included Transport Minister Patrick Schnieder, Hesse Minister-President Boris Rhein, Frankfurt Lord Mayor Mike Josef, Supervisory Board chair Michael Boddenberg and architect Christoph Mäckler.
- Regular operation starts April 23. All 57 airlines relocating permanently move in four waves, concluding by June 9. Condor will switch in summer 2027.
- Facilities: fully automated luggage check-in, security checks with CT scanners, 64 stores and restaurants.
- Groundbreaking October 15, 2015; up to 3,000 tradespeople at peak. Initial capacity up to 19 million passengers per year (Piers G, H, J); a possible second phase adding Pier K could raise it to up to 25 million. Fraport invested approximately EUR 4 billion. Built by wholly owned subsidiary Fraport Ausbau Süd GmbH (FAS), "on time without exceeding the budget" despite Covid-19, Russia's war against Ukraine and supply-chain disruption.
- Rhein called it "Europe's largest privately funded infrastructure project".

wikis.title: Frankfurt Airport to open Terminal 3 with 19 million passenger capacity in 2026
wikis.summary: International Airport Review (8 Oct 2025) reports Fraport confirmed Terminal 3 will open on 22 April 2026 after final inspections, with test operations beforehand.
wikis.body:
- Published 2025-10-08 (Gabriel Higgins). Fraport confirmed Terminal 3 at Frankfurt Airport (FRA) opens officially on 22 April 2026 after authority inspections including fire protection; no longer classed a construction site.
- Remaining work: installation of 21 security check lanes with CT scanners, food and retail areas, baggage handling system testing. Between 27 January and 16 April 2026 around 8,000 volunteer test passengers will simulate operations.
- Construction began October 2015, despite COVID-19, the war in Ukraine and supply chain disruption. Initial configuration with Piers G, H and J: capacity up to 19 million passengers per year. Built by Fraport Ausbau Süd GmbH (FAS); technical director Harald Rohr said it was implemented "on schedule and on budget".
- Airlines will move from Terminal 2 in four phases between mid-April and early June 2026; terminal handles Schengen and non-Schengen flights. CEO Dr Stefan Schulte: groundbreaking was ten years ago.

wikis.title: Newcastle to Sydney high-speed rail development phase begins
wikis.summary: Australian Government media release (24 Feb 2026) announcing a $659.6 million two-year development phase for Newcastle-Sydney High Speed Rail and release of the business case.
wikis.body:
- Media release, Tuesday 24 February 2026, Minister Catherine King. Development phase for High Speed Rail between Newcastle and Sydney begins.
- Travel time about one hour Newcastle to Central Sydney; Central Coast to Sydney or Newcastle about 30 minutes.
- $659.6 million, two-year development phase to make Line 1 construction ready (design, approvals, scope, cost); public and private financing options to be assessed; a future government investment decision follows once scope, cost and risk are finalised.
- Business case by the High Speed Rail Authority released: boosts the economy by $250 billion over 50 years and over 99,000 new jobs.

wikis.title: Australia begins development for Newcastle-Sydney high-speed rail
wikis.summary: Railway-News (24 Feb 2026) reports the start of the AUD 659.6 million two-year development phase for the Newcastle-Sydney line, the first stage of a potential east-coast network.
wikis.body:
- Published 24 Feb 2026 by Tiana May. Newcastle-Sydney is identified as the first stage of a potential east-coast high-speed rail network.
- About one hour Newcastle to central Sydney; about 30 minutes from Central Coast to either city.
- Two-year development phase funded with 659.6 million AUD to make the first corridor "construction ready" (detailed design, environmental approvals, scope, cost estimates), following Infrastructure Australia advice; financing options to be assessed before a later investment decision.
- Business case by the High Speed Rail Authority: approximately 250 billion AUD to the national economy over 50 years and more than 99,000 jobs.
- Quote from Minister Catherine King on delivery and planning.

wikis.title: The Muraba Veil: Dubai's ultra-slim residential tower set for 2028
wikis.summary: PropNewsTime (updated 28 Apr 2025) describes the planned 380 m, 22.5 m wide Muraba Veil tower on the Dubai Water Canal, expected to complete in December 2028.
wikis.body:
- Last updated 28th Apr, 2025. Dubai plans the Muraba Veil, "one of the world's thinnest skyscrapers", along the Dubai Water Canal.
- Height 380 m (1,247 ft), width only 22.5 m (73 ft); 74 floors above ground and five basement levels; 131 apartments of 2, 3, 4 and 5 bedrooms with large private terraces; prices from AED 18 million.
- Collaboration between Muraba and Spanish firm RCR Arquitectes; engineering by WSP and Arup. Project value estimated at AED 775.8 million (about USD 211.2 million), according to the Dubai Land Department.
- Facade: movable stainless steel mesh inspired by Mashrabiya, allowing residents to adjust privacy and encouraging natural ventilation to reduce air-conditioning need.
- Amenities: private underground wellness spa, residents-only cinema, fine-dining restaurant, inner courtyards with gardens and swimming pools.
- "Construction is expected to be completed by December 2028."

wikis.title: Africa's biggest airport being built in Ethiopia for $12.5 billion
wikis.summary: CNN Travel (23 Apr 2026) covers Bishoftu International Airport, its funding gap, Zaha Hadid Architects design, resettlement controversy and regional competition.
wikis.body:
- Published Apr 23, 2026 (Daniel Olivares Gallego). Bishoftu International Airport, nearly 30 miles southeast of Addis Ababa; works began January 2026; PM Abiy Ahmed Ali called it "the largest aviation infrastructure project in Africa's history".
- Scheduled to open in 2030 (phase I) with two runways and capacity for 60 million passengers a year, growing to 110 million (Atlanta's Hartsfield-Jackson had 106 million in 2025). Cargo capacity of 3.73 million tons annually.
- Cost $12.5 billion. State-owned Ethiopian Airlines leads; CEO Mesfin Tasew said it "will invest 30% of its equity"; the other $8 billion is yet to be secured, with the US, China and Italy in negotiations. Brookings' Signé: closing $8 billion in one year is "ambitious"; delay would make the 2030 target "very difficult to hold".
- Design by Zaha Hadid Architects (Cristiano Ceccato): X-shaped terminal of 660,000 sq m inspired by the Great Rift Valley with a central spine and four piers; up to 80% transit passengers; naturally ventilated walkways and courtyards; site almost 400 m lower in elevation than Bole, so aircraft take off more efficiently per ZHA. Sustainability: local materials, solar energy, stormwater system feeding wetlands.
- Controversy: reportedly displaced over 15,000 people from over 9,000 acres; Ethiopian Airlines says it spends $350 million on resettlement, building 1,400 homes with services; some residents told local media they received no compensation, which the city administration denied.
- Regional context: Rwanda's $2 billion Bugesera Airport, Ouagadougou-Donsin, upgrades in Casablanca, Cairo, Nairobi. Tasew wants it to be for Africa what Dubai or Doha is for the Middle East.

wikis.title: Ethiopian Airlines marks groundbreaking of Bishoftu International Airport
wikis.summary: Ethiopian Airlines press release (10 January 2026) announcing construction start of Bishoftu International Airport, phase one due 2030 for 60 million passengers.
wikis.body:
- Addis Ababa, 10 January 2026. Construction began that day after a groundbreaking ceremony attended by PM Dr. Abiy Ahmed, ministers and executives; the airport design was unveiled and the resettlement and livelihood restoration project for affected communities described as successfully completed.
- CEO Mesfin Tasew: "a new chapter"; the airport is a key player in implementing the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA); Ethiopian celebrates 80 years of service.
- "Phase One of the project is expected to be completed by 2030 and will accommodate 60 million passengers annually and when fully completed it will have the capacity to handle 110 million passengers."
- Airline background: more than 26,000 employees, flights to more than 160 destinations, Vision 2035 plan, multi-hub strategy (Lomé, Lilongwe, Lusaka, Kinshasa).

wikis.title: Toronto's 106-storey Pinnacle SkyTower tops out
wikis.summary: RENX (23 Mar 2026) reports Pinnacle SkyTower has topped out at 106 storeys as Canada's tallest building, due for completion in 2026 with first residents in the fall.
wikis.body:
- Published Mar. 23 2026 (Steve McLean). Pinnacle SkyTower topped out at 106 storeys, now the tallest building in Canada and the first residential building in North America at 106 storeys; top floor level with the CN Tower main observation deck.
- Designed by Hariri Pontarini Architects at the foot of Yonge Street; scheduled completion this year; first residents (up to the 56th floor) move in this fall. 958 units; 12-sided tapered design; originally 95 storeys before permission to go taller.
- Developer Pinnacle International will release the final block of condos (previously held-back top floors); VP Anson Kwok says "well-sold", no incentives, less aggressive pricing amid a condo slump.
- Amenities: 80,000 sq ft; 223-room Le Méridien Toronto Pinnacle Hotel in the podium opening this fall; top-floor restaurant.
- Wider site: Prestige (65 storeys, 496 units) completed; the Toronto Star's 25-storey former office building converted to a 468-room hotel (about two years); street work finishing in 2027; proposed 92-storey, 847-unit tower on the north parcel, launch expected once market conditions improve.

wikis.title: Pinnacle One Yonge, Toronto (Wikipedia)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the six-tower Pinnacle One Yonge development in Toronto, including the 106-storey SkyTower, Canada's tallest building since 2026.
wikis.body:
- Mixed-use development at 7 Yonge Street, Toronto; six skyscrapers from 22 to 106 storeys. Developer Pinnacle International; architect Hariri Pontarini Architects; structural engineer Jablonsky, Ast and Partners. Construction started 2018; SkyTower estimated completion September 2026.
- SkyTower: 351.4 m (1,153 ft), 106 floors, tallest in Canada since 2026 (preceded by One Bloor West). Prestige (65 storeys, 216.2 m) completed 2022.
- Planned 4,600 m2 community space, 7,400 m2 retail, 93,000 m2 offices and 2,500 apartments.
- Original plans (early 2020): 95-storey 313 m tower, 65-storey Prestige, 80-storey tower; 2,200 apartments. November 2022 application to raise SkyTower from 95 to 106 storeys (313 m to 353 m) and the third tower from 80 to 92 storeys; Planning recommended approval November 2023; March 2025 proposal for 356 m. SkyTower passed its 100th storey December 2025 and reached its top floor in March 2026.

wikis.title: Egypt unveils $15bn New Delta megaproject to expand farmland
wikis.summary: Arab News (17 May 2026) reports El-Sisi inaugurated the 2.3 million-acre New Delta project in Dabaa, with infrastructure investments of 800 billion Egyptian pounds ($15 billion).
wikis.body:
- Updated 17 May 2026. President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi (per Reuters) said the New Delta project will transform desert west of the mouth of the Nile into arable land, with infrastructure investments worth 800 billion Egyptian pounds ($15 billion), at the inauguration of the 2.3 million-acre megaproject in Dabaa.
- Includes advanced irrigation systems, wastewater treatment plants, tied to Egypt's Vision 2030. Authorities have completed cultivation of hundreds of thousands of acres.
- Context: April launch of "The Spine" mixed-use city (over 1.4 trillion Egyptian pounds; Talaat Moustafa Group with National Bank of Egypt); S&P affirmed Egypt at "B/B" stable.

wikis.title: Al-Sisi directs acceleration of New Delta project and expanded land reclamation
wikis.summary: Daily News Egypt (24 Nov 2025) reports El-Sisi told officials to speed up the New Delta agricultural project, with the drainage-water conveyance system about 85% complete.
wikis.body:
- Last updated November 24, 2025. El-Sisi met Water Resources Minister Hani Sweilam, presidential adviser Amir Sayed Ahmed, Armed Forces Engineering Authority head Walid Mohamed Aref and Bahaa El-Ghannam of the "Future of Egypt" project.
- The northern water-supply corridor was reviewed; the 166-kilometre agricultural drainage-water conveyance system supplying the New Delta station is roughly 85% implemented with 12 lifting stations. He directed construction on schedule and strict prevention of encroachments on the Nile, and more private-sector participation.
- Ghannam: reclamation projects in Al-Khufra and along the Dakhla-Owaynat road expected to launch early next year; feasibility studies under way for an agricultural project in Senegal and other African countries.

wikis.title: Army Corps proposes $52 billion storm surge barriers for New York-New Jersey waterways
wikis.summary: Gothamist (26 Sep 2022) reports the Army Corps' HATS report tentatively selecting Alternative 3B: 12 storm surge gates and 41+ miles of coastal barriers over 14 years of construction.
wikis.body:
- Published Sep 26, 2022 (Nathan Kensinger). The US Army Corps of Engineers released a report detailing a $52 billion plan for New York City metro storm-surge protection, from the NY & NJ Harbor & Tributaries Focus Area Feasibility Study (HATS), a study begun after Hurricane Sandy. Tentatively selected plan: Alternative 3B, picked from five options.
- 14-year construction; 12 storm surge gates across large waterways plus coastal barriers across more than 41 miles of shoreline, including seawalls/floodwalls in East Harlem, Lower Manhattan, southern Brooklyn and the entire Rockaway Peninsula. Public comment through January 6, 2023; final designs anticipated to begin in 2025, construction in 2030.
- Benefit: could reduce coastal-storm economic damages 2044-2093 by an average of $6.2 billion a year. Comparable to the $14.5 billion New Orleans system (133 miles) built after Katrina.
- Gates: largest are a dual system on the Arthur Kill and Kill Van Kull and a gate at the entrance to Jamaica Bay; others at Flushing Creek, Newtown Creek, Gowanus Canal, Sheepshead Bay, Gerritsen Creek, Shellbank Basin, Hawtree Creek, head of Jamaica Bay, and the Hackensack River (NJ); a tidal gate on Coney Island Creek. 31+ miles of onshore defences, including 22+ miles from Bath Beach to Far Rockaway, 5.7 miles in Lower Manhattan, 4.7 miles in East Harlem, 8 miles in Jersey City. Gates not intended for sea level rise or rainfall flooding (e.g. Hurricane Ida 2021).
- History: study funding halted February 2020 after then-President Trump mocked the largest alternative (a $119 billion five-mile barrier from Sandy Hook to Breezy Point); restarted October 2021; 3B selected July 2022.
- Concerns: Riverkeeper called HATS "fatally flawed"; NRDC, Gowanus Canal Conservancy, Guardians of Flushing Bay, Newtown Creek Alliance raised concerns on habitats and trapped runoff/sewage; three gate sites are Superfund sites. Largest environmental impact expected in Jamaica Bay (moderately high). Waterfront Alliance welcomed the shift to a hybrid approach.

wikis.title: Surrey-Langley SkyTrain on track for late 2029 opening
wikis.summary: Surrey Now-Leader (28 Jan 2026) reports the project's January 26 council update: construction progress in 2025, 2026 plans, and a late 2029 opening for the 14 km line.
wikis.body:
- Published Jan 28, 2026 (Tom Zytaruk). Executive project director Gilles Assier updated Surrey council-in-committee on January 26: the Whalley-Langley City line is on track to open in late 2029.
- 2026: most guideway foundations and substructure completed this year; all stations under construction in the first half. Testing and commissioning in 2028. Line: 14 km, eight stations, three transit exchanges.
- History: business case approved and procurement began summer 2022; BC Hydro utility relocations started January 2024; contracts announced August; major construction began fall 2024.
- 2025 progress: guideway foundations more than 70% complete by end of year; 10 km of underground electrical power work complete; more than 40% of guideway columns completed; four launching gantries in operation (Surrey Sprinter, Fleetwood Flyer, Clayton Clipper, Langley Launcher).
- Stations: Green Timbers (140 St), 152 Street, Fleetwood (160 St), Bakerview-166 Street, Hillcrest-184 Street, Clayton (190 St), then Langley's Willowbrook (196 St) and Langley City Centre (203 St). Public art artists to be announced.

wikis.title: Surrey Langley SkyTrain project overview
wikis.summary: Official project overview: a 16 km Expo Line extension (Dave Barrett Extension) with eight stations, a $5.996 billion budget and late 2029 in-service date.
wikis.body:
- Extends the Expo Line 16 kilometres, mainly along Fraser Highway on an elevated guideway from King George Station in Surrey to 203 Street in Langley City. Named the Dave Barrett Extension; eight stations and three transit exchanges (Bakerview-166 Street, Willowbrook, Langley City Centre).
- Budget $5.996 billion (capital costs and active transportation investments). Current anticipated in-service date: late 2029.
- Surrey, Langley City and Langley Township population projected to grow by 420,000 people and add 147,000 jobs by 2050.
- Adds 14 km of active transportation paths, bike racks and enclosed bike parking; areas around all eight stations designated transit-oriented development areas.

wikis.title: Seine-Nord Europe Canal breaks ground after 20-year delay
wikis.summary: Euronews (27 Sep 2024) reports work has begun on the 107 km, EUR 5.1bn Seine-Nord Europe Canal due to complete in 2030.
wikis.body:
- Published 27/09/2024 (Garfield Myrie). Work is underway on France's Seine-Nord Europe Canal (SNEC), a 107 km new trade route between France, Belgium and the Netherlands, "completed in 2030".
- Currently limited by the narrower Canal du Nord, which struggles with super-sized cargo ships. Project got the green light in 2003 but was stalled by decades of political wrangling over funding and route.
- EUR 5.1bn investment by the French government, local authorities and the EU. Analysts suggest it could remove as many as a million heavy goods vehicles from French roads each year. Involves as many as sixty bridges, three canal bridges, seven locks, 700 hectares of environmental plantation. New canal 54 metres wide, part of the Seine-Escaut waterway.
- Arcadis France (CEO Nicolas Ledoux) is leading the project.

wikis.title: The Seine-Nord Europe Canal: Here we go (Seine-Scheldt, 2022 update)
wikis.summary: Seine-Scheldt EEIG news item on the 15 September 2022 progress meeting for the 107 km, EUR 5 billion Seine-Nord Europe Canal.
wikis.body:
- Meeting on 15 September 2022 in Amiens (fifth anniversary of the "Yes to the Canal" mobilisation, September 2017, Peronne). The canal is the future central 107 km link of the Seine-Scheldt cross-border waterway; estimated cost EUR 5 billion; almost 500 people mobilised.
- Funding: EU grant EUR 2.1 billion (Connecting Europe Facility, decision 27 June 2019); State EUR 1.1 billion; local authorities EUR 1.1 billion (financing agreement 22 November 2019, Nesle).
- Environment: over 10,000 trees planted; 165 hectares of wetland restoration out of more than 1,100 hectares planned. Sector 1 (18 km Compiegne to Passel) authorisation obtained 8 April 2021; sectors 2, 3, 4 (89 km Passel to Aubencheul-au-Bac) authorisation aimed at March 2024.
- Schedule: 2022 quays at Ribecourt and Pimprez, new road, 3 bridges on RD 66, Oise relocation, weir and siphon; 2023 Montmacq lock; 2024 canal earthworks; sectors 2-4 work in 2024-2025; full swing until 2030 when the whole network enters service.

wikis.title: Hagia Sophia dome restoration to withstand earthquakes
wikis.summary: Medievalists.net (12 May 2025) reports Turkish authorities launched a dome restoration to reinforce Hagia Sophia against earthquakes, with no completion timeline.
wikis.body:
- May 12, 2025. Turkish authorities launched an extensive restoration of the dome of the nearly 1,500-year-old Hagia Sophia (built 537 under Justinian I; cathedral, mosque, museum, mosque again since 2020).
- Begins with a temporary roof structure; existing lead cover removed and restored; weak points identified through seismic simulations reinforced. "No timeline has been set for the project's completion", expected to take several years.
- Ahmet Gulec (scientific board, to Daily Sabah): "The dome isn't perfectly round"; some areas filled with rubble or patched with wood; work to balance the structure.
- History: original dome collapsed in 558; earthquake damage in 989 and 1346; Mimar Sinan added buttresses in the 16th century.

wikis.title: Hagia Sophia begins extensive dome restoration for earthquake resilience
wikis.summary: Jerusalem Post (25 Apr 2025) reports Turkey's Culture and Tourism Ministry 50-year plan, with dome restoration scheduled to begin April 14, 2025 from the exterior.
wikis.body:
- April 25, 2025. The Culture and Tourism Ministry initiated a 50-year plan to reinforce Hagia Sophia, focusing on the dome, walls and minarets; restoration began about three years ago and is set to be the largest in its history; dome restoration scheduled to commence on April 14, 2025.
- Work is from the exterior to protect interior mosaics; lead covering removed, damaged lead repaired or replaced; Ottoman-era-consistent materials and techniques (Ahmet Gulec).
- A steel platform system on four columns, 43.5 m tall, inside the mosque keeps worship and visits going; a 41 m tower crane with 60 m boom east of the building; temporary steel structure and tarp cover the dome; a digital twin was made; after completion the covering, platform and crane are dismantled.
- Context: 7.8 magnitude earthquake in southern Turkey in 2023; fears of an expected Istanbul earthquake (Mehmet Selim Okten). UNESCO World Heritage listing 1985.

wikis.title: Norway is building the world's longest, deepest undersea road tunnel (Rogfast)
wikis.summary: CNN Travel (2 Dec 2025) describes Rogfast, a 27 km undersea road tunnel reaching 392 m below sea level, due in 2033 at about NOK 25 billion.
wikis.body:
- Published Dec 2, 2025 (Jacopo Prisco). Rogfast ("Rogaland fastforbindelse"): 27 km (17 miles), up to 392 m (1,286 ft) below sea level; two tubes each with two lanes, road traffic only; a double roundabout about halfway (cited as 230 m and 260 m deep) connects to Kvitsoy.
- Construction started January 2018, halted late 2019 over predicted cost overruns; slated for completion in 2033 at approximately NOK 25 billion (about $2.4 billion).
- Cuts Bergen/Stavanger travel by around 40 minutes by replacing ferries; part of the 1,100 km E39 coastal highway revamp (21 hours today, seven ferries; ferry-free not expected before 2050).
- Built from both ends to meet within 5 cm; Skanska builds the 9 km northern section; Hexagon laser scanning (2 million data points per second). Challenges: saltwater leaks, grouting to seal rock at 300 m below sea level; longitudinal ventilation with jet fans plus shaft ventilation.
- Comparisons: Seikan Tunnel 53.85 km (undersea 23.3 km, 240 m deep); Channel Tunnel 50.46 km (undersea 37.9 km, 115 m deep).

wikis.title: Rogfast (Wikipedia)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on Rogfast, the Rogaland subsea road tunnel in Norway: 2017 plan, 2019-2020 halt and cost rise, contracts, and 2033 opening.
wikis.body:
- Subsea road tunnel between Randaberg (near Stavanger) and Bokn, with a 4.1 km spur to Kvitsoy; 27 km, minimum elevation -392 m; part of E39; operator Norwegian Public Roads Administration; tolled; opening 2033.
- Approved by the Storting May 2017 (planned finish 2025-26), cost NOK 16.8 billion; work began 4 January 2018. Halted October 2019 over cost overruns after only two bids for the Kvitsoy spur; April 2020 estimate NOK 25 billion; late November 2020 government approved NOK 24.8 billion (state NOK 9.9 billion, NOK 14.9 billion tolled loan). By March 2022 opening delayed to 2033.
- Contracts: Skanska northern part December 12, 2022 (nearly NOK 5 billion); Implenia Norge southern part January 9, 2023 (NOK 4 billion); Implenia/Stangeland middle part June 11, 2024 (NOK 6.2 billion). As of November 2023 Kvitsoy tunnel blasting done (about 800 blasts over 3.5 km).

wikis.title: Height approved for Dubai's Burj Azizi, world's second tallest tower
wikis.summary: Gulf News (18 Feb 2025) reports the 725 m, 131-storey Burj Azizi height received all approvals, with 2028 completion and off-plan sales starting.
wikis.body:
- Last updated Feb 18, 2025 (Manoj Nair). 725 m Burj Azizi on Sheikh Zayed Road got all approvals (Dubai Civil Aviation Authority, Dubai Municipality); CEO Farhad Azizi: height "fully confirmed and will remain unchanged". Completion set for 2028; 131 storeys.
- Burj Khalifa is 828 m; Merdeka 118 is 678.9 m; Shanghai Tower 632 m. Azizi bought the plot in 2022 (earlier owned by Meydan City Corp.).
- Prices: Dh7,149 to Dh34,000 psf; apartments from Dh7.5 million to Dh156m. Global sales launch in Dubai, Hong Kong, London, Mumbai, Singapore, Sydney, Tokyo.
- Challenges: tall tower on narrow plot, wind load, elevators (partnership with Kone), 1,000+ parking spaces. Record targets: observation deck level 130, hotel lobby level 111, nightclub 126, restaurant 122, hotel room 118; luxury mall; amenity floor every 20 residential floors.

wikis.title: Burj Azizi (Wikipedia)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on Burj Azizi, a 725 m, 133-floor megatall under construction on Sheikh Zayed Road, Dubai.
wikis.body:
- Under construction; 725 m architectural height (roof 665 m, observatory 649 m); 133 floors; 44 lifts; floor area 279,200 m2; architect AE7; developer Azizi Developments; main contractor Gardinia Contracting. Estimated completion 2030 (infobox); construction started 29 August 2016, restarted August 21, 2024. Formerly Entisar Tower.
- History: Meydan Group announced Entisar Tower in 2012 (570 m, 122 storeys); groundbreaking 2016; halted 2017 (stop-work order, payment dispute); Azizi Developments acquired it 2018; rebranded Burj Azizi January 2024; construction restarted 2025 ("citation needed"). Named after Mirwais Azizi.
- As of May 2026, raft foundation and nine-basement automated car park in progress with around 750 workers on site daily.

wikis.title: Reinventing the Rigid Airship: LTA's Pathfinder 1 (Akron Roundtable)
wikis.summary: Ideastream listing (21 Nov 2025) for a 52-minute Akron Roundtable talk by LTA Research CEO Brett Crozier on building and flight-testing the Pathfinder 1 airship.
wikis.body:
- Published November 21, 2025; 52:17 recording. Brett Crozier, CEO of LTA Research, leads a team building next-generation airships to complement humanitarian aid delivery and reduce aviation's carbon footprint. Bio: 30-year US Navy veteran, commanded USS Blue Ridge and USS Theodore Roosevelt, retired 2022.
- Program: Akron was once the "Airship Capital of the World" (USS Akron and Macon built in the Akron Airdock). Crozier shares the path to building and flight testing Pathfinder 1, "the largest flying aircraft in the world", and how modern materials, fly-by-wire controls and advanced monitoring transform the concept.

wikis.title: Airships may soon be built in Akron again (Cleveland Fed)
wikis.summary: Cleveland Fed (26 Mar 2025) reports president Beth Hammack toured LTA Research's Akron facility, where the company hopes to restore airship production.
wikis.body:
- 03.26.2025. Tour on March 4, 2025. The Goodyear Zeppelin Corporation built the 1,175-foot-long Akron Airdock nearly 100 years ago; two dirigibles were built there in the 1930s.
- LTA Research has facilities in Ohio, California and Nevada; nearly a third of its 300 employees work in Ohio. It is testing proof-of-concept airship Pathfinder 1 in California; the Akron team supports it and researches technology for future airships expected to be built in Akron. Uses lasers to weld titanium parts; machine scans parts; electric motors, with a smaller carbon footprint than traditional aviation. LTA says airships may be used for consumer and cargo transport and humanitarian aid.

wikis.title: Ontario Line likely to open in the early 2030s, with possible DVP shutdown for bridgework
wikis.summary: Metrolinx CEO Michael Lindsay said on 18 Feb 2026 the Ontario Line is trending towards early 2030s civil completion, later than the 2031 target, and that Don Valley Parkway bridge work could 'potentially' require a shutdown.
wikis.body:
- Reported by Liam Casey, The Canadian Press, posted Feb 18, 2026 (last updated February 19).
- The province will not commit to an opening date for the Ontario Line under construction in Toronto.
- Lindsay: "Based on where civil infrastructure is at this point, we think we're still trending towards the early 2030s to be done with civil infrastructure." Testing would then begin. This is potentially later than the 2031 target.
- Metrolinx announced the project in 2019 with an initial opening of 2027.
- Lessons from two other projects: the Eglinton Crosstown LRT opened earlier in February 2026, six years after its original schedule and 15 years after construction began; the Finch West LRT opened late 2025 and had early problems, largely trains performing poorly in wintry conditions. Metrolinx wants to "front load systems integration considerations" to reduce testing and conditioning time.
- Lindsay and Premier Doug Ford said ground has been broken on the elevated portion and construction is beginning on four new stations.
- Line: more than 15 km, 15 new stations, nearly 400,000 trips a day; runs from Exhibition Place in the west to the old Science Centre near midtown.
- Route needs three bridges over the Don River beside the Don Valley Parkway; asked whether this could shut the DVP, Lindsay said "potentially": "we are building the Bloor viaduct again three times for this project."
- Politics: interim Liberal Leader John Fraser said the province is bad at managing projects; NDP Leader Marit Stiles called it shaping up as a "money pit" and again asked for a public inquiry into Metrolinx (Ford has said he would not call one).
- Precedent: a two-lane shutdown on the six-lane Gardiner Expressway led the province to pay $73 million for 24-hour crews; the lanes opened last year.

wikis.title: Ontario Line could open later than 2031 target, Metrolinx says
wikis.summary: Canadian Press report (Globe and Mail) that Metrolinx will not commit to an Ontario Line opening date, points to early 2030s civil completion, and warns the DVP could be shut for bridge work.
wikis.body:
- By Liam Casey, The Canadian Press, published February 18, 2026.
- Metrolinx CEO Michael Lindsay: plan is to open by the early 2030s, potentially later than the 2031 target; "trending towards the early 2030s to be done with civil infrastructure", then testing.
- Originally supposed to open in 2027 (announced 2019).
- Eglinton Crosstown LRT opened earlier in the month, six years late and 15 years after construction began; Finch West LRT opened late last year with early problems in wintry conditions.
- Elevated section groundbreaking; four new stations starting; line runs Exhibition Place to the old Science Centre, more than 15 km, 15 stations, nearly 400,000 trips a day.
- Three Don River bridges needed; DVP shutdown "potentially" required.
- Opposition: John Fraser (interim Liberal) and Marit Stiles (NDP) criticised management; Stiles called for a public inquiry; a Gardiner two-lane shutdown cost the province $73 million for round-the-clock crews.

wikis.title: Berlin TXL: $8 billion plan to turn Tegel Airport into an eco city
wikis.summary: CNN Travel (Oct 2022) on the roughly $7.9 billion redevelopment of the former Berlin Tegel Airport into a residential smart city, university campus and innovation hub, with a gallery of other repurposed airports.
wikis.body:
- By Tom Page, CNN Travel, published Oct 3, 2022.
- The $7.9 billion project includes a residential smart city with approximately 5,000 homes, a university campus and an innovation hub. Construction is underway with completion scheduled for the end of the 2030s.
- Residential Schumacher Quartier: car-free streets, bicycle/e-bike/scooter use encouraged, delivery robots being explored for groceries; "sponge city" concept with no rainwater flowing into sewers (retained, reused, soaked away or evaporated).
- Urban Tech Republic (nearly four times the size of the residential area): BHT University (Berlin University of Applied Sciences and Technology) takes over hexagonal Terminal A, Terminal B becomes a startup centre with conference centre and showrooms, Terminal D a laboratory hub; a "living lab street" will test mobility tech. Terminals are protected buildings, so nearby streets and sidewalks will use recycled runway concrete.
- Consultant Johanna Sonnenburg (TU Berlin): held up for years while Berlin Brandenburg Airport was completed; ideas are innovative but less cutting edge than when developed; "Tegel is not very well connected" - no rail link, only the Schumacher Quartier will have an underground connection.
- Other repurposed airports mentioned: Tempelhof (park since 2010, 386 ha), Kai Tak (cruise terminal 2013), Hellinikon (Athens, reportedly EUR 8 billion redevelopment, first phase targeted 2025), Stapleton (Denver), Galeville (Shawangunk Grasslands NWR), Quito old airport (park after 2013), Brooks City (San Antonio, 1,300 acres), Downsview Toronto proposal (homes for over 80,000 residents).

wikis.title: Berlin TXL handover of keys: former Tegel Airport passed to Tegel Projekt GmbH
wikis.summary: Press release of 5 August 2021 on the symbolic key handover of the former Tegel Airport to Tegel Projekt GmbH to start Berlin TXL - The Urban Tech Republic and Schumacher Quartier, with clearance progress and a 2027 outlook.
wikis.body:
- Berlin, 5 August 2021: Governing Mayor Michael Müller handed the site to Tegel Projekt GmbH.
- Over about 20 years, a 500-hectare site becomes a climate-neutral, low-car, water-sensitive residential quarter for more than 10,000 people, a research and industrial park (Urban Tech Republic) with a university campus, and a 150-hectare landscape area run by Grün Berlin GmbH. Schumacher Quartier: over 5,000 flats, described as the world's largest urban timber construction quarter and sponge city project. Over 140 individual innovations are cited.
- Handover: 59 buildings, approx. 60,000 keys, 42 km of water pipes, ~10 km each of electricity and heating/cooling networks; the terminal ensemble by Gerkan, Marg und Partner (completed 1975) will be preserved.
- Explosive ordnance clearance began May 2021 on ~22,000 m2 (80% cleared); 350 pieces of ammunition (almost 900 kg) and almost 30,000 kg of scrap found; work to complete by September; further clearance to end of 2022.
- Guided tours from 14 August; events include a Freedom Dinner on the runway (7 Aug) and the Sonambiente festival (21 Aug-5 Sep). All plots to be rented or granted under heritable building rights; no sales.
- Outlook for 2027, "provided the planning and construction process runs smoothly": first tenants move into Schumacher Quarter flats; education campus and central park complete; Startup and Congress Centre opens in Terminal B; Berlin University of Applied Sciences starts teaching in Terminal A with 13 degree programmes (2,500 students); Berlin Fire and Rescue Services Academy moves into hangars.

wikis.title: Dubai selects teams for key contracts of $22B Strategic Sewerage Tunnels project
wikis.summary: ENR, 1 July 2026: Dubai Municipality picked two consortia to bid on Packages W and J of the $22 billion Dubai Strategic Sewerage Tunnels PPP.
wikis.body:
- By Gary Lakes, ENR, July 1, 2026. In early June Dubai Municipality selected two consortia; ultimate investment is $22 billion under a PPP framework.
- Package W (Warsan, ~$3 billion): led by Etihad Water & Electricity with Tamasuk Holding and Alkhorayef Water & Power; EPC team China Civil Engineering Construction Corp., Shanghai Tunnel Engineering, China Railway 114th Bureau Group; operator likely Veolia.
- Package J (Jebel Ali, ~$2 billion): led by Vision Invest and Suez Water Co.; EPC by China State Construction Engineering Corp. and DeTech Contracting.
- A Links package (over 200 km of deep tunnels linking existing facilities) is under tender. Packages were reconfigured and retendered in November 2025.
- Tunnels 3 m in diameter up to 90 m deep; two main tunnels: Bur Dubai Deep Tunnel (50 km) and Deira Deep Tunnel (25 km), gravity-fed; more than 150 legacy pumping stations to be decommissioned; earth pressure balance TBMs. Urgency followed April 2024 flooding.
- Capex for these sections $8 billion, lifecycle $22 billion; 30-year DBFOM concession, 80:20 debt-to-equity. Tunnel contracts expected to be awarded in January 2030; completion of tunnel infrastructure targeted for 2030-2056.

wikis.title: Dubai Strategic Sewerage Tunnel megaproject planned as 'development of the century'
wikis.summary: WaterWorld, 13 July 2017: Dubai's AED30 billion (US$8bn) deep-tunnel wastewater system, feasibility complete, construction expected as soon as 2019.
wikis.body:
- By Tom Freyberg, WaterWorld, July 13, 2017.
- Plans for a deep-tunnel wastewater treatment system costing AED30 billion (US$8bn) were progressing, with construction "expected to start as soon as 2019". Feasibility studies were said to be complete.
- Dubbed the 'development of the century'; to run over six years in two phases: first in Deira District, second in Bur Dubai. The two tunnels support Dubai's 50-year master plan and cover the two key catchments.
- Expected to enable wastewater reuse and generate "millions of cubic metres of irrigation water" (per WAM). A total of 100 pumping stations are expected to be replaced. Dubai Municipality director general Hussain Nasser Lootah said it would significantly reduce running costs.
- In May 2016 Parsons won the Dubai Municipality contract for feasibility studies, preliminary design and tender preparation, to be followed by programme management of detailed design and construction supervision.
- Regional comparisons: Abu Dhabi's STEP ($1.9 billion, started 2008, 41 km sewer tunnel plus 43 km link sewers, capacity 1.7 million m3/day by 2030); Qatar's IDRIS ($2.7 billion) reportedly suspended by Ashghal.

wikis.title: HRBT Expansion completion pushed back about 18 months to 2027
wikis.summary: WTKR report that VDOT revised the Hampton Roads Bridge-Tunnel expansion agreement, moving substantial completion to Feb. 26, 2027 and final completion to Aug. 27, 2027.
wikis.body:
- VDOT news release: completion of the Hampton Roads Bridge-Tunnel (HRBT) expansion pushed back by about 18 months; the comprehensive agreement (which had incentives for on-schedule completion) was revised for unforeseen circumstances.
- New "substantial completion" date Feb. 26, 2027 (tunnel usable, some construction remaining); final completion Aug. 27, 2027. Could be finished sooner: the contractor has a $90 million early completion incentive if substantial completion is reached by September 2026.
- Revisions let the project finish "nearly" within the original $3.9 billion budget.
- Christopher Hall, VDOT Hampton Roads district engineer: milestones include a 15-acre North Island expansion, reassembling the second largest tunnel boring machine in North America, the largest continuous concrete pour in VDOT history, and boring/building nearly 90% of the first of two new tunnels. First time a tunnel of this size is built between two man-made islands with this technology; launch pits are "a football field in size 60 to 80 feet" deep. The first bored tunnel breakthrough was expected within weeks.
- Page shows no explicit posting date.

wikis.title: HRBT Expansion newsroom: 2025-2026 press coverage of the Hampton Roads Bridge-Tunnel expansion
wikis.summary: Newsroom listing of headlines and excerpts (Nov 2025 to Aug 2026) about the $3.9 billion Hampton Roads Bridge-Tunnel expansion on I-64.
wikis.body:
- Newsroom index of press items, latest dated August 6, 2026 (WAVY): project is "another day closer to its substantial completion"; $3.9 billion; VDOT project director Ryan Banas calls it the largest highway construction effort in Virginia's history; goal is easing I-64 congestion.
- Scope: two new tunnels and trestle bridges to double driving lanes over a roughly 10-mile stretch of I-64 from Mallory Street in Hampton to Patrol Road in Norfolk. The two new tubes will carry four eastbound lanes; existing tunnels carry westbound traffic.
- TBM "Mary" (on site since 2022) completed its second and final tunnel (a three-mile journey) with final breakthrough reported Jan. 9, 2026; final shield piece extracted Jan 14; dismantled on South Island by March 10, 2026. Tunnel outfitting underway; full completion "expected in Spring 2027" (Virginia Peninsula Chamber, Apr 6, 2026).
- New tunnels will have an egress corridor emergency exit (Apr 5, 2026).
- July 27, 2026: first new westbound I-64 lanes opened in Norfolk (Oates Creek to Bay Avenue).
- About 100,000 tons of demolished bridge material will go to artificial reefs in the Chesapeake Bay (May-June 2026).
- Other items: welcome centre open house May 6, 2026; Nov 19, 2025 stoppage caused miles of I-64W congestion.

wikis.title: Chongqing East railway station
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the elevated Chongqing East station in Nan'an District, opened 27 June 2025 with 29 tracks and 15 platforms.
wikis.body:
- Major passenger station in Nan'an District, Chongqing, one of three main passenger hubs of the Chongqing network; on opening, per Time Out, "one of the largest passenger stations in the world" (flagged 'better source needed').
- Location planned (Chaoyuan New Area) published November 2018; construction officially began 22 November 2018 alongside the Yu-Qian Intercity Railway; by April 2024 roofing, fit-out and M&E were in progress. Opened to passengers 27 June 2025 (Chongqing-Xiamen high-speed railway, Chongqing East to Qianjiang section).
- Layout: elevated; 29 tracks, 15 platforms (14 island, 1 side), six through tracks; storage and maintenance yards. Operator China Railway Chengdu Group; classification Special Class; station code 30074.
- Lines: East Ring Line, Yuxiang HSR (Chongqing-Qiannan); Zhengyu and Yukun HSRs under construction.
- Metro station beneath: Line 6 branch opened 27 June 2025; Lines 24 and 27 under construction; Line 8 in unapproved long-term planning.
- Transit-oriented development planned (hotels, offices, shopping, culture). Expected times after full completion: about 1 hour to Wanzhou, Qianjiang, Chengdu, Guiyang; 3 hours to Wuhan, Kunming, Changsha; 6 hours to Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou.

wikis.title: New Valley Project (Toshka Project), Egypt
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on Egypt's canal system carrying Lake Nasser water to irrigate Western Desert land, begun 1997, and its shortfalls as of April 2012.
wikis.body:
- Also Toshka Project; original owner Egyptian Government; construction began 1997 when the government decided to develop a "new valley" for agricultural and industrial communities.
- Canal inlet 8 km north of Toshka Bay on Lake Nasser; meant to run west to the Darb el-Arbe'ien route then north to Baris Oasis, 310 km. As of April 2012 still 60 km short.
- Mubarak Pumping Station inaugurated March 2005; intended to transform 2,340 km2 (588,000 acres) of desert into farmland. Revived by President el-Sisi; half the land to go to college graduates, 1 acre each, funded by the Long Live Egypt Fund.
- Problems: high salinity and underground aquifers; clay soils stalling irrigation machines. "The only objective met up to April 2012" was diversion of water into the little Sheikh Zayed Canal built. Toshka Lakes are a by-product of Lake Nasser's rise.

wikis.title: Mubarak Pumping Station: centerpiece of the Toshka Project
wikis.summary: Bright Hub Engineering article on the Toshka Project's goals and the engineering of the Mubarak Pumping Station, with its 2011 status.
wikis.body:
- Toshka aimed by 2020 to turn half a million acres of desert into arable land; approved 1997, inaugurated Jan. 9, 1997 by President Mubarak; expected to house over three million residents by 2020 and add 10% to Egypt's arable land.
- Mubarak Pumping Station: cost $436 million, completed March 2005, in the lake and surrounded by water; 24 vertical pumps (18 running, 3 maintenance, 3 reserve); 50 m deep intake channel; capacity 1.2 million m3 of water per hour; canal about 30 m wide named for Sheikh Zayed al Nahyan, with UAE financial backing.
- Engineering: steel mini-piles (cost-effective, earthquake-resistant) and a jointless underwater design watertight from 0 to 50 C; ASCE named it one of the five most outstanding civil engineering achievements of 2005. Builders named: Hamza Associates/Lahmeyer design JV; Arabian International, Skanska, Hitachi built.
- Status in 2011: Mubarak overthrown; controversy over his holdings; a land dispute with Saudi Kingdom Holdings paused development; the 2020 completion described as "a serious challenge".

wikis.title: 2026 Nepal-Tibet floods: overview, background and cause
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article (part 1 of 2) on the 26 August 2026 glacier-collapse flood and debris flow that destroyed Gyirong Port and struck the Trishuli River valley in Nepal and Tibet.
wikis.body:
- Event: morning of 26 August 2026, flash floods and debris flows (also called Bhotekoshi or Rasuwa flood) destroyed Gyirong Port on the China-Nepal border and hit dozens of settlements along a 72 km stretch of the Trishuli River. The page notes it is a current disaster and information may change.
- Infobox tolls (rising): deaths 1,453+ (1,410 Nepal, 43 China); injuries 9,287+; missing 6,664+ (6,145 Nepal, 519 China). Damage: Nepal NPR 400 billion+ (US$2.64 billion+); China CNY 450 million+ (US$67.08 million+). Some victims' bodies were carried 240 km into India. Cause "under investigation".
- Cause: glacier collapse on the north face of Langtang Lirung widely thought to be the proximate cause. Seismic event Ms 5.2 at 02:52 UTC (08:37 NPT); USGS analysis said the seismic event was generated by the collapse, not before it; GFZ recorded Mw 5.7. A second landslide (Ms 4.2) three hours later. No rain reported at Rasuwa headquarters. Seven minutes later a camera captured floodwaters destroying Gyirong Port.
- Background: Gyirong crossing accounted for 30% of Nepal-China trade; over 100,000 crossings in first half of 2026. A July 2025 glacial lake outburst had washed away the border bridge; the 2015 Langtang landslide killed over 350.
- Warning: early warning system built for monsoon/glacial-lake floods did not detect it in time; upstream stations swept away; first text alerts by 09:15, 679,295 messages in one minute.
- Climate: researchers differ on attributing it directly to climate change; BBC, CNN, NPR researchers said it probably increased likelihood.

wikis.title: Rasuwagadhi Hydroelectric Project (111 MW), Nepal
wikis.summary: Company page for the 111 MW run-of-river Rasuwagadhi plant in Rasuwa district, Nepal, with key features and milestones through commercial operation on 31 December 2024.
wikis.body:
- Rasuwagadhi Hydropower Company Limited developed the 111 MW run-of-river project in Gosaikunda Rural Municipality, Rasuwa; 130 km north of Kathmandu to Syabrubesi then ~16 km to the site. Financing debt:equity 60:40.
- Annual generation 613.875 GWh (dry months 84.318 GWh, wet 529.557 GWh); gross head 167.9 m; design discharge 80 m3/s; headworks about 400 m downstream of the confluence of Kerung Khola and Lende Khola (Nepal-China/Tibet boundary rivers); headrace tunnel 4,185 m (dia 6.0 m); 715 m tailrace; underground powerhouse; 3 Francis turbines of 38.5 MW; 10 km 132 kV double-circuit transmission line.
- Milestones: PPA with NEA signed 14 Nov 2011 (revised RCOD 30 April 2023); EPF loan agreement 8 Dec 2011; consultant SMEC International (Australia) 3 Dec 2012; generation license 6 Dec 2012; civil EPC with China International Water and Electric Corp signed 5 Jan 2014; electromechanical with Voith Hydro (India) 31 July 2015; transmission contract with Mudbhary & Joshi (2017) terminated 6 July 2022 and replaced by Royal Construction Company on 1 Nov 2022.
- 2024: transmission line accepted 15 June; civil works taken over 1 Sept; 132 kV grid available 10 Nov; Unit 1 synchronized 20 Nov; commercial generation started 31 December 2024.

wikis.title: Katse Dam, Lesotho
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the 185 m concrete arch Katse Dam on the Malibamatso River, part of the Lesotho Highlands Water Project supplying water to South Africa.
wikis.body:
- Concrete double-curvature arch dam, Malibamatšo River, Lesotho; height 185 m, length 710 m; reservoir 1.950 km3, 3,580 ha; opened 1996; second largest double-curvature arch dam in Africa after Tekezé Dam.
- Part of a larger project to eventually include five large dams. Potential identified by Ninham Shand in 1953 to supplement water for the Witwatersrand; World Bank arranged the treaty between South Africa and Lesotho.
- Built by a consortium of Bouygues, Concor, Group 5, Hochtief, Impregilo, Kier Group and Sterling International; completed 1996, reservoir filled by 1997; total project cost US$8 billion.
- Water goes through a 45 km, 4 m diameter tunnel to a hydroelectric station near Muela; gravity flow to South Africa. Delivery began 22 January 1998; about 30 m3/s supplied; South Africa pays Lesotho $35 million per year plus a variable royalty.
- Impacts: induced seismicity; displaced farmers struggled to re-establish livelihoods; plant rescue and Katse Botanical Gardens; corruption scandal with convictions and at least one company debarred by the World Bank.

wikis.title: Lesotho Highlands Development Authority: LHWP homepage
wikis.summary: LHDA homepage describing the Lesotho Highlands Water Project and showing Phase II progress percentages and dam levels.
wikis.body:
- The Lesotho Highlands Water Project (LHWP) is multi-phased, to provide water to South Africa's Gauteng region and generate hydro-electricity for Lesotho; established by the 1986 Treaty between Lesotho and South Africa; harnesses the Senqu/Orange River through a series of dams. Phase I completed 2003, inaugurated 2004; Phase II underway.
- Phase II progress shown (updated 04-03-2026): Advanced Infrastructure 97%, Polihali Dam 44%, Polihali Transfer Tunnel 51%, Senqu major bridge 98%, Khubelu & Mabunyaneng bridges 70%.
- Reservoir levels (updated 13-09-2026): Katse Dam 79.05% of capacity, Mohale Dam 100.12%.

wikis.title: Coastal Japan turns to forests to blunt tsunami risks (Chinju no Mori / Morino Project)
wikis.summary: Mongabay/Eco-Business feature (Aug. 20, 2026) on the Chinju no Mori Project's Miyawaki-method tree planting as tsunami barriers alongside the concrete seawalls most Tohoku towns chose.
wikis.body:
- By Jonathan Vit, Mongabay.com, Aug. 20, 2026. The Chinju no Mori (Morino) Project has planted more than 680,000 trees over 14 years along Japan's coast; at Minamisoma, more than 1,000 volunteers planted more than 12,000 trees. Mayor Kazuo Monma spoke.
- Uses the Miyawaki method (dense mix of 20+ species); critics say many claims lack scientific evidence (Journal of Applied Ecology study). Secretary-general Makoto Shinkawa.
- Background: March 2011 magnitude 9 quake and tsunami up to 40 m, more than 19,700 killed along 2,000 km of coast. Since then about 1.4 trillion yen (US$8.2 billion) spent on 432 km of concrete seawalls at over 620 locations (MLIT and Reconstruction Agency data).
- Research (Jeremy Bricker, Univ. of Michigan; tsunamis of 1896, 1933, 1960, 2011): seawalls over 5 m reduced deaths and destruction, smaller walls often had the opposite effect; forests dissipate energy of smaller events.
- Inspiration: Amaterasu-mioya Shrine and its "chinju no mori" guardian forest in Otsuchi survived the 22 m wave; only 2 of 27 coastal Tohoku shrines were lost.
- Obstacles: municipalities disagree over species (black pine vs broadleaf evergreens); Sendai plants both and says forests alone "cannot completely stop large tsunamis"; many towns chose concrete only.

wikis.title: Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism (Japan)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on MLIT, the Japanese ministry formed on 6 January 2001, its organization and external agencies.
wikis.body:
- MLIT (Kokudokotsusho) is responsible for one-third of all laws and orders in Japan and is the largest Japanese ministry by employees, second-largest executive agency after Defense.
- Formed in the administrative reforms of January 6, 2001 by merging the Ministry of Transport, Ministry of Construction, Hokkaido Development Agency and National Land Agency; English name changed from "Ministry of Land, Infrastructure and Transport" on January 8, 2008. Headquarters 2-1-3 Kasumigaseki, Chiyoda-ku, Tokyo.
- Ministers listed: Tatsunori Ibayashi (Minister); state ministers Takashi Otsuka and Ichiro Tsukada.
- Bureaus include Policy, City, Water and Disaster Management, Road, Housing, Railway, Maritime, Ports and Harbours, Civil Aviation, Hokkaido.
- External agencies: Japan Coast Guard, Japan Meteorological Agency, Japan Tourism Agency, Japan Transport Safety Board.

wikis.title: Long Thanh International Airport ready for first flight on December 19
wikis.summary: Vietnam Government News (Dec 15, 2025): PM Pham Minh Chinh told builders Long Thanh must be ready for a first flight on Dec 19 and commercial operation in the first half of 2026.
wikis.body:
- VGP, Kim Anh, December 15, 2025. PM Pham Minh Chinh visited the site on December 14; airport is Viet Nam's largest aviation infrastructure project, in Dong Nai province about 40 km east of Ho Chi Minh City.
- Technical test flight expected December 15; first official flight December 19, 2025; commercial operation "in the first half of 2026".
- 15,000 experts, engineers and workers involved. Only three of 15 packages completed, 12 under construction; PM urged acceleration on runways, connecting roads, terminals and taxiways. Fourth sub-project (ground services) inspected.
- Developed by Airports Corporation of Viet Nam; Phase 1 designed for about 25 million passengers a year, operations expected 2026; fully built capacity up to 100 million passengers annually.

wikis.title: Long Thanh International Airport
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the airport under construction 40 km east of Ho Chi Minh City, with its December 2025 technical opening, planned December 2026 commercial opening, phases and costs.
wikis.body:
- Under construction in Long Thanh, Dong Nai, about 40 km east of Ho Chi Minh City; second airport for the metro area after Tan Son Nhat (which handled 40.7 million passengers in 2023 against ~30 million design capacity). IATA LTH, ICAO VVLT; operator Airports Corporation of Vietnam.
- Approved 4 January 2021; construction began 5 January; phase 1 originally to finish by September 2025, now expected late 2026.
- 19 December 2025: ceremonial "technical opening" with first landings (Vietnam Airlines charter, then Vietjet Air and Bamboo Airways technical flights). Full commercial operations "scheduled to commence in December 2026" (infobox: planned 1 December 2026).
- Design capacity over 100 million passengers and five million tonnes of cargo a year; "the most expensive infrastructure project in Vietnam's history"; hub for Vietnam Airlines.
- Four phases: phase 1 about US$4.6 billion, ~5,580 ha, 25 million passengers and 1.2 million tonnes cargo, one terminal, one 4,000 m x 60 m runway; remaining three phases by 2035 at US$18.7 billion. Planned links: Thu Thiem-Long Thanh Light Rail, North-South Express Railway.

wikis.title: Saudi's NEOM halts work on The Line until after 2030
wikis.summary: Semafor exclusive (22 May 2026): NEOM delays further work on The Line and Red Sea tourism destinations until at least after 2030, while spending about $3 billion on OXAGON.
wikis.body:
- By Matthew Martin, Semafor, May 22, 2026, citing people familiar with the matter.
- NEOM has delayed further work on The Line, "the planned 170-kilometer long dual skyscrapers once projected to cost more than $1 trillion", until at least after 2030, as the Public Investment Fund shifts spending to ports and data centers. Tourism destinations on the Red Sea coast also postponed until after 2030; Trojena (earlier due to host the 2029 Asian Winter Games) gets no new investment until after 2030.
- The Line's twin mirrored skyscrapers are to be significantly redesigned; unclear when the redesign will be done or when new funding will be allocated.
- NEOM plans about $3 billion more for OXAGON, the industrial city with a Red Sea port, with utilities and data connectivity to attract AI firms' data centers.
- Result of a strategic review by CEO Aiman al-Mudaifer (appointed last year). Population target by 2030 now up to 100,000 (once 1.5 million, revised to 300,000 two years earlier).
- Context: PIF to stop funding LIV Golf after $5 billion; the Mukaab in Riyadh put on hold; widening deficits and the Iran war. NEOM did not respond to a request for comment.

wikis.title: Further doubts over Saudi Arabia's Neom gigaproject
wikis.summary: New Civil Engineer (1 June 2026) on reports that Neom and The Line have stalled, with contract terminations for Webuild and doubts from a former PR representative.
wikis.body:
- By Tom Pashby, 01 Jun 2026. Neom, made of regions Magna, Oxagon, Sindalah, Trojena with The Line as flagship (described as 300 m wide, 500 m tall, 170 km long), "appears to have stalled completely" per a PR professional who previously represented it, who said "I doubt it will go ahead at all".
- Suspension first reported by Semafor and BBC; on 22 May Semafor reported postponements to after 2030, with $3bn still for Oxagon port. BBC (25 May) said The Line "is being turned into something considerably more prosaic".
- Webuild: March 2026 statement that Neom terminated for convenience its $4.7bn contract for Trojena's artificial lake (three dams and 'The Bow'); 21 May 2026 update that Neom terminated the Neom Connector High-Speed Line contract effective May 27, 2026, works about 20% complete, residual backlog about EUR 1bn. All Webuild activities for Neom concluded.
- Firms known to have worked on the project include Mott MacDonald, Jacobs, Aecom, Bechtel, Keller, AtkinsRealis, Webuild, Systra, Egis, Turner & Townsend, Archirodon, Deme. Jacobs' web page on Oxagon/DataVolt work now 404s.
- Controversies cited: removal of the Huwaitat people, worker deaths claims (ITV: 21,000, which Saudi authorities called "misinformation"), al-Muwaila village displacement (ALQST), CEO Nadhmi Al-Nasr's departure in November 2024.

wikis.title: Gross Dam construction milestone (Denver Water)
wikis.summary: Denver Water (20 July 2026): final roller-compacted concrete placed on 3 June 2026, bringing Gross Dam to 470 feet.
wikis.body:
- By Jay Adams, July 20, 2026. On June 3, 2026 workers placed the final load of roller-compacted concrete, bringing Gross Dam to 470 feet; RCC used over three years to raise, thicken and lengthen the dam.
- Project designed to nearly triple Gross Reservoir's capacity, increase Denver Water's reservoir storage by 11%.
- One more foot of conventional protective concrete over the next year gives a final height of 471 feet.
- Program manager Jeff Martin: dam transformed from a gravity dam to an arch dam, "the first time that we know that this dam transformation has ever been done in the world."

wikis.title: Gross Reservoir dam raise hits major construction milestone
wikis.summary: International Water Power (June 12, 2026): Kiewit completed all RCC placement at the Gross Reservoir Expansion Project; overall completion expected October 2027.
wikis.body:
- Kiewit completed all roller compacted concrete placement; the dam is 130 ft (40 m) higher, at 470 ft (143 m), the tallest dam in Colorado. One vertical foot of structural concrete slabs remains.
- As of June 2026: over 744,000 cu yd (569,000 m3) of RCC and 59,000 cu yd (45,000 m3) of conventional concrete facing placed. One of the largest RCC dam projects underway in the US.
- Remaining: crest, spillway and stilling basin structural works, and mechanical, electrical, instrumentation and security systems. Overall construction expected complete October 2027.

wikis.title: Uttarakhand tunnel rescue (Silkyara Bend-Barkot tunnel, November 2023)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the 12 November 2023 tunnel collapse in Uttarkashi that trapped 41 workers, all rescued on 28 November 2023.
wikis.body:
- 12-28 November 2023 (16 days): a section of the Silkyara Bend-Barkot tunnel (Char Dham project, National Highway 134; planned 4.5 km, saving about 20 km) collapsed at around 05:30 IST during construction, trapping 41 workers; blockage 60 m long. Built by Navayuga Engineering Construction Ltd under NHIDCL.
- Agencies: NDRF, SDRF, Uttarakhand Police, Army engineers, Border Roads Organisation Project Shivalik; Australian experts Arnold Dix and Chris Cooper.
- Rescue: Operation Zindagi; augers and drilling machines failed (one broke 47 m in on 25 November); pipes supplied oxygen and food; vertical drilling also started. On 28 November "rat-hole" miners broke through manually and pushed a pipe; all 41 confirmed rescued around 20:50 IST. 40 declared fit by 1 December.
- Cause/investigation: weak rock (meta-siltstone and phyllites) near the Main Central Thrust, no escape shafts; NHAI ordered a safety audit of 29 tunnels; the detailed probe report found negligence by NHIDCL, the construction firm and the supervising engineer, but no significant action yet (21 minor collapses previously flagged).
- Aftermath: breakthrough of the two ends reported 16 April 2025.

wikis.title: NDRF: Silkyara tunnel collapse operation
wikis.summary: NDRF operations page summarising its role in the 17-day rescue of 41 workers from the Silkyara-Barkot tunnel, Uttarkashi, in November 2023.
wikis.body:
- On 12 November 2023 the partial collapse of the Silkyara-Barkot Tunnel, Uttarkashi, entrapped 41 workers on the Silkyara side.
- Two well-equipped NDRF teams took part in the 17-day-long rescue, jointly with NHIDCL, RITES, NHAI, RVNL, SJVNL, KRCL, BRO, ITBP, SDRF, PWD, Air Force, State Police, rat miners and state administration.
- Using different cutting and drilling methods, all 41 trapped persons were rescued.

wikis.title: E&O says Andaman Island Phase 2 reclamation to be completed by end-2027
wikis.summary: The Edge Malaysia (Feb 26): E&O expects Phase 2 reclamation of Penang's Andaman Island to finish by end-2027, about a year ahead of schedule.
wikis.body:
- Eastern & Oriental Bhd (E&O) expects Phase 2 reclamation completed by end-2027 (December 2027), about a year ahead of the earlier end-2028 expectation; infrastructure works targeted for 2029 (Tee). MD Kok Tuck Cheong said additional financing, likely bank borrowings, would be sought (amount undisclosed) for the 507-acre Phase 2.
- In September last year E&O secured RM780 million from AmBank Group for Phase 2.
- Andaman Island: 760-acre reclamation off Gurney Drive, Penang. Phase 1 (253 acres, GDV RM20 billion) has launched six projects (The Meg, Arica, Senna, Fera, The Lume, Maris); Phase 2 (507 acres) estimated GDV RM40 billion.
- E&O Q3 FY2026 (to Dec 31, 2025): net profit RM63.51 million (from RM30.9 million); revenue RM243.92 million (+45.41%); nine-month net profit RM159.17 million.
- Page date given only as "Feb 26" (year 2026 implied by site date, not stated in article text).

wikis.title: Highest bridge in the world opens in China: Huajiang Grand Canyon Bridge
wikis.summary: Smithsonian (Oct 1, 2025): the Huajiang Grand Canyon Bridge in Guizhou opened Sept 28, 2025, about 2,050 feet above the Beipan River, surpassing Beipanjiang Bridge.
wikis.body:
- By Sonja Anderson, October 1, 2025. Opened to traffic September 28 after more than three years of construction; about 2,050 feet above the Beipan River (per China Daily). The Empire State Building would fit beneath with about 600 feet to spare.
- Beats Beipanjiang (Duge) Bridge, about 1,854 feet, the record holder since 2016. Guizhou has more than 32,000 bridges built or in development. China now has the world's seven highest bridges, three in Guizhou.
- Cuts valley crossing from two hours to two minutes (CCTV). Suspension bridge with two lanes each direction; tourist attraction with glass elevator to a cafe in a tower and planned bungee jumping.
- Chief engineer Yang Jian: "It turns an impassable gorge into a passage." Context: a bridge under construction in Qinghai collapsed in August, killing at least 12 workers; engineers describe a top-down infrastructure approach.

wikis.title: Huajiang Canyon Bridge
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the suspension bridge in Guizhou, opened 28 September 2025, world's highest bridge at 625 m deck-to-river.
wikis.body:
- Carries S57 Liuzhi-Anlong Expressway across the Beipan River (Guanling-Zhenfeng counties). Total length 2,890 m; main span 1,420 m; towers 262 m and 205 m; clearance below 625 m (2,051 ft); 4 lanes.
- Builder Guizhou Bridge Group; construction 18 January 2022 to 28 September 2025; cost 2.1 billion RMB. Load test 21-25 August 2025; opened 28 September 2025. First tower reached 199 m on 21 April 2023.
- Surpassed the Duge Bridge (200 km upstream). Motives: revitalising remote, poor Guizhou and tourism. Crossing time cut from 70 minutes to just over one minute.
- Features: fibre-optic load cell cable in three of 217 cable strands; karst groundwater diverted to a 4,000 m3 reservoir feeding the service area, farmland and a ~300 m wide water curtain up to nearly 100 m high (described by state media as the world's highest artificial waterfall) with light shows twice daily; glass walkway, glass elevator, tower coffeehouse 800 m above valley floor, bungee and paragliding facilities.

wikis.title: Titans host media tour at new Nissan Stadium, scheduled to open in 2027
wikis.summary: Tennessee Titans article (Mar 3, 2025): project about one-third complete and on schedule for February 2027 completion.
wikis.body:
- By Jim Wyatt, Mar 03, 2025. Project executive Kellen DeCoursey: three-year project roughly one-third complete; on schedule; completion February 2027.
- 850 workers on site weekly, peak 1,700. New stadium rises to 235 feet versus 150 feet for the current one; located roughly 100 feet from it, with a pedestrian parkway to the west.
- By end of 2025 a building "basically to the roof level"; then exterior work (windows, metal panels); interior finishing in 2026. Crews on site at all hours (Reggie Polk, Tennessee Builders Alliance).
- Groundbreaking was February 2024 (related items: over 700 community members, Amy Adams Strunk, Gov. Bill Lee, Mayor Freddie O'Connell); Mosh Pit section sold out.

wikis.title: Titans' new enclosed stadium on track for February 2027 completion
wikis.summary: AP report via NFL.com (2026) that the Titans' new Nissan Stadium remains on schedule, with keys due in February and a $2.1 billion cost.
wikis.body:
- Associated Press, Nashville. CEO Burke Nihill: "We're going to get keys to this building in February." Groundbreaking Feb. 29, 2024; team moves in for the 2027 season.
- Cost $2.1 billion, including $1.2 billion combined state and local bonds.
- Locker room with 68 fixed lockers, about 50% more space than the stadium opened in 1999; underground player parking; 44 escalators and 27 elevators (versus six elevators now).
- Roof: cables raised starting in May, all translucent roof panels installed by October at the latest; two layers like Allegiant Stadium; project manager Kellen DeCoursey: "We're the second building that's fully enclosed." Interior work sheltered by boat wrap.
- Page's publish date not shown (related items dated March 2026).

wikis.title: New Manila International Airport completion delayed to 2028
wikis.summary: Reuters via Khaleej Times (27 Aug 2024): San Miguel Corp says the Bulacan airport will be delayed to 2028 mainly due to sand shortages.
wikis.body:
- Published Tue 27 Aug 2024. San Miguel Corp confirmed a BusinessWorld report that completion of the New Manila International Airport in Bulacan would slip to 2028, mainly from difficulty sourcing sand used as backfill.
- Project cost: Php740 billion ($13.15 billion). The Manila Bay reclamation projects' suspension limited access to sand.
- SMC also expected MRT Line 7 in Bulacan to be delayed to 2028 over the alignment and location of San Jose del Monte Station. SMC's half-year net income jumped 66 per cent.

wikis.title: MetroLink enabling works could start in 2027, says Transport Minister
wikis.summary: Irish Times report (3 Oct 2025) on Transport Minister Darragh O'Brien's timeline for Dublin's MetroLink after planning permission was granted.
wikis.body:
- Published Fri 3 Oct 2025 by The Irish Times. Minister for Transport Darragh O'Brien said "enabling" works could start in two years (2027), with construction getting under way in 2028, "with a fair wind".
- Planning permission was granted "on Thursday"; he hoped there would be no legal challenge (judicial review). Absent one, MetroLink could be completed by 2035. He said the rail link from Swords (north Dublin) to Charlemont, near Ranelagh, could open in phases.
- He said: "This [project] is happening", after many previous announcements and cancellations.
- Funding: the Government pledged EUR 2 billion under the revised National Development Plan (announced in July), covering initial works over the next five years; "not a blank cheque".
