- Formerly American Copper Buildings / 626 First Avenue; two luxury towers in Murray Hill/Kips Bay; developer JDS Development, architect SHoP Architects; 761 rental units, 20% affordable; west tower 540 ft (48 floors), east 470 ft (41 floors); 824,000 sq ft.
- Site: former Con Edison Kips Bay Generating Station; Sheldon Solow bought it, sold the southwest corner to the School Construction Authority in 2010 for $33.25 million and the remaining plot to JDS and Largo in 2013 for $172 million.
- Timeline: construction began mid-2014, copper cladding mid-2015, towers topped out late 2015 and early 2016, skybridge installation began January 2016; name released April 2016; West opened April 2017, East late 2018; cafe Hole in the Wall June 2019.
- Financing/sale: $500 million AIG mortgage plus $160 million mezzanine loan (December 2016); contract to sell to Black Spruce Management and Orbach Affordable Housing Solutions for about $850 million (December 2021); JPMorgan $675 million financing (March 2022).
- Design: copper on north and south facades, glass on east and west; three-story skybridge about 300 ft above ground.

wikis.title: Jakarta to break ground on giant sea wall in September (Jakarta Post)
wikis.summary: Jakarta Post, 21-22 Jan 2026: Jakarta plans to begin its 19 km segment of the giant sea wall in September, per Governor Pramono Anung.
wikis.body:
- The Jakarta administration is set to begin the giant sea wall along the city's northern coast in September (2026), part of President Prabowo Subianto's 500-kilometer megaproject to protect flood-prone communities from Banten to East Java against rising seas.
- Governor Pramono Anung "fully supports the project"; Jakarta's stretch is 19 km, up from an initial 12 km, projected at around US$1 billion annually over eight years of construction. Whole project expected to cost up to $80 billion and take around 20 years.
- Prabowo last year asked the city to fund the Jakarta segment, citing its "very large regional budget"; Pramono says Jakarta is committed to helping finance it.
- Pramono reiterated a hybrid design combining concrete with nature-based solutions such as mangrove restoration: "I will still develop mangrove ecosystems along Jakarta's sections of the wall". (Premium article; text partial.)

wikis.title: Jakarta sets September 2026 groundbreaking for Giant Sea Wall (Investortrust)
wikis.summary: Investortrust.id, 20 Jan 2026: Governor Pramono says Jakarta plans a September 2026 groundbreaking while awaiting central-government direction.
wikis.body:
- Pramono Anung said on Tuesday Jan 20, 2026 that Jakarta plans to start groundbreaking for the Giant Sea Wall in September 2026 while awaiting final direction from the central government. Scope expanded from 12 km to 19 km ("whether it is 12 or 19 kilometers, Jakarta is ready").
- Meanwhile Jakarta prioritises NCICD coastal defenses (National Capital Integrated Coastal Development); the Ancol phase is complete and entering beautification; he asked for parks, not only concrete.
- Kadin Indonesia gives conditional support, asking for sound economic calculations "so it does not become another debt problem like the high-speed rail" (Carmelita Hartoto, Nov 13, 2025); no commitment to direct involvement.
- Minister Agus Harimurti Yudhoyono (Oct 21, 2025): meant to protect around 50 million people on Java's northern coast from tidal flooding and land subsidence; warns against rushing.
- Prabowo has estimated up to $80 billion and 15 to 20 years, up to 535 km from Banten to East Java; Jakarta Bay construction 8 to 10 years.

wikis.title: Camp Century (Wikipedia): US Army ice-cap base in Greenland, 1959-1967
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on Camp Century, the nuclear-powered US Army subsurface research base in Greenland and its link to Project Iceworm.
wikis.body:
- Abandoned Arctic US military scientific research base in Greenland, 205 km east-northeast of Pituffik Space Base; operated 1959 to 1967; 21 tunnels totalling 9,800 feet (3.0 km); powered by a nuclear reactor (PM-2A semi-mobile). Publicized as a demonstration of affordable ice-cap outposts and a research base.
- Per documents declassified in 1996 it was a preliminary camp for Project Iceworm (survivable nuclear missile launch sites); missiles were never fielded and Danish consent was never sought. Iceworm was aborted when the ice sheet proved less stable than assessed.
- Construction began without explicit permission from Denmark, creating a dilemma for PM H. C. Hansen. Cut-and-cover trenches under steel arches (longest 1,100 ft); projected lifespan ten years, manned five, abandoned after eight; trenches compressed within four years, requiring snow trimming; reactor shut down after over three years due to accelerated compression; sewage sump problems (liquid waste permeated up to 170 feet by 1962).
- Science: ice cores gave stable isotope analyses for climate models; soil in samples suggests the site was ice-free as recently as 400,000 years prior. Since 2017 the Geological Survey of Denmark and Greenland runs the Camp Century Climate Monitoring Program.
- Hazardous waste remains buried under the ice and is an environmental concern. October 1965: the US Army concluded subsurface ice camps feasible and nuclear power advantageous.

wikis.title: The Army once built an underground ice fortress (Task & Purpose)
wikis.summary: Task & Purpose, Oct 27 2022: history of Camp Century in Greenland and the secret Project Iceworm.
wikis.body:
- Camp Century: almost two miles of tunnels in Greenland ice, space for 200 soldiers and scientists, about 800 miles from the North Pole, powered by a portable nuclear reactor. Construction June 1959 to October 1960; more than 100 miles inland from Thule Air Base; supplies hauled on tracked "heavy swings" at 2 mph, a 70-hour trip; the reactor equipment and fuel weighed 330 tons.
- Trenches dug with Swiss-built snow plows; largest "Main Street" over 1,000 feet, covered with steel arches and snow; prefabricated buildings inside (sleeping quarters, labs, mess hall, hospital, laundry, recreation hall, chapel, barbershop); well for water.
- Publicly run by the Army's Polar Research and Development Center as a science and weather station; core samples used to study weather patterns (1960 Popular Science). Secretly Project Iceworm: up to 600 modified Minuteman missiles across 52,000 square miles of tunnels with 11,000 personnel.
- Iceworm abandoned in 1963: Air Force and Navy wanted control, Denmark would not allow nuclear weapons, and the ice kept shifting. Camp closed in 1966 (per this article); tunnels collapsed, leaving toxic waste including 47,000 gallons of radioactive waste. In 2016 scientists reported warming could eventually expose it.

wikis.title: Ryugyong Hotel (Wikipedia): unfinished pyramid skyscraper in Pyongyang
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the 330 m Ryugyong Hotel in Pyongyang, begun in 1987, halted 1992, exterior completed 2011.
wikis.body:
- 330 m (1,080 ft) unfinished pyramid-shaped skyscraper in Pyongyang, North Korea; 105 floors above ground, 3 below; 360,000 m2; architect Baikdoosan Architects & Engineers; developer Orascom Group (from 2008). Status on hold; construction started 28 August 1987, topped out 1992, exterior completed 14 July 2011; completion estimate unknown.
- Planned as a mixed-use development; work halted in 1992 amid North Korea's economic crisis after the Soviet Union's dissolution; stood as a windowless concrete shell for over a decade; construction resumed 2008. Planned opening 2012 (centenary of Kim Il Sung's birth), partial opening announced for 2013 then cancelled. In 2018 an LED display was fitted, showing propaganda animations and film scenes.
- Reportedly a Cold War response to the 1986 Westin Stamford in Singapore; aimed to attract $230 million in foreign investment. Japanese newspapers estimated cost at $750 million (2 percent of North Korea's GDP). Late 1990s inspection by the European Chamber of Commerce in Korea concluded it was irreparable (per Marcus Noland); a 2008 government official said it was unfinished because North Korea "ran out of money".
- Design: three wings each 100 m long and 18 m wide, sloping at 75 degrees; truncated cone of eight rotating floors plus six static; originally five revolving restaurants and 3,000 or 7,665 rooms. Previously considered the tallest unoccupied building until Goldin Finance 117.

wikis.title: The Rocky History of the Ryugyong Hotel, 1987-2019 (Koryo Tours)
wikis.summary: Koryo Tours blog (12 Jul 2018, updated May 2019): timeline of the Ryugyong Hotel from 1987 to 2019.
wikis.body:
- 1987: construction begins, funding backed by the Soviet Union, planned completion for the 13th World Festival of Youth and Students in June 1989 (would have been the world's tallest hotel).
- 1987-1992: construction on schedule, pyramid takes shape with a detached "pyramid top" for a revolving restaurant. 1992: construction ceases, unclad concrete for over ten years (Daily Mail called it "The Hotel of Doom").
- 2008: restarts with Egyptian company Orascom on the outer cladding; opening date 2012, pushed to 2013. 2011: exterior complete, construction ceases a second time with no opening date.
- 2018: entrance driveway completed; the pyramid top lit up as a North Korean flag image, then the front surface revealed to be LED panels; late 2018 lit every evening 7pm-10pm.
- 2019 (updated May): still empty and awaiting interior fitting; originally five revolving restaurants, now two planned. Simon Cockerell and Hannah Barraclough reached the top in 2012 and, per the blog, remain the only foreigners to have done so.

wikis.title: Commonwealth Fusion Systems to build world's first commercial fusion power plant in Virginia
wikis.summary: CFS press release (Dec. 17, 2024) announcing the ARC grid-scale fusion plant at the James River Industrial Center, Chesterfield County, Virginia.
wikis.body:
- Dec. 17, 2024: CFS, "the largest private fusion company", said it will build the first grid-scale commercial fusion power plant, ARC, at the James River Industrial Center in Chesterfield County, Virginia; CFS will independently finance, build, own and operate it.
- Agreement with Dominion Energy Virginia (current site owner) for non-financial collaboration: development and technical expertise and leasing rights.
- ARC will generate about 400 megawatts, "enough energy to power large industrial sites or about 150,000 homes"; expected to deliver power to the grid in the early 2030s; expected to generate billions of dollars in economic development and hundreds of jobs.
- SPARC demonstration machine at Devens, Massachusetts is expected to produce first plasma in 2026 and net fusion energy shortly after; CFS has raised more than $2 billion since its 2018 founding.
- Quote, Bob Mumgaard (CEO): "In the early 2030s, all eyes will be on the Richmond region ... as the birthplace of commercial fusion energy."

wikis.title: Commonwealth Fusion Systems' ARC fusion power plant in Virginia
wikis.summary: New Atlas report that Commonwealth Fusion Systems plans to build a grid-scale fusion power plant (ARC) in Chesterfield County, Virginia.
wikis.body:
- Commonwealth Fusion Systems (CFS) announced plans to build "the world's first grid-scale fusion power plant" near Richmond, Virginia.
- After more than 100 locations worldwide were scouted, CFS chose a 100-acre (40.5-ha) plot in Chesterfield County. The ARC facility ("Affordable, Robust, Compact") would occupy 25 acres of it.
- Aim: a continuous 400 megawatts of clean power by the early 2030s; if successful it could power 150,000 homes.
- The SPARC tokamak design uses high-temperature superconducting magnets designed by CFS to confine plasma at over 100 million degrees Celsius in a donut-shaped vessel. The goal is a steady burn producing electricity continuously.
- Any disruption (loss of power, mechanical failure) would cool the plasma in milliseconds and stop the reaction.
- Challenges noted: high-energy neutrons degrade reactor materials, so maintenance is a constant concern; tritium fuel is mildly radioactive and needs careful handling. Plasma containment was only recently "conquered": KSTAR managed a 48-second continuous plasma burn in February 2024, the longest to date.
- The article says a single gram of fuel can produce as much energy as 10 tons (9 tonnes) of coal.
- The name ARC is shared with the fictional reactor of Marvel's Tony Stark; the real one is about the size of a warehouse.

wikis.title: April 9, 1965: first game in the Houston Astrodome, Astros vs. Yankees
wikis.summary: SABR game account of the Astros' 12-inning exhibition win over the Yankees that opened the Astrodome, attended by President Lyndon Johnson.
wikis.body:
- Date: Friday, April 9, 1965; Houston Astros beat the New York Yankees in the first professional baseball game played indoors. Written by Rory Costello (SABR Games Project).
- President Lyndon B. Johnson attended, telling Astros president and co-owner Judge Roy Hofheinz "Roy, I want to congratulate you; it shows so much imagination." Texas governor John Connally threw the ceremonial first ball. One of seven times a US president attended a major-league ballpark's debut.
- Yankees manager Johnny Keane led off Mickey Mantle, who opened with a single off Dick Farrell. Mel Stottlemyre started for New York.
- Mantle homered in the sixth for the first run (the ball "barely made it into the first row of seats"); Houston tied it with an unearned run in the bottom of the sixth.
- Extra innings: in the bottom of the 12th, off Pete Mikkelsen, Jimmy Wynn singled and stole second, and Nellie Fox's two-out bloop single scored him. Game time 2 hours 34 minutes. Hal Woodeshick threw five scoreless innings for Houston.
- Fox, 37, had said before the game "I have retired as a player."
- Visibility: fielders complained the ball blended into the roof girders; Maris said "The ball blends into the girders." Paul Richards urged a money-back guarantee; Saturday and Sunday were cloudy and the roof was soon painted.
- Listed baseball capacity per some accounts was 46,000. LBJ and party left before the top of the ninth.

wikis.title: The Astrodome: overview of the first multipurpose domed stadium
wikis.summary: Texas State Historical Association handbook entry on the Houston Astrodome's financing, construction, features, events and later decline.
wikis.body:
- The Astrodome, "the first fully air-conditioned, enclosed, domed, multipurpose sports stadium in the world", was officially named Harris County Domed Stadium when it opened in April 1965.
- Financing: bond issue approved July 26, 1958; $22 million general obligation bonds approved January 31, 1961 (Roy M. Hofheinz led the covered-stadium idea); $9 million more approved December 22, 1962. Ground broken January 3, 1962; construction began March 18, 1963 and took two years.
- Cost: stadium structure $20 million; overall more than $40 million ($31.6 million from two county bond issues, $3.75 million from state highway department and city of Houston). Houston Sports Association leased it for forty years and added $6 million (apartments, restaurants, cushioned seats, $2 million scoreboard).
- First event: April 9, 1965, Astros vs. Yankees exhibition. First football game September 11, 1965 (Tulsa 14, Houston 0). Oilers moved in for 1968.
- Specs: baseball seating 52,000, football about 62,000; constant 73F, 50 percent humidity; clear span 642 feet, inside height 208 feet. Roof painted after outfielders lost fly balls; grass died, so AstroTurf (Chemstrand) was used from 1966.
- 1988-89: $100 million renovation (+10,000 seats, 72 luxury boxes).
- Events: 1966 Ali-Williams fight, 1968 UCLA-Houston "Game of the Century", 1973 King-Riggs "Battle of the Sexes", MLB All-Star Games 1968 and 1986, 1971 Final Four, 1989 NBA All-Star Game, 1992 Republican convention.
- Decline: Oilers left after 1996; Astros played last game there October 9, 1999, moving to Enron Field.

wikis.title: 262 Fifth Avenue, Manhattan residential skyscraper
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the 860-foot, 26-apartment pencil tower at 262 Fifth Avenue, its development history, design and reception.
wikis.body:
- Residential skyscraper on Fifth Avenue, Manhattan; developed by Boris Kuzinez (Five Points Development), designed by Russian firm Meganom, executive architect SLCE Architects. 860 feet (260 m), 54 stories, 26 apartments.
- History: Kuzinez bought 260, 262 and 264 Fifth Avenue in 2015-2016 for a total of $101.8 million, plus air rights for $5.8 million. September 2016 filing: 54 stories, 928 feet. Demolition done by September 2017; DOB approved plans the next month (then up to 41 apartments, 1,009 feet).
- Work appeared stalled in 2019; site at 260 Fifth Avenue sold to Amir Loloi for $52.5 million in mid-2021; excavation by November 2021; foundation work began 2022.
- Between August and December 2022 height cut from 1,043 to 860 feet; in mid-2023 apartments cut from 41 to 26. November 2023: Madison Realty Capital and Cottonwood Group lent a combined $180 million.
- Topped out April 2024; in December 2024 the NY Attorney General's office allowed unit sales to begin and five apartments were marketed.
- Details: 139,168 sq ft residential, average apartment about 3,200 sq ft, at least one four-story unit, 10,850 sq ft retail, rooftop infinity pool; slabs mostly 45 by 45 feet; height-to-width ratio about 19:1 (pencil tower).
- Reception: criticized for blocking views of the Empire State Building from south of 28th Street including most of Madison Square Park; design criticized (Curbed's Christopher Bonanos on the pencil look); few units relative to height.

wikis.title: Meganom nears completion of 262 Fifth Avenue
wikis.summary: ArchDaily news piece (December 24, 2025) on the design and engineering of Meganom's 262 Fifth Avenue tower in Manhattan.
wikis.body:
- Moscow-based Meganom is nearing completion of the residential skyscraper at 262 Fifth Avenue for client Five Points Development; project dates back to 2015.
- Team: Norm Architects (interior), SLCE Architects (architect of record), untitled architecture (architectural supervision and project management).
- 860 feet, 52 stories (per this article), 26 residential units in about 140,000 sq ft; apartments conceived as elevated "shelves" framing city views, inspired by aeronautics.
- Structure: backbone supporting attached floor modules, reinforced concrete core plus two parallel walls along Fifth Avenue; core pushed outward for clear-span apartment layouts. Six mechanical floors act as outriggers; wind-tunnel tested (including aeroelastic studies); a void acts as windbreak and a damper sits on the upper mechanical floor. Tapering high-strength concrete walls with 97 ksi rebar.
- Foundation rests on Manhattan schist (40-60 tons per square foot allowable bearing).
- Facade: curtain wall on north and south, glass panels up to 20 feet high and 8.5 feet wide, triple-glazed low-iron Low-E glass.
- Systems: hydronic radiant heating; micro-climate HVAC giving fresh air every hour (three times NYC health-code requirement) with energy recovery; photovoltaic glass and Passive House principles.

wikis.title: Inauguration of Mareterra by Prince Albert II of Monaco
wikis.summary: Short Mareterra notice that the new Monaco district was officially inaugurated on December 4, 2024.
wikis.body:
- On December 4, 2024, Mareterra was officially inaugurated by H.S.H. Prince Albert II of Monaco and the princely family.
- Plaques were unveiled for the "Piscine Princesse Charlene", the "Place Princesse Gabriella" and the "Esplanade et Promenade Prince Jacques".
- The page says that nine years after the signing of the Concession Treaty, the new district of Monaco "has become a reality".

wikis.title: Prince Albert inaugurates Mareterra, Monaco's new eco-district
wikis.summary: Monaco Reporter article on the December 4, 2024 inauguration of the EUR 2 billion Mareterra sea-reclaimed district and its features.
wikis.body:
- Mareterra, described as a EUR 2Bn environmentally friendly development announced in 2013 and started in 2015, was inaugurated ahead of schedule on Wednesday, December 4, 2024, by Prince Albert with Princess Charlene and children Jacques and Gabriella.
- It is the Principality's 11th district, developed by SAM L'Anse du Portier; a 6-hectare area (3% added land; Monaco is 1.98 sq km) built into the sea. Green spaces now account for almost 20% of territory. Lead developer Patrice Pastor; Guy Thomas Levy-Soussan managing director.
- Built to the Environmental High Quality standard.
- Contents: 500 m waterfront promenade, small port with 16 berths for boats up to 16 m, park, underground parking; 110 sea-view apartments including Le Renzo (62 m high, 125 m long, raised five meters on columns, 50 apartments, none smaller than 400 sqm, penthouse quadruplex); four townhouses; 10 villas of 0.2 hectares with 1,500-2,000 m2 living space; over 4,000 m2 of commercial space for about a dozen restaurants and shops.
- Reportedly most residences are sold, mostly to European clients, at prices up to EUR 120,000 per square meter.
- Architects named: Denis Valode and Jean Pistre, Renzo Piano Building Workshop, Stefano Boeri, Tadao Ando, Norman Foster (Yacht Club of Monaco), landscape artist Michel Desvigne.

wikis.title: Shanghai World Financial Center
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the Shanghai World Financial Center supertall in Pudong: history, construction, design and the aperture change.
wikis.body:
- Supertall mixed-use skyscraper in Pudong, Shanghai; designed by Kohn Pedersen Fox, developed by Mori Building Company, structural engineer Leslie E. Robertson Associates, main contractors China State Construction Engineering Corporation and Shanghai Construction (Group) General Co. Offices, hotel, conference rooms, ground-floor mall.
- Infobox: tip 494.3 m, roof 487.4 m, 101 floors (3 below ground), cost RMB 8.17 billion (US$1.20 billion), floor area 381,600 m2.
- Foundation stone laid 27 August 1997; the 1997 Asian financial crisis halted work after foundations. On 13 February 2003 Mori increased height to 492 m and 101 stories from an initial 460 m, 94-story plan; construction resumed 16 November 2003.
- A fire on 14 August 2007 (noticed on the 40th floor) was extinguished by 17:45; damage slight, nobody injured; cause unknown, preliminary investigation suggested workers' welding.
- Topped out 14 September 2007 at 492 m, then 2nd tallest building in the world (after Taipei 101), tallest by roof height only and tallest in mainland China. Declared complete 17 July 2008; opened 28 August 2008; observation floors opened 30 August 2008.
- Park Hyatt Shanghai: 174 rooms on floors 79-93. Observation deck at 474 m, since closed permanently in 2023 after Shanghai Tower (completed 2016; exceeded SWFC's height in 2013) and COVID-19 cut visitors.
- Design: original circular aperture 46 m in diameter was protested (including by mayor Chen Liangyu) as resembling the Japanese flag; on 18 October 2005 KPF submitted a trapezoidal aperture instead. Nicknamed "the bottle opener".
- Named best completed skyscraper of 2008 by architects. With Shanghai Tower and Jin Mao Tower forms the first adjacent grouping of three supertall skyscrapers.

wikis.title: Shanghai World Financial Center (KPF project page)
wikis.summary: Kohn Pedersen Fox project page describing the Shanghai World Financial Center's program, form, structure and awards.
wikis.body:
- KPF calls it one of its most recognized award-winning projects, a symbol of commerce and culture since completion in 2008; "a virtual city within a city" with offices, retail and the Park Hyatt Shanghai on floors 79-93.
- SWFC Sky Arena on the uppermost floors; a 100th-floor Sky Walk almost 500 meters above the city.
- Form: a square prism (earth) intersected by two cosmic arcs (heavens), carving a square sky portal at the top.
- Structure, with Leslie E. Robertson Associates: replaced the original concrete frame with a diagonal-braced frame with outrigger trusses, reducing building weight by more than 10%.
- Client Mori Building Company; team Shanghai Modern (architect of record), Irie Miyake (executive architect), Tony Chi (interior). Size 381,600 m2; 174 rooms.
- Awards: CTBUH 2018 10 Year Award; Guinness World Records 2009 Highest Observation Deck and Tallest Hotel; MIPIM Asia 2009; AIA New York State 2009 awards; International High-Rise Award 2010 finalist.

wikis.title: Guggenheim Museum Bilbao
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on Frank Gehry's Guggenheim Museum Bilbao: founding, opening, architecture, expansion plan and visitor numbers.
wikis.body:
- Museum of modern and contemporary art in Bilbao, Spain, affiliated with the Solomon R. Guggenheim Foundation; inaugurated 18 October 1997 by King Juan Carlos I with an exhibition of 250 works. Architect Frank Gehry; beside the Nervion River. 1,305,003 visitors in 2025; director Miren Arzalluz.
- Founding: in 1991 the Basque Government proposed a Guggenheim museum in the decrepit port; it agreed to pay US$100 million construction cost, a $50 million acquisitions fund, a $20 million one-time fee and subsidize the $12 million annual budget. Built by Ferrovial at a cost of $89 million. On 13 October 1997 two ETA militants shot dead a Basque policeman who interrupted an attempt to set up grenade launchers.
- Architecture: clad in glass, titanium and limestone; atrium nicknamed "The Flower". 32,500 m2 site, 24,000 m2 total, 11,000 m2 exhibition space in nineteen galleries (largest 130 m x 30 m). Philip Johnson called it "the greatest building of our time". Built on time and budget, using CATIA software.
- Urdaibai expansion: in 2008 the museum looked at a 5,000 m2 expansion; by 2022 Biscay government planned EUR 40 million; after backlash (Greenpeace, SEO/BirdLife, WWF) the Foundation announced in December 2025 it was abandoned.
- Most frequently named important work since 1980 in the 2010 World Architecture Survey. Foundation used more than 25,000 tonnes of concrete.

wikis.title: Reflections on twenty years of the Guggenheim Museum Bilbao
wikis.summary: Guggenheim Checklist article (October 18, 2017) collecting recollections from architects, curators and directors on the Bilbao museum's 20th anniversary.
wikis.body:
- By Caitlin Dover. States the museum opened October 19, 1997 (the page's own date) with a curving titanium form; Frank Gehry's building became one of the best-known in the world.
- Herbert Muschamp (New York Times) quoted: Bilbao became "a pilgrimage town" and "Have you been to Bilbao?" a shibboleth in architectural circles.
- Contributors quoted: Steven Holl (visited 1992 mudflat site, amazed in 1998); Neri Oxman ("engineered like a symphony but experienced like a late quartet"); Nancy Spector (worked with the building from "a sketch on a napkin"); Richard Armstrong (the museum "introduced a new kind of space to the museum-going public" and made Bilbao "an obligatory stop for millions of visitors"); Karole Vail; Juan Ignacio Vidarte, Director General.
- Common themes: economic and cultural importance for Bilbao, a new concept of the museum experience, and the building as a catalyst for art.

wikis.title: Demolition of the Nakagin Capsule Tower begins in Tokyo
wikis.summary: Dezeen report (12 April 2022) that dismantling of Kisho Kurokawa's Nakagin Capsule Tower in Ginza had begun.
wikis.body:
- Demolition of the metabolist Nakagin Capsule Tower in Tokyo began 12 April 2022; interiors were already being emptied ("looks like a demolition site") ahead of asbestos removal, then removal of the capsules, then demolition of the concrete towers. Expected to take until the end of 2022.
- Reason given: decay of its concrete and steel structure. Plans to disassemble were confirmed the previous year; residents crowdfunded to preserve, donate or relocate capsules.
- Built 1972 in Ginza to Kisho Kurokawa's design: two interconnected concrete towers with 140 prefabricated steel capsules bolted on. Each capsule with a round window measures 2.5 m by four metres. Capsules were meant to be replaced every 25 years but lack of funding meant this never happened.
- The Nakagin Capsule Tower A606 Project (representative Akiko Ishimaru) is restoring capsule A606 as a "mobile capsule" honouring Kurokawa's "architecture in motion"; it documented the building with measurements, photos, video and 3D scans.
- Kurokawa (died 2007) pioneered Metabolism with Kiyonori Kikutake and Fumihiko Maki. Dezeen notes wider threats to 20th-century architecture, especially brutalism.

wikis.title: Nakagin Capsule Tower
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on Kisho Kurokawa's Nakagin Capsule Tower in Ginza, Tokyo: design, capsules, Metabolism context and 2022 demolition.
wikis.body:
- Former mixed-use residential and office tower in Ginza, Tokyo, designed by Kisho Kurokawa (structural engineer Gengo Matsui); built 1970-1972; demolished 2022; described as the world's first example of capsule architecture and a rare remaining example of Japanese Metabolism.
- Attempts to raise funds and campaigns to preserve it as a landmark were unsuccessful; 23 component units were earmarked for preservation and later repurposing.
- Structure: two interconnected concrete towers of 11 and 13 floors, 140 self-contained prefabricated capsules in total, three bridge decks (6F, 9F, 12F). Floor area 3,091.23 m2.
- Capsules: 2.5 m x 2.5 m x 4.0 m with a 1.3 m circular window and in-unit bathroom; each attached by only four high-tension bolts so one could be removed without affecting others. No additional capsules were produced and none was ever replaced. Structural elements fireproofed with sprayed asbestos 45 mm thick.
- Target occupants: bachelor Tokyo salarymen; built-in stove, refrigerator, TV, reel-to-reel tape deck.
- Metabolist movement launched in 1960 by Kurokawa, Kiyonori Kikutake, Masato Otaka, Fumihiko Maki, Noboru Kawazoe, Kenji Ekuan and Kiyoshi Awazu; Kurokawa began exploring capsule architecture with the Takara Beautilion at Expo '70 in Osaka.

wikis.title: Constellation seeks FERC help for 2027 Crane plant restart
wikis.summary: World Nuclear News (1 April 2026) on Constellation's plan to restart the Crane Clean Energy Center (Three Mile Island 1) in 2027 despite possible grid connection delays.
wikis.body:
- Constellation Energy still expects to restart the Crane Clean Energy Center (formerly Three Mile Island unit 1) in 2027 despite possible grid connection delays.
- CEO Joseph Dominguez said the company would file a request with FERC to transfer capacity injection rights from its Eddystone plant to Crane. Quote: "we continue to expect to start this unit in 2027."
- Constellation announced the restart in 2024 (reactor closed in 1999) after a 20-year power purchase agreement with Microsoft. Crane would add 835 megawatts. Target was originally 2028, brought forward to 2027 after PJM approved its early interconnection request.
- David Dardis told Reuters at CERA Week that PJM said some transmission upgrades would take until 2031.
- Eddystone (Pennsylvania) has two 380 MW units (3 and 4) kept online beyond planned retirement by emergency orders from US Energy Secretary Chris Wright; latest order issued February, in force until 24 May.
- The restart receives federal support through the US Department of Energy's loan programme.

wikis.title: Crane Clean Energy Center one year after restart announcement
wikis.summary: Constellation press release (Sept. 23, 2025) on progress restarting Three Mile Island Unit 1 as the Crane Clean Energy Center.
wikis.body:
- One-year anniversary of Constellation's announcement to restart Three Mile Island Unit 1, renamed Crane Clean Energy Center; plant was retired for economic reasons in 2019; restart backed by a 20-year power purchase agreement with Microsoft.
- Restart accelerated to 2027. Staffing nearly 80%, 500 full-time employees on site; second Initial License Training class in early 2026.
- Inspections of steam generators, main generator, emergency diesel generators and underground piping completed or near completion; training center and control room simulator upgraded.
- PJM gave accelerated approval of the interconnection request; NRC filings on track with a Restart Panel; NRC approved renaming to "Christopher M. Crane Clean Energy Center".
- Independent study: about 3,400 direct and indirect jobs, over $16 billion added to Pennsylvania GDP, more than $3 billion state and federal tax revenue. More than $1 million charitable giving over five years.
- Constellation says uprates plus the restart could add up to 2,000 megawatts of baseload capacity. Quotes from CEO Joe Dominguez and Governor Josh Shapiro.

wikis.title: Port Polska airport to open in 2032 with 34 million capacity
wikis.summary: Rus Tourism News (May 28, 2026) on the planned 2032 opening of Poland's new central airport with 34 million passengers a year of capacity.
wikis.body:
- Port Polska's new airport is set to open in 2032 with capacity for 34 million passengers a year, per a senior figure involved, confirmed at a parliamentary infrastructure committee session.
- Dariusz Kus, board member at Centralny Port Komunikacyjny (CPK), the delivering company: "We are building in options for a larger airport at opening."
- Designed with expansion options built in from the start; described as one of the largest transport schemes in Poland and intended as a major hub.
- CPK says it is a broader transport project linking aviation with rail and road connections. 2032 remains the current milestone.

wikis.title: Poland's CPK sets out $10B tender pipeline for 2026
wikis.summary: Paywalled Aviation Week teaser: CPK plans tenders worth over $10 billion in 2026, targeting a 2032 opening.
wikis.body:
- Only a teaser is available (subscription required). Published September 9, 2025 by David Casey in Aviation Daily.
- Centralny Port Komunikacyjny (CPK) is described as "Poland's flagship transport infrastructure project combining a new international airport with a nationwide high-speed rail and road network".
- It has unveiled plans to launch tenders worth more than $10 billion next year (2026) as it targets a 2032 opening.

wikis.title: DC Tower 2 in Vienna's Donau City
wikis.summary: Construction Kenya article (updated August 15, 2025) on DC Tower 2, a 174-metre, 53-floor Vienna skyscraper due in 2026.
wikis.body:
- DC Tower 2 in Donau City near the Danube: 174 metres, 53 floors, scheduled for completion in 2026; would be Austria's second-tallest skyscraper after DC Tower 1 (250 m); neighbours DC Tower 3.
- Originally designed as a twin to DC Tower 1; reshaped after advice from Vienna's Urban Planning Advisory Board; Dominique Perrault revised the plans.
- Mix: retail, restaurants, offices and roughly 470 rental apartments with private loggias.
- Peri GmbH supplied climbing formwork for the core (split into four work areas); Porr AG main contractor.
- Facade to include what the article calls Europe's first photovoltaic solar panels on a high-rise.
- Fact sheet: developer Commerz Real; general contractor S+B Gruppe AG; building contractor Porr AG.

wikis.title: DC Tower 2 Vienna (MAX FRANK project page)
wikis.summary: MAX FRANK project entry on DC Tower 2 and its supply of Egcobox thermal-break balcony connectors for loggias.
wikis.body:
- DC Tower 2 is under construction next to Austria's tallest building, Donau City Tower 1 (opened 2014), at approx. 180 meters after an architectural redesign; the third tower was "due for completion in 2022".
- 53 floors, almost 52,000 m2 usable space: retail, gastronomy, offices and circa 470 rental apartments with loggias.
- MAX FRANK Austria supplied circa 5,800 Egcobox thermally insulating cantilever connector units for the loggias, adapted to the geometries and delivered to the Oberndorfer precast plant. Meets Austrian OIB fire requirements (REI90, insulation body A2 non-combustible).
- Client/developer Commerz Real; general contractor S+B Gruppe AG; architect Dominique Perrault; structural planner ghp gmeiner|haferl & partner.

wikis.title: NASA FAQs on the International Space Station transition plan and deorbit
wikis.summary: NASA FAQ explaining why and how the ISS will be operated through 2030 and then deorbited by the SpaceX-built U.S. Deorbit Vehicle, and what follows in low Earth orbit.
wikis.body:
- The 2022 ISS Transition Plan: the US plans to shift low Earth orbit operations to commercially owned and operated destinations; NASA aims to be "one of many customers" and to focus human missions on the Moon and Mars. Commercial stations are planned before the ISS deorbit to avoid a service gap.
- NASA has committed to fully use and safely operate the station through 2030. Its lifetime is limited by the primary structure (modules, radiators, truss) from dynamic loading and thermal cycling. Continuous human presence: more than 23 years per this page, assembly from 1998.
- The station will be deorbited in a controlled manner; shared responsibility of NASA, CSA, ESA, JAXA and Roscosmos. Studies of using up to three Progress spacecraft showed a new or modified vehicle is needed, so NASA is procuring the U.S. Deorbit Vehicle (USDV); "SpaceX has been selected" to develop and deliver it.
- Alternatives rejected: disassembly and return (initial assembly took 27 shuttle flights, 13 years, 161 EVAs; modules not designed for disassembly; smaller items may be preserved with the Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum); boost to higher orbit (needs 120-140 m/s delta-V for 100-year orbit, 760 m/s for over 10,000 years vs 57 m/s for controlled deorbit; debris impact interval falls from about 51 years at 415 km to under four years at 800 km); random re-entry (US Government requires a 1-in-10,000 public risk limit, ISS too large).
- Station: about 257 miles (415 km) altitude, mass more than 945,000 lbs (430,000 kg); orbital life without reboosts roughly one to two years.
- Method: natural orbital decay, lowering altitude with current propulsion, then a large re-entry burn after crew return, targeting an uninhabited ocean area.

wikis.title: ISS prepares for new commander, enters final five years of planned operations
wikis.summary: Spaceflight Now (December 5, 2025) on the ISS commander handover, plans to deorbit around 2030, CASIS extension and the Soyuz pad damage.
wikis.body:
- After 25 years of continuous human presence, the ISS heads into its final half decade; NASA and partners plan to intentionally deorbit it "around 2030 or shortly thereafter". SpaceX contracted for up to $843 million to build the United States Deorbit Vehicle, guiding a splashdown in an uninhabited part of the Pacific.
- On Sunday, Dec. 7 NASA astronaut Mike Fincke takes over as ISS Commander from cosmonaut Sergey Ryzhikov, who with Alexey Zubritsky and Jonny Kim undocks Monday, ending a 245-day mission. Expedition 73 crew portrait Nov. 27, 2025 marked Fincke's 500 cumulative days in space.
- Funding from the recent budget bill and NASA Administrator nominee Jared Isaacman's pledge to "maximize the scientific value of every dollar" mean a busy final five years.
- CASIS extended its cooperative agreement with NASA to manage the ISS National Laboratory through 2030: up to 50 percent of cargo flight allocation and US crew time; more than 940 payloads launched since 2011.
- After the Soyuz MS-28 launch (Chris Williams, Sergey Kud-Sverchkov, Sergei Mikaev), the mobile service platform at Site 31 collapsed into the flame duct; one source told Anatoly Zak repairs could take "up to two years". Roscosmos said it would be fixed "in the nearest time".
- Reboost is partly done by a SpaceX Cargo Dragon (CRS-33), which NASA said will undock in late January 2026; a spokesperson said "there are no expected impacts" to reboost and attitude control.

wikis.title: Excavation completed on DUNE caverns at Sanford Underground Research Facility
wikis.summary: Fermilab press release (August 15, 2024) on the ribbon-cutting marking completion of excavation for LBNF/DUNE underground caverns in Lead, South Dakota.
wikis.body:
- Aug. 15, 2024, Lead, S.D.: ribbon-cutting at SURF, "Into the Depths of Discovery", hosted by Fermilab and the South Dakota Science and Technology Authority, marks completion of the three-year excavation for LBNF/DUNE, led by DOE's Fermilab.
- Held one mile beneath the surface in the northern detector cavern. Excavation covered two seven-story caverns for particle detectors plus a smaller central utility cavern.
- Each detector will be filled with 17,000 tons of liquid argon cooled to minus 184 degrees Celsius to record neutrino interactions.
- Science aims: why the universe contains matter, how an exploding star creates a black hole, whether neutrinos connect to dark matter.
- Quotes: Derek Passarelli (DOE) "a remarkable engineering feat"; Lia Merminga, Fermilab director, "an important step in making LBNF/DUNE a world-class international underground science facility".
- Ribbon cut by Merminga and SURF director Mike Headley; attendees included Sen. Mike Rounds, Rep. Dusty Johnson, Lt. Gov. Larry Rhoden.

wikis.title: Event marks excavation completion on DUNE caverns (SURF release)
wikis.summary: Sanford Underground Research Facility's account of the August 15, 2024 ribbon-cutting for the completed LBNF/DUNE caverns, with excavation figures.
wikis.body:
- Ribbon-cutting on Thursday, August 15, 2024 at SURF in Lead, S.D. for completion of excavation for LBNF/DUNE, an international project led by Fermilab; hosted with the SDSTA and attended by state, federal and DOE officials.
- Event held one mile beneath the surface at the northern detector cavern; two seven-story detector caverns plus a smaller central utility cavern. Each detector to hold 17,000 tons of liquid argon at minus 184 degrees Celsius.
- Teams worked 4,850 feet below the surface since 2021; over 800,000 tons of rock excavated and moved to the former surface mining area known as the Open Cut. Heavy mining equipment was dismantled, taken underground piece by piece and reassembled.
- Collaboration: more than 1,400 scientists and engineers from over 200 institutions in over 35 countries, and CERN.
- Quotes from Derek Passarelli, Lia Merminga and Mike Headley (SURF laboratory director and SDSTA executive director), who called SURF "America's Underground Lab".

wikis.title: Quebec approves interior renovations at Montreal's Olympic Stadium
wikis.summary: CBC News (July 16, 2026) on Quebec's approval of interior modernization of the Olympic Stadium, with reopening planned for 2028.
wikis.body:
- The Quebec government approved plans to modernize the inside of Montreal's Olympic Stadium (first reported by La Presse, confirmed by Radio-Canada). Cost unknown; Tourism Minister Amelie Dionne expected to issue a statement Friday.
- Scope per Radio-Canada: refurbishing the stands, creating VIP boxes and premium spaces, upgrading restrooms and food concession stands. The stadium currently has 56,000 seats.
- Renovations expected to be completed by 2028, in time for the planned reopening. Long-term goal: large-scale shows and sporting events; CF Montreal is particularly interested as MLS adopts a winter schedule (its current home Stade Saputo is open to the elements).
- Roof work continues: the $870-million project, approved in early 2024, replaces the 27,000-square-metre canvas and the technical ring.

wikis.title: New roof for Montreal's Olympic Stadium to cost $870 million
wikis.summary: Global News (Nov. 29, 2024) on the $870-million project to dismantle and replace the Olympic Stadium roof, with reopening set for 2028.
wikis.body:
- Work to dismantle the roof of Montreal's Olympic Stadium was almost complete; the top has been removed and final parts are being disassembled.
- In 2026 work on the new roof starts at ground level, to be assembled there and raised in 2027. The stadium is set to reopen to the public in 2028.
- Price: $870 million for the entire project; Nadir Guenfoud of the Olympic Park cited almost 300 people contributing so far.
- Third roof in the stadium's 48-year history; the first two were plagued with tearing and partial collapses, including Jan. 18, 1999, when part of the structure collapsed under snow during a car show.
- Some question the price for a stadium not consistently used since the Expos last played in 2004. Guenfoud: "There is no reason to think that Montreal cannot host these type of events if it has a proper stadium."
- New permanent fixed roof with a green translucent window; officials hope to double visitors to the Olympic Park.

wikis.title: Grenfell Tower fire: overview, building, renovation and start of the fire
wikis.summary: First part of the Wikipedia article on the 14 June 2017 Grenfell Tower fire covering the overall outcome, the tower's history, 2015-16 cladding renovation, prior warnings and the fire's start.
wikis.body:
- On 14 June 2017 a fire broke out at 00:54 BST in the 24-storey Grenfell Tower, North Kensington, West London, burning 60 hours. 72 died (70 at the scene, two later in hospital), more than 70 injured, 223 escaped. The deadliest UK structural fire since Piper Alpha (1988) and worst UK residential fire since the Blitz. Over 250 London Fire Brigade firefighters and 70 engines attended. Cause: electrical fault in a refrigerator, with spread largely exacerbated by flammable exterior cladding.
- Inquiry opened 14 September 2017; phase 1 report October 2019 found the exterior did not comply with regulations and the fire service was too late advising evacuation; final report published 26 February 2025 (the infobox says 4 September 2024), with the Government accepting all 58 recommendations. Police cases not expected before end of 2026, trials from 2027. April 2023 civil settlement with 900 people by 22 organisations. Demolition began September 2025, expected to take two years.
- Building: part of Lancaster West Estate; designed 1967 by Clifford Wearden and Associates, built 1972-74, 220 ft 10 in (67.30 m); 120 flats later 129 housing up to 600 people; "stay put" policy, one central staircase, no central alarm, no sprinklers.
- Renovation 2015-16: new windows, heating and aluminium composite cladding (Arconic Reynobond PE with polyethylene core; Celotex RS5000 PIR insulation). Rydon won for 8.7 million pounds; Harley Facades fitted cladding at 2.6 million pounds; a more fire-resistant alternative was refused due to cost.
- Warnings: Grenfell Action Group blog, expired extinguishers, a June 2016 assessor flagging 40 serious issues, November 2016 fire deficiency notice; May 2017 LFB warned all 33 London councils about panels.
- Start: around 00:50 a fridge-freezer caught fire in flat 16 on the fourth floor (resident Behailu Kebede).
- Aftermath: UK cladding crisis, over 5 billion pounds pledged since 2017 (estimates 15-50 billion).

wikis.title: London Fire Brigade page on the Grenfell Tower fire
wikis.summary: Short London Fire Brigade page on the 2017 Grenfell Tower fire, the Grenfell Memory Project and the brigade's responses to the inquiry.
wikis.body:
- On 14 June 2017 a fire broke out at Grenfell Tower in North Kensington killing 72 people; "one of the worst UK fires in living memory".
- Grenfell Memory Project: aims to create a lasting legacy honouring the 72 lives lost; a formal consultation is open.
- The Grenfell Tower Inquiry examined the circumstances of the fire and has been "a catalyst for deep institutional transformation within the Brigade".
- Listed LFB responses: to Inquiry Phase 2 (14 February 2025); update that phase 1 recommendations were completed with further changes to come (13 March 2024); response to Phase 1 (30 October 2019).

wikis.title: Tokyo Skytree
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on Tokyo Skytree, the 634 m broadcasting and observation tower in Sumida, Tokyo: dates, design, earthquake resistance and naming.
wikis.body:
- Broadcasting and observation tower in Sumida, Tokyo; 634.0 m (antenna spire), tallest tower in Japan and, per the page, tallest tower in the world (displacing Canton Tower) and third tallest structure behind Merdeka 118 and Burj Khalifa. Roof 495.2 m, top floor 451.3 m, 13 lifts.
- Construction started 14 July 2008; topped out 18 March 2011; completed 29 February 2012; opened 22 May 2012. Cost 65 billion JPY. Architect Nikken Sekkei, contractor Obayashi, developer/owner Tobu Railway.
- Primary TV and radio broadcast site for the Kanto region because Tokyo Tower no longer gives complete digital coverage. Funded by Tobu Railway and six terrestrial broadcasters headed by NHK.
- Design published 24 November 2006, three concepts: neofuturistic plus traditional Japanese beauty; catalyst for revitalization; disaster prevention.
- Observatories at 350 m (up to 2,000 people) and 450 m (900 people), glass floor section and spiral skywalk.
- Earthquake resistance: central reinforced-concrete shaft, oil dampers between 125 m and 375 m, tuned mass damper; designers say dampers can absorb 50 percent of quake energy.
- Colour "Skytree White" (aijiro); LED illumination alternating sky-blue Iki and purple Miyabi (published 16 October 2009).
- Name chosen by public vote, announced 10 June 2008, about 33,000 of 110,000 votes (30%); height 634 m chosen for Musashi (mu-sa-shi).

wikis.title: Tokyo Sky Tree to open on 22 May 2012 (Embassy of Japan feature)
wikis.summary: Embassy of Japan in the UK web-magazine feature (May 2012) on Tokyo Sky Tree's opening, height, purpose, name and structure.
wikis.body:
- Tokyo Sky Tree opens Tuesday 22 May 2012; at 634 metres the tallest freestanding tower in the world and second tallest structure after Burj Khalifa (829.84 m). In Sumida Ward, Tokyo.
- Main purpose: relay TV and radio signals as Tokyo Tower (333 m) no longer provides adequate coverage; also restaurant, cafes, and an observation deck with a glass floor. Intended to help revitalise the city and contribute to disaster prevention; design combines futuristic and traditional Japanese elements.
- Colour officially "Sky Tree White" based on aijiro; sky-blue and purple LEDs.
- Name decided by public vote, announced 10 June 2008 with over 33,000 votes (30%); 634 m chosen to be memorable (6 mu, 3 sa, 4 shi = "Musashi").
- Structure: Knuckle Wall foundation; steel tubes around a concrete core structurally separate in the mid-section, designed to offset each other in an earthquake.
- Thousands of visitors expected in opening weeks; tickets already reserved.

wikis.title: Ciel Dubai Marina, the world's tallest hotel, welcomes first guests
wikis.summary: The National (Nov 15, 2025) report on Ciel Dubai Marina, 377 m, opening as the world's tallest hotel.
wikis.body:
- First guests checked into Ciel Dubai Marina, standing 377 metres and overtaking the 356-metre Gevora Hotel (also Dubai). 82 floors, 1,004 rooms and suites.
- Also claims world's highest infinity pool: Tattu Sky Pool on level 76, 310 metres above the city. Tattu Dubai (first international branch of Manchester-born Asian chain) opened October 10 on level 74; Tattu Sky Lounge & Terrace on level 81 with 360-degree views.
- Managed by The First Group Hospitality under IHG's Vignette Collection.
- Dining: West 13 (Mediterranean), East 14 (Asian), Risen Cafe & Artisanal Bakery. Spa and 24-hour gym on level 61; access and free transfers to Soluna Beach Club on Palm Jumeirah; links to Dubai Marina Mall, tram and metro.
- Cost Dh2 billion ($544 million); originally scheduled to open the previous year. Dubai's skyline has eight of the world's 10 tallest hotels (e.g. Rose Rayhaan 333 m, Burj Al Arab 321 m).
- Managing director Heinrich Morio quoted on welcoming guests.

wikis.title: Ciel Dubai Marina, Vignette Collection debuts as world's tallest hotel (IHG release)
wikis.summary: IHG news release (17 November 2025) announcing the opening of the 377 m Ciel Dubai Marina and describing its venues.
wikis.body:
- DUBAI, 17 November 2025: Ciel Dubai Marina is officially open within IHG's Vignette Collection, billed as the world's tallest hotel; project led by developer The First Group.
- 82 floors rising 377 meters; home to one of the world's highest infinity pools.
- Venues: Tattu (level 74 restaurant; level 76 Tattu Sky Pool, "the world's highest infinity pool"; level 81 Sky Lounge & Terrace); West 13 (Mediterranean); East 14 (buffet-style Asian); Risen Cafe and Artisanal Bakery.
- Spa on Level 61 from February 2026; 24-hour gym; access to Soluna Beach Club on Palm Jumeirah; family facilities (Splash Pad, Kids Club); Nest lounge on Level 16 for business travellers and Executive Club guests.
- Quote from Managing Director Heinrich Morio.

wikis.title: Westminster tube station
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on Westminster London Underground station: 1868 sub-surface platforms and the 1999 deep-level Jubilee line station rebuilt with Portcullis House.
wikis.body:
- London Underground station in the City of Westminster, fare zone 1, served by Circle, District and Jubilee lines; 4 platforms; near Houses of Parliament, Big Ben, Westminster Abbey, London Eye. Entries and exits 2023: 19.17 million; 2024: 18.78 million; 2025: 18.56 million.
- Two parts: sub-surface platforms opened 24 December 1868 (as Westminster Bridge) by the District Railway, then eastern terminus (extended to Blackfriars 30 May 1870); deep-level platforms opened 22 December 1999 on the Jubilee line extension. Outer Circle ran from 1 February 1872 (ended 31 December 1908); Middle Circle from 1 August 1872 (ended 30 June 1900).
- The Jubilee line originally was not planned to pass Westminster; Docklands redevelopment redirected the route via Westminster to connect Waterloo and London Bridge.
- For the extension the sub-surface station was rebuilt with Portcullis House above it; both designed by Michael Hopkins & Partners. The 39-metre (128 ft) deep "station box" was the deepest excavation in central London.
- Big Ben's clock tower stands only 34 m from the station box; 50-metre steel tubes with grout injection (22 occasions, January 1996-September 1997) limited movement to a maximum 35 mm versus at least 120 mm without.

wikis.title: Bechtel's Jubilee Line Extension project, London
wikis.summary: Bechtel project page describing its fast-track completion of the Jubilee Line Extension for the December 1999 millennium deadline.
wikis.body:
- Jubilee Line Extension: London, completed 1999; "the largest addition to the London Underground in more than 25 years" and one of the UK's biggest construction projects, but severely behind schedule because of tunneling and signaling problems.
- Fixed deadline of December 1999 tied to the Millennium Dome in Greenwich (now The O2). Bechtel was hired for a fast-track push and, with partners, finished the extension and operational commissioning in 14 months.
- 10 miles (16 km) linking Green Park in the West End to Greenwich and Stratford; $5.3 billion; 11 stations (6 brand new, 5 substantially enlarged or rebuilt). The Jubilee is the only London Underground line connecting with every other line.
- Highlights: rebuilding Westminster Station next to the Houses of Parliament; archaeological investigations at three historic station sites; four Thames crossings and tunneling at depths up to 30 meters.

wikis.title: Thessaloniki opens its metro after 38 years
wikis.summary: Euronews (30 Nov 2024) on the opening of Thessaloniki's 9.6 km driverless metro line, long delayed by archaeological finds and contractor collapse.
wikis.body:
- Thessaloniki, Greece's second-largest city, inaugurated a new metro on Saturday (30 Nov 2024) by PM Kyriakos Mitsotakis: 9.6 km, driverless trains, platform screen doors, 13 stations. Free for four days, then 0.60 euro tickets.
- First conceived more than a century ago; first tunnel dug in 1986; construction began in earnest in 2003 and unearthed antiquities (Roman-era thoroughfare, ancient Greek burial sites, mosaics; over 300,000 finds per Minister Christos Staikouras). Project nearly abandoned in 2013; in 2015 the Central Archaeological Council agreed to detach and reposition antiquities, one at Venizelos station.
- Tunnels bored deeper than planned to preserve finds, adding cost and delay. Contractor AEGEK collapsed during the crisis begun in 2009.
- Cost so far three billion euros for the first line and most of a second line under construction, due in a year. Consortium: Aktor (Greece), Webuild (Italy), Hitachi Rail (Japan).
- Compared with Rome's Metro Line C (construction began 2006, also slowed by finds).

wikis.title: Melbourne Port Rail Transformation Project completed
wikis.summary: VINCI news item (1 Feb 2024) that Seymour Whyte handed over 2.7 km of new rail infrastructure at the Port of Melbourne.
wikis.body:
- Australia, 01 February 2024: Seymour Whyte (VINCI Construction) handed over 2.7 km of new rail infrastructure in the port, including a new rail terminal.
- Goal: increase ship-to-rail capacity and reduce trucks on the metropolitan road network.
- Over two years of works: two new rail sidings for 600 metre long trains, 1.2 km of roads for heavy vehicles built and relocated, 70,000 sq. metres of pavement for containers.

wikis.title: Port of Melbourne Port Rail Transformation Project overview
wikis.summary: Port of Melbourne's summary of its Port Rail Transformation Project (PRTP) to move more containers by rail at Swanson Dock.
wikis.body:
- The Port of Melbourne announced a rail solution to meet the needs of a growing port and to reduce truck movements in Melbourne's inner western suburbs. The PRTP will increase rail terminal capacity and improve rail terminal operations, moving more containers by rail and bypassing inner-Melbourne roads.
- Comparison given: a 600 metre long train can carry 84 TEU versus about three TEU for an average B-Double truck.
- Funding: an amendment to the Pricing Order effective from 1 June 2020 that includes an increase in the tariff on full import containers of $9.75 per TEU ("less than five cents on the wholesale price on an average sized television").

## Key elements
- Commercial: the port is restructuring rail land and asset arrangements for leaseholders in the Swanson Dock East Precinct so rail land and assets are provided on the same basis as wharf and road.
- Operations: new working arrangements between the port and Rail Terminal Operators at most current and all future port rail terminals, for transparency.
- Infrastructure: a new Coode Road rail terminal interfacing with Swanson Dock East International Container Terminal, with two new rail sidings each able to handle 600 metre trains; a new road for uninterrupted east/west container movement without trucks exiting to Footscray Road (replacing the section of Coode Road to be closed); modifications to Swanson precinct common user sidings for 600 metre trains; a new track linking the Swanson and Appleton lead tracks; upgrades to the Swanson lead track.

## Indicative timing (financial year)
- Existing land and asset acquisition 2019-2020; new land and asset arrangements 2020; rail terminal improvements 2021-2023; operating protocol implementation 2020-2023.

## Latest news
- A section of Coode Road between Dock Link Road and Phillips Road is being permanently closed; a new east-west connection, Intermodal Way, opens. Three-stage road changes between late March and early April 2023, with a permanent switch scheduled for early April 2023. Access to all terminals stays open.
- The PRTP is the cornerstone of the port's rail access strategy "Our Plan for Rail".

wikis.title: Senna Tower, Balneario Camboriu (Wikipedia)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the under-construction supertall residential Senna Tower in Balneario Camboriu, Brazil.
wikis.body:
- Status: under construction; residential skyscraper in neo-futurist style, in Balneario Camboriu, Brazil. Original name Triumph Tower.
- Height and floors: infobox gives 544 m architectural height (Skyscraper Center) and 153 floors; text says a planned height of 544 m (1,785 ft) and 154 floors. Concrete frame, 8 elevators. Cost listed as US$545 million.
- Architect listed: Lalalli Senna; structural engineer WSP Global / FG Empreendimentos; developer FG Empreendimentos and the Senna family.
- Will be the first residential building in Latin America to use a tuned mass damper and, per the article, the world's first supertall residential building certified LEED Platinum. Once completed it will be "by far the tallest in Brazil".
- Announced 17 September 2024 by FG Empreendimentos and the Senna family, on Atlantic Avenue along the beach. At completion it would be the first or second tallest residential building in the world, pending the final height of Burj Binghatti Jacob & Co Residences in Dubai, and the tallest building outside Asia.
- Program: private apartments plus a skyline observation point, heated pool, wellness center, gym, tennis courts, leisure and gastronomy areas open to the public, and an immersive educational space about Ayrton Senna. Received architectural and construction authorizations from the local prefecture.
- Idealized in 2019 as Triumph Tower with 204 apartments and 24 duplex and triplex units. Broke ground in the second half of 2025.

wikis.title: Senna Tower: race for the world's tallest residential building (blog)
wikis.summary: Portuguese-language university civil-engineering blog post (4 December 2025) describing the Senna Tower project in Balneario Camboriu.
wikis.body:
- The post says Senna Tower aims to reach 550 m and the title of the world's tallest residential building; its design is based on the Fibonacci sequence and golden ratio; inspired by Ayrton Senna's "hero's journey".
- To be built in Balneario Camboriu, north coast of Santa Catarina, with 228 units: 204 apartments of up to 400 m2, 18 suspended mansions of 420 to 563 m2, 4 duplex penthouses of 600 m2 and 2 triplex mega-penthouses of 903 m2.
- Developed via a partnership between the Graciola family (FG Empreendimentos, the builder), the Senna family (represented by Lalalli Senna, the driver's niece) and Hang; the site comes from a partnership between Luciano Hang and Francisco Graciola.
- Investment: R$ 3 billion; delivery is "prevista" (planned) between 2033 and 2035.
- Framed as a homage to Ayrton Senna, a national hero and three-time Formula 1 world champion.
- Written by Joao Antonio de Sousa Martins for the blog of PET Engenharia Civil UFC; published 4 December 2025.

wikis.title: Citicorp Center engineering crisis (Wikipedia)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia account of the 1978 discovery of a structural wind-load flaw in Citicorp Center (now Citigroup Center), New York, and its secret repair.
wikis.body:
- In July 1978 a possible structural flaw was found in Citicorp Center, recently completed in New York City. After investigations the building was found to be in danger of possible collapse; workers surreptitiously made repairs over the following months. Structural engineer William LeMessurier used unconventional features: a raised base on four offset stilts, diagonal bracing, and a roof tuned mass damper (the first building to use active mechanical stabilization).
- Princeton undergraduate Diane Hartley investigated the building's integrity for quartering winds; NJIT student Lee DeCarolis also chose it for a report, and his professor John Zoldos expressed reservations; DeCarolis contacted LeMessurier.
- LeMessurier learned that changes had been made in construction without his approval: Bethlehem Steel proposed changing the chevron braces from welded to bolted joints to save money, accepted by his office but unknown to him.
- Estimates suggested that if the mass damper lost power, a 70 mph (110 km/h) quartering wind could topple the building. Reinforcement was done at night while offices operated by day; a backup generator was added and the city had evacuation plans. Hurricane Ella threatened during the retrofit but changed course. The repair was kept secret until 1995.
- A later NIST reassessment found the quartering wind loads were not the threat LeMessurier and Hartley thought, and recommended reevaluating whether the retrofit was warranted.
- Background: 59-story tower at 601 Lexington Avenue, designed by Hugh Stubbins with Emery Roth & Sons; dedicated 12 October 1977. Stilts sit under the centers of each face because of the agreement with St. Peter's Lutheran Church at the northwest corner.

wikis.title: CNN: the Citicorp Center skyscraper's 1-in-16 collapse risk
wikis.summary: CNN Style feature (15 Aug 2025) on the 1978 discovery that New York's Citicorp Center was vulnerable to wind, drawing on a new book, The Great Miscalculation.
wikis.body:
- Citicorp opened its 59-floor, 915-foot tower on October 12, 1977, the tallest new NYC skyscraper since the early 1930s; the $128-million building is now 601 Lexington.
- Unknown to owners and occupants, it was far more vulnerable to wind than believed: if a storm cut power to the stabilizing device, a strong enough gust could topple it, and winds that strong occur in New York on average every 16 years. The engineer realized this in July 1978, during hurricane season. Welders corrected it under cover of darkness within months; a newspaper strike kept the story hidden until the mid-1990s.
- The article draws on "The Great Miscalculation: The Race to Save New York City's Citicorp Tower" by Michael M. Greenburg, on William LeMessurier, who blew the whistle on himself.
- Design origin: holdout St. Peter's Lutheran Church, whose new church had to be distinct from the tower, so architect Hugh Stubbins and LeMessurier designed a tower on four stilts, with columns at the middle of each face. Chevron bracing divided the tower into six independent segments; columns were drilled about 50 feet into bedrock. A tuned mass damper (400-ton concrete block on a film of oil) reduced sway. Groundbreaking 1974.
- Two college students helped uncover the flaw.

wikis.title: Subsidence (Wikipedia)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia overview of subsidence, the downward vertical movement of the Earth's surface, with causes and examples.
wikis.body:
- Subsidence is downward vertical movement of the Earth's surface from natural processes and human activities, with little or no horizontal movement (which distinguishes it from slope movement).
- Processes: dissolution of carbonate rock by groundwater; gradual sediment compaction; withdrawal of fluid lava; mining; pumping of groundwater or petroleum; tectonic warping (tectonic subsidence).
- Pumping of groundwater or petroleum has led to subsidence of as much as 9 meters (30 ft) in many places, with costs in the hundreds of millions of US dollars. Groundwater-related subsidence is likely to increase with population and economic growth; one estimate has 80% of serious land subsidence problems associated with excessive groundwater extraction.
- Examples in the lead: the Crooked House pub (Staffordshire) from 19th-century mining subsidence, and the Mam Tor road near Castleton, Derbyshire. San Joaquin Valley subsidence is covered under groundwater-related subsidence.
- Drainage of lowlands (coastal or delta plains) aerates soil, leading to oxidation of organic material.

wikis.title: Iraq's Al Faw Grand Port project nears first-phase completion (Maritime Executive)
wikis.summary: Maritime Executive report (30 July 2023) that Iraq's Al Faw Grand Port is nearly two-thirds complete.
wikis.body:
- Iraq's Transport Minister Razzak Al-Saadawi said phase one is nearly two-thirds complete: "About 68 percent of the five berths in Faw has been completed after it was only 19 percent 3 years ago." Berth one expected to receive its first vessel soon in trial operation.
- Phase one completion date set for 2025, including a five-berth container terminal with initial capacity of 3.5 million TEU per year.
- Construction began almost a decade earlier and has had considerable delays, partly due to funding and political issues.
- Masterplan: container, dry bulk and oil terminals with total capacity of 99 million tons per year, plus a dry dock and naval base. Road and rail links through Iraq to Turkey and Europe; a 36-mile road to Umm Qasr; a 745-mile rail and motorway project ("The Development Road", $17 billion) linking Faw to Turkey.
- South Korea's Daewoo E&C builds phase one under a $2.7 billion contract awarded four years earlier. Phase two (not yet initiated) is an industrial area with refinery and steel plant; phase three is Al Faw New City (housing, commercial center, school, mosques).

wikis.title: Grand Faw Port (Wikipedia)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on Grand Faw Port, a large port under construction on Iraq's Faw peninsula near Basra.
wikis.body:
- Under construction on the coast of Iraq near Al-Faw, at the northern tip of the Gulf of Basra; meant to be the southern terminal of the Development Road; a strategic national project planned to become the largest port in the Middle East.
- Infobox: 54 km2 free trade area; berths Phase I: 5 (completed), Phase II: 30 (by 2030), Phase III: 100 (by 2045); channel draft 11 m in Phase I (2013-2019) and 19.8 m in Phase II (2020-2025); operated by State Company for Iraqi Ports.
- History: project idea dates to after WWII, revived in the 1970s, halted by the Iran-Iraq war. A private proposal targeted operation by 2038 but the Ministry of Transport rejected it and expanded the size from 12 to 54 km2 with about 100 berths, power and desalination plants, refineries and a petrochemical plant. Iraq also plans a naval base.
- Officially proposed in 2010; delays from conflict, cash shortages and low oil prices. In 2020 PM Mustafa al-Kadhimi launched phase two; South Korea's Daewoo Engineering won $2.7 billion contracts in December.
- Breakwaters, costing over 1 billion dollars, are recognized by Guinness World Records as the world's longest at 14.523 km, built by Daewoo E&C, GCPI (Iraq) and TECHNITAL (Italy). Initial five berths, roads and a tunnel to Umm Qasr port were under construction.

wikis.title: Berlin Brandenburg Airport: overview and planning history (Wikipedia, part 1)
wikis.summary: First part of the Wikipedia article on Berlin Brandenburg Airport (BER): lead, capacity, and the history of planning, site choice and failed privatisation.
wikis.body:
- BER is an international airport at Schoenefeld in Brandenburg, 18 km south-east of Berlin's centre, and a base for Condor, easyJet, Eurowings, Ryanair (ends 24 October 2026 per infobox) and Sundair. IATA BER, ICAO EDDB. Infobox: 2025 passengers 26,050,880 (+2.3%).
- Replaced Tempelhof (closed 2008), Schoenefeld and Tegel (2020). At opening theoretical capacity 46 million a year: Terminal 1 28 million, Terminal 2 (opened 24 March 2022) 6 million, Terminal 5 (former Schoenefeld terminals) 12 million; planned expansion to 58 million by 2035.
- Originally planned to open October 2011, five years after construction started in 2006; delays due to "poor construction planning, execution, management, and corruption". Operating licence May 2020; opened for commercial traffic 31 October 2020, 14 years after construction began and 29 years after planning began. Terminal 5 incorporated 25 October 2020; Tegel transition completed 8 November 2020.
- History: after 1989-1990 Berlin planned a single large airport. Holding company BBF founded 2 May 1991 (Berlin 37%, Brandenburg 37%, Federal Republic 26%). On 28 May 1996 Schoenefeld was chosen as site over Sperenberg and Juterbog options.
- Privatisation: Hochtief consortium chosen 19 September 1998; contract annulled 3 August 1999 after IVG's lawsuit; joint Hochtief/IVG bid February 2002; board scrapped privatisation on 22 May 2003; the two received about EUR 50 million compensation. BBF Holding became Flughafen Berlin Brandenburg GmbH (FBB), publicly owned.

wikis.title: Kvesheti-Kobi road: first section to open in 2025 (Georgia Today)
wikis.summary: Georgia Today (7 March 2025) on progress of Georgia's Kvesheti-Kobi highway providing access to Gudauri.
wikis.body:
- Georgian Roads Department said a 5 km section of the new Kvesheti-Kobi road will open in 2025, providing access to Gudauri.
- The full 23 km highway is being built in two phases. Phase one: a 9 km tunnel by China Railway Tunnel Group Co., completed in 2024, overall progress 79%, cost 909 million GEL. Phase two: 12.7 km with five bridges and four tunnels, by China Railway 23rd Bureau Group, 50% complete, cost GEL 316.7 million; one bridge will be the highest in Georgia at 166 m tall and 426 m long.
- No exact date for completing the entire highway; the department disclosed it will be operational "next year".

wikis.title: Kvesheti-Kobi Road Project (official site)
wikis.summary: Official project site describing the 23 km Kvesheti-Kobi road in Georgia, its scope, funding and benefits.
wikis.body:
- Plan: 23 km 2-lane asphalt-concrete road, 5 bridges and 5 tunnels, plus repair of 1 bridge, pedestrian crossings and paths. Commissioned by the Roads Department of the Ministry of Infrastructure; total value 1.240 billion Lari; funded by the Asian Development Bank and the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development; monitored by UBM International United Consultants Inc.
- Benefits claimed: new road shortens Kvesheti to Kobi travel time by 45 minutes (15 minutes instead of 1 hour); route shorter by 11 km; safe in any season, avoiding avalanche and heavy snow danger; a new 5 km road to Gudauri and visitor center; 10 revived villages. Locals are cut off for almost 100 days a year.
- Two lots: lot 1, a 9 km tunnel by China Railway Tunnel Group Co., Ltd. (CRTG) with tunnel boring machine technology; lot 2, the access road section by China Railway 23rd Bureau Group Co. Procurement followed ADB rules; lowest-price qualified bidders won.

wikis.title: Internationales Congress Centrum Berlin (Wikipedia)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on ICC Berlin, the closed 1979 high-tech convention centre in West Berlin and its redevelopment.
wikis.body:
- Former convention centre in Westend, Berlin, next to Messe Berlin, at Messedamm 22. Designed by Ralf Schueler and Ursulina Schueler-Witte; construction 1975 (text also says 1973) to 1979; opened 1979; closed 2014. High-tech architecture, aluminium facade.
- 313 m long, 80 m wide, 40 m tall; 80 halls and rooms; capacity up to 20,000; main auditorium planned for 5,000. Cost almost one billion marks, the most expensive construction in West Berlin then.
- Built in the enclave of West Berlin as a Cold War soft-power counterpart to East Berlin's Palace of the Republic (begun 1973); the ICC opened in 1979, three years after the Palace of the Republic opened.
- Regular operations ended 10 April 2014 because ageing technical systems needed extensive renovation; asbestos raises projected cost. Protected monument since 2019. Berlin launched a redevelopment process in 2024; in June 2026 the Project Partnership Quartier ICC received an official recommendation for reuse for events and creative industries; "still in development".
- Appears in The Apple (1980), Wings of Desire (1987), The International (2009); Grateful Dead played there 19 and 20 October 1990.

wikis.title: Deccan Chronicle: Polavaram completion by July 2027
wikis.summary: Deccan Chronicle (8 Dec 2025) on Andhra Pradesh's push to finish the Polavaram irrigation project before Godavari Pushkaralu in July 2027.
wikis.body:
- The state water resources department and central agencies are racing to complete the multi-purpose Polavaram irrigation project before the Godavari Pushkaralu in July 2027, on direction of Chief Minister N. Chandrababu Naidu, although the scheduled completion date is end of December 2027. Officials say 80% of headworks are done.
- Command area: new 7.2 lakh acres and stabilisation of 13.5 lakh acres; Right Main Canal works almost complete, Left Main Canal still in progress.
- Dam storage: initial height 41.11 m gives about 124.2 tmc-ft; final 45.72 m gives 194.6 tmc-ft.
- Progress: diaphragm wall 50,858 of 65,352 sq-m (78%), target Feb 2026; ECRF Dam Gap-1 (+25m to +38.32m) by March 2026; Gap-II by July 2027 (target December 2027). Land acquisition: 91,127 of 1,00,099 acres, rest by March 2026. Resettlement: 38,060 displaced families; 14,385 shifted, 23,675 to be shifted by March 2027; housing to 15,439, 18,921 more by March 2027.

wikis.title: Polavaram Project: infobox and history (Wikipedia, part 1)
wikis.summary: First part of the Wikipedia article on the Polavaram multi-purpose dam project on the Godavari River in Andhra Pradesh.
wikis.body:
- Under-construction multi-purpose irrigation project on the Godavari in Eluru and Polavaram districts, Andhra Pradesh; National Project status. Construction began 2003; opening "2029 July (Expected)" per infobox; hydroelectric, irrigation and water supply.
- Dam: concrete spillway 1,128 m, non-overflow concrete dam 140 m, earth-cum-rock-fill dam 2,454 m; length 3,722 m; height 39.28 m; spillway capacity 3,600,000 cusecs. Reservoir 194 tmcft at FRL 150 ft msl; catchment 307,800 km2; surface 600 km2. Backwater spreads up to about 150 km (into Chhattisgarh and Odisha).
- Power: APGENCO, 12 x 80 MW Kaplan turbines, 960 MW under construction, 2.29 billion kWh a year, commission 2026.
- History: first proposal July 1941 (Madras Presidency, L. Venkatakrishna Iyer); estimated Rs 129 crore in 1946-47; foundation stone 1980 (T. Anjaiah); Polavaram Project Authority constituted May 2014; Transstroy sought extension in Dec 2017; new spillway contract to Navayuga Engineering January 2018; diaphragm wall completed 11 June 2018; on 7 January 2019 a Guinness record of 32,100 m3 of concrete in 24 hours.

wikis.title: Tokyo: overview (Wikipedia, part 1)
wikis.summary: First part of the Wikipedia article on Tokyo, Japan's capital, giving its status, governance and history summary.
wikis.body:
- Capital and most populous city of Japan; city proper population over 14 million as of 2023; Greater Tokyo Area 33 million as of 2025, third-most populous metropolitan area in the world.
- At the head of Tokyo Bay in the Kanto region on Honshu; Japan's economic center and seat of government and the Emperor. Administered by the Tokyo Metropolitan Government (23 special wards, western commuter towns, two island chains); since 1943 governed more like a prefecture. Wards mentioned: Chiyoda (National Diet Building, Imperial Palace), Shinjuku (administrative center), Shibuya (commerce).
- Infobox: established 1457; nickname "The Big Mikan".
- History: originally Edo; political prominence from 1603 as seat of the Tokugawa shogunate; by mid-18th century over one million people. After the Meiji Restoration (1868) the capital moved to Edo, renamed Tokyo ("Eastern Capital"). Damaged by the 1923 Great Kanto earthquake and WWII bombing; rapid reconstruction from the late 1940s fueled the "Japanese economic miracle".

wikis.title: Millau Viaduct (Wikipedia)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the Millau Viaduct, the cable-stayed motorway bridge across the Tarn gorge in France.
wikis.body:
- Multiple-span cable-stayed viaduct carrying 4 lanes of the A75 autoroute over the Tarn valley at Millau-Creissels, Aveyron. Designers: Norman Foster (architect) and Michel Virlogeux (structural engineer). Concrete and steel.
- Total length 2,460 m; width 32.05 m; max pylon height 343 m above ground; main span 342 m (spans 204 m, 6 x 342 m, 204 m); deck about 270 m above the valley below. Design life 120 years.
- Cost EUR 394 million; construction began 16 October 2001 (infobox); inaugurated 14 December 2004; opened to traffic 16 December 2004; toll from EUR 8.30. Builder and maintainer: Compagnie Eiffage du Viaduc de Millau.

wikis.title: Eiffage Genie Civil: Millau Viaduct
wikis.summary: Eiffage's page on building the Millau Viaduct in three years (2001-2004).
wikis.body:
- Eiffage says it took exactly three years to build the world's highest viaduct, enabled by the steel deck it proposed and installed. Delivered December 2004.
