- Vision: reinstate the Cathedral, Whare Karakia Nui, as "an awe-inspiring symbol of life, regeneration and healing". It is the seat of the Anglican faith in Christchurch and has been part of the city's identity for 150 years; severely damaged in the Christchurch earthquakes.
- It will look as it did before, retaining heritage features, but "stronger, safer and more functional, flexible and comfortable". The rebuild delivers the main Cathedral and Tower with north, south and west porches.
- 700,000 people visited each year pre-earthquakes.
- Approach: collaborative design and construction planning because of uncertainty; heritage fabric is catalogued and stored when deconstructed, and protected by stabilising and weather-proofing.
- A timelapse of the Nave covers 1 January to 25 May 2023.

wikis.title: Oosterweel Link (Antwerp Ring Road completion)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the Oosterweel Link, the Flemish project first proposed in 1996 to complete the Antwerp R1 ring road, with its early history and costs.
wikis.body:
- Construction project first proposed in 1996 to complete the R1 Antwerp Ring Road; responsible body is the Flemish Government controlled Antwerp Mobility Management Company (BAM, renamed Lantis in 2019). The article carries maintenance notes (needs citations; needs updating, tagged March 2017).
- Route: connects the Expressweg (E34) near Blokkersdijk via a toll tunnel (Oosterweeltunnel) under the Scheldt, then a dual-layered tunnel under the Albert Canal, joining the ring at Merksem and Deurne.
- Cost estimated at 10 billion euros ("the project of the century"). A 2010 Transport & Mobility Leuven analysis found infrastructure costs about five times the societal benefits; road pricing had a significant positive effect on congestion.
- Part of the Antwerp Masterplan of sixteen infrastructure projects.
- History: 1996 governor Camille Paulus mentioned a multimodal traffic model; a 5 km tunnel was proposed; October 1998 Flemish government decided to complete the ring; June 1999 ABM studied 6 layouts (one bridge, five tunnels); 14 January 2000 a 7th option, a viaduct over docks and canal, was proposed and chosen on 7 April 2000 (estimated 0.55 billion euro, inauguration expected 2005); Masterplan approved 15 December 2000; BAM created; 2001 tender to TV SAM (0.59 billion euro, 6 years, later deemed unrealistic); 2004 cost estimate 0.95 billion euro; February 2005 the city ordered a study of a tunnel alternative and BAM said a tunnel would raise the price to 2 billion euros.

wikis.title: Vistula Spit canal (Nowy Świat ship canal), Poland
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the 1.5 km canal across the Vistula Spit opened 17 September 2022, its history, costs and concerns.
wikis.body:
- Canal across the Polish Vistula Spit creating a second connection between the Vistula Lagoon and Gulf of Gdańsk, so ships can reach the port of Elbląg without the Russian Strait of Baltiysk, saving a 100 km journey.
- 1,536 m long, one lock; ships up to 4 m draft, 100 m length, 20 m beam. Part of a planned 22.88 km waterway to Elbląg. Construction began 4 October 2019 (tree cutting from February 2019); officially inaugurated 17 September 2022; "further works will continue".
- History: idea dates to 1577 (King Stephen Báthory); revived 1945 by Eugeniusz Kwiatkowski; final decision 10 November 2006 by PM Jarosław Kaczyński.
- Works: breakwater forebay of 10,000 concrete blocks, shipping channel and locks, roads, two swing bridges (southern completed June 2021), and an artificial island of about 180 ha in the lagoon (started 30 May 2020, tentative name Aestian Island).
- Costs: October 2019 contract with a Polish-Belgian consortium for 992 million PLN (230 million euro); total project expected 2 billion PLN.
- Concerns: Russia objected on security and environmental grounds; environmental worries about phosphorus in lagoon sediments and cyanobacteria.

wikis.title: Panama Supreme Court overturns law blocking canal reservoir
wikis.summary: ENR report on the 2 July 2024 ruling striking down Law 20 of 2006, clearing the way for a Rio Indio reservoir for the Panama Canal.
wikis.body:
- July 3, 2024: on July 2 Panama's Supreme Court plenary ruled Law 20 of June 21, 2006 unconstitutional, restoring a 1999 law that set the limits of the canal's hydrographic basin.
- This lets the Panama Canal Authority (ACP) build a reservoir on the Rio Indio, outside the current watershed, to meet water needs for the next half century. Initial estimate about $900 million and five years; update 7/9/24: ACP now estimates $1.6 billion and six years.
- Lawyer Publio Cortés filed the challenge in December (argued watershed changes must originate with the ACP board); Juan Ramón Sevillano filed a similar claim in January.
- Background: historic drought and El Niño last year cut Gatun Lake levels and transits. Neopanamax transits rise to 35 per day on Aug. 8; maximum draft boosted to 47 on July 11. Administrator Ricaurte Vásquez Morales said climate change remains a key concern.

wikis.title: Panama Canal Authority sees Rio Indio project as answer to future droughts
wikis.summary: FreightWaves report on the ACP administrator's roundtable on the $1.6 billion Rio Indio reservoir and canal recovery from drought.
wikis.body:
- August 26, 2024, by Noi Mahoney: ACP administrator Ricaurte Vasquez spoke at a roundtable marking the canal's 110th anniversary. The canal connects 180 maritime routes to 1,920 ports in 170 countries, carrying nearly 3% of global maritime trade; 8,549 employees.
- Last year was the worst drought since 1950, with water levels almost 6 feet lower in January than January 2023.
- Proposed $1.6 billion Rio Indio reservoir: dam the Indio River and drill a 5-mile tunnel to Gatun Lake; could take five years or more and allow up to 15 additional transits per day. Local farmers and communities face flooding risk and have criticised it.
- On July 2 the Supreme Court reinstated a law expanding the watershed by 1.4 million acres beyond the 741,316 acres previously managed.
- Other options: dredging, moving water intakes, controlling Gatun Lake salinity.
- Transit slots were cut from 36 to as few as 18 by Feb. 1; back to 36 per day from September; draft back to 50 feet. Tonnage fell 1.5% in fiscal 2023 but revenue was $4.9 billion (+14.9%). LNG shippers expected to return.

wikis.title: Honolulu rail to begin passenger operations June 30, 2023
wikis.summary: HART announcement that the first phase of Honolulu's rail transit opens for interim passenger service on June 30, 2023.
wikis.body:
- Announced Wednesday, May 10, 2023 by Mayor Rick Blangiardi: the first phase will begin interim passenger operations at 2 p.m. on June 30, 2023, with a grand opening celebration at Hālawa station earlier that day.
- Phase one covers roughly 11 miles between Kualaka'i Station in East Kapolei and Hālawa Station near Aloha Stadium; service to additional stations further east is "scheduled to commence in phases over the coming years".
- Mayor: "we are turning the page on the largest public works project in Hawaii's history."

wikis.title: English Channel tunnel opens, May 6, 1994
wikis.summary: History.com entry on the 1994 opening of the Channel Tunnel, its scale, cost and early troubles.
wikis.body:
- Published November 24, 2009; last updated May 27, 2025.
- In a May 6, 1994 ceremony led by Queen Elizabeth II and French President Francois Mitterrand, the rail tunnel was officially opened, connecting Britain and the mainland "for the first time since the Ice Age".
- Connects Folkestone, England, with Coquelles, France, 31 miles apart; cut travel to 35 minutes and eventually London-Paris to two-and-a-half hours. World's longest undersea tunnel: 23 miles under water, average depth 150 feet below the seabed.
- About 30,000 people, 6,000 cars and 3,500 trucks per day. Two rail tunnels plus one service tunnel; 15,000 employed at peak; ten people killed during construction.
- History: Albert Mathieu planned a tunnel in 1802; Colonel Beaumont bored over a mile in 1880; the tunnels were begun in June 1988.
- Cost $16 billion, roughly twice the original estimate, and a year behind schedule. Eurotunnel announced a huge loss one year into service; a debt-for-shares swap saved it; first net profit in 1999. Freight suspended six months after a lorry fire in November 1996. In 1996 the ASCE named it one of the Seven Wonders of the Modern World.

wikis.title: Channel Tunnel: overview and early history (Wikipedia)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia's opening sections on the Channel Tunnel: specifications, traffic, and the history of proposals from 1802 to the 1920s.
wikis.body:
- 50.46 km (31.35 mile) railway tunnel under the English Channel connecting Folkestone, UK with Coquelles, France. Opened 1994; "the only fixed link between Great Britain and the European mainland". Longest underwater section of any tunnel: 37.9 km (23.5 miles); depth 75 m below sea level, averaging 45 m below the seabed; third-longest railway tunnel in the world.
- Two single-track running tunnels (7.6 m wide) and a service tunnel (4.8 m); 270 cross passages; 25 kV AC. Designed for 200 km/h, limited to 160 km/h for safety. Work began 1 December 1987 (infobox). Engineer: TransManche Link; owner Getlink; operators include Eurostar, DB Cargo UK, Getlink.
- 2017 traffic: Eurostar 10.3 million passengers; freight 1.2 million tonnes; LeShuttle 10.4 million passengers in 2.6 million cars and 51,000 coaches, plus 1.6 million heavy goods vehicles carrying 21.3 million tonnes.
- Modern project initiated by Eurotunnel in 1988, completed 1994 at final cost of £4.65 billion (equivalent to £9.8 billion in 2025). Economic assessments found only limited positive impact on the British economy; disruptions from faults, fires, weather and unauthorised access by migrants.
- Key dates: 1802 Albert Mathieu proposal; 1875 Channel Tunnel Company trials; 1882-83 British TBM bored 1,840 m and French 1,669 m before abandonment in 1883 over military invasion fears; January 1975 UK-France scheme cancelled; February 1986 Treaty of Canterbury; June 1988 tunnelling starts in France; December 1990 service tunnel breakthrough; May 1994 opened; June 1994 freight, November 1994 passenger trains; November 1996 HGV shuttle fire; November 2007 High Speed 1 opened; September 2008 another fire; December 2009 Eurostar trains stranded by snow.
- Earlier proposals: 1839 Thomé de Gamond surveys and 1856 proposal to Napoleon III (170 million francs); 1866 Henry Marc Brunel's seabed survey; 1907 Méliès film; 1919 Lloyd George promoted the idea.

wikis.title: Surat Diamond Bourse
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the Surat Diamond Bourse in Gujarat, described as the world's largest office building.
wikis.body:
- Diamond trade centre in DREAM City, Surat, Gujarat, India, designed by Morphogenesis (architects Manit Rastogi and Sonali Rastogi). Floor space 660,000 sq m (7,100,000 sq ft); 15 floors, 81.9 m high; grounds 14.38 hectares. Cost ₹3,200 crore (US$330 million).
- Timeline: foundation stone 15/16 February 2015; construction started 25 October 2017; overall structure completed May 2022; construction finished 26 July 2023; Guinness World Records declared it the world's largest office building, surpassing The Pentagon, on 22 August 2023; inaugurated 17 December 2023 by Prime Minister Narendra Modi after a delay from the planned November 2023. COVID-19 slowed construction.
- Nine interconnected 15-floor towers with 4,200 offices (28 to 700 sq m); central corridor; nine Panchtattva courts; 131 elevators; two-level parking for 4,500 cars and 10,000 two-wheelers; central air-conditioning; conference halls, banks, customs clearance house, National Diamond Research Institute, convention centre. Pre-certified green building by IGBC.
- Reception: "lukewarm" among diamond traders because of the outskirts location and poor connectivity compared with Mumbai's Bharat Diamond Bourse; SDB announced incentives to shift business to Surat.

wikis.title: How India built the world's biggest office (The B1M)
wikis.summary: The B1M article/video on the design and construction of the Surat Diamond Bourse.
wikis.body:
- 10 January 2024, Ian Parkin; video narrated by Fred Mills.
- In December 2023 the Surat Diamond Bourse (SDB) took the title of world's largest office building from the Pentagon: over 7 million sq ft, nearly 70,000 workers, 10,000 m2 of restaurants and cafes, parking for 5,000 cars and 10,000 motorbikes, 131 elevators, nine courtyard gardens, on a 35 acre high-security compound.
- Full occupancy was guaranteed before construction. About 90 percent of the world's diamonds are cut and polished in Surat, but merchants travelled 200+ km to Mumbai to trade; nearly five thousand diamond businesses formed the SDB.
- Requirements: 4,700 offices with ambient daylight, coping with humid heat and monsoon, 67,000 workers a day. Morphogenesis (Manit Rastogi) targeted seven minutes from the gate to any office; plan of nine 15-storey towers flanking a 400 m central spine, aligned north to south for daylight; the spine funnels prevailing winds for 50 percent of cooling needs.
- Construction: ground broke December 2017; 6,000 people took four and a half years. During covid all materials were sourced within 500 km; a factory was built on site for unitised glazing.

wikis.title: Brightline West breaks ground on Las Vegas to Southern California high-speed rail
wikis.summary: Brightline West press release (April 22, 2024) on the groundbreaking, route, stations, funding and benefits of its 218-mile high-speed rail system.
wikis.body:
- LAS VEGAS (April 22, 2024): Brightline West broke ground on what it calls the nation's first true high-speed rail system connecting Las Vegas to Southern California. 218 miles, built in the median of I-15, zero-emission fully electric trains capable of 200 miles per hour; two hours between Southern California and Las Vegas, "almost half the time as driving".
- Funding: $3 billion from the Bipartisan Infrastructure Bill; rest privately funded, with $3.5 billion in private activity bonds from USDOT. Total $12 billion infrastructure investment; over $10 billion economic impact, more than 35,000 jobs (10,000 direct union construction, 1,000 permanent).
- Speakers included Pete Buttigieg, Wes Edens, Gov. Joe Lombardo, Senators Cortez Masto and Rosen; over 600 attended.
- Construction: zero grade crossings; 700,000 concrete ties, 2.2 million tons ballast, 63,000 tons of steel rail; 322 miles of overhead lines; 3.4 million sq ft retaining walls; 160+ structures; Buy America compliant.
- Stations: Las Vegas (110 acres, ~80,000 sq ft), Victor Valley in Apple Valley (300 acres, ~20,000 sq ft, future link to High Desert Corridor and California High Speed Rail), Hesperia (I-15 median at Joshua Street, local service), Rancho Cucamonga (5 acres, ~80,000 sq ft, near Ontario airport, co-located with Metrolink). Vehicle maintenance facility 200,000 sq ft on 238 acres in Sloan, Nev., 100+ permanent employees.
- Market: over 50 million trips a year between the regions; 4.7 million international travelers to Las Vegas; about 17 million Southern California residents within 25 miles of stations.

wikis.title: Brightline West High-Speed Rail Project, USA (Railway Technology)
wikis.summary: Railway Technology project profile of the 218-mile Las Vegas to Rancho Cucamonga high-speed line, expected in 2028.
wikis.body:
- Page dated July 26 2024 (Surya Akella). 218 miles (351 km) between Las Vegas, Nevada and Southern California; expected investment $12bn; construction started April 2024; expected completion 2028; contractors listed: Grimshaw, Arup, Siemens Mobility, Atlas Technical Consultants, HNTB.
- Services projected for 2028 to serve the Los Angeles Summer Olympic Games; about 11 million passengers annually; Las Vegas to Rancho Cucamonga about two hours and ten minutes, twice as fast as driving; 35,000+ construction jobs and 1,000 permanent.
- Runs in the I-15 median without grade crossings; stations in Las Vegas, Apple Valley, Hesperia, Rancho Cucamonga; 160+ structures; 200,000 ft2 maintenance facility in Sloan on 238 acres.
- MOUs with California agencies: January 2019 (Las Vegas to Apple Valley) and April 2021 (Apple Valley to Rancho Cucamonga).
- Trains: American Pioneer 220 (AP 220), up to 220 mph (354 km/h), seven cars, 434 to 450 passengers.
- Environmental: reduce greenhouse gas emissions by more than 400,000tpa and vehicle miles by more than 700 million a year; 16,000 fewer short-haul flights; aims for 100% emission-free power by 2045.
- Financing: $3bn from Bipartisan Infrastructure Bill and $3.5bn in USDOT private activity bonds; the remainder privately funded.

wikis.title: Embassy of the United States, London
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the US embassy in London, its history of locations, the Nine Elms building opened 2018, demonstrations and security.
wikis.body:
- The embassy is in Nine Elms (33 Nine Elms Lane), the largest American embassy in Western Europe, overlooking the Thames; open to the public since 13 December 2017; formally opened 16 January 2018. Ambassador Warren Stephens (since 2025).
- History: John Adams opened the first American legation in London in 1785 at 9 Grosvenor Square; upgraded to an embassy in 1893; moved several times (Victoria Street 1883-1912, 4 Grosvenor Gardens 1912, 1 Grosvenor Square 1938). Winfield House in Regent's Park has been the ambassador's residence since 1955.
- The 30 Grosvenor Square chancery by Eero Saarinen opened 1960, leased from the Duke of Westminster for a symbolic peppercorn rent; gilded aluminum eagle by Theodore Roszak with a wingspan of over 11 metres; Grade II listed October 2009; served as chancery until 2017; reopened in 2025 as The Chancery Rosewood hotel.
- Demonstrations: March 1968 (some 10,000) against the Vietnam War; 2020 George Floyd protests; 6 November 2024 Just Stop Oil painted the compound wall; 10 April 2025 Greenpeace UK activists poured red dye into the water, six arrested.
- Security tightened in the 1980s-90s and after 11 September 2001.

wikis.title: Regional San EchoWater Project completed on schedule and under budget
wikis.summary: Sacramento Area Sewer District press release (May 15, 2023) on completion of the $1.7 billion EchoWater wastewater plant expansion.
wikis.body:
- May 15, 2023: Regional San's $1.7 billion, decade-long EchoWater Project was completed in spring 2023, on schedule and under budget. The expanded tertiary treatment facility is now the second largest of its kind in the nation.
- Regional San treats an average of 135 million gallons a day from 1.6 million people. Upgraded process removes 99 percent of ammonia and 89 percent of nitrogen (GM Christoph Dobson). Treated water goes to the Sacramento River and recycled uses, incl. the Harvest Water project.
- Began in 2010 when the Central Valley Regional Water Quality Control Board issued new treatment requirements. 22 individual projects; 41,350 tons of steel, 225,000+ cubic yards of concrete; centerpiece Biological Nutrient Removal complex about the size of 18 football fields.
- Original estimate as much as $2.1 billion; final about $1.7 billion. Nearly $1.4 billion in low-interest Clean Water State Revolving Fund financing, saving ratepayers more than a half-billion dollars in interest. Media event Friday, May 19, near Elk Grove; punch list items to wrap up.

wikis.title: Sacramento completes $1.7 billion EchoWater project
wikis.summary: Short Water Finance & Management item noting completion of Regional San's $1.7 billion EchoWater plant expansion.
wikis.body:
- August 14, 2023, WFM Staff: Sacramento Regional County Sanitation District (Regional San) completed its $1.7 billion, decade-long plant expansion, named the EchoWater Project, in spring 2023, "on schedule and under budget".
- The story says the region can expect big changes in how wastewater is treated and reused. The full article is archived behind an email gate; tags include Carollo, wastewater treatment and water reclamation.

wikis.title: 220 Central Park South: overview, site and architecture (Wikipedia)
wikis.summary: Opening sections of Wikipedia's article on 220 Central Park South, the 70-story Billionaires' Row residential tower in Manhattan.
wikis.body:
- Residential skyscraper on Central Park South between Broadway and Seventh Avenue, on Billionaires' Row. Designed by Robert A.M. Stern Architects with SLCE Architects as architect of record; interiors by Thierry Despont; structural engineer DeSimone; contractor Lendlease. Owner/developer Vornado Realty Trust; cost $1.4 billion.
- 70-story, 950-foot (290 m) tower on 58th Street (21st-tallest in New York City) plus an 18-story section on Central Park South ("The Villas"); limestone facade; 118 apartments, mostly duplexes; porte-cochère, wine cellar, private dining rooms, recreational facilities. Upper floors about 7,500 sq ft each, slenderness ratio 18:1 ("pencil towers").
- Timeline: site held a rent-stabilized 1954 complex acquired in 2005; tenant lawsuit delayed demolition to 2012; dispute with Extell over views for Central Park Tower; groundbreaking 2013; designs released early 2014 and approved that March; work on the base started 2015; first residents moved in 2018; completed 2019.
- Sales: secretive process with many anonymous buyers; two units sold for over $100 million, including a $238 million unit bought by Kenneth C. Griffin in 2019, the most expensive home sold in the US at the time.

wikis.title: 220 Central Park South, New York City (CTBUH Skyscraper Center entry)
wikis.summary: Skyscraper Center database entry giving height, floors, completion year, function, structure and project team for 220 Central Park South in New York City.
wikis.body:
- Location: 220 Central Park South, New York City, United States. Status: Completed; completion 2019.
- Global height rank listed as 294.
- Height: 289.6 m / 950 ft to tip; 289.6 m / 950 ft architectural; 276 m / 906 ft to highest occupied floor.
- Floors: 65 above ground.
- Function: residential. Structural material: all-concrete.
- Owner/developer: Vornado Realty Trust. Structural engineer: DeSimone Consulting Engineering. MEP engineer: Cosentini Associates. Main contractor: Lendlease Corporation.
- Consultants: code - Code Consultants, Inc.; damping - Motioneering; environmental, geotechnical and quantity surveyor - Langan Engineering; facade - Heintges Consulting Architects & Engineers and Enclos Corp.; interiors - The Office of Thierry W Despont Ltd.; wind - RWDI.
- Suppliers: cladding - Vetter Stone Company; dampers - A&H Tuned Mass Dampers and ITT Enidine; formwork - Doka GmbH.
- Related news item (9 November 2022): a full-floor penthouse of just over 5,000 square feet on Billionaire's Row at 220 Central Park South sold for US$72 million.

wikis.title: Why Sydney's skyline is short compared to other cities
wikis.summary: ABC News explainer on Sydney's history of building height limits and two proposed CBD towers of 305 m and 309 m.
wikis.body:
- Posted 19 July 2024 (ABC News, by Sam Nichols).
- Two tower proposals in Sydney's CBD, at 305 m and 309 m, would match Sydney Tower and, if approved, be the city's tallest. One is Lendlease's planned O'Connell Precinct; another is a proposed Dexus tower.
- According to one analysis, Sydney ranks 41st globally by number of buildings over 150 m and has 15 over 200 m. Melbourne ranks 23rd with 77 over 150 m, 29 over 200 m and one over 300 m. Australia's tallest building is Surfers Paradise's Q1 at 322.5 m.
- History: in 1912 NSW parliament limited new Sydney buildings to 150 m (fire and public health concerns, and fear of becoming a "morally suspect city" like New York, per a 2011 University of Sydney paper). The limit remained until 1957.
- Currently the maximum height is no more than 235 m, a requirement introduced with aviation authorities because of Kingsford Smith Airport. Architect Philip Vivian says the height limit is based on the underside of Centrepoint Tower (now Sydney Tower), meant to stay the highest point.
- Since the mid-to-late 2010s, case-by-case exemptions have been allowed, including 271 m Crown Sydney and 263 m Salesforce Tower.
- In 2021 the City of Sydney said the state government approved a planning framework allowing buildings up to 310 m if criteria (sun access, wind, airport regulation) are met.
- Mayor Clover Moore, Vivian and Property Council NSW executive director Katie Stevenson welcomed the proposals.

wikis.title: Skyscrapers set to reshape Sydney skyline
wikis.summary: City of Sydney media release on Council endorsing planning changes for a 310 m tower at 56-60 Pitt Street and a proposed 319 m tower at 1-25 O'Connell Street.
wikis.body:
- Published 3 July 2025.
- Council endorsed proposed planning-rule changes raising the maximum permitted height at 56-60 Pitt Street to 310 m and increasing floor space, to enable a 70-storey commercial building, with a new public plaza and a pedestrian through-site link connecting Pitt Street to Spring and Gresham streets.
- A proposal for a second 300 m-plus tower is being finalised before public consultation: 1-25 O'Connell Street, expected to hold a 319 m, 71-storey tower built by Lendlease, providing 150,000 square metres of commercial floor space, a public through-site link, a shared loading dock and adaptive reuse of heritage buildings.
- Both sites are in the northern tower cluster of Central Sydney.
- Lord Mayor Clover Moore said the proposal fits the Central Sydney Planning Strategy, described as the most significant review of city-centre planning in over 45 years, which balances height growth with sunlight to Hyde Park, Wynyard Park and the Royal Botanic Garden.

wikis.title: GMP Architekten's renovation of the Santiago Bernabeu
wikis.summary: Dezeen Future Stadium article on the over EUR 1 billion renovation of Real Madrid's Estadio Santiago Bernabeu for full-time use.
wikis.body:
- Published 23 July 2026 (Dezeen, Tom Ravenscroft), part of the Future Stadium series.
- Renovation by GMP Architekten with L35 and Ribas & Ribas; costing over EUR 1 bn; stadium originally opened in 1947. GMP director Martin Glass: the big driver is "full-time use".
- Goals: enhance Real Madrid's brand and commercial potential while keeping the "identity, soul and character" of the structure.
- Facade: original concrete structure entirely wrapped in stainless steel louvres.
- Retractable pitch stacked in an underground "greenhouse" on one side because the site is surrounded by roads and residential areas, and a public metro line lies 50 m under the other side. A retractable roof allows concerts and large events.
- Museum built as a 150 m-long cantilevered bridge between two existing concrete stair towers; Glass says only the Prado has more visitors in Spain, with prices around 35 euros. Also restaurants, a brewery, Starbucks and the Bernabeu Market; a panoramic viewpoint is planned.
- Set to host games at the 2030 World Cup. Photography by Marcus Bredt.

wikis.title: Santiago Bernabeu redevelopment on the home stretch
wikis.summary: StadiumDB December 2023 report on progress, cost rise and remaining work on Real Madrid's Bernabeu redevelopment.
wikis.body:
- Dated 15.12.2023 (StadiumDB.com, Miguel Ciolczyk Garcia).
- Shareholders agreed to a third loan of EUR 370 million, raising total project cost to over EUR 1 billion.
- Works delayed several times (supply chains hit by the war in Ukraine, the pandemic); planned opening postponed, now set for spring 2024.
- Done recently: museum enlarged, hospitality area rebuilt, retractable roof installed, new car park opened.
- Remaining: VIP area, commercial area with a large Real Madrid shop, entertainment area. The 360-degree scoreboard, weighing 330 tonnes, is being changed in size from 7 to 11 metres; the Operational Control Unit is being enlarged.
- Facade of 14,000 plates: alignment is poor according to the club, causing a conflict with the architects; it lets too much light through.
- The Madrid regional authority tendered a EUR 68 million extension of Santiago Bernabeu metro station (tripling its area); work expected as early as 2024.

wikis.title: MSG Sphere creators withdraw plans for London venue
wikis.summary: Dezeen report of 9 January 2024 that Madison Square Garden Entertainment withdrew its Stratford MSG Sphere London application.
wikis.body:
- Published 9 January 2024 (Dezeen, Lizzie Crook).
- MSG withdrew from the Planning Inspectorate process, calling it "a political football between rival parties", after a five-year planning process; Sphere Entertainment will not take part in the call-in process.
- London mayor Sadiq Khan rejected the proposal in October, citing "unacceptable harm to hundreds of residents", after a WSP report commissioned by the GLA "identified significant errors and omissions". In November Michael Gove told the London Legacy Development Corporation not to deny planning permission until he had reviewed it.
- Proposed 2018 for Stratford near the Olympic Park; would have been 120 m wide and 90 m tall with illuminated screens; designed by Populous. It won permission in 2022 (6-4 vote, 852 objections, 355 supportive responses).
- Would have been the second Sphere after Las Vegas. MSG says it will focus on "forward-thinking cities"; it is reportedly planning a 120 m K-pop sphere in Hanam, South Korea (per The Korea Economic Daily).

wikis.title: Newham Mayor's statement on the withdrawal of MSG Sphere proposals
wikis.summary: Newham Council statement by Mayor Rokhsana Fiaz welcoming MSG's withdrawal of its Stratford MSG Sphere planning application.
wikis.body:
- Published 12 Jan 2024 by Newham Council.
- Mayor Rokhsana Fiaz OBE called the withdrawal "a fantastic outcome" for communities in Stratford, Maryland and the Stratford Olympic Park area.
- She said "Newham is not another Las Vegas" and that the structure, "some 100 meters high and 120 meters wide", would have caused significant light intrusion and negative health impacts for residents. The council had campaigned against it for five years.
- She said the campaign was not anti-business but investment cannot come at residents' health and well-being.
- The council will now campaign for the site to be designated a housing and employment inclusion zone, for affordable homes and jobs.

wikis.title: 2023 Las Vegas Grand Prix
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the 2023 Formula One Las Vegas Grand Prix, held 18 November 2023 on the Las Vegas Strip Circuit.
wikis.body:
- Formula 1 Heineken Silver Las Vegas Grand Prix 2023, held November 18, 2023 at the Las Vegas Strip Circuit, Paradise, Nevada; race 21 of 22 in the 2023 F1 season and the first running of the Las Vegas Grand Prix.
- Street circuit, 6.201 km (3.853 mi), 17 corners and a 1.9 km (1.2 mi) straight down the Strip; 50 laps, 309.958 km. It starts in a former parking lot bought by Formula One for $240 million, now the pits and paddock. Attendance 315,000. Weather clear.
- Result: Max Verstappen (Red Bull-Honda RBPT) won, Charles Leclerc (Ferrari) second, Sergio Perez (Red Bull) third. Leclerc took pole (1:32.726); Carlos Sainz qualified second but started twelfth after a grid penalty. Fastest lap: Oscar Piastri (McLaren), 1:35.490 on lap 47. Perez secured second in the Drivers' Championship.
- Before the race Verstappen led with 524 points; Red Bull led the Constructors' with 782.
- Practice: FP1 (16 Nov) red-flagged after Sainz hit a loose metal cover on the track surface, damaging his and Esteban Ocon's cars; Sainz needed a third energy store, causing a 10-place grid penalty. FP2 was delayed two and a half hours for drain-cover checks. Fans were ejected at 1:30 and $200 merchandise vouchers were given; a class action was launched on behalf of 35,000 fans. Ferrari's Fred Vasseur criticised the drain covers; Toto Wolff praised the organisers.
- On March 5, 2024 the BBC reported FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem allegedly tried to pressure officials over certifying the circuit; the FIA later cleared him.
- Tyres: Pirelli C3, C4, C5.

wikis.title: Las Vegas Grand Prix date set for Nov. 18, 2023
wikis.summary: LVSportsBiz report of 20 September 2022 announcing the Saturday-night F1 Las Vegas Grand Prix on Nov. 18, 2023 and describing the course.
wikis.body:
- Published September 20, 2022 (Alan Snel, LVSportsBiz.com).
- Race set for a Saturday night start at 10PM on Nov. 18, the weekend before Thanksgiving 2023. Opening ceremony Nov. 15, practice Nov. 16, qualifying Nov. 17.
- Formula 1 president/CEO Stefano Domenicali: the race will "take F1 race weekends to the next level".
- Course: 3.8-mile, 14-turn counter-clockwise route including Koval Lane, Sands Avenue and Harmon Avenue, with a 1.2-mile southbound section of Las Vegas Boulevard on the Strip. The full route was to be paved in the second quarter of 2023.

wikis.title: DAMAC unveils The Delmore, designed by Zaha Hadid Architects
wikis.summary: Press release of 26 February 2025 announcing The Delmore, a 12-story oceanfront condominium at 8777 Collins Avenue, Surfside, and start of construction.
wikis.body:
- Dated February 26, 2025 (Mann Report newswire).
- DAMAC International (Dubai-headquartered; founder Hussain Sajwani) launched The Delmore, a 12-story ultra-luxury boutique oceanfront condominium at 8777 Collins Avenue, Town of Surfside, Miami; its real estate entry into the United States. Sales exclusively by Douglas Elliman.
- Construction begun; anticipated completion 2029.
- Designed by Zaha Hadid Architects (its second residential project in Miami); interior designer Hirsch Bedner Associates. Two-acre site with 200 linear feet of beachfront.
- 37 mansions, no more than four per floor, four to five bedrooms, averaging 7,000 sq ft, penthouses from 10,000 sq ft; prices start at $15 million. More than 55,000 sq ft of amenities. A 75-foot acrylic see-through pool suspended 125 feet in the air; sculptural facade with staggered terraces and shell-shaped fins.
- DAMAC also announced a $20 billion investment in data centers across the American Sunbelt and Midwest.

wikis.title: Foundation permit approved for The Delmore in Surfside
wikis.summary: Florida YIMBY report of 4 August 2025 on the foundation permit and construction schedule of DAMAC's The Delmore at 8777 Collins Avenue.
wikis.body:
- Published August 4, 2025 (Florida YIMBY, Oscar Nunez).
- The Town of Surfside approved the foundation permit for The Delmore, DAMAC International's 12-story oceanfront condominium designed by Zaha Hadid Architects.
- Deep-soil mixing by Keller North America is more than one-third complete, expected to finish in the fall; piling follows, foundations over 100 feet below grade. Vertical construction expected to begin in the third quarter of 2026. DAMAC has invested over $25 million so far.
- 37 full- and half-floor residences averaging over 7,000 sq ft, four to five bedrooms, from $15 million; no more than two per floor in each wing. Amenities over 55,000 sq ft including a 75-foot indoor lap pool and resident restaurant with a "Michelin-starred menu". Completion expected in 2029.
- Off-site sales gallery at 301 71st Street, Miami Beach. Jeffery Rossely (DAMAC) said it is committed to construction "irrespective of the current market slowdown".

wikis.title: Woolworth Tower Residences (ENR New York Best Project 2019)
wikis.summary: ENR 2019 Best Project write-up on converting the upper floors of the Woolworth Building in New York into luxury residences.
wikis.body:
- ENR New York's 2019 Best Projects, dated September 24, 2019.
- Owner: BlackRock. Lead design firm: SLCE Architects. General contractor/CM: CNY. Civil: Langan. Structural: Gilsanz Murray Steficek LLP. MEP: AKF Group LLC. Design architect: The Office of Thierry W. Despont Ltd. Owner's rep: Gardiner & Theobald.
- The 62-story Woolworth Building (world's tallest in 1913, Cass Gilbert neo-Gothic) became mixed-use: office tenants up to the 29th floor, residences above, including a five-level 9,000-sq-ft penthouse with private elevator. Project started early 2016.
- No external hoist or crane was possible (landmark facade, partly occupied, new crane rules); crews used an internal hoist and a chain-fall system in an empty elevator shaft.
- Scope: gut renovation of 110,000 sq ft; $22-million terra-cotta facade restoration; new MEP incl. a new mechanical floor; reinforced pinnacle on floors 50-58; new lobby and two residential elevators; amenities including wine rooms, yoga and fitness studios and restored historic sub-cellar pool.

wikis.title: Woolworth Tower Residences records first closing of $7.55M
wikis.summary: CityRealty item of 13 June 2018 on the first sale at The Woolworth Tower Residences, 2 Park Place, plus building history and amenities.
wikis.body:
- Dated Wednesday, Jun 13, 2018 (CityRealty, Michelle Sinclair Colman).
- First closing: James R. Schnepper bought a two-bedroom, two-and-a-half-bath 38th-floor residence for $7.55M ($2,963/ft2), 96% of the $7.85M asking price.
- Residences: 33 condominium apartments by architect Thierry W. Despont atop the 60-story Woolworth Building facing City Hall Park; 14 then for sale, from a two-bedroom on the 34th floor asking $7.45M to a four-bedroom, 6,095 SF full-floor simplex on the 40th asking $21.325M.
- Amenities: 55-foot saltwater lap pool (once Woolworth's private pool), fitness center on the 30th floor, wine cellar and tasting room (a locker for up to 185 bottles per residence), attended parking, residents' lobby, 29th-floor Gilbert Lounge.
- History: designed by Cass Gilbert, built 1910-1912 at 233 Broadway; originally planned at 420 feet, grew to 792 feet; commissioned by Frank W. Woolworth, dubbed "The Cathedral of Commerce"; tallest in the world until the 1930 race between 40 Wall Street and the Chrysler Building; owned by the Woolworth company until 1998.

wikis.title: Reinventing Woolworth: adaptive reuse of a historic skyscraper
wikis.summary: Gilsanz Murray Steficek post (29 Oct 2015) introducing a CTBUH Journal case study on converting the Woolworth Building's upper floors to luxury residences.
wikis.body:
- Dated October 29, 2015.
- The CTBUH Journal published a case study of the redevelopment GMS is undertaking with Alchemy Properties and SLCE Architects at the Woolworth Building, covering structural and logistical issues and the sustainability case for repurposing.
- Repositions an underused 1913 office tower (once packed with dentists' and barbershops' offices) as luxury homes, after multiple structural design iterations over 17 years.
- The 792 ft (241 m) "Cathedral of Commerce" will include some of the highest-altitude residences in the city, including a 6-story, $110 million "Castle in the Sky" penthouse.
- Methods were designed around 100-year-old documents; modern systems interact with historic riveted framing and structural terracotta, under strict landmark preservation guidelines.

wikis.title: Omniturm, Frankfurt
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the 190 m mixed-use Omniturm skyscraper in Frankfurt designed by Bjarke Ingels Group and completed in 2019.
wikis.body:
- Skyscraper at Grosse Gallusstrasse 16-18, Frankfurt am Main, Germany; status completed.
- Built by Tishman Speyer Properties from early 2016 (infobox: construction started 2017), completed and inaugurated 2019. Height 189.9 m (190 m / 620 ft); sixth-tallest building in Frankfurt and Germany upon completion. 49 storeys.
- Architect: Bjarke Ingels Group; structural engineer PfeiferINTERPLAN. Name from Latin omnis "everyone", alluding to mixed office and residential use.
- Design: a "swing" halfway up; spiral axis shift creates terraces for the living area between the 14th and 23rd floors, offset by more than 5 m at largest.
- Areas: 43,850 m2 rentable office, 8,175 m2 living space, 1,579 m2 publicly accessible; leasable area over 54,100 m2 with about 44,200 m2 flexible office and 147 premium apartments (about 8,200 m2).
- Owner: Commerz Real (investment manager for Commerzbank), which bought it in 2018.

wikis.title: OMNITURM (Frankfurt, 2019) - Structurae data sheet
wikis.summary: Structurae database entry with dates, dimensions, materials and project participants for the Omniturm in Frankfurt.
wikis.body:
- Location: Grosse Gallusstrasse 16-18, Frankfurt, Hesse, Germany. Works began 2016; completion December 2019; status in use. Function: office and apartment building; reinforced and precast concrete structure.
- Dimensions: height 190 m; base 40 m x 30 m; 46 piles, diameter 1.2 m / 1.5 m, length 12-27 m. Listed with a 2020 award (details for registered users).
- Participants: owner Tishman Speyer GmbH & Co.; architecture BIG Bjarke Ingels Group; structural design B+G Ingenieure Bollinger und Grohmann; wind analysis Wacker Ingenieure; structural engineering Professor Pfeifer und Partner; contractor Adolf Lupp GmbH + Co. KG.
- Includes a Wikipedia excerpt: 49 storeys, 43,850 m2 office, 8,175 m2 living space, 147 apartments, bought by Commerz Real in 2018. Data sheet published 30/09/2020, updated 04/10/2020.

wikis.title: Suburban Rail Loop, Melbourne (overview, description and background)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia part 1 on Melbourne's Suburban Rail Loop: sections, cost, schedule, political opposition and the history of Melbourne orbital transport.
wikis.body:
- Rapid transit system under construction in Melbourne, Victoria; three sections: SRL East (Cheltenham to Box Hill, 26 km, 6 stations, work began 2022, planned opening 2035), SRL North (Box Hill to Melbourne Airport, 34 km, 7 stations, planned 2043 in infobox; text says construction not expected before the 2030s, completion by 2053, may be split in two) and SRL West (undefined, no timeframe).
- East and North together form a 60 km fully automated underground orbital line with 13 stations connecting eight existing rail lines and three university campuses. Estimated cost $31-58 billion. Owner VicTrack; operator TransitLinX (John Holland and RATP Dev); 4-car driverless Alstom Metropolis trains; Alstom Urbalis Forward signalling; 25 kV AC.
- Announced by the Andrews Labor government before the 2018 state election. Praised for vision; criticised for political motives, business-case transparency, prioritisation and cost.
- First $3.6 billion tunnel contract signed December 2023 with Suburban Connect. The Coalition opposes it: Brad Battin (Jan 2025) and then Jess Wilson (leader from November 2025) pledged to halt it if elected in 2026; federal Coalition vowed to scrap $2.2 billion federal funding before the 2025 election, which it lost.
- As of September 2026, six SRL East stations are under construction and tunnel boring began in September 2026, first from Burwood towards Glen Waverley.
- Background: Melbourne's radial rail network; failed orbital lines (Outer Circle 1888-1891, closed by 1897; Inner Circle opened 1888, closed to passengers 1941); M80 Ring Road (1989-1999); EastLink (2008).

wikis.title: LNG Canada achieves first production in Kitimat, B.C.
wikis.summary: CBC News report of 23 June 2025 that LNG Canada safely achieved first LNG production at Kitimat.
wikis.body:
- Posted Jun 23, 2025 (CBC News).
- LNG Canada confirmed it "safely achieved its first production" at its Kitimat facility, about 650 km northwest of Vancouver; it expects to load first cargoes by the middle of 2025.
- Gas arrives via the Coastal GasLink pipeline from near Dawson Creek, is cooled and shipped to Asian markets. First large-scale Canadian LNG project to produce and first major North American LNG facility with direct Pacific access.
- Expected to export 14 million tonnes a year, about 300 ongoing jobs and an estimated $575 million annually for 40 years (B.C. government); a proposed Phase 2 would double to 28 million tonnes.
- Costs $40 billion, described as the "largest single private sector investment in the history of the country", backed by Shell, Petronas, PetroChina, Mitsubishi Corporation and Korea Gas Corp. Partners still considering Phase 2.
- Kitimat Mayor Phil Germouth praised the company's work with communities and First Nations. LNG is cooled to about -160 C; the "clean" label is disputed by some analysts, and fracking is linked to earthquakes in the Peace River region. Two smaller B.C. LNG export facilities are under construction (Woodfibre LNG and another).

wikis.title: $1.3B Harbor Bridge opens in Texas after series of delays
wikis.summary: Construction Dive report of 1 July 2025 on the opening of the new Harbor Bridge in Corpus Christi and its history of delays.
wikis.body:
- Published July 1, 2025 (Construction Dive, Julie Strupp).
- The $1.3 billion Harbor Bridge opened Saturday in Corpus Christi, Texas, replacing the original bridge (high accident rates: no shoulders, steep grade, reverse curve, no pedestrian/bike access). Described as the longest concrete segmental cable-stayed span in North America; 538-foot towers let taller ships pass the ship channel; just over 6 miles of bridge and connecting roadway; shared-use path, community plaza. Expected service life 170 years.
- Built by FlatironDragados; the old structure was demolished as part of the scope. Southbound lanes opened; northbound scheduled for early July.
- Originally due 2020. Delays: cost disputes over permitting and right-of-way, COVID-19, replacement of the engineer of record, an April 2023 crane fire injuring two at Whataburger Field, and Texas DOT concerns in 2022 with FlatironDragados and Arup (notice of default over five design issues; work shut down in August 2022). Disputes and claims were settled in October 2023.
- Mayor Paulette Guajardo: the bridge solidifies Corpus Christi as an energy hub.

wikis.title: New Harbor Bridge in Corpus Christi opens after decade-long construction
wikis.summary: KRIS 6 News report on the opening of Corpus Christi's Harbor Bridge, its cost overrun and delays.
wikis.body:
- KRIS 6 News (José Luis Martínez); no date shown; refers to a ribbon-cutting originally set for May 10, 2025 that was postponed.
- The $1.2 billion project broke ground in 2016 to replace the old Harbor Bridge (higher-than-average accident rates, limited navigational clearance); it lets the Port of Corpus Christi take larger vessels including bigger crude tankers and potentially container ships. Completed shortly after the Ship Channel Improvement Project.
- Originally due to open in 2020 with a $900 million budget; final cost about $1.2 billion, about $300 million over.
- In November 2019 TxDOT suspended design work over safety concerns about engineering firm FIGG Group, implicated in the 2018 Florida International University pedestrian bridge collapse (6 killed, 10 injured). TxDOT later reviewed the built portions and found them safe; further delays came from weather, permitting and construction.

wikis.title: On this day, October 9, 1888: the Washington Monument opens to the public
wikis.summary: Fox News history item (9 October 2024) on the construction timeline and dimensions of the Washington Monument.
wikis.body:
- Published October 9, 2024 (Erica Lamberg, Fox News).
- The marble-faced granite obelisk honouring George Washington, built in two phases (1848 and 1884), dedicated 1885, opened to the public on Oct. 9, 1888.
- Stands 555' 5 1/8" tall and weighs 81,120 tons; marble blocks 15' thick at the base to 18" at the top; the marble changes colour at 150 feet, where construction stopped between 1856 and 1876. 896 steps to the observation level; there is also an elevator.
- Timeline: Washington National Monument Society formed in 1833 (John Marshall, James Madison and others); bonded agents collecting funds in 1835; Robert Mills's design selected Nov. 18, 1845; cornerstone laid July 4, 1848 before 20,000 people; Congress appropriated $2 million on Aug. 2, 1876; Thomas Lincoln Casey engineer-in-charge; staircase and elevator frames from February 1880; capstone and aluminum point set Dec. 6, 1884.
- Construction took nearly four decades, hit by controversy and lack of funds.

wikis.title: Schlaich Bergermann Partner's Danube Valley Bridge opens in Austria
wikis.summary: Architectural Record article on the Danube Valley Bridge in Linz, described as the longest earth-anchored suspension bridge in the world.
wikis.body:
- Architectural Record (Matthew Marani). The Danube Valley Bridge in Linz, Austria, completed October 2024 and designed by Schlaich Bergermann Partner (SBP), is "the longest earth-anchored suspension bridge in the world"; opened to the public in November 2024 as part of the first phase of the A26 Linz motorway.
- Began in 2003 with a competition for a pylon-free bridge; winning team SBP with Gerkan, Marg & Partners and Baumann + Obholzer Ingenieure. Nearly 1,000-foot-long single wide-deck suspension bridge anchored in the rocky slopes; composite prefabricated steel and concrete. SBP director Mathias Widmayer: two anchorage points rather than four.
- Work began 2019 with anchor blocks (hundreds of grouted anchors, some over 200 feet, 785 cubic yards of concrete). Main cable installation began end of 2021: 12 parallel spiral cables, each nearly 6 inches in diameter, over 1,600 feet long; hangers about 80 feet apart.
- Steel box and cross girders made in northern Italy by Maeg Costruzioni, assembled into nine 80-foot-wide segments up to 350 tons each; seven placed from a stilt pontoon on the Danube. In fall 2022 3-inch precast slabs were placed, then the deck poured and mastic asphalt applied.

wikis.title: New Linz Danube Valley Bridge opens to traffic
wikis.summary: The International (Vienna) report of 15 November 2024 on the opening of the Linz Danube Valley Bridge, first phase of the A26 Westring.
wikis.body:
- Dated 15 November 2024 (The International).
- The Linz Danube Valley Bridge, first phase of the A26 Westring, opens Friday from 6:00 PM after a completion ceremony the previous month. It connects Linz with the Muhlviertel and cost EUR 305 million; initially one lane each direction.
- Spans more than 300 metres, the fourth river crossing in Linz, without supporting pillars, a "true" suspension bridge; Asfinag calls it "one of a kind in this dimension worldwide". Ramp tunnel system totals 3.2 km.
- Whole Westring expected to cost at least EUR 1.2 billion, possibly more. It has faced opposition from environmental activists; the "Initiative Verkehrswende jetzt!" planned a "public walk" that the State Police Directorate prohibited.

wikis.title: Klamath River dams fully removed ahead of schedule
wikis.summary: California Governor's office release of 2 October 2024 announcing completion of Klamath River dam removal.
wikis.body:
- Dated Oct 2, 2024 (Governor of California).
- Governor Newsom announced the Klamath River restoration project completed the final work removing the dams, called the largest such project in American history, ahead of schedule and on budget. Restoration of 2,200 acres of formerly submerged land continues for several years.
- Removal restores nearly 400 miles of habitat for salmon and other species. In August the governor announced fish could swim freely for the first time in more than 100 years.
- The river, once the third-largest salmon-producing river on the West Coast, declined after dam construction began in 1918.
- Quotes from Karuk Chairman Russell "Buster" Attebery and Yurok Chairman Joseph L. James on the tribally led effort; Newsom convened leaders in 2020 and pushed federal approvals; land returned to the Shasta Indian Nation.

wikis.title: Tribes celebrate end of largest dam removal project in US history
wikis.summary: CBS Sacramento/AP piece (2 October 2024) on completion of Klamath River dam removal and the tribal campaign behind it.
wikis.body:
- Updated October 2, 2024 (AP via CBS Sacramento).
- The largest dam removal in U.S. history was completed Wednesday, a victory for tribes who fought for decades through protests, testimony and lawsuits to free hundreds of miles of the Klamath River near the California-Oregon border.
- PacifiCorp built the four hydroelectric dams between 1918 and 1962; they blocked a river once the third-largest salmon producer on the West Coast and produced only enough power for about 70,000 homes, with no irrigation, drinking water or flood control (per the Klamath River Renewal Corporation, whose CEO Mark Bransom credited tribal activism).
- Since breaching, fish regained habitat and water temperature fell and quality improved (Michael Belchik, Yurok Tribe). Advocates are now turning to revegetation and restoration.
- Profile: Karuk member Molli Myers organised about 25 tribal members to fly to Scotland in 2004 to protest at the Scottish Power (then PacifiCorp's parent) stockholders meeting, motivated by a salmon die-off two years earlier.

wikis.title: Ethiopia inaugurates the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam
wikis.summary: Ecofin Agency report of 9 September 2025 on the GERD inauguration and Egypt and Sudan's water concerns.
wikis.body:
- Tuesday, 09 September 2025 (Ecofin Agency).
- Ethiopia officially inaugurated the $4 billion Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD) on September 9, 2025, on the Blue Nile about thirty kilometres from the Sudanese border, after more than a decade of construction. Africa's largest hydroelectric dam; targeted capacity 5,000 megawatts; reservoir of 74 billion cubic metres.
- Egypt depends on the Nile for nearly 90% of its freshwater; per its ministry it has under 60 billion m3 a year against needs of about 114 billion, and fears uncoordinated filling. Sudan is divided between support and mistrust, worried about its downstream dams and farmland.
- Project launched 2011; 2015 declaration of principles signed by the three countries; Ethiopia began filling unilaterally in 2020; in 2021 the UN recommended African Union-led talks, with no significant progress recorded.

wikis.title: Icon of the Seas
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on Royal Caribbean's Icon of the Seas, lead ship of the Icon class and the largest cruise ship by gross tonnage.
wikis.body:
- Royal Caribbean International cruise ship, lead of the Icon class, built by Meyer Turku in Finland; 248,663 GT; length 364.75 m; beam 48.47 m; 20 decks; speed 22 knots; capacity 5,610 passengers at double occupancy, 7,600 maximum; crew 2,350. Six multi-fuel Warstila engines (LNG or distillate), first Royal Caribbean vessel with such technology; three 20 MW ABB Azipods.
- Timeline: order announced October 2016; steel cutting June 2021; keel laid 4 April 2022; launched 9 December 2022; first sea trials 19 June 2023; handed over 27 November 2023; arrived PortMiami 10 January 2024; christened 23 January 2024 by Lionel Messi; maiden voyage and service began 27 January 2024 from PortMiami.
- Features: Aquadome, The Pearl, Absolute Zero ice rink, Surfside, The Hideaway with first suspended infinity pool, Thrill Island (six water slides), Swim & Tonic, 670 m jogging track; seven pools; company claims tallest waterfall and slide and largest waterpark on a cruise ship. Designers include Wilson Butler Architects, 3Deluxe, RTKL and Skylab Architecture.
- Incidents: a passenger reportedly jumped in May 2024 and died; a fire was reported 25 June 2024 at Costa Maya, Mexico.

wikis.title: Icon of the Seas officially named in Miami
wikis.summary: Karryon report of 26 January 2024 on the gala naming ceremony of Icon of the Seas with Lionel Messi.
wikis.body:
- 26 Jan 2024 (Karryon News Desk).
- Lionel Messi joined Royal Caribbean International at the naming ceremony in Miami on the eve of first sailing on 27 January; hosted by Mario Lopez in the AquaDome. Present: Michael Bayley, Jason Liberty, Captain Henrik Loy, Meyer Turku and Inter Miami CF representatives.
- Ship described as the world's largest cruise ship: six waterslides, "Crown's Edge" experience (154 feet above the ocean), seven pools including the first suspended infinity pool at sea, more than 40 restaurants, bars and lounges, eight neighbourhoods. Seven-night Eastern or Western Caribbean cruises from Miami, including Perfect Day at CocoCay.
- When revealed in October 2022 it produced the highest single-day bookings and busiest booking week in the cruise line's then 53-year history.
- Messi: "Everything I've seen on Icon of the Seas is next level." Jason Liberty: "the culmination of more than 50 years of dreaming, innovating".

wikis.title: CIPESS meeting of 6 August 2025 approves the Strait of Messina Bridge
wikis.summary: Italian Government release on CIPESS approving the final project for the Strait of Messina bridge at EUR 13.532 billion.
wikis.body:
- 6 August 2025 (governo.it). CIPESS, chaired by Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni with secretary Alessandro Morelli, approved the final project for a permanent Sicily-Calabria link across the Strait of Messina.
- Cost EUR 13.532 billion, fully covered by public funding already available through the 2024 and 2025 budget laws.
- Provided for in a 1971 regulation and relaunched by the Government in 2022. Would be the world's longest single-span bridge: 3,300 metres, two 399-metre towers, three traffic lanes each direction (including emergency lane), two service lanes and two rail tracks with walkways.
- About 40 km of road and rail links (80% in tunnels) to the Calabria "Mediterranean" motorway, Villa S. Giovanni and Reggio Calabria stations, and in Sicily the Messina-Catania and Messina-Palermo motorways and a new Messina station.
- Described as strategic for the Mezzogiorno and trans-European networks.

wikis.title: Eurolink and Stretto di Messina sign Strait of Messina Bridge contract
wikis.summary: Webuild press release of 6 August 2025 on the contract addendum and CIPESS design approval for the record-span Strait of Messina Bridge.
wikis.body:
- August 06, 2025 (Webuild Group), Rome. The bridge "has officially entered the implementation phase" after CIPESS approved the Definitive Design; Eurolink (general contractor led by Webuild) signed a EUR 10.6 billion addendum with concessionaire Stretto di Messina, effective on publication of the approval in the Official Gazette.
- Deck spans 3,666 m; central suspended span 3,300 m, one kilometre longer than the current record-holder Canakkale Bridge in Turkey. Deck about 60 m wide, three vehicle lanes each way, two rail lines, two service lanes; capacity up to 200 trains a day and 6,000 vehicles an hour.
- Steel towers 399 m; cables 1.26 m in diameter and 5,320 m long; clearance 72 m above sea level over 600 m width. Designed for seismic activity and extreme winds, with an intelligent monitoring system.
- Eurolink partners: Webuild, Sacyr, IHI, Condotte, Itinera; designer COWI.
- Complementary works: over 40 km of roads and rail; Calabria 10 km roads, 2.7 km rail, a multifunctional centre at Piale, Villa San Giovanni; Sicily 10.4 km roads, 17.5 km rail and three Messina stations (Papardo, Annunziata, Europa). Excavation estimated at 12 million m3 in Sicily and 4.5 million in Calabria.

wikis.title: SIS Building (MI6), Vauxhall Cross, London
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the MI6 headquarters at 85 Albert Embankment, Vauxhall, its design, construction and history.
wikis.body:
- Government office building, headquarters of the Secret Intelligence Service (SIS/MI6) since 1994, at 85 Albert Embankment, Vauxhall, London beside Vauxhall Bridge. Postmodern; architect Terry Farrell and Partners; main contractor John Laing plc; owner HM Government.
- Background: SIS moved from 54 Broadway to Century House in 1964; a 1985 NAO report called Century House "irredeemably insecure".
- Site: formerly Vauxhall Pleasure Gardens, later a glass factory, vinegar works and gin distillery. Bought 1983 by Regalian Properties; Terry Farrell won the competition. Margaret Thatcher approved the SIS purchase in 1988. NAO final cost GBP 135.05 million (site and basic building) or GBP 152.6 million including special requirements.
- Design: influenced by 1930s industrial modernism and Mayan and Aztec temples; 60 roof areas; 25 types of glass; triple-glazed windows; large parts below street level; two moats; rumoured tunnel under the Thames to Whitehall (rumour).
- Completed April 1994, opened by Queen Elizabeth II on 14 July 1994. In September 2000 it was attacked with a Russian-made weapon (per the article).
- Nicknames: Legoland, Ceausescu Towers, Babylon-on-Thames, Vauxhall Trollop, The Ziggurat.

wikis.title: Replacement of the Spitallamm dam by KWO
wikis.summary: Short swissdams blog note that Kraftwerke Oberhasli AG is replacing the 1932 Spitallamm dam with a new arch dam from 2019 to 2025.
wikis.body:
- Kraftwerke Oberhasli AG (KWO) replaces the Spitallamm dam from 2019 to 2025.
- The existing dam was completed in 1932 and now needs strengthening (page text, in French: "besogneux de confortement").
- It is being replaced by a new arch dam; the old wall is preserved and later flooded.
- Link given to KWO's project page (grimselstrom.ch). Image courtesy of KWO.

wikis.title: Spitallamm dam, Grimsel: Implenia reference
wikis.summary: Implenia project page on the joint-venture replacement of the Spitallamm dam on Lake Grimsel with a new double-curvature arch dam.
wikis.body:
- Client: Kraftwerke Oberhasli AG (KWO), which is also designer and construction manager. A joint venture of Frutiger AG (project lead), Implenia and Ghelma AG Baubetriebe builds it; Implenia holds 42.5%.
- Contract volume around CHF 100 million in total; Implenia's share of services listed as 98 M CHF.
- The existing Spitallamm dam was completed in 1932. The new double-curvature arch dam is built directly in front of it; the old dam stays in place and will be flooded later, with a tunnel balancing the water level hydraulically.
- New dam has the same crest height as the existing arch-gravity dam and allows a later height increase to enlarge Lake Grimsel.
- Figures: max height 113 m, crest length 212 m, crest width 8 m, max footing width 20 m, concrete volume more than 223,000 m3.
- Site on the Grimsel Pass road, roughly 1,650 m (Gerstenegg) to 1,980 m (Grimsel Hospice) above sea level.
- Timing: building began in summer 2019 (start of construction May 2019); "scheduled to be completed in 2026"; facts box gives completion October 2025; status "Under construction".
- Implenia cites its earlier Vieux Emosson dam height-increase project.

wikis.title: Taipei Performing Arts Center (Wikipedia)
wikis.summary: Encyclopedia entry on the OMA-designed performing arts center in Shilin, Taipei, which opened officially on 2 July 2022.
wikis.body:
- Located at No. 1 Jiantan Rd., Shilin District, Taipei; accessible from Jiantan Station of Taipei Metro. Former name Taipei Arts Center (2004-2014). Owner: Department of Cultural Affairs, Taipei City Government.
- Architect: Office for Metropolitan Architecture (David Gianotten and Rem Koolhaas); structural engineer Evergreen Consulting Engineering.
- Timeline: groundbreaking 28 February 2012; topped out 27 August 2014; facade revealed 31 August 2016; trial opening March-May 2022; officially opened 2 July 2022.
- Cost: infobox NT$6.75 billion; history text says the structure was built for NT$5.4 billion.
- Capacity 3,100 in the infobox; total space area 50,000 m2.
- Design: geometric shapes with a cube-shaped structure; sphere-shaped Globe Playhouse (800 seats); asymmetrical Grand Theater (1,500 seats); Blue Box for experimental performances (500 seats).

wikis.title: OMA's Taipei Performing Arts Center completes (Dezeen)
wikis.summary: Dezeen report of 13 May 2022 on the completion of OMA's Taipei Performing Arts Center ahead of its planned August 2022 opening.
wikis.body:
- Completed ahead of an official opening then stated as 7 August 2022. Commissioned by Taipei City Government in 2009; construction began 2012; originally slated for completion in 2015, topped out August 2014.
- 59,000 m2 cultural landmark; three auditoriums protrude from a central cuboid volume, in the Shilin Night Market area. Led by Rem Koolhaas with managing partner David Gianotten.
- Theatres: 800-seat spherical Globe Playhouse supported on two columns; 1,500-seat Grand Theater; 800-seat Blue Box. The Grand Theater and Blue Box sit opposite each other on the same level and can be combined into a "Super Theater".
- The central section is raised to form a covered plaza and holds entrances, foyers and backstage areas. A public walkway, the Public Loop, runs through the backstage areas with windows, up to a rooftop viewing point.
- Quote, Koolhaas: "We want to contribute to the history of the theatre." He said contemporary performance theatres are "increasingly becoming standardised".
- Quote, TPAC CEO Austin Wang: "much more than the sum of its three theaters".
- Credits include executive architect Kris Yao | ARTECH, Arup (structure/MEP/fire), Inside Outside (landscape/interior), photography by Chris Stowers.

wikis.title: Habitat 67 (Wikipedia)
wikis.summary: Encyclopedia entry on Moshe Safdie's Habitat 67 housing complex in Montreal, built for Expo 67, covering its history, design, cost and legacy.
wikis.body:
- Housing complex at Cite du Havre, Montreal, Quebec (2600 Avenue Pierre-Dupuy), designed by Moshe Safdie; originated in his McGill University master's thesis, then an amended version was built for Expo 67 (April-October 1967). Structural engineer August Komendant; construction by Anglin-Norcross Ltd.
- Construction 1964-1967. Infobox cost CA$12.4 million (1967); text also gives about CA$22.4 million for the reduced development. Original plans called for 1,200 homes at $45 million.
- Design: 354 identical prefabricated concrete modules (11.7 m x 5.3 m x 3 m) in three pyramids up to 12 storeys, making 146 residences of one to eight modules each; originally 158 apartments, some since joined. Each unit has a roof-terrace garden of roughly 20 to 90 m2. Brutalist and Metabolist style; floor area 29,700 m2; 3 lifts.
- Financed by the federal government; tenants formed a limited partnership that bought it from Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation in 1985. Designated Montreal heritage monument (2009).
- Safdie's goal of affordable housing "largely failed"; per-unit cost of about $140,000 prevented a larger complex.
- Access: guided tours offered; in 2023 the 777 Casino bus route extension gave public transport for the first time.
- Legacy: 2017 Canada Post stamp for Expo 67's 50th anniversary; 2017 UQAM exhibition; 2023 Safdie Architects with Epic Games modelled the original larger vision in Unreal Engine. Judged both success ("redefined urban living") and failure to revolutionize modular housing; The Walrus called it a "failed dream"; Christopher Alexander criticised it as "banal and deadening". Won a March 2012 online Lego Architecture poll.
- Appears in Leonard Cohen's "In My Secret Life" video and the 1977 film The Disappearance.

wikis.title: Habitat 67 (Tourisme Montreal)
wikis.summary: Tourism-board article describing Moshe Safdie's Habitat 67 and its guided tours, updated 19 August 2024.
wikis.body:
- Habitat 67 was built as a pavilion for Expo 67; began as Safdie's master's thesis at McGill (he was 24 then, 29 when it opened). On Cite du Havre, a man-made peninsula partly made from Montreal metro excavation material.
- 12 storeys of 354 grey-beige modules stacked in a pyramidal cluster forming 148 residences (158 apartments in 1967). 15 model residences of 1 to 4 modules each, with terraces and views on three sides.
- Modules were cast on site and delivered by crane, with pre-assembled kitchens and fibreglass washrooms; central heating, air conditioning and "racetrack wiring".
- Designated historical monument; on a 2017 Canada Post stamp; about 40 staff work there today. Safdie pitched Habitat Puerto Rico and Habitat New York, but modular and prefab "did not take off as imagined".
- Tours: 90 minutes, French and English, May to November, includes Safdie's four-module penthouse (restored over two years, completed 2018). Reservations mandatory.

wikis.title: Gural's group wins Flatiron Building auction
wikis.summary: The Real Deal report of 23 May 2023 that Jeffrey Gural's group won the second Flatiron Building auction with a $161 million bid.
wikis.body:
- On Tuesday (23 May 2023) a group led by Jeffrey Gural, long-time majority owners, bid $161 million on the steps of the New York County courthouse; bidding started at $50 million. Five other bidders fell short; Jacob Garlick did not show up.
- The earlier auction had ended in chaos when Garlick bid $190 million but failed to put down a deposit; the Gural group declined its runner-up option at $189.5 million.
- New rules required the winner to pay the court-appointed referee $100,000 at the end.
- Auction resolved a lawsuit between majority owners (GFP Real Estate, Sorgente Group, Newmark, ABS Partners) and Nathan Silverstein, who owns the remaining 25%; a partition auction let owners bid with their stakes.
- Gural: "I still think we overpaid, but we overpaid by a lot less." He suggested half residential/half office or all residential; renovation could cost around $100 million per Gural. Attorneys are pursuing Garlick for the $19 million deposit.
- Building: vacant, 175 Fifth Avenue.

wikis.title: Flatiron Building sells at auction for $161 million (NY1)
wikis.summary: NY1 report of 24 May 2023 on Jeffrey Gural winning the Flatiron Building auction at $161 million.
wikis.body:
- Jeffrey Gural won Tuesday's auction outside 60 Centre Street, Lower Manhattan, with a $161 million bid; he was part of the ownership group before it went to auction.
- He wants to turn half or all of the building into apartments: "residential is easier"; needs a special city permit for residential conversion.
- Building empty since 2019 when MacMillan Publishers left; it occupied all 21 office floors. Owners spent nearly $100 million on renovations; a disagreement among owners led a judge to order the auction early in 2023.
- March auction: Jacob Garlick, of Virginia venture firm Abraham Trust, bid $190 million but lacked the 10% down payment; Gural's group is suing him for the $19 million deposit.
- Scaffolding could come down "in as soon as a couple of months"; the building still needs extensive repairs.

wikis.title: Golden Gate Bridge district approves $1B seismic retrofit work
wikis.summary: Marin Independent Journal report of 24 October 2025 on the bridge district authorizing about $1.01 billion for the final phase of the Golden Gate Bridge seismic retrofit.
wikis.body:
- The Golden Gate Bridge, Highway and Transportation District board voted Friday to authorize about $1.01 billion: an $864 million contract with Halmar International LLC (New York), a $41.3 million contingency, and a $141.7 million budget increase from district reserves.
- Original estimate about $880 million; higher cost blamed on post-pandemic construction price increases. Expected to take more than 10 years.
- Split in two: "contract 1" expected to begin early 2026 and last six years; "contract 2" at an estimated additional $900 million follows, about five more years.
- Contract 1 funding: $395.7 million federal Bridge Investment Program grant, $200 million Caltrans Federal Highway Bridge Program, $274.3 million district reserves. The grant was potentially at stake after a US DOT April letter warning about DEI policies; the district removed DEI language from policy documents.
- Four-phase retrofit launched in 1997 after the 1989 Loma Prieta earthquake; about $260 million of upgrades done 2001-2014 at viaducts and Fort Point Arch.
- Final phase: strengthen main span, two side spans, both towers and south tower pier; steel plates at tower bases, tower truss strengthening, new expansion joints, 255 floor beams retrofitted and 38 absorption devices installed.

wikis.title: Golden Gate Bridge seismic retrofit secures $1 billion for final phase (Roads & Bridges)
wikis.summary: Roads & Bridges piece of 6 November 2025 on the additional $1 billion approved for the decade-long final phase of the Golden Gate Bridge seismic retrofit, citing The Mercury News and SF Gate.
wikis.body:
- An additional $1 billion was allocated to the Golden Gate Bridge Seismic Retrofit Construction Project; total cost now exceeds $1.8 billion versus the original $880 million estimate, driven by post-pandemic construction inflation.
- Final phase starts early 2026 and takes 10 years, in two subphases: "Contract 1" lasts six years; the second, expected to cost $900 million, follows for five more years.
- District approved an $864 million contract with Halmar International LLC, a $41.3 million contingency, and a $141.7 million budget increase from district reserves.
- Work: steel plate reinforcements on the suspension bridge and two towers, truss and floor beam strengthening, energy dissipation devices, new expansion joints; towers and side spans first as they are less flexible than the main span. SF Gate reported lane closures mainly on weeknights 9 p.m. to 5 a.m.
- Background: program began in 1997 after the 1989 Loma Prieta earthquake; more than $260 million of upgrades in 2001 to 2014. The bridge is described as six miles from the San Andreas Fault.

wikis.title: Amtrak: design unveiled for New York Penn Station overhaul
wikis.summary: Amtrak media release of 8 June 2026 in which USDOT, Amtrak and Penn Transformation Partners (Halmar and Skanska) unveil renderings for the redevelopment of New York Penn Station.
wikis.body:
- Unveiled by U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean P. Duffy, Amtrak Board special advisor Andy Byford and Penn Transformation Partners (PTP), a Halmar and Skanska joint venture serving as master developer.
- Aims: serve more than 600,000 daily commuters; Madison Square Garden stays in place and the arena and all railroads keep operating during construction. "Breaking ground by the end of 2027"; 100 percent union-built.
- USDOT took control of the project in April 2025 and gave Amtrak $43 million in grant funding; PTP was selected in May 2026 and USDOT added $200 million for design and permitting. Deputy Secretary Steve Bradbury: nearly a quarter-billion dollars invested so far.
- Design: single-level, ADA-compliant concourse of stone and bronze with soaring ceilings; grand entrance on Eighth Avenue to a new train hall; expanded track capacity with at least limited through-running; MSG gets new cladding. The Infosys Theater on 8th Avenue is replaced by an art deco facade. A square structure of about 90 feet tall and 150,000 gross square feet surrounds the MSG cylinder from 31st to 33rd Street. Scores of track-level columns removed.
- Funding: primarily federal grants to Amtrak, plus federal loans, private financing and PTP equity; USDOT is investing nearly $5 billion into the Northeast Corridor.
- Lead design architect Vishaan Chakrabarti (PAU); PTP CEO Peter E. Cipriano; Chief Commercial Officer Magnus Eriksson.

wikis.title: Penn Transformation Partners named master developer for New York Penn Station
wikis.summary: Amtrak media release of 20 May 2026 announcing Halmar and Skanska's Penn Transformation Partners as master developer team for the Penn Station renovation.
wikis.body:
- USDOT Secretary Sean P. Duffy and the Amtrak Board selected Penn Transformation Partners (Halmar and Skanska) as the private master developer.
- Plans: grand Eighth Avenue entrance to a new train hall; open concourses; expanded track capacity including at least limited through-running; new retail and wayfinding; Madison Square Garden kept with new cladding; improved subterranean structure.
- Bidders were assessed on best value, new revenue streams for Amtrak, concourse capacity, safe operations, growth and user experience.
- FRA announced $200 million more via the Partnership-Northeast Corridor Program for design and permitting. Groundbreaking targeted "before the end of 2027".
- Next steps: contract negotiations, permits, FRA-led Service Optimization Study, design, financial and commercial close.
- Timeline: April 2025 USDOT and Amtrak took control from the MTA; May 2025 Andy Byford appointed; August 2025 schedule and $43 million grant; October 2025 P3 advisors named (Hunton Andrews Kurth legal, KPMG financial, AECOM/LIRO JV project/construction manager; AKRF environmental consultant).

wikis.title: JPMorganChase opens new global headquarters at 270 Park Avenue
wikis.summary: JPMorganChase story of 21 October 2025 on the grand opening of its 60-story headquarters tower at 270 Park Avenue in New York.
wikis.body:
- Opened 21 October 2025; 60 stories, 2.5 million sq ft, designed for 10,000 employees (of 24,000 in New York City) by year-end.
- Construction created 8,000 jobs across 40 local unions. Vista Site Selection study: the firm contributes $42 billion annually to the city's economy and supports 40,000 more jobs.
- 2.5 times more outdoor public space than the previous building, incl. a public plaza on Madison Avenue and wider sidewalks; fan column structure and triangular bracing; 285,000 sq ft of client entertainment space; eight trading floors; 50,000 connected devices.
- Sustainability: city's largest all-electric tower, net zero operational emissions, 100% renewable hydroelectric power; targets LEED Platinum v4 and WELL; water use cut more than 40%; 97% of demolition materials recycled.
- Renovations start at 383 Madison Avenue across the street; work with the MTA on Midtown infrastructure and access to Grand Central.
- Quote, Jamie Dimon: "For more than 225 years, JPMorganChase has been deeply rooted in New York City."

wikis.title: JPMorgan seeks to attract staff with $3 billion skyscraper (CNBC)
wikis.summary: CNBC report of 21 October 2025 on JPMorgan Chase opening its $3 billion, 60-story Park Avenue headquarters as a recruiting tool.
wikis.body:
- New 60-story, $3 billion headquarters in Midtown Manhattan; holds 10,000 workers; opened at a ribbon cutting with Jamie Dimon, Gov. Kathy Hochul and Lord Norman Foster on 21 October 2025.
- David Arena (head of global corporate real estate): "We think of the building as a recruitment tool"; a model for future offices worldwide.
- Features: biometric access, building app to order food and reserve rooms, a drone port for package deliveries, a Michelin-starred vegan restaurant, an Airstream cafe with protein shakes, an English-style pub; 50% more hospitality space than any previous JPMorgan property.
- About 97% of material from the demolished old building was recycled. Construction required 8,000 workers and added $2.6 billion to the city's economy, per the bank.
- Bank upgraded 125,000 workstations in Bangalore, Tokyo, Paris and Mexico City in five years, 75,000 more planned. Dimon, 69, reiterated he intends to step down within five years.

wikis.title: KONE reopens its mine elevator test laboratory in Tytyri, Finland
wikis.summary: Elevator Today report of 29 March 2017 on KONE's renewed high-rise elevator test lab in a working limestone mine in Tytyri, 350 m deep.
wikis.body:
- KONE unveiled its renewed high-rise elevator test facility in Tytyri, Finland, after extensive renovations. It reaches 350 meters depth, is part of a working limestone mine and hosts the world's deepest elevator test shaft.
- 11 elevator shafts with combined length of 1.6 km: seven for super-tall and mega-tall testing, four for mid- and low-rise.
- Tests: speeds up to 70 km/hour (about 19 m/s) at conventional acceleration; free-fall tests up to 90 km/hour (26 m/s). Free-fall test drops a 10,000 kg elevator frame into a 200 meter shaft to test safety gear.
- Used to test the carbon fiber hoisting technology KONE UltraRope, ride comfort, aerodynamics and robot-aided installation.
- The Tytyri lab first opened in 1997; part of a global test network at seven R&D sites in Finland, Italy, China, USA, Mexico and India.
- Quote, CTO Tomio Pihkala: "At Tytyri we can push the limits of elevator physics like at no other place in the world."

wikis.title: Antwerp Port House by Zaha Hadid Architects (ArchDaily)
