- Terminal 5 expansion: $1.2 billion, construction March 2019, completed 2023; 10 new widebody gates, 25% more international gate capacity, amenity areas up 75%, $3.5 million art program.
- Runway 9C-27C finished 2020, capping a $6 billion, 16-year airfield reconfiguration; city reported a 64% reduction in delays.
- Delay causes: FAA environmental review took four years, approval November 2022; May 2024 agreement between Mayor Brandon Johnson and airlines changed sequence to Satellite 1, then Global Terminal, then second satellite, pushing completion from 2032 to 2034.

wikis.title: O'Hare redevelopment timeline pushes back to 2034
wikis.summary: Urbanize Chicago (10 Sept 2024) on the new phasing plan that extends the $8.5 billion O'Hare 21 expansion to 2034.
wikis.body:
- Timeline for O'Hare's $8.5 billion expansion and rebuild extended to 2034; recently expected 2032; when announced in 2018, completion was supposed to be 2026.
- In May 2024 Mayor Brandon Johnson and the airlines agreed to build the first satellite, then the Global Terminal, then the second satellite last (original plan: both satellites and connecting tunnel first).
- Satellite Concourse 1: designed by SOM with Ross Barney Architects, JGMA and Arup; adds 19 gates; completion as an extension of Concourse C in 2028. Work began March 2023 with temporary taxiways, a grade-separated roadway, reconfiguration of Taxiway B and three temporary gates off Concourse C (opened spring 2024).
- Global Terminal (Studio ORD) on track to finish 2032; Satellite 2 pushed to 2034.

wikis.title: Korea Football Park opens in Cheonan
wikis.summary: Seoul Economic Daily (7 April 2026) on the official opening of the Korea Football Association's Korea Football Park in Cheonan.
wikis.body:
- Official opening ceremony at 2 p.m. on 7 April 2026 at Korea Football Park, Cheonan, South Chungcheong Province; jointly built by the KFA and Cheonan City.
- Approximately 145,000 pyeong (about 479,000 square meters), total cost approximately 400 billion won ($290 million); 11 football pitches (including a small stadium and an indoor pitch), four futsal courts, five tennis courts. Stadium, accommodation, training grounds and indoor pitch began operating in fall 2025.
- KFA President Chung Mong-gyu: a hub where players, coaches and administrators can "research and grow"; a "Korean-style development model built on artificial intelligence and scientific research". FIFA President Gianni Infantino sent a video message.
- Three functional spaces: Landmark (national team competitiveness), Campus (education of coaches, referees, analysts), Playground (fans and community). Reachable from anywhere in the country in about two hours.
- Opening match: Korea Football Park U-18 Champions Cup final, FC Seoul U-18 vs Jeonbuk Hyundai U-18.

wikis.title: Korea Republic opens new national training centre with FIFA Forward support
wikis.summary: FIFA news (8 April 2026) on the opening of the Korea Football Park national training centre in Cheonan, partly funded through FIFA Forward.
wikis.body:
- The KFA opened Korea Football Park at Cheonan, South Chungcheong, built with support of the FIFA Forward Programme; aims to improve national teams' training conditions and nurture youth players, coaches and referees, with access for clubs and the public.
- Comprises seven football pitches, two small stadiums, a football museum and player accommodation. FIFA Forward supported funding for five of the pitches and the museum. The city of Cheonan built an adjacent facility with a further five pitches, an indoor sports centre, tennis courts and futsal pitches.
- KFA President Chung Mong Gyu: a core hub to "research and grow", with a "Korean-style development model built on artificial intelligence and scientific research".
- Infantino: Korean football is "an example of how to manage, develop and invest in football"; wished Korea luck at the FIFA World Cup 2026, their eleventh successive appearance and twelfth overall, a record for Asian teams.

wikis.title: Russia launches Vostok Oil project with first Arctic crude loading
wikis.summary: gCaptain (7 Sept 2026) on Rosneft loading the first Vostok Oil crude at Bukhta Sever after Putin commissioned the project on 6 September.
wikis.body:
- Rosneft loaded the first cargo onto the 69,000-dwt ice-class tanker Valentin Pikul at the new Bukhta Sever terminal on the Kara Sea after President Putin formally commissioned the project on September 6 (2026). The roughly 120,000-dwt Aframax Akademik Gubkin waited for a second cargo. Both built at Zvezda; Valentin Pikul (delivered late 2024, 257 m, Arc6) took almost seven years with help from Samsung Heavy Industries.
- Vostok Oil: largest oil development in Russia since Soviet-era West Siberia; investment estimated at more than $100 billion; resource base exceeds 6 billion tonnes; Rosneft targets up to 100 million tonnes a year. Earlier plans: 30 million tonnes exports initially, then 50 and 100 million tonnes, timeline uncertain.
- Infrastructure: 770-km Vankor-Payakha-Bukhta Sever trunk pipeline including a 5.8-km pipeline beneath the Yenisei near Dudinka (construction started 2023). Over 2 million tonnes of supplies shipped to Sever Bay in 2023-2024; more than 700 supply voyages in 2024.
- Trafigura (10% from 2020, sold July 2022) and a Vitol-led consortium (5%) exited after the invasion of Ukraine.
- Rosneft ordered 10 high-ice-class tankers from Zvezda, envisaged about 50 vessels. Putin: "the first – yet very important – step". Sechin: "birthday of the new Russian oil province".

wikis.title: Rosneft ships first crude from $157 billion Vostok Oil project
wikis.summary: OilPrice.com (7 Sept 2026) on Rosneft's first Vostok Oil crude shipment despite sanctions and the exit of Western partners.
wikis.body:
- Rosneft shipped the first crude cargo from Vostok Oil (fields in Krasnoyarsk Krai, Eastern Siberia). Peak production expected at 50-100 million tons a year (up to 2 million bpd). Sechin: 2,000 wells drilled, combined reserves some 7 billion tons of low-sulfur crude.
- Price tag was the ruble equivalent of $157 billion in 2019; lifetime operating costs estimated at $170 billion in 2021.
- Western partners Trafigura and Vitol pulled out in 2022; Rosneft sold some assets to focus on Vostok and used domestically developed drilling tech (rigs able to drill wells up to 6,000 metres).
- The first shipment "should have been sent on its way in 2024", so a two-year delay. Original plans: 600,000 barrels/day in 2024, 1 million in phase two, ultimately 2 million at peak.
- First cargo loaded on a Russia-flagged Arc7 ice-class tanker at Sever. Sechin said Asia is the obvious destination, though oil from the Taymyr Peninsula fields would flow "in the western direction" (per a Bloomberg report).
- Putin: part of efforts to develop Siberia, the Arctic and the Far East, including the Trans-Arctic Transport Corridor.

wikis.title: San Francisco's Millennium Tower leaning fix substantially completed
wikis.summary: SF Standard (21 June 2023) on the $100 million pile upgrade meant to stop the Millennium Tower's sinking and tilting being substantially completed.
wikis.body:
- A $100 million effort to address sinking and tilting at Millennium Tower, 301 Mission St., SoMa, was substantially completed (per the homeowners association) earlier in June 2023: 18 concrete piles driven into bedrock, shifting part of the load onto them.
- Ron Hamburger (Simpson Gumpertz & Heger): "No one had ever done this for a 60-story structure and 18 million pounds of load"; technique is underpinning. The fix is a scaled-down version of an original 52-pile proposal; installing those piles caused additional sinking, and work paused for months in 2021.
- Non-structural work and restoration of Fremont and Mission streets to finish by August. HOA president Howard Dickstein: the upgrade will "restore our building's reputation and the value of condominiums".
- Litigation against the developer was settled in 2020. Building opened 2009, tallest residential high-rise in San Francisco; 419 units sold for about $750 million by Millennium Partners. Subject to a 10-year monitoring plan; retrofit also makes it more earthquake-resistant.

wikis.title: After 15 years, settlement arrested at San Francisco's Millennium Tower
wikis.summary: ENR (21 June 2023) on completion of load transfer to 18 new bedrock piles at the Millennium Tower under the $100 million foundation upgrade.
wikis.body:
- Load fully transferred to 18 new perimeter piles driven to bedrock; $100-million foundation upgrade on the 645-ft, 58-story building. As of June 19 survey data show settlement "has indeed been arrested" and the building "has risen slightly out of the ground" (engineer Ronald Hamburger, SGH). Building had 30 in. of tilt to the northwest over 15 years and has begun slowly recovering; 7 in. of tilt occurred during the upgrade work.
- Fix began fall 2020; original scheme had 52 piles; initial pile driving triggered extra settlement, Hamburger halted repairs voluntarily in August 2021; homeowners asked to scale down; 18 piles chosen (studied six to 52). Revised permit issued last August (2022).
- Piles socketed more than 30 ft into rock that starts 220 ft below grade: six along Mission, 12 along Fremont; support a new mat collar. Load transfer: January phase (six piles to 500 kips each), June 10 second stage (12 piles to 500 kips), June 15 final stage (all 18 to 1,000 kips), completed June 19, at 100 kips per day.
- Contractor Legacy Foundations (Shimmick Construction). Settlement attributed to densification of Marine/Colma sands. Building remained occupied; completion forecast for late August or early September (2023).

wikis.title: Hong Kong airport's new three-runway system opens
wikis.summary: SCMP (28 Nov 2024) brief on the launch of Hong Kong International Airport's HK$141.5 billion three-runway system.
wikis.body:
- The three-runway system at Hong Kong International Airport launched on Thursday (article published 28 Nov 2024), advancing the city's status as a global transport and aviation hub.
- Cost HK$141.5 billion (US$18.1 billion); started in 2016; "completed within schedule and budget".
- A third runway began operations in 2022; the final stage, reconfiguration of the centre runway, has recently been completed, so all three runways operate simultaneously from Thursday.
- Only a teaser is visible: the article's discussion of opportunities and challenges is not in the text.

wikis.title: Hong Kong Airport's new $18 billion three-runway system now receiving planes
wikis.summary: Simple Flying (28 Nov 2024) on HKG's official launch of its three-runway system and its traffic recovery.
wikis.body:
- HKG officially launched its three-runway system; at the inauguration three aircraft took off and landed simultaneously. Worth $18 billion, took 13 years from public consultation to full operation.
- North runway commissioned November 2022; Centre Runway then closed for reconfiguration (levelling pavement, new entry/exit taxiways, wrap-around taxiways). Flight checks in September and a crash and rescue exercise in October.
- Chief Executive John Lee: will increase capacity and facilitate airline growth. Airport aims in about 10 years to serve 120 million passengers and handle 10 million tonnes of cargo annually. AAHK chairman Fred Lam expects it to give impetus to the Airport City development.
- 2023: 40 million passengers and 276,000 flight movements (about 600% and 100% up on 2022). October 2024: 4.5 million passengers (+21% year on year) versus 5.4 million in October 2019. Incheon handled 55.7 million and Changi 58.5 million in 2023.

wikis.title: One World Trade Center officially opens, November 3, 2014
wikis.summary: History.com entry on the opening of One World Trade Center on the site of the Twin Towers and its design and construction history.
wikis.body:
- One World Trade Center officially opened in Manhattan on November 3, 2014, replacing the Twin Towers destroyed on September 11, 2001. Condé Nast announced it would move its HQ there, occupying floors 20 through 44.
- 2002: Lower Manhattan Development Corporation held an architect competition; Daniel Libeskind won and became master planner. His asymmetrical tower reached a spire of 1,776 feet; Gov. Pataki dubbed it the "Freedom Tower".
- 2004: Silverstein's preferred architect David Childs took over; his symmetrical design unveiled in 2005. NYPD requested a windowless, solid concrete base, criticized by NYT critic Nicolai Ourousoff.
- Cornerstone 2004, construction began summer 2006; tower "topped off" August 2012; spire installed May 2013.
- Offers floor-to-ceiling 360-degree views of Manhattan, Long Island, New Jersey and New York Harbor.

wikis.title: One World Trade Center Fast Facts (CNN)
wikis.summary: CNN fast facts on One World Trade Center: dimensions and a timeline from the 2001 planning to the 2025 WTC Command facility.
wikis.body:
- Tallest building in the United States and second-tallest in the Western Hemisphere. Height 1,362 ft (South Tower height); 1,368 ft with observation deck; 1,776 ft with antenna (year of the Declaration of Independence); 200-ft-square base; 104 stories.
- Timeline: fall 2001 LMDC formed; February 2003 Libeskind's "Memory Foundations" selected; July 2003 David Childs (SOM) selected for Freedom Tower; December 19, 2003 plans unveiled; July 4, 2004 20-ton granite cornerstone laid; May 4, 2005 redesign announced for security; April 26-27, 2006 financing agreement with Larry Silverstein and construction begins; March 26, 2009 no longer called Freedom Tower; May 10, 2013 last pieces of a 408-foot spire bolted, reaching 1,776 ft.
- March 2014 trespassers arrested for climbing the building; November 3, 2014 opens when first tenant Condé Nast moves in; November 12, 2014 two window washers rescued from 68th floor; May 29, 2015 One World Observatory opens (about 1,250 ft up); September 8, 2018 WTC Cortlandt subway station reopens; April 4, 2025 new NYPD WTC Command facility announced.
- Designed to be "the safest commercial structure in the world"; underground Vehicle Screening Center.

wikis.title: Brooklyn Tower (9 DeKalb Avenue): design, history and sales
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the 74-story, 1,035-foot Brooklyn Tower in Downtown Brooklyn, built around the landmark Dime Savings Bank Building, covering design, financing, construction, loan default and sales.
wikis.body:
- **What**: supertall mixed-use, primarily residential skyscraper in Downtown Brooklyn, New York City (formerly 340 Flatbush Avenue Extension and 9 DeKalb Avenue; also 55 and 85 Fleet Street). Developed by JDS Development Group. Tallest building in Brooklyn, first Brooklyn supertall, and tallest in NYC outside Manhattan.
- **Size**: 74 floors, roof 1,035 ft (315 m); floor area 555,734 sq ft. Tower built 2018-2022; topped out October 28, 2021. Architect SHoP Architects; structural engineer WSP Global; contractor JDS Construction; neo-Art Deco style.
- **Dime Savings Bank Building**: designed by Mowbray and Uffinger, built 1906-1908 (opened December 19, 1908), expanded 1931-1932, NYC landmark designated July 19, 1994 (facade and interior). Preserved at the tower's base; clad in Pentelic marble (about 2,000 tons); banking room about 16,750 sq ft with a rotunda of twelve red marble columns.
- **Units and space**: about 150 condominiums and 425 rental apartments (466,000 sq ft); up to 140,000 sq ft commercial space; 120,000 sq ft of amenities including three roof pools over the bank, an indoor 75-ft lap pool, a 66th-floor basketball court advertised as the tallest residential basketball court, an 85th-floor lounge. 30 percent of apartments allocated to affordable housing under the 421-a program.
- **History**: JDS and Chetrit bought 340 Flatbush Avenue Extension in June 2014 for $43.5 million; acquired the bank building from JPMorgan Chase for $90 million in December 2015. Landmarks Preservation Commission approved modifications in April 2016. Bank OZK/Melody Finance $135 million loan February 2017; foundation work began June 2017; superstructure mid-2018. April 2019 loans: $240 million mezzanine from Silverstein Capital and $424.1 million senior loan from Otera Capital.
- **Completion and sales**: Life Time Fitness became first commercial tenant in May 2022 (100,000 sq ft, later downsized to 80,000 sq ft on seven floors in March 2025). Crown completed February 2023. Sales of condos began early 2022; only 18 of 148 sold through April 2024. In March 2024 JDS defaulted on the $240 million mezzanine loan; Silverstein paid $672 million to take over the unsold apartments in the following July. Condo sales resumed June 2025 (Corcoran Sunshine); the fitness center was still not open then. The penthouse was listed December 2025 and unsold in April 2026.
- **Sway**: the tower was observed swaying in high winds less than two years after the developer said it would not; a time-lapse video was widely viewed.
- **Reception**: called "neo Art Deco" by Architectural Digest; Woods Bagot's lobby/amenity design was an Interior Design Best of Year honoree in 2022.

wikis.title: JDSPulse critique of the Brooklyn Tower (9 DeKalb) delays and problems
wikis.summary: A July 7, 2025 opinion-style article listing delays, financial trouble and resident complaints at Michael Stern's Brooklyn Tower.
wikis.body:
- Published Brooklyn, NY, July 7, 2025 by JDSPULSE; critical of Michael Stern of JDS Development.
- Says the tower was pitched as Brooklyn's first supertall with a historic bank dome, pools, terraces and a members'-club style fitness center.
- Says construction was declared complete in 2022 but the building only received its official Certificate of Occupancy on April 25, 2025, as an extension of a temporary permit; residents moved in under TCOs.
- Says Stern defaulted in 2024 on a $240 million mezzanine loan and JDS lost control of the project to Silverstein Capital Partners.
- Pools: a 23-meter indoor pool and three outdoor pools were marketed; the article says they remained closed through 2023 and early 2025 with no confirmed opening date.
- Life Time fitness center: promised at over 100,000 sq ft and slated for 2023; opening pushed to mid-2026 and size cut to 80,000 sq ft; residents offered temporary off-site gym memberships.
- Resident complaints: noisy, vibrating elevators that stall, cracked tiles, peeling grout and paint, failing intercoms and FOB keys, unopened terraces and dog run.
- Silverstein offered discounts on common charges, temporary compensation, off-site gyms, and promised to "complete everything by 2026".

wikis.title: One Za'abeel, Dubai
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on One Za'abeel, a two-tower Dubai complex joined by The Link, a record-setting cantilever completed December 2023.
wikis.body:
- Mixed-use complex in the Za'abeel district of Dubai, UAE; construction began January 2016, completed December 2023, officially opened 10 February 2024.
- Two towers: One Za'abeel Tower (68 floors, 305 m) and One Za'abeel The Residences (59 floors, 235 m; 264 apartments), joined by The Link 100 m above ground.
- The Link is 230 m long with a cantilever of about 66-67.5 m, described as the world's largest of its kind. Guinness World Records recognized it as the longest cantilever building (title dated March 1, 2024).
- The Link was lifted in two phases over 16 days without disrupting four lanes of traffic: an 8,500+ tonne steel structure over 12 days using over 110 jacks, then a 900-tonne cantilever section over four days.
- Architect Nikken Sekkei; developer Ithra Dubai (subsidiary of Investment Corporation of Dubai); main contractor ALEC Engineering & Contracting.
- Includes a One&Only vertical resort, 94 private residences, SIRO lifestyle hotel, restaurants (e.g. La Dame de Pic, Sagetsu by Tetsuya, StreetXO), an infinity pool and observation points on The Link, about 26,000 m2 of offices over 17 levels.
- Integrated into the Dubai World Trade Centre Authority Free Zone in 2024 (Decree No. 18 of 2024).
- Awards: CTBUH Award of Excellence for Best Tall Building in the Middle East & Africa 2024; BNC Publishing "Best Innovation Project of the Year" in November 2020.

wikis.title: One Za'abeel wins Guinness World Record for Longest Cantilevered Building
wikis.summary: Press release dated Dubai, 26 Mar 2024 announcing the Guinness title for The Link at One Za'abeel.
wikis.body:
- Dubai, 26 Mar 2024: One Za'abeel, developed by ICD (Investment Corporation of Dubai), achieved the Guinness World Records title "Longest Cantilevered Building" for its sky concourse, The Link; title cemented 1 March 2024.
- The Link is 230 m long, 100 m above ground, with a cantilever extending 67.277 m beyond the main tower.
- Built in two phases over 16 days without disrupting 4 lanes of live traffic: phase one lifted a steel structure over 8,500 tonnes over 12 days with over 110 jacks; phase two lifted the 900+ ton cantilevered structure over four days.
- The Link houses 8 Michelin-inspired restaurants, the UAE's longest suspended infinity pool and a destination bar, with 360-degree views.
- Quotes from Issam Galadari (Director, One Za'abeel Holdings) and Shaddy Gaad (Guinness World Records).

wikis.title: 40 Leadenhall Street, London
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on 40 Leadenhall (Stanza London), a 35-floor City of London office skyscraper completed 2024.
wikis.body:
- Commercial skyscraper on Leadenhall Street in the City of London, also known as Stanza London. Architect Make Architects; height 155 m (170 m AOD); 35 floors; offices 890,000 sq ft, retail 20,000 sq ft; cost £875 million (estimate).
- The Leadenhall Triangle site was bought by Henderson Global Investors in June 2011 for around £190 million.
- October 2013 planning application (max 170 m AOD); permission granted by the City of London Corporation on 29 May 2014.
- After Brexit the developer said construction would go ahead only once enough office space was pre-let. In October 2019 M&G and Prudential bought the site and would fund construction for £875 m (final development value £1.4 bn). Build started 2020 after Keltbray cleared the site, with no pre-let; completed 2024.
- Design: vertical slices ranging from 7 to 34 storeys at the Leadenhall Street end.
- Tenants listed: Acrisure RE, Ark Syndicate Management, Chubb, Huckletree, Kirkland & Ellis (floors 15-34), McGill, Monex, NKSJ / Sompo Japan, Shawbrook Bank.

wikis.title: How BIM helped build 40 Leadenhall Street
wikis.summary: Trimble blog (August 13, 2024) on steel contractor William Hare's use of Tekla and Trimble Connect at 40 Leadenhall Street.
wikis.body:
- Trimble blog, August 13, 2024. 40 Leadenhall Street is nicknamed the 'Gotham City' project and is one of the largest buildings to have received planning permission in the City of London; 155 m, stepped design toward the Thames, 820,000 sq ft over 34 storeys.
- William Hare handled structural connection design, steel fabrication and installation; Focchi was principal glazing contractor.
- Chris Grime (William Hare Engineering Manager) credits 3D BIM workflows, IFCs and Trimble Connect with keeping construction on schedule.
- Complex elements: two curved first-floor walkways with a spiral staircase, bespoke handrailing and a heavily loaded plate girder framework.
- Tekla Structures models drove fabrication (NC data) and lotting models for deliveries and site progress.
- Expected completion Q4 2024. William Hare won the Public Vote in the 2024 UK Tekla Awards.

wikis.title: East Side Access: history, planning and early construction (part 1)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the LIRR East Side Access project to Grand Central Madison, covering its 1960s-70s origins, stalling, revival and early tunnelling.
wikis.body:
- East Side Access brought Long Island Rail Road trains into a new terminal (Grand Central Madison) under Grand Central in Manhattan via the 63rd Street Tunnel; owner MTA, operator LIRR. Work began September 2007; opened January 25, 2023; 2 mi line, 6.1 mi of track, third-rail 750 V DC; projected ridership 162,000 daily.
- **Origins**: proposals for an LIRR terminal in eastern Midtown arose in 1963; a third and fourth track were added to the 63rd Street tunnel plans in 1966. The 1968 MTA Program for Action proposed a terminal at Third Avenue and 48th Street. Construction of the East River tunnel began 1969; the tunnel was "holed through" October 10, 1972.
- **Grand Central chosen**: after residents' opposition, a 1976 "Grand Central Alternative" was published and in 1977 the MTA board voted to use Grand Central.
- **Stalled**: the 1975 fiscal crisis cancelled the LIRR project; the lower tunnel level was finished anyway, leaving an 8,600-foot "tunnel to nowhere" dormant for three decades. The subway level opened 1989.
- **Revival**: plans in 1995; Senator Al D'Amato sought federal money in 1997; the 1999 capital budget proposed a $1.6 billion LIRR connection; final environmental impact assessment released March 2001, recommending a new station under Grand Central because it was cheaper and less disruptive to Metro-North. After September 11, 2001 the MTA said it would accelerate construction. Final design approved 2002.
- **Construction**: Full funding grant agreement signed December 2006. Manhattan tunnel contract awarded to Dragados/Judlau in July 2006 (total contract $428 million), using two 640-ton tunnel boring machines; first launched September 2007 and reached Grand Central in July 2008; second completed its tunnel September 30, 2008; average 50 feet per day. After Hurricane Sandy (2012) the project was prioritized so LIRR trains could be diverted while East River Tunnels were renovated.
- The Manhattan station has two caverns, each with 1,020-foot platforms, about 100 feet deep, plus storage tracks to 38th Street.

wikis.title: MTA East Side Access project page
wikis.summary: MTA project page (updated Mar 11, 2025) describing the completed East Side Access project and Grand Central Madison.
wikis.body:
- Updated Mar 11, 2025. Status: Complete. Location: Manhattan, Queens. Type: System Expansion.
- Described as the MTA's largest capital project: 40 miles of new tracks, a new terminal beneath Grand Central, and modernization of the busiest intersection of passenger train lines in North America (Harold Interlocking).
- Timeline: 1998 decision to complete; 2001 Environmental Impact Statement approved and construction began; 2007 tunnelling began in Manhattan and Queens; January 2023 Grand Central Madison opened; February 2023 full LIRR service to Grand Central began.
- Grand Central Madison is a new terminal along Madison Avenue between 43 and 48 Streets; service saves commuters up to 40 minutes per day. About 45% of LIRR commuters are expected to go to it.
- Benefits listed: direct connection for all 11 LIRR lines; a 350,000-sq-ft terminal; over 160,000 passengers per day; two new tunnels increase capacity to and from Manhattan by 50%; less crowding at Penn Station.

wikis.title: Phoenix Hill Sports Park, Chengdu
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the Chengdu Phoenix Hill Sports Park, a stadium and arena complex designed by HKS, opened 2022.
wikis.body:
- Sports complex in Jinniu District, Chengdu, Sichuan, China; designed by HKS Architects; constructed 2010-2021, officially opened 2022. (The article carries a "needs more citations" notice.)
- 50,695-seat FIFA-standard football stadium, home of Chengdu Rongcheng FC (Chinese Super League).
- 15,000-seat NBA-standard basketball arena (Jinqiang International Event Center Arena), home of the Sichuan Blue Whales (CBA); hosted the 2021 Summer World University Games basketball and concerts.
- Events: 2021 Summer World University Games basketball; Westlife's The Wild Dreams Tour concert on September 20, 2023.
- Future plans (marked citation needed): a sports museum and hotel complex.

wikis.title: Mumbai Coastal Road
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on Mumbai's Coastal Road (Sambhaji Maharaj Coastal Road), its planning, cost, legal delays, design and phase I opening on 11 March 2024.
wikis.body:
- Planned 29.2 km-class coastal road linking Marine Lines in the south to Kandivali in the north; projected 130,000 vehicles daily; expected to cut South Mumbai-Western Suburbs travel from 2 hours to 40 minutes. Estimated cost ₹13,060 crore (US$1.4 billion), up from ₹12,721 crore because GST on construction rose from 12% to 18% and an unplanned water pipeline had to be shifted. First phase (10.58 km, Princess Street flyover to the Worli end of the Bandra-Worli Sea Link) inaugurated 11 March 2024.
- **Planning**: Wilbur Smith and Associates proposed a road in 1962; Maharashtra CM Prithviraj Chavan proposed a coastal road in 2011; a 2012 committee advised a 35.6 km freeway costing ₹10,000 crore. Clearances: MoEF 8 June 2015 and final 11 May 2017; foundation stone 16 December 2018.
- **Contracts and start**: awarded October 2018 in four packages (Larsen and Toubro packages 1 and 4, ₹7,489 crore; Hindustan Construction Company/Hyundai Development Company packages 2 and 3, ₹2,126 crore). Construction began 13 October 2018, expected complete 2022. The Bombay High Court halted work in April 2019 and cancelled the environmental approvals on 16 July 2019; work was halted; BMC fined contractors ₹31 crore in total for missing the deadline.
- **Design**: 111 hectares reclaimed (largest in independent India), 70 hectares for green space; 7.47 km promenade (first 5.5 km opened August 2025); 8.5 m seawall; 16 floodgates; 10 bus bays; underground parking for 1,856 vehicles; twin tunnels of about 2.07 km between Girgaon Chowpatty and Priyadarshini Park (outer diameter 12.19 m, up to 72 m deep, described as India's first undersea tunnels; Saccardo ventilation, a first in India). Eight lanes including 2 BRT lanes; AECOM general consultant.
- 14 May 2023: CM Eknath Shinde announced the road would be named after Chattrapati Sambhaji Maharaj. Worli interchange redesigned as a 120-metre bow-string bridge after fishermen's protests.
- BMC's Ashwini Bhide: aim is to decongest roads; first phase expected to cut Princess Street to Sea Link travel from 35-45 minutes at peak to under 10.

wikis.title: Etihad Rail passenger service launch schedule (June 2026)
wikis.summary: Khaleej Times article dated 23 Jun 2026 on Etihad Rail's passenger launch: Abu Dhabi-Fujairah from June 30, network launch September 30, 2026.
wikis.body:
- PUBLISHED Tue 23 Jun 2026 (updated same day), by Bahni Bandyopadhyay.
- First phase of passenger services begins June 30 between Abu Dhabi and Fujairah (journey 1 hour 45 minutes); the passenger network is formally launched September 30, 2026.
- Dubai and Al Dhaid stations open September 30, 2026; Al Dhafra region stations December 30, 2026; route completes at Sharjah station on March 30, 2027.
- Announced as Sheikh Khalid bin Mohammed bin Zayed Al Nahyan inaugurated the new passenger station in Mohammed bin Zayed City, Abu Dhabi.
- Tickets on the Abu Dhabi-Fujairah route start from Dh55 (Comfort Class) and Dh120 (Premium Class); fleet of 13 trains, up to 400 passengers each; bookings via the Etihad Rail app and website from June 23, 2026.
- The passenger project was part of the "Fifty Projects" announced in 2021; stations offer cafes, restaurants and retail.

wikis.title: Etihad Rail passenger service set to launch in 2026
wikis.summary: The National article (May 15, 2025) confirming Etihad Rail's passenger service would launch in 2026, with station and speed details.
wikis.body:
- The National, May 15, 2025: Etihad Rail said in an X post that the UAE-wide passenger line will start operations in 2026, confirmed by an Etihad Rail media relations agency; first revealed May 9 in a post about a meeting with Sheikh Hamdan bin Zayed.
- Plans for the passenger line were unveiled in 2021.
- In January (2025) Etihad Rail said the first four passenger stations would be in Abu Dhabi, Dubai, Sharjah and Fujairah; Fujairah in Sakamkam, Sharjah near the airport and University City; Dubai station "believed" to be near Jumeirah Golf Estates (Wasl said the station is being built within the development).
- Trains to travel at 200kph carrying up to 400 passengers; Abu Dhabi-Dubai about 57 minutes; Abu Dhabi-Fujairah 105 minutes.
- Separately in January Etihad Rail announced an electrified high-speed Abu Dhabi-Dubai service (30 minutes); construction not yet started and no launch date given.

wikis.title: Onkalo spent nuclear fuel repository, Finland
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on Posiva's Onkalo deep geological repository at Olkiluoto, its history, construction phases, costs and criticism.
wikis.body:
- Deep geological repository for final disposal of spent nuclear fuel near the Olkiluoto Nuclear Power Plant, Eurajoki, west coast of Finland; described as the world's first long-term disposal facility for spent nuclear fuel. Built and operated by Posiva (owned by Fortum and TVO); based on the KBS-3 method. "Onkalo" means "small cave" or "cavity".
- **History**: 1994 Nuclear Energy Act amendment required Finnish waste to be disposed of in Finland; site screening began 1983; Olkiluoto selected in 2000, ratified by government May 2001. Building permit August 2003, excavation from 2004. Construction licence issued 12 November 2015. Trials began August 2024 with empty canisters in the burial chambers.
- **Phases**: Phase 1 (2004-2009) access tunnel to 420 m; Phase 2 (2009-2011) to final depth 520 m; Phase 3 (2015-2017) repository construction; Phase 4 encapsulation and burial "will begin in 2026". Operational by 2026 and decommissioned by 2100 per the article.
- **Process**: twelve fuel assemblies go in a boron steel canister inside a copper capsule, each placed in its own hole and overpacked with bentonite clay. Construction cost so far around €1 billion; operating for 100 years and closing estimated at an additional €4 billion; the State Nuclear Waste Management Fund holds about €1.4 billion.
- **Criticism**: a 2012 KTH Stockholm study questioned copper capsule corrosion-proofness; SKB follow-up studies refuted it; a 2019 study concluded radiation should not significantly damage canisters during 100,000 years.
- **In media**: documentary Into Eternity (2010), book Deep Time Reckoning (2020) by Vincent Ialenti, Robert Macfarlane's Underland.

wikis.title: Posiva begins drilling disposal holes at Onkalo
wikis.summary: American Nuclear Society news item dated August 31, 2026 on Posiva starting to drill final disposal holes at Finland's Onkalo repository.
wikis.body:
- Nuclear News, August 31, 2026: "Last week" Posiva began drilling holes for final disposal at Onkalo near the Olkiluoto plant.
- The German-made Deposition Hole Boring Machine (made by Herrenknecht) took about 10 hours for the first hole: 8.4 m deep, 1.75 m diameter, in 1.9-billion-year-old bedrock. First hole intended for an iron-copper canister of spent fuel, though test holes have been drilled since 2022.
- The Radiation and Nuclear Safety Authority of Finland gave a favorable safety assessment earlier in August (2026).
- Precision: hole centre point cannot deviate more than 25 mm from vertical centre line. The machine is about 9 m long, over 3 m wide, almost 4 m tall, 78 metric tons, with a 22-ton energy unit and 18.5-ton separator.
- The first three holes will be measured before continuing; Posiva hopes to produce about two finished holes per week once routine.
- About 30 deposition holes will be in a 330-metre disposal tunnel at about 450 m depth; about 100 tunnels totalling 35 km (22 miles) are estimated over the 100-year operating life.
- Posiva construction manager Kimmo Lehtola: "this day has been much anticipated by our team."

wikis.title: Little Island at Pier 55, Manhattan
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on Little Island, the Heatherwick-designed park on the Hudson River atop 132 'tulip' pots, opened May 21, 2021 at a reported $260 million.
wikis.body:
- Public park on the Hudson River near West 13th Street, Meatpacking District/Chelsea, Manhattan; designed by Heatherwick Studio; commissioned by Barry Diller (with Diane von Furstenberg's foundation). 2.4 acres, capacity 1,000; two esplanades at Little West 12th and West 14th Streets; a 687-seat amphitheater ("The Amph"), small stage and concession stands.
- **Structure**: 132 pot-shaped "tulips" (15 to 62 ft above mean waterline) on 267 or 280 concrete pilings reaching at most 200 ft into the riverbed; designed against a 500-year flood; Arup structural design; pots made by Fort Miller Company (upstate New York), assembled by Weeks Marine, barged from Port of Coeymans in about 14 hours. Landscape architect Signe Nielsen; over 350 species of flora, 114 trees and 66,000 bulbs at opening.
- **Timeline**: plans arose November 2014 as "Pier 55"; construction was to begin 2015 with completion 2018 or 2019. Lawsuits by the City Club of New York delayed it; plans scrapped September 2017 after lawsuits and cost overruns (costs had reached $200 million). Revived the next month when Gov. Andrew Cuomo agreed to fund it ($50 million in April 2018, conditional on a city match). Construction began April 2018; symbolic cornerstone December 2018; renamed Little Island in 2019; opened May 21, 2021.
- **Costs**: initial concept was a $35 million structure; early estimates $130-160 million; Diller's foundation gave $100 million plus $30 million planned, city $17 million and state $18 million promised; new estimate $250 million; "It ultimately cost $260 million." Diller's foundation total contribution estimated at $380 million, of which $120 million is upkeep.
- **Lease terms**: at least 51 percent of tickets must be under 30 dollars, including free tickets.

wikis.title: Queen's Wharf Brisbane opening date announced (30 Jun 2024)
wikis.summary: Queen's Wharf Brisbane news post announcing that the first phase of the $3.6 billion precinct opens Thursday, August 29, 2024, with a phased rollout.
wikis.body:
- News dated 30 Jun '24: The Star Brisbane at Queen's Wharf released the attractions opening on Thursday, August 29, 2024 as first phase of a multi-phased reveal of the $3.6 billion entertainment precinct (not all opening that day). Quotes from Star Brisbane CEO Daniel Finch.
- From late August into September and through the rest of 2024 new restaurants, bars, public spaces will open across the previously underutilised 12 hectares of river's edge.
- **First phase (August-September 2024)**: 7.5 hectares of public space including Neville Bonner Bridge (linking to South Bank), upgraded Bicentennial Bikeway, Miller Park, Sky Deck viewing platform, Leisure Deck on Level Seven; The Landing green space after Riverfire; The Star Grand with 340 hotel rooms including four penthouses and Sokyo; Event Centre with a 1,440-seat ballroom; The Terrace Dining (Level Four); Level Five and Six: LiveWire, Sports Bar, Fat Noodle, Food Quarter, Cherry, Main Casino Floor and Premium Gaming Rooms (subject to regulatory approvals).
- **Later phases**: Dorsett and Rosewood hotel tower, Velo Cafe, luxury retail, heritage buildings, gymnasium.
- Finch also stressed The Star's remediation plan, subject to regulatory approvals.

wikis.title: Building Australia's $3.6bn Queen's Wharf megaproject (The B1M)
wikis.summary: Sponsored (Nemetschek Group) B1M article on how Queen's Wharf Brisbane's AUD 3.6bn build uses information modelling software.
wikis.body:
- Contains paid promotion for Nemetschek Group; narrated by Fred Mills.
- Queen's Wharf spans 26 hectares of land and water, described as the largest district development in the southern hemisphere. Led by Destination Brisbane Consortium; AUD 3.6BN; six new towers, restored heritage buildings; hotels, apartments, 12 football pitches of public space, a new bridge; aims to attract more than 1.5 million extra tourists and create over 8,000 jobs.
- Excavation: a 26-metre hole with almost half a million cubic metres removed, for a five-storey basement car park; material sent to Brisbane Airport reclamation and the BNE Auto Mall; excavation completed 2019, works at street level by end of 2020.
- Lead architect Cottee Parker; 16 software tools across 39 companies; DBM Vircon manages over 340 models and processes 215 models weekly. Nemetschek products used: Graphisoft Archicad, Solibri (error checking), Bluebeam Revu (cut drawing review time by 50%), dRofus (data). About 10,000 times more documents than a domestic building. Information modelling continues over a 99-year lease.

wikis.title: Germany's first 3D-printed house opens in Beckum
wikis.summary: Construction Index report (28 Jul 21) on Peri's 3D-printed single-family house in Beckum, North Rhine-Westphalia.
wikis.body:
- 28 Jul 2021: Peri's 3D-printed single-family house in Beckum, North Rhine-Westphalia, is ready for occupancy; officially opened by minister Ina Scharrenbach. Subsidised by the state's 'Innovative Building' funding programme.
- Printed with a Cobod BOD2 concrete printer (Peri acquired a stake in Cobod in 2018); printing started 17 September 2020. Printing mortar 'i.tech 3D' from HeidelbergCement; mixing technology from M-Tec Mathis Technik; approval support by Schiessl Gehlen Sodeikat; approval tests by Centrum Baustoffe Munchen of TU Munich.
- Designed by Mense-Korte Ingenieure & Architekten (Waldemar Korte quoted).
- Peri's Thomas Imbacher: the project shows the technology "is ready for the market"; Peri has since printed the largest apartment building in Europe in Wallenhausen and the first residential building in Tempe, Arizona.

wikis.title: PERI press release: Germany's first printed house officially opened
wikis.summary: PERI press release dated 28 July 2021 on the official opening of the 3D-printed house in Beckum.
wikis.body:
- 28 July 2021, Weissenhorn/Beckum: the single-family house printed by PERI with a COBOD BOD2 printer was officially opened by Ina Scharrenbach, NRW Minister for Home, Municipal Affairs, Construction and Equality; state-subsidised under "Innovative Building".
- Minister: "The three Ds - digital, dynamic, print-ready - have been implemented in Beckum"; only more housing provides affordable rents.
- Thomas Imbacher (PERI): the technology is ready for the market; PERI has since printed Europe's largest apartment building in Wallenhausen and the first residential building in Tempe, Arizona.
- Planned by MENSE-KORTE ingenieure+architekten. Printing started September 17, 2020; mortar "i.tech 3D" (HeidelbergCement), mixing technology from m-tec mathis technik; approval support by Schiessl Gehlen Sodeikat, tests by Centrum Baustoffe Munchen (TU Munich).

wikis.title: Otis completes Empire State Building elevator modernization with glass mast car
wikis.summary: Otis press release (Oct 14, 2019) on the custom glass elevator to the 102nd floor Observatory and the completed modernization.
wikis.body:
- NEW YORK, Oct. 14, 2019 (PRNewswire): Otis delivered and installed a custom-made glass elevator (Otis Gen2 with steel-reinforced flat belts) to carry visitors to the renovated 102nd floor Observatory, essentially completing one of the largest and most complex modernization projects in Otis's 166-year history.
- Runs between the 86th and 102nd floors with a light show on the hoistway wall and a curated soundtrack; the 102nd floor landing has glass hoistway walls.
- Otis installed the original elevators in 1931; Empire State Realty Trust entrusted the modernization to Otis eighty years later; it began in 2011.
- Otis ReGen drive uses 50-75 percent less energy than the original system; CompassPlus dispatching is 50 percent faster at peak times.
- The elevators carry 10 million tenants, guests and visitors each year. Quotes from Tom Vining (Otis Americas) and Jean-Yves Ghazi (Observatory).

wikis.title: Custom glass mast car tops off Empire State Building modernization (FacilitiesNet)
wikis.summary: FacilitiesNet case study dated December 12, 2019 on Otis's glass elevator to the Empire State Building's 102nd floor Observatory.
wikis.body:
- December 12, 2019, Elevators case study. Otis installed the original elevators in 1931; 80 years later Empire State Realty Trust entrusted it with modernization (begun 2011).
- A custom-made Otis Gen2 glass elevator with steel-reinforced flat belts carries visitors between the 86th and 102nd floors, with a light show projected on the hoistway wall and curated soundtrack; the 102nd floor landing has glass hoistway walls.
- Otis ReGen regenerative drive uses 50 to 75 percent less energy than the original system; CompassPlus dispatching improves peak travel times (text repeats the Otis release).

wikis.title: Brooklyn Bridge opens (History.com, May 24, 1883)
wikis.summary: History.com 'This Day in History' entry on the May 24, 1883 opening of the Brooklyn Bridge and its construction under John, Washington and Emily Roebling.
wikis.body:
- The Brooklyn Bridge over the East River opened May 24, 1883, connecting New York and Brooklyn; dedication presided over by President Chester A. Arthur and Governor Grover Cleveland. Largest suspension bridge built to that date, with a 1,595-foot span; "the world's first steel suspension bridge".
- Designed by John A. Roebling (born Germany 1806), who was fatally injured (toes crushed by a boat; died of tetanus three weeks later) just before construction began in 1869; he was the first of more than two dozen people who died building it. Son Washington A. Roebling (32) became chief engineer.
- Foundations: timber caissons sunk to 44 feet (Brooklyn) and 78 feet (New York); more than a hundred workers suffered compression sickness; Washington became bedridden in 1872. Wife Emily Roebling effectively took over as chief engineer and spokesperson; she was given the first ride across, with a rooster in her lap. Each of four main cables has 19 strands of 278 wires.
- Within 24 hours an estimated 250,000 people walked across. Called "eighth wonder of the world". In 1898 Brooklyn merged with New York City to form Greater New York.

wikis.title: Brooklyn Bridge (Wikipedia)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the Brooklyn Bridge, its 1870-1883 construction, design, later changes, renovations and cultural role.
wikis.body:
- Cable-stayed suspension bridge across the East River between Manhattan and Brooklyn; opened May 24, 1883, the first fixed East River crossing and longest suspension bridge in the world then; main span 1,595.5 ft (486.3 m), total length 6,016 ft, towers 272 ft, deck 127 ft above mean high water. Renamed the Brooklyn Bridge officially in 1915. Daily traffic 121,930 (2019).
- Designed by John A. Roebling; chief engineer son Washington Roebling, assisted by Emily Warren Roebling. Construction started 1870, overseen by the New York Bridge Company (controlled by Tammany Hall) and took thirteen years amid controversies.
- Construction: caissons in compressed air caused decompression sickness (Between January 25 and May 31, 1872, Dr. Smith treated 110 cases; three died); by 1876 three workers had fallen from the towers and nine died in other accidents; an estimated 27 men died overall. Main cables strung from 1876-1878.
- After opening: on May 30, 1883 a stampede at the Brooklyn approach killed at least twelve; the bridge carried horse-drawn vehicles and elevated railway lines until 1950. P.T. Barnum's Jumbo led 21 elephants over it. Five daily inspectors after 1901 cost $250,000 a year. Renovated in the 1950s, 1980s and 2010s; project cost rose from $508 million in 2010 to $811 million in 2016. Designated National Historic Landmark (January 29, 1964), NYC landmark (August 24, 1967).
- Only passenger vehicles, pedestrians and bicycles permitted; the article also covers stunts, crimes and love locks (removal costs $100,000 per year).

wikis.title: Virgin Hyperloop completes first test with passengers (CNN)
wikis.summary: CNN Business article (Nov 8-9, 2020) on Virgin Hyperloop's first passenger ride on its 500 m Las Vegas test track.
wikis.body:
- PUBLISHED Nov 8, 2020, updated Nov 9, 2020, by Matt McFarland, CNN Business.
- Virgin Hyperloop gave the first ride on its test track Sunday in Las Vegas; the pod reached only 100 mph on the 500 meter track versus the 600 mph advocates have promised. The article says it will be "years" before the public can potentially ride.
- First riders: CTO Josh Giegel and Director of Passenger Experience Sara Luchian, in a two-person pod with seat belts and small windows. Future commercial pods would seat 25 to 30 people, carrying "tens of thousands of passengers per hour".
- Hurdles: the company still needs to raise money for a six-mile, $500 million test facility in West Virginia to certify the technology; Walder believes certification in 2025 or 2026 and hyperloop projects before the decade ends.
- Background: Elon Musk announced a concept in 2013; in 2017 he tweeted "verbal govt approval" for a Washington-New York tunnel (29 minutes), which is mired in environmental review; the Boring Company builds a Las Vegas "Loop". Virgin Hyperloop was founded as Hyperloop Technologies in 2014; Richard Branson joined the board in 2017 and the name changed.

wikis.title: Virgin Hyperloop tests first passenger journey in Nevada (CNBC)
wikis.summary: CNBC article (Nov 9, 2020) on the first human ride in a hyperloop pod: 500 m in 15 seconds at about 100 mph.
wikis.body:
- Published Mon, Nov 9 2020, by Sam Shead. Virgin Hyperloop announced Sunday it transported two staff members (CTO Josh Giegel and passenger experience director Sara Luchian) 500 meters in 15 seconds at a test site outside Las Vegas, reaching around 100 mph (160 km/h), versus the 1,000-kmh-plus speeds it hopes for. The site had already completed over 400 unoccupied tests.
- Hyperloop fires a pod through a low-pressure tunnel using electric propulsion and electromagnetic levitation. Elon Musk said in 2013 it would allow Los Angeles to San Francisco in about 30 minutes. The article says Virgin Hyperloop is the only company to have tested with passengers.
- Richard Branson: "we have shown that this spirit of innovation will in fact change the way people everywhere live, work, and travel". The article says it is unclear whether the concept will be safe at full speed; Virgin Hyperloop has raised over $400 million.

wikis.title: KPIX footage: Transamerica Pyramid construction nears completion (1972)
wikis.summary: Bay Area Television Archive catalogue entry for a Feb 15, 1972 KPIX-TV news report on the Transamerica Pyramid nearing completion.
wikis.body:
- Item: 3:07 KPIX-TV newsfilm dated 2/15/1972, reporter Ben Williams, showing construction nearing completion at 600 Montgomery Street, San Francisco; includes an interview with a construction team member about modern safety features.
- Notes: the first tenant to open for business was Crocker Bank, with a ribbon cutting and Open Day on November 27, 1972. The Pyramid was San Francisco's tallest skyscraper from 1972 until 2017, when Salesforce Tower surpassed it.
- 16mm color reversal print scanned in 4K in September 2024; copyright CBS5 KPIX-TV.

wikis.title: Transamerica Pyramid, San Francisco (Wikipedia)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the 48-story, 853 ft Transamerica Pyramid at 600 Montgomery Street, completed 1972, with its history, design and recent ownership.
wikis.body:
- Pyramid-shaped 48-story modernist skyscraper at 600 Montgomery Street, San Francisco Financial District; 853 ft (260 m); construction started December 1969, completed 1972; cost US$32 million. Architects William Pereira and Harry D. Som; contractor Dinwiddie Construction. Tallest San Francisco building from 1972 until Salesforce Tower surpassed it in 2017/2018. Eighth-tallest in the world on completion.
- Commissioned by Transamerica CEO John (Jack) R. Beckett, who chose the pyramid to let light in to the street. Built on the site of the Montgomery Block (demolished 1959). Detractors called it "Pereira's Prick".
- Transamerica was acquired by Aegon in 1999 and left the building in 2011. In 2020 Aegon sold it to SHVO and Deutsche Finance America for $650 million; in 2022 Norman Foster was hired for a $250 million renovation. "As of April 2026" acquired by Yoda PLC (Cyprus-based, led by Ioannis Papalekas).
- Features: top 212 ft spire; virtual observation deck (27th-floor deck closed 2001 per official site); "Crown Jewel" beacon lit at Christmas, Independence Day and 9/11 anniversary; 3,678 windows; crushed-quartz facade; 9-ft-thick foundation from a 3-day continuous pour; half-acre Redwood Park at the base.
- Thought to have been an intended target of the foiled 1995 Bojinka plot; one of 39 SF high rises flagged by the USGS as potentially vulnerable due to a flawed welding technique.

wikis.title: Crown Sydney (One Barangaroo)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on Crown Sydney, the 271.3 m, 75-floor WilkinsonEyre tower at Barangaroo: planning, licence controversy, construction and design.
wikis.body:
- Skyscraper in Barangaroo, Sydney (also One Barangaroo, informally "Packer's Pecker"); designed by WilkinsonEyre; 271.3 m (890 ft), 75 floors; tallest in Sydney, 4th tallest in Australia. Developed by Crown Resorts: hotel, apartments, casino and hospitality. Construction began October 2016, topped out March 2020, inaugurated to the public 28 December 2020.
- **Background**: hotel concepts from 2010; Crown presented a A$1 billion+ proposal in February 2012; NSW government received a $100 million upfront licence fee (Deloitte calculated a $250 million alternative offer superior); casino licence approval November 2013; final approval June 2016. Millers Point Fund's legal challenge dismissed in August 2016.
- **Licence**: a 2020 inquiry (Patricia Bergin) led to ILGA banning Crown from opening the casino in December 2020 after money-laundering admissions on 17 November 2020; Bergin reported on 1 February 2021 that Crown was unsuitable. Blackstone takeover accepted February 2022 (A$8.9 billion). Conditional licence June 2022, opening August 2022; unconditional licence reinstated 23 April 2024.
- **Construction**: Lendlease main contractor; excavation 2016-2017; cranes February-March 2018; about 7,000 triangular glass panels; top-down core construction.
- **Design**: 2013 competition (WilkinsonEyre chosen unanimously, May 2013); three twisting "petals" with 60-degree twist; floor area 146,500 m2.

wikis.title: Dubai Creek Tower (Wikipedia)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the proposed Calatrava-designed Dubai Creek Tower, its 2016 groundbreaking, foundations, delays and 2024 redesign.
wikis.body:
- Proposed supported observation tower at Dubai Creek Harbour, Dubai; architect Santiago Calatrava; developer Emaar Properties; listed cost US$1 billion (preliminary AED 3.67 billion); construction start October 11, 2016; estimated completion 2030.
- Emaar talked about a minimum height of at least 1,300 metres; in February 2024 it was reportedly reduced to less than the Burj Khalifa. Minaret-inspired design with cable stays and an oval "bud" with ten observation decks including The Pinnacle Room.
- Groundbreaking attended by Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum in October 2016; foundations completed by BESIX subsidiary Six Construct in May 2018; main construction never began; as of July 2019 the tender was ongoing.
- 4 April 2020 Emaar halted construction due to COVID-19 (no activity for almost two years); renders removed from the website in July or August 2020. August 2023: redesign confirmed. February 2024: Alabbar said height would be reduced; construction restarted March 2024. January 2026: Alabbar said the tender would launch within three months; June 2026: he said the tender was delayed.

wikis.title: Emaar to tender Dubai Creek Tower within three months (Khaleej Times)
wikis.summary: Khaleej Times report (14 Jan 2026) that Emaar founder Mohamed Alabbar says a tender for the redesigned Dubai Creek Tower will be issued within three months.
wikis.body:
- PUBLISHED Wed 14 Jan 2026, by Waheed Abbas. Alabbar, speaking at the Dubai International Project Management Forum: "The tender for the Creek Tower will be offered in three months. We have changed the design, even though the previous one had already been announced."
- Emaar first unveiled the tower before the Covid-19 pandemic, promoting it as surpassing the Burj Khalifa; the project was put on hold as the design was revised. Alabbar declined to disclose construction details or cost.
- Alabbar: "After the Burj Khalifa, altitude alone is no longer enough." Mentions Saudi Arabia's Kingdom Tower (mile-high) with construction reported to have resumed.
- Also: Dubai Square project launched November 2025 at Dubai Creek Harbour, with Dubai Square Mall scheduled to open within three years, estimated cost Dh180 billion.

wikis.title: Dubai Creek Tower pile cap completed (Emaar, Oct 2018)
wikis.summary: Emaar press release dated OCT 01, 2018 on completion of the Dubai Creek Tower pile cap two months ahead of schedule.
wikis.body:
- OCT 01, 2018: concrete placement for the pile cap completed two months ahead of schedule; pouring began September (2017) and passed 50 per cent in January 2018.
- Pile cap about 20 m thick, multi-layered reinforced concrete; 50,000 cubic meters of concrete (about 120,000 tonnes, "the weight of the CN Tower") and about 16,000 tonnes of steel reinforcement (just over twice the Eiffel Tower).
- Groundbreaking October 2016 by Sheikh Mohammed; 145 barrette piles tested to a world-record load of 36,000 tonnes and laid 72 metres deep. Over 450 skilled professionals on site.
- Designed by Santiago Calatrava Valls; observation decks include the Pinnacle Room and VIP Observation Garden Decks; located in the 6 sq km Dubai Creek Harbour near Ras Al Khor Wildlife Sanctuary.

wikis.title: Wood City Supercell, Helsinki (ark)
wikis.summary: Short ark.fi project page for Wood City Supercell, an eight-storey wooden office building in Helsinki's Jatkasaari, completed 2021.
wikis.body:
- Offices by Anttinen Oiva Architects (Selina Anttinen, Vesa Oiva, Teemu Halme), at Jatkasaarenlaituri 1, Helsinki; gross area 13,000 m2; completion 2021.
- Eight-storey office building in the Jatkasaari district that "holds the record for being the largest in Finland when measured in the quantity of wood used".
- A related article (1.2.2021) says the wooden block is an example of the new scale of wooden urban building and that since January 2021 it has been occupied by mobile game company Supercell. Published in 2-2021, Tradition and Renewal.

wikis.title: Wood City, Helsinki: Supercell's wood headquarters and Finnish wood construction
wikis.summary: Wood magazine article (Puuinfo, published 16.9.2021) on the Wood City project in Jätkäsaari, Helsinki, focused on the Supercell office building's structure, collaboration, safety and moisture management.
wikis.body:
- Wood City is a series of wood buildings in the Jätkäsaari district of Helsinki, a collaboration of SRV and Stora Enso. Article text by Mia Heiskanen and Heidi Tetteh; first published June 2021 in Wood magazine 1/2021.
- Completed: two residential apartment buildings (phase 1) and an office building (phase 2); a hotel is "still planned" (phase 3). All buildings are eight storeys. A shared three-storey car park (170 spaces) is part of phase 2.
- The office is the new headquarters of Supercell and is "the largest wood office building in Finland as measured by the amount of wood used", said to bind the CO2 equivalent of a year's driving for 600 passenger cars.
- Structure: ground floor, basement and stiffening shafts are concrete; floors 1-7 are wood with load-bearing LVL pillars, beams and slabs; wood-clad facades. LVL from Stora Enso's Varkaus facility (wood mostly from private forest owners in Savo); CLT from a Stora Enso facility in Sweden.
- Supercell aimed at "the world's best work environment"; the project promoted an open office culture and collaboration. Biggest change: team-space layout changes in December 2018 while the concrete frame was being poured. Subcontractors met in Last Planner sessions twice a week. A 1:1 scale model of a team space was built; quality walks and gates were used.
- Site culture: SRV's first stocking-foot site office, a grill area, a monthly lunch of a subcontractor worker management team, lunches offered by Supercell.
- Safety: SRV accident rate on the site was zero; site average 17.88 over 475 thousand hours worked; 1,278 safety observations in 2019, highest across SRV sites.
- Moisture management: detailed plan, weekly rounds reported to the Helsinki Building Inspectorate; site received the 2020 Rakentamisen Ruusu award.
- Facts: developer Supercell Oy; architect Anttinen Oiva Arkkitehdit Oy; main contractor SRV Rakennus Oy; schedule 6/2018 - 12/2020; total area 19,150 brm2 (office 13,650, parking 5,500); volume 61,200 rkm3; 8 floors + basement, 7 lifts. Wood City to be presented at Wood Day on November 4, 2021.

wikis.title: 51WORLD unveils all-element virtual scenarios at Earth Clone 3
wikis.summary: GlobeNewswire release (6 Jan 2020) on 51WORLD's digital-twin 'all-element virtual scenarios' launched at the Earth Clone 3 event in Shanghai on December 18, and the rename from 51VR.
wikis.body:
- 51WORLD (previously 51VR) unveiled its all-element virtual scenarios at the Earth Clone 3 (EC3) press conference at the InterContinental Shanghai Hongqiao NECC on December 18; more than one thousand experts attended.
- The scenarios combine virtual reality, geographic information, physical simulation and interaction, aimed at smart cities, smart transportation, smart vehicle, real estate, etc. Founder and CEO Archer Li presented a city-level Shanghai demo (HD graphics, large scale, real-time rendering, rapid auto-generation of city models).
- Data from satellite remote sensing, tilt photography, urban GIS/DEM, high-precision maps and BIM/CAD is processed with self-developed tools "ten times faster (or even more)" than by hand.
- Five levels: L1 preliminary simulation scene, rapid automatic urban grid; L2 detailed buildings, roads, greenery, traffic flow; L3 more realistic with dynamic lights, shadows, traffic flow; L4 for simulation and AI training with traffic signals, vehicles, pedestrians; L5 replicates the real world to every detail incl. lighting and physical conditions.
- Cases: an IOC management digital twin platform for Huawei's Shenzhen headquarters; an intelligent traffic digital twin cloud control platform with China Transinfo; a micro-urban real-time traffic flow with Beijing Transport Institute. Customers can use SuperAPI; 51Cloud is a real-time cloud rendering platform; 2019 was the first year of commercialized 5G.
- After the keynote, the name 51VR was officially upgraded to 51WORLD. Afternoon fora covered smart city, smart transportation and digital real estate.

wikis.title: 51WORLD digital twin for Shanghai city rail at the 2023 Infrastructure Quality Enhancement Design Exhibition
wikis.summary: 51WORLD Medium post (Jul 4, 2023) on the digital twin system it built with Shanghai Shentie shown at the 2023 Shanghai Infrastructure Quality Enhancement Design Exhibition.
wikis.body:
- The "Integrated Innovation, City Creation" 2023 Shanghai Infrastructure Quality Enhancement Design Exhibition opened at the Shanghai City Planning Exhibition Center; organized by the Shanghai Municipal Planning and Natural Resources Bureau, Shanghai City Construction Investment Group, Shanghai Shentong Metro Group and Shanghai Shentie Investment. Described as the first Shanghai exhibition focused on planning and design of municipal infrastructure.
- Deputy Mayor Zhang Xiaohong announced the opening; Wang Weiren, Zhang Yuxin and Li Xiangning (chief curator, Tongji University) took part. Sections: Prologue, Leaping Forward on the Road, Source of a Better Life, City Renewal Network.
- Highlight: a digital twin system developed by 51WORLD with Shanghai Shentie, guided by the Planning and Natural Resources Bureau, with three-dimensional scenes at macro (Shanghai overall), meso (four lines) and micro (sixteen stations) levels. At station level visitors get aerial and roaming views and can adjust sunlight and weather (rain, clouds).
- Interactive, two-way; visitors can give feedback via questionnaires. "In the future, more city rail transit systems will grow within the digital twin system."

wikis.title: SoFi Stadium: overview, design, financing and construction (Wikipedia, part 1)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia's account of SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, California: specs, design, awards, site history, financing and start of construction.
wikis.body:
- Multi-purpose stadium in Inglewood, California on the former Hollywood Park Racetrack site; opened September 8, 2020 (groundbreaking November 17, 2016; built 2016-2020). Capacity 70,240, expandable to over 100,000; translucent ETFE roof. Home of the Los Angeles Rams and Los Angeles Chargers; LA Bowl 2021-2025.
- Hosted Super Bowl LVI (2022), the 2023 College Football Playoff National Championship, WrestleMania 39, the 2023 CONCACAF Gold Cup final, and eight 2026 FIFA World Cup matches including the US opening match vs Paraguay. Will host Super Bowl LXI in 2027 and the opening ceremony and swimming for the 2028 Summer Olympics.
- Design by HKS: canopy of 302 ETFE panels (46 openable) on a cable net, about a million square feet, with 27,000 LED pucks; YouTube Theater attached (6,000 seats). Infinity Screen by Samsung: double-sided 4K HDR, 2.2 million pounds (1,000 t), 80 million pixels, 260-speaker JBL system and 56 5G antennas. Artificial turf because two NFL teams share it. Open sides allowed the first NFL lightning delay on October 4, 2021.
- Awards include StadiumDB "Stadium of the Year", 2021 ASCE Outstanding Architectural Engineering Project.
- Cost: estimated $5-6 billion; $2.66 billion at construction start; NFL debt ceiling raised to $4.963 billion (March 2018); another $500 million loans in May 2020, total $5.5 billion, "the most expensive stadium ever built".
- History: Hollywood Park raced 1938 to December 2013. Kroenke bought 60 acres in 2014; on January 5, 2015 Stockbridge Capital and Kroenke Sports & Entertainment partnered; Inglewood City Council approved 5-0 on February 24, 2015; NFL approved relocation 30-2 on January 12, 2016 over a rival Carson plan ($1.85 billion). Turner Construction and AECOM Hunt built it; HKS designed it (announced July 14, 2016).

wikis.title: SoFi Stadium: the story of an LA icon
wikis.summary: Discover Los Angeles guide (Apr 6, 2026) to SoFi Stadium's design, events, tours, shop and food.
wikis.body:
- Opened September 2020 in Inglewood; home of the Rams and Chargers; developed by E. Stanley Kroenke. 3.1 million sq ft, "the largest in the NFL"; seats 70,000 (expandable to 100,000), 260+ luxury suites, 13,000+ premium seats.
- Hosted Super Bowl LVI (2022), CFP National Championship (January 2023), CONCACAF Gold Cup Final (July 2023); a 2026 World Cup host venue; co-hosts Opening and Closing Ceremonies of the 2028 Summer Olympics. Centerpiece of the 298-acre Hollywood Park (retail, offices, hotel, 2,500 residences, parks).
- Design by HKS; seating bowl 100 feet below grade due to FAA height limits near LAX; landscape by Studio-MLA; 25-acre Lake Park with a 5.5-acre lake of reclaimed water.
- Infinity Screen by Samsung: 70,000 sq ft, dual-sided, 122 feet above the field, spans 120 yards, weighs 2.2 million pounds, 268 speakers.
- Events named: Blackpink, The Weeknd, George Strait & Chris Stapleton, Hard Summer, Shakira with Black Eyed Peas, Chris Brown. Stadium tours and Rally Days; The Equipment Room team store (daily 11:30am-6pm); LA Eats menus by Jon Shook and Vinny Dotolo.

wikis.title: Afsluitdijk causeway reinforcement wins second place in 2025 Jan Agema Award
wikis.summary: Rijkswaterstaat news (20 October 2025) on the Afsluitdijk reinforcement placing second in the 2025 Jan Agema Award, with details of the Levvel design.
wikis.body:
- Announced at Waterbouwdag on Thursday, 9 October 2025. The Jan Agema Award is given once every five years for the best, most innovative recent hydraulic engineering project; 13 submitted, 3 nominated; winner was the Borssele Wind Energy project.
- Jury: praised "the innovative reinforcement with an eye for landscape, ecology, and the specially developed Levvel blocks, which are being emulated worldwide."
- Afsluitdijk completed 1932; the Levvel consortium (BAM, Van Oord, Rebel, Invesis) started reinforcement in 2019 and completed it in 2023 for Rijkswaterstaat. Design was tested extensively in the Delta Flume; the dike lies between 2 Natura 2000 areas.
- Innovations: Levvel block on the lower slope, ribbed Basalton-Quattroblock facing on the upper slope; approximately 60% less concrete than a traditional design; placement machines Ballerina and Titan; a semi-automatic factory for 70,000 Levvel blocks; 32 km of dike.
- Video transcript: standards based on a once-in-10,000-year superstorm; protects against sea level rise (0.35 m) until at least 2050; some parts (revetment) built to last 100 years; "Adaptive Delta Management".

wikis.title: Afsluitdijk dike reinforcement project by consortium Levvel
wikis.summary: Project page describing why and how the Afsluitdijk was reinforced with Levvel-blocs and Quattroblocks between 2019 and 2023.
wikis.body:
- Consortium Levvel (BAM, Van Oord and Rebel) was commissioned by Rijkswaterstaat to reinforce the Afsluitdijk so it can withstand surge overflows. Status: "Ready".
- Why: the dike has protected the Netherlands since 1932 but "no longer complies with current legislated water safety standards"; climate change brings sea level rise and more extreme weather.
- How: on the Wadden Sea side, raise the dike by almost two metres; Quattroblocks on the top, Levvel-blocs on the bottom (a smaller Quattroblock version between Kornwerderzand and the Frisian coast). The IJsselmeer side can withstand 10 litres of water per second per metre. A recreational cycling and hiking path on the Wadden Sea side.
- Levvel-blocs: 200,000 m3 less concrete, 56% less CO2 emissions; 6,500 kg each; interlock like Lego; rough top and notches let salt-tolerant plants return. 70,000 blocs total; crane pontoon Titan places 35 metres per day; about 100 blocks per day made in an automated plant in Harlingen (demolished after the project); blocks shipped and placed from the water so the dike stays open to traffic.
- Adaptive Delta Management: complies with standards until at least 2050; sea-side revetment lasts at least 100 years.
- When: work started in 2019 and was completed in 2023.

wikis.title: Central Park Tower commences closings
wikis.summary: Extell press release (Feb 25, 2021) announcing closings began at Central Park Tower, the tallest residential building in the world at 1,550 feet.
wikis.body:
- Published Feb 25, 2021 (PRNewswire). Extell Development Company said Central Park Tower, "the tallest residential building in the world at 1,550 feet", commenced closings and would welcome its first residents. Quote from founder and chairman Gary Barnett.
- Awarded the 2021 Award of Excellence by the CTBUH as "The Best Tall Building 400 meters and above". Designed by Adrian Smith + Gordon Gill Architecture; interiors by Rottet Studio.
- 179 two-to-eight-bedroom residences starting on the 32nd floor, from 1,435 sq ft to over 17,500 sq ft.
- Central Park Club: about 50,000 sq ft over three floors; the 100th floor is "the highest private residential club in the world"; a 14th-floor screening room and lounges; 16th-floor fitness and wellness; outdoor terrace with pool.
- Base: Nordstrom's first full-line department store, about 320,000 sq ft, seven storeys, opened in 2019, with resident access programming. Entrances on 57th and 58th Streets.

wikis.title: Central Park Tower: overview, site and history (Wikipedia, part 1)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia intro to the 1,550 ft Central Park Tower at 217 West 57th Street, Manhattan, with its specs, site and construction timeline.
wikis.body:
- Residential supertall at 217 West 57th Street on Billionaires' Row; designed by Adrian Smith + Gordon Gill Architecture; 1,550 ft (472.4 m), 98 above-ground stories plus three basements (top story numbered 136).
- Second-tallest building in New York City, the US and the Western Hemisphere; 15th tallest in the world; tallest primarily residential building in the world and tallest outside Asia by roof height.
- Developed by Extell Development Company and Shanghai Municipal Investment Group. Nordstrom store in the basement and first five stories opened in 2019. Cantilever over the Art Students League building. 179 condominiums averaging 5,000 sq ft; amenity floors 14-16 and a private club on floor 100. Main contractor Lendlease; structural engineer WSP Global; 11 elevators; 1,285,308 sq ft floor area.
- Construction started September 17, 2014 (excavation May 2014, above-ground early 2015); topped out September 17, 2019; completed 2020. Cost $3 billion. Delays arose when two buildings (225 West 57th Street and 1780 Broadway) were considered for landmark status. Controversies included the cantilever and the death of a security guard.

wikis.title: 111 West 57th Street (Steinway Tower): overview and architecture (Wikipedia, part 1)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia intro to 111 West 57th Street, the SHoP-designed residential tower atop Steinway Hall in Manhattan.
wikis.body:
- Also called Steinway Tower; Billionaires' Row skyscraper. Developed by JDS Development Group (Michael Stern) and Property Markets Group (Kevin P. Maloney). Architect SHoP Architects; structural engineer WSP; MEP Jaros, Baum & Bolles. Cost $2 billion; 59 units; 14 elevators; construction began July 8, 2015; topped out October 2019; completed 2022.
- Height 1,428 ft (435 m); roof slab 1,257 ft 6 in; 84 stories (top numbered 91; some floor numbers skipped); tower site about 59 by 75 ft; "the thinnest skyscraper in the world with a width-to-height ratio of about 1:24".
- Base: Steinway Hall (Warren & Wetmore, completed October 27, 1925 for Steinway & Sons), a NYC landmark, renovated 2019-2021; the tower is a Neo-Art Deco design.
- Neighbors: Carnegie Hall, 57th Street subway station (F, M); part of Billionaires' Row with 432 Park Avenue, 220 Central Park South, Central Park Tower, One57.

wikis.title: 10 facts about Steinway Tower (111 West 57th Street), the world's thinnest skyscraper
wikis.summary: Architizer Journal list (updated November 2021) of ten facts about SHoP Architects' Steinway Tower in Manhattan.
wikis.body:
- Topped out (concrete form) in April 2019; exterior hoist dismantled by March 2021; the building is described as complete. JDS Development's Michael Stern and Property Markets Group's Kevin Maloney called the superstructure completion "a major construction milestone".
- Width-to-height ratio approx. 1:24, the world's most slender skyscraper; 1,428 ft (435 m), taller than 432 Park Avenue (1,396 ft) and ONE57 (1,005 ft).
- 82 floors: first 5 for shared recreation and high-end retail, upper 77 luxury apartments. On Billionaires' Row.
- Highest apartment expected to fetch at least $100 million; 220 Central Park South penthouse sold for $238 million to Ken Griffin.
- Bronze and terracotta facade referencing New York art deco; 49,000 cubic yards of concrete (per YIMBY); form inspired by early-20th-century towers; uses the air rights of Steinway Hall (sold to the developers in 2013); aligned with the axis of Central Park.

wikis.title: China signals 'new era' for architecture with 500m skyscraper cap and copycat ban
wikis.summary: CNN Style article (Jun 6, 2020) on Chinese government guidelines capping skyscrapers at 500 m and banning copycat buildings.
wikis.body:
- A circular from China's housing ministry and the National Development and Reform Commission, issued "earlier this year", bans skyscrapers taller than 500 m (1,640 ft) and "plagiarism, imitation and copycat behavior", and proposes heritage protection, a credit system for designers and chief architects. It formalizes trends including Beijing height limits and a 2016 directive against "oversized, xenocentric, weird" buildings.
- Of 10 completed buildings above 500 m, half are in mainland China (Shanghai Tower 632 m; Ping An Finance Center 599 m).
- CTBUH: new buildings of 200 m+ in China fell almost 40% last year. Beijing CBD cap 180 m (2018 JLL report). Wuhan Greenland Center cut from 636 m to under 500 m; Suzhou Hungnam Center from 729 m to 499 m.
- About 70 Chinese 200 m+ buildings are "on hold", three expected over 500 m including Tianjin's Goldin Finance 117. Experts (Li Shiqiao, Fei Chen) call the cap "quite arbitrary" and say the document is about culture and context; Xiongan is cited as a low-rise "new paradigm".

wikis.title: China bans new super skyscrapers over 500 metres
wikis.summary: SCMP report (7 Jul 2021) on the NDRC order ending approvals of buildings above 500 m and restricting towers above 250 m.
wikis.body:
- NDRC order issued late Tuesday: buildings taller than 500 m (1,640 ft) will no longer be approved; towers over 250 m "must be strictly limited"; those over 100 m must match the scale and fire rescue capacity of their locations.
- Came two months after the unexplained wobbling of the 72-storey SEG Plaza in Shenzhen; cited concerns on safety and a glut of office space.
- China is home to almost half of the world's 100 tallest buildings (44 per CTBUH) and five of the 10 tallest 500 m-plus structures, all completed in the past six years.
- Knight Frank's Martin Wong: limited impact, as popular floor plates lie between 180 and 200 metres.

wikis.title: Tottenham Court Road station, London (Wikipedia)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia history of Tottenham Court Road interchange station, including its Crossrail/Elizabeth line rebuild.
wikis.body:
- Interchange station in St Giles and Soho for the Central and Northern lines and the Elizabeth line; fare zone 1; at St Giles Circus, second Elizabeth line entrance at Dean Street. 6 platforms; 60.81 million London Underground entries/exits in 2025.
- Opened 30 July 1900 (Central London Railway); Northern line (CCE&HR) 22 June 1907 (called Oxford Street until 3 September 1908); Elizabeth line 24 May 2022.
- Escalators replaced lifts from 1926. Early 1980s: Eduardo Paolozzi mosaics.
- Crossrail rebuild: 500 million pound upgrade taking eight years; Astoria theatres and original Central line entrance demolished. Upon completion in 2017: ticket hall six times larger, Hawkins\Brown entrances, step-free access, Daniel Buren artwork; the western entrance and Crossrail platforms handed over to TfL in early 2021. Platforms 230 m long under Soho Square.
- Elizabeth line central section opened 24 May 2022 (Paddington to Abbey Wood); direct services to Reading, Heathrow, Stratford, Shenfield from 6 November 2022. Over-station developments: 92 homes (Galliard Homes) and @sohoplace theatre (Derwent London), opened 15 October 2022.

wikis.title: Tottenham Court Road Crossrail station construction finished
wikis.summary: Construction Index news (15 Feb 21) that construction at the Elizabeth line Tottenham Court Road station is complete, 12 weeks before handover to TfL.
wikis.body:
- Laing O'Rourke was awarded Crossrail contract C422 in Jul 2012, when work and line opening were meant to finish in 2018. The station reached the T-12 landmark (12 weeks from handover to TfL); focus turns to testing and commissioning.
- Railway "currently expected to open in the first half of 2022". Custom House handed over first; Farringdon reached T-12 before Christmas. Trial Running to start later in the year.
- Crossrail chief executive Mark Wild and Laing O'Rourke's Declan Mcgeeney quoted; challenges included the line's only curved platform to avoid Centre Point's foundations.
- Will be an interchange between the Northern, Central and Elizabeth lines.

wikis.title: Port City Colombo, Sri Lanka special economic zone (Wikipedia)
