wikis.summary: Wikipedia overview of Port City Colombo, a multi-services special economic zone on reclaimed land beside Galle Face Green, with its incentive regime.
wikis.body:
- Multi-services SEZ on reclaimed land adjacent to Galle Face Green, Colombo; established 17 September 2014; area 2.69 km2; sea area to be reclaimed 269 ha. Land reclamation completed as of January 2019. Cost slated at US$ 15 billion in 2017; a FDI-funded Public Private Partnership.
- Five precincts: Financial District, Central Park Living, Island Living, the Marina, International Island; over 6.4 million sq m of new development.
- May 2021: Parliament approved the Port City Commission Bill; SEZ governed by the Colombo Port City Economic Commission (Act No. 11 of 2021). Initial incentives: tax holidays of 25 to 40 years for 'Businesses of Strategic Importance', unrestricted FX in sixteen currencies, 100 percent foreign ownership, five- to ten-year visas.
- Under the IMF Extended Fund Facility (2023-2025) concessions were revised; new tax-holiday approvals suspended; September 2025 Regulation No. 01 of 2025: per KPMG Sri Lanka, primary BSIs get 8 to 15 year corporate-tax holidays, secondary BSIs 7.5 percent for four years.
- April 2025: hosted the Regional Competition of the FinTech World Cup with FASL. Site of the future Colombo International Financial Centre.

wikis.title: Heatherwick's Vessel at Hudson Yards opens to the public
wikis.summary: Dezeen report (15 March 2019) on the opening of Thomas Heatherwick's Vessel climbable structure at Hudson Yards, New York.
wikis.body:
- Vessel, designed by Heatherwick Studio, opened 15 March 2019 with timed free tickets from 12pm, alongside the other Hudson Yards phase one public spaces. 154 staircases, 80 landings, a mile of walkways; 150 feet high and 150 feet wide at the top, narrow at the base; a sloping elevator to the top. First unveiled September 2016.
- Stuart Wood: "It's not a building, it's not a sculpture, it's not an artwork... we're thinking of this as a piece of furniture." References the Spanish Steps in Rome. Copper-coloured metal soffits, concrete inside. A public competition would decide its permanent name.
- Setting: landscaped plaza by Nelson Byrd Woltz; Hudson Yards built over a 28-acre active rail yard, "the largest private development in the US". 15 Hudson Yards and The Shed (programming from 5 April 2019); second phase adds eight towers.

wikis.title: The Vessel at Hudson Yards reopens with safety netting
wikis.summary: CNN report (Oct 27, 2024) on the Vessel reopening with netting more than three years after suicides forced its closure.
wikis.body:
- Reopened Monday (article dated Oct 27, 2024) with newly installed safety netting; opened March 2019; 150-foot-tall; owned by Related Companies.
- Closed January 2021 after three suicides, reopened with security and other measures; closed for over three years after a 14-year-old's suicide in July 2021. Four suicides in total forced closure.
- Hudson Yards COO Andrew Rosen: the solution "balances all the aesthetic concerns... and also provide that safety". Heatherwick Studio designed the "bespoke" netting and said it was "pleased".
- Critics (Jacob Alspector, Matt Shaw) say the netting addresses safety but the structure remains "gaudy and ungainly"; early warnings about low barriers were ignored.

wikis.title: 18 Hanover Square, Mayfair: development timeline (Buildington)
wikis.summary: Buildington's timeline of news for Great Portland Estates' Hanover Square scheme in Mayfair from 2015 to 2021.
wikis.body:
- Scheme by The GHS Limited Partnership (Great Portland Estates joint venture), a 223,600 sq ft prime mixed-use development.
- 2015-2017: GPE working with Westminster to improve the scheme; New Bond Street buildings demolished (Jan 2017). 23/04/2018: 57,200 sq ft pre-let to Kohlberg Kravis Roberts & Co. 31/10/2018: land buy back from Transport for London completed. 07/03/2019: 53,900 sq ft pre-let to Glencore UK Limited.
- Topping out on Thursday 4 April 2019 at nine storeys. 22/05/2019: delayed Crossrail opening beneficial to site.
- 2020: first retail unit handed over to Canali; floors five to eight completed; practical completion of Grade II* listed 20 Hanover Square (6,300 sq ft office) 17/09/2020; scheme expected complete by October 2020; office building 87% pre-let.
- 11/11/2020: 111,500 sq ft of 134,200 sq ft offices pre-let. 10/03/2021: 9,350 sq ft restaurant at 20 Hanover Square let to Colonial Property Co. 22/09/2021: 6,000 sq ft flagship store at 70/71 New Bond Street let.

wikis.title: GHS completes office leasing at 18 Hanover Square, W1
wikis.summary: GPE news release (12 May 2021) on the final office letting at 18 Hanover Square, Mayfair, and the wider 1.3-acre scheme.
wikis.body:
- Published 12 May 2021. The GHS Limited Partnership (a Great Portland Estates joint venture) completed office leasing of 18 Hanover Square with a 16,500 sq ft first-floor letting to an undisclosed financial services company, less than six months after practical completion.
- Two earlier pre-lettings of c.111,000 sq ft to Kohlberg Kravis Roberts & Co. Partners LLP and Glencore UK Limited. Total contracted office rent 14.8 million pounds (ahead of March 2021 ERV); weighted average unexpired lease term 15.7 years.
- 18 Hanover Square is a nine-storey building incorporating the eastern entrance to the Elizabeth Line's Bond Street station, at the heart of a 1.3-acre mixed-use development.
- Also: 1 Medici Courtyard (seven storeys, 31,000 sq ft flagship retail on New Bond Street, 33,300 sq ft offices above; second floor 9,000 sq ft let to Lexington Partners LP, third under offer); six luxury apartments, all sold; 6,200 sq ft offices in Grade II* listed 20 Hanover Square (under offer) plus a restaurant let to Colonial Property Co.

wikis.title: Australia 108, Melbourne: Skyscraper Center building data
wikis.summary: Skyscraper Center (CTBUH/CVU) data page for Australia 108, a completed 2020 residential tower at 70 Southbank Boulevard, Melbourne.
wikis.body:
- Global height rank 176. Height to tip 318.7 m / 1,046 ft; architectural 316.7 m / 1,039 ft; occupied 312.4 m / 1,025 ft.
- 100 floors above ground (the page also shows 1 below ground); status Completed, completion 2020; city Melbourne, Australia; address 70 Southbank Boulevard; function Residential. Photo credits Peter Bennetts, Fender Katsalidis, Willem-Dirk du Toit.
- Most of the page text is generic definitions of the CVU metrics; most other data is behind CVU membership.

wikis.title: Australia 108, Melbourne (Wikipedia)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on Australia 108, the 100-floor residential supertall in Southbank, Melbourne, with its design history.
wikis.body:
- Formerly 70 Southbank Boulevard; residential supertall in Southbank, Melbourne. 316.7 m (1,039 ft) architectural, 1,105 apartments over 100 floors; 11 lifts; 558 parking spaces. Designed by Fender Katsalidis Architects; developer Aspial Corporation (World Class Land); contractor Brookfield Multiplex; services engineer Norman Disney & Young. Cost about AUD $900 million.
- Construction started October 2015; topped out June 2020, then the tallest building in Australia by roof height (surpassing Eureka Tower) and second-tallest by full height (behind Q1 Tower); completed September 2020; opened in stages 2018-2020.
- History: site bought by Fender Katsalidis in April 2008 for A$14.2 million. 2009 plan: A$400 million, 226 m, 72-level (532 apartments). 2012 revision: mixed-use residential and hotel, 388 m, 108 levels, approved by the Victorian Government in March 2013 but shelved four months later after struggling with VicRoads and the Civil Aviation Safety Authority conditions. Reduced to its final form and ministerial approval in June 2014. Penthouse sold for A$25 million record price in April 2015.

wikis.title: Finances behind the $1.97 billion Allegiant Stadium
wikis.summary: Las Vegas Review-Journal breakdown (August 27, 2020) of the funding and costs of Allegiant Stadium.
wikis.body:
- Allegiant Stadium cost $1.97 billion to build. Article by Richard N. Velotta, August 27, 2020.
- Revenue $1.952 billion: $1.02 billion Raiders' equity (includes loans authorized by Senate Bill 1 and personal seat license revenue); $750 million Clark County bond proceeds and room-tax revenue; $200 million NFL G-4 loan program financing.
- Expenses $1.9696 billion: $1.405 billion construction; $240.9 million design, engineering and soft costs; $157.3 million furniture, fixtures and equipment; $77.8 million land; $60 million premium seating and marketing; $28.6 million utility and infrastructure.

wikis.title: Allegiant Stadium welcomes Raiders fans: On This Day
wikis.summary: FOX5 short piece (Jul. 31, 2025) marking the July 31, 2020 opening of Allegiant Stadium for the Raiders' first home game.
wikis.body:
- "On July 31, 2020, Allegiant Stadium opened its doors for Las Vegas Raiders fans for the team's first game on home turf" (as the piece words it).
- The project took three years, nine months and one day to complete and cost $1.9 billion, listed among the most expensive stadiums in the world.

wikis.title: Shanghai Tower, Pudong (Wikipedia)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the 632 m Shanghai Tower in Lujiazui, Shanghai: specifications, ownership, construction and observation decks.
wikis.body:
- 128-story, 632 m (2,073 ft) megatall skyscraper in Lujiazui, Pudong; tallest building in China; per the article, third-tallest by architectural top and second-tallest by highest occupied floor. Tallest and largest LEED-CS Platinum-certified building in the world from 2016 to 2025. Designed by Gensler (Marshall Strabala, Jun Xia) with TJAD.
- Cost: infobox CNY 15.9 billion; text gives an estimated US$2.4 billion. Owned by Shanghai Tower Construction and Development (consortium incl. Shanghai Chengtou, Shanghai Lujiazui Finance & Trade Zone Development, Shanghai Construction Group, which was main contractor).
- Timeline: groundbreaking 29 November 2008 (infobox says 1 November 2008); topped out 4 August 2013; considered complete September 2014 (infobox 31 August 2014); public use February 2015 rather than the originally scheduled November 2014. Observation deck opened July 2016; 118th/119th floor decks open since 26 April 2017; "Top of Shanghai" at 562 m on level 121 made it the highest observation deck (beating Burj Khalifa's 555 m). J Hotel on the 120th floor opened 2021.
- World's fastest elevators (20.5 m/s) until 2017. Nine zones of office, retail and leisure; tallest of the triple-adjacent supertalls with Jin Mao Tower and Shanghai World Financial Center. Floor area 380,000 m2 above grade; 128 floors above ground, 5 below. CTBUH: "one of the most sustainably advanced tall buildings in the world."

wikis.title: New Rothera Research Station wharf ready for RRS Sir David Attenborough
wikis.summary: BAM press release (16 April 2020) on the completed 74 m, 40 million pound wharf at BAS Rothera Research Station in Antarctica.
wikis.body:
- 16 April 2020: polar ships moored for the first time at the new 40 million pound wharf at British Antarctic Survey's Rothera Research Station; RRS James Clark Ross used it to re-supply the station.
- Built by BAM with Sweco, technical advisors Ramboll, cost management by Turner & Townsend; completed a second six-month construction season in the Antarctic austral summer. Part of the Antarctic Infrastructure Modernisation Programme (AIMP), commissioned by UKRI's NERC. Replaces a smaller 1980s structure.
- 74 metre wharf designed for the RRS Sir David Attenborough; bigger crane and enhanced cargo handling.
- Logistics: 45-tonne steel frames test-assembled in the UK; materials shipped 11,000 km; second season began November with 2,000 tonnes of snow cleared; installed the final 14 frames and all facing sheet piles (over 1,000 tonnes of steel), then backfilled. Strict biosecurity and environmental training; risks from weather, icebergs, whales and seals.
- Quotes from Martha McGowan (BAM), David Seaton (BAS) - completed "to schedule and to budget" - and Graham Hopper (BAM).

wikis.title: The B1M: the world's most extreme construction site (Rothera wharf, Antarctica)
wikis.summary: The B1M video page (9 October 2019, 771,744 views) on BAM and BAS building the new wharf at Rothera Research Station.
wikis.body:
- BAS partnered with BAM and Ramboll to upgrade sites in Antarctica. NERC invested more than 300 million pounds over seven years across BAS's sites; many upgrades revolve around the RRS Sir David Attenborough (launch in 2020), 30 m longer than the James Clark Ross, requiring larger wharves.
- Rothera is on Adelaide Island off the Antarctic Peninsula, more than five hours by plane from the nearest town; population more than 100 in summer.
- Challenges: orcas and leopard seals restrict diving; icebergs could damage the wharf under construction. The team spent 12 months in the UK planning with designers in The Hague and Camberley, built digital models, and test-assembled the whole prefabricated wharf in the steelwork fabricator's yard in Southampton.
- Biosecurity: 10 weeks inspecting and cleaning equipment from Teesport. First season done; return in November 2019 to complete the wharf and begin phase two (research station updates, expected to take four seasons).

wikis.title: One Park Drive, Wood Wharf, London (Wikipedia)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on One Park Drive, Herzog & de Meuron's cylindrical 205 m residential tower at Wood Wharf, Canary Wharf.
wikis.body:
- Residential skyscraper in the south-west corner of Wood Wharf, Canary Wharf estate, Isle of Dogs; Herzog & de Meuron's first residential development in the UK; likened to Marina City in Chicago. Cylindrical, 57 storeys (infobox), 484 private apartments and penthouses; 205 m (673 ft), ninth-tallest building in the UK as of 2023.
- Construction started 2016; completed 2021 (per Skyscraper Center); main contractor Canary Wharf Contractors; executive architect Adamson Associates; structural engineer AKT II; floor area 54,656 m2; planning reference PA/15/00018 (detailed approval announced 28 July 2015). Sub-penthouses on floor 55 launched September 2022; duplex penthouses on floors 56-57 launched October 2022.
- Awards: two International Property Awards 2021; two British Homes Awards 2021; two golds at WhatHouse? Awards 2021; Best Large Housing Scheme by New London Architecture 2022; penthouse Best Apartment at the Evening Standard New Homes Awards and gold for Best Interior Design at WhatHouse? Awards 2023.

wikis.title: Step inside One Park Drive, Herzog & de Meuron's first UK residential tower
wikis.summary: Wallpaper* article (last updated 14 October 2022) on One Park Drive in Canary Wharf welcoming its first residents.
wikis.body:
- One Park Drive has "just welcomed its first residents". Herzog & de Meuron's first residential high-rise in the UK, in Canary Wharf; about 58 floors, geometric articulated facade; interiors by Goddard Littlefair and Bowler James Brindley.
- Abstractly circular floorplates; amenities include reception, 24/7 concierge, lounge, cinema, library, health club.
- Four apartment categories: lower Loft, middle Cluster, upper Bay and Panoramic penthouses. Interior materials: exposed concrete walls, profiled timber panelling, natural stone.
- "Now over 70 per cent sold"; joins recent work such as 10 Park Drive by Stanton Williams.

wikis.title: The B1M: Building London's multi-faceted skyscraper, One Park Drive
wikis.summary: The B1M video page (04 September 2019, 263,914 views) on One Park Drive and the Wood Wharf district in Canary Wharf.
wikis.body:
- One Park Drive is the centrepiece of Wood Wharf, a district built partly on land reclaimed from the Thames; rising over 200 m. Designed by Herzog and de Meuron; cylindrical, 58 storeys, 215-metre profile as stated by the video page (one of the UK's tallest residential skyscrapers).
- Wood Wharf: decade-long development from 2015 by Canary Wharf Group: up to 3,600 homes, 2.8 million sq ft offices, up to 490,000 sq ft retail, GP surgery, two-form entry primary school, over eight acres of public space. Canary Wharf: One Canada Square completed 1990, then the UK's tallest building.
- Facade in three parts: lower loft apartments with wrap-around terraces, a pixelated middle section with private balconies, upper floors offset to give double-height terraces (similar to 56 Leonard in New York).
- Built on land reclaimed from the south dock: sheet piling in 2016 formed a lagoon, fill from the Isle of Wight was pumped in, and over 57 million litres of water were pumped out over more than a week. Rises alongside 12 other structures in phase one.

wikis.title: Herzog & de Meuron unveils cylindrical One Park Drive skyscraper at Canary Wharf
wikis.summary: Dezeen article (21 July 2021) on the nearly complete 58-storey, 205 m One Park Drive residential tower.
wikis.body:
- 58-storey, 205 m cylindrical residential tower, 484 apartments, in Wood Wharf, Canary Wharf; developer Canary Wharf Group. Photography by Lee Mawdsley.
- Studio: "the circular form of the new tower clearly distinguishes itself from its orthogonal neighbours". Most apartments have straight edges; Brian De'ath (Canary Wharf Group): "It looks like a round building, but doesn't have the issues of breaking a round building into apartments."
- Four sections: lowest nine floors with rounded plates and curved balconies; 22 floors of smaller studio to two-bed apartments with a boxy exterior; top 25 floors with twisted curved walls. Ground floors have lobby and cinema, then gym and pool (interiors GA Design). Lower apartments by Bowler James Brindley, upper by Goddard Littlefair. Seven duplex penthouses on the top two floors were still to be completed "later this year", designed by Herzog & de Meuron.
- First UK residential skyscraper by the Swiss studio (founded 1978 by Jacques Herzog and Pierre de Meuron).

wikis.title: AC Hotel NoMad modular hotel canceled, condo planned
wikis.summary: The Real Deal reports the planned 26-story modular AC Hotel at 842 Sixth Avenue was canceled and the site sold for a condo.
wikis.body:
- Hung Pin Hung's Brooklyn-based Pro-H Development plans a residential condo on the site of what would have been the 26-story AC Hotel NoMad, per a developer representative. Construction "is expected to start in the spring".
- Pro-H bought the site at 842 Sixth Avenue from developer Robert Chun for $30 million, per city records. The Chun family had owned it since the early 1990s.
- In 2017 the family filed plans for a Marriott hotel with 168 rooms, between West 29th and West 30th streets. Design: Danny Foster & Architecture; components were to be built in Poland.
- Work never got off the ground; Google Maps images showed the site empty as of May 2024.
- Lender Avana Capital filed to foreclose in December (2023), claiming Chun defaulted and owed $33 million; the case settled in August (2024).
- It would have been the world's tallest prefab hotel, topping the 19-story CitizenM at 189 Bowery by 114 feet.
- Modular method was relatively new when plans were announced in 2019. Richard Born (BD Hotels, builder of Pod BK) said he "would not do a 25-story modular building". CitizenM's Bowery hotel opened more than a year later than scheduled.
- As of 2019 Marriott had completed 31 modular hotels in the U.S.; construction takes about half the time versus traditional building.

wikis.title: 842 Sixth Avenue condo on the former modular hotel site (CityRealty)
wikis.summary: CityRealty, 2 April 2026, on the 27-story condo at 842 Sixth Avenue in NoMad, built on the site once planned for the world's tallest modular hotel.
wikis.body:
- A condo tower at 842 Sixth Avenue is gearing up for a sales launch: 94 condo units and ground-floor retail, topped out at 27 stories, 329 feet high. Designed by Isaac & Stern Architects, developed by Pro-H Development; between West 29th and 30th Streets at the edge of the Flower District.
- Design: low-rise podium, setback at the seventh floor, open-air loggias with plantings, vegetated walls at the base, faint Art Deco accents. Average unit about 900 sq ft; 3-5 apartments per floor on levels 3-27 plus a ground-floor duplex; amenities include a pet spa, shared garden, fitness center, lounge, rooftop terrace with Empire State Building views.
- History: in 2017 Robert and Helen Chun filed plans for a 25-story, 168-key AC Hotel NoMad by Danny Forster & Architecture, which would have been the world's tallest modular hotel; construction stalled at the foundation stage after the pandemic hit. Lender Avana Capital filed to foreclose in December 2023; Pro-H acquired the site for $30 million in September 2024, and the completed foundation let construction pick up quickly.
- Neighbor The NOMA (55-unit condo, 2017) averages $1,684 per sq ft in recent sales. The City Council approved the Midtown South Mixed-Use Plan rezoning 42 blocks for over 9,500 new housing units (about 3,000 affordable).

wikis.title: Beijing Daxing International Airport opens
wikis.summary: CNBC reports the opening of Beijing Daxing airport on 25 Sep 2019, its size, cost and China's air travel demand.
wikis.body:
- Beijing Daxing International Airport opened Wednesday 25 Sept 2019, inaugurated by President Xi Jinping ahead of the PRC's 70th anniversary on Oct. 1.
- Starfish-shaped, in southern Beijing; built to handle 72 million passengers a year (key points), described as able to handle up to 100 million travelers a year.
- Meant to ease pressure on Beijing Capital, which handled more than 100 million passengers last year.
- Designed by the late Zaha Hadid; five concourses and four runways, plans for up to three more, to handle 620,000 flights a year.
- Cost about $17 billion per the airport; completed in less than five years.
- IATA expects China to overtake the U.S. as largest aviation market around 2024 / mid-2020s and ~1.6 billion air travelers a year by 2037.
- China Southern and China Eastern will use it; British Airways and Finnair are planning to fly from it.

wikis.title: Beijing Daxing International Airport (Wikipedia)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on Beijing Daxing International Airport: history, design, construction, opening and cost.
wikis.body:
- IATA PKX, ICAO ZBAD; one of two international airports serving Beijing, on the Beijing/Langfang (Hebei) border, nicknamed "the starfish" for its terminal shape.
- Completed 30 June 2019; opening ceremony 25 September 2019 (six days before the PRC's 70th anniversary), attended by Xi Jinping; first commercial flight 26 September 2019.
- Covers 2,679 hectares, four civilian runways (one 3,400 m, three 3,800 m); nearby Nanjiao Airport is a military base and potential 5th runway. 46 km south of Beijing.
- Terminal of 700,000 m2, described as the world's largest single-building airport terminal. The article cites facility cost CN¥80 billion (US$11.4 billion) in the lead, but its construction section says the airport itself cost CN¥120bn (about US$17bn), with peripheral projects CN¥330bn, total CN¥450bn (US$63bn).
- History: third Beijing airport proposed 2008; approved by the NDRC on 22 December 2014; construction began 26 December 2014 (chief engineer Guo Yanchi); final construction phase January 2019.
- Design: terminal by Zaha Hadid Architects with ADPI, executed by BIAD; master plan by NACO; central hub with six curved spokes; Lead 8 designed the integrated service building.
- Hub for SkyTeam airlines and some Oneworld members; China United Airlines relocated fully after opening. 2025 stats: 53,618,949 passengers, 345,791 aircraft movements.
- As of 14 September 2026 it had handled over 1.68 million flights and 237 million passengers.

wikis.title: One Vanderbilt skyscraper (Wikipedia)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on One Vanderbilt, the 62-story KPF-designed supertall next to Grand Central Terminal that opened in 2020.
wikis.body:
- 62-story supertall at 42nd Street and Vanderbilt Avenue, Midtown Manhattan; designed by Kohn Pedersen Fox for developer SL Green Realty; opened 2020.
- Roof 1,301 ft (397 m), spire 1,401 ft (427 m); city's fourth-tallest building after One World Trade Center, Central Park Tower and 111 West 57th Street. Top floor numbered 73; 49 elevators; floor area 1,750,212 sq ft.
- Facade mostly glass with terracotta spandrels, meant to harmonize with Grand Central Terminal; wedge-shaped void at the base; interior spaces up to 105 ft high. Top stories hold Summit One Vanderbilt observation deck; second floor has the Le Pavillon restaurant; lobby has a bank branch and entrance to the terminal/subway.
- Timeline: SL Green acquired the site 2001-2011 and announced plans in 2012; a zoning amendment failed in 2013; TD Bank signed as anchor tenant May 2014; approved a year later; groundbreaking October 2016; topped out 17 September 2019; COVID-19 delayed completion; building opened September 2020, observation deck 13 months later.
- Air rights: normal limit about 600 ft; SL Green transferred air rights from the Bowery Savings Bank Building and got more from the city for transit and public-space improvements.
- Team: Severud Associates (structural), Langan (civil), Jaros, Baum & Bolles (MEP), Tishman Construction (contractor), Hines (project manager). Early plans called for 67 stories.
- Replaced five Terminal City-era structures; Vanderbilt Avenue between 42nd and 43rd streets became a 14,000 sq ft pedestrian plaza (PWP Landscape Architecture).

wikis.title: Tax incentives for the Forest City Special Financial Zone (EY Malaysia)
wikis.summary: EY Malaysia tax alert on the incentives announced for the Forest City Special Financial Zone in Iskandar Puteri, Johor.
wikis.body:
- On 20 September 2024 the Finance Minister II launched the Forest City Special Financial Zone (SFZ) and announced tax incentives. Forest City is four man-made islands with duty-free status in Iskandar Puteri, Johor. The SFZ was first announced by PM Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim in August "last year" (2023).
- Incentives: 0% tax rate under the Single-Family Office Scheme (coordinated by the Securities Commission, SC); special 15% individual income tax rate for knowledge workers, including Malaysians working in the SFZ; 5% concessionary rate for financial global business services, fintech and foreign payment system operators; special deductions on relocation costs, enhanced industrial building allowances and withholding tax exemptions for banks, insurers, capital market intermediaries and other eligible financial entities.
- Forest City is "set to be the first location in Malaysia to offer a 0% tax rate for Family Offices". SC issued an FAQ on 23 September 2024.
- 0% rate for eligible Single-Family Office Vehicles: 10 years initial, extendable another 10 years, subject to conditions. Applications go to the SC; the scheme is targeted to be operational by the first quarter of 2025.

wikis.title: Forest City Special Financial Zone announced (press release)
wikis.summary: Forest City Malaysia press release on the official announcement of the Forest City Special Financial Zone in Johor.
wikis.body:
- Dateline Iskandar Puteri, Malaysia, 3 Oct 2024: Forest City Special Financial Zone (SFZ) was officially announced, witnessed by the Regent of Johor, HRH Tunku Ismail; the Second Minister of Finance and the State Minister of Johor attended the press conference.
- Aim: become a "highland of financial innovation", attract financial institutions. The Second Minister of Finance called Forest City the first location in Malaysia to offer a zero tax rate for family offices.
- Positioned as complementing Singapore, "rather than competing", a financial "dual-core engine" for ASEAN.
- Forest City is applying for "Malaysian Digital Status"; qualified companies would enjoy a 10-year corporate income tax exemption. In July 2024 Forest City Island 1 was listed as a duty-free island.
- Johor State Government plans to set up the Investment Malaysia Coordination Center (IMFC) in Forest City, called a "special zone within a special zone".
- Source is a company press release (Forest City Malaysia) with promotional claims.

wikis.title: Australia 108 skyscraper completed in Melbourne (Dezeen)
wikis.summary: Dezeen on Fender Katsalidis's Australia 108, a 319 m, 100-storey Melbourne residential tower with a cantilevered golden star.
wikis.body:
- Fender Katsalidis has completed Australia 108 in Melbourne: 319 metres, 100 storeys, "the tallest residential building in the southern hemisphere" (Dezeen, 4 May 2021).
- A golden star ("the Starburst") cantilevers six metres outward about two-thirds of the way up, informed by the Commonwealth Star on the Australian flag.
- Rectangular ribbed, fully glazed form with horizontal white bands; stands near the studio's 297 m Eureka Tower.
- 1,105 apartments across 90 residential floors, plus dining spaces, gyms, cantilevered pools, spas, event spaces and a double-height sky garden. A heritage facade is incorporated into the base, framed by stacked green canopies enclosing a ten-storey car park.
- Q1 Tower in Surfers Paradise is 322.5 m overall but topped by a spire; roof height only 245 m.

wikis.title: Keys handed over for Quay Quarter Tower (AMP)
wikis.summary: AMP press release of 19 April 2022 announcing Multiplex completed Quay Quarter Tower, a 50-storey adaptive re-use tower at 50 Bridge Street, Sydney.
wikis.body:
- 19 April 2022: Multiplex completed construction of AMP Capital's Quay Quarter Tower, a 50-storey Premium grade office building at 50 Bridge Street, Sydney CBD.
- Four-year build; a 45-year-old 45,000 m2 office building became 89,000 m2 of office space plus a 4,000 m2 retail podium. 89 per cent pre-leased (Deloitte, Corrs Chambers Westgarth, AMP and AMP Capital, EQT, Johnson Winter & Slattery, The Work Project).
- Multiplex: some 35,000 people worked on the project; "the most complex build ever undertaken in Australia". Retained 68% of the existing core; "top down, bottom up" method.
- Saved more than 8,000 tonnes of embodied carbon, described as a world-first for an office tower of this scale.
- Designed by 3XN with BVN: "jenga-like" five shifting glass volumes stacked with atriums and a continuous spiral staircase. One acre of urban green space. Ratings: 6 Star Green Star, 5.5 Star NABERS Energy, 4 Star NABERS Water, WELL.
- Part of the 11,000 m2 Quay Quarter Sydney precinct (33 Alfred Street tower, Quay Quarter Lanes with 104 apartments). Owned by AMP Capital Wholesale Office Fund and Dexus Wholesale Property Fund; Rest Super to become one-third owner.

wikis.title: Quay Quarter Tower (Wikipedia)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on Quay Quarter Tower, Sydney's redeveloped AMP Centre, the world's first upcycled skyscraper.
wikis.body:
- 50 Bridge Street, Sydney. Built as the AMP Centre in 1976 (45 floors, roof 188 m, tallest in Sydney until the MLC Centre in 1977); redeveloped 2018-2021 and reopened as Quay Quarter Tower in early 2022 at 216 m (709 ft), 54 floors.
- Called the world's first upcycled skyscraper, retaining 68% of the existing structure; the core, 66% of columns, beams and slabs and 95% of internal walls kept. Floor space doubled to about 90,000 m2.
- 2013: BVN designed the precinct masterplan; 3XN's winning design revealed 24 September 2014, BVN executive architect. Approval finalised November 2015; construction began early 2018 (Multiplex); topped out early 2021.
- Awards: International High-Rise Award (November 2022), World Building of the Year at the World Architecture Festival (December 2022), CTBUH best new tall building (2023).
- Owners: AMP Capital Wholesale Office Fund, Dexus Wholesale Property Fund and Rest; tenants include AMP, Corrs, Deloitte, EQT, Johnson Winter Slattery.

wikis.title: Eko Atlantic City opening ceremony (BellaNaija)
wikis.summary: BellaNaija photo report on the February 2013 inauguration of the first phase of Eko Atlantic City in Lagos.
wikis.body:
- Published 22 February 2013: the first phase of Eko Atlantic City "was inaugurated in Lagos yesterday" at an event with top dignitaries: former US President Bill Clinton, Nigerian President Goodluck Jonathan, former Lagos governor Bola Tinubu and Lagos governor Babatunde Fashola.
- Eko Atlantic is described as a planned district of Lagos built on land reclaimed from the Atlantic Ocean, still under development, anticipating 400,000 residents and a daily flow of 250,000 commuters.
- Its main purpose is said to be stopping erosion of the Lagos coastline, giving a positive environmental impact.

wikis.title: Eko Atlantic (Wikipedia)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on Eko Atlantic, the planned city in Lagos built on land reclaimed from the Atlantic Ocean.
wikis.body:
- Planned city in Lagos State, Nigeria, on a peninsula of reclaimed land; expects at least 250,000 residents and 150,000 daily commuters (article's figures). Aimed at stopping erosion of Lagos's coast (Bar Beach erosion of about 30 m a year).
- Developer South Energyx Nigeria Ltd (Chagoury group subsidiary); public-private partnership with Lagos State Government as strategic partner. Contractor: China Communications Construction Group (CCCC); consultants Royal Haskoning and ar+h Architects.
- Reclaims 9 km2 in front of Bar Beach; roughly 10 km2 total, 10 districts, planned 3,000 buildings and 400,000 homes. About 8.4-8.5 km revetment ("Great Wall of Lagos") protects it. Reclamation reported to cost around $6B.
- Land pricing: Phases 1 and 2 plots from about 2,200 m2, from $1,150 per m2; Phase 3 from about 1,200 m2 at $1,050 per m2.
- Timeline: 2009 Clinton Global Initiative Commitment Certificate; 21 February 2013 ceremony marking reclamation attended by Jonathan, Bill Clinton, Fashola, Tinubu; March 2014 developer said "The first residential tower will open in 2016"; by November 2020 a few buildings, notably Eko Pearl Towers, completed; EDGE certification from IFC.
- Controversy: nearby residents say construction caused erosion and surges; in August 2012 an ocean surge swept 16 people into the sea, killing several; 29 April 2024 demolition of Landmark beach began for the Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway.

wikis.title: Star Wars: Galaxy's Edge opening dates revealed (StarWars.com)
wikis.summary: StarWars.com news post, 7 March 2019, giving the phased opening dates and reservation rules for Star Wars: Galaxy's Edge.
wikis.body:
- Announced 7 March 2019: Star Wars: Galaxy's Edge opens ahead of schedule on May 31 (2019) at Disneyland Resort, California and August 29 (2019) at Disney's Hollywood Studios, Florida. Disney says it is "debuting early because of high guest interest".
- Phase one: Millennium Falcon: Smugglers Run, food and beverages, merchant shops. Phase two, "opening later this year": Star Wars: Rise of the Resistance, called "the most ambitious, immersive and advanced attraction ever imagined".
- Disneyland: between May 31 and June 23, 2019 guests need theme park admission plus a no-cost reservation, subject to availability; guests at the three Disneyland Resort hotels get a designated reservation. No reservation offered or required at Walt Disney World at that time; park admission required. Capacity limited; access may be restricted depending on demand.

wikis.title: Inside Disney's $1 billion Star Wars: Galaxy's Edge (CNBC)
wikis.summary: CNBC preview of Star Wars: Galaxy's Edge at Disneyland and Walt Disney World ahead of the May 31, 2019 opening.
wikis.body:
- Disneyland's Galaxy's Edge (Anaheim, California) opens May 31 (2019); covers 14 acres and cost an estimated $1 billion per USA Today. Walt Disney World's billion-dollar version opens Aug. 29.
- Set on the planet Batuu (not in the films; in the book "Thrawn: Alliances"), with Black Spire Outpost as a smugglers' stop.
- Two phases: phase one (May 31) includes Millennium Falcon: Smugglers Run (100-foot ship, six-seat cockpit simulator: pilots, gunners, flight engineers), shops, and restaurants (Oga's Cantina, Ronto Roasters, "Blue Milk"); phase two "later this year" brings Star Wars: Rise of the Resistance in the Resistance Forest, a ride with Kylo Ren, a Star Destroyer, and animatronic Stormtroopers.
- Shops include Droid Depot and Savi's Workshop - Handbuilt Lightsabers; Play Disney Parks app. Single-day ticket starts at $107 for adults.
- Disney calls the additions "the largest and most technologically advanced single-themed land expansions ever in a Disney park". Disney parks and resorts brought in more than $20 billion in revenue in 2018 and $4.5 billion operating profit.

wikis.title: 100 Liverpool Street (New London Architecture)
wikis.summary: NLA project entry for the conversion of a 1980s building into British Land's 100 Liverpool Street in the City of London.
wikis.body:
- Conversion of a "tired 1980's building" into British Land's first ultra-low carbon building; first major UK development with a converged network and smart-enabled infrastructure; reused the existing frame to provide over 40% additional net internal area.
- Over 20,000 sq ft of terraces with landscaped gardens and views to St Paul's. Certified BREEAM 'Outstanding', Wired 'Platinum', WELL 'Gold'; all electricity from renewable sources.
- Over 520,000 sq ft of office space plus three levels of shops, bars and restaurants and a rooftop restaurant; curved glazed facade. New London Awards 2021 winner, Working category.
- Status built; City of London; 69,000 sq m; completed September 2020; 100 Broadgate, Liverpool St, EC2M 2AU. Client British Land; architect Hopkins Architects; structural engineer AKT II; wind consultant RWDI. Page last updated 13/01/2025.

wikis.title: 100 Liverpool Street (Hopkins Architects)
wikis.summary: Hopkins Architects' project page for the redevelopment of 100 Liverpool Street, London, completed 2020.
wikis.body:
- Location London; 69,000 m2; client British Land; year 2020. Awards listed include Stirling Prize 2022 shortlisted, RIBA National Award, RIBA London Regional Award, New London Award (Working winner), City of London Building of the Year, Building Magazine Project of the Year, BCI Award, Civic Trust Award.
- Stripped the 1980s building back to its structural frame, relocated cores to the perimeter for open flexible floors, added a central atrium; sinuous glazed facade replaced the old cladding.
- Rooftop restaurant and large 9th-floor terrace with views to St Paul's. Three additional office floors added while keeping foundations and a large proportion of the steelwork, reducing embodied carbon and letting Network Rail retail below keep trading. Total 520,000 sq ft lettable office space; top five floors set back with planted terraces; new escalators and walkways in Octagon Mall.
- 50% of the original superstructure re-used. BREEAM Outstanding and WELL Gold. Interiors with Universal Design Studio.
- Quote from Nigel Webb, British Land: "It will set the benchmark for British Land buildings going forward."

wikis.title: 100 Liverpool Street shortlisted for Stirling Prize (Dezeen)
wikis.summary: Dezeen on Hopkins Architects' reuse of a 1980s office block as 100 Liverpool Street, London, shortlisted for the 2022 RIBA Stirling Prize.
wikis.body:
- Hopkins Architects reused elements of a 1980s office block (originally by Arup Associates) for British Land; shortlisted for the RIBA Stirling Prize, one of six. Developed with Universal Design Studio; forms a gateway to the Broadgate Estate beside Liverpool Street Station.
- Now 48,000 square metres of flexible offices on a podium of restaurants and retail; stone facade replaced with glass and aluminium; colonnaded walkway wraps the building.
- All original foundations kept plus half the superstructure; 50 per cent of the superstructure replaced to reorganise the layout. Cores moved from the facade to reduce the deep plan (originally 40 m deep at the narrowest); atrium with statement staircase added.
- Low-carbon steps: steel and composite steel frames, GGBS cement substitute where concrete needed. Claimed embodied carbon 389 kg CO2 per m2 versus 600 kg in the LETI 2020 target. Heat recovery systems for hot water; efficient form factor.

wikis.title: Copenhagen abandons 2025 CO2-neutrality goal (CPH Post)
wikis.summary: The Copenhagen Post reports the city has dropped its 2025 CO2-neutrality target after the ARC incinerator gave up applying for state carbon-capture funds.
wikis.body:
- Aug 23, 2022: Copenhagen, which unveiled the 2025 CO2-neutrality goal in 2009, says it is "no longer realistic", per mayor Sophie Haestorp Andersen, after the ARC incinerator in Amager gave up applying for state funds for a carbon capture plant on its chimneys.
- Andersen: "it doesn't mean we can't get there in 2026, 2027 or 2028". City has cut CO2 emissions by 80 percent, above the 70 percent target for this year; full neutrality would need ARC to access the state's 8 billion kroner CCS fund.
- Per Energywatch.dk, ARC lacks the necessary equity capital. ARC has a demo capture plant running; a bigger plant is scheduled next year, with a full-scale plant planned for 2025.
- City technical mayor Line Barfoed says the state set criteria it knew ARC could not meet. Climate minister Dan Jorgensen replied that such demands on finances are standard, and that other plants (e.g. Vestforbraending in Glostrup) qualified.
- New vision: Copenhagen should contribute positively to climate calculations by 2035 at the latest.

wikis.title: Copenhagen will fail its 2025 carbon-neutrality goal (TheMayor.EU)
wikis.summary: TheMayor.EU, 24 Aug 2022, on Copenhagen conceding it cannot reach climate neutrality by 2025 because ARC will not seek carbon-capture funding.
wikis.body:
- Mayor Sophie Haestorp Andersen announced at the start of the week that Copenhagen cannot meet its goal of climate neutrality by 2025, set in 2009.
- Cause described as bureaucratic and financial: district heating and power company ARC (Amager Resource Centre) decided not to seek government funding because it cannot meet national equity standards; its carbon-capture plant would be essential for the last stretch to a 100% CO2 reduction.
- City has already cut CO2 emissions by 80 percent; ARC has a demo capture plant working.
- Mayor in a Facebook post set a new ambition: climate-positive by 2035. She told DR Nyheder the target could still be reached in "2026, 2027 or 2028"; the article says there is hope before 2030.
- Line Barfoed (city technical mayor) blamed the national government for setting financial requirements ARC could not meet.

wikis.title: Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macau Bridge (Wikipedia)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the 55 km Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macau Bridge-tunnel system: planning, construction, cost and layout.
wikis.body:
- 55 km (34 mi) bridge-tunnel system: three cable-stayed bridges, an undersea tunnel and four artificial islands; called the longest sea crossing and longest open-sea fixed link. Connects Hong Kong and Macau with Zhuhai. Design life 120 years.
- Cost CNY 127 billion (US$18.8 billion); Main Bridge estimated CNY 51.1 billion (US$7.56 billion) via bank loans shared by mainland China, Hong Kong and Macau.
- Originally set to open late 2016; construction began 15 December 2009 (mainland side; Hong Kong section began December 2011 after a legal challenge over environmental impact); completed 6 February 2018; inaugurated 23 October 2018 by Xi Jinping and opened to the public 24 October 2018. 19 workers died during construction.
- Sections: Main Bridge 29.6 km (22.9 km bridge plus 6.7 km immersed tunnel between Blue Dolphin and White Dolphin islands; cable-stayed spans of 280-460 m), Hong Kong Link Road 12 km, Zhuhai Link Road 13.4 km. A 3 km Macau Bridge Link opened October 2024.
- Background: Gordon Wu (Hopewell) proposed the concept in the 1980s; talks stalled after Tiananmen 1989; 2003 coordination group formed.
- The bridge itself uses right-hand traffic, so Hong Kong and Macau drivers switch sides at crossing viaducts. Tolls CNY 80-300; 2024 daily average 10,600 vehicles and 78,000 passenger trips. HZMBus "golden buses" shuttle takes about 40 minutes.

wikis.title: China's president opens long-delayed southern sea bridge (Al Jazeera)
wikis.summary: Al Jazeera, 24 Oct 2018, on Xi Jinping opening the Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macau Bridge and the political and environmental debate around it.
wikis.body:
- Xi Jinping opened the long-delayed, over-budget 55 km Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macau Bridge on Tuesday (23 Oct 2018); public use from the next day. Billed as a step in making the Pearl River Delta/Greater Bay Area (about 69 million people) a technology hub. Final cost estimate $20.2bn (correction: an earlier version said $2.2bn).
- Construction started nine years earlier; supposed to finish by 2016; delays tied to Hong Kong construction and environmental standards inflated costs.
- Cuts driving time from Hong Kong International Airport to Zhuhai from four hours to 45 minutes; six-lane highway.
- Critics: analyst Philip Bowring called it "a grand political gesture", "certainly not a commercial gesture". Environmentalist Roy Tam says Chinese White Dolphin numbers around North Lantau have declined significantly.
- Transport operators had expected two months' notice but learned a week before; SCMP citing a government source said late notice was a security precaution. Xi opened it near Zhuhai and was not expected to visit Hong Kong or Macau.
- Transport secretary Frank Chan Fan said it would facilitate personnel exchange.

wikis.title: Sixth Street Viaduct, Los Angeles (Wikipedia)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the Sixth Street Viaduct in Los Angeles: the 1932 original, its demolition, the 2022 replacement and later vandalism.
wikis.body:
- Connects 6th Street in the Arts District with Whittier Boulevard in Boyle Heights, spanning the LA River, US 101, I-5 and rail lines. Original opened November 9, 1932; closed January 27, 2016; demolition began February 5, 2016 (nine months). Replacement opened July 9, 2022.
- Reason: alkali-silica reaction in the concrete caused cracking; estimated 70% probability of collapse in a major earthquake within 50 years.
- Replacement designed by Michael Maltzan with HNTB (contractors Skanska, Stacy and Witbeck); several years-long delays and multimillion-dollar cost increases; single-direction bike lanes with bollards criticized as unsafe.
- A park under the bridge: construction began August 2023, planned to finish in 2026.
- By June 13, 2024 wire thieves had stripped 38,000 ft of copper wiring, leaving the LED lighting dark; theft and vandalism continued; by February 2026 almost 7 miles of wire stolen; street takeovers occur.
- The original appeared in many films, TV shows and music videos (e.g. Grease, Terminator 2).

wikis.title: LA's Sixth Street Viaduct opens to the public (NBC Los Angeles)
wikis.summary: NBC Los Angeles report of 10 July 2022 on the opening of the new Sixth Street Viaduct after three days of celebrations.
wikis.body:
- The Sixth Street Viaduct, connecting Boyle Heights and the downtown Arts District, "officially opened Sunday night" (July 10, 2022) after three straight days of community celebrations. Pedestrians and bicyclists 11 a.m.-4 p.m.; vehicle traffic from 7 p.m.
- Roughly $588 million, the largest bridge project in city history; ran years over schedule. Demolition began in 2016 with a projected 2019 completion for a then-$449 million effort; later pushed to late 2020, then COVID delays.
- Funded by the Federal Highway Transportation Administration, Caltrans and the city; officials said it had the largest number of women workers of any US public works project.
- "Ribbon of Light" design with 20 sweeping arches by HNTB and Michael Maltzan. City Engineer Gary Lee Moore said the bridge is seismically strong. Mayor Eric Garcetti: "It is in many ways the embodiment of what Los Angeles strives to be".
- Original (1932) was torn down due to alkali-silica reaction; seen in Grease and Terminator 2. City plans a 12-acre park under the bridge.

wikis.title: Collins House Melbourne (Wikipedia)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on Collins House Melbourne, a slim 190 m residential pencil tower at 464-466 Collins Street completed in 2019.
wikis.body:
- Private residential high-rise at 464-466 Collins Street, Melbourne; developed by Asian Pacific Group and Golden Age, designed by Bates Smart; main contractor Hickory Group.
- Height 190 m (620 ft), 57 floors in the infobox (text says about 280 apartments across 56 levels); floor area 28,775 m2; 280 rooms, 107 parking spaces.
- Launched 2013; approved by then-Planning Minister Matthew Guy in February 2014 as part of a "Super Tuesday" that approved five skyscrapers.
- 11.8 m wide at its narrowest; described as one of the world's slimmest skyscrapers, a "pencil tower".
- Construction began February 2016; completed 2019.

wikis.title: Collins House project (Hickory)
wikis.summary: Hickory contractor's project page for the Collins House high-rise at 466 Collins Street, Melbourne, completed September 2019.
wikis.body:
- Location 466 Collins Street, Melbourne. Developer: Golden Age, Asian Pacific Group and Deague Group; architect Bates Smart; structural engineer 4D Workshop; services engineer Murchie Consulting; development manager Time and Place.
- Construction duration 29 months; completion September 2019.
- Described as 60 levels, 184 metres, 259 luxury apartments (two and three bedrooms and double-storey lofts) over one basement level. Incorporates the heritage facade of the historic Maker's Mark building.
- Communal facilities: Collins Terrace on Level 3 and the St James Club on Level 27.
- Features: "slimmest tower project in Australia"; cantilever at L14, 4.5 m over the adjoining building; programme reduced by up to 30% using Hickory's volumetric structural system (HBS); single tower crane; conventional formwork to level 14, then prefabricated Hickory structural units; fully automatic car storage.

wikis.title: Walt Disney World (Wikipedia)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on Walt Disney World Resort near Orlando: planning, 1971 opening, expansions and scale.
wikis.body:
- Resort complex about 20 miles (32 km) southwest of Orlando, Florida; opened October 1, 1971; operated by Disney Experiences. About 27,000 acres; four theme parks (Magic Kingdom 1971, EPCOT 1982, Hollywood Studios 1989, Animal Kingdom 1998), two water parks, 31 Disney-owned resort hotels. In 2024 the most visited vacation resort in the world, over 49 million average annual attendance; largest single-site employer in the US.
- Planning: in 1959 Walt Disney Productions began searching for land (only 5% of Disneyland visitors came from east of the Mississippi); Walt flew over the Orlando site in November 1963; dummy corporations acquired 27,443 acres beginning April 1964, some land for as little as $100 an acre. Official reveal November 15, 1965 with Governor Haydon Burns. Walt died December 15, 1966; brother Roy O. Disney came out of retirement to finish it. Construction began 1967; the EPCOT city concept was dropped.
- Reedy Creek Improvement Act signed May 12, 1967 by Gov. Claude Kirk; Florida Supreme Court in 1968 allowed tax-exempt bonds.
- Opening: Magic Kingdom, Polynesian Village and Contemporary resorts opened October 1, 1971 to about 10,000 guests; grand opening ceremony October 23-25 where Roy Disney dedicated it as "Walt Disney World". Fort Wilderness opened a month later.
- EPCOT Center: groundbreaking October 1, 1979, opened October 1, 1982, cost $1.5 billion (Disney about $1.2 billion).

wikis.title: Walt Disney World's opening, Oct 1-Dec 31, 1971 (WDWNT)
wikis.summary: WDWNT history article detailing Walt Disney World's opening day and first three months in 1971, including prices and Magic Kingdom layout.
wikis.body:
- Published October 9, 2020, part of a year-by-year "Timekeeping" series. On October 1, 1971 crowds feared in the hundreds of thousands (per newspapers and Florida Highway Patrol) did not come; about 10,000 people visited the Magic Kingdom by day's end. The star-studded events came later in the month.
- Parking 50 cents; access from the Transportation and Ticket Center by monorail (Orange, Green, Gold, Blue in service) or ferries (Ports O' Call and Southern Seas, 250 guests each).
- Prices: adult general admission $3.50 (Child 3-11, Junior 12-17, Adult 18+); 7 Adventure book $4.50 adult, 11 Adventure book $5.75; individual tickets A 10 cents, B 25 cents, C 50 cents, D 75 cents, E 90 cents (adult).
- Main Street, U.S.A. had sponsored shops (Town Square Cafe by Oscar Mayer, Hallmark Card Shop, Refreshment Corner by Coca-Cola). Railroad had one stop with three trains (Walter E. Disney, Lilly Belle, Roger E. Broggie). Adventureland had the Jungle Cruise and Tropical Serenade among few attractions; Frontierland had three at opening.
- Layout essentially the same as today's but smaller.

wikis.title: 53 West 53 skyscraper (Wikipedia)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on 53 West 53 (53W53, formerly Tower Verre), Jean Nouvel's supertall next to MoMA in Midtown Manhattan.
wikis.body:
- Supertall at 53 West 53rd Street beside MoMA; developed by Pontiac Land Group and Hines; designed by Jean Nouvel (AAI Architects architect of record); structural engineer WSP Global; contractor Lendlease. Height 1,050 ft (320 m), twelfth-tallest completed building in the city as of January 2025.
- 77 stories, top numbered 87 (some floor numbers skipped, matching MoMA's). Concrete diagrid facade, north and south facades slope inward to five spires; curtain wall of 5,747 triple-glazed panels made in Germany.
- 145 condominiums with interiors by Thierry Despont; amenities on floors 12-16, lounge on 46-47. MoMA gallery space (about 40,000 sq ft) on floors 2, 4 and 5; 11,000 sq ft restaurant "53" by Lionel Ohayon; 9,000 sq ft lobby.
- Timeline: Tower Verre announced 2007 at 1,250 ft alongside a MoMA expansion; shortened by 200 ft in 2009 after protests; financing delayed construction until 2013; work began late 2014, sales the next year; topped out mid-2018; completed early 2020, with a majority of units unsold at completion.

wikis.title: Closings commence at 53W53 (CityRealty)
wikis.summary: CityRealty piece on the start of condo closings at 53W53 above MoMA, with listings and amenities.
wikis.body:
- The Hines-led development team "commenced closings" at 53W53 (53 West 53rd Street) earlier in the month; the building is ready to welcome its first residents. Height 1,050 ft; diagrid designed with Jean Nouvel.
- Availabilities range from $3.5 million for a one-bedroom to $63.82 million for a four-bedroom duplex penthouse (PH76, 7,973 sq ft). Other listings: #38B $6.55M, #37C $7.625M, #32A $9.61M, #30B $9.975M, rental #19E $12,500/month.
- Interiors by Thierry Despont; model units on the 36th floor by Andre Fu and by Roman and Williams.
- Each unit includes a Perpetual Benefactor W53 membership to MoMA. Over 30,000 sq ft of amenities: double-height lounge facing Central Park, wellness center managed by The Wright Fit, 65-foot lap pool, squash court, golf simulator, private screening room and theater, wine tasting room.

wikis.title: One Thousand Museum, Miami (Wikipedia)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on One Thousand Museum, Zaha Hadid Architects' 62-story residential tower on Biscayne Boulevard in Miami, completed 2019.
wikis.body:
- High-rise condominium (the "Scorpion Tower") at 1000 Biscayne Boulevard opposite Museum Park; Zaha Hadid Architects (architect of record ODP Architects); developer 1000 Biscayne Tower, LLC; structural engineer DeSimone; contractor Plaza Construction. Completed 2019; 62 stories, 707 ft (215 m).
- Zaha Hadid's first residential tower in the Western Hemisphere and one of her final projects. Curving exoskeleton of about 5,000 glass fiber reinforced concrete pieces shipped from Dubai; allows fewer interior columns.
- Foundation auger-cast piles over 170 ft deep set a Miami-Dade record. Topped out February 2018.
- 84 residences: a two-story duplex penthouse, 4 townhouses, 10 full-floor residences, 70 half-floor units; roughly double the cost per sq ft of nearby condos; rooftop pool, spa, possibly a helipad. PBS' Impossible Builds called it "one of the most complex skyscrapers ever to make it off the drawing board".

wikis.title: One Thousand Museum completion (designboom)
wikis.summary: designboom, 2 July 2019, on the announced completion of Zaha Hadid's One Thousand Museum residential tower in Miami.
wikis.body:
- One Thousand Museum, "Zaha Hadid's first and only residential skyscraper in the United States", has announced completion: 62 stories with 84 half- and full-floor residences; amenities include a multimedia theater, aquatic center with indoor pool and a private vault. Named for its location opposite Museum Park; views over Biscayne Bay.
- Construction began August 2015 with 10,000 cubic yards of concrete for the foundation; from August 2016 to December 2017 one floor was poured about every eight days; topped out early 2018 with a private helipad (the "only residential helipad on the east coast"); height 709 ft (216 m).
- The tower has received its TCO (temporary certificate of occupancy). Turnkey residences by B&B Italia, Roche Bobois and Artefacto to be released "this summer"; prices for 4- to 6-bed condos from the mid-$5Ms to over $20 million.

wikis.title: Salesforce Tower (Wikipedia)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on Salesforce Tower, the 61-story Pelli-designed tallest building in San Francisco, opened 2018.
wikis.body:
- 61-story supertall at 415 Mission Street, San Francisco (formerly Transbay Tower); architectural height 1,070 ft (326 m), roof 970 ft; 1,400,000 sq ft; cost US$1.1 billion; designed by César Pelli (Pelli Clarke Pelli), developed by Hines and Boston Properties; contractors Clark Construction and Hathaway Dinwiddie; engineer Magnusson Klemencic.
- As of 2024 tallest building in San Francisco and second-tallest in California and west of the Mississippi after the Wilshire Grand Center. Last Pelli building completed in his lifetime.
- Obelisk shape with aluminum fins; LED light sculpture of 11,000 LEDs visible up to 30 miles away; 61st floor "Ohana Floor" lounge.
- Timeline: Transbay plan adopted 2005; Transbay Terminal demolished 2011; site sold for US$192 million; groundbreaking March 27, 2013; Salesforce signed a 714,000 sq ft lease on April 11, 2014 (US$560 million over 15.5 years from 2017); first tenants January 8, 2018, 97% leased; original proposal was 1,200 ft. May 2019 Boston Properties bought Hines' remaining 5%.
- Recognition: CTBUH "Best Tall Building Worldwide" 2019; BOMA TOBY award 2025 (over 1 million sq ft).

wikis.title: Facebook opens Frank Gehry-designed MPK20 (NBC Bay Area)
wikis.summary: NBC Bay Area, 31 March 2015, on Facebook's new Frank Gehry-designed MPK20 building opening in Menlo Park.
wikis.body:
- Facebook's new Menlo Park campus building MPK20 is open (staff moved in March 30, 2015): 430,000 square feet, LEED gold certified, large open floor plan and multi-story windows, designed by Frank Gehry.
- Gehry: "From the start, Mark wanted a space that was unassuming, matter-of-fact and cost effective... It is not a grand design statement". Mark Zuckerberg wrote that the building "isn't fancy. That's on purpose."
- Features a nine-acre green rooftop park by CMG Landscape Architects with more than 400 trees, and work by 15 artists (onsite murals on themes such as systems, networks and communities). Hashtags #mpk20 and #mpk20firstlook.

wikis.title: InterContinental Shanghai Wonderland opens as IHG's 200th InterContinental hotel
wikis.summary: IHG's 15 November 2018 news release announcing the grand opening of InterContinental Shanghai Wonderland, built into a former quarry.
wikis.body:
- IHG announced "today" (release dated 15 November 2018) the grand opening of InterContinental Shanghai Wonderland, the 200th hotel for the InterContinental brand worldwide.
- Developed by Shimao Group and managed by IHG; built into the side wall of a formerly abandoned quarry in Southwestern Shanghai, beside Tianma Pit at the Sheshan Mountain Range.
- Stretches 88 metres underground; nominated as one of the architectural wonders of the world by the National Geographic Channel's MegaStructures series.
- Mostly subterranean: two floors above ground and 16 below ground, including 2 floors underwater.
- 336 rooms and suites with views of waterfalls and cliffs. The underwater loft has two levels: a landing deck at water level with outdoor terrace and bedroom, and an underwater living room encased in a turquoise aquarium. Bottom-floor rooms get around-the-clock butler service.
- Club InterContinental lounge sits just above water level; InterContinental Concierge uses the "In-the-Know" approach.
- Lin Wang, Chief Marketing Officer, Greater China, IHG: joining forces with Shimao Group again; IHG has grown since entering the Chinese market in 1984.
- InterContinental Hotels & Resorts was founded in 1946 by aviation pioneer Juan Trippe.

wikis.title: InterContinental Shanghai Wonderland (Wikipedia)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the quarry hotel in Songjiang, Shanghai, covering its history, design and construction.
wikis.body:
- Five-star hotel and "earthscraper" in Songjiang, Shanghai, about 50 km (30 miles) from the city centre; also called Tianma Pit Hotel, Shimao Quarry Hotel or Pit Pegasus Hotel.
- Started operations 20 November 2018; managed by InterContinental; owner Shimao Group. Built on an abandoned quarry; some rooms are underwater. Wikipedia gives 337 rooms.
- Design and construction had many delays before 2013, then progressed swiftly; fit-out was in 2017. Design was shortlisted at the World Architecture Festival in 2009.
- According to Shanghaiist, Shanghai Shimao Property Group invested US$555 million.
- Architects: JADE+QA (concept and facade, led by Martin Jochman, who designed the concept while working with Atkins), ECADI (local architect: design development, construction documents, structure, MEP), Atkins. Interior design: CCD (Cheng Chung Design) and AB Concept.
- 18 stories, 16 below ground including two projected underwater floors; two floors are above the 88 m deep quarry. The quarry is partly filled with water to make an artificial lake. "S"-shaped design with sequential hanging gardens; a glass atrium resembles an artificial waterfall.

wikis.title: Sydney Opera House officially opened, 20 October 1973
wikis.summary: NSW State Archives 'on this day' note on the official opening of the Sydney Opera House by Queen Elizabeth II.
wikis.body:
- On 20 October 1973 the Sydney Opera House was officially opened by Queen Elizabeth II.
- Work began in 1959 and was completed in 1973 at a cost of $102 million.
- The opening was celebrated with fireworks and a performance of Beethoven's Symphony No. 9; a two-week festival of events followed.
- The first public performance was the month before, on 28 September 1973.
- It stands on Tubowgule land of the Gadigal people.
- Related archive records mentioned: the 'Gold Book' (1959 ceremony to commemorate the commencement), Jorn Utzon's 1958 'Red Book', the 'Brown Book' competition conditions; Fort Macquarie (built 1817-1821, demolished 1901) and the Tram Depot (opened 1902, pulled down 1958) previously stood at Bennelong Point.
- Page published 5 Dec 2022.

wikis.title: Sydney Opera House opens, October 20, 1973 (HISTORY)
wikis.summary: HISTORY.com entry on the dedication of the Sydney Opera House by Queen Elizabeth II on 20 October 1973.
wikis.body:
- After 15 years of construction, the Sydney Opera House was dedicated by Queen Elizabeth II on October 20, 1973.
- Cost given as $80 million; designed by Danish architect Jorn Utzon; funded by profits of the Opera House Lotteries; built on Bennelong Point, Sydney, Australia.
- Known for its geometric roof shells; contains several large auditoriums and presents an average of 3,000 events a year to an estimated two million people.
- First performance in the complex: the Australian Opera's production of Prokofiev's War and Peace in the 1,547-seat Opera Theatre.
- Described as Sydney's best-known landmark.
- Page published July 21, 2010; last updated May 27, 2025.

wikis.title: Hoover Dam chronology (Bureau of Reclamation)
wikis.summary: Bureau of Reclamation timeline of Hoover Dam from 1540 exploration of the Colorado River to the 1985 50th anniversary.
wikis.body:
Key dates from the chronology:
- 1902: Reclamation Act signed by Theodore Roosevelt. 1905-1907: Colorado River breaks into the Imperial Valley, creating the Salton Sea.
- 1918: Arthur P. Davis proposes a dam of unprecedented height in Boulder Canyon.
- 1922: Colorado River Compact signed by the seven basin states in Santa Fe, November 24th; Fall-Davis report recommends a high dam near Boulder Canyon.
- 1928: Boulder Canyon Project Act signed by President Calvin Coolidge, December 21st. 1929: declared effective June 25th.
- 1931: bids opened March 4; contract awarded to Six Companies March 11; notice to proceed April 20.
- 1932: river diverted around the dam site, November 14th. 1933: first concrete placed June 6th.
- 1935: dam starts impounding water in Lake Mead February 1st; last concrete May 29th; President Franklin D. Roosevelt dedicates the dam September 30th.
- 1936: first generator (N-2) in full operation October 26th; further generators added through 1939.
- 1939: installed capacity of 704,800 kilowatts made Hoover Powerplant the largest hydroelectric facility in the world until surpassed by Grand Coulee Dam in 1949.
- 1941: Lake Mead 580 feet deep, 120 miles long; dam closed to the public December 7th for WWII.
- 1947: Congress designates the structure "Hoover Dam".
- 1961: final generating unit (N-8) on line December 1st; installed capacity 1,334,800 kilowatts.
- 1985: 50th anniversary; majority of the project cost repaid to the Federal Treasury.
Last updated 7/13/22.

wikis.title: The Hoover Dam (Herbert Hoover Presidential Library)
wikis.summary: Presidential library page on how Herbert Hoover's role led to the Colorado River Compact, the Boulder Canyon Project Act and Hoover Dam.
wikis.body:
- Named in honor of President Herbert Hoover, who played a crucial role in its creation; still "considered an engineering marvel" 85 years after completion.
- Disastrous early-1900s floods and irrigation experiments led southwestern residents to seek federal help; the main obstacle was allocating water rights among seven basin states (meetings in 1918, 1919, 1920 failed to reach consensus).
- As Secretary of Commerce from 1921, Hoover proposed the dam; on December 17, 1921 President Harding appointed him chair of the Colorado River Commission.
- Colorado River Compact signed in Santa Fe on November 24, 1922: splits the basin into upper and lower halves without individual state quotas (Hoover's compromise).
- Swing-Johnson bills 1922-1928 were rejected until the Boulder Canyon Project Act, largely written by Hoover and Interior Secretary Hubert Work, signed by Coolidge on December 21, 1928.
- June 25, 1929: President Hoover proclaimed the Compact effective. Construction began 1930; dedicated 1935; generators online 1937. In 1947 Congress "restored" Hoover's name to the dam.
- Cost $49 million for the dam (about $1 billion adjusted); power plant and generators an additional $71 million; power sales paid back construction with interest by 1987.
- Today: controls flooding, irrigates more than 1.5 million acres, supplies water to more than 16 million people, power for over 500,000 homes.

wikis.title: Leeza SOHO (Wikipedia)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on Leeza SOHO, a 207 m Zaha Hadid Architects office tower in Beijing with the world's tallest atrium, opened 19 November 2019.
wikis.body:
- Leeza SOHO (Li Ze Tower), a 207 m (679 ft) commercial skyscraper in the Lize Financial Business District, Beijing.
- SOHO China acquired land use rights in 2013 for 1.922 billion RMB (US$288 million). Construction began 2015; topped out September 2017; opened 19 November 2019.
- 46 floors (+4 underground); floor area 172,800 m2. Architects Zaha Hadid and Patrik Schumacher (Zaha Hadid Architects); structural engineer Bollinger + Grohmann; main contractor China State Construction Engineering Corp.
- Third of three ZHA buildings developed by SOHO China, after Galaxy SOHO and Wangjing SOHO.
- Central atrium 194 m (636 ft) tall, the tallest in the world, a title previously held by the Burj Al Arab; twists 45 degrees over the height to bring natural light to all floors; four sky bridges and a double-insulated glass facade.
- At the intersection of Beijing Subway Lines 14 and 16 (Lize Shangwuqu station); a Daxing Airport Express platform is to open in 2026, with Line 11 and Line 25 extensions planned.

wikis.title: Zaha Hadid Architects completes Leeza SOHO tower in Beijing (designboom)
wikis.summary: Designboom report on the opening of Leeza SOHO with the world's tallest atrium, including design and sustainability details and project data.
wikis.body:
- Leeza SOHO, by Zaha Hadid Architects (ZHA), has opened in China with the world's tallest atrium; it anchors Beijing's new Fengtai business district, a financial and transport hub between the city centre and the new international airport.
- 45-storey, 172,800 sqm tower giving small and medium-sized businesses flexible grade A office space.
- Site is next to the district rail station at the intersection of five new subway lines under construction and is diagonally dissected by an underground subway service tunnel; the design divides the volume into two halves under a single facade shell. The atrium is 194.15 m and rotates as the tower rises to realign upper floors with Lize Road; skybridges on levels 13, 24, 35 and 45. It is meant to work as a public square, and as a thermal chimney with integrated ventilation.
- Double-insulated unitized glass curtain wall: glazing u-value 2.0 W/m2K, shading coefficient 0.4; envelope u-value 0.55 W/m2K. Designed to achieve LEED gold; 3D BIM energy management; heat recovery, water collection, grey water flushing, green roof with photovoltaic array. 2,680 bicycle parking spaces below ground plus EV charging.
- Project data: top of facade 199.99 m; top of atrium 194.15 m; floor-to-floor 4.1 m; 45 floors above and 4 below ground; site area 14,365 sqm; project start October 2013; siteworks start April 2015; completion 19 November 2019.
- Team: design Zaha Hadid and Patrik Schumacher; project director Satoshi Ohashi; executive architect Beijing Institute of Architectural Design; structure Bollinger + Grohmann (early stages).

wikis.title: Bloomberg London (Wikipedia)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on Bloomberg's European headquarters at 3 Queen Victoria Street, City of London, designed by Foster and Partners and opened in 2017.
wikis.body:
- Office building at 3 Queen Victoria Street in the City of London, opened October 2017; Bloomberg L.P.'s European headquarters, on the former site of Bucklersbury House.
- Designed by Foster and Partners with structural engineer AKT II; built by Sir Robert McAlpine at a cost of 1 billion pounds. Won the RIBA Stirling Prize in 2018.
- Two buildings divided by a covered arcade with restaurants that reinstates part of Watling Street, an ancient Roman road; linked by bridges. Digs on the site found Roman-era wooden writing tablets ("Bloomberg tablets").
- Clad in 9,600 tonnes of Derbyshire sandstone with bronze ventilation fins; a 210 m helical bronze "ramp"; houses 4,000 staff; artwork by Olafur Eliasson and "Forgotten Streams" by Cristina Iglesias.
- Energy: 98.5% BREEAM score, the highest design-stage score for a major office development; 500,000 LEDs; rainwater feeds vacuum toilets. Criticised as wasteful (600 tonnes of Japanese bronze, 10,000 tonnes of imported Indian granite).
- New Bank and Monument station entrance (Waterloo & City line, four escalators, two lifts, step-free); construction began November 2015; opened December 2018 by Sadiq Khan and Michael Bloomberg.
- The London Mithraeum, a Roman temple, was relocated close to its original site beneath the building and is open to the public; also the Bloomberg Space for artworks.

wikis.title: Foster + Partners' Bloomberg headquarters, the "world's most sustainable office" (Dezeen)
wikis.summary: Dezeen, 4 October 2017, on the newly completed Bloomberg European headquarters in London and its BREEAM Outstanding rating.
wikis.body:
- Dezeen, 4 October 2017: first photos of Norman Foster's newly completed European HQ for Bloomberg, which "claims to be the world's most sustainable office building".
- BREEAM rating Outstanding, score 98.5 per cent, the highest achieved so far by a major office development. Designed to use 73 per cent less water and 35 per cent less energy than a standard office.
- Bronze blades on the facade open and close with the weather for natural ventilation; petal-design ceiling panels with 500,000 LEDs combine heating, cooling and acoustic functions; smart sensors adjust airflow, expected to cut CO2 by 300 tonnes a year; rainwater and grey water feed vacuum toilets, saving 25 million litres a year.
- Sits between St Paul's Cathedral and the Bank of England on the site of an ancient Roman temple; the Temple of Mithras (discovered 1954) returns to its original site in a double-height basement.
- Over 3.2 acres; 102,200 square metres of office and retail space; two triangular-plan buildings clad in Yorkshire sandstone [sic] and bronze fins; brass ramp; the Bloomberg Arcade reinstates a Roman road; three new public plazas, a theatre, and a new Bank station entrance.
- To be officially opened on 24 October 2017.

wikis.title: Bloomberg's European HQ / Foster + Partners (ArchDaily)
wikis.summary: ArchDaily project page for Bloomberg's European headquarters in London by Foster + Partners, 2017.
wikis.body:
- Architects Foster + Partners; client Bloomberg LP; London; area 102,190 m2; year 2017; structural engineer AKT II; quantity surveyor AECOM; lighting engineer Tillotson Design Associates.
- Architects' description: respectful of its location near the Bank of England, St. Paul's Cathedral and St. Stephen's Walbrook; "a natural extension of the City".
- BREEAM Outstanding rating, "the highest design-stage score ever achieved by any major office development".
- Published on October 25, 2017.

wikis.title: Dalston Lane completed: world's largest CLT structure (Waugh Thistleton)
wikis.summary: Waugh Thistleton's 30 June 2017 news item announcing completion of Dalston Lane, described as the world's largest CLT structure.
wikis.body:
- Dalston Lane, "the world's largest CLT structure", has been completed, delivering 121 new affordable and private-for-rent homes plus 3500m2 of commercial space.
- Uses over 4,500m3 of CLT; the structure consumes less than half the embodied carbon of an equivalent concrete frame.
- Carbon stored in the timber is 3756 TCO2e; the equivalent of 2325 trees were used, which the architects say can be regrown in 3 hours in the German and Austrian forests they come from.

wikis.title: Dalston Works CLT housing in east London (Dezeen)
wikis.summary: Dezeen, 1 November 2017, on the completed 10-storey Dalston Works cross-laminated timber apartment complex by Waugh Thistleton.
wikis.body:
- Completed 10-storey carbon-neutral apartment complex in Dalston, London, by Waugh Thistleton, which claims it is the "world's largest cross-laminated timber building"; 33.8 metres tall.
- Walls' frames, party walls, floors, ceilings, stairs and lift core are wood and glue, brick-clad; structure is five times lighter than concrete, which allowed building higher near a planned Crossrail route.
- Timber frame has 50 per cent less embodied CO2 than a concrete frame and locks in 2,600 tonnes of CO2.
- Prefabricated off site; assembly took 374 days.
- Cluster of buildings of five to ten storeys; GBP 24 million mixed-use development by Regal London: 121 apartments (102 build-to-rent via Go Native, interiors by Conran Contracts; two-bedroom around GBP 2,190 per month), 1,500 m2 restaurant/retail, and a 3,500 m2 flexible workspace hub.
- Comparison: Hawkins\Brown's The Cube in Shoreditch is 0.8 m shorter (hybrid timber with steel and concrete core); a 10-storey CLT building, 5 King Street, was planned in Brisbane for 2018.
- Andrew Waugh: "Dalston Works demonstrates the possibilities of engineered, cross-laminated timber as a cost efficient, and desperately necessary, viable alternative to the polluting technologies of concrete and steel."

wikis.title: 22 Bishopsgate (Wikipedia)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the 278 m, 62-storey London skyscraper 22 Bishopsgate (formerly The Pinnacle), its stalled construction, redesign and completion in 2020.
wikis.body:
- Commercial skyscraper in Bishopsgate, City of London; completed 2020; 278 m (912 ft), 62 storeys; architect PLP Architecture; WSP structural and services engineer; main contractor Multiplex. Second tallest building in the UK and seventeenth tallest in Europe.
- Replaced The Pinnacle (KPF design, nicknamed "The Helter Skelter", 288 m after being scaled down from 307 m), on which construction started in 2008 but was suspended in 2012 after the Great Recession with only the concrete core of the first seven storeys done. Planning approved April 2006.
- Original funding: Arab Investments / Economic Development Corporation of Saudi Arabia invested 500 million pounds for a majority stake; a 140 million pound HSH Nordbank loan; work halted March 2012 over pre-let problems.
- February 2015: site bought by an Axa Real Estate-led consortium in a deal worth 550 million pounds; redesigned with a simpler exterior; planning approved November 2015; the old core was removed by December 2015 and construction of the new building began January 2016. April 2016: Lipton Rogers and Axa IM - Real Assets to complete the 1 billion pound development in 2019.
- Construction continued despite the June 2016 EU referendum leave vote. A November 2016 plan to cut height by 23 m (59 floors) was approved February 2017 but withdrawn; the 62-storey, 278 m scheme is being built. In 2017 a suspended girder from the site struck Leadenhall Tower; nobody was hurt.
- Facilities: about 61 levels mostly offices; bike park for over 1,000 bicycles; food "marketplace"; public gym with glass climbing wall; free public viewing gallery on the 58th floor at 254 m, the highest viewing gallery in the UK and highest free one in Europe (free as a planning condition).
- Foundations: longest piles in the UK as of March 2009 (48.5 m below sea level, 65.5 m below ground).

wikis.title: Zeitz MOCAA to open in Cape Town, designed by Heatherwick Studio
wikis.summary: Zeitz MOCAA announcement of 13 July 2017 that the Heatherwick-designed contemporary African art museum will open at Cape Town's V&A Waterfront on 22 September 2017.
wikis.body:
- Announced 13 July 2017: Zeitz Museum of Contemporary Art Africa opens to the public at Cape Town's V&A Waterfront on Friday, 22 September 2017; "the world's largest museum dedicated to contemporary art from Africa and its Diaspora".
- 9,500 square metres over nine floors carved from the historic grain silo (disused since 1990, once the tallest building in South Africa) with a cathedral-like atrium cut from its 42 tubes; 6,000 sq m of exhibition space in 80 galleries, rooftop sculpture garden, restaurant and bar, shop, reading rooms; centres for Photography, Curatorial Excellence, the Moving Image, Performative Practice, Art Education and the Costume Institute.
- Cost R500-million (30 million pounds), announced November 2013; a partnership between the V&A Waterfront and Jochen Zeitz; not-for-profit; Mark Coetzee Executive Director and Chief Curator.
- Thomas Heatherwick: the silo was "made from 116 vertical tubes" [sic vs 42 elsewhere in the release]; the challenge was to carve galleries from the "10-storey-high tubular honeycomb" without destroying its authenticity.
