- The Zeitz Collection was founded in 2002 by Jochen Zeitz. V&A Waterfront draws up to 100,000 people a day.

wikis.title: Zeitz Museum of Contemporary Art Africa (Wikipedia)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on Zeitz MOCAA in Cape Town, opened 22 September 2017 in a converted grain silo by Heatherwick Studio.
wikis.body:
- Public non-profit museum in the Silo District at the V&A Waterfront, Cape Town; opened September 22, 2017 as the largest museum of contemporary art from Africa and its diaspora. Waterfront receives around 24 million visitors per year.
- Founders: Mark Coetzee, Jochen Zeitz and the V&A Waterfront (David Green). Koyo Kouoh was Executive Director and Chief Curator from 6 May 2019 until her passing in May 2025.
- The Waterfront invested more than R500 million; Zeitz has loaned his art collection for his lifetime.
- Building: conversion of the 57 m tall grain silo built 1921-1924 by indentured labourers; Heatherwick Studio (introduced to it in 2006 and 2011 by Ravi Naidoo of Design Indaba); conversion began 2014; 42 concrete cylinders carved out with concrete-cutting techniques; remaining shafts capped with strengthened glass; pillowed glass panels on upper floors. 9,500 sqm, nine floors, 6,000 sqm of exhibition space, sculpture garden. The upper part is The Silo Hotel (opened March 2017). On the RIBA International List 2018.
- Includes the Centre for Art Education, a fellowship programme, an atelier artist residency, shop, rooftop restaurant and coffee shop. Lists past exhibitions, e.g. Senzeni Marasela's Waiting For Gebane (18 Dec 2020 - 29 Aug 2021) and Joel Andrianomearisoa's The Five Continents of All Our Desires (2 Aug 2022 - 25 Jul 2023).

wikis.title: Docklands Light Railway (Wikipedia): overview, origins and early history
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on London's automated Docklands Light Railway: system facts, planning origins from the 1970s, construction and the 1987 opening and early extensions.
wikis.body:
- Automated light metro in London; owner Docklands Light Railway Ltd (part of Transport for London); 3 lines, 45 stations, 38 km (24 mi), 149 vehicles, 3-5 minute headway; third rail 750 V DC; began operation 31 August 1987; operated by KeolisAmey (Keolis 70%, Amey 30%) 2014-2033; ridership 97.8 million (2024/25); all stations step-free.
- Planning: in the early 1970s Travis Morgan & Partners proposed a "minitram" system for the Docklands; a 1976 plan for a Jubilee line extension would have cost about 325 million pounds (later estimated 450 million); the Thatcher government halted it and insisted on a lower-cost option.
- July 1981: London Docklands Development Corporation (LDDC) established, commissioning light rail options. The Minories option (high-level, on the site of the old Minories station) became Tower Gateway; the central Isle of Dogs route was chosen, though a 1981 report warned Canary Wharf would be "very isolated with poor traffic prospects" without extensive development. Final report June 1982.
- Funding: Departments of Environment and Transport agreed 77 million pounds with a 1987 deadline and no ongoing subsidy. Initially planned manual with some street running; northern terminus changed to Stratford and an automated system was pushed by the LDDC. 1984 contract to GEC / John Mowlem; Acts of Parliament in 1984 and 1985; construction from 1985; two thirds of the route on disused or underused railway.
- Opening: formally opened by Queen Elizabeth II on 30 July 1987; passenger services began 31 August 1987. Initial system: routes Tower Gateway and Stratford to Island Gardens; 13 km, 15 stations; 11 P86 stock units from Linke-Hofmann-Busch; driverless with a Passenger Service Agent ("Train Captain") on board.
- 1991: tunnel extension to Bank (this article gives a cost of 295 million pounds), Canary Wharf station rebuilt with six platforms on three tracks; extension east toward Beckton followed.

wikis.title: Building an Urban Railway: 30 Years of the DLR (The B1M)
wikis.summary: The B1M article of 13 September 2017 on the history of the Docklands Light Railway from its 1987 opening through its extensions.
wikis.body:
- Published 13 September 2017 (author given as Tom Ravenscroft). DLR is a driverless automated light metro designed to rejuvenate London's Docklands, a low-cost alternative to extending the Underground; opened 1987 with 11 trains serving 15 stations, now (2017) 145 trains and 45 stations.
- Ridership: 6.7M in the first year, 122M in 2016.
- July 1981: LDDC created; wanted a highly visible, automated, driverless, futuristic system. Government specified a 77 million pound budget; eight miles of track on disused viaducts and existing formations plus new elevated concrete viaducts; not connected to the Tube; terminus at the disused Minories station.
- 31 August 1987: opened with lines Tower Gateway-Island Gardens and Stratford-Island Gardens.
- 1991: Bank extension, 149 million pounds, 1.3 km tunnel; original fleet sold to Essen, Germany for its tram system; Canary Wharf opened 1991 as the largest station (six platforms, three tracks). March 1994: Beckton extension added 11 stations; 15 to 28 stations in 7 years.
- 3 December 1999: Lewisham extension, 4.2 km, 200 million pound project, the first PFI on a UK railway; Island Gardens rebuilt underground; five stations added.
- 2 December 2005: London City Airport branch, 140 million pounds; 2009: Woolwich Arsenal extension, 180 million pounds.
- 2011: Canning Town-Stratford International extension before the 2012 Olympics, seven stations, total 45.
- Extensions discussed: Lewisham to Forest Hill, east to Dagenham Dock, Thamesmead, and Bank to Charing Cross and Victoria.

wikis.title: King Power Mahanakhon (Wikipedia)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the 314 m mixed-use Mahanakhon skyscraper in Bangkok, its history, design and 2018 sale to King Power.
wikis.body:
- Mixed-use skyscraper (residential, retail, hotel, observatory) in the Silom/Sathon business district of Bangkok, formerly MahaNakhon; 314 m (1,030 ft) roof height; 77-78 floors (article gives both); 150,000 m2; architect Ole Scheeren; developer Pace Development; structural engineer Arup.
- Details announced 27 May 2009; groundbreaking 20 June 2011; CUBE building finished October 2013; topped off at 314 m in April 2015; completed April 2016 (CTBUH recognised it as tallest in Thailand on 4 May 2016). Infobox opening date 29 August 2016; the article text also says it was opened in December 2016 by Managing Director Kipsan Beck, and mentions a major opening event in late 2017.
- Total project value reached 21 billion baht (US$620 million). Sold freehold from March 2014. Residences priced about US$1,100,000 to US$17,000,000.
- Tallest in Thailand until Magnolias Waterfront Residences at ICONSIAM (317 m) in 2018.
- Purchased by King Power group from Pace Development's Sorapoj Techakraisri in April 2018, hence the rename.
- Design: square glass-curtain-walled prism with a pixelated ribbon swirling around the exterior, a cuboid-surfaced helix cut into the side.

wikis.title: MahaNakhon's spectacular grand opening (The Nation)
wikis.summary: The Nation, 29 August 2016, on the light-show grand opening of MahaNakhon, Thailand's tallest building.
wikis.body:
- Bangkok's skyline was lit "last night" by the grand opening of MahaNakhon, Thailand's tallest building, with the "MahaNakhon Bangkok Rising the Night of Light" light show.
- Pharrell Williams was in Bangkok; his "Williams Family Kitchen", opened with Dean & Deluca, is part of the building.
- Luxury mixed-use, 77 floors, 314.2 metres, on Sathorn Road business district; developer Pace Development, a listed developer.
- Contains restaurants, cafes and marketplace; The Ritz-Carlton Residences and a hotel managed by The Ritz-Carlton Hotel Company (Marriott International with Ian Schrager); multi-level roof-top Terrace Bar and observation deck.

wikis.title: Royal Hospital for Children and Young People, Edinburgh (Wikipedia)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on Edinburgh's new paediatric hospital at Little France, its procurement, delays and opening.
wikis.body:
- Paediatric hospital at 50 Little France Crescent, Edinburgh (Edinburgh BioQuarter, part of the Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh campus), managed by NHS Lothian; replaced the Royal Hospital for Sick Children (the Sick Kids) at Sciennes; 167 beds in the infobox (the text says 233 beds); cares for patients from birth to around 16.
- 2005: NHS Lothian decided to move the Sick Kids; business case approved by the Scottish Government in January 2012; procured under the non-profit distributing model in 2015; design by HLM Architects; construction by Brookfield Multiplex at a cost of 150 million pounds, begun February 2015.
- August 2016: delay announced due to adverse weather and two of the project's builders entering administration. May 2017: named Royal Hospital for Children and Young People.
- Emergency department was to transfer 9 July 2019, but two weeks before, faults in the air conditioning and then drainage were found, estimated to cost 90 million pounds to fix.
- Officially opened / founded 23 March 2021 (per the article). Also houses the Department of Clinical Neurosciences (from the Western General) and CAMHS (from the Royal Edinburgh Hospital). 112 disabled parking spaces on site.
tags: royal hospital for children and young people

wikis.title: Princess Royal officially opens the RHCYP and Department of Clinical Neurosciences (Edinburgh BioQuarter)
wikis.summary: Edinburgh BioQuarter news item on HRH The Princess Royal's official opening of the Royal Hospital for Children and Young People and the Department of Clinical Neurosciences.
wikis.body:
- NHS Lothian welcomed HRH The Princess Royal to officially open the RHCYP and the Department of Clinical Neurosciences (DCN) on Edinburgh BioQuarter, on the 75th anniversary of the NHS (per chief executive Calum Campbell; the COVID pandemic had delayed the official opening).
- The building first opened its doors in July 2020, with all services transferred by March 2021.
- The children's hospital is physically connected to the Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh, putting paediatric care, specialist neonatal care, neurosciences and both Emergency Departments on one site, reducing emergency transfers.
- DCN treats patients from the Borders, Dumfries & Galloway, Forth Valley, Fife and Lothian: population 1.6 million; 2.8 million for some specialist services.
- Visit: tour, Dalhousie Ward and Play Teams, magician Tricky Ricky funded by Edinburgh Children's Hospital Charity, an EMG demonstration, and the Neurorehabilitation Ward. Facilities include one of the UK's largest Art and Therapeutic Design programmes. Afternoon activities with charity partners including Kindred.
tags: royal hospital for children and young people

wikis.title: Battersea Power Station Phase One, Circus West Village (Buro Happold)
wikis.summary: Buro Happold project page on its engineering role in Phase One (Circus West Village) of the Battersea Power Station regeneration, London.
wikis.body:
- Client Battersea Power Station Development Company (BPSDC); architects SimpsonHaugh and Partners (RS1-A) and dRMM (RS1-B); Buro Happold duration 2012-2016; services include structural, facade, fire, bridge/civil and water engineering.
- Regeneration: 42-acre former brownfield site, seven phases, more than 8 million ft2 of mixed-use development and more than 19 acres of parkland; described as a 9 billion pound scheme, served by a Zone 1 Northern Line extension, with restoration of the Grade II* listed power station.
- Phase One, Circus West Village, completed 2017; 865 new homes, home to 800 residents (the page elsewhere says more than 1,800), bars, restaurants, cinema and theatre, a new Thames Clipper jetty; 25,000 ft2 of shops and food and beverage; 450 new permanent jobs, 37 per cent filled by local people.
- Two structural blocks over a common two-level basement: RS1-A more than 300 m long by just over 20 m wide, 8 to 18 storeys; RS1-B (Faraday House) uniform nine storeys, about 115 m by 15 m.
- Buro Happold was lead consultant for the basement (site-wide car park, podium areas, a temporary energy centre); facade challenge was the double-skin "wintergarden" balconies; a "kit of parts" construction scheme helped meet the programme.

wikis.title: Battersea Power Station Phase 1: Circus West Village (SimpsonHaugh)
wikis.summary: SimpsonHaugh's project page for Circus West, the first completed phase of Battersea Power Station's regeneration, finished September 2017.
wikis.body:
- First phase completed at Battersea Power Station; a new neighbourhood on the western side of the power station, with links to the riverfront and Battersea Park and refurbished railway arches for a village hall and restaurant.
- Main building Circus West: 17 storeys, 327 metres long, tapering footprint; 752 new homes (1-3 bedroom apartments, townhouses, penthouses), residents' garden and lounge, health suite, offices, shops, bars, restaurants and a riverside park.
- Amenities: 15,000 sq ft gym, indoor pool, health spa, 5,000 sq ft private residents' club with bar, dining space, library and cinema; podium-level private garden.
- Double-skin glass facade in articulated horizontal glass ribbons; winter gardens.
- Project data: client Battersea Power Station Development Company; area 90,112 sq m; start 2011; completion September 2017; structural engineer Buro Happold; services engineer Hoare Lea; cost manager Gardiner & Theobald; award 2018 MSA Multiple Residences - Built.

wikis.title: Beirut Terraces (Wikipedia)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on Beirut Terraces, a 26-floor Herzog & de Meuron residential tower in central Beirut completed in 2017.
wikis.body:
- Residential skyscraper at 1399 Fouad Najjar Street, Minet el-Hosn, Beirut Central District, across from the ruined Holiday Inn Beirut and south of the Platinum Tower.
- 26 floors; 119.5 m architectural height (tip 121.5 m); construction 2011, completed 2017.
- Architect Herzog & de Meuron; developer Benchmark; structural engineer Arup (design) and Khatib & Alami (engineer of record); main contractor MAN Enterprise; owners DIB Tower SAL and TOWN Tower SAL; materials aluminium, concrete, glass.
- Design inspired by Beirut's classic and contemporary history: a stack of layers formed by terraces and overhangs projecting differently; overhangs shade and reduce solar gain; floor slabs extend at least 60 cm around the perimeter to ease facade construction and upkeep and protect tenants from direct heat.

wikis.title: 347 Beirut Terraces (Herzog & de Meuron)
wikis.summary: The architects' project page for Beirut Terraces, a 119 m layered residential tower in Beirut (project 2009-2012, realization 2012-2016).
wikis.body:
- Project 2009-2012; realization 2012-2016; Beirut, Lebanon.
- Site: in a portion of a Beirut master plan for office and residential high-rises near a new yacht marina; the design was influenced by the layers of the city's history (Phoenician, Roman, Mamluk, Ottoman and Colonial remains); mentions the 2005 assassination of Prime Minister Rafik Hariri by a car bomb in front of St. Georges Hotel.
- Multilayered 119-metre high-rise; five principles: layers and terraces, inside and outside, vegetation, views and privacy, light and identity. Projecting or set-back living areas create terraces and overhangs; each unit is unique.
- Vegetation on terraces provides shade and privacy; a water feature in the main entry lobby; sea views to the north and the green boulevard to the east.
- Slabs protrude at least 60 cm around the circumference; thick floor plates use thermal mass to store cold at night; perforations in overhangs modulate light and sun.
- Structure: five modular floors repeated in different combinations; carried by the core and a regular column grid spanning up to 14.7 metres, so apartment walls are non-structural.

wikis.title: David Miller Architects revamps Lord's Cricket Ground Media Centre (Architects' Journal)
wikis.summary: AJ Specification case study, 17 October 2017, on the refurbishment of Lord's Media Centre by David Miller Architects, completed April 2017.
wikis.body:
- The 1999 Media Centre at Lord's (Future Systems, engineered by Arup; RIBA Stirling Prize winner in 1999) is an all-aluminium, semi-monocoque building built and fitted out by a shipyard using boatbuilding technology.
- David Miller, project architect on the original at Future Systems, was approached by the MCC in 2015 (via David Miller Architects, DMA) for a full upgrade and redesign.
- Method: modelled the aluminium shell from 2D fabrication drawings, laser-scanned the interior to find voids, pushed the internal shell outward: usable floor area up 15 per cent.
- Larger areas for reporters and photographers, bigger and more broadcast boxes, relocated refreshment area, new M&E, new lifts and stairs, and a new 30 m, 23-tonne steel camera gantry suspended and cantilevered from beneath the shell, closer to Jan Kaplicky's original concept, lost to value engineering in the 1990s.
- Project data: two phases of six months each in the cricket off-season (phase 1 November 2015 to April 2016); completion April 2017; 900 m2 gross internal area; construction cost 4 million pounds; client Marylebone Cricket Club; structural engineer Elliott Wood; M&E Long and Partners; QS Gardiner & Theobald; main contractor Knight Harwood; Revit and Navisworks.

wikis.title: How BIM helped refurbish Lord's Media Centre (David Miller Architects)
wikis.summary: David Miller Architects news post of 8 May 2017 on using BIM and scanning for the 4 million pound refurbishment of the J.P. Morgan Media Centre at Lord's.
wikis.body:
- The J.P. Morgan Media Centre at Lord's won the RIBA Stirling Prize in 1999; designed by Future Systems, engineered by Arup; described as the first all-aluminium, semi-monocoque building in the world, built and fitted out in two boatyards. It stands 15 metres above the ground and is supported solely by its two lift shafts.
- MCC turned to David Miller, original project architect, to lead the 4 million pound refurbishment to increase space for broadcast and print media.
- DMA digitally scanned the structure inside and out because original plans were 2D; the 3D models identified an additional 15% of internal floor space.
- Robert Ebdon, Head of Estates at MCC: part of a wider investment masterplan for Lord's, "the Home of Cricket".

wikis.title: 56 Leonard Street (Wikipedia)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on 56 Leonard Street, the Herzog & de Meuron 'Jenga Building' condominium tower in Tribeca, Manhattan, completed in 2017.
wikis.body:
- Residential condominium in Tribeca, Manhattan; 821 ft (250 m), 57 stories (infobox says 60 floors); colloquially the "Jenga Building"; completed 2017; tallest structure in Tribeca. Herzog & de Meuron describe it as "houses stacked in the sky".
- Architects Herzog & de Meuron with Goldstein, Hill & West Architects as architect of record; developer Alexico Group (Izak Senbahar); structural engineer WSP.
- History: land and air rights bought in 2007 from the New York Law School for US$150 million; foundation work in 2008 but project put on hold; construction resumed October 2012; 2013 US$350 million loan led by Bank of America; 70% sold by May 2013, 92% sold in seven months per Senbahar. June 2013: a penthouse went into contract for US$47 million, the most expensive residence sold below Midtown Manhattan.
- Interior: 17,000 ft2 of amenity space on the ninth and tenth floors including a 75 ft pool and 25-seat screening room; ten elevators; eight full-floor apartments at the top (5,200 to 6,400 ft2, 14-to-19 ft ceilings); black granite double-height lobby.
- Anish Kapoor sculpture at the base unveiled February 2023: 19 ft high, 48 ft curved length, 40 tons, commissioned in 2008 at an estimated US$8-10 million.
- The article also records that on September 2, 2022 Gustavo Arnal, CFO of Bed Bath & Beyond, died in a fall from his 18th-floor apartment.

wikis.title: 56 Leonard Street / Herzog & de Meuron (ArchDaily)
wikis.summary: ArchDaily project listing for 56 Leonard Street, New York, by Herzog & de Meuron, 2017 (metadata only).
wikis.body:
- Apartments in New York, United States; architects Herzog & de Meuron; year 2017.
- Client: Izak Senbahar, Alexico Group LLC; executive architect Goldstein and Associates, Hill & West Architects; photographs by Hufton+Crow and Iwan Baan; manufacturers Laufen, Soprema.
- Materials: glass, concrete. Published on May 22, 2017.
- The page has no descriptive text beyond these project specifications.

wikis.title: Five years on: the day Louvre Abu Dhabi opened its doors (The National)
wikis.summary: The National, 11 November 2022, looking back at the 11 November 2017 opening of Louvre Abu Dhabi on its fifth anniversary.
wikis.body:
- Louvre Abu Dhabi welcomed its first public visitors on November 11, 2017, five years before the article (11 November 2022); described as the Arab world's first universal museum.
- It was also 15 years since the project was first approved by the French Parliament and the Louvre Museum signed a Dh1.92 billion agreement allowing Abu Dhabi's museum to use its name for three decades.
- Opening ceremony: traditional Emirati dances beneath Jean Nouvel's dome, a flypast by an Etihad A380 and a light show. Director Manuel Rabate: "You see people from all over the world... mesmerised by the dome, the artworks, by the Children's Museum." Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid: the museum will be a "meeting point for lovers of art, culture and beauty all around the world".
- First special exhibition: From One Louvre to Another: Opening a Museum for Everyone, with 150 masterpieces from the Palace of Versailles and Louvre Museum. Leonardo's La Belle Ferronniere was loaned until 2019; for the fifth anniversary the Louvre loaned Leonardo's Saint John the Baptist, which arrived the week before.

wikis.title: Louvre Abu Dhabi to welcome visitors from November (Louvre press room)
wikis.summary: Announcement dated 6 September 2017 that Louvre Abu Dhabi opens to the public on 11 November 2017, with details of its architecture and collection.
wikis.body:
- Abu Dhabi, 6 September 2017: Louvre Abu Dhabi announced it will open on 11 November 2017; "the first museum of its kind in the Arab world", a universal museum on shared human stories. Opening celebrations include symposiums, performances, concerts, dance and visual arts.
- Designed by Pritzker Prize winning architect Jean Nouvel as a museum city (Arab medina) under a 180-metre dome of almost 8,000 unique metal stars that creates a moving "rain of light". Also a Children's Museum, restaurant, boutique and cafe.
- Galleries are chronological and thematic in 12 chapters, starting in the "Great Vestibule". Works cited: the Bactrian Princess, sarcophagi of Princess Henuttawy, a Decadrachm coin of Syracuse, a Leaf from the "Blue Quran", Japanese Namban screens, an Ottoman Turban Helmet, a Van Risenburgh red Chinese lacquer chest, and Manet's the Gypsy, Gauguin's Children Wrestling, Mondrian's Composition with Blue, Red, Yellow and Black; a monumental Ai Weiwei work.
- Site-specific works: Jenny Holzer's three engraved stone walls For Louvre Abu Dhabi (2017); Giuseppe Penone's Leaves of Light (bronze tree with mirrors) and Propagation (porcelain tiles from Sheikh Zayed's fingerprint, made with Sevres workshops).
- Quotes from Mohamed Khalifa Al Mubarak (TCA Abu Dhabi/TDIC) and French Culture Minister Francoise Nyssen, who calls it a milestone ten years after the intergovernmental agreement.

wikis.title: Statue of Liberty dedicated, October 28, 1886 (HISTORY)
wikis.summary: HISTORY.com entry on the dedication of the Statue of Liberty in New York Harbor by President Grover Cleveland on 28 October 1886.
wikis.body:
- The Statue of Liberty, a gift of friendship from the people of France, was dedicated in New York Harbor by President Grover Cleveland on October 28, 1886; originally "Liberty Enlightening the World"; proposed by French abolitionist Edouard de Laboulaye to commemorate the Franco-American alliance in the Revolution.
- Designed by Frederic-Auguste Bartholdi; 151-foot statue; steel framework designed by Eugene-Emmanuel Viollet-le-Duc and Alexandre-Gustave Eiffel.
- Timeline: February 1877 Congress approved Bedloe's Island site; May 1884 statue completed in France; three months later cornerstone of the pedestal laid; June 1885 arrived dismantled in more than 200 packing cases; last rivet fitted October 28, 1886.
- 1903: bronze plaque with Emma Lazarus's "The New Colossus" placed in the pedestal. 1892: Ellis Island opened (more than 12 million immigrants over 32 years). 1924: national monument. 1956: Bedloe's Island renamed Liberty Island. Major restoration in the 1980s.
- Page published February 09, 2010; last updated August 17, 2026 (as shown).

wikis.title: Platov International Airport, Rostov-on-Don
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on Platov International Airport in Rostov Oblast, Russia: its naming, opening on 7 December 2017, facilities and suspension of flights since 24 February 2022.
wikis.body:
- Airport (IATA ROV, ICAO URRP) near the stanitsa of Grushevskaya, Aksaysky District, Rostov Oblast, Russia, near Novocherkassk northeast of Rostov-on-Don; operator Airports of Regions. It replaced the old Rostov-on-Don Airport. Named after Matvei Platov, a Russian general commanding the Don Cossacks.
- Runway 05/23, 3,600 m (11,811 ft), concrete/asphalt; elevation 65 m (213 ft). Capacity of the project: 5 million passengers per year. Hub for Azimuth.
- Name: originally "Yuzhny" (Southern); in the naming vote "Platov" led with 40%, versus 27% and 34% cited for "Yuzhny" and "Rostov-on-Don International". Officially named by the Government of the Russian Federation on 20 January 2017.
- Opening: construction finished end of September 2017; Rosaviation approved it on 16 October; test flights on 18 November (Airbus A319 of Rossiya, Sukhoi Superjet 100 of Azimuth); 150 volunteers tested equipment on 24 November; IATA code ROV moved to Platov on 27 November (old airport became RVI). Officially opened 7 December 2017 at 11:00am with a Pobeda Boeing 737-800 from Moscow-Vnukovo. Old airport was to close on 1 March 2018. Described as the most expensive airport in Russia at time of construction.
- Traffic: 3,236,000 passengers in the first year (2018); 2,086,000 in 2020 (-32%).
- Facilities: passenger terminal 50,000 m2 with 9 air-bridges and 9 bus gates; cargo terminal; VIP terminal of 2,880 m2 opened early 2018; parking for up to 2,500 cars. Shuttle buses from Rostov-on-Don centre, about 1 hour, 05:00-23:00 every half hour.
- Closure: all civilian flights suspended since 24 February 2022 (with other southern Russian airports, without prior notice) due to the Russian invasion of Ukraine; still closed for security reasons as of late 2025, with Rosaviatsiya dismissing reports of a near-term reopening.
- Pre-2022 airlines included Aeroflot, Air Serbia, Azimuth, and others.

wikis.title: Platov Airport celebrates first year of operation
wikis.summary: Press release dated 7 December 2018 on Platov Airport's first anniversary, with first-year traffic figures and route growth.
wikis.body:
- Published 7 December 2018 by Platov International Airport (Airports of Regions Holding). Received its first scheduled passenger flight on 7 December 2017.
- Anniversary events: festive terminal decorations, photo exhibition (official opening December 2017 to the three-millionth passenger in November 2018), greeting-sticker board, DJ, special hand-baggage tags, holiday luggage stickers designed by Rostov artist Maxim Ilyinov.
- Traffic 7 Dec 2017 to 7 Dec 2018: over 3.23 million passengers, 20% above the prior comparable figure; 764 thousand international (+20.2%), 2.47 million domestic (+20.2%). Annual traffic first exceeded 3 million on 27 November; the three-millionth passenger flew to Samara with Azimuth.
- 20 new destinations in the first year; new international lines to Alanya, Batumi, Bologna, Djerba, Minsk and Dalaman.
- Transfer traffic: 79.5 thousand passengers January-November, 85% above 2017, largely travellers between Russian cities and Georgia and Armenia.
- FIFA World Cup 2018: 257.8 thousand passengers during the Rostov matches (+51%); record 19.7 thousand passengers and 212 flights on 23 June, the Mexico vs Republic of Korea match day, twice normal summer load.
- Quote from Executive Director Alexander Serov: "The first year of Platov Airport's operations demonstrated that construction of an absolutely new airport was justified..."
- Built under a public-private partnership with the Russian Government, Rostov Region government and Airports of Regions (strategic shareholder Renova Group); the largest infrastructure project of the Rostov Region, in Aksaisky District, 4 km north of Grushevskaya.

wikis.title: What happened to BD Bacata, Colombia's tallest skyscraper
wikis.summary: ArchDaily article on BD Bacata's still-unset opening date, investor concerns and planned December completion.
wikis.body:
- ArchDaily, by Nicolas Valencia, published 04 July 2026 (AI-translated from Spanish).
- In early 2016 ArchDaily reported BD Bacata (216 m) complete with opening months away; "an official opening date has yet to be set".
- Atrio Towers (268 m, Rogers Stirk Harbour + Partners and El Equipo de Mazzanti) is under construction in Bogota and will surpass it.
- Funded by real estate crowdfunding; investors seek information. In March 2017 El Espectador reported investor concerns over delayed returns; representatives said progress was being made on wall finishes, paving and flooring (85%) and bathroom tiling and fixtures (95%).
- Venerando Lamelas, president of BD Promotores, told La Republica and W Radio the delay is due partly to excavation ("We realized that the conditions for building the foundations were highly complex") and that the project would be "100% completed" by December of this year.
- Downtown Bogota; over 115,000 m2: 405 apartments, 117 offices, 319 hotel rooms, 6,500 m2 retail, 700 parking spaces.
- A related piece notes designers Alonso & Balaguer, manager BD Promotores Colombia, builder Prabyc Ingenieros; two towers, south tower at floor 67 (last habitable), north tower 28 floors built at that point.

wikis.title: BD Bacata skyscraper, Bogota
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on BD Bacata, a two-tower mixed-use crowdfunded skyscraper complex in Bogota, its construction timeline and stalled completion.
wikis.body:
- Mixed-use complex at Calle 19 #5-20, Santa Fe, Bogota, Colombia. South tower 67 floors, 216 m; north tower 56 floors, 167 m. Architect Grupo Alonso Balaguer; structural engineer/builder Prabyc Ingenieros; developer BD Promotores. Hotel by Eurostars (364 rooms per text; infobox lists 300). Tallest in Colombia since 2 April 2015 (infobox), previous record Torre Colpatria, 196 m.
- Named after the old Hotel Bacata on the site, demolished October 2011. First crowdfunded skyscraper, financed by over 3,800 ordinary Colombians; first skyscraper built in Colombia in 35 years.
- Materials: 56,000 m3 concrete, 25,000 m2 glass, 11,500 tonnes steel. Seven basements built top-down; about 300 piles 40 m deep.
- Timeline: above-grade construction began 15 April 2014; surpassed Colpatria in storeys on 19 April 2015 and height on 2 June 2015; south tower final slab 24 July 2015; north tower final slab 20 December 2015; structural work completed 24 February 2016 with inauguration scheduled for the following year.
- Delays: works halted in early 2018 due to financing difficulties; in March 2019 resumption announced with completion targeted in the second half of 2020; suspended again during COVID-19 lockdown, completion indefinite.
- Main investor Venerando Lamelas stopped disbursing funds to Prabyc; Total Co took over recovery in the final quarter of 2024 to complete unfinished South Tower floors; by early 2026 it reported 30% of the work remained. 133 billion COP of debt registered.

wikis.title: New Karolinska Solna hospital (Skanska project page)
wikis.summary: Skanska Sweden project page for New Karolinska Solna, a completed public-private-partnership university hospital.
wikis.body:
- Project status: Completed. Client: Stockholms lans landsting. Service: Construction Management. Segment: Hospitals. City Solna, Stockholm County, Sweden.
- "The first patients arrived at New Karolinska Solna (NKS) at the end of November 2016", offered customized care in "one of the world's most sustainable university hospitals".
- Skanska's largest project ever; operated and financed under a public-private partnership.
- Page has a 25-image gallery (intensive care, AGV robots, heating and cooling system, art installations, emergency department, etc.); start and completion dates are blank.

wikis.title: New Karolinska Solna University Hospital PPP case study
wikis.summary: Wikibooks casebook entry on the New Karolinska Solna hospital public-private partnership: scope, actors, risks, timeline and contract structure.
wikis.body:
- Case study by Katherine Wilson and Muhammet Mustafa Sever (George Mason University, Public-Private Partnership Policy course, Dr. Jonathan Gifford).
- Scope: 12 floors, 320,000 m2 total area incl. 2-level underground parking, about 8000 rooms, 36 operating theaters, 8 radiation units, 168 doctor's surgeries; aimed for LEED Gold. Overall investment of $3.0 billion, contract to 2040; "considered the world's largest hospital public-private partnership (P3)". Controversies noted: tax evasion allegations and lack of competition at procurement.
- Scale (Skanska's largest project): contract value SEK 14.5 billion (~$1.3 bn); 7,174,500 m of rebar; about 444,000 m2 of earth and rock excavated; 8,000 doors; about 1,400 people involved; 32 nationalities; 30 km of geothermal drilling.
- Actors: Region Stockholm (owner), Karolinska Institutet; project company Swedish Hospital Partners AB (formed April 2010, 50% Skanska, 50% Innisfree); White Tengbom (architect), Coor Service Management (operation and maintenance); lenders include EIB, NIB, BBVA, Nordea and others.
- Timeline: SNUS investigation initiated end of 2001, report November 2002; conclusion favouring a new hospital April 2008; P3 procurement decided 10 June 2008; contract awarded 4 May 2010 (majority) and 8 June (all parties); financial close 30 June 2010; groundbreaking 3 September 2010 by Crown Princess Victoria; garage first completed December 2012 (per table); technological building 2014; first patients 2016; final building handed over December 2017, three months ahead of the agreed March 2018 date; all seven phases handed over on schedule.
- Contract: DBFOM; Region Stockholm makes annual availability payments to SHP through 2040 and keeps ownership of the property.

wikis.title: thyssenkrupp MULTI elevator named to TIME's 25 Best Inventions of 2017
wikis.summary: thyssenkrupp Elevator press release dated 2017-11-17 announcing that TIME named its rope-less, sideways-moving MULTI elevator to its 25 Best Inventions of 2017.
wikis.body:
- Press release dated 2017-11-17: TIME named thyssenkrupp Elevator's MULTI to its "25 Best Inventions of 2017".
- MULTI: "the world's first rope-less and sideways-moving elevator system"; unveiled in June; moves both horizontally and vertically.
- Claims: needs fewer and smaller shafts and can increase a building's usable area by up to 25% (elevator-escalator footprints can take up to 40% of a high-rise's floor space); works like a metro system inside a building, up to 50% higher transport capacity, shorter waits; peak power reduced by as much as 60% versus conventional systems.
- Global debut as a fully functional unit on 22 June 2017 at the 246-metre test tower in Rottweil, Germany, with 12 test shafts and speeds up to 18 m/s. First commercial home planned in Berlin at OVG Real Estate's East Side Tower.
- Quote from CEO Andreas Schierenbeck: "We believe MULTI is a genuine game-changer that will truly transform the way people move, work and live in our built environment."

wikis.title: thyssenkrupp Test Tower, Rottweil
wikis.summary: Autodesk article on the 246 m thyssenkrupp test tower in Rottweil, Germany, its membrane facade, MULTI elevator testing and BIM-based fast construction.
wikis.body:
- Tower in Rottweil near Stuttgart, Germany: 246 m (807 ft), Germany's highest public observation platform, 12 shafts for testing high-speed elevators.
- MULTI elevator: first of its kind, operates in three shafts, cableless, powered by electromagnets, changes direction with an exchanger; several cars in one shaft; maximum wait 30 seconds; braking energy recovered to heat rooms. Tower manager Beate Hohnle quoted.
- Facade: largest building built with an exterior membrane, a fiberglass fabric net designed by architects Dr. Werner Sobek and Helmut Jahn; varying mesh widths; spiral form offsets wind-vortex vibrations; a vibration damper can simulate hurricanes.
- About 2,700 metric tons of steel in walls and ceilings; shell built by Zublin using slip forming, three shifts, seven days a week, 24 hours; modelled in Autodesk Revit with Navisworks clash detection; QR codes on components.
- Built in record time of about two years; opening ceremony in autumn 2017.
- Near 10,000 engineering students at surrounding universities.

wikis.title: Dubai Opera
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on Dubai Opera, a 2,000-seat multi-format performing arts centre in Downtown Dubai that opened 31 August 2016.
wikis.body:
- Multi-format venue in The Opera District, Downtown Dubai, developed by Emaar Properties; announced by Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum in March 2012; construction started April 2013; completed August 2016; opened 31 August 2016 with Placido Domingo. First season included Bizet's The Pearl Fishers and Jose Carreras.
- Size 60,000 m2; seating about 2,000 (also described as 1,901); flat floor of 1,800 m2. Converts between theatre, concert hall and banquet/event hall using hydraulic lifts and seating wagons moving 900 seats.
- Designed by Atkins, principal architect Janus Rostock; theatre consultant Theatre Projects; main contractor Consolidated Contractors Company; stage engineering by ThyssenKrupp. Designed to resemble a dhow.
- Earlier proposal for a Zaha Hadid cultural centre on Dubai Creek (announced 2008) was shelved in the property crash.
- Jasper Hope named chief executive January 2015; Paolo Petrocelli head as of 2023. First Emirati singer Hussain Al Jassmi on 10 October 2016; Les Miserables ran three weeks; BBC Proms Dubai 2017; longest run Phantom of the Opera late 2019; 2023-24 season record 250,000 audience members.

wikis.title: Placido Domingo to open Dubai Opera
wikis.summary: Gulf News article announcing Dubai Opera's 31 August opening performance by Placido Domingo and its first-season line-up.
wikis.body:
- Dubai Opera, in Downtown Dubai, "will open on August 31" with a performance by tenor Placido Domingo; first season runs until the end of 2016.
- Jose Carreras brings his final tour, A Life in Music.
- 49 performances listed, including Anoushka Shankar, Emirati singer Hussain Al Jassimi, Bizet's The Pearl Fishers, Rossini's The Barber of Seville, Opera without Words, Giselle and Coppelia by The Russian State Ballet and Orchestra of Siberia, Mozart Gala, Impossible (illusionists), Sara Baras's Voces, Suite Flamenca, The Nutcracker on Ice and Slava's Snowshow.
- Dates for all performances yet to be announced; tickets at dubaiopera.com. (Page shows "Last updated: September 15, 2018", though it describes 2016.)

wikis.title: Harbin Opera House by MAD completes
wikis.summary: Dezeen article of 16 December 2015 on MAD's completed Harbin Opera House in north-east China.
wikis.body:
- By Amy Frearson, Dezeen, 16 December 2015. Beijing studio MAD completed the opera house in Harbin, with an undulating form wrapping two concert halls and a large public plaza.
- First and largest building MAD designed for Harbin Cultural Island, an arts complex among the wetlands of the Songhua River.
- 79,000 m2, three-petalled plan: grand theatre up to 1,600, intimate hall of 400, and public plaza; exterior of white aluminium panels and glass, roof of ice-inspired glass pyramids; rooftop terrace as performance space and observation platform.
- Grand theatre enclosed in Manchurian Ash wood ("emulating a wooden block that has been gently eroded away"); second theatre has a soundproof glass wall backdrop.
- Founder Ma Yansong: "We envision Harbin Opera House as a cultural center of the future..."

wikis.title: Harbin Opera House / MAD Architects
wikis.summary: ArchDaily project page for MAD Architects' completed Harbin Opera House (2015), part of Harbin Cultural Island in China.
wikis.body:
- ArchDaily project page, published December 16, 2015. Architects: MAD Architects (directors Ma Yansong, Dang Qun, Yosuke Hayano). Location Harbin, China; year 2015; area listed as 850000 ft2.
- Text from the architects: in 2010 MAD won the international open competition for Harbin Cultural Island, a master plan for an opera house, a cultural center and the surrounding wetland landscape along the Songhua River. The opera house is the focal point, about 850,000 sq ft of a 444-acre site; grand theater over 1,600 patrons, smaller theater 400.
- Credits: photographs Hufton+Crow and Adam Mork; stage mechanical engineers Chinese PLA General Armament Institute of Engineering Design; landscape Turenscape and Earthasia; acoustics Zhang Kuisheng Acoustical Design Research Studio; BIM Gehry Technologies; manufacturers Kalzip, Nuprotec, Sika.

wikis.title: Govett-Brewster Art Gallery and Len Lye Centre
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the Govett-Brewster Art Gallery in New Plymouth, New Zealand, including its Len Lye Centre extension opened 25 July 2015.
wikis.body:
- Contemporary art museum in New Plymouth, Taranaki, New Zealand, core-funded by New Plymouth District Council.
- Origin: Monica Brewster (nee Govett) transferred GBP 50,000 in 1962 to establish a public art gallery; first director John Maynard appointed 1967 (aged 24); the converted Regent cinema (architect Terry Boon) opened 22 February 1970 with Leon Narbey's Real Time.
- 1998 extension by Boon Cox Goldsmith Jackson to hold the Len Lye Foundation Collection.
- Len Lye Centre: extension designed by Andrew Patterson of Pattersons Associates to display the works of Len Lye (born Christchurch 1901; film-maker and kinetic sculptor); opened 25 July 2015, "the first gallery in New Zealand to be dedicated to a single artist".
- Awards: 2009 Arts Foundation of NZ Governor's Award; 2011 Big 'A' Creative NZ Arts for All Award; 2016 Designers Institute of NZ Best Design Award, Large Brand Identity.
- Directors run from Maynard (1967-71) to Zara Stanhope (2021-2026) and Megan Dunn (2026-).

wikis.title: Govett-Brewster Art Gallery / Len Lye Centre opening July 2015
wikis.summary: e-flux announcement dated April 26, 2015 that the Govett-Brewster Art Gallery and its Len Lye Centre extension would open in July 2015.
wikis.body:
- e-flux announcement, April 26, 2015: after "more than a decade of blood, sweat and tears" the gallery and new extension, the Len Lye Centre, "will be opening in July this year".
- Gallery: New Zealand's museum of contemporary art in New Plymouth, Taranaki; opened 1970; founded 1962 from a vision of Monica Romaine Brewster (nee Govett, 1886-1973).
- Len Lye (1901-80) spent his career in London and New York; in 1977 the gallery presented "Kinetic Works", the first survey of his work anywhere and his first exhibition in his homeland. Months before his death in 1980 he set up the Len Lye Foundation and chose the gallery as home for his work.
- Len Lye Centre: mirror-finished building by Patterson Associates Ltd; exhibition spaces, archive room, education studio and a dedicated 62-seat cinema.
- Address: Corner of Devon St West and Queen St, New Plymouth 4342. The gallery would recruit curatorial, technical and commercial staff.

wikis.title: Inaugural transit of the expanded Panama Canal begins
wikis.summary: Panama Canal Authority release of 26 June 2016 on the first transit of the expanded canal by COSCO Shipping Panama.
wikis.body:
- Dated 26 June 2016. Early Sunday morning the inaugural transit began: Neopanamax vessel COSCO Shipping Panama (originally Andronikos, renamed) through the new Atlantic-facing Agua Clara Locks; to reach the Pacific-facing Cocoli Locks that afternoon for the official inauguration ceremony.
- Vessel left Piraeus on June 11 carrying 9,472 TEUs; 299.98 m long, 48.25 m beam.
- President Juan Carlos Varela and Administrator/CEO Jorge L. Quijano honoured almost 40,000 workers. Quijano: in 2015 the original canal set a tonnage record of 340.8 million PC/UMS; 170 reservations received for the expanded canal.
- Expansion Program: largest enhancement since the canal's 1914 opening; new locks at both ends, more than 150 million cubic meters excavated, a second lane of traffic doubling cargo capacity. Locks are 70 feet wider and 18 feet deeper; water-saving basins recycle 60 percent of water per transit. Studied for a decade with more than 100 studies.

wikis.title: Panama Canal Expansion Wraps Up
wikis.summary: ENR article of 2016-06-15 on the final stretch of the $5.4-billion Panama Canal third-lane expansion ahead of its 26 June inauguration.
wikis.body:
- ENR, by Scott Blair, 2016-06-15. The 10-year, $5.4-billion effort to add a third set of locks reached a milestone on June 9 when tugboats guided the 255 m bulk carrier Baroque into the first lock, the first full-scale test; ACP's Ilya Espino de Marotta: "Everything worked according to plan." Inauguration and first commercial passage scheduled June 26.
- Three 1,400-ft locks at each end for New Panamax ships (366 m long); gates 10 m wide, 57.6 m long, 33 m high, moving like pocket doors; 16 gates opened and closed more than 100 times in commissioning; each gate about four minutes.
- Contractor consortium GUPC (Sacyr, Salini Impregilo, Jan De Nul, Constructora Urbana): peak about 13,000 workers, still about 4,000; demobilization staff of 300; about 96 buildings (430,000 sq ft) being fitted out; 4.7 million cu m of concrete; 250,000 tons rebar, 71,000 tons steel in gates and 152 valves; lock chambers fill in seven minutes; basins cut freshwater use up to 60%. More than 50,000 people employed over six years; three-year maintenance period.
- Problems: last year a crack in a concrete sill on the Pacific side caused seepage (five more sills reinforced); with earlier concrete-mix issues and a GUPC stoppage in early 2014, about one and a half years added to the schedule; arbitration ongoing, budget could swell.

wikis.title: Neuschwanstein Castle (Bavarian Palace Administration)
wikis.summary: Official Bavarian Palace Administration page on Neuschwanstein Castle: history, construction, rooms and visitor information.
wikis.body:
- Begun by King Ludwig II of Bavaria in 1869 and never completed; seen as a monument to medieval culture and kingship. Modelled partly on the Wartburg (renovated 1867) and Wagner stage sets (Lohengrin, Tannhauser); built on the remains of two small medieval castles above the Pollat Gorge.
- Construction commenced September 1869; Gateway Building completed 1873; Ludwig's rooms in the Palas ready in 1884; the Bower completed 1891 in simplified form; keep with chapel never built. Throne Hall added 1881.
- Ludwig died 13 June 1886 at Berg Palace; the castle opened to the public from 1 August 1886 and was named Neuschwanstein only after his death.
- Since 2025 the palaces of Ludwig II (Neuschwanstein, Linderhof, Herrenchiemsee, King's House on Schachen) are UNESCO World Heritage Sites.
- Visitor info: guided tours only (about 30 minutes, German and English; audioguides in 19 languages); open daily 28 March-15 October 9am-6pm, 16 October-27 March 10am-4pm; admission 2026 21 euros regular, 20 reduced, under 18 free; tickets online at hohenschwangau.de (booking fee 2.50 euros). Address Neuschwansteinstr. 20, 87645 Schwangau.

wikis.title: Neuschwanstein Castle
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on Neuschwanstein Castle, King Ludwig II's 19th-century historicist palace in Bavaria, its design, construction and visitor numbers.
wikis.body:
- Historicist palace in the foothills of the Alps in Bavaria, Germany (Schwangau, above Hohenschwangau, near Fussen); UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2025 as part of "The Palaces of King Ludwig II of Bavaria". Guinness World Records is cited as calling it, at 65 m (213 ft), the tallest castle in the world.
- Commissioned by Ludwig II as a retreat and in honour of Richard Wagner; three-winged complex built 1869-1892 to plans by Eduard Riedel in Neo-Romanesque style; construction started 5 September 1869; opened to the public shortly after Ludwig's death in 1886. Paid from his personal fortune and extensive borrowing, not public funds.
- Inspirations: Ludwig's 1867 trips to the Wartburg (May) and Chateau de Pierrefonds (July). Built over the ruins of Vorder- and Hinterhohenschwangau; first called New Hohenschwangau Castle, renamed Neuschwanstein after his death.
- Visitors: more than 61 million since opening; over 1.3 million annually, up to 6,000 a day in summer; guided tours only.
- Noteworthy rooms: throne room, bedroom, minstrels' hall.

wikis.title: Golden Gate Bridge opens
wikis.summary: HISTORY.com entry on the opening of San Francisco's Golden Gate Bridge on May 27, 1937.
wikis.body:
- Published February 09, 2010, last updated August 17, 2026. Golden Gate Bridge opened to the public 27 May 1937 after five years of construction; about 200,000 walked it on "Pedestrian Day"; vehicles from 28 May. 4,200-foot suspension bridge connecting San Francisco and Marin County; longest in the world until the Verrazano-Narrows Bridge in 1964.
- Bridging the strait was proposed as early as 1872; in 1921 Joseph Strauss proposed a suspension-cantilever for $27 million. Design evolved with consulting engineer Leon S. Moisseiff and architect Irving F. Morrow (Art Deco; helped choose "international orange"). Strauss chief engineer from 1929.
- Financing: Golden Gate Bridge and Highway District formed 1928; in November 1930 voters approved a $35 million bond 3-1, repaid through tolls.
- Construction began January 5, 1933; challenges of tides, storms, fog, blasting rock 65 feet below water; eleven men died.

wikis.title: Golden Gate Bridge opened on May 27, 1937 (ABC7)
wikis.summary: ABC7 San Francisco anniversary piece of May 27, 2019 on the Golden Gate Bridge opening in 1937.
wikis.body:
- Published Monday, May 27, 2019, on the 82nd anniversary. About 200,000 people crossed on May 27, each paying a toll of $0.25; more than 2 billion vehicles since.
- Chief engineer Joseph Strauss on opening day: "The Golden Gate Bridge, the bridge which could not and should not be built... stands before you in all its majestic splendor, in complete refutation of every attack made upon it."
- Strauss began efforts in 1916 and faced 16 years of opposition (Great Depression cost, Department of War shipping concerns, ferry industry, unpopular original design, per PBS). Consultants helped redesign; International Orange chosen after seeing the red primer on steel beams.
- After four years of construction it was the longest suspension bridge at 4,200 feet, a record until 1964. Opening ceremony lasted a week; first day pedestrians only.

wikis.title: Ice Hotel 365 opens in Sweden
wikis.summary: WorldArchitecture.org article of Dec 09, 2016 on Ice Hotel 365, a permanent year-round ice hotel in Jukkasjarvi, Sweden, opened 16 October 2016.
wikis.body:
- Opened 16 October 2016 in Jukkasjarvi on the Torne River, Sweden; designed by Swedish architect and sustainability designer Hans Eek. Built on the ice-storage site next to the existing Ice Hotel; open 365 days a year; interior at -5 degrees Celsius; in summer the arched roof is covered in grass.
- 2,100 m2, 55 rooms (20 suites, 9 luxury suites, 11 art suites), Icebar, ice sculpture gallery, sculpting class studio, event space. Over 40 designers, architects and artists designed interiors.
- Classic winter Ice Hotel holds about 35 ice rooms, main hall and chapel; the 27th Icehotel to be completed December 16 with 55 rooms in total. About 30,000 liters of Torne River water turned into snow plus several tons of river ice.
- Sustainability: energy-saving schemes since 2008 with energy partner Gavle Energi. Quote from Creative Director Arne Bergh on the sun making year-round art possible.

wikis.title: Torre Reforma, Mexico City
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on Torre Reforma, a 57-story, 246 m office skyscraper on Paseo de la Reforma in Mexico City.
wikis.body:
- Office skyscraper at Paseo de la Reforma #483, Mexico City; 807 ft (246 m) to spire, 244 m to roof, 57 floors; construction began May 2008 (infobox 2008), completed 2016; owner Fondo Hexa; architects LBR&A; structural engineer Arup and DITEC.
- Tallest in Mexico from July 2015 to May 2016 (surpassed by Torre KOI); tallest in Mexico City upon completion, exceeding Torre BBVA Bancomer (771 ft) and Torre Mayor (739.5 ft); "currently the second tallest building after Torre Mitikah completed in 2020".
- 45,000 m2 office, 2,500 m2 retail, 2,500 m2 gym; 28 lifts (infobox 27) up to 6.8 m/s; underground garage for 1,161 vehicles; LEED Platinum in 2016.
- Historic 1930s Casa Austin was conserved as the main entrance rather than demolished.

wikis.title: Torre Reforma / LBR&A
wikis.summary: ArchDaily project page for Torre Reforma, a 2016 skyscraper by LBR&A in Mexico City, published August 04, 2016.
wikis.body:
- Architects LBR&A, architect in charge Benjamin Romano; year 2016; area 89,657 m2; photographs Alfonso Merchand; published on ArchDaily August 04, 2016.
- Architects' text: on Paseo de la Reforma; a "turning point for vertical urban growth" in Mexico City; ground site of 2,800 m2, "extremely small for a high-rise building of roughly 87,000 m2".
- Credits: structural design ARUP New York and Dr. Rodolfo Valles Mattox/DITEC; MEP ARUP Los Angeles; wind study Alan G. Davenport Wind Engineering Group (University of Western Ontario); facade HEG; foundation CIMESA; robotized parking Wohr Parking Systems.

wikis.title: Dongdaemun Design Plaza, Seoul
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on Dongdaemun Design Plaza (DDP), Zaha Hadid's neofuturistic design landmark in Seoul, inaugurated 21 March 2014.
wikis.body:
- Urban development landmark in Dongdaemun, Seoul, designed by Zaha Hadid (with Samoo), concept "Metonymic Landscape"; centrepiece of South Korea's fashion hub. Construction started 2009; inaugurated 21 March 2014; cost $451 million; floor area 86,574.7 m2; SEGD Merit Award 2015.
- Replaced Dongdaemun Stadium (first modern stadium in Korea, 1925 to demolition in 2007). Seoul invited architects to a design competition in February 2007; Hadid's design won. Cited as one of the reasons for Seoul's World Design Capital designation in 2010.
- Features: three underground and four above-ground levels, main building 280 m long; exhibition hall, design museum, design lab, design market open 24 hours, Dongdaemun History and Culture Park; BIM, mega-truss and space frame; double-skin facade, solar panels, water recycling. Connected to Dongdaemun History & Culture Park Station (Lines 2, 4, 5). Managed by the Seoul Design Foundation.
- Critics challenge the eventual removal of street vendors as a "repressive relocation".

wikis.title: Dongdaemun Design Plaza (DDP), Seoul Solution
wikis.summary: Seoul Solution policy case on how Seoul demolished Dongdaemun Stadium and built the Dongdaemun Design Plaza as a design and fashion hub.
wikis.body:
- Policy page dated 2014-12-22, last update 2017-12-12. Because Dongdaemun Stadium deteriorated and the area was declining into a slum, the Seoul Metropolitan Government decided to demolish it and build the DDP as a centre for design and fashion industry and a history and culture park.
- Called "the most successful urban development project ever attempted in Seoul"; eight strategic objectives (creative design, design industry base, knowledge exchange, designer network, cultural hub, tourism landmark, place identity, trading area promotion).
- History: fortress wall (Joseon Dynasty) demolition began 1889; Gyeongseong Sports Complex built 1925 on the site, later Dongdaemun Sports Complex, diminished after Jamsil Sports Complex in 1984. Gwangjang Market formed 1905; Miliore mall 1998.
- Process: 2006 General Downtown Creation Plan; fortress wall excavation announced 18 September 2006, total budget KRW 24.3 billion; idea contest November 2006; international design competition followed.

wikis.title: Abu Dhabi Airport Terminal A to open 1 November 2023
wikis.summary: Abu Dhabi Media Office release of 16 October 2023 on the opening of Terminal A at Abu Dhabi International Airport on 1 November 2023.
wikis.body:
- Dated 16 October 2023. Terminal A begins operations 1 November 2023; Etihad Airways ceremonial flight 31 October. Airlines move in three phases over two weeks: Wizz Air Abu Dhabi and 15 other international airlines from 1 November; Etihad 16 daily flights from 9 November and fully operational 14 November with Air Arabia Abu Dhabi and 10 others; 28 airlines fully operational from 14 November.
- Readiness trials ended 17 October with more than 11,000 volunteers.
- 35,000 m2 retail with 163 shops and food and beverage outlets (Gucci, Yves Saint Laurent, Ferragamo, world's first Muji airport store, Starbucks, McDonalds, Todd English's first airport restaurant), two spas, a 138-bedroom hotel.
- "First in the world to include all nine biometric airport touchpoints"; baggage system up to 19,200 bags per hour. X-shaped building with four themed piers (desert, sea, city, oasis). Quote from Elena Sorlini, Managing Director and Interim CEO of Abu Dhabi Airports.

wikis.title: Abu Dhabi International Airport schedules new terminal opening for November 2023
wikis.summary: International Airport Review article (2023-09-05) on Abu Dhabi Airports' announcement that Terminal A opens in early November 2023.
wikis.body:
- Dated 2023-09-05. Terminal A (known as Midfield Terminal Building during construction) scheduled to operate in early November 2023.
- 742,000 sqm built-up area, "among the largest airport terminals in the world"; up to 45 million passengers per year, 11,000 travellers per hour, 79 aircraft at once.
- Interconnected biometric systems, self-service kiosks, advanced baggage handling; won international design awards; glass exterior.
- Sustainability: energy-efficient lighting, HVAC, sustainable materials; car park roof 3 MW solar PV plant saving nearly 5,300t of CO2 annually.
- 163 retail and food and beverage outlets, lounges, spas. Chairman Sheikh Mohammed bin Hamad bin Tahnoon Al Nahyan: opening "turns over a new page in Abu Dhabi's 55-year aviation history".

wikis.title: New Royal Adelaide Hospital emergency department opens
wikis.summary: ABC News report of 5 Sep 2017 on the new Royal Adelaide Hospital's emergency department opening as patients move from the old hospital.
wikis.body:
- Posted Tue 5 Sep 2017. The old emergency department closed at 6:59am; the new one, with 65 cubicles, opened at 7:00am, as the patient move entered its second day. SA Health said the move was on track to finish the next day; first 130 patients moved by ambulance the previous day.
- Emergency physician Dr Megan Brooks and Professor Bob Dunn quoted; "Nearly a million patients have come through this department over the past [14 years]."
- Nurse Jennifer Jones, 46, worked at the old hospital since age 22; called the closure emotional. The new hospital is at the other end of North Terrace.

wikis.title: New Royal Adelaide Hospital handed over for September opening
wikis.summary: ABC News report of 14 Jun 2017 on the new Royal Adelaide Hospital being handed over to the SA Government ahead of a September opening.
wikis.body:
- Posted Wed 14 Jun 2017. Testing and commissioning complete (90-day); hospital handed over from the construction consortium to the South Australian Government. Consortium CEO Duncan Jewell quoted.
- Emergency department to open September 5; patients moved from the old hospital (eastern end of North Terrace) to the new one (western end) over three days, September 4-6; some day surgery, oncology, radiology from mid-August. New hospital has 120 more beds.
- Handover triggers a daily cost of about $1 million for taxpayers while unused. Opposition spokesman Stephen Wade: additional $90 million brings total cost overrun to more than $730 million.
- $2 billion hospital originally due April the previous year; Premier Jay Weatherill said delay cost was borne by the builder to the tune of $400 million. Health Minister Jack Snelling said safety issues including a cooling system had been rectified.

That castle is home to the magnificent wizard Howl, infamous for both his magical prowess and for being a womanizer—or so the rumor goes in Sophie Hatter's small town. Sophie, as the plain daughter of a hatmaker, does not expect much from her future and is content with working hard in the shop. However, Sophie's simple life takes a turn for the exciting when she is ensnared in a disturbing situation, and the mysterious wizard appears to rescue her. Unfortunately, this encounter, brief as it may be, spurs the vain and vengeful Witch of the Waste—in a fit of jealousy caused by a past discord with Howl—to put a curse on the maiden, turning her into an old woman. In an endeavor to return to normal, Sophie must accompany Howl and a myriad of eccentric companions—ranging from a powerful fire demon to a hopping scarecrow—in his living castle, on a dangerous adventure as a raging war tears their kingdom apart. [Written by MAL Rewrite]

## Background
Howl No Ugoku Shiro premiered at the Venice Film Festival in 2004 and was later released to Japanese theaters in November, making it one of only three Studio Ghibli films not to be released in July. In 2004 the film won the Osella Awards for Technical Achievement in the 61st Venice Film Festival, the Best Japanese Movie Overall in the Mainichi Film Awards and an Excellence Prize, Animation in the Japan Media Arts Festival. In 2005 the film won the Animation of the Year in the Tokyo International Anime Fair and the Audience Award in the Maui Film Festival. In 2006 it was nominated for the Best Animated Feature in the 78th Academy Award, but lost to the movie Wallace and Gromit: The Curse of the Were-Rabbit .

wikis.title: DanTysk offshore wind farm formally opened
wikis.summary: Vattenfall press release of 30 April 2015 on the formal opening of the 288 MW DanTysk offshore wind farm west of Sylt.
wikis.body:
## Event
- Vattenfall press release dated 30 April 2015: representatives from government, industry and project partners gathered in Hamburg to mark the formal opening of the DanTysk offshore wind farm.
- Attendees named: German Federal Minister for Economic Affairs Sigmar Gabriel, Swedish Minister for Enterprise and Innovation Mikael Damberg, Hamburg Mayor Olaf Scholz, Schleswig-Holstein Prime Minister Torsten Albig, Vattenfall CEO Magnus Hall and SWM CEO Dr Florian Bieberbach.

## Facts and figures
- Located 70 kilometres west of Sylt Island; the first infrastructure project jointly implemented by Vattenfall and SWM (Stadtwerke Muenchen) in Germany's energy transition.
- Vattenfall holds 51% of DanTysk Offshore GmbH (construction and operation), SWM 49%.
- 80 Siemens wind turbines in the 3.6 MW class, total installed capacity 288 MW.
- Capital investment more than EUR 1 billion.
- Generates climate-neutral power equal to the annual consumption of more than 400,000 average households.
- Offshore construction started in February 2013.
- Sandbank offshore wind farm: green light from both companies in August 2014, also 288 MW, to be built near DanTysk in summer 2015, investment roughly EUR 1.2 billion.

## Quotes
- Gabriel: by 2030 there should be 15 gigawatts of installed offshore capacity; together with DanTysk, Germany will by the end of 2015 generate green power from more than 3,000 megawatts of installed offshore capacity.
- Hall: Vattenfall is "the second largest operator of offshore wind in the world".
- Bieberbach: DanTysk is SWM's first finalized offshore wind farm and its largest completed renewable project to date in capital investment and capacity; from May its renewable assets including the DanTysk share would meet the needs of all private households, underground, tram and electric vehicles in Munich.
- Gunnar Groebler (Head of Business Area Wind): the first large offshore project in Germany brought to a successful conclusion with SWM.

wikis.title: DanTysk offshore wind farm project profile
wikis.summary: Power Technology profile (May 2015) of the 288 MW DanTysk North Sea wind farm: ownership, contractors, grid connection and construction timeline.
wikis.body:
## Key data
- 288 MW project in the North Sea Exclusive Economic Zone, 70 km west of Sylt, northern Germany; area about 71 km2.
- Owner DanTysk Offshore Wind; Vattenfall 51% (construction and maintenance), Stadtwerke Muenchen (SWM) 49%. Estimated investment EUR 1bn ($1.4bn), "more than EUR 1bn".
- Annual output 1,320 GWh; enough for more than 400,000 houses at 2,500 kWh per home per year. SWM aimed at powering 800,000 Munich households with renewable energy.
- 80 Siemens SWT-3.6-120 turbines (3.6 MW, 120 m rotor) at depths of 21 m to 31 m. Grid connector TenneT.
- First power to the German grid in December 2014; formal commissioning in April 2015.

## History
- 2007: Vattenfall acquired the project from developer Geo Gesellschaft fuer Energie und Oekologie. July 2010: SWM bought 49%.
- Construction started March 2012 (per this page); offshore work began February 2013; all 80 foundations installed by December 2013; turbine installation March 2014 to end of 2014; offshore accommodation platform construction began 2015.

## Contractors
- Siemens Energy: turbines (contract October 2010), installation, commissioning, maintenance.
- Strukton Systems and Hollandia joint venture: 155kV/33kV offshore substation (December 2010 turnkey contract); Seaway Heavy Lifting subcontractor. Substation has three decks, a tank station and a helipad, installed 2013.
- Aarsleff Bilfinger Berger joint venture: 80 monopile foundations (April 2011).
- Swire Blue Ocean heavy-lift vessel Pacific Orca (161.9 m, 1,200 t capacity; built by Samsung Heavy Industries, delivered 2012) carried turbines from Esbjerg, where they were preassembled (agreement February 2011).

## Grid
- Power goes to TenneT's SylWin alpha HVDC converter platform, then by a 160 km sea cable and 45 km land cable to a new substation in Buettel, Schleswig-Holstein.

wikis.title: Felbermayr multimodal heavy haulage of two autoclaves for FACC
wikis.summary: Felbermayr news item (12 December 2017) on moving two 160 t and 140 t autoclaves by water and road to FACC sites in Austria.
wikis.body:
- Published December 12, 2017. In late November 2017 Felbermayr moved two autoclaves from Aschach an der Donau to two destinations in the Innviertel region, Austria, for aeroplane-component maker FACC (Reichersberg and Ort im Innkreis sites). Autoclaves are used for thermal processing of lightweight fibre-composite parts under overpressure.
- Autoclaves weigh 160 and 140 tons, are 20.5 and 18.5 m long, about 6.5 m in diameter.
- Water leg: about 800 km from the manufacturer in Coesfeld (D) to Aschach an der Donau (A), shipped from the port of Luedinghausen near Dortmund by Felbermayr subsidiary Haeger & Schmidt Logistics.
- At Aschach a crawler crane transshipped them onto two flat bed trailers.
- Road leg: 100 km, four days. Obstacles: structurally insufficient bridges (crossed with a "bridge crossing system", a bridge built on top of the bridge transferring load to the ground via the piers), some 150 power and telephone lines that were too low, many traffic signs and roundabouts; steel plates protected curbs and underground gas lines.
- The 160-ton autoclave was placed on its foundations in Reichersberg with a lift mast. Project took four days of transport and several months of lead time, with "several dozen companies" coordinated.

wikis.title: FACC expands and installs new autoclaves
wikis.summary: CompositesWorld item (published 12/04/2017) on FACC's up-to-EUR 100 million expansion and the delivery of two new autoclaves to its Upper Austrian sites.
wikis.body:
## Expansion
- Published 12/04/2017. FACC AG (Ried im Innkreis, Austria) says more than 41,000 aircraft are needed by the year 2036 and has started expanding.
- CEO Robert Machtlinger: up to 100 million Euro ($118.5 million USD) over the next three years in a large-scale investment program.
- Order level more than $5 billion USD; existing capacities "fully stretched for the next seven years". Focus on Reichersberg and Ort im Innkreis. Corporate strategy "Vision 2020" aims at sales of one billion Euro by fiscal year 2020/2021; current annual turnover more than 700 million Euro.
- First step: an additional 6,400 m2 production area, construction started recently.

## Autoclave delivery
- One of the two pressure vessels is 19.9 m long and 6.1 m in diameter, the largest operating at FACC to date.
- Built by German manufacturer Scholz (Coesfeld); loaded on a barge at Luedinghausen port on November 13, arrived Aschach an der Donau on November 27; Felbermayr transferred them onto two flatbed trailers for the last leg to Reichersberg and Ort im Innkreis.
- Vehicles 38.5 m long, 6.5 m wide, 232 tons; tractor units more than 800 hp each. Bridges were reinforced beforehand; electricity and telephone lines raised; road signs, traffic lights, lamp posts and fences removed.

## About FACC
- Fibre-composite components for aviation (fuselage, wings, engine parts, cabins); suppliers to Airbus, Boeing, Bombardier, Embraer, Sukhoi, COMAC. Turnover 705.7 million Euros in business year 2016/17; about 3,300 employees.

wikis.title: Walking excavator (Wikipedia)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on walking excavators, both the historic walking draglines and the modern spider excavators pioneered by Menzi Muck and Kaiser.
wikis.body:
- Term covers two forms: historic walking power shovels/draglines (early 20th century, enormous, slow) and the contemporary all-terrain "spider excavator".
- Modern type: excavator "house" sits on articulated limb-like extensions, with or without wheels; each moves independently. Legs/wheels vary from three (Menzi Muck 5000T2) to four; legs fixed or telescoping; most have powered wheels.
- First development along this line: 1966, Edwin Ernst Menzi (1897-1984) and Joseph Kaiser (1928-1993) built a prototype for work on mountain slopes. Kaiser AG (Schaanwald, Liechtenstein) and Menzi Muck AG (Kriessern, Switzerland) then developed excavators separately.
- Not widely used because of relatively small mobility gain, most excavation being in urban areas, and high cost of electro-hydraulic controls and maintenance.
- Figures: Kaiser AG turnover nearly 60 million Swiss francs in 2007 and 70 million in 2014; Menzi Muck AG 56.93 million francs in 2013.
- Menzi Muck with ETH Zurich demonstrated a remotely operated excavator at Bauma 2019. In January 2026 the UK rail regulator granted engineering acceptance for the first Menzi Muck 545X RRV in the UK, built for Arbor Division Ltd (designed by Excav8 and King Rail).
- Big Brutus: tracked walking power shovel built 1962, 9,300,000 lb plus 1,700,000 lb ballast, 0.22 mph. Big Muskie: built 1969, "world's largest ever dragline excavator", 487 ft long, 13,500 short tons, 220 cu yd bucket, top speed 0.1 mph.

wikis.title: Shinjuku Station, Tokyo (Wikipedia)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on Shinjuku Station: history, operators and lines, platforms, and passenger figures for the world's busiest railway station.
wikis.body:
## Overview
- Major railway hub in Tokyo, connecting central/eastern Tokyo with Western Tokyo; straddles the Shinjuku and Shibuya special wards.
- Used by an average of 3.59 million people per day in 2018, "the world's busiest railway station by far" (registered with Guinness World Records).
- JR East station plus adjacent private railways have 35 platforms, with another 17 (52 total) reachable through hallways to five directly connected stations; the complex has "well over 200 exits".
- Operators: JR East (Chuo Main, Chuo Rapid, Chuo-Sobu, Saikyo, Shonan-Shinjuku, Yamanote), Keio, Odakyu (Odawara Line), Toei Subway (Oedo, Shinjuku), Tokyo Metro (Marunouchi).
- JR East part: eight ground-level island platforms (16 tracks); the JR section alone handles about 1.5 million passengers a day; opened 1 March 1885; FY2024 1,333,618 daily (in the infobox, different counting basis); station code SJK. Odakyu: opened 1927, FY2024 450,952 daily; Keio (opened 1915): 728,874 daily FY2024 and 788,567 for the Keio complex in 2019; Tokyo Metro Marunouchi opened 15 March 1959, 199,942 daily.

## History
- 1885: opened on Nippon Railway's Akabane-Shinagawa line (now Yamanote); 1889 Kobu Railway (now Chuo Main Line) to Tachikawa; 1915 Keio Line; 1927 Odakyu Odawara Line.
- 1933: planner Kensaburo Kondo designed a major revamp incl. a west-side square completed 1941; plans suspended by WWII but influenced the layout.
- 1952: Seibu Shinjuku Line extended to Seibu Shinjuku station. 8 August 1967: a jet-fuel freight train collided and caught fire on the Chuo Rapid tracks. 1968-69: student protests; on 21 October 1968, 290,000 marchers took over the station.
- 5 May 1995: Aum Shinrikyo attempted a cyanide gas attack in an underground concourse toilet; staff extinguished the device.
- April 2016: JR terminal expansion completed (32-story office tower, bus and taxi terminals). 2020: east-west free passageway opened, cutting 10 minutes off crossing. July 2021: major redevelopment began, "expected to continue until 2047".
- The 1973 Shinkansen Basic Plan still specifies the station as the southern terminus of the Joetsu Shinkansen; the link was never built, the right of way remains reserved.

wikis.title: Busiest railway station: Shinjuku Station (Guinness World Records)
wikis.summary: Guinness World Records entry naming Shinjuku Station as the busiest railway station with 2,704,703 average daily passengers in 2022.
wikis.body:
- Record: busiest railway station (including subways): Shinjuku Station, Tokyo, Japan; average daily passenger throughput 2,704,703 in 2022.
- Located on the boundary between the Shinjuku and Shibuya wards; serves JR East, Keio Corporation, Odakyu Electric Railway, Toei Subway and Tokyo Metro.
- 2022 numbers are down around 20 percent from pre-pandemic levels but up significantly on 2020 and 2021.
- Closest competitor: Gare du Nord, Paris, around 600,000 people a day.

wikis.title: Antonov An-124 Ruslan (Wikipedia)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the Antonov An-124 Ruslan heavy strategic airlifter: development, post-Soviet history, design and specifications.
wikis.body:
## Overview
- Large four-engined strategic airlifter designed in the 1980s by the Antonov design bureau in the Ukrainian SSR; NATO name Condor; "Ruslan" means "lion". Second heaviest gross weight production cargo airplane and heaviest operating cargo aircraft (behind the destroyed An-225 Mriya, its enlarged derivative); the largest military transport aircraft in service.
- Manufactured 1982-2004; introduced 1986; 57 built (citation needed); first flight 24 December 1982 (per this page). Primary user Russian Aerospace Forces; also Volga-Dnepr Airlines, Antonov Airlines, Maximus Air.

## Development
- Design began 1971 as Izdeliye 400 (An-40 in the West) to fix a shortfall in heavy airlift in Soviet Military Transport Aviation (VTA), whose largest aircraft were about 50 An-22 turboprops. A declassified 1975 CIA analysis said the USSR did "not match the US in ability to provide long-range heavy lift support". Lead designer Viktor Tolmachev.
- Two final assembly lines: Aviastar-SP (Ulyanovsk, Russia) and Kyiv Aviation Plant AVIANT (Ukraine); over 100 factories supplied components. Facilities built from 1973; first airframe manufacturing 1979; Western debut at the 1985 Paris Air Show.
- Civil certification issued to Antonov on 30 December 1992. By July 2013, 26 were reportedly in commercial service with ten more on order; 26 in 2019.
- April 2008: Russia and Ukraine agreed to resume production; the An-124-150 variant (150 tonne lift) announced May 2008. May 2009: United Aircraft Corporation said no production planned 2009-2012. August 2014: resumption reported shelved over Russia-Ukraine tensions. January 2019: Antonov revealed plans to restart production without Russian support. 2018: GE Aviation reportedly studied CF6 re-engining for CargoLogicAir.
- Russian replacement design: TsAGI's An-124-102 Slon (announced at MAKS 2017), to carry 150 t over 3,800 nmi, powered by PD-35 engines; first aerodynamic test cycle completed, announced 26 March 2020.

## Design
- Resembles the Lockheed C-5 (rear door, control surfaces) but with a conventional tail; fly-by-wire hybrid controls; about 5% carbon-fibre composites; titanium cargo floor. Carries up to 150 tonnes internally; fully pressurised upper deck for 88 passengers; main cargo deck only partly pressurised (24.6 kPa); cargo compartment 36 x 6.4 x 4.4 m, about 20% larger than the C-5's. No in-flight refuelling.
- Four Lotarev/Progress D-18T turbofans of 238-250 kN each, thrust reversers.

## Specifications (An-124-100M)
- Crew eight; length 69.1 m, span 73.3 m, height 21.08 m, wing area 628 m2; empty weight 181,000 kg; max takeoff weight 402,000 kg; max landing weight 330,000 kg; fuel capacity 210,172 kg.

wikis.title: First flight of the Antonov An-124 Ruslan
wikis.summary: Vintage Aviation News piece (26 December 2025) on the An-124's first flight on 26 December 1982, its development and specifications.
wikis.body:
- Published December 26, 2025. The An-124 Ruslan ("Lion", NATO name Condor) first flew on December 26, 1982, 43 years earlier.
- Designed by the Antonov bureau in the Ukrainian SSR; development began 1971 (Izdeliye 400) to fill a heavy-airlift shortage in Soviet Military Transport Aviation; assembly of the first began 1979. Western debut at the 1985 Paris Air Show.
- Called the heaviest operating aircraft with the second heaviest gross weight of any plane flying today (behind the destroyed An-225 Mriya) and the largest military transport still in service.
- 57 airframes built; flies with the Russian Aerospace Forces, Volga-Dnepr Airlines and Antonov Airlines.
- May 1987 record: 10,881 nautical miles without refuelling, 25 hours 30 minutes, takeoff weight 455,000 kg.
- Recent humanitarian use: COVID-19 and post-earthquake supplies.
- Specs: crew of eight; 88 passengers upper aft plus 350 in the hold; payload 264,555 lb; length 226 ft 8 in, wingspan 240 ft 6 in, height 69 ft 2 in; four Progress D-18T engines of 51,000 lb thrust each; cruise 500-537 mph; range 2,000 nm with max payload; ceiling 39,000 ft.

wikis.title: Caterpillar 797 ultra-class haul truck (Wikipedia)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the Caterpillar 797 series mining haul trucks: generations, powertrain, tires, manufacturing, cost and competitors.
wikis.body:
## Overview
- Series of off-highway, ultra-class, two-axle, mechanical-drive haul trucks built by Caterpillar Inc. (assembly in Decatur, Illinois) for mining and heavy construction; in production since 1998. The 797F offers up to 400 short tons (363 t) payload, the highest among mechanical-drive haul trucks.

## Generations
- Development began 1997 for a 360 short ton (327 t) truck; first use of CAD tools extensively for a Caterpillar truck. First 797 unveiled September 29, 1998 in Decatur; third and fourth units entered service at Bingham Canyon Mine, Utah, second quarter 1999; marketed in North America 2000, worldwide 2001.
