wikis.title: San Diego International Airport terminal projects
wikis.summary: SAN Airport's page describing its terminal redevelopment work - the New Terminal 1 and the existing Terminal 2 East and Terminal 2 West - for concessionaires, contractors and tenants.
wikis.body:
## Overview

- "San Diego International Airport (SAN) is undergoing significant terminal renovations to enhance passenger experiences and operational efficiency."
- The page is aimed at "Concessionaires, Contractors, and Tenants involved with or affected by these developments" and covers three terminals: New Terminal 1, Terminal 2 East and Terminal 2 West.

## New Terminal 1

- "A comprehensive redevelopment of the existing Terminal 1, aimed at improving passenger flow, increasing gate capacity, and enhancing amenities", executed in phases "to minimize disruptions".
- 30 gates, "with 19 opening in 2025 and the remaining 11 by 2028, replacing the outdated 1967 facility".
- 13-lane security checkpoint; more gate-area seating, up to two airline or common-use lounges, a children's play area, and a post-security outdoor patio with views of the airfield, San Diego Bay and downtown.
- 30 restaurants and retail stores, including Puesto, Cutwater Spirits, Novecientos Grados by Tony Hawk and SIP Wine and Beer Bar.
- New on-airport access road bypassing N. Harbor Drive; parking plaza with up to 5,200 spaces and 185 EV charging stations; bicycle lanes and a pedestrian path, "with space reserved for a future public transit connection".
- Five commissioned artists will create installations. Architecture described as a "Glassy Garden Pavilion".
- Sustainability: goal of LEED Gold certification, 100% carbon-free electricity, rainwater harvesting, electric shuttle services and an underground fuel distribution system.
- Concession design guidance is the 2022 Concession Design Manual.

## Terminal 2 East and Terminal 2 West

- Both are existing terminals whose concession guidance is the 2014 Concession Design Manual; the page describes their layouts and what concessionaires are expected to do.

## Other

- The page links to "Non-terminal Projects" and the Air Incentives Program.
- Footer: SDCRAA, P.O. Box 82776, San Diego, California 92138-2776; "© 2026 San Diego County Regional Airport Authority."

wikis.title: New Terminal 1 at San Diego International Airport
wikis.summary: The phased redevelopment of SAN's Terminal 1, its gates, amenities, dining, access road, art and sustainability goals.
wikis.body:
- "The New Terminal 1 is a comprehensive redevelopment of the existing Terminal 1, aimed at improving passenger flow, increasing gate capacity, and enhancing amenities. The project is being executed in phases to minimize disruptions and ensure a seamless transition."
- Architecture "reflects San Diego's natural and cultural heritage, featuring sunlit spaces and regional design influences." Passengers enter via sky bridges or escalators into a bright ticketing hall with art glass walls; the concourse runs east-west with dining halls, retail and departure lounges; arriving passengers are guided past concessions to baggage claim.
- Gates: "30 New Gates: The terminal will feature 30 gates, with 19 opening in 2025 and the remaining 11 by 2028, replacing the outdated 1967 facility."
- 13-lane security checkpoint "designed to expedite passenger processing".
- Seating and lounges: more gate-area seating, up to two airline or common-use lounges, a children's play area.
- Outdoor patio: post-security, with views of the airfield, San Diego Bay and downtown.
- Dining and retail: 30 restaurants and retail stores, "including local favorites like Puesto, Cutwater Spirits, Novecientos Grados by Tony Hawk, and SIP Wine and Beer Bar."
- Transportation and parking: a new on-airport entrance road to bypass local traffic on N. Harbor Drive; a parking plaza with up to 5,200 spaces including 185 EV charging stations; bicycle lanes and a pedestrian path connecting to surrounding communities, "with space reserved for a future public transit connection."
- Art and design: five commissioned artists will create installations throughout the terminal; the terminal is designed as a "Glassy Garden Pavilion" with light-filled spaces, an outdoor dining terrace and bay views.
- Sustainability: LEED Gold certification goal, 100% carbon-free electricity, rainwater harvesting systems, electric shuttle services and an underground fuel distribution system.
- Concessionaires "are expected to create strong, unique identities that align with the Terminal's design standards, as outlined in the 2022 Concession Design Manual."

wikis.title: Terminal 2 East (T2E) key features
wikis.summary: SAN's description of Terminal 2 East's ticketing lobby, concourse and concession expectations.
wikis.body:
- "Terminal 2 East (T2E) features a light-filled ticketing lobby inspired by the sun, sand, and sea, with access via sky bridge or escalators."
- "The space transitions from a grand entry to more intimate concourse areas with lower ceilings and hold rooms. A central dining cove with airfield views anchors the concessions."
- "Concessionaires are expected to create a strong, unique presence through thoughtful signage and storefront design within a neutral framework." Guidance: the 2014 Concession Design Manual.

wikis.title: Terminal 2 West (T2W) key features
wikis.summary: SAN's description of Terminal 2 West's lobby, concourses, the Sunset Cove hub and concession expectations.
wikis.body:
- "Terminal 2 West (T2W) features a bright, spacious lobby inspired by the sun, sand, sea, and aviation. Passengers enter via sky bridge or escalators, with clear views to TSA checkpoints and baggage claim."
- "The north and west concourses include hold rooms, amenities, and concessions, all connected by 'Sunset Cove' - a dramatic, two-story central hub with airfield views, dining, art, and passenger services."
- "Concessionaires are expected to establish a strong, distinct identity using cohesive signage and storefront design within a neutral architectural framework." Guidance: the 2014 Concession Design Manual.

wikis.title: Otay Mesa East Port of Entry
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the planned Otay Mesa East border crossing between San Diego and Tijuana, its lanes, cost and repeatedly pushed-back opening.
wikis.body:
## What it is

- "The Otay Mesa East Port of Entry is a planned border crossing between San Diego and Tijuana, approximately two miles east of the existing Otay Mesa Port of Entry."
- It "will connect the Otay Centenario borough of Tijuana with East Otay Mesa in unincorporated San Diego County, an as-yet undeveloped area slotted for future development including a business park."
- "Although the crossing will allow cars and pedestrians, it is mainly designed for trucks and commercial vehicles."
- Coordinates: 32°33'11"N 116°54'21"W (32.5530, -116.9058), San Diego, California, United States. Categorised as proposed infrastructure.

## Agreement and design

- "In July 2014, Mexican Undersecretary of Infrastructure of the Secretariat of Communications and Transportation Raúl Murrieta Cummings and the Secretary of the California Department of Transportation (Caltrans), Brian P. Kelly, signed a memorandum of understanding to build and put the new port of entry into operation."
- "It was expected to be ready as early as 2017, and provide 27 northbound lanes from Tijuana to San Diego and 8 southbound lanes."
- "The cost is estimated to be 2 billion Mexican pesos (about 99 million US dollars)."

## Construction and schedule

- "Construction began at the initial ground breaking in August 2022, after long delays."
- "Although earlier estimates suggested the project would be completed by late 2024, more recent estimates suggest construction may not be complete until 2026."
- "As of 2024, it is expected to open in 2028, with tolls to help fund the project."

## Cited sources

- References include a 2022-08-22 Caltrans item, "U.S., Mexico Break Ground on New Otay Mesa East Port of Entry"; a 2023-07-06 San Diego Union-Tribune piece, "Future Otay Mesa East border crossing may open later than expected"; and a 2024-06-28 cbs8.com piece, "More delays for opening of Otay Mesa East Port of Entry".
- External link: "Otay Mesa East Port of Entry / State Route 11 Presidential Permit Application", 2007, SANDAG and Caltrans.

wikis.title: Downtown COASTER Platform project
wikis.summary: NCTD's project page for a new downtown San Diego COASTER station near the Convention Center, with its elements, cost, funding and timeline.
wikis.body:
## What the project is

- "The Downtown Platform Project will add a new COASTER station in downtown San Diego parallel to Harbor Drive in downtown San Diego near the Gaslamp Quarter and the San Diego Convention Center."
- It creates "a one-seat ride from Oceanside to Petco Park, the San Diego Convention Center, the Gaslamp Quarter, The Rady Shell, and other downtown destinations."
- "This station will improve passenger and freight operations along the Los Angeles-San Diego-San Luis Obispo (LOSSAN) corridor, which is the second busiest intercity rail corridor in the country."

## Project details

- A new 850-foot station platform "with the capacity to accommodate eight passenger cars", stretching between 1st and 5th Avenues near two existing MTS Trolley stations.
- Reconfiguration of the existing track used by BNSF Railway, a new siding track (pocket track), and extension of railroad signaling and dispatching systems.
- Signal equipment upgrades at five grade crossings: Kettner Blvd., Market Street, Front Street, First Avenue and Fifth Avenue.
- Railroad switch and signal upgrades at Broadway.
- Pedestrian and cyclist safety improvements at First Avenue and Fifth Avenue.

## Project area figures

- San Diego Convention Center: "hosted over 836,000 individuals attending 143 events with a total tax revenue of $29M in fiscal year 2019".
- Petco Park: "approximately 2.4M individuals attended 81 baseball games in 2019".
- Gaslamp Quarter: "draws an average of 9M visitors from 166 countries annually".
- The Rady Shell at Jacobs Park: open-air amphitheater and "architectural wonder" opened in 2021.

## Benefits

- Part of a group of Trade Corridor Enhancement Program (TCEP) projects funded by the California Transportation Commission (CTC). "The primary benefit of the TCEP program of projects is increased freight frequencies, which is key to improving the supply chain, reducing inflation, and meeting climate action goals."

## Status and timeline

- "The Project has completed the preliminary design phase and received the necessary environmental permits."
- "Design of the Project is planned to be completed in April 2025. Construction is expected to start in fall 2025, and the station is anticipated to be open to passengers in early 2027."

## Cost and funding

- "The Project, which costs $33 million for design and construction, is fully funded."
- "It was included in a December 2020 grant for $106 million, NCTD received from the California Transportation Commission to fund a slate of improvement projects to the LOSSAN corridor."
- "NCTD has entered into a design-build project management contract with BNSF for the construction of the Project."

wikis.title: Hillcrest Medical Campus Redevelopment, UC San Diego Health
wikis.summary: UC San Diego Health's page on the redevelopment of its 62-acre Hillcrest medical campus, including the newly opened McGrath Outpatient Pavilion.
wikis.body:
## The project

- "The Hillcrest Medical Campus Redevelopment Project represents a reimagining of how academic medicine can better serve you, your family and the whole community."
- "The redevelopment of the 62-acre Hillcrest medical campus is a major step forward for UC San Diego Health and health care in central San Diego and beyond. With modern, state-of-the-art facilities and upgraded infrastructure, we will enhance the vitality and creativity of the region's only academic medical center."
- The campus will continue to deliver "all the critical care services that define our more than 50-year commitment to the community", including a Level 1 Trauma Center, Regional Burn Center and Comprehensive Stroke Center, and an Emergency Department "with more than 50,000 patient visits per year".
- "We've been a beacon of hope and healing in Hillcrest since 1966, when the university began operating the former county hospital."

## McGrath Outpatient Pavilion (now open)

- "McGrath Outpatient Pavilion opened on UC San Diego Health's Hillcrest Medical Campus on July 28, 2025."
- Six floors, 250,000 square feet, at 4250 1st Ave., San Diego, CA 92103. It "houses key clinical programs that have either relocated or expanded from their previous locations", and outpatient clinical staff relocated there.
- Services listed: audiology; comprehensive breast center; digestive diseases (colorectal); ear, nose and throat care; infusion therapy; lab services; multi-specialty cancer care; neurology and neurosurgery; orthopedics; outpatient surgery; pain management procedures; perinatology; pharmacy; plastic surgery; radiation therapy; radiology and advanced imaging; trauma and burn surgery; urology; vascular surgery.
- Patient parking and drop-off are in the adjacent new parking structure at 4245 1st Ave., on level PL; "There is a charge for valet and self-parking at this location."

## Canyon wildlife

- "The natural canyon areas around the medical campus are home to many native plant and wildlife species. To protect this vibrant biodiversity, we designated 20-plus acres as 'Canyon District' land use, which will remain natural open space." Barriers, signage, lighting and landscaping near the Canyon District are being planned.

## Rankings mentioned on the page

- "UC San Diego Health is again ranked the No. 1 hospital system in San Diego by U.S. News & World Report for 2026-27", one of only 20 health systems nationwide on the "Best Hospitals" Honor Roll and nationally ranked in eight medical and surgical specialties.

wikis.title: Kindred Affordable Apartments tops out in downtown San Diego
wikis.summary: News report that VCC Construction has completed framing on the eight-story Kindred Affordable Apartments in San Diego's Cortez Hill, with the project's size, unit mix and funding.
wikis.body:
## The milestone

- "Construction has reached a major milestone at Kindred Affordable Apartments in downtown San Diego, where VCC Construction has completed framing on the eight-story affordable housing development."
- "The topping-out milestone marks the completion of the building's structural frame and moves the project closer to its planned opening in early 2027."

## The development

- Located in the Cortez Hill neighborhood; the 138,000-square-foot development "will transform the former site of the County of San Diego's Family Court into an affordable, intergenerational community for seniors and families with low incomes."
- Developed by BRIDGE Housing in partnership with the San Diego Housing Commission (SDHC). It "will include 126 rental homes, community spaces, resident services offices, outdoor courtyards, parking and approximately 4,400 square feet of commercial space."
- "The project will provide 125 affordable apartments and one unrestricted manager's unit. The affordable homes will remain restricted for 99 years for households earning no more than 60% of San Diego's Area Median Income, currently $99,240 annually for a family of four."
- Built "in a transit-oriented area with access to public transportation, jobs, schools, parks and other community resources."

## Funding and partners

- SDHC awarded 84 housing vouchers: "63 vouchers are designated for seniors who have previously experienced homelessness, while 21 will assist eligible families with low incomes."
- SDHC also provided "a loan of up to $7.955 million using federal, state and local resources", including HUD's HOME Investment Partnerships Program, California's Local Housing Trust Fund and the City of San Diego's Affordable Housing Fund.
- "The County of San Diego contributed $4 million from its Innovative Housing Trust Fund and provided the development site as part of its initiative to use excess county-owned land for affordable housing."
- "Additional financing includes more than $17.7 million in recycled tax-exempt Multifamily Housing Revenue Bonds from the state", part of a bond recycling partnership involving SDHC, the City of San Diego and the California Housing Finance Agency.
- Project team: BRIDGE Housing as developer, SDHC as financing and development partner, VCC Construction as general contractor.
- San Ysidro Health will provide supportive services, "including medical and social services through the San Diego Program of All-Inclusive Care for the Elderly (PACE) for seniors who have experienced homelessness", plus case management and social services for all residents.

## Quotes

- San Diego Mayor Todd Gloria: "This project represents what can happen when public agencies and nonprofit partners work together to deliver much-needed housing. I look forward to continued collaboration to ensure we are serving our shared constituents."
- Colin Miller, SDHC senior vice president of real estate development: "Kindred Apartments will transform this site into a vibrant community that brings seniors and families together and provides housing stability in a shared place to call home."
- BRIDGE Housing President and CEO Ken Lombard said affordable housing "provides more than shelter by supporting healthier families, stronger communities and opportunities for residents of all ages."

wikis.title: Downtown San Diego station (planned COASTER stop)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the planned Downtown San Diego COASTER commuter rail station, its layout, funding and shifting opening date.
wikis.body:
## Station facts

- "Downtown San Diego station is a planned Coaster commuter rail station in San Diego, California."
- Infobox: location San Diego, California; coordinates 32°42'29"N 117°09'44"W (32.7080, -117.1622); owner North County Transit District; line BNSF San Diego Subdivision; 1 side platform; 2 tracks; accessible: Yes; opening 2027.
- Future services: COASTER, with Santa Fe Depot as the preceding station (toward Oceanside) and this station as the terminus.

## The project

- "The station will be built in conjunction with upgrades to the BNSF Railway corridor and adds a pocket track to allow greater service frequencies."
- "A new passenger platform will be located between 1st and 5th Streets."
- "The station is in the vicinity of the Gaslamp Quarter, San Diego Convention Center, and Petco Park; it will further provide connections to the San Diego Trolley at the adjacent Convention Center station and Gaslamp Quarter station."
- "Improvements were funded partly by a Trade Corridor Enhancement Program grant, derived from Road Repair and Accountability Act revenues, and partly by BNSF."

## Schedule

- "As of February 2026, construction on the Downtown Platform is scheduled to begin in the spring. After 18 months of construction, the station will likely open in late-2027 or early-2028."
- Categorised under "Railway stations scheduled to open in 2027".

## Cited sources

- Phil Diehl, "Transit district to increase Coaster commuter train service this fall", San Diego Union-Tribune, June 27, 2021.
- Vanessa Paz, "New Downtown COASTER stop to connect Oceanside and the Gaslamp by 2027 | On the Move", CBS8, November 12, 2025.
- Jacob Smith, "San Diego Downtown COASTER Stop Planned For 2027", Hoodline, November 12, 2025.
- "Long-sought Coaster extension to San Diego Convention Center will break ground this year", San Diego Union-Tribune (retrieved February 24, 2026).
- SMA Rail Consulting, "California Passenger Rail Network Schematics", Caltrans, April 2016, p. 26.

wikis.title: Coaster extension to the San Diego Convention Center to break ground in 2026
wikis.summary: San Diego Union-Tribune report on NCTD's $33 million Coaster extension from Santa Fe Depot to the convention center, its delayed groundbreaking and expected 2027-28 opening.
wikis.body:
## The project

- "The $33 million project will extend the Coaster commuter rail line from its existing terminus at Santa Fe Depot to San Diego's waterfront convention center."
- Supporters call the project - "which is fully funded and designed" - "the biggest boost to local transit since the Blue Line trolley line was extended north four years ago to University City and La Jolla."
- "The new Coaster convention center station will be just steps from Petco Park, the Gaslamp Quarter, the Rady Shell and other nearby attractions", letting riders avoid walking nearly a mile, transferring to the trolley or taking a car from Santa Fe Depot.
- "A key feature of the project will be an 850-foot platform extending from First Avenue to Fifth Avenue. New bicycle and pedestrian infrastructure will also be added along those two streets."
- New signals at Kettner Boulevard, Market Street, Front Street, First Avenue and Fifth Avenue.
- "The extension project will also add a second rail track in part of downtown - making it easier for freight trains to travel through the area from the Port of San Diego to Los Angeles and other points north."
- NCTD is partnering with BNSF Railway, "a freight operator taking the lead on project construction", along with the city, the Port of San Diego and San Diego Gas & Electric.

## Schedule

- NCTD officials said Wednesday "they plan to break ground on the convention center extension by the end of this year and have it operating by late 2027 or early 2028."
- They "had hoped to break ground this spring but had to delay that plan so they could analyze potential relocation of utilities between Harbor Drive and Tony Gwynn Drive."
- Shawn Donaghy, NCTD chief executive: "It is unlikely that construction will start in spring of 2026, as these utility reviews are critical to the project. While we are hopeful that the project will be complete in 2027, it is more likely at this point that it will be late 2027 to early 2028."
- "Construction is expected to last about 18 months." Any delay in reaching agreement on utility relocations "would delay groundbreaking".

## Funding

- "The $33 million being spent on the project comes from a $106 million grant NCTD got in 2020 from the California Transportation Commission to enhance the San Diego-Los Angeles rail corridor."
- Since securing the funding, NCTD "has completed design work, signed a memorandum of understanding with the city on cycling infrastructure and worked with SDG&E on utilities infrastructure issues", said Mary Dover, NCTD's chief of staff.

## Ridership and service

- The extension "is expected to boost ridership beyond the 871,000 it had in 2024", and to reduce road congestion by persuading more residents of Oceanside, Carlsbad and other North County cities to take the Coaster.
- "Currently, the last northbound Coaster train leaves Santa Fe Depot at 8:40 p.m. on Sunday, 9:20 p.m. Monday through Thursday and 10:40 p.m. on Friday and Saturday."
- "The Coaster now has eight stations along its 41-mile route." NCTD has also discussed stations at the Del Mar Fairgrounds and Camp Pendleton, "but no progress has been made on those."
- "An extension to the Convention Center has been an ambition of NCTD since shortly after the Coaster began running in 1995. But formal efforts to make it happen didn't begin until 2020."

## Reaction

- Michael Trimble, executive director of the Gaslamp Quarter Association: "More convenient rail access gives people a real alternative to driving downtown. That means a better visitor experience, less time in traffic, fewer parking headaches and more time enjoying the Gaslamp."
- RideSD, a local transit advocacy group, hailed the project but said the Coaster needs to run more frequently and for more of the day: "An extension that increases ridership should go hand-in-hand with improved hours and frequency, so the Coaster can provide North County residents with meaningful access to downtown's vibrant bar & food scene."

wikis.title: CTA breaks ground on the Red Line Extension at the future Michigan Avenue station
wikis.summary: CTA press release announcing the groundbreaking of the 5.5-mile Red Line Extension from 95th to 130th Street, with the project's scope, timeline, jobs and contracting goals.
wikis.body:
## The groundbreaking

- "Mayor Brandon Johnson today joined U.S. Sen. Dick Durbin, members of the Illinois congressional delegation, Federal Transit Administration officials, Chicago Transit Authority (CTA) Acting President Nora Leerhsen and other dignitaries to break ground on the largest and most transformational capital construction project in CTA history, the Red Line Extension (RLE) Project."
- Sub-headline: "Promised nearly 60 years ago, project will extend the CTA's Red Line from 95th Street to 130th Street and will include four new, fully accessible stations at 103rd, 111th, Michigan & 130th streets."
- The project "will provide the Far South Side of Chicago with rapid rail transit for the first time".

## Project scope

- Build a 5.5-mile extension of the Red Line starting at 95th Street Terminal to the vicinity of 130th Street.
- Four new accessible stations near 103rd Street, 111th Street, Michigan Avenue (near 116th) and 130th Street, "each of which will include bus, bike, pedestrian and parking facilities."
- "Build a new rail yard and related rail facilities near 120th Street to improve operational efficiency for the entire Red Line and CTA system."

## Benefits claimed

- "Once the extension opens, it is expected to provide up to an hour of time savings roundtrip to riders traveling between the future 130th station and the Loop."
- Stations will offer plaza areas with seating and amenities; "All stations will receive commissioned, one-of-a-kind artwork that will be developed with feedback from people in the neighborhood areas around the stations."
- "More than 12,500 construction jobs and an estimated 59,800 indirect jobs are expected to be created."
- "Because of the improved transit options, an estimated 25,000 additional jobs to become available within an hour commute or less".

## Timeline

- Advance construction work has been under way, "including demolition of properties acquired to build the project and relocation of utility poles and other equipment where the new track will be built."
- "With construction beginning in spring 2026", upcoming work includes drilling where new elevated track columns will be located, and pouring concrete for track foundations and columns.
- "Station construction will begin in 2027."
- "The new extension and stations are expected to be completed and in service in 2030."

## Workforce and small business goals

- CTA and design-build contractor Walsh-VINCI Transit Community Partners "committed to creating pathways for Chicagoans to receive training and access to jobs". CTA has contracted with Chicago Women in Trades, HIRE 360 and Metropolitan Family Services.
- Walsh-VINCI workforce goals as a percentage of total labor hours: design - Service Area Economically Disadvantaged Area (EDA) 10 percent of total design hours; construction - Careers Opportunity Goal 10 percent of total trade labor hours, Service Area EDA 35 percent, Union Apprentice 15 percent.
- Disadvantaged Business Enterprise (DBE) goals: "25 percent for project design and 22 percent for project construction." Supportive services include the "Driving Small Businesses the Distance" monthly webinar, the Small Business Educational Series and "Building Small Businesses".

## Quotes

- Mayor Brandon Johnson: "Today's groundbreaking demonstrates our shared commitment to transit equity and opportunity for every Chicagoan. Far South Side residents have waited decades for this vital rail service to come to life."
- CTA Acting President Nora Leerhsen: "This historic CTA project finally delivers on the transit promises made to the residents of Roseland, Pullman, Washington Heights and surrounding neighborhoods decades ago."
- U.S. Sen. Dick Durbin, U.S. Sen. Tammy Duckworth, U.S. Reps. Mike Quigley (D-IL-05), Robin Kelly (D-IL-02), Jonathan L. Jackson (D-IL-01) and Jesús "Chuy" García (D-IL-04), and Aldermen Anthony A. Beale (9th), Ronnie L. Mosley (21st) and Peter Chico (10th) also gave statements.
- Alderman Beale cited "more than $1 billion in investment that has already created thousands of jobs" in the Far South Side; Alderman Chico mentioned "the new Illinois Quantum and Microelectronics Park" in the 10th Ward.
- Dan Walsh Jr., president of Walsh Construction's transportation division and lead partner of Walsh-VINCI Transit Community Partners: "Walsh Construction, VINCI Construction and our entire design-build team are committed to delivering a safe, reliable, high-quality project."

wikis.title: Opening the Obama Presidential Center - FAQ
wikis.summary: Obama Foundation FAQ giving the Obama Presidential Center's grand opening dates, what is on campus, and how and when Museum tickets go on sale.
wikis.body:
## Opening dates

- "The Obama Presidential Center Grand Opening Ceremony will be held on June 18, 2026. This event will serve as a celebration to mark the campus's official opening. The invite-only event will be livestreamed for all to enjoy."
- "The public will be able to start visiting the campus and Museum on June 19, 2026."
- "Obama Presidential Center Opening Weekend festivities will take place June 20 and 21, 2026 with an array of public celebrations to welcome the community and guests from around the world to Chicago's South Side."

## The campus

- "Most of the Obama Presidential Campus is free, open to the public and does not require tickets."
- Features listed: original works of art commissioned specifically for the campus; the Women's Garden, the Eleanor Roosevelt Fruit and Vegetable Garden and the John Lewis Plaza; the Great Lawn and walking paths on the Wetland Walk; a Playground and "the newest branch of the Chicago Public Library"; a Cafe, a Restaurant, a Picnic Area and a store.
- "A variety of programs, tours, and events will be available across campus throughout the year. Some programs and events may require separate registration or tickets."

## Museum tickets

- "To visit the Museum, you will need to purchase tickets for a timed entry. Museum tickets will go on sale in May. Guests with tickets can begin to visit the Museum on June 19, 2026."
- "We recommend reserving your tickets online in advance to secure your preferred time. We can not guarantee availability if you buy tickets in person."
- "Information about ticket options will be made available before they go on sale in May. Ticket pricing is in line with other Chicago museums, and includes everyday discounts and designated free days for Illinois residents."

## School visits

- "School visits will officially launch fall semester of 2026, with the ability to reserve your spot beginning in the spring of 2026." Questions go to education@obama.org.

wikis.title: UChicago Medicine breaks ground on Illinois' first freestanding cancer center
wikis.summary: University of Chicago news story on the groundbreaking of UChicago Medicine's $815 million standalone cancer care and research pavilion in Hyde Park.
wikis.body:
## The groundbreaking

- "The University of Chicago Medicine broke ground on its $815 million project to build the state's first standalone structure dedicated to cancer care and research."
- Subhead: "Chicago mayor, other leaders gather to celebrate $815 million South Side project."
- "The Sept. 19 event included remarks from Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson, Attorney General Kwame Raoul and University of Chicago and health system leaders. It also featured performances by the Chicago Mass Choir and a ceremonial bell ringing."

## The building

- 575,000 square feet, seven storeys, to be built on the flagship Hyde Park campus on the South Side.
- "Expected to open to patients in spring 2027."
- Includes 80 inpatient beds, 90 outpatient exam rooms and dedicated imaging, infusion and clinical trial spaces.
- The team of "more than 200 people currently works in more than five different buildings on the Hyde Park campus"; the new facility "will be the central point of cancer research efforts, new therapy development, clinical advancements and other discoveries."
- Features listed: streamlined access to diagnostic and treatment innovations to bring clinical trials to historically underrepresented populations; work in cancer metabolomics, big data and artificial intelligence; an on-campus "molecule to medicine" therapy development pipeline with UChicago's Pritzker School for Molecular Engineering and Argonne National Laboratory; and support services from cancer screenings to lifestyle classes, nutrition education, survivor support, music therapy, fitness classes and a retail store selling cancer-specific products such as wigs or clothing with openings for ports.
- "The new building's additional inpatient beds will allow UChicago Medicine to open other rooms for patients with complex or acute care needs" in organ transplants, digestive diseases, cardiology, orthopedics and trauma care.

## Approvals and project team

- "The building proposal was approved by the Illinois Health Facilities and Services Review Board in June 2023."
- "Key partners in the project include architect CannonDesign and Turner Construction, both of which are working with diverse firms to build the pavilion."
- "Involving more than 500 construction jobs, at least 41% of the contract construction dollars will go to minority- and women-owned firms", with onsite minority and female worker goals and Chicago residency goals.

## Cancer rates cited

- "The CDC estimates cancer rates will grow by 49% between 2015 and 2050 in the U.S."
- "On the South Side, where cancer rates are expected to climb 19% in the next decade alone, compared with 9% in the rest of the Chicago area. South Side residents are twice as likely to die from cancer as people living in the rest of the country."
- "UChicago Medicine is one of 72 hospitals in the U.S. and one of only two in Illinois designated by the National Cancer Institute as delivering cutting-edge cancer care."

## Quotes

- Tom Jackiewicz, president of the University of Chicago Health System: "This project represents our latest bold move to make an even bigger difference in cancer care and research."
- Kunle Odunsi, director of the UChicago Medicine Comprehensive Cancer Center, cited "our 49-year status as a National Cancer Institute-designated Cancer Center and newest member of the prestigious National Comprehensive Cancer Network".
- Nita Karnik Lee, associate director of the Comprehensive Cancer Center Office of Community Engagement and Cancer Health Equity, described planned community spaces offering "cooking classes, support groups, music therapy and fitness classes."
- Cancer survivor Candace Henley, chair of UChicago Medicine's Community Advisory Council: "This hospital is allowing those of us who have felt invisible to now be seen, to now have access, to now have resources and state-of-the-art care."

## Note

- "This story was adapted from the UChicago Medicine website."

wikis.title: IAH Terminal B Transformation progress
wikis.summary: Houston Airports newsroom article on construction progress at George Bush Intercontinental Airport's $2.5 billion Terminal B Transformation and what the finished terminal will contain.
wikis.body:
## Progress

- "From the upper level of the new Terminal B Central Processor at George Bush Intercontinental Airport (IAH), sunlight now floods through newly installed curtainwall glass."
- "The curtainwall installation marks a major milestone in the Terminal B Transformation Project; a collaboration between United Airlines and Houston Airports to reimagine one of the airport's original terminals."
- "Structural steel defines new concourses, and crews are actively installing mechanical systems, flooring and interior finishes."
- Houston Airports Director of Aviation Jim Szczesniak toured the site with United leaders: "That view says it all... Every pane of glass represents progress for Houston and the passengers who will experience a modernized terminal built for decades ahead."

## North Concourse

- "The new Terminal B North Concourse will span approximately 765,000 square feet across three levels, replacing the original 1969-era flight stations with two new passenger concourses."
- "22 gates will serve United's growing fleet as part of the airline's United NEXT initiative."
- "A 54,000-square-foot United Club at the mezzanine level will offer panoramic airfield views - the largest in United's system."
- Also: "a Sensory Room for passengers with hidden disabilities, a United-branded interactive park that combines art and technology, and quiet zones for relaxation."
- "Two new concessions hubs will offer more than 115,000 square feet of dining and retail space supported by advanced food service technology", with an upgraded baggage handling system beneath.

## South Concourse

- "The Terminal B South concourse will modernize 18 E175 gates, replacing older layouts with upgraded hold rooms designed around United's 'gate of the future' standards."

## Central Processor

- "At the heart of the project is the Central Processor - the architectural centerpiece of the transformation."
- "The expansion and renovation, totaling more than 440,000 square feet, will support future growth to 36 million passengers annually."
- Includes "a new baggage claim hall, modern ticketing lobby, expanded security checkpoint and enhanced airline and airport support areas", a streamlined third-floor security checkpoint, direct connections to concessions and concourses, and "improved roadway flow with expanded curbsides, updated signage and intuitive wayfinding."

## Cost and schedule

- "The $2.5 billion Terminal B Transformation is one of the most significant airport projects in the country."
- "When it opens in 2026, Terminal B will look and function entirely differently from the facility built more than half a century ago."
- "Completion is scheduled for fall 2026."
- Szczesniak: "This transformation is about more than infrastructure. It's about creating a passenger experience that feels distinctly Houston and is built for the future."

wikis.title: Full financing of the first phase of the George R. Brown Convention District Transformation
wikis.summary: Houston First press release announcing a roughly $1.38 billion bond sale that fully funds phase one of the George R. Brown Convention Center transformation, with the bond structure and what the phase builds.
wikis.body:
## The announcement

- "The City of Houston and Houston First Corporation today announced the successful sale of approximately $1.38 billion of Hotel Occupancy Tax and Special Revenue Bonds to fully fund the first phase of the Convention District Transformation Project."
- Subhead: "Sale of Hotel Occupancy Tax and Special Revenue Bonds Secures Project Funds." Dateline HOUSTON (April 1, 2026).

## What phase one builds

- "GRB South, a new 700,000-square-foot building that will directly connect to the existing George R. Brown Convention Center, as well as a new 100,000-square-foot pedestrian plaza connecting the facility to Toyota Center."
- "The initial expansion will feature two exhibition halls, flexible indoor/outdoor and atrium space, the largest ballroom in Texas, and dedicated ground-level spaces for retail and restaurants, all designed with inspiration drawn from Houston's bayous and native prairie landscape."
- "On schedule to open in May 2028, the building's environmental footprint will be reduced by incorporating low-carbon materials, high-efficiency building systems, and native landscaping in a new expansive living roof, with potential solar integration."
- Project team: "global real estate firm Hines as development manager, Populous as architect of record, and Gilbane | Flintco as construction manager under a joint venture."

## Funding mechanism

- "As authorized by Senate Bill 1057, signed into law in 2023 and authored by then-Senator Whitmire, the project will be funded by the state's portion of incremental Hotel Occupancy Tax revenue growth within a three-mile radius of the convention center for 30 years, estimated to total roughly $2 billion. This funding mechanism ensures no burden on local taxpayers."
- Houston First and the City structured the financing for "affordability, flexibility, and multiple pathways to access future funding."

## The bond sale

- "$149 million of tax-exempt and $52.9 million of taxable Senior Lien revenue refunding bonds, which closed on March 25, 2026, and $1.096 billion of tax-exempt First Lien Revenue and Refunding bonds and $78 million of tax-exempt Second Lien revenue bonds, which closed on April 1, 2026."
- "Bond proceeds will be used to refund existing debt, refund subordinate lien notes outstanding, and provide permanent financing for the transformational George R. Brown expansion."
- "For its senior lien series of bonds (Series A & B), Houston received a full notch upgrade from the rating agency S&P, from A to AA-."
- "The combined four series generated significant investor demand, with 115 different accounts participating, generating over $15.8 billion of priority orders and representing approximately 10.4 times the amount of bonds offered for sale."
- Tender process: "The City received nearly 480 offers from bondholders during the tender process for a total of roughly $208 million, or 22% of the outstanding principal of the relevant bonds."
- "The bonds were underwritten through a syndicate led by joint senior managers J.P. Morgan Securities and Ramirez & Co., Inc., which also served as Dealer-Managers for the tender transaction."

## Quotes

- Houston Mayor John Whitmire: "The overall success of this bond sale speaks to the confidence the markets have in Houston as a city moving in the right direction. This project has been a priority of mine since I was a state senator."
- Michael Heckman, President and CEO of Houston First: "This is a highly complicated and ambitious project, but we have set a standard for how to move an initiative of this scale forward efficiently and effectively and bring it to market."
- Drew Masterson, CEO of Masterson Advisors LLC: "This was the most complex transaction that I have worked on in my 42 years in the bond business... the new revenue stream that the Mayor procured for the project is heavily backloaded over 30 years and we needed $1.14 billion for the project up front."

wikis.title: Houston Ship Channel Expansion (Project 11) overview
wikis.summary: Port Houston's project overview of the Houston Ship Channel Expansion - Project 11 - covering what is being widened and deepened, segment by segment, plus its environmental features and authorization history.
wikis.body:
## The project

- "As the local sponsor of this crucial federal waterway, Port Houston is partnering with the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers to expand the channel."
- "The Houston Ship Channel expansion - Project 11 - is widening the channel by 170 feet along its Galveston Bay reach, from 530 feet to 700 feet and deepening some upstream segments to 46.5 feet, alongside other safety and efficiency improvements, and crafting new environmental features."
- "Dredging began in 2022 and with the help of our partners, we are expediting the process to complete the work in 2029."
- Tagline: "Bigger. Better. Safer."

## Why the page says it matters

- The channel "has more deep-draft ship visits than any other port in the country, and nearly 200,000 barge transits every year as well."
- "The Port of Houston drives $987 billion in annual national economic value, sustains more than three million U.S. jobs, and is the nation's number one port in total waterborne tonnage."
- "There are more than 200 public and private facilities along the Houston Ship Channel."

## Project segments

- Bolivar Roads to Redfish: approximately 11.5 miles; widen channel to 700 feet; bend easings.
- Redfish to Bayport Ship Channel: "Currently not in the proposed federal plan, so must be built by local interests"; approximately 8.3 miles; widen to a minimum of 700 feet; bend easings.
- Bayport Ship Channel to Barbours Cut: "Currently not in the proposed federal plan, so must be built by local interests"; approximately 5 miles; widen to 700 feet.
- Bayport Ship Channel: approximately 4 miles; widen to approximately 455 feet; modify channel entrance to reduce shoaling.
- Barbours Cut Ship Channel: widen to approximately 455 feet; modify channel entrance; perform advanced maintenance for flare.
- Boggy Bayou (BW 8) to Sims Bayou: widen to approximately 530 feet through the Greens Bayou confluence; deepen from existing 41 feet to 46.5 feet from Boggy Bayou to Hunting Bayou (last Turning Basin before reaching Washburn Tunnel).
- Sims Bayou to IH 610: deepen from existing 37 feet to 41.5 feet.
- IH 610 to Turning Basin: deepen from existing 39 feet to potential 41.5 feet; increase Brady Island Turning Basin.

## Environmental components

- Marsh creation: dredged material "will be used to build three new marshes, for up to 800 total acres, providing a combination of wetlands and shallow open water habitat for wildlife."
- Bird island construction: new bird islands from dredged material "anticipated to be up to 20 acres in total", supported by the Beneficial Use Group (BUG), which includes Port Houston and state and federal environmental agencies.
- New oyster reef: "approximately 375 acres of substrate for natural recruitment and settlement of oysters to mitigate for those displaced by channel modifications."
- Marsh/bird island construction: "This triangular-shaped marsh will have a bird island at each corner."
- Air quality: expansion "is expected to improve regional air quality by reducing ship emissions... through more efficient vessel movements and avoiding congestion within the Port of Houston."

## The "Texas Chicken" maneuver

- "This maneuver is unique to the Houston Ship Channel. Ships from opposing directions in the channel meet each other head-on but still safely pass each other, as hydrodynamic forces keep the vessels from touching! This maneuver is successfully performed every day, and it's necessary in relatively narrow channels like ours."

## Study, authorization and funding

- "Port Houston began planning the latest improvements to the Houston Ship Channel in 2010, working in collaboration with Congress, the Army Corps of Engineers and channel stakeholders."
- The Corps completed its five-year Project 11 feasibility study, the Houston Ship Channel Mega Study; "In April 2020, the Chief of Engineers signed the final Chief's Report for the project."
- "The Houston Ship Channel Expansion Channel Improvement project was authorized in the Water Resources and Development Act of 2020 as part of a larger legislative package passed by Congress in December."
- "On January 19, 2021, the Port of Houston was notified by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) that it was awarded a 'new start' designation and $19.5 million in federal funds to begin construction of the project."

## Latest news listed on the page

- October 27, 2025: "Port Houston Completes its Portion of Project 11 Dredging"
- May 22, 2025: "Port Houston Announces $131M in USACE workplan for Houston Ship Channel Construction and Maintenance"
- May 5, 2025: "Houston Ship Channel Ranked #1 U.S. Waterway"

wikis.title: Up First: US-Iran Talks Delayed, Vance Peace Architect, Obama Presidential Center Opens
wikis.summary: Apple Podcasts page for an episode of NPR's Up First covering the shaky Iran deal, Vance's negotiating role and the Obama Presidential Center opening.
wikis.body:
## Episode

- Show: "Up First from NPR" (channel NPR Podcasts, updated daily). Episode title: "US-Iran Talks Delayed, Vance Peace Architect, Obama Presidential Center Opens".
- Published June 19, 2026 at 9:59 AM UTC. Length 13 min. Rating: Clean.
- Hosts listed: A Martínez, Ayesha Rascoe, Leila Fadel, Michel Martin, Scott Simon, Steve Inskeep.

## What the episode covers

- "The deal to end the war with Iran is already looking shaky, with Vice President Vance delaying his trip to Switzerland to start negotiations and Israel still bombing Lebanon even though the deal says that has to stop."
- "Vance is supposed to lead difficult negotiations with Iran, but he has limited diplomatic experience with a 60 days goal of going through a long list of tough issues still left to settle."
- "And the Obama Presidential Center opens to the public in Chicago today, where Obama used the dedication to tell people not to miss the past, but to remember what is still possible."

## Chapters

- (0:00) Introduction; (02:19) US-Iran Talks Delayed; (05:55) Vance Peace Architect; (09:16) Obama Presidential Center Opens.

## Credits

- Edited by Kate Bartlett, Dana Farrington, Megan Pratz, Mohamad ElBardicy and Lindsay Totty; produced by Ziad Buchh and Ava Pukatch; director Christopher Thomas; engineering support from Simon-Laslo Janssen; technical director Carleigh Strange; executive producer Jay Shaylor.

wikis.title: DFW Airport completes Terminal F module moves
wikis.summary: DFW Airport newsroom release on finishing the move of six prefabricated modules that form the first phase of its new Terminal F, with the terminal's size, cost and schedule.
wikis.body:
## The milestone

- "On Aug. 8, the airport completed the last of six module moves that make up the structure for Terminal F."
- "The modules, some nearly as large as a football field, were moved overnight during a two-week period using self-propelled modular transporters along one of DFW's airside taxiways. The structures were then placed onto the foundations constructed at the Terminal F site."
- "This is DFW's third project to deploy the innovative module-based method to reconstruct or expand its terminal facilities, with the most recent moves being the largest modules for a terminal expansion at any airport."
- "The modules for Terminal F are approximately four times larger than the structures moved earlier this year for the ongoing expansion of Terminal C. The largest of the six modules measured 278 feet long by 136 feet wide and weighed 3,320 tons - about as heavy as 12 Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner widebody aircraft."
- Subhead: "Project Takes Modular Construction at Airports to New Heights with Size and Scale of Structures."

## Terminal F

- "In May, DFW and American Airlines announced the decision to expand the scope and accelerate the phasing of the new Terminal F."
- "The first phase of the Terminal F expansion program is anticipated to open with 15 gates in 2027."
- "The estimated $4 billion Terminal F is planned to ultimately deliver a total of 31 gates to be serviced entirely by American Airlines, expand capacity for international operations and widebody aircraft, and include areas to facilitate parking, ticketing, check-in, security screening and baggage operations."
- "American will return some gates in other areas of the airport, which will help facilitate the growth of other airlines at DFW as well."
- "In addition to a new centralized Skylink Station, which is included with the first phase of construction, the final configuration will provide a walking connection with Terminal D."

## Project team

- "The design-build team for the first phase of Terminal F is Innovation Next+, a joint venture comprised of Archer Western Construction, Turner Construction Company, Phillips May Corporation, H. J. Russell & Company and CARCON Industries, with PGAL, Gensler and Muller2 as design team members."

## Quotes

- DFW CEO Chris McLaughlin: "This milestone reflects the dedication and vision of the many teams who are building the future of our airport... By embracing modular construction, we are finding smarter ways to deliver results faster, with less impact on travelers."
- Mohamed Charkas, DFW's Executive Vice President of Infrastructure and Development: "DFW is at the forefront of innovation in terminal construction, continually redefining what's possible. The time we save using modular construction techniques is crucial for fostering the growth of our community and supporting our airline partners."

## About DFW (from the release)

- "Centered between owner cities Dallas and Fort Worth, Texas", DFW's "historic $12 billion capital plan - DFW Forward - is set to transform the customer experience and plan for the future with monumental upgrades and expansions underway across DFW's terminals, airfield and roadway infrastructure."

wikis.title: DART Silver Line launches October 25
wikis.summary: DART news release announcing the October 25, 2025 launch of the 26-mile Silver Line regional rail service linking seven cities and DFW International Airport.
wikis.body:
## The launch

- "Dallas Area Rapid Transit (DART) will launch the Silver Line regional rail service on Saturday, October 25, 2025." Dateline: DALLAS, October 8, 2025.
- Subhead: "New 26-mile commuter rail strengthens North Texas' economy, expands mobility, and prepares region for projected growth."
- "Spanning over 26 miles, the Silver Line connects Plano, Richardson, Dallas, Addison, Carrollton, Coppell, Grapevine, and DFW International Airport."
- "The Silver Line features state-of-the-art Stadler trains, fully accessible stations, and direct transfers to DART Light Rail, bus routes, and DFW terminals."

## Service at a glance

- Start date: Saturday, October 25, 2025.
- Frequency: "Every 30 minutes during weekday peak hours; every 60 minutes off-peak and on weekends."
- Hours: 4 a.m. to 1 a.m. daily.
- Connections: DART Light Rail lines, bus routes, DFW airport terminals, Trinity Metro TexRail service.

## The line

- "Each station was designed with input from the cities along the rail corridor, reflecting local character, community feedback, and accessibility features."
- "The line connects residents to key employment centers and educational destinations, including The University of Texas at Dallas."
- "The Silver Line is rail service built for longer distances and faster connections than DART's light rail system. It also links to North Texas' expanding trail network."
- "Originating from the Cotton Belt Corridor plan, the line reflects years of planning to expand mobility, ease congestion, and prepare for future growth across the region."
- Trains "will feature comfortable seating, bicycle racks, overhead luggage racks, USB phone chargers and ADA-compliant boarding."

## Opening celebrations

- "To mark the start of service, DART will offer free Silver Line rides from October 25 through November 8."
- "Public station celebrations will be held at each of the 10 Silver Line stations on October 25, featuring live music, cultural performances, family-friendly activities, and community programming."
- "A detailed advisory with schedules and event information will follow in coming weeks."

## Quotes

- Nadine Lee, DART President & CEO: "The Silver Line is a centerpiece of our Point B vision to make DART your first-in-mind mobility partner. By connecting key employment centers, neighborhoods, and the world's third-busiest airport, this project will be a catalyst for economic growth."
- Gary Slagel, DART Chairman of the Board: "Our focus is on reliability and convenience. With predictable schedules, modern trains, and seamless connections, the Silver Line is built to meet the needs of both daily riders and occasional travelers."

## About DART (from the release)

- DART "operates Light Rail, Trinity Railway Express regional rail, bus routes, GoLink on-demand service, and paratransit, moving more than 220,000 passengers daily across a 700-square-mile, 13-city region including Addison, Carrollton, Cockrell Hill, Dallas, Farmers Branch, Garland, Glenn Heights, Highland Park, Irving, Richardson, Rowlett, Plano, and University Park."
- Rider resources: DART.org/SilverLine, the GoPass app, customer service at 214-979-1111.

wikis.title: Silicon Valley BART extension
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on VTA's BART Silicon Valley Extension Program - the three-phase extension of BART from Fremont into Santa Clara County - covering its phases, funding history and delays.
wikis.body:
## Overview

- "The Silicon Valley BART extension (officially VTA's BART Silicon Valley Extension Program, commonly known as BART Silicon Valley) is an ongoing effort to expand the Green and Orange Line service by Bay Area Rapid Transit (BART) into Santa Clara County via the East Bay from its former terminus at the Fremont station in Alameda County. Planned since at least 1981, the project has seven stations in three sequential phases."
- "The Santa Clara Valley Transportation Authority (VTA) built the Berryessa Extension and intends to build the final downtown San Jose extension, but BART operates and maintains the completed portion of the extension and will also do so for the final phase when completed."
- The article carries a maintenance banner: "This article needs to be updated... (August 2023)".

## Infobox

- Status: "revenue service (to Berryessa)"; "Tunnel boring machine testing and pit excavation at Santa Clara station site; design and engineering elsewhere (to Santa Clara)".
- Locale: southern Alameda County and Santa Clara County. Termini: Fremont and Santa Clara. Stations: "7 + 2 potential infill". Depot: Newhall. Services: 2.
- Work began October 1, 2009. Planned opening 2037 (to Santa Clara). Opened March 25, 2017 (to Warm Springs) and June 13, 2020 (to Berryessa).
- Track gauge 5 ft 6 in (1,676 mm); electrification third rail, 1 kV DC. Website http://www.vta.org/bart/.
- The route map marks Irvington as 2031 and 28th Street/Little Portugal, Downtown San José, Diridon and Santa Clara as 2036; Calaveras is marked "proposed".

## Phases table

| Phase | Name | Length | Groundbreaking | Opening | Cost ($ billions) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Warm Springs (WSX) | 5.4 mi (8.7 km) | Sep 30, 2009 | Mar 25, 2017 | 0.79 |
| 2 | Berryessa (SVX Phase 1) | 10 mi (16 km) | Apr 12, 2012 | Jun 13, 2020 | 2.3 |
| 3 | Downtown San Jose/Santa Clara (SVX Phase 2) | 6 mi (9.7 km) | Jun 14, 2024 | 2037 (planned) | 12.7 |

- Notes: Irvington and Calaveras are future infill stations; "Groundbreaking for the construction of the Fremont subway section occurred in 2009. Preliminary site preparation work for the Paseo Padre/Washington grade separation project began in June 2005"; "Preliminary subsurface exploration started in late January 2019."

## Funding history

- "Santa Clara County was originally planned to be part of the BART system, but local governments did not approve."
- "In 2000, Santa Clara County voters approved a 30-year half-cent sales tax increase to fund BART, which took effect in April 2006."
- "The Federal Transit Administration issued a 'Not Recommended' rating in January 2004", concerned "about the ability of VTA to operate BART and other bus services at the same time."
- A 2006 half-cent general sales tax measure was defeated "by a margin of 58% to 42%" on June 6, 2006. "In December 2006, the VTA board authorized $135 million in contract amendments to continue engineering work and environmental clearance."
- "By a two-thirds majority, Santa Clara County voters approved Measure B in November 2008, implementing a 30-year, 1/8-cent local sales tax dedicated solely to funding the operating and maintenance costs... The 2008 Measure B sales tax took effect in July 2012."
- "The economy worsened in 2009, and the 2000 sales tax was projected to generate $7 billion - short of the originally expected $11 billion. As a consequence, the number of planned stations was reduced." The line from Berryessa to downtown San Jose "was delayed until 2026, pushed back from 2025."
- "VTA awarded $770 million to Skanska-Shimmick-Herzog in 2011 for the first phase of the Berryessa Extension... and the federal government granted $900 million for the project in 2012."
- For phase II: "A half-cent 30-year sales tax passed in the 2016 elections, to raise $6.0 to $6.5 billion with up to 25% of this (or $1.6 billion) for BART. VTA also sought $1.5 billion from New Starts, and $750 million from the California Cap and Trade program."
- "In 2018, VTA was awarded $2.6 billion for the project from the state's Transit and Intercity Rail Capital Program funded by the 2017 gas tax bill. In August 2019, the VTA received $125 million from the FTA under a new accelerated funding program."
- "$140 million was included in the version of the American Rescue Plan Act of 2021 passed by the House of Representatives, but was dropped in the Senate."
- "In August 2024, the FTA made a commitment to grant $5 billion for Phase II. VTA plans to apply for a Full Funding Grant Agreement from the FTA after covering existing funding gaps."

wikis.title: Warm Springs extension (Phase 1)
wikis.summary: The 5.4-mile BART extension from Fremont to Warm Springs/South Fremont, built for $790 million and opened in 2017.
wikis.body:
- "The first phase, known as the Warm Springs Extension, was built by BART at a cost of $790 million, terminating at the new Warm Springs/South Fremont station. Construction began in 2009, and the extension and new station opened in 2017."
- "The 5.4-mile-long (8.7 km) extension to Warm Springs was constructed by BART south from the existing Fremont station (opened in 1972) to the new Warm Springs/South Fremont station; revenue service began in March 2017."
- "The original estimate was $890 million, but the cost of the subway segment under Lake Elizabeth was reduced by 45% from the original estimate of $249 million to $136 million, bringing the total cost to $790 million."
- "The Warm Springs/South Fremont station opened on March 25, 2017. The extension broke ground in 2009, and was originally scheduled for completion in 2014. Construction of the station began in 2011, and was expected to take three and a half years. However, the opening was delayed repeatedly, and ultimately pushed back to spring 2017."
- Phases table: groundbreaking Sep 30, 2009; opening Mar 25, 2017; cost $0.79 billion; Irvington listed as a future infill station.

wikis.title: Berryessa extension (BART Silicon Valley Phase I)
wikis.summary: The $2.3 billion, 10-mile extension to Milpitas and Berryessa/North San José, opened to riders on June 13, 2020.
wikis.body:
- "The $2.3-billion second phase, known as BART Silicon Valley Phase I or the Berryessa Extension, includes two new stations, Milpitas and Berryessa/North San José. Construction began in 2012, and the extension and its two new stations were inaugurated on June 12, 2020, while service for the public began on the next day."
- "Many credited the former Mayor of San Jose, Ron Gonzales, with bringing this project to fruition."
- "The 10-mile-long (16 km) Berryessa extension to north San Jose encompasses the Milpitas station and the Berryessa station. A proposed infill station at Calaveras Boulevard in downtown Milpitas has been deferred until the city secures funding. Milpitas Station connects to VTA's Milpitas light rail station (formerly known as Montague station) near the Great Mall of the Bay Area via a pedestrian bridge."
- "Originally the entire Silicon Valley Extension from Fremont to Santa Clara was proposed as one megaproject, but lower than expected federal funding and sales tax revenue eliminated some stations from the original project and caused the division into two phases... The Phase 1 scope was set by what VTA could afford."
- "A local industrial park sued in 2011, without success, on environmental grounds claiming that the extension would reduce vehicular access."
- "The project saw numerous delays, and completion was pushed back many times from the originally-planned 2016."
- "Milpitas and Berryessa/North San José stations opened on June 13, 2020." Phases table: groundbreaking Apr 12, 2012; cost $2.3 billion.

wikis.title: Downtown San Jose/Santa Clara extension (BART Silicon Valley Phase II)
wikis.summary: The third phase, a largely underground 6-mile extension to Santa Clara with four new stations, its single-bore tunnel decision and repeated delays.
wikis.body:
- "The $12.7 billion third phase to downtown San Jose, known as BART Silicon Valley Phase II, is undergoing the early stages of construction, but funding has not been fully finalized. Targeted for completion in 2037, it would add three new subway stations south of Berryessa: 28th Street/Little Portugal, Downtown San José, Diridon, and a surface station in Santa Clara. Initial testing and preliminary construction activities began in January 2019, with excavation of the tunnel boring machine entrance pit in progress as of late 2025."
- "The final Downtown San Jose/Santa Clara leg has been planned through downtown San Jose to Santa Clara at an estimated cost of $6.8 billion. This third phase, 6 miles (9.7 km) long, is largely underground, featuring a 5-mile-long (8.0 km) tunnel."
- Route: south from Berryessa, into a tunnel crossing the Bayshore Freeway, to a 28th Street/Little Portugal station, then west under Santa Clara Street to a Downtown San Jose subway station interchanging with VTA light rail, then underground to San Jose Diridon station ("a transfer point to Amtrak, Caltrain, Altamont Corridor Express, VTA light rail and bus, and the planned California High-Speed Rail system"), then surfacing to the site of the current Santa Clara Caltrain Station.
- "The original proposal had additional subway stations between Alum Rock and Downtown at Civic Plaza/SJSU and Plaza de César Chávez, but these were consolidated into a single station to cut costs."
- "A 40-acre (16 ha) BART maintenance yard would also be created at Newhall as part of this phase, using land just south of Santa Clara station that was purchased by VTA from Union Pacific. Like the Berryessa Extension, it would be built by VTA, but operated by BART."
- Tunnel design dispute: "In late 2017, a disagreement arose between VTA and BART over whether the tunnel should have a single bore or dual bores. VTA favored a single 45-foot-wide (14 m) bore, configured as a double-deck stack... BART preferred dual bores... The twin bores would each be 20 feet (6.1 m) wide, and separated horizontally." "The design decision was postponed for three months; in March, BART and VTA reached agreement on a single bore. The $125 million contract for engineering the single bore tunnel was awarded to a joint venture bid placed by London-based Mott MacDonald and San Francisco-based PGH Wong Engineering."
- "Initial construction and soil sampling began in January 2019. In September, it was announced that the project would be delayed three to four years, with revenue service to begin in 2029-2030."
- "On October 15, 2021, VTA announced that it would award construction contracts for this phase's stations in summer 2022. In May 2022, the first major contract... was awarded to Kiewit Shea Traylor Joint Venture, a joint venture between Kiewit Corporation, J. F. Shea Co. and Traylor Brothers, Inc. KSTJV will bore the 4-mile tunnel from Berryessa to Diridon, and construct the 1-mile above-ground track from Diridon to Santa Clara."
- "In October 2023, it was announced that the project would be further delayed until 2036."
- "In June 2025, agency staff recommended that the Kiewit Shea Traylor contract be terminated, and a new contractor found, because the agency and the contractor could not agree on costs. This was estimated to add 18 months of delay."
- Phases table: groundbreaking Jun 14, 2024; opening 2037 (planned); cost $12.7 billion.

wikis.title: Texas Instruments begins production at its Sherman, Texas 300mm fab
wikis.summary: TI news release announcing the start of production at SM1, its new 300mm semiconductor fab in Sherman, Texas, and the site's and company's wider expansion plans.
wikis.body:
## What's new

- "Texas Instruments (TI) today announced the start of production at its newest semiconductor fab in Sherman, TX, just three and a half years after breaking ground."
- "Leaders from TI were joined by local and state elected officials to celebrate the opening of this state-of-the-art 300mm semiconductor fab in North Texas." Photo captions name TI President and CEO Haviv Ilan, Texas Governor Greg Abbott and Sherman Mayor Shawn Teamann at the ribbon-cutting ceremony.
- "The new facility, called SM1, will ramp according to customer demand, ultimately producing tens of millions of chips daily that go into nearly every electronic device - from smartphones, automotive systems, and life-saving medical devices to industrial robots, smart home appliances, and data centers."
- Subhead: "State-of-the-art wafer fab will produce tens of millions of chips daily that go into nearly every electronic device."
- Dated 17 DEC 2025, filed under Manufacturing.

## Why it matters

- "As the largest foundational semiconductor manufacturer in the U.S., TI produces analog and embedded processing chips critical for virtually all modern electronic devices."
- TI "is building on its nearly 100-year legacy of innovation by expanding its 300mm semiconductor manufacturing footprint. By owning and controlling its manufacturing operations, process technology and packaging, TI has greater control of its supply."

## TI in Sherman

- "TI's mega-site in Sherman includes future plans for up to four connected wafer fabs that will be constructed and equipped in alignment with market demand. Combined, this site will support as many as 3,000 direct jobs, along with thousands of additional jobs in support industries."
- "TI's investment in Sherman is part of the company's broader plans to invest more than $60 billion across seven semiconductor fabs in Texas and Utah, making this the largest investment in foundational semiconductor manufacturing in U.S. history."
- "With 15 manufacturing sites around the world, TI's internal operations build on decades of proven and reliable manufacturing expertise."

## Quote

- Haviv Ilan, president and CEO: "The start of production at our newest wafer fab in Sherman, TX represents what TI does best: owning every part of the manufacturing process to deliver the foundational semiconductors that are vital for nearly every type of electronic system... We're proud to have called North Texas home for nearly a century."

## Related releases listed

- "Texas Instruments opens its second assembly and test factory in Melaka, Malaysia", 06 Nov 2025.
- "Texas Instruments plans to invest more than $60 billion to manufacture billions of foundational semiconductors in the U.S.", 18 Jun 2025.

wikis.title: Fort Worth Convention Center expansion
wikis.summary: Visit Fort Worth's page on the Fort Worth Convention Center expansion and renovation, setting out its two phases, costs and completion dates.
wikis.body:
## The project

- "The expansion and renovation of the Fort Worth Convention Center is at the heart of more than $2 billion in investments in our downtown. The Center will be open during construction, with completion in early 2030."
- Tagline: "Modern Meetings. Room to Roam." The page states the centre is "OPEN through Construction".

## Phases

- Phase 1, "Completion Winter 2025", a $95 million investment: contemporary food and beverage facilities; straighten Commerce Street "to make way for new hotel"; expanded southeast entrance by the Water Gardens and Texas A&M - Fort Worth; increase loading docks from 7 to 11 "and eventually to 13".
- Phase 2, "Completion Early 2030", a $606 million investment: replace the outdated arena with modern, flexible meeting space and a large ballroom; renovate existing exhibit space, meeting rooms and ballroom; "Fresh design shaped by customer input".

## Convention Center District

- "Surrounded 4,000 hotel rooms in the downtown core"; adjacent to the Texas A&M Fort Worth campus, the Water Gardens and Main Street leading to Sundance Square.
- 10-minute drive to the historic Stockyards to the north; 10-minute drive to museums, the zoo and botanic garden to the west; 5-minute walk to rail connections to DFW Airport; at the intersection of Interstates 30 and 35.

## About Fort Worth (from the page)

- "Nation's 10th largest city with a population near 1 million."
- "DFW Airport serves 90 domestic destinations - four hours or less to every major U.S. city and the world's first carbon neutral airport."
- "All central tourism districts are within 10 minutes of each other"; the Stockyards National Historic District is "the most visited western heritage district in the U.S."; Dickies Arena is "one of the top music and sports venues in the world"; home to American Airlines; "5 World Class Museums".

wikis.title: Fort Worth Convention Center expansion phase 1
wikis.summary: The $95 million first phase of the Fort Worth Convention Center expansion, due to complete in winter 2025.
wikis.body:
- "Phase 1 Overview: Completion Winter 2025"; "$95 million investment".
- Contemporary food & beverage facilities.
- "Straighten Commerce Street to make way for new hotel".
- "Expanded southeast entrance by Water Gardens and Texas A&M - Fort Worth".
- "Increase loading docks from 7 to 11 and eventually to 13".

wikis.title: Fort Worth Convention Center expansion phase 2
wikis.summary: The $606 million second phase of the Fort Worth Convention Center expansion, due to complete in early 2030.
wikis.body:
- "Phase 2 Overview: Completion Early 2030"; "$606 million investment".
- "Replace outdated arena with modern, flexible meeting space and large ballroom".
- "Renovate existing exhibit space, meeting rooms and ballroom" and "Renovate and modernize exhibit space, meeting rooms and ballroom".
- "Fresh design shaped by customer input".

wikis.title: What's inside Waterline, Texas' tallest building
wikis.summary: KUT report on the opening of the Waterline tower in downtown Austin - its height, construction figures, tenants, rents and link to The Confluence project.
wikis.body:
## The building

- "The Waterline tower is officially open in Austin, making it the tallest building in Texas and the 24th tallest in the United States."
- "The building at Cesar Chavez and Red River streets stands at over 1,000 feet, which is like three University of Texas at Austin towers stacked on top of each other and then some."
- "It took over four years to complete, with construction crews putting in 4.5 million hours of labor and using enough concrete to fill about 46 Olympic-sized swimming pools, according to DPR, Waterline's construction company."
- "The elevator ride from the lobby to the top floor takes over one minute."
- "The building has offices, residential space, a luxury hotel, a rooftop restaurant with Japanese-inspired cuisine, a coffee shop and a Mexican restaurant, Alteño, created by Michelin-starred chef Johnny Curiel."
- "DPR finished the project two months ahead of schedule. The residential component was the last to be completed, and residents were able to move in early, said Emory Sweeney, the project superintendent with DPR."
- "The hotel, operated by luxury hotel chain 1 Hotels, opened Sept. 3."
- Nearly 6,800 workers "helped lay the concrete".

## Living at Waterline

- "The cheapest available apartment is a 778-square-foot one-bedroom and one-bath, which costs $4,027 a month, including mandatory fees, according to Bosque at Waterline's website."
- "The most expensive apartment listed is a 1,606-square-foot two-bedroom and two-bath. It's listed for $12,357. The penthouses, that occupy floors 69 to 72, do not have prices listed online."
- Parking is extra: "from $225 a month for an unreserved spot to $1,250 a month for a private garage."
- Amenities include a pool deck, a spa, an infrared sauna, a golf simulator, a gym and a poker room. "An amenity space near the top floor overlooks Lady Bird Lake and I-35."

## Connection to The Confluence

- "Part of the building's allure is its location next to Lady Bird Lake and its proximity to The Confluence. This recently completed $91.5 million project restored 13 acres along Waller Creek and connected the space to nearby trails and bikeways, according to the city of Austin's website."
- "The waterline developers donated at least $695,000 to the Waller Creek Delta project and the Waterloo Greenway Conservancy, according to public records. The figure does not include development-related payments."
- "According to Austin Watershed Protection, Waterloo Greenway has a policy of keeping details of donor gifts private, so the full amount donated is unclear."

## Quotes

- Turner Kerr, project manager for DPR: "It's tens of thousands of people that are putting in the effort to make this project become a reality. And then afterwards everybody in Austin gets to enjoy it."
- Kerr: "The nice thing about construction, especially when you're building the tallest building in Austin, you can pretty much drive around anywhere and point up to it and be like, 'I built that.'"

## Related coverage listed

- "It's a 45-second elevator ride to the top of the new tallest building in Texas" - "After four years of construction, the 74-story Waterline tower has reached its final height. It will be divided into offices, residences, shops and restaurants, all with separate entrances and parking."

wikis.title: TxDOT breaks ground on the I-35 Capital Express Central project
wikis.summary: TxDOT news release on the groundbreaking of the $5.6 billion I-35 Capital Express Central project in Austin, its scope, contractors and schedule.
wikis.body:
## The groundbreaking

- "The Texas Department of Transportation was joined by Texas Transportation Commission Chairman J. Bruce Bugg, Jr., Commissioner Robert Vaughn, Sen. Judith Zaffirini and other partners to break ground on the I-35 Capital Express Central project in Austin."
- Subhead: "Safety and mobility improvements include two non-tolled high-occupancy-vehicle lanes in each direction, widened bridges and enhanced bike and ped paths."

## Scope

- "This I-35 Texas Clear Lanes project will add two non-tolled high-occupancy-vehicle (HOV) managed lanes in each direction from US 290 East to SH 71/Ben White Boulevard."
- "The project will also lower the mainlanes from Airport Boulevard to Lady Bird Lake, remove the upper decks, provide opportunities for deck plazas, improve transit connections, add boulevard-style segments through downtown and enhance pedestrian and bicycle paths along the corridor."
- "The project includes more than 19 miles of new shared-use paths, as well as widened and enhanced east-west crossings, and new bicycle-pedestrian crossings at 3rd Street, 15th Street and 41st Street."

## Cost and schedule

- Chairman Bugg: "Currently, TxDOT has under contract over $53 billion under construction across Texas. Last week we broke ground on the start of the $13 billion NHHIP project in Houston, and today we are breaking ground on the $5.6 billion Capital Express Central project, bringing that total of construction and planned projects to $71.6 billion."
- "Construction on the Central project started in October 2024 with the reconstruction of the Martin Luther King Jr. Boulevard Bridge. The contractor is Harper Brothers, LLC."
- "The next segment to begin construction will be at Lady Bird Lake (Holly Street to SH 71/Ben White Boulevard) in early 2025. The contractor is Balfour Beatty."
- "Construction along the entire corridor is expected to be complete in 2033, weather permitting."

## Quotes

- Sen. Judith Zaffirini: "I-35, and this particular project is of such significance and such importance. The impact will be statewide, nationwide, and international.
