- The David Rubenstein Treehouse is Harvard's first university-wide conference center.
- It opened in October 2025 and hosts events ranging in size from 20 up to 755 people.
- It incorporates space for visiting scholars, industry partners and guests "to convene, collaborate and foster connections."
- Designed by Studio Gang, the expressive mass timber structure features a double-height lobby that extends outdoors through two covered porches that can be used year-round.

wikis.title: The Atlas hotel
wikis.summary: The ERC's 246-room boutique hotel, which opened earlier in the year with two dining concepts.
wikis.body:
- The Atlas is a boutique hotel that opened earlier this year.
- Designed by Marlon Blackwell Architects, with interiors for the lobby, corridors and guestrooms by INC Architecture & Design.
- It features 246 rooms and an array of amenities, including two dining concepts by the James Beard-nominated Pearl & Law Hospitality, the team behind Dorchester's Comfort Kitchen.
- Ama at The Atlas, the hotel's signature restaurant concept, and Foxglove Terrace, a rooftop restaurant and bar, both opened in the spring.

wikis.title: Verra apartments
wikis.summary: The ERC's 343-apartment residential community, designed by MVRDV, which opened last year.
wikis.body:
- Verra is the ERC's 343-apartment community, which opened last year.
- It offers "thoughtfully designed studios through two-bedroom apartments with an emphasis on comfort, warmth and hospitality."
- Verra features sweeping views of Boston and Cambridge alongside "a curated collection of best-in-class amenities."
- Designed by MVRDV; it "is already helping shape the neighborhood's energy and sense of community."

wikis.title: Street-level shops, restaurants and cafes
wikis.summary: The ERC's retail program of street-level shops and eateries, prioritising local Boston operators.
wikis.body:
- Tishman Speyer's retail program "has prioritized beloved Boston operators with deep local followings to create a vibrant, inclusive district that authentically connects to Allston-Brighton and the broader Boston community."
- In addition to Comfort Kitchen's Ama restaurant and Foxglove Terrace, the ERC is home to Harvard's COOP bookstore and apparel shop, Revival Café, Phin Coffee House and a Little Sprouts daycare center.
- The first phase includes 40,000 square feet of retail and restaurants.

wikis.title: Allstonway and public open space
wikis.summary: More than two acres of publicly accessible open space at the ERC, centred on the Allstonway, which opened in May.
wikis.body:
- Two acres of activated publicly accessible open space, with the new Allstonway as its centerpiece.
- The Allstonway opened in May and was designed by SCAPE.
- It connects the neighborhood to the Charles River, "bringing people of all ages together through public art, landscaping, walking paths, comfortable seating and year-round programming such as farmer's markets, concerts and outdoor fitness classes."

wikis.title: Phillip and Susan Ragon Building Project at Massachusetts General Hospital
wikis.summary: Mass General Brigham's project page for the Phillip and Susan Ragon Building, a new clinical care building on Cambridge Street in Boston, with its programme, by-the-numbers figures, regulatory history, phased timeline and community benefits.
wikis.body:
## About the project

- "Mass General has begun construction on a state-of-the-art new building," described as ushering in the next generation of health care while reinforcing commitments to workforce, neighbors and communities.
- The Ragon Building "will strengthen our ability to deliver exceptional health care," enliven the West End and Beacon Hill neighborhoods, provide job opportunities for those historically underrepresented in the trades, and make "an unprecedented $62 million investment in our local communities."
- Massachusetts General Hospital has embarked on a multi-year construction project for a state-of-the-art clinical care building along Cambridge Street.
- The facility will be situated entirely on Mass General's campus, on a parcel framed by Cambridge, North Grove, Parkman and Blossom streets.

## What the building enables

- Address growing demands for delivering the highest level of care and services
- Alleviate ongoing capacity challenges in the hospital's Emergency Department and inpatient units
- Accommodate new and rapidly evolving technologies
- Enable consolidation and organization of related services
- Create a comfortable, efficient and positive healing environment for patients and families
- Prepare for patient surges related to disease outbreaks or natural- or human-made disasters

## Programme

- Home to the Mass General Brigham Cancer Institute and the Corrigan Minehan Heart Center.
- 482 single-bed inpatient rooms located in the two towers, enabling Mass General to decommission outmoded space in older hospital facilities and convert double inpatient rooms into single-patient rooms.
- Spacious operating/interventional and procedural rooms, imaging facilities, infusion rooms, exam rooms and clinical support space for pharmacy and dietary, plus an education center and auditorium.
- Six levels of underground parking for 864 vehicles "for patients and families only—no staff parking," replacing spaces in the outdated Parkman Garage, which will be demolished; parking space for 566 bicycles.

## By the numbers

- 1.05 million square feet of space
- 5 continuous podium level floors above street level
- 2 inpatient towers
- 6 below-ground levels for parking and support services
- 482 new private single-bed rooms
- 23 cardiovascular OR/interventional procedure rooms
- 100 infusion bays
- 120 exam rooms
- 13 imaging modalities
- 864 parking spaces
- 566 bicycle parking spaces
- 46,000 square feet of public space
- 1,000 new jobs

## Timeline

- "The entire project... will likely involve approximately 8.5 years of phased construction."
- Design, planning and the multi-step regulatory approval process took place over the last several years; next steps involve preparing and clearing much of the site, "which is likely to begin in summer 2022."
- **Phase 1** — creating the below-ground parking levels and then erecting the tower closest to the Blossom Street side of the parcel. Expected to last approximately four years, with the initial first side of the building opening in 2027.
- **Phase 2** — demolition of the Parkman Garage and construction of the second tower on the North Grove side. Expected to be completed three years later, with an expected opening in 2030.
- "This timeline is dependent on many factors."

## Regulatory history

- **Institutional Master Plan (IMP):** Mass General submitted its Institutional Master Plan Notification Form (IMPNF) to the Boston Planning & Development Agency (BPDA) on February 20, 2019. After a 30-day comment period with public meetings, the BPDA issued a Scoping Determination. Mass General submitted its IMP on April 23, 2021, followed by a 75-day comment period and multiple public meetings. The IMP, which has a term of 10 years, was approved on October 14, 2021 by the BPDA Board and on November 17, 2021 by the Boston Zoning Commission.
- **Large Project Review:** initiated through a Project Notification Form submitted jointly with the IMPNF on February 20, 2019. A Draft Project Impact Report was prepared based on the BPDA's Scoping Determination issued April 19, 2019 and submitted April 23, 2021. The BPDA Board approved the project on October 14, 2021, concurrently with the IMP. Further BPDA design review and supplemental permitting followed, including approvals by the Public Improvement Commission and Boston Water and Sewer Commission; review by the Boston Landmarks Commission was required to approve demolition of the site's aged buildings.
- **MEPA review:** required because the project needed a Determination of Need from the Department of Public Health and exceeded at least one MEPA review threshold for transportation. An Environmental Notification Form was submitted to the Executive Office of Energy and Environmental Affairs (EEA) on February 20, 2019. The Secretary of EEA issued a Certificate on May 24, 2019 requesting information for the Draft Environmental Impact Report, submitted April 23, 2021. A further Certificate issued June 16, 2021 requested a Final Environmental Impact Report, submitted October 8, 2021; the final Certificate issued November 15, 2021 determined the Final EIR adequately and properly complied with MEPA, allowing Mass General to proceed to state permitting.

## Sustainability and resilience

- The building will be resilient, "able to withstand major flooding and high winds, serving as a critical resource for patients, families, staff and the community during a disaster."
- It will be powered almost entirely using renewable electricity, with a plan to achieve net zero carbon in both operations and construction.

## Neighborhood benefit

- Retail space and a restaurant on the ground floor will "augment the activity and enrich the vitality of the area."
- A glass pavilion — the North Anderson Street arcade — will create an open feel from Cambridge Street back toward the Bulfinch lawn and the Bulfinch Building; inside will be curated exhibits developed with the West End Museum and the Museum of African American History.
- The facade of the former Winchell School — later known as Ruth Sleeper Hall — will be incorporated into the facility at the corner of Blossom and Parkman streets, where the school had been situated.
- Mass General is creating a West End senior/community center and food bank, and providing financial support to the West End Museum, the Museum of African American History, the Old West Church and the Esplanade Association.
- The hospital will pursue an anchor strategy focused on hiring a workforce including a significant percentage of people of color and women, working with diverse engineers and consultants, and offering training and apprenticeship opportunities.
- Space on the building's street level will be reserved for the MBTA to use as a future subway station headhouse for the proposed Red-Blue Connector; the page also mentions "a proposed new T stop" on Cambridge Street.
- MGH Community Health Impact Funds: "an historic $62 million investment to diverse communities and organizations in Boston and the North Suffolk region."

## Construction updates listed

- Two-Week Look Ahead: 9/14/26 to 9/27/26 (Updated: 9/10/26)
- MGH Front Entrance Coordination Project: Need-to-know and FAQs (Updated: 3/6/25)
- Logistics Planning Update 2023-2024 (Updated: 10/6/23)
- Environmental Dust, Noise and Vibration Monitoring Program (Updated: 10/3/22)
- Patient Safety Campus Construction Information (Updated: 10/22)

wikis.title: White Stadium, Franklin Park, Boston
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on White Stadium in Boston's Franklin Park, covering its 1949 construction, decline, the $325 million 2025-2027 renovation for Boston Legacy FC and Boston Public Schools, the litigation over it, its design and its tenants.
wikis.body:
## Overview

- White Stadium, formally the George R. White Memorial Stadium, is a 10,519-seat stadium in Franklin Park, Boston, Massachusetts. Address: 450 Walnut Avenue. Owner: Boston Public Schools.
- Originally constructed between 1947 and 1949 for the use of Boston Public Schools athletics, "the stadium is currently closed and undergoing a renovation that will turn it into an 11,000-seat venue shared with Boston Legacy FC of the National Women's Soccer League."
- Opened 1949; renovated 2025–2027. Cost: $1 million (original 1949 cost); $325 million (2027 renovation cost).
- Tenants: Boston Public Schools athletics (1949-2024; planned for 2027); Boston Legacy FC (NWSL) (planned for 2028).

## History

- Financed by the George Robert White fund, the cost was originally estimated at between $350,000 and $450,000, but the final amount ballooned to $1,000,000 (equivalent to $14,000,000 in 2025), a figure city clerk and former acting mayor John Hynes blamed on Mayor James Michael Curley.
- On October 1, 1949, after twice being postponed due to weather, the opening football games were: Boston Technical High School over Boston College High School 12–6; Dorchester High over Boston Trade 18–0; Boston English over Roxbury Memorial High School 12–6; Boston Latin School over Boston Commerce 33–6.
- In 1970, a proposal was made to enlarge the stadium to 50,000 seats as a potential home for the New England Patriots, though the Patriots ultimately chose to build Foxboro Stadium.
- Around the time of the Boston busing crisis interest in high school football waned; games were marred by low attendance and violent incidents. By the 1980s the stadium had deteriorated: the scoreboard was unusable due to vandalism and the locker rooms lacked working showers and toilets. A fire in the 1990s led to the entire eastside grandstand being condemned and permanently closed off.
- A $4.2 million renovation project concluded in 1990, outfitting the stadium with new and updated athletic facilities and bleachers.
- In 2009, then-Mayor Thomas Menino tried to organize a renovation funded by Northeastern University to move Huskies football to the stadium, abandoned when the university shut its football program later that year.
- Businessman John Fish lobbied for a $45 million renovation and expansion plan starting in 2013, but the project was shelved by then-Mayor Marty Walsh citing budget concerns.
- White Stadium was proposed to be renovated and used as a venue for equestrian events as part of Boston's bid for the 2024 Summer Olympics; that plan was shelved when the Olympic bid was dropped.

## Renovation

- In 2023 the city of Boston announced a $30 million renovation to prepare for the arrival of an NWSL expansion team set to start play in 2026. The owners of the team, eventually christened Boston Legacy FC, were the only group to respond to the city's RFP for a renovation partner.
- The renovation would include additional seats to bring capacity to 11,000 to meet league minimum standards, plus new facilities for Boston Public Schools athletics including new locker rooms, sports-medicine facilities, study spaces, and replacement of the unmaintained six-lane track with a new eight-lane track at regulation size. It will also include water fountains and restrooms for the public, accessible from the park outside the stadium.
- The project, championed by Mayor Michelle Wu, is a public-private partnership in which Boston Public Schools retains ownership and scheduling priority, leasing the stadium to Boston Legacy for a maximum of 20 games and 20 practices per year.
- Some neighborhood organizations and the Emerald Necklace Conservancy opposed the renovation; it was repeatedly criticized during the 2025 Boston mayoral election by candidate Josh Kraft "as expensive, unpopular, and detrimental to communities living near the stadium." Kraft, whose family's New England Revolution was attempting to build a stadium in nearby Everett, dropped out after finishing a distant second to Wu in the preliminary election, and the Revolution filed an amicus brief in support of the project in 2026.
- The Franklin Park Coalition and Boston Preservation Alliance supported the plan once the city addressed their concerns. A 2024 survey commissioned by the Franklin Park Coalition and a 2025 poll by Emerson College Polling found a majority of Boston residents polled supported the renovation plans.
- In February 2024 the Emerald Necklace Conservancy and a group of local residents filed a lawsuit claiming the renovation was illegal; the plaintiffs were denied a preliminary injunction, a Suffolk Superior Court judge ruled for the city in all pretrial motions, and the lawsuit was dismissed in March 2025. That decision was unanimously upheld by the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court in August 2026, "clearing the project to proceed as planned, albeit with delays that pushed the planned re-opening of the stadium to 2027 and Boston Legacy FC's first game there to 2028."
- Demolition work for the project was completed by mid-2025. By 2026, estimates for the stadium revitalization had risen to $325 million, with $135 million committed in public funding from the City of Boston and $190 million in private funding from the owners of Boston Legacy FC.

## Design

- White Stadium sits at the northern corner of Franklin Park near Egleston Square, at the meeting point of the Roxbury and Jamaica Plain neighborhoods and near Dorchester and Mattapan on the other side of the park. The site was chosen to use Franklin Park's natural landscape to protect attendees from the elements while orienting the playing field in the sun.
- Designed by the firm Desmond & Lord, it was originally constructed to hold 10,519 patrons. The structure consisted of a pair of twin clamshell bleacher sections mirrored on either side of the playing field and track; the design was said to be borrowed from a stadium at Brown University while the locker rooms were inspired by those at Yankee Stadium.
- The Boston Preservation Alliance called White Stadium "a rare example of Streamline Art Deco architecture in New England with a hint of Bauhaus influence".
- The 2020s renovation demolished the condemned, fire-damaged east grandstand and gutted the west grandstand, while preserving the original Art Deco clamshell west wall and the ticketing booths and entry gates on the north side. The track and field were torn up and rebuilt from scratch to install new drainage and expand the track to eight lanes at regulation size.
- The project will add a restaurant and public gathering space to the south end of the site; rebuilt grandstands on either side will add canopies above the bleachers; movable bleachers can be added on top of the track to bring spectators closer to the field during soccer and football games, and retracted when the track is in use.

## Tenants

- Originally built for Boston public school teams, most notably football; the English–Latin football rivalry game drew a sellout crowd and a half-million TV viewers when played at White in 1950. In track and field, 14 Boston schools were competing at White following the stadium's opening. Franklin Park's cross country course, used by local schools and for MIAA state meets, encircles the stadium.
- By the time the rebuild project began in 2024, high school football in Boston was "at a nadir due to waning interest and poor infrastructure"; only Boston Latin School and Boston Latin Academy were using White Stadium as a home field. The English–Latin game had long been played at Harvard Stadium, and other Thanksgiving rivalry games moved elsewhere, such as the 100th East Boston-South Boston game moving due to poor field conditions.
- Boston Legacy FC plan to move in in 2028 after the renovation concludes. The team provided the majority of the funding, including money to build professional-level infrastructure in the rebuilt west grandstand. Its lease permits up to 20 home games per year, with BPS athletics using the stadium on all other days. Football games will be prohibited until after the conclusion of Legacy FC's season due to risk of field damage, although this is not planned to conflict with the football teams' Thanksgiving or postseason games; no such restrictions apply to high school soccer or track.

## Other events

- A rally by the Black Panther Party was held in the park on July 27, 1969, at 2 p.m.
- "Uptown in the Park," a three-part series of funk/soul and jazz concerts to benefit Elma Lewis School of Fine Arts, was held in the park in 1974: on July 7, Sly and the Family Stone with Tower of Power, Hues Corporation, Donald Byrd and the Blackbyrds, and Richard Pryor; on August 25, Funkadelic with The Voices of East Harlem, The Isley Brothers, Gil Scott-Heron, Mandrill and Bar-Kays; a September 2 concert featuring the Ohio Players, Staple Singers, Bobbi Humphrey and Bobby Womack was canceled.
- The 1992 IAAF World Cross Country Championships were held at Franklin Park; the course, covered in mud and snow from an unusually early winter storm, concluded with its final stretch and finish line running down the center of White Stadium.
- White Stadium has historically served as the start and finish line for the annual Boston Half, previously known as the B.A.A. Half Marathon.

wikis.title: New Stadium at RFK Campus, Washington, D.C.
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the New Stadium at RFK Campus, the planned $3.8 billion indoor home of the Washington Commanders scheduled to open in 2030, covering its approval history, financing, design and the surrounding mixed-use development.
wikis.body:
## Overview

- New Stadium at RFK Campus (nickname: New RFK Stadium) is the project name for an indoor stadium in Washington, D.C. scheduled to open in 2030.
- Address: 2400 East Capitol Street SE, Washington, D.C. Owner: Government of DC. Operator: Washington Commanders. Type: multi-purpose stadium. Events: American football, soccer, concerts. Roof: skylight. Capacity: 65,000.
- Groundbreaking planned 2027; opening planned 2030. Cost: US$3.8 billion. Architectural style: neoclassical. Architect: HKS. Project manager: District PM Alliance. General contractors: Clark, Mortenson, SmootDC. Tenant: Washington Commanders (NFL) (c. 2030). Website: OurRFK.DC.gov.
- Public transit: Metro Blue, Orange and Silver lines at Stadium–Armory; Metrobus C41, C51, D24.
- It will serve as the home venue of the Washington Commanders and host other sports and public events, succeeding the former RFK Stadium — home of the team from 1961 to 1996 when they were known as the Redskins — along the Anacostia River in the city's Hill East neighborhood.
- The stadium "will be among the most expensive ever built and will anchor adjacent mixed-use development."

## History

- In the early 2010s the Redskins began searching for a site to replace Northwest Stadium in Landover, Maryland, considering Oxon Cove Park in Maryland and Sterling, Dumfries and Woodbridge in Virginia, but ultimately desired the former RFK Stadium site. RFK Stadium, considered the "spiritual home" of the team by its owners, hosted their games from its 1961 opening until 1996; it closed in 2019 due to its age and poor condition and was deconstructed in 2025.
- The campus had been managed by the National Park Service since the District of Columbia Stadium Act of 1957 (H.R. 1937). On July 27, 2023, Congress introduced the D.C. Robert F. Kennedy Memorial Stadium Campus Revitalization Act (H.R. 4984), proposing transfer of control to the DC city government through a 99-year lease and permitting mixed-use development. It passed the House of Representatives on February 28, 2024, the Senate on December 21, 2024, and was signed into law by president Joe Biden on January 6, 2025.
- On April 28, 2025, DC mayor Muriel Bowser, NFL commissioner Roger Goodell and Commanders owner Josh Harris held a joint press conference announcing the RFK Campus as the site for the stadium.
- U.S. president Donald Trump suggested blocking the deal in July 2025 unless the Commanders returned to the Redskins branding, and later stated a desire for the stadium to be named after him.
- The project was tentatively approved by the DC Council in August 2025, with another vote finalizing it the following month.
- Work on foundational infrastructure began in April 2026, with groundbreaking scheduled for early 2027.

## Financing and operations

- The stadium will be financed through a public-private partnership, with the government of DC owning it and the Commanders managing it.
- The Commanders are slated to contribute $2.7 billion for construction, a parking garage and any additional cost overrun; DC is to spend $500 million on infrastructure by way of the Sports Facilities Fee, $356 million on another parking garage by way of Events DC bonds, and $202 million on public utilities by way of general taxes.
- DC is planning an expansion of the nearby Stadium–Armory Metrorail station and a new Metrobus rapid transit line mirroring the route of the former DC Streetcar, to reduce traffic congestion and reliance on parking.
- The Commanders will collect revenue from personal seat licenses (PSL), tickets and parking, with DC anticipating over $5 billion in sales taxes raised over 30 years. Around 8,000 parking spots will be available on opening day.
- The stadium is expected to host up to 200 additional events annually, such as concerts, Olympic events, college sports, international soccer and rugby matches, and other ceremonies and gatherings. It is in consideration to host Super Bowl LXV and the 2031 FIFA Women's World Cup final, with the NWSL team Washington Spirit suggested as a possible additional tenant.

## Design

- An indoor stadium designed by HKS in a neoclassical style inspired by the original RFK Stadium, featuring an exterior of colonnades in a wave pattern and a skylight roof made from cable-netted ETFE.
- Managed by District PM Alliance, a joint venture between Brailsford & Dunlavey, Creative Artists Agency Icon and McKissack & McKissack; constructed by Clark Construction, Mortenson Construction and SmootDC.
- The playing surface has not been decided upon, with natural grass preferred by the Commanders.
- Seating capacity of 65,000 plus upwards of 5,000 standing-room only, with a section designed to replicate the bouncing stands RFK Stadium was known for.
- The top row of seating will be below 130 ft (40 m) to comply with DC's Height of Buildings Act, with the stadium sunken into the ground and fused with RFK Stadium's original foundation.
- The site, "considered an eastern gateway into Capitol Hill and downtown DC as part of the L'Enfant Plan monumental axis," lies along the western bank of the Anacostia River adjacent to the D.C. Armory, approximately 2 miles (3.2 km) east of the United States Capitol and National Mall. It is bordered by C Street to the north and Independence Avenue to the south, with the streets converging at the Whitney Young Memorial Bridge.
- A balcony on the stadium's western entrance will overlook the plaza and offer views of the Capitol building and Washington Monument down East Capitol Street.

## Mixed-use development

- The stadium will eventually anchor approximately 180 acres (0.73 km2) of adjacent mixed-use development featuring housing, hotels, restaurants, shops, offices, parks and public spaces across five districts.
- The Commanders are to oversee development of the Plaza and Riverfront districts.
- The DC Department of Parks and Recreation (DPR) will develop the Recreation district — adding an $89 million indoor gymnasium and sports facility to the existing Fields at RFK recreation center — the Kingman Commons district, expanding on the bordering Kingman Park residential neighborhood to the northwest, and the Anacostia Commons, a protected riparian zone along Kingman Lake containing a section of the Anacostia Riverwalk Trail.
- Around 6,000 residences are expected across Kingman Commons and the Plaza and Riverfront districts, with 30% designated affordable.
- Over a third of the campus will be dedicated to green space, with heritage trees preserved. A grass plaza west of the stadium, the Festival Plaza, will host public events, markets and concerts.
- The Commanders will move their corporate headquarters next to the stadium while retaining football operations and their training facility in Ashburn, Virginia.
- Due to phased zoning approval, full district construction is expected to take until 2040.

wikis.title: Monumental Sports & Entertainment unveils vision for brand-new Capital One Arena
wikis.summary: MSE press release announcing a 20-year Capital One naming rights extension and new renderings for the transformed Capital One Arena in downtown Washington, D.C., with the project's scope, schedule and upgrades.
wikis.body:
## The announcement

- WASHINGTON, D.C. (August 11, 2026) — Monumental Sports & Entertainment (MSE) and Capital One "unveiled the next chapter of Capital One Arena: a world-class, next-generation sports and entertainment destination."
- MSE and Capital One have entered into a 20-year naming rights extension for the reimagined Capital One Arena.
- "With the completion of the arena transformation just over a year away," MSE released new renderings showing the building's new exterior and a first look at upgraded experiences on the District Level (previous 100 Level) and Terrace Level (previous 400 Level), "slated to debut ahead of the 2027 season."

## The project

- The arena anchors MSE and Capital One's shared vision for a sports, entertainment and business district in the heart of the nation's capital, created in partnership with the District.
- "Once the $1 billion+ project is completed," the transformed arena will host approximately 250 events annually.
- It serves as home of the NHL's Washington Capitals, the NBA's Washington Wizards and Georgetown men's basketball, while also hosting a slate of games for the WNBA's Washington Mystics plus concerts, family shows and live entertainment.
- The venue is set to host the 2027 NCAA Division I Men's Ice Hockey Championship ("Frozen Four") and the 2028 NCAA Division I Women's Basketball Regional ("Sweet 16" and "Elite 8").
- With Phase Two of construction underway, "the full transformation remains on schedule for completion ahead of the 2027–28 NBA and NHL seasons."

## Upgrades

- A reimagined District Level and Terrace Level, a premium culinary and beverage program for every guest, expanded entrances and easier-to-navigate connection points, and new gathering spaces within the arena complex.
- The Capital One cardholder entrance will be relocated to F Street and will be accessible to cardholders for all events, expanding a benefit previously available only during Capitals and Wizards games.
- **Enhanced Concourse Experience** — "transforms the concourse from a place of passage into a destination in itself... the concourse is part of the event."
- **Premium for Every Guest** — elevated culinary experiences, destination bars and refined hospitality extending premium-quality experiences beyond premium ticket holders.
- **The Best View Belongs to Everyone** — "the new Visibowl creates an immersive, first-of-its-kind viewing experience," with dramatic sightlines directly into the arena from the heart of the concourse.
- **One Connected Arena** — expanded entrances, new vertical circulation and seamless connections between the District Level and Terrace Level.
- **A Place to Gather** — four distinct districts in the District Level, new social destinations, Center Stage Bars, and a Food Hall spanning the entire length of the F Street side of the building on the Terrace Level.

## The partnership

- The naming rights extension builds on nearly a decade of collaboration between MSE and Capital One.
- The partnership extends across MSE's integrated sports, entertainment and media platform, including the Capitals, Wizards, Mystics and Monumental Sports Network (MNMT).
- Capital One cardholders will enjoy exclusive access, benefits and experiences at the arena, including the new dedicated cardholder entrance open for all events beginning fall 2027, special discounts throughout the venue, and additional offerings to be announced.
- Capital One has "more than 32,000 local associates who live, work, and commute across the DMV," and in 2025 alone supported the Washington metro area with over $7.2 billion in community development financing targeting affordable housing, economic development, revitalization/stabilization and community services, including supporting the creation or preservation of over 31,000 affordable housing units. It also provided $17.2 million in direct charitable contributions and 35,980 associate volunteer and pro bono hours.
- Capital One Financial Corporation (NYSE: COF) had $484.3 billion in deposits and $673.8 billion in total assets as of June 30, 2026, and is headquartered in McLean, Virginia.

## Quotes

- Jim Van Stone, President of Business Operations and Chief Commercial Officer at MSE: "Washington is entering an extraordinary new era, and the completely reimagined Capital One Arena will reflect the ambition, energy, and global stature of the city it represents... We're excited to partner with Capital One, a leading financial institution founded and headquartered right in our backyard."
- Byron Daub, Vice President, Sponsorships and Experiential Marketing at Capital One: "Capital One has called the Washington region home for more than three decades, and we're proud to continue investing in its future... This revitalization can help strengthen the surrounding neighborhood, support local businesses and create new opportunities across this important region."

Updates are directed to DistrictMomentum.com.

wikis.title: VPRA announces rail service changes for Long Bridge Project construction
wikis.summary: Virginia Passenger Rail Authority news release announcing Amtrak and VRE schedule changes from January 12, 2026 to accommodate daytime construction work windows on the Long Bridge Project through 2030.
wikis.body:
## The announcement

- RICHMOND — The Virginia Passenger Rail Authority (VPRA) "today announced plans for passenger rail service changes to accommodate the Long Bridge Project, the flagship project of the state's Transforming Rail in Virginia (TRV) initiative to expand passenger rail service in the Commonwealth."
- The changes will impact Amtrak and VRE services.
- As the Long Bridge Project enters full construction, major construction activities require daytime "work windows" through the construction zone in Washington, D.C. The work must be carried out during the daytime because noise and vibration ordinances in Washington, D.C. prohibit certain work at night.
- VPRA coordinated service planning with Amtrak, NCDOT, CSX, NS and Virginia Railway Express (VRE), who jointly developed a plan to preserve service.
- **Work windows will begin January 12, 2026, and will continue until the project's completion in 2030.**
- Schedule changes seek to preserve optimal times for Amtrak service while protecting the highest ridership "peak" for VRE's morning and evening commuter trains. CSX has also rescheduled its freight traffic to accommodate the work window.

## The Long Bridge Project

- "One of the largest railroad construction projects undertaken in the Commonwealth in decades."
- It includes much more than a new two-track passenger rail bridge across the Potomac River: in its entirety it encompasses construction of a total of seven new bridges, five for rail and two for pedestrians and cyclists.
- In Washington, DC, these bridges stretch from just south of L'Enfant Plaza across Maine Avenue, the Washington Channel and I-395 to the Potomac River.

## Factors considered in the service plan

- Preserving as much of the current service — passenger and freight — as possible, with the least impactful changes in schedule.
- Creating the longest possible work window without interruptions; crews will be working on the Long Bridge Project and also on the Alexandria Fourth Track project and VRE's L'Enfant project, both critical connections to the Long Bridge Project.
- Scheduling the daily work window around Washington, DC's noise and vibration restriction, which prohibits crews from working between 7 pm and 7 am.
- Looking beyond Virginia at other large East Coast infrastructure projects, most notably large-scale Amtrak Northeast Corridor projects outside Baltimore and New York, whose schedule changes impact service to and from Virginia.
- VPRA and partners will continue to measure performance and update schedules as operating conditions change, communicating via local media, social media, email blasts, website updates and station pop-ups.

## Quotes

- DJ Stadtler, Executive Director of VPRA: "While we are thrilled with the progress of the Long Bridge Project, we understand that these necessary service changes will be difficult for a number of our passengers... we evaluated every possible scenario to limit the disruptions while providing our construction teams with the work window they need to safely complete the project on time and on budget."
- Amtrak EVP of Strategy and Planning Jennifer Mitchell: "Amtrak is proud to support VPRA with the Long Bridge Project, a transformative investment in rail infrastructure that will unlock new capacity, improve service reliability, and stimulate economic opportunity for generations to come."
- VRE Acting CEO Dallas Richards: "With the completion of the Long Bridge Project and other improvements along the corridor, we look forward to expanding VRE service to include our first-ever weekend and late-night service."

## About the organizations (as given)

- VPRA was established in 2020 to promote, sustain and expand passenger and commuter rail service in the Commonwealth. Virginia first launched state-supported service in 2009 with one roundtrip between Washington, DC and Lynchburg, VA; service has grown to eight roundtrips daily with stops at 17 stations in Virginia plus Washington, DC along four corridors.
- VRE, "the nation's 13th largest commuter rail service," connects Central and Northern Virginia with the District of Columbia. Its two lines, Manassas and Fredericksburg, serve 19 stations, including two — L'Enfant and Union Station — in D.C.

wikis.title: DC Water launches tunnel boring machine Mary on the Potomac River Tunnel Project
wikis.summary: DC Water news release on the launch of tunnel boring machine Mary, starting excavation on the $819 million Potomac River Tunnel Project, with the machine's specifications, route and the tunnel's pollution-reduction targets.
wikis.body:
## The milestone

- "In a defining moment for one of the District's largest infrastructure investments, DC Water has marked its next major milestone in the Potomac River Tunnel Project."
- The first tunnel boring machine, Mary, "has launched her northbound journey breaking through the soil to signal the start of excavation."
- The first turn of Mary's drill-like cutterhead underground represents "the transition from years of planning and preparation to active tunnel construction on the $819 million project."
- DC Water Chief Executive Officer and General Manager David L. Gadis: "Launching Mary is a significant step forward for this project and for the future of the Potomac River. This moment reflects years of planning, and the incredible coordination, engineering, and dedication required to bring a machine of this scale to life underground. It's how we turn planning into progress."

## The machine

- As Mary advances, additional sections called gantries will be attached one by one until fully assembled. The gantries support power, ventilation, material transport and worker access, forming a continuous underground operation.
- Once fully assembled, she will be "a 21-foot diameter, 1,200-ton, 700-foot-long mammoth tunneling machine."
- Preparations included constructing a 100-foot-deep overflow mining shaft and excavating a starter tunnel. The front portion of Mary was lowered and assembled inside the shaft and starter tunnel earlier this year.
- At the front is the cutterhead; behind it the front and middle shields, "huge, heavy-duty steel cylinders for the crew and equipment"; trailing behind are the initial gantries.
- During the launch the first concrete tunnel ring is installed and connected to a thrust frame, allowing the TBM's hydraulic jacks to push the machine forward. As the cutterhead rotates it excavates the ground while crews build the tunnel lining behind it using precast concrete segments.

## Route

- Mary will bore approximately 2.4 miles north from West Potomac Park to Georgetown University, excavating through the District's hard bedrock.
- Her sister machine, Emily, is scheduled to arrive from Germany later this spring and will excavate south toward Joint Base Anacostia-Bolling, completing the full 5.5-mile tunnel system.

## Purpose

- The Potomac River Tunnel is part of DC Water's Clean Rivers Program, a long-term initiative to reduce pollution in the Potomac River and Chesapeake Bay.
- Currently about 650 million gallons of untreated combined stormwater and sewer overflow enter the river each year.
- Once completed, the 5.5-mile tunnel system will reduce overflow volume by 93% and cut the number of overflow events from 74 to just four in a typical year.

wikis.title: South Central Extension/Downtown Hub light rail opens June 7, 2025
wikis.summary: City of Phoenix news release announcing the June 7, 2025 opening of the 5.5-mile South Central Extension/Downtown Hub light rail project, with its new two-line system, features, budget and workforce figures.
wikis.body:
## The opening

- The City of Phoenix and Valley Metro Rail "will soon expand into south Phoenix with the opening of the South Central Extension/Downtown Hub (SCE/DH) light rail project on Saturday, June 7, 2025."
- A ribbon cutting and community celebration "filled with local culture and excitement" is being planned for that day.
- Mayor Kate Gallego: "It's a big day for Phoenix as we celebrate the upcoming opening of the South Central light rail extension. This fresh segment of our transit system will connect thousands of residents to jobs, health care, and social opportunities in downtown and beyond. A reality in 2025 instead of the originally planned 2034 opening date, the South Central extension also brings with it new and improved public infrastructure—from great bike lanes and additional shade structures to beautiful artwork along the corridor."

## The route and the two-line system

- The 5.5-mile extension will operate between downtown Phoenix along Central and 1st avenues, continuing south to Baseline Road.
- The expansion introduces a two-line rail system intersecting at the new transit hub in downtown Phoenix:
  - **A Line:** between Gilbert Road/Main Street in Mesa and the Downtown Hub
  - **B Line:** between Metro Parkway in northwest Phoenix and Baseline Road/Central Avenue
  - **The Downtown Hub** consists of four platforms on Washington, Jefferson, Central and 1st avenues where riders transfer between the A and B lines

## Why the corridor

- Selected as a priority corridor after a comprehensive analysis; the expansion "addresses critical transportation needs in an area where 44% of residents have limited or no access to personal vehicles."
- It connects historically underserved communities to regional destinations including downtown Phoenix, the airport area, educational institutions and key employment centers.
- The extension is expected to add more than 8,000 daily riders to the light rail system, which currently serves approximately 35,000 boardings per day.

## Project features

- 18 community-driven public art installations created by artists who are predominantly local
- Eight new stations
- 14 new trains
- 110-space park-and-ride facility at Baseline Road/Central Avenue
- Enhanced bike lanes and pedestrian pathways
- Over 550 new trees and desert-adapted landscaping providing shade
- Comprehensive utility upgrades, replacing more than 30 miles of underground infrastructure

## Budget and funding

- Federal grants cover more than half the project's $1.34 billion budget; additional funding sources include Phoenix Transportation 2050 and regional Proposition 400 funds.

## Workforce and economic impact

- Valley Metro and the City of Phoenix, alongside construction contractor Kiewit, implemented targeted workforce development initiatives.
- The project employed over 5,000 local workers, with south Phoenix residents contributing more than 470,000 work hours.
- Programs ranged from youth STEM engagement to craft workforce development.
- Valley Metro Rail has attracted more than $17.5 billion in public and private investment development since service began in 2008.
- Future economic development in the area will be guided by the South Central Transit-Oriented Development Community Plan, approved by Phoenix City Council in spring 2022.

## Background given on the funding programmes

- **T2050:** In August 2015 Phoenix voters approved Transportation 2050, a 35-year citywide transportation plan overseen by the Citizens Transportation Commission, funded by a 7/10ths of a cent city sales tax that started Jan. 1, 2016; over the life of the plan the funds are estimated to generate about $16.7 billion, more than half the plan's overall cost, with an additional $14.8 billion from federal and county funds, passenger fares and other sources.
- **Valley Metro:** progress continues on additional high-capacity transit extensions in planning or under construction "to create a 50-mile rail system by 2030"; Valley Metro receives capital, bus and paratransit operations funds from Prop. 400, the 20-year regional half-cent transportation sales tax, and voters continued the 20-year regional funding support with the passage of Prop. 479 in 2024.

- Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. (TSMC) "has pushed up the mass production schedule for its second wafer fab in the U.S. state of Arizona to the second half of 2027 from the previously planned 2028," Chairman C.C. Wei (魏哲家) said Thursday.
