wikis.title: I-10 Broadway Curve Improvement Project completed
wikis.summary: ADOT news release announcing that the I-10 Broadway Curve Improvement Project in the Phoenix area is complete and all lanes are open, listing the project's major components, funding and delivery team.
wikis.body:
## Completion

- The Arizona Department of Transportation (ADOT) has completed the I-10 Broadway Curve Improvement Project, "providing motorists a less traffic-congested, shorter commute times and safer driving experience through one of the busiest stretches of Interstate 10 in the Phoenix area."
- All major construction work has been completed and all lanes on I-10 through the Broadway Curve area are open. Motorists may still see crews conducting finishing touches such as planting bushes and completing some wall and barrier work.
- Construction began in summer 2021 and was completed on May 31, 2025.
- The project expanded capacity along 11 miles of I-10 from just south of Ray Road to Interstate 17 near Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport.

## Traffic figures

- More than 300,000 vehicles pass through the I-10 Broadway Curve area on an average weekday.
- That number is expected to increase by 25%, or by 75,000 more vehicles, by 2040.

## Quote

- ADOT Director Jennifer Toth: "As the largest urban freeway reconstruction project in Arizona, the benefits are endless for everyone who relies on our highway system — that includes motorists and the thousands of businesses along the corridor. By improving safety and reducing congestion, this project supports our agency's vision to safely connect people and empower the economy. We're already seeing results."

## Major components

- Adding additional travel and HOV lanes in both directions on I-10 between US 60 and I-17 by Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport
- Construction of Collector Distributor (CD) roads to separate mainline traffic from traffic entering and exiting the freeway
- Construction of new 48th Street and Broadway Road bridges
- Rebuilding the I-10 interchange with SR 143 and constructing new HOV flyover ramps connecting I-10 and SR 143
- Widening the I-10 bridge over the Salt River to make room for additional travel lanes
- Constructing two new multi-use bridges over I-10 between Baseline and Broadway roads
- Constructing several sound and barrier walls throughout the project area

## Funding and delivery

- Funded by federal funds, the Maricopa Association of Governments' Prop 400 (a dedicated half-cent sales tax approved by Maricopa voters in 2004), and local funds.
- Built using a public-private partnership combining design and construction in a single contract.
- Developers: a joint venture of Pulice, FNF Construction and Flatiron Constructors, known as Broadway Curve Constructors.
- Designers: T.Y. Lin International Group, Stanley Consultants and Aztec Engineering.
- The project is identified in MAG's Regional Transportation Plan; MAG identified the need to reduce travel times on I-10 during peak hours, improve airport access, support ridesharing and transit, and prepare the region for future growth projections.

wikis.title: Future West Terminal at Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport
wikis.summary: Phoenix Sky Harbor's project page for a planned new terminal on the airport's west side, with its timeline, likely cost and funding, and FAQs on gates, airlines and construction impacts.
wikis.body:
## The project

- A future terminal on the west side of the airport is described as "a key component of Phoenix Sky Harbor's long-range plan to support passenger growth," with additional capacity needed as passenger traffic and aircraft size increase.
- The new terminal will be built on the west side of the airport between Terminal 3 and Taxiway U.
- It will be the first new terminal construction since Terminal 4 opened in 1990. The Terminal 3 Modernization Program was completed in 2020.

## Timeline (subject to change)

- A collaborative visioning phase for the terminal and its design started in early 2026; a design procurement process is anticipated in 2027; and construction could begin in late 2029, with a potential late 2033 opening.
- Planning 2025 – 2026
- Design Procurement 2027
- Design 2028 – 2030
- Construction 2029 – 2033
- Opening 2033

## Cost and funding

- The final project cost has not yet been determined; the project "could likely cost around $4.5 billion."
- The actual budget will be set as part of the terminal planning process taking place in 2026.
- Funding will come from passenger facility charges, bonds and airport funding. No tax dollars will be used.

## Still undetermined

- Number of concourses and gates remains to be determined, based on day-one passenger demand expected in 2033; the design will be modular to accommodate more concourses as the need arises.
- Airline assignments have not yet been determined.
- The passenger split between Terminal 3, Terminal 4 and the new terminal has not been determined.
- The terminal's name or number has not yet been determined.

## Construction impacts

- Some roadway construction will be required during construction; the airport will communicate changes in advance and work to minimize inconvenience. The PHX Sky Train will continue offering terminal access and helping reduce roadway impacts.

## Why a new terminal

- Terminals 3 and 4 are fully built out and cannot accommodate more gates, so the airport must expand its facilities to meet demand.

The page links to a press release, "New Terminal Coming to America's Friendliest Airport" (May 7, 2024).

wikis.title: RTD service changes taking effect September 27, 2026
wikis.summary: RTD Denver news release detailing the September 27, 2026 service changes, including rail adjustments during the Downtown Rail Reconstruction Project, a new SkyRide route to Denver International Airport and the start of East Colfax BRT service.
wikis.body:
## Headline changes

- DENVER (Sept. 9, 2026) — The Regional Transportation District (RTD)'s next service changes take effect Sunday, Sept. 27, and "will continue rail options to support customers during the Downtown Rail Reconstruction Project." The agency is maintaining the level of service hours since the June service changes took effect.
- The T (Temporary) Line will operate from Lincoln Station to Alameda Station, replacing some service formerly offered by the suspended H Line. It will continue to run at regular intervals of every 15 or 30 minutes during peak periods of customer demand.
- RTD is introducing SkyRide service – Route AL – in response to community and stakeholder requests, offering hourly service between Longmont and Denver International Airport. The route will start at 8th and Coffman and include stops at the Niwot and Lafayette Park-n-Rides, among others.
- The initial service on East Colfax Bus Rapid Transit (BRT) will begin along Colfax Avenue starting Sept. 27. Route 15 and Route 15L will use the new center bus-only lanes between Broadway and Colorado Boulevard, with customers boarding and exiting at the new stations in the center of Colfax Avenue.
- RTD adjusts its schedule three times a year — typically in January, May or June, and either August or September — accounting for traffic patterns, economic conditions and customer feedback.

## Rail services

- The L Line will remain suspended through the completion of the Downtown Rail Reconstruction Project.
- The C Line will be permanently reinstated once the Downtown Rail Reconstruction is completed, travelling between Littleton•Mineral Station and Union Station, and replacing the D Line.
- The R and T lines will undergo minor schedule changes, with the T Line also extending northbound beyond I-25•Broadway Station to also serve Alameda Station.
- The A Line will undergo schedule changes affecting early morning and evening service frequencies, with 30-minute frequencies beginning at 7:30 p.m. instead of 6:30 p.m. from Union Station.

## Bus services

- Schedule adjustments: routes 0, 0B, 1, 9, 10, 11, 14, 15, 20, 32, 37, 42, 45, 52, 53, 65, 72, 83L, 105, 120, 120L, 153, 204, 206, 323, AB, DASH, FREE, LD, LX, NB and SKIP.
- Route adjustments: 9, 10, 15, 20, 32, 52, 53, 59, 72, 73, 83L, 225, ART, DASH, JUMP and NB.
- Seasonal adjustments: 11, 20, 24, 35, 42, 45, 51, 65, 73, 225, DASH, NB and SKIP.
- Service increase: 35, 51 and ILFX.
- SkyRide Route AL is introduced, making hourly connections between Longmont and Denver International Airport.

## CTE grant funding

- RTD applied for the Clean Transit Enterprise (CTE) grant and was awarded $9.25 million in 2026 through funding by oil and gas production fees.
- RTD is required to apply the funds toward expanding transit services through increases to service frequency, the length of time services are offered, or expanding the service area.
- Since the June 2026 service changes, routes continuing their increased service frequencies due to the funding include the 16th Street FreeRide and bus routes 19, 21, 22, 37, 53, 80, LD3/287, and the ART.

## Access-a-Ride and customer tools

- Customers who use Access-a-Ride should be aware that any reductions or improvements to regular bus and rail routes may also affect paratransit service availability; RTD says it will communicate any changes.
- RTD encourages customers to use the new NextRide mobile app to plan travel adjustments, receive Service Alerts, purchase and store digital fare, and report security concerns. RTD Customer Care: 303.299.6000 (Mondays-Fridays 6 a.m.-8 p.m., weekends/holidays 9 a.m.-6 p.m.); dial 711 for the speech and hearing impaired.

Written by Tara Broghammer.

wikis.title: New Denver Broncos stadium at Burnham Yard: FAQs
wikis.summary: The Broncos' new-stadium FAQ page explaining why Burnham Yard was chosen as the preferred site for a stadium-anchored mixed-use district, how it would be funded and designed, and what happens next.
wikis.body:
## The site

- Burnham Yard, "the Broncos' preferred site for a new stadium," is located less than a mile southeast of Empower Field at Mile High along the I-25 corridor in Denver's urban core, between 6th and 13th avenues to the south and north and bordered by Seminole Road and Osage Street to the west and east.
- The Broncos selected Burnham Yard as the preferred site for a stadium-anchored mixed-use community "following a comprehensive and collaborative evaluation process spanning several years."
- Other locations considered included Empower Field at Mile High's existing footprint; the Broncos narrowed options to the current site as well as Denver, Lone Tree and Aurora before identifying Burnham Yard.
- The entire area for the new stadium and mixed-use development is more than 100 acres. The organization has an agreement with the state of Colorado to purchase the 58-acre parcel of Burnham Yard at cost, as well as an agreement in concept to purchase 25 acres from Denver Water; various private real estate acquisitions will make up the rest.
- Burnham Yard is "a downtown railyard that predates Colorado statehood." For nearly 150 years it was a major center of activity for Denver. It ceased operations in 2016, and Union Pacific Railroad sold the site to the state in 2021. History Colorado will be the main point of contact for cultural and heritage resources related to the site.
- The site was chosen in part for accessibility and connectivity along the I-25 corridor; the stadium and mixed-use district will anchor redevelopment as a transit-oriented neighborhood with multi-modal transit options (including RTD light rail) and a walkable neighborhood adjacent to public transportation.

## Why a new stadium

- "When the Broncos' lease at Empower Field at Mile High expires with the Metropolitan Football Stadium District after the 2030 season, the facility will be 30 years old, which is a common inflection point for professional sports venues to undergo a complete replacement or extensive renovation."
- Shortly after the Walton-Penner Family Ownership Group purchased the Broncos in 2022, the team began exploring future stadium possibilities: surveying more than 10,000 season ticket members, conducting more than 100 focus groups, interviewing team partners, consulting experts and visiting several new stadiums and developments.
- According to market research conducted by the Broncos, the majority of fans and stakeholders preferred a new stadium in a near-downtown location as well as a roof covering, with a retractable roof being the No. 1 option. Survey participants showed overwhelming support for a mixed-use development while also valuing site accessibility and non-gameday amenities.

## Funding

- The new stadium and mixed-use district "will be funded through a private investment from the Walton-Penner Family Ownership Group."
- "The city of Denver and state of Colorado will provide support for public improvements benefiting the community year-round with no new taxes."

## Next steps and timing

- The preferred-site announcement "marks the next step forward and a meaningful checkpoint in a comprehensive process," which now focuses on deeper civic and community engagement, higher-level site design and planning, and the necessary agreements and approvals. "There is a long way to go and a lot of work to do."
- No specific timelines have been discussed for a potential groundbreaking. "The targeted completion for a new stadium would be the 2031 NFL season," aligned with the expiration of the current lease at Empower Field at Mile High, which runs through 2030; the Broncos also have the option to extend the lease if needed.
- The Broncos formally informed the Denver City Council on Sept. 9 that they are committed to engaging in a strong and inclusive Community Benefits Agreement process; the CBA will include partnering with registered neighborhood organizations to study redevelopment options for the mixed-use district.

## Design

- Initial stadium design concepts call for a retractable roof featuring the latest technology, allowing games to be played in the elements while maximizing the year-round flexibility of the stadium.
- The Broncos have prioritized natural grass in the initial design and planning.
- The stadium "will showcase innovative technology and modern amenities"; further details will be shared as the project advances.
- The Broncos have partnered with Tryba, a Denver firm, for the site's master plan, and Manica, "a globally renowned firm," for the stadium design. The team is in the preliminary stages of stadium design and looks forward to sharing initial renderings in the near future.
- Initial plans for the mixed-use community hub feature restaurants, retail outlets, hotel and housing options, office spaces, entertainment venues, dynamic public spaces and more.

## Empower Field at Mile High

- If a new stadium is built and the Empower Field lease is closed (currently set to expire after the 2030 NFL season), the land the stadium is on and the surrounding parking lots will revert back to city ownership, and the city will work with the community on a plan for the 80 acres.

wikis.title: Ceremonial groundbreaking for the future Betty Knoebel Arena
wikis.summary: National Western press release on the ceremonial groundbreaking for the Betty Knoebel Arena at the National Western Center in Denver, and the launch of the Fritz & Betty Knoebel Equestrian Scholarship Program.
wikis.body:
## The groundbreaking

- Denver, CO — "The National Western celebrated philanthropists Fritz and Betty Knoebel and the future home of the Betty Knoebel Arena during a ceremonial groundbreaking at the National Western Center."
- The arena will be part of the planned Equestrian Center, and "acknowledges Betty Knoebel's love of horses as well as her legacy of philanthropy and transformational support of higher education and medical research."
- **Construction on the Equestrian Center is expected to begin in early 2027.**
- Wes Allison, President and CEO of National Western: "The Betty Knoebel Arena will be an important part of the National Western Center and the future of the National Western Stock Show. It will give us new opportunities to showcase equestrian sport, welcome competitors and audiences from around the country, and create memorable experiences for generations to come. We are incredibly grateful to Betty and the Knoebel family for investing not only in this facility, but in the young people who will shape the future of agriculture and the equine industry."

## Scholarship programme

- As part of the celebration, the National Western and Knoebel Foundation announced the Fritz & Betty Knoebel Equestrian Scholarship Program, supporting students pursuing equine sciences and related fields.
- The gift is an endowment intended to offer annual scholarships in perpetuity.
- The program's inaugural scholarship recipients were recognized during the event, with 10 students each receiving a $10,000 scholarship.

## The wider redevelopment

- The Betty Knoebel Arena "represents a significant investment in facilities that support the National Western Stock Show and year-round activities."
- The transformation of the National Western Center is a multiphase redevelopment that includes new event and agricultural facilities, transportation and infrastructure improvements, and revitalization of the South Platte River.

## About the National Western (as given)

- A Denver-based charitable organization dedicated to strengthening American agriculture through youth education, scholarships, and livestock, equestrian, farming, ranching and animal stewardship enrichment programs.
- Best known for producing the annual National Western Stock Show — "the 121st anniversary is Jan. 9-24, 2027" — the organization also operates The Legacy, "a premier year-round destination for events, exhibitions and Western experiences."

wikis.title: A's Ballpark in Las Vegas: ballpark experience site
wikis.summary: The Athletics' ballpark experience site for the new Las Vegas ballpark, describing the venue's design and 2028 opening plus its premium clubs, suites and priority ticket access.
wikis.body:
## The ballpark

- "The new A's ballpark is bringing Major League Baseball to the heart of the Las Vegas Strip."
- It is rising on the historic site of the former Tropicana Hotel.
- Designed by Bjarke Ingels, his firm BIG, and HNTB, "the ballpark features a striking, climate-controlled design with sweeping roof panels and one of the largest cable-glass windows in North America."
- With 80% of seats inside the foul poles, "fans will feel closer than ever to the action."
- Opening in 2028.

## Tickets

- A Priority Access list offers "priority access to purchase for just $19.01," giving early access to tickets in the new ballpark before the general public, with a dedicated representative to guide buyers through ticket options. "Limited availability."
- Premium spaces are on sale now.
- The page carries a message signed by Jason Green, Chief Ticketing Officer.

The site also lists sections for the Experience Center, Construction, The Ballpark, In The Community, In The News and FAQ, and a ballpark livestream.

wikis.title: Legends Lounge
wikis.summary: A social destination with premium seating behind home plate at the south end of the main concourse.
wikis.body:
- The Legends Lounge is "a vibrant social destination located at the south end of the main concourse featuring premium seating directly behind home plate."
- "Designed for game-connected socializing," it pairs views with a lively atmosphere, including a main bar and two terrace bars.
- It offers an all-inclusive culinary experience with interactive stations "serving approachable favorites made for sharing and grazing, along with complimentary beer, wine, and soda."

wikis.title: Diamond Club
wikis.summary: An all-inclusive social hub for premium ticket members adjacent to the Athletic Club behind home plate.
wikis.body:
- Developed by Aramark and Guidara "to further amplify the stadium's premium hospitality program."
- An all-inclusive social hub for premium ticket members, located adjacent to the Athletic Club behind home plate.
- Members "will enjoy a food and beverage experience featuring Vegas-inspired food stations inclusive of locally curated dishes, chef's specials, and a bold selection of elevated game day favorites."

wikis.title: Dugout Clubs
wikis.summary: Seating directly behind the dugouts along the first and third baselines with exclusive amenities.
wikis.body:
- Located directly behind the dugouts along the first and third baselines.
- They "offer some of the closest seats to the action in Major League Baseball, along with exclusive amenities and access."
- Dugout Club members will enjoy a private VIP entrance, access to a dedicated concourse, and all-inclusive food and non-alcoholic beverages.

wikis.title: Athletic Club
wikis.summary: The ballpark's most exclusive space, designed by Will Guidara for premium season-ticket members behind home plate.
wikis.body:
- "The Athletic Club is designed by Will Guidara to be the most exclusive space in the ballpark, with access reserved for A's premium season-ticket members seated behind home plate."
- Members will enjoy a private restaurant and supper club offering a multi-course, table-service menu.
- It also has an upscale lounge featuring small plates and a full bar with craft beer, curated wines and premium cocktails.

wikis.title: Executive Suites
wikis.summary: Private suites for up to 16 guests with parking passes, VIP entrance and a chef-driven multi-course menu.
wikis.body:
- Executive Suites at the new A's Ballpark are pitched for hosting client events or celebrating with friends.
- Each suite accommodates up to 16 guests and includes 4 on-site parking passes with access to the private VIP entrance.
- The culinary program delivers "a progressive, multi-course menu of chef-driven, seasonal creations directly to your suite as the game unfolds."
- Complimentary non-alcoholic beverages are included all evening, with premium spirits, beer and wine available for purchase.

wikis.title: Hard Rock Las Vegas
wikis.summary: Wikipedia's article on Hard Rock Las Vegas, the casino hotel resort under construction on the former Mirage site on the Las Vegas Strip, with its history, guitar tower and opening plans.
wikis.body:
## The resort

- "Hard Rock Las Vegas is a casino hotel resort under construction at the center of the Las Vegas Strip in Paradise, Nevada." Address 3400 South Las Vegas Boulevard; coordinates 36°07′16″N 115°10′31″W.
- Owned by Vici Properties and leased by Hard Rock International (operating licence holder; Seminole Tribe of Florida). Architect: Klai Juba Wald Architecture + Interiors. Main contractor: The PENTA Building Group. Website www.hardrockvegas.com.
- Infobox: opened Q4 2027 (expected); theme rock and roll; approx. 3,700 rooms; gaming space 174,000 sq ft (16,200 m2); signature attractions Hard Rock Live and West Theater (proposed); land-based casino; previous name The Mirage (1989–2024).
- An image is captioned "Under construction (March 2026)."
- "A previous casino resort, The Mirage, opened on the site in 1989 and will be incorporated into the new project."
- It is the second Hard Rock gaming property in the Las Vegas Valley; the earlier Hard Rock Hotel & Casino operated from 1995 to 2020.

## History

- The earlier Hard Rock Hotel & Casino operated east of the Strip from 1995 to 2020, with Hard Rock International involved only through licensing and branding.
- In 2019, with plans to rename the original Hard Rock as Virgin Hotels Las Vegas, Hard Rock International expressed interest in buying a Strip property; in May 2020 it bought the naming rights for a future Las Vegas property and development rights from Juniper Capital.
- The Mirage opened on November 22, 1989 and later came under MGM Resorts International ownership.
- "Hard Rock announced in December 2021 that it would rebrand the Mirage as Hard Rock Las Vegas."
- Vici Properties completed a $17 billion acquisition of MGM's properties, including the Mirage, in April 2022; Hard Rock took over the Mirage's operations in December 2022 after a $1.075 billion deal with MGM, leasing the property from Vici.
- The Mirage closed on July 17, 2024, and work on the Hard Rock project began one day after the closure.

## Construction

- The Mirage structures receive a full renovation, with hotel rooms completely remodeled and the casino and convention facilities expanded.
- A guitar-shaped hotel tower, akin to the Seminole Hard Rock Hotel & Casino Hollywood in Broward County, Florida, is being built on the former site of the Mirage's volcano attraction; demolition of the volcano was among the first tasks.
- "The guitar tower is expected to rise 660 feet (200 m)." Hard Rock previously proposed a larger 998-foot (304 m) tower, "which was rejected by Clark County officials."
- Construction of the tower is expected to take two and a half years; most of the pilings were in place as of January 2025.
- Rooms in the guitar tower increased from 596 to 675, with expanded pool and spa amenities in the updated plans.
- "The final structural beam was installed at the top of the newly-built 42-story guitar-shaped hotel tower on May 1, 2026."

## Opening plans

- "The $4 billion Hard Rock Las Vegas is expected to open in the fourth quarter of 2027," several months later than previously scheduled.
- Expected to employ up to 6,000 workers; will open with a 174,000 sq ft casino featuring 2,000 slot machines and 212 table games, and approximately 3,700 rooms including those in the guitar tower.
- Like the original off-Strip property, the new resort is expected to feature music memorabilia, "though not to the same extent."
- On opening, the Hard Rock-Treasure Island Tram (previously the Mirage-Treasure Island Tram) will reopen.
- "On July 17, 2026, as construction was underway, Hard Rock proposed a 2,000-seat, five-story live theater with a karaoke room in the second floor behind the Guitar Hotel known as West Theater, alongside a guitar museum and a sportsbook facing the Strip with 88,650 square feet (8,236 m2)."
- The resort is also planned to have a 5,000-seat Hard Rock Live arena.

wikis.title: New Customs and Border Protection facility opens at Harry Reid International Airport
wikis.summary: Harry Reid International Airport's newsroom announces the grand opening of a new CBP facility for the airport's general aviation and private jet operations.
wikis.body:
## What happened

- Harry Reid International Airport, Signature Aviation and U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) "celebrated the grand opening of a new facility dedicated to the airport's general aviation and private jet operations."
- Published on September 18, 2026.

## The facility

- Serves international arrivals on the west side of the airfield, "away from bustling commercial operations."
- Separates international general aviation and cargo processing from international commercial airline arrivals.
- The airport says this helps improve operational efficiency, reduces congestion and creates a more seamless experience for all travelers.

## Context given

- As Las Vegas has evolved into "the sports and entertainment capital of the world," general aviation has become increasingly important to airport operations as high-profile events draw private jets to LAS.
- The facility allows processing of arrivals from abroad without taking away space or resources from commercial operations.
- The page ends by pointing to photos of the new CBP facility.

wikis.title: Groundbreaking for the major construction stage of Second Avenue Subway Phase 2
wikis.summary: New York's Governor's office announces the groundbreaking of the Second Avenue Subway Phase 2 tunnel-boring launch site, the award of Contract 3, and the project's budget, savings and schedule.
wikis.body:
## The announcement

- Dated JUNE 8, 2026, Albany, NY. "Governor Kathy Hochul today joined leadership from the Metropolitan Transportation Authority (MTA), elected officials and Harlem community leaders to break ground on the major construction stage of the transformative Second Avenue Subway Phase 2 project."
- The groundbreaking occurred where, "in early 2027, the state-of-the-art tunnel-boring machine (TBM) will be lowered into the ground and begin mining the new subway tunnels from 120 Street and 2nd Avenue to 125 Street and Malcolm X Boulevard."
- "Following the resumption of federal funding to the project in April," the MTA has awarded the next major contract to construct the final tunnel section of this phase from 105 Street to 110 Street, including the future 106 St Station, using a "cut and cover" approach.
- Advanced utility relocations are on track to complete early, "allowing pending work on this project to start six months faster than originally scheduled."
- The release notes the project is "Funded in Part by Revenues from Congestion Pricing" and will serve "100,000 East Harlem Daily Riders."

## Contracts, budget and schedule

- Phase 2 is divided into four contracts, "compared to 10 in Phase 1."
- Tunnel boring is part of Contract 2, valued at $1.97 billion, including shaft excavation for the TBM, controlled blasting for future stations, and asbestos and lead abatement in the existing 1970s tunnels.
- Contract 3, announced at the groundbreaking, "will construct the structural shells of the new 106 St Station and associated tunneling, connecting the existing tunnels north and south of the station," with work expected to begin in the coming months.
- "The entire Second Avenue Subway Phase 2 project is budgeted at $6.968 billion and is on track for revenue service in 2032."

## Tunnel boring machines

- "The state-of-the-art variable-density Tunnel Boring Machines will be delivered early next year."
- Weighing more than one and a half million pounds, equipped with 23-foot tungsten carbide cutter heads; able to toggle between drills for hard rock and for soft soil or sand, and reinforcing the tunnel lining behind them.
- The TBM will launch from the 120 Street site and travel to 125 Street and Malcolm X Boulevard.

## Cost savings

- Lessons from Phase 1 deliver "more than $1 billion in savings."
- Measures: addressing utility relocation requirements upfront; reuse of a tunnel segment built in the 1970s from 110 Street to 120 Street along Second Avenue; early real estate acquisition; best-value performance-based contracts and design-build; close coordination of contracts; and reduction in back-of-house, ancillary spaces and station sizes.

## About Phase 2

- Extends Q train service from 96 Street north to 125 Street and then west on 125 Street to Park Avenue, "approximately 1.5 miles in total."
- Three new accessible stations at 106 Street, 116 Street and 125 Street; one-seat rides from East Harlem to the Upper East Side, West Midtown and Coney Island, "shortening travel times by up to 20 minutes."
- Direct passenger connection with the existing 125 St station on the Lexington Avenue subway line, plus an entrance at Park Avenue for transfers to Metro-North's Harlem-125 Street Station and connections to the 4 5 6 lines and the M60 Select Bus Service to LaGuardia Airport.
- Each station will have above-ground ancillary buildings housing ventilation, mechanical and electrical equipment, with space for possible ground-floor retail and community uses.
- "The expansion will serve 300,000 daily riders when combined with Phase 1."
- East Harlem "has one of the largest concentrations of affordable housing in the United States and where 70 percent of residents rely on transit." A 20 percent local hiring goal applies to the project.
- Sections of 1970s tunnelling will be adapted and used in Phase 2, including for the 116 St station.

## Possible next phase

- Hochul and the MTA are "already scoping and designing a potential next phase of the Q train westward across 125th St to Broadway with three new stations and more than 160,000 daily riders."
- After an MTA feasibility study announced by the governor in 2024, "this year's FY27 enacted state budget secured $25 million to conduct preliminary engineering and design of a tunnel extension and approval of an efficient environmental review process."

## History given

- In the 1920s the Second System proposal (which became the IND subway) included Second Avenue service; in 1948 New York City voters approved bonding for the line, left unbuilt after the start of the Korean War; in 1972 construction commenced in East Harlem but was abandoned in 1975 during the city's fiscal crisis.
- Governor Hochul: "The last groundbreaking for a second avenue subway in East Harlem was 54 years ago, only for the project to be abandoned and this community left behind."

## Quotes

- Governor Kathy Hochul: "The Second Avenue Subway will change everything for East Harlem, saving people precious time and making possible opportunities that have for too long been out of reach for too many."
- MTA Chair and CEO Janno Lieber: "It was 80 years ago they started knocking down the Second Avenue El -- an entire lifetime. Today's groundbreaking is another major step toward transit justice for East Harlem, the City's most transit-dependent community."
- President of MTA Construction & Development Jamie Torres-Springer: "By applying lessons learned from Phase 1, we're delivering this project better, faster, and cheaper—with more than $1 billion in savings to date."
- U.S. Senator Charles Schumer says he secured "$3.4 billion in federal funding—the largest Capital Investment Grant in history at the time," and that on completion "more than 300,000 New Yorkers will benefit from almost two miles of new track, six new stations, and one fully refurbished station."
- Supporting statements also came from Senator Kirsten Gillibrand, Rep. Adriano Espaillat, State Senators José M. Serrano and Cordell Cleare, Assemblymembers Edward Gibbs and Jordan J.G. Wright, Manhattan Borough President Brad Hoylman-Sigal, City Comptroller Mark Levine, Council Majority Leader Shaun Abreu, Council Member Yusef Salaam, New York Building Congress President Carlo A. Scissura and Building and Construction Trades Council President Gary LaBarbera.

wikis.title: Port Authority Bus Terminal
wikis.summary: Wikipedia's article on Manhattan's Port Authority Bus Terminal: its 1950 opening, later expansions, chronic congestion, and the $10 billion replacement now under way.
wikis.body:
## The terminal

- "The Port Authority Bus Terminal (colloquially known as the Port Authority and by its acronym PABT) is a bus terminal located in Manhattan in New York City. It is the busiest bus terminal in the world by volume of traffic, serving about 8,000 buses and 225,000 people on an average weekday and more than 65 million people a year."
- At 625 Eighth Avenue between 40th and 42nd Streets, one block east of the Lincoln Tunnel and one block west of Times Square; owned by the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey.
- 223 departure gates, 1,250 parking spaces, nine platform levels, plus commercial and retail space.

## History

- Opened December 15, 1950 as the Mid-Manhattan Bus Terminal (now the South Wing), built to consolidate private terminals across Midtown; architect Walter McQuade, groundbreaking January 27, 1949, superstructure by Turner Construction for about $9.2 million.
- Expanded from 1959–1963 (rooftop bus levels and a 1,000-space parking deck); the North Wing opened in 1979, adding 50 percent more capacity; a $52 million seismic retrofit of the South Wing followed in 2007.
- Greyhound moved in in May 1963, consolidating long-distance service at the terminal.
- The terminal declined from the mid-1960s, with high crime (3,300 crimes reported in 1983) and overcrowding investigations in the 1970s.

## Capacity problems

- The terminal has reached peak-hour capacity, causing congestion and overflow on local streets; it allows no layover parking, so buses park on local streets or deadhead through the Lincoln Tunnel.
- On-time performance fell from 92 percent in 2012 to 85 percent in the first quarter of 2014.
- A planned $800 million bus garage was scrapped in October 2011 over budget constraints; air-rights tower deals with Vornado Realty Trust collapsed in November 2011.

## Replacement

- "In January 2021, the PANYNJ released plans for reconstructing the terminal on the same site, with expansion of bus layover facilities." Foster + Partners and Epstein Global were hired in August 2022.
- Revised plans of January 2024 include 3.5 acres of parks, a glass atrium, a main entrance on 41st Street and two office buildings of at least 60 stories; the terminal was then planned to cost $10 billion, with new ramps by 2028 and the terminal itself by 2032.
- The City Planning Commission approved the plans in October 2024, federal approval came that December, and a $1.89 billion federal grant was disbursed in January 2025. "Work began on May 29, 2025, when a groundbreaking ceremony for a temporary terminal on Dyer Avenue between 37th and 39th streets was hosted."

## Services and art

- Gates 1–85 on the Subway Level serve long-distance buses and jitneys; Gates 200–425 serve short-haul commuter lines. NJ Transit accounts for 70 percent of the terminal's traffic.
- Underground passageways connect to the subway at Times Square–42nd Street and 42nd Street–Port Authority Bus Terminal.
- Artworks include George Segal's The Commuters (1982), George Rhoads's 42nd Street Ballroom (1983), a Ralph Kramden statue, Triple Bridge Gateway (2009) and a 6,000 sq ft LED mediamesh facade added in July 2011.

wikis.title: Port Authority Bus Terminal: history, expansions, replacement plans and operations
wikis.summary: The main text of Wikipedia's Port Authority Bus Terminal article, covering the terminal's construction from 1950, its expansions and decline, the planned $10 billion replacement, and its gates, operators and capacity problems.
wikis.body:
## The terminal

- "The Port Authority Bus Terminal (colloquially known as the Port Authority and by its acronym PABT) is a bus terminal located in Manhattan in New York City. It is the busiest bus terminal in the world by volume of traffic, serving about 8,000 buses and 225,000 people on an average weekday and more than 65 million people a year."
- Located at 625 Eighth Avenue between 40th Street and 42nd Street, "one block east of the Lincoln Tunnel and one block west of Times Square." Coordinates 40°45′24″N 73°59′28″W.
- Owner: Port Authority of New York and New Jersey (PANYNJ); one of its three bus terminals, with the George Washington Bridge Bus Station and Journal Square Transportation Center.
- 223 departure gates, 1,250 car parking spaces, 9 platform levels, plus commercial and retail space. "In 2011, there were more than 2.263 million bus departures from the terminal."
- Infobox: opened December 15, 1950; rebuilt 1963 (parking decks), 1979 (annex), 2007 (seismic retrofit).
- "Opened in 1950, the terminal was built to consolidate several private terminals spread across Midtown Manhattan. A second wing, extending to 42nd Street, was added in 1979. Since then, the terminal has reached peak hour capacity, leading to congestion and overflow on local streets." It does not allow layover parking, so buses use local streets and parking lots or deadhead through the tunnel.

## Before PABT

- Several terminals were scattered through Midtown, some in hotels: the All American Bus Depot on West 42nd, the Consolidated Bus Terminal on West 41st and the Hotel Astor Bus Terminal on West 45th (per the Federal Writers' Project's 1940 New York: A Guide to the Empire State); the Dixie Bus Center opened in 1930 and operated until 1959.
- Greyhound Lines had its own facility next to Pennsylvania Station and "did not move into the Port Authority Bus Terminal until May 1963," when all long-distance bus service to the city was consolidated at the terminal.

## Planning and construction

- The Lincoln Tunnel opened in 1937; within a year and a half, five companies ran 600 interstate bus trips through it daily.
- A large terminal near the tunnel mouth was first mandated in December 1939 after the city announced a ban on commuter buses in congested Midtown; the ban, due in January 1941, was blocked by Justice John E. McGeehan.
- In July 1940, at Mayor Fiorello H. La Guardia's request, the Port of New York Authority began a survey of bus traffic. In December 1940 Times Square Terminal Inc. applied to build a $4 million terminal from 41st to 42nd Streets; Borough President Stanley M. Isaacs proposed a $600,000 tube to the Lincoln Tunnel; the city approved both in January 1941.
- World War II delayed plans; in June 1944 New York State allocated $180,000 for a feasibility study. Greyhound initially opposed the terminal but withdrew its opposition in late 1947.
- The New York City Board of Estimate approved construction in January 1947, on the block bounded by 40th and 41st Streets and Eighth and Ninth Avenues. Land acquisition began two months later, and $16.3 million in bonds were issued in July 1947.
- In March 1948 a 500-spot rooftop parking lot was added to the design; the agency began relocating the first of 450 displaced families in November 1948.
- "Walter McQuade designed the terminal, with Vincent Marchesani as the assistant architect." Groundbreaking was January 27, 1949.
- First steel beams installed November 1949; Turner Construction won the superstructure contract for about $9.2 million that December; the frame topped out in March 1950; a labor strike caused slight delay. "The project had employed 1,055 men and used 1.53 million bricks and 1.22 million square feet (113,000 m2) of concrete."

## The original terminal

- The Mid-Manhattan Bus Terminal (now the South Wing), built in the International Style, opened on December 15, 1950.
- Four stories, 200 by 800 feet (61 by 244 m), 65 feet (20 m) tall, with a 500-space parking lot and 50 stores; ground level 40 slips for long-haul buses plus an auxiliary platform for 15 more; second level the main concourse with ticket offices, waiting rooms, baggage check, restaurants, shops and a 300-seat newsreel theater; third story the suburban concourse with 72 loading and 15 unloading slips; fourth story for short-haul buses.
- Pipes embedded in the reinforced-concrete ramps kept them ice-free; a rooftop heliport was proposed during construction, and a ramp to the 42nd Street and Eighth Avenue subway station was authorized just before opening.
- "During its first year, the Port Authority Bus Terminal accommodated 40 million passengers; the terminal's construction was credited with diverting 5,000 buses per day from street-level bus stops."
- It recorded a net loss during its first five years, due in part to high operating expenses, debt charges and interest costs.

## Expansions

- September 1959: the Port of New York Authority announced $19 million to increase capacity by 50 percent, converting the rooftop parking lot to 25 long-haul and 32 short-haul bus spaces, with a new 1,000-space lot above. That December it approved $24 million for the expansion and ramp widening.
- The expansion topped out in June 1961; a bridge to the Lincoln Tunnel was installed two months later; $25 million in bonds were sold in January 1962; new ramps finished the next month; the first 300 parking spaces opened April 1962; new loading slips were in full operation by April 1963.

## Decline

- From the mid-1960s the terminal had a reputation as a "derelict's haven" at night; extra officers were stationed there in January 1967 and a CCTV system was added in 1966.
- By 1975 the terminal still handled an average of 250,000 passengers daily, though bus numbers had begun declining in 1968; hundreds of crimes were recorded yearly by the late 1970s.
- In March 1975 a federal judge ruled the PANYNJ "was not competent to" allocate loading space; a subsequent study found 750 to 800 buses in a typical morning carrying 35,000 passengers. The Interstate Commerce Commission opened an overcrowding investigation, cancelling its hearing after the annex was announced.
- Trailways began a rent strike in 1977 over dilapidation and high rent, ending it under threat of eviction.

## Northern annex

- Irving Maidman proposed a second terminal to the north in 1956; the PANYNJ considered extending to 42nd Street from January 1965 and announced plans in 1970 for a north annex ($80 million) with a $50 million office tower above.
- The expansion was announced in May 1975 by chairman William J. Ronan at a cost of $137.5 million, including a glass curtain wall replacing the original curved facade, a new wing with four above-ground concourses and one basement, improved subway access and a tunnel to the Lincoln Tunnel. Tolls on six bridges and tunnels were raised 50 percent to fund it, and $22 million more was allocated that August.
- The facility handled 7,000 buses per day in 1977, giving buses seven minutes to load and unload in rush hours.
- "The North Wing was opened in 1979," increasing capacity by 50 percent, with a facade of 27 steel X-shaped trusses. In 2008 Virtualtourist listed the terminal among the "World's Top 10 Ugliest Buildings and Monuments." The annex included 50 loading slips with space for 25 more.

## Later years

- Crime rose after the north wing: 2,800 crimes reported in 1979 and 3,300 in 1983.
- A 1997 study coordinated by Professor Marcus Felson of Rutgers University identified design and supervision changes to reduce crime.
- In 2007 the South Wing underwent a seismic retrofit in a $52 million building-code project. PKSB Architects, hired in 1995 for a titanium facade, entrance canopy and stainless steel cladding, saw that project completed in 2008.
- On September 11, 2001 the terminal closed; partial service resumed September 13 at 5:00 a.m., two hours after the Lincoln Tunnel reopened.

## Air rights and a West Side depot

- In 1999 a 35-story building, 7 Times Square, was proposed over the North Wing with a golf driving range over the South Wing; it was put on hold in 2001 after the dot-com bust.
- The PANYNJ worked with Vornado Realty Trust between 2000 and 2011. In November 2007 it announced terms for nearly $500 million in a lease arrangement for an office tower with 1.3 million sq ft of commercial space (vanity address 20 Times Square), 60,000 sq ft of new retail in the terminal and 18 additional departure gates for 70 more buses carrying up to 3,000 passengers per hour; construction was expected to begin in 2009 or 2010 and take four years. Richard Rogers of Rogers Stirk Harbour + Partners won the competition with a 45-story, 855-foot tower. The agreement expired in August 2009, was extended to August 2011, and the new backers pulled out in November 2011.
- In June 2014 the PANYNJ sold nearby property for $115 million rather than the anticipated $100 million, indicating higher air-rights values.
- A joint city–PANYNJ study identified Galvin Plaza (39th to 40th Streets between Tenth and Eleventh Avenues) as a preferred bus depot location, without capacity for charter and tour buses.
- In August 2011 the PANYNJ cited an $800 million "new bus garage connected to the Port Authority Bus Terminal, which will serve as a traffic reliever to the Lincoln Tunnel and midtown Manhattan streets, saving two-thirds of the empty bus trips" among reasons for toll increases; construction was scrapped in October 2011 over budget constraints.
- In April 2012 developer Larry Silverstein proposed a bus garage with a residential tower at 39th Street and Dyer Avenue; "The proposal has not progressed any further." In 2014 the PANYNJ applied for a $230 million Federal Transit Administration grant for the garage.

## Replacement

- June 2013: the PANYNJ commissioned an 18-month study of reconfiguration, expansion and replacement options, a $5.5 million contract to Kohn Pedersen Fox and Parsons Brinckerhoff.
- 2016: development teams were invited to propose replacements. May 2019: environmental review began, with four public hearings planned in July and September 2019; three plans were considered.
- "In January 2021, the PANYNJ released plans for reconstructing the terminal on the same site, with expansion of bus layover facilities."
- August 2022: Foster + Partners (Boston-based per the article) and Epstein Global were hired to design the new terminal; $65 million was allocated the next year.
- January 2024: the Federal Transit Administration approved a draft environmental impact report. Revised plans called for 3.5 acres (1.4 ha) of parks, a glass atrium, a main entrance on 41st Street, two office buildings of at least 60 stories on 40th and 42nd streets, permanent closure of part of 41st Street from Eighth to Ninth avenues, and a separate bus storage and staging building. "At the time, the new terminal was planned to cost $10 billion; new ramps to the terminal were to be completed by 2028, while the terminal itself was planned to be finished by 2032."
- The New York City Planning Commission approved the plans in October 2024 and federal approval followed that December. In January 2025 the U.S. Department of Transportation disbursed a $1.89 billion grant.
- "Work began on May 29, 2025, when a groundbreaking ceremony for a temporary terminal on Dyer Avenue between 37th and 39th streets was hosted."

## Art and advertising

- George Segal's The Commuters, three weary bus passengers and a clock salvaged from the original terminal, was unveiled in the main ticket area in 1982.
- George Rhoads's rolling ball sculpture 42nd Street Ballroom was installed on the main floor of the North Wing in 1983.
- A statue of Jackie Gleason as Ralph Kramden stands in front of the South Wing's main entrance, presented by "the People of TV Land."
- Triple Bridge Gateway by Leni Schwendinger Light Projects was completed in 2009 under the ramps.
- In July 2011 PABT gained "the world's largest mediamesh," a 6,000 sq ft LED-embedded stainless steel facade wrapping the corner of 42nd Street and Eighth Avenue.

## Configuration and services

- There was no departure board for many years; in 2015 both the Port Authority and NJ Transit installed screens listing scheduled departures, though buses are not tracked so delays are not shown.
- Tickets are sold on the South Wing main level; Greyhound, Trailways and Short Line have additional counters. NJ Transit has a customer service counter and ticket vending machines; since 2009 passengers must buy a ticket before boarding NJT buses; contactless payment is accepted.
- Gates: 223 of saw-tooth (pull-in) or island platform (pull-through) design. Gates 1–85 on the Subway Level are used mainly for long-distance travel, including buses to Canada, jitneys, and overnight (1 a.m. to 6 a.m.) commuter lines; Gates 200–425 serve short-haul commuter lines from 6 a.m. to 1 a.m.
- Retail includes franchise stores (Heartland Brewery, Au Bon Pain, Jamba Juice, Starbucks, Hudson News, Duane Reade, GNC), a USPS branch and Frames bowling alley on the 2nd floor.
- The second-floor women's restroom is the terminal's busiest and is used as a makeup counter. A lawsuit filed in 2014 alleged plainclothes officers targeted homosexual or effeminate men in the men's restrooms; five officers of about 1,700 accounted for 70 percent of public lewdness arrests in 2014. "The Port Authority Police Department ended the practice in 2022."
- Operators listed include commuter lines (Academy Bus, Coach USA, Community Coach, Rockland Coaches, Short Line, Suburban Trails, Community Lines, Lakeland Bus Lines, Martz Trailways, New Jersey Transit routes 101–199, OurBus, Spanish Transportation, Trans-Bridge Lines), Olympia Trails to Newark Airport, intercity operators (Adirondack Trailways, C&J, Coach Company, Fullington Trailways, Greyhound Lines, OurBus Prime, Peter Pan Bus Lines, Short Line) and sightseeing (Gray Line New York, The RIDE).
- A note states NJT bus operations make up 70 percent of the terminal's traffic, with about 79,000 NJT riders and 30,000 private-line commuters each morning.

## Connections and capacity

- Underground passageways connect to the 1, 2, 3, 7, A, C, E, N, Q, R, W and S subway trains at Times Square–42nd Street and 42nd Street–Port Authority Bus Terminal; several NYC bus routes stop outside; NY Waterway's 42nd Street shuttle also serves it.
- "PABT is the gateway for most bus and jitney traffic entering Manhattan with more than 190,000 passengers on 6,000 bus trips made through the Lincoln Tunnel and terminal daily."
- The exclusive bus lane (XBL), first implemented in 1970 after studies from 1964, serves weekday eastbound buses 6 a.m. to 10 a.m., fed by the New Jersey Turnpike at Exits 16E and 17 and New Jersey Route 3; it "serves over 1,800 buses and 65,000 bus commuters on regular weekday mornings," with over 100 carriers using it. The contraflow lane runs 2.5 miles (4.02 km).
- As of 2013 NJ Transit operated fifty-seven interstate routes through the Lincoln Tunnel.
- Congestion at the capacity-constrained terminal causes delays and overflow; on-time performance fell from 92 percent in 2012 to 85 percent in the first quarter of 2014. In December 2011 the New Jersey Assembly passed a resolution calling on the PANYNJ to address congestion. The Tri-State Transportation Campaign proposed reconfiguration and expansion, a PM westbound XBL, other Manhattan bus stops and a new storage depot. In May 2012 the NJDOT commissioner suggested some NJ Transit routes could start or end elsewhere in Manhattan, notably the East Side.
- In 2011 Megabus began using streets and sidewalk at the terminal with NYCDOT permission, opposed by the PANYNJ on safety grounds and by rent-paying long-haul companies; the permission was withdrawn later that year, and Megabus now largely uses street stops near the Javits Center and Penn Station.

wikis.title: Port Authority Bus Terminal article: references, external links and navigation
wikis.summary: The second part of the Wikipedia page, which is the article's citation list, external links, navigation boxes and categories rather than article text.
wikis.body:
## What this part contains

- This part of the page holds the tail of the reference list, the external links, Wikipedia navigation templates and the article's categories; it contains no article prose.
- Cited sources are largely New York Times, New York Herald Tribune, Wall Street Journal, The Record (Bergen County), The Star-Ledger, Crain's New York and Port Authority of New York and New Jersey publications, dated from the 1940s to 2026.
- Reports cited include "Improving Trans-Hudson Bus Access" (ITE Journal, May 1987), TCRP Report 90 on New York bus lanes and limited-stop service, "The Lincoln Tunnel Exclusive Bus Lane" (PANYNJ, 2009), a "Lincoln Tunnel HOT Lane Feasibility Study" (PANYNJ, 2009), the Hudson County Bus Circulation and Infrastructure Study (NJTPA, November 2007) and the Jersey City Local Bus Study (NJ Transit, November 2009).
- Citations on the restroom-arrests lawsuit include The Appeal (July 12, 2019), The New York Times (October 8, 2014) and "Port Authority Settlement Will End Undercover Bathroom Patrols" (The New York Times, June 1, 2022).

## External links listed

- Wikimedia Commons media related to Port Authority Bus Terminal; Port Authority Bus Terminal Website; Port Authority Bus Terminal History; PATH station details; New Jersey Transit station details; "Competition for a Bus Terminal Replacement"; "Guide to the Port Authority Bus Terminal"; "Buses, The Lincoln Tunnel, and The Port Authority Bus Terminal."

- 1950 establishments in New York City; 42nd Street (Manhattan); Bus stations in New York City; Eighth Avenue (Manhattan); Hell's Kitchen, Manhattan; Lincoln Tunnel; NJ Transit Bus Operations; NJ Transit bus stations; Port Authority of New York and New Jersey; Transit hubs serving New Jersey; Transportation buildings and structures in Manhattan.

wikis.title: Roberts Children's Health at Children's Hospital of Philadelphia
wikis.summary: CHOP's giving page for Roberts Children's Health, the renovated flagship hospital and new inpatient tower opening in 2028, with its gift, size and planned features.
wikis.body:
## The project

- "A transformational gift of $125 million from Aileen and Brian Roberts and their family is partially funding Roberts Children's Health at CHOP, opening in 2028."
- CHOP has been "a world leader in pediatric health" for nearly 170 years.
- The project covers a renovated and redesigned flagship hospital on CHOP's Philadelphia Campus plus "a more than 1 million-square-foot new inpatient tower."
- The new building, currently under construction, "will rise more than 20 stories" and "will be the tallest medical building in West Philadelphia."
- Key figures given: 2028 opening, 20+ stories high, 1 million+ square feet.

## Milestone

- "On January 28, 2026, the final structural beam was placed at the top of Roberts Children's Health." A video by CHOP's patient reporters, the Breakthrough News Crew, covers the milestone.
- In the video, Jennifer Hart, MSN, RNC-NIC, says teams "run simulations, drills, and virtual reality tours so teams can practice pretend scenarios for all aspects of patient care" — "like a giant rehearsal, testing rooms, equipment, and technology."
- Hart: "Every patient will have a private room with advanced technology to make care faster and easier," and families can work remotely, order food, exercise, meditate "even get a haircut right in the hospital."
- Monica Jones describes family involvement as honouring "CHOP's long-standing commitment to including families as essential members of the care team."

## Highlights listed

- Dramatically increased capacity across the expansion and subsequent renovations, with hundreds of private rooms equipped with the latest digital tools.
- Lush outdoor green spaces; mental health resources.
- More than 30 procedure and imaging rooms for cardiology, neurology and other specialties.
- Simulation spaces for family education on complex patient needs.
- A new Family Amenities Suite with flexible spaces for fitness, meditation and entertainment.
- Expanded parking with interior connectivity to other buildings on the Philadelphia Campus.
- A centralized third-floor connector with dining options and areas for relaxation and meditation.
- Cardiac operating and imaging complex; configurable advanced surgical suites.
- Emergency Department staffed 24/7 by attending physicians and nurses specially trained in pediatric emergency medicine.

## Quote

- Madeline Bell, CEO, Children's Hospital of Philadelphia: Roberts Children's Health "will provide an environment where children and families receive the most cutting-edge care and the very best experience, ultimately helping more children realize the hope of a healthy future."

wikis.title: 76ers and Flyers unveil first look at new Philadelphia arena
wikis.summary: The Flyers' news release on the first exterior renderings of the proposed privately funded arena on the Spectrum grounds in South Philadelphia, scheduled to open in 2030.
wikis.body:
## Announcement

- The Philadelphia 76ers and Philadelphia Flyers "today unveiled the first exterior renderings of the proposed new arena, which will also serve as home to Philadelphia's WNBA team, planned for the historic Spectrum grounds in South Philadelphia." Dated September 08, 2026.
- "Scheduled to open in 2030, the arena is designed to deliver a next-generation fan experience and amplify the energy of Philadelphia sports, concerts, live entertainment and community programming."
- Targeted to open ahead of the 2030 inaugural season of Philadelphia's WNBA expansion team as well as the respective NBA and NHL seasons.
- Comcast will own the naming rights; the arena is to be formally named at a later date.

## Economics

- "Philadelphia's largest fully privately funded project in the city's history."
- Anticipated to create nearly 15,000 jobs and generate nearly $6 billion in economic activity over the next 10 years, with hundreds of millions in new tax revenue directly benefiting the School District of Philadelphia and the city.

## Design

- Global design firm Populous and architect Moody Nolan were selected by the 76ers and Flyers.
- The architecture "draws inspiration from the shape of the Spectrum, which hosted the Flyers and the 76ers for nearly three decades, and reimagines it through a contemporary design lens."
- The exterior will be defined by "stacked, cantilevered bands that break down the scale of a typical arena."
- Fan plazas outside; a broad arrival stair at the front echoing landmarks such as the steps at the Philadelphia Museum of Art.
- Over a half-acre of outdoor space, with flexible fan-friendly areas and options for food-and-beverage pavilions extending the restaurant footprint.
- The renderings reflect fan feedback and stakeholder input; fan surveys, focus groups, community engagement and public review "will continue throughout the design and approval process."

## Quotes

- Josh Harris, Co-Founder of Harris Blitzer Sports & Entertainment and Managing Partner of the 76ers: "Philly fans deserve the best arena in the world, and we are excited to partner with Comcast to deliver just that. This privately funded arena will be the home to moments and memories that define this city for generations." He thanks partners David Blitzer, David Adelman, Brian Roberts and Dan Hilferty, and Mayor Parker and Council President Kenyatta Johnson.
- Brian Roberts, Chairman of Comcast Corporation: "This is a new era for Philadelphia sports. To build our future where Ed Snider and the Spectrum made history makes this project truly special."

## More information

- Updates at https://www.ThePhillyArena.com.

wikis.title: Penn's Landing Park, Philadelphia
wikis.summary: The project website for Penn's Landing Park, an 11.5-acre civic park under construction over I-95 on Philadelphia's Delaware River waterfront, with its amenities, schedule and related South Street Pedestrian Bridge.
wikis.body:
## The park

- "Penn's Landing Park is a new 11.5-acre civic park under construction along Philadelphia's Central Delaware Waterfront."
- Built atop a new expanded cap over Interstate 95 and Christopher Columbus Boulevard; it "will reconnect Center City neighborhoods to the Delaware River."
- "Set to open in 2029/2030."
- Created by the Delaware River Waterfront Corporation (DRWC), which has led citywide engagement efforts with community organizations.

## Amenities listed

- Open lawns for festivals, performances and everyday gatherings.
- Year-round café with rotating food trucks and seasonal offerings.
- Nature-inspired play space for kids of all ages and abilities.
- Reimagined RiverRink with winter ice skating and warm-weather activities (roller skating, markets, movie nights).
- Interactive water feature for summer.
- Welcoming pavilion with café seating, restrooms, rentals and flexible indoor and outdoor spaces.
- Outdoor amphitheater for concerts, cultural events and community performances.

## South Street Pedestrian Bridge

- Part of PennDOT's CAP project and DRWC's park work, the bridge "will extend across Columbus Boulevard, creating a direct, safe, and scenic link from South Street to the Waterfront."
- "The bridge will be installed during a single overnight operation in Winter 2027 and is expected to open to the public in late 2027 to early 2028."

## I-95 CAP construction

- Construction has begun on the I-95 Central Access Philadelphia (CAP) project, which includes Penn's Landing Park and an extension of the South Street Pedestrian Bridge.
- A timelapse video from PennDOT shows the partial demolition of I-95 between Chestnut and Walnut Streets.
- Information at 95revive.com; PennDOT hotline 1-215-513-1399 or info@95revive.com.

## Background given

- "In 2011, the future of Penn's Landing was first envisioned in the Master Plan for the Central Delaware," a roadmap for waterfront development between Port Richmond and Pennsport.
- After a three-year study with community input, designers and engineers confirmed a new park space was possible at the waterfront; this section states "Construction is scheduled to start in 2023."
- The project also includes a new trail along Columbus Boulevard.
- DRWC's engagement team is led by PennPraxis, Little Giant Creative, SEAMAAC, Make the World Better Foundation, and the Village of Arts & Humanities.
- Planning boards are posted from the April 18, 2023 I-95 CAP pre-construction meeting and an October 17, 2019 meeting.

wikis.title: William H. Gray III 30th Street Station redevelopment project schedule
wikis.summary: The project website's schedule page for the redevelopment of Philadelphia's William H. Gray III 30th Street Station, with its phasing and two dated updates.
wikis.body:
## Schedule as stated

- The redevelopment "began Fall 2021 by starting the design phase that preserves the historic significance of the station."
- Concurrently, PIP began to maintain the facility, operations and concessions in Fall 2021 and "will continue in this role through 2071."
- "Beginning in 2023, the project will be constructed in phases to maintain Amtrak operations with the full station renovation anticipated to be complete in 2028."

## Update (January 2026)

- The station redevelopment project "continues to progress."
- The South Station Retail Concourse is anticipated to open to the public "in late 2026," with construction continuing through 2028.

## Update (February 2025)

- "The first phase of the Station redevelopment project is underway."
- The South Station Retail Concourse was then anticipated to open to the public in 2026, with construction continuing through 2027.

wikis.title: Nu Stadium, Miami Freedom Park
wikis.summary: Wikipedia's article on Nu Stadium, Inter Miami's soccer-specific stadium in Miami Freedom Park, covering its long site search, construction, naming and opening events.
wikis.body:
## The stadium

- "Nu Stadium is a soccer-specific stadium in Miami, Florida, United States. Opened in April 2026, the 26,700-seat stadium is the home field of Inter Miami of Major League Soccer (MLS), replacing the interim Chase Stadium in Fort Lauderdale."
- Nicknamed "The House that Messi Built" in the infobox.
- Address 1900 NW 37th Avenue, Miami Freedom Park; coordinates 25°47′35″N 80°15′32″W.
- Owner and operator: Inter Miami. Capacity 26,700. Grass surface. Architects: MANICA Architecture and Arquitectonica. Website nustadium.com.
- Groundbreaking August 28, 2023; opened April 4, 2026. Tenant: Inter Miami (MLS) (2026–present).
- Public transit: Tri-Rail, Miami Metrorail and MIA Mover at the Miami Intermodal Center.
- "It is the centerpiece of Miami Freedom Park—a mixed-use development near Miami International Airport that will include office, retail, and commercial space, as well as public parks."
- The stadium was unveiled by team co-founder David Beckham in 2018 and approved by Miami City Council in 2022.

## Earlier proposed sites

- **PortMiami (2014):** On March 25, 2014 Beckham announced plans for a 25,000-seat stadium at PortMiami next to the Miami Heat's American Airlines Arena, at the southwest corner of Dodge Island. On April 8, 2014 Miami-Dade commissioners refused to relocate a fuel-spill facility needed for the plan; Royal Caribbean Cruises formed the Miami Seaport Alliance to oppose it. Commissioners voted 11–1 against the PortMiami site on May 20, 2014. On February 3, 2015 commissioners voted unanimously to recommend FIU Stadium as a temporary home.
- **Museum Park boat slip (2014):** Mayor Carlos A. Giménez proposed filling a boat slip between American Airlines Arena and Museum Park on May 5, 2014; Beckham's group made it "Plan A" on May 19. Plans of May 22, 2014 had a 20,000-seat stadium on 4.2 acres of the 19-acre park while adding 8.5 acres by filling the basin. Mayor Regalado and City Manager Daniel Alfonso turned the proposal down on June 10, 2014 after the city said the sides were "too far apart" on rent.
- **Little Havana / Marlins Park (2014–2015):** MLS president Mark Abbott said in June 2014 the league was not interested in the Marlins Park site. In March 2015 commissioners asked Mayor Gimenez to negotiate over a county parcel west of Marlins Park; a tentative deal announced July 17, 2015 was pulled from the December 1, 2015 commission agenda, with Commissioner Francis Suarez citing the group's inability to secure deals with private landowners. Commissioner Don Garber said in August 2014 the league "will not expand to Miami unless we have a downtown site for the stadium." In May 2015, University of Miami President Donna Shalala met Beckham's group about a possible joint stadium with the Miami Hurricanes.
- **Overtown (2015):** On December 4, 2015 Beckham's group announced a contract to buy a privately owned block at 650 NW 8th Street near Culmer station, I-95 and the Miami River, plus a letter of intent for the county-owned block to the south; MLS's governing board endorsed the location on December 5. The private land purchase was completed by March 24, 2016 and 3 acres of county land acquired on June 6, 2017. After Jorge Mas joined the team, the group announced it would abandon Overtown for a larger development near Miami International Airport.

## Freedom Park (2018 onward)

- In July 2018 Beckham and Mas unveiled plans for a 25,000-seat stadium as part of Freedom Park at the city-owned Melreese Country Club: 131 acres of public land with 1 million sq ft of office, retail and commercial space, 750 hotel rooms, 23 acres of public soccer fields plus the 10.5-acre stadium, and 58 acres of public park, with annual installment payments of $20 million for 30 years for city park improvements.
- A November 2018 referendum on negotiating a no-bid lease "passed with 60% of the vote."
- The PGA Tour Latinoamérica moved the Shell Championship from Melreese to Trump National Doral Miami Golden Palm in October 2018.
- In June 2019 Beckham projected the stadium would open by 2022. On August 20, 2019 Mayor Francis Suarez confirmed soil contamination at Melreese was worse than thought; per CBS Miami, "arsenic contamination levels are more than twice what is allowed by law."
- "On April 28, 2022, the Miami City Council voted 4–1 to grant Inter Miami a 99-year lease for the Melreese site, with the stadium projected to open in the 2025 MLS season."

## Construction and naming

- Melreese Golf Course shut on March 19, 2023; construction of Miami Freedom Park began in August 2023 "with intentions to open in 2026."
- On August 8, 2024 Governor Ron DeSantis announced an $8 million grant from the Governor's Job Growth Grant Fund for road infrastructure around the stadium.
- "On March 3, 2026, the team announced a naming rights deal with Brazilian financial technology company Nubank, under which the stadium will be known as Nu Stadium."
- On March 27, 2026 Inter Miami named part of the east stand the "Leo Messi Stand," covering blocks 117–121 of the lower bowl and 217–223 of the upper bowl.

## Opening and first events

- Inaugural match on April 4, 2026 against Austin FC, a 2–2 draw; Guilherme Biro scored the first goal in the stadium's history and Lionel Messi scored the first Inter Miami goal there. Attendance 26,412.
- First Inter Miami win at the stadium: May 17, 2026, 2–0 over the Portland Timbers before 26,715 fans.
- First international game: June 5, 2026, Peru beat Haiti 2–1 before 26,700 fans.
- Mexican country musician Carín León was the first musical artist to perform there, on June 28, 2026.

## Transportation

- Near Miami International Airport and the Miami Intermodal Center, served by the MIA Mover, Metrorail, Tri-Rail and express bus service to Miami Beach.
- "A 1,450-foot, grade-separated pedestrian bridge linking the transit hub with Miami Freedom Park will begin construction in 2027 and be completed by the second quarter of 2029."
- Tri-Rail runs special trains for weekend matches departing 45 minutes after the final whistle; the club offers a $10 beverage and concessions voucher to fans showing proof of public transport use.
- "The stadium has over 4,500 on-site parking spaces, the largest capacity at any MLS stadium," plus 2.51 miles (4.04 km) of new roadways (marked "better source needed").

wikis.title: New Concourse K at Miami International Airport
wikis.summary: Miami International Airport's project page for the new Concourse K, giving its cost, schedule, contractors and scope.
wikis.body:
## Project

- The new Concourse K at Miami International Airport (MIA) is described as "a transformative infrastructure project marking a significant milestone in MIA's ambitious $9 billion Future-Ready Modernization in Action plan."
- Investment of $600.6 million, designed to meet growing demand for passenger traffic.
- The Modernization in Action plan positions MIA to accommodate 77 million passengers and 5 million tons of cargo by 2040.
- MIA recorded nearly 56 million passengers and more than 3 million U.S. tons of freight in 2024 alone.

## Schedule and team

- Construction "is set to begin following a ceremonial groundbreaking this summer and is scheduled for completion by Spring 2029."
- General contractor: Lemartec-NV2A JV, LLC. Lead architect: Perez & Perez Architects Planners, Inc.

## Scope

- Expansion of the existing South Terminal: a new 3-level Concourse K with six contact (domestic) gates, "with the potential for future international capabilities."
- Associated aircraft apron and jet fuel hydrant system.
- Modernized zoned holdrooms catering to different passenger needs, from seating arrangements to workstations.
- New 2-level Ground Support Equipment (GSE) facility with office areas, storage and maintenance spaces.
- Baggage handling system (BHS) modifications in the existing Central and South Terminals, including a new crossover from the Central Terminal to the South Terminal and utility modifications for new conveyors; installation of two new make-up carousels.
- Envision LEED Silver certification for sustainable infrastructure.

wikis.title: Groundbreaking of Cruise Terminal G at PortMiami
wikis.summary: Miami-Dade County's press release on the groundbreaking ceremony for PortMiami's new Cruise Terminal G for Royal Caribbean Group, with its cost, capacity and completion date.
wikis.body:
## The event

- "Today, Miami-Dade County Mayor Daniella Levine Cava, Miami-Dade Board of County Commissioners, PortMiami Director and CEO Hydi Webb, and Royal Caribbean Group Chairman and CEO Jason Liberty led a groundbreaking ceremony for the future new Cruise Terminal G at PortMiami." Release dated 2026-01-08.

## The terminal

- Delivered by Lemartec-NV2A Joint Venture in partnership with Perez & Perez Architects & Planners; design-build delivery of a cruise terminal for Royal Caribbean Group "designed to meet LEED certification and the capacity to accommodate up to 7,000 passengers."
- Will include a multi-level parking garage, an intermodal facility "and other critical infrastructure to support large cruise ships such as the Icon-class vessels."
- "With a total investment of $345 million, this world-class complex will be dedicated to Royal Caribbean Group while maintaining multi-vessel functionality."
- Designed as a single-berth terminal for efficient embarkation and disembarkation.
- "The future Cruise Terminal G is slated for completion in late 2027."
- Funding is provided "through a partnership between Miami-Dade County and Royal Caribbean Group."

## Quotes

- Mayor Daniella Levine Cava: "This world-class facility will enhance Miami-Dade County's skyline while marking another milestone in PortMiami's evolution. Our modern terminals are transforming how we do business and move people, delivering greater efficiency through innovative technology."
- Royal Caribbean Group Chairman and CEO Jason Liberty: "Cruise Terminal G represents a major investment in Miami's future. Built with advanced technology and sustainable design, this new facility will deliver a smarter, faster, more seamless experience for guests sailing with our industry-leading brands: Royal Caribbean, Celebrity Cruises, and Silversea."
- Lemartec-NV2A Joint Venture: "Cruise Terminal G will be a world-class gateway to the sea, creating jobs and driving economic growth. This iconic addition to PortMiami secures Miami's place as the Cruise Capital of the World® for generations to come."

## About the parties (as given)

- PortMiami is "the Cruise Capital of the World® and Cargo Gateway of the Americas," contributing $61 billion annually to the local economy and supporting more than 340,000 jobs.
- Royal Caribbean Group (NYSE: RCL) has a global fleet of 69 ships across five brands, including Royal Caribbean, Celebrity Cruises and Silversea, plus Perfect Day at CocoCay and the Royal Beach Club collection, and owns a 50% joint venture interest in TUI Cruises.
- Media contact: Freddy Pereira, 786-626-9725.

wikis.title: Waldorf Astoria Hotel and Residences Miami
wikis.summary: Wikipedia's article on the under-construction Waldorf Astoria supertall skyscraper in downtown Miami, with its dimensions, schedule, team and sales.
wikis.body:
## The building

- "The Waldorf Astoria Hotel and Residences is a supertall skyscraper currently under construction in Miami, Florida." Status: under construction. Type: residential, hotel, retail.
- Location: 330 Biscayne Boulevard, Miami, Florida — on Biscayne Boulevard between NE 3rd and 4th Streets in the Central business district of Greater Downtown Miami, across from Bayfront Park. Coordinates 25°46′39″N 80°11′20″W.
- Built on the former site of the once-proposed Empire World Towers, "which were proposed and ultimately cancelled in the 2000s."
- Infobox: construction started 2022, estimated completion 2027, roof height 1,041 ft (317 m), floor count 100.
- Architect: Carlos Ott Architect. Developers: Property Markets Group, Greybrook Realty Partners, S2 Development. Main contractor: John Moriarty and Associates. Website: waldorfresidencesmiami.com.

## Height and schedule as described in the text

- "It will be the tallest building in the Southern United States, surpassing the 1,020-foot (311 m) Bank of America Plaza in Atlanta, and the 1,030-foot (314 m) Waterline tower nearing completion in Austin, Texas."
- Planned to rise to the maximum allowable height in downtown Miami of 1,049 ft (320 m) above sea level, or about 1,040 ft (317 m) above ground, making it the tallest building in Miami and Florida, surpassing the Panorama Tower built in 2017 and the 940-foot (286 m) Cipriani Residences Miami, which topped out in early 2026.
- "Construction began in late 2022 and is expected to top out in 2026 and be completed by January 2028." (The infobox instead gives estimated completion 2027.)
- An infobox image is captioned "Waldorf Astoria Miami in July 2026."

## Design

- The design incorporates deconstructivist elements, "resembling the City of Capitals skyscrapers in MIBC with its composition of stacked and cantilevered boxes."
- Nine cubes of 10 to 11 floors each, comprising nearly 100 stories of condominium and hotel space, topped by a five-floor penthouse with over 30,000 square feet (2,800 m2).
- Named after the Waldorf Astoria New York; worldwide Waldorf Astoria hotels are managed under the Hilton Hotels group.

## Sales

- "All one bedroom apartments in the skyscraper have been sold before construction was even completed. Prices now start at $3.3 million for a two bedroom apartment."
- "The five story, 33,000+ square foot penthouse atop of the structure was also sold for an undisclosed amount. It is the largest residential unit south of New York City."

wikis.title: MARTA Rapid A-Line bus rapid transit project
wikis.summary: MARTA's project page for the Rapid A-Line BRT route in Atlanta, covering its alignment, funding, schedule and service features.
wikis.body:
## Overview
