- EOLE was "declared of public utility on January 31, 2013" and extends the RER E westward to Mantes-la-Jolie in Yvelines, with 55 kilometres of new or renovated tracks, intended as an alternative to the congested central section of the RER A.
- Travel time between Mantes-la-Jolie and La Défense "should drop to 40 minutes from the current 55".
- In May 2024 three new stations opened — Neuilly-Porte Maillot, La Défense and Nanterre-la-Folie — initially with off-peak trains only; regular all-day service to Nanterre-la-Folie came in December 2024.
- The final phase involves "renovating and modernizing the 47 kilometers of existing tracks between Nanterre and Mantes-la-Jolie", serving Houilles - Carrières-sur-Seine, Poissy, Villennes-sur-Seine, Vernouillet-Verneuil, Les Clairières de Verneuil, Les Mureaux, Aubergenville-Elisabethville, Epône-Mézières, Mantes Station and Mantes-la-Jolie, the new terminus.
- Official project website: www.rer-eole.fr.

wikis.title: RER E extension to Mantes-la-Jolie: official service date
wikis.summary: The article itself: the EOLE project's second phase, with commercial service to Mantes-la-Jolie announced for 28 February 2027 and a gradual ramp-up of frequencies.
wikis.body:
## The EOLE project

- EOLE (East-West Express Delivery) is an Île-de-France project "declared of public utility on January 31, 2013", extending the RER E westward to Mantes-la-Jolie in Yvelines.
- "With a total of 55 kilometers of new or renovated tracks, the new RER E line is meant to give users an alternative to the RER A, whose central segment is regularly congested."
- "In the coming months, thanks to this extension, travel time between Mantes-la-Jolie and La Défense should drop to 40 minutes from the current 55."

## 2024 milestones

- Three new stations opened in May 2024: Neuilly-Porte Maillot, La Défense and Nanterre-la-Folie. "However, initially, trains only ran during off-peak hours."
- "It wasn't until December 2024 that this extension to Nanterre-la-Folie hit its stride, offering regular all-day service without the need to change trains."

## The final phase

- Mantes-la-Jolie "will be the new terminus and the final stop of the EOLE project".
- The extension "involves renovating and modernizing the 47 kilometers of existing tracks between Nanterre and Mantes-la-Jolie".
- Stations served include Houilles - Carrières-sur-Seine (connections to RER A and Transilien Line L), Poissy (connections to RER A and T13), Villennes-sur-Seine, Vernouillet-Verneuil, Les Clairières de Verneuil, Les Mureaux, Aubergenville-Elisabethville, Epône-Mézières, Mantes Station, and Mantes-la-Jolie (connections to Transilien lines J and N).

## Service date

- "At the Île-de-France Mayors' Fair, held on June 2 in Paris, project managers said the RER E will begin commercial service as far as Mantes-la-Jolie on February 28, 2027."
- "Please note that the rollout will be gradual. Starting February 28, 2027, four trains per hour will serve Mantes-la-Jolie. The ramp-up is expected to continue through the end of 2029, or perhaps into early 2030, with six trains per hour at peak times, according to the Mantes-la-Jolie website."
- Practical information given: official website www.rer-eole.fr. Published by Caroline de Sortiraparis, "Updated on August 18, 2026 at 04:10 p.m.".

wikis.title: Site listings following the article
wikis.summary: This part of the page holds only Sortiraparis's related-article and city-guide listings, with no content about the RER E extension.
wikis.body: This part of the source contains no article text about the RER E extension. It is made up of the site's repeated teaser listings for unrelated Sortiraparis articles (Paris weather forecasts, transport disruption round-ups, Pope Leo XIV's September 2026 visit to Paris, things to do in Paris), plus the live feed, city-guide links and footer.

wikis.title: Inside the Tour Triangle construction site in Paris
wikis.summary: France 3 Paris Île-de-France report from the Tour Triangle building site, giving its height, cost, floors, completion date of early 2027 and the judicial investigation hanging over the project.
wikis.body:
## The tower

- "Avec ses 180 mètres de hauteur, la tour Triangle va bientôt tutoyer la tour Montparnasse. Car déjà 35 des 44 étages ont été construits."
- A triangle rising 180 metres beside the périphérique at the porte de Versailles, in the 15th arrondissement of Paris.
- "90 000 mètres carrés sont construits, dont trois-quarts de bureaux. Un gratte-ciel à 700 millions d'euros."
- More than 650 workers are on site every day between 7h and 22h.

## Schedule

- Mourad Akl, directeur général du projet Triangle, Unibail-Rodamco-Westfield: "On est aujourd'hui au niveau du 35e étage. La forme extérieure, le gros œuvre et les façades sont prévus d'être achevés en fin d'année. On attaque toutes les finitions intérieures, les corps d'état architecturaux, la décoration, et tous les systèmes climatiques à l'intérieur pour une livraison finale début 2027."

## Contents of the building

- At street level: shops; a crèche halfway up; a hotel and restaurants; then a cultural centre and offices. The tower will have 44 floors in total.
- The entrance hall, with an XXL ceiling height, will be open to the public "comme dans un centre commercial".
- Jean Di Paolo, chef de chantier de la Tour Triangle-Besix, on the structure: "La difficulté de cette structure est la gestion des déformations. C'est un triangle. On a un noyau dur qui se trouve au centre, et des planchers qui se trouvent plus ou moins nord et sud... C'est comme un bateau : de temps en temps, ça bouge un peu plus à droite, de temps en temps, un peu plus à gauche."

## Environmental claims

- According to the project's promoters, everything is done to limit the building's impact: lifts that recover energy, specific glazing, and solar panels on the south façade to limit air-conditioning costs.
- Mourad Akl: "C'est une façade qu'on appelle 'la double peau', qui va bloquer 90 % des apports solaires tout en laissant pénétrer la lumière naturelle au quotidien pour limiter les besoins en éclairage artificiel. C'est une enveloppe qui est deux à trois fois plus efficace que les façades classiques."
- On neighbours' complaints that the tower glitters and dazzles: "On est sur des degrés de réflexion entre 25 et 28. Et donc, dans la lignée d'un immeuble comme le tribunal de grande instance dans le 17e arrondissement."

## The legal case

- The skyscraper "est menacé par l'ouverture d'une enquête et de soupçons de malversations".
- Built without a tender or an architecture competition, the project was the subject of a complaint filed by the association Anticor in 2020. "En avril dernier, le parquet financier auditionnait Elisabeth Borne, ancienne directrice de l'urbanisme à Paris."
- Olivier Rigaud, cofondateur du Collectif contre la Tour Triangle: "Une instruction a été ouverte au parquet national financier en 2021. On attend avec impatience que le procureur de la République financier décide d'ouvrir une procédure en jugement qui nous permettra ensuite de voir cette affaire jugée."
- A linked article on the page: "Tour Triangle à Paris : une information judiciaire ouverte pour des soupçons de favoritisme".
- Report by F. Hovasse, M. Tafnil and E. Peraud; article by Marc Taubert, with a 3 min 34 s video.

wikis.title: Construction begins on Torch Tower at TOKYO TORCH
wikis.summary: Mitsubishi Estate press release announcing the start of construction on Torch Tower, set to be Japan's tallest building at about 390 m, within the TOKYO TORCH redevelopment in front of Tokyo Station.
wikis.body:
## Groundbreaking

- "Mitsubishi Estate Co., Ltd. held a groundbreaking ceremony on September 27, 2023, to announce the start of construction of Torch Tower, the highest building in Japan once complete, in the 'TOKYO TORCH' district in front of the Nihonbashi Exit of Tokyo Station." It is being developed jointly with related rights holders.

## The TOKYO TORCH district

- A large-scale mixed-use redevelopment of approximately 3.1 hectares, "the largest site around the Tokyo Station", and the fourth project in the Chain Urban Renaissance Project in Otemachi. Four buildings are being developed over 10 years while maintaining the district's critical infrastructure, including a sewage pumping station and electricity substation.
- Tokiwabashi Tower was completed at the end of June 2021; the Zenigamecho Building at the end of March 2022.
- "Construction of Torch Tower and the substation building are scheduled for completion at the end of March 2028 together with TOKYO TORCH Park, a large 7,000 m2 plaza in the center of the district."

## Torch Tower

- "The Torch Tower is as the highest building in Japan at approximately 390 meters."
- A high-rise office building of approximately 6,700 m² on standard floors, with a large-scale commercial facility, an observation deck, a residence, an ultra-luxury hotel and a 2,000-seat hall, connected by the central plaza, an aerial walkway in the low-rise area and a rooftop garden.
- Usage composition: observatory (61-RF) with outdoor space; rental housing (59-60F), "the first luxury residence in Otemachi, Yurakucho and Marunouchi area"; hotel (53-58F); office (7-52F); Grand Hall (3-6F), a large-scale entertainment hall with approximately 2,000 seats; retail/park (B1-6F), with an outdoor plaza of approx. 2.0 ha.

## History of the district

- In the Edo period (1603-1867) people from all over Japan gathered in the district around Tokiwabashi Gate, the main entrance to Edo Castle. During the rapid growth of the 1960s the district was developed with infrastructure such as a sewage pumping station and an electricity substation, and office buildings such as the Nippon Building, "which was said to be the largest building in the East at the time".

## Environmental certifications

- Five environmental certifications obtained to date, plus two new international ones: LEED® BD+C (CS, Core & Shell) Gold precertification from the U.S. Green Building Council, and precertification for office use under the WELL Building Standard™ from the International WELL Building Institute. "Gold level certification is expected upon completion of construction."
- LEED precertification praised the openness to visitors through plaza and aerial walkways, high-efficiency equipment, and "efficient reuse of rainwater and wastewater". WELL precertification praised attention to health and safety, universal design, and preparedness for emergencies such as natural disasters.
- Peter Templeton, president and CEO of the U.S. Green Building Council: "Congratulations to Mitsubishi Estate by achieving LEED precertification for its iconic TOKYO TORCH Torch Tower."
- Rachel Hodgdon, IWBI President and CEO, congratulated Mitsubishi Estate "for achieving the WELL precertification for the office space of Japan's tallest skyscraper".
- The district is connected by two lines to a main substation in the Kanto region with a direct connection to Torch Tower, "ensuring a stable power supply".

## Project overview (from the table)

- Project name: Otemachi 2-chome Tokiwabashi area first class urban area redevelopment project (Executor: Mitsubishi Estate Co., Ltd.). Site: Otemachi 2-chome, Chiyoda-ku and Yaesu 1-chome, Chuo-ku, Tokyo. Site area approx. 31,400 m²; gross floor area approx. 740,000 m².
- Tokiwabashi Tower (Building A): office, retail, parking etc.; approx. 146,000 m²; 38 floors above ground / 5 below / approx. 212 metres; construction started January 2018, completed end of June 2021; construction by Toda Corporation.
- Torch Tower (Building B): office, rental housing, hotel, hall, retail, parking etc.; approx. 553,000 m²; 62 floors above ground / 4 below / approx. 390 metres; construction started September 2023, completion end of March 2028 (planned); construction by Shimizu Corporation.
- Electricity Substation (Building C): retail, electrical substation, parking etc.; approx. 20,000 m²; Phase I from January 2018 completed end of June 2021, Phase II from September 2023 to end of March 2028 (planned).
- Building For Sewage Bureau (Building D): office, sewage pumping station, parking etc.; approx. 30,000 m²; approx. 53 metres; construction April 2017 to end of March 2022.
- Design and supervision by Mitsubishi Jisho Design Inc. (with Nihon Suiko Sekkei Co., Ltd. for Building D).
- Related rights holders: Mitsubishi Estate Co., Ltd., Tokyo Century Corporation, Tokyo Metropolitan Government Bureau of Sewerage, Daiwa Securities Group Inc., Isetan Mitsukoshi Holdings Ltd., TEPCO Power Grid, Inc., Otemachi Development Co., Ltd., Urban Renaissance Agency, and others.
- A note says: "The information given in this press release is subject to change as studies and discussions continue."

## Community programmes

- TOKYO TORCH Park, partly opened in advance, hosts collaborations with local communities across Japan, including a koi pond and koi art playground equipment from Ojiya City, Niigata; gold ore from Sado Island; zoysia from Tsukuba City; a green area from Susono City, Shizuoka; and a giant Akabeko from Fukushima Prefecture (some items not currently in place).
- The TOKYO TORCH Market has been held since September 2021 with local communities, in cooperation with Agri Innovation Design.

## Marunouchi context

- Under "MARUNOUCHI REDESIGN" and "Marunouchi Next Stage", Yurakucho and the Tokiwabashi area are designated priority improvement areas, with "approximately 600 to 700 billion yen (our share)" invested in rebuilding and software development through 2030.
- The pipeline listed gives Torch Tower a total floor area of 553,000 m² and "Completion: FY2027".

wikis.title: Port Houston completes its portion of Project 11 dredging
wikis.summary: Port Houston press release announcing completion of its dredging for the Houston Ship Channel Expansion Project 11, widening the Galveston Bay reach, with the environmental features, economic estimates and navigation changes that follow.
wikis.body:
## The milestone

- Port Houston, working with the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE), "has completed its portion of the Houston Ship Channel Expansion Project 11".
- Construction of channel improvements began in 2022; the project "has reached its most important milestone dredging completion of the widening of the Galveston Bay reach from Bolivar Roads to Morgans Point. With this work done, Port Houston-led project dredging of the Houston Ship Channel is complete."
- The channel through Galveston Bay is widened "from 530 feet to 700 feet".
- Port Commission Chairman Ric Campo commended "the incredible Port Houston team, our bipartisan federal and local delegations, and our industry and federal partners", calling it "a testament to the hard work of all the individuals involved in the project".

## Remaining work

- "While Port-led dredging is now complete for navigation, some beneficial use aspects of the project remain under construction, including marsh areas that are being built with dredged material."
- The USACE "will lead the remaining portions of the project, which are scheduled to be completed in 2029".

## Environmental features

- Project 11 dredged material in the Galveston Bay area was used, to the extent possible, to construct environmental features that "will ultimately include approximately 10 acres of bird islands, 276 acres of marsh, and 324 acres of oyster reefs".
- Vessel nitrogen oxide emissions "are expected to be reduced by between three percent and seven percent".
- Dredges contracted for the first three segments were equipped with Tier 3 or Tier 4 engines or scrubbers.

## The channel and economics

- "The 52-mile-long Houston Ship Channel serves more than 200 private facilities and eight public terminals", in industries from petrochemicals and heavy machinery to consumer goods and energy.
- In a report released earlier this year, the USACE recognized the channel as the busiest waterway in the United States, "handling approximately 12% of the nation's total waterborne tonnage".
- A 2022 third-party economic impact study: the channel "supports 3.37 million jobs nationwide and generates $906 billion in annual economic activity in the United States".
- "A draft study by the Perryman Group estimates that by 2040, Segment 1 of Project 11 alone will generate $60.95 billion in statewide economic benefit and add 440,665 jobs in Texas." Port Houston anticipates publishing the study when finalized.

## Navigation changes

- Based on Project 11 improvements, research initiatives and full mission bridge simulations, the Houston Pilots have revised their Navigation Safety Guidelines.
- "Daylight restricted vessels now have up to an additional two and a half hours to transit into and out of port each day", allowing more time for two-way vessel movements; harbor assist tug and dock operations are expected to see greater predictability, reduced congestion and improved asset utilization.
- Earlier project phases let the Pilots increase permissible container ship size at Bayport Container Terminal: "vessels between 15,000 and 17,000 TEU - matching the capacity of the Panama Canal - can now safely call Bayport".

## Background and awards

- Planning of Project 11 began in 2010, "when Port Houston leadership, working with Congress and the USACE, recognized the need to widen and deepen the channel". The team accelerated the project "by working in parallel versus typical sequential steps related to specific federal authorizations".
- Awards include the 2025 Environmental Excellence Award from the Western Dredging Association (WEDA) and the 2025 Texas ASCE Outstanding Civil Engineering Achievement Award (OCEA).
- About Port Houston: it has owned and operated the public wharves and terminals along the Houston Ship Channel for more than 100 years; the Port of Houston "supports the creation of nearly 1.5 million jobs in Texas and 3.37 million jobs nationwide, and economic activity totaling $439 billion in Texas and $906 billion in economic impact across the nation".
- Contact: Lisa Ashley-Daniels, Director, Public Relations.

wikis.title: The Employment Situation - April 2023 (BLS news release)
wikis.summary: The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics news release for April 2023, reporting a 253,000 rise in nonfarm payroll employment and a 3.4 percent unemployment rate, with the full household and establishment survey tables.
wikis.body:
## Headline figures for April 2023

- "Total nonfarm payroll employment rose by 253,000 in April, and the unemployment rate changed little at 3.4 percent, the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reported today."
- Unemployed persons 5.7 million; the unemployment rate "has ranged from 3.4 percent to 3.7 percent since March 2022".
- Labor force participation rate 62.6 percent and employment-population ratio 60.4 percent, both unchanged and below their February 2020 levels of 63.3 percent and 61.1 percent.
- The 253,000 gain compares with an average monthly gain of 290,000 over the prior 6 months.

## Where the jobs were

Professional and business services +43,000 (professional, scientific and technical services +45,000; temporary help services -23,000), health care +40,000, leisure and hospitality +31,000, social assistance +25,000, financial activities +23,000, government +23,000, mining/quarrying/oil and gas extraction +6,000. Construction, manufacturing, wholesale and retail trade, transportation and warehousing, information and other services were little changed.

## Pay and hours

Average hourly earnings for all private nonfarm employees rose 16 cents, or 0.5 percent, to $33.36, up 4.4 percent over 12 months; production and nonsupervisory earnings rose 11 cents to $28.62. The average workweek was unchanged at 34.4 hours.

## Revisions

February was revised down 78,000 to +248,000 and March down 71,000 to +165,000, leaving the two months combined 149,000 lower than previously reported.

## Other measures

Alternative measures of labor underutilization for April 2023, seasonally adjusted: U-3 (official rate) 3.4 percent, U-6 6.6 percent. Long-term unemployed (27 weeks or more) 1.2 million, 20.6 percent of the unemployed. Persons not in the labor force who want a job rose 346,000 to 5.3 million.

## Dates

Embargoed until 8:30 a.m. (ET) Friday, May 5, 2023; release number USDL-23-0871. "The Employment Situation for May is scheduled to be released on Friday, June 2, 2023, at 8:30 a.m. (ET)."

## About this source

A 39-page PDF split into three parts: part 1 has the release text, summary tables A and B, an eight-question FAQ and the technical note; part 2 has household data tables A-3 through A-16 and the start of Table B-1; part 3 has the rest of the establishment data tables B-1 through B-9. The household survey samples about 60,000 households; the establishment survey covers about 122,000 businesses and government agencies representing approximately 666,000 worksites. March and April establishment figures are preliminary, and the data reflect March 2022 benchmark levels and updated seasonal adjustment factors.

wikis.title: The Employment Situation - April 2023: BLS news release text, summary tables and technical note
wikis.summary: The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics news release for April 2023, giving the month's payroll and unemployment figures, industry detail, earnings and hours, revisions, summary tables A and B, an FAQ and the technical note.
wikis.body:
## Release details

- "Transmission of material in this news release is embargoed until 8:30 a.m. (ET) Friday, May 5, 2023". Release number USDL-23-0871. Source file is a 39-page PDF posted at dol.gov.
- Contacts: household data (202) 691-6378, cpsinfo@bls.gov; establishment data (202) 691-6555, cesinfo@bls.gov; media (202) 691-5902, PressOffice@bls.gov.
- "The Employment Situation for May is scheduled to be released on Friday, June 2, 2023, at 8:30 a.m. (ET)."

## Headline

"Total nonfarm payroll employment rose by 253,000 in April, and the unemployment rate changed little at 3.4 percent, the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reported today. Employment continued to trend up in professional and business services, health care, leisure and hospitality, and social assistance."

## Household survey data (April 2023)

- Unemployment rate 3.4 percent; unemployed persons 5.7 million; both changed little. The rate "has ranged from 3.4 percent to 3.7 percent since March 2022".
- Rates by group, all little or no change: adult men 3.3 percent, adult women 3.1 percent, teenagers 9.2 percent, Whites 3.1 percent, Blacks 4.7 percent, Asians 2.8 percent, Hispanics 4.4 percent.
- Job losers and persons who completed temporary jobs fell by 307,000 to 2.6 million.
- Persons jobless less than 5 weeks fell by 406,000 to 1.9 million; long-term unemployed (27 weeks or more) little changed at 1.2 million, 20.6 percent of the total unemployed.
- Labor force participation rate 62.6 percent and employment-population ratio 60.4 percent, both unchanged and both below their pre-pandemic February 2020 levels of 63.3 percent and 61.1 percent.
- Part time for economic reasons 3.9 million, little changed.
- Persons not in the labor force who currently want a job rose by 346,000 to 5.3 million; marginally attached rose by 191,000 to 1.5 million; discouraged workers little changed at 364,000.

## Establishment survey data (April 2023)

- Total nonfarm payroll employment +253,000, against an average monthly gain of 290,000 over the prior 6 months.
- Professional and business services +43,000 (prior 6-month average 25,000); professional, scientific and technical services +45,000; temporary help services -23,000, down 174,000 since its peak in March 2022.
- Health care +40,000 (prior 6-month average 47,000): ambulatory health care services +24,000, nursing and residential care facilities +9,000, hospitals +7,000.
- Leisure and hospitality +31,000, largely food services and drinking places +25,000; prior 6-month average 73,000 per month; the industry remains 402,000, or 2.4 percent, below its February 2020 level.
- Social assistance +25,000 (prior 6-month average 21,000); individual and family services +21,000.
- Financial activities +23,000, with insurance carriers and related activities +15,000 and real estate +9,000.
- Government +23,000 (prior 6-month average 52,000); government employment is 301,000, or 1.3 percent, below February 2020.
- Mining, quarrying, and oil and gas extraction +6,000, up 102,000 since a recent low in February 2021, nearly all in support activities for mining.
- Little changed: construction, manufacturing, wholesale trade, retail trade, transportation and warehousing, information, other services.

## Earnings and hours

- Average hourly earnings for all private nonfarm employees +16 cents, or 0.5 percent, to $33.36; up 4.4 percent over the past 12 months.
- Production and nonsupervisory employees +11 cents, or 0.4 percent, to $28.62.
- Average workweek unchanged at 34.4 hours; manufacturing workweek little changed at 40.2 hours with overtime at 2.9 hours; production and nonsupervisory workweek edged down 0.1 hour to 33.8 hours.

## Revisions

February was revised down by 78,000, from +326,000 to +248,000, and March was revised down by 71,000, from +236,000 to +165,000; "employment in February and March combined is 149,000 lower than previously reported."

## Summary table A (household data, seasonally adjusted, thousands)

- April 2023: civilian noninstitutional population 266,443; civilian labor force 166,688 (participation rate 62.6); employed 161,031 (employment-population ratio 60.4); unemployed 5,657 (rate 3.4); not in labor force 99,755. Change from March 2023: labor force -43, employed +139, unemployed -182, rate -0.1, not in labor force +214.
- Unemployment rates by educational attainment, 25 years and over, April 2023: total 2.9; less than a high school diploma 5.4 (up 0.6 over the month); high school graduates no college 3.9; some college or associate degree 2.9; bachelor's degree and higher 1.9.
- Reason for unemployment, April 2023: job losers and completed temporary jobs 2,642 (-307); job leavers 790; reentrants 1,761; new entrants 531.
- Duration: less than 5 weeks 1,866 (-406); 5 to 14 weeks 1,915; 15 to 26 weeks 679; 27 weeks and over 1,156.
- Part time for economic reasons 3,903 (-199); slack work or business conditions 2,760; could only find part-time work 817; part time for noneconomic reasons 21,796.
- Marginally attached 1,480 (+191); discouraged workers 364 (+13).

## Summary table B (establishment data, seasonally adjusted)

- Over-the-month change April 2023 (thousands): total nonfarm +253; total private +230; goods-producing +33; mining and logging +7; construction +15; manufacturing +11; private service-providing +197; wholesale trade -2.2; retail trade +7.7; transportation and warehousing +10.6; utilities +1.0; information +1; financial activities +23; professional and business services +43 (temporary help services -23.3); private education and health services +77 (health care and social assistance +64.2); leisure and hospitality +31; other services +5; government +23.
- Three-month average change: total nonfarm 222; total private 182 (against 295 and 223 for March 2023).
- Hours and earnings, all employees, total private, April 2023: average weekly hours 34.4; average hourly earnings $33.36; average weekly earnings $1,147.58; index of aggregate weekly hours (2007=100) 114.9, +0.2 percent over the month; index of aggregate weekly payrolls 183.3, +0.7 percent.
- Diffusion index over a 1-month span: total private (250 industries) 57.4; manufacturing (72 industries) 45.1.
- "p Preliminary" marks March and April figures. "Data have been revised to reflect March 2022 benchmark levels and updated seasonal adjustment factors."

## Frequently asked questions

Eight questions cover why there are two monthly measures of employment (an over-the-month change of about 130,000 is statistically significant in the establishment survey, versus about 600,000 in the household survey), whether undocumented immigrants are counted (likely at least some, but legal status is not identified), why the establishment survey revises (twice in the succeeding 2 months, plus an annual benchmark), small-firm coverage (about 40 percent of the sample has fewer than 20 employees), the birth-death adjustment, the fact that unemployment is not limited to insurance recipients, the treatment of people who want a job but are not looking, and the effects of severe weather.

## Technical note

- The household survey (CPS) samples about 60,000 eligible households and is conducted by the U.S. Census Bureau for BLS; its data appear in the "A" tables.
- The establishment survey (CES) surveys about 122,000 businesses and government agencies representing approximately 666,000 individual worksites, about one-third of all nonfarm payroll jobs; its data appear in the "B" tables.
- Reference periods: household survey, the calendar week containing the 12th of the month; establishment survey, the pay period including the 12th.
- Industries are classified using the 2022 version of the North American Industry Classification System.
- Reliability: the confidence interval for the monthly change in total nonfarm employment is on the order of plus or minus 130,000; at an unemployment rate of around 6.0 percent, the 90-percent confidence interval for the monthly change in unemployment is about +/- 300,000 and for the rate about +/- 0.2 percentage point. BLS analyses are generally conducted at the 90-percent level of confidence.

## Tables begun in this part

Table A-1 (employment status of the civilian population by sex and age), Table A-2 (by race, sex, and age) and the start of Table A-3 (Hispanic or Latino population by sex and age). Table A-2 example, Asian, April 2023 seasonally adjusted: civilian labor force 11,396; participation rate 64.9; employed 11,073; employment-population ratio 63.1; unemployed 323; unemployment rate 2.8.

wikis.title: California High-Speed Rail Authority 2025 Supplemental Project Update Report
wikis.summary: The Authority's August 2025 supplemental report to the California Legislature, presenting a reassessed program with three buildout scenarios - Merced-Bakersfield, Gilroy-Bakersfield and Gilroy-Palmdale - their costs, ridership, revenue and funding needs, plus the policy and funding changes the Authority says it needs.
wikis.body:
## The report

- "2025 SUPPLEMENTAL PROJECT UPDATE REPORT" of the California High-Speed Rail Authority, led by CEO Ian Choudri with Tom Richards as board chair. The capture covers the first 50 pages of a 112-page PDF: the CEO letter, the statutory-requirements tables, Chapters 1 to 3 and the start of Appendices A and B.
- It presents "early results from the holistic reassessment of the high-speed rail program" that Choudri ordered, and says its scenarios "are intended to support the Newsom Administration and California State Legislature's discussions as they evaluate the next steps for the program".

## The three scenarios

| Scenario | Cost | Funding needed | 40-year net operating profit/loss |
|---|---|---|---|
| Merced - Bakersfield | $36.75bn | $8.59bn | -3.8 |
| SF - Gilroy - Bakersfield | $54.38bn | $26.22bn | +47.5 |
| SF - Gilroy - Bakersfield (incl. Merced) | $58.10bn | $29.94bn | +45.9 |
| SF - Gilroy - Palmdale | $87.12bn | $58.96bn | +98.1 |
| SF - Gilroy - Palmdale (incl. Merced) | $90.85bn | $62.69bn | +96.8 |

(Figures in $ billions; costs include a P65 level of contingency.)

- **Merced - Bakersfield**, the statutorily required 171-mile early operating segment, has "an updated revenue service start date of January 1, 2032". Ridership 1.6-2.2 million a year on eight round trips a day; passenger revenue $39.28-$55.60 million against operations and maintenance of $120.60-$122.10 million, a recovery ratio of 45.27% to 74.31%. The Authority states plainly that it "would not be able to cover its total operational expenses" as a standalone line. Reassessment offset "$14.28 billion in cost increases, which is a cost savings of 30 percent", against roughly $51 billion otherwise.
- **Gilroy - Bakersfield** would run through to San Francisco over Caltrain: ridership 8.71-11.83 million, passenger revenue $623.72-$882.93 million, O&M $419.19-$435.47 million, recovery ratio 163.61%-257.39%; $54.4 billion, operational by early 2038.
- **Gilroy - Palmdale** adds Metrolink/Surfliner and, via the High Desert Corridor, Brightline West connections: ridership 12.46-17.94 million, passenger revenue $1.1-$1.6 billion, O&M $602-$635 million, recovery ratio 191.93%-314.52%; $87.12 billion, operational in early 2038.
- Gilroy - San Jose improvements on the Union Pacific line are excluded from those costs and "may range from $3.0 billion to $6.0 billion".

## Funding

- Current capital funding of $28.16 billion, including an estimated $5.5 billion from Cap-and-Invest through 2030 and "the $4.0 billion in federal funding, currently the subject of litigation". The Governor's proposal to extend Cap-and-Invest to 2045 at "at least $1.0 billion" a year would add at least $15 billion, "bringing the Authority's total capital funding to $43.16 billion".
- Chapter 3 sets out repayment terms from 15 to 45 years: financing Gilroy - Bakersfield over 15 years would cost $2.29 billion a year against $1.63 billion over 30 years.
- SB 198 (2022) prioritized the Merced - Bakersfield EOS and "imposed a $500 million cap on Authority expenditures outside the Central Valley"; the Authority asks the Legislature to remove or adjust it. Its June 26, 2025 Request for Expressions of Interest for P3s "yielded 31 responses".

## Policy asks and the federal grant fight

- SB 131, signed June 30, 2025, gave targeted CEQA streamlining for high-speed rail stations and maintenance facilities; the Authority also asks for a CEQA exemption for clean power interconnection, permitting reform for a long linear project, dedicated court resources for the "nearly 2,300 parcels required for the initial 119-mile segment and an estimated 530 for the extensions", and enforceable third-party timelines.
- The FRA "issued a decision to terminate the cooperative agreements" for the $928.62 million FY10 grants and the nearly $3.1 billion Federal-State Partnership grant on July 16, 2025, "even though no fraud, waste, or abuse was identified"; the Authority sued on July 17, 2025 under the Administrative Procedure Act, and the funds will not be transferred to another grantee while litigation is pending.

## Benefits claimed

Nearly $22 billion in economic output generated since the project began; a construction fleet producing "62 percent less emissions than a typical California construction fleet"; more than 400 avoided air-pollution deaths over a 50-year operational period; and, by scenario, economic output during construction of $65.95 billion (284,000 job years) to $138.01 billion (594,000 job years).

## Contradictions within the report

- The Gilroy - Bakersfield with Merced Extension text gives passenger revenue as "$626 billion to $886 billion", while Table 1.3 for the same scenario gives "$626.03 to $886.20" under the heading "($ in millions)".
- The CEO's letter looks to "a future by 2038 to 2039 when operations are already connecting the Central Valley to population centers", while Chapter 1 sets "a target operational date of 2038" and separately says the Authority "aims to have these operational within the next 15 years".
- The letter says the Merced - Bakersfield segment will "begin operations by 2032"; Chapter 1 says completion "prior to 2033, with an updated revenue service start date of January 1, 2032".
- Statutory requirement (F) appears in the requirements table as milestones "during the prior year" and "in the coming year", while Appendix A quotes the statute as "the prior two-year period" and "the coming two-year period".

## Dates

The report identifies itself as "the supplemental August 2025 PUR". The only dated item is the acting chief counsel's memo, "DATE: August 15, 2025". No publication or last-updated date is stated for the document itself.

wikis.title: 2025 Supplemental Project Update Report: CEO letter, statutory requirements and the three buildout scenarios
wikis.summary: Part 1 of the California High-Speed Rail Authority's 2025 Supplemental Project Update Report, covering the CEO's letter and program reassessment, the statutory requirements tables, the Merced-Bakersfield, Gilroy-Bakersfield and Gilroy-Palmdale business cases with their costs and ridership, the environmental and economic benefits, and the start of the policy chapter.
wikis.body:
## The document

- Title page: "2025 SUPPLEMENTAL PROJECT UPDATE REPORT", California High-Speed Rail Authority. The capture is noted as "[PDF, 112 pages; text of the first 50]".
- Board of Directors: Tom Richards (Chair), Nancy Miller (Vice Chair), Ernesto M. Camacho, Emily Cohen, Martha M. Escutia, Henry Perea, Lynn Schenk, Anthony Williams. Ex officio: Honorable Juan Carrillo, Honorable Lena Gonzalez. Chief Executive Officer: Ian Choudri.
- Mission statement: the Authority "is responsible for planning, designing, building, and operating the first high-speed rail system in the nation."
- Contents: Chapter 1 (Connecting the Central Valley to San Francisco and Los Angeles County), Chapter 2 (Policy and Funding Changes to Accelerate Project Delivery), Chapter 3 (Funding to Deliver California High-Speed Rail), and Appendices A through L plus endnotes.
- The report says the statutory requirements are satisfied "from both the March 2025 PUR and the supplemental August 2025 PUR", with "[a]dditional clarification ... where the Authority will provide more information in the 2026 Business Plan". No day-level publication date is stated in this part.

## Headline figures

- Current capital funding: "$28.16 billion in capital funding, which includes an estimated $5.5 billion from Cap-and-Invest through 2030 and retention of federally awarded funds." The Governor's FY 2025-26 budget proposal to extend Cap-and-Invest through 2045 with at least $1.0 billion a year "would provide at least $15 billion in additional funding for the program, bringing the Authority's total capital funding to $43.16 billion."
- "For purposes of this report, the Authority included the $4.0 billion in federal funding, currently the subject of litigation, as part of its total capital funding figures."
- Merced - Bakersfield: 171-mile early operating segment, now estimated at $36.75 billion, revenue service start date of January 1, 2032.
- San Francisco - Gilroy - Bakersfield: $54.38 billion, operational by early 2038.
- San Francisco - Gilroy - Palmdale: $87.12 billion, operational in early 2038.
- Gilroy - San Jose improvements are "additional costs not included in the scenarios, which may range from $3.0 billion to $6.0 billion."
- Table 1.5 (cost / funding needed / 40-year net operating profit or loss, $ in billions): Merced - Bakersfield 36.75 / 8.59 / -3.8; SF - Gilroy - Bakersfield 54.38 / 26.22 / +47.5; SF - Gilroy - Bakersfield incl. Merced 58.10 / 29.94 / +45.9; SF - Gilroy - Palmdale 87.12 / 58.96 / +98.1; SF - Gilroy - Palmdale incl. Merced 90.85 / 62.69 / +96.8. Construction cost estimates "include a P65 level of contingency".

## Contradictions and inconsistencies within this part

- Units in the Merced-extension text: the Gilroy - Bakersfield with Merced Extension passage says ridership "would result in similar passenger revenue of $626 billion to $886 billion", while Table 1.3 for the same scenario gives "$626.03 to $886.20" with the heading "($ in millions)".
- Opening date wording: the CEO's letter says "I see a future by 2038 to 2039 when operations are already connecting the Central Valley to population centers and innovation hubs", while Chapter 1 states the Gilroy - Bakersfield and Gilroy - Palmdale segments would be "operational by early 2038" and sets "a target operational date of 2038"; the same Chapter 1 passage also says the Authority "aims to have these operational within the next 15 years".
- Merced - Bakersfield completion: the CEO's letter says the Authority "is on track to complete that segment and begin operations by 2032", while Chapter 1 says it will be completed "within the original schedule envelope and prior to 2033, with an updated revenue service start date of January 1, 2032".
- Statutory requirement (F) is listed in the requirements table as "A summary of milestones achieved during the prior year and milestones expected to be reached in the coming year", while Appendix A quotes Section 185033.5 as "milestones achieved during the prior two-year period and milestones expected to be reached in the coming two-year period".
- Scenario naming: Chapter 1's third scenario is "Gilroy - Palmdale", but Table 1.6's emissions rows label the same cases "SF - Gilroy -Palmdale - Victorville".

wikis.title: Letter from the CEO and the program reassessment
wikis.summary: Ian Choudri's letter opening the report, the holistic reassessment he ordered and the four-step 'right-sizing' process.
wikis.body:
- Pull quote: "I see clearer now more than ever the potential for this transformational project, one that can reshape the state and our society for the better. I see a future by 2038 to 2039 when operations are already connecting the Central Valley to population centers and innovation hubs, offering new career opportunities, economic mobility, affordable housing, and a cleaner environment."
- Choudri says he stepped into the CEO role "last September". He writes that "No other true high-speed rail project in North America is under active construction, let alone made as much tangible progress as California's" and that the Authority is "preparing to procure the track, equipment, and materials required to launch the nation's first high-speed track and systems installation within the next year."
- He lists the program's hurdles as "a lack of continuous political support, insufficient jurisdictional authority, costly and duplicative regulatory requirements, and chronic underfunding", and compares the difficulties to "the Interstate Highway System to the Big Dig, the Northeast Corridor, or the Hoover Dam".
- At his direction the Authority undertook "a holistic reassessment of the entire program", reviewing the organizational structure, culture, suitability of the design criteria, scope of what was being built, cost estimates, procurement strategy, ridership projections, risks, and the overall delivery timeline.
- "As required by statute, the Authority is currently focused on completion of the 171-mile Merced – Bakersfield early operating segment (EOS) and is on track to complete that segment and begin operations by 2032." Appendix B provides the evaluation and "incorporates recommendations from the Authority's Office of the Inspector General."
- The segments with business cases are listed as Merced - Bakersfield, Gilroy - Bakersfield and Gilroy - Palmdale. The letter ends "Let's go build it."
- "Right-Sizing the Program" describes four steps taken "[o]ver the past six months": completing design reviews to minimize costs; making trade-off decisions for greater efficiency; sequencing construction and making funding go further; and reviewing estimating methods for greater reliability using "a bottom-up method to assess design, materials, and labor components of each scope element".
- Photo captions in this part record construction facts: a worker ties rebar on the Tied Arch Bridge over State Route 43 in Fresno County; "The Conejo Viaduct, west of State Route 43 in Fresno County, will be 2,000 feet long when complete"; "Workers have placed the remaining 112 girders over the San Joaquin Valley Railroad for the Hanford Viaduct"; "The Kimberlina Viaduct in Kern County will take high-speed trains over Kimberlina Road. It was completed in February 2023"; "The Avenue 56 Grade Separation in Tulare County was completed in June 2025 and spans a length of 219 feet."

wikis.title: Statutory requirements tables
wikis.summary: Where the report says each statutory requirement of the Project Update Report is answered, across the March 2025 and August 2025 reports.
wikis.body:
The tables list requirements for Project Update Reports and where the March 2025 PUR and the supplemental August 2025 PUR satisfy each. A legal memo from the acting chief counsel is in Appendix A.

General requirements (March 2025 PUR / August 2025 PUR):
- (A) Overall progress summary - CEO Letter pages V to VII and Chapter 2 pages 9 to 17 / Appendix B pages 37-50 and Appendix E pages 60-63.
- (B) Baseline budget by segment or contract from the Revised 2012 Business Plan - Chapter 3 pages 19 to 30 / Appendix B page 49.
- (C) Current and projected budget - Chapter 3 pages 19 to 30 / Appendix B pages 41-42 and Appendix C pages 51-52.
- (D) Expenditures to date - Chapter 3 pages 19 to 30 / Appendix B pages 41-42, Appendix C pages 51-52.
- (E) Comparison of current and projected work schedule with the 2012 baseline - Appendix D page 55 / Appendix D page 59.
- (F) Milestones achieved and expected - Chapter 2 pages 9 to 17 / Appendix B pages 37-50, Appendix E pages 60-63.
- (G) Issues identified in the prior two-year period - Chapter 4 pages 33 to 40.
- (H) Risks and mitigation - Chapter 4 pages 33 to 40 / Appendix F pages 64-70.

AB 95 requirements (A) to (G) - the 119-mile dual track segment from Madera to Poplar Avenue, right-of-way and advance engineering for the Merced and Bakersfield extensions, the agreements with the San Joaquin Joint Powers Authority and San Joaquin Regional Rail Commission, an updated cost estimate with a stated probability level, a funding plan, and additional milestones - are all marked "*" for March 2025 and answered in Appendix B pages 41-47 in August 2025.

SB 198 cost and funding requirements (A) to (E) are likewise marked "*" for March 2025 and answered at Appendix B pages 41-42; (F) progress on milestones cites the CEO letter pages V to VIII and Chapter 2 pages 9 to 17 for March, and the CEO letter pages IX to XI, Appendix B pages 44-45, Appendix E pages 60-63 and Appendix I pages 78-80 for August; (G) funding commitments beyond Merced to Bakersfield cites Chapter 3 page 23. SB 198 delivery schedules are answered "More information will be available in the 2026 Business Plan."

The footnote explains: "*Indicates where previously the Authority stated in the 2025 March PUR it would update its cost and schedule estimates, as well as operating agreement schedules, ridership, and additional milestones required later this year with a supplemental report."

wikis.title: Scenario 1: Merced - Bakersfield (project underway)
wikis.summary: The cost, schedule, ridership, revenue and recovery ratio for the statutorily required 171-mile early operating segment.
wikis.body:
- "The Merced - Bakersfield scenario, as shown in Exhibit 1.0, is now estimated to cost $36.75 billion."
- "By resequencing work, refining design criteria, and adopting innovative engineering methods, the Authority was able to offset $14.28 billion in cost increases, which is a cost savings of 30 percent. Without the program reassessment, scope increases, inflation (bringing prices from 2022 to 2024) and added cost and contingency for the Central Valley would have increased the Merced – Bakersfield segment costs to approximately $51 billion."
- Risks are outlined in Appendix F, "such as ongoing tariff and trade wars".
- The Authority "is set to complete the 119-mile Central Valley Segment (CVS) currently under construction and the Merced and Bakersfield extensions within the original schedule envelope and prior to 2033, with an updated revenue service start date of January 1, 2032."
- Table 1.0, "Merced – Bakersfield 2030 Financial Outlook ($ in millions)", figures in 2024 tax dollars: passenger revenue $39.28 to $55.60; ancillary revenue net income $15.99 to $34.02; operations and maintenance $120.60 to $122.10; recovery ratio 45.27% to 74.31%.
- Passenger revenue is based on "projected annual high speed rail ridership figures of 1.6 million to 2.2 million", from "eight round trips per day of high-speed rail only service". Ancillary revenue sources given as parking, retail, advertising and broadband.
- "These estimates indicate that this specific scenario would not achieve a positive profitable outcome ... the Merced – Bakersfield corridor operating as a standalone high-speed rail line with transfer connections to other rail services would not be able to cover its total operational expenses. The Authority will continue to explore contracting for service by a third-party, such as the San Joaquin Joint Powers Authority".
- "Assuming a baseline of at least $1.0 billion per year in Cap-and-Invest program funding through 2045, as contained in the Governor's proposal, the Merced – Bakersfield segment will no longer have a budgetary funding gap. However, the Authority will need to work with the Administration and Legislature to solve the timing of future cash receipts with capital expenses".
- Table 1.5 gives this scenario a funding need of $8.59 billion and a 40-year net operating profit/loss of -3.8 ($ in billions).

wikis.title: Scenario 2: Gilroy - Bakersfield (San Francisco to Bakersfield)
wikis.summary: The second business case, extending the system north to Gilroy for through service to San Francisco over Caltrain.
wikis.body:
- The Authority "would sequence construction to leverage Central Valley infrastructure while extending the high-speed rail system north and west to Gilroy. High-speed trains would continue to San Francisco, utilizing existing Caltrain infrastructure and a coordinated state solution to connect to the section from San Jose to Gilroy."
- Construction on this extension can start "while work on the section from the Central Valley Wye to Bakersfield is underway". The scenario "would also rely on improvements between Gilroy and San Jose and on Caltrain electrification to run hourly through service to San Francisco."
- Ridership 8.71 million to 11.83 million, giving passenger revenue of $623.72 million to $882.93 million a year. Ancillary revenue around $89 million to $196 million. Operating and maintenance costs $419.19 million to $435.47 million. Recovery ratio "between 164 percent and 257 percent" (Table 1.1 gives 163.61% to 257.39%).
- "This segment is estimated to cost $54.4 billion and would be operational by early 2038." To help fund it "the state could re-sequence the Merced extension. These savings could be reallocated toward building the system to Gilroy."
- Direct high-speed rail service to San Francisco is described as "a transformative opportunity to engage the private sector through potential public-private partnership (P3) delivery models."
- With the Merced extension included: ridership 8.77 million to 11.91 million; ancillary revenue about $92 million to $202 million; O&M rising to $441 million to $457 million; recovery ratio between 157 percent and 246 percent (Table 1.3: 156.79% to 246.45%); cost estimated at $58.1 billion, operational by early 2038. The text states the passenger revenue as "$626 billion to $886 billion" while Table 1.3 gives $626.03 to $886.20 in millions.

wikis.title: Scenario 3: Gilroy - Palmdale (San Francisco to Los Angeles County)
wikis.summary: The largest business case, extending infrastructure to Palmdale with Metrolink and Brightline West connections.
wikis.body:
- The scenario extends high-speed rail infrastructure to Palmdale, leveraging Central Valley infrastructure and relying on other improvements between Gilroy and San Francisco.
- "Two hourly high-speed trains would operate from San Francisco to Palmdale, one as a limited-stop express. With the High Desert Corridor, one train per hour would continue to Victor Valley, where passengers could connect with Brightline West service to Rancho Cucamonga and Las Vegas. At Palmdale, trains could connect with a Metrolink/Surfliner express service to Los Angeles and San Diego".
- Ridership 12.46 million to 17.94 million; passenger revenue $1.1 billion to $1.6 billion annually (Table 1.2: $1,109.35 to $1,641.23 million); ancillary revenue around $110 million to $254 million (Table 1.2: $110.40 to $253.70 million); operating and maintenance costs between $602 million and $635 million (Table 1.2: $602.48 to $635.52 million); recovery ratio 191 percent to 314 percent (Table 1.2: 191.93% to 314.52%).
- "The Gilroy – Palmdale scenario is estimated to cost $87.12 billion and would be operational in early 2038."
- With the Merced extension: ridership 12.52 million to 18.02 million, passenger revenue $1.1 billion to $1.6 billion (Table 1.4: $1,111.69 to $1,640.70 million), ancillary revenue around $114 million to $260 million, O&M rising to $625 million to $658 million, recovery ratio between 186 percent and 304 percent (Table 1.4: 186.18% to 304.06%); cost estimated at $90.85 billion, operational by early 2038.
- The report notes possible "mutually beneficial operational upgrades with existing rail operators — such as potential improvements along the Union Pacific corridor in the north and with Metrolink and LOSSAN services in Southern California".
- Conclusion: "completing the Gilroy – Palmdale segment would provide statewide rail service to a majority of Californians and promises the highest return on investment for the state; and completing the Gilroy – Bakersfield scenario is a cost-effective way to achieve profitable commercial operations at the earliest possible opportunity with less additional funding needed." The Authority remains "statutorily obligated to prioritize delivery of the Merced – Bakersfield segment and plans to do so unless otherwise directed by the Legislature."

wikis.title: Gilroy - San Jose improvements and the 2038 target
wikis.summary: The Union Pacific corridor work the northern scenarios depend on, and its cost range excluded from the scenarios.
wikis.body:
- "Successful implementation of the Gilroy – Bakersfield and Gilroy – Palmdale scenarios will depend on a coordinated state solution to access and improve the Union Pacific rail line between Gilroy and San Jose."
- "Building on past investments in Caltrain electrification, and in partnership with regional agencies, a joint improvement and electrification of the rail line will be necessary to enable high-speed rail service to reach San Jose and San Francisco."
- "The Authority is prepared to work with state and regional partners to define the extent of the improvements and the additional costs not included in the scenarios, which may range from $3.0 billion to $6.0 billion."
- "Connecting California's Population Centers by Early 2038": "By strategically focusing on building high-speed rail segments from Gilroy to Bakersfield and Gilroy to Palmdale, the Authority aims to have these operational within the next 15 years, with a target operational date of 2038." Detailed project schedules are in Appendix C.
- A rendering caption notes "This future blended corridor in San Mateo will feature Caltrain and high-speed rail."

wikis.title: Environmental and economic benefits
wikis.summary: The report's claimed emissions reductions, avoided vehicle miles and flights, and economic output and job years for each scenario.
wikis.body:
- "The California high-speed rail system will form the backbone of the state's zero-emission transit network and is currently the largest greenhouse gas (GHG) reduction project in the state's GHG investment portfolio."
- "Avoided air pollutant emissions due to high-speed rail operation can save more than 400 air pollution related deaths and avoid hundreds of thousands of cases of asthma over a 50-year operational period."
- The Authority's construction equipment fleet produces "62 percent less emissions than a typical California construction fleet", and through a Voluntary Emissions Reduction Agreement the Authority "has provided more than 200 zero-emission vehicles to local agencies".
- "Since the high-speed rail project began, it has generated nearly $22 billion in economic output, which encompasses direct, indirect, and induced benefits."
- Table 1.6, Emissions Avoided by Year - annual VMT avoided / GHG reduced from VMT (MTCO2e) / flights avoided / GHG reduced from flights / total GHG avoided:
  - 2030, Merced - Bakersfield: 236,377,620 / 71,717 / 664 / 4,860 / 76,577.
  - 2040, SF - Gilroy - Bakersfield: 826,012,491 / 231,269 / 5,810 / 42,538 / 273,807.
  - 2040, SF - Gilroy - Bakersfield (including Merced): 843,936,739 / 236,288 / 5,801 / 42,475 / 278,762.
  - 2040, SF - Gilroy - Palmdale - Victorville: 1,440,138,157 / 403,214 / 14,334 / 104,954 / 508,168.
  - 2040, SF - Gilroy - Palmdale - Victorville (including Merced): 1,460,735,967 / 408,981 / 14,312 / 104,791 / 513,772.
- Table 1.7, Economic Output and Job Years - total economic output during construction / employment creation (job years): Merced - Bakersfield $65.95 billion / 284,000; Gilroy (SF) - Bakersfield $88.31 billion / 380,000; Gilroy (SF) - Bakersfield including Merced $94.49 billion / 407,000; Gilroy (SF) - Palmdale $132.11 billion / 569,000; Gilroy (SF) - Palmdale including Merced $138.01 billion / 594,000.

wikis.title: Chapter 2: funding stability, regulatory streamlining and the federal grant lawsuit
wikis.summary: The policy changes the Authority asks for - stable Cap-and-Invest funding, CEQA streamlining, environmental permitting reform - and its litigation against the FRA's grant termination.
wikis.body:
## Stable and secured funding

- "Governor Gavin Newsom proposed extending the Cap-and-Invest program to 2045 with an annual allocation of at least $1.0 billion for high-speed rail. This proposal guarantees at least $1.0 billion a year for 15 years for the program."
- "Currently, the Authority receives 25 percent of the quarterly auction proceeds, which has been subject to market volatility."
- Secured funding "would allow the Authority to explore federal loan programs like Railroad Rehabilitation and Improvement Financing (RRIF) and Transportation Infrastructure Finance and Innovation Act (TIFIA) over the long term".

## Regulatory streamlining

- "On June 30, 2025, the Governor signed Senate Bill 131, which contained targeted California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) streamlining for high-speed rail stations and maintenance facilities by reducing environmental review requirements."
- The Authority asks the Legislature to enact "a CEQA exemption for clean power interconnection". The project is committed to "100 percent renewable energy".
- International comparisons cited: Spain's Renfe Alta Velocidad Española "sources nearly all its electricity from renewable energy, much of it solar and wind"; France's Train à Grande Vitesse network "has moved toward contracts with renewable energy providers and has begun exploring on-site solar generation along right-of-way corridors"; "Japan's Shinkansen operators are investing in carbon neutrality through renewable energy procurement and energy efficiency improvements".
- "California high-speed rail is projected to eliminate more than a hundred million tons of greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions by shifting travelers from cars and airplanes to trains powered with 100 percent renewable energy."
- Permitting friction: "If construction in a habitat area pauses for more than 30 days, as can easily happen along a long linear site, permit conditions require new surveys for individual protected animals before construction resumes." The Authority recommends programmatic agreements or multi-year biological opinions.

## Federal grant funding litigation

- "In 2010 and 2011, FRA awarded the Authority two grants under the 2010 Consolidated Appropriation Act (FY10 Grant) totaling $928.62 million. More recently, in December 2023, the Authority was awarded nearly $3.1 billion from the Biden Administration through the Federal-State Partnership for Intercity Passenger Rail Grant Program (FSP Grant)."
- "In June 2025, under the Trump Administration, the Federal Railroad Administration (FRA) completed a federal grant compliance review and, on July 16, 2025, issued a decision to terminate the cooperative agreements for the Federal State Partnership and FY 10 grants — even though no fraud, waste, or abuse was identified."
- "On July 17, 2025, the Authority filed a lawsuit in federal court challenging FRA's decision to terminate the grant funding, asserting that the termination violates the Administrative Procedure Act because it was arbitrary and capricious, and the asserted reasons were pretextual, reflecting the Trump Administration's hostility to California and the high-speed rail program."
- "Since then, the Authority and the FRA have reached agreement that the obligated and contingent funds under both cooperative agreements will not be transferred to another grantee, except through a new Notice of Funding Opportunity, while litigation is pending."

## Court resources for property acquisition

- "In 2015, for instance, the assignment of only a single visiting retired judge to Kings County nearly halted adjudication, causing significant delays and resource inefficiencies."

wikis.title: 2025 Supplemental Project Update Report: third-party streamlining, funding scenarios and Appendices A-B
wikis.summary: Part 2 of the California High-Speed Rail Authority's 2025 Supplemental Project Update Report, covering right-of-way and third-party delays, the SB 198 spending cap, the international high-speed rail comparison, Chapter 3's long-term funding and P3 scenarios, and the start of Appendices A and B.
wikis.body:
## What this part covers

The second half of the capture runs from the middle of Chapter 2 (property acquisition and third-party coordination) through Chapter 2's international comparison, all of Chapter 3 on funding, and into Appendix A (statutory requirements and legal memo) and Appendix B (Merced - Bakersfield ridership, revenue, cost and schedule), stopping partway through Appendix B's cost-saving opportunities.

## Figures stated here

- "With nearly 2,300 parcels required for the initial 119-mile segment and an estimated 530 for the extensions to Merced and Bakersfield, the need for reliable, efficient adjudication processes remains high."
- "Senate Bill (SB) 198, enacted in 2022, prioritized construction of the 171-mile Merced – Bakersfield early operating segment (EOS) and imposed a $500 million cap on Authority expenditures outside the Central Valley."
- "The Authority's June 26, 2025, Request for Expressions of Interest for public-private partnerships yielded 31 responses from a wide range of industry participants."
- Table 3.0 annual funding commitments including debt service, in $ billions: SF - Gilroy - Bakersfield ($54.38 cost, $26.22 needed) 2.29 over 15 years to 2045, 1.98 over 20 years to 2050, 1.63 over 30 years to 2060, 1.39 over 45 years to 2075, +47.5 40-year net operating profit; SF - Gilroy - Bakersfield including Merced ($58.10 / $29.94) 2.58 / 2.22 / 1.83 / 1.56, +45.9; SF - Gilroy - Palmdale ($87.12 / $58.96) 5.10 / 4.37 / 3.60 / 3.06, +98.1; SF - Gilroy - Palmdale including Merced ($90.85 / $62.69) 5.39 / 4.61 / 3.80 / 3.24, +96.8.
- "The Authority also evaluated the potential cumulative returns from the first 40 years of high-speed rail operating profits under each funding scenario, ranging from $45.9 billion to $98.1 billion."
- Table B.0, "Merced to Bakersfield 2030 Net Proceeds Outlook ($ in millions)" in 2024 tax dollars, repeats Table 1.0: passenger revenue $39.28 to $55.60; ancillary revenue net income $15.99 to $34.02; O&M $120.60 to $122.10; recovery ratio 45.27% to 74.31%, on ridership of 1.6 million to 2.2 million.
- Appendix B states the 171-mile EOS assumed "hourly service at speeds up to 220 miles per hour" and "was never intended to operate as a stand-alone system".

## Dates stated

The chief counsel's memo in Appendix A is dated August 15, 2025 ("DATE: August 15, 2025 ... FROM: Thomas Fellenz, Acting Chief Counsel"). No publication or last-updated date for the report itself is stated in this part.

wikis.title: Property acquisition, court resources and third-party streamlining
wikis.summary: The right-of-way adjudication bottleneck and the framework the Authority asks for to hold third parties to schedule.
wikis.body:
- On orders of possession: "What is most urgently needed is not final resolution of compensation, but the timely and impartial issuance of orders of possession — legal determinations that allow construction to proceed while final valuation is adjudicated. When these orders are delayed, the impacts ripple across project schedules, increase mobilization and holding costs, and divert resources away from construction activities."
- "With nearly 2,300 parcels required for the initial 119-mile segment and an estimated 530 for the extensions to Merced and Bakersfield, the need for reliable, efficient adjudication processes remains high. Moreover, as the project advances toward future segments in the Central Valley and beyond that need will only grow."
- Suggested remedies: "dedicated procedural tracks for infrastructure-related acquisitions, or a regional or centralized forum model", including "dedicated court resources in the counties where the properties are located."
- On third parties (railroads, utility providers, local agencies): "recurring delays related to reviews, approvals, agreements, and permitting, often stemming from inconsistent engagement or lack of adherence to schedules, continue to disrupt right-of-way acquisition, utility relocation, and overall construction sequencing", with timelines "treated as aspirational rather than binding" and "some entities routinely pass costs to the Authority with little scrutiny".
- The framework asked for includes defined and binding timelines that can be tracked and enforced, mandatory participation in coordination meetings and transparent progress reporting, streamlined permitting pathways, cost containment policies preventing unchecked cost transfers, and clear escalation and oversight mechanisms.

wikis.title: SB 198's spending cap and private-sector interest
wikis.summary: The 2022 law's $500 million cap outside the Central Valley, the change the Authority asks for, and the response to its 2025 P3 solicitation.
wikis.body:
- "Senate Bill (SB) 198, enacted in 2022, prioritized construction of the 171-mile Merced – Bakersfield early operating segment (EOS) and imposed a $500 million cap on Authority expenditures outside the Central Valley."
- "While this focus has facilitated progress on the EOS, it is critical that the project be responsive to evolving funding opportunities, market dynamics, and ridership potential."
- "To provide flexibility for project sequencing and unlock private sector engagement, the Legislature could modify SB 198 to remove or adjust the current spending cap outside the Central Valley."
- "The Authority's June 26, 2025, Request for Expressions of Interest for public-private partnerships yielded 31 responses from a wide range of industry participants. Consistent industry engagement had highlighted the critical nature of stable funding, emphasizing how a credible state backstop allows the private sector to invest at scale".
- The Authority "will continue to evaluate significant potential for commercialization and monetization opportunities that can generate additional funding for project delivery."

wikis.title: International high-speed rail comparison
wikis.summary: Table 2.0's cost per mile, delivery time, length and constraints for six high-speed rail projects including California's.
wikis.body:
Table 2.0: International High-Speed Rail Projects - cost per mile (2025 prices, in millions) / total years to plan and build / route length / miles of tunnelling / environmental and geographic constraints:

- Spain Madrid - Barcelona: ~$75 / 16 years / 385 miles / 32 miles / mountain ranges, archaeological sites.
- HS1 (UK): ~$202 / 9 years / 68 miles / 25 miles / urban density, River Thames crossing, protected landscapes, wetlands, archaeological and cultural heritage sites.
- Taiwan High-Speed Rail: ~$134 / 17 years / 214 miles / 31 miles / typhoons, earthquakes, narrow corridor.
- California High-Speed Rail: ~$212 / 15 years / 500 miles (Phase 1) / 50 miles / wetlands, farmland, seismic zones, CEQA & NEPA.
- HS2 (UK): ~$613 / 24 years / 140 miles / 30 miles / ancient woodlands, urban tunnelling, political opposition.
- Beijing - Shanghai High-Speed Rail: ~$61 / 7 years / 819 miles / 50 miles / high land acquisition pressure, river crossings, flood plains.

Commentary: "The most critical factor for the successful development and delivery of high-speed rail is strong political support combined with a firm funding commitment." China's success is attributed to "centralized planning, the establishment of consistent technical standards, and standardized approaches, all supported by robust national funding", while "California's project experienced fluctuating levels of support at the national level". "Projects in regions such as California, Japan, and the UK have also taken longer to complete due to challenging terrain, varied land uses, extensive environmental mitigation, and heightened public scrutiny." More detail is in Appendix H. The table image is sourced to UK.GOV.

Photo captions here: local and state leaders celebrated the completion of the Tulare Street Grade Separation with a ribbon-cutting in Fresno's Historic Chinatown in July 2025; "The Tulare Street Undercrossing, completed in July 2025, reconnects Fresno's historic Chinatown and downtown".

wikis.title: Chapter 3: funding options and repayment scenarios
wikis.summary: How the state could structure new funding over 15 to 45 years, with the annual commitments and 40-year operating profits for each buildout.
wikis.body:
- "The Authority's current funding, coupled with the Governor's proposal to dedicate at least $1.0 billion annually from the Cap-and-Invest program to high-speed rail through 2045, is projected to be sufficient to complete the 171-mile Merced – Bakersfield early operating segment and begin operations within the Authority's schedule window."
- Extending the project to Gilroy - Bakersfield and Gilroy - Palmdale "would also require a new funding commitment from the state combined with other public and private funding sources."
- The comparison used: "Much like a homeowner taking out a mortgage, the state has several funding options available, each with different timelines and total repayment costs." Funding could be structured "over a period of 15 to 45 years", supporting "'PayGo' expenditures through 2038, as well as financing program covering both the principal construction costs and the interest accrued over time."
- "A 15-year repayment schedule minimizes interest accumulation but requires the highest annual payments. At the other end of the spectrum, a 45-year repayment period offers the lowest recurring payments but has the highest total cost due to accumulated interest." Example: "financing the Gilroy – Bakersfield segment over 15 years would cost $2.29 billion per year, compared to $1.63 billion per year over a 30-year term."
- Table 3.0 (all $ in billions; annual funding commitment includes debt service; construction costs include a P65 contingency; funding needed derived from existing funding of $28.16 billion and excluding the proposed incremental $15.0 billion from Cap and Invest and reserved Capital Outlay Support and Administrative costs; cumulative profit assumes an operational start of early 2038):
  - SF - Gilroy - Bakersfield: cost 54.38, funding needed 26.22; 2.29 (to 2045, 15 years), 1.98 (2050, 20 years), 1.63 (2060, 30 years), 1.39 (2075, 45 years); 40-year net operating profit +47.5.
  - SF - Gilroy - Bakersfield (including Merced): 58.10, 29.94; 2.58 / 2.22 / 1.83 / 1.56; +45.9.
  - SF - Gilroy - Palmdale: 87.12, 58.96; 5.10 / 4.37 / 3.60 / 3.06; +98.1.
  - SF - Gilroy - Palmdale (including Merced): 90.85, 62.69; 5.39 / 4.61 / 3.80 / 3.24; +96.8.
- "Costs and schedules described in this report are contingent on affirmative state action on funding and on streamlining construction as described in Chapter 2."
- Conclusion: "Without state action on long-term funding and removal of obstacles as outlined in this chapter to improve project construction efficiency, there are no guarantees the faster delivery and cost savings laid out in this report could be achieved." "Connecting profitable service to San Jose, San Francisco, and the broader Bay Area economic hub is within reach by early 2038".

wikis.title: What is a public-private partnership
wikis.summary: The report's definition of a P3 and its lists of California and US examples.
wikis.body:
- "A public-private partnership (P3) is a collaborative, contractual arrangement between a government entity (federal, state, or local) and a private organization used as a proven innovative mechanism for public infrastructure projects. P3 partnerships bring together the strengths of public and private participants to share risks, access expertise, and improve cost efficiencies."
- California examples: Presidio Parkway (San Francisco), Long Beach Civic Center, Long Beach Court Building, UC Merced.
- Rest of the U.S. examples: Moynihan Station (New York City), Eagle P3 Rail Project (Denver, Colorado), New Terminal 1 at JFK, Major Bridges Project (Pennsylvania DOT).
- Elsewhere in Chapter 3: "Private investors and industry partners are more likely to engage and partner to deliver the California high-speed rail project if the state demonstrates a long-term funding commitment. Such a commitment could encourage the private sector to offer additional financing and equity investment in exchange for operational rights."
- A photo caption notes the Presidio Parkway image is sourced to the Bay Area Council, and that "Located in Kings County, the Hanford Viaduct will allow high-speed trains to cross over Grangeville Boulevard, San Joaquin Valley Railroad, and State Route 198."

wikis.title: Appendix A: statutory basis and the chief counsel memo
wikis.summary: The legal memo confirming the report's contents and the Public Utilities Code sections that govern Project Update Reports.
wikis.body:
- Memo: "DATE: August 15, 2025 / TO: File / FROM: Thomas Fellenz, Acting Chief Counsel / SUBJECT: Review of Supplemental 2025 Project Update Report". He confirms the revised cost and schedule estimates, operating agreement update, ridership and additional milestones are provided, and that "other elements required pursuant to CA Public Utilities Code section 185033 are included therein".
- The Project Update Report is a biennial report to the Legislature submitted in odd-numbered years; business plans are submitted in even-numbered years. "Together, these two reports fulfill the requirements of Government Code 16724.4 which relates to annual reporting requirements associated with voter approved bond measures."
- June 2015 (AB 95) added Section 185033.5 to the Public Utilities Code, requiring a Project Update Report "[o]n or before March 1, 2017, and every two years thereafter", approved by the Secretary of Transportation, listing requirements (A) through (H) - overall progress; baseline budget from the Revised 2012 Business Plan; current and projected budget; expenditures to date; schedule comparison; "[a] summary of milestones achieved during the prior two-year period and milestones expected to be reached in the coming two-year period"; issues identified in the prior two-year period; and risks and mitigation.
- June 2022 (SB 198) added Section 185033.7, specifying delivery schedules (A) through (G) - the 119-mile dual track segment "from Madera to Poplar Avenue, which means Avenue 19 in the County of Madera to one mile north of the Tulare-Kern County line southward to north of Bakersfield, currently near Poplar Avenue"; right-of-way, planning and advance engineering for the Merced and Bakersfield extensions; agreements with the San Joaquin Joint Powers Authority and the San Joaquin Regional Rail Commission on the Merced connection and on planning, funding and operation of Merced - Bakersfield services; an updated cost estimate with a stated probability level; a funding plan including additional federal awards; and additional milestones.
- SB 198 also set cost and funding requirements (A) through (G): estimated and actual civil works costs; right-of-way, acquisitions, utilities and third-party agreement costs; contract costs including contingencies for change orders; other costs including rolling stock, interim use and stations; costs reported comparably across reports; milestone progress; and funding commitments beyond the Merced to Bakersfield segment.

wikis.title: Appendix B: Merced - Bakersfield ridership, revenue and cost-saving opportunities
wikis.summary: The updated analysis of the early operating segment, why it is not self-sustaining, and the cost-saving strategies proposed.
wikis.body:
- The appendix addresses the statutory requirements for the Merced - Bakersfield segment. In the March 2025 PUR the Authority "committed to releasing an updated project schedule including the new procurement sequencing plan, updated capital costs that incorporate revised engineering and financial assumptions, and updated ridership and revenue figures based on the refined model."
- "The original strategic vision for the Merced – Bakersfield high-speed rail early operating segment (EOS) assumed the availability of supporting infrastructure necessary to run hourly service at speeds up to 220 miles per hour. This 171-mile EOS was never intended to operate as a stand-alone system; rather, it was designed to demonstrate the early benefits of high-speed rail while the broader statewide network was being built. That vision depended on improved connecting services, such as Altamont Corridor Express (ACE) and San Joaquins, to deliver passengers to and from Merced."
- Table B.0, "Merced to Bakersfield 2030 Net Proceeds Outlook ($ in millions)", 2024 tax dollars: passenger revenue $39.28 to $55.60; ancillary revenue net income $15.99 to $34.02; operations and maintenance $120.60 to $122.10; recovery ratio 45.27% to 74.31%, based on ridership of 1.6 million to 2.2 million.
- "Although the original vision for Merced – Bakersfield is not projected to be self-sustaining under current conditions, the 171 miles of infrastructure in the Central Valley provide a strong foundation for improving statewide rail connectivity and are essential for future system expansion."
- Status: "With 119 miles of civil works nearing completion, advanced design taking place on extensions and stations, and the railhead construction project close to completion, the Authority is well positioned to achieve this goal." The Authority's primary goal is "to complete the current construction packages and progress quickly to track laying, rail systems, and operations."
- The Authority "looks forward to collaborating with the California State Transportation Agency (CalSTA) and other state partners", with findings "expected to be included in a future Business Plan".
- Cost-saving opportunities listed so far: "Initial Track Infrastructure" - near-term schedule and cost savings "by using an optimized track schematic, under which track configuration is determined based on delivering full operational utility while reducing costly redundancies"; and "Station Development" - "a phased approach to station development", a "building block approach [that] enables future expansion and customization of stations in response to increasing demand."

wikis.title: NVIDIA launches the Rubin AI compute platform at CES 2026
