wikis.title: Narnia: The Magician's Nephew (upcoming Greta Gerwig film)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the upcoming Netflix film Narnia: The Magician's Nephew, covering its cast, production history, filming and its 2027 theatrical and streaming release dates.
wikis.body:
## Overview

- "Narnia: The Magician's Nephew is an upcoming high fantasy film written for the screen, co-produced, and directed by Greta Gerwig", based on the 1955 novel *The Magician's Nephew*, "the sixth published and first chronological novel" in *The Chronicles of Narnia* by C. S. Lewis.
- It "will be the fourth film adaptation" of the series, following a trilogy of films produced by Walden Media.
- Countries: United States, United Kingdom. Language: English.

## Release

- "Following IMAX previews on February 10, 2027", the film "is scheduled to be released theatrically worldwide excluding France on February 12, before streaming on Netflix on April 2."
- Infobox release dates: February 12, 2027 (United States); April 2, 2027 (Netflix).
- "It will be the first film by Netflix to receive a wide theatrical release" and its "first foray into releasing a movie into theaters exclusively for a minimum of 45 days."
- Earlier plan: it "was previously scheduled to release exclusively on 1,000 IMAX screens on November 26, 2026, followed by a debut on Netflix on December 25, 2026, before *The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth* (2026) took over the release dates."
- June 2026: Sony Pictures announced as handler of international theatrical distribution.
- July 2026: Netflix announced the film "would forgo a theatrical release in France, instead premiering on the streaming service on April 2."
- The page describes the excluded territories two ways. The body says Sony's international rights "would extend only to territories outside North America and France where Netflix operates, meaning China, Belarus and Russia would be excluded from the pact." The infobox note says the Sony deal "excludes France, where Netflix will premiere it direct-to-streaming, as well as China and Russia" (Belarus not mentioned).

## Credits and figures

- Directed and written by Greta Gerwig. Produced by Mark Gordon, Amy Pascal, Vincent Sieber-Smith and Greta Gerwig.
- Cinematography: Seamus McGarvey. Editing: Nick Houy, Andrew Weisblum. Music: Mark Ronson, Andrew Wyatt.
- Production companies: The C.S. Lewis Company, eOne Films, Pascal Pictures, Midnight Road Entertainment.
- Distributors: Netflix (United States and Canada); Sony Pictures Releasing International (International).
- Budget: $200 million, cited to Deadline Hollywood, December 26, 2025.
- No runtime or gross given.

## Cast (as listed)

- David McKenna as Digory Kirke; Beatrice Campbell as Polly Plummer; Emma Mackey as Jadis, "the future White Witch and the last Queen of Charn"; Carey Mulligan as Mabel Kirke, Digory's mother; Ciarán Hinds; Daniel Craig as Andrew Ketterley, Digory's uncle; Meryl Streep as Aslan, "the great lion who was responsible for creating Narnia."
- Also listed: Kobna Holdbrook-Smith, Denise Gough, Susan Wokoma, Tom Bonington as Mr. Potts, Ava Jager as Violet Plummer (Polly's sister), Gerard Monaco, James Murray, Samantha Spiro.

## Background and development

- Walden Media's contract on the film rights expired in 2011; in October 2013 the C. S. Lewis Company agreed with The Mark Gordon Company to adapt the 1953 novel *The Silver Chair*. In December 2013 David Magee was announced as screenwriter. In July 2014 the official Narnia website ran a fan contest to name the Lady of the Green Kirtle.
- The producers called that film a "reboot" because of a new creative team, "although it was still a narrative successor" to the previous three films.
- August 2016: TriStar Pictures and Entertainment One set to finance and distribute the fourth film. April 2017: Joe Johnston hired to direct *The Silver Chair*.
- October 2018: Netflix and eOne made a multi-year deal with the C.S. Lewis Company for Narnia films and TV.
- July 2023, following the release of *Barbie*: Gerwig signed a deal with Netflix to write and direct two films in the series, with Gordon, Douglas Gresham, Amy Pascal and Sieber producing.
- December 2024: Pascal said filming "was expected to start in July 2025"; The Times reported filming would take place at Shepperton Studios; Jason Isaacs revealed Gerwig "was rumored" to be adapting *The Magician's Nephew* first.
- March and April 2025: Production Weekly and Production List listings referred to the production as *Narnia: The Magician's Nephew*; the subject and full title were confirmed in mid-2025.

## Casting timeline

- January 2025: open casting calls for a young boy and young girl "were quietly released".
- March 2025: Charli XCX "was in talks"; Daniel Craig "had been offered a role".
- Early April 2025: Meryl Streep "was in talks to voice Aslan and was confirmed to be voicing the character the following year"; later that month Emma Mackey cast as the White Witch "over Margaret Qualley and Charli".
- May 2025: Carey Mulligan cast as Mabel Kirke. July 2025: David McKenna, Beatrice Campbell and Tom Bonington. September 2025: Denise Gough. October 2025: Craig's casting confirmed, Ava Jager joined. February 2026: Susan Wokoma, Gerard Monaco, James Murray, Samantha Spiro. May 2026: Ciarán Hinds and Kobna Holdbrook-Smith "rounded out the cast."

## Filming and post-production

- Principal photography began August 11, 2025, with location filming around Bank Station and The Royal Exchange in London and set filming at Shepperton Studios.
- Further scenes shot in the Castlefield area of Manchester the same month.
- "By October 1, with location shooting complete, studio filming at Shepperton and Longcross Studios was expected to continue to December 2025."
- Filming wrapped January 31, 2026.
- "According to Deadline Hollywood, a cast member sustained an injury during filming which caused a production delay of six weeks."
- October 2025: Mark Ronson and Andrew Wyatt reported to be co-composing the score, having previously worked with Gerwig on *Barbie*.

wikis.title: The Thomas Crown Affair (1968 film)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on Norman Jewison's 1968 heist film The Thomas Crown Affair, covering its plot, cast, production and Boston locations, release, reception, Oscar-winning score and its remakes.
wikis.body:
## Overview

- "The Thomas Crown Affair is a 1968 American heist film directed by Norman Jewison and written by Alan R. Trustman. Starring Steve McQueen, Faye Dunaway, Paul Burke, and Jack Weston, the film follows Vicki Anderson (Dunaway), who is hired to investigate the culprits of a multi-million dollar bank heist orchestrated by Thomas Crown (McQueen)."
- "The film was nominated for two Academy Awards, winning Best Original Song for Michel Legrand's \"The Windmills of Your Mind\". A remake was released in 1999, and a second remake is set to be released in 2027. A Hong Kong version of the movie was released in 1987 under the title Easy Money, starring Michelle Yeoh as Thomas Crown's female version."
- Infobox: produced by Norman Jewison; cinematography Haskell Wexler; edited by Hal Ashby, Ralph E. Winters and Byron Brandt; music by Michel Legrand; production companies The Mirisch Corporation, Simkoe, Solar Productions; distributed by United Artists; release date June 19, 1968; running time 102 minutes; country United States; language English; budget $4.3 million; box office $14 million.

## Plot (as summarised by the article)

Bored multi-millionaire Thomas Crown masterminds "a five-man heist of $2.66 million from a Boston bank", the getaway driver dumping the money in a cemetery trash can; none of the men meet Crown or each other. Crown retrieves it and deposits it in a numbered Geneva account over several trips. Independent investigator Vicki Anderson, contracted by the bank's insurance company for "10% of the stolen money if she recovers it", narrows a list of customers making recent Geneva trips, identifies Crown and guesses his cellular method. A cat-and-mouse game becomes an affair, complicating her vow to help detective Eddy Malone. A reward of $25,000 entices getaway driver Erwin Weaver's wife to inform; Weaver only ever heard his employer's voice, and does not recognise Crown. Vicki uses the IRS as leverage; Malone refuses a deal. Crown stages an identical second robbery and tells Vicki where the drop will be to test her. At the cemetery stakeout Crown sends a messenger in his Rolls-Royce with a telegram inviting her to bring the money and join him or keep the car "as a consolation prize"; she tears it up as he escapes overhead.

## Cast

Steve McQueen as Thomas Crown; Faye Dunaway as Vicki Anderson; Paul Burke as Detective Eddy Malone; Jack Weston as Erwin Weaver; Biff McGuire as Sandy; Addison Powell as Abe; Gordon Pinsent as Jamie; Yaphet Kotto as Carl; Sidney Armus as Arnie; Richard Bull as booth guard; Peg Shirley as Honey; Tom Rosqui as private detective; Michael Shillo as Swiss banker; Astrid Heeren as Gwen.

## Production details

- The split-screen technique "was inspired by the breakthrough Expo 67 films In the Labyrinth and A Place to Stand", the latter debuting Christopher Chapman's "multi-dynamic image technique". McQueen saw an advance screening of A Place to Stand and told Chapman he was impressed; "the following year, Norman Jewison incorporated the technique into the film by inserting split screen scenes into the already finished product."
- The chess scene's game "is based on a game played in Vienna in 1898 between Gustav Zeissl and Walter von Walthoffen", played on "a Cantonese Export 1820-1850 \"Burmese\" Pattern chess set."
- "McQueen performed his own stunts, which include playing polo and driving a dune buggy at high speed along the Massachusetts coastline."
- Vicki Anderson's car, "one of those red Italian things", "is the first of only ten Ferrari 275 GTB/4S NART Spiders built"; McQueen later acquired one. The dune buggy was a Meyers Manx. "Crown's two-door Rolls-Royce Silver Shadow carried the Massachusetts vanity license plate \"TC 100\" for the film."
- "Sean Connery had been the original choice for the title role, but turned it down—a decision he later regretted. Johnny Carson also turned down the role."

## Filming locations

Shot primarily on location in Boston and surrounding Massachusetts and New Hampshire: the Second Harrison Gray Otis House, 85 Mt. Vernon Street, Beacon Hill (Crown's home); the first robbery at the then Beverly National Bank (renamed Boston Mercantile Bank) at North Beverly Plaza, Beverly; the second robbery at 55 Congress Street, Boston (now 44 Water Street, offices of Brown Brothers); car theft in downtown Beverly across from City Hall; money dumpings at Mount Auburn Cemetery, Cambridge; polo at the Myopia Hunt Club, South Hamilton; golf at Belmont Country Club; auctions in the St. James Ballroom at the Eben Jordan Mansion, 46 Beacon Street; the dune buggy on Crane Beach, Ipswich; the Schweizer SGS 1-23 H glider flown at Salem, New Hampshire; the meat shop at Blackstone and North Street in the North End; the rain walk in Copp's Hill Cemetery; the formal-dress kiss at the top of Acorn Street, "a narrow, cobblestone lane often called \"the most photographed street in America\"". Other locations: the Allston-Brighton tollbooths (demolished 2016), Anthony's Pier 4, Boston Common, the old Boston Police Headquarters on Berkeley Street, Cambridge and Linden Streets in Allston, Copp's Hill Terrace, the North End Greenmarket, South Station, the Tobin Bridge, the Prudential Tunnel, the then-Dewey Square Tunnel ("a feat technically impossible since McQueen drove into the Prudential Tunnel one scene earlier"), the Marliave Restaurant rooftop, the Charles River footpath between the Weeks Footbridge and the Anderson Bridge, and Dulles International Airport in Virginia "with signage making it look as if it were in Boston".

## Release

- "The Thomas Crown Affair had its world premiere in Boston on June 19, 1968, with openings in Los Angeles and New York on June 26, 1968, and a nationwide release in August 1968."
- The release "introduced United Artists' new logo that shows the iconic Transamerica \"T\" and the byline, \"Entertainment from Transamerica Corporation\"."
- "The Thomas Crown Affair made its American television premiere on NBC Saturday Night at the Movies in September 1972."
- Home media: DVD by MGM Home Entertainment in February 1999 (commentary by Jewison, trailer); Blu-ray on February 1, 2011; "On February 13, 2018, Kino Lorber (under license from MGM) released a Blu-ray 50th anniversary edition with six extra features", including commentary by Lem Dobbs and Nick Redman.

## Reception

- Box office: "$14 million on a $4.3 million budget."
- "Reviews at the time were mixed." Roger Ebert gave two-and-a-half stars of four, calling it "possibly the most under-plotted, underwritten, over-photographed film of the year. Which is not to say it isn't great to look at. It is." Pauline Kael called it "pretty good trash".
- Rotten Tomatoes: 70% from 40 reviews, average 6.5/10; consensus "Steve McQueen settles into the role with ease and aplomb, in a film that whisks viewers into an exotic world with style and sex appeal." Metacritic: 66 of 100 from 7 critics, "generally favorable".

## Accolades

- Academy Awards: Best Original Score for a Motion Picture (Not a Musical), Michel Legrand — nominated; Best Song – Original for the Picture, "The Windmills of Your Mind" (music Michel Legrand, lyrics Alan and Marilyn Bergman) — won.
- British Academy Film Awards: Anthony Asquith Award for Original Film Music.
- Golden Globe Awards: Best Original Score – Motion Picture; Best Original Song – Motion Picture ("The Windmills of Your Mind").
- Laurel Awards: Top Action-Drama — 5th place; Top Male Dramatic Performance.

## Soundtrack

- Album by Michel Legrand and Noel Harrison; released 1968 (original) and June 10, 2014 (expansion); recorded 1968; length 70:39 (expansion); labels United Artists Records (original) and Quartet (expansion).
- "The music was composed and conducted by Michel Legrand, scoring his first major American film." Jewison had hoped to hire Henry Mancini, who was unavailable and recommended Legrand; Legrand "wrote his music as long pieces rather than specifically to scene timings, with the film later edited to the music by Legrand, Jewison and editor Hal Ashby."
- Legrand had to replace "Strawberry Fields Forever", the temp track for the glider scene; on Quincy Jones' advice he wrote "The Windmills of Your Mind" and "His Eyes, Her Eyes" with the Bergmans. Noel Harrison sang the former "after Jewison failed to get his friend Andy Williams to do it"; Legrand performed the latter.
- The score was recorded in Hollywood with Vincent DeRosa, Bud Shank, Carol Kaye, Emil Richards, Ray Brown and Shelly Manne, while the United Artists LP re-recording was made in France. "Jewison said it was the favorite score for any of his films."
- Reissues: Rykodisc CD in 1998 with five dialogue excerpts plus "Moments of Love" and "Doubting Thomas"; Varèse Sarabande in 2004 without the dialogue; a 2014 Quartet Records limited edition adding the film version. The expanded track listing runs from "The Windmills of Your Mind" (2:24) to "All My Love, Tommy" (3:07).

## In popular culture

- The kissing scene on the poster "was used in Hal Ashby's satirical film Being There (1979). Ashby was The Thomas Crown Affair's associate producer and editor."
- Madonna's 1998 video for "The Power of Good-Bye" is based on the chess scene, which is also parodied in Austin Powers: The Spy Who Shagged Me (1999).

## Remakes

- 1999 film: starring Pierce Brosnan, Rene Russo and Denis Leary, with Faye Dunaway as Crown's therapist; set in New York rather than Boston, with the theft of "a priceless painting, a Monet, instead of cash", and "the complete lack of violence in Thomas Crown's crimes."
- Planned sequel: announced in January 2007, "loosely based on Topkapi (1964)"; by January 2009 Brosnan confirmed his involvement with Paul Verhoeven directing; Verhoeven left by April 2010 "citing creative differences and scheduling conflicts". Angelina Jolie and Charlize Theron were discussed for roles. In April 2013 Brosnan acknowledged development hell. "In April 2014, John McTiernan revealed that he had written a treatment for the script, titled Thomas Crown and the Missing Lioness", with an initial script by John Rogers from a story with Harley Peyton and additional material by Nick Meyer, Michael Finch and Karl Gajdusek.
- 2027 film: Michael B. Jordan pitched a new adaptation to MGM in 2016; "In April 2023, after having acquired MGM, Amazon announced plans to reboot the franchise". "On September 11, 2024, it was announced that Michael B. Jordan had returned to direct and star in the new film, with Drew Pearce writing. On April 25, 2025, The Thomas Crown Affair was announced for a release date for March 5, 2027."

The capture contains some unrendered citation markup inside the accolades table.

wikis.title: The Thomas Crown Affair (1999 film)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on John McTiernan's 1999 remake The Thomas Crown Affair, covering its plot, cast, script changes from the 1968 film, filming, paintings used, soundtrack, box office, reviews and the planned 2027 reboot.
wikis.body:
## Overview

- "The Thomas Crown Affair is a 1999 American romantic heist film directed by John McTiernan and written by Leslie Dixon and Kurt Wimmer. It is a remake of the 1968 film of the same title. Starring Pierce Brosnan, Rene Russo, and Denis Leary, it follows Thomas Crown, a bored billionaire who steals a painting from the Metropolitan Museum of Art and is pursued by an insurance investigator, with the two falling in love."
- "Produced by United Artists and Irish DreamTime, the film was released on August 6, 1999. It grossed $125.3 million worldwide, against a budget of $48 million, and received generally positive reviews from critics."
- Infobox: directed by John McTiernan; screenplay Leslie Dixon and Kurt Wimmer; based on the story by Alan Trustman; produced by Pierce Brosnan and Beau St. Clair; cinematography Tom Priestley Jr.; edited by John Wright; music by Bill Conti; production companies United Artists and Irish DreamTime; distributed by MGM Distribution Co. (US/Canada) and United International Pictures (international); release date August 6, 1999; running time 113 minutes; budget $48 million; box office $125.3 million. (The Box office section instead gives a worldwide total of $124.3 million — $69.3 million domestic and $55.0 million overseas.)

## Plot (as summarised by the article)

Thieves enter the Metropolitan Museum of Art inside a Trojan horse and are caught; in the confusion billionaire Thomas Crown, "the crime's secret mastermind", steals Monet's San Giorgio Maggiore at Dusk. NYPD Detective Michael McCann investigates "the theft of the $100 million artwork" alongside insurance investigator Catherine Banning. Crown lends a Pissarro to fill the gap; Banning deduces he is driven "not by money but by the sheer thrill of the crime", copies his keys and finds a taunting fake Monet painted over a copy of Poker Sympathy from the Dogs Playing Poker series. They become lovers while the cat-and-mouse game continues, including a trip to Martinique. McCann shows Banning photographs of Crown with another woman, Anna. The forgery could only have been made by someone with access to the original; imprisoned forger Heinrich Knutzhorn says nothing but seems to recognise it. Crown offers to return the Monet and names a rendezvous; Banning tells McCann. At the museum, Banning learns Anna painted the fake and that Knutzhorn is her father, "a former business partner of Crown, who became her guardian". Crown blends into a crowd of bowler-hatted lookalikes "à la René Magritte's 1964 painting The Son of Man", sets off smoke bombs and the fire alarm; the sprinklers wash his donated Pissarro clean to reveal the real Monet beneath. Crown has meanwhile taken a second painting, the one Banning said she would have chosen; it is not covered by her employer. A bowler-hatted courier delivers it to her; she sends it to McCann and flies back to London, where Crown appears in the seat behind her.

## Cast

Pierce Brosnan as Thomas Crown; Rene Russo as Catherine Banning; Denis Leary as Detective Michael McCann; Ben Gazzara as Andrew Wallace; Frankie Faison as Paretti; Fritz Weaver as John Reynolds; Charles Keating as Golchan; Mark Margolis as Knutzhorn; Faye Dunaway as Psychiatrist; Esther Cañadas as Anna Knudsen.

## Development and script amendments

- "At first, director John McTiernan was unavailable for the remake"; Brosnan and his fellow producers considered Mike Newell, Andrew Davis and Roger Donaldson "before returning to their original choice."
- McTiernan "changed the theme of the central heist and a number of key scenes", judging that audiences "would be less forgiving of Thomas Crown if he staged two armed bank robberies for fun as Steve McQueen did in the original, rather than if he staged an unarmed art heist."
- "He wrote the heist based on the Trojan horse theme and on a technical failure of thermal cameras." The rewritten polo match struck him as cliché and was replaced by a catamaran race. "Originally, an elaborate 30-page sequence of the theft of the final painting was planned, although McTiernan removed this in favor of a simple mystified response by Denis Leary's character Michael McCann when asked how it was taken."

## References to the 1968 film

- Faye Dunaway, the original's Vicki Anderson, plays Crown's psychiatrist. "The Windmills of Your Mind" plays during the ballroom scene, elsewhere as background music, and over the closing credits. "Both films share a nearly identical scene with Crown playing high-stakes golf, and in both films Crown pilots a glider for recreation."

## Filming

- "Filming took place in several parts of New York City, including Central Park in 1998. The corporate headquarters of Lucent Technologies stood in for Crown's suite of offices."
- The Metropolitan Museum of Art declined the producers' request ("respectfully declined"), so the crew built their own museum on a soundstage with artisans hired for realism. Another scene was shot at the main research library of the New York Public Library.
- "The glider scenes were shot at Ridge Soaring Gliderport, Eagle Field in Pennsylvania and at Corning-Painted Post Airport in New York." The two aero-tow shots came from different airports with different tow planes; the initial takeoff was shot at the Harris Hill Soaring Center at the National Soaring Museum in Elmira, New York. "The glider pilot was Thomas L. Knauff, a world record holder, and a member of the US Soaring Hall of Fame."

## Paintings

Copies were supplied by "Troubetzkoy Paintings" in New York. The paintings are: San Giorgio Maggiore at Twilight by Claude Monet (National Museum and Art Gallery, Cardiff); Wheatstacks by Monet (Getty Museum, Los Angeles); Noon: Rest From Work (After Millet) by Van Gogh, "The painting Crown admires and calls \"his haystacks\"" (Musée d'Orsay); The Artist's Garden at Eragny by Camille Pissarro; The Son of Man by René Magritte; Banks of the Seine at Argenteuil by Édouard Manet, "The second painting to go missing" (Courtauld Institute of Art Gallery, London); The Intervention of the Sabine Women by Jacques-Louis David (Louvre); a painting in the style of Coolidge's Dogs Playing Poker "but it is not one of Coolidge's works"; and The Caliph of Constantine by Théodore Chassériau (Palace of Versailles). (The plot section calls the stolen Monet "San Giorgio Maggiore at Dusk", this list "at Twilight".)

## Soundtrack

- Album by Bill Conti, Sting and Nina Simone; released September 7, 1999 (original) and March 8, 2002 (re-release); recorded 1999; length 37:44; labels Ark 21 (original) and Pangaea (re-release).
- "The soundtrack was composed by Bill Conti and arranged by Jack Eskew. It features a variety of jazz arrangements which harken back to the original film's version." The film ends with a reprise of "Windmills of Your Mind" sung by Sting. Nina Simone's "Sinnerman" (from Pastel Blues, 1965) is used throughout, mostly its non-vocal parts, with the vocal "Oh sinnerman, where are you gonna run to?" in the final scenes.
- Track listing: "Windmills of Your Mind" (Sting); "Sinnerman" (Nina Simone); "Everything (...Is Never Quite Enough)" (Wasis Diop); "Caban La Ka Kratchie" (Georges Fordant); then Bill Conti's "Black & White X 5", "Never Change", "Meet Ms. Banning", "Goodnight/Breaking & Entering", "Glider Pt. 1", "Glider Pt. 2", "Cocktails", "Quick Exit".

## Release

- "The Thomas Crown Affair premiered on July 27, 1999, and was theatrically released in the United States on August 6, 1999 by United Artists and Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer."
- Home media: "released on VHS and DVD in the LaserDisc format on January 4, 2000 in the United States by MGM Home Entertainment", the DVD including comments from McTiernan. "When the film was broadcast on TBS, the Pepsi One logo on the can from which Catherine Banning (Rene Russo) drinks had to be deleted."

## Reception

- Box office: "$69.3 million domestically (United States and Canada) and $55.0 million in other territories, for a worldwide total of $124.3 million, against a budget of $48 million. It peaked at No. 4, in its first week of release, and spent its first seven weeks in the Top 10 at the domestic box office."
- Rotten Tomatoes: "69% of 102 critics' reviews are positive, with an average rating of 6.4/10"; consensus: "Sleek, stylish, and painlessly diverting, The Thomas Crown Affair is a remake of uncommon charm." Metacritic 72 of 100 from 23 critics. CinemaScore "B+".
- David Edelstein (Slate) called it unnecessary but positive: "We didn't need it, but we got it anyway--and it's pretty terrific."
- Owen Gleiberman (Entertainment Weekly) gave it a B+, praised the light touch, called it an improvement in several ways, but criticised it as "built out of spare parts we've seen in countless other films".

## Accolades

- 2000 Blockbuster Entertainment Awards: Favourite Actor – Drama/Romance, Pierce Brosnan — won; Favourite Supporting Actor, Denis Leary — won; Favourite Actress, Rene Russo — nominated.
- Hollywood Makeup Artist and Hair Stylist Guild Award: Best Contemporary Hair Styling – Feature, Enzo Angileri — won.
- Golden Satellite Award: Best Original Score, Bill Conti — nominated.

## Future

- A sequel announced in January 2007 "would be a loose remake of the 1964 film Topkapi"; Brosnan said in January 2009 Paul Verhoeven was attached, and Verhoeven said in 2010 he left "due to script changes and a change in the regime". Angelina Jolie and Charlize Theron were rumoured. In April 2013 Brosnan acknowledged development hell.
- "The initial script was penned by John Rogers from a story he had co-written with Harley Peyton while additional material was provided by Nick Meyer, Michael Finch and Karl Gajdusek."
- "In the April 2014 edition of Empire, two months after completing a one-year prison term on multiple felony convictions, John McTiernan revealed that he had written a script while incarcerated, for a sequel called Thomas Crown and the Missing Lioness."
- Michael B. Jordan pitched a new adaptation to MGM in 2016; by April 2023 Amazon announced a reboot through Amazon Studios. "The Thomas Crown Affair is scheduled to be released in the United States on March 5, 2027."

wikis.title: The Exorcist (1973 film)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia's article on The Exorcist, William Friedkin's 1973 horror film from William Peter Blatty's novel, covering its casting, punishing production and supposed curse, December 1973 release, box office, controversies, awards and franchise.
wikis.body:
## Overview
- The source is the English Wikipedia article on *The Exorcist*, the 1973 American supernatural horror film directed by William Friedkin and produced by William Peter Blatty from his own 1971 novel. Parts 1 and 2 hold the article (plot, cast, production, the purported curse, release, reception, controversies, themes, litigation, legacy, accolades and the franchise); part 3 holds the references, bibliography, external links and categories.

## Key facts
- Released in the United States by Warner Bros. on December 26, 1973; running time 122 minutes; infobox budget $12 million and box office $441.3 million. Stars Ellen Burstyn, Max von Sydow, Lee J. Cobb, Kitty Winn, Jack MacGowran, Jason Miller and Linda Blair.
- Principal photography began August 14, 1972; scheduled for 85 days, it "took over 200 days to wrap", going $2.5 million over an initial $4.2 million budget. Locations included Georgetown in Washington, D.C., New York interiors and Mosul and Hatra in Iraq, where daytime temperatures reached 130 degrees F (54 degrees C).
- Injuries and deaths around the production (Burstyn's fractured coccyx, Blair's fractured lower spine and scoliosis, the deaths of Jack MacGowran and Vasiliki Maliaros) fed a belief the film was cursed; Friedkin said he "definitely believe[s] in demonic possession", while Blatty and historian Sarah Crowther attributed the stories to publicity and a long, punishing shoot - and the page records Friedkin's 2018 claim that Burstyn was not injured at all, against her own account.
- Box-office figures as the page gives them: $1.9 million in the first week from 30 screens; $193 million by the end of the original run (lead); $232.6 million lifetime in the United States and Canada and, "as of 2025", $430 million worldwide (body), against the $441.3 million / $441 million in the infobox and lead. Warner Bros. used four-wall distribution, a first for a major studio.
- Reception was mixed on release - from Kauffmann's "the scariest film I've seen in years" to Canby's "elegant occultist claptrap" - with strong audience reactions (fainting, vomiting, riots in queues), Catholic and Protestant criticism, an R-rating controversy, and bans or prosecutions in Boston, Hattiesburg, Tunisia and several UK councils. Its later standing: Rotten Tomatoes 78% of 177 reviews (8.50/10), Metacritic 83/100, National Film Registry induction in 2010.
- Awards: ten Academy Award nominations, the first horror film nominated for Best Picture, with wins for Blatty's adapted screenplay and for Best Sound; four Golden Globes including Best Motion Picture - Drama; four Saturn Awards.
- Franchise: *Exorcist II: The Heretic* (1977), *The Exorcist III* (1990), *Exorcist: The Beginning* (2004), *Dominion* (2005), the Fox series (2016-2017), *The Exorcist: Believer* (2023), and Mike Flanagan's *The Exorcist: Martyrs*, "set to release in theaters on March 12, 2027".

## Date wording
- The parts give no publication or last-updated date for the page itself; only dated maintenance tags ("Use mdy dates from February 2026") and "as of 2025" statements appear.

wikis.title: The Exorcist (1973) - film, plot, cast and production
wikis.summary: The first part of the Wikipedia article on The Exorcist, covering the film's credits, plot, casting, direction, filming and effects, the troubled production and purported curse, post-production, music, releases and its opening box office.
wikis.body:
## Film
- *The Exorcist* is "a 1973 American supernatural horror film directed by William Friedkin and produced by William Peter Blatty, who adapted his own 1971 novel".
- Infobox: screenplay by Blatty; editors Evan A. Lottman, Norman Gay, Bud S. Smith and supervising editor Jordan Leondopoulos; music Jack Nitzsche; cinematography Owen Roizman; production company Hoya Productions; distributed by Warner Bros.; release date December 26, 1973; running time 122 minutes; country United States; language English; budget $12 million; box office $441.3 million.
- Stars Ellen Burstyn, Max von Sydow, Lee J. Cobb, Kitty Winn, Jack MacGowran, Jason Miller and Linda Blair; it follows a girl's demonic possession and an exorcism by two Catholic priests.
- The lead states production "took twice as long as scheduled and cost almost three times the initial budget", that the many mishaps "led to a belief that the film was cursed", that Warner Bros. booked it under four-wall distribution rental agreements ("a first for any major studio"), and that "at the end of its original theatrical run, the film grossed $193 million, and has a lifetime gross of $441 million with subsequent re-releases".
- It was the first horror film nominated for the Academy Award for Best Picture (ten nominations in all); Blatty won Best Adapted Screenplay and the sound engineers Best Sound. It was the highest-grossing R-rated horror film (unadjusted) until 2017's *It*, and was selected for the National Film Registry in 2010.

## Plot (as the page summarizes it)
- Priest Lankester Merrin finds a talisman at an archaeological dig at Hatra in northern Iraq; in Georgetown, Washington, D.C., actress Chris MacNeil's 12-year-old daughter Regan plays with a spirit board and contacts "Captain Howdy". Director Burke Dennings is found dead at the bottom of the stairs beneath Regan's window with his head turned backward.
- Father Damien Karras, a Jesuit psychiatrist in a crisis of faith, records Regan speaking a language a linguist identifies as "perfect English being spoken backwards", sees "help me" appear on her stomach from the inside, and concludes an exorcism is warranted. Merrin dies of a heart attack during the ritual; Karras takes the demon into himself and jumps from the window to his death, and Dyer gives him last rites.

## Cast
- Ellen Burstyn (Chris MacNeil), Max von Sydow (Merrin), Jason Miller (Karras), Lee J. Cobb (Lt. William F. Kinderman), Kitty Winn (Sharon Spencer), Jack MacGowran (Burke Dennings), Linda Blair (Regan), Father William O'Malley (Father Dyer), Father Thomas Bermingham, Vasiliki Maliaros and others.
- The demon Pazuzu is voiced by Mercedes McCambridge, with vocal effects by Ron Faber and its face by Eileen Dietz; the "spider walk" was performed by stunt double Ann Miles. Uncredited cast includes Blatty himself as Fromme and Paul Bateson as a radiologist's assistant.

## Development and writing
- Aspects of Blatty's novel were inspired by the 1949 exorcism performed by Jesuit William S. Bowdern; the novel sold poorly until Blatty discussed the devil on *The Dick Cavett Show*, after which it topped the *New York Times* best seller list.
- Lew Grade made a modest offer for the rights; a co-production with Paul Monash collapsed over script differences.
- The screenplay narrows the novel's focus, tones down the sexual content, drops Regan's constant diarrhea and removes the novel's counterbalancing natural explanations for her symptoms.

## Casting
- Jack Nicholson was considered for Karras and Paul Newman was interested before Blatty hired Stacy Keach; Audrey Hepburn, Anne Bancroft and Jane Fonda were considered for Chris and rejected the part; Carol Burnett was turned down by the studio; Burstyn got the part over studio head Ted Ashley's opposition.
- Jason Miller, a playwright who had studied three years for the Jesuit priesthood, told Friedkin "[Karras] is me"; after a screen test the studio bought out Keach's contract.
- Regan: Pamelyn Ferdin was "too familiar", Denise Nickerson's family found the script too dark, and Janet Leigh would not let Jamie Lee Curtis audition. Linda Blair, 12, came in with her mother Elinore; Friedkin recalled her as "[S]mart but not precocious ... cute but not beautiful", and the page quotes their exchange about the crucifix scene verbatim.
- Mercedes McCambridge "ate raw eggs, drank whiskey and chainsmoked cigarettes" for Pazuzu's voice and was credited only after Screen Actors Guild arbitration; her name was on all but the first 30 prints, and the dispute blocked a soundtrack album with dialogue.
- Eileen Dietz, 15 years Blair's senior, doubled Blair in violent scenes and appears as Pazuzu's face. Blair estimates Dietz is in 17 seconds of the film; Dietz claimed in the media to have performed all the possession scenes; "the studio ultimately measured her screen presence at 28.25 seconds".
- Warner Bros. wanted Marlon Brando as Merrin; Friedkin refused and cast Max von Sydow, inspired by a Philippe Halsman photograph of Pierre Teilhard de Chardin, over Blatty's choice Paul Scofield.

## Direction
- Directors considered included Mike Nichols, Arthur Penn, Stanley Kubrick, John Boorman and Peter Bogdanovich; the studio hired Mark Rydell before Blatty insisted on Friedkin, which the studio accepted after *The French Connection*'s success and Best Picture win.
- "[P]roduction costs soon exceeded the initial $4.2 million ($23.8 million in 2024) budget."
- Friedkin manipulated performances: he slapped O'Malley to get his reaction in Karras's death scene, fired blanks without warning to shock Miller, and had the vomit (porridge coloured like pea soup) hit Miller's face after rehearsing it hitting his chest. Crew nicknamed him "Wacky Willy"; Dietz recalled "People were literally placing bets on what he would reshoot next."

## Cinematography, locations and effects
- Owen Roizman shot everything except the Iraqi prologue (Billy Williams), aiming for an available-light look; Friedkin "demanded complete realism", making the reflective kitchen set "virtually impossible" to light.
- Principal photography began August 14, 1972. Interiors were shot in New York (CECO Studios, Goldwater Memorial Hospital, Bellevue, Fordham's Keating Hall); the opening was shot in and near Mosul, Iraq, where Friedkin negotiated with local Ba'ath Party officials, hired local crew and taught filmmaking; the dig site is Hatra, and daytime temperatures reached 130 degrees F (54 degrees C), limiting shooting to dawn and dusk.
- The MacNeil house exterior was a home at 36th and Prospect streets in Washington, with an added mansard roof, a rubber-padded staircase and an eastward false-front extension for Karras's fall. Georgetown locations included Healy Hall, Lauinger Library, Dahlgren Chapel and The Tombs pub.
- The bedroom was chilled to -20 degrees F (-29 degrees C) by a $50,000 ($284,000 in 2024) refrigeration system; only three minutes of filming at a time were possible and about five shots a day, the sequence taking a month, filmed in script order.
- The 80-pound (36 kg) Blair wore a bodysuit with hooks for monofilament wires for the levitation; the wires had to be painted out "practically ... frame by frame".
- Merrin's arrival scene, shot on von Sydow's first day, was inspired by Rene Magritte's 1954 painting *Empire of Light*; the crew had a full day to light it and Friedkin was satisfied with the first take.
- The head-spinning used a life-size animated dummy built by makeup artist Dick Smith with effects supervisor Marcel Vercoutere, tested by turning its head in a taxi. Kermode says its repeat during the exorcism was added on set, against Blatty's argument that "supernatural doesn't mean impossible".
- The crucifix scene runs 50 seconds; Blatty pleaded with Friedkin to stop "destroying the film", and later found its popularity "terribly depressing".
- The angiography scene, not in the novel, was the scene audiences found most disturbing; it has been called "irresponsible" (Graeme Garden, *New Scientist*) and, per Friedkin's 2012 DVD commentary, was used in radiological training films for years.
- The spider-walk was performed by Ann Miles after two weeks' practice, without the harness Vercoutere designed; Friedkin cut it before the premiere and denied filming it until Kermode found the footage in the Warner Bros. archives in the mid-1990s; it was restored in the 2000 cut. Credit was long misattributed to Sylvia Hager.
- Smith aged von Sydow about 30 years in close-ups with four hours of makeup daily; Pauline Kael called it "one of the most convincing aging jobs I've ever seen". Blair wore green contact lenses; the "HELP ME" letters were scratched into a latex stomach and heated to disappear, then the film was reversed.

## Production difficulties and the purported curse
- Scheduled for 85 days of principal photography, the film "took over 200 days to wrap", went $2.5 million ($14.2 million in 2024) over budget and cost the studio $12 million ($68 million in 2024).
- A bird flew into a circuit breaker, starting a fire that destroyed all the house sets except Regan's room, delaying shooting six weeks; another set was damaged by sprinklers; the 10-foot Pazuzu statue was shipped to Hong Kong instead of Iraq, costing two weeks.
- Burstyn fractured her coccyx in the scene where Regan throws Chris backward, was unable to film for two weeks and used crutches for the rest of the shoot, with chronic problems since; the page also records Friedkin saying in 2018 that she did not make an insurance claim, was not injured and did not miss any shooting, and that he "would rather have had one [take] that risked hurting her a little, not injuring her", while Burstyn believes there should have been padding.
- Blair fractured her lower spine on the loosely strapped rocking bed (the take is in the film) and developed scoliosis and a lifelong aversion to cold. A carpenter cut off his thumb; a lighting technician lost a toe.
- Deaths connected with the production: MacGowran a week after finishing his scenes; Maliaros before the film was finished; a night watchman, the refrigeration system operator and an assistant cameraman's newborn; Blair's grandfather; von Sydow's brother. Years later Paul Bateson, the angiography technician, was convicted of murdering journalist Addison Verrill.
- Friedkin told *Castle of Frankenstein*: "I'm not a convert to the occult ... but after all I've seen on this film, I definitely believe in demonic possession". Father Bermingham blessed the cast and crew rather than exorcising the set.
- Sarah Crowther believes the curse stories were spread by the studio; Blatty said Friedkin started them and that "if you shoot something for a year, people are going to get hurt, people are going to die", joking in 2000 "There is no Exorcist curse. I am The Exorcist curse!"

## Post-production, sound and music
- Four editors worked on the film - Leondopoulos (supervising), Norman Gay, Evan Lottman and Bud Smith - and shared the editing Oscar nomination; Smith also made the "flash face" trailer, which Warner Bros. feared would scare audiences too much.
- Friedkin felt the 140-minute cut was perfect; the studio insisted on two hours and he cut roughly 10-12 minutes over Blatty's objections, including the original ending with Dyer and Kinderman and a scene where Karras and Merrin discuss the demon's motive.
- Sound effects by Ron Nagle, Doc Siegel, Gonzalo Gavira and Bob Fine mixed bees, dogs, hamsters and pigs into the demon's voice; the head-rotation sound was a twisted leather wallet. The four-month sound process finished just before release.
- Wilson Bryan Key alleged subliminal imagery; Friedkin said subliminal editing was done "for dramatic effect", while Blatty said in 1999 "[t]here are no subliminal images. If you can see it, it's not subliminal."
- Title sequence by Dan Perri, keeping the novel cover's Weiss Initials typeface, with an "implied sunrise" fading from black and white to colour over 30 seconds.
- Music: Friedkin found Mike Oldfield's *Tubular Bells* in the studio's music library; Lalo Schifrin's score was rejected and the tapes thrown away in the studio parking lot; Bernard Herrmann turned the job down after a rough cut. The film uses Penderecki (Cello Concerto No. 1, *Polymorphia*), Webern's *Five Pieces for Orchestra* and original music by Jack Nitzsche - "only 17 minutes of music in the two-hour film". Henze's *Fantasia for Strings* plays over the closing credits. A 1998 restored soundtrack included three pieces from Schifrin's rejected score; Waxwork Records reissued the score in 2017.

## Releases
- Warner Bros. scheduled release for December 26, 1973 after post-production delays; Friedkin believed the date hurt it commercially and had wanted a March release like *The Godfather*. The first run lasted 105 weeks. A 1979 re-release in 70 mm expanded the 1.75:1 ratio to 2.20:1; a longer cut, "The Version You've Never Seen" (later "Extended Director's Cut"), was released theatrically in 2000.
- Home media: 25th anniversary box set (1998, VHS and DVD) with the original ending as a special feature; the 2000 cut on VHS and DVD; DVD/Blu-ray as the "Extended Director's Cut" in 2010; a 40th-anniversary Blu-ray in 2013; *The Exorcist: The Complete Anthology* on DVD in 2006 and Blu-ray in 2014; both cuts on Ultra HD Blu-ray on September 19, 2023 for the 50th anniversary.

## Box office (opening)
- Warner Bros. had low expectations; the film was not previewed for critics and opened on 30 screens in 24 theaters, grossing $1.9 million in its first week (a $70,000 per-theater average) and $7.4 million nationwide within a month, expanding to a 366-screen wide release. By February it accounted for 15 percent of the distributor's grosses in key markets.
- No theaters in Black neighbourhoods were booked initially; after the Westwood theater was overwhelmed by moviegoers from South Central, it was booked there. Black enthusiasm "has been credited with ending mainstream studio support for blaxploitation movies".

wikis.title: The Exorcist (1973) - box office, reception, controversies and legacy
wikis.summary: The second part of The Exorcist article: its full box office, mixed reviews, extreme audience reactions, religious and rating controversies, later reputation, themes, lawsuits, legacy, awards and the franchise.
wikis.body:
## Box office (continued)
- The film took second place among 1974 US and Canadian distributor rentals (behind *The Sting*'s $68.5 million), became Warner Bros.' highest-grossing film at the time and eventually the highest-grossing 1973 release. Warner Bros. kept more than usual by using four-wall distribution, "the first time a major studio had done that", and made theaters commit to at least 24 weeks.
- Overseas rentals of $46 million gave a worldwide total of $112.3 million ($604 million in 2024); it became the highest-grossing film in Japan with over $8.2 million in rentals in its first 11 weeks.
- After reissues it has grossed $232.6 million in the United States and Canada - adjusted for inflation the ninth highest-grossing film of all time there and the top-grossing R-rated film - and, "as of 2025", $430 million worldwide ($2.31 billion in 2024). (The article's infobox and lead instead give $441.3 million / $441 million.)

## Initial critical response
- Reviews were mixed. Stanley Kauffmann (*The New Republic*): "This is the scariest film I've seen in years"; Arthur D. Murphy (*Variety*): "an expert telling of a supernatural horror story"; Joe Dante in *Castle of Frankenstein* called it "an amazing film"; Roger Ebert gave four stars but asked "Are people so numb they need movies of this intensity in order to feel anything at all?"
- Judith Crist called it "half-successful"; Pauline Kael called it "shallowness that asks to be taken seriously"; Vincent Canby (*The New York Times*) dismissed it as "a chunk of elegant occultist claptrap"; Andrew Sarris called it "a thoroughly evil film"; Jon Landau (*Rolling Stone*) called it "nothing more than a religious porn film"; Michael Dempsey (*Film Quarterly*) "the trash bombshell of 1973".

## Audience reaction
- *Newsweek*, February 2, 1974: "On December 26 a movie called The Exorcist opened in theatres across the country and since then all Hell has broken loose."
- Audiences screamed and fled the only sneak preview. Queues formed in 6 degrees F (-14 degrees C) cold in New York; crowds outside theaters sometimes rioted; Burstyn recalled a report of moviegoers queuing in Montreal at 4 a.m.
- Many viewers fainted; a woman in New York was said to have miscarried; a man was carried out on a stretcher after 20 minutes; a Toronto theater manager said "We have a plumber practically living here now"; some theaters arranged for ambulances to be on call. Many found the angiography the most unsettling scene.
- Some Catholic viewers had spiritual crises and parishes fielded calls about exorcisms; Rev. Richard Woods of Loyola of Chicago said "It stirs up memories of all those descriptions of hell that you got from nuns."
- In 1975 *The Journal of Nervous and Mental Disease* published a psychiatrist's paper documenting four cases of "cinematic neurosis" triggered by the film.
- Jason Zinoman: the film "was one of the rare horror movies that became part of the national conversation"; journalists complained coverage distracted from Watergate, and William Paul wrote the audience "had become a spectacle equal to the film".

## Religious response
- Friedkin: "One of the best things that could happen is if the Pope denounces it." The Catholic Film Newsletter rated it A-IV (adults only, with reservations) and faulted it for suggesting exorcisms were common and possibly encouraging belief in the occult.
- Priests criticised the priests' conduct: Woods said "They departed from the ritual in the most stupid and reckless manner"; Eugene Kennedy called its view of good and evil "immature".
- Kael asked whether "American Catholics [are] willing to see their faith turned into a horror show", while calling the film "the biggest recruiting poster the Catholic Church has had since ... Going My Way". A later historian found the Church privately considered it faith-affirming.
- Tunisia banned the film before its 1975 release as "unjustified propaganda in favor of Christianity". The Jesuit magazine *America* ran priests' commentaries in February 1974 with a reply from Blatty. Billy Graham told the *National Enquirer* "the Devil is in every frame of that film"; *The Christian Century* denounced it as "hardcore pornography".

## Rating controversy and bans
- MPAA ratings board head Aaron Stern told Friedkin it was "an important film" and would get an R as submitted. Critic Roy Meacham argued in February 1974 that the MPAA had yielded to Warner Bros. pressure; Washington authorities later invoked a local ordinance over the crucifix scene and police warned theaters that staff admitting minors would be arrested. Ebert found the R "stupefying"; later ratings chair Richard Heffner said "How could anything be worse than this? And it got an R?"
- Boston's attempted ban was blocked by a court on obscenity grounds, though authorities told theaters not to admit minors. In Hattiesburg, Mississippi, police arrested the projectionist and manager after the first showing and a jury fined the theater $100; the Mississippi Supreme Court overturned the conviction in 1976 under *Miller v. California*.
- UK release March 1974 drew protests from the Nationwide Festival of Light; some councils banned it (Dinefwr Borough and Ceredigion in Wales). Released on UK home video in 1981, it was withdrawn in 1988 after BBFC director James Ferman vetoed a certificate; it was passed uncut at 18 in 1999, and Channel 4 first showed it on UK terrestrial television in 2001.

## Later reputation and themes
- It was the top-grossing R-rated horror film for almost half a century; *The Sixth Sense* (1999) and then *It* (2017) passed it as highest-grossing supernatural horror film.
- Rotten Tomatoes: 78% of 177 reviews positive, average 8.50/10; the director's cut 88% from 82 reviews (7.30). Metacritic: 83 out of 100 from 22 critics, "universal acclaim". Gene Siskel named it a top-five film of 1973; Mark Kermode believes it the best film ever made; *Rolling Stone* ranked it No. 1 in a 2022 list of 101 best horror movies.
- Themes discussed: social anxiety after the upheavals of the late 1960s; Stephen King calls it "a social horror film if there ever was one"; readings around Watergate, second-wave feminism (Peter Biskind: "a male nightmare of female puberty"), Barbara Creed's counter-reading of Pazuzu as female, and Joseph Laycock on "folk piety" against rationalised religion.

## Litigation
- November 1973: Blatty sued the studio and Friedkin over billing, settling for the "William Peter Blatty's The Exorcist" line. February 1974: Dietz's nondisclosure dispute, in which SAG ruled her contract not binding.
- 2001: Blatty and Friedkin sued Warner Bros. over promotion profits and again over licensing deals, including the sale of television rights to Turner Network Television; Blatty made a criminal complaint to the FBI, which closed the case in 2002; the suits were settled confidentially two years later. In 2012 Blatty sued again for access to the studio's records.

## Legacy
- *Cinefantastique*: "The Exorcist has done for the horror film what 2001 did for science fiction". Studios funded similar films (*The Omen*, *The Sentinel*, *Burnt Offerings*, *Audrey Rose*, *The Amityville Horror*); well-known actors began taking horror roles; avant-garde scoring (Penderecki) spread to films such as *The Shining*.
- *Exorcist II: The Heretic* (1977) was one of the first sequels a studio commissioned for a major film not planned to have one.
- Cultural references include political cartoons, Maureen Dowd's 1998 column, *Square Pegs*, *Evil*, Pantera's *Vulgar Display of Power* (1992), *Saturday Night Live* parodies in its first season and in 2023, *Ghostbusters* (1984) and *Repossessed* (1990); in 2023 a protist was named *Daimonympha friedkini*.
- In 2015 the District of Columbia put a commemorative plaque on the Exorcist steps, unveiled with Blatty and Friedkin present the day before Halloween.

## Accolades
- Ten Academy Award nominations and two wins: Best Adapted Screenplay (Blatty) and Best Sound (Robert Knudson and Chris Newman); nominations for Picture, Director, Actress (Burstyn), Supporting Actor (Miller), Supporting Actress (Blair), Art Direction, Cinematography and Editing.
- Four wins from seven Golden Globe nominations, including Best Motion Picture - Drama, Best Director, Best Screenplay and Best Supporting Actress (Blair); a BAFTA soundtrack nomination; a DGA nomination; four Saturn Awards (Best Horror Film, Writing, Make-up, Special Effects); a WGA nomination; National Film Registry induction.
- AFI lists: No. 3 in "100 Years...100 Thrills"; Regan MacNeil No. 9 villain.

## Related media
- *Exorcist II: The Heretic* (1977, Boorman, with Richard Burton); Blatty's novel *Legion* (1983) became *The Exorcist III* (1990), which he wrote and directed with George C. Scott as Kinderman; prequels *Exorcist: The Beginning* (2004, Renny Harlin) and *Dominion: Prequel to the Exorcist* (2005, Paul Schrader).
- A 2020 reboot announcement was replaced by a Blumhouse/Morgan Creek sequel trilogy directed by David Gordon Green with Burstyn returning and Leslie Odom Jr. co-starring; *The Exorcist: Believer* was released in October 2023, after which the trilogy was scrapped and the franchise rebooted with *The Exorcist: Martyrs* from Mike Flanagan, "set to release in theaters on March 12, 2027". As of March 2026 *Deadline* reported Flanagan had added eleven long-time collaborators to the cast, including Rahul Kohli, Kate Siegel and Carla Gugino.
- Fox's television series *The Exorcist* (2016-2017) revealed Angela Rance as the adult Regan, making it a direct sequel; it was cancelled after two seasons. Blatty's script was published in 1974, 1998 and 2000.
- The part closes with See also links, the article's lettered notes and the start of the reference list. No publication or last-updated date is stated.

wikis.title: The Exorcist (1973) - references, works cited and page footer
wikis.summary: The closing part of The Exorcist article: its reference list, book bibliography, external links, franchise and Friedkin navigation boxes, and the category footer.
wikis.body:
## References
- The part is mostly the article's rendered reference list, ending with citations of Blatty's published screenplays (*William Peter Blatty on The Exorcist: From Novel to Film*, 1974; *The Exorcist/Legion - Two Classic Screenplays*, 1998; *The Exorcist*, Faber & Faber, 2000) and a *Variety* report that Fox cancelled *The Exorcist* series after two seasons.

## Works cited
