wikis.title: Exorcist: The Beginning (2004 film)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on Renny Harlin's 2004 Exorcist prequel, covering its plot, cast, its troubled production as a reshoot of Paul Schrader's Dominion, release, box office and largely negative reception.
wikis.body:
## Overview

- "Exorcist: The Beginning is a 2004 American supernatural horror film serving as a prequel to The Exorcist (1973), and the fourth installment in The Exorcist film series. Directed by Renny Harlin, the film stars Stellan Skarsgård, Izabella Scorupco and James D'Arcy."
- "The film follows Father Lankester Merrin, whose faith has been renounced after his experiences in World War II, as he works as an archeologist and discovers dark occurrences while excavating in Kenya."
- "The film was retooled from Paul Schrader's nearly-completed Dominion: Prequel to the Exorcist, which Morgan Creek Productions executives feared would be unsuccessful. Morgan Creek commissioned The Beginning with the emphasis of featuring more scares and gore. In addition to Harlin replacing Schrader, Hawley rewrote William Wisher and Caleb Carr's original script, while Mark Goldblatt and Todd E. Miller replaced Tim Silano as editors."
- "Exorcist: The Beginning was released in the United States on August 20, 2004, by Warner Bros. Pictures. The film received negative reviews from critics and grossed over $78 million against a $50 million production budget. Dominion was released the following year to slightly more favorable reviews."
- Infobox: screenplay Alexi Hawley; story William Wisher and Caleb Carr; based on characters by William Peter Blatty; produced by James G. Robinson; cinematography Vittorio Storaro; edited by Mark Goldblatt and Todd E. Miller; music by Trevor Rabin; production company Morgan Creek Productions; distributed by Warner Bros. Pictures; release date August 20, 2004; running time 114 minutes; budget $50 million; box office $78.1 million.

## Plot (as summarised by the article)

A prologue in the Byzantine era shows an injured priest crossing a battlefield, an impaled priest holding a Pazuzu head pendant, and hundreds of Byzantine soldiers crucified upside down. In Cairo in 1949, Father Lankester Merrin is haunted by a wartime incident in the occupied Netherlands where SS Lieutenant Kessel forced him to take part in arbitrary executions to spare a village. Antiquities collector Semelier sends him to a British dig at Derati in the Turkana region of British Kenya, where "a Christian Byzantine-era church built circa 500 AD—long before Christianity had reached that region of Africa" has been uncovered, to recover a demon relic before the British find it. At the site Merrin meets excavator Jefferies, doctor Sarah Novak, guide Chuma and Father Francis; diggers are fleeing because the church is thought cursed. The buried church is pristine, its angel statues pointing spears downward and its cross inverted, as if the sculptors "were trying to depict the angels restraining something beneath the church." Lead archaeologist Bession, committed to a Nairobi asylum, has carved a swastika into his chest, speaks in Kessel's voice and cuts his throat saying he is "free"; Father Gionetti says he was "touched" rather than possessed and gives Merrin the Roman ritual of exorcism. A boy, James, is killed by hyenas; his brother Joseph enters a fugue state; a stillborn baby is born covered in maggots. Merrin finds a cave temple to Pazuzu used for human sacrifice, and empty graves where plague victims were supposedly buried. Francis explains that 1,500 years earlier an army led by two priests sought the origin of evil there; Justinian ordered a church built over the site and buried; a vague Vatican reference found in 1893 drew four priests who vanished with the local tribesmen, after which the Vatican staged the false graveyard and the plague story. "Francis reveals that it is believed that the valley in Derati was the traditional spot of Lucifer's fall after the war in Heaven." Jefferies is found tied up in the church with his organs pecked out by crows. Sarah proves to be Bession's wife and the possessed one; she kills Francis and dies after Merrin exorcises her. The British soldiers and local tribes annihilate each other; only Merrin and Joseph remain. Back in Rome, Merrin tells Semelier he could not find the relic, and Semelier replies: "But you found something... didn't you?"

## Cast

Stellan Skarsgård as Father Lankester Merrin; Izabella Scorupco as Sarah; James D'Arcy as Father Francis; Remy Sweeney as Joseph; Julian Wadham as Major Granville; Andrew French as Chuma; Ralph Brown as Sergeant Major; Ben Cross as Semelier; David Bradley as Father Gionetti; Alan Ford as Jefferies; Antonie Kamerling as Lieutenant Kessel; Eddie Osei as Emekwi; Israel Aduramo as Jomo; Patrick O'Kane as Bession; James Bellamy as James; Rupert Degas as Pazuzu (uncredited).

## Production

- "Producer James G. Robinson first began development on an untitled prequel to The Exorcist (1973) in 1997, with the first draft of the screenplay penned by William Wisher Jr."
- "In October 1999, Morgan Creek Productions hired Tom McLoughlin to helm the film", with production slated for the following spring in Africa; McLoughlin left over script issues.
- "In October 2001, numerous publications reported that John Frankenheimer was on board as director, with a new screenplay revised by Caleb Carr. Liam Neeson was attached to portray... Merrin." Blatty was not expected to take part. After a July 2003 release date was set, Frankenheimer stepped down "due to his declining health and was replaced by Paul Schrader."
- Gabriel Mann joined in April 2002; the next month the film was titled Exorcist: The Beginning and Skarsgård (replacing Neeson) and Billy Crawford were cast.
- "Principal photography on Schrader's film began on November 11, 2002, in Morocco with Vittorio Storaro handling cinematography duties." Six weeks in Morocco and two months in Rome; "By the time filming had wrapped in February 2003, six writers had contributed to the screenplay and the budget had nearly doubled."
- "An early cut of Schrader's film that ran at 130 minutes was shown to the studio in early 2003. The cut was widely derided due to a lack of scares and gore." The studio's re-edit plan was opposed by Schrader; additional photography grew "bigger and bigger". Schrader said he faithfully adapted Carr's screenplay and that the studio had "buyer's remorse".
- Sheldon Kahn was brought in to re-cut without Schrader, who was "livid" and reportedly demanded Kahn leave. "Carr was expected for rewrites, but instead the studio opted to fire Schrader and scrap the film entirely in August 2003. Morgan Creek searched for a new director starting in October."
- "Renny Harlin was among the directors who met with Robinson and suggested rewriting the script, casting new actors and adding more action." Harlin oversaw rewrites by Skip Woods, then by Alexi Hawley and himself. "Skarsgård and Julian Wadham were the only cast members retained from the original shoot." Makeup effects artist Gary J. Tunnicliffe confirmed involvement in November 2003.
- Filming under Harlin began in winter 2003 in Rome. "Two weeks into production, the director's leg was shattered after being struck by a car, resulting in a two-week hiatus for filming. Harlin shot six weeks on crutches." Production ran twelve weeks; work continued into June 2004 and "The film was finished mere days before its official release."
- "After initially being given a $35 million budget under Schrader's direction, the reshoots and post-production work ballooned the film's budget to over $90 million." (The infobox gives the budget as $50 million.)

## Release

- Theatrical release August 20, 2004 by Warner Bros. Pictures.
- Home media: DVD and VHS on March 1, 2005; first Blu-ray on September 23, 2014; "Sony Pictures Home Entertainment re-released the film on October 13, 2020."

## Reception

- Box office: "$41.8 million in the United States and Canada, and $36.2 million in international territories, for a worldwide total of $78.1 million. On its opening weekend, the film grossed $18 million, earning the top spot at the box office."
- Rotten Tomatoes: "11% of 132 critics' reviews are positive, with an average rating of 3.6/10"; consensus: "A mediocre, gory horror film, nowhere near the quality of the 1973 original." Metacritic 30 of 100 from 22 critics, "generally unfavorable". CinemaScore "C".
- "Blatty said that watching Exorcist: The Beginning was his \"most humiliating professional experience\"", while calling Dominion "a handsome, classy, elegant piece of work". Roger Ebert: "I've seen both versions and much prefer Schrader's, and yet it must be said that Harlin did not prostitute himself in his version".
- "Exorcist: The Beginning was nominated for two Golden Raspberry Awards, Worst Director and Worst Remake or Sequel, but lost to two other Warner Bros. films, Catwoman and Scooby-Doo 2: Monsters Unleashed, respectively, at the 25th Golden Raspberry Awards."

The capture's cast section contains unrendered wikitext markup alongside the rendered list.

wikis.title: The Exorcist: Believer
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the 2023 film The Exorcist: Believer - its plot, cast, development under the $400 million Universal/Peacock rights deal, filming, release, box office, hostile reviews, and the cancelled sequels replaced by Mike Flanagan's reboot.
wikis.body:
## Overview
- 2023 American supernatural horror film directed by David Gordon Green, who co-wrote the screenplay with Peter Sattler from a story by Scott Teems, Danny McBride and Green, based on characters by William Peter Blatty.
- "The sixth installment in The Exorcist franchise, it serves as a legacy sequel to The Exorcist (1973)."
- Stars Leslie Odom Jr., Lidya Jewett, Olivia O'Neill (film debut), Jennifer Nettles, Norbert Leo Butz and Ann Dowd; Ellen Burstyn and Linda Blair reprise their roles from the original film.
- Production companies Morgan Creek Entertainment, Blumhouse Productions and Rough House Pictures; distributed by Universal Pictures. Cinematography Michael Simmonds; edited by Tim Alverson; music by David Wingo and Amman Abbasi.
- Release date October 6, 2023. Running time 111 minutes. Budget $30 million; box office $137 million.
- Plot: after his pregnant wife is fatally injured in a Haiti earthquake, photographer Victor Fielding raises daughter Angela alone in Georgia; Angela and her friend Katherine West go missing after a seance and return possessed, leading to an ecumenical exorcism in which Katherine is dragged to Hell and Angela revives.

## Cast
- Leslie Odom Jr. (Victor Fielding), Lidya Jewett (Angela Fielding), Olivia O'Neill (Katherine West), Jennifer Nettles (Miranda West), Norbert Leo Butz (Tony West), Raphael Sbarge (Pastor Don Revans), Okwui Okpokwasili (Dr. Beehibe), Danny McCarthy (Stuart), E. J. Bonilla (Father Maddox).
- Linda Blair as Regan MacNeil; Ann Dowd as Ann, a nurse; Ellen Burstyn as Chris MacNeil; Tracey Graves as Sorenne Fielding; Celeste Oliva as Detective Konik; Lize Johnston as Lamashtu.
- Helen Leahey served as the "primary source" of the demon's voice, the final effect created with additional voicework by J. Moliere and audio processing by sound mixer Paul Urmson.

## Development
- August 2020: Morgan Creek Entertainment reported to be producing a new franchise installment, with a tentative 2021 theatrical window. /Film's Ben Pearson noted the studio had said it would "never attempt to remake The Exorcist" but would obtain the "blessings of their library titles' original creators".
- December 2020: clarified as a sequel to the original film, with David Gordon Green in early negotiations to direct; Jason Blum, David Robinson and James Robinson producing.
- July 2021: a trilogy of sequels reported in concurrent development, Green directing the first from a script co-written with Peter Sattler and an original story with Scott Teems and Danny McBride. The film is a direct sequel to The Exorcist and "the story does not acknowledge the events of the other four films in the franchise".
- Joint-venture productions between Blumhouse and Morgan Creek with Universal distributing; "Universal collaborated with Peacock to purchase distribution rights for $400 million total", parts two and three optioned as potential Peacock exclusives. By October 2021 Green intended to direct all three, with outlines completed for the latter two.
- Executive producers: Green, McBride, Couper Samuelson and Stephanie Allain. Before the rights were acquired, the writing team and Blum spent early 2020 devising the story over Zoom.
- "The Exorcist: Believer was the last film produced by James G. Robinson before his death in February 2026."

## Casting and filming
- Ellen Burstyn reprised Chris MacNeil; Ann Dowd, Lidya Jewett, Olivia Marcum and Okwui Okpokwasili were cast; Raphael Sbarge joined as a pastor; Jennifer Nettles has a "primary role"; Helen Leahey was cast as the main voice of the demon.
- Linda Blair's cameo "was filmed in secret and not in the script". Green: "I told Ellen that Linda had agreed to do this... The moment that you see Linda take a knee and take her hand is the first time they'd communicated in many, many years. It was the first take".
- February 2022: Burstyn said she had completed her part; the team worked around her age and COVID-19 risks rather than waiting until after Halloween Ends (2022).
- Linda Blair served as an on-set "advisor"; Green told Total Film: "she was not interested in a significant role... We brought her in as an advisor because we're dealing with young people, and we want to take them to dangerous places safely".
- Principal photography began November 2022 in Atlanta and Savannah, Georgia on a $30 million budget; Burstyn was brought in that month for reshoots; in mid-December production shut down early for the holidays after Odom had an "unspecified health issue"; filming concluded in early March 2023.

## Release
- Released in the United States on October 6, 2023, moved up a week from October 13 "to avoid competition with the concert film Taylor Swift: The Eras Tour".
- Home media: digital October 24, 2023; streaming exclusively on Peacock in the US from December 1, 2023; Blu-ray, DVD and 4K UHD on December 19, 2023.
- In 2025 a haunted house attraction called Universal Horror Unleashed features characters from the film.

## Box office
- Grossed $65.5 million in the United States and Canada and $71.4 million in other territories, for a worldwide total of $137 million.
- Projected at $30-36 million from 3,663 theaters; made $11.8 million on its first day including $2.9 million in Thursday previews, and debuted to $26.5 million, topping the box office and the best opening of the franchise, "but was noted as disappointing given mid-$30 million projections and the $400 million Universal spent to acquire the rights". Second weekend $11 million, behind Taylor Swift: The Eras Tour.

## Critical response
- Rotten Tomatoes: 22% of 250 critics positive, average 4.4/10; consensus says it "earns points for trying to take the franchise back to its terrifying roots, but a lack of new ideas - and scares - make this an inauspicious start to a planned new trilogy."
- Metacritic 39 out of 100 from 54 critics, "generally unfavorable"; CinemaScore "C" (the same as The Exorcist III and Exorcist: The Beginning); PostTrak 61% positive.
- The article quotes William Friedkin, via friend and critic Ed Whitfield: "if there's a spirit world, and I can come back, I plan to possess David Gordon Green and make his life a living hell."
- Owen Gleiberman (Variety): it "feels about as dangerous as a crucifix dipped in a bottle of designer water". David Rooney (The Hollywood Reporter) called it "hella disappointing". David Fear (Rolling Stone) called it a "borderline incoherent mess". John Mulderig (Catholic Review) judged it "best dismissed as a bit of chaotic schlock". Stephanie Zacharek (Time) wrote that Burstyn "said yes to the wrong Exorcist sequel".
- More positive: Paul Asay in Plugged In praised its theme of faith and community; USA Today's Brian Truitt gave three out of four, noting Burstyn's limited screen time but saying "at least this franchise still has a prayer". Olly Richards (Empire) found Burstyn's role "gimmicky rather than essential".

## Accolades
- Hollywood Music in Media Awards, November 15th, 2023 - Best Original Score in a Horror Film (David Wingo and Amman Abbasi) - nominated.
- Golden Raspberry Awards, March 9th, 2024 - nominated for Worst Picture, Worst Director, Worst Screenplay, Worst Screen Combo ("Any 2 Money-Grubbing Investors Who Donated to the $400 Million for Remake Rights to The Exorcist") and Worst Prequel, Remake, Rip-off, or Sequel.

## Cancelled sequels and the reboot
- July 2021: two sequels confirmed in development with Green, McBride, Sattler and Teems. The first, The Exorcist: Deceiver, was originally scheduled for theaters on April 18, 2025; Green said in a 2024 Indiewire interview it would have been set in Europe and focused on Ann Dowd's Nurse Ann.
- After Believer's reception, The Hollywood Reporter sources said a creative re-think was near certain and Green had expressed doubt about participating; in January 2024 Green stepped down from Deceiver and the film was removed from the schedule.
- By May 2024 Mike Flanagan was in talks to write, direct and produce the next Exorcist film; confirmed later that month, with Deceiver and the planned trilogy officially cancelled and the franchise rebooted.
- The new film was slated for March 13, 2026, removed from Universal's schedule in June 2025 - Flanagan said on Tumblr it would not start production until after his Carrie miniseries and there was "no way it's coming out next March" - and was later rescheduled for theatrical release on March 12, 2027.

wikis.title: Sonic the Hedgehog 3 (film) - Wikipedia article
wikis.summary: Wikipedia's article on the 2024 film Sonic the Hedgehog 3, covering its credits, plot, cast, development, filming and animation, music, release, box office, critical response, awards and the fourth film.
wikis.body:
## The film

- "A 2024 action-adventure comedy film based on the Sonic video game series", the third in the Sonic film series, directed by Jeff Fowler and written by Pat Casey, Josh Miller and John Whittington; story by Casey and Miller; based on Sonic the Hedgehog by Sega. Known in Japan as Sonic x Shadow TOKYO MISSION.
- Produced by Neal H. Moritz, Toby Ascher, Toru Nakahara and Hitoshi Okuno; production companies Original Film, Marza Animation Planet and Blur Studio; distributed by Paramount Pictures. Cinematography Brandon Trost; editing Al LeVine; music Tom Holkenborg. Running time 110 minutes; countries United States and Japan; language English.
- Jim Carrey, Ben Schwartz, Lee Majdoub, Natasha Rothwell, Adam Pally, Shemar Moore, Colleen O'Shaughnessey, James Marsden, Tika Sumpter and Idris Elba reprise their roles; Krysten Ritter and Keanu Reeves join, Reeves as Shadow the Hedgehog and Carrey in a dual role as Ivo and Gerald Robotnik. Sonic, Tails and Knuckles face Shadow, who allies with the Robotniks to pursue revenge against humanity.

## Dates

- Announced in February 2022 during ViacomCBS's investor event, before the release of Sonic the Hedgehog 2.
- Reeves reported cast as Shadow on April 15, 2024; Carrey confirmed returning in February 2024.
- Principal photography was scheduled for August 31, 2023 in London and delayed to September; filming with physical actors started November 29, 2023; Fowler announced the wrap on March 29, 2024.
- Premiered at the Empire Leicester Square in London on December 10, 2024 and at the TCL Chinese Theatre in Los Angeles on December 16; released in the United States on December 20, 2024.
- Home media: digital January 21, 2025; disc formats April 15; Paramount+ in the US and Canada from February 18, 2025.
- A fourth film entered development in December 2024, "set for release on March 19, 2027"; Kristen Bell was announced as the voice of Amy Rose on February 18, 2026.

## Money

- Budget $122 million. Box office $492.2 million worldwide: $236.1 million in the United States and Canada and $256 million elsewhere.
- Opening weekend $60.1 million from about 3,800 theaters against a $55-60 million projection, with $6.5 million in Thursday previews, a franchise record.
- Became the highest-grossing film in the franchise, the second-highest-grossing video game film at the time (until A Minecraft Movie passed it in April 2025) and the tenth-highest-grossing film of 2024. Deadline Hollywood calculated a net profit of $123.6 million. By March 4 it had reached $485.7 million and overtaken Bruce Almighty as Carrey's highest-grossing film.

## Making it

- The plot draws on Sonic Adventure 2 (2001) and Shadow the Hedgehog (2005), with elements such as the ARK space station and Maria's terminal illness dropped to fit the film's 1970s setting.
- Carrey, who had said he was considering retiring, returned saying "I bought a lot of stuff and I need the money, frankly"; Fowler printed the script in 24-carat ink after Carrey's "gold ink" remark.
- Animation was produced by six studios - Rising Sun Pictures, Rodeo FX, Industrial Light & Magic, Fin, Marza Animation Planet and Paramount's in-house team - working in tandem with the Knuckles series, with the in-house team owning the Sonic assets to keep costs down.
- Tom Holkenborg's score incorporates Crush 40's "Live & Learn" from Sonic Adventure 2 as a leitmotif for Shadow; Jelly Roll released the single "Run It" on November 21, 2024, and the soundtrack album came out on Milan Records on December 20, 2024.

## Reception and awards

- Rotten Tomatoes 85% of 151 reviews (the article elsewhere cites an 86% score when calling it the site's highest-rated video game film as of January 2025, tied with Werewolves Within); Metacritic 56/100 from 28 critics; CinemaScore "A"; PostTrak 89% positive. Praise centred on Carrey's and Reeves's performances.
- Jim Carrey won Favorite Villain at the Nickelodeon Kids' Choice Awards on June 21, 2025, where the film took five further nominations; it was nominated for Best Game Adaptation at the Golden Joystick Awards on November 20, 2025.

## About this capture

The source is one long Wikipedia page split into four parts: all article text is in part 1, while parts 2 to 4 hold citation markup, the rendered reference list, external links, navigation boxes and categories. The capture gives no publication or last-edited date, only the permanent link oldid=1375452794.

wikis.title: Sonic the Hedgehog 3 (2024): plot, cast, production, release, box office and awards
wikis.summary: The main text of the Wikipedia article on the 2024 film Sonic the Hedgehog 3, covering its credits and infobox figures, plot, cast, development, filming and animation, music, release, box office, critical response, accolades and the planned fourth film.
wikis.body:
## Infobox / credits

- Directed by Jeff Fowler; screenplay by Pat Casey, Josh Miller and John Whittington; story by Pat Casey and Josh Miller; "Based on Sonic the Hedgehog by Sega".
- Produced by Neal H. Moritz, Toby Ascher, Toru Nakahara and Hitoshi Okuno. Executive producers Haruki Satomi, Shuji Utsumi, Yukio Sugino, Fowler, Tommy Gormley and Tim Miller.
- Starring (per end credits) Jim Carrey, Ben Schwartz, Krysten Ritter, Lee Majdoub, Natasha Rothwell, Adam Pally, Shemar Moore, Colleen O'Shaughnessey, James Marsden, Tika Sumpter, Idris Elba and Keanu Reeves.
- Cinematography Brandon Trost; edited by Al LeVine; music by Tom Holkenborg.
- Production companies Original Film, Marza Animation Planet and Blur Studio (a hidden note in the source says the credits state "In association with Sega Sammy Group", indicating financing only); distributed by Paramount Pictures.
- Release dates: December 10, 2024 (Empire Leicester Square); December 20, 2024 (United States). Running time 110 minutes. Countries United States and Japan. Language English.
- Budget $122 million. Box office $492.2 million.
- "A 2024 action-adventure comedy film based on the Sonic video game series", the third in the Sonic film series. Known in Japan as Sonic x Shadow TOKYO MISSION.

## Plot

In 1974 a meteorite carrying the alien hedgehog Shadow crash-lands in Oklahoma and is seized by the U.S. military; Professor Gerald Robotnik experiments on Shadow at a Guardian Units of Nations (G.U.N.) facility under Captain Walters, and Shadow befriends Gerald's granddaughter Maria, who is accidentally killed in an explosion during an escape attempt. In 2024 Shadow is released from a G.U.N. prison facility off the coast of Japan. Sonic, Tails and Knuckles - "Team Sonic" - are recruited by G.U.N. Director Rockwell to apprehend Shadow in Tokyo. Commander Walters is fatally wounded by Dr. Ivo Robotnik's drones and gives Sonic a keycard. Gerald, revealed as the mastermind, needs two keycards to activate the Eclipse Cannon, an orbiting laser weapon he designed for G.U.N., and claims he will destroy G.U.N.'s London headquarters. Sonic uses the Master Emerald and the seven Chaos Emeralds to become superpowered and fights Shadow, then persuades him to stop the cannon. Gerald reveals he means to destroy Earth; Tails, Knuckles and Ivo knock him into the reactor core and steer the beam away, slicing off part of the Moon. Ivo and Shadow move the melting core away from Earth before it explodes. In a scene after the film Sonic is ambushed outside New York by an army of Metal Sonics and saved by Amy Rose; Shadow is shown to have survived.

## Cast

- Voice: Ben Schwartz as Sonic the Hedgehog; Keanu Reeves as Shadow the Hedgehog; Colleen O'Shaughnessey as Miles "Tails" Prower; Idris Elba as Knuckles the Echidna.
- Live action: Jim Carrey in a dual role as Dr. Ivo Robotnik and Prof. Gerald Robotnik; James Marsden as Tom Wachowski; Tika Sumpter as Maddie Wachowski; Lee Majdoub as Agent Stone; Krysten Ritter as Director Rockwell; Natasha Rothwell as Rachel; Shemar Moore as Randall Handel; Adam Pally as Wade Whipple; Alyla Browne as Maria Robotnik; Tom Butler as Commander Walters; James Wolk as a young Captain Walters; Jorma Taccone as Kyle Lancebottom; Cristo Fernandez as brothers Pablo and Juan, and Sofia Pernas as Gabriella, in the in-universe telenovela La Ultima Pasion.

## Development and casting

- March 2020: James Marsden confirmed he had signed on for multiple sequels. February 2022: the third film was formally announced during ViacomCBS's investor event, with the Knuckles series for Paramount+ developed simultaneously. Budget $122 million. Paul Greenberg and Oren Uziel received off-screen additional literary material credit.
- April 2022: Carrey announced he was considering retiring from acting; producers said the role would not be recast. Carrey said he would need "the angels bring some sort of script that's written in gold ink"; Fowler printed the script in 24-carat ink, which he estimates would be worth about $100,000. Carrey was confirmed to be returning in February 2024 and said: "I came back to this universe because, first of all, I get to play a genius, which is a bit of a stretch. And, you know, it's just... I bought a lot of stuff and I need the money, frankly".
- April 15, 2024: Keanu Reeves reported as cast as the voice of Shadow. Fowler said there was an "obvious corollary" with the John Wick films, which served as a "perfect, albeit unconventional, 'audition'".
- February 2024: Krysten Ritter, Alyla Browne, James Wolk, Sofia Pernas, Cristo Fernandez and Jorma Taccone cast in undisclosed roles; Browne's role revealed as Maria on February 16.

## Writing

The film draws on the video games Sonic Adventure 2 (2001) and Shadow the Hedgehog (2005). Miller framed the adaptation question as "how dark can it get" while remaining PG-rated. Elements used include the Chao, placed in a Chao Gardens-themed restaurant in Tokyo. Gerald, Maria and Shadow living on the ARK space station and Maria's terminal illness from the games were dropped as incompatible with the 1970s setting and unneeded. A "guns, lots of guns" line for Shadow was considered as a Reeves homage and rejected; the film instead references Speed (1994) and mirrors the Neo/Agent Smith fight from The Matrix in the final duel. Fowler said the inclusion of the TikTok meme "Shadow loves Latinas" was a way to "honor what fans know and love".

## Filming, voice recording and animation

- Principal photography was originally scheduled to begin August 31, 2023 in London, England, but was delayed to September. Production with physical actors started November 29, 2023, announced with a teaser image of Shadow's stand-in statue. Schwartz began recording by mid-February 2024. Marsden said filming was completed by March 14; Fowler revealed the film had wrapped on March 29. (The article's lead summarizes this as filming for animated characters beginning in September 2023 because of the 2023 SAG-AFTRA strike, filming with actors that November in London, and production ending by March 2024.)
- Brandon Trost returned as cinematographer; Luke Freeborn was production designer.
- Carrey spent three hours in makeup for each Gerald session and helped design his prosthetics; actor Brendan Murphy doubled for whichever character Carrey was not playing. Shooting Carrey as both characters on the same day was not feasible, so the crew took notes and panorama photographs to keep the set consistent.
- Clem Yip was animation supervisor. Animation was produced by six studios: Rising Sun Pictures, Rodeo FX, Industrial Light & Magic, Fin, Marza Animation Planet and the in-house team at Paramount, in a "speedboat vendor" strategy. The in-house team built and owned the Sonic assets and distributed them to vendors, which "helped the production keep costs down and move faster". The in-house team worked on both the film and the Knuckles series as a cost-cutting measure. Trost said the filming crew's work constituted around 30% of the content in a final frame.

## Music

Tom Holkenborg returned to score and had finished work by July 2024. Crush 40 vocalist Johnny Gioeli said in December 2023 that there had been talks of including "Live & Learn" from Sonic Adventure 2 and confirmed its inclusion in February 2024; it is introduced as a riff Maria plays on her guitar and becomes a leitmotif for Shadow, with a vocal version remixed by the composer used in the duel. Jelly Roll released the single "Run It" on November 21, 2024. The film also features "Neon" by One Ok Rock. The soundtrack album was released by Milan Records on December 20, 2024.

## Release and marketing

- Premiered at the Empire Leicester Square in London on December 10, 2024 and at the TCL Chinese Theatre in Los Angeles on December 16; released in the United States by Paramount Pictures on December 20, taking over the original release date of Smurfs (2025). Screened in 4DX and other premium formats but forewent an IMAX release; Paramount held a fan event on December 19.
- Marketing: first-look footage at CinemaCon in April 2024; first tease of Reeves posted to the film's TikTok on August 25, captioned "foreSHADOWing"; first trailer and teaser poster August 27; second trailer November 25, unlocked via a Sega Genesis cartridge minigame using a cheat code from Sonic the Hedgehog 3 (1994). Tie-ins included Jakks Pacific toys, a Reebok sneaker line, McDonald's Happy Meal toys, AMC novelty popcorn buckets, the stop-motion short "A Very Sonic Christmas" (December 11, 2024) and Shadow Generations downloadable content on December 12 with a Tokyo level and Reeves reprising his voice.
- Home media: digital download January 21, 2025; Ultra HD Blu-ray, Blu-ray and DVD April 15; streaming on Paramount+ in the United States and Canada from February 18, 2025. Its UK digital release debuted atop the Official Film Chart.

## Box office

- "$236.1 million in the United States and Canada, and $256 million in other territories, for a worldwide total of $492.2 million"; tenth highest-grossing film of 2024 both in the US and Canada and worldwide. Deadline Hollywood calculated net profit as $123.6 million and ranked it tenth among 2024's "Most Valuable Blockbusters".
- Projected $55-60 million from 3,800 theaters; $6.5 million from Thursday previews, a franchise record; $25.7 million Friday against Sonic the Hedgehog 2's $26.3 million; $60.1 million three-day opening weekend, first place and the second-highest December debut for a PG film behind The Chronicles of Narnia: The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe ($65.6 million).
- Second weekend $37 million (first place); at $136 million in the US and Canada it pushed Reeves's lifetime earnings in the region past $3 billion. Third weekend $21.4 million (second), fourth $11.3 million (third), sixth $10.6 million.
- By its fifth weekend it passed its predecessor at $420 million to become the highest-grossing film in the franchise; in its seventh it reached $462.5 million worldwide, the second-highest-grossing video game film ever, ahead of Pokemon Detective Pikachu (2019) and behind The Super Mario Bros. Movie (2023), a record held until A Minecraft Movie surpassed it in April 2025. By March 4 it had grossed $485.7 million, overtaking Bruce Almighty (2003) as Carrey's highest-grossing film.

## Critical response

- Rotten Tomatoes: 85% of 151 critics' reviews positive; consensus: "With a double helping of Jim Carrey's antics and a quicksilver pace befitting its hero, Sonic the Hedgehog 3 is the best entry in this amiable series yet." The article adds that as of January 2025 it was tied with Werewolves Within (2021) as the site's highest-rated video game film "with an 86% score", a figure that differs from the 85% given in the same paragraph.
- Metacritic: 56 out of 100 based on 28 critics, "mixed or average". CinemaScore "A", matching the previous two films; PostTrak 89% positive.
- Praise focused on Reeves and Carrey: Owen Gleiberman (Variety), Rachel Labonte (Screen Rant), Marc Deschamps (ComicBook.com), Glenn Kenny (The New York Times), Matt Donato (IGN and The A.V. Club), The Hollywood Reporter and Jesse Hassenger (Polygon). Andrew Pulver (The Guardian) was largely critical of the performances, Pete Hammond (Deadline Hollywood) found Carrey's fourth-wall breaking less impactful after Deadpool, and Wendy Ide (The Observer) wrote "two Jim Carreys, each of them turning every individual line of dialogue into an extravagant pantomime of gurning and grandstanding, is categorically one too many". A. A. Dowd of IGN called the CGI "much more pleasing" than in previous Sonic films, while Christian Zilko (IndieWire) criticized it.

## Accolades (as tabulated)

- Nickelodeon Kids' Choice Awards, June 21, 2025: Favorite Movie - Nominated; Favorite Movie Actor (Jim Carrey) - Nominated; Favorite Male Voice from an Animated Movie (Ben Schwartz) - Nominated; Favorite Male Voice from an Animated Movie (Keanu Reeves) - Nominated; Favorite Villain (Jim Carrey) - Won; Favorite Song from a Movie ("Run It" - Jelly Roll) - Nominated.
- Golden Joystick Awards, November 20, 2025: Best Game Adaptation - Nominated.

## Sequel

In September 2024 producer Toby Ascher stated intent for additional Sonic films; Elba and Reeves expressed interest in a spin-off. In December 2024 a fourth Sonic film entered development, "set for release on March 19, 2027". In January 2025 Carrey said he was "open to the idea" of returning. On February 18, 2026 it was announced that Kristen Bell had joined the sequel's cast as the voice of Amy Rose.

## Notes

A footnote states that Sonic the Hedgehog "was developed by Sonic Team, published by Sega, directed and programmed by Yuji Naka, designed by Hirokazu Yasuhara, and illustrated by Naoto Ohshima".

wikis.title: Sonic the Hedgehog 4 (film)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the upcoming film Sonic the Hedgehog 4: cast, development out of Sonic the Hedgehog 3, filming in 2026, marketing and its March 19, 2027 release date.
wikis.body:
## Overview
- "Sonic the Hedgehog 4 is an upcoming American action-adventure comedy film based on the Sonic video game series", directed by Jeff Fowler.
- Produced by Neal H. Moritz, Toby Ascher and Toru Nakahara for Original Film; distributed by Paramount Pictures. Cinematography by Brandon Trost; edited by Al LeVine.
- Infobox release date: March 19, 2027. Country United States, language English.
- Reported in development in December 2024, just before the release of Sonic the Hedgehog 3; principal photography began in March 2026 and wrapped in May; the cast was confirmed in March 2026 alongside the title announcement.
- "The film will draw elements from the video game Sonic CD (1993)."

## Cast
- Returning: Jim Carrey, Ben Schwartz, Idris Elba, Keanu Reeves, James Marsden, Tika Sumpter, Colleen O'Shaughnessey and Lee Majdoub. Kristen Bell joins the voice cast as Amy Rose. Ben Kingsley, Matt Berry, Nick Offerman and Richard Ayoade are cast in undisclosed roles.
- Voices: Ben Schwartz (Sonic the Hedgehog), Kristen Bell (Amy Rose), Idris Elba (Knuckles the Echidna, with "the Flames of Disaster"), Keanu Reeves (Shadow the Hedgehog, of Project Shadow), Colleen O'Shaughnessey (Miles "Tails" Prower).
- Live-action: Jim Carrey (Dr. Ivo Robotnik), James Marsden (Tom Wachowski, sheriff of Green Hills, Montana), Tika Sumpter (Maddie Wachowski), Lee Majdoub (Agent Stone).
- Metal Sonic will appear; "It is currently unknown whether he will be voiced or be a non-speaking character".

## Development
- September 2024: producer Toby Ascher said additional installments were planned. November 2024: Fowler revealed Sonic the Hedgehog 3 would tease new characters for a fourth film; its mid-credits scene features Amy Rose saving Sonic by smashing an army of Metal Sonics.
- Writers Pat Casey and Josh Miller said Amy had been considered for a larger role in the third film but was excluded so the script could focus on Shadow.
- December 2024: the fourth film was officially greenlit, with Fowler returning to direct and Toku Nakahara, Neal H. Moritz and Toby Ascher returning to produce. Later that month Casey and Miller expressed interest in taking Sonic to worlds beyond Earth.
- January 2025: concept art for Sonic the Hedgehog 3 released online by Tacit Sign Studio, including Amy and Metal Sonic scenes not in the final film, fuelled theories that the fourth film would take inspiration from Sonic CD - the games debut of both characters. Miller said it could not be openly discussed; Fowler said their simultaneous introduction was intended to "honor that chronology" but that the story would not be solely based on CD.

## Casting, filming and voice recording
- Keanu Reeves, Idris Elba and Jim Carrey had expressed interest in returning. February 2026: Kristen Bell cast as Amy with Ben Schwartz returning. March 2026: journalist Jeff Sneider indicated Ben Kingsley was cast in "a key role"; the rest of the cast was revealed later that month, including Nick Offerman (who, with Bell, had appeared alongside Schwartz in Parks and Recreation), plus Matt Berry and Richard Ayoade in undisclosed roles.
- In a January 2025 interview Fowler said someone could be cast as the voice of Metal Sonic, as the possibility was likely to be raised during scripting.
- Principal photography began March 2, 2026, announced by Fowler on social media with a picture of him holding Amy's hammer; filming took place at Shinfield Studios in Berkshire and wrapped May 15, 2026, announced on Instagram with a photo of Fowler next to a Metal Sonic prop.
- May 27, 2026: Ben Schwartz posted a photo with Fowler and editor Al LeVine in a vocal recording booth, confirming voice recording had begun. June 3, 2026: Kristen Bell posted a photo in a recording studio about to record her lines as Amy.

## Release and marketing
- Scheduled for release in the United States on March 19, 2027 by Paramount Pictures.
- A teaser trailer was released on March 19, 2026, featuring Jim Carrey as Dr. Ivo Robotnik. Carrey's return was considered notable given a February 2026 appearance at the Academie des Arts et Techniques du Cinema that "sparked conspiracies of cloning or impersonation" and his past mentions of retirement. The Chaos Emeralds in the teaser and the use of the "Sonic Boom" theme from Sonic CD also drew commentary.
- Footage featuring Carrey was showcased at CinemaCon in April 2026 and more footage was privately shown at CineEurope in June 2026.

wikis.title: Godzilla (2014 film)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia's article on Godzilla, the 2014 Legendary/Warner Bros. reboot directed by Gareth Edwards, covering its plot, decade-long development, production, May 2014 release, $529 million box office and reception.
wikis.body:
## Overview
- The source is the English Wikipedia article on *Godzilla*, the 2014 monster film directed by Gareth Edwards, produced by Legendary Pictures and distributed by Warner Bros. Pictures (Toho in Japan) - a reboot of Toho's franchise, its 30th film and the first Monsterverse entry. Part 1 runs from the lead to the theatrical release, part 2 from home media through reception, accolades and sequels, and part 3 holds the references, bibliography, external links and categories.

## Key facts
- Premiered at the Dolby Theatre in Hollywood on May 8, 2014 and released wide on May 16, 2014 in 2D, 3D, RealD 3D, IMAX 3D and 4DX; China June 13 and Japan July 25, 2014. Running time 123 minutes, rated PG-13.
- Screenplay by Max Borenstein from a story by David Callaham, after drafts and rewrites by Callaham, David S. Goyer (uncredited), Drew Pearce, Frank Darabont and Tony Gilroy (uncredited). Stars Aaron Taylor-Johnson, Ken Watanabe, Elizabeth Olsen, Juliette Binoche, Sally Hawkins, David Strathairn and Bryan Cranston; T.J. Storm did Godzilla's motion capture.
- Budget $160 million with a $100 million print and advertising budget; Legendary financed 75% and Warner Bros. 25%. Legendary estimated a $380 million break-even; the film grossed $93.2 million in its North American opening weekend, $200.7 million domestically and $529 million worldwide, with *Deadline Hollywood* estimating a $92.3 million net profit.
- Reception: Rotten Tomatoes 76% of 330 reviews (6.7/10 average), Metacritic 62/100 from 48 critics, CinemaScore "B+"; praise for direction and effects, criticism of the characters and Godzilla's screen time.
- Production: the project began in 2004 as Yoshimitsu Banno's IMAX 3D short *Godzilla 3D to the Max*, moved to Legendary in 2009 and was announced March 29, 2010; Edwards was announced in January 2011; principal photography ran March 18 to mid-July 2013 in Vancouver and Hawaii under the working title "Nautilus". Toho's licence required a nuclear origin and a Japanese setting; the U.S. Army required removing a reference to the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki in return for assistance.
- Godzilla was designed at 350 feet (106.7 m) and "finally turned out to be 355 feet (108.2 meters)"; the roar was rebuilt over six months, the 50th version being used.
- Legacy: the film's success "prompted Toho to produce a reboot of their own", *Shin Godzilla* (2016); Legendary's Monsterverse followed with *Godzilla: King of the Monsters* (May 31, 2019), *Godzilla vs. Kong* (2021), *Godzilla x Kong: The New Empire* and *Godzilla x Kong: Supernova*, set for March 26, 2027.

## Date wording
- The parts give no publication or last-updated date for the page itself; the footer carries only an oldid, and dated maintenance tags ("Use mdy dates from April 2021") are not revision dates.

wikis.title: Godzilla (2014 film) - film, plot, cast and production
wikis.summary: The first part of the Wikipedia article on Gareth Edwards' 2014 Godzilla, covering the film's credits, plot, cast, influences, development, writing, creature design, filming, music, marketing and theatrical release.
wikis.body:
## Film
- *Godzilla* is "a 2014 monster film directed by Gareth Edwards", produced by Legendary Pictures and distributed by Warner Bros. Pictures (worldwide) and Toho (Japan); a reboot of Toho's Godzilla franchise, its 30th film, and the first entry in Legendary's Monsterverse.
- Screenplay by Max Borenstein, story by David Callaham, based on Godzilla by Toho Co., Ltd; producers Thomas Tull, Jon Jashni, Mary Parent and Brian Rogers; cinematography Seamus McGarvey; editing Bob Ducsay; music Alexandre Desplat.
- Stars Aaron Taylor-Johnson, Ken Watanabe, Elizabeth Olsen, Juliette Binoche, Sally Hawkins, David Strathairn and Bryan Cranston.
- Infobox: release dates May 8, 2014 (Dolby Theatre) and May 16, 2014 (United States); running time 123 minutes; countries United States and Japan; languages English and Japanese; budget $160 million; box office $529.1 million.
- The lead states the film "received generally positive reviews", praised for direction, visual effects, music, cinematography, respect for the source material and Cranston's performance, while the script, characters and Godzilla's screen time were criticised. Its success "prompted Toho to produce a reboot of their own", *Shin Godzilla* (2016). Sequel *Godzilla: King of the Monsters* released May 31, 2019.
- Early project history: began in 2004 under executive producer Yoshimitsu Banno as a short IMAX 3D film, transferred to Legendary in 2009; announced March 2010; Edwards announced as director January 2011; principal photography March to July 2013 in the United States and Canada.

## Plot (as the page summarizes it)
- 1954: Godzilla is lured to Bikini Atoll in an attempt to kill him with a nuclear weapon. 1999: Monarch scientists Ishiro Serizawa and Vivienne Graham investigate a skeleton in a collapsed Philippine uranium mine and find two spores; the Janjira Nuclear Power Plant in Japan collapses, killing Sandra Brody.
- 2014: Joe and Ford Brody find a chrysalis that has fed on the reactors for fifteen years; a winged MUTO (Massive Unidentified Terrestrial Organism) emerges and Joe dies. A second, larger wingless female MUTO emerges from a spore at Yucca Mountain and attacks Las Vegas; their signals are a mating call.
- Admiral Stenz approves luring the monsters out with nuclear warheads; the monsters converge on San Francisco, Godzilla defeats the MUTOs, the warhead is taken out to sea, and Godzilla returns to the sea as the media dub him the "King of the Monsters".

## Cast and characters
- Aaron Taylor-Johnson as Navy EOD LT Ford Brody; the role "was reportedly offered to Joseph Gordon-Levitt in 2012, but he declined", with Henry Cavill, Scoot McNairy and Caleb Landry Jones on the 2013 shortlist. CJ Adams plays Ford as a boy.
- Ken Watanabe as Dr. Ishiro Serizawa, named after director Ishiro Honda and the 1954 film's Dr. Daisuke Serizawa; Watanabe on the nuclear element: "If you are telling the Godzilla story, you cannot separate it from the nuclear element".
- Elizabeth Olsen as Elle Brody; Juliette Binoche as Sandra Brody; Sally Hawkins as Dr. Vivienne Graham (cast last, during principal photography); David Strathairn as Admiral William Stenz; Bryan Cranston as Joe Brody, who wore a wig after finishing *Breaking Bad* days before filming and later called killing Joe off early a "narrative mistake".
- T.J. Storm provided Godzilla's motion capture (joining after principal photography had finished, without meeting Edwards or the actors); Matt Cross and Lee Ross played the MUTOs.
- Franchise actor Akira Takarada was cast as an immigration officer but cut; Edwards called cutting the scene his "biggest regret", and Takarada remains in the closing credits.

## Influences
- Edwards cited *Godzilla* (1954): "Godzilla is a metaphor for Hiroshima in the original movie. We tried to keep that". Other cited influences: *Alien*, *Jaws*, *Close Encounters of the Third Kind*, *Jurassic Park*, Spielberg's style, Katsuhiro Otomo's *Akira*, and late-1970s/early-1980s action films.
- Real events cited as influences on the destruction scenes: the 2004 Indian tsunami, Hurricane Katrina and the Fukushima nuclear disaster.

## Development
- TriStar's 1998 Hollywood *Godzilla* led to a cancelled trilogy, and TriStar's remake/sequel rights expired on May 20, 2003; Toho released *Godzilla: Final Wars* in 2004 and put the franchise on hiatus.
- *Godzilla 3D To The Max*: in August 2004 Yoshimitsu Banno secured rights from Toho for an IMAX 3D short remaking *Godzilla vs. Hedorah*; Peter Anderson joined in 2005, Kerner Optical in 2007, and the licence was renegotiated in Tokyo in autumn 2007 for a feature-length 3D release. After Kerner's 2008 financial trouble, Rogers, Anderson and proposed director Keith Melton met Legendary in 2009; Legendary green-lit production in 2010. Banno died on May 7, 2017.
- Legendary announced its acquisition of the Godzilla licence on March 29, 2010 with Warner Bros. co-producing and co-financing; Legendary financed 75% of the budget and Warner Bros. 25%, with RatPac-Dune Entertainment holding a minority stake. Thomas Tull: "Our plans are to produce the Godzilla that we, as fans, would want to see."
- A 2012 release date was targeted at the 2010 3D Summit but missed. Gareth Edwards was announced as director in January 2011; a teaser directed on the Warner Bros. lot was shown at San Diego Comic-Con in July 2012.

## Writing
- David Callaham pitched and wrote the first draft in 2010; David S. Goyer did three or four weeks of uncredited "script doctoring" from July 2011; Max Borenstein was hired in November 2011; Drew Pearce polished it in October 2012, ageing the principal characters; Frank Darabont was hired for a final rewrite in January 2013, and Tony Gilroy contributed uncredited rewrites.
- Toho's licensing conditions were "that Godzilla is born of a nuclear incident and that it is set in Japan". Legendary rejected a Siberian carcass origin after learning *Man of Steel* had a similar scene. The US Army reviewed the script and, in return for production assistance, "required deleting a reference to the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki".
- Edwards on the theme: "Godzilla is definitely a representation of the wrath of nature ... He's the punishment we deserve."

## Creature design
- Tull insisted the design stay consistent with Toho's: "Godzilla had to look like Godzilla. Period."
- The filmmakers specified Godzilla would be 350 feet (106.7 m) tall, the tallest incarnation to date at the time; "the height of the creature finally turned out to be 355 feet (108.2 meters)".
- Fighting mechanics were based on bears and Komodo dragons per VFX chief Jim Rygiel; face elements drew on bears, dogs and eagles; motion capture by The Imaginarium with consultation from Andy Serkis.
- The roar was rebuilt by sound designers Erik Aadahl and Ethan Van der Ryn over six months of a three-year production; it keeps the original's key and cadence, "going from a C to a D", and the final version was the 50th produced; tested on a Rolling Stones tour speaker array, they estimated it could be heard 3 miles (4.83 km) away.
- The MUTOs took over a year to design; Edwards credited artist Matt Allsopp with "80 to 90 percent" of the design. They are sexually dimorphic - a larger eight-limbed female and a smaller winged male - and cause electromagnetic interference as a side effect of feeding on radiation.

## Pre-production, casting disputes and filming
- September 2012: Legendary announced a May 16, 2014 theatrical release in 3D, later also IMAX 3D.
- January 2013: Mary Parent joined as producer and Dan Lin, Roy Lee and Doug Davison were dismissed; Legendary filed a 'Complaint for Declaratory Relief' in California State Court on January 9; the three counter-claimed; Legendary lost an appeal in March 2014, and the parties settled in June 2015 on the eve of trial, terms undisclosed.
- Principal photography began March 18, 2013 in Vancouver under the working title "Nautilus", with locations including the Vancouver Convention Centre, BC Place, Cypress Provincial Park, Steveston in Richmond (a battle scene with about 200 soldiers), Vancouver Island and Coquitlam; sets at Burnaby's Canadian Motion Picture Park included a San Francisco Chinatown street and a 400-foot (120 m) section of the Golden Gate Bridge.
- Further filming in Honolulu in June and July 2013; over 2,000 people applied at an open casting call on June 2, 2013 and over 200 extras were hired; principal photography wrapped the weekend of July 13-14 per *The Hollywood Reporter*.
- Shot digitally on Arri Alexa with Panavision C-Series anamorphic lenses; 1954 sequences used vintage early-1960s lenses; though made for 3D it "received a predominantly 2D release".
- The U.S. Navy cooperated, with filming aboard the USS Carl Vinson, USS Nimitz and USS Ronald Reagan and part of the opening on the USS Missouri at Pearl Harbor; the U.S. Army provided three technical advisors; the U.S. Marine Corps declined after reviewing the script.

## Visual effects, post-production and music
- VFX supervised by Jim Rygiel, with MPC, Double Negative, Weta Digital, Amalgamated Dynamics, ComputerCafe/CafeFX, Lidar VFX, Scanline VFX, Stereo D and The Third Floor; production completed in the last week of March 2014. Title sequence by Kyle Cooper; sound mixed by Gregg Landaker in Dolby Atmos at Warner Bros. Burbank.
- Alexandre Desplat composed and conducted the score, described by him as "non-stop fortissimo, with lots of brass, Japanese drums, and electric violin"; released by WaterTower Music on May 13, 2014. The film also features Ligeti's *Requiem*, Dusty Springfield's 1969 "Breakfast in Bed" and Elvis Presley's "(You're the) Devil in Disguise".

## Marketing and merchandise
- Print and advertisement budget of $100 million. Promotions ran from the 2010 San Diego Comic-Con T-shirt and augmented-reality booth through a July 2012 SDCC teaser (featuring a "gigantic centipede-like monster" conceived only for the teaser), the 2013 "Godzilla Encounter" warehouse exhibit and viral sites godzillaencounter.com and mutoresearch.net.
- The first official trailer went online December 10, 2013 with *The Hobbit: The Desolation of Smaug*, passing nine million YouTube views within two days; the second trailer (February 25, 2014) recorded 13 million views within three days. Trailer, TV spot and poster won Golden Trailer Awards.
- Cross-promotions with Snickers and a Fiat 500L commercial. Legendary's Applied Analytics Group used software named "Eddington"; Tull credited it when the film beat a predicted $60 million opening weekend "by over $30 million".
- In July 2014 Japan completed a 6.6 meters (22 ft) statue in Tokyo Midtown.
- Licensed merchandise from Bandai America, NECA, Jakks Pacific, Bioworld, Trevco, Rubie's and Sideshow Collectibles; a novelization by Greg Cox (Titan Books, May 2014); a tie-in graphic novel *Godzilla: Awakening* released May 7, 2014; mobile game *Godzilla Smash 3* released May 2014.

## Release
- Red carpet premiere at the Dolby Theatre in Hollywood on May 8, 2014, with an "Aftermath Afterparty" featuring a 22-foot Godzilla statue made of rubble at the El Capitan Theatre.
- Wide release worldwide in 2D, 3D, RealD 3D, IMAX 3D and 4DX on May 16, 2014; rated PG-13 by the MPAA "for intense sequences of destruction, mayhem and creature violence"; released in China on June 13 and Japan on July 25, 2014.
- Toho screened the film early in April 2014 and responded positively; Edwards: "I got an e-mail saying they thought it was fantastic!" The section on home media begins here and continues in the next part.

wikis.title: Godzilla (2014 film) - home media, reception, accolades and sequels
wikis.summary: The second part of the Godzilla (2014) article: home video releases, box office and critical reception, commentary from Godzilla authors, awards, and the Monsterverse sequels.
wikis.body:
## Home media
- Released on Blu-ray and DVD in North America on September 16, 2014, and for digital HD download on August 26, 2014; Target's exclusive Blu-ray included a 30-minute featurette *Godzilla: Rebirth of an Icon*. Thomas Tull confirmed plans for a future extended cut.
- US and Canada video sales: DVD $17.8 million and Blu-ray $27.5 million, totalling $45.3 million.
- Toho released it in Japan on February 25, 2015, including a five-disc limited edition with an exclusive S.H. MonsterArts figure; a 4K Blu-ray followed on March 23, 2021 to mark *Godzilla vs. Kong*.

## Box office
- In January 2014 John Furrier wrote in *Forbes* that *Godzilla* would be "the biggest box office bomb of 2014"; Legendary estimated the film needed to gross $380 million worldwide to break even.
- Opened with $9.3 million from North American Thursday screenings and $93.2 million for the weekend - the fifth highest opening weekend of 2014, a record debut for a disaster film and a creature feature, and the highest May opening for a Warner Bros. film at the time; about half the gross came from 3D screenings. It dropped 66% in its second weekend against *X-Men: Days of Future Past*.
- Domestic total $200.7 million, "the lowest total ever for a movie that opened above $90 million", finishing 13th for 2014 in North America.
- International: $103.4 million in its opening weekend outside China and Japan; opened in China on June 13 with a $10.9 million opening day (the largest of 2014 there) and $37 million for the weekend, finishing at $77.6 million; opened at number one in Japan on July 25 with $6.95 million and finished just shy of $30 million there.
- Worldwide total $529 million (international $324-328 million), the 14th highest-grossing film of 2014; *Deadline Hollywood* estimated a net profit of $92.3 million shared between Warner Bros. and Legendary.

## Critical response
- Rotten Tomatoes: 76% of 330 critics' reviews positive, average rating 6.7/10, consensus that the film "satisfyingly restores the franchise's fire-breathing glory". Metacritic: 62 out of 100 from 48 critics, "generally favorable". CinemaScore: "B+".
- Positive: Alex Pappademas (*Grantland*) called it "the first truly joyous popcorn action movie of the season"; Richard Roeper gave it a B+; Keith Uhlich (*The A.V. Club*) named it the second-best film of 2014; Michael Phillips (*Chicago Tribune*) 3.5 stars ("Is there enough Godzilla in Godzilla? Folks, there is."); Matt Zoller Seitz 3.5 out of 4.
- Critical: Stephanie Zacharek (*Village Voice*) on spectacle where "nothing has any weight"; A. O. Scott (*New York Times*) called it "at once bloated and efficient" with "thin" characterization; Tom Russo (*Boston Globe*) called it "an uneven spectacle"; David Blaustein (ABC News Radio) 3.5 out of 5, "very good, but not great".
- Japanese critics praised the effort "to honor the spirit and visual style of the Japanese series" but criticised the handling of anti-nuclear themes; illustrator Yuji Kaida called it "a real kaiju eiga (monster movie) that honored the original".

## Other responses
- William Tsutsui found the Godzilla faithful to 1960s-70s Toho versions but said the film loses his Japanese identity by casting him as a "defender of the United States"; Ed Godziszewski felt it offered only "superficial lip service" on nuclear weapons; David Kalat praised the "modern American context" and the film's treatment of the military while criticising Godzilla's "almost no screen-time"; Steve Ryfle argued "America is incapable of making an honest Godzilla" and concluded "the latest Godzilla reboot is about nothing".
- Juliette Binoche said Quentin Tarantino told her he cried watching it: "the first time I've ever cried during a 3D blockbuster."
- In 2023 *Mutotylaspis*, a paguroid hermit crab from middle Cretaceous (Albian) deposits of Vladimir Oblast, was named after the MUTOs.

## Accolades
- 2014: 15th Golden Trailer Awards - nominations for Best Summer 2014 Blockbuster Trailer ("Ravaged/Event"), Best Sound Editing and Best Action TV Spot ("Fight"); wins for Best Summer 2014 Blockbuster TV Spot, Best International Poster and Best Summer 2014 Blockbuster Poster. Golden Schmoes nominations (including Best Line of the Year, "Let them fight"); three Teen Choice nominations; a Hollywood Post Alliance sound nomination; World Soundtrack Academy Film Composer of the Year won by Alexandre Desplat; 22nd Annual Japan Cool Content Contribution Award won by Alex Garcia.
- 2015: nominations at the Fangoria Chainsaw Awards, Houston Film Critics Society, IFMCA, Japan Academy Prize (Outstanding Foreign Language Film), 41st Saturn Awards (Best Science Fiction Film and Best Music) and 36th Young Artist Awards (Carson Bolde).

## Sequels
- Legendary announced plans in October 2015 for a shared franchise leading to *Godzilla vs. Kong*; Thomas Tull resigned from Legendary in January 2017 but stayed as producer of what was revealed as the "Monsterverse".
- Edwards left the sequel in May 2016; Michael Dougherty and Zach Shields wrote *Godzilla: King of the Monsters*, with Dougherty announced as director in January 2017; it filmed in Atlanta from June to September 2017 and was released May 31, 2019, followed by *Godzilla vs. Kong* (2021) and *Godzilla x Kong: The New Empire*. "The next installment, *Godzilla x Kong: Supernova*, will release on March 26, 2027."

## Notes and references
- A footnote explains the film is the second Godzilla film completely produced by an American studio, after the 1998 TriStar film, and that earlier American releases merged new Western footage with Japanese footage; *Invasion of Astro-Monster* was the first Japanese-American co-production (Toho and UPA).
- The part ends in the raw wikitext reference list (cites to US Army, Bloody Disgusting, Box Office Mojo and others). No publication or last-updated date is stated for the page.

wikis.title: Godzilla: King of the Monsters (2019 film) - Wikipedia article
wikis.summary: Wikipedia's article on the 2019 Monsterverse film Godzilla: King of the Monsters, covering its credits, plot, cast, development and filming, music, marketing, release, box office, critical response and awards.
wikis.body:
## The film

- "A 2019 American monster film directed and co-written by Michael Dougherty", screenplay by Dougherty and Zach Shields, story by Max Borenstein, Dougherty and Shields, based on Godzilla, King Ghidorah, Mothra and Rodan by Toho Co., Ltd.
- Sequel to Godzilla (2014), the third film in Legendary's Monsterverse franchise and the 35th film in the Godzilla franchise; released as Godzilla II: King of the Monsters in selected markets.
- Production company Legendary Pictures; distributed by Warner Bros. Pictures worldwide and Toho in Japan. Running time 131 minutes; country United States; language English.
- Stars Kyle Chandler, Vera Farmiga, Millie Bobby Brown, Bradley Whitford, Sally Hawkins, Charles Dance, Thomas Middleditch, Aisha Hinds, O'Shea Jackson Jr., David Strathairn, Ken Watanabe and Zhang Ziyi. Music by Bear McCreary; cinematography by Lawrence Sher.
- Plot: eco-terrorists release King Ghidorah, who awakens other "Titans" worldwide, forcing Godzilla and Mothra to engage Ghidorah and Rodan.

## Dates

- Release dates given in the infobox: May 13, 2019 (Beijing) and May 31, 2019 (United States); the red-carpet premiere was in Beijing on May 13, 2019 and a second at Grauman's Chinese Theatre on May 18, 2019.
- Originally scheduled for June 8, 2018, pushed in May 2016 to March 22, 2019 and later to May 31, 2019.
- Principal photography began June 19, 2017 in Atlanta, Georgia under the working title Fathom, with shooting in the Historic Center of Mexico City August 19-22, 2017; Dougherty announced the wrap on September 27, 2017. Post-production ended in November 2018.
- Home media: Digital HD August 13, 2019; disc formats August 27, 2019; Japan December 18, 2019; HBO debut January 2020.
- Sequel Godzilla vs. Kong released March 24, 2021 internationally and March 31, 2021 in the United States, in theaters and on HBO Max simultaneously.

## Money

- Budget stated as $170-200 million, with the article's footnote recording $170 million (Entertainment Weekly, Box Office Mojo, Deadline Hollywood), $185 million (other analysts per Deadline) and $200 million (Hindustan Times, July 2018; echoed by Variety, June 2019). Marketing costs reported at $100-150 million.
- Box office $387.3 million worldwide: $110.5 million in the United States and Canada and $276.8 million elsewhere. The same section also states the film grossed "$130 million internationally and $177.8 million including North American tallies" with China at $70 million, a set of figures that does not line up with the totals given just above it.
- Opening weekend $47.8 million in the United States and Canada against a $55-65 million projection, from 4,108 theaters; first day $19.6 million including $6.3 million in Thursday previews. Called a box office disappointment and the lowest-grossing Monsterverse film. Break-even estimates differ: $550-600 million (Erik Childress, Rotten Tomatoes) versus about $400 million (Chris Agar, Screen Rant).
- U.S./Canada home video sales of $36.6 million (DVD $12.9 million, Blu-ray $23.6 million).

## Reception and awards

- Rotten Tomatoes 42% of 353 reviews, average 5.1/10; Metacritic 48/100 from 46 critics; CinemaScore "B+"; PostTrak 85% positive.
- Awards listed include wins at the Indiana Film Journalists Association (motion-capture performances), the IFMCA (Bear McCreary, Film Composer of the Year), the Golden Trailer Awards (2021 TV spot), the Hollywood Professional Association (sound) and the Reel Music Awards, plus nominations at the Saturn Awards, People's Choice Awards, Blue Ribbon Awards and the Golden Raspberry Awards.

## Credits dispute recorded by the article

The final billing credits name Legendary Pictures as the sole production studio with Toho and Huahua Media "in association with", while secondary sources also credit Toho and Wanda Qingdao Studios; the article notes Wanda Qingdao is a filming facility and the film was shot in Atlanta and Mexico. Toho covered twenty-five percent of production costs; Huahua Media took a stake in April 2019, after production was complete, for Chinese marketing and a box-office share.

## About this capture

The source is one long Wikipedia page split into four parts: the article text is in part 1, while parts 2 to 4 hold only citation markup, the rendered reference list, navigation boxes and categories. The capture gives no publication or last-edited date, only the permanent link oldid=1374341932.

wikis.title: Godzilla: King of the Monsters (2019): plot, cast, production, release and reception
wikis.summary: The main text of the Wikipedia article on the 2019 film Godzilla: King of the Monsters, covering its credits and infobox figures, plot, cast, development and filming, marketing, release, box office, critical response and awards.
wikis.body:
## Infobox / credits

- Directed by Michael Dougherty; screenplay by Michael Dougherty and Zach Shields; story by Max Borenstein, Michael Dougherty and Zach Shields.
- "Based on Godzilla, King Ghidorah, Mothra and Rodan by Toho Co., Ltd."
- Produced by Mary Parent, Alex Garcia, Thomas Tull, Jon Jashni, Brian Rogers.
- Starring Kyle Chandler, Vera Farmiga, Millie Bobby Brown, Bradley Whitford, Sally Hawkins, Charles Dance, Thomas Middleditch, Aisha Hinds, O'Shea Jackson Jr., David Strathairn, Ken Watanabe, Zhang Ziyi.
- Cinematography Lawrence Sher; edited by Roger Barton, Richard Pearson, Bob Ducsay; music by Bear McCreary.
- Production company Legendary Pictures; distributed by Warner Bros. Pictures (worldwide) and Toho (Japan).
- Release dates: May 13, 2019 (Beijing); May 31, 2019 (United States). Running time 131 minutes. Country United States. Language English.
- Budget $170-200 million. Box office $387.3 million.
- Described as "a 2019 American monster film", a sequel to Godzilla (2014), the third film in Legendary's Monsterverse franchise and the 35th film in the Godzilla franchise. Released as Godzilla II: King of the Monsters in selected markets.

### Budget figures the page gives differently

A footnote states Entertainment Weekly, Box Office Mojo and Deadline Hollywood reported the production budget as $170 million; Deadline also noted other analysts marked it at $185 million; the Hindustan Times reported $200 million in July 2018, a figure Variety echoed in June 2019. Marketing costs are reported as ranging $100-150 million.

### Production-company credits the page says conflict

Notes state the final billing credits name Legendary Pictures as the sole production studio, with Toho Co., Ltd. and Huahua Media given an "in association with" credit, while secondary sources credit Toho and Wanda Qingdao Studios as production companies; the article says the latter is a filming facility, not a production company, and that the film was shot in Atlanta and parts of Mexico, not Qingdao. The Hollywood Reporter is cited as verifying Huahua Media took a "major" financial stake in April 2019, after development, principal photography and post-production were complete, its role extending only to marketing in China and a share of worldwide box office. Twenty-five percent of production costs were covered by Toho.

## Plot

Five years after the revelation of giant monsters called "Titans", Monarch paleobiologist Dr. Emma Russell and her daughter Madison witness the birth of a larval Mothra; Emma calms it with the "Orca", a device emitting bioacoustic frequencies. Eco-terrorists led by former British Army Colonel Alan Jonah abduct them. Monarch recruits Emma's ex-husband Dr. Mark Russell. In Antarctica, Emma frees the three-headed Titan codenamed "Monster Zero", which kills Dr. Vivienne Graham. Emma argues the Titans must be awakened to heal the Earth. She awakens Rodan in Mexico; the U.S. military's prototype "Oxygen Destroyer" seemingly kills Godzilla; Monster Zero is identified as King Ghidorah, an alien seeking to xenoform Earth. Dr. Ishiro Serizawa sacrifices himself detonating a nuclear warhead to revive Godzilla. Madison uses the Orca at Fenway Park in Boston; Godzilla and Mothra fight Ghidorah there; Mothra sacrifices herself and transfers her energy to Godzilla, who vaporizes Ghidorah and Emma. End credits show Titans healing Earth, a suspected second Mothra egg, Titans converging on Skull Island and cave paintings of Godzilla and a Kong-like Titan; a post-credits scene has Jonah purchasing Ghidorah's severed left head in Mexico.

## Cast (selected)

- Kyle Chandler as Dr. Mark Russell; Vera Farmiga as Dr. Emma Russell; Millie Bobby Brown as Madison Russell, "Emma and Mark's 12-year-old daughter" (Lexi Rabe as young Madison).
- Bradley Whitford as Dr. Rick Stanton; Sally Hawkins as Dr. Vivienne Graham; Charles Dance as Alan Jonah; Thomas Middleditch as Sam Coleman; Aisha Hinds as Colonel Diane Foster; O'Shea Jackson Jr. as Jackson Barnes; David Strathairn as Admiral William Stenz; Ken Watanabe as Dr. Ishiro Serizawa; Zhang Ziyi as Dr. Ilene Chen and Dr. Ling Chen.
- Hawkins, Strathairn and Watanabe reprise roles from Godzilla (2014). Joe Morton appears as an older Dr. Houston Brooks, a character from Kong: Skull Island. T.J. Storm reprises Godzilla via motion capture; Jason Liles, Alan Maxson and Richard Dorton portray King Ghidorah's heads (Dorton left, Liles middle, Maxson right); Liles also performs Rodan.
- Farmiga described her character as "a DJ for the monsters" and said the film may pass the Bechdel test.

## Development and writing

- The sequel was announced by Legendary after Godzilla (2014) opened to "$103 million internationally", with a trilogy planned and Gareth Edwards attached.
- At San Diego Comic-Con in July 2014, Legendary confirmed it had acquired the rights to Rodan, Mothra and King Ghidorah from Toho, with a teaser ending "Let them fight".
- August 2014: release announced for June 8, 2018, with Max Borenstein returning to write.
- October 2015: Legendary announced Godzilla vs. Kong, "then-set for a 2020 release date", and a shared franchise "centered around Monarch".
- May 2016: Warner Bros. pushed the film from June 8, 2018 to March 22, 2019; shortly afterward Edwards left.
- October 2016: Dougherty and Shields hired to write; a day later Dougherty was reported in negotiations to direct. December 2016: title announced as Godzilla: King of the Monsters. January 2017: Dougherty confirmed as director.
- Legendary's "only mandate" was to include Monarch, Rodan, Mothra and King Ghidorah; a writers' room of ten writers built on Dougherty's two-page treatment, and the script "took a year to come together". Borenstein had originally written Mechagodzilla into the film; Dougherty scrapped the character.
- Dougherty: "I would call (my movie) the Aliens to Gareth's Alien."

## Creature design

The film reclassifies the monsters from "MUTOs" to "Titans". Dougherty added the 1954 dorsal plates to Godzilla's design; Legacy Effects provided designs for Mothra and King Ghidorah; Tom Woodruff Jr. and Amalgamated Dynamics provided Rodan. Non-Toho Titans named: Baphomet, Typhon, Abaddon, Bunyip, Methuselah, Behemoth, Scylla, Tiamat, Leviathan and Mokele-Mbembe. Budget prevented acquiring further Toho characters such as Anguirus, Biollante and Gigan.

## Filming and post-production

- Principal photography began June 19, 2017 in Atlanta, Georgia, under the working title Fathom.
- Parts were shot in the Historic Center of Mexico City between August 19-22, 2017.
- Dougherty announced the film had wrapped on September 27, 2017.
- Visual effects by Moving Picture Company (MPC), DNEG, Method Studios, Raynault VFX, Rodeo FX and Ollin VFX; Guillaume Rocheron main VFX supervisor. Post-production officially ended in November 2018. An earlier cut was "nearly three hours long".
- The film is dedicated to executive producer Yoshimitsu Banno and original Godzilla suit performer Haruo Nakajima, "both of whom died in 2017".

## Music

On July 21, 2018 Dougherty revealed Bear McCreary would score the film, incorporating Akira Ifukube's themes. In April 2019 WaterTower Music released "Old Rivals" and a cover of Blue Oyster Cult's "Godzilla" by Serj Tankian, with contributions from Brendon Small, Gene Hoglan and other members of Dethklok. The Japanese band Alexandros contributed the single "Pray" for the Japanese release, released May 13, 2019. The soundtrack was released by Waxwork Records in 2019 on a triple LP.

## Marketing and merchandise

First trailer shown at San Diego Comic-Con and released online July 21, 2018; a new trailer premiered at Comic Con Experience on December 9, 2018; first teaser poster December 10, 2018; final trailer released online April 23, 2019. Huahua Media invested an undisclosed sum to market the film in China. A Godzilla head was built on top of the Cinerama Dome in May 2019. Prequel graphic novel Godzilla: Aftershock released May 2019 (written by Arvid Nelson, illustrated by Drew Edward Johnson); novelization May 31, 2019; art book The Art of Godzilla: King of the Monsters June 4, 2019; S.H. MonsterArts figures June 2019.

## Release

- Released May 31, 2019 in IMAX, 3D, Dolby Cinema, RealD 3D, 4DX and ScreenX by Warner Bros., except in Japan where Toho distributed. Rated PG-13 in the United States for "sequences of monster action, violence, and destruction, and for some language."
- Red-carpet premiere in Beijing May 13, 2019; second premiere at Grauman's Chinese Theatre, Hollywood, May 18, 2019. A private press screening was held at Toho Studios in Tokyo in April 2019; a VIP press screening in Los Angeles on May 17, 2019. In June 2019 the film received a one-month theatrical extension in China.
- Home media: Digital HD August 13, 2019; DVD, Blu-ray, Blu-ray 3D and Ultra HD Blu-ray August 27, 2019; Toho editions in Japan December 18, 2019; pay cable debut on HBO January 2020. U.S./Canada video sales: DVD $12.9 million, Blu-ray $23.6 million, "totaling $36.6 million".

## Box office

- "$110.5 million in the United States and Canada, and $276.8 million in other territories, for a worldwide total of $387.3 million."
- Break-even estimates differ: Erik Childress of Rotten Tomatoes estimated $550-600 million; Chris Agar of Screen Rant estimated $400 million worldwide "just to make its money back".
- Projected $55-65 million from 4,108 theaters; made $19.6 million on its first day including $6.3 million from Thursday previews; debuted to $47.8 million, first place but "below expectations". Fell 67% to $15.5 million (fourth), then $8.1 million (seventh).
- China previews on May 25, 2019 grossed $2.5 million; $12.7 million from 51 countries Thursday and $31.4 million from 75 countries Friday; in China "$54.15 million through Friday and Saturday".
- The article also states the film "ended up grossing a total of $130 million internationally and $177.8 million including North American tallies, far below projections", with largest markets China ($70 million), the United Kingdom ($4.4 million), France ($2.6 million) and South Korea ($2.2 million) - figures that sit alongside the $276.8 million international / $387.3 million worldwide totals given earlier in the same section. International play dropped 64% to $47.1 million in the second weekend, a ten-day running total of $213.7 million.
- Called "a box office disappointment" and "the lowest-grossing film in the Monsterverse".

## Critical response

- Rotten Tomatoes: 42% of 353 critics' reviews positive, average rating 5.1/10; consensus: "Godzilla: King of the Monsters delivers spectacular kaiju action -- and reaffirms that cutting-edge effects are still no substitute for a good story."
- Metacritic: 48 out of 100 based on 46 critics, "mixed or average".
- CinemaScore "B+"; PostTrak 85% overall positive, average 4.5 out of 5 stars, 75% "definite recommend".
- Characterizations of the reception differ by outlet: The Observer said reviews were "mixed to negative", The Indian Express "largely negative", Screen Rant "so negative", Yahoo! Finance a "pretty mixed bag"; Scott Mendelson of Forbes said "mixed reviews", later "mixed-negative reviews".
- Individual reviews cited: Benjamin Lee (The Guardian) 2/5; Chris Evangelista (/Film) 6.5/10; Kate Erbland (IndieWire) "C-"; Ben Travis (Empire Online) 1/5; Scott Collura (IGN) 7.8/10; Alonso Duralde (TheWrap) praised an "all-thriller-no-filler approach".

## Accolades (as tabulated)

- Australian Effects & Animation Festival, August 16, 2019 - MPC Film for Feature Films, VFX - Bronze.
- Blue Ribbon Awards, February 18, 2020 - Best Foreign Film - Nominated.
- Golden Raspberry Awards, March 16, 2020 - Worst Prequel, Remake, Rip-off or Sequel - Nominated.
- Indiana Film Journalists Association, December 16, 2019 - Best Vocal / Motion Capture Performances - Won.
- IFMCA, February 20, 2020 - Best Original Score for a Fantasy/Science Fiction/Horror Film (Bear McCreary) - Nominated; Film Composer of the Year (McCreary) - Won.
- Golden Trailer Awards, May 29, 2019 - two nominations; July 22, 2021 - Best Fantasy Adventure TV Spot - Won, plus one nomination.
- Guild of Music Supervisors Awards, February 13, 2019 - Best Music Supervision for Trailers - Nominated.
- Hollywood Professional Association, November 21, 2019 - Outstanding Sound, Theatrical Feature - Won.
- People's Choice Awards, November 10, 2019 - Favorite Action Movie of 2019 and Favorite Female Movie Star of 2019 (Millie Bobby Brown) - Nominated.
- Reel Music Awards, March 23, 2020 - Original Score (McCreary) - Won.
- Rondo Hatton Classic Horror Awards, April 6, 2020 - Best Film - Runner-up.
- Saturn Awards, September 13, 2019 - four nominations (Best Fantasy Film; Millie Bobby Brown; Bear McCreary; special effects).
- Young Entertainer Awards, November 6, 2021 - Best Supporting Young Actor, Feature Film (Gabriel L. Silva) - Nominated.

## Sequel

Godzilla vs. Kong was "theatrically released internationally on March 24, 2021, and released in the United States on March 31, 2021, simultaneously in theaters and on HBO Max"; the article's lead states it "was released on March 24, 2021".
