wikis.title: Star Wars: The Last Jedi
wikis.summary: Wikipedia's article on Star Wars: The Last Jedi, Rian Johnson's 2017 sequel-trilogy film, covering its credits and figures, plot, cast, production and filming locations, release, record box office, acclaimed reviews and divided audience response.
wikis.body:
## The film

- "Star Wars: The Last Jedi, also known as Star Wars: Episode VIII - The Last Jedi, or simply The Last Jedi, is a 2017 American epic space opera film written and directed by Rian Johnson", the second film of the sequel trilogy and eighth episode of the "Skywalker saga". Produced by Lucasfilm with Kathleen Kennedy and Ram Bergman, executive produced by J. J. Abrams, distributed by Walt Disney Studios Motion Pictures. Music by John Williams, cinematography by Steve Yedlin, editing by Bob Ducsay. Running time 152 minutes.
- Cast: Mark Hamill, Carrie Fisher, Adam Driver, Daisy Ridley, John Boyega, Oscar Isaac, Andy Serkis, Lupita Nyong'o, Domhnall Gleeson, Anthony Daniels, Gwendoline Christie, Kelly Marie Tran, Laura Dern and Benicio del Toro. "The film is dedicated to Fisher, who died in December 2016."
- Story: Rey seeks Luke Skywalker's help on Ahch-To while Leia, Finn and Poe try to escape a First Order pursuit of the dwindling Resistance fleet; Kylo Ren kills Snoke, Holdo destroys the First Order flagship at lightspeed, and Luke holds off the First Order on Crait as a Force projection before dying on Ahch-To.

## Dates and figures

- Premiere at the Shrine Auditorium, Los Angeles, on December 9, 2017; United States release December 15, 2017, moved from an original May 26 date to avoid Pirates of the Caribbean: Dead Men Tell No Tales. Home media March 13 (digital) and March 27, 2018 (disc).
- Second unit filming at Skellig Michael from September 14, 2015; principal photography began at Pinewood Studios on February 10, 2016 under the working title Space Bear and wrapped July 22, 2016, with location work in Dubrovnik, Ireland, the Salar de Uyuni in Bolivia and Mexico.
- Budget given as "$414.6 million (gross)" and "$343.2 million (net)"; the page says the film needed to gross $800 million worldwide to break even.
- Box office: $1.334 billion in the infobox and lead, while the reception section gives $620.2 million in the United States and Canada plus $712.5 million elsewhere "for a worldwide total of $1.333 billion". It was the highest-grossing film of 2017 and the ninth-highest-grossing film of all time, with a $450.8 million worldwide opening, a $220 million domestic opening weekend and a net profit of $417 million ($417.5 million per Deadline Hollywood).

## Reception

Rotten Tomatoes 91% of 483 reviews positive (average 8.1/10); Metacritic 84 from 56 critics, "universal acclaim"; CinemaScore "A" and PostTrak 89% positive. User scores on aggregator sites were far more negative, and Rotten Tomatoes said in 2019 the film had been "seriously targeted" by review bombing. George Lucas called the film "beautifully made". Kelly Marie Tran's casting as Rose Tico drew a racist and misogynistic backlash that led her to quit social media, and Johnson, Hamill and Boyega defended her. The film received four Academy Award nominations (Best Original Score, Best Sound Editing, Best Sound Mixing, Best Visual Effects) and two BAFTA nominations, and won at the Empire Awards (Best Film and Best Director among others), the Saturn Awards (Best Actor, Best Screenplay, Best Editing) and the AARP Movies for Grownups Awards. The Rise of Skywalker followed.

## Rest of the page

Two of the capture's four parts are raw citation markup and the reference list; the last is external links, Star Wars and Lucasfilm navigation templates, and the page's portals and categories.

wikis.title: Star Wars: The Last Jedi - plot, cast, production, release, box office and reception
wikis.summary: Part 1 of Wikipedia's article on Star Wars: The Last Jedi, holding the infobox, lead, plot, cast, production and filming, music, marketing, release, box office, critical and audience response, the harassment of Kelly Marie Tran, the full awards table and the sequel.
wikis.body:
## Infobox

- Written and directed by Rian Johnson; based on characters by George Lucas; produced by Kathleen Kennedy and Ram Bergman.
- Starring Mark Hamill, Carrie Fisher, Adam Driver, Daisy Ridley, John Boyega, Oscar Isaac, Andy Serkis, Lupita Nyong'o, Domhnall Gleeson, Anthony Daniels, Gwendoline Christie, Kelly Marie Tran, Laura Dern and Benicio del Toro.
- Music by John Williams; cinematography Steve Yedlin; edited by Bob Ducsay. Production company Lucasfilm Ltd.; distributed by Walt Disney Studios Motion Pictures.
- Release dates: December 9, 2017 (Shrine Auditorium) and December 15, 2017 (United States). Running time 152 minutes (a hidden note in the page source gives the exact runtime as 151 minutes and 38 seconds). Country United States; language English.
- Budget: "$414.6 million (gross)" and "$343.2 million (net)". Box office $1.334 billion.

## Lead

"Star Wars: The Last Jedi, also known as Star Wars: Episode VIII - The Last Jedi, or simply The Last Jedi, is a 2017 American epic space opera film written and directed by Rian Johnson." It is the second installment of the sequel trilogy after The Force Awakens (2015) and the eighth episode of the nine-part "Skywalker saga". "The film is dedicated to Fisher, who died in December 2016." J. J. Abrams executive produced; John Williams returned to compose the score. "A number of scenes were filmed at Skellig Michael in Ireland during pre-production in September 2015, but principal photography began at Pinewood Studios in England in February 2016 and wrapped that July." It "premiered in Los Angeles on December 9, 2017, and was released in the United States on December 15", grossed $1.334 billion worldwide, was the highest-grossing film of 2017 and the ninth-highest-grossing film of all time by the end of its run, is the second-highest-grossing Star Wars film and "turned a net profit of $417 million". It received four nominations at the 90th Academy Awards, including Best Original Score and Best Visual Effects, and two at the 71st British Academy Film Awards. The Rise of Skywalker concluded the trilogy in 2019.

## Plot

Shortly after the Battle of Starkiller Base, the Resistance evacuates its base as the First Order fleet arrives; against Leia's orders Poe Dameron leads a costly counterattack that destroys a First Order dreadnought. The First Order tracks the fleet through hyperspace; Kylo Ren hesitates to fire on the lead ship after sensing Leia, but his wingmen destroy the bridge, killing most of the Resistance leadership, and Leia survives being dragged into space by using the Force, with Vice-Admiral Holdo taking command. On Ahch-To, Luke Skywalker refuses to help before agreeing to give Rey three lessons; Rey and Kylo begin communicating through the Force, and Luke confesses he briefly contemplated killing Kylo on sensing Snoke's corruption of him. Yoda's spirit destroys the Jedi library with lightning and encourages Luke to learn from failure. Finn, Rose and BB-8 go to the casino town of Canto Bight and meet the hacker DJ; they infiltrate Snoke's flagship and are captured by Captain Phasma. Poe mutinies against Holdo's evacuation plan and is stunned by Leia; DJ sells the evacuation plan to General Hux. Kylo kills Snoke instead of Rey, and the two defeat the Praetorian Guard before Rey refuses his offer to rule the galaxy and they break Luke's lightsaber between them. Holdo sacrifices herself by slicing through Snoke's flagship at lightspeed. On Crait, Luke appears and holds off the First Order, revealed to be a Force projection; he dies peacefully on Ahch-To, becoming one with the Force. At Canto Bight, a stablehand moves a broom with the Force and gazes into space.

## Cast

Mark Hamill as Luke Skywalker (and voicing Dobbu Scay, named after editor Bob Ducsay); Carrie Fisher as General Leia Organa; Adam Driver as Kylo Ren; Daisy Ridley as Rey; John Boyega as Finn; Oscar Isaac as Poe Dameron; Andy Serkis as Supreme Leader Snoke; Lupita Nyong'o as Maz Kanata; Domhnall Gleeson as General Hux; Anthony Daniels as C-3PO; Gwendoline Christie as Captain Phasma; Kelly Marie Tran as Rose Tico; Laura Dern as Vice-Admiral Amilyn Holdo; Benicio del Toro as DJ.

Also: Frank Oz returns as Yoda as a Force spirit; Joonas Suotamo takes over Chewbacca from Peter Mayhew, who was credited as "Chewbacca consultant" because of chronic knee and back pain; Billie Lourd, Mike Quinn and Timothy D. Rose reprise Connix, Nien Nunb and Admiral Ackbar, with Tom Kane voicing Ackbar; Amanda Lawrence, Mark Lewis Jones and Adrian Edmondson; BB-8 puppeteered by Dave Chapman and Brian Herring with initial voice work by Ben Schwartz and final sound effects voiced by Bill Hader through a synthesizer; Jimmy Vee as R2-D2, taking over from Kenny Baker, "who died in August 2016"; Veronica Ngo as Paige Tico. Cameos include Justin Theroux, Lily Cole, Joseph Gordon-Levitt (voice, Slowen Lo), Warwick Davis, Gareth Edwards, Edgar Wright, Joe Cornish, Hermione Corfield, Noah Segan, Jamie Christopher, Hugh Skinner, Hamill's children Griffin, Nathan and Chelsea, and Prince William, Prince Harry and Gary Barlow as stormtroopers; Tom Hardy also filmed a stormtrooper cameo that "was dropped from the final cut".

## Development and writing

Disney announced a new trilogy after buying Lucasfilm in October 2012. In June 2014 Rian Johnson was reported to be in talks to write and direct Episode VIII and to write a treatment for Episode IX, with Ram Bergman producing; Johnson confirmed in August 2014. In January 2015 Bob Iger said Episode VIII would be released in 2017; in December 2015 Kathleen Kennedy said the film had not been mapped out and that Abrams was collaborating with Johnson, who would work with then-Episode IX director Colin Trevorrow. Abrams was an executive producer with Tom Karnowski and Jason McGatlin. The title was announced in January 2017.

Johnson had his story group watch Twelve O'Clock High (1949), The Bridge on the River Kwai (1957), Gunga Din (1939), Three Outlaw Samurai (1964), Sahara (1943) and Letter Never Sent (1960). He wrote the mirrored-Rey scene to symbolise her search for identity, and made her parents "nobodies" because it would be "the hardest thing" she and the audience could hear, likening it to Luke learning Vader is his father in The Empire Strikes Back. During production Hamill disagreed with Luke's direction and later said he regretted making his misgivings public.

## Casting

In September 2015 Disney shortlisted Gina Rodriguez, Tatiana Maslany and Olivia Cooke for the female cast; Benicio del Toro confirmed his involvement, denying he was a villain, and Hamill was confirmed. Joaquin Phoenix was courted for DJ but passed. Gugu Mbatha-Raw was rumoured in October 2015. In November 2015 Kennedy announced at The Force Awakens's London premiere that the entire cast would return plus "a handful" of new members. Laura Dern and Kelly Marie Tran were confirmed in February 2016; Tran's role as Rose Tico, described by Johnson as the film's largest new role, was announced at Star Wars Celebration Orlando in April 2017. Frank Oz's name was left out of pre-release billing to keep Yoda's return secret.

## Filming

Second unit photography began at Skellig Michael, Ireland on September 14, 2015, planned for five days but cancelled on the first day for poor weather. Work began on the 007 Stage at Pinewood Studios on November 15, 2015; Rick Heinrichs was production designer. Production slipped from January to February 2016 for script rewrites, with a possible union strike threatening further delay. On February 10, 2016 Bob Iger confirmed principal photography had begun under the working title Space Bear. Additional filming took place in Dubrovnik, Croatia from March 9 to 16, in Ireland in May (Malin Head, County Donegal, and Ceann Sibeal, County Kerry), at the Salar de Uyuni salt flats in Bolivia for the Crait battle, and in Mexico. Principal photography wrapped on July 22, 2016, though as of early September Nyong'o had not filmed her scenes. In February 2017 it was announced that sequences were shot in IMAX. The original script called for 160 sets; 125 were built on 14 sound stages at Pinewood. Creature designer Neal Scanlan said the film has more practical effects than any Star Wars film, with 180 to 200 creatures, and Yoda was created with puppetry rather than CGI.

## Music and marketing

Kennedy confirmed Williams's return at Star Wars Celebration Europe in July 2013; Williams confirmed at a Tanglewood concert in August 2016 that he would record "off and on" from December 2016 to March or April 2017, and recording was confirmed underway on February 21, 2017, with Williams and William Ross conducting. In place of a spotting session he was given a temp track of his own earlier scores. The soundtrack was released by Walt Disney Records on December 15, 2017. Australia Post released stamp packs on September 19, 2017 and Royal Mail eight stamps designed by Malcolm Tween on October 12. Tie-in books released with the film included The Last Jedi: The Visual Dictionary, the prequel Cobalt Squadron and the novella collection Canto Bight; as with The Force Awakens there was no official tie-in game, with content added to Star Wars Battlefront II instead.

## Release

World premiere at the Shrine Auditorium in Los Angeles on December 9, 2017; United States release December 15 in IMAX and 3D. "The film was originally scheduled to be released in the United States on May 26; however, it was pushed back to December to avoid competition with Pirates of the Caribbean: Dead Men Tell No Tales (2017)." Home media: digital HD and 4K on March 13, 2018; Ultra HD Blu-ray, Blu-ray and DVD on March 27; included in the 27-disc Skywalker Saga box set released March 31, 2020.

## Box office

The reception section gives "$620.2 million in the United States and Canada, and $712.5 million in other territories, for a worldwide total of $1.333 billion", while the infobox and lead give $1.334 billion. Worldwide opening $450.8 million, the eighth-biggest of all time, including $40.6 million from IMAX. "It was estimated that the film would need to gross $800 million worldwide to break even"; it passed $1 billion on December 31, 2017, the third Star Wars film to do so. Deadline Hollywood calculated a net profit of $417.5 million, first on its 2017 "Most Valuable Blockbusters" list.

- United States and Canada: pre-sales opened October 9, 2017 and crashed ticket sites; tracking suggested around $200 million from 4,232 theaters. It made $45 million from Thursday previews (second-highest ever behind The Force Awakens's $57 million), $104.8 million on its first day and $220 million over the weekend, both second-highest of all time, with a $25 million IMAX opening. It fell 76% on its second Friday, "the worst Friday-to-Friday drop in the series", and 67% in its second weekend to $71.7 million while staying at number one; $52.4 million in the third weekend brought the domestic total to $517.1 million, passing Beauty and the Beast (2017) as 2017's highest; it then made $23.6 million and was passed by Jumanji: Welcome to the Jungle and Insidious: The Last Key.
- Other countries: $60.8 million from 48 markets in the first two days, led by the United Kingdom ($10.2 million), Germany ($6.1 million), France ($6 million), Australia ($5.6 million) and Brazil ($2.5 million); $230 million outside the US and Canada by the end of the weekend, with all-time opening records in France, Germany, Spain, the United Kingdom and Finland; $76.1 million in the second weekend. As of January 21 the largest markets were the United Kingdom ($109.3 million), Germany ($79.8 million), France ($63.5 million), Japan ($60.8 million) and Australia ($43.5 million). China: a $28.7 million opening weekend, showtimes cut by 90% a week later, $910,000 in the third weekend for ninth place, and $42.5 million in total.

## Critical and audience response

Rotten Tomatoes: "91% of 483 critics' reviews are positive, with an average rating of 8.1/10", with the consensus quoted on the page. Metacritic: 84 out of 100 from 56 critics, "universal acclaim"; Metacritic analysis found it the 25th-most mentioned film on "best of the year" lists and 22nd-most on "best of the decade" lists. Praise from Matt Zoller Seitz (RogerEbert.com, 4/4), Peter Travers (Rolling Stone, 3.5/4), Richard Roeper (Chicago Sun-Times, 3.5/4), Will Gompertz (BBC News, 4/5) and Alex Leadbeater (Screen Rant, Snoke's death "the best movie twist in years"); criticism from Richard Brody (The New Yorker), Kate Taylor (The Globe and Mail, 2/4) and Owen Gleiberman (Variety). George Lucas, not involved in production, "described The Last Jedi as 'beautifully made' shortly after its release", a warmer reaction than he gave The Force Awakens.

Audience polling was highly positive: CinemaScore "A", PostTrak 89% overall positive with a 79% "definite recommend" and a rare five-star rating, and SurveyMonkey 89% positive. User scores on Rotten Tomatoes and Metacritic were far more negative; reviewers speculated about vote brigading by internet groups and bots, with analysis from Quartz and Bleeding Cool, and Rotten Tomatoes said in 2019 that the film had been "seriously targeted" by review bombing. Scott Mendelson of Forbes called the negative reaction "alleged". Divisive points included Rey's parents being insignificant, Snoke's underdevelopment and Luke's characterisation.

## Harassment

"The casting of Asian-American actress Kelly Marie Tran as Rose Tico spurred both a racist and misogynistic backlash against the film"; Tran was accused of representing "forced diversity" by "social justice warriors" and quit social media after extensive harassment. She was the first woman of colour to have a lead role in a Star Wars film; John Boyega faced similar abuse over The Force Awakens. Rian Johnson, Hamill and Boyega defended her.

## Accolades table

Wins listed: AARP Movies for Grownups Awards (February 5, 2018) Best Movie for Grownups; BMI Film Music Award (May 9, 2018) for John Williams; Empire Awards (March 18, 2018) Best Film, Best Director (Rian Johnson), Best Actress (Daisy Ridley), Best Visual Effects and Best Costume Design (Michael Kaplan); Golden Trailer Awards (June 6, 2017) Best Fantasy/Adventure Poster for the "Teaser"; Saturn Awards (June 27, 2018) Best Actor (Mark Hamill), Best Screenplay (Rian Johnson) and Best Editing (Bob Ducsay); Teen Choice Awards (August 12, 2018) Choice Fantasy Actress (Carrie Fisher).

Nominations listed include: Academy Awards (March 4, 2018) Best Original Score (John Williams), Best Sound Editing (Matthew Wood and Ren Klyce), Best Sound Mixing (David Parker, Michael Semanick, Ren Klyce and Stuart Wilson) and Best Visual Effects (Ben Morris, Mike Mulholland, Neal Scanlan and Chris Corbould); British Academy Film Awards (February 18, 2018) Best Sound and Best Special Visual Effects; Art Directors Guild (January 27, 2018), Costume Designers Guild (February 20, 2018), Cinema Audio Society (February 24, 2018), Golden Reel Awards (February 18, 2018), Visual Effects Society Awards (February 13, 2018, four categories), Make-Up Artists and Hair Stylists Guild (February 24, 2018), London Film Critics' Circle (January 28, 2018), Florida Film Critics Circle (December 23, 2017), Georgia Film Critics Association (January 12, 2018), BET Awards (June 24, 2018, Lupita Nyong'o), Grammy Awards (February 10, 2019), Hugo Awards (August 19, 2018), Nebula Awards (May 19, 2018), MTV Movie & TV Awards (June 18, 2018), Nickelodeon Kids' Choice Awards (March 24, 2018), International Film Music Critics Association Awards (February 22, 2018) and World Soundtrack Awards (October 17, 2018).

## Sequel

"The Last Jedi was followed by The Rise of Skywalker, the conclusion of the sequel trilogy. Despite a mixed critical reception, The Rise of Skywalker was a financial success." The part ends with a Wikipedia maintenance notice about duplicated citations.

## What this part is

No prose from the article. The capture holds the closing fields of a citation to The A.V. Club piece "Mark Hamill regrets ever making his debates with Rian Johnson about Luke Skywalker public" (dated March 12, 2018), long runs of blank wikitext, and the opening of a citation to Alissa Wilkinson's Vox article "CinemaScore, Rotten Tomatoes, and movie audience scores, explained" (August 13, 2018).

wikis.title: The Last Jedi article: reference list, external links and the sequel-trilogy navigation box
wikis.summary: Part 3 of the capture is the article's numbered reference list, its external links, and the start of the Star Wars sequel trilogy navigation template.
wikis.body:
## What this part is

Mostly the numbered reference list. The opening fragment is the end of the Vox citation about audience scores, quoting: "But with Rotten Tomatoes, Metacritic, and IMDB scores, that's not necessarily the case. None of these sites require users to prove that they've seen the film. All a person has to do is register for an account on the site."

## Sources cited in this block

Box Office Mojo; Irish Examiner (September 15, 2015, "Bad weather halts Star Wars filming on Skellig Michael"); Evening Standard (December 17, 2015, Kathleen Kennedy confirming the entire cast would return); Vanity Fair (cameos, December 17, 2017; four exclusive covers, May 23, 2017; "the Definitive Preview", May 24, 2017); Comicbook.com; Variety (Rose as the "Biggest New Part", April 14, 2017; Kelly Marie Tran on online harassment, August 21, 2018); The Verge (February 15, 2016, filming started); Entertainment Weekly (spoiler-talk pieces, December 16, 2017; Star Wars Celebration updates, July 17, 2016); British Film Institute; Bloomberg Businessweek; The A.V. Club (March 12, 2018); Empire (del Toro casting, September 7, 2015); Star Wars News Net; StarWars.com; The Hollywood Reporter (new release date, January 20, 2016); Deadline Hollywood (December 17, 2017, "'The Last Jedi' Opening To $219M" and a piece deciphering online user reviews); Boxoffice Pro; Syfy Wire; Vox, BBC News, CNET, The Daily Telegraph, The Washington Post, The New York Times, Screen Rant, Inverse, The Straits Times and IGN on the backlash; and Chris Kempshall's 2023 book The History and Politics of Star Wars: Death Stars and Democracy (pp. 202-207), quoted: "These attacks were then expanded outwards to focus on the character of Rose Tico in The Last Jedi and Kelly Marie Tran who played her."

## External links

The Last Jedi at StarWars.com, at Lucasfilm.com, on Wookieepedia, at IMDb and at Disney A to Z.

## Star Wars sequel trilogy navigation box

wikis.title: Star Wars: The Rise of Skywalker (2019 film)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia's article on Star Wars: The Rise of Skywalker - its credits and budget, plot, cast, the switch from Colin Trevorrow to J. J. Abrams, filming, its December 2019 release, $1.077 billion gross, mixed reviews and awards.
wikis.body:
## The film

- A 2019 American epic space opera film produced, co-written and directed by J. J. Abrams, "the third and final installment of the Star Wars sequel trilogy" and the last episode of the nine-part "Skywalker saga".
- Screenplay by Chris Terrio and Abrams; story by Derek Connolly, Colin Trevorrow, Abrams and Terrio. Produced by Lucasfilm and Bad Robot, distributed by Walt Disney Studios Motion Pictures. Music by John Williams, his last score for the franchise. Running time 141 minutes.
- Cast includes Carrie Fisher (through unreleased footage from The Force Awakens; she died in December 2016), Mark Hamill, Adam Driver, Daisy Ridley, John Boyega, Oscar Isaac, Naomi Ackie, Domhnall Gleeson, Richard E. Grant, Keri Russell, Kelly Marie Tran, Ian McDiarmid and Billy Dee Williams.

## Dates

- Premiered at the Dolby Theatre in Hollywood on December 16, 2019; released in the United States on December 20, 2019. It had first been dated May 24, 2019 before swapping with Aladdin.
- Principal photography began August 1, 2018 at Pinewood Studios and wrapped February 15, 2019; post-production finished November 25, 2019.
- Home media: Digital HD released four days before its March 17, 2020 date because of COVID-19; disc release March 31, 2020; Disney+ May 4.

## Money

- Budget listed as "$593.7 million (gross)" and "$490.2 million (net)"; with the net figure "it is the third most-expensive film ever made".
- Grossed $515.2 million in the United States and Canada and $561.8 million elsewhere, $1.077 billion worldwide - the seventh highest-grossing film of 2019 and the lowest-grossing of the sequel trilogy. Deadline Hollywood put the net profit at $300 million. Opening weekend $177.4 million domestic, $373.5 million worldwide.

## Production history

- Colin Trevorrow was announced as director in August 2015 and left in September 2017 over creative differences with Kathleen Kennedy; Abrams returned on September 12, 2017 and the release moved to December 2019. The title was announced at Star Wars Celebration in April 2019, where the teaser also revealed Palpatine's return.

## Reception

- Rotten Tomatoes 51% (average 6.1/10) from 522 reviews; Metacritic 53 out of 100 from 61 critics; "the lowest-rated of the nine main Star Wars films on both sites". CinemaScore "B+", the lowest among the franchise's live-action films.
- Three Academy Award nominations (Original Score, Visual Effects, Sound Editing) and three BAFTA nominations; won five Saturn Awards including Best Science Fiction Film.

## About the capture

- Part 2 of the capture is the remainder of the reference list plus navigation boxes and categories; the article text is in part 1. The page states no last-edited date.

wikis.title: Star Wars: The Rise of Skywalker (2019 film): plot, cast, production, release, reception and accolades
wikis.summary: Wikipedia's article body on Star Wars: The Rise of Skywalker, covering its credits and infobox figures, plot, cast, the change of director from Colin Trevorrow to J. J. Abrams, filming, marketing, box office, critical and audience response, its awards table and planned follow-ups.
wikis.body:
## Film and credits

- "Star Wars: The Rise of Skywalker, also known as Star Wars: Episode IX – The Rise of Skywalker, is a 2019 American epic space opera film produced, co-written, and directed by J. J. Abrams"; the third and final installment of the sequel trilogy after The Force Awakens (2015) and The Last Jedi (2017), and the last episode of the nine-part "Skywalker saga".
- Screenplay by Chris Terrio and J. J. Abrams; story by Derek Connolly, Colin Trevorrow, J. J. Abrams and Chris Terrio; based on characters by George Lucas. Produced by Kathleen Kennedy, J. J. Abrams and Michelle Rejwan.
- Cinematography Dan Mindel; edited by Maryann Brandon and Stefan Grube; music by John Williams. Production companies Lucasfilm and Bad Robot; distributed by Walt Disney Studios Motion Pictures.
- Release dates: December 16, 2019 (Dolby Theatre) and December 20, 2019 (United States). Running time 141 minutes. Country United States, language English.
- Budget given in the infobox as "$593.7 million (gross)" and "$490.2 million (net)"; the body says "With a net budget of approximately $490.2 million, it is the third most-expensive film ever made".
- Box office $1.077 billion.
- Cast listed: Carrie Fisher, Mark Hamill, Adam Driver, Daisy Ridley, John Boyega, Oscar Isaac, Anthony Daniels, Naomi Ackie, Domhnall Gleeson, Richard E. Grant, Lupita Nyong'o, Keri Russell, Joonas Suotamo, Kelly Marie Tran, Ian McDiarmid and Billy Dee Williams.

## Plot

- A year after the Battle of Crait, the resurrected Emperor Palpatine sends a message of revenge. Kylo Ren finds a Sith wayfinder leading to Exegol, where Palpatine reveals himself as the power behind Snoke and the First Order and offers Ren an armada of Star Destroyers if he kills Rey.
- Rey, Poe, Finn, Chewbacca, BB-8 and C-3PO travel to Pasaana, find a dagger with Sith text and the remains of the Sith assassin Ochi; then to Kijimi, where Babu Frik extracts the wayfinder coordinates from C-3PO's memory. Ren reveals Palpatine is Rey's grandfather; General Hux is revealed as the First Order spy and is killed by Allegiant General Pryde.
- On a moon in the Endor system Rey finds the wayfinder in the wreckage of the second Death Star; Ren destroys it, Leia distracts him through the Force as she dies, Rey impales then heals him, and he reclaims his identity as Ben Solo.
- At Exegol Palpatine senses Rey and Ben as "a dyad in the Force" and drains their power; the spirits of deceased Jedi place their power within Rey, who deflects his lightning onto him. Ben revives Rey and dies. Rey later buries Luke and Leia's lightsabers at Luke's homestead on Tatooine and answers "Rey Skywalker".

## Cast details

- Carrie Fisher as Leia Organa: "Fisher, who died in December 2016, appears through the use of repurposed unreleased footage from The Force Awakens." A note adds that Billie Lourd portrays her mother's character in a short flashback using footage from Return of the Jedi, and that unseen Last Jedi footage was considered but not used.
- Mark Hamill as Luke Skywalker; Adam Driver as Ben Solo / Kylo Ren; Daisy Ridley as Rey, "the paternal granddaughter of Palpatine"; Cailey Fleming and Josefine Irrera Jackson as young Rey; John Boyega as Finn (former stormtrooper FN-2187); Oscar Isaac as Poe Dameron; Anthony Daniels as C-3PO; Naomi Ackie as Jannah (former stormtrooper TZ-1719 of Kef Bir); Domhnall Gleeson as General Hux; Richard E. Grant as Allegiant General Pryde; Lupita Nyong'o as Maz Kanata; Keri Russell as Zorii Bliss; Joonas Suotamo as Chewbacca; Kelly Marie Tran as Rose Tico; Ian McDiarmid as Emperor Palpatine; Billy Dee Williams as Lando Calrissian.
- Billie Lourd, Greg Grunberg and Harrison Ford reprise Kaydel Ko Connix, Snap Wexley and Han Solo. Other appearances: Dominic Monaghan, Shirley Henderson (Babu Frik), Billy Howle and Jodie Comer as Rey's parents Dathan and Miramir, Liam Cook as Ochi, Denis Lawson (Wedge Antilles), Warwick Davis (Wicket), and cameos by John Williams, Kevin Smith, Michael Giacchino, Lin-Manuel Miranda, Jeff Garlin, Ed Sheeran and others. Vocal cameos include Hayden Christensen, James Earl Jones, Andy Serkis, Ewan McGregor, Alec Guinness (digitally altered archive audio), Frank Oz, Liam Neeson and Samuel L. Jackson.
- "The Rise of Skywalker marks the final film acting role for voice actor Tom Kane", following his retirement after a stroke in November 2020 and his death in May 2026.

## Development

- October 2012: George Lucas sold Lucasfilm to the Walt Disney Company; Disney announced the sequel trilogy. June 2014: Rian Johnson announced to write a story treatment for Episode IX; in April 2017 he denied involvement, saying the information was outdated.
- August 2015: Colin Trevorrow announced as director, writing with Derek Connolly. Their script, titled Star Wars: Duel of the Fates, included elements used to some extent in the final film.
- Late April 2017: Disney announced a May 24, 2019 release date. August 2017: Jack Thorne to rewrite the script. September 5, 2017: Lucasfilm said Trevorrow had left over creative differences; The Hollywood Reporter reported his relationship with Kathleen Kennedy had become unmanageable. David Fincher discussed the job and declined.
- September 12 [2017]: J. J. Abrams announced as director and the release date moved to December 20, 2019. The story team met George Lucas before writing the new script; Abrams co-wrote with Chris Terrio while Trevorrow and Connolly retain story credits.
- Working titles Black Diamond, then TrIXie in 2018. The title The Rise of Skywalker was announced at Star Wars Celebration in Chicago in April 2019.

## Casting

- Carrie Fisher died on December 27, 2016. January 2017: Lucasfilm said there were no plans to digitally generate her performance as in Rogue One (2016). July 2018: Abrams announced that unused Force Awakens footage would be used. Todd Fisher said in November 2019 that "she was going to be the big payoff in the final film".
- July 2018: Keri Russell in talks; Billy Dee Williams confirmed to return as Lando, onscreen for the first time since Return of the Jedi (1983). Late August 2018: Deadline reported Dominic Monaghan and Matt Smith cast; Smith denied involvement in 2019 and later said he had been in talks for an unrealized "transformative" part; Shawn Levy confirmed the casting when casting Smith in Star Wars: Starfighter (2027).
- April 2019: the teaser trailer revealed Ian McDiarmid's return as Palpatine, on-screen for the first time since Revenge of the Sith (2005).

## Filming and post-production

- Principal photography began August 1, 2018 at Pinewood Studios in Buckinghamshire, England, with filming also in Wadi Rum, Jordan (the desert planet Pasaana); it wrapped on February 15, 2019.
- The crew had three fewer months than on The Force Awakens; Maryann Brandon was sent to cut on set a third of the way through production. The Ben/Rey kiss was filmed with and without the kiss and included at the last minute.
- Two weeks of reshoots at Pinewood in July 2019 with Hamill, Ridley and Isaac; further reshoots at Bad Robot between late September and mid-October.
- Visual effects by Industrial Light & Magic, supervised by Roger Guyett. "The film finished post-production on November 25, 2019." A script John Boyega left in a hotel room was listed on eBay for around £65 and bought back by a Disney employee.

## Music

- January 2018: John Williams confirmed to return; the next month he said it would be his last Star Wars score (he later composed the theme for the Disney+ miniseries Obi-Wan Kenobi). August 2019: about 35 of an expected 135 minutes of music written. Scoring began in July 2019, conducted by Williams and William Ross over six months. Soundtrack album released by Walt Disney Records on December 20, 2019.

## Marketing and tie-ins

- Abrams headed a panel on April 12, 2019 at Star Wars Celebration in Chicago, where the title was revealed. A new poster and "sizzle reel" were released at D23 on August 24, with the footage public two days later.
- Publishing campaign "Journey to Star Wars: The Rise of Skywalker" announced May 4, 2019. The prequel graphic novel The Rise of Kylo Ren ran December 18, 2019 to March 11, 2020 (Charles Soule, Will Sliney). The novelization by Rae Carson was released March 19, 2020 and details that Palpatine transferred his consciousness into a clone body and that Rey's father was a failed clone. The junior novel by Michael Kogge followed on April 21, 2020. A five-issue Marvel adaptation planned for mid-2020 was cancelled, then scheduled for February 2025; IDW released a separate graphic novel adaptation in 2021.
- Games: a free Ajan Kloss level for Star Wars Battlefront II (2017); Fortnite Battle Royale cosmetics in December 2019 and an in-game preview event on December 14.

## Release

- Originally planned for May 24, 2019, then pushed to December 20, swapping dates with Aladdin. World premiere at the Dolby Theatre in Hollywood on December 16.
- Disney reportedly held no test screenings, showing it only to Abrams' friends and family and a terminally ill fan, and issued a warning about strobe-like flashing lights.
- Home media: Digital HD scheduled for March 17, 2020 but released four days early because of the COVID-19 pandemic; DVD, Blu-ray and 4K Ultra HD on March 31; on Disney+ on May 4, reportedly two months ahead of schedule.

## Box office

- Grossed $515.2 million in the United States and Canada and $561.8 million in other territories for $1.077 billion worldwide, "making it the seventh highest-grossing film of 2019" and the lowest-grossing of the sequel trilogy. Deadline Hollywood calculated a net profit of $300 million.
- Pre-sale tickets went on sale October 21, 2019. First day $89.6 million including $40 million from Thursday previews, the sixth-highest opening day of all time; opening weekend $177.4 million, the third-highest ever for a December release and 12th-best of all time. Christmas Day $32 million; five-day total $138.8 million including $76 million for the weekend; third weekend $34.5 million, first place, dethroned in the fourth weekend by 1917 (2019). Crossed $1 billion on January 14, 2020, Disney's seventh film of 2019 to do so.
- The article also says that at the end of its run it was "third highest-grossing film of 2019 in this region behind Avengers: Endgame and The Lion King" (United States and Canada).
- International: $59.1 million on its first day in 46 countries; opened to $198 million overseas and $373.5 million worldwide, "coming in below projections and 47% lower than The Last Jedi's total". Biggest opening totals: UK $26.8 million, Germany $21.8 million, France $15.2 million, Japan $14.6 million, Australia $12.6 million, China $12.1 million.

## Critical and audience response

- Rotten Tomatoes: 51% approval, average 6.1/10, from 522 reviews; consensus: "The Rise of Skywalker suffers from a frustrating lack of imagination, but concludes this beloved saga with fan-focused devotion." Metacritic: 53 out of 100 from 61 critics ("mixed or average reviews"). "It is the lowest-rated of the nine main Star Wars films on both sites."
- Reviews quoted: Richard Roeper (three stars out of four), A. A. Dowd (C+), Michael Phillips, Mick LaSalle ("a disappointment"; "Sit through a so-so 110 minutes to get to a strong half hour"), Owen Gleiberman, Nicholas Barber, Scott Mendelson, Justin Chang, Richard Brody and Brian Tallerico (2.5/4).
- Kelly Marie Tran, who had around ten minutes of screen time in The Last Jedi, "appears for about a minute" here; Chris Terrio attributed the reduction to the difficulty of using Carrie Fisher's archive footage in scenes planned for both characters.
- CinemaScore "B+", the lowest among the franchise's live-action films; PostTrak four stars out of five with 70% "definite recommend"; parents 5 stars, children under 12 4.5 stars, 80% of males and 84% of females positive.
- The "Want to See" percentage was review bombed on Rotten Tomatoes, dropping as low as 5% within a day. The line "Somehow, Palpatine returned" became an internet meme; Ian McDiarmid commented in 2025 that "I think he's dead."

## Accolades (table)

- Academy Awards, February 9, 2020: nominated for Best Original Score (John Williams), Best Sound Editing (Matthew Wood, David Acord) and Best Visual Effects (Roger Guyett, Neal Scanlan, Patrick Tubach, Dominic Tuohy).
- British Academy Film Awards, February 2, 2020: nominated for Best Sound, Best Original Score and Best Special Visual Effects.
- Saturn Awards, October 26, 2021: won Best Science Fiction Film, Best Director (Abrams), Best Music (Williams), Best Make-up (Amanda Knight, Neal Scanlan) and Best Special Effects; nominated in six further categories.
- Also: Artios Awards (January 30, 2020) Zeitgeist Award won; Dragon Awards (September 6, 2020) Best Science Fiction or Fantasy Movie won; Lumiere Awards (January 22, 2020) Best 2D to 3D Conversion won; Grammy Awards (March 14, 2021) and Hugo Awards (August 1, 2020) nominations; several Golden Trailer Awards wins in 2021; Visual Effects Society Awards (January 29, 2020) one win, three nominations; Art Directors Guild, Costume Designers Guild and Kids' Choice nominations.
- The article's lead says it "won five awards at the 46th Saturn Awards, including Best Science Fiction Film".

## Future

- November 2021: Kathleen Kennedy said Lucasfilm had been discussing the future of the sequel trilogy's characters. At Star Wars Celebration Europe in 2023 a new film directed by Sharmeen Obaid-Chinoy was announced following Rey rebuilding the Jedi Order, with Ridley reprising the role.
- Adam Driver sought a spin-off titled The Hunt for Ben Solo, developed with Steven Soderbergh and Jules Asner with a script by Scott Z. Burns; Lucasfilm greenlit it but Bob Iger and Alan Bergman ultimately rejected it.

wikis.title: How to Train Your Dragon (2010 film)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the 2010 DreamWorks Animation film How to Train Your Dragon: plot, voice cast, production, music, release, box office, reception, accolades and the franchise it started.
wikis.body:
## Overview
- 2010 American animated fantasy film directed by Chris Sanders and Dean DeBlois, written by Sanders, DeBlois and Will Davies, based on the 2003 novel by British author Cressida Cowell.
- Produced by DreamWorks Animation (producer Bonnie Arnold); distributed by Paramount Pictures.
- Edited by Darren T. Holmes and Maryann Brandon; music by John Powell.
- Running time 98 minutes. Country: United States. Language: English.
- Infobox budget $165 million; infobox box office $494.9 million.
- Release dates: March 21, 2010 (Gibson Amphitheater premiere); March 26, 2010 (United States).
- Story set in Berk, "a mythical Viking village"; Hiccup injures a rare Night Fury dragon, refuses to kill it and befriends it.

## Voice cast
- Jay Baruchel as Hiccup Horrendous Haddock III; America Ferrera as Astrid Hofferson; Gerard Butler as Stoick the Vast; Craig Ferguson as Gobber the Belch.
- Jonah Hill as Snotlout Jorgenson; Christopher Mintz-Plasse as Fishlegs Ingerman; Kristen Wiig as Ruffnut Thorston; T.J. Miller as Tuffnut Thorston.
- Randy Thom provides the vocal effects for Toothless and for Stormfly, Astrid's Deadly Nadder.
- Also David Tennant (Spitelout Jorgenson), Ashley Jensen (Phlegma the Fierce), Robin Atkin Downes (Ack), Philip McGrade (Starkard), Kieron Elliott (Hoark the Haggard).

## Production
- The book series came to the attention of DreamWorks Animation executives in 2004; after Over the Hedge, producer Bonnie Arnold chose the property when co-president of production Bill Damaschke asked what she wanted to do next.
- Original directors were Peter Hastings, Lorna Cook and David Soren; earlier versions followed the novel closely, but DreamWorks decided the story "skewed too much towards younger viewers", the three were removed and given "Special Thanks" credit. Damaschke hired Chris Sanders, who called Dean DeBlois (his Lilo & Stitch collaborator) to co-direct.
- DeBlois described the original plot as "heavily loyal to the book", regarded as too "sweet" and "whimsical".
- In the novel Toothless is thought to be a Common or Garden Dragon; in the film he is an injured Night Fury, "the rarest species of all dragons".
- Cinematographer Roger Deakins was hired as visual consultant to help with lighting and look and to "add a live-action feel".
- Research went into depicting flight and fire; Toothless's design combined dragon traits in a "black panther-inspired design" with large ears and eyes to convey emotion.
- The directors brought the secondary cast (Mintz-Plasse, Hill, Wiig, Miller) together in recording sessions to use their improvisation.

## Music
- John Powell's sixth DreamWorks Animation collaboration, after Antz, The Road to El Dorado, Chicken Run, Shrek and Kung Fu Panda.
- Orchestral score with "exotic Scottish and Irish tones" using penny whistle and bagpipes; Icelandic singer Jonsi wrote and performed the song "Sticks & Stones".
- Score released by Varese Sarabande on March 23, 2010.
- Powell earned his first Academy Award nomination for the score, losing to Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross for The Social Network.

## Release
- US premiere March 21, 2010 at the Gibson Amphitheatre in Universal City, California; theatrical release March 26, 2010.
- Originally scheduled for November 20, 2009, pushed back to avoid competition with Planet 51 and other November family films.
- Digitally re-mastered into IMAX 3D and released to 186 North American IMAX theaters and approximately 80 outside North America.
- A month before release, DreamWorks Animation CEO Jeffrey Katzenberg protested Warner Bros.' conversion of Clash of the Titans to 3D and its release one week after the film; theater executives accused Paramount of "high-pressure tactics" to favour it over Clash of the Titans and Alice in Wonderland, since multiplexes often had one 3D screen.
- Home media: single-disc DVD, two-disc DVD pack and Blu-ray/DVD combo in Canada and the US on October 15, 2010, with the sequel short Legend of the Boneknapper Dragon; "As of February 2012, 9.7 million home entertainment units were sold worldwide"; reissued on Blu-ray May 27, 2014.
- Distribution rights bought by DreamWorks Animation from Paramount in July 2014 and moved to 20th Century Fox, reverting to Universal Studios in 2018; Universal released a 4K Ultra HD Blu-ray on January 22, 2019 alongside How to Train Your Dragon 2, the first DreamWorks Animation catalog titles in that format.

## Box office
- Topped the North American box office with $43.7 million in its first weekend.
- Grossed $217.6 million in the United States and Canada and $277.3 million in foreign countries for a worldwide total of $494.9 million; the lead states the film earned "$495 million" and calls it the tenth-highest-grossing film of 2010.
- Called DreamWorks Animation's highest-grossing film in the American and Canadian box office other than the Shrek films, and the fifth-highest-grossing animated film of 2010 behind Toy Story 3 ($1,063.2 million), Shrek Forever After ($752.6 million), Tangled ($576.6 million) and Despicable Me ($543.1 million).
- "As of 2019", the series had grossed over $1 billion worldwide.

## Reception
- Rotten Tomatoes: 99% of 210 critics positive, average 7.9/10; consensus "Boasting dazzling animation, a script with surprising dramatic depth, and thrilling 3-D sequences, How to Train Your Dragon soars." "As of September 2025" it is DreamWorks Animation's highest-rated film on the site.
- Metacritic: 75 out of 100 from 37 reviews, "generally favorable". CinemaScore grade "A".
- Positive quotes include Variety's Matt Risley ("undoubtedly Dreamworks' best film yet, and quite probably the best dragon movie ever made") and James Berardinelli (3.5/4). Roger Ebert and A. O. Scott felt character and story development were sidelined for spectacle; Roger Moore of the Orlando Sentinel gave 2.5 of 4; Village Voice's Ella Taylor called it "adequate but unremarkable".

## Accolades
- At the 83rd Academy Awards: nominations for Best Animated Feature and Best Original Score.
- Fourteen Annie Award nominations (winning ten), two British Academy Film Awards, one Critics' Choice Movie Awards and one Golden Globe Award nomination.

## Franchise and other media
- Sequels How to Train Your Dragon 2 (2014) and How to Train Your Dragon: The Hidden World (2019); five short films: Legend of the Boneknapper Dragon (2010), Book of Dragons (2011), Gift of the Night Fury (2011), Dawn of the Dragon Racers (2014) and Homecoming (2019).
- A live-action remake was released in 2025, "to be followed by a remake of the second film in 2027". The remake was announced in development in February 2023, produced by Marc Platt Productions and distributed by Universal, DeBlois writing and directing; originally set for March 14, 2025, delayed to June 13 that year due to the 2023 SAG-AFTRA strike; Mason Thames and Nico Parker cast as Hiccup and Astrid, Butler reprising Stoick.
- A television series premiered on Cartoon Network in Autumn 2012, set between the first and second films, with Baruchel, Ferrera, Mintz-Plasse and Miller reprising roles.
- Activision's How to Train Your Dragon game released March 23, 2010 for Wii, Xbox 360, PS3 and Nintendo DS; School of Dragons, a free-to-play 3D MMO, released July 17, 2013 at San Diego Comic-Con.
- How to Train Your Dragon Arena Spectacular, with 24 animatronic dragons, premiered March 2, 2012 in Melbourne, Australia.
- Announced January 2024: How to Train Your Dragon: Isle of Berk, one of five lands at Universal Orlando's Universal Epic Universe, which opened May 22, 2025, with five attractions including Hiccup's Wing Gliders, Dragon Racer's Rally, Fyre Drill, the Viking Training Camp and a twenty-minute stage show.
- HarperCollins Children's Books published a storybook version in 2010, adapted by Rennie Brown with illustrations by Michael Koelsch.

wikis.title: How to Train Your Dragon 2 (2014 film)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on DreamWorks Animation's 2014 sequel written and directed by Dean DeBlois - its story, voice cast, production and animation technology, Cannes and June 2014 release, acclaim, $622 million gross and awards.
wikis.body:
## The film

- A 2014 American animated fantasy film written and directed by Dean DeBlois, based on Cressida Cowell's book series, produced by DreamWorks Animation and distributed by 20th Century Fox; the sequel to How to Train Your Dragon (2010) and second in the trilogy. Producer Bonnie Arnold, editor John K. Carr, composer John Powell. 102 minutes. Budget $145 million; box office $622 million.
- Set five years after the first film, it follows 20-year-old Hiccup, his mother Valka and the warlord Drago Bludvist, who wants to conquer the world with a dragon army. Stoick the Vast is killed by the brainwashed Toothless, and Hiccup becomes chieftain of Berk.
- Jay Baruchel, Gerard Butler, Craig Ferguson, America Ferrera, Jonah Hill, Christopher Mintz-Plasse, Kristen Wiig and T.J. Miller reprise their roles, with Cate Blanchett (Valka), Djimon Hounsou (Drago) and Kit Harington (Eret) joining.

## Production

- Announced on April 27, 2010; DeBlois had begun the outline in February 2010 at Skywalker Ranch. He accepted on condition he could make a trilogy, citing The Empire Strikes Back (1980) and My Neighbor Totoro (1988) as his main inspirations.
- The team researched Norway - Oslo, Bergen and the fjords - and DeBlois, Gregg Taylor and Roger Deakins went on to Svalbard. Guillermo del Toro suggested killing Stoick rather than Gobber, and received a "Thank you" credit.
- The first DreamWorks Animation film to use "scalable multicore processing", developed with Hewlett-Packard, and the studio's first to use its new Premo and Torch animation and lighting software through the whole production; over 500 people worked on it.
- John Powell scored the film with a 120-piece orchestra and 100-voice choir at Abbey Road Studios in April 2014, with two original songs written with Jónsi.

## Release and reception

- Screened at the 2014 Cannes Film Festival - the Release section says out of competition on May 16, 2014, the lead says it premiered May 21, 2014, and the infobox gives May 20, 2014 - and released in the United States on June 13, 2014, also in IMAX 3D internationally.
- Rotten Tomatoes 92% from 184 critics (average 7.8/10); Metacritic 77 from 48 critics; CinemaScore "A".
- $177 million in North America and $445 million elsewhere for $622 million worldwide (the same section elsewhere gives $438 million internationally) - the second-highest-grossing animated film of 2014 behind Big Hero 6 and the twelfth-highest-grossing film of the year. Deadline Hollywood estimated a $107.3 million profit. Its $25.9 million China opening weekend was the country's biggest ever for an animated film.
- Won the Golden Globe for Best Animated Feature and six Annie Awards including Best Animated Feature; nominated for the Academy Award for Best Animated Feature.

## After the film

- How to Train Your Dragon: The Hidden World was released on February 22, 2019.
- Universal Pictures announced a live-action remake on April 2, 2025, scheduled for June 11, 2027, with Cate Blanchett returning as Valka, Ólafur Darri Ólafsson as Drago and Phil Dunster as Eret.

wikis.title: How to Train Your Dragon 2 (2014 film) - plot, production, release, reception and accolades
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the 2014 DreamWorks Animation sequel written and directed by Dean DeBlois, covering its story, voice cast, animation technology, Cannes and US release, reviews, $622 million box office and awards.
wikis.body:
## The film

- "How to Train Your Dragon 2 is a 2014 American animated fantasy film written and directed by Dean DeBlois, based on the book series by Cressida Cowell." Produced by DreamWorks Animation, it is the sequel to How to Train Your Dragon (2010) and the second installment in the How to Train Your Dragon trilogy.
- Produced by Bonnie Arnold; edited by John K. Carr; music by John Powell. Distributed by 20th Century Fox.
- Release dates in the infobox: May 20, 2014 (Cannes) and June 13, 2014 (United States). Running time 102 minutes. Country United States; language English.
- Budget $145 million; box office $622 million.
- "Set five years after the events of the first film, it follows 20-year-old Hiccup and his friends as they encounter Valka, Hiccup's long-lost mother, and Drago Bludvist, a vengeful madman who wants to conquer the world by use of a dragon army."
- It grossed $622 million, "becoming the 12th-highest-grossing film of 2014". It won the Golden Globe for Best Animated Feature and six Annie Awards including Best Animated Feature, and was nominated for the Academy Award for Best Animated Feature.
- The final installment in the trilogy, How to Train Your Dragon: The Hidden World, was released in 2019 (on February 22, 2019, "the release date had been changed multiple times due to various distributor changes"). A live-action remake is scheduled for release in 2027.

## Voice cast

- Jay Baruchel as Hiccup Horrendous Haddock III; America Ferrera as Astrid Hofferson; Cate Blanchett as Valka Haddock, with Mary Jane Wells providing Valka's singing voice during "For the Dancing and the Dreaming"; Gerard Butler as Stoick the Vast; Craig Ferguson as Gobber the Belch; Jonah Hill as Snotlout Jorgenson; Christopher Mintz-Plasse as Fishlegs Ingerman; Kristen Wiig and T.J. Miller as the fraternal twins Ruffnut and Tuffnut Thorston; Djimon Hounsou as Drago Bludvist; Kit Harington as Eret, son of Eret; Randy Thom as vocal effects for Toothless and Stormfly.

## Video game

- A video game based on the film, also called How to Train Your Dragon 2, was released in June 2014 by Little Orbit. Developed by Torus Games, it was available for Xbox 360, Nintendo 3DS, Wii, Wii U and PlayStation 3.

## Live-action remake

- On April 2, 2025 Universal Pictures announced a live-action remake of How to Train Your Dragon 2, following the live-action remake of the first film, scheduled for release on June 11, 2027.
- In January 2026 it was revealed that Cate Blanchett would reprise her role as Valka and that Ólafur Darri Ólafsson had been cast as Drago. Phil Dunster was later announced as Eret.

## Contradictions inside the page

- Cannes date: the infobox gives the Cannes release date as May 20, 2014; the lead says the film "premiered at the 2014 Cannes Film Festival on May 21, 2014"; the Release section says it "was screened out of competition on May 16, 2014, at the 2014 Cannes Film Festival".
- International gross: the Box office section says the film grossed "$445 million in other countries" for a $622 million worldwide total, then says it earned "$438 million" internationally against How to Train Your Dragon's $277 million.

wikis.title: Plot of How to Train Your Dragon 2
wikis.summary: The film's story as the article summarises it, from Berk five years on to Stoick's death and Hiccup becoming chieftain.
wikis.body:
- Five years after the Viking villagers of Berk and the dragons have made peace, Hiccup and his Night Fury best friend Toothless map out unexplored lands. Hiccup's father Stoick the Vast pressures him to succeed as chieftain, although Hiccup is uncertain whether he is ready.
- Investigating a burnt forest, Hiccup and his girlfriend Astrid are ambushed by dragon trappers led by Eret, who works for the warlord Drago Bludvist, who plots to enslave all dragons as soldiers. Stoick fortifies Berk and explains he once met Drago at a chieftain gathering, where Drago offered protection in exchange for service; when denied, Drago had his dragons attack, leaving Stoick the sole survivor.
- Hiccup flies off to change Drago's mind and instead meets a mysterious dragon rider who is his mother Valka, presumed dead after being taken by a dragon during a raid. Valka rescues dragons from Drago and brings them to an island nest formed of ice by a massive ice-breathing alpha dragon, a Bewilderbeast, which controls smaller dragons with hypnotic sound waves. Stoick and Gobber track Hiccup there and Stoick and Valka reunite.
- Astrid and the other riders force Eret to lead them to Drago, who captures them and tries to execute Eret; Astrid's dragon Stormfly saves him, and Eret helps them escape. Drago directs his armada to attack the nest.
- Drago unveils his own Bewilderbeast, which kills the alpha and takes control of all the dragons. Drago cites his family's deaths from dragon attacks in his childhood and his desire to conquer the world. His Bewilderbeast hypnotizes Toothless and forces him to kill Hiccup, but Stoick takes the fatal blast; Hiccup drives Toothless away out of grief, and Drago rides Toothless to conquer Berk.
- After a Viking funeral for Stoick, Valka reminds Hiccup that his father believed he could unite humans and dragons. Hiccup and his allies return to Berk on baby dragons, immune to the Bewilderbeast's influence. Hiccup frees Toothless, who enters a glowing, super-powered dominant state, breaks the Bewilderbeast's control over the other dragons and fires a massive blast breaking its left tusk; the defeated Bewilderbeast retreats to the sea with Drago.
- Hiccup is officially made chieftain of Berk, Valka stays with her son, and the dragons accept Toothless as the new alpha.

wikis.title: Development, casting and research
wikis.summary: How the sequel was announced and shaped - DeBlois's trilogy condition, his Empire Strikes Back and Totoro inspirations, the Norway and Svalbard research trip, and Guillermo del Toro's story note.
wikis.body:
- The sequel was announced on April 27, 2010 after the success of the first film. Jeffrey Katzenberg, DreamWorks Animation's CEO: "How to Train Your Dragon … has become DreamWorks Animation's next franchise. We plan to release the sequel theatrically in 2013".
- DeBlois had started drafting the outline in February 2010 at Skywalker Ranch during the final sound mix of the first film. The film was originally scheduled for June 20, 2014 but in August 2013 the date was moved forward one week to June 13, 2014.
- DeBlois wrote, directed and executive produced. Bonnie Arnold returned as producer; Chris Sanders, co-director and co-writer of the first film, acted only as an additional executive producer because of his involvement with The Croods (2013).
- "When offered the sequel, DeBlois accepted it on condition he could turn it into a trilogy." His pivotal inspirations were The Empire Strikes Back (1980) and My Neighbor Totoro (1988). DeBlois: "What I loved especially about Empire is that it expanded Star Wars (1977) in every direction: emotionally, its scope, characters, fun. It felt like an embellishment and that's the goal."
- The entire original voice cast returned. On June 19, 2012 Kit Harington was announced as one of the film's antagonists; at the 2013 San Diego Comic-Con, Cate Blanchett and Djimon Hounsou were announced as Valka and Drago Bludvist.
- Where the first film was set in a generic North Sea environment, the team focused on Norway; about a dozen of them made a week-long research trip touring Oslo, Bergen and the fjords. DeBlois, DreamWorks head of feature development Gregg Taylor and visual consultant Roger Deakins then went on to Svalbard to see polar bears in the wild with armed guides.
- DeBlois said he had learned from Lilo & Stitch (2002) that "if you set an animated film in a place you want to visit, there's a chance you might get to go there"; he had wanted to visit Svalbard since hearing of its stark beauty from backpackers met on earlier visits to Iceland to work with Sigur Rós on the documentary Heima (2007).
- An early draft had Gobber the Belch killed by the brainwashed Toothless rather than Stoick. Guillermo del Toro, shown the outline, suggested killing Stoick instead, as Stoick had "exhausted" his narrative contribution and would be a "crutch" for Hiccup as chief; DeBlois agreed and del Toro was given a "Thank you" credit.

wikis.title: Animation technology
wikis.summary: The new DreamWorks production workflow, scalable multicore processing with Hewlett-Packard, and the Premo and Torch software used on the film.
wikis.body:
- Over the five years before release, DreamWorks Animation "had substantially overhauled its production workflow and animation software".
- How to Train Your Dragon 2 was the first DreamWorks Animation film to use "scalable multicore processing", developed with Hewlett-Packard - called by Katzenberg "the next revolution in filmmaking" - which "enabled artists for the first time to work on rich, complex images in real time, instead of waiting eight hours to see the results the next day".
- It was also the studio's first film to use its new animation and lighting software through the entire production. Programs named Premo and Torch "allowed much more subtlety, improving facial animation and enabling 'the sense of fat, jiggle, loose skin, the sensation of skin moving over muscle instead of masses moving together.'"
- By completion, over 500 people had worked on the film at DreamWorks Animation's Glendale headquarters and its branch offices at PDI/DreamWorks in Redwood City and DreamWorks India in Bangalore.
- During a November 2013 visit to DreamWorks Animation, U.S. President Barack Obama tried a motion capture camera of the kind used to capture live-action reference performance for the film.

wikis.title: Music of How to Train Your Dragon 2
wikis.summary: John Powell's score, the Abbey Road recording sessions, the Jónsi songs and the soundtrack releases.
wikis.body:
- John Powell, who earned his first Academy Award nomination for the original film's music, returned to score the sequel. He described the project as "a maturation story" and said he tried to achieve the same maturation in his music by developing further every aspect of his compositions from the first film.
- Recording took place during April 2014 at Abbey Road Studios in London with a 120-piece orchestra, a 100-voice choir, and ethnic instruments including Celtic harp, uilleann bagpipes, tin whistle, bodhrán and Highland bagpipes, the latter performed by pipers from the Scottish group Red Hot Chilli Pipers. The ensemble was conducted by Gavin Greenaway.
- Sigur Rós's lead vocalist Jónsi, who wrote and performed "Sticks & Stones" for the first film, provided two new original songs with Powell: "For the Dancing and the Dreaming" (performed by Gerard Butler, Craig Ferguson and Mary Jane Wells) and "Where No One Goes" (performed by Jónsi).
- Belarusian-Norwegian artist Alexander Rybak, who voices Hiccup in the Norwegian dub, wrote and performed "Into a Fantasy", "which is only featured in the European versions of the film".
- The soundtrack album was released on June 13, 2014 by Relativity Music Group, with over an hour of Powell's score plus additional music by Anthony Willis and Paul Mounsey and the two original songs; "Into a Fantasy" was released separately as a single. A deluxe edition of previously unreleased music was released by Varèse Sarabande in May 2022.

wikis.title: Release, home media and box office
wikis.summary: The Cannes screening, US premiere and IMAX 3D release, the home video releases, and the film's takings in North America and abroad.
wikis.body:
## Release

- "The film was screened out of competition on May 16, 2014, at the 2014 Cannes Film Festival." (The lead instead gives a Cannes premiere of May 21, 2014, and the infobox a Cannes release date of May 20, 2014.)
- In the United States it premiered on June 8, 2014 at the Regency Village Theater in Los Angeles and was theatrically released on June 13, 2014. It was digitally remastered into IMAX 3D and released to international theaters on June 13, 2014.
- An advance screening for military members and their families was held on June 4, 2014 at Joint Base McGuire-Dix-Lakehurst, attended by DeBlois, Baruchel and Ferrera.

## Home media

- Released digitally on October 21, 2014 and on DVD and Blu-ray (both 2D and 3D) on November 11. The Blu-ray and digital releases came with a new animated short, Dawn of the Dragon Racers (2014), in which Hiccup and friends compete to become the first Dragon Racing Champion of Berk.
- A double DVD pack with the film and Dawn of the Dragon Racers was sold exclusively at Walmart. As of February 2015, 7.5 million home entertainment units had been sold worldwide.
- On January 22, 2019, Universal Pictures Home Entertainment released a 4K Ultra HD Blu-ray version alongside its predecessor, "making them the first catalog DreamWorks Animation films to be released on that format".

## Box office

- Grossed $177 million in North America and $445 million in other countries, for a worldwide total of $622 million - the second-highest-grossing animated film of 2014 behind Big Hero 6 and the twelfth-highest-grossing film of the year in any genre.
- The article also says it earned $177 million in the US against $217 million for its predecessor, but performed much better internationally, "earning $438 million to How to Train Your Dragon's $277 million". Deadline Hollywood estimated a profit of $107.3 million after all expenses.
- In the United States and Canada it earned $18.5 million on its opening day and opened at number two behind 22 Jump Street with $49,451,322. Second weekend: number three with $24,719,312. Third weekend: number three with $13,237,697. Fourth weekend: number five with $8,961,088.
- "Its $25.9 million opening weekend in China was the biggest-ever for an animated film in the country, surpassing the record previously held by Kung Fu Panda 2."

## Critical response

- Rotten Tomatoes: 92% approval from 184 critics, average 7.8/10. Consensus: "Exciting, emotionally resonant, and beautifully animated, How to Train Your Dragon 2 builds on its predecessor's successes just the way a sequel should."
- Metacritic: 77 out of 100 from 48 critics, "generally favorable". CinemaScore opening-weekend grade "A"; audiences 47% female and 53% male, with under-25s giving A+.
- Peter Debruge (Variety) at Cannes called it "DreamWorks Animation's strongest sequel yet—one that breathes fresh fire into the franchise, instead of merely rehashing the original. Braver than Brave, more fun than Frozen, and more emotionally satisfying than so many of its live-action counterparts".
- Peter Travers (Rolling Stone), three and a half of four: "Dragon 2, like The Empire Strikes Back, takes sequels to a new level of imagination and innovation."
- Stephen Holden (The New York Times) was negative: "The story seems to be going somewhere until it comes to a halt with the inevitable showdown between the forces of darkness and the forces of light."
- A. A. Dowd (The A.V. Club) gave it a B−: "There aren't just more dragons, but more characters, more plot, more everything. The trade-off is that the charm of the original gets a little lost." Inkoo Kang (The Wrap) was mixed; Stephen Whitty (Newark Star-Ledger) gave two and a half of four: "This was not a sequel that anybody needed, outside of the accountants."
- Four-star and near-perfect reviews came from Colin Covert (Star Tribune), Bill Zwecker (Chicago Sun-Times), John Semley (The Globe and Mail) and Bill Goodykoontz (The Arizona Republic, four of five), among many three-and-a-half and three-star notices.
