wikis.title: Supergirl (2026 film)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia's article on Supergirl, the 2026 DC Universe film directed by Craig Gillespie and starring Milly Alcock, with its production history, June 2026 release, box office and reception.
wikis.body:
## Overview
- The source is the English Wikipedia article on *Supergirl*, a 2026 American superhero film based on the DC Comics character Kara Zor-El, directed by Craig Gillespie, written by Ana Nogueira and produced by Peter Safran and James Gunn of DC Studios. It is the second DC Universe (DCU) film, part of "Chapter One: Gods and Monsters", adapted from Tom King and Bilquis Evely's 2021-22 miniseries *Supergirl: Woman of Tomorrow*.
- Part 1 holds the article itself (plot, cast, production, release, reception, future); parts 2 and 3 are its reference list, external links, navigation boxes and categories.

## Key facts
- Premiered at the Plaza at 300 Ashland in Brooklyn on June 22, 2026; released theatrically in the United States by Warner Bros. Pictures on June 26, 2026, in IMAX. Running time 108 minutes. Digital release July 28, 2026; 4K Ultra HD, Blu-ray and DVD September 8.
- Stars Milly Alcock as Kara Zor-El / Supergirl, with Matthias Schoenaerts (Krem of the Yellow Hills), Eve Ridley (Ruthye Marye Knoll), David Krumholtz (Zor-El), Emily Beecham (Alura In-Ze), David Corenswet (Superman) and Jason Momoa (Lobo); Seth Rogen has a voice cameo.
- Budget given as "$170-186 million" in the infobox; the article notes a report at the start of December 2025 of a $200 million budget "which Gunn disputed", and a subsequently reported net budget of $170 million.
- Box office $126.4 million worldwide ($72.4 million US/Canada, $54 million elsewhere) against a reported break-even of about $315 million; opened to $38 million domestically ($68 million worldwide) after a $13 million first day, and fell 76% in weekend two. Projected studio losses were reported as $85-125 million.
- Reception: Rotten Tomatoes 53% of 372 reviews (average 5.5/10); Metacritic 50/100 from 56 critics; CinemaScore "B-". Described by the article as "a box-office flop".
- Production: principal photography January 13 to about May 10, 2025, at Warner Bros. Studios Leavesden and London, and in Scotland; composer changed twice (Ramin Djawadi to Tom Holkenborg to Claudia Sarne); after a December 2025 test screening DC Studios took over post-production and released its own cut rather than Gillespie's 11-minutes-longer version.
- In May 2026 Safran said Alcock's Supergirl would have a major role in the DCU beyond *Man of Tomorrow* (2027).

## Date wording
- The page gives no publication or last-updated date for itself; its footer carries only an oldid, and its maintenance categories ("Use mdy dates from July 2026") are not stated as a revision date.

wikis.title: Supergirl (2026 film)
wikis.summary: The Wikipedia article on the 2026 DC Universe film Supergirl, covering its plot, cast, development and production, marketing, release, box office and critical reception.
wikis.body:
## Film
- *Supergirl* is a 2026 American superhero film based on the DC Comics superheroine Kara Zor-El / Supergirl, directed by Craig Gillespie and written by Ana Nogueira; it is the second film in the DC Universe (DCU), part of "Chapter One: Gods and Monsters".
- Produced by Peter Safran and James Gunn of DC Studios; production companies DC Studios, Troll Court Entertainment and The Safran Company; distributed by Warner Bros. Pictures.
- Infobox credits: cinematography Rob Hardy; editing Tatiana S. Riegel and Fred Raskin; music Claudia Sarne; running time 108 minutes; country United States; language English.
- Release dates given as June 22, 2026 (Brooklyn, premiere) and June 26, 2026 (wide release).
- Infobox budget "$170-186 million"; box office "$126.4 million".
- Adapted from the 2021-22 comic book miniseries *Supergirl: Woman of Tomorrow* by Tom King and Bilquis Evely.

## Cast
- Milly Alcock as Kara Zor-El / Supergirl - raised on a chunk of destroyed Krypton, "a more jaded person than her cousin"; Gunn envisioned her as a "pixie-ish, but very attitudinal character"; Gunn and Gillespie described her as an antihero.
- Matthias Schoenaerts as Krem of the Yellow Hills, leader of the Brigands, "a group of space pirates and human traffickers".
- Eve Ridley as Ruthye Marye Knoll; David Krumholtz as Zor-El; Emily Beecham as Alura In-Ze; David Corenswet as Kal-El / Clark Kent / Superman; Jason Momoa as Lobo, "an alien mercenary and bounty hunter from the utopian planet Czarnia" (Momoa played Aquaman in the DCEU from 2016 to 2023).
- Also Ferdinand Kingsley as Elias Knoll, Diarmaid Murtagh as Drom Baxton, and Clara Rosager, Heather Agyepong and Alice Hewkin as the Sklarian Raiders; Seth Rogen has a voice cameo as a small alien on a space bus; Krypto returns from *Superman* (2025).

## Plot (as summarized by the page)
- Zor-El separates Argo City from Krypton before the planet's core explodes; Kryptonite radiation later kills the citizens, and Kara and her dog Krypto are sent to Earth, greeted by Kal-El.
- In the present Kara is celebrating her 23rd birthday off-world; Krem hijacks her ship and shoots Krypto with a poisonous dart, leaving him "only three days left to live"; Kara pursues Krem for the antidote with Ruthye, aided by Lobo, and ultimately kills Krem herself before saving Krypto.

## Background and development
- Oren Uziel was hired by Warner Bros. in August 2018 to write a Supergirl film; production was tentatively scheduled to begin in early 2020 but was put on hold due to the COVID-19 pandemic.
- February 2021: Sasha Calle cast as Supergirl for *The Flash* (2023) on a multi-film DCEU contract. Tatiana Siegel of *Rolling Stone* reported in August 2022 that the film was unlikely to move forward under David Zaslav, and it "was quietly canceled around that time".
- Gunn and Safran announced as co-chairs/co-CEOs of DC Studios at the end of October 2022.
- January 31, 2023: the DCU slate was unveiled including the *Woman of Tomorrow* adaptation; Gunn called it "a big science fiction epic film" with a more "hardcore" Kara.
- November 2023: Ana Nogueira revealed as screenwriter; Gunn called the film a "beautiful, star-spanning tale" and moved it up as the second DCU film after *Superman* on the strength of her script. Nogueira said her initial pitch already changed the comic by having Supergirl, not Ruthye, kill Krem.

## Pre-production and casting
- By January 2024 Milly Alcock, Emilia Jones, Cailee Spaeny and Meg Donnelly were considered; Alcock and Donnelly screen-tested in costume on the *Superman* set in Atlanta, and Alcock was cast at the end of the month. Gunn had first mentioned Alcock to Safran over a year earlier after *House of the Dragon*.
- April 2024: Craig Gillespie in talks to direct; DC Studios EVP Chantal Nong revealed as executive producer. He was confirmed the next month, when the film was given a release date of June 26, 2026.
- September 2024: Schoenaerts cast as Krem; filming expected to begin in January 2025 in the United Kingdom. Eve Ridley cast as Ruthye at the end of October 2024. Momoa reported as Lobo in December.
- Costume designer Anna B. Sheppard, production designer Neil Lamont. Alcock's cape was made from 16 meters of the same material used for Christopher Reeve's Superman cape. Some Lobo designs reviewed in pre-production "were criticized by some who believed they were created with artificial intelligence (AI)".
- Cited inspirations: *True Grit* (1968 novel), *Logan* (2017), *John Wick* (2014), and *The Fifth Element* (1997); Gillespie estimated nine distinct worlds, each with their own languages.

## Filming and post-production
- Principal photography began January 13, 2025, at Warner Bros. Studios Leavesden and London, England; shot on the Sony Venice 2 with Panavision Ultra Panatar II anamorphic lenses, and digital IMAX cameras were also used.
- Gunn and Safran said filming was halfway done at the end of February 2025; Momoa and Krumholtz wrapped in April; filming was taking place in Scotland by the end of April and wrapped by May 10. Filming "was also expected to occur in Iceland".
- Visual effects supervisor Geoffrey Baumann, with work by Digital Domain, Framestore and Industrial Light & Magic.
- June 2025: Gunn announced the title had been shortened to *Supergirl*.
- The film "was reported at the start of December [2025] to have a $200 million budget, which Gunn disputed; it was subsequently reported to have a net budget of $170 million."
- Jeff Sneider reported a test screening in the week of December 15, 2025; *The Hollywood Reporter* later reported DC Studios took control of post-production afterwards, enlisting writer Jeremy Slater. By early 2026 two cuts were tested - Gillespie's, 11 minutes longer with more of Krem, and the studio's, which "scored slightly above" and was used.

## Music and marketing
- Ramin Djawadi revealed as composer in December 2025, replaced by Tom Holkenborg in February 2026, with Claudia Sarne taking over by the following month; soundtrack released by WaterTower Music on June 26, 2026.
- Songs in the film but not on the album include "This Summer" (Sleigh Bells), "Le Temps de l'amour" (Francoise Hardy), "Silver Lining" (Rilo Kiley), "The Middle" covered by Kelty Greye and KidMotel, and the "Original Superman Theme" by John Williams. "The Middle" was picked by Gunn from about 45 songs in contention; a planned "Girls Just Wanna Have Fun" cover was scrapped.
- First poster released July 2025 ("Look Up" graffitied to "Look Out"); logo and suit shown at CCXP in Brazil in early December 2025; teasers and a "Truth, Justice, Whatever" poster followed, and the first full trailer, set to "Call Me" by Blondie, was released December 11.
- Warner Bros. and DC Studios collaborated with over 80 brands on a $100 million promotional campaign; the marketing budget "was reported to be $120 million".

## Release and reception
- World premiere at the Plaza at 300 Ashland in Brooklyn on June 22, 2026; US theatrical release June 26, in IMAX. Digital download July 28, 2026; 4K Ultra HD, Blu-ray and DVD on September 8.
- Grossed $72.4 million in the US and Canada and $54 million elsewhere, for $126.4 million worldwide; with a net production budget of $170-186 million the film "reportedly needed to gross around $315 million worldwide to break even".
- After the opening weekend it was reported the film was projected to lose the studio $85-125 million (TheWrap headline "to Lose $85 Million"; Deadline "To Lose $125M").
- Projected US/Canada opening of $40-55 million from 3,600 theaters; estimates were lowered after $13 million on the first day (including $7.8 million in previews); it opened to $38 million domestically and $68 million worldwide, then dropped 76% to $9.6 million domestically in its second weekend, reaching $100.5 million worldwide.
- Rotten Tomatoes: 53% of 372 critics' reviews positive, average rating 5.5/10. Metacritic: 50 out of 100 from 56 critics, "mixed or average". CinemaScore "B-"; 52% of PostTrak respondents would definitely recommend it.
- Mixed and negative reviews quoted from David Rooney (*The Hollywood Reporter*), Pete Hammond (*Deadline*), Owen Gleiberman (*Variety*, "numbingly flat"), Tomris Laffly (RogerEbert.com, 1.5/4, "shallow blockbuster that never takes flight"), Clarisse Loughley (*The Independent*, 2/5, "the superhero equivalent of a Vegas impersonator") and Amy Nicholson (*Los Angeles Times*, "hot mess"); positive from Kate Erbland (IndieWire), Peter Bradshaw (*The Guardian*, 3/5), David Fear (*Rolling Stone*) and Leila Latif (*Empire*, 3/5).

## Future
- In May 2026 Safran said Alcock's Supergirl "would have a major role in the future of the DCU" beyond her return in the *Superman* follow-up film *Man of Tomorrow* (2027).

wikis.title: A Quiet Place Part II (2020 film)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia's article on A Quiet Place Part II, John Krasinski's sequel to A Quiet Place: its credits and plot, the Western New York shoot, a year of COVID-19 release delays, record pandemic-era box office and its reviews and awards.
wikis.body:
## The film

- **A Quiet Place Part II**, a 2020 American post-apocalyptic horror film written, directed and co-produced by **John Krasinski**, sequel to *A Quiet Place* (2018), based on characters by Bryan Woods and Scott Beck.
- Emily Blunt (Evelyn), Millicent Simmonds (Regan), Noah Jupe (Marcus) and Krasinski (Lee) return; **Cillian Murphy** (Emmett) and **Djimon Hounsou** (the Man on the Island) join.
- Cinematography Polly Morgan; editing Michael P. Shawver; music Marco Beltrami. Produced by Michael Bay, Andrew Form, Brad Fuller and Krasinski for Paramount Pictures, Platinum Dunes and Sunday Night Productions.
- Running time **97 minutes**; United States; American Sign Language and English. Budget **$55-61 million** in the infobox and lead, **$61 million** in the Production section - "over three times the original's $17 million".

## Dates

- World premiere in New York City (Lincoln Center) **March 8, 2020**.
- Release was set for March 2020, then postponed to **September 4, 2020**, **April 23, 2021** and **September 17, 2021**, before Krasinski announced on **March 4, 2021** that it would move up to **May 28, 2021**, the Memorial Day weekend, in 3,752 US and Canadian theaters plus 12 other markets.
- Paramount+ and digital **July 13, 2021**, 45 days after the theatrical debut; disc **July 27, 2021**.
- *A Quiet Place Part III*, announced by Paramount in **October 2025**, is scheduled for **July 30, 2027** and is described as "the third and final film following the original film's family".

## Money

- Worldwide gross **$297.5 million** in the infobox and lead; the box office section gives **$297.4 million** - $160.1 million in the US and Canada and $137.3 million elsewhere.
- Opening: $19.3 million first day including $4.8 million in Thursday previews (both pandemic highs), **$48.0 million** three-day and **$57.5 million** four-day Memorial Day weekend - the biggest opening weekend since *Sonic the Hedgehog* in February 2020. First pandemic-era film to pass **$100 million** domestically, on June 11, 2021.

## Reception

- Rotten Tomatoes **91%** (366 reviews, 7.5/10); Metacritic **71/100** (57 critics); CinemaScore **A-**, up from the first film's B+. The article calls the reviews "mostly positive" while noting The Independent said critics were divided.
- Wins include the Hollywood Critics Association Midseason Awards for Millicent Simmonds (Best Actress) and Cillian Murphy (Best Supporting Actor), and the Critics' Choice Super Award for Best Horror Movie. BAFTA nominated the sound team; the Saturn Awards nominated the film and three of its actors.

## Making it

- Krasinski's starting idea was "to make Millie [Simmonds] the lead of the movie"; original writers Scott Beck and Bryan Woods declined to return, preferring original ideas. He wrote a draft in three and a half weeks and was confirmed as director in February 2019.
- Filming ran **47 days** from July 15, 2019 across Western New York (Buffalo, Lackawanna, Dunkirk, Akron, Olcott and more) and the Hudson Valley, investing over $10 million in Upstate New York with 400 hires and 300 background actors.
- Polly Morgan shot on 35 mm, with night and stage work making up 75% of screen time; the first film's sound team of Erik Aadahl, Ethan Van der Ryn and Brandon Proctor returned and were told to "follow the rules" of the original.

wikis.title: A Quiet Place Part II - film article from plot to sequel plans
wikis.summary: The body of the Wikipedia article on John Krasinski's 2020 film A Quiet Place Part II: credits, plot, cast, development and filming, cinematography and sound, marketing, the chain of COVID-19 release postponements, box office, reviews and awards.
wikis.body:
## Infobox

- **A Quiet Place Part II**, "2020 film by John Krasinski". Written and directed by **John Krasinski**, based on characters by **Bryan Woods and Scott Beck**.
- Produced by Michael Bay, Andrew Form, Brad Fuller and John Krasinski. Cinematography **Polly Morgan**; edited by **Michael P. Shawver**; music by **Marco Beltrami**.
- Production companies **Paramount Pictures**, **Platinum Dunes** and **Sunday Night Productions**; distributed by Paramount Pictures.
- Release dates: **March 8, 2020** (New York City), **May 28, 2021** (United States).
- Running time **97 minutes**; country United States; languages American Sign Language and English.
- Budget **$55-61 million**; box office **$297.5 million**.

## Lead

- A 2020 American post-apocalyptic horror film, sequel to *A Quiet Place* (2018), following the same family "as they continue to navigate a post-apocalyptic world inhabited by blind aliens with an acute sense of hearing". Emily Blunt, Millicent Simmonds, Noah Jupe and Krasinski reprise their roles; Cillian Murphy and Djimon Hounsou join.
- Paramount began developing a sequel in **April 2018**; by August Krasinski was writing; in **February 2019** he was confirmed to direct. His starting idea was making Simmonds the lead. Production ran in Western New York from **June to September 2019**.
- Budget "around $55-61 million, over three times the original's $17 million".
- World premiere in New York City **March 8, 2020**; after more than a year of pandemic postponements, released in US theaters **May 28, 2021**; on Paramount+ 45 days after the theatrical debut. It "set several box office records, including the biggest opening weekend during the course of the pandemic, and grossed $297.5 million worldwide".
- *A Quiet Place Part III*, "the third and final film following the original film's family, is scheduled to be released on July 30, 2027".

## Figures the article gives more than one way

- **Worldwide gross**: infobox and lead say **$297.5 million**; the box office section says **$297.4 million** ($160.1 million US and Canada, $137.3 million elsewhere).
- **Budget**: infobox and lead say **$55-61 million**; the Production section says the film "was produced under Paramount Pictures with a budget of $61 million".
- **Critical response**: the article says it "received mostly positive reviews from film critics", but also that "The Independent wrote that critics were divided".
- **Original release date**: the Release section says the film was "Originally set for May 15, 2020 and March 20, 2020"; the Postponement section says the studio "initially planned to release the film in theaters globally starting on March 18, 2020", with the UK and Australia on March 19 and the US and Canada on March 20.

## Plot (as summarised in the article)

- In Millbrook, New York, the Abbott family - Evelyn, Lee, deaf daughter Regan, and sons Marcus and Beau - are at a Little League game when a meteor-like object falls and hostile blind alien creatures with armoured skin, speed, strength and acute hearing begin attacking anything that makes noise.
- Over a year later, with Lee and Beau dead, Regan modifies her cochlear implant to emit the high-frequency signal that disrupts the aliens. The surviving Abbotts leave, Marcus steps in a bear trap, and they shelter in an abandoned steel foundry with Emmett, a former friend living in a soundproof bunker.
- Marcus hears "Beyond the Sea" looping on a radio station; Regan reads it as a signal from survivors on the Norwalk Islands and sets out to broadcast the high-frequency weapon from the island's radio tower. Emmett rescues her and joins the mission.
- At a marina they are ambushed by looters; Emmett draws aliens who kill the attackers, and a drowning creature reveals the aliens cannot swim. On the island, the colony's leader explains the National Guard tried evacuations by boat once the government learned this, but only two of twelve boats made it.
- An alien reaches the island on a drifting boat and kills the leader; Regan broadcasts the signal, incapacitating it, and kills it with a metal rod. Marcus hears the broadcast at the foundry, plays it on a portable radio and shoots the weakened alien. Regan leaves her implant connected to the station microphone so the signal keeps broadcasting.
- Footnotes: Lee and Beau's deaths were depicted in *A Quiet Place* (2018); the Man on the Island's name is revealed to be Henri in *A Quiet Place: Day One*.

## Cast

- Emily Blunt as Evelyn Abbott; Cillian Murphy as Emmett; Millicent Simmonds as Regan Abbott; Noah Jupe as Marcus Abbott; Djimon Hounsou as the Man on the Island; John Krasinski as Lee Abbott.
- Also Scoot McNairy (Marina Man), Alice Sophie Malyukova (Girl at Marina), Dean Woodward (Beau Abbott - played in the first film by his real-life older brother Cade Woodward), Okieriete Onaodowan (Ronnie, a police officer), Zachary Golinger (Emmett's young son), Lauren Ashley Cristiano (Emmett's deceased wife), Wayne Duvall (Roger, a grocery store owner), Barbara Singer (Woman in Store).

## Development and casting

- The first film cost **$17 million**, opened to **$50.2 million** in the US and Canada in April 2018 "well above a mid-$20 million forecast", and totalled **$188 million** domestically and **$340.9 million** worldwide. Paramount Chair and CEO Jim Gianopulos announced a sequel later that April.
- Krasinski had considered the first film "as a one-off" and initially told Paramount to find another writer and director. Scott Beck and Bryan Woods did not return; Woods said they were not interested in a franchise approach and would rather "create original ideas", and Beck said "Instead of focusing on sequels per se, it's about investing back into the ecosystem of original ideas in a massive marketplace."
- Three months after release Krasinski began brainstorming; Paramount rejected other pitches as too franchise-oriented. He said "I had this small idea, which was to make Millie [Simmonds] the lead of the movie... her character opens the door to all the themes I was dealing with in the first movie." He was writing by August 2018 and produced a draft in three and a half weeks.
- February 2019: Krasinski confirmed as director, with Blunt, Simmonds and Jupe reprising. March: Cillian Murphy joined - "For me, Emmett represents where the heart of the world lies right now, which is: finally feeling like they've all given up." June: Brian Tyree Henry added, but he left over scheduling and was replaced by Djimon Hounsou in August.
- Krasinski wrote himself in because the first film "was such a personal experience" and his "love letter" to his children: "It was really important for me to continue the metaphor and we actually start dealing with how this all started."
- Simmonds, who is deaf, said her character "has a lot of pressure to become an adult very quickly", worked with an ASL coach on clean signing and articulation, and felt "a sense of pressure" representing deaf and hard of hearing people. Syfy Wire wrote that deafness and American Sign Language "are inherently linked to the heroism of its heroine".

## Filming

- Production began June 2019; filming officially commenced **July 15**, running **47 days** through Western New York including Akron, Olcott, Dunkirk, Lackawanna and Buffalo, plus Erie County, North Tonawanda and Barcelona Harbor in Westfield, Chautauqua County.
- Stage work at Buffalo FilmWorks in South Buffalo; an abandoned Bethlehem Steel plant in Lackawanna was a location; the northbound South Grand Island Bridge was shut for 13 hours for one of the last shoots.
- Also filmed in the Hudson Valley - Dover, Pawling and New Paltz, where the Wallkill Valley Rail Trail bridge from the first film was revisited.
- The production "invested over $10 million in Upstate New York, created 400 hires, and involved 300 background actors". Production finished by late September.

## Cinematography

- Polly Morgan replaced Charlotte Bruus Christensen, continuing 35 mm film: "Although A Quiet Place 2 is a horror, it looks pretty and engaging, with a nostalgic look that you would find hard to achieve digitally."
- "Extensive dark situations" - night scenes and stage work comprising **75% of screen time** - used Kodak Vision3 500T 5219; Vision3 250D 5207 was mainly for day exteriors. Cameras were Panavision Panaflex Millennium XL2 with T-Series anamorphic lenses adjusted to match the first film's C-Series lenses. Lighting and shooting the furnace setting was among her hardest tasks.
- Krasinski "wanted to always keep the camera moving and create long 'oners' to play with rhythm and tension"; Morgan used tracking vehicles at full speed carrying jibs, cranes and Steadicam vests.

## Sound design

- Supervising sound editors **Erik Aadahl** and **Ethan Van der Ryn** and re-recording mixer **Brandon Proctor** returned. Krasinski told them to "follow the rules" set in the first film: "What we found was by doing that, and not trying to be cool, we ended up uncovering way more stuff than we ever would've been able to."
- Van der Ryn and Aadahl told Headliner Magazine: "We started hearing stories after the first film that people were afraid to eat their popcorn in the theatre!... We were able to literally make the audience hold their breath."

## Marketing

- A 30-second teaser ran before select screenings of *Black Christmas* (released December 13, 2019), went online less than a week later, and a full trailer followed on **January 1, 2020**. A 30-second Super Bowl TV spot on **February 2, 2020** revealed Krasinski had reprised his role in a newly filmed flashback.
- Early March 2020: "survival room" experiences in New York and Los Angeles, costing Paramount less than a million dollars, with 7,000-8,000 people expected. Emily Blunt promoted the film on *Jimmy Kimmel Live!* on March 10 in a parody commercial for "A Quiet Plane". A double-feature event with collector's prints had been planned for March 18, 2020.
- After the postponement, Paramount's marketing team offered *A Quiet Place Part II* virtual backgrounds for Zoom. A final trailer preceded the May 2021 release; The A.V. Club's William Hughes called it a retread whose notable element was the message that the film was the "experience that theaters are made for".

## Release and the postponements

- World premiere at Lincoln Center, New York City, **March 8, 2020**. Paramount released it in theaters **May 28, 2021**; The New York Times called it "one of the first major films to receive an exclusive theatrical release from a Hollywood studio in the not-quite-post-coronavirus era". Paramount+ followed 45 days later.
- Date chain given: originally May 15, 2020 and March 20, 2020; postponed to **September 4, 2020**; then **April 23, 2021**; then **September 17, 2021**; then moved up to **May 28, 2021**.
- Paramount had already spent around **60%** of its global prints and advertising budget, which made Deadline Hollywood call the delay "truly a shocker". The studio said on March 6 it would not reschedule, then pulled the film worldwide on March 12. Krasinski said he wanted moviegoers to see it together and that the pandemic was not the right time.
- The July 2020 move to April 2021 came with US and Canadian theaters closed nearly four months; Variety reported "Paramount did not want A Quiet Place Part 2 to stay on Labor Day weekend and have the pressure of being the first new movie out of the gate during the pandemic".
- The January 2021 move to September 2021 came amid a US infection surge, with Variety reporting "Around 65% of movie theaters remain closed". It followed delays to *No Time to Die*, *Ghostbusters: Afterlife*, *Morbius*, *Cinderella* and *The King's Man*.
- **March 4, 2021**: Krasinski announced the move up to May 28, 2021, the start of Memorial Day weekend. Boxoffice Pro: "This marks the first time post-pandemic that a theatrically exclusive major studio tentpole has moved a planned release up by this many months rather than back", and it would be "the first live-action tentpole exclusively in theaters" since *Tenet* in August 2020. The same day Universal moved *F9* from late May to June 25; Paramount pushed its own *Infinite* off May 28. Deadline said theaters reopening in New York City from the weekend of March 5, 2021 encouraged the move.
- Because the theatrical window shrank from 90 days to 45, Krasinski, Blunt and producers including Michael Bay, whose pay depends on box-office receipts, asked Paramount to compensate them.
- Paramount+ window: announced February 2021; Deadline called it "a clear sign that Paramount is committed to theatrical, but still open to the future of streaming". By contrast Warner Bros. put its 2021 slate on HBO Max day-and-date and Universal went to VOD after 17 days; Variety said "Paramount's strategy may be received the most favorably among film exhibitors" (45 days for tentpoles, 30 for other titles). Boxoffice Pro noted the first film had grossed 94% of its $188 million domestic total by day 45.
- Theatrical release in **3,752** US and Canadian theaters, plus 12 other markets on opening weekend including China "as a last-minute addition".
- Home media: digital **July 13, 2021** (also Paramount+ that day); 4K Ultra HD, Blu-ray and DVD **July 27, 2021**.

## Box office

- **$160.1 million** US and Canada, **$137.3 million** other territories, **$297.4 million** worldwide.
- Pre-pandemic forecasts: Boxoffice Pro predicted a $72 million opening; February tracking had $55-60 million. Deadline's Anthony D'Alessandro: "A Quiet Place Part II is currently strong with females under 25, African Americans and Hispanic demos, but overall I hear it's strong with all quads."
- 2021 forecasts: Boxoffice Pro $30-50 million opening and $75-125 million total; IndieWire predicted $40-50 million, citing "a core male audience that skews younger with minority moviegoers". Fandango said US advance sales were double those for the planned March 2020 date and higher than the first film's in 2018.
- Actual: **$19.3 million** first day including **$4.8 million** Thursday previews (above the first film's $4.3 million; both pandemic highs); **$48.0 million** three-day opening and **$57.5 million** over the four-day Memorial Day frame, topping the box office and the biggest opening weekend since *Sonic the Hedgehog* in February 2020. Second weekend $19.5 million, second behind *The Conjuring: The Devil Made Me Do It*. Crossed **$100 million** domestic on **June 11**, the first film of the pandemic era to do so, and retook first place in its third weekend with $12 million, beating newcomer *In the Heights*.

## Critical response

- Rotten Tomatoes: **91%** of 366 critics' reviews positive, average 7.5/10; consensus "A nerve-wracking continuation of its predecessor, A Quiet Place Part II expands the terrifying world of the franchise without losing track of its heart." Metacritic **71 out of 100** from 57 critics ("generally favorable"). CinemaScore **A-**, up from the first film's B+. PostTrak: 83% positive, 63% "definitely recommend".
- Peter Bradshaw (The Guardian), 4/5: "a really effective and engrossing followup, with an absolutely sensational 'prelude' sequence at the top of the movie", while noting borrowings from *Alien*, *Jurassic Park* and *Jaws*; he called Simmonds "an excellent performer: bold, confident and forthright".
- Jeannette Catsoulis (The New York Times), positive: the film "has also largely replaced the hushed horror of the original with full-on action. Faster, coarser and far noisier, Part II sacrifices emotional depth for thriller setups", and "remains hobbled by a script that resolves two separate crises while leaving the movie itself in limbo".
- Justin Chang (NPR): "an unexpectedly resonant film for the present moment as this country slowly emerges from a crisis", praising Krasinski as "a ruthlessly efficient visual storyteller" and comparing him to Hitchcock.
- Bloody Disgusting 3.5/5, "a satisfying, worthwhile sequel"; The A.V. Club B-, "a part two in the classic, traditional sense, echoing without quite amplifying the pleasures of its predecessor"; io9 called it "a quintessential great sequel"; Nick Allen (RogerEbert.com) 3/4, faulting Krasinski for not taking risks but praising "incredibly robust and kinetic" action. The film ranks on Rotten Tomatoes' Best Horror Movies of 2021.

## Accolades

- Hollywood Critics Association Midseason Awards (July 1, 2021): **Best Actress - Millicent Simmonds (won)**; **Best Supporting Actor - Cillian Murphy (won)**; nominations for Best Picture, Best Supporting Actress (Emily Blunt), Best Filmmaker and Best Screenplay (John Krasinski).
- People's Choice Awards (December 7, 2021): nominated Best Drama Movie of 2021 and Best Drama Actress (Emily Blunt).
- British Academy Film Awards (March 13, 2022): nominated Best Sound - Erik Aadahl, Michael Barosky, Brandon Procter, Ethan Van der Ryn.
- Critics' Choice Super Awards (March 17, 2022): **Best Horror Movie (won)**; nominated Best Actor in a Horror Movie (Murphy) and Best Actress in a Horror Movie (Simmonds).
- MTV Movie & TV Awards (June 5, 2022): nominated Most Frightened Performance (Simmonds). Saturn Awards (October 25, 2022): nominated Best Horror Film, Best Actress in a Film (Blunt), Best Performance by a Younger Actor (Noah Jupe and Millicent Simmonds).
- The series received the Seal of Authentic Representation from the Ruderman Family Foundation for Simmonds's portrayal of Regan as an actor with a disability with at least five lines of dialogue; Krasinski received an Excellence in Directing prize from The Media Access Awards for disability inclusion.

## Sequel

- May 2021: Blunt revealed Krasinski had plans for a third film and that it was intended to be a trilogy, after seeing how the second was received. July 2021: she confirmed he was working on a third instalment, separate from the spin-off *A Quiet Place: Day One*, again intending to direct.
- **October 2025**: Paramount Pictures announced *A Quiet Place Part III* for **July 30, 2027**.

wikis.title: Filming in Western New York and the Hudson Valley

- Production began June 2019; filming officially commenced **July 15, 2019** and ran **47 days**.

wikis.title: Look and sound of the film

- Polly Morgan replaced Charlotte Bruus Christensen as cinematographer and kept the first film's 35 mm film: "Although A Quiet Place 2 is a horror, it looks pretty and engaging, with a nostalgic look that you would find hard to achieve digitally."
- Night scenes and stage work made up **75% of screen time** and used Kodak Vision3 500T 5219; Vision3 250D 5207 was used mainly for day exteriors.

- Sound: supervising sound editors Erik Aadahl and Ethan Van der Ryn and re-recording mixer Brandon Proctor returned. Krasinski told them to "follow the rules" of the first film - "by doing that, and not trying to be cool, we ended up uncovering way more stuff".

wikis.title: A year of COVID-19 postponements, then a move up
wikis.summary: The film's release-date chain from March 2020 to May 2021, and the 45-day Paramount+ window.
wikis.body:
- World premiere at Lincoln Center, New York City, **March 8, 2020**.
- Planned global theatrical release **March 18, 2020**, with the UK and Australia on March 19 and the US and Canada, including Dolby Cinema and IMAX, on March 20. The Release section separately says the film had been "Originally set for May 15, 2020 and March 20, 2020".
- Paramount said on **March 6** it would not reschedule; on **March 12** it pulled the film worldwide. About **60%** of the global prints and advertising budget had already been spent, which Deadline Hollywood called "truly a shocker". Krasinski said he wanted moviegoers to see the film together and the pandemic was not the right time.
- **April 2020**: rescheduled to **September 4, 2020**, Labor Day weekend - which Deadline called "typically the deadest period ever for moviegoing".
- **July 2020**: moved to **April 23, 2021**, with US and Canadian theaters closed nearly four months; Variety said Paramount "did not want A Quiet Place Part 2... [to] have the pressure of being the first new movie out of the gate during the pandemic".
- **January 2021**: moved to **September 17, 2021** amid a US infection surge, with Variety reporting "Around 65% of movie theaters remain closed".
- **March 4, 2021**: Krasinski announced a move up to **May 28, 2021**, Memorial Day weekend - per Boxoffice Pro "the first time post-pandemic that a theatrically exclusive major studio tentpole has moved a planned release up by this many months rather than back", and "the first live-action tentpole exclusively in theaters" since *Tenet*. Universal moved *F9* to June 25 the same day and Paramount shifted its own *Infinite* off the date.
- Streaming: announced February 2021, Paramount+ 45 days after theaters - against Warner Bros.' day-and-date HBO Max slate and Universal's 17-day VOD window. Because the window shrank from 90 to 45 days, Krasinski, Blunt and producers including Michael Bay asked to be compensated.
- Opened in **3,752** US and Canadian theaters plus 12 other markets, China added at the last minute. Digital and Paramount+ July 13, 2021; disc July 27, 2021.

wikis.title: Box office records of the pandemic era
wikis.summary: Forecasts, the opening weekend figures and the domestic $100 million milestone.
wikis.body:
- Final totals: **$160.1 million** US and Canada, **$137.3 million** elsewhere, **$297.4 million** worldwide (infobox: $297.5 million).
- Forecasts before the 2020 postponement: Boxoffice Pro $72 million opening; February tracking $55-60 million; Deadline's Anthony D'Alessandro said it was "strong with females under 25, African Americans and Hispanic demos, but overall... strong with all quads".
- Forecasts for 2021: Boxoffice Pro $30-50 million opening, $75-125 million total; IndieWire $40-50 million. Fandango reported US advance sales double those for the March 2020 date and higher than the first film's.
- Opening: **$19.3 million** first day, including **$4.8 million** in Thursday previews - both the highest of the pandemic, beating the first film's $4.3 million preview. **$48.0 million** three-day weekend, **$57.5 million** over the four-day Memorial Day frame, number one and the biggest opening weekend since *Sonic the Hedgehog* in February 2020.
- Second weekend $19.5 million, second to *The Conjuring: The Devil Made Me Do It*. Crossed **$100 million** domestically on **June 11**, the first pandemic-era film to do so. Third weekend $12 million, back at number one ahead of *In the Heights*.

wikis.title: Reviews and awards
wikis.summary: Aggregate scores, what critics singled out, and the film's wins and nominations.
wikis.body:
- Rotten Tomatoes **91%** from 366 reviews (7.5/10), consensus: "A nerve-wracking continuation of its predecessor, A Quiet Place Part II expands the terrifying world of the franchise without losing track of its heart." Metacritic **71/100** from 57 critics. CinemaScore **A-** (up from the first film's B+); PostTrak 83% positive, 63% definite recommend.
- The article says reviews were "mostly positive" and that Screen Rant credited the "two-pronged story" and Murphy's character, while noting The Independent wrote that critics were divided.
- Peter Bradshaw (The Guardian) 4/5 praised "an absolutely sensational 'prelude' sequence" and Simmonds as "bold, confident and forthright", while noting borrowings from *Alien*, *Jurassic Park* and *Jaws*.
- Jeannette Catsoulis (The New York Times) called it "wonderfully acted and intuitively directed" but "Faster, coarser and far noisier", sacrificing "emotional depth for thriller setups" and "hobbled by a script that resolves two separate crises while leaving the movie itself in limbo".
- Justin Chang (NPR) called it "unexpectedly resonant... as this country slowly emerges from a crisis" and Krasinski "a ruthlessly efficient visual storyteller". Bloody Disgusting 3.5/5; The A.V. Club B-; io9 "a quintessential great sequel"; RogerEbert.com 3/4.
- Wins: Hollywood Critics Association Midseason Awards Best Actress (Millicent Simmonds) and Best Supporting Actor (Cillian Murphy), July 1, 2021; Critics' Choice Super Award for Best Horror Movie, March 17, 2022.
- Nominations: HCA Best Picture, Best Supporting Actress (Blunt), Best Filmmaker and Best Screenplay (Krasinski); People's Choice Best Drama Movie and Best Drama Actress; BAFTA Best Sound (Erik Aadahl, Michael Barosky, Brandon Procter, Ethan Van der Ryn); Critics' Choice Super Awards acting categories; MTV Most Frightened Performance (Simmonds); Saturn Awards Best Horror Film, Best Actress (Blunt) and Best Performance by a Younger Actor (Jupe, Simmonds).
- The series received the Ruderman Family Foundation's Seal of Authentic Representation for Simmonds's Regan; Krasinski received an Excellence in Directing prize from The Media Access Awards for disability inclusion.

wikis.title: A Quiet Place: Day One (2024 film)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the 2024 prequel film A Quiet Place: Day One, covering its cast, production, release, box office, critical reception and awards.
wikis.body:
## Overview

- "A Quiet Place: Day One is a 2024 American apocalyptic horror film, written and directed by Michael Sarnoski, based on a story he conceived with John Krasinski. It is the third installment in the A Quiet Place film series, and a prequel spinoff of the first film."
- It stars Lupita Nyong'o "as a terminally ill woman during the early stages of an invasion in New York City by blind extraterrestrial creatures with an acute sense of hearing", with Joseph Quinn and Djimon Hounsou, "who reprises his role from A Quiet Place Part II".

## Infobox

- Directed by Michael Sarnoski; screenplay by Michael Sarnoski; story by John Krasinski and Michael Sarnoski; based on A Quiet Place by Bryan Woods and Scott Beck.
- Produced by Michael Bay, Andrew Form, Brad Fuller. Starring Lupita Nyong'o, Joseph Quinn, Djimon Hounsou. Cinematography Pat Scola. Edited by Gregory Plotkin and Andrew Mondshein. Music by Alexis Grapsas.
- Production companies Paramount Pictures, Platinum Dunes, Sunday Night Productions; distributed by Paramount Pictures.
- Release dates: June 26, 2024 (Tribeca); June 28, 2024 (United States). Running time 99 minutes. Country United States. Language English. Budget $67 million. Box office $261.8 million.

## Plot (as summarised by the article)

Sam, a terminally ill cancer patient living in a hospice outside New York City with her cat Frodo, is taken by the nurse Reuben to a marionette show in Manhattan when meteor-like objects fall and alien creatures attack. Survivors shelter in the puppet theatre with Henri; military helicopters warn civilians to stay silent, and fighter jets destroy the bridges off Manhattan. Reuben is killed when the building's generator activates. Sam heads for Harlem while the military prepares a boat evacuation from the South Street Seaport, "as the creatures are unable to swim"; she is separated from Frodo in a stampede. Eric, an English law student, finds Frodo and joins her. They shelter in a ruined church; Eric fetches medication and sees "a group of creatures led by a larger one feeding on the remains of an organic egg-like pod". Sam wants to revisit the Harlem jazz club where her late father played and to eat pizza at Patsy's; Patsy's has been destroyed, so Eric collects pizza elsewhere. Sam gives Eric her sweater and Frodo and distracts the creatures with car alarms; Eric and Frodo swim to the boat, where Henri has also arrived, and Eric finds Sam's note asking him to care for Frodo. Sam listens to Nina Simone's "Feeling Good", then unplugs her headphones and lets the music play as a creature appears behind her.

## Cast

- Lupita Nyong'o as Samira ("Sam"), a cancer patient
- Joseph Quinn as Eric, a British law student that Sam befriends
- Alex Wolff as Reuben, a nurse at the hospice
- Djimon Hounsou as Henri, "Originally credited as \"Man on the Island\" in A Quiet Place Part II"
- Eliane Umuhire as Zena; Ronnie Le Drew as Puppeteer

## Development

- "In November 2020, Paramount Pictures announced a spinoff film set within the same world as A Quiet Place (2018), with Jeff Nichols set to write and direct, based on a story by John Krasinski." In May 2021 Krasinski said Nichols' completed script had gone to the studio; by October 2021 Nichols dropped out "to focus on a different project at Paramount", and in January 2022 Sarnoski replaced him, having been approached after his debut feature Pig (2021).
- Co-production between Platinum Dunes and Sunday Night Productions, with Bay, Form, Fuller and Krasinski producing. Sarnoski cited Children of Men (2006) as an inspiration for the look.
- Nyong'o and Quinn joined in November 2022. Nyong'o asked to change the cat because of a fear of cats, "which she overcame with exposure therapy; by the end of production, she adopted a cat of her own." Paramount executives wanted a computer-generated Frodo; Sarnoski insisted on a real cat. "Frodo was played by two cats named Nico and Schnitzel." Scripted hissing and back-arching were cut because handlers could not train it and the production avoided CGI.
- Sam and Frodo are named after Samwise Gamgee and Frodo Baggins. Alex Wolff was cast in January 2023; Hounsou's Part II character is revealed as "Henri"; Denis O'Hare was cast but cut from the final film.

## Filming

- "Principal photography took place from February 6 to April 11, 2023, in London, though the film is set in New York City."
- Production designer Simon Bowles; cinematographer Pat Scola. The Warner Bros. Studios, Leavesden backlot "was used to recreate four NYC blocks, each two stories high, including Mott Street in Chinatown and parts of Harlem, the Lower East Side, and the Upper East Side." Patsy's Pizzeria's exterior was recreated from the production's photography of the real restaurant.
- Loetta's Jazz Club interiors were shot at the George Tavern in Stepney; subway interiors at London Charing Cross with exteriors at Canary Wharf tube station; the office lobby chase at One Canada Square; the cathedral scene at St. Sophia's Greek Orthodox Cathedral of Divine Wisdom. Bowles built SketchUp 3D models of the sets.
- Industrial Light & Magic completed the visual effects. Budget $67 million. Alexis Grapsas composed the score in post-production.

## Release

- World premiere at the Tribeca Festival on June 26, 2024, "as a special presentation taking place after the festival itself, which was held from June 5–16"; US release June 28, 2024.
- "It was previously scheduled to be released on March 31, 2023, then on September 22, 2023, and on March 8, 2024."
- Digital download July 30, 2024; DVD, Blu-ray and Ultra HD Blu-ray October 8, 2024.

## Box office

- "$138.9 million in the United States and Canada, and $122.9 million in other territories, for a worldwide total of $261.8 million." Deadline Hollywood calculated net profit as $83.6 million.
- Released alongside Horizon: An American Saga – Chapter 1; projected $40–50 million from 3,707 theaters. It made $22.5 million on day one including $6.8 million in Thursday previews ("the best of the series"), then opened to $52.2 million, the franchise's best opening weekend, second behind Inside Out 2.
- Deadline's Anthony D'Alessandro credited heat waves, walk-up business (66% bought tickets the day of the screening) and diverse turnout (32% Hispanic and Latino, against the first film's 28%). "IMAX and Premium Large Formats (PLFs) accounted for 39% of the earnings, with IMAX specifically earning 11% of the weekend take."
- Second weekend $20.6 million (third place); third weekend $11.4 million (fourth).
- Internationally "$45.5 million from 59 overseas markets, a 4% increase over the opening weekend of Part II", biggest markets China ($9.8 million), Mexico ($4.7 million), the UK ($3.9 million), Australia ($2.6 million), South Korea ($2.5 million).

## Critical response

- Rotten Tomatoes: "86% of 281 critics' reviews are positive, with an average rating of 7.1/10", consensus: "Grounded in raw humanity by Lupita Nyong'o and Joseph Quinn, this sideways entry into A Quiet Place finds fresh notes of fright to play amongst the silence."
- Metacritic: 68 out of 100 from 53 critics, "generally favorable". CinemaScore "B+" (same as the first film); PostTrak 79% overall positive, 59% definite recommend.
- Entertainment Weekly gave it a B+. RogerEbert.com, two and a half stars: "There are enough interesting ideas and at least two confident performances holding A Quiet Place: Day One together, even if it sometimes feels like a first draft of a richer, more complex final film." Peter Bradshaw (The Guardian), three of five: "It's an efficient, if familiar, spectacle of suspense." Variety's Peter Debruge criticised that most of the film was "tiptoeing through a mostly off-screen apocalypse".

## Accolades (as tabled)

- Astra Film Awards, December 8, 2024 — Best Performance in a Horror or Thriller — nominated.
- Astra Creative Arts Awards — Best Sound.
- Astra Midseason Movie Awards, July 3, 2024 — Best Horror — won.
- Fangoria Chainsaw Awards, October 13, 2024 — Best Lead Performance.
- Hollywood Music in Media Awards, November 20, 2024 — Best Original Score – Horror/Thriller Film — Alexis Grapsas.
- Las Vegas Film Critics Society, December 14, 2024 — Best Animal Performance — Frodo the Cat.
- NAACP Image Awards, February 22, 2025 — Outstanding Actress in a Motion Picture.
- Saturn Awards, February 2, 2025 — Best Horror Film; Best Actress in a Film.

wikis.title: Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Mutant Mayhem
wikis.summary: Wikipedia's article on the 2023 animated reboot Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Mutant Mayhem, covering its credits, plot, voice cast, production and animation, release, box office, reviews, awards and the sequel, short, series and game that followed.
wikis.body:
## The film

- "Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Mutant Mayhem is a 2023 American animated superhero comedy film directed by Jeff Rowe", co-written with Seth Rogen, Evan Goldberg, Dan Hernandez and Benji Samit, and "a reboot of the related film series". Story by Brendan O'Brien, Rogen, Goldberg and Rowe; based on the characters by Peter Laird and Kevin Eastman.
- Produced by Rogen, Goldberg and James Weaver through Point Grey Pictures, with Paramount Pictures and Nickelodeon Movies; distributed by Paramount Pictures.
- Voices: Nicolas Cantu, Brady Noon, Micah Abbey and Shamon Brown Jr. as the Turtles, with Jackie Chan (Splinter), Ayo Edebiri (April O'Neil), Ice Cube (Superfly), Giancarlo Esposito, Rogen, John Cena, Paul Rudd, Post Malone, Rose Byrne, Natasia Demetriou, Hannibal Buress and Maya Rudolph. "Mutant Mayhem marks the first time all four Turtles are portrayed by teenage actors."
- Score by Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross, with classic East Coast hip-hop songs. Cinematography Kent Seki; editing Greg Levitan. Running time 99 minutes.
- Budget $70 million; box office $182 million ($118 million in the United States and Canada, $63.2 million elsewhere).

## Dates

- Work-in-progress screening at the Annecy International Animation Film Festival on June 12, 2023, followed by a six-minute standing ovation.
- United States theatrical release August 2, 2023; United Kingdom July 31, 2023. The date moved from an original August 11, 2023 to August 4 and then two days earlier again.
- Digital download September 1, 2023; Paramount+ from September 19; disc release December 12, 2023.
- Follow-ups: sequel greenlit July 2023 and now set for August 13, 2027 (after October 9, 2026 and September 17, 2027); the short Chrome Alone 2 - Lost in New Jersey released December 19, 2025; the series Tales of the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles on Paramount+ from August 9, 2024, concluding December 2025 after cancellation; the game Mutants Unleashed released October 18, 2024.

## Production

The reboot was pushed by Brian Robbins after the 2014 and 2016 films, with Playmates Toys advising an animated film; Rogen was brought in during 2018 and Rowe soon after, and the project was reported in June 2020. Rowe aimed at "the ultimate teenage coming-of-age film", citing Stand by Me and Lady Bird. Shredder was written out as the villain in favour of Superfly, and in July 2022 Rogen told Rowe the film was "fundamentally broken", leading to a complete rewrite over four months. The cast, revealed at the Nickelodeon Kids' Choice Awards on March 4, 2023, recorded together in groups with heavy improvisation. Animation was by Mikros Animation and Cinesite in a sketchbook style Rowe called the film's "North Star", built on a custom Arnold-based shader with scribbles and cross-hatching.

## Reception

Rotten Tomatoes 95% of 251 reviews positive (average 7.6/10); Metacritic 74 from 47 critics; CinemaScore "A"; PostTrak 88% positive. The opening weekend took $28 million ($43 million over five days), fourth behind Barbie, Meg 2: The Trench and Oppenheimer; The Hollywood Reporter reported the SAG-AFTRA strike may have cost about 15% of earnings. In China it made $310,000 in its opening weekend. Deadline calculated a net profit of $204.5 million, fourth on its 2023 "Most Valuable Blockbusters" list. The film was nominated for Best Animated Feature at the Critics' Choice Awards (January 14, 2024), Annie Awards (February 17, 2024, five nominations) and Producers Guild of America Awards (February 25, 2024), among many critics' awards; it won the Heartland Film Festival's Truly Moving Picture Award in 2023.

## Rest of the page

The later parts of the capture are raw wikitext section comments, the numbered reference list, external links, the Turtles and studio navigation templates, and the page's portals and categories.

wikis.title: Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Mutant Mayhem - film article (plot through accolades and follow-ups)
wikis.summary: Part 1 of Wikipedia's article on the 2023 animated film Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Mutant Mayhem, with the infobox, plot, voice cast, production, music, themes, release, box office, critical response, the full accolades table and the announced sequel, short film, TV series and video game.
wikis.body:
## Infobox

- Directed by Jeff Rowe. Screenplay by Seth Rogen, Evan Goldberg, Jeff Rowe, Dan Hernandez and Benji Samit; story by Brendan O'Brien, Rogen, Goldberg and Rowe.
- Based on Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles characters by Peter Laird and Kevin Eastman.
- Produced by Seth Rogen, Evan Goldberg and James Weaver.
- Starring Nicolas Cantu, Brady Noon, Micah Abbey, Shamon Brown Jr., Jackie Chan, Ayo Edebiri, Ice Cube, Giancarlo Esposito, Seth Rogen, John Cena, Paul Rudd, Post Malone, Rose Byrne, Natasia Demetriou, Hannibal Buress and Maya Rudolph.
- Cinematography Kent Seki; edited by Greg Levitan; music by Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross.
- Production companies Paramount Pictures, Nickelodeon Movies and Point Grey Pictures; distributed by Paramount Pictures.
- Release dates: June 12, 2023 (Annecy) and August 2, 2023 (United States). Running time 99 minutes. Country United States, language English.
- Budget $70 million. Box office $182 million.

## Lead

"Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Mutant Mayhem is a 2023 American animated superhero comedy film directed by Jeff Rowe"; it is "a reboot of the related film series". Plans for an animated Turtles film with Rogen began in 2018; the film was announced in June 2020. Animation was by Mikros Animation and Cinesite. After a work-in-progress screening at Annecy on June 12, 2023 it was released by Paramount in the United States on August 2. It "was a box office success, grossing $182 million worldwide against its $70 million budget", and its nominations include Best Animated Feature at the 29th Critics' Choice Awards, 51st Annie Awards and 35th Producers Guild of America Awards. "A sequel is set for August 13, 2027. A follow-up television series, Tales of the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles, debuted on Paramount+ in August 2024, and ran for two seasons before concluding in December 2025."

## Plot

TCRI executive Cynthia Utrom sends a squad after rogue scientist Baxter Stockman, who has created a mutagenic ooze; Baxter is killed in an explosion and the mutagen falls into New York City's sewers, mutating four turtle brothers - Leonardo, Raphael, Donatello and Michelangelo - and the rat Splinter, who adopts and trains them in ninjutsu. Fifteen years later they meet teenage aspiring journalist April O'Neil while recovering her stolen moped, and set out to stop the thief "Superfly", who proves to be a mutant fly leading a mutant gang living on an abandoned ship in Staten Island and planning to mutate every animal on Earth. After the Turtles are captured and rescued, the gang turns on Superfly, who becomes a whale-like kaiju; the Turtles use TCRI retro-mutagen to revert him. The Turtles enroll at April's high school, while Cynthia, holding the unmutated Superfly, plans to recapture them with the aid of "the mysterious Shredder".

## Voice cast

Nicolas Cantu as Leonardo (two katana, romantic interest in April); Brady Noon as Raphael (sai, "fight first, ask questions later"); Micah Abbey as Donatello (bo staff, likes anime and video games); Shamon Brown Jr. as Michelangelo (nunchucks, wants to be a stand-up comedian); Jackie Chan as Splinter; Ayo Edebiri as April O'Neil; Ice Cube as Superfly; Giancarlo Esposito as Baxter Stockman; Seth Rogen as Bebop; John Cena as Rocksteady; Paul Rudd as Mondo Gecko; Post Malone as Ray Fillet; Rose Byrne as Leatherhead; Natasia Demetriou as Wingnut; Hannibal Buress as Genghis Frog; Maya Rudolph as Cynthia Utrom; MrBeast as a Times Square bystander; Kevin Eastman as a human who assists Splinter; Alex Hirsch as Scumbug; Bobby Wagner as "Man Who Thought a Giant Rat Was a Big Cat But It Was Actually a Rat".

## Development

Brian Robbins felt the film series needed a reboot after the 2014 film and Out of the Shadows (2016); Playmates Toys advised that it be animated. In 2018 Robbins discussed the project with Nickelodeon Animation Studio's Ramsay Naito; Rogen was chosen and Rowe joined soon after. In June 2020 Deadline Hollywood reported Nickelodeon Animation was developing a CG-animated Turtles film for Paramount, with Rowe directing from a screenplay by Brendan O'Brien and Point Grey producing. Rogen told Collider in August 2020 that "the 'Teenage' part of Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles was always the part that stuck out to me the most". Rogen posted a teaser image in June 2021; by October 2021 the working title was Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: The Next Chapter; the final title was set by August 2022. Kyler Spears joined as co-director; J.J. Villard designed the logo. "Overall, the budget was $70 million at minimum."

## Writing

Rowe compared the film to Stand by Me (1986) and Lady Bird (2017), aiming at "the ultimate teenage coming-of-age film". Shredder was originally the main villain but was written out; Superfly was originally going to be a mutated Baxter Stockman. An early draft was more of a high school film. In July 2022 Rogen texted Rowe that the film was "fundamentally broken"; "in the next four months, the film was completely rewritten and boarded into its final state".

## Casting and voice recording

The Turtles' voice cast was revealed at the Nickelodeon Kids' Choice Awards on March 4, 2023, along with the other cast members. It "marks the first time all four Turtles are portrayed by teenage actors". Hundreds auditioned; Rowe narrowed the field to ten before a chemistry table read. Rowe wrote a letter to Jackie Chan; Ice Cube signed on after hearing the name Superfly. Kevin Eastman's cameo is credited as "Good Human", cast as an homage to Stan Lee's Marvel cameos. Unusually for animation, the cast recorded in groups, with up to seven actors in a session and a lot of improvisation, an approach Rogen drew from recording The Lion King (2019).

## Design, animation and cinematography

Rowe wanted the film to resemble concept art and his teenage school-notebook sketches, calling the sketch look the film's "North Star". Production designer Yashar Kassai cited the 1987 television series and the classic toyline, plus Wong Kar-wai films such as Chungking Express (1994) and the street photography of Alex Webb. Lead character designer Woodrow White gave the Turtles teenage builds, Splinter a kataginu cut from a bathrobe and sweatpants, with Jeff Bridges's Dude and Danny DeVito as references and Jackie Chan's Police Story (1985) and Rumble in the Bronx (1995) for his fighting style. Animation was by Mikros Animation (Montreal and Paris), hired in 2022 for the bulk of the work, and Cinesite (Vancouver and Montreal), which produced nearly 25 minutes. Mikros's test shot was 40 seconds of Donatello talking; visual effects supervisor Matthieu Rouxel quoted Rowe: "If the picture looks like a 2D painting when it is not moving, that means we are good". Mikros built a shader from the Autodesk Arnold toonshader with developer Marcel Reinhard, adding scribbles, cross-hatching, stepping and colour transitions. Cinesite brought in five traditional 2D effects animators and Toon Boom Animation software. Head of cinematography Kent Seki used a cinema verite handheld style influenced by Emmanuel Lubezki and Spike Jonze, contrasted with camera language influenced by early Paul Thomas Anderson and Robert Elswit's Boogie Nights (1997).

## Music and themes

The score by Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross, with Gabe Hilfer as music supervisor, was announced in May 2023; the score album was released by Reznor's label The Null Corporation on July 28, 2023. The film features classic East Coast hip-hop, with an official Spotify playlist. Goldberg described the film as about a father, his four sons and the importance of family; acceptance is a major theme, and Rowe said the parallel with a first-generation parent "wasn't the intention, but it became highlighted through execution."

## Release

- Work-in-progress screening at the Annecy International Animation Film Festival on June 12, 2023; TheWrap said the cut had "just a few scenes of rough animation but was otherwise complete". It received a six-minute standing ovation.
- A screening at the Paramount lot in Los Angeles on July 29, 2023 was billed as a "special family screening"; The Hollywood Reporter described it as essentially a premiere that the cast could not attend because of the SAG-AFTRA strike.
- Theatrical release in the United States on August 2, 2023, in formats including Dolby Cinema, 4DX and RealD 3D. "It was originally scheduled for release on August 11, 2023, but was later pushed a week forward to August 4, 2023 before being pushed forward again by two days to its final date." In the United Kingdom it was released on July 31, 2023.
- Marketing: over 400 licensees; Deadline Hollywood estimated the promotional partner campaign was worth $100 million and drew over 3 billion impressions. A teaser trailer came out March 6, 2023 set to A Tribe Called Quest's "Can I Kick It?"; extended footage at CinemaCon on April 27, 2023; the full trailer on May 31, 2023; a Mutant Mayhem Experience ran July 23 to August 1, 2023 in New York City and Los Angeles.
- Home media: digital download September 1, 2023; Paramount+ streaming from September 19; Ultra HD Blu-ray, Blu-ray and DVD on December 12, 2023, with three behind-the-scenes featurettes and a tutorial on drawing Leonardo.

## Box office

"$118 million in the United States and Canada, and $63.2 million in other territories, for a worldwide total of $182 million." Deadline Hollywood calculated the film's net profit as $204.5 million across box office, merchandise, television, streaming and home media, placing it fourth on its 2023 "Most Valuable Blockbusters" list. It was projected at around $30 million from 3,851 theaters over a five-day opening; it made $10.2 million on day one (including $3.85 million from Tuesday previews), $28 million in the opening weekend and $43 million over five days, finishing fourth behind Barbie, Meg 2: The Trench and Oppenheimer. Second and third weekends: $15.7 million and $8.4 million. The Hollywood Reporter said the SAG-AFTRA strike potentially cut earnings by 15%, with insiders speculating a $7-10 million setback. In China it made $310,000 over its three-day opening weekend, ninth place.

## Critical response

Rotten Tomatoes: "95% of 251 critics' reviews are positive, with an average rating of 7.6/10", consensus quoted in full on the page. Metacritic: 74 out of 100 from 47 critics, "generally favorable". CinemaScore "A"; PostTrak 88% positive with 70% definite recommendations. Positive notices from Justin Chang (Los Angeles Times), Tom Jorgensen (IGN, 8/10), Charlotte O'Sullivan (Evening Standard, 4/5), John Nugent (Empire, 4/5), Rafael Motomayor (/Film, 9/10), Liz Miller (Consequence, A-) and Pete Hammond (Deadline). More critical: Brian Tallerico (RogerEbert.com, 2.5/4), Peter Debruge (Variety) and Nick Schager (The Daily Beast).

## Accolades table

The page tabulates awards with ceremony dates, including: Heartland Film Festival 2023 Truly Moving Picture Award (Won); Hollywood Professional Association Awards, November 28, 2023, Outstanding Color Grading - Animated Theatrical Feature, Mitch Paulson (Company 3), Nominated; Boston Society of Film Critics, December 10, 2023, runner-up for Best Animated Film; nominations at the Washington D.C. Area (December 10, 2023), Chicago (December 12, 2023), St. Louis (December 17, 2023), Florida (December 21, 2023), Georgia (January 5, 2024), Seattle (January 8, 2024), Austin (January 10, 2024) and Houston (January 22, 2024) critics' awards; AWFJ EDA Awards January 3, 2024 (Best Animated Film; Best Animated Female, Ayo Edebiri); Astra Film and Creative Arts Awards January 6, 2024; Critics' Choice Movie Awards January 14, 2024 (Best Animated Feature); Black Reel Awards January 16, 2024 (Outstanding Voice Performance, Edebiri); Kansas City Film Critics Circle January 27, 2024 (runner-up); London Film Critics' Circle and Saturn Awards February 4, 2024; ADG Awards February 10, 2024 (Yashar Kassai); Annie Awards February 17, 2024 (five nominations including Best Animated Feature, directing for Jeff Rowe and Kyler Spears, writing, music for Reznor and Ross, production design and editorial); Visual Effects Society Awards February 21, 2024 (four nominations, including Superfly and Midtown Manhattan); Producers Guild of America Awards February 25, 2024; Cinema Audio Society Awards March 2, 2024; ACE Eddie Awards and Satellite Awards March 3, 2024; Artios Awards March 7, 2024; ICG Publicists Awards March 8, 2024; NAACP Image Awards March 16, 2024; Critics' Choice Super Awards April 4, 2024 (Best Superhero Movie; Best Actress in a Superhero Movie, Edebiri); Nickelodeon Kids' Choice Awards July 13, 2024 (Favorite Animated Movie; Favorite Male Voice, Brady Noon and Jackie Chan; Favorite Female Voice, Edebiri). All entries are "Nominated" except the Heartland win and the two runner-up placements.

## Future

- Sequel: greenlit in July 2023, a month before release, with Shredder as the main antagonist; Rowe returning as director with co-directors Spears and Kassai, Point Grey co-producing with Rogen, Goldberg, Weaver, Josh Fagen and Ramsay McBean. "The film was originally set to release in theaters on October 9, 2026, but it was later pushed back to September 17, 2027, before being moved up to August 13, 2027." In December 2025 Rogen and Point Grey were in discussions with Paramount Skydance about a third film.
- Short film: Chrome Alone 2 - Lost in New Jersey, reported in May 2025 for an Annecy debut in June 2025, directed by Kent Seki and written by Andrew Joustra; released in theaters on December 19, 2025 with The SpongeBob Movie: Search for SquarePants.
- Television series: Tales of the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles, announced with the sequel in July 2023 as a two-season 2D animated Paramount+ series bridging the film and its sequel, with Christopher Yost and Alan Wan as executive producer and showrunner; it "debuted on Paramount+ on August 9, 2024, and concluded in December 12, 2025 after being cancelled."
- Video game: Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Mutants Unleashed, a 3D beat 'em up platformer by A Heartful of Games, published by Outright Games, released October 18, 2024 for Nintendo Switch, PlayStation 4 and 5, Xbox One, Xbox Series X/S and Microsoft Windows.
