wikis.title: Untitled Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Mutant Mayhem sequel
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the upcoming sequel to Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Mutant Mayhem - its premise, returning voice cast, development and animation troubles, marketing changes and its August 13, 2027 release date.
wikis.body:
## Overview
- "The untitled Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Mutant Mayhem sequel is an upcoming American animated superhero film directed by Jeff Rowe", based on the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles characters by Peter Laird and Kevin Eastman.
- Sequel to Mutant Mayhem (2023). Produced by Seth Rogen, Evan Goldberg, James Weaver, Josh Fagen and Ramsay McBean; production companies Nickelodeon Movies and Point Grey Pictures; distributed by Paramount Pictures. Cinematography by Kent Seki.
- Infobox release date: August 13, 2027. Country United States, language English.
- Premise: "The Turtles face off against a new and deadly foe: the Shredder."
- Mikros Animation returns to provide animation; Rowe sought "a villain-forward film".

## Voice cast
- Micah Abbey as Donatello, "the tech guru of the Turtles who uses a bo staff", with a liking for anime and video games.
- Shamon Brown Jr. as Michelangelo, the jokester who uses nunchucks and wants to be a stand-up comedian.
- Nicolas Cantu as Leonardo, the leader who uses two katana and has a romantic interest in April O'Neil.
- Brady Noon as Raphael, the muscle who uses a pair of sai, with a "fight first, ask questions later" attitude.

## Development
- June 2022: then-Paramount CEO Brian Robbins said there were plans for multiple feature follow-ups to the then-upcoming Mutant Mayhem.
- July 2023: Rowe expressed interest in returning for a sequel featuring the Shredder; later that month Variety reported a sequel film and the Paramount+ animated series Tales of the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles had been greenlit, with Rowe returning to direct and the Point Grey producers returning alongside Ramsay McBean, who had been an executive producer on Mutant Mayhem.
- April 2024: Kyler Spears and Yashar Kassai - Mutant Mayhem's co-director and production designer - reported as joining Rowe as co-directors.
- July 2024: Rogen said the film had been titled and an animatic completed.
- December 2024: Mikros Animation announced it would return to lead animation.
- February 2025: Mikros' parent Technicolor Group was reported to be shutting down operations immediately "due to financial struggles and failures to find new investors", halting Mikros' global work on current projects including this sequel. In March 2025, Rodeo FX was reported to have acquired Mikros' Paris and Canadian operations and would resume paused projects.
- CinemaCon 2026: during the Paramount presentation, Rogen announced the film would feature Krang as an additional antagonist.

## Writing and animation
- Writing had already begun by 2023. Shredder was originally the main villain of Mutant Mayhem but was written out because Rowe wanted a villain "who the Turtles could relate to and be tempted by".
- Rowe wanted a depiction of the Shredder that is unique but faithful to the original character, and "a more intimidating presence than Mutant Mayhem's villain, Superfly".
- Kent Seki again serves as head of cinematography.

## Casting and recording
- Abbey, Brown Jr., Cantu and Noon reprise their roles; "Voice recording had already begun by 2025."

## Release
- Scheduled for theatrical release in the United States on August 13, 2027. It was previously scheduled for October 9, 2026 and September 17, 2027. According to Animation Magazine, "unspecified delays in physical animation production" led to the first release date push.

## Marketing and future
- December 2025: Paramount reported not to be renewing its agreement with Playmates Toys, "ending the company's nearly 40-year long tenure as the manufacturer of Turtles toys". February 2026: Mattel announced as acquiring the franchise's master license, with the partnership beginning with toys based on this sequel in 2027.
- "By December 2025, Rogen and Point Grey Pictures were in discussions with Paramount Skydance to produce a third film in the series."

wikis.title: The Simpsons Movie (2007)
wikis.summary: The English Wikipedia article on The Simpsons Movie, covering the 2007 film's credits, plot, its long development and much-rewritten screenplay, animation, music, marketing, record-setting box office, reviews and the 2027 sequel.
wikis.body:
## The film

- *The Simpsons Movie* is "a 2007 American animated comedy film directed by David Silverman and based on the animated television series *The Simpsons* created by Matt Groening", produced by 20th Century Fox Animation and Gracie Films and distributed by 20th Century Fox.
- Eleven credited screenwriters: James L. Brooks, Matt Groening, Al Jean, Ian Maxtone-Graham, George Meyer, David Mirkin, Mike Reiss, Mike Scully, Matt Selman, John Swartzwelder and Jon Vitti. Music by Hans Zimmer, with the *Simpsons* theme by Danny Elfman.
- Premiered in Springfield, Vermont on July 21, 2007 - winner of a contest among 16 Springfields, beating Springfield, Illinois by 15,367 votes to 14,634 - and released in the United States on July 27. Running time 87 minutes; budget $75 million; box office $536.4 million.
- Rated PG-13 by the MPAA for "irreverent humor throughout"; passed PG uncut by the BBFC.
- The plot has Homer's dumping of a silo of pig waste into Lake Springfield lead the EPA, under Russ Cargill, to seal the town under a glass dome; the family flee to Alaska before Homer and Bart destroy the dome with the EPA's own bomb.

## Production

Considered since early in the series and green-lit by 20th Century Fox in 1997, the film only moved after the voice cast signed on in 2001. The writers spent six months on a plot from late 2003, split the outline into seven 25-page sections, and rewrote the screenplay over 100 times; at one point it was a musical. Animation began in January 2006 at Film Roman and Rough Draft Studios in California with overseas work at AKOM and Rough Draft in Seoul, in 2.40:1 widescreen using Toon Boom Harmony and Opus. Editing continued as late as May 2007, and Groening said enough material for two more films was cut - including cameos by Minnie Driver, Edward Norton, Isla Fisher, Erin Brockovich and Kelsey Grammer as Sideshow Bob. Green Day and Tom Hanks appear as themselves, and Albert Brooks voices Russ Cargill.

## Release and reception

- Opening day in the United States $30,758,269; opening weekend $74,036,787 from 5,500 screens at 3,922 theatres, against Fox's $40 million expectation, setting records for a non-CG animated film and for a film based on a television series.
- International opening $96 million from 71 territories, including $27.8 million in the United Kingdom. It closed December 20, 2007 with $183.1 million in the United States and $536.4 million worldwide.
- The lead calls it "the eighth-highest-grossing film of 2007, as well as at the time the second-highest-grossing traditionally animated film and the highest-grossing film based on an animated television series, two records later overtaken by *Demon Slayer: Kimetsu no Yaiba - The Movie: Infinity Castle* in 2025."
- Rotten Tomatoes 87% from 220 reviews (average 7.5/10); Metacritic 80/100 from 36 critics; CinemaScore "A−". It won Best Comedy Film at the British Comedy Awards and was nominated for Best Animated Feature Film at the 65th Golden Globe Awards and four Annie Awards, all lost to *Ratatouille*.

## Sequel

Announced by 20th Century Studios on Instagram on September 29, 2025 as *The Simpsons 2* with a July 23, 2027 release, later delayed to September 3, 2027 to avoid competition with *A Minecraft Movie Squared*; the official title *The New Simpsons Movie* was confirmed at the 2026 D23 Expo in August 2026.

## Note on the page's own figures

The infobox gives a running time of 87 minutes, while the article quotes Peter Bradshaw saying "Eighty-five minutes [was] not long enough to do justice to 17 years of comedy genius".

The second part of the capture is the external links, franchise navigation boxes and category list; it states no publication or last-updated date.

wikis.title: The Simpsons Movie (2007): plot, production, release and reception
wikis.summary: Part 1 of the English Wikipedia article on The Simpsons Movie, covering the 2007 film's credits and infobox figures, plot, voice cast, development and animation, editing, music, themes, marketing, box office, reviews, awards and the announced sequel.
wikis.body:
## The film

- *The Simpsons Movie* is "a 2007 American animated comedy film directed by David Silverman and based on the animated television series *The Simpsons* created by Matt Groening".
- Screenplay by James L. Brooks, Matt Groening, Al Jean, Ian Maxtone-Graham, George Meyer, David Mirkin, Mike Reiss, Mike Scully, Matt Selman, John Swartzwelder and Jon Vitti. Produced by Brooks, Groening, Jean, Scully and Richard Sakai. Edited by John Carnochan; music by Hans Zimmer (with the note "The Simpsons Theme by Danny Elfman").
- Production companies 20th Century Fox Animation and Gracie Films; distributed by 20th Century Fox.
- Release dates: July 21, 2007 (Springfield) and July 27, 2007 (United States). Running time 87 minutes. Country United States; language English. Budget $75 million; box office $536.4 million.
- Starring Dan Castellaneta, Julie Kavner, Nancy Cartwright, Yeardley Smith, Hank Azaria, Harry Shearer, Pamela Hayden, Tress MacNeille and Albert Brooks.
- The plot follows the Simpson family after Homer's reckless actions lead to Springfield being encased under a massive glass dome by the Environmental Protection Agency.
- "The screenplay was rewritten over a hundred times, which continued after work on the film's animation began in 2006", and hours of finished material was cut, including cameos from Erin Brockovich, Minnie Driver, Isla Fisher, Edward Norton and Kelsey Grammer (who would have reprised Sideshow Bob). Green Day and Tom Hanks voice themselves in the final cut.
- It grossed $536.4 million worldwide against a $75 million budget, "becoming the eighth-highest-grossing film of 2007, as well as at the time the second-highest-grossing traditionally animated film and the highest-grossing film based on an animated television series, two records later overtaken by *Demon Slayer: Kimetsu no Yaiba - The Movie: Infinity Castle* in 2025."
- It was nominated for Best Animated Feature Film at the 65th Golden Globe Awards.
- "A sequel, titled *The New Simpsons Movie*, is scheduled for release on September 3, 2027."

## Plot

Green Day drown when pollution in Lake Springfield erodes their barge. Lisa and her boyfriend Colin convince the town to clean up the lake; Grampa prophesies a disaster involving a "twisted tail", "a thousand eyes", the people being "trapped forever" and the warning "eepah". Homer adopts a pig, "Plopper", and dumps a silo of its waste in the lake. EPA head Russ Cargill has President Arnold Schwarzenegger seal Springfield under a giant glass dome. The family escape to Alaska; Cargill tricks Schwarzenegger into ordering the town's demolition, and the Simpsons see Tom Hanks advertising a "new Grand Canyon" on the site. Homer, after an epiphany induced by an Inuk shaman, returns; he and Bart use a motorcycle to carry the EPA's time bomb up the side of the dome, and Bart throws it through the hole seconds before it detonates, shattering the dome. Maggie knocks Cargill out with a rock, and the town praises Homer as a hero.

## Notable numbers

- Budget $75 million; worldwide gross $536.4 million; US gross $183.1 million.
- Opening day in the United States $30,758,269; opening weekend $74,036,787 on 5,500 screens at 3,922 theatres, against Fox's expectation of $40 million.
- International opening $96 million from 71 overseas territories, including $27.8 million in the United Kingdom.
- 98 characters have speaking parts; the angry-mob shot features cameos from more than 320 characters.
- 7-Eleven spent approximately $10 million converting 12 stores into Kwik-E-Marts, for a 30% profit increase at those stores.

## Internal tension worth noting

The infobox gives a running time of 87 minutes, while the article quotes *The Guardian*'s Peter Bradshaw saying "Eighty-five minutes [was] not long enough to do justice to 17 years of comedy genius".

wikis.title: Development of a Simpsons film
wikis.summary: The abandoned earlier attempts and how the 2007 film was finally set up, staffed and written.
wikis.body:
- A film adaptation had been considered since early in the series (1989-present). Groening felt a feature would let them increase the show's scale and animate sequences too complex for television, and intended it to be made after the show ended, "but that [...] was undone by good ratings".
- There were attempts to adapt the fourth-season episode "Kamp Krusty", but expanding it to feature length proved difficult. Groening also wished to make *Simpstasia*, a parody of *Fantasia* (1940), never produced. An anthology-style *Treehouse of Horror* film was briefly suggested but not pursued. Phil Hartman wished to make a live-action Troy McClure film, with Josh Weinstein proposing the plot of "A Fish Called Selma"; the project was cancelled after Hartman's death in 1998.
- "The project was officially green-lit by 20th Century Fox in 1997, and Groening and James L. Brooks were set to produce the film."
- The voice cast signed on in 2001 and work then began on the screenplay. Groening and Brooks invited Mike Scully and Al Jean (who continued as showrunner on the series) to produce, and signed series director David Silverman to direct. The writing team drew on the show's early seasons: David Mirkin, Mike Reiss, George Meyer, John Swartzwelder and Jon Vitti, with Ian Maxtone-Graham and Matt Selman joining later. Sam Simon did not return, having left the show over creative differences in 1993.
- Conan O'Brien expressed interest but joked "I worry that the Simpsons-writing portion of my brain has been destroyed after 14 years". Brad Bird said he had "entertained fantasies of asking if [he] could work on the movie" but lacked time because of *The Incredibles* (2004) and *Ratatouille* (2007).
- The producers arranged a deal with Fox letting them abandon production at any point if the screenplay was unsatisfactory.
- Work on the screenplay continued from late 2003 in the small bungalow where Groening first pitched *The Simpsons* in 1987. The writers spent six months discussing a plot. Scully suggested a story in which Steven Spielberg would try to blow up Springfield to shoot a film with Tom Hanks; Groening introduced the pet-pig idea, inspired by a pig-waste management story he read in the news. Jean's manatee idea became the episode "The Bonfire of the Manatees"; a *Truman Show*-like idea was rejected because the Simpsons should "never become aware of themselves as celebrities", and was later used in *The Simpsons Game* (2007). Hank Scorpio was originally to return as the main antagonist before Russ Cargill was created.
- The outline was split into seven sections; Jean, Scully, Reiss, Swartzwelder, Vitti, Mirkin and Meyer wrote 25 pages each and merged them a month later into one "very rough draft". The screenplay was rewritten over 100 times, and at one point the film was a musical before the songs were shortened and dropped.
- Groening quote: "If every episode of The Simpsons is a celebration, which we try to make it, then the movie is like a big celebration. It's a way of honoring the animators [...] It's a way of honoring the writers [...] and it's a way of honoring all the great actors."

wikis.title: Animation and casting
wikis.summary: How the film was animated, by which studios and with what tools, and how the cast and guest voices were recorded.
wikis.body:
## Animation

- Animation began January 2006, with the *Itchy & Scratchy* short the first scene storyboarded. Groening rejected live-action or CGI, calling the animation "deliberately imperfect" and "a tribute to the art of hand-drawn animation".
- Produced in a widescreen 2.40:1 aspect ratio, to distinguish it from the series' then 4:3 fullscreen look, and coloured with the largest palette the animators had ever had. Much of the animation used Wacom Cintiq tablets.
- Work was divided among four studios: Film Roman in Burbank, California and Rough Draft Studios in Glendale, California, with overseas animation at AKOM and Rough Draft's division in Seoul, South Korea. Storyboarding, character design, background layout, general animation and animatics were done in America; the overseas studios completed camera work, inbetweening and digital ink and paint.
- Silverman said that unlike the series where "you [have] to pick and choose", the film let them "lavish that attention [on] every single scene"; characters have shadows, unlike in the show. Inspirations included *The Incredibles*, *The Triplets of Belleville* (2003) and *Bad Day at Black Rock* (1955) for staging, *Dumbo* (1941) and *Pluto's Judgment Day* for a dream sequence, and *It's a Mad, Mad, Mad, Mad World* (1963) for crowd scenes.
- Mike B. Anderson, Lauren MacMullan, Rich Moore and Steven Dean Moore each directed around a quarter of the film's animation under Silverman. The software used was a combination of Toon Boom Harmony and Toon Boom Opus.

## Casting

- The staff referenced a poster featuring more than 320 *Simpsons* characters for crowd scenes; Groening said they tried to include every character, with 98 having speaking parts.
- Albert Brooks was cast as Russ Cargill after telling the staff he wanted to be part of the film; for "about a week" he was to reprise Hank Scorpio.
- The cast did the first of three table readings in May 2005 and recorded every week from June 2006 until the end of production. James L. Brooks directed them for the first time since the show's early seasons. Castellaneta found the sessions "more intense" and "more emotionally dramatic" than the series; some scenes, such as Marge's video message, were recorded over one hundred times.
- Green Day were cast in the opening concert scene, having asked to guest star. Tom Hanks accepted "after just one phone call". Philip Rosenthal voices the father in the "new Grand Canyon" commercial.
- Cut guests: Minnie Driver (a grievance counsellor), Edward Norton (the man crushed by the dome, doing a Woody Allen impression, re-recorded by Castellaneta because the voice was too distracting), Isla Fisher, Erin Brockovich and Kelsey Grammer as Sideshow Bob. Johnny Knoxville was touted as a possible guest.
- Arnold Schwarzenegger is president rather than the incumbent George W. Bush because, per Groening, "in two years ... the film [would be] out of date"; the president was designed as an altered Rainier Wolfcastle with more wrinkles under the eyes and a different hairstyle.

wikis.title: Editing and cut material
wikis.summary: The changes made during production and after test screenings, and what was removed from the film.
wikis.body:
- Storylines, jokes and characters were regularly rewritten, with edits continuing into 2007 "with some edits taking place as late as May, two months before the film was released". James L. Brooks said "70 percent of the things in [one of the trailers]—based on where we were eight weeks ago—are no longer in the movie." Groening said enough material for two more films was cut.
- Marge originally had the prophetic vision in church; the writers considered this too dark and changed it to Grampa.
- Lisa's love interest Colin was previously named Dexter and Adrien and his appearance was completely altered; an idea to make Milhouse the love interest was dropped because "the audience was not as familiar with [his] long-standing crush on [Lisa] as [they had] thought".
- A car chase in which Homer throws flaming mummies at the EPA was replaced with motel and carnival scenes.
- Bart's naked skateboard scene was Groening's idea, with Mike Scully suggesting showing Bart's penis for two seconds; storyboard artist Martin Archer devised the way to cover the genitals. The crew worried about an R rating, wanting PG-13, and got away with it because it was not live-action and not Homer.
- March 2007 preview screenings in Portland, Oregon and Phoenix, Arizona led to further changes, including deleting Kang and Kodos criticizing the film during the end credits, and toning down scenes because some of Homer's behaviour was found too unlikable.
- Russ Cargill was redesigned several times, originally an older man whose speech patterns Albert Brooks based on Donald Rumsfeld; the older model was used by Burger King for the action figure.
- Cargill's closing scene with Bart and Homer was added to resolve his story, and the "Spider-Pig" gag was a late addition. An excised scene had Mr. Burns remind viewers it was their last chance for a refund. Other deletions: Homer's encounter with a sausage truck driver, a Plopper scene at the end, and a news report on the dome's effect on farming and sports - all on the DVD. Several musical numbers were cut, including a song about Alaska with music by Dave Stewart of Eurythmics; Jean said it "got pretty far along in the animation, and then we got scared that the movie began to drag in that section."

wikis.title: Music and themes
wikis.summary: Hans Zimmer's score, Green Day's theme recording, and the film's environmental and religious themes.
wikis.body:
## Music

- James L. Brooks chose Hans Zimmer, a good friend and regular collaborator. Zimmer called the score a "unique challenge" and said he had to "try and express the style of The Simpsons without wearing the audience out". He used Danny Elfman's original opening theme sparingly and created themes for each family member, with Homer's leitmotif a major focus and smaller themes for Bart and Marge.
- Regular series composer Alf Clausen was not asked to score the film: "sometimes you're the windshield, sometimes you're the bug".
- Green Day recorded its own version of the *Simpsons* theme and released it as a single. Zimmer turned the Spider-Pig song into a choral piece as a joke he never intended to be used, and had to write foreign-language lyrics for the 32 dubbed versions; Spanish was the hardest, and the same choir learned the piece for each dub.

## Themes

- Al Jean described the film's message as "a man should listen to his wife". The film parodies religion and environmentalism.
- Environmentalism runs through Homer's polluting of Lake Springfield, Green Day's cameo, Lisa's activism and her romance with Colin, and the villain heads the EPA. Reviewer Ed Gonzalez argued the plot satirizes the government's reaction to Hurricane Katrina. Ian Nathan of *Empire* said this gave the film an "overt political agenda [which] border[s] on polemic". James D. Bloom of Muhlenberg College wrote that the opening Green Day scene "sets in motion a plot expressly built around cultural agenda-setting".
- Religion appears in Grampa's possession and Marge's belief it is a message from God. Groening joked the film "posit[s] the existence of a very active God". Mark I. Pinsky said it "treats genuine faith with respect, while keeping a sharp eye out for religious pretension and hypocrisy of all kinds".
- Trees are a motif, implemented in every important or emotional scene; an apple tree was inserted behind Lisa and Colin at their first meeting as a reference to Adam and Eve and the Garden of Eden.

wikis.title: Release, premiere and marketing
wikis.summary: The Springfield premiere contest, ratings, the worldwide promotional campaign and the home video release.
wikis.body:
## Theatrical

- On April 1, 2006, 20th Century Fox announced a worldwide release of July 27, 2007; the film was released a day earlier in Australia and the United Kingdom.
- Fox held a competition among 16 Springfields across the United States to host the American premiere, each producing a film and the result decided by a vote on the USA Today website. Springfield, Minnesota dropped out on May 31, 2007. The winner, announced July 10, was Springfield, Vermont, which beat Springfield, Illinois by 15,367 votes to 14,634. The other 14 entrants held smaller screenings on July 26. Springfield, Vermont hosted the world premiere on July 21 "with a yellow carpet instead of the traditional red".
- Rated PG-13 by the MPAA for "irreverent humor throughout", as the staff had expected. The British Board of Film Classification passed it as a PG with no cuts; a BBFC spokeswoman said of Bart's nude scene, "natural nudity with no sexual content is acceptable in PG films".

## Marketing

- 7-Eleven converted 11 US stores and one in Canada into Kwik-E-Marts at a cost of approximately $10 million, selling "Squishees", "Buzz Cola", "Krusty-O's" cereal and "Pink Movie Donuts"; the promotion produced a 30% profit increase at those stores. Homer performed an animated monologue on *The Tonight Show with Jay Leno* for July 24, 2007.
- 20th Century Fox erected a giant pink donut at Springfield in Canterbury, New Zealand; a double-decker-bus-sized inflatable Spider Pig floated next to Battersea Power Station in London; and an image of Homer was painted next to the Cerne Abbas Giant in Dorset, which "caused outrage amongst local neopagans who performed 'rain magic' to try to get it washed away".
- Tie-ins: McFarlane Toys action figures; EA's *The Simpsons Game* (plot not based on the film); a Samsung *Simpsons Movie* phone; a limited-edition *Simpsons Movie* Xbox 360; Ben & Jerry's "Duff & D'oh! Nuts" ice cream; Windows Live Messenger content; Burger King toys and adverts; and JetBlue sweepstakes plus a dedicated in-flight channel.

## Home media

- Released on DVD and Blu-ray worldwide on December 3, 2007 and on December 18 in the United States by 20th Century Fox Home Entertainment, with producer and animator commentaries, six short deleted scenes and promotional material. An unfinished deleted scene of the Springfield Anthem appeared on *The Simpsons The Complete Tenth Season* box set.
- The Empire State Building was illuminated yellow, "the first time the building had ever been used as part of a film promotion". In the United Kingdom Fox launched a £5 million advertising campaign and signed a £1.6 million deal with Yoplait for a *Simpsons Movie* design on Frubes. In its first week the DVD topped the US chart and generated $11.8 million in rental revenue.

wikis.title: Box office and critical response
wikis.summary: The film's opening records and grosses, the aggregate scores and the range of published reviews.
wikis.body:
## Box office

- Opening day in the United States: $30,758,269, "the 25th-highest, and fifth-highest non-sequel opening day revenue of all time".
- Opening weekend: $74,036,787 from 5,500 screens at 3,922 theatres, first at the box office - the tenth-highest opening weekend of all time for July, the highest among non-sequels, and the highest animated TV adaptation of all time, surpassing *The SpongeBob SquarePants Movie*. Fox had expected $40 million.
- Records set: highest-grossing opening weekend for a non-CG animated film and for a film based on a television series, surpassing *Mission: Impossible 2* (2000); third-highest opening weekend for an animated film.
- International: opened first with $96 million from 71 overseas territories, including $27.8 million in the United Kingdom, "the second-highest UK opening ever for a 20th Century Fox film", contributing to over half of the record 5.5 million people attending British cinemas that weekend. Australia $13.2 million, the third-highest opening weekend in the country and the highest for an animated film.
- Top territories outside the United States: the United Kingdom $78.4 million overall and Germany $36.3 million.
- Closed December 20, 2007 with $183.1 million in the United States and $536.4 million worldwide, the eighth-highest-grossing film worldwide and the tenth-highest-grossing in the United States of 2007.

## Critical response

- "Mostly positive reviews." Rotten Tomatoes: 87% of 220 critics' reviews positive, average 7.5/10, with the consensus that the film "contains the hearty laughs, biting satire, and honest portrayal of an American family that makes the show so popular". Metacritic: 80 out of 100 from 36 critics, "generally favorable". CinemaScore: "A−".
- *The Guardian* and *The Times* both gave four out of five stars. James Bone (*The Times*) said it "boasts the same sly cultural references and flashes of brilliance". Peter Bradshaw (*The Guardian*) said it "gives you everything you could possibly want" and that "Eighty-five minutes [was] not long enough to do justice to 17 years of comedy genius".
- Roger Ebert gave three out of four stars, calling it "radical and simple at the same time, subversive and good-hearted, offensive without really meaning to be". Richard Corliss (*Time*) said it "doesn't try to be ruder or kinkier, just bigger and better". Randy Shulman praised Kavner, who "gave what must be the most heartfelt performance ever". Claudia Puig (*USA Today*) said the story did "warrant a full-length feature".
- Mixed and negative: Kirk Honeycutt (*The Hollywood Reporter*) said "little has been gained bringing the Simpsons to the screen"; Brian Lowry (*Variety*) called it "clever, irreverent, satirical and outfitted" but "just barely" able to sustain the length; Luke Davies (*The Monthly*) said "it makes the film feel like three episodes strung together"; Ian Nathan (*Empire*) compared it to New Coke, saying "it utterly failed"; David Edwards wrote it "isn't a terrible film, just a terribly disappointing one"; Carina Chocano (*Los Angeles Times*) negatively compared it to *South Park: Bigger, Longer & Uncut* (1999).

wikis.title: Accolades and the sequel
wikis.summary: The awards the film won and was nominated for, and the long road to The New Simpsons Movie.
wikis.body:
## Accolades

- Won Best Comedy Film at the British Comedy Awards, Best Animation at the inaugural ITV National Movie Awards, and Best Movie at the UK Nickelodeon Kids Choice Awards, beating *Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix*, *Pirates of the Caribbean: At World's End* and *Shrek the Third*.
- The trailer won a Golden Trailer Award for Best Animated/Family Film Trailer at the 8th Annual Golden Trailer Awards; the film's website won a Webby Award at the 12th Annual Webby Awards for "Best Movie and Film Website". *Forbes* named it the third best film of the year based on box office and Metacritic score.
- Nominated in four categories at the 35th Annie Awards - Best Animated Feature, Directing, Writing and Voice Acting (Julie Kavner) - all won by *Ratatouille*.
- Also nominated for Best Animated Feature Film at the 65th Golden Globe Awards, the BAFTA for Best Animated Film, the Producers Guild Award, the Satellite Award, the Chicago Film Critics Association Award and the Broadcast Film Critics Association Award.
- Before release it was nominated at the 2007 MTV Movie Awards for "Best Summer Movie You Haven't Seen Yet" (won by *Transformers*), lost the Teen Choice Award for "Choice Summer Movie - Comedy/Musical" to *Hairspray*, and was nominated for Favorite Movie Comedy at the People's Choice Awards, losing to *Knocked Up*.

## Sequel

- In 2014 Brooks said Fox had requested a second film but there were no immediate plans. In December 2014 Jean wrote on Twitter that the episode "The Man Who Came to Be Dinner" (produced in 2012, originally set to air in May 2013) had been held back because it was being considered for a sequel as it was "cinematic"; he cited fears the film would be considered "not canonical".
- July 2017: Silverman and Jean said a sequel was in early development and stressed the toll the first film took. August 10, 2018: a sequel reported in development. July 22, 2019: Groening said he had "no doubts" Disney would produce one. July 2021: Jean said discussions had stalled due to the COVID-19 pandemic. May 2024: Jean said "I want to see the animation business completely returned to what it was before the pandemic."
- On September 29, 2025 a sequel with the working title *The Simpsons 2* was announced by 20th Century Studios on Instagram, with a pink donut and the tagline "Homer's coming back for seconds", confirming a theatrical release on July 23, 2027. The release was later delayed to September 3 "to avoid competition with *A Minecraft Movie Squared*". In August 2026, at the 2026 D23 Expo, the official title was confirmed as *The New Simpsons Movie*.

No published or last-updated date is stated.

wikis.title: The New Simpsons Movie (upcoming 2027 film)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the upcoming sequel to The Simpsons Movie, covering its long development history, the 2025 announcement, the 2026 title reveal and its September 3, 2027 release date.
wikis.body:
## Overview

- "The New Simpsons Movie is an upcoming American animated comedy film based on the Fox animated sitcom The Simpsons created by Matt Groening."
- "Produced by 20th Century Animation and Gracie Films, it is the second feature film adaptation of the series and the sequel to The Simpsons Movie (2007)."
- Distributed by 20th Century Studios. Country: United States. Language: English.
- "On September 29, 2025, Disney, which acquired 21st Century Fox in 2019, officially announced the sequel, with the working title of The Simpsons 2. The official title was announced in August 2026."
- Infobox release date: September 3, 2027. The infobox leaves writer, screenplay, story, producer, starring, cinematography, editing, music, runtime, budget and gross blank, each marked "MUST HAVE RELIABLE SOURCE".

## Release

- "The New Simpsons Movie is scheduled to be released in the United States on September 3, 2027."
- "It was previously scheduled for a July 23, 2027 release, taking over a date that Disney had originally reserved for an untitled Marvel Studios film."

## Development

- 2014: James L. Brooks said 20th Century Fox "had approached him and requested a second film based on The Simpsons", with no immediate plans: "We've been asked to [develop it], but we haven't. We're doing a lot of other stuff".
- December 2014, before the season 26 episode "The Man Who Came to Be Dinner": writer Al Jean wrote on Twitter that the episode (produced in 2012, originally set to air in 2013) "had been held back by himself and Brooks because it was being considered for adaptation into a sequel film as the episode was 'cinematic'." Jean later cited fear that the film would be considered "not canonical" with the TV series and the potential backlash of a "memory wipe".
- July 2017, at the 10th anniversary of The Simpsons Movie: Jean and David Silverman "said that a sequel film was in the early stages of development and stressed the toll production of the first picture took on the entire staff."
- August 10, 2018: "it was reported that a sequel was in development."
- July 22, 2019: Matt Groening "stated that he had 'no doubts' that The Walt Disney Company, which acquired 21st Century Fox early that year, would likely produce a sequel one day."
- July 2021: Jean said discussions "had stalled due to the COVID-19 pandemic."
- May 2024: Jean said, "I want to see the animation business completely returned to what it was before the pandemic. And then, I think if that was the case, it would make sense to do The Simpsons theatrically".
- September 2025: Disney announced the sequel with the working title The Simpsons 2.
- August 2026: "at the 2026 D23 Expo, the official title was confirmed as The New Simpsons Movie."

## Notes from the page's other listings

- Referenced article titles include "First 'New Simpsons Movie' Footage Features Baseball Shenanigans" (TheWrap, August 14, 2026).
- Navigation boxes list the film under 20th Century Animation, Gracie Films, Matt Groening films and Disney theatrical animated features, all dated 2027.
- Categories include "Films with screenplays by James L. Brooks" and "Films with screenplays by Matt Groening", though the infobox writer fields are empty.

wikis.title: Frozen (2013 film)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia's article on Frozen, the 2013 Walt Disney Animation Studios musical fantasy film directed by Chris Buck and Jennifer Lee, covering its plot, voice cast, long development history, production, release, box office, reception, awards and legacy.
wikis.body:
## The film

- "Frozen is a 2013 American animated musical fantasy film produced by Walt Disney Animation Studios, loosely inspired by Hans Christian Andersen's 1844 fairy tale 'The Snow Queen'." Directed by Chris Buck and Jennifer Lee, written by Lee, story by Buck, Lee and Shane Morris; produced by Peter Del Vecho.
- Voices: Kristen Bell (Anna), Idina Menzel (Elsa), Jonathan Groff (Kristoff), Josh Gad (Olaf), Santino Fontana (Hans), with Alan Tudyk, Ciaran Hinds, Maurice LaMarche and Jennifer Lee among others.
- Score by Christophe Beck; songs by Robert Lopez and Kristen Anderson-Lopez. Running time 102 minutes; country United States; language English.
- Budget $150 million (infobox). Box office $1.280 billion (infobox); the reception section gives $400.7 million in North America and an estimated $880 million elsewhere for $1,280,802,282 worldwide.

## Dates the page gives

- Premiere at the El Capitan Theatre, Hollywood/Los Angeles, on November 19, 2013.
- The infobox gives release dates of November 19, 2013 (El Capitan Theatre) and November 22, 2013 (United States); the release section says the film "was released theatrically in the United States on November 27, 2013" after "a five-day limited release there beginning on November 22", and the lead says the general theatrical release was November 27. The box-office section says it "opened on November 22, 2013, at the El Capitan Theatre in Hollywood for a five-day limited release and earned $342,839 before its wide opening on November 27."
- Announced on December 22, 2011 under the new title Frozen with a release date of November 27, 2013.
- Home media: digital download February 25, 2014; Blu-ray and DVD March 18; sing-along reissue November 18, 2014; 4K Ultra HD in 2019.
- It passed $1 billion on March 2, 2014, its 101st day of release, and $400 million in North America on April 25, 2014.

## Production

Disney explored Andersen material from the late 1930s and shelved The Snow Queen repeatedly (a project scrapped in late 2002 after Glen Keane "reportedly quit"). Development restarted in 2008 when John Lasseter brought Chris Buck back to the studio; the film became computer-animated in 3D, Jennifer Lee joined as screenwriter in March 2012 and was promoted to co-director in August 2012 (announced that November), "making her the first woman to direct a full-length animated film from Walt Disney Animation Studios". Breakthroughs were making Anna and Elsa sisters, the song "Let It Go", the Hans twist and "For the First Time in Forever", written in June 2013. Research trips went to Jackson Hole, Quebec City's Ice Hotel and Norway; Arendelle is based on Norwegian landmarks and the film draws on Sami culture. New tools included a snowflake generator producing 2,000 unique shapes and the Matterhorn snow simulator, used in at least 43 scenes; Elsa's hair has 420,000 strands; the ice-palace shot took 30 hours to render each frame on 4,000 computers. It was the studio's last film to use Pixar RenderMan. The film was dubbed into 41 languages, with over 900 voices in about 1,300 recording sessions.

## Reception and records

- Rotten Tomatoes: 89% of 251 reviews positive, average 7.7/10; Metacritic 75 from 48 reviews; CinemaScore A+.
- It is listed as the fifth-highest-grossing film, highest-grossing animated film and highest-grossing 2013 film, overtaken as highest-grossing animated film by The Lion King remake in August 2019. Japan was its biggest market after North America at $247.6 million.
- Home video: 3.2 million units on day one, over 18 million units by 2015, $308,026,545 in US home-media sales by the end of 2014; the all-time bestselling US Blu-ray release by July 2018 with over 7.5 million units.
- Awards: Academy Awards for Best Animated Feature and Best Original Song ("Let It Go"), the Golden Globe for Best Animated Feature Film, the BAFTA for Best Animated Film, five Annie Awards, Critics' Choice Awards, and two Grammy Awards.
- Criticism recorded: the Lino DiSalvo "keep them pretty" remark and Disney's response; debate over perceived LGBTQ parallels; the Jaime Ciero "Let It Go" lawsuit filed November 24, 2017 and dropped in May 2019; and Disney's trademark suit against Phase 4 Films over Frozen Land, settled with a $100,000 payment due January 27, 2014.

## Legacy and franchise

"Frozen-mania" among children in 2014, a merchandise shortage resolved by early November 2014 after over three million costumes were sold in North America, park attractions and a Broadway musical announced in January 2014. The franchise includes Frozen Fever (2015), Olaf's Frozen Adventure (2017), Frozen 2, "released on November 22, 2019", and Frozen 3, "scheduled to be released in November 2027", with a fourth film in development.

## Rest of the page

The final parts of the page are the numbered reference list, external links, and Disney, director and award navigation templates plus the page's categories.

wikis.title: Frozen (2013 film): plot, cast, production and release
wikis.summary: Wikipedia's article on the 2013 Disney animated film Frozen, part 1: infobox credits and figures, the plot, voice cast, production history (development, writing, casting, animation, technology, Scandinavian and Sami inspiration, music and sound, localization), and its theatrical and home-media release.
wikis.body:
## What the page covers

Part 1 of the Wikipedia article "Frozen (2013 film)", described in the page's own subtitle as a "2013 film by Chris Buck and Jennifer Lee".

## Infobox

- Directed by Chris Buck and Jennifer Lee; screenplay by Jennifer Lee; story by Chris Buck, Jennifer Lee and Shane Morris.
- Based on "The Snow Queen" by Hans Christian Andersen.
- Produced by Peter Del Vecho. Starring Kristen Bell, Idina Menzel, Jonathan Groff, Josh Gad, Santino Fontana.
- Cinematography: Scott Beattie (layout), Mohit Kallianpur (lighting). Edited by Jeff Draheim.
- Music by Christophe Beck (score), Robert Lopez and Kristen Anderson-Lopez (songs).
- Production company Walt Disney Animation Studios; distributed by Walt Disney Studios Motion Pictures (a note says it was distributed under the Walt Disney Pictures banner).
- Release dates: November 19, 2013 (El Capitan Theatre) and November 22, 2013 (United States).
- Running time 102 minutes. Country: United States. Language: English.
- Budget $150 million. Box office $1.280 billion.

## Lead

- "Frozen is a 2013 American animated musical fantasy film produced by Walt Disney Animation Studios, loosely inspired by Hans Christian Andersen's 1844 fairy tale 'The Snow Queen'."
- Anna (Bell), princess of Arendelle, travels with the iceman Kristoff (Groff), his reindeer Sven and the snowman Olaf (Gad) to find her estranged sister Elsa (Menzel) after Elsa accidentally traps the kingdom in eternal winter.
- The film "underwent several story treatments before it was commissioned in 2011".
- "Following its world premiere at the El Capitan Theatre in Los Angeles on November 19, 2013, Frozen had its general theatrical release on November 27."
- It "grossed over $1.280 billion worldwide, becoming the highest-grossing animated film until the remake of The Lion King overtook this position in August 2019"; it finished its run as the highest-grossing film of 2013 and the fifth-highest-grossing film of all time.
- Franchise: the short Frozen Fever (2015), the featurette Olaf's Frozen Adventure (2017), and two feature sequels, Frozen 2 (2019) and "the upcoming Frozen 3 (2027)".
- Accolades listed: Academy Awards for Best Animated Feature and Best Original Song ("Let It Go"), the Golden Globe for Best Animated Feature Film, the BAFTA for Best Animated Film, and two Grammy Awards.

## Plot

Elsa of Arendelle has magical ice and snow powers; after she injures her younger sister Anna, trolls led by Grand Pabbie heal Anna and erase her memories of the magic, and the sisters are isolated. Their parents die in a shipwreck. On Elsa's coronation day Anna falls for Prince Hans of the Southern Isles; Elsa's powers are revealed, she is accused of witchcraft by the Duke of Weselton, and she flees to the North Mountain, building an ice palace while Arendelle freezes. Anna, Kristoff, Sven and Olaf reach the palace; Elsa accidentally freezes Anna's heart and casts her out, creating a giant snow monster. Grand Pabbie says only "an act of true love" can thaw Anna. Hans reveals he plotted to rule Arendelle. Anna steps between Hans and Elsa and freezes solid; her heroism is "an act of true love" and she thaws. Elsa ends the winter, Hans is arrested and exiled, and Kristoff is appointed royal ice deliverer.

## Voice cast

Kristen Bell as Anna, an 18-year-old princess (Livvy Stubenrauch as 5-year-old Anna, with Katie Lopez singing; Agatha Lee Monn as 9-year-old Anna); Idina Menzel as Elsa, the 21-year-old queen (Eva Bella as 8-year-old Elsa, Spencer Lacey Ganus as 12-year-old Elsa); Jonathan Groff as Kristoff (Tyree Brown as 8-year-old Kristoff); Josh Gad as Olaf; Santino Fontana as Hans; Alan Tudyk as the Duke of Weselton; Ciaran Hinds as Grand Pabbie; Chris Williams as Oaken; Maia Wilson as Bulda; Paul Briggs as Marshmallow; Maurice LaMarche as King Agnarr; Jennifer Lee as Queen Iduna. Sven's grunts and snorts were provided by Frank Welker, uncredited.

## Production background

- Walt Disney Productions began exploring a live-action/animated biographical film of Hans Christian Andersen in late 1937; in March 1940 Walt Disney proposed a co-production with Samuel Goldwyn. The project halted in 1942 after the United States entered World War II; Goldwyn produced the 1952 live-action Hans Christian Andersen, and Disney shelved unfinished projects including The Snow Queen.
- Walt Disney Feature Animation developed a new adaptation in the late 1990s; the project was scrapped in late 2002 when Glen Keane "reportedly quit" for the project that became Tangled (2010). Harvey Fierstein pitched a version and was turned down; Paul and Gaetan Brizzi, Dick Zondag and Dave Goetz "reportedly tried their hands at it, but failed". After unsuccessful attempts from 2000 to 2002 the project was shelved again.
- Michael Eisner suggested John Lasseter at Pixar; Pixar-Disney negotiations collapsed in January 2004; Bob Iger negotiated Disney's purchase of Pixar in January 2006 for $7.4 billion, and Lasseter became chief creative officer of Pixar and Disney Animation.
- Producer Peter Del Vecho on the adaptation: "Hans Christian Andersen's original version of The Snow Queen is a pretty dark tale and it doesn't translate easily into a film. For us the breakthrough came when we tried to give really human qualities to the Snow Queen."

## Development and writing

- Development began in 2008 when Lasseter convinced Chris Buck to return from Sony Pictures Animation; Buck pitched The Snow Queen among other ideas in September 2008. Development began as Anna and the Snow Queen, planned as traditional animation; Josh Gad says Megan Mullally was going to play Elsa at that stage. By early 2010 the project was "in development hell".
- On December 22, 2011, after the success of Tangled, Disney announced the new title Frozen and a release date of November 27, 2013. A month later it was confirmed the film would be computer-animated in stereoscopic 3D. The Lopezes began writing songs in January 2012. On March 5, 2012 it was announced Buck would direct, with Lasseter and Del Vecho producing.
- Jennifer Lee was brought in as screenwriter in March 2012; the team "essentially started over and ... had 17 months".
- Key changes: Anna rewritten as Elsa's younger sibling; a "Sister Summit" convened at the studio; the song "Let It Go" reimagined Elsa as sympathetic and led Lee to "rewrite the first act"; the twist that Prince Hans is the villain, Hans written as "sociopathic" and "twisted"; Olaf changed from Elsa's obnoxious sidekick to Anna's; story artist John Ripa solved the climax.
- Lee was promoted to co-director in August 2012 (announced that November), "making her the first woman to direct a full-length animated film from Walt Disney Animation Studios".
- The team thought the story was "cracked" by November 2012, but in late February 2013 it "wasn't working" and rewriting continued February through June 2013. In June, five months before the announced release date, "For the First Time in Forever" was written, which Lopez said "became the linchpin of the whole movie". Test screenings were held that month in Phoenix, Arizona.

## Casting

Kristen Bell was cast as Anna on March 5, 2012, and was called in to re-record dialogue "probably 20 times". Idina Menzel, cast as Elsa, had auditioned for Tangled; she and Bell sang "Wind Beneath My Wings" as a duet at an early table read. Additional casting was announced between December 2012 and June 2013: Jonathan Groff, Alan Tudyk, Santino Fontana and Josh Gad.

## Animation, design and technology

- Art director Michael Giaimo researched Scandinavia, visited Solvang, California, and focused on Norway. Disney sponsored three research field trips: Jackson Hole, Wyoming (deep snow); Quebec City's Ice Hotel (light on snow and ice); and Norway.
- The animation team had a schedule of less than 12 months; Lee estimated the team at 600 to 650 people, "including around 70 lighting people[,] 70-plus animators", and 15 to 20 storyboard artists.
- Supervising animators included Hyrum Osmond (Olaf), Rebecca "Becky" Bresee (Anna) and Wayne Unten (Elsa). A live reindeer named Sage was brought into the studio as reference for Sven.
- Giaimo's influences included Jack Cardiff's Black Narcissus (1947) and Ted D. McCord's The Sound of Music; Frozen was produced in CinemaScope, "the first animated film completely produced in CinemaScope since 2000's Titan A.E.".
- Costumes: character designer Jean Gillmore served as costume designer, melding "the historic silhouettes of 1840 Western Europe (give or take), with the shapes and garment relationships and details of folk costume in early Norway, circa 19th century", mainly wool with velvet, linen and silk.
- Title change from The Snow Queen to Frozen; Del Vecho said the film keeps the title The Snow Queen in some countries.
- Technology: Caltech professor Kenneth Libbrecht instructed the effects group; a snowflake generator randomly created 2,000 unique snowflake shapes. The snow simulator Matterhorn, built on the material point method with help from UCLA mathematicians, was used in at least 43 scenes. Other tools: Spaces, Flourish, Snow Batcher and Tonic. Elsa's hair contains 420,000 computer-generated strands versus about 100,000 on an average human. The film has 312 character rigs and 245 cloth costume rigs. Fifty effects and lighting artists worked on the single shot of Elsa building her ice palace; "It required 30 hours to render each frame, with 4,000 computers rendering one frame at a time." Frozen was the last Walt Disney Animation Studios film to use Pixar RenderMan; the studio switched to Hyperion with Big Hero 6.

## Scandinavian and Sami inspiration

Arendelle was based on Norway, with locations inspired by Akershus Fortress in Oslo, Nidaros Cathedral in Trondheim and Bryggen in Bergen; Arendelle itself was inspired by Naeroyfjord, a branch of Sognefjorden and a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Sami elements include reindeer transport, the ice cutters' clothing, parts of the score and duodji-inspired decoration; the team visited Rorosrein, a Sami family-owned company in Plassja.

## Music and sound

- Songs by Robert Lopez and Kristen Anderson-Lopez. About 23 minutes of the film are musical numbers; collaboration required two-hour transcontinental videoconferences nearly every weekday for about 14 months. They wrote 25 songs, eight were used; with a reprise of "For the First Time in Forever" and Demi Lovato's credits cover of "Let It Go" there are ten songs. Seven of the 17 unused songs were later released on the deluxe-edition soundtrack.
- Christophe Beck was hired to score the film in February 2013. On September 14, 2013 it was announced that Sami musician Frode Fjellheim's "Eatnemen Vuelie" would be the opening song. Norwegian linguist and composer Christine Hals assisted with an Old Norse song for Elsa's coronation; the Cantus choir was recorded in Trondheim.
- Vocal tracks were recorded from October 2012 at Sunset Sound in Hollywood under sound engineer David Boucher; dialogue was recorded mainly at the Roy E. Disney Animation Building in Burbank. Dave Metzger of Salem, Oregon, arranged and orchestrated. Final orchestrations were recorded at the Eastwood Scoring Stage on the Warner Bros. lot with an 80-piece orchestra and 32 vocalists; songs were recorded July 22 to 24, 2013, and Beck's score on September 3-6 and 9-10. The final re-recording mix was in Dolby Atmos.
- Sound designer Odin Benitez recorded snow and ice effects at a frozen lake at Mammoth Mountain, California; Foley artists received daily deliveries of 50 pounds (22.6 kg) of snow and ice, and five versions of nearly every footstep on snow were recorded. Elsa's footsteps in the ice palace took eight attempts and ended as a mix of three sounds.

## Localization

Frozen was translated and dubbed into 41 languages (The Lion King had been localized into 15); about 200 singers auditioned for the 41 Elsa slots, Elsa's singing and speaking roles were cast separately for almost 15 versions, and the international cast totalled over 900 people across about 1,300 recording sessions. The Italian version received an award for best foreign dubbing worldwide. The page tabulates the film's title in each language, including French "La Reine des neiges" (The Snow Queen), German "Die Eiskonigin - Vollig unverfroren" (The Ice Queen - Unfrozen), Japanese "Ana to Yuki no Joo" (Anna and the Snow Queen), Korean "Gyeoul Wangguk" (The Kingdom of Winter), Russian "Kholodnoe syertse" (Cold Heart) and Mandarin "Bing xue qi yuan" (Magical Tales of Ice and Snow). Unofficial dubs exist in Albanian, Arabic (TV), Karachay-Balkar, Persian and Tagalog.

## Release and home media

- "Frozen was released theatrically in the United States on November 27, 2013, with Get a Horse! (a new Mickey Mouse animated short film)." The premiere was at the El Capitan Theatre in Hollywood on November 19, 2013, "with a five-day limited release there beginning on November 22 before its wide release". (The infobox instead gives the release dates as November 19, 2013 at the El Capitan Theatre and November 22, 2013 in the United States; the lead says the general theatrical release was November 27.)
- "Let It Go" and "In Summer" were previewed at the 2013 D23 Expo, where Menzel performed "Let It Go" live. A teaser trailer was released on June 18, 2013, and the trailer on September 26, 2013. Merchandise went on sale November 6, 2013.
- A sing-along version opened in 2,057 US theaters on January 31, 2014; after the film's wide Japanese release on March 14, 2014, a Japanese sing-along version followed on April 26; a UK sing-along version was released on November 28, 2014.
- Home media: digital download February 25, 2014; Blu-ray and DVD March 18 [2014]; a sing-along reissue announced August 12, 2014 and released on DVD and digital download November 18 of that year; a 4K Ultra HD Blu-ray version in 2019.

wikis.title: Frozen (2013 film): home-media sales, box office, reception, criticism, accolades and legacy
wikis.summary: Part 2 of Wikipedia's Frozen (2013 film) article, covering home-video and streaming figures, the Phase 4 Films lawsuit, worldwide and territory box office, critical response, criticisms, the 'Let It Go' lawsuit, awards, cultural impact, franchise spin-offs and sequels.
wikis.body:
## Home media sales

- Frozen sold 3.2 million units on its Blu-ray and DVD release day; the page calls it "one of the decade's biggest home-video sellers and Amazon's best-selling children's disc of all time", and its digital-download version "the fastest-selling digital release of all time".
- It finished its first US week at number one in unit sales, selling more than three times as many units as the other 19 titles in Nielsen's sales chart combined; 3,969,270 Blu-ray units ($79,266,322) in the first week, half of opening home-media sales.
- By May 4, 2014 it had topped the U.S. home-video sales charts for six of its seven weeks of release.
- United Kingdom: number one on the Official Video Chart; over 500,000 copies in its two-day opening (March 31 - April 1, 2014); more than 1.45 million units in its first three weeks and 2014's biggest-selling video title.
- Japan: 2,025,000 Blu-ray-DVD combination sets in four weeks, the fastest-selling home video to reach two million copies, surpassing Spirited Away's record of 11 weeks; it holds Japan's first-day and first-week home-video sales records.
- By the end of 2014 it had $308,026,545 in U.S. home-media sales; over 18 million units sold by 2015; by July 2018 it was the all-time bestselling Blu-ray release in the United States with over 7.5 million units, "slightly ahead of Avatar".
- Nielsen Media Research calculated 3.056 billion minutes of viewing time between January and June 2025, the ninth most-streamed film in that period.

## Lawsuit against Phase 4 Films

The Walt Disney Company filed a trademark-infringement suit in California federal court in late December 2013 against Phase 4 Films over The Legend of Sarila, retitled Frozen Land in the United States with a similar logo. The case settled by late January 2014: the film had to be distributed under its original title, Phase 4 could not use confusingly similar trademarks or logos, had to pay Disney $100,000 by January 27, 2014, and make "all practicable efforts" to remove Frozen Land copies from stores and online distributors before March 3 of that year.

## Box office

- Original theatrical release: $400.7 million in North America and an estimated $880 million elsewhere, for a worldwide total of $1,280,802,282. Deadline Hollywood estimated a profit of over $400 million.
- Records claimed: fifth-highest-grossing film, highest-grossing animated film, highest-grossing 2013 film, third-highest-grossing Walt Disney Pictures release, eighth-highest-grossing Disney-distributed film.
- Opening weekend worldwide: $110.6 million. It passed $1 billion on March 2, 2014, its 101st day of release - the eighteenth film in cinematic history, seventh Disney-distributed film, fifth non-sequel film, second Disney-distributed 2013 film after Iron Man 3, and first animated film since Toy Story 3.
- Bloomberg Business reported in March 2014 that outside analysts projected total cost at $323 million to $350 million for production, marketing and distribution, and revenue of $1.3 billion across tickets, digital downloads, discs and television rights.

### North America

- "Frozen opened on November 22, 2013, at the El Capitan Theatre in Hollywood for a five-day limited release and earned $342,839 before its wide opening on November 27." It earned $243,390 over that three-day weekend, the seventh-largest per-theater average.
- Wide opening day: $15.2 million (including $1.2 million from Tuesday late-night shows), a record pre-Thanksgiving Wednesday opening ahead of Tangled ($11.9 million) and second-largest overall behind Catching Fire ($20.8 million).
- Three-day weekend $67.4 million (second place, a Walt Disney Animation Studios opening-weekend record); five-day $93.6 million. Female audiences were 57 percent and family audiences 81 percent of the first weekend.
- Second wide weekend: down 53 percent to $31.6 million but rose to first place, a record post-Thanksgiving weekend ahead of Toy Story 2 ($27.8 million). It was the first film since Avatar to reach first place in its sixth weekend of wide release and stayed in the top 10 for sixteen consecutive weekends, "the longest run by any film since 2002".
- On April 25, 2014 it became the nineteenth film to gross $400 million in North America and the fifteenth without a major re-release. Box Office Mojo estimated over 49 million tickets sold in North America.
- It is listed as the twenty-sixth-highest-grossing film in North America, third-highest-grossing 2013 film, fifth-highest-grossing animated film, twelfth-highest-grossing 3-D film and second-highest-grossing Walt Disney Animation Studios film.

### Outside North America

- Highest-grossing animated film in South Korea, Denmark and Venezuela; highest-grossing Walt Disney Animation Studios film in more than 45 territories.
- It opened outside North America on the same weekend as the wide North American release with $16.7 million from sixteen markets, and topped the international box office on January 10-12, 2014 ($27.8 million) and February 7-9, 2014 ($24 million).
- Largest openings: China (five-day, $14.3 million), Russia and the CIS ($11.9 million including previews), Japan (three-day, $9.73 million). Top markets after North America: Japan ($247.6 million), South Korea ($76.6 million), and the United Kingdom, Ireland and Malta ($65.7 million).
- In Japan it is listed as the third-highest-grossing film of all time, second-highest-grossing imported film behind Titanic, and highest-grossing Disney film; it topped Japan's box office for sixteen consecutive weekends until Maleficent passed it.

### Pre-release commercial forecasts

Ray Subers (Box Office Mojo) predicted $185 million in North America; Boxoffice forecast $170,000,000; Chris Agar of ScreenRant did not expect it to pass Catching Fire; Clayton Dillard (Slant) and Brad Brevet (Ropeofsilicon.com) commented on the marketing. After the $93.6 million Thanksgiving opening, most watchers predicted $250-$300 million in North America, with Box Office Mojo repeating $250 million.

## Critical response

- Rotten Tomatoes: "89% of 251 critics' reviews are positive, with an average rating of 7.7/10"; consensus: "Beautifully animated, smartly written, and stocked with singalong songs, Frozen adds another worthy entry to the Disney canon."
- Metacritic: score of 75 from 48 reviews, "generally favorable reviews". CinemaScore: a rare A+ grade.
- Fandango surveys of 1,000 ticket buyers: 75 percent had seen the film at least once and 52 percent twice; 55 percent named "Let It Go" their favourite song, "Do You Want to Build a Snowman?" 21 percent and "For the First Time in Forever" nine percent.
- Ranked the seventh-best film of 2013 by Richard Corliss of Time and Kyle Smith of the New York Post.
- Positive notices quoted from Alonso Duralde (TheWrap), Todd McCarthy (The Hollywood Reporter: "You can practically see the Broadway musical Frozen is destined to become"), Scott Mendelson (Forbes), the Los Angeles Times, Owen Gleiberman (Entertainment Weekly, B+), Richard Corliss, Richard Roeper, Michael Phillips, Stephen Holden and Emma Dibdin (Digital Spy, five out of five).
- Mixed and negative: Scott Foundas (Variety) called it "formulaic"; The Seattle Times gave two out of four stars; Joe Williams (St. Louis Post-Dispatch) faulted the plot; Christy Lemire gave two-and-a-half out of four on RogerEbert.com.
- Norwegian Sami media cited the film for showcasing Sami culture; Sami President Aili Keskitalo praised composer Frode Fjellheim in her 2014 New Year's speech.

## Criticism

- Portrayal of emotions: head of animation Lino DiSalvo was accused of sexism for saying "Historically speaking, animating female characters are really, really difficult, because they have to go through these range of emotions, but you have to keep them pretty". A Disney spokesperson told Time the quote was widely misinterpreted; Lee said it was taken out of context; in an August 2014 interview DiSalvo said translating emotional range onto a CG character is "one of the most difficult parts of the process. Male. Female. Snowman. Animal."
- Perceived LGBTQ parallels: some conservative Christian commentators said the film promotes homosexuality, reading Elsa's difference and "Let It Go" as allusions to coming out; others saw Elsa as a role model for LGBT youth. Akash Nikolas wrote in The Atlantic about Disney films appealing to queer children; Robert Geal wrote in Film International that the film perpetuates conservative notions of sexuality and gender. Lee was noncommittal: "I don't like to say anything [...] let the fans talk. I think it's up to them."
- "Let It Go" lawsuit: Chilean singer Jaime Ciero sued Demi Lovato, Idina Menzel, Walt Disney Animation Studios and others on November 24, 2017, alleging infringement of his 2008 song "Volar". In May 2018 the court released songwriters Robert Lopez and Kristen Anderson-Lopez because of the three-year statute of limitations; Ciero dropped the suit in May 2019.

## Accolades

Two nominations and the Best Animated Feature award at the 71st Golden Globe Awards (the first Walt Disney Animation Studios film to win that category); Academy Awards for Best Animated Feature and Best Original Song ("Let It Go"); the BAFTA Award for Best Animated Film; five Annie Awards including Best Animated Feature; Critics' Choice Awards for Best Animated Feature and Best Original Song; nominations at the Satellite Awards. At the 57th Annual Grammy Awards the soundtrack won Best Compilation Soundtrack For Visual Media and was nominated for Best Score Soundtrack For Visual Media (Christophe Beck as composer), and "Let It Go" won Best Song Written For Visual Media (Anderson-Lopez and Lopez as songwriters, Menzel as performer).

## Cultural impact

- In spring and summer 2014 the film's popularity with children in the US and UK was widely noted; The Guardian called it "Frozen-mania". Commentators included UK prime minister David Cameron and actors Ben Affleck, Kevin Costner and Vince Vaughn.
- In an April 2014 NPR interview with Terry Gross the Lopezes said they were "just trying to tell a story that resonated" and "didn't suck".
- Joel Stein of Time wrote in May about his son Laszlo; Kristen Bell told the boy: "I did not know that people would not let it go. No pun intended."
- In a December 2014 Hollywood Reporter interview Lee described apologising to parents still listening to the songs, and spoke about using the film's female characters to inspire her daughter.
- In a mid-2014 BabyCenter list of the 100 most-used baby names, Elsa ranked 88th, its first appearance on that chart. On the 2014 year-end Google list Frozen was the year's most-searched film, and Google Play named the film and its soundtrack movie and album of the year. The Writers Guild Foundation listed Frozen among the best scripts of 2010s film and television.
- The film became the subject of academic publications; the University of East Anglia hosted "Symfrozium", a May 12, 2015 academic conference.

## Franchise

- In January 2014 Iger announced a Broadway musical adaptation; he moved from calling Frozen's "franchise potential" in February 2014 to "probably" one of Disney's "top five franchises" in May.
- A US and international merchandise shortage in April 2014 pushed limited-edition doll and costume resale prices over $1,000 on eBay; by the time it was resolved in early November 2014 Disney had sold over three million Frozen costumes in North America. Park meet-and-greet waits regularly exceeded four hours in February 2014.
- Disney Parks staged Frozen Summer Fun at Disney's Hollywood Studios; on September 12, 2014 Disney announced Epcot's Maelstrom would close and be replaced by a Frozen attraction opening in early 2016; a live Frozen musical stage show opened at the Hyperion Theater in Disney California Adventure on May 27, 2016, replacing Aladdin. By August 2014 Random House had sold over eight million Frozen-related books; tour operators added Norway tours.
- Once Upon a Time ran a Frozen-inspired arc in its fourth season, broadcast September to December 2014. ABC aired the special The Story of Frozen: Making a Disney Animated Classic on September 2, 2014, where Lasseter announced the short Frozen Fever, which debuted in theaters with Cinderella on March 13, 2015. Disney on Ice premiered a touring show at Amway Center, Orlando, on September 4, 2014.
- Olaf's Frozen Adventure was announced during The Making of Frozen: Return to Arendelle for winter 2017; in June 2017 Lasseter said the 21-minute special would have a limited theatrical release; it premiered with Pixar's Coco on November 22, 2017 and aired on ABC on December 14. Arendelle appears in the 2019 game Kingdom Hearts III with the film's voice cast.
- Musical parody: Wicked Frozen premiered in New York City in November 2014, satirising both Frozen and Wicked; Time Out described it as "Like an ice capade infused with psychedelic drugs".
- Sequels: "Frozen 2, a feature-length sequel, was released on November 22, 2019. It outgrossed the first film at the box office... Frozen 3 is scheduled to be released in November 2027, while a fourth film is in development."

## Note on this part

The rest of this part is the article's numbered reference list (publication citations), plus "See also" links to List of Disney animated films based on fairy tales and List of Disney theatrical animated feature films.
