wikis.title: Frozen 2 (2019 film)
wikis.summary: The English Wikipedia article on Frozen 2, the 2019 Walt Disney Animation Studios sequel, covering its credits, plot, production, music, themes, release, box office and reception.
wikis.body:
## The film

- *Frozen 2* (stylized *Frozen II*) is "a 2019 American animated musical fantasy film produced by Walt Disney Animation Studios", the second film in the *Frozen* franchise after the 2013 film, set three years after it.
- Directed by Chris Buck and Jennifer Lee, written by Lee from a story with Marc Smith, Kristen Anderson-Lopez and Robert Lopez, produced by Peter Del Vecho, with the voices of Kristen Bell, Idina Menzel, Josh Gad and Jonathan Groff.
- Christophe Beck scored the film; Anderson-Lopez and Lopez wrote the songs. Running time 103 minutes; budget $150 million (the page also says "approximately $150 million").
- Premiered November 7, 2019 at the Dolby Theatre in Hollywood, Los Angeles, and released in the United States on November 22, 2019, having been moved forward five days from November 27.
- Grossed $1.453 billion worldwide - $477.4 million in the United States and Canada, $976.3 million elsewhere - and passed $1 billion globally on December 15, 2019.
- Reviews were "generally positive": Rotten Tomatoes 77% from 336 reviews (average 6.7/10), Metacritic 64/100 from 47 critics, CinemaScore A-.
- It was nominated for Best Original Song at the 92nd Academy Awards, with eight Annie Award nominations (two wins), a BAFTA, two Critics' Choice and two Golden Globe nominations.
- A sequel, *Frozen 3*, "is set for release on November 24, 2027", and a fourth film is in development.

## Production

Greenlit after a March 12, 2015 announcement at Disney's annual shareholders' meeting, following 2014 statements from Alan F. Horn and Bob Iger that a sequel would not be forced. Voice recording began in September 2017; Allison Schroeder joined the script in August 2018. The team researched in Norway, Finland and Iceland, and worked with Sámi experts through Verdett, an advisory group formed by agreement between the Walt Disney Company, the Saami Council and the Sámi parliaments of Finland, Norway and Sweden. About 800 people, 80 of them animators, worked on the film; after a San Diego test screening the team created 61 new shots and redid another 35. A documentary series, *Into the Unknown: Making Frozen 2* - 1,300 hours shot over 115 days, edited to six episodes - was released June 26, 2020.

## Themes

The Northuldra are modelled on the Sámi, and the dam subplot is read as alluding to Norway's Virdnejávr Dam, built on the Altaelva river from 1979 to 1981. Critics quoted include Inkoo Kang on reparations and colonialism, Jennifer Baldwin on trauma and environmental repair, and Lauren Dundes on gender.

## Internal contradictions

- The lead says the film "was translated into 46 languages"; the release section says it was localized "into 45 languages by its original theatrical release date".
- It is called the third-highest-grossing film of 2019 worldwide, and separately the fourth highest-grossing film of 2019 in the United States and Canada.
- The page calls it the second-highest-grossing animated film of all time, and reports that according to Disney - which did not count the 2019 *Lion King* remake as animated - it was the highest-grossing animated film at that time.

The second part of the capture is the article's citation list, works cited, further reading, external links, navigation boxes and categories; it states no publication or last-updated date.

wikis.title: Frozen 2 (2019 film): plot, production, release and reception
wikis.summary: Part 1 of the English Wikipedia article on Frozen 2, giving the film's credits and infobox figures, plot, voice cast, production, music, thematic analysis, marketing and release, and its box office and critical reception.
wikis.body:
## The film

- *Frozen 2* (stylized *Frozen II*) is described as "a 2019 American animated musical fantasy film produced by Walt Disney Animation Studios", the second film in the *Frozen* franchise, following the 2013 film.
- Directed by Chris Buck and Jennifer Lee; screenplay by Lee, "from a story they conceived with Marc Smith, Kristen Anderson-Lopez, and Robert Lopez"; produced by Peter Del Vecho.
- Voices of Kristen Bell, Idina Menzel, Josh Gad and Jonathan Groff. Cinematography Mohit Kallianpur; edited by Jeff Draheim; Christophe Beck (score), Robert Lopez and Kristen Anderson-Lopez (songs).
- Distributed by Walt Disney Studios Motion Pictures, "distributed under the Walt Disney Pictures banner".
- Release dates given in the infobox: November 7, 2019 (Dolby Theatre) and November 22, 2019 (United States).
- Running time 103 minutes; country United States; language English; budget $150 million; box office $1.453 billion.
- Set three years after the events of the first film.
- A sequel, *Frozen 3*, "is set for release on November 24, 2027", and "a fourth film is in development".

## Plot

Agnarr tells Elsa and Anna that their grandfather King Runeard built a dam in the Northuldra homeland, the Enchanted Forest; a fight followed, Runeard died, the elemental spirits of earth, fire, water and air disappeared and a wall of mist trapped everyone in the forest. Three years after Elsa's coronation she hears a voice, awakens the spirits and the kingdom is evacuated. Elsa, Anna, Olaf, Kristoff and Sven travel to the forest, broker a truce between Arendellian soldiers and the Northuldra, and learn their mother Iduna was Northuldran. Elsa reaches Ahtohallan, tames the water spirit Nøkk, and learns the dam was a ruse to weaken the Northuldra and that Runeard murdered their leader. Elsa freezes; Anna lures the earth giants (Jötunn) into destroying the dam; Elsa thaws, freezes the resulting flood and saves Arendelle, revives Olaf, and abdicates to Anna, becoming protector of the Enchanted Forest. A post-credits scene has Olaf recount the events to Marshmallow and the Snowgies.

## Figures the page gives

- Budget "approximately $150 million".
- About 800 people, 80 of them animators, worked on the film.
- 1,300 hours of documentary footage shot in 115 days.
- Trailer released February 13, 2019; viewed 116.4 million times in its first 24 hours.
- Worldwide gross $1.453 billion: $477.4 million in the United States and Canada, $976.3 million in other territories.

## Contradictions within the page

- Language count: the lead says the film "was translated into 46 languages", while the release section says it "was localized by Disney Character Voices International into 45 languages by its original theatrical release date" (it adds that *Frozen* had been translated into 41 languages).
- Ranking for 2019: the lead and box office section call it "the third-highest-grossing film of 2019" (worldwide), while the box office section also says it left theatres by March 19, 2020, "making it the fourth highest-grossing film of 2019 in the United States and Canada".
- Highest-grossing animated film: the page calls it "the second-highest-grossing animated film of all time", and separately reports that "according to Disney (who did not consider the 2019 Lion King remake an animated film but a live-action reboot), Frozen 2 was the highest-grossing animated film (surpassing Frozen) at that time".

wikis.title: Frozen 2 voice cast
wikis.summary: The voice actors the article lists for Frozen 2 and the characters they play.
wikis.body:
- Idina Menzel as Elsa, queen of Arendelle and Anna's older sister, with magical ice powers; Mattea Conforti and Eva Bella as young Elsa.
- Kristen Bell as Anna, princess of Arendelle, who becomes queen after Elsa's abdication; Hadley Gannaway and Livvy Stubenrauch as young Anna.
- Josh Gad as Olaf, a snowman created by Elsa.
- Jonathan Groff as Kristoff, an ice harvester and Anna's boyfriend; Groff also voices Sven and several other reindeer.
- Martha Plimpton as Northuldra chief Yelena; Sterling K. Brown as Arendelle lieutenant Mattias; Jason Ritter as Ryder; Rachel Matthews as Honeymaren, Ryder's sister.
- Evan Rachel Wood as Iduna, with Delaney Rose Stein as young Iduna; Alfred Molina as Agnarr, with Jackson Stein as young Agnarr; Jeremy Sisto as Runeard; Ciarán Hinds as the Rock Troll head Pabbie; Aurora as "the voice"; Alan Tudyk as a guard, a Northuldran leader and an Arendellian soldier; Paul Briggs reprising Marshmallow in the post-credits scene.
- The voice of Agnarr "was changed from Maurice LaMarche to Molina". Wood "was cast because her voice resembled Menzel and Bell's".

wikis.title: Conception and development of Frozen 2
wikis.summary: How the article says the sequel came about, from 2014 statements through the March 2015 announcement to script, casting and test screenings.
wikis.body:
- March 31, 2014: producer Peter Del Vecho said he, Chris Buck and Jennifer Lee collaborated well and he envisioned another *Frozen*-related project.
- The following month, Walt Disney Studios chairman Alan F. Horn said a sequel would not be immediately forthcoming because the studio was focused on the Broadway musical adaptation.
- In a May 2014 CNBC interview with David Faber, Disney CEO Bob Iger said the company would not force a sequel, and that the franchise "is something that is kind of forever for the company", similar to *The Lion King*.
- June 10, 2014: Lee confirmed CCO John Lasseter had authorized her and Buck to explore a possible sequel. Buck: "The one thing that we did right away was to figure out what would be satisfying for Anna and Elsa at the end of the movie." They decided to end with Anna becoming queen and Elsa "free".
- March 12, 2015: Iger, Lasseter and Josh Gad announced at Disney's annual shareholders' meeting in San Francisco that a full-length sequel was in development, with Buck and Lee directing and Del Vecho producing. Lasseter: "At the Walt Disney Animation Studio, as with Pixar, when we do a sequel, it is because the filmmakers who created the original have created an idea that is so good that it's worthy of these characters."
- The team travelled to Norway, Finland and Iceland for background research and made Elsa a "mythic hero" and Anna a "fairytale hero".
- Allison Schroeder was hired in August 2018 to assist Lee with the script; Lee was credited as screenwriter and Schroeder with additional screenplay material. Budget approximately $150 million.
- Voice recording began September 2017 (Menzel started a couple of weeks later because of a concert tour). In July 2018 *Variety* reported Wood and Brown were in talks.
- First completed scenes were test screened at the Annecy International Animated Film Festival in June 2019, where Becky Bresee and effects-animation head Marlon West said the film was "still in production, with seven weeks of animation to be completed and 10 weeks of special effects".
- Filmmakers worked with Sámi experts through Verdett, an advisory group resulting from an agreement between the Walt Disney Company, the Saami Council and the Sámi parliaments of Finland, Norway and Sweden.
- Anderson-Lopez confirmed Elsa would have no female love interest; Lee told *The New York Times*' Maureen Dowd that Elsa's main audience did not seem ready for such a relationship. Lee said the film would not take elements from *Once Upon a Time*'s Frozen storyline.
- After a first test screening in San Diego, adults liked the film but children found it hard to follow; the team clarified the Voice's identity and Elsa's transformation, added comedy and shots of Bruni the fire salamander, and replaced an expository scene with Olaf's recap of *Frozen*. Animators created 61 new shots and redid another 35; about a dozen animators and artists worked two months on an Olaf resurrection scene that was cut.
- The last major animation scene completed was "Show Yourself"; Del Vecho said it "required all of the resources at the studio" to finish on time.

wikis.title: Design and animation of Frozen 2
wikis.summary: The costume design, animation staff and software the article credits for Frozen 2.
wikis.body:
- Designer Griselda Sastrawinata-Lemay said the costume and character design process was the most intricate of any animated film; the team used Marvelous Designer, a CGI program, to drape clothing.
- Anna's outfit was inspired by the Norwegian folk *bunad* worn during the 1840s and 1850s. Anna lost her *Frozen* pigtail braid because she is three years older. Elsa's ageing was inspired by Alexander McQueen and Elie Saab; designers created a tailored coat with a double-panel cape and epaulettes.
- Embroidery used a curve-based method: a program interpreted two-dimensional designs as line strokes rendered as curves, supporting free-form stitching with threads of various widths, colours and densities.
- About 800 people, 80 of them animators, were involved. Tony Smeed and Becky Bresee were heads of animation; Hyun-Min Lee replaced Bresee as supervising animator for Anna; Wayne Unten again supervised Elsa; Steve Goldberg supervised visual effects; Scott Beattie was director of cinematography layout and Mohit Kallianpur director of cinematography lighting.
- Unten showed animators scenes of superheroes such as Frozone as examples of what to avoid. Elsa's movements were modelled on modern dance, particularly Martha Graham's work. The personal flurry effect was difficult enough that the directors had Elsa put a permafrost coating on Olaf instead.
- The effects team used two internally developed applications, Vegetation Asset and Fire Tree. Anna's hair was animated with Quicksilver, developed for *Moana* (2016); Elsa's hair used the lighting software Beast. Animators spent about eight months creating Nøkk, with effects supervised by Erin Ramos; a tool called Swoop was developed for Gale, the wind spirit.
- *Frozen*'s greatest difficulty was winter snow; *Frozen 2* is set in fall and its main challenge was depicting wind consistently.

wikis.title: Frozen 2 music and soundtrack
wikis.summary: The songwriters, score and soundtrack album details the article gives.
wikis.body:
- Robert Lopez and Kristen Anderson-Lopez returned from *Frozen* to write the songs, and Christophe Beck returned as composer.
- The soundtrack album was released on November 15, 2019, after the release of Panic! at the Disco's version of "Into the Unknown". The seven-song album also contains a remix of "Reindeer(s) Are Better Than People" from *Frozen*.
- Beck said the score conveys Elsa and Anna's emotional growth, "matured and introduc[ing] more sophisticated musical concepts and thematic elements", and wanted it to reflect the film's complex, intense imagery.
- Anderson-Lopez described the album's theme as a "meta-story". A camera crew sent to the Lopez home in Brooklyn was found intrusive, and the composers did most of their work off-camera.
- The Voice's four-note call, derived from the Latin sequence "Dies irae", is delivered in a manner resembling the Scandinavian music form kulning.
- Lopez said the first draft of "Show Yourself" was very different from its final version.

wikis.title: Thematic analysis of Frozen 2
wikis.summary: Readings of the film the article reports, on the Sámi, colonialism and reparations, environmental trauma and gender.
wikis.body:
- The Northuldra are modelled on the Sámi people, indigenous to Scandinavia and north-western Russia. The article notes that in 1609 King Christian IV of Denmark wrote that the Sámi were adept at magic and that no mercy should be granted in cases involving Sámi sorcery, and that Nordic missionaries confiscated or destroyed religious items and sites and built churches to supplant Sámi shamanism.
- The dam subplot is said to allude to Norway's Virdnejávr Dam: a hydroelectric power station was built on the Altaelva river in Norway from 1979 to 1981, and the dam flooded a Sámi village, disrupting traditional hunting and herding.
- Trude Fonneland wrote that a female divinity emphasized female contributions, with themes of unity, courage, hope, friendship and truth.
- *Slate* critic Inkoo Kang said the film was obviously influenced by Sámi history but the Northuldra may also be read as displaced Native Americans, with Arendelle representing the United States' colonial past, "evocative of the embellished life of Pocahontas", and that the film promotes reparations for past atrocities.
- Matt Goldberg wrote that the ending's symbolism is undercut by Elsa saving Arendelle instead of the kingdom being rebuilt elsewhere.
- Jennifer Baldwin described the film as being about trauma, transformation and faith communities' more active role in environmental repair, and said it encourages audiences to adopt sustainable practices; the article adds the film can introduce young children to environmental issues such as climate change.
- Sociologist Lauren Dundes wrote of Elsa and the mythological horse Nøkk that "her skills as a horse whisperer do not threaten men's ascendancy [...] These themes show how Disney balked at modernizing Elsa, retreating to outdated conceptions of gender roles". Nia Kurniawati wrote that the film's feminist message was subtle and realistic.
- The article notes racial issues are "mitigated" by making Elsa and Anna half Northuldran, with their mother depicted as a heroine who saved King Agnarr.

wikis.title: Frozen 2 marketing, release and home video
wikis.summary: Trailer, brand partnerships, premiere, theatrical and home releases, and the Disney+ date change.
wikis.body:
- A *Frozen 2* DVD appears in the 2016 film *Zootopia*, alongside *Moana* and the unproduced *Gigantic*, before the first trailer.
- The first trailer was released February 13, 2019 and was viewed 116.4 million times in its first 24 hours, "the most-watched animated film trailer until the teaser of Inside Out 2 (2024) surpassed that record in November 2023".
- Neil deGrasse Tyson commented that "water crystals have hexagonal 'six-fold' symmetry" but the preview poster had a four-sided snowflake; Lee replied that it was not really a snowflake, the four sides representing the four elemental spirits and its centre Elsa, the fifth spirit.
- Disney partnered with 140 other brands worldwide, "the highest number of brands for a Disney animated film", including Enterprise Rent-A-Car, McDonald's and Lego. Cast appearances included a Friendsgiving stunt night on ABC, introductions on *The Masked Singer* and a Women of Impact program on Nat Geo Wild. In November 2019 Bell said of the cast's schedules: "Time [was] not there".
- The 103-minute film premiered November 7, 2019 at the Dolby Theatre in Hollywood, Los Angeles. It was initially scheduled for release on November 27 but "was moved forward five days, to November 22, 2019".
- A sing-along version was released January 17, 2020. The film was localized into 45 languages by its original theatrical release date; a Northern Sami version, *Jikŋon 2*, was released to honour the people's contributions.
- Walt Disney Studios Home Entertainment released it for digital download February 11, 2020 and on Blu-ray and DVD February 25, alongside 4K Ultra HD Blu-ray, Ultimate Collector's Edition and 4KUHD Blu-ray SteelBook editions. Special features include a sing-along audio recording, a presentation of the Nordic mythology behind the Enchanted Forest, musical clips, 29 translated versions of "Into the Unknown", and deleted music and scenes.
- The Disney+ premiere, initially scheduled for June 26, 2020, was moved up to March 15 in the United States and March 17 in Canada, the Netherlands, Australia and New Zealand due to the COVID-19 pandemic.
- Documentary series: Megan Harding, working with Lincoln Square Productions, commuted from New York City to Burbank, California and shot 1,300 hours of footage in 115 days between December 2018 and the November 2019 world premiere, edited down to six episodes of about 35 to 45 minutes. Her crew was asked to leave only once, when the production team decided the mysterious voice's identity. *Into the Unknown: Making Frozen 2* was released June 26, 2020.

wikis.title: Frozen 2 box office
wikis.summary: The domestic, international and worldwide grosses and opening figures the article reports.
wikis.body:
- Grossed $477.4 million in the United States and Canada and $976.3 million in other territories, for a worldwide total of $1.453 billion.
- Called the third-highest-grossing film of 2019, the tenth-highest-grossing film of all time and the second-highest-grossing animated film of all time. It passed $1 billion globally on December 15, 2019.
- *Deadline Hollywood* calculated net profit as $599 million, placing it second on their list of 2019's "Most Valuable Blockbusters".
- According to Disney, which did not count the 2019 *Lion King* remake as an animated film but a live-action reboot, *Frozen 2* was the highest-grossing animated film at that time, surpassing *Frozen*.
- Comscore analyst Paul Dergarabedian said the film was "perfectly positioned to play well into 2020"; its success was attributed to a release date near Thanksgiving.
- Released November 22, 2019 alongside *A Beautiful Day in the Neighborhood* and *21 Bridges* in 4,440 theatres: 2,500 in 3D, 800 in premium large format (including 400 IMAX) and 235 in D-Box/4DX.
- First day $41.8 million, including $8.5 million from Thursday night previews; debut weekend $130 million, "the highest opening for an animated film that month". Audience mostly female, approximately 70 percent families.
- Second weekend $85.6 million, down 34 percent, with $125 million over the five-day Thanksgiving weekend; third weekend $34.7 million. Domestic gross topped $400 million by December 29. It left theatres by March 19, 2020, the fourth highest-grossing film of 2019 in the United States and Canada.
- Worldwide opening weekend $228.2 million in 37 markets, for a global debut total of $358.5 million, surpassing the 2019 *Lion King* remake as the highest-grossing opening for an animated title until *The Super Mario Bros. Movie* (2023).
- Best all-time animated opening in the United Kingdom ($17.8 million) and France ($13.4 million); biggest start for a Pixar or Disney Animation title in China ($53 million), Japan ($18.2 million), Germany ($14.9 million) and Spain ($5.8 million); third-biggest opening of any film in South Korea ($31.5 million).
- Second week in the United Kingdom $11.4 million, for $35.3 million there. By January 5, 2020 offshore gross exceeded $875.3 million. As of July 2021 top international markets were Japan ($122.6 million), China ($122.3 million), South Korea ($95.5 million), the United Kingdom ($69.7 million), Germany ($60.6 million) and France ($53.9 million).

wikis.title: Frozen 2 critical response and accolades
wikis.summary: Aggregate scores, named critics' praise and criticism, and the awards the article lists.
wikis.body:
- Generally positive reviews. Rotten Tomatoes: 77% approval based on 336 professional reviews, average rating 6.7/10, with the consensus "Frozen II can't quite recapture the showstopping feel of its predecessor, but it remains a dazzling adventure into the unknown." Metacritic: 64 out of 100 from 47 critics, "generally favorable". CinemaScore average grade A− (lower than *Frozen*'s A+); PostTrak 4.5 out of five stars on opening day.
- Manohla Dargis (*The New York Times*): "Frozen II continues in the same nonthreatening, emancipatory vein, jumping to life when Elsa responds to the siren's call. As before, the songs by Kristen Anderson-Lopez and Robert Lopez are pleasantly melodious with lyrics that can have the quality of a confession, as if a friend were sharing her inner-voice struggles." She called the narrative a "pink world of adventure and aspirational uplift".
- Nell Minow (RogerEbert.com) noted the film's frank depiction of issues understandable by all ages and its autumnal palette, but criticized the excessively detailed narrative.
- Peter Travers (*Rolling Stone*) called the animation stunning and the music "tantalizing earworms"; Simran Hans (*The Guardian*) compared the narrative to real-world climate change efforts; Todd McCarthy (*The Hollywood Reporter*) praised its "catchy songs", "easy-to-like characters" and "astonishing backdrops".
- John Anderson (*The Wall Street Journal*) said the sequel was not innovative and criticized its flawed narrative and low-quality music compared with *Frozen*. Ben Travis (*Empire*) said the narrative relied too much on mythology and hazy backstories. Oliver Jones (*Observer*) said the film's energy and originality were overly focused on the sisters. Reviewers for the *Los Angeles Times* and *The Washington Post* cited its complicated story and dark tone.
- Accolades: a Best Original Song nomination at the 92nd Academy Awards; eight Annie Award nominations (winning two); a British Academy Film Award; two Critics' Choice Movie Awards; and two Golden Globe Awards.

wikis.title: Frozen 2 article: citations, works cited and navigation
wikis.summary: Part 2 of the Wikipedia article on Frozen 2, which is the reference apparatus - citation list, works cited, further reading, external links, navigation boxes and categories - with no further article prose.
wikis.body:
This part of the page carries no article text about the film; it is the citation list and site apparatus.

## Works cited

- Baldwin, Jennifer (2020). "Trauma, Eco-spirituality, and Transformation in *Frozen 2*: Guides for the Church and Climate Change". *Dialog: A Journal of Theology* 59 (2), Wiley-Blackwell, pp. 60-61.
- Dundes, Lauren (2020). "Elsa as Horse Whisperer in Disney's *Frozen 2*: Opportunity 'Nokk's to Quash Gender Stereotypes". *Social Sciences* 86 (9), McDaniel College, p. 11.
- Fonneland, Trude (2020). "Religion-Making in the Disney Feature Film, *Frozen II*: Indigenous Religion and Dynamics of Agency". *Religions* 11 (9), University of Tromsø, p. 430.
- Kittelsen, Theodor; Østby, Leif (1975). *Theodor Kittelsen*. Dreyer. ISBN 978-8-20901-226-0.
- March, Julia (2019). *Disney Frozen 2: The Magical Guide*. Dorling Kindersley. ISBN 978-0-241-35767-5.
- Wilkins, Jonathan (2019). *Frozen 2: The Official Movie Special*. Titan Publishing Group. ISBN 978-1-78773-227-8.

## Further reading and external links

## Apparatus

wikis.title: Frozen 3 (upcoming Disney animated film)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on Frozen 3, the upcoming Walt Disney Animation Studios sequel written and directed by Jennifer Lee, covering its cast, development, marketing and November 24, 2027 release date.
wikis.body:
## Overview

- "Frozen 3 (stylized as Frozen III) is an upcoming American animated musical fantasy film written and directed by Jennifer Lee."
- "Produced by Walt Disney Animation Studios, it is the third feature film in the Frozen franchise, following Frozen II."
- "Kristen Bell, Idina Menzel, Josh Gad, and Jonathan Groff will reprise their roles from the previous films, with a new cast member set to join the franchise. The film's antagonist will be Elsa and Anna's mysterious family member."
- Distributed by Walt Disney Studios Motion Pictures; a note adds it is "Distributed by Walt Disney Studios Motion Pictures through the Walt Disney Pictures banner."
- Country: United States. Language: English. The infobox leaves producer, cinematography, editing, music, runtime, budget and gross blank, each marked "MUST HAVE RELIABLE SOURCE".

## Release

- Infobox release date: November 24, 2027.
- "Frozen 3 is scheduled to be theatrically released in the United States by Walt Disney Pictures on November 24, 2027."

## Voice cast

- Kristen Bell as Anna; Idina Menzel as Elsa; Josh Gad as Olaf; Jonathan Groff as Kristoff.

## Development

- "In February 2023, during the Q1 earnings call, Disney CEO Bob Iger announced that a sequel to Frozen 2 (2019) was in active development."
- "Shortly thereafter, MovieWeb exclusively reported that Josh Gad would return as the voice of Olaf in the film."
- June 2023: "Jennifer Lee revealed that she would not be returning to direct."
- August 2024, at the D23 convention: "Lee showed the first look concept art of the film."
- September 2024: "it was revealed that Lee would be directing the film after all, with her stepping down as Chief Creative Officer for Walt Disney Animation Studios."
- November 2025: "Gad was officially confirmed to be reprising his role, alongside Idina Menzel and Kristen Bell, while Once Upon a Studio (2023) director Trent Correy signed on as the film's co-director."
- February 2026: "Gad began recording voice work for his role as Olaf."

## Marketing

- In an interview with License Global "that same month" (the page's wording, following the February 2026 item), Paul Glitter, "the executive vice president of global brand commercialization at Disney Consumer Products, revealed that a new Frozen short film would be released in October."
- Glitter said: "we're excited to kick off the countdown to Frozen 3 with a new short this October, ahead of our biggest ever cross-company movie marketing campaign in 2027."
- "The first trailer was released at D23 in August 2026 and attendees secretly filmed it illegally during the event. Many people then posted it to social media. Disney hasn't released the official teaser trailer on YouTube yet."

## Sequel (Frozen 4)

- "In November 2023, Disney CEO Bob Iger announced that a fourth Frozen film was in active development."
- "At the 2024 D23 convention, Lee confirmed that a fourth film was being planned. The film was officially confirmed the following month with Lee and Marc Smith set to write the script."

## From the cited article titles on the page

- "Kristen Bell, Idina Menzel & Josh Gad Net Record-Breaking Pay For Frozen 3 & 4" (Screen Rant, November 20, 2025) and "Disney Megadeal: Kristen Bell, Josh Gad, Idina Menzel Score $60 Million Packages for 'Frozen' 3 and 4" (TheWrap, November 19, 2025).
- "'Frozen 3' 'Royal Wedding' Between Anna and Kristoff Is Crashed by New Villain in First-Look" (The Hollywood Reporter, August 15, 2026).

wikis.title: The Lord of the Rings: The Two Towers (2002 film)
wikis.summary: The English Wikipedia article on The Lord of the Rings: The Two Towers, covering the 2002 Peter Jackson film's credits, plot, cast, its departures from Tolkien, the New Zealand production and Weta's Gollum, and its record-setting box office and acclaim.
wikis.body:
## The film

- "*The Lord of the Rings: The Two Towers* is a 2002 epic fantasy film directed by Peter Jackson from a screenplay by Fran Walsh, Philippa Boyens, Stephen Sinclair, and Jackson, based on 1954's *The Two Towers*", the second instalment of the trilogy and the sequel to *The Fellowship of the Ring* (2001).
- Produced by Barrie M. Osborne, Fran Walsh and Peter Jackson; cinematography Andrew Lesnie; edited by Michael J. Horton; score by Howard Shore. WingNut Films and New Line Cinema; distributed by New Line Cinema.
- Premiered 5 December 2002 at the Ziegfeld Theatre in New York City, released 18 December 2002 in the United States and 19 December 2002 in New Zealand. Running time 179 minutes; budget $94 million.
- "The Two Towers was financed and distributed by American studio New Line Cinema, but filmed and edited entirely in Jackson's native New Zealand, concurrently with the other two parts of the trilogy" - the trilogy was shot between 11 October 1999 and 22 December 2000.

## Production

Alan Lee's 1:35-scale Helm's Deep was among the first miniatures built and part of the 45-minute video that sold the project to New Line; Jackson planned the battle with 40,000 toy soldiers, and the battle took about three months to film with 500 extras. Edoras took six months to build on Mount Sunday. Weta Digital doubled its staff of 260 and produced "73 minutes of digital effects with 800 shots". Gollum, begun in late 1998, was to be solely CGI until Jackson saw Andy Serkis's audition tape; the model was redesigned in 2001 and every earlier shot reanimated over Christmas 2001 in two months, with skin tones taking four hours a frame to render. Treebeard took 28 to 48 hours a frame, with a 14-foot puppet built for the scenes with Merry and Pippin.

## Reception

- Opened to $26 million on its first day, $62 million over its US and Canadian opening weekend and $101.5 million over five days; $99.4 million overseas from 25 countries, then "the highest international opening weekend", and a $189.9 million worldwide opening, then the highest of all time.
- The highest-grossing film of 2002 worldwide. Rotten Tomatoes 95% from 288 reviews; Metacritic 87/100 from 39 reviews ("universal acclaim"); CinemaScore "A".
- At the 75th Academy Awards it won Best Visual Effects and Best Sound Editing from six nominations including Best Picture. Other wins include two BAFTAs, a Grammy for Howard Shore's score, a Hugo Award, an MTV Movie Award for Gollum and four Saturn Awards. "My precious." is #85 on AFI's 100 Years...100 Movie Quotes.
- Home video: 3.5 million DVD units in five days and $22.8 million in rentals, breaking *The Bourne Identity*'s record; 16.4 million copies and $305.4 million by December 2003, second only to *Finding Nemo* for 2003. The extended edition (18 November 2003) added 44 minutes of new material for a 235-minute runtime.

## Conflicting figures the page gives

- Worldwide gross of the original run: "$923 million" in the lead versus "$942.3 million" in the box office section.
- Total after re-releases: "$944 million" in both the lead and the box office section, versus "$945.1 million" in the infobox.
- Academy Award Best Picture nominees: "Fran Walsh, Philippa Boyens, Stephen Sinclair and Peter Jackson" in the accolades list versus "Barrie M. Osborne, Fran Walsh and Peter Jackson" in the accolades table.
- BAFTAs: the list credits three wins including Orange Film of the Year; the table lists only Best Costume Design and Best Special Visual Effects as wins and does not include Orange Film of the Year.

The second part of the capture is Middle-earth navigation boxes and the category list; no published or last-updated date is stated.

wikis.title: The Lord of the Rings: The Two Towers (2002): plot, cast, production, release and reception
wikis.summary: Part 1 of the English Wikipedia article on The Lord of the Rings: The Two Towers, covering the 2002 film's credits and infobox figures, plot, cast, differences from Tolkien's novel, production design, filming, visual effects, score, release, box office, reviews and awards.
wikis.body:
## The film

- "*The Lord of the Rings: The Two Towers* is a 2002 epic fantasy film directed by Peter Jackson from a screenplay by Fran Walsh, Philippa Boyens, Stephen Sinclair, and Jackson, based on 1954's *The Two Towers*, the second volume of the novel *The Lord of the Rings* by J. R. R. Tolkien." It is the sequel to 2001's *The Fellowship of the Ring* and the second instalment of the trilogy.
- Produced by Barrie M. Osborne, Fran Walsh and Peter Jackson. Cinematography Andrew Lesnie; edited by Michael J. Horton; music by Howard Shore. Production companies WingNut Films and New Line Cinema; distributed by New Line Cinema.
- Release dates: 5 December 2002 (Ziegfeld Theatre), 18 December 2002 (United States), 19 December 2002 (New Zealand). Running time 179 minutes. Countries New Zealand and United States; language English. Budget $94 million; box office $945.1 million.
- Ensemble cast: Elijah Wood, Ian McKellen, Liv Tyler, Viggo Mortensen, Sean Astin, Cate Blanchett, John Rhys-Davies, Bernard Hill, Christopher Lee, Billy Boyd, Dominic Monaghan, Orlando Bloom, Hugo Weaving, Miranda Otto, David Wenham, Brad Dourif, Karl Urban and Andy Serkis.
- "The Two Towers was financed and distributed by American studio New Line Cinema, but filmed and edited entirely in Jackson's native New Zealand, concurrently with the other two parts of the trilogy."
- At the 75th Academy Awards it was nominated for six awards including Best Picture, winning Best Sound Editing and Best Visual Effects. *The Return of the King* followed in 2003.

## Plot

Three intercut storylines: Frodo and Sam journey toward Mordor with Gollum as their guide; Merry and Pippin escape the Uruk-hai into Fangorn Forest, meet Treebeard and rouse the Ents to storm Isengard; Aragorn, Legolas and Gimli reach Rohan, are reunited with the resurrected Gandalf, free Théoden from Saruman's control and fight the Battle of Helm's Deep. Faramir captures Frodo and Sam and takes them to Osgiliath before releasing them; Gollum, feeling betrayed, resolves to reclaim the Ring by leading them to "her" at Cirith Ungol.

## Contradictory figures in the page

- **Original-run worldwide gross**: the lead says "It grossed $923 million worldwide during its original theatrical run", while the box office section says "The film went on to gross $348.9 million in North America and $592.7 million internationally for a worldwide total of $942.3 million against a budget of $94 million."
- **Total gross after re-releases**: the lead says "Following subsequent re-releases, it has grossed $944 million" and the box office section gives "$350 million in the United States and Canada and $593 million in the rest of the world for a worldwide total of $944 million", while the infobox states "$945.1 million".
- **Best Picture nominees**: the accolades list names "Best Picture (Fran Walsh, Philippa Boyens, Stephen Sinclair and Peter Jackson, producers)", while the accolades table gives the Academy Award Best Picture nominees as "Barrie M. Osborne, Fran Walsh and Peter Jackson".
- **BAFTA count**: the bulleted list credits three British Academy Film Awards (Best Costume Design, Best Special Visual Effects, Orange Film of the Year), while the table lists Best Costume Design and Best Special Visual Effects as wins with Best Film, Best Direction, Best Cinematography, Best Editing, Best Makeup and Hair, Best Production Design and Best Sound as nominations, and does not list Orange Film of the Year.

wikis.title: Cast of The Two Towers
wikis.summary: The ensemble cast and their characters, plus the extended-edition-only role and the cameos.
wikis.body:
- Viggo Mortensen as Aragorn, "the heir-in-exile to Gondor's throne who has come to Rohan's defence". According to Peter Jackson, *The Two Towers* is centred around Aragorn.
- Elijah Wood as Frodo Baggins; Sean Astin as Samwise Gamgee.
- Andy Serkis as Gollum (voice/motion capture), "originally known as Sméagol, who owned the Ring for 500 years".
- Ian McKellen as Gandalf the White; John Rhys-Davies as Gimli, also voicing Treebeard; Orlando Bloom as Legolas; Christopher Lee as Saruman the White.
- Bernard Hill as Théoden - "Kevin Conway was offered the role but he declined."
- Billy Boyd as Peregrin Took; Dominic Monaghan as Meriadoc Brandybuck; Brad Dourif as Gríma Wormtongue.
- Miranda Otto as Éowyn - "Uma Thurman was offered the role but turned it down and later regretted it."
- David Wenham as Faramir; Karl Urban as Éomer; Liv Tyler as Arwen; Hugo Weaving as Elrond; Cate Blanchett as Galadriel; Sean Bean as Boromir, appearing in flashbacks "more prominently in the film's extended edition".
- Craig Parker as Haldir; John Leigh as Háma; Bruce Hopkins as Gamling; John Bach as Madril; Nathaniel Lees as Ugluk.
- Appearing only in the Extended Edition: John Noble as Denethor.
- Cameos in the Battle of Helm's Deep: Peter Jackson as a man on top of the gate throwing a spear; his children and Elijah Wood's sister as young refugees in the caves behind the Hornburg; Alan Lee and Dan Hennah as soldiers preparing for battle; Hamish Duncan, "the son of a producer's friend", as a reluctant young Rohirrim warrior; Daniel Falconer as an Elvish archer.

wikis.title: Changes from Tolkien's novel
wikis.summary: How the film departs from The Two Towers, including the Warg attack, the Elves at Helm's Deep, Faramir's arc and the meaning of the title.
wikis.body:
- "Screenwriters did not originally script The Two Towers as its own film; The Lord of the Rings trilogy was initially written as a two-part series to be produced by Miramax, with parts of The Two Towers written as the conclusion to The Fellowship of the Ring."
- A new subplot has Aragorn fall over a cliff during a Warg attack on the refugees and be assumed dead; "Jackson stated that he added it to create tension."
- A larger change was planned in which Arwen and Elrond would visit Galadriel and Arwen would accompany an army of Elves to Helm's Deep. The script changed during shooting, "both from writers coming up with better ideas to portray the romance between Aragorn and Arwen, as well as poor fan reaction." The new scene of Arwen leaving for the West was created, the conversation scene became a flashback to Rivendell, and the Elrond-Galadriel conversation was edited to be telepathic. One change already filmed could not be reversed: the Elven warriors at Helm's Deep, which Jackson and Boyens defended as "romantic and stirring" and a reference to events in the Appendices of *The Return of the King*.
- Treebeard does not immediately decide to go to war; Boyens describes this as making Merry and Pippin "more than luggage".
- "The filmmakers' decision to leave Shelob for the third film meant that Faramir had to become an obstacle for Frodo and Sam." In the book Faramir quickly recognises the Ring as a danger and lets them go; in the film he first decides the Ring should go to his father Denethor and takes them to Osgiliath, which they do not visit in the book, changing his mind after the Nazgûl attack. Boyens contends the changes "were needed to keep the Ring menacing". Wenham said he had not read the book before the script; when he later raised the difference, the writers explained that if he said "I wouldn't pick that thing up even if it lay by the wayside", it "would basically strip the One Ring of all corruptive power".
- The title's meaning was changed: Tolkien's note at the end of *The Fellowship of the Ring* identified the towers as Minas Morgul and Orthanc, while "Jackson's film names them instead as Orthanc and Barad-dûr, symbolic of an evil alliance out to destroy Men". The film also depicts Saruman openly as Sauron's servant, whereas the novel suggested a rivalry, with Saruman "afraid of the prospect of being at war with Sauron, if Rohan and Gondor fell".

wikis.title: Production design
wikis.summary: How Helm's Deep, Edoras, the armies and the Mordor and Gondor locations were designed and built.
wikis.body:
- Alan Lee joined the project in late 1997 and Helm's Deep "was the first structure he was tasked to design. At 1:35 scale, it was one of the first miniatures built for the film, and was part of the 45-minute video that sold the project to New Line Cinema." It drew on an illustration Lee had done for the book, though "the curved wall featured in the film was proposed by fellow illustrator and designer John Howe". Jackson used the miniature to plan the battle "using 40,000 toy soldiers".
- Helm's Deep was built at Dry Creek Quarry with a gate, ramp and wall including a removable section and a tower on a second level. "A 1:4-scale miniature of Helm's Deep that ran 50 feet (15 m) wide was used for forced perspective shots, as well as the major explosion sequence."
- John Howe was the basic designer of the evil forces; the Uruk-hai were "the first army approved by Jackson", and Howe designed a special crossbow for them "which was significant because it did not require external tools to rearm". 100 Elven suits of armour were made with emphasis on autumnal colours, plus 250 suits for the Rohirrim. Rohan's designs were based on Germanic and Anglo-Saxon patterns; most weapons were designed by John Howe and forged by Peter Lyon, with "[e]ach sword [taking] 3 to 6 days to make."
- "The exterior of the Rohirrim's capital of Edoras, including its thatched roofs, took six months to build on Mount Sunday", in New Zealand's Canterbury Region of South Island. The interiors doubled as offices and lunch halls; the Hall of Edoras interior was filmed at Stone Street Studios with tapestries designed by Lee, and Théoden's wooden throne was partly created by Lee's daughter.
- Barad-dûr is fully seen in a tracking shot, "a design which Howe called a mockery of Gothic Cathedrals". Howe and Lee created the Black Gate - "though a typo in the script made the miniature into two" - and Osgiliath, "a ruined city reflecting London during the Blitz or Berlin in 1945", built on a backlot around a bridge and reusing some of Moria.

wikis.title: Principal photography
wikis.summary: The shared shoot for the trilogy, the injuries sustained and the three-month Helm's Deep battle filming.
wikis.body:
- "The Two Towers shared principal photography with The Fellowship of the Ring and The Return of the King. The trilogy was filmed between 11 October 1999 and 22 December 2000."
- The Rohan scenes were shot earlier in the production, during which Viggo Mortensen, Orlando Bloom and John Rhys-Davies's stunt double Brett Beattie sustained many injuries. "Mortensen broke two toes when he kicked an Orc helmet while filming the scene in which he, Legolas, and Gimli find the remains of the Uruk-hai" - a shot included in the film. Bloom fell off his horse and cracked three ribs, and Beattie dislocated his knee, leading Jackson to call them "The Walking Wounded".
- "The filming of the Battle of Helm's Deep took approximately three months, with most of the nighttime shots handled by John Mahaffie." Mortensen chipped a tooth and Bernard Hill's ear was slashed. The sequence "features 500 extras, who insulted each other in Māori", and improvised moments such as the Uruk-hai stamping their spears. There was "alleged annoyance among the film's crew for the strength of the gates, which were claimed to be too reinforced during the Battering Ram scene". Mortensen "head bumped" the stunt team as a sign of respect.
- "Wood and Astin were joined by Serkis on 13 April 2000."
- "Brad Dourif reportedly spent considerable time researching and developing the British accent used for his portrayal of Gríma Wormtongue."

wikis.title: Visual effects, Gollum and Treebeard
wikis.summary: Weta Digital's work on the film, how Andy Serkis's Gollum was created, and the Treebeard puppet.
wikis.body:
- Jim Rygiel served as visual effects supervisor, "while newcomer Joe Letteri joined the visual effects team to supervise Andy Serkis's motion capture performance in the creation of the character Gollum. During the production of The Two Towers Weta Digital doubled their staff of 260. In total, they have produced 73 minutes of digital effects with 800 shots."
- The film was Weta's "first challenge in creating a battle scene, as well as creating two digital characters who needed to act rather than be a set piece, unlike the previous film's Cave Troll and Balrog."
- **Gollum**: "Weta began animating Gollum in late 1998 to convince New Line they could achieve the effect." Serkis provided voice and movements on set and later performed in a motion capture suit; his scenes were filmed twice, with and without him. Gollum was originally to be solely CGI, but Jackson was impressed by Serkis's audition tape. The CGI model was redesigned in 2001 when Serkis was cast as Sméagol; "[o]ver Christmas 2001, the crew reanimated all the previous shots accordingly within two months", and the original model "can still be glimpsed briefly in the first film". The CGI Gollum was rotoscoped and animated over the takes that included Serkis; his face was animated manually using recordings of Serkis as a guide. "Gino Acevedo supervised realistic skin tones, which took four hours per frame to render."
- The film depicts Gollum with a split personality, established in "perhaps the most celebrated scene" in the film where Sméagol and Gollum argue, conveyed "by contrasting camera angles and by Serkis altering his voice and physicality for each persona". The key scene "was written and directed by Fran Walsh" and is one of Jackson's favourites.
- **Treebeard**: "took between 28 and 48 hours per frame to render". A 14-foot-tall puppet on a wheel was built for scenes with Merry and Pippin; "Weta took polyurethane moulds of tree bark and applied them to the sculpt of Treebeard to create his wooden skin." Monaghan and Boyd "sat on bicycle seats concealed in Treebeard's hands to avoid discomfort and were left alone on set sitting in the puppet's hands during breaks." The puppet was shot against bluescreen.

wikis.title: Howard Shore's score
wikis.summary: The composition, performers and the Rohirric funeral song in the extended edition.
wikis.body:
- "The musical score for The Two Towers was composed, orchestrated, and conducted by Howard Shore, who also composed the music for the other two films in the series."
- "The scores for its predecessor and sequel won Academy Awards for Best Score, but the soundtrack for The Two Towers was not nominated. Initially there was confusion over the score's eligibility due to a new rule applying to sequels, but the academy declared it eligible."
- Performed by the London Philharmonic Orchestra, London Voices and the London Oratory School Schola, with soloists including soprano Isabel Bayrakdarian and Irish fiddler and violinist Dermot Crehan, who also played the Hardanger fiddle "used in conjunction with the various Rohan themes". Recorded at Abbey Road Studios.
- "The funeral song that Éowyn sings during her cousin Théodred's entombment in the extended edition is styled to be a traditional song of the Rohirrim and has lyrics in their language, Rohirric (represented by Old English). The text was written by Philippa Boyens, not by Tolkien, and was translated by David Salo. The tune is a variation on a theme of the rímur Icelandic folk tradition."
- The film won a Grammy Award for Best Score (Howard Shore).

wikis.title: Release, marketing and home media
wikis.summary: Trailer dates, the VHS/DVD release and its records, the extended edition and later Blu-ray editions.
wikis.body:
- "The teaser trailer premiered in theatres on 3 July 2002 with the release of *Men in Black II*. The theatrical trailer was then released theatrically on 4 October 2002 with the debut of *Red Dragon*."
- Released on VHS and DVD on 26 August 2003 in the United States by New Line Home Entertainment. The date "was originally intended to be a simultaneous worldwide release, but due to a bank holiday weekend in the United Kingdom, some British outlets began selling DVDs as much as four days earlier, much to the ire of the UK distributor, Entertainment in Video, which had threatened to withhold advance supplies of subsequent DVD releases."
- "During its first five days of release, the DVD release sold over 3.5 million units. The film also generated $22.8 million in rentals, breaking *The Bourne Identity*'s record for having the biggest rentals of any DVD release. By December 2003, it was reported that The Two Towers sold 16.4 million copies and earned $305.4 million in sales revenue, becoming the second-highest selling home video release of 2003, after *Finding Nemo*."
- An extended edition was released on VHS and DVD on 18 November 2003 "with 44 minutes of new material, added special effects and music, plus 12 minutes of fan-club credits. The runtime expanded to 235 minutes."
- Theatrical Blu-ray of the trilogy released in the US in April 2010, with the individual *Two Towers* disc in September 2010; extended Blu-ray editions in the US and Canada in June 2011; Ultra HD Blu-ray on 30 November 2020 in the United Kingdom and 1 December 2020 in the United States, with both theatrical and extended cuts.

wikis.title: Box office, critical response and accolades
wikis.summary: The film's opening records and grosses, the aggregate scores and named reviews, and its awards.
wikis.body:
## Box office

- Opened 18 December 2002 with $26 million on its opening day, "making it the second-highest opening Wednesday, behind *Star Wars: Episode I – The Phantom Menace*". It earned $62 million in its opening weekend in the US and Canada, the fifth-highest opening weekend of that year and the third-highest for a New Line Cinema film. It made $101.5 million over its five-day Wednesday opening and topped the box office for three weekends before being beaten by *Just Married*.
- Outside the US and Canada it earned $99.4 million from 25 countries in its opening weekend, "making it the highest international opening weekend", for a combined worldwide opening of $189.9 million, "the highest worldwide opening weekend of all time" until 2003, when the records passed to *The Matrix Reloaded* and *The Matrix Revolutions*.
- Opening day records in Germany, Austria, Finland, the Netherlands, Switzerland, Belgium, Sweden and Norway, a single-day record in Denmark, and opening weekend records in the United Kingdom, Spain, France, Mexico, Norway, Switzerland, Denmark, Germany and South Korea. In the Netherlands it made $2.2 million in four days; in the United Kingdom $13.7 million in its opening weekend and $20.9 million over five days, topping the box office for four weeks until overtaken by *8 Mile*.
- Totals: "$348.9 million in North America and $592.7 million internationally for a worldwide total of $942.3 million against a budget of $94 million", the highest-grossing film of 2002 worldwide, with Box Office Mojo estimating over 57 million tickets sold in the US in its initial run. After reissues, "$350 million in the United States and Canada and $593 million in the rest of the world for a worldwide total of $944 million" - against the infobox figure of $945.1 million and the lead's "$923 million worldwide during its original theatrical run".

## Critical response

- Rotten Tomatoes: 95% approval from 288 reviews, consensus "The Two Towers balances spectacular action with emotional storytelling, leaving audiences both wholly satisfied and eager for the final chapter." Metacritic: 87 out of 100 from 39 reviews, "universal acclaim". CinemaScore: "A", up from the previous film's "A−".
- Roger Ebert (*Chicago Sun-Times*), three stars of four: "one of the most spectacular swashbucklers ever made", though "not faithful to the spirit of Tolkien".
- Nev Pierce (BBC), four of five, called Gollum "the first believable CG character" and Helm's Deep "one of the finest, most expansive combat sequences ever filmed".
- Philip French (*The Observer*) called it a "stunning visual epic", relating its visual style to Caspar David Friedrich, the Pre-Raphaelites, Art Nouveau illustration and John Martin.
- Joe Morgenstern (*The Wall Street Journal*): "Seldom has a popular entertainment set its stage so carefully or evocatively, with such lavish respect for its audience."
- Alexander Walker (*Evening Standard*) called Helm's Deep "probably the greatest battlepiece composed for the screen since Eisenstein's *Ivan the Terrible*".
- David Ansen (*Newsweek*) on Gollum: "In an epic drenched in medievalism, he's the dangerously ambiguous voice of the modern."
- Caroline Westbrook (*Empire*), five of five: "It may lack the first-view-thrill and natural dramatic shape of Fellowship, but this is both funnier and darker than the first film".
- Peter Bradshaw (*The Guardian*), three of five, called it "a very watchable, distinctive, if over-extended FX spectacle" but dismissed the subject as "lots and lots of interminable nerdish nonsense".
- CNN named the Battle of Helm's Deep one of the greatest screen battles of all time; *Entertainment Weekly* named Gollum the third favourite computer-generated film character in 2007. In 2025 the film ranked number 43 on the "Readers' Choice" edition of *The New York Times*' list of "The 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century".

## Accolades

- Academy Awards: won Best Visual Effects (Jim Rygiel, Joe Letteri, Randall William Cook, Alex Funke) and Best Sound Editing (Ethan Van der Ryn, Michael Hopkins); nominated for Best Picture, Best Art Direction (Grant Major; Dan Hennah and Alan Lee), Best Film Editing (Michael J. Horton) and Best Sound (Christopher Boyes, Michael Semanick, Michael Hedges, Hammond Peek). The bulleted list names the Best Picture nominees as Walsh, Boyens, Sinclair and Jackson; the table names Barrie M. Osborne, Fran Walsh and Peter Jackson.
- BAFTA: won Best Costume Design (Ngila Dickson and Richard Taylor) and Best Special Visual Effects; the bulleted list also credits Orange Film of the Year, voted by the public. Nominations in the table include Best Film, Best Direction, Best Cinematography, Best Editing, Best Makeup and Hair, Best Production Design and Best Sound.
- Also won: Empire Award for Best Picture; Grammy for Best Score (Howard Shore); Hugo Award for Best Dramatic Presentation - Long Form; 2003 MTV Movie Award for Best Virtual Performance (Gollum); Saturn Awards for Best Fantasy Film, Best Costume (Ngila Dickson), Best Supporting Actor (Andy Serkis) and Best Make-up (Peter Owen and Peter King). Golden Globe nominations for Best Motion Picture - Drama and Best Director.
- AFI's 100 Years...100 Movie Quotes: "My precious." at #85.

wikis.title: The Two Towers article: Middle-earth navigation boxes and categories
wikis.summary: Part 2 of the Wikipedia article on The Lord of the Rings: The Two Towers, consisting entirely of the Tolkien and Middle-earth navigation boxes and the page's category list, with no article prose.
wikis.body:
This part carries no article text about the film; it is navigation and site apparatus.

- Navigation boxes list Middle-earth games and adaptations: role-playing games (*The One Ring Roleplaying Game*, *Adventures in Middle-earth*), board games (*Middle Earth*, *War of the Ring*, *Gondor: The Siege of Minas Tirith*, *Sauron*, *Lord of the Rings*), card games (*Middle-earth Collectible Card Game*, *The Lord of the Rings Trading Card Game*, *The Lord of the Rings: The Card Game*) and other games (*Middle-earth Strategy Battle Game*, *Lego The Lord of the Rings*), alongside the wider *Lord of the Rings* franchise boxes.
- The page ends with its category list, which includes "Films shot at Stone Street Studios", "Films shot in England", "Films shot in New Zealand", "The Lord of the Rings (film series)", "Middle-earth (film franchise) films", "New Line Cinema films", "WingNut Films films", "Films that won the Best Sound Editing Academy Award", "Films that won the Best Visual Effects Academy Award", "Hugo Award for Best Dramatic Presentation, Long Form–winning works" and "Nebula Award for Best Script–winning works", plus hidden maintenance categories.

wikis.title: The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King (2003 film)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia's article on The Return of the King - its credits, plot, differences from Tolkien's book, New Zealand production, December 2003 release, more than $1.1 billion gross, acclaim and its clean sweep of eleven Academy Awards.
wikis.body:
## The film

- A 2003 epic fantasy film directed by Peter Jackson from a screenplay with Fran Walsh and Philippa Boyens, based on the third volume of Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings and the final installment of the trilogy after The Two Towers (2002).
- Produced by Barrie M. Osborne, Walsh and Jackson for WingNut Films and New Line Cinema, which also distributed. Cinematography Andrew Lesnie, editing Jamie Selkirk, music Howard Shore. Running time 201 minutes; countries New Zealand, Germany and the United States.
- Ensemble cast including Elijah Wood, Ian McKellen, Viggo Mortensen, Sean Astin, Andy Serkis, Liv Tyler, Cate Blanchett, Bernard Hill, Billy Boyd, Dominic Monaghan, Orlando Bloom, Miranda Otto, David Wenham, Karl Urban, John Noble, Ian Holm and Sean Bean.

## Dates

- Premiered at the Embassy Theatre in Wellington on 1 December 2003, released 17 December 2003 in the United States and 18 December 2003 in New Zealand.
- Filmed across New Zealand between 11 October 1999 and 22 December 2000, with 2003 pick-ups that ended on 27 June 2003; the film was completed on 12 November 2003.
- Extended Edition (252 minutes) released 14 December 2004; Ultra HD Blu-ray 30 November 2020 (UK) and 1 December 2020 (US).

## Money

- Budget $94 million. Initial release grossed $377 million in the United States and Canada and $741.9 million elsewhere, $1.118 billion worldwide, crossing $1 billion in the weekend of 20–22 February 2004 - the second film to do so after Titanic. With reissues the totals are $387 million and $761 million, given as a worldwide $1.149 billion.
- The highest-grossing film of 2003, the highest-grossing entry in the trilogy and New Line Cinema's highest-grossing film. Opening weekend $72.6 million; five-day Wednesday opening $125.1 million.

## Production notes

- The three films were written and shot simultaneously, a first. The film has 1,489 visual effect shots, nearly three times the first film's; the Pelennor battle grew from 60 planned shots to 250 and from 50,000 to 200,000 digital characters.
- Many book events are compressed or cut, including the Scouring of the Shire; Saruman's death appears only in the Extended Edition.

## Reception and awards

- Rotten Tomatoes 94% from 304 reviews; Metacritic 94 out of 100 from 41 reviews; CinemaScore "A+". The most common criticism was the running time, particularly the epilogue.
- Nominated for eleven Academy Awards and won all eleven at the 76th Academy Awards, including Best Picture - the first fantasy film to win it - tying Ben-Hur and Titanic for most wins. Also four Golden Globes, five BAFTAs, nine Saturn Awards, two Grammy Awards, two MTV Movie Awards, the New York Film Critics Circle Best Picture, the Nebula Award for Best Script and the Hugo Award for Best Dramatic Presentation, Long Form.

## About the capture

- Part 1 holds the article through the positive reviews, part 2 the negative reviews, rankings and awards table, and part 3 navigation templates and categories. The page states no last-edited date.

wikis.title: The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King (2003 film): plot, cast, production, release, box office and reviews
wikis.summary: The first part of Wikipedia's article on The Return of the King, covering its credits and figures, plot, cast, differences from Tolkien's book, design, filming, pick-ups, editing, effects, score, home media, box office records and critical reviews.
wikis.body:
## Film and credits

- "The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King is a 2003 epic fantasy film directed by Peter Jackson from a screenplay he wrote with Fran Walsh and Philippa Boyens", based on 1955's The Return of the King, the third volume of Tolkien's novel, and the sequel to The Two Towers (2002).
- Produced by Barrie M. Osborne, Fran Walsh and Peter Jackson. Cinematography Andrew Lesnie; edited by Jamie Selkirk; music by Howard Shore. Production companies WingNut Films and New Line Cinema; distributed by New Line Cinema.
- Release dates: 1 December 2003 (Embassy Theatre), 17 December 2003 (United States), 18 December 2003 (New Zealand). Running time 201 minutes. Countries New Zealand, Germany, United States; language English.
- Budget $94 million; box office $1.149 billion (infobox).
- Ensemble cast: Elijah Wood, Ian McKellen, Liv Tyler, Viggo Mortensen, Sean Astin, Cate Blanchett, John Rhys-Davies, Bernard Hill, Billy Boyd, Dominic Monaghan, Orlando Bloom, Hugo Weaving, Miranda Otto, David Wenham, Karl Urban, John Noble, Andy Serkis, Ian Holm and Sean Bean.
- "At the 76th Academy Awards, it won all 11 awards for which it was nominated, including Best Picture, the first fantasy film to do so", tying Ben-Hur (1959) and Titanic (1997) for most wins.

## Plot

- Sméagol kills his cousin Déagol for the One Ring and becomes Gollum. Centuries later Gandalf takes Pippin to Minas Tirith after Pippin looks into Saruman's palantír; Pippin lights the beacons to call Rohan.
- Frodo and Sam are led towards Mordor by Gollum, who frames Sam and later lures Frodo into Shelob's lair; Sam drives Shelob off and rescues Frodo from Orcs.
- Denethor sends Faramir on a suicide charge and falls into madness, dying on his pyre. Théoden leads Rohan's charge and is mortally wounded by the Witch-king, whom Éowyn slays with Merry's help; Aragorn arrives with the Army of the Dead.
- At Mount Doom Gollum bites off Frodo's finger and falls into the lava with the Ring, destroying it and Sauron. Aragorn is crowned and marries Arwen; four years later Frodo leaves for the Undying Lands with Bilbo, Gandalf and the Elves, giving Sam the Red Book of Westmarch.

## Cast details

- Elijah Wood (Frodo), Viggo Mortensen (Aragorn), Sean Astin (Sam), Andy Serkis (Sméagol/Gollum), Ian McKellen (Gandalf the White), John Rhys-Davies (Gimli, also voicing Treebeard), Orlando Bloom (Legolas), Billy Boyd (Pippin), Dominic Monaghan (Merry), Bernard Hill (Théoden), Miranda Otto (Éowyn), David Wenham (Faramir), Karl Urban (Éomer), Hugo Weaving (Elrond), Liv Tyler (Arwen), Cate Blanchett (Galadriel), John Noble (Denethor), Ian Holm (Bilbo), Sean Bean (Boromir), Marton Csokas (Celeborn), Lawrence Makoare (the Witch-king and Gothmog, the latter voiced by Craig Parker), Thomas Robins (Déagol).
- The Extended Edition adds Christopher Lee (Saruman), Brad Dourif (Gríma) and Bruce Spence (the Mouth of Sauron).
- Cameos by Peter Jackson, Richard Taylor, Gino Acevedo, Rick Porras, Andrew Lesnie, Royd Tolkien, Christian Rivers and Howard Shore; Sean Astin's daughter plays Elanor. Closing credits show a sketched portrait of each cast member by Alan Lee, an idea suggested by Ian McKellen.

## Differences from the book

- The film includes scenes from the middle of The Two Towers (Shelob's attack, the palantír subplot) because Jackson realigned events to the Appendices' timeline rather than the book's interlaced order.
- Saruman's murder by Gríma (Extended Edition only) is moved into the Isengard visit because the Scouring of the Shire was cut. Denethor refuses to light the beacons in the film, so Pippin's secret lighting was invented for the movie; Denethor jumps from the Citadel as well as burning on the pyre.
- The muster of Rohan, the Drúedain subplot and the Red Arrow are cut; Théoden's death speech is delivered to Éowyn instead of Merry; Éowyn's presence on the battlefield is known to the audience in advance.
- Gollum's fall was rewritten because a simple slip was felt anticlimactic; an earlier plan had Frodo push him, dropped because it would look like murder.
- Omitted after the fall of Barad-dûr: the camp at Cormallen, Aragorn and Arwen's wedding, Théoden's funeral, the journey back through Rivendell and Bree, and the Scouring of the Shire, "which was seen by the screenwriters as anticlimactic". The article also summarises the Appendix A epilogues for Sam, Aragorn, Merry, Pippin, Legolas, Gimli and Frodo.

## Production

- The three films were written and shot simultaneously - "the first where three separate entries were written and shot simultaneously (excluding pick up shoots)". Filming took place across New Zealand "between 11 October 1999 and 22 December 2000, with pick up shoots for six weeks in 2003 before the film's release".
- The Return of the King was originally the second of two planned films under Miramax Films from January 1997 to August 1998.
- Design by Alan Lee and John Howe, built by Weta Workshop under Richard Taylor with Grant Major and Dan Hennah. The Minas Tirith soundstage was built at Dry Creek Quarry outside Wellington from the Helm's Deep set; its 8 m Gate had engravings inspired by the Baptistry of San Giovanni and its streets by Siena. The Citadel interior's colours were influenced by Charlemagne's Chapel.
- Shelob was designed in 1999, body based on a tunnelweb spider. The Dead Men's underground city was influenced by Petra; the Haradrim drew on Kiribati and Aztec influences after Philippa Boyens raised concerns about African influences being offensive.

## Filming and pick-ups

- Shot during 2000, though Astin's coverage of Gollum separating Frodo and Sam was filmed on 24 November 1999. Hobbiton was shot in January 2000 at a Matamata farm; the Battle of the Black Gate in April at the Rangipo Desert, a former minefield, with New Zealand soldiers as extras; Paths of the Dead scenes in June including Pūtangirua Pinnacles; Shelob scenes in July; Isengard in August and September; Edoras exteriors in October, with the Ride of the Rohirrim filmed in Twizel with 150 extras on horseback.
- The 2003 pick-ups were filmed in the Wellington studio car park over two months and ended on 27 June 2003; they included Aragorn's coronation, Mount Doom scenes, Théoden's death and all the Witch-king's scenes, plus the new character Gothmog. For the Extended DVD, in March 2004 Jackson shot skulls rolling for the avalanche scene - "the final piece of footage ever shot for the trilogy".

## Editing, effects and sound

- Post-production began in November 2002 with a 4½ hour assembly cut by Annie Collins; Théoden's charge went from 150 minutes of takes to 90 seconds. Three weeks were spent on the last 45 minutes. The Saruman scene was cut despite pick-ups and dubs, upsetting fans and Christopher Lee. The film was completed on 12 November 2003, and Jackson first saw it end to end on 1 December at the Wellington premiere.
- "The Return of the King contains 1,489 visual effect shots, nearly three times the number from the first film and almost twice that of the second", with Jim Rygiel as visual effects supervisor. Planned Pelennor shots rose from 60 to 250 and 50,000 characters to 200,000; Weta delivered 100 shots a week. 450 motions were recorded for the MASSIVE digital horses.
- Miniatures included a 1:72 Minas Tirith 7 m high and 6.5 m in diameter, and 80,000 skulls for the City of the Dead. The miniatures team finished in November with the Black Gate after 1000 days of shooting; the final digital effects shot, the Ring's destruction, was done on 25 November.
- Sound: a Tasmanian devil for Shelob's shriek, a lion roar for the mûmakil; mixing began 15 August and finished 15 November.

## Score

- Composed by Howard Shore, writing seven minutes of music per day. Performed by the London Philharmonic Orchestra, London Voices and the London Oratory School Schola, with 85 singers in the mixed choir and over fifty in the boy choir; one piece needed a specially built fiddle with four pairs of strings.
- Billy Boyd, Viggo Mortensen and Liv Tyler sing on screen; soloists include Renée Fleming, Ben Del Maestro, Sissel Kyrkjebø and James Galway. The end title song "Into the West", by Shore with lyrics by Fran Walsh and performed by Annie Lennox, won the Oscar for Best Original Song and a Grammy for Best Film Song; it was partly inspired by the death from cancer of young New Zealand filmmaker Cameron Duncan.

## Release and home media

- World premiere at Wellington's Embassy Theatre on 1 December 2003, with an estimated "over 100,000 people" lining the streets, more than a quarter of the city's population.
- Theatrical edition on VHS and DVD on 25 May 2004. Extended Edition (252 minutes) released 14 December 2004 in the UK and US; the Blu-ray Extended Edition is given as 264 minutes, and the US Extended Edition released in June 2011 as 263 minutes. The final 11 minutes list the fan-club charter members.
- A collectors' box set added a Minas Tirith sculpture and a 50-minute documentary. A Limited Edition followed in August 2006. Theatrical Blu-ray 6 April 2010 (trilogy set) and 14 September 2010 individually. Ultra HD Blu-ray on 30 November 2020 (UK) and 1 December 2020 (US).

## Box office

- Initial release: "$377 million in the United States and Canada and $741.9 million in other countries for a worldwide total of $1.118 billion". It crossed $1 billion in the weekend of 20–22 February 2004, the second film to do so after Titanic in 1998.
- Following reissues: "$387 million in the United States and Canada and $761 million in the rest of the world for a worldwide total of $1.149.4 billion" [as written].
- The highest-grossing film of 2003, the second highest-grossing film of the 2000s, the highest-grossing entry in the trilogy and New Line Cinema's highest-grossing film; 27th highest-grossing film of all time unadjusted. Time Warner's highest-grossing film worldwide for eight years until Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows – Part 2 in 2011. Box Office Mojo estimates over 61 million US tickets sold.
- Set an opening Wednesday record with $34 million; about $8 million came from midnight showings. Opening weekend $72.6 million; five-day Wednesday opening $125.1 million, a record until Shrek 2 five months later. First day outside the US and Canada $23.5 million from 19 countries, with a record $125.9 million five-day international weekend and $250.1 million combined - then the highest worldwide opening weekend. Records set in the UK ($26.5 million in five days), Germany, Spain, Sweden, Denmark, Switzerland and New Zealand ($1.7 million in four days).
- The trilogy is called the highest-grossing motion picture trilogy worldwide with over $2.9 billion; estimated non-box-office income would bring the trilogy total to about $6 billion on an investment of $300 million ($426 million including marketing).

## Critical response

- Rotten Tomatoes 94% from 304 reviews; Metacritic 94 out of 100 from 41 reviews ("universal acclaim"); CinemaScore "A+", the highest grade in the trilogy.
- Five-star and rave reviews from Alan Morrison (Empire), Nev Pierce (BBC), James Christopher (The Times), Elvis Mitchell (The New York Times) and Philip French (The Observer); Roger Ebert gave three and a half stars out of four.

wikis.title: The Return of the King: negative reviews, rankings and the awards table
wikis.summary: The second part of the captured page finishes the reception section with negative reviews and later rankings, then lists the film's awards - eleven Academy Award wins, BAFTAs, Golden Globes and Saturn Awards - before the references and navigation templates.
wikis.body:
## Negative reviews

- Tom Charity in Time Out: "Some story strands are crudely abbreviated; others fail to develop elements that were already well-established. Given the inordinate running time, it's hard to avoid the feeling that we've already been here, done this."
- Jonathan Romney in The Independent objected to "all these intrepid, largely beautiful Europeans boldly fending off the nameless, numberless hordes from the other side of the world" and to "the film's self-important solemnity, its hyperbolic over-insistence".
- Antonia Quirke in the Evening Standard said Mortensen's Aragorn "doesn't have half of the gravitas of Sean Bean's Boromir in the first film".
- "The most common criticism ... was its running time, particularly the epilogue". Joel Siegel of Good Morning America, who gave it an 'A', said: "If it didn't take forty-five minutes to end, it'd be my best picture of the year."

## Later rankings

- February 2004: voted eighth on Empire's 100 Greatest Movies of All Time from readers' lists, forcing the magazine to abandon its one-year eligibility rule.
- 2007: Total Film named it the third best film of the past decade, behind The Matrix and Fight Club.
- July 2025: ranked number 15 on the "Readers' Choice" edition of The New York Times' "The 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century".

## Academy Awards

- Nominated for eleven awards and won all eleven at the 76th Academy Awards in 2004, sharing the record for highest Academy Award totals with Titanic and Ben-Hur.
- Wins: Best Picture (Barrie M. Osborne, Peter Jackson, Fran Walsh), Best Director (Jackson), Best Adapted Screenplay (Walsh, Boyens, Jackson), Best Art Direction (Grant Major, Dan Hennah, Alan Lee), Best Costume Design (Ngila Dickson, Richard Taylor), Best Film Editing (Jamie Selkirk), Best Makeup (Richard Taylor, Peter King), Best Original Score (Howard Shore), Best Original Song (Walsh, Shore, Annie Lennox), Best Sound Mixing (Christopher Boyes, Michael Semanick, Michael Hedges, Hammond Peek) and Best Visual Effects (Jim Rygiel, Joe Letteri, Randall William Cook, Alex Funke).

## Other awards listed

- British Academy Film Awards: won Best Film, Best Adapted Screenplay, Best Cinematography (Andrew Lesnie) and Best Special Visual Effects; nominated for Best Direction, Best Actor in a Supporting Role (Ian McKellen), Best Costume Design, Best Editing, Best Makeup and Hair, Best Original Music, Best Production Design and Best Sound.
- Golden Globe Awards: won Best Motion Picture – Drama, Best Director, Best Original Score and Best Original Song.
- Saturn Awards: won Best Fantasy Film, Best Director, Best Actor (Elijah Wood), Best Supporting Actor (Sean Astin), Best Writing, Best Make-up, Best Music and Best Special Effects; nominated for Best Actor (Viggo Mortensen), Best Supporting Actor (Andy Serkis, Ian McKellen), Best Supporting Actress (Miranda Otto) and Best Costume Design.
- Summary text: "The film won four Golden Globes ..., five BAFTAs, two MTV Movie Awards, two Grammy Awards, nine Saturn Awards, the New York Film Critics Circle award for Best Picture, the Nebula Award for Best Script, and the Hugo Award for Best Dramatic Presentation, Long Form."

## Rest of the part

- A "See also" list (The Hobbit film series, the 1977, 1978 and 1980 animated adaptations, List of films considered the best, List of Academy Award records), two notes pointing to The Two Towers (2002) and The Fellowship of the Ring (2001), the article's reference list, external links (official website, IMDb, Metacritic) and large Tolkien navigation templates.

- Ends with the article's categories, including "WingNut Films films" and "English-language drama films", and hidden maintenance categories such as "Use British English from August 2025" and "Use dmy dates from August 2024".
