wikis.title: The Hobbit: The Battle of the Five Armies (2014 film)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia's article on Peter Jackson's 2014 fantasy film The Hobbit: The Battle of the Five Armies - credits, plot, cast, development, release dates, box office totals and critical reception.
wikis.body:
## The film

- **The Hobbit: The Battle of the Five Armies**, a 2014 fantasy film directed by **Peter Jackson** from a screenplay by Fran Walsh, Philippa Boyens, Jackson and Guillermo del Toro, based on the 1937 novel *The Hobbit* by J. R. R. Tolkien.
- Sequel to 2013's *The Hobbit: The Desolation of Smaug*, the final instalment of *The Hobbit* trilogy and a prequel to Jackson's *The Lord of the Rings* trilogy (2001-2003).
- Cinematography Andrew Lesnie; editing Jabez Olssen; music Howard Shore. Produced by Carolynne Cunningham, Zane Weiner, Fran Walsh and Peter Jackson for New Line Cinema, Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer Pictures and WingNut Films; distributed by Warner Bros. Pictures.
- Running time **144 minutes**; New Zealand and United States; English; budget **$209-300 million**.
- Stars Martin Freeman (Bilbo), Ian McKellen (Gandalf), Richard Armitage (Thorin), Evangeline Lilly (Tauriel), Luke Evans (Bard), Lee Pace (Thranduil), Benedict Cumberbatch (Smaug / Sauron), with Cate Blanchett, Ian Holm, Christopher Lee, Hugo Weaving and Orlando Bloom.

## Dates

- **1 December 2014** - world premiere at Leicester Square, London.
- **11 December 2014** - New Zealand; **12 December** - United Kingdom; **17 December** - United States; **18 December** - Greece; **26 December** - Australia; **23 January 2015** - China.
- The film had first been dated **18 July 2014** before moving to December.
- Home media: digital 6 March 2015, US DVD/Blu-ray 24 March 2015, Extended Edition 17 November 2015, Ultra HD Blu-ray 30 November / 1 December 2020. A one-night extended-edition re-release ran on 13 October 2015.

## Money

- Worldwide gross **$962.2 million** in the lead and box office section ($255.1 million US and Canada, $707.1 million elsewhere), against **$962.7 million** in the infobox; "over $956 million" in the original theatrical release. Second-highest-grossing film of 2014 behind *Transformers: Age of Extinction*.
- Deadline Hollywood put net profit at **$103.4 million**, fourteenth among 2014's "Most Valuable Blockbusters". Pundits had projected $1 billion; The Hollywood Reporter blamed "plunging exchange rates around the globe", costing Warner Bros. and MGM nearly $90 million.
- Biggest markets: China $121.7 million; UK, Ireland & Malta $61.3 million; Australia $27 million. Home video earned $70.3 million on 3.4 million copies.

## Reception

- Rotten Tomatoes 59% (265 reviews, 6.30/10); Metacritic 59/100 (46 critics); CinemaScore A-. The lead calls the reviews mixed; contemporary reports ranged from "generally positive" (MTV) to "a flawed but fitting finale" (Los Angeles Times).
- Nominated for **Best Sound Editing** at the 87th Academy Awards; listed as the 2014 Saturn Award winner for Best Fantasy Film.

## Production notes

- Planned as two films until Jackson confirmed a third on 30 July 2012; titled *There and Back Again* in August 2012 and renamed *The Battle of the Five Armies* in April 2014 because Bilbo had already reached Erebor by the second film.
- Howard Shore's score added themes for Dain, Gundabad (with didgeridoos) and the dwarves' war preparations; Billy Boyd wrote and sang "The Last Goodbye" over the end credits.
- The Extended Edition is rated **R** by the MPAA for "some violence" - the only Middle-earth film with a restricted rating - MA15+ in Australia and 15 by the BBFC.

wikis.title: The Hobbit: The Battle of the Five Armies - film article, plot through accolades
wikis.summary: The body of the Wikipedia article on the 2014 Peter Jackson film The Hobbit: The Battle of the Five Armies: infobox credits, plot, cast, development and score, marketing and releases, ratings, box office, critical response and awards.
wikis.body:
## Infobox

- **The Hobbit: The Battle of the Five Armies**, "2014 fantasy film directed by Peter Jackson".
- Directed by **Peter Jackson**; screenplay by **Fran Walsh, Philippa Boyens, Peter Jackson and Guillermo del Toro**; based on *The Hobbit* by J. R. R. Tolkien.
- Produced by Carolynne Cunningham, Zane Weiner, Fran Walsh and Peter Jackson. Cinematography **Andrew Lesnie**; edited by **Jabez Olssen**; music by **Howard Shore**.
- Production companies **New Line Cinema**, **Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer Pictures** and **WingNut Films**; distributed by **Warner Bros. Pictures**.
- Release dates: **1 December 2014** (London premiere), **11 December 2014** (New Zealand), **17 December 2014** (United States).
- Running time **144 minutes**; countries New Zealand and United States; language English.
- Budget **$209-300 million**; box office **$962.7 million**.

## Lead

- Based on the 1937 novel *The Hobbit*; sequel to 2013's *The Hobbit: The Desolation of Smaug* and the final instalment in *The Hobbit* trilogy, acting as a prequel to Jackson's *The Lord of the Rings* trilogy (2001-2003).
- Story: Bilbo Baggins and Thorin Oakenshield's company take possession of the treasure in the Lonely Mountain as factions of dwarves, elves and men clash over it, "while the orc Azog the Defiler and his forces make their move upon them".
- Premiered in London on 1 December 2014, released 11 December in New Zealand and 17 December in the United States by Warner Bros. Pictures.
- "The film received mixed reviews from critics and grossed $962.2 million worldwide, making it the second-highest-grossing film of 2014." Nominated for Best Sound Editing at the 87th Academy Awards.

## Contradictory figures in the article

- **Worldwide gross**: the infobox says **$962.7 million**; the lead and the box office section say **$962.2 million** ($255.1 million US and Canada plus $707.1 million elsewhere). The box office section also says "In its original theatrical release, it grossed over $956 million".
- **Opening date in North America**: the box office section says "It opened on 16 December 2014 across 3,100 theatres and widened to 3,875 the following day", then that it "topped the box office on its opening day (Wednesday, 17 December 2014)".
- An international-rollout sentence reads "Through 14 December 2015, it had an opening weekend total of $122.2 million from 37 countries", in a passage otherwise about December 2014.

## Plot (as the article summarises it)

- Smaug burns Laketown; Bard escapes prison and kills him with the black arrow. Smaug's falling body crushes the Master of Laketown and his cronies fleeing with the town's gold; Bard leads the survivors to the ruins of Dale. Thorin hunts obsessively for the Arkenstone, which Bilbo has hidden, and seals the mountain.
- Galadriel, Elrond and Saruman free Gandalf at Dol Guldur, defeat the Nazgul and face a formless Sauron, whom Galadriel banishes to the East. Azog marches on Erebor and sends Bolg to Mount Gundabad for a second army; Legolas and Tauriel see it march, with orc berserkers and giant bats.
- Thranduil's elf army reaches Dale to reclaim treasure held by the dwarf king Thror; Bard's attempt to negotiate fails; Gandalf's warning about Azog is dismissed by Thranduil; Bilbo smuggles the Arkenstone out to Thranduil and Bard.
- Dain's dwarf army arrives; Azog's forces interrupt the looming battle; Gandalf persuades Thranduil to join against Azog, who splits his army to attack Dale.
- Thorin regains his sanity and rides with Dwalin, Fili and Kili to Ravenhill. Azog kills Fili; Bolg kills Kili and is killed by Legolas; the Great Eagles arrive with Radagast and Beorn; Thorin kills Azog but is fatally wounded and reconciles with Bilbo. Thranduil tells Legolas to seek "a ranger in the north who goes by the name Strider".
- Dain becomes king in Erebor; Bilbo returns to the Shire, keeps the ring secret from Gandalf, stops the auction of his belongings, and sixty years later receives Gandalf on his "111th" birthday.
- Footnotes state the Arkenstone find was depicted in *The Hobbit: The Desolation of Smaug* (2013) and the birthday visit in *The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring* (2001).

## Cast

- Martin Freeman (Bilbo Baggins), Ian Holm (Old Bilbo), Ian McKellen (Gandalf the Grey), Richard Armitage (Thorin II Oakenshield), Orlando Bloom (Legolas), Evangeline Lilly (Tauriel), Luke Evans (Bard the Bowman), Benedict Cumberbatch (Smaug / Sauron), Lee Pace (Thranduil).
- Dwarves and others: Graham McTavish (Dwalin), Ken Stott (Balin), Aidan Turner (Kili), Dean O'Gorman (Fili), Mark Hadlow (Dori), Jed Brophy (Nori), Adam Brown (Ori), John Callen (Oin), Peter Hambleton (Gloin), William Kircher (Bifur), James Nesbitt (Bofur), Stephen Hunter (Bombur), Billy Connolly (Dain II Ironfoot).
- Also Manu Bennett (Azog the Defiler), Cate Blanchett (Galadriel), Hugo Weaving (Elrond), Christopher Lee (Saruman the White), Sylvester McCoy (Radagast the Brown), John Tui (Bolg), Mikael Persbrandt (Beorn), Stephen Fry (Master of Lake-town), Ryan Gage (Alfrid Lickspittle), Mark Mitchinson (Braga), John Bell (Bain), Peggy and Mary Nesbitt (Sigrid and Tilda), Simon London (Feren).
- Cameos: Peter Jackson's and Andy Serkis's daughters as girls rowing away during Smaug's attack; movement coach Terry Notary and stand-in Jamie Haugh as Laketown refugees; Conan Stevens, who was to play Bolg, as the Keeper of the Dungeons, an orc captain holding Gandalf hostage; the sons of key second assistant director Guy Campbell, casting director Miranda Rivers and Weta Workshop founder Richard Taylor as hobbit children in the auction scene.

## Development

- *The Hobbit* was originally planned as two films; Jackson confirmed a third on **30 July 2012**. He said it would contain the Battle of the Five Armies and draw heavily on Tolkien's appendices published at the back of *The Return of the King*, using mostly footage shot for the first two films but requiring additional filming.
- Titled *There and Back Again* in **August 2012**; in **April 2014** Jackson renamed it *The Battle of the Five Armies*, saying the old title might have suited a two-part adaptation's second half, but felt misplaced once Bilbo had already reached Erebor in the second film.
- Shaun Gunner, chairman of The Tolkien Society, backed the change: "The Battle of the Five Armies much better captures the focus of the film but also more accurately channels the essence of the story."

## Score

- Howard Shore composed the score, as on the previous films. Conrad Pope (who conducted) and James Sizemore orchestrated for the New Zealand Symphony Orchestra and two Gamelan orchestras; the London Voices and Tiffin boys' choir were recorded at AIR Lyndhurst, London.
- New themes for Dain, Gundabad (with a "chorus" of didgeridoos) and the dwarves' war preparations; the score otherwise blends and clashes existing themes toward a resolution.
- Billy Boyd, Peregrin Took in *The Lord of the Rings*, wrote and recorded "The Last Goodbye" for the end credits.

## Marketing and tie-ins

- Teaser trailer **28 July 2014** with *Guardians of the Galaxy*, *Into the Storm* and *If I Stay*; second theatrical trailer **6 November 2014** with *Interstellar* and *The Hunger Games: Mockingjay - Part 1*.
- Wellington Phoenix wore a one-off film-themed jersey on 13 December 2014.
- For the Japanese release on 13 December, Warner Bros. worked with mobile gaming company A-Lim to add Bilbo, Gandalf and Legolas to *Brave Frontier* as Vortex Dungeon units from the end of December; the campaign ran until February 2015.
- Smaug appeared on *The Colbert Report* on 12 December 2014, animated by WETA and voiced by Cumberbatch.
- Video games: the tie-in fighting game *The Hobbit: Battle of the Five Armies - Fight for Middle Earth* launched with the film on Android and iOS to negative reviews; *Middle-earth: Shadow of Mordor* came out for Windows, PlayStation 4 and Xbox One in October 2014 and for PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360 on 21 November, its events set directly after Sauron fled to Mordor.

## Theatrical release

- Initially set for **18 July 2014**, then pushed to **17 December**. World premiere at Leicester Square, London, **1 December 2014**.
- Opened **11 December 2014** in New Zealand, **12 December** in the United Kingdom, **17 December** in the United States, **18 December** in Greece, **26 December** in Australia, and **23 January 2015** in China.
- An extended edition had a one-night-only re-release on **13 October 2015** with a special greeting from Peter Jackson.

## Home media

- Digital release **6 March 2015**; DVD and Blu-ray **24 March 2015** in the United States, topping the home video sales chart in its opening week. It earned **$70.3 million** on **3.4 million copies**, the ninth best-selling title of 2015.
- Extended Edition with 20 minutes of extra footage and original music: Digital HD **20 October 2015**, DVD/Blu-ray/Blu-ray 3D **17 November 2015** in the US and **23 November 2015** in the UK.
- Ultra HD Blu-ray **30 November 2020** in the UK and **1 December 2020** in the US, with the rest of the trilogy in theatrical and extended cuts.

## Ratings

- The theatrical version is PG-13; the Extended Edition was rated **R** by the MPAA for "some violence" - "the only Middle Earth film to have a restricted rating and, one of the few films based on a children's book to have an R rating".
- The Australian Classification Board gave MA15+ for "strong fantasy violence"; the BBFC gave a 15 certificate for "strong violence", and 12A to the theatrical version.

## Box office

- Grossed **$255.1 million** in the US and Canada and **$707.1 million** elsewhere for **$962.2 million** worldwide; "over $956 million" in the original theatrical release, the second-highest-grossing film of 2014 behind *Transformers: Age of Extinction*.
- Deadline Hollywood calculated net profit of **$103.4 million** after production budgets, marketing, talent participations and other costs, ranking it fourteenth on its 2014 "Most Valuable Blockbusters" list.
- It did not reach $1 billion despite projections. The Hollywood Reporter blamed "plunging exchange rates around the globe" and said Warner Bros. and MGM would take in nearly $90 million less than expected. Forbes still called the trilogy "an unmitigated financial grand-slam for all parties".
- **US and Canada**: lowest-grossing of the three *Hobbit* films and of the six Middle-earth adaptations, but the sixth-highest-grossing film of 2014 domestically. $11.2 million from Tuesday late-night shows (of which $2.5 million, "just over 22%", from IMAX), breaking *The Desolation of Smaug*'s $8.8 million Middle-earth preview record. $24.5 million on opening day Wednesday 17 December (third-highest Middle-earth Wednesday opening, behind *The Return of the King*'s $34.5 million and *The Two Towers*' $26.2 million). $57.4 million three-day and $89.1 million five-day opening - second-biggest five-day in the franchise, above *The Desolation of Smaug*'s $86.1 million, below *An Unexpected Journey*'s $100.2 million - though the three-day figure under-performed expectations. December IMAX opening record of $13.4 million (previously *Mission: Impossible - Ghost Protocol*). 3-D was 49% of the gross; IMAX 15%, $13.4 million over five days and $7.4 million over three; premium large format 8%, $7.2 million from 396 theatres. Passed $100 million on its seventh day, 23 December 2014, the third film of 2014 to do so in under a week after *Mockingjay - Part 1* ($168.7 million) and *Guardians of the Galaxy* ($134.4 million). Number one for three consecutive weekends until *Taken 3*.
- **Other countries**: opened 10 December 2014 in 11 European markets for $11.3 million and 11 December in 17 more for $13.7 million, a two-day total of $26.6 million, topping every territory. Opening weekend $122.2 million from 37 countries on 15,395 screens, 71% ($86.7 million) from 3-D, below *An Unexpected Journey* ($138 million) and *The Desolation of Smaug* ($135.4 million) in dollar terms. December IMAX opening record of $6.4 million on 160 screens. Second weekend $109 million from 19,315 screens (down 13%); third weekend $89 million; first place outside North America for four consecutive and five weekends in total.
- Records: all-time Warner Bros. opening in Russia ($13.8 million), Argentina ($2.1 million), Sweden and Finland; 2014 opening records in Germany ($20.5 million), France ($15.1 million) and Spain ($6.3 million); best Middle-earth opening in the UK ($15.2 million) and Mexico ($6.3 million); second-biggest Warner Bros. opening ever in Brazil ($6.8 million, behind *Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows - Part 2*). Australia: opening-day record $5.6 million on 26 December, behind *Deathly Hallows - Part 2* ($7.092 million), *The Avengers* ($6.0 million) and *The Desolation of Smaug* ($5.9 million), then $10.1 million opening weekend. China: all-time Warner Bros. opening record of $49.8 million (previously *Pacific Rim*), with $6.8 million from IMAX, then the second-highest IMAX three-day gross behind *Transformers: Age of Extinction*'s $10 million. Other openings: Korea $10.4 million, Poland $5.6 million, Italy $5.6 million, Malaysia $3 million, Taiwan $2.8 million.
- Largest total markets: China ($121.7 million), the UK, Ireland & Malta ($61.3 million), Australia ($27 million).

## Critical response

- Rotten Tomatoes: **59%** from 265 reviews, average 6.30/10, consensus "Though somewhat overwhelmed by its own spectacle, The Hobbit: The Battle of the Five Armies ends Peter Jackson's second Middle-earth trilogy on a reasonably satisfying note". Metacritic: **59 out of 100** from 46 critics. CinemaScore opening-weekend grade **A-**, the same as its predecessor.
- Early coverage: MTV reported reviews "generally positive", praising "its energy, shorter running time and satisfying closure"; IBT said reviews were mostly positive; CBS News reported critics saying it "will satisfy fans" but "otherwise, it may be worth waiting until it's available to rent"; Oliver Gettel of the Los Angeles Times summarised the consensus as "a flawed but fitting finale to The Hobbit trilogy".
- Positive: Scott Foundas (Variety) - "at once the trilogy's most engrossing episode, its most expeditious (at a comparatively lean 144 minutes) and also its darkest". Todd McCarthy (The Hollywood Reporter) - "After six films, 13 years and 1031 minutes of accumulated running time... a film that may be the most purely entertaining of any in the collection." Andrew Pulver (The Guardian) - "a fitting cap to an extended series". Chris Tilly (IGN Movies) - "a little too much padding... But the central battle is indeed spectacular". Russell Baillie (The New Zealand Herald) - "something less than the supposed 'defining chapter'... But action-wise, it certainly goes out with a very pleasing bang."
- Negative: Inkoo Kang (TheWrap) - "The 144-minute running time showcases Jackson's worst tendencies: eons-long battle scenes, sloppy and abrupt resolutions, portentous romances, off-rhythm comic timing, and, newly in this case, patience-testing fan service." Tim Robey (The Daily Telegraph) - "a paragraph on steroids", "a series of stomping footnotes in search of a climax". Nicholas Barber (BBC) called it "a colossal technical achievement" but criticised "its repetitive battle scenes and a lack of plot". Nicolas Rapold (The New York Times) - "somewhere along the way, Mr. Jackson loses much of the magic."

## Accolades

- One Academy Award nomination, for **Best Sound Editing**, plus praise from the Broadcast Film Critics Association and groups including the Heartland Film Festival, Phoenix Film Critics Society and Hollywood Makeup Artist and Hair Stylist Guild.
- A navigation box on the page lists the film as the **Saturn Award for Best Fantasy Film** winner for 2014.

wikis.title: From two films to three, and the title change
wikis.summary: How the third Hobbit film came about and why it was renamed from There and Back Again.
wikis.body:
- *The Hobbit* was originally planned as a two-part film; Jackson confirmed a third on **30 July 2012**, making it a trilogy.
- Jackson said the third film would contain the Battle of the Five Armies and "make extensive use of the appendices that Tolkien wrote to expand the story of Middle-earth (published in the back of The Return of the King)", using footage shot for the first two films but requiring additional filming.
- Titled *There and Back Again* in **August 2012**.
- In **April 2014** Jackson renamed it *The Battle of the Five Armies*, saying the original title might have suited the second half of a two-part adaptation covering both Bilbo's arrival at and departure from Erebor, but felt misplaced once Bilbo had already arrived at Erebor in the second film of three.
- Shaun Gunner, chairman of The Tolkien Society, supported the change, saying the new title "much better captures the focus of the film but also more accurately channels the essence of the story".

wikis.title: Howard Shore's score and 'The Last Goodbye'
wikis.summary: Who wrote, orchestrated and performed the film's music, and the new themes it introduced.
wikis.body:
- Howard Shore composed the score, as on all the previous films.
- Conrad Pope, who conducted the orchestra, and James Sizemore orchestrated for the New Zealand Symphony Orchestra and for two Gamelan orchestras.
- The London Voices and the Tiffin boys' choir were recorded at AIR Lyndhurst, London.
- New themes were written for Dain, for Gundabad (featuring a "chorus" of didgeridoos) and for the dwarves' war preparations; otherwise the score focuses on "blending and clashing the themes against one another, eventually bringing the themes to a resolution".
- Billy Boyd, who played Peregrin Took in *The Lord of the Rings*, wrote and recorded "The Last Goodbye" for the end credits.

wikis.title: Releases, home media and the R-rated extended edition
wikis.summary: Cinema dates by country, the home video schedule, and the ratings the extended cut received.
wikis.body:
- Originally dated **18 July 2014**, moved to **17 December 2014**. World premiere at Leicester Square, London, **1 December 2014**.
- Cinema openings: New Zealand 11 December 2014; United Kingdom 12 December; United States 17 December; Greece 18 December; Australia 26 December; China 23 January 2015. An extended edition had a one-night-only re-release on 13 October 2015 with a greeting from Peter Jackson.
- Home media: digital 6 March 2015; US DVD and Blu-ray 24 March 2015, topping the home video sales chart in its opening week and earning **$70.3 million** on **3.4 million copies**, the ninth best-selling title of 2015. Extended Edition (20 minutes of extra footage and original music) on Digital HD 20 October 2015, DVD/Blu-ray/Blu-ray 3D 17 November 2015 in the US and 23 November 2015 in the UK. Ultra HD Blu-ray 30 November 2020 (UK) and 1 December 2020 (US) with the rest of the trilogy.
- Ratings: theatrical PG-13, but the Extended Edition was rated **R** by the MPAA for "some violence" - "the only Middle Earth film to have a restricted rating and, one of the few films based on a children's book to have an R rating". The Australian Classification Board gave MA15+ for "strong fantasy violence"; the BBFC gave 15 for "strong violence" (and 12A to the theatrical cut on 28 November 2014).

wikis.title: Box office performance
wikis.summary: Grosses, opening records and the shortfall against the $1 billion mark.
wikis.body:
- Totals: **$255.1 million** US and Canada, **$707.1 million** elsewhere, **$962.2 million** worldwide (the infobox says $962.7 million); "over $956 million" in the original theatrical release, the second-highest-grossing film of 2014 behind *Transformers: Age of Extinction*.
- Deadline Hollywood put net profit at **$103.4 million**, fourteenth on its 2014 "Most Valuable Blockbusters" list. The Hollywood Reporter attributed the missed $1 billion to "plunging exchange rates around the globe", costing Warner Bros. and MGM nearly $90 million; Forbes called the trilogy "an unmitigated financial grand-slam for all parties".
- North America: $11.2 million in Tuesday late-night shows (Middle-earth preview record, beating *The Desolation of Smaug*'s $8.8 million); $24.5 million opening Wednesday; $57.4 million three-day and $89.1 million five-day opening; December IMAX opening record $13.4 million; 3-D 49% of gross, IMAX 15%, premium large format 8% ($7.2 million from 396 theatres); passed $100 million on day seven, 23 December 2014; number one for three weekends until *Taken 3*. It is the lowest-grossing of the three *Hobbit* films and of the six Middle-earth adaptations domestically, but the sixth-highest-grossing film of 2014 there.
- International: $26.6 million from 28 markets over 10-11 December; $122.2 million opening weekend from 37 countries and 15,395 screens, 71% from 3-D, below both predecessors in dollars; $109 million second weekend from 19,315 screens; $89 million third; number one outside North America for five weekends in total.
- Opening records: all-time Warner Bros. in Russia ($13.8 million), Argentina ($2.1 million), Sweden, Finland and China ($49.8 million, beating *Pacific Rim*); 2014 records in Germany ($20.5 million), France ($15.1 million) and Spain ($6.3 million); best Middle-earth opening in the UK ($15.2 million) and Mexico ($6.3 million); Brazil's second-biggest Warner Bros. opening ($6.8 million); Australian opening-day record $5.6 million.
- Largest markets overall: China $121.7 million; UK, Ireland & Malta $61.3 million; Australia $27 million.

wikis.title: Critical reception and awards
wikis.summary: Aggregate scores, the split between favourable and unfavourable reviews, and the film's award recognition.
wikis.body:
- Rotten Tomatoes **59%** from 265 reviews (average 6.30/10), consensus: "Though somewhat overwhelmed by its own spectacle, The Hobbit: The Battle of the Five Armies ends Peter Jackson's second Middle-earth trilogy on a reasonably satisfying note". Metacritic **59/100** from 46 critics. CinemaScore **A-**, matching its predecessor. The lead calls the reviews "mixed".
- Favourable: Scott Foundas (Variety) called it "the trilogy's most engrossing episode, its most expeditious (at a comparatively lean 144 minutes) and also its darkest"; Todd McCarthy (The Hollywood Reporter) said that after "six films, 13 years and 1031 minutes" it "may be the most purely entertaining of any in the collection"; Andrew Pulver (The Guardian) called it "a fitting cap"; Chris Tilly (IGN) praised the "spectacular" central battle despite "padding"; Russell Baillie (The New Zealand Herald) said it "goes out with a very pleasing bang".
- Unfavourable: Inkoo Kang (TheWrap) listed "eons-long battle scenes, sloppy and abrupt resolutions, portentous romances, off-rhythm comic timing, and... patience-testing fan service"; Tim Robey (The Daily Telegraph) called it "a paragraph on steroids" and "a series of stomping footnotes in search of a climax"; Nicholas Barber (BBC) praised a "colossal technical achievement" but faulted "repetitive battle scenes and a lack of plot"; Nicolas Rapold (The New York Times) wrote that "Mr. Jackson loses much of the magic".
- Awards: one Academy Award nomination, Best Sound Editing (87th Academy Awards), plus recognition from the Broadcast Film Critics Association, Heartland Film Festival, Phoenix Film Critics Society and the Hollywood Makeup Artist and Hair Stylist Guild. A navigation box lists it as the 2014 Saturn Award winner for Best Fantasy Film.

wikis.title: Avengers: Endgame
wikis.summary: Wikipedia's article on the 2019 Marvel Studios film Avengers: Endgame, covering its plot, cast, production, release, record box office, reception and its 2026 Encore re-release and sequels.
wikis.body:
## The film

- "Avengers: Endgame is a 2019 American superhero film based on the Marvel Comics superhero team the Avengers ", produced by Marvel Studios, distributed by Walt Disney Studios Motion Pictures, "the direct sequel to Avengers: Infinity War (2018) and the 22nd film in the Marvel Cinematic Universe (MCU)". Directed by Anthony and Joe Russo, written by Christopher Markus and Stephen McFeely, produced by Kevin Feige, shot by Trent Opaloch, edited by Jeffrey Ford and Matthew Schmidt, scored by Alan Silvestri.
- Running time 181 minutes; budget "$356-400 million"; box office "$2.799 billion". Premiered at the Los Angeles Convention Center on April 22, 2019 and released in the United States on April 26, 2019, as part of Phase Three of the MCU.
- Story: "the surviving members of the Avengers and their allies attempt to reverse Thanos 's actions in Infinity War , which erased half of all life in the universe" - a time heist through earlier MCU films that ends with Natasha Romanoff's sacrifice on Vormir, Tony Stark's death using the Infinity Stones, and an elderly Steve Rogers passing his shield to Sam Wilson.
- Cast led by Robert Downey Jr., Chris Evans, Mark Ruffalo, Chris Hemsworth, Scarlett Johansson, Jeremy Renner, Don Cheadle, Paul Rudd, Brie Larson, Karen Gillan, Danai Gurira, Benedict Wong, Jon Favreau, Bradley Cooper, Gwyneth Paltrow and Josh Brolin, with dozens of returning MCU actors and a posthumous, digitally de-aged Stan Lee cameo in his final film appearance.

## Making and marketing

Announced in October 2014 as Avengers: Infinity War - Part 2 and later retitled, with the Russos hired in April 2015 and Markus and McFeely a month later. "Principal photography began on August 10, 2017, under the working title Mary Lou 2 at Pinewood Atlanta Studios", shot back-to-back with Infinity War and "with ARRI Alexa IMAX 2D cameras, the first time a Hollywood feature film was shot entirely with IMAX digital cameras"; it wrapped January 11, 2018, with re-shoots into January 2019 and location work in Atlanta, New York state, Durham Cathedral and St Abbs, Scotland. The film has "200 de-aging and aging shots". "The marketing campaign for Endgame cost over $200 million, the most for any Marvel Studios film"; the first trailer (December 7, 2018) was "viewed 289 million times in its first 24 hours".

## Box office and reception

- "Avengers: Endgame grossed $858.4 million in the United States and Canada and $1.941 billion in other territories for a worldwide total of $2.799 billion ", opening worldwide with $1.2 billion and a US opening weekend of $357.1 million from a then-record 4,662 theaters. It reached $2 billion in 11 days and was the highest-grossing film of all time until Avatar's 2021 re-release.
- Rotten Tomatoes: "an approval rating of 94% , with an average score of 8.2/10 based on 551 reviews"; Metacritic 78/100 from 57 critics; CinemaScore A+. Reviews ranged from Glen Weldon's "extended victory lap for the Marvel Cinematic Universe" to Anthony Lane's verdict that a viewer "can easily duck out during the middle hour".
- It was nominated for Best Visual Effects at the 92nd Academy Awards, won an Annie Award and two Critics' Choice Awards, and its Wikipedia page "was the most-viewed article of 2019 , with 44.2 million views".

## Encore and sequels

"Endgame will be re-released in theaters on September 25, 2026, under the title Avengers Endgame: Encore ", with new footage, a custom introduction and a new post-credits scene adding two minutes (five in Infinity Vision/IMAX screenings with an exclusive Doomsday look). Joe Russo called it "required viewing" for Avengers: Doomsday, which is "scheduled to be released on December 18, 2026, with Secret Wars following on December 17, 2027"; the Russos direct both, with Downey cast as Doctor Doom.

## About the page

The article is listed in 82 languages. Most of its length is citation apparatus: three of the five parts of this capture are raw `<ref name=...>{{Cite ...}}</ref>` definitions grouped by section, followed by the rendered numbered reference list, external links (official website, IMDb, Disney A to Z, the archived script) and the Avengers and Marvel Cinematic Universe navigation boxes. Citations run from the 2010s to August 2026.

wikis.title: Avengers: Endgame (2019 film)
wikis.summary: The full Wikipedia article on Avengers: Endgame - its infobox, plot, cast, production, music, marketing, release including the 2026 Encore re-release, box office, critical response, accolades and sequels.
wikis.body:
## The film

- "Avengers: Endgame is a 2019 American superhero film based on the Marvel Comics superhero team the Avengers ." Produced by Marvel Studios and distributed by Walt Disney Studios Motion Pictures, it is "the direct sequel to Avengers: Infinity War (2018) and the 22nd film in the Marvel Cinematic Universe (MCU)", directed by Anthony and Joe Russo and written by Christopher Markus and Stephen McFeely.
- Infobox: based on Avengers by Stan Lee and Jack Kirby; produced by Kevin Feige; cinematography Trent Opaloch; edited by Jeffrey Ford and Matthew Schmidt; music by Alan Silvestri; release dates April 22, 2019 (Los Angeles Convention Center) and April 26, 2019 (United States); running time 181 minutes; country United States; language English; budget "$356-400 million"; box office "$2.799 billion".
- Premise: "the surviving members of the Avengers and their allies attempt to reverse Thanos 's actions in Infinity War , which erased half of all life in the universe."
- Development history in the lead: announced in October 2014 as Avengers: Infinity War - Part 2, a title Marvel later removed; the Russos joined in April 2015 and Markus and McFeely a month later; filming began in August 2017 at Pinewood Atlanta Studios in Fayette County, Georgia, shooting back-to-back with Infinity War, and ended in January 2018, with additional filming in Metro and downtown Atlanta, New York state, Scotland and England; the official title was announced in December 2018. "With an estimated budget range of $356-400 million, Endgame is one of the most expensive films ever produced."
- Reception in the lead: positive reviews praising direction, acting, score, action, visual effects and emotional weight; "[i]t grossed nearly $2.8 billion worldwide, surpassing Infinity War ' s entire theatrical run in eleven days"; "the highest-grossing film of all time from July 2019 to March 2021, when it was surpassed by the previous record-holder, Avatar (2009)"; nominated for Best Visual Effects at the 92nd Academy Awards.
- "An extended version , subtitled Encore , will be released in theaters in September 2026 in anticipation of the film's two sequels, Avengers: Doomsday and Avengers: Secret Wars , which are respectively scheduled for release in December 2026 and 2027."

## Sequels (compressed)

In May 2018 Disney CEO Bob Iger said Marvel Studios was focusing on new characters and franchises after Endgame but another Avengers film could happen; the Russos said shortly after the premiere that they were not opposed to returning but had no plans; Feige said in January 2021 another Avengers film would happen eventually. At the 2022 San Diego Comic-Con Feige announced Avengers: The Kang Dynasty and Avengers: Secret Wars to conclude Phase Six, with the Russos not returning; Destin Daniel Cretton was set to direct The Kang Dynasty from a script by Jeff Loveness, and Michael Waldron to write Secret Wars. By November 2023 Cretton had stepped down and Waldron replaced Loveness. "Jonathan Majors , who portrayed Kang the Conqueror and was expected to appear in both films, was fired by Disney and Marvel Studios in December 2023 after he was convicted of assault . By then, Marvel was referring to The Kang Dynasty internally as Avengers 5 ." At the 2024 Comic-Con the Russos were announced as directors of the next two films; Avengers 5 was retitled Avengers: Doomsday with Doctor Doom as antagonist rather than Kang, Downey cast as Doom in both films, and McFeely joining as co-writer, with Chris McKenna and Erik Sommers also working on the scripts. Numerous MCU cast members reprise their roles in Doomsday along with actors from 20th Century Fox's X-Men series; Evans reprises Rogers despite his "definitive ending" in Endgame, the Russos calling him "the character that changed our lives... it was always going to come back". Feige described Doomsday as "picking up" where Endgame ended. "Doomsday is scheduled to be released on December 18, 2026, with Secret Wars following on December 17, 2027."

## Notes in this part

Explanatory notes identify Thanos's erasure as "the Blip" depicted in Infinity War, Lang's entrapment at the end of Ant-Man and the Wasp (2018), the 2012 New York trip as "[d]uring the events of The Avengers (2012)", the 2013 Asgard trip as Thor: The Dark World (2013), Morag as depicted in Guardians of the Galaxy (2014), and point to the "Avengers assemble scene" article.

wikis.title: Plot
wikis.summary: The article's plot summary, from Thanos's death through the time heist to Tony Stark's sacrifice and Steve Rogers passing on the shield.
wikis.body:
- "In 2018, 23 days after Thanos erased half of all life in the universe", Carol Danvers rescues Tony Stark and Nebula from deep space. They rejoin Bruce Banner, Steve Rogers, Thor, Natasha Romanoff, James Rhodes and Rocket on Earth, find Thanos on an uninhabited planet, and learn he has destroyed the Infinity Stones; "[e]nraged, Thor decapitates Thanos."
- Five years later Scott Lang escapes the Quantum Realm, having experienced only five hours. Theorizing that the Quantum Realm allows time travel, the team persuades a reluctant Stark to help; Stark, Rocket and Banner - who has merged his intelligence with the Hulk's strength - build a time machine. "Banner theorizes that altering the past will not affect the present, since any changes will create alternate realities ." Banner and Rocket recruit "an overweight, despondent Thor" at New Asgard in Norway; Romanoff recruits Clint Barton in Tokyo, "who became a vigilante after his family was erased".
- 2012 New York: Banner convinces the Ancient One to hand over the Time Stone after promising to return the Stones to their proper points in time; Rogers retrieves the Mind Stone from Hydra sleeper agents; Stark and Lang fail to steal the Space Stone, "allowing 2012-Loki to escape with it". 1970 Camp Lehigh: Stark obtains an earlier Space Stone and meets his father Howard; Rogers steals Pym Particles from Hank Pym and sees Peggy Carter.
- 2013 Asgard: Rocket extracts the Reality Stone from Jane Foster while Frigga encourages Thor, who retrieves Mjolnir. 2014: Nebula and Rhodes steal the Power Stone on Morag before Peter Quill; on Vormir, Red Skull says the Soul Stone "can be acquired only by sacrificing a loved one", and Romanoff sacrifices herself so Barton can take it. Nebula's cybernetic implants link with her past self, letting 2014-Thanos learn of his future success and the Avengers' plan; he captures Nebula and sends 2014-Nebula forward in time.
- In the present the Stones go into a gauntlet built by Stark, Banner and Rocket; Banner, "who has the most resistance to radiation", undoes the disintegrations. 2014-Nebula brings 2014-Thanos and his warship forward; he destroys the Avengers Compound. Present-day Nebula turns 2014-Gamora and kills 2014-Nebula. Thanos overpowers Stark, Thor and "a Mjolnir-wielding Rogers" and summons his army, "intent on using [the Stones] to destroy the universe and create a new one". Stephen Strange arrives with sorcerers, the restored Avengers, the Guardians, the Ravagers and the armies of Wakanda and Asgard; Danvers destroys Thanos's warship but he seizes the gauntlet. "Stark steals the Stones and uses them to disintegrate Thanos and his army, sacrificing himself."
- After Stark's funeral, Thor appoints Valkyrie king of New Asgard and joins the Guardians; Rogers returns the Stones and Mjolnir and stays in the past with Carter; "[i]n the present, an elderly Rogers passes his shield to Sam Wilson."''

wikis.title: Cast and characters
wikis.summary: The billed cast with the filmmakers' comments on each character's arc, plus the reprising actors, stand-ins and cameos.
wikis.body:
- **Robert Downey Jr. as Tony Stark / Iron Man** - per the Russos, "Downey was the only actor to receive the entire screenplay". Markus and McFeely knew Stark's death was inevitable as a "[move] to selflessness": "It's a good death. It doesn't feel like a tragedy. It feels like a heroic, finished life." Joe Russo said Stark "always knew he was going to die because he could never reconcile that notion in himself of not protecting the universe" and was "the most formidable of all of them [...] because of his heart"; the Russos sought Downey's approval for an arc developed since Captain America: Civil War (2016).
- **Chris Evans as Steve Rogers / Captain America** - Markus described him as "moving toward some sort of enlightened self-interest"; McFeely knew Rogers "was going to get his dance" promised in The First Avenger (2011) and initially planned to kill him before choosing the shield handover to Sam Wilson. Patrick Gorman "provided an on-set reference for an elderly Steve Rogers."
- **Mark Ruffalo as Bruce Banner / Hulk** - balances both sides through gamma experimentation, based on his "Professor Hulk" comic identity; Anthony Russo called him "the sole character who is actually forging into a bright new future".
- **Chris Hemsworth as Thor** - wields Stormbreaker, now "an overweight, drunken ruler of Asgard's refugees in Tønsberg, Norway". Anthony Russo: "it's not a gag. It's a manifestation of where he is on a character level ... a very common sort of response to depression and pain." Hemsworth underwent "around three hours of hair and makeup" plus a large silicone prosthetic suit, calling himself "Lebowski Thor"; Thor was initially to revert to his "old chiseled self" mid-film but Hemsworth wanted to keep the new physique.
- **Scarlett Johansson as Natasha Romanoff / Black Widow** - Joe Russo: "She's the watcher on the wall still" and "the only way to bring the community back is for her to sacrifice herself"; McFeely noted her "abusive, terrible, mind-control background". Johansson trained with plyometrics, Olympic weightlifting, gymnastics and a time-restricted diet under trainer Eric Johnson, with whom she had worked since Iron Man 2 (2010).
- **Jeremy Renner as Clint Barton / Hawkeye** - the cold open with his family's disintegration was originally meant for Infinity War but moved because it was "going to blunt the brutality of what [Thanos] did".
- **Don Cheadle as James Rhodes / War Machine**, **Paul Rudd as Scott Lang / Ant-Man** (played as a baby by twins Bazlo and Loen LeClair, at 12 by Jackson A. Dunn and at 93 by Lee Moore, "Moore's final film before his death in August 2018"), **Brie Larson as Carol Danvers / Captain Marvel** (her scenes filmed before Captain Marvel, whose directors Anna Boden and Ryan Fleck attended and blessed the characterization), **Karen Gillan as Nebula** (a redemption arc; several scenes with Downey "most of which were improvised"), **Danai Gurira as Okoye**, **Benedict Wong as Wong**, **Jon Favreau as Happy Hogan**, **Bradley Cooper as Rocket** (Sean Gunn again the on-set stand-in and motion reference), **Gwyneth Paltrow as Pepper Potts** (in a Rescue-based exosuit; she said it would be her final major MCU appearance), and **Josh Brolin as Thanos** (executive producer Trinh Tran suggested killing Thanos in the first act; the younger version was nicknamed "Warrior Thanos"; Brolin also did the motion capture and Joe Russo stood in for some Nebula scenes).
- Reprising from Infinity War: Benedict Cumberbatch, Chadwick Boseman, Tom Holland, Zoe Saldaña, Elizabeth Olsen, Anthony Mackie, Sebastian Stan, Tom Hiddleston, Pom Klementieff, Dave Bautista, Letitia Wright, William Hurt, Cobie Smulders, Winston Duke, Tom Vaughan-Lawlor, Jacob Batalon, Vin Diesel, Chris Pratt, Samuel L. Jackson, Ross Marquand, Michael James Shaw, Terry Notary and Kerry Condon (F.R.I.D.A.Y.), with Monique Ganderton again providing motion capture for Proxima Midnight.
- Reprising from other MCU films: Evangeline Lilly, Tessa Thompson, Rene Russo, John Slattery, Tilda Swinton, Hayley Atwell, Marisa Tomei, Taika Waititi, Angela Bassett, Michael Douglas, Michelle Pfeiffer, Linda Cardellini, Maximiliano Hernández, Frank Grillo, Robert Redford, Callan Mulvey and Ty Simpkins. Sean Gunn was credited as Kraglin "although he is not clearly visible in the film"; Natalie Portman appears via deleted Thor: The Dark World footage and a voiceover; "James D'Arcy reprised his role as Edwin Jarvis from the MCU television series Agent Carter , the first time a character introduced in an MCU television series appeared in an MCU film."
- Others: Hiroyuki Sanada as the Yakuza boss Akihiko; Lexi Rabe as Morgan Stark (Katherine Langford's older Morgan was cut); Emma Fuhrmann as an older Cassie Lang; "Avengers co-creator Stan Lee had a posthumous cameo ... digitally de-aged as a car driver in 1970, in his final film appearance"; Ken Jeong and Yvette Nicole Brown cameos; Joe Russo (credited as Gozie Agbo) as a grieving gay man, "the first appearance of an openly homosexual character in an MCU film"; Ava and Lia Russo; Thanos creator Jim Starlin as a grieving man; and a non-speaking Howard the Duck cameo.

wikis.title: Production
wikis.summary: Development from the 2014 two-part announcement through back-to-back filming, re-shoots, visual effects and de-aging.
wikis.body:
- "In October 2014, Marvel Studios announced a two-part sequel of Avengers: Age of Ultron (2015) entitled Avengers: Infinity War ." Part 1 was set for May 4, 2018 and Part 2 for May 3, 2019, to be filmed back-to-back. The Russos were hired in April 2015 and Markus and McFeely signed the next month. Feige said they would be "two distinct" projects, not one story split in two; the Russos decided to rename them in May 2016 and Marvel left the second film untitled that July, withholding the title "to avoid giving away plot details".
- "Principal photography began on August 10, 2017, under the working title Mary Lou 2 at Pinewood Atlanta Studios in Fayette County, Georgia , with Trent Opaloch the director of photography ." The film and Infinity War "were shot with ARRI Alexa IMAX 2D cameras, the first time a Hollywood feature film was shot entirely with IMAX digital cameras". August filming took place in the Gulch area of downtown Atlanta near the Five Points MARTA station and in Piedmont Park.
- Feige said the films were originally to be shot simultaneously but ended up back-to-back: "It became too complicated to cross-board them like that". Anthony Russo had preferred simultaneous shooting for financial and logistical reasons.
- "The 2013 Asgard scenes were shot at Durham Cathedral in Durham , England during production of Infinity War in early May 2017." Production wrapped on January 11, 2018, with additional filming in New York's Dutchess and Ulster counties in June 2018; re-shoots ran from September 7 to October 12, 2018, with more in January 2019. Location shooting also took place in St Abbs, Scotland, "which doubled for New Asgard in Norway". "Evans and Hemsworth earned $15 million each for the film."
- The official title and the April 26, 2019 US date "were revealed with the film's first trailer in December 2018".
- Visual effects vendors: Industrial Light & Magic, Weta Digital, DNEG, Framestore, Cinesite, Digital Domain, Rise, Lola VFX, Cantina Creative, Capital T, Technicolor VFX and Territory Studio. Lola handled de-aging; "the film has 200 de-aging and aging shots". Downey, Evans, Ruffalo, Hemsworth, Johansson and Renner were de-aged to their 2012 appearances; Douglas, Slattery and Lee were de-aged for the 1970 New Jersey scene; Lola aged Evans for the final scene with make-up and a stand-in. Editors: Jeffrey Ford and Matthew Schmidt.

wikis.title: Music
wikis.summary: Alan Silvestri's score, its themes and borrowings, and the soundtrack release.
wikis.body:
- Alan Silvestri, composer of The Avengers, "was announced in June 2016 to be returning to score Infinity War and Endgame ". The Russos began work with him on the Endgame score in early November 2018; it was completed in late March 2019.
- "A soundtrack album with Silvestri's score was released digitally by Hollywood Records on April 26, 2019, with a physical release on May 24." A video for "Portals", composed for the climactic "Avengers assemble" scene, was released on June 13.
- Silvestri described the score as having the franchise's most versatile tone, "ranging from 'thunderous percussion and powerful brass' for the action scenes to minimalist, jazz-inspired music for Ant-Man and the Quantum Realm", reprising themes from the previous Avengers films and Captain America: The First Avenger, including his Thanos and Infinity Stones material from Infinity War. He found writing the music to end Captain America's story poignant, having "been on this journey with him since the beginning".
- The film also used Christophe Beck's Ant-Man (2015) theme, Michael Giacchino's Doctor Strange (2016) theme and Pinar Toprak's Captain Marvel theme, plus the songs "Come and Get Your Love" by Redbone and "It's Been a Long, Long Time" by Jule Styne and Sammy Cahn.

wikis.title: Marketing
wikis.summary: The record-cost campaign, the decision to hide dead characters, and the two trailers and their viewing records.
wikis.body:
- "The marketing campaign for Endgame cost over $200 million, the most for any Marvel Studios film." Promotional partners included Stand Up to Cancer, Mastercard, Ulta Beauty, the Audi e-tron GT concept car (which appears in the film), McDonald's, GEICO, Coca-Cola, Google, General Mills, Hertz, Ziploc, Oppo and Synchrony Financial.
- A year before release, Germain Lussier of io9 asked whether the characters killed in Infinity War would appear in posters and toy campaigns; Feige said in June 2018 that the dead characters would not be featured in marketing. He presented a behind-the-scenes video at CineEurope and said the campaign would begin at the end of 2018. In early December 2018 Graeme McMillan of The Hollywood Reporter described "fevered anticipation" that was mostly "fan-created" and urged Marvel to release no trailers at all.
- "The first trailer for the film was released on December 7, 2018." Marvel's Dustin Sandoval said the team omitted the "title or hashtag" in trailer posts so fans would not be spoiled by seeing it "at the end". Richard Newby called it "a somber glimpse of a universe made unrecognizable"; Austen Goslin of Polygon tied the title to lines in Infinity War and Age of Ultron. "The trailer was viewed 289 million times in its first 24 hours and was the most-viewed trailer in that time period, surpassing the record of Avengers: Infinity War (230 million views). It set a record for Twitter conversation for a film trailer in the first 24 hours, generating 549,000 mentions." By January 3, 2019, BoxOffice's "Trailer Impact" metric found 77-78 percent of surveyed viewers expressed interest in seeing the film.
- "The second trailer for the film and its theatrical release poster were released on March 14, 2019." All 13 actors on the poster received top billing except Danai Gurira, whose name appeared in the bottom billing block with Wong, Favreau and Paltrow; the omission drew fan criticism and Marvel released an updated poster later that day with Gurira in the top billing. The second trailer "was viewed 268 million times in the first 24 hours, becoming the second-most-viewed trailer in that time period".

wikis.title: Release, the 2026 Encore re-release and home media
wikis.summary: The April 2019 premiere and worldwide rollout, the June 2019 re-release, the September 2026 Encore version and the home-video editions.
wikis.body:
- "Avengers: Endgame premiered at the Los Angeles Convention Center on April 22, 2019." Disney converted Hall K with Dolby and QSC Audio, installing "a 70-foot (21-metre) screen, Dolby Vision projectors, and a Dolby Atmos sound system", and held the red carpet and after-party there.
- Release dates: Australia, China and other parts of Asia and Europe on April 24; the United Kingdom on April 25; the United States and India on April 26; Russia on April 29 - in IMAX and 3D. It had originally been scheduled for May 3 in the US. "Radio Liberty alleged that the Russian government postponed the film's release in that country to promote Russian-produced films." The film is part of Phase Three of the MCU.
- After the Spider-Man: Far From Home trailer released on May 6, it was added to the end of Endgame screenings with a message from Tom Holland. In June, Feige announced a re-release "with seven minutes of new post-credits footage, including a Stan Lee tribute, an unfinished deleted scene, and the opening scene of Far From Home", with a limited-edition poster; it began June 28 in 1,040 US theaters.
- **Encore.** "Endgame will be re-released in theaters on September 25, 2026, under the title Avengers Endgame: Encore , in anticipation of the sequel Avengers: Doomsday being released in December 2026." It features new footage, a custom introduction and a new post-credits scene, "amounting to two additional minutes". Joe Russo called the re-release "critically important" and "required viewing" to follow Doomsday, the new footage acting as a narrative bridge; commentators questioned whether the amount of new footage justified the "hype". Encore received an IMAX release and Disney's Infinity Vision certification for premium large formats; those screenings add "an additional exclusive look at Doomsday", three more minutes, "for a total of five additional minutes". "The trailer for Encore received 77 million views in 24 hours, the most for any re-release trailer and four times as much as the previous record holder, the trailer for the May 2026 re-release of the 1986 film Top Gun (19 million views)", and was noted for more saturated colour grading than the original release.
- **Home media.** Digital download July 30, 2019; Ultra HD Blu-ray, Blu-ray and DVD on August 13; streaming exclusive to Disney+ from November 12, 2019. Extras include featurettes, audio commentary, deleted scenes and a blooper reel. Despite the IMAX 1.90:1 photography, "the home-media release has the cropped 2.39:1 aspect-ratio version"; the IMAX Enhanced version reached Disney+ on November 12, 2021. "The film earned $107.8 million from DVD and Blu-ray sales in the U.S."''

wikis.title: Box office
wikis.summary: Worldwide and domestic grosses, pre-sale records, opening-weekend records and the biggest international markets.
wikis.body:
- "Avengers: Endgame grossed $858.4 million in the United States and Canada and $1.941 billion in other territories for a worldwide total of $2.799 billion ." It was the highest-grossing film of all time until surpassed by Avatar (2009) after that film's 2021 re-release in China, and was the second-highest-grossing film in the US and Canada; the article adds that Gone with the Wind (1939) remains the highest-grossing film adjusted for inflation and that Endgame "is the fifth-highest-grossing film of all time worldwide".
- "The film had a worldwide opening of $1.2 billion, the biggest of all time , and nearly double Infinity War ' s previous record of $640 million." It is "the fastest film to reach the $1 billion and $1.5 billion marks, doing so in five and eight days respectively". Deadline Hollywood estimated it would break even five days after release, "unheard of for a major studio tentpole during its opening weekend", and calculated a final net profit of $890 million, first on its list of 2019's "Most Valuable Blockbusters".
- On May 4 it passed Infinity War's entire theatrical run; it reached $2 billion in 11 days (Avatar took 47) as the fifth film to do so, and $2.5 billion in 20 days (Avatar: 72).
- **Pre-sales.** Ranked second by IMDb and first by Fandango and Atom Tickets among 2019's most anticipated films. When US pre-sales opened April 2, 2019, Atom and Fandango had long waits and "AMC Theatres ' website and app crashed for several hours"; Fandango said it broke The Force Awakens's 24-hour record in six hours; Atom said it outsold Aquaman (2018) fourfold; Regal said Endgame sold more tickets in eight hours than Infinity War in its first week. Pre-sales totalled $120-140 million. In India it "sold one million tickets in one day" across English, Hindi, Tamil and Telugu screenings, "18 tickets ... every second"; in China pre-sales opened April 12 with "a record one million ... sold in six hours" and $114.5 million (RMB 770 million) in pre-sales.
- **United States and Canada.** Tracking on April 4 projected $200-250 million for the opening weekend, with insiders expecting $260-300 million. It played in 4,662 theaters, 410 in IMAX - "the widest release ever", beating Despicable Me 3's 4,529. It earned "$357.1 million in its opening weekend , breaking Infinity War ' s record by nearly $100 million", with records for Friday ($157.5 million including $60 million in Thursday previews), Saturday ($109.3 million) and Sunday ($90.4 million), and a weekend gross higher than the previous all-films combined high of $314 million. Its $76,601 per-theatre average broke the nationwide record ($59,982 for The Force Awakens) and the inflation-adjusted record held by Return of the Jedi (about $66,400 in 1983). It made $36.9 million the next Monday and $33.1 million Tuesday; $147.4 million in weekend two for a 10-day total of $621.3 million (fastest to $600 million); $64.8 million in weekend three, tying The Force Awakens's 16 days to $700 million; was dethroned in weekend four by John Wick: Chapter 3 - Parabellum; crossed $800 million with $17.2 million ($22.3 million over the four-day Memorial Day weekend); earned $6.1 million in the tenth-weekend re-release, up 207 percent; and "earned $1.2 million in its thirteenth weekend, breaking Avatar ' s all-time record".
- **Other territories.** Projected around $680 million internationally over five days. In China it took "a record $107.5 million (RMB 719 million) ... on its first day", including $28.2 million from midnight, 3am and 6am screenings, beating The Fate of the Furious's $9.1 million; local scores were 9.1 on Douban and 9.3 on Maoyan. Its global first day was $169 million, "the highest total of all time", with India ($9 million), South Korea ($8.4 million, "the largest non-holiday single-day gross ever"), Australia ($7.1 million), France ($6 million) and Italy ($5.8 million) next. It opened with $866 million overseas, setting best-ever opening records in China ($330.5 million, RMB 2.22 billion), the UK ($53.8 million), South Korea ($47.4 million), Mexico ($33.1 million), Australia ($30.8 million), Brazil ($26 million), Spain ($13.3 million), Japan ($13 million) and Vietnam ($10 million), and earned $21.6 million in its first four days in Russia. First-week top markets: China ($459.4 million), UK ($68.2 million), South Korea ($60.3 million), Mexico ($48.6 million), India ($40.9 million). A week after release it was the highest-grossing foreign film ever in China and India; its international running total passed $1.569 billion in the second weekend, overtaking Titanic. By January 2021 its top international markets were China ($632 million), the UK ($115 million), South Korea ($105 million), Brazil ($86 million) and Mexico ($78 million).

wikis.title: Critical response and accolades
wikis.summary: Aggregator scores, audience grades, a range of reviews from praise to criticism, and the film's awards and rankings.
wikis.body:
- "Review aggregator Rotten Tomatoes reported an approval rating of 94% , with an average score of 8.2/10 based on 551 reviews", with the consensus: "Exciting, entertaining, and emotionally impactful, Avengers: Endgame does whatever it takes to deliver a satisfying finale to Marvel's epic Infinity Saga ." Metacritic gave "a score of 78 out of 100 based on 57 critics", indicating "generally favorable" reviews. CinemaScore audiences gave an A+, "the third Marvel film to receive the grade after The Avengers and Black Panther (2018)"; PostTrak audiences gave five stars out of five and an 85-percent "definite recommend".
- Positive reviews: Glen Weldon (NPR) called it "an extended victory lap for the Marvel Cinematic Universe writ large"; Peter Travers (Rolling Stone) gave four out of five, noting the film jokes about "the clichéd time travel plot"; Peter Debruge (Variety) called it "a more fan-facing three-hour follow-up, rewarding loyalty"; J. R. Kinnard (PopMatters): "Big budget action filmmaking doesn't get much better than this."; Todd McCarthy (The Hollywood Reporter) singled out "the character acting, especially from Downey, Ruffalo, Evans, Hemsworth, Brolin, and Paul Rudd"; Richard Roeper (Chicago Sun-Times) gave four stars for its "emotional punch" and "universally stellar performances".
- Mixed and negative: A. O. Scott (The New York Times) called it "a monument to adequacy, a fitting capstone to an enterprise that figured out how to be good enough for enough people enough of the time"; Justin Chang (Los Angeles Times) said it "achieves and earns its climactic surge of feeling, even as it falls just short of real catharsis"; Brian Tallerico and Matt Zoller Seitz (RogerEbert.com) both preferred it to Infinity War, Seitz calling much of it "a laid-back Richard Linklater movie with superheroes"; Joe Morgenstern (WSJ) called the final battle "inevitably unwieldy [...] but thrilling all the same"; Richard Brody (The New Yorker) said "[t]he Russos have peculiarly little sense of visual pleasure"; Anthony Lane (The New Yorker) was negative: "you can easily duck out during the middle hour, do some shopping, and slip back into your seat for the climax. You won't have missed a thing."
- **Accolades.** "At the 92nd Academy Awards , Avengers: Endgame received a nomination for Best Visual Effects ." Other nominations include an Annie Award (won), a British Academy Film Award and three Critics' Choice Movie Awards (winning two). "Its Wikipedia page was the most-viewed article of 2019 , with 44.2 million views." It ranked 41st in a March 2020 Empire poll of the 100 greatest films of the 21st century, and the Avengers' assembling moment was one of five finalists for an Oscars Cheer Moment in the "Oscars Fan Favorite" contest for the 94th Academy Awards in February 2022.
