wikis.title: Delcy Rodríguez
wikis.summary: Wikipedia biography of Delcy Rodríguez, the Venezuelan lawyer and PSUV politician who became the country's interim president on 5 January 2026 after United States strikes captured Nicolás Maduro.
wikis.body:
## Who she is

- Delcy Eloína Rodríguez Gómez, born 18 May 1969 in Caracas, is a Venezuelan lawyer, politician and diplomat, interim president of Venezuela since 2026 "following the United States intervention in Venezuela" and "the first woman in Venezuelan history to perform the duties of the presidency".
- A member of the United Socialist Party of Venezuela (PSUV), and 24th Vice President of Venezuela under Nicolás Maduro since 14 June 2018. Sister of Jorge Rodríguez, President of the National Assembly since 2021; daughter of Socialist League founder Jorge Antonio Rodríguez, murdered in 1976 in DISIP custody.
- Law degree from the Central University of Venezuela in 1993; she also studied at the Sorbonne and, per the infobox, Birkbeck, University of London (MS) - though the lead says she did not graduate from either.

## Career

- Minister for Presidential Affairs February-August 2006 under Hugo Chávez; Minister of Communication and Information 2013-2014; Minister of Foreign Affairs December 2014 - June 2017, the first woman in that post in Venezuela's history; President of the Constituent National Assembly 2017-2018; Vice President from June 2018; Minister of Economy and Finance 2020-2024; Minister of Petroleum and Hydrocarbons 2024 - 11 March 2026.
- As foreign minister she clashed publicly with Mauricio Macri at the 2015 Mercosur summit and with OAS Secretary General Luis Almagro, whom she called a "liar, dishonest, a criminal, and a mercenary".
- As vice president she headed the SEBIN intelligence service, which the United Nations found had committed crimes against humanity to crush political dissent.
- She has been sanctioned by Colombia, Canada, Mexico, the European Union, Switzerland and the United States; in February 2026 EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said she would propose lifting the EU sanctions.
- The 2020 "Delcygate" affair concerned her stop at Madrid-Barajas Airport on 20 January 2020 and an alleged sale of 104 bars of Venezuelan gold to Spanish businessmen for $68.5 million.

## Interim presidency

- On 3 January 2026 at about 2:00 AM VET the United States struck targets in Venezuela including Caracas, detained Maduro and took him to New York City. The Constitutional Chamber of the Supreme Tribunal of Justice ordered Rodríguez to assume the office as interim president that day; she was sworn in on 5 January 2026 by her brother Jorge Rodríguez.
- She called Maduro Venezuela's "only president"; the article says "both he and Rodríguez claim that he remains the legal officeholder", while Trump said she had been "sworn in" and would do "whatever the US asks". The European Union said on 5 January 2026 that it does not recognize her legitimacy; the United States formally recognized her authority on 12 March 2026.
- Her government released political prisoners on 8 January, signed the Amnesty Law for Democratic Coexistence on 30 January 2026, reformed the Organic Law on Hydrocarbons on 29 January 2026 to end PDVSA's monopoly, and announced $300 million received on 20 January 2026 from a $500 million oil export agreement with the United States.
- Foreign visits as acting president: Grenada (9-10 April 2026), Barbados (27 April 2026), The Hague (May 2026, the Essequibo dispute with Guyana), India (4 June 2026, meeting Narendra Modi) and Suriname (10 September 2026). She "will attend the general debate of the eighty-first session of the United Nations General Assembly in New York City and will meet President Donald Trump there."

## Conflicting statements in the article

- The Delcygate section says she has been barred from EU territory since November 2017, while the Sanctions section dates the EU sanctions and travel ban to June 2018.
- The infobox credits her with an MS from Birkbeck, University of London; the lead says she did not graduate from Birkbeck or the Sorbonne.

wikis.title: Delcy Rodríguez - life, political career and interim presidency of Venezuela
wikis.summary: Wikipedia biography of Delcy Eloína Rodríguez Gómez, the Venezuelan lawyer and PSUV politician who became interim president in January 2026 after the United States captured Nicolás Maduro.
wikis.body:
## Who she is

- "Delcy Eloína Rodríguez Gómez (born 18 May 1969) is a Venezuelan lawyer, politician, and diplomat who has been interim president of Venezuela since 2026, following the United States intervention in Venezuela. She is the first woman in Venezuelan history to perform the duties of the presidency."
- A member of the United Socialist Party of Venezuela (PSUV); 24th Vice President of Venezuela under Nicolás Maduro since 14 June 2018, succeeding Tareck El Aissami. Her infobox lists her own vice president as "Herself".
- Born in Caracas, Republic of Venezuela. Parents Jorge Antonio Rodríguez and Delcy Gómez; brother Jorge Rodríguez. Domestic partners listed as Fernando Carrillo (2004-2007) and Yussef Abou Nassif Smaili (2017-2026).
- Party: PSUV (2012-2018, 2018-present); other political affiliation MSV (2018).
- Education in the infobox: Central University of Venezuela (BA) and Birkbeck, University of London (MS). Occupation: lawyer, diplomat, politician.

## Offices held (infobox)

- President of Venezuela, interim, from 5 January 2026, preceded by Nicolás Maduro. A note says she was "Designated by the Supreme Tribunal of Justice to ensure administrative continuity on 3 January, formally sworn in two days later."
- Vice President of Venezuela, from 14 June 2018, preceded by Tareck El Aissami.
- Minister of Petroleum and Hydrocarbons, 27 August 2024 - 11 March 2026; preceded by Pedro Tellechea, succeeded by Paula Henao.
- Minister of Economy and Finance, 10 September 2020 - 27 August 2024; preceded by Simón Zerpa, succeeded by Anabel Pereira Fernández.
- President of the Constituent National Assembly, 4 August 2017 - 14 June 2018; preceded by "Position re-established; Luis Miquilena (1999)", succeeded by Diosdado Cabello.
- Minister of Foreign Affairs, 26 December 2014 - 21 June 2017; preceded by Rafael Ramírez, succeeded by Samuel Moncada.
- Minister of Popular Power for Communication and Information, 3 August 2013 - 13 October 2014; preceded by Ernesto Villegas, succeeded by Jacqueline Faría.
- Minister for Presidential Affairs, February 2006 - August 2006 under Hugo Chávez; preceded by Haiman El Troudi, succeeded by Adán Chávez.

## Personal life

- She was the romantic partner of Venezuelan actor and model Fernando Carrillo until 2007.
- "Rodríguez is a follower of Indian guru Sathya Sai Baba."

## Contradictions inside the page

- Education: the infobox credits her with an MS from Birkbeck, University of London, while the lead says she "studied labor law in Sorbonne University in Paris and social policy in Birkbeck, University of London, but did not graduate from either of them"; the Early life section mentions only the Sorbonne and says she did not graduate.
- EU entry ban: the Delcygate section says "since November 2017, Rodríguez has been prohibited from entering the territory of the European Union", while the Sanctions section says she was sanctioned by the European Union in June 2018, "shortly after being named Vice President of Venezuela", with an asset freeze and travel ban.
- Who is president: Donald Trump announced she had been "sworn in" as president, while Rodríguez herself described Maduro as Venezuela's "only president", and the article says "both he and Rodríguez claim that he remains the legal officeholder."
- The infobox gives her as interim president from 5 January 2026, while the Supreme Tribunal ordered her to assume the office on 3 January 2026.

wikis.title: Early life and family
wikis.summary: Rodríguez's birth in Caracas, her father's death in DISIP custody, and her legal education and academic work.
wikis.body:
- Born 18 May 1969 in Caracas. Sister of Jorge Rodríguez Gómez, a psychiatrist serving as President of the National Assembly of Venezuela since 2021. Mother Delcy Gómez.
- Her father, Jorge Antonio Rodríguez, was a founder of the Socialist League, a Marxist political party in Venezuela. He "was murdered in 1976, while he was incarcerated and being tortured by the Directorate of Intelligence and Prevention Services (DISIP) for his leadership role in the kidnapping of American executive and alleged CIA spy William Niehous." The lead says she was seven years old at the time.
- "According to The Washington Post, a person who had held repeated conversations with Rodríguez stated that Rodríguez had lived in Santa Monica, California during her college years."
- She graduated with a law degree from the Central University of Venezuela (UCV) in 1993 and was active as a student leader there. She then studied labor law at Sorbonne University in Paris but did not graduate.
- She served as a professor at UCV and was president of the union within the Venezuelan Association of Labor Lawyers.

wikis.title: Political career before the vice presidency (2002-2018)
wikis.summary: Her entry into politics during the 2002 coup attempt, early government posts, her short stint as Minister for Presidential Affairs, and her time as foreign minister and president of the Constituent Assembly.
wikis.body:
## Entry into politics

- She became involved in national politics during the 2002 Venezuelan coup attempt, and "has stated that her decision to enter politics was motivated by revenge for the death of her father while in the custody of pro-American intelligence agents."
- While in London during the crisis, she and her mother symbolically took over the Venezuelan Embassy in London to protest the de facto government of Pedro Carmona, coordinating interviews with the BBC, CNN and other international media.
- She joined the General Coordination of the Vice Presidency in 2003, became Director of International Affairs at the Ministry of Energy and Mines, and in 2005 was appointed Vice-minister for European Affairs.

## Minister for Presidential Affairs (2006)

- She served February to August 2006; "Her tenure was short-lived due to reported tensions with president Hugo Chávez", reportedly refusing to show the "personal homage" expected by the president.
- Profiles in Tal Cual and El Estímulo say she disregarded established hierarchies and kept a direct attitude that alienated the presidential inner circle. On an official visit to Moscow in 2006 she reportedly argued heatedly with Chávez and swore at him; "Chávez dismissed her, and she had to return immediately to Venezuela."

## 2007-2014

- In 2007 she was General Coordinator to the Vice-President of Venezuela while her brother held the vice presidency.
- In August 2013 Maduro appointed her Minister of Popular Power for Communication and Information, reaffirmed in 2014 and held until October 2014.

## Minister of Foreign Affairs (2014-2017)

- Appointed in December 2014, succeeding Rafael Ramírez Carreño; "Rodríguez became the first woman to hold this position in Venezuela's history."
- December 2015: at the 49th Summit of Mercosur heads of state in Asunción she clashed with Argentine president Mauricio Macri over political prisoners, accusing him of meddling, of endorsing political violence against Chavismo, of criticising Hebe de Bonafini, of releasing officials responsible for dictatorship-era torture and of vetoing human rights laws - claims Clarín characterised as factual errors. Maduro later praised her for metaphorically "sending Macri to the showers".
- At the same summit she presented agency photographs of Leopoldo López and opposition protestors attacking public buildings, saying they evidenced López's responsibility for "attacks against essential public services and Venezuelan universities". Argentine Foreign Minister Susana Malcorra said the accusations were incorrect, overly aggressive and based on inaccurate information.
- 2016: she accused OAS Secretary General Luis Almagro of "international bullying" over his attempt to suspend Venezuela from the OAS, and in March 2016 called his report part of a "complex intervention strategy with medium and long-term consequences", telling the assembly that over 70% of Almagro's tweets criticised the Venezuelan government and its citizens.
- June 2016: at the 195th anniversary of the Battle of Carabobo, Maduro awarded her the Military Order of National Defense, Commander Degree, First Class, for "defending the interests of the nation in the face of attacks from the right". At the XXV Ibero-American Summit in Cartagena de Indias she told Peru's president Pedro Pablo Kuczynski to "see more of the reality of the people of Latin America".
- Brazil, Argentina and Paraguay deliberated on suspending Venezuela from Mercosur over compliance with trade, political, democratic and human rights requirements; Venezuela did not acknowledge the suspension and sought to keep the pro tempore presidency until 30 December 2016.
- December 2016: after the suspension she tried to force entry into a Mercosur meeting in Buenos Aires she had not been invited to, accompanied by Bolivian foreign minister David Choquehuanca, and was blocked by riot police at the San Martín Palace. She said she was "struck" by police and a doctor had to immobilize her arm; when she got in, the meeting room was empty because the other foreign ministers had moved.
- June 2017: she left the Chancellor role to stand in the National Constituent Assembly elections, having been a member of the Presidential Commission for the Constituent Assembly. Maduro honoured her on 22 June with the Saber Order of the Liberator Simón Bolívar of the Battle of Carabobo. Samuel Moncada succeeded her.
- At a 2017 OAS meeting she called Almagro a "liar, dishonest, a criminal, and a mercenary, a traitor to everything that represents the dignity of a Latin American diplomat", drawing criticism from Uruguayan Foreign Minister Rodolfo Nin Novoa; in June 2017 she criticised Kuczynski after he proposed international intervention in Venezuela.

## President of the Constituent Assembly (2017-2018)

- Elected in July 2017 as a deputy for Caracas to the National Constituent Assembly and chosen as its president on its establishment in August 2017 at the Federal Legislative Palace.
- In January 2018 Maduro announced her as president of the then-to-be-legalized Somos Venezuela Movement (MSV). In February 2018 she resigned from the PSUV to join the MSV under statutes prohibiting dual membership; she re-entered the PSUV in October 2018.

wikis.title: Vice President of Venezuela (2018-2026)
wikis.summary: Her appointment as vice president, her control of the SEBIN intelligence service, her economy and petroleum portfolios, and reported back-channel contacts before Maduro's capture.
wikis.body:
- Appointed Vice President of Venezuela by Maduro on 14 June 2018, succeeding Tareck El Aissami. She also became head official of the Bolivarian Intelligence Service (SEBIN), which depends on the vice presidency. "During Rodríguez's time as head of SEBIN, the United Nations found the agency had committed crimes against humanity with the intent of crushing political dissent."
- December 2018: she welcomed Turkish president Recep Tayyip Erdoğan on his official visit to Venezuela. November 2022: she visited the Sheikh Zayed Grand Mosque in Abu Dhabi.
- Photographs in the article show her with Lula da Silva and Emmanuel Macron at the 3rd EU-CELAC summit in Brussels on 17 July 2023, and with Russian Deputy Prime Minister Dmitry Chernyshenko in Moscow on 26 September 2024.
- "Reporting from late 2025 suggests she established private communication channels with international intermediaries. Analysts point to a clandestine meeting on the island of Bonaire in November 2025 as a pivotal moment where she reportedly discussed 'stabilization protocols' for Venezuela's energy sector in the event of a power vacuum."

## Minister of Economy and Finance (2020-2024)

- Served 10 September 2020 to 27 August 2024, appointed by Maduro.
- In July 2021 she took part in the Annual Assembly of Fedecámaras - "the first instance in two decades that a high-ranking official from the national executive attended this event", which convenes leaders of the country's main corporations. She highlighted private sector engagement in unlocking Venezuela's productive capacity but urged the business community to refrain from political involvement. Fedecámaras has historically been viewed by Chavismo as part of the opposition, "often being described as the 'parasitic bourgeoisie'".

wikis.title: Capture of Nicolás Maduro and Rodríguez's assumption of power (January 2026)
wikis.summary: The US strikes of 3 January 2026, the Supreme Tribunal ruling making her interim president, her swearing-in on 5 January and the reactions to it.
wikis.body:
- "On 3 January 2026, at approximately 2:00 AM VET, the United States carried out several strikes in Venezuela, including the capital of Caracas, and detained President Maduro and transported him to New York City."
- Rodríguez was granted presidential powers under Article 233 of the Venezuelan Constitution, under which the vice president takes charge if there is a presidential vacancy. She initially demanded proof that Maduro was still alive.
- US President Donald Trump announced that Secretary of State Marco Rubio had made contact with her and that she had been "sworn in" as president, and that she told Rubio she would do "whatever the US asks", adding that she was gracious but "really doesn't have a choice".
- According to The New York Times, she "had earned the respect of American officials due to increasing Venezuela's oil production and stabilizing its economy, despite harsher US sanctions", and has a reputation among Venezuelan and foreign business leaders as a technocrat.
- According to the Financial Times, her brother Jorge Rodríguez had held talks with the US government in 2025 to have her lead a post-Maduro transitional government, "although those talks had included Maduro being allowed to go into exile instead of being captured".
- The Venezuelan military announced it would recognize her as acting president and called for a return to normalcy; she also received a pledge of loyalty from Assemblyman Nicolás Maduro Guerra, the president's son.
- On 3 January 2026 the Venezuelan government declared a state of emergency (estado de conmoción) suspending constitutional guarantees and authorizing detention without judicial warrant of individuals expressing support for the military operation.

## Supreme Tribunal ruling

- On 3 January the Constitutional Chamber of the Supreme Tribunal of Justice ordered Rodríguez to "assume and exercise, as interim president, all the powers, duties, and faculties inherent to the office of President of the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela, in order to guarantee administrative continuity and the comprehensive defense of the nation."
- The ruling rested on an expansive interpretation of constitutional provisions on state continuity and the role of the executive vice president: Maduro's capture was an extraordinary situation that could not immediately be treated as an absolute absence, since it involved no resignation, death, removal or declaration of permanent incapacity. The court found a temporary inability to exercise the office and authorized her to assume the functions of acting president "without initially establishing a fixed term".

## Inauguration and reactions

- On Venezolana de Televisión she described Maduro as Venezuela's "only president", called for calm and unity while Maduro remained under US detention, and said Venezuela would never be the colony of any nation. She also said that "governments around the world are shocked that the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela has become the victim and target of an attack of this nature, which undoubtedly has Zionist undertones".
- She was sworn in as acting president on 5 January 2026 by her brother Jorge Rodríguez, president of the National Assembly, and announced a week of national mourning for those killed in the American strike.
- On inauguration day armed colectivos were deployed in the streets; fourteen journalists were detained and later released without being formally presented before a court, and CNN journalist Stefano Pozzebon was deported from Venezuela.
- Speaking at the European Commission, spokesperson Anitta Hipper announced on 5 January 2026 that the European Union does not recognize the legitimacy of Rodríguez as the country's acting head of government.

wikis.title: Policies of the Rodríguez interim government in 2026
wikis.summary: Her government's restart of relations with the United States, oil reforms and sales, amnesty law, social missions, health and education plans, and foreign visits.
wikis.body:
## Relations with the United States

- On 8 January her government released nine foreign and Venezuelan political prisoners; Donald Trump announced he had cancelled a second wave of attacks because of the gesture. The US and the Rodríguez government began discussions to restart diplomatic relations and possibly reopen the U.S. embassy, closed since 2019.
- On 16 January she met CIA director John Ratcliffe in Caracas on intelligence cooperation, economic stability and action against drug traffickers. On 13 February she met a delegation led by U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright on energy cooperation.
- On 12 March the United States formally recognized her authority.

## Energy policy

- On 6 January 2026 Trump stated that Venezuela's "interim authorities" would deliver between 30 and 50 million barrels of oil to the United States and that the proceeds would remain under U.S. control, presenting it as part of the post-transition energy framework. On 7 January PDVSA confirmed it was "conducting negotiations with the United States for the sale of oil volumes", calling it a "strictly commercial" transaction under legal criteria, without confirming Trump's figure.
- On 20 January 2026 Rodríguez announced that $300 million had been received from the first U.S.-facilitated sales of Venezuelan crude, part of a $500 million oil export agreement between Venezuela and the United States.
- On 29 January 2026 she signed a reform to the Organic Law on Hydrocarbons, approved by the National Assembly, ending PDVSA's monopoly over oil production and sales, allowing private domestic and foreign companies to manage production and commercialization, reducing fiscal and administrative burdens on operators and expanding the Ministry of Petroleum's powers to authorize partnerships and contracts with international firms.
- In early 2026 the U.S. Department of the Treasury partially eased sanctions on Venezuela's energy sector through new OFAC general licenses, including GL 46.

## Domestic measures

- In early 2026 she issued decrees eliminating or restructuring several Bolivarian social programs created under Chávez and Maduro; at least seven missions and foundations, including the New Frontier for Peace Socialist Mission Foundation, were dismantled or reorganized.
- On 30 January 2026 she announced and signed the Amnesty Law for Democratic Coexistence, granting amnesty for political offenses and politically motivated acts of violence committed since 1999. "With the law in place, Venezuela has effectively acknowledged that the government has held political prisoners."
- On 14 January 2026 she launched the Plan por la Salud y la Vida ("Health and Life Plan") to strengthen primary health care services.
- On 7 April 2026 the government implemented a plan that restored 1,700 schools throughout the country.

## Foreign visits

- First overseas visits as acting president: Grenada on 9-10 April 2026 and Barbados on 27 April 2026.
- In May 2026 she travelled to The Hague to represent Venezuela in the dispute with Guyana over Essequibo.
- On 4 June 2026 she paid a state visit to India, meeting Prime Minister Narendra Modi in New Delhi.
- On 10 September 2026 she flew to Suriname and met President Jennifer Geerlings-Simons to discuss oil, gas and hydrocarbons agreements.
- "Rodríguez will attend the general debate of the eighty-first session of the United Nations General Assembly in New York City and will meet President Donald Trump there."
- A photograph shows her with Colombian president Gustavo Petro on 24 April 2026.

wikis.title: Sanctions on Rodríguez and the Delcygate affair
wikis.summary: The countries that sanctioned her, moves to lift those sanctions after she took office, and the 2020 Madrid airport scandal involving Venezuelan gold.
wikis.body:
## Sanctions

- Colombia included her on a list of people banned from entering the country, along with (as of 2019) approximately 200 other Maduro government supporters and associates.
- September 2017: Canada sanctioned her for her role in Venezuela's constitutional crisis.
- April 2018: the Mexican Senate approved a Point of Agreement rejecting the presidential elections scheduled for 20 May, froze the assets of Maduro administration officials including Rodríguez and barred them from entering Mexico.
- June 2018: shortly after being named Vice President, she was one of eleven Venezuelan officials sanctioned by the European Union, with assets frozen and a travel ban, for "undermin[ing] democracy and the rule of law in Venezuela".
- July 2018: Switzerland sanctioned her, freezing assets and imposing a travel ban, citing the same reasons as the EU.
- September 2018: the United States sanctioned her for "corruption and humanitarian issues" by adding her to OFAC's Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons List.
- After her ascension to the interim presidency her cabinet asked the European Commission to lift the EU sanctions; "The Commission has yet to respond." In February 2026 EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said she had accepted Spain's request and would propose lifting sanctions against Rodríguez.

## Delcygate

- In January 2020 a controversy emerged in Spain over her presence at Madrid-Barajas Airport, where she was purported to have met Spanish politician José Luis Ábalos. The article says that "since November 2017, Rodríguez has been prohibited from entering the territory of the European Union". Ábalos denied having met her.
- The incident took place on 20 January, when an aircraft registered TC-AKE and flying the Turkish flag arrived at the terminal; on recognizing Rodríguez among the passengers, Spanish authorities decided to prevent her entry. Also on the flight were Kenny Antonio Díaz, Alejandra Carolina Bastidas, Yussef Abou Nassif Smaili (her partner), Jorge Andrés Giménez (president of the Venezuelan Football Federation) and minister Félix Plasencia.
- "The scandal originated from a covert visit by Delcy Rodríguez to Spain, during which she allegedly facilitated the fraudulent sale of 104 bars of Venezuelan gold to Spanish businessmen for $68.5 million." The transaction was purportedly conducted through the Spanish Ministry of Transport with the involvement of then-Transport Minister José Luis Ábalos, who is under investigation as part of the Koldo Case; El Confidencial reported she offered the gold bars to Spanish entrepreneurs at meetings arranged with Ábalos, with the approval of Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez.
- The Guardia Civil's Central Operative Unit (UCO) found communications on Spanish businessman Víctor de Aldama's phone linking him to Rodríguez about the purchase of Venezuelan gold. A contract dated 27 December 2019 set delivery of the gold between 27 December 2019 and 6 January 2020, shortly before her secret trip to Madrid, "which was officially described by La Moncloa as a 'technical stopover'".
- According to Diario de Cuba the connection underscored the alleged lack of commitment by the Spanish government to a democratic transition in Venezuela; a 2020 U.S. government official said Spain was a significant barrier within the EU in confronting the Venezuelan government. The opposition Partido Popular accused Sánchez of deceit about the purpose of the visit and said it would launch a political, judicial and international campaign over Delcygate.
- A photograph shows Rodríguez with Ursula von der Leyen, Charles Michel and Pedro Sánchez in Brussels in 2023, "five years after European sanctions against Rodríguez".

## Rules

- "This market will resolve to “No” if the United States takes a qualifying military action against Iran by the specified date, 11:59 PM Iran Standard Time. Otherwise this market will resolve to “Yes.”"
- "A qualifying military action refers to an air strike or a surface-to-surface missile strike, initiated by the United States, that directly impacts Iran. An air strike includes bombs, air-to-surface missiles, and air-launched drones. A surface-to-surface missile strike includes one-way attack drones and surface-to-surface missiles such as cruise or ballistic missiles."
- Not qualifying: munitions destroyed or intercepted before impact; surface-to-air missile strikes; small-arms fire; ground incursions; cyber operations; naval gunfire and artillery fire; howitzers, artillery pieces, mortars and rocket artillery (e.g. MLRS); minor surface-to-surface strikes including short range loitering munitions, FPV drones and ATGM strikes; "Any threat, authorization, or announcement of force that has not been executed."
- "“Iran” refers to the terrestrial territory of Iran, including its internal waters. Iran’s maritime territory and airspace are not encompassed."
- Where sources conflict the market stays open until a consensus forms or "3 full calendar days (Iran Standard Time) from the date of the first credibly reported evidence of the action".
- Resolution sources: "official information from the governments and militaries of the United States and Iran and a consensus of credible reporting."

## Site note on Middle East markets

> "The promise of prediction markets is to harness the wisdom of the crowd to create accurate, unbiased forecasts for the most important events to society. That ability is particularly invaluable in gut-wrenching times like today. After discussing with those directly affected by the attacks, who had dozens of questions, we realized that prediction markets could give them the answers they needed in ways TV news and 𝕏 could not."

The 60-day framework, intended to halt military operations across fronts including Lebanon, reopen the Strait of Hormuz, and advance nuclear talks, collapsed amid mutual violations, Iranian strikes on shipping, and renewed US strikes through July and into September. Limited exchanges of attacks, expanded US sanctions, and proxy-related tensions in Lebanon continue to define the environment. Regional mediators have floated renewed diplomatic channels, yet no comprehensive agreement has taken hold."

wikis.title: 2026 Iran war
wikis.summary: Wikipedia's article on the war between the United States and Israel and Iran and its allies that began on 28 February 2026, covering its course to September 2026, casualties, impacts, diplomacy and reactions.
wikis.body:
## The war

- "Since 28 February 2026, the United States and Israel have been at war with Iran and its regional allies." Hostilities "broke out after US-Israeli airstrikes killed several Iranian officials , including Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei", launched "amid ongoing US-Iran negotiations regarding Iran's nuclear program". The infobox gives the date as "28 February 2026 - present (6 months, 3 weeks and 2 days)", the location as "Middle East" and the status as "Ongoing", with the Strait of Hormuz crisis, the resumption of the Hezbollah-Israel conflict, a US-led economic isolation campaign against Iran, and the escalation of the Yemeni civil war and Bab al-Mandab crisis listed under it.
- Sides: the United States, Israel, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Kuwait, Bahrain, Yemen (PLC), Iranian separatist groups and the United Kingdom against Iran and the Axis of Resistance - Yemen (SPC), Hezbollah, the Popular Mobilization Forces and the Islamic Resistance in Iraq - with a long list of "[o]ther parties" marked "dubious - discuss". Footnotes record that Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Kuwait and Bahrain also struck Iran or Iran-backed militias covertly before Saudi Arabia acknowledged joint strikes on 29 July 2026; Kuwait denied the reports.
- Codenames: "Operation Epic Fury" (US), "Operation Roaring Lion" (Israel), "Operation True Promise IV" (Iran). The war is also called the "Third Gulf War", the "Third Imposed War" in Iranian state media, and the "Ramadan War".

## Course of the fighting

- Trump authorized Operation Epic Fury on 27 February at 3:38 p.m. EST (11:08 p.m. IRST); strikes began the next day "around 9:45 am. IRST (1:15 am. EST)". The Israeli Air Force said it struck "500 military targets in Iran in the largest combat sortie in its history" and used "over 1,200 bombs in 24 hours". The initial strikes killed Ali Khamenei and other senior officials; cyberattacks caused a near-total internet blackout "lasting over 60 hours with connectivity dropping to as low as 1% of normal levels" (a later section puts connectivity at 4% of ordinary levels and the blackout beyond 240 hours, "the second longest ever").
- Iran replied within hours against Israel, US bases and Gulf states, and shipping through the Strait of Hormuz "slowed to a standstill, with 150 freight ships, including oil tankers, stalled". Hezbollah resumed fire on Israel on 2 March; Israel authorized a ground invasion of Lebanon on 3 March and launched it on 17 March. USS Charlotte sank the Iranian frigate IRIS Dena about "40 nautical miles (74 km; 46 mi) south of Galle , Sri Lanka", killing 104.
- Mojtaba Khamenei was elected supreme leader on 8 March. Through March the US and Israel struck Kharg Island, South Pars, Natanz (with bunker busters on 21 March) and Iranian leadership figures including Ali Larijani; Iran struck Dimona, Prince Sultan Air Base and, disputedly, Diego Garcia. Admiral Brad Cooper said the US "had struck more than 8,000 Iranian military targets, including 130 vessels", and CENTCOM later said "over 11,000 targets". The Houthis joined on 28 March.
- A two-week ceasefire mediated by Pakistan began on 7-8 April; Israel and the US said it excluded Lebanon, "contradicting the Pakistani mediators and Iran", and Israel's "Operation Eternal Darkness" killed "at least 357 people" there. The Islamabad talks of 11-13 April failed, and rival blockades followed - a US naval blockade from 13 April and Iran's closure of the strait, "a dual blockade" in The Guardian's words. Trump and Pezeshkian signed the Islamabad Memorandum at Versailles on 17 June, suspending hostilities for 60 days; it collapsed on 7-8 July when the IRGC attacked commercial vessels in the strait. After a military lull in August and Trump's 20 August "economic D-day" sanctions threat, hostilities resumed on 1 September 2026, with the US reclassifying the engagement from "Operation Epic Fury" to "Overseas Operations".

## Casualties, costs and impacts

- The infobox gives competing counts: per the US, "19-23 soldiers and 1 contractor killed", "820 military personnel wounded" and "97 aircraft lost or damaged"; per Israel, 40 soldiers, 1 contractor and 31 civilians killed with "7,841 injured"; per Iran, "3,528 people killed" and "27,170 injured"; per HRANA "3,684 killed"; per OCHA "3,400+ civilians killed" and "33,000+ civilians injured"; per the US and Israel, "6,000+" Iranian military personnel killed. Kuwait, Bahrain, Saudi Arabia and the UAE report their own dead and injured.
- US losses and strain: "at least 228 structures or pieces of equipment at US bases across the Persian Gulf" damaged per Washington Post satellite analysis; 42 US aircraft destroyed or damaged per a May Congressional Research Service report; about 65% of 2,330 Patriot interceptors used between February and July; roughly 80% of THAAD missiles used as of 5 August; around 25% of Reaper drones lost as of 14 August.
- Cost: "[a]s of June 2026 ... the cost of the war to the US was estimated at $113.3 billion", with a $1.5 trillion Pentagon request for the next fiscal year; Iran's government spokesperson estimated "$270 billion, or 90% of the estimated Iranian GDP in 2026" for 40 days of war; a mid-September CBO report put US costs at "at least $38 billion" and rising "roughly $3 billion per month".
- In Iran, "138,000 civilian sites ... were damaged", with reconstruction estimated at 2-5 years, and many heritage sites including Chehel Sotoun, Golestan Palace and the Rafi'-Nia synagogue were damaged or destroyed. Lebanon said "over one million people, one-sixth of the population, had been displaced". Iran fired 650 missiles at Israel in the 40 days to the 8 April ceasefire, killing 24 civilians and injuring more than 7,000. Globally, oil and gas prices surged and the IEA's Fatih Birol called it the "greatest global energy security challenge in history".

## Diplomacy, reactions and analysis

The UN secretary-general and several countries condemned the US-Israeli strikes while the Security Council condemned Iran's strikes on Gulf states. Most countries called for peace; US public opinion was mostly against the war and Congress failed to pass a War Powers Resolution, while "Israeli opinion was overwhelmingly in favor". Analysts disagree on the outcome: some say Iran's survival and its use of the strait showed the limits of American power, others point to severe Iranian losses, and in August Reuters' Ron Bousso "described the conflict as a stalemate". Legal experts warn Trump's threats against Iranian infrastructure "could constitute war crimes under the Rome Statute".

## About the page

The article carries a merge proposal for "United States war crimes in Iran strikes" ("Proposed since September 2026") and an open requested move to "Iran War", is listed in 93 languages, and includes an infobox map of reported strike sites dated from 2 March to 29 March 2026 sourced largely to ISW updates and news outlets, extensive lettered notes, and a long reference list whose citations run into late September 2026.

## What this part holds

( Discuss ) Proposed since September 2026." and "A request that this article title be changed to Iran War Iran War is under discussion . Please do not move this article until the discussion is closed."

wikis.title: 2026 Iran war: infobox, lead, background and the first two weeks of fighting
wikis.summary: The main body of the Wikipedia article on the 2026 Iran war up to mid-March: the infobox (dates, belligerents, commanders, casualties), the lead, the war's names, background on Iran-US/Israel relations and nuclear activity, the prelude, and hostilities from 27 February to 13 March 2026.
wikis.body:
## Overview

- The article covers a war that, it says, has run "Since 28 February 2026", in which "the United States and Israel have been at war with Iran and its regional allies". Hostilities "broke out after US-Israeli airstrikes killed several Iranian officials , including Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei", launched "amid ongoing US-Iran negotiations regarding Iran's nuclear program".
- The war is described as part of a Middle Eastern crisis sparked by the Gaza war, following the Twelve-Day War, and preceded by "the largest US military buildup in the region since the 2003 invasion of Iraq".
- Stated US justifications: a response to the crackdown on anti-government protests in Iran, preventing Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon, regime change, and "taking Iran's oil and gas resources". Critics "have rejected these justifications, maintaining that the attack initiated a war of aggression , in violation of international law".
- Iran, "[f]ollowing a decentralized strategy", replied with missile and drone attacks on Israel, US bases and US allies in the Middle East, blocked the Strait of Hormuz and "subsequently claim[ed] sovereignty over it in late March". The UAE, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and Bahrain then attacked Iran after strikes on their territory. Fighting between Hezbollah and Israel resumed two days after Khamenei's assassination; Israel "began occupying southern Lebanon in March". A Houthi escalation of the Yemeni civil war "in September started the Strait of Bab al-Mandab crisis".
- Economic impact given in the lead: "the largest supply disruption of the global oil market", disruption of natural gas, fertilizer, aviation and tourism, and financial-market volatility. "As of June 2026 [ update ] , the cost of the war to the US was estimated at $113.3 billion", while "the Trump administration requested $1.5 trillion for the Pentagon over the next fiscal year, which would set a record in modern US military spending if approved by Congress".
- Diplomacy in the lead: the UN secretary-general and several countries condemned the US-Israeli strikes; the UN Security Council "passed a resolution condemning Iran's retaliatory strikes on Gulf states"; "A two-week ceasefire beginning on 8 April came under strain after Iran responded to Israeli attacks on Lebanon by resuming its blockade"; after "the failure of the Islamabad Talks on 12-13 April" the US imposed its own naval blockade; "A memorandum to end the war was signed on 17 June by the presidents of the US and Iran, lifting the dual blockade"; on 28 June the US and Iran "agreed to cease their exchange of attacks"; "On 8 July, the ceasefire deal between the US and Iran collapsed after Iran initiated attacks on commercial vessels in the Strait of Hormuz to assert Iranian sovereignty over the Strait of Hormuz, surprising U.S. officials and interrupting a brief diplomatic lull."

## Names

- US codename for the initial strikes: "Operation Epic Fury"; Israel's: "Operation Roaring Lion", said to be in line with "Operation Rising Lion" for its strikes during the Twelve-Day War in June 2025. Iran codenamed its response "Operation True Promise IV" (Persian: عملیات وعده صادق ۴, romanized: Amaliyat-e Va'deh-ye Sadegh 4).
- "American media outlets have generally referred to the conflict as the Iran war." It has also been called the "Third Gulf War" (Gulf War III) after the Gulf War (1990-1991) and the Iraq War/Second Gulf War (2003-2011); Iranian state media call it the "Third Imposed War", with the Iran-Iraq War (1980-1988) and the Twelve-Day War as the "First" and "Second"; and, because it began during Ramadan, it "has sometimes been called the 'Ramadan War'".

## Navigation content in this part

The part also carries the article's campaign navbox, listing sub-articles such as Timeline, Casualties, Order of battle, Prelude, strike articles by country, "Sinking of IRIS Dena", "Strait of Hormuz crisis", "Naval blockade of Iran", "Operation Project Freedom", "Battle of Khiam", "Battle of Bint Jbeil", "Crossing of the Litani River", "2026 Israel-Lebanon ceasefire", "2026 Iran war ceasefire", "Islamabad Talks", "Islamabad Memorandum", "UNSC Resolution 2817" and "2026 alleged Iranian plot to assassinate Donald Trump".

Listed as "Other parties: [ dubious - discuss ]": Azerbaijan, Egypt, Iraq, Kurdistan Region, Jordan, Lebanon, Oman, Palestine, Qatar, Syria, Turkey.

wikis.title: Casualties and losses as the infobox reports them
wikis.summary: The infobox's casualty and equipment-loss figures, each attributed to the party or body that reports it.
wikis.body:
The infobox gives competing counts, each under whose figure it is.

**Per US - United States:** "19-23 soldiers and 1 contractor killed"; "820 military personnel wounded"; "5 contractors injured"; "97 aircraft lost or damaged"; "217+ U.S. structures and 11 assets damaged or destroyed (May 2026)".

**Per Israel - Israel:** "40 soldiers and 1 contractor killed"; "31 civilians killed"; "7,841 injured (including 1,468 military personnel)"; "23 aircraft lost or damaged".

**Per Saudi Arabia:** "3 civilians killed and 23 injured". **Per United Arab Emirates:** "2 soldiers, 1 civilian contractor and 13 civilians killed, 246 injured". **Per Bahrain:** "2 civilians killed and 51 injured". **Per Kuwait:** "4 soldiers and 8 civilians killed, 82 soldiers and 108 civilians injured".

**Per PJAK and PDKI:** Coalition of Political Forces of Iranian Kurdistan "10 fighters killed". **Per PFF:** People's Fighters Front "8 fighters killed".

**Per OSINT - United States:** "US 5th Fleet Naval base in Bahrain rendered inoperable"; "12+ radar and satellite systems destroyed or damaged".

**Per Iran - Iran:** "3,528 people killed"; "27,170 injured". **Per internal sources:** Hezbollah "1,000+ fighters killed"; Hamas "3 members killed"; Popular Mobilization Forces "80 fighters killed, 270 injured (April 2026)" and "20 fighters killed, 32 injured (July 2026)".

**Per HRANA:** "3,684 killed (1,249 military personnel, 1,721 civilians, and 714 unclassified)". **Per OCHA:** "3,400+ civilians killed"; "33,000+ civilians injured".

**Per US and Israel - Iran:** "6,000+ military personnel killed"; "~15,000 military personnel wounded"; "190+ ballistic missile launchers destroyed"; "155 naval vessels destroyed or damaged"; "9 IRGC-linked oil tankers destroyed or damaged". Hezbollah: "2,500 fighters killed".

The box points to separate lists for naval and aviation losses and to a casualties article for other countries' counts.

wikis.title: Background: Iran's relations with the United States and Israel
wikis.summary: The article's historical background, from the 1953 coup to Netanyahu's lobbying of Trump in early 2026.
wikis.body:
- A US- and UK-backed coup d'etat in 1953 deposed prime minister Mohammad Mosaddegh over his nationalization of the oil industry, strengthening Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi; Israel kept ties with Iran under its "alliance of the periphery" strategy. The 1979 revolution replaced the Shah with an Islamic republic; Iran cut ties with the US and Israel and held US embassy staff hostage, releasing them after the Algiers Accords (1981), in which the US agreed not to intervene in Iranian affairs.
- During the Iran-Iraq War the US supported Iraq. "In 1988, a US warship struck an Iranian mine , and the US responded by attacking Iran's navy . A few months later, the US mistakenly shot down a civilian Iranian flight." Iran started a ballistic missile program to deter Iraqi missile attacks during the 1980-88 war and to compensate for lacking a modern air force under sanctions.
- "Starting in 1985, Iran began engaging in proxy conflicts throughout the Middle East", forming the informal 'Axis of Resistance' against American, Israeli, Saudi, Emirati and sometimes Turkish influence.
- 2002: Iran's covert nuclear program first revealed; Iran denied seeking a weapon. 2003: the AMAD Project suspended after Khamenei's fatwa against nuclear weapons. 2005: US sanctions on the nuclear program begin; 2006: UN Security Council sanctions. US and Israeli cyberwarfare against Iranian nuclear facilities; Israel assassinated several Iranian nuclear scientists. UNSC concern from 2006 led to the JCPOA between Iran, the P5+1 and the EU in 2015.
- January 2020: Trump ordered the assassination of Qasem Soleimani, commander of the Quds Force. After the October 7 attacks and the start of the Gaza war, Israel fought Iran-backed militias including Hamas, Hezbollah and the Houthis; Israeli strikes on the Iranian consulate in Damascus and the assassinations of Ismail Haniyeh and Hassan Nasrallah in 2024 drew Iranian strikes on Israel in April and October. In June 2025 Israel launched the Twelve-Day War against Iranian military and nuclear facilities; the US joined by striking nuclear facilities, and it ended in a ceasefire.
- "In early 2026, Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu lobbied President Donald Trump for a joint military strike on Iran, specifically targeting its leadership." After high-level meetings in February, Trump authorized "Operation Epic Fury", "with reports citing Israeli intelligence provided by Netanyahu as a decisive factor in the decision".

wikis.title: Nuclear activity in the Middle East
wikis.summary: The article's account of Iran's nuclear program, sanctions and IAEA findings, and of Israel's undeclared nuclear weapons.
wikis.body:
**Iran's program.** Enrichment has been part of Iranian national development plans since the Shah's regime; Iran kept the program after 1979 and "has long denied seeking nuclear weapons, saying its enrichment efforts were to generate nuclear power for civilian use". Despite Iran's compliance with the JCPOA, Trump withdrew the US in 2018, re-imposed sanctions and adopted "maximum pressure"; the Biden administration kept most sanctions; Trump continued the approach in his second term. "In September 2025, the UN reimposed sanctions on Iran using the 'snapback' mechanism", weakening the currency, raising prices for meat, rice and other staples, freezing assets abroad, suspending arms transactions and adding ballistic-missile penalties. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called the December 2025 collapse of the Iranian currency the strategy's "grand culmination".

At his State of the Union Address in February 2026 Trump "claimed Iran had restarted its nuclear program and was developing missiles capable of striking the US". The article says this contradicted his earlier claim that the program was "obliterated" and US intelligence reports that Iran posed no threat to the US and "needed until 2035 to build such missiles to do so".

**IAEA.** "On 12 June 2025, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) found Iran non-compliant with its NPT safeguards agreement for the first time since 2005." Days later it was reported Iran had stored highly enriched uranium in an underground facility undamaged by the 2025 US bombings. Iran then denied the IAEA access to bombed facilities while allowing access to unaffected ones; Mohammad Eslami, head of the Atomic Energy Organization of Iran, said inspections of struck facilities would wait until the IAEA set rules for the post-war situation and condemned the attacks. "In February 2026, Iran informed the IAEA that normal safeguards were 'legally untenable and materially impracticable' as a result of threats and 'acts of aggression'", leaving the IAEA unable to verify suspension of enrichment or the stockpile's status, "though it found no evidence Iran was weaponizing". Analysts in the UK and US called the strategy "nuclear hedging"; the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists said Iran was using enrichment and stockpiles as negotiating leverage and was willing to dilute or export higher-enriched uranium for sanctions relief and protection from attack.

**Israel.** "Israel is widely believed to possess nuclear weapons , with an estimated stockpile of between 90 and 400 nuclear warheads", and "is the only nuclear-armed country that does not officially acknowledge its nuclear weapons capability". Some scholars argue this incentivized Iran's program, as deterrence balance or a regional arms race. Israel rejects calls to join the NPT or negotiate a Middle East nuclear weapon free zone, frustrating US and UK diplomacy; scholars suggest US tacit acceptance is "a double standard that undermines its diplomatic credibility" in nonproliferation talks.

wikis.title: Prelude to the war
wikis.summary: The excerpted prelude section: the January 2026 crackdown, the US buildup and the February negotiations that ran until the strikes.
wikis.body:
- Marked as "an excerpt from Prelude to the 2026 Iran war".
- "Tension between Iran and the United States during negotiations over Iran's nuclear program intensified in January 2026 when Iranian security forces massacred anti-government protesters."
- "The US began its greatest buildup of military assets in the region since the Iraq War in 2003 . The US accused Iran of building up its nuclear and missile programs to threaten the United States and its allies. Iran accused the US of disinformation . Gulf states like Qatar predicted that escalations could severely harm the region . Negotiations regarding the Iranian nuclear program were held in February until the US and Israel commenced military strikes in Iran on 28 February 2026."
- A caption states that Netanyahu "successfully lobbied the Trump administration for military intervention. (Pictured in July 2025)".

wikis.title: First three days of war (27 February - 1 March 2026)
wikis.summary: The opening strikes, the killing of Ali Khamenei, the cyberattacks and internet blackout, and Iran's first retaliation.
wikis.body:
- "On 27 February at 3:38 p.m. EST (11:08 p.m. IRST ), Trump, traveling on Air Force One to Texas , authorized Operation Epic Fury." US missiles, drones and Israeli fighter jets "began striking Iran the next day, around 9:45 am. IRST (1:15 am. EST)". The strikes came during nuclear negotiations and "coincided with the holy month of Ramadan".
- The Israeli Air Force said it struck "500 military targets in Iran in the largest combat sortie in its history"; Iranian naval vessels were also targeted; Israel said it used "over 1,200 bombs in 24 hours". US strikes came from planes based around the Middle East and from aircraft carriers.
- "Initial strikes killed Iran's supreme leader Ali Khamenei and other top Iranian officials , and hundreds of Iranians were killed or injured. The Iranian Red Crescent said 24 provinces were affected."
- Cyberattacks hit Iranian infrastructure, media and phone apps with messages urging Iranians to rise up; they caused "a near-total internet blackout in Iran, lasting over 60 hours with connectivity dropping to as low as 1% of normal levels". Iran restricted internet access "allowing access only to government-approved users until 26 May".
- On 28 February Trump said the purpose of the strikes was regime change, citing Iran's support for Hamas and Hezbollah, killings of protesters, chants of "Death to America", an alleged history of attacking US civilians and soldiers, and the Iran hostage crisis. Israeli defense minister Israel Katz called the strikes a "pre-emptive attack" intended to "remove threats to...Israel". "Iran denied that it intended to attack the US."
- Iran replied within hours with missiles and drones (Operation True Promise IV; state media called the events the Ramadan War). Early targets were American radars in the region, which "degraded missile-warning capability". Iran struck Tel Aviv and Haifa and targets across the Persian Gulf: Manama, Kuwait International Airport, Abu Dhabi, Riyadh and Eastern Province in Saudi Arabia, and Erbil International Airport and the US Consulate General in Erbil.
- "On 1 or 2 March, Iran struck the radar bases for US THAAD missile defense systems in Jordan, the UAE and Saudi Arabia, destroying at least one." On 1 March Iran launched missiles and drones at Bahrain, Israel, Jordan, Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the UAE.
- The UK reported "missiles fired in the direction of Cyprus", but "don't believe they were targeted at Cyprus"; the presidents of Cyprus and Northern Cyprus denied any missiles were fired at Cyprus. The Palau-flagged Skylight and Marshall Islands-flagged MKD VYOM tankers were targeted off Oman's coast. "Shipping through the Strait of Hormuz slowed to a standstill, with 150 freight ships, including oil tankers, stalled."
- Keir Starmer said the US could use British bases for "defensive" strikes on Iran and disclosed that Ukrainian and other specialists would aid Gulf efforts against Iranian drones. Mohammed bin Salman, with US backing, vowed force against Iranian incursions, calling Iranian strikes "cowardly". Trump announced the US had accepted an Iranian proposal to negotiate; Ali Larijani ruled out talks.

wikis.title: End of the first week (2-6 March 2026)
wikis.summary: Strikes on Kuwait, Qatar and Iranian sites, the Hezbollah-Israel exchange, the Akrotiri drone strike and the sinking of IRIS Dena.
wikis.body:
- 2 March: the US embassy in Kuwait was struck and closed indefinitely. The US-flagged tanker Stena Imperative and Honduras-flagged tanker Athe Nova were struck. An advisor to an IRGC commander "said he would set fire to any ship coming through the Strait of Hormuz, and added that no oil would leave the area". Qatari air defenses shot down two Iranian Su-24 bombers. Qatar's defense ministry said Ras Laffan Industrial City, its main gas facility, and the Mesaieed Industrial Area were hit by Iranian drones; satellite imagery analysis by the Energy Economics and Society Research Institute found Ras Laffan appeared undamaged before the "unprecedented shutdown" that pushed fuel prices higher.
- The US and Israel attacked the Natanz Nuclear Facility; Iranian media reported damage to the Khatam-al-Anbia and Gandhi hospitals. "In a friendly fire incident, the pilot of an F/A-18 of the Kuwait Air Force shot down three US F-15E fighters."
- Hezbollah began firing rockets and missiles at Israel in retaliation for the killing of Khamenei, calling it a "defensive act" after more than a year of Israeli attacks despite a 2024 truce and saying the move was unrelated to the war. Lebanon banned military activities by Hezbollah. An IDF spokesperson called the attack "an official declaration of war by Hezbollah" and vowed to "neutralize" the threat; Israel struck southern Lebanon, Beirut and the Beqaa Valley, saying it killed Hezbollah intelligence head Hussein Makled and Adham Adnan al-Othman of Palestinian Islamic Jihad's Al-Quds Brigades.
- "The Royal Air Force station at Akrotiri , Cyprus, was targeted by a drone strike causing damage to a runway"; another strike on Cyprus led Greece to announce frigates and F-16s to defend the island. The Iraqi Guardians of Blood Brigades claimed attacks on the US Victory Base near Baghdad International Airport and Erbil; the Islamic Resistance in Iraq claimed 23 drone strikes on US assets in Erbil.
- 3 March: US and Israeli strikes destroyed the SNSC headquarters, the Expediency Discernment Council building in Tehran and "what Israeli officials described as an alleged underground nuclear weapons facility called Min Zadai". Their proximity to the Bushehr Nuclear Power Plant, "about 12 km (7.5 mi) away", prompted Rosatom to suspend construction on new units and evacuate non-essential staff. A CIA site in the US embassy in Riyadh was hit by Iranian drones. US officials said Iran's naval capabilities were severely damaged, mainly in the Gulf of Oman. Debris from an airstrike damaged Golestan Palace, a UNESCO World Heritage Site; UNESCO said damaging such sites is against international law. Israel Katz authorized a ground invasion of Lebanon with the 91st Division to establish a "security layer" against Hezbollah; Lebanon reported attacks reaching Kfarkela and Qouzah. Israel said it killed Daoud Alizadeh, commander of the Quds Force's Lebanon branch, in Tehran.
- Western diplomats said Qatar had struck Iran after Iran attempted to strike Doha's airport; Qatar denied joining the "campaign targeting Iran". Iran warned it would hit all economic hubs in the Middle East and that any defensive European military involvement would be an act of war.
- 4 March: Marco Rubio announced the US-Israeli attacks would increase in intensity. Israeli attacks hit the Basij headquarters. The IDF said an F-35I "Adir" shot down an Iranian Yak-130, "the first time that an F-35 shot down a crewed fighter jet in air-to-air combat, and the first time the IAF shot down an aircraft since 1985". Iran struck Al Udeid Air Base and Aramco's Ras Tanura oil refining facility. The US ordered non-essential workers in Cyprus to evacuate. A ballistic missile from Iran was intercepted by NATO air defenses entering Turkish airspace; Turkey asserted self-defense after the missile landed in Dortyol, Hatay Province, and Mark Rutte said NATO was committed to defending Turkey.
- The Iranian frigate IRIS Dena was sunk in the Indian Ocean by the US Navy submarine USS Charlotte "about 40 nautical miles (74 km; 46 mi) south of Galle , Sri Lanka", while returning from the International Fleet Review 2026 and Exercise MILAN at Visakhapatnam; the exercise required ships to carry no ammunition and "the US likely knew the Dena was defenseless". It was "the first ship sunk by a submarine in active combat since the Falklands War , and the first by an American submarine since World War II"; 104 Iranians were killed.
- 5 March: Azerbaijan said drones from Iran struck its Nakhchivan exclave, damaging an airport and injuring two civilians. Starmer confirmed UK bases on Cyprus would defend Jordan's airspace from Iranian drones; Italy, the Netherlands and Spain said they would send warships to defend Cyprus, and Ireland said it was willing to join the European defense coalition around the island if asked. The IDF killed Hamas official Wassim Attallah al-Ali in Beddawi, Lebanon.
- 6 March: Trump said there were "no time limits" for how long the war could continue. The Iranian tanker IRIS Bushehr was interned by the Sri Lanka Navy, "marking the first instance of a warship being interned in a neutral country since World War II".

wikis.title: Second week (7-13 March 2026)
wikis.summary: Carrier reinforcements, Mojtaba Khamenei's designation as supreme leader, strikes on oil and heritage sites, and falling Iranian launch rates.
wikis.body:
- 7 March: the US sent a third aircraft carrier, USS George H. W. Bush, to the Middle East; the British carrier HMS Prince of Wales was placed on advanced readiness. Iranian president Masoud Pezeshkian apologized for strikes on neighboring countries, citing "miscommunication in the ranks", and said they would not be targeted unless the US attacked from them; attacks continued, "highlighting limited control over the IRGC chief Ahmad Vahidi".
- 8 March: "Khamenei's second son, Mojtaba , was designated as Iran's new supreme leader." US Central Command posted on X urging "civilians in Iran to stay at home" and alleging "[t]he Iranian regime is knowingly endangering innocent lives".
- Israeli airstrikes hit Iranian oil storage facilities, killing four people; strikes on fuel depots near Tehran caused a "river of fire" along the streets, thick black smoke over the city and "toxic acidic rain" in the surrounding area. US Central Command announced the death of a seventh US service member. The UK said it intercepted an Iranian drone heading to Iraq and would send a Merlin helicopter to detect aerial threats. The Iranian Red Crescent Society said "65 schools and 32 medical facilities had been targeted, and more than 10,000 civilian sites damaged".
- 9 March: NATO confirmed a second ballistic missile intercepted in Turkish airspace; Turkey deployed six F-16s and air defense systems to Northern Cyprus. Trump claimed "the war is very complete, pretty much" after speaking with Putin, and "we already won the war in many ways". After Syrian president Ahmed al-Sharaa backed Lebanon's aim to disarm Hezbollah, the group targeted Inkhil in Syria. "About a dozen B-1B bombers arrived at bases in Europe."
- Strait of Hormuz transits "dropped significantly since the start of the war"; GPS jamming "of uncertain origin" disrupted ship navigation near the strait. The US State Department designated the Muslim Brotherhood branch in Sudan a terrorist organization.
- 10 March: an IRGC commander said Iran was "only firing missiles with payloads of 1,000 kg or more"; AFP reported Iran's attacks were the "most intense and heaviest" since the war began, a shift "from saturating air defenses to high-impact penetration strikes". General Dan Caine "acknowledged that Iran was fighting back, but not harder than the US expected". Shells from Lebanon landed in Serghaya, "20 km (12 mi) from Damascus". Israel issued an urgent evacuation notice for Beirut's southern suburbs.
- Defense analyst AJ Jaff reported "Iran's ballistic missile launch rate fell 92% from day one of the war (480 to 40) and the drone launch rate fell 92% (720 to 60)".
- 11 March: 14 US bombers deployed to RAF Fairford in the UK, following Hegseth's statement that it was the "most intense day of strikes inside Iran". Israel reportedly struck the Parchin military complex. A Bank Sepah branch in Tehran was hit, prompting an IRGC warning that it could strike US or Israeli banks in the region. Iran hit Stryker, a US medical supply company, with a cyberattack.
- 12 March: UNICEF reported "300 children had been killed, thousands injured, hundreds of thousands displaced, and millions unable to attend schools". Iranian deputy intelligence minister Akbar Ghaffari was killed in an airstrike. An Iranian attack set two tankers on fire off the Iraqi coast, killing one person. The Safavid-era Rashk-e Jenan was destroyed by US-Israeli strikes; other damaged buildings included the Chehel Sotoun pavilion, Rakib Khaneh Mansion, Timurid Hall, Ashraf Hall and the Ali Qapu palace - many protected by Blue Shield International, which called damaging them a war crime.
- French soldiers were injured in a drone strike at a base in Iraqi Kurdistan; Macron announced on 13 March that a soldier had been killed.
- 13 March: "to alleviate the economic costs of the war, the US temporarily lifted restrictions on the sale of Russian oil". Iran announced a coordinated offensive by its navy, army and Hezbollah against Israel and US bases. Israel reported 58 people hospitalized after a missile strike. Kuwait said defense equipment and its main airport were attacked and power lines went out of service. Missiles entering Turkish airspace were intercepted, with explosions heard near Adana. Israel struck IRGC checkpoints after tip-offs from informants, and Reuters reported strikes on Basij positions used to suppress Iranian protests.

wikis.title: 2026 Iran war: fighting from mid-March onward, casualties, impacts and reactions
wikis.summary: The Wikipedia article's account of the war from the third week of March 2026 through September, with the April ceasefire and Islamabad Memorandum, casualty and stockpile figures, impacts on Iran, Israel, Lebanon and the Gulf, economic and environmental effects, reactions, diplomacy and analysis.
wikis.body:
## Overview of this part

This part runs from the third week of the war (14 March 2026) to "Renewed hostilities (1 September - present)", then covers casualties and damages, direct impacts by country, economic and environmental impacts, reactions, diplomatic efforts, the June 2026 Memorandum of Understanding and analysis.

## Impacts outside Iran (compressed)

**Israel.** Israel declared a nationwide state of emergency, "saying that the strikes on Iran were the largest that it had ever launched"; schools and workspaces closed and public gatherings were cancelled. "In the 40 days from the start of the war through the 8 April ceasefire , there were a total of 650 missile attacks from Iran to Israel, the majority of which carried cluster munitions. About 16 of the missiles that made it past Israeli missile defenses carried conventional warheads, while 50 had cluster munitions. The attacks killed a total of 24 people, all of them civilians, and resulted in more than 7,000 injuries. Of the 24 civilians killed, 14 were struck by conventional explosive warheads and 10 by cluster submunitions. Two of the deaths were inside a sheltered space."

**Palestine.** Israel's Coordinator of Government Activities in the Territories closed multiple aid crossings in Gaza, interrupting circulation on the Egypt-Gaza border; Israeli forces suspended UN humanitarian movements and postponed staff rotations, medical evacuations and returns into Gaza, which OCHA condemned. Settler violence in the occupied West Bank increased under the renewed state of emergency, and road closures delayed medics; on 10 March the EU called the Israeli actions unacceptable and warned that "impunity for such acts risks provoking further violence".

**Lebanon.** "Lebanon stated in March that over one million people, one-sixth of the population, had been displaced."

**Persian Gulf Arab states.** The Gulf states began prosecuting civilians and foreign citizens who shared unverified rumours about the Iranian attacks; Bahrain's Cyber Crime Directorate arrested people who allegedly expressed "their support for the Iranian shelling targeting the Kingdom of Bahrain", calling it treason. Trump said "Even if we knew Gulf countries would be hit, big deal we did what we have to do". Saudi Arabia invoked its Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement with Pakistan, which deployed "some 8,000 troops, a squadron of 16 aircraft, and two squadrons of drones". On 28 May Trump threatened to "blow up" Oman if it failed to "behave", after reports of Iran-Oman talks about jointly charging a toll for ships in the strait.

## Economic impacts (compressed)

- "[O]il and gas prices surged, aviation and tourism were disrupted, and financial markets shuddered." IEA head Fatih Birol called it the "greatest global energy security challenge in history".
- Iranian government spokesperson Fatemeh Mohajerani "estimated the direct and indirect cost of 40 days of war by $270 billion, or 90% of the estimated Iranian GDP in 2026"; the Foundation for Defense of Democracies estimates "damages of up to $300 billion, with a middle estimation range of $144 billion".
- The Center for American Progress said that as of 14 July "Americans had paid more than $68 billion in extra costs for gas and diesel since the beginning of the war"; other reports put the cost to the US government at "approximately $40 billion as of July".
- Houthi-controlled Yemen threatened shipping in the Gulf of Aden and Red Sea, threats suspended since 10 October 2025; as of mid-April Red Sea traffic had not stopped but stayed below historic levels. On 15 March the AP reported the Houthis' weapons stockpile was running low and Iran could not resupply them.
- "Three Amazon Web Services data centers in the United Arab Emirates were struck and damaged as a result of drone strikes", causing "sparks and fire" and "major structural damage" to two, internal water up to 4 cm, and complete early-March outages of S3 storage, EC2 compute and DynamoDB in the region.
- In mid-September the US House of Representatives voted a third time to end the war, after a CBO report warned the conflict "had already cost at least $38 billion", was depleting defensive missile stockpiles "to the point of a five-year rebuild", and would add "roughly $3 billion per month".

## Environmental impacts (compressed)

Airstrikes on industrial and fuel hubs "released a chronic toxic cocktail of benzene, heavy metals, and persistent 'forever chemicals' ( PFAS ), triggering 'black rain' in major cities". High oil prices lifted oil-company profits and planned expansion projected to exceed the IEA's regular scenario - "a 5.9% increase in oil and gas production in the 2020s, leading to a 2.9 °C (5.2 °F) global temperature increase".

## Reactions (compressed)

Reactions came from states, faith leaders and global bodies, with protests and unrest. Some US allies supported the attack, others hesitated; "[o]pinion in the Global South was less favorable"; most countries called for peace. Saudi Arabia, Egypt and the Gulf states criticized the Iranian attacks; in Europe most condemned the Iranian retaliatory strikes; in Oceania most countries supported the strikes. Within Iran opinion was divided: "[m]illions of Iranians and Iraqis and many international leaders and dignitaries attended the state funeral of Ali Khamenei", while others hoped for regime change; "[a]n anti-government uprising hoped for by the United States and Israel did not materialize, with some analysts saying that the attacks had bolstered the government's domestic popularity". US public opinion was mostly against the war and split by party; Congress failed to pass a War Powers Resolution; "Israeli opinion was overwhelmingly in favor of the war". Reuters reported higher oil prices, inflation and cost of living in the US.

## Diplomacy and the June 2026 Memorandum of Understanding (compressed)

- Excerpted from the negotiations article: talks began after a Trump letter to Khamenei setting a 60-day deadline; after it passed in June 2025 Israel launched the Twelve-Day War. "As of June 28, 2026 [ update ] , there were three rounds of talks before the Islamabad talks that led to the Islamabad Memorandum , and two rounds of technical talks." First round in Oman on 12 April 2025 (Steve Witkoff and Abbas Araghchi), second in Rome on 19 April 2025, a third in Muscat about a week later, with an expert-level meeting led by Michael Anton for the US and Majid Takht-Ravanchi for Iran.
- "[A]fter concluding that continued hostilities would risk economic calamity", Trump signed the MOU at the Palace of Versailles on 17 June 2026, following an earlier digital signing by the two foreign ministers. The US and Iran "agreed to suspend hostilities for 60 days and to establish a framework for a permanent peace under which the US would make major financial and political concessions to the Islamic Republic of Iran."
- "The memorandum began to collapse on 7 July 2026, when Iranian forces attacked three commercial vessels in the Strait of Hormuz, including a Qatari LNG tanker, setting it ablaze and damaging other ships." Iranian officials told The New York Times that internal inquiries traced the decision to Hossein Taeb, head of the Basij and former Revolutionary Guards' intelligence chief. US airstrikes followed within a day, "effectively ending the ceasefire".

## Analysis (compressed)

Some analysts argued Iran's ability to preserve the Islamic Republic, strike American bases and disrupt the strait showed the limits of American military power; others cautioned against treating the Islamic Republic's survival as a strategic victory given severe losses to Iran's conventional capabilities. Michael Froman of the Council on Foreign Relations said after the first ceasefire it was "simply too soon to tell" whether the war advanced American interests. In August, Reuters columnist Ron Bousso "described the conflict as a stalemate in which neither side had shown a convincing strategy for breaking the deadlock". International law experts warned Trump's threats to destroy Iranian infrastructure "could constitute war crimes under the Rome Statute" and be actionable under universal jurisdiction.

A note at the end of the part defines the war's location as "[p]rimarily the Persian Gulf and the Levant , as well as Cyprus ( Akrotiri and Dhekelia ) and the South Caucasus ."

wikis.title: Third week of the war (14-20 March 2026)
wikis.summary: Kharg Island and South Pars strikes, the killing of Ali Larijani, Israel's ground invasion of southern Lebanon and Trump's break with allies.
wikis.body:
- Analysts found "little evidence of significant defections in the Iranian military", "which have been considered a necessary condition for regime change".
- "The US conducted an attack on Kharg Island , a key oil export hub home to 90 percent of Iran's oil exports. Over 90 military sites were targeted; oil infrastructure was not targeted 'for reasons of decency', according to Trump."
- 14 March: Kata'ib Hezbollah security commander Abu Ali al-Askari killed in an airstrike in Baghdad. The Royal Tulip Al Rasheed Hotel in Baghdad's Green Zone was hit by a drone while hosting an EU and Saudi delegation; unclaimed, but suspected Iranian given a similar attack on the US embassy 48 hours earlier.
- 16 March: China and US-aligned NATO nations in Europe rejected Trump's call for military support to reopen the Strait of Hormuz; Trump called the decision a "very foolish mistake". Press secretary Karoline Leavitt said the administration would not rule out a military draft, though it was not "part of the current plan".
- 17 March: Trump posted on Truth Social renouncing NATO's assistance and criticizing Japan, South Korea and Australia for refusing to join the attacks, declaring the US "[does] not need the help of anyone". Israeli airstrikes targeted senior Iranian officials including Ali Larijani and Basij chief Gholamreza Soleimani; Iranian state media later confirmed both deaths. Iran's retaliatory missile barrage killed two Israeli civilians in Ramat Gan. "The same day, Israel launched a ground invasion of southern Lebanon."
- 18 March: Israel struck the South Pars natural gas field and neighbouring refineries "with US coordination"; Iran retaliated against "the world's largest LNG production facility in Qatar", while "Trump claimed he had no knowledge of the South Pars attack". Israel said it killed Iranian intelligence minister Esmaeil Khatib; Pezeshkian confirmed the killing. A hair salon in Beit Awwa was struck, killing four women - Israeli authorities said most likely cluster munitions, Palestinian authorities said an errant Israeli interceptor.
- 19 March: a US F-35 made an emergency landing after a suspected Iranian hit (Tasnim released video, described as "the first case of a damaged stealth fighter in combat"). A BAZAN Group refinery in Haifa was hit in an Iranian missile attack retaliating for South Pars. Netanyahu said "You can't make a revolution from the air" and "there must be a ground component-I won't share with you all the options". The US began an aerial campaign against Iranian vessels and drones in the strait.

wikis.title: Fourth week (21-27 March 2026)
wikis.summary: Bunker-buster strikes on Natanz, the disputed missile attack on Diego Garcia, Trump's 48-hour ultimatum over the strait and the strike on Prince Sultan Air Base.
wikis.body:
- Admiral Brad Cooper said the US military "had struck more than 8,000 Iranian military targets, including 130 vessels".
- 21 March: US strikes on the Natanz Nuclear Facility using bunker buster bombs. Russia condemned them as a "blatant violation of international law"; the IAEA urged restraint "to avoid any risk of a nuclear accident". Iran struck Dimona, injuring at least 78, saying it targeted the Shimon Peres Negev Nuclear Research Center.
- CNN and The Wall Street Journal, citing unnamed US officials, reported Iran "unsuccessfully attempted to strike the joint US-UK military base at Diego Garcia"; one missile broke apart mid-flight, another was intercepted by an SM-3 from a US warship. Israel said Iran used a two-stage intercontinental ballistic missile; Iran denied it, calling it "an Israeli false flag attack"; the UK foreign secretary confirmed and denounced the attack and expanded US permission to bomb certain targets from UK bases. "No evidence has been presented that the alleged Iranian missiles neared Diego Garcia or that one was intercepted."
- The Houthis warned they would respond to escalation against Iran and told Bahrain and the UAE, the two Arab countries offering to join the Strait of Hormuz campaign, that they "will be the first to lose in this battle". Lebanon's government expelled the Iranian ambassador.
- Trump issued an ultimatum threatening to strike Iran's power plants unless it opened the strait within 48 hours; Iran threatened to close it "completely" and to strike energy and desalination facilities. Reza Pahlavi called on Trump and Netanyahu to target the military while sparing civilian infrastructure "Iranians will need to rebuild our country." Halfway through the deadline Trump postponed the power-plant strikes for five days and said the US was negotiating; Iran denied any talks, calling him "deceitful", and rejected a US 15-point peace plan, insisting Lebanon be part of any ceasefire.
- 24 March: Israel or its allies shot down an Iranian missile over Lebanon at high altitude - per the Lebanese army the first such shootdown over Lebanese territory in the conflict, and the missile was not targeting Lebanon. A US strike on the Habbaniya military base in Al Anbar Governorate "killed seven members of the Iraqi Armed Forces and injured 13 others"; prime minister Mohammed Shia' al-Sudani summoned the US chargé d'affaires.
