Iranian state media threatened Iran could seize Bahraini and Emirati territory and signalled readiness to close the Bab al-Mandab Strait with the Houthis. Israel said it killed Iran's top naval commander Alireza Tangsiri, whom Katz called "directly responsible" for the strait's closure.
- 27 March: a day after Trump and Hegseth announced the "neutralization" of Iran's military, an Iranian missile and drone strike on Prince Sultan Air Base "damaged several US refueling aircraft and injured at least 15 US soldiers", also damaging an E-3 Sentry; analyst Cedric Leighton called it "a serious blow to [US] surveillance capabilities". Iran blocked two Chinese ships from entering the strait and sought to formalize transit fees. Katz vowed to "intensify and expand" attacks in Iran. The Shahid Khondab Heavy Water Complex in Arak and the Ardakan yellowcake plant in Yazd Province were confirmed damaged in Israeli airstrikes.

wikis.title: Fifth week (28 March - 3 April 2026)
wikis.summary: The Houthis enter the war, US marines deploy, strikes on universities and the Karaj bridge, and the downing of a US F-15E.
wikis.body:
- 28 March: the Houthis joined the war, launching a ballistic missile at Israel targeting "sensitive" military sites - intercepted, no casualties - then a second at Eilat. Yemen's internationally recognized government condemned Iran's "frequent attempts to drag Yemen" into conflict "through its terrorist militias".
- "2,500 US marines from the 31st Marine Expeditionary Unit arrived in the Middle East", expected to help open the strait. CENTCOM said it had struck "over 11,000 targets in Iran since the beginning of the war". Joint US-Israeli airstrikes damaged residential and civilian facilities including the Iran University of Science and Technology; Iran threatened to attack Israeli and American colleges across the Middle East. Airstrikes hit "a 10,000-cubic-metre (350,000 cu ft) water reservoir in Haftkel , in Khuzestan province". An Iranian missile struck a chemical plant in the Ne'ot Hovav industrial zone, injuring one and raising fears of a hazardous leak. A PMF convoy was seen entering Khorramshahr. "Eleven-year-old child soldier Alireza Jafari was killed in an Israeli drone strike 'while serving' at a checkpoint on a Tehran highway"; Amnesty International called Iran's organized recruitment of children a war crime.
- 29 March: Trump said he would prefer to "take the oil in Iran ", proposing to take Kharg Island, claiming the US could capture it "very easily".
- 30 March: Trump said that without a deal and a reopened strait the US would strike all of Iran's power plants, oil wells, Kharg Island and possibly all desalination plants, though feasibility was contested. Turkey and NATO intercepted "the fourth missile directed towards Turkish territory"; Iran denied firing it, calling it a false flag. The US flew B-52 bombers over Iranian territory for the first time and used bombers against an ammunition depot and air base in Isfahan. Gulf states reportedly pushed Trump to continue the war "until there are significant changes in Iran's leadership". American journalist Shelly Kittleson was kidnapped in Baghdad by Kata'ib Hezbollah, which demanded the release of detained members.
- 1 April: Mehr News Agency reported former foreign minister Kamal Kharazi seriously injured and his wife killed in an airstrike on his home; Iranian officials called it an attempt to derail diplomacy, noting Kharazi was overseeing a possible meeting with JD Vance. Airstrikes on Hengam Island caused seven injuries. Netanyahu said the strikes had eliminated Iran's ability to produce nuclear weapons and ballistic missiles, removing "two existential threats". Late that day Trump said the strikes had "dramatically curtailed" Iranian missile and drone systems and that attacks would escalate over the next two to three weeks to "bring them back to the Stone Ages , where they belong".
- 2 April: two US strikes on the B1 bridge between Tehran and Karaj, "described as the highest bridge in the Middle East, reportedly killed eight people and wounded 95 others, causing it to collapse"; experts assessed it as a possible war crime and Trump celebrated it. Many families had gathered in the parks below to celebrate Sizdah Be-dar. Iran revealed major damage to the Pasteur Institute of Iran. Hegseth boasted of "death and destruction from the sky all day long". The IDF said a strike near Kermanshah killed Iranian ballistic missile chief Makram Atimi and several battalion commanders. An Iranian missile damaged an Israeli drone factory in Petah Tikva. Army chief Amir Hatami said that if US forces invaded, "not a single person" among them would survive.
- 3 April: Iranian forces shot down a USAF F-15E Strike Eagle over Kohgiluyeh and Boyer-Ahmad province, "the first incident of its kind in more than 20 years"; the pilot was rescued the same day and the WSO, missing, was rescued alive 48 hours later in a "high-stake" operation with US special forces supported by 155 aircraft. A US A-10 was downed near the strait and its crew member rescued. Iran released video it said showed the downing by a surface-to-air missile. Tehran's Shahid Beheshti University was hit, bringing universities struck to "more than 30, according to the Iranian Minister of Science".

wikis.title: Sixth week (4-7 April 2026) and Trump's 'whole civilization' post
wikis.summary: Strikes on Bushehr's auxiliary building and Mahshahr, the F-15E rescue operation, senior IRGC deaths, the destroyed Tehran synagogue and Trump's Truth Social threat.
wikis.body:
- 4 April: explosions reported at an auxiliary building of the Bushehr Nuclear Power Plant and at the Mahshahr Special Petrochemical Zone; the Mahshahr airstrikes "killed at least five and injured 170 others". An Iranian missile hit near the IDF's HaKirya headquarters in Tel Aviv.
- 5 April: the second crew member of the F-15E downed on 3 April was recovered after heavy fighting, in an operation that damaged helicopters, saw an A-10 Thunderbolt II shot down and two C-130 Hercules destroyed, killed three IRGC members and injured several American service members.
- 6 April: the IRGC announced that Major General Majid Khademi, head of its intelligence organization, was killed in a joint US-Israeli airstrike, saying he had "played a major role in Iran's intelligence and security apparatus over nearly five decades"; Israel said Quds Force commander Yazdan Mir was also killed. Before Trump's infrastructure deadline, Israel struck the South Pars Petrochemical facility in Asaluyeh; the IAF said "85% of Iran's petrochemical exports" were now offline. "At least 34 people, including six children, were killed in US-Israeli airstrikes across Iran", including on Sharif University of Technology and residential areas; vice president Mohammad Reza Aref called the alleged bunker-buster use "a symbol of Trump's madness and ignorance".
- 7 April: the Rafi'-Nia synagogue in central Tehran was destroyed in an airstrike; Israel said it was collateral damage and never the direct target. US forces began strikes on Kharg Island, and Iran said its restraint in targeting regional oil infrastructure would no longer apply. Trump posted to Truth Social that "a whole civilization will die tonight, never to be brought back again", causing international concern he would use nuclear weapons; Amnesty International's Secretary General said the statement "may constitute a threat to commit genocide", right-wing commentators and many Democrats condemned it and some called for removal under the 25th Amendment. The White House denied considering nuclear weapons and later said "only the president knows" what he would do. "A leaked US intelligence report concluded that Iran retained 70% of missiles and launchers at this point, despite Trump claims regarding 'destruction' of Iran's military."

wikis.title: Ceasefire, dual blockade and the Islamabad Memorandum (8 April - 19 June 2026)
wikis.summary: The Pakistani-mediated two-week ceasefire, Israel's Operation Eternal Darkness in Lebanon, the failed Islamabad talks, the rival blockades and the memorandum signed at Versailles.
wikis.body:
- 7 April: Trump announced a US-Iran agreement based on "the 10-point proposal mediated by Pakistani prime minister Shehbaz Sharif and Field Marshal Asim Munir"; the US, Israel and Iran agreed to a two-week ceasefire under which Iran would reopen the strait. Afterwards Iran's Lavan Island oil refinery and Sirri Island crude export facilities were struck with no claim of responsibility - "later revealed to have been done secretly by the UAE" - and Iran continued strikes on Gulf Arab states.
- Israel and the US asserted the ceasefire did not include Lebanon, "contradicting the Pakistani mediators and Iran". Hezbollah said it had halted attacks. Israel launched "Operation Eternal Darkness", which it said targeted all Hezbollah command and control centres in southern Lebanon, Beirut and the Beqaa Valley; local observers said the attacks were not targeted. They were the largest since the war began, "killing at least 357 people and injuring more than 1,200", with 92 killed and at least 740 injured in Beirut alone. Iran threatened to attack Israel "if the aggressions against dear Lebanon are not brought to an immediate end" and paused Strait of Hormuz traffic; Hezbollah fired rockets at northern Israel over "ceasefire violations".
- 11 April: Trump said US forces had started "clearing" the strait; Iran claimed an American ship turned back after a warning. The WSJ reported US Navy destroyers entered the strait for the first time in the war and that Iran threatened to attack them, accusing the US of a ceasefire violation; CENTCOM said the ships were minesweeping. The Islamabad talks - "the highest-level discussions between the two since the 1979 Islamic Revolution" - lasted 21 hours; JD Vance announced no agreement was reached and that Iran refused "to accept our terms", and Trump said he no longer cared about negotiations.
- Trump declared a US Navy blockade of "all Ships trying to enter, or leave, the Strait of Hormuz" from 13 April, stopping any ships that paid tolls to Iran; CENTCOM clarified it would apply only to ships to or from Iranian ports. The IRGC Navy said any military vessel approaching would meet a "severe response". "Iran had 13 days of oil storage capacity, forcing it to shut down its oil fields and potentially damaging them", with an analyst estimating lost import and export capacity of "US$435 million per day".
- 16 April: Trump announced a ten-day Israel-Lebanon truce; Iran allowed commercial passage during it while Trump kept the blockade, and Iran reimposed restrictions. The US said its blockade had intercepted 23 ships; Iran seized two cargo ships while Trump claimed total control of the strait. The Guardian called it a "dual blockade". Israel and Lebanon later agreed a three-week ceasefire extension.
- 8 June: the IDF struck military sites in Iran with explosions in Tehran, Isfahan and Tabriz, triggering an exchange; two Iranian soldiers were killed; Iran then said it had ceased military action, and Israel stopped strikes at Trump's request.
- 9 June: the NYT reported an American crew rescued after a helicopter went down near the strait - CENTCOM said rescued by a US Navy drone boat "for the first time". Trump said Iranians shot it down and pledged a response; a US official blamed a Shahed one-way attack drone; Iran said it did not deliberately target it. CENTCOM later launched "self-defense" strikes; one damaged water reservoir tanks in Sirik, and Iran said 20,000 people lost access to drinking water.
- 14 June: Iran said the draft US deal had Tehran agreeing not to produce or acquire nuclear weapons and the US allowing it to dilute its highly enriched uranium stockpile inside Iran. Trump and Iran announced an agreement to end the war and reopen the strait, and Trump authorized lifting the blockade. 15 June: Vance said the memorandum was digitally signed the previous day. 17 June: Trump and Pezeshkian signed the Islamabad Memorandum, Trump signing "during dinner with French president Emmanuel Macron at the Palace of Versailles after the G7 summit". 18 June: Pakistan said Tehran would reopen the strait "instantly" and the blockade end "immediately"; CENTCOM removed the blockade. 19 June: Trump announced a renewed Israel-Hezbollah ceasefire facilitated by the US, Qatar and Iran - but on 20 June Hezbollah announced an attack on Israeli forces trying to capture Ali al-Taher in Nabatieh while Israel kept striking southern Lebanon.

wikis.title: Collapse of the June ceasefire, August lull and renewed hostilities
wikis.summary: July's tanker attacks and US strikes, the August operational standoff and 'economic D-day', and the resumption of fighting from 1 September 2026.
wikis.body:
**July.** "On July 8, 2026, the IRGC launched targeted kinetic attacks against commercial vessels in the Strait of Hormuz, abruptly ending the short-lived diplomatic respite created by the June ceasefire." After three foreign commercial ships allegedly avoided pre-approved transit routes, Tehran defended the offensive as an assertion of sovereignty over the corridor. The US struck Iranian missile, drone and radar installations along the strait and on Qeshm Island. On 12 July Iran launched ballistic missiles and drone swarms at US installations in Bahrain, Kuwait, Jordan, Qatar and Oman. On 22 and 23 July the US ran a two-day wave of strikes on IRGC and Artesh command nodes in southern and western Iran. On 20 July the Houthis declared a blockade targeting shipping headed for Saudi Arabia, leading to border skirmishes after Saudi forces intercepted an aircraft "purportedly carrying Iranian military advisors to Sanaa". By the last week of July the US was "forced into an unexpected operational drawdown ... due to the extreme fatigue of regional logistics networks and growing service casualties".

**August.** A brief operational standoff, with "a sharp decline in direct kinetic engagements and an end to Iranian drone attacks against Gulf Arab states"; the US carried out extensive naval de-mining to clear shipping lanes. "On 20 August, declaring ' economic D-day ,' Trump announced that any nation trading with the Iran would be sanctioned." The Islamabad Memorandum "completely expired without a long-term peace deal", with backchannel diplomacy resuming through Pakistani and Qatari mediation.

**1 September - present.** Hostilities resumed on 1 September 2026. "The US reclassified the engagement from 'Operation Epic Fury' to 'Overseas Operations' based on the enforcement of a strict naval blockade." Through September the IRGC used drone strikes and projectiles against commercial oil tankers using the southern Omani route under US escort, while the Houthis struck infrastructure and oil refineries in Saudi Arabia, including Yanbu and Riyadh. Through Qatari intermediaries, Iran's Supreme National Security Council under Mohsen Rezaee demanded "a complete lifting of the naval blockade , the unfreezing of sanctioned financial assets , and an end to all wars against its proxies".

wikis.title: Casualties, opening deception and US losses and stockpiles
wikis.summary: How the first-day strikes were concealed, US base damage and deaths, aircraft losses, and the depletion of American interceptor stockpiles.
wikis.body:
- The US and Israel killed many Iranian commanders on the first day by making Iran believe strikes were not imminent, so senior officials kept gathering in person; leaked information about a US F-22 deployment hid that preparations were further along at other bases, and Trump-Netanyahu calls before the war were not publicized "to diminish the possibility of an Iranian first strike". IDF spokesperson Effie Defrin said months of joint "strategic and operational deception" of satellite imagery preceded the war; he and chief of staff Eyal Zamir drove their official cars home and returned without them so imagery would not show the base full or warplanes armed. "Three separate gatherings of Iranian officials were hit within half a minute of each other in the opening strike."
- Strikes hit IRGC bases, border guard posts and security facilities to enable possible ground incursions by Kurdish separatists in the northwest and Baloch separatists in the southeast; no cross-border operations by either were reported, though Iran attacked both, reportedly killing Kurdish fighters of the Coalition of Political Forces of Iranian Kurdistan and Baloch fighters of the People's Fighters Front.
- "Analysis of satellite images by The Washington Post revealed damage to at least 228 structures or pieces of equipment at US bases across the Persian Gulf, far more than the Trump administration has admitted to."
- 1 March: "six US soldiers were killed amid more than 30 injured in an Iranian drone attack near Camp Arifjan in Port Shuaiba, Kuwait" - Army Reserve soldiers of the 103rd Expeditionary Sustainment Command, headquartered in Des Moines, Iowa. 8 March: CENTCOM reported a National Guard soldier died during a medical emergency. A 1st Space Brigade soldier wounded at Prince Sultan Air Base on 1 March died of his injuries on 9 March.
- "According to a May report by the Congressional Research Service, 42 U.S. military aircraft were destroyed or damaged." CSIS data indicate "about 65 percent of the 2,330 US Patriot interceptor missiles available at the beginning of the conflict ... were used between February and July, leaving less than 850 missiles remaining."
- The US Strategic Petroleum Reserve "dropped to its lowest level in four decades, with possibility of permanent damage to the caverns if the withdrawals continue".
- The war exposed weapons stockpile shortages: "[a]fter less than five months of the war, US was already running out of ammunition against a middle-tier adversary", which could limit deterrence of Russia and China; Leon Panetta called it a "dangerous moment". As of 5 August 2026 the US "had reportedly used roughly 80% of its THAAD missiles"; a 4 August Reuters report said it had burned through "virtually all" of its PrSM and ATACMS munitions and "a little less than half" of its global Tomahawk supply; as of 14 August it had "reportedly lost around 25% of their Reaper drones".
- On 6 August, per the Washington Post, Trump and Hegseth clashed at Camp David over "extreme missile shortages", Trump saying he felt misled and Hegseth blaming deputy Stephen Feinberg; Trump denied the report and threatened long prison sentences for leaks. The administration subjected about 50 members of the Joint Chiefs of Staff to polygraph tests over leaks. The Pentagon transferred weapons from Asia and Europe to the Middle East; an interceptor shortage reportedly persuaded Trump to call off a planned major attack, and the administration blamed Biden's arms transfers to Ukraine. On 17 September Lockheed Martin received the first batch of Patriot interceptor parts from General Motors, less than a month after their manufacturing agreement.

wikis.title: Impact on Iran: leadership, civilian life and cultural heritage
wikis.summary: The succession after Khamenei's death, conditions for Iranian civilians during the blackout and strikes, and damage to historic and religious sites.
wikis.body:
**Leadership.** Khamenei's death triggered an election for a new supreme leader; under the constitution an Interim Leadership Council - President Masoud Pezeshkian, Chief Justice Gholam-Hossein Mohseni-Eje'i and Ayatollah Alireza Arafi - was established on 1 March to exercise head-of-state functions. "Mojtaba Khamenei was elected on 8 March 2026 to replace his father as supreme leader", and the IRGC and top leaders including Ghalibaf, Larijani and Pezeshkian pledged allegiance. In late March the NYT described Iran's leadership as "paralyzed with severely disrupted decision-making process", with damaged communications causing "paranoia and internal power struggles". "As of 21 May, Khamenei remains in hiding and the de facto ruler is uncertain", with the IRGC under hardliner general Ahmad Vahidi, cited as the formulator of Iran's military and negotiation stance; The Telegraph revealed "a shadowy partnership with the retired IRGC commander-in-chief Mohammad Ali Jafari".

**Civilian life.** UN Human Rights Chief Volker Türk said the "reckless" war is disproportionately impacting civilians in the Middle East and beyond. "138,000 civilian sites in Iran were damaged during the conflict, with estimated time of reconstruction being 2-5 years." Tehran "reportedly became a ghost town"; prisoners in Evin Prison have received limited bread and water since the war began; schools closed while banks and government offices ran at reduced capacity and subway and bus services continued. During the "near total" internet blackout NetBlocks reported connectivity "dropped to 4% of ordinary levels"; as the blackout "exceeded 240 hours, making it the second longest ever", the government handed out "white sim cards" bypassing filters to supporters. As news of Khamenei's death broke, security forces deployed against an uprising, with footage showing them firing on celebrants in the streets and at people chanting from their windows. In the first two weeks of March "over 70,000 Afghan refugees returned to Afghanistan, frequently under forced circumstances"; UNHCR's Arafat Jamal noted limited options amid Afghanistan-Pakistan confrontations. The Guardian reported the war has overshadowed executions of political prisoners, including those involved in the January 2026 protests, and rights groups said sentencing and hangings surged with little due process.

**Iranian military.** On 26 March it was reported that children as young as 12 "may join Iran's war support", raising child-soldier concerns; days later rights groups said an 11-year-old was killed on duty at a Tehran checkpoint. On 29 March footage showed Iraq's PMF deployed in Iran. A leaked US intelligence report concluded in May that "Iran retained 70% of missile and launchers relative to pre-war status". Iran "has become more skilled as the war progressed, learning how to evade American air defenses", extended the conflict across most of the Middle East and enlisted allied militia in Iraq and Yemen.

**Cultural heritage.** Multiple historic and cultural sites including UNESCO World Heritage Sites were damaged; "[t]he most affected was Chehel Sotoun and its rich ayeneh-kari". On 2 March a strike on Arg Square damaged Golestan Palace, prompting a UNESCO statement of concern; on 5 March the Azadi Sport Complex was bombed; an 8 March strike on Falak-ol-Aflak, "marked with a blue shield emblem", damaged several sections; strikes on Isfahan on 9 March damaged Naqsh-e Jahan Square, Chehel Sotoun, Ali Qapu, the Shah Mosque, Jameh Mosque and Teymouri Hall. On 11 March UNESCO urged protection for damaged and at-risk sites in Iran, Israel, Lebanon and the rest of West Asia. On 17 March blast waves and shrapnel damaged palaces at the Sa'dabad Complex; Russia's foreign ministry reported strikes in Tehran on 1 April damaged the St. Nicholas Orthodox Church and its auxiliary buildings; on 7 April the Rafi'-Nia synagogue "was fully destroyed by the IAF".

wikis.title: 2026 Iran war: explanatory notes and the start of the reference list
wikis.summary: The Wikipedia article's footnotes - covert Gulf participation, which countries were drawn in, operation-name glossaries and incident clarifications - followed by the beginning of its numbered reference list.
wikis.body:
## What this part holds

Two things: the article's "Notes" section (lettered footnotes attached to the infobox and body) and the opening stretch of the numbered "References" list.

The notes carry facts not stated elsewhere, mainly about which states took part covertly and about disputed incidents. The reference list is citation data - author, headline, outlet, publication and retrieval dates - for news and think-tank sources dated across 2026 (the citations in this part run from March to late September 2026) plus older background sources.

## Glossary notes

- Operation Roaring Lion: "Hebrew : מִבְצַע שְׁאָגַת הָאֲרִי , romanized : Mivtsá She'agát Ha'arí" (given twice).
- Operation True Promise IV: "Persian : عملیات وعده صادق ۴ , romanized : Amaliyat-e Va'deh-ye Sadegh 4"; a note adds that "Previously, Iran had launched I , II , and III on a more limited scale."
- Ramadan War: "Persian : جنگ رمضان , romanized : Jang-e Ramazān".
- A note explains the 2006 UNSC problems were "uranium enrichment and reprocessing" in that year's second resolution, "additionally use or attempted use of 'heavy water'".
- A note says the Houthis are "[s]ometimes included in the 'Axis of Resistance'".
- A note on US munitions: since late 2023 the US military has deployed reserves across the Red Sea, Israel's defence, Ukraine and troop protection in the Middle East, with "rapid consumption of advanced interceptor missiles, raising concerns among experts about the ability of defense companies to replenish stocks", and replacement will take time, "as will increasing supplies for potential future conflicts, such as with China in the Taiwan Strait".
- A comparison note recalls the 2010 sinking of the South Korean corvette ROKS Cheonan, which an international investigation attributed to a North Korean Yeono-class midget submarine torpedo, "though North Korea denied any responsibility".
- Casualty pointers: notes refer readers to "Casualties of the 2026 Iran war" for the US, Israel and totals; one note states "104 sailors killed and 32 injured off the coast of Sri Lanka."
- A note records that Israel "had initially conducted bombings against Iran and its allies since the beginning of the war but later refrained from attacks on Iran since July."
- A note records Iran's confirmation of the Qatari claim on 15 August 2026: "One Iranian fighter jet pilot was killed in the strike. Iran accused Qatar Armed Forces of capturing three Iranian fighter jet pilots."

wikis.title: Covert and acknowledged Gulf participation
wikis.summary: Footnotes describing secret Saudi, Emirati, Kuwaiti and Bahraini strikes on Iran and on Iran-backed militias, and the denials.
wikis.body:
- **Saudi Arabia:** "On 29 July 2026, Saudi Arabia publicly participated in joint strikes with the United States against Iran-backed Iraqi militias." Earlier, Reuters, citing Western and Iranian officials, reported the Saudi Air Force launched numerous unpublicized "tit-for-tat" strikes on Iranian soil in late March 2026, in retaliation for Iranian attacks on Saudi Arabia; The New York Times, citing US officials, corroborated Saudi strikes on Iran. Reuters also reported Saudi strikes on Iran-backed Iraqi militias near the Iraqi-Saudi border "around the time of the 7 April ceasefire".
- **United Arab Emirates:** The Wall Street Journal and Bloomberg, citing "people familiar with the matter", and The New York Times, citing current and former US officials, reported that "the UAE discreetly carried out retaliatory attacks against Iran, including a strike on an oil refinery at Lavan Island on 8 April."
- **Kuwait:** Per the WSJ, Kuwait launched attacks on Iran-backed Iraqi militias from its own territory. Iraqi officials reported at least two rocket attacks from Kuwaiti territory in April; per Reuters "it was unclear whether they were launched by the Kuwaiti Armed Forces or the US military". "On 1 May, Kuwait said its soldiers exchanged fire with six members of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps, and arrested four, during an Iranian raid on Bubiyan Island ." In July the WSJ reported Kuwaiti airstrikes inside Iran; Kuwait denied this, saying it had not taken part in operations against Iran and had not allowed its territory to be used for offensive operations against any neighbouring country.
- **Bahrain:** "According to The Wall Street Journal , Bahrain launched airstrikes inside Iran in July 2026."
- Cited reporting behind these notes includes Reuters' "Exclusive: Saudi Arabia launched covert attacks on Iran as regional war widened, sources say" (12 May 2026), the NYT's "Saudi Arabia and U.A.E. Carried Out Secret Attacks in Iran, U.S. Officials Say" (14 May 2026), the WSJ's "The U.A.E. Has Been Secretly Carrying Out Attacks on Iran" (11 May 2026) and "Bahrain, Kuwait Warplanes Struck Iran in Rare Gulf Retaliation" (24 July 2026), and the NYT's "Saudi Arabia Reluctantly Enters U.S.-Iran War" (29 July 2026), which said the joint strikes "marked the first time the kingdom acknowledged direct involvement in the U.S. war effort".

wikis.title: Other countries and territories drawn into the war
wikis.summary: Footnotes on when the Houthis, Lebanon, Iraq, Azerbaijan, Egypt, Jordan, Oman, Qatar, Syria, Turkey and the British Indian Ocean Territory entered or were hit.
wikis.body:
- Houthis (Yemen, SPC): "Since 28 March"; see "Houthis in the 2026 Iran war".
- Hezbollah/Lebanon: "Since 2 March"; both Israel and Iran "have attacked Lebanon during the war" (see "2026 Lebanon war").
- Iraq: notes point to "2026 United States-Israeli strikes on Iraq", to "Iraq in the 2026 Iran war" for attacks on Iraqi facilities outside the Kurdistan Region, and to "2026 Iranian strikes on the Kurdistan Region".
- Azerbaijan: see "2026 Iranian strikes on Azerbaijan".
- Egypt: "On 29 July, two floating LNG storage tankers, the Energos Winter and the GasLog Salem , were struck by drones at the Egyptian port of Damietta ." Two Iranian officials told the New York Times the strike was "designed to show that global shipping and energy supplies could be more deeply disrupted if Iran chose to escalate."
- Jordan, Oman, Qatar: notes point to "2026 Iranian strikes on Jordan", "...on Oman" and "...on Qatar"; Palestine to "2026 Beit Awwa salon strike".
- Syria: see "Syria in the 2026 Iran war" for shelling by Hezbollah and drone attacks by groups affiliated with the Islamic Resistance in Iraq.
- Turkey: see "2026 interceptions of Iranian missiles in Turkey".
- British Indian Ocean Territory: "There are disputed accounts on whether the British Indian Ocean Territory was attacked in March 2026. Iran denied attacking the Diego Garcia military base, while the United Kingdom confirmed the attack without providing evidence it took place."
- Iranian separatists: cited notes report "Ten Kurdish fighters killed in clashes with IRGC" (Kurdistan Human Rights Network, 2 July 2026) and the People's Fighters Front confirming "deaths of four members in Saravan drone strike" (Hengaw, 28 July 2026).

wikis.title: Reference list (opening stretch)
wikis.summary: What the article's numbered citations consist of and the kinds of claims they support.
wikis.body: The rest of this part is the numbered reference list: news and analysis citations with author, headline, outlet and dates. Examples in this stretch include the WSJ's "Why Israel Is Sitting Out the Latest U.S. Bombing Campaign in Iran" (21 July 2026), AP's "Iran launches renewed missile attacks as US and Saudis strike Tehran-backed militias in Iraq" (29 July 2026), Reuters' "Egypt confirms drone caused fire on two gas vessels at Damietta" (30 July 2026), El Pais' report on the worst strike against Iraq's army since the war began, quoting "Why did the Americans attack us?" (27 March 2026), The Guardian's "Mojtaba Khamenei was hurt in strike that killed his father, Iran's Cyprus ambassador confirms" (11 March 2026), ABC News' "Who is running Iran right now? Trump, security officials offer different accounts", the NYT's "A New Era and New Leadership: The Generals Who Are Running Iran" (23 April 2026), the Washington Post's "More U.S. troops have died amid Iran war than Pentagon has disclosed publicly" (18 September 2026), and reporting on NATO's interception of a second Iranian ballistic missile over Turkey and the deployment of six Turkish F-16s to Northern Cyprus (9 March 2026).

wikis.title: 2026 Iran war: tail of the reference list
wikis.summary: A short closing fragment of the Wikipedia article's citation list, with news references dated 9-11 March 2026.
wikis.body:
This part is only the tail of the article's numbered reference list - no article prose. The citations it contains are:

- "Israeli Army Intercepts Iranian Drone over Southern Syria: Report", Al Jazeera English, 10 March 2026.
- Todd South, "B-1s And B-52s Bombers Pour into Europe for Ops Against Iran", Air & Space Forces Magazine, 9 March 2026.
- "Trade Disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz Due to Attacks on Commercial Ships", PortWatch, International Monetary Fund, 28 February 2026.
- Chris Baraniuk, "GPS Jamming: The Invisible Battle in the Middle East", BBC News, 10 March 2026.
- "Saudi Arabia Welcomes US Designation of Sudanese Muslim Brotherhood as Terrorist Organization", Arab News, 11 March 2026.
- "U.S. Designates Sudanese Islamic Movement and Its Armed Wing as Terrorist Entity", Sudan Tribune, 9 March 2026.
- Hamza Hendawi, "US Says Iran's IRGC-Trained Sudanese Muslim Brotherhood Members Fighting Alongside Army", The National, 11 March 2026.
- Chandrashekar Srinivasan, "With Missiles Carrying 1,000 kg Explosives, A New Tactical Phase For Iran", NDTV, 10 March 2026.
- A truncated citation to Bel Trew, 10 March 2026.

The fragment cuts off mid-citation.

wikis.title: Iran War 2026 - Day 204 Update, 19 September 2026 (GlobalSecurity.org)
wikis.summary: GlobalSecurity.org's daily operational report for Day 204 of the 2026 Iran war, with a metrics dashboard, executive summary and sections on coalition and Iranian operations, proxies, the Strait of Hormuz and oil, the nuclear file, Iran's internal situation and international and US politics.
wikis.body:
## The report
- "Iran War 2026 -- Day 204 Update", 19 September 2026, 0800 ET, "Data cutoff: 0500 ET". Part of GlobalSecurity.org's daily update series (with a Daily Update Calendar, Order of Battle, Key Facilities and Satellite Imagery Gallery).
- Report information: "This operational report is updated daily by 0800 ET. Data cutoff for this report is 0500 ET on the date of publication." Figures are "subject to revision".
- "Page last modified: 09-19-2026 12:00:00 Zulu". Site maintained by John Pike; copyright 2000-2026 GlobalSecurity.org.

## Headline state of the war on Day 204
- The fire pause "entered a tenth day with no Iranian ballistic missile or drone attack on any host state reported through the early morning cutoff of 19 September"; elsewhere the report says the pause "has now survived ten days and two nights". The 20 missiles at Muwaffaq Salti on the night of 8-9 September remain the most recent confirmed launch event at a state.
- No American or coalition strike ashore in Iran was announced; the Coalition Operations section calls this "the twelfth consecutive operational period without an announced strike ashore", while the dashboard entry for the 17-18 September window describes "an eleventh consecutive operational period".
- The report repeatedly stresses a "breakdown in public accounting": irreconcilable Hormuz datasets, unreconciled casualty figures and an air-defence assessment more than six months old.

## Citations listed by the report
- Sources cited include CNBC, Finance Feeds, Cornerstone Futures, UN News, Democracy Now!, NBC News, NPR, Townhall, UPI, Iran Wire, Shabtab News, USNI News, Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty, Reuters via gCaptain, Bloomberg via gCaptain, OilPrice.com, Al Jazeera, TASS, AFP via France 24, Arab News, Anadolu via A News, Amnesty International and CBS News, dated 16-18 September 2026.
- One cited headline, "Brent Falls to $101.92, Third Straight Session of Losses" (Cornerstone Futures, 18 September 2026), differs from the report's own figure of a $102.41 settlement on 18 September.

wikis.title: Campaign dashboard metrics
wikis.summary: The report's metric table for Day 204, most entries 'not reported' with standing baselines carried forward.
wikis.body:
- Coalition sorties (cumulative): not reported between 17 and 18 September; the DoD Inspector General's quarterly report through 30 June, published 16 September, supplies "approximately 36,000 combat sorties between 28 February and 7 April". No new CENTCOM press release in the window; public activity limited to "the standing Strait of Hormuz blockade tally of 103 commercial vessels redirected as of 15 September"; cumulative sites struck since strikes resumed 7 July remains "approximately 400 or more Iranian sites".
- Coalition aircraft losses: not reported; baseline is the Inspector General's "approximately 57 aircraft lost or damaged through 30 June", with KC-135 losses put at 7 to 12 depending on source and MQ-9 losses exceeding 30. The IRGC's fourth shootdown claim in three days - an MQ-9 said destroyed over Qeshm Island on 16 September at 0229 local by "a new integrated air defense system" - "remains unconfirmed by imagery, wreckage serial number or CENTCOM response".
- Iranian air defenses degraded: not reported as a percentage; "CENTCOM's last assessment of approximately 90 percent degradation stands from 14 March and is now more than six months old".
- Iranian ballistic missile launches: not reported; no salvo at a host state for a tenth consecutive day. The Congressional Budget Office assessment "of between one-half and two-thirds of certain missile defense interceptor inventories consumed since June 2025 stands".
- Iranian drone launches: not reported; no drone attack on a host state for a fourteenth consecutive day; "the theater's drone activity remained Houthi, directed at Saudi Arabia".
- Launch rates vs Day 1: not reported as rates; the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs' last published comparison placed ballistic launches "down 86 percent from Day 1 levels" and drone launches "down 83 percent".
- US military KIA: "18 since 28 February, unchanged in the window". Unreconciled figures stand: the Inspector General records 14 killed and 417 wounded through 30 June; a combined figure of 18 dead and 758 wounded; Reuters "more than 800 injured"; an independent compilation of 820 as of 8 September; no departmental reconciliation.
- Israeli KIA: "32 or more IDF military personnel since 2 March 2026, unchanged".
- Iranian military casualties: not reported; standing figures are Reuters' 13 killed in 1 September strikes, Iran's Ministry of Health "at least 18 killed nationwide" from those strikes, JINSA's "1,221 or more Iranian military deaths within a total of 3,724 or more killed", and Iran International's "4,700 or more security personnel killed".
- Civilian casualties (Iran): not reported; baselines are HRANA's 3,636, the Foundation of Martyrs' 3,468, Al Jazeera's 12 August compilation of "at least 3,527 killed and more than 27,000 wounded", JINSA's "3,724 or more killed and 26,580 or more wounded", and US and Israeli estimates of "6,000 or more".
- Hormuz shipping traffic: Reuters (Kpler data) recorded four commodity vessel transits on 15 September; Windward (AIS plus satellite imagery) recorded 12 on Wednesday 16 September; Energy Secretary Wright said on Fox Business on 16 September that 18 million barrels went through the previous day with American military assistance and that the seven-day average is "approximately 11 million barrels a day"; CENTCOM told RFE/RL the cumulative figure is "thousands of commercial ships and nearly one billion barrels of oil". Iran's Persian Gulf Strait Authority non-compliant vessel list stands at "77 to 78 entries"; the Joint Maritime Information Center's "SEVERE" rating of 13 September stands.
- Brent crude: settled at $102.41 on 18 September, "down 2.3 percent for a third consecutive session"; WTI settled at $100.04, down 1.84 percent; Oman crude above $130 and Shanghai INE elevated; Brent is down about $3.42 from the 16 September close of $105.83 but "approximately 55 percent above the roughly $66 at which it stood immediately before the war and approximately 14 percent below the March peak of $119"; US retail diesel "above $6.30 a gallon"; Saudi Arabia moved "reportedly 2.8 million barrels per day" through Hormuz over six days before 18 September against 700,000 bpd in August.

wikis.title: Coalition operations
wikis.summary: A twelfth silent period ashore, the static counter-reconstitution and nuclear files, and the munitions shortfall.
wikis.body:
- "No American or coalition strike on Iranian territory ashore was announced between the 18 and 19 September cutoffs. This is the twelfth consecutive operational period without an announced strike ashore." No new centcom.mil press release; public activity was the blockade tally, "the September 15 figure of 103 commercial vessels redirected".
- "The command publishes blockade and throughput claims and does not publish engagements, and engagements reach the record when a correspondent is briefed." No US-contracted vessel strike confirmed after Fox News' 16 September report. "The destruction of the two IRGC boats on 14 September remains the most recent announced American kinetic action" with no death figure published by either party.
- Adm. Brad Cooper made no public statement, a fourth day; the closed conference of military chiefs he hosted in Germany produced no communique.
- Missile infrastructure: no strike reported; "the counter-reconstitution file has been static for twelve consecutive operational periods". Munitions: the Inspector General's finding of "strategic inventory shortfalls" stands without a remediation plan; CBO's one-half to two-thirds interceptor consumption stands; CSIS estimates "fewer than 830 Patriot interceptors remaining of a pre-war 2,330".
- Nuclear sites: no strike reported "and none has been reported since 7 July"; "The five presidential threats against the Pickaxe Mountain complex stand unexecuted." Vice President Vance's 15 September formulation - that the first phase destroyed the nuclear program and the second is to "ensure that they're not able to rebuild", with the war entering "a different phase" in coming months - "remains unelaborated by any official".
- Leadership: no Iranian military or political figure reported killed or targeted; Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei made no public statement.
- Naval and port: no strike announced, no Iranian naval vessel lost, no new blockade or boarding incident; cyber threat tracking reported 16 September continues to be monitored by the Coast Guard, FBI and DHS with no attribution.
- Israeli posture: no Israeli operation against Iran; activity remained directed at Hezbollah in Lebanon; the Israel Atomic Energy Commission's "will do it again if needed" stands as the most recent declaratory position.

wikis.title: Iranian retaliation and the fire pause
wikis.summary: A tenth day with no Iranian fire at a host state, and a diplomatic rather than kinetic response.
wikis.body:
- "Iran did not fire at a host state for a tenth consecutive day." No ballistic salvo at any of the six Arabian Peninsula Gulf states, Jordan or Israel between the 18 and 19 September cutoffs; no drone attack on a host state for a fourteenth consecutive day; no Iranian fire into Iraq in the window; the two-day sequence of Iranian fire into Kurdistan that ended 15 September was not renewed.
- The pause "has now survived ten days and two nights of accumulated pressure", including the UN fact-finding mission's war crimes findings of 17 September, the White House response of 18 September, Amnesty International's findings, the Basij mobilization of 18 September "with up to 330,000 announced participants", and "the Federal Reserve's monetary policy reversal citing Middle East tension".
- Diplomatically, Foreign Minister Araghchi reiterated in Beijing that "Iran has agreed a plan with Oman to reopen the Strait of Hormuz", a claim "no Omani official has yet confirmed". "The expulsion of a Swedish diplomat in response to a Swedish expulsion of an Iranian embassy employee stands as the sole retaliatory act recorded in the window."
- "Whether the pause continues through the day and whether it reflects calculation, capability or opportunity remains the standing question."

wikis.title: Proxy activity: Hezbollah, Iraqi militias, Houthis, Hamas
wikis.summary: The Axis of Resistance file, with the Houthis the most active front.
wikis.body:
- Hezbollah claimed no fire in the window and the IDF reported none from Lebanese territory; "The ceasefire of April continues to hold notwithstanding Israeli strikes reported on multiple towns across south Lebanon on 16 September."
- Iraqi militias: no attack on American or coalition positions reported. "The disarmament file remains stalled with no handover expected before 30 September, the date by which American anti-ISIS coalition troops are expected to fully depart Iraq." Iraq's East-West pipeline attack investigation continues with no attribution.
- Houthis: "The Houthis remain the war's most active theater." Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree's claimed operations of 16 September against the Aramco facility at Yanbu and Khamis Mushait air base, and the claim of a Saudi F-15 downed over Marib province, stand as previously reported; no new operation announced. "The American-Houthi channel opened by the meeting at the United States Embassy in Muscat over the weekend remains under way, with Houthi representatives having told American officials that they have no intention of attacking American vessels."
- Hamas and Gaza: no development bearing on the Iran war; "The standing assessment that Iranian material and financial support to Hamas has not been restored to pre-war levels is unchanged."

wikis.title: Maritime and economic domain
wikis.summary: Irreconcilable Hormuz transit data, the Saudi pipeline recovery and oil prices, and the Federal Reserve's rate rise.
wikis.body:
- The transit datasets remain unreconciled: Reuters four commodity transits on 15 September; Windward 12 on 16 September; Energy Secretary Wright's 18 million barrels with American assistance and a seven-day average of about 11 million barrels a day "cannot be reconciled to either dataset". "The gap remains the dark fleet and the standing qualification on every published Hormuz figure."
- Brent "fell more than two percent on the announcement that Aramco has begun selling twenty million barrels to Asian refiners via the Oman route and ship-to-ship transfer". "Four supertankers capable of carrying eight million barrels loaded at Ras Tanura and Juaymah on Tuesday." Riyadh seeks to restore about half the East-West pipeline's capacity "within days and full operation within six weeks". Yanbu's storage "stood below 15 million barrels, a few days of cover at the current export rate".
- Physical market above futures: Oman crude above $130 and "Shanghai INE reaching a record $138.50"; "the $391,000 difference between the Persian Gulf to China VLCC rate and the Gulf of Oman to China route stands as the market's price for the strait".
- "The Federal Reserve raised the federal funds target range by a quarter point to 3.75-4.00 percent on 16 September by a vote of 12 to 0." Chairman Kevin Warsh said "tension in the Middle East" is one of three factors that "lend themselves to a firm unanimous decision today" - "the first Federal Reserve invocation of the war as a factor in monetary policy".

wikis.title: Nuclear status
wikis.summary: The standing IAEA and Security Council picture, unchanged in the window.
wikis.body:
- "No Iranian or Agency verification step was announced between the 17 and 18 September cutoffs." The General Conference in Vienna continues through 18 September. The Board of Governors referral of Iran to the Security Council stands from 9 September.
- The Security Council vote on the 1737 Committee Panel of Experts was scheduled for 17 September at an unspecified hour and had not been reported through the 18 September 0500 ET cutoff; "The procedural pattern of the last three Iran meetings is for 11 votes in favour against China and Russia, with Pakistan and Somalia abstaining, and a veto is expected." The Panel of Experts mandate "expires on 26 or 27 September depending on source".
- No Iranian step toward NPT withdrawal, expulsion of the Agency presence or resumption of enrichment was announced.
- Technical picture: the IAEA has conducted no verification activities in Iran under the NPT safeguards agreement since 28 February "other than a single Bushehr inspection in June" and has been denied access to more than 20 declared nuclear sites and one location outside facilities. The enriched-uranium stockpile is assessed to be in country, "including 184.1 kilograms enriched to up to 20 percent and 440.9 kilograms enriched to up to 60 percent"; the Agency cannot verify the location or status of "more than 200 kilograms of the 60 percent material believed to survive at Isfahan and Natanz". Grossi stated on 7 September that it is "more than a year since the Agency lost continuity of knowledge" over those stocks.

wikis.title: Iranian internal situation
wikis.summary: The Basij mobilization of 18 September and Iran's deteriorating economic indicators.
wikis.body:
- The response to "the Kurdish strike and general closure of 17 September", announced as the largest Basij mobilization in recent periods, "took place as scheduled on 18 September with the announced scale of up to 330,000 participants".
- The exercise was titled "313,000-Strong Exercise of Iran's Jan-Fadayans" and was attended by Basij chief Hossein Taeb and IRGC Greater Tehran commander Hassan Hassanzadeh. The Basij then declared that "pro-regime street deployments will continue indefinitely" and that "preliminary and advanced training programs for recruits covering ground, air and naval domains have been established".
- Economic indicators: the rial traded at "2,311,000 to the dollar on 16 September, down 43.99 percent over six months" (the executive summary says the rial is "below 2.3 million to the dollar"); household inflation 89 percent year on year in August, food and beverage inflation 127.5 percent; Health Minister Mohammad Reza Zafarghandi said on 14 September that "32 types of medicine are in short supply"; average Iranian crude loadings have fallen approximately 85 percent.
- Mahan Air announced on 16 September it is cancelling all Iran-Turkey flights from 21 September, and Georgia will suspend sanctioned Iranian carriers from the same date. Oil Minister Mohsen Paknejad said on 16 September that "some lost production capacity would return by year's end and the remainder in the first half of 2027".
- "No executions or new death sentences were reported in the window, and the standing execution rate recorded on 16 September at one every 9.6 hours stands as the most recent assessment."

wikis.title: International response, US policy and the war crimes findings
wikis.summary: The UN and Amnesty findings, the White House response, China's position and the state of US domestic politics.
wikis.body:
- The UN Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Iran reported on 17 September "reasonable grounds to believe United States forces committed war crimes in two strikes and that Iranian authorities committed crimes against humanity during the suppression of the winter protests".
- The mission's findings against Iran "name 87 officials for criminal investigation and documented 377 protest deaths including 56 children"; its findings against the United States "name a primary school in which approximately 120 children died and a sports center where tungsten pellets were dispersed over a residential area" (the dashboard describes "approximately 120 schoolchildren at Minab and 22 civilians at Lamerd").
- Amnesty International's report of 16 September "names 62 security force commanders and 25 Ministry of Interior officials for criminal investigation"; the casualties section of the same report instead says Amnesty's report "named 87 Iranian officials for criminal investigation".
- The White House responded on 18 September that "the UN Human Rights Council has accomplished nothing for human rights while spouting unserious nonsense for decades" and that "the only party committing war crimes in the conflict has been the Iranian regime." No formal Iranian, European or Gulf response had been published by the cutoff.
- China: Wang Yi's position of 16 September is called "the most complete statement of any external power" - willing to cooperate with Iran, urging the strait open "at an early date", not wanting tensions to spread to Yemen and the Red Sea, urging Tehran and Washington back to "the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding", and saying the Middle East security architecture needs reform; the meeting was "a week before President Xi is received in Washington".
- Secretary-General Guterres said on 16 September the UN can offer a negotiating platform "but they have to want it". The Gulf-Iran foreign ministers' meeting postponed from 14 September after Bahrain's withdrawal has not been rescheduled.
- US domestic: Congress in recess after its 15 September vote on the third war powers resolution; "The House adjourned after voting 220 to 204 to limit the President's power to strike Iran, with seven Republicans breaking ranks", and Rep. Thomas Massie introduced articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Speaker Mike Johnson: "Iran will not have a nuclear weapon. That's taken care of, and now we got to get gas prices down." Regular gasoline stood at $4.37 a gallon against $3.19 a year earlier.
- President Trump said on 16 September the United States is "hopefully toward the end" of its war on Iran and that he has spoken with Iranians "directly", reiterating the conflict will end after the November elections while allowing for an earlier solution; Vice President Vance said the war will enter "a different phase" and that withdrawal "would mean necessarily a worldwide energy crisis".
- Sanctions: no OFAC Iran-related action between the 17 and 18 September cutoffs; the most recent designation remains "the 14 September amendment adding the Bank Vostok designation under Operation Economic Outcast".

wikis.title: Super Bowl LXI
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on Super Bowl LXI, the NFL championship game for the 2026 season scheduled for February 14, 2027 at SoFi Stadium, covering host selection, the logo, ESPN/ABC broadcasting, advertising rates and international coverage.
wikis.body:
## Overview

- "Super Bowl LXI is the upcoming American football championship game of the National Football League (NFL) for the 2026 season."
- "The game will be played on February 14, 2027, at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, California."
- "This will be the ninth Super Bowl hosted by the Greater Los Angeles area, and the second at this venue, the first being Super Bowl LVI in 2022."
- "It will also be the first Super Bowl to be played on both Valentine's Day and Presidents' Day weekend."
- "The game is planned to be nationally televised by ESPN and ABC."
- Preceded by Super Bowl LX, followed by Super Bowl LXII.
- Infobox announcers: Joe Buck (play-by-play), Troy Aikman (analyst), Lisa Salters and Laura Rutledge (sideline reporters), Russell Yurk (rules analyst). The infobox leaves rating, share, commercial, radio announcers, team records, coaches and referee blank.

## Host selection

- "The league has made all decisions regarding hosting sites from Super Bowl LVII onward. There is no bidding process per site: the league selects a potential venue unilaterally, the chosen team puts together a hosting proposal, and then the league votes to determine whether it is acceptable."
- "On December 13, 2023, the NFL announced that SoFi Stadium, home of both the Los Angeles Rams and the Los Angeles Chargers, was selected as the Super Bowl site."

## Logo

- "The official logo for Super Bowl LXI was unveiled by the game's broadcaster ESPN on February 8, 2026, during a special post-Super Bowl LX edition of SportsCenter with Scott Van Pelt from SoFi Stadium."
- "It was formally unveiled during a press conference in Los Angeles the following day, accompanied by an introductory video narrated by Inglewood-based rapper D Smoke."
- "Keeping with the tradition established at Super Bowl LVI, the logo features Roman numerals with imagery representing the host city/region, in this case being waves - reflecting Southern California's surfing culture and the 'grit and tenacity of Los Angeles'."

## US television

- "Super Bowl LXI is scheduled to be televised nationally by ABC and ESPN in English and ESPN Deportes in Spanish."
- "It will be the fourth Super Bowl to be broadcast as part of the current 11-year NFL television contract, which allows a four-year rotation between CBS, Fox, NBC and ABC/ESPN."
- The page dates ABC's last Super Bowl two ways: the lead says "the first time ABC will air the Super Bowl since Super Bowl XL in 2006", while the broadcasting section says "the first time ABC will have aired the Super Bowl since 2005's Super Bowl XL". Both say it is "the first time that ESPN will air a live Super Bowl in the United States in English."
- "Univision will also carry a separate Spanish broadcast on broadcast television."
- "ESPN's president of content Burke Magnus stated that its popular Peyton and Eli altcast would 'definitely be a part' of the game." The infobox lists ESPN2 carrying the Manningcast.
- Cable/streaming listed: ESPN, ESPN2 (Manningcast), ESPN Deportes; ESPN Unlimited and NFL+ for streaming.
- "In January 2025, ESPN named E:60 producer Andy Tennant as vice president of Super Bowl production."
- "In March 2025, ESPN hired former Fox Sports director Artie Kempner to serve as the new director for Monday Night Football beginning in the 2025 season"; Magnus cited his previous Super Bowl telecasts at Fox alongside Joe Buck and Troy Aikman, "who themselves moved from Fox to ESPN and MNF in 2022".
- "ESPN and ABC will broadcast programming from Santa Monica State Beach during Super Bowl week, which will feature Disney promotional presences and other entertainment."

## Promotion

- "Promotional efforts began a year in advance: ESPN aired a special SportsCenter with Scott Van Pelt from SoFi Stadium following its Super Bowl LX post-game coverage to launch a year-long countdown to Super Bowl LXI."
- "The following day, ESPN aired studio shows from its Los Angeles studio, SoFi Stadium, and Disneyland, and cross-promotional content appeared on ABC programming such as Good Morning America."
- "This included the premiere of a commercial that reimagines the 'I'm going to Disneyland/Disney World!' commercials with Disney characters and personalities instead going to Super Bowl LXI."
- "On February 11, 2026, the Walt Disney Company announced a company-wide 'Year of the Super Bowl' campaign, which will include cross-promotion across its various platforms and properties, and on-air initiatives across ESPN programming during the year prior to the game."

## Advertising

- "Disney charged an average rate of $8.5-10 million for a 30-second advertisement during Super Bowl LXI."
- "The company had initially attempted to charge a $10 million rate on par with NBC's rates for Super Bowl LX, along with requiring advertisers to commit to an equivalent spend across other Disney platforms, but became more willing to negotiate after a lukewarm reception from advertisers."
- "Disney CFO Hugh Johnston stated that 58 individual brands had purchased advertisements during the game, including nine first-time advertisers."

## Radio and international

- "Westwood One holds the national radio rights to the game."
- United Kingdom: free-to-air on 5; Ireland: Virgin Media Television.
- Latin America: ESPN and Disney+.
- Germany and Austria: RTL. Serbia: Arena Sport.
- Africa: ESPN Africa, and Disney+ in South Africa.

wikis.title: 2026-27 NHL season
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the upcoming 2026-27 NHL season: the 84-game schedule and new CBA, coaching and front-office changes, arena and outdoor games, and the league's Canadian, US, local and international media deals.
wikis.body:
## Overview
- "The 2026-27 NHL season is the upcoming 110th season of operation (109th season of play) of the National Hockey League (NHL)."
- Duration given in the infobox: September 29, 2026 - June 2027. Games: 84. Teams: 32.
- "The season will feature an 84-game regular season schedule for the first time since 1993-94."
- The regular season is scheduled to begin September 29, 2026 and end April 10, 2027; the Stanley Cup playoffs are "planned to begin in April 2027, ending with the Stanley Cup Final in June".
- Infobox TV partners: Sportsnet / SN1 / SN360, TVA Sports (Canada); ESPN / ABC / ESPN2, TNT/TBS/truTV, NHL Network (United States). Streaming: Sportsnet+, Amazon Prime Video (Canada); ESPN app / Hulu / Disney+, HBO Max (United States); DAZN internationally (NHL.TV excluded in Denmark, Finland, Norway and Sweden).
- Infobox draft: top draft pick Gavin McKenna, picked by the Toronto Maple Leafs. The 2026 NHL entry draft took place June 26-27 at KeyBank Center in Buffalo, New York.
- Arena change: "planned to be the last season the Calgary Flames will play their home games at Scotiabank Saddledome before moving to Scotia Place".
- Uniforms: on August 19, 2026 the league announced the "Hometown Remix" program, jerseys for all 32 teams meant to invoke the "fans, city, and local culture" of the franchises.
- See-also links: 2026-27 NHL transactions, 2026 in sports, 2027 in sports.

wikis.title: 2026-30 collective bargaining agreement and EBUG rules
wikis.summary: The new four-year NHL-NHLPA CBA that expands the season to 84 games and replaces amateur emergency backup goaltenders.
wikis.body:
- "On June 27, 2025, the league and the NHL Players' Association agreed on a new four-year collective bargaining agreement (CBA) that will take effect from the 2026-27 to 2029-30 seasons."
- The 2026-27 regular season expands from 82 to 84 games, "featuring two more divisional games"; preseason games drop from 6 to 4.
- The season also ends the use of amateur emergency back-up goaltenders (EBUGs) supplied by the home team; teams must hire their own emergency goaltender who travels with the team and may have other non-player team duties.
- To prevent "ringers", a team's EBUG must not have played professional hockey at any level in the previous three seasons, cannot have played a single NHL game under a standard player contract, cannot have played more than 80 professional games in their career, and cannot be on any NHL team's reserve list or restricted free agent list.
- A team that signs three or more goaltenders must still hire a permanent EBUG but need not have them present for a game. EBUGs must wear 00 as their uniform number.

wikis.title: Coaching changes for 2026-27
wikis.summary: The five head-coaching changes listed for the off-season, with the firings, records and replacements.
wikis.body:
- Edmonton Oilers: Kris Knoblauch to Mike Babcock. Knoblauch fired May 14, 2026, two weeks after elimination from the 2026 Stanley Cup playoffs; 135-77-21 in parts of three seasons with two consecutive Stanley Cup Final appearances (2024, 2025). Babcock, most recently Columbus Blue Jackets coach during part of the 2023 offseason, was cleared by the NHLPA and NHL in an investigation on June 18 and named head coach June 23.
- Los Angeles Kings: Jim Hiller to D. J. Smith (interim) to Peter Laviolette. Hiller fired March 1, 2026 after a 24-21-14 start including 2-5-1 in his final eight games; 93-58-24 in parts of three seasons, losing to Edmonton in the first round both times. Smith named interim the same day, finished 11-6-6, swept in the first round. Laviolette (New York Rangers 2023-2025) named head coach June 9.
- Toronto Maple Leafs: Craig Berube to Jim Hiller. Berube fired May 13, 2026; 84-62-18 in two seasons, second round in 2025, missed playoffs in year two. Hiller named head coach June 17.
- Vancouver Canucks: Adam Foote to Manny Malhotra. Foote fired May 19, 2026 after a 25-49-8 season, last in the NHL. Malhotra, head coach of the AHL Abbotsford Canucks and a Canucks player 2010-2013, named June 1.
- Vegas Golden Knights: Bruce Cassidy to John Tortorella to Ryan Craig. Cassidy fired March 29, 2026 with eight games left after a 32-26-16 start; 178-99-43 in just under four seasons, three playoff appearances and the 2023 Stanley Cup. Tortorella (Philadelphia 2022-2025) signed for the remainder of the season and playoffs, finished 7-0-1 and reached the 2026 Stanley Cup Final, losing to the Carolina Hurricanes; on June 16 Vegas announced he would not return. Ryan Craig, coach of the AHL Henderson Silver Knights and a Vegas assistant 2017-2023, named June 17.

wikis.title: Front office and general manager changes
wikis.summary: The general manager changes across seven teams ahead of the 2026-27 season.
wikis.body:
- Colorado Avalanche: Chris MacFarland to Joe Sakic. MacFarland left June 2, 2026 to become president of hockey operations and GM of the Nashville Predators; Sakic, the Avalanche's president of hockey operations and GM from 2014 to 2022, re-assumed the role the same day.
- Detroit Red Wings: Steve Yzerman to Shawn Horcoff (interim). On July 15, 2026 Detroit announced Yzerman would step down as GM to become senior advisor to owner Christopher Ilitch, staying until a successor was found; Horcoff named interim GM on September 15.
- Nashville Predators: Barry Trotz to Chris MacFarland. Trotz announced on February 2, 2026 his intention to retire as GM and serve as an advisor through the end of his contract; MacFarland named president of hockey operations and GM June 2.
- New Jersey Devils: Tom Fitzgerald to Sunny Mehta. Fitzgerald fired April 6, 2026 after a 40-34-3 start; GM since 2020 and president of hockey operations since 2024, with two playoff berths in six completed seasons. Mehta, assistant GM of the Florida Panthers and a Devils executive 2014-2017, named GM April 16.
- St. Louis Blues: Doug Armstrong to Alexander Steen. Armstrong signed a three-year extension as president of hockey operations June 13, 2024, with Steen named special assistant intended to become GM from 2026-27. On April 24, 2026 the Blues confirmed Steen would succeed Armstrong on July 1; on June 30 the Blues announced Steen had officially begun his GM duties that day.
- Toronto Maple Leafs: Brad Treliving to Ryan Hardy and Brandon Pridham (co-interim) to John Chayka. Treliving fired March 30, 2026 after a 31-30-13 start; GM since 2023 with playoff berths in two completed seasons. Chayka, Arizona Coyotes GM 2016-2020, named GM May 3.
- Vancouver Canucks: Patrik Allvin to Ryan Johnson. Allvin fired April 17, 2026, the day after the season ended; GM since 2022 with one playoff appearance. Johnson, assistant GM and GM of the AHL Abbotsford Canucks, promoted May 14.

wikis.title: Regular season and international games
wikis.summary: The season's start and end dates and the two European regular-season series.
wikis.body:
- The regular season is scheduled to begin on September 29, 2026 and end on April 10, 2027.
- The Seattle Kraken and Carolina Hurricanes are scheduled to play two games against each other on November 12 and 14, 2026 at Veikkaus Arena in Helsinki, Finland.
- The Chicago Blackhawks and Ottawa Senators are scheduled to play two games against each other on December 18 and 20, 2026 at PSD Bank Dome in Dusseldorf, Germany.

wikis.title: Outdoor games and the 2027 All-Star Game
wikis.summary: The season's three scheduled outdoor games and the return of the All-Star Game at UBS Arena.
wikis.body:
- "The league has scheduled three outdoor games this season":
  - 2026 Heritage Classic, October 25, at Princess Auto Stadium in Winnipeg, Winnipeg Jets hosting the Montreal Canadiens.
  - 2027 NHL Winter Classic, "scheduled for December 31, at Rice-Eccles Stadium in Salt Lake City", Utah Mammoth hosting the Colorado Avalanche.
  - 2027 NHL Stadium Series, February 20, at AT&T Stadium in Arlington, Texas, Dallas Stars hosting the Vegas Golden Knights.
- The 2027 All-Star Game is scheduled for February 7 at UBS Arena in Elmont, New York, home of the New York Islanders - "played for the first time since 2024". The league held the 4 Nations Face-Off in 2025, then players took part in the 2026 Winter Olympics; a 2026 All-Star Game at UBS Arena had been planned as an Olympic "send-off" but was dropped.

wikis.title: Canadian media rights
wikis.summary: The first season of the 12-year Rogers renewal, the end of CBC's involvement, and the Sportsnet, Amazon and TVA packages.
wikis.body:
- First season of a 12-year renewal of the NHL's Canadian broadcast rights with Rogers Sports & Media; Amazon Prime Video and TVA Sports renewed their sub-licensing agreements with Rogers for the entire 12 years.
- CBC Sports will no longer sub-license NHL coverage, "ending the CBC's 74-year relationship with the league"; it will replace Hockey Night in Canada with a new primetime sports block focusing on Canadian athletes while keeping ownership of the Hockey Night in Canada brand, to be used in "different ways".
- Saturday night games rebranded Saturday Night Hockey on the four regional Sportsnet feeds, SN1 and SN360, with weekly doubleheaders featuring at least one Canadian team per matchup; Sportsnet can flex more regional games to national telecasts and has its own Tuesday opening-night doubleheader featuring Canadian teams for the first time since 2021-22.
- Citytv and Omni Television will no longer carry broadcasts, "ending all free-to-air television coverage of the NHL in Canada"; Sportsnet confirmed the cancellation of Omni's Hockey Night in Canada: Punjabi Edition on August 14, 2026.
- TVA Sports will offer French-language broadcasts of up to 350 regular season games per season; nationally televised Montreal Canadiens regular games rise from 22 to 32, including the season opener, Monday night and Saturday night games, plus "tentpole" events and the playoffs.
- Streaming: Sportsnet+ takes over Monday Night Hockey from Amazon Prime Video; Amazon Prime Video takes over Wednesday Night Hockey from Sportsnet and will produce all its games in English and French.
- Postseason split: in round one Sportsnet has the first three series choices, Amazon the fourth and fifth, Sportsnet the remaining three; in round two Sportsnet picks first and second, Amazon third, Sportsnet the fourth. Sportsnet exclusively televises the conference finals and the Stanley Cup Final. TVA Sports produces French-language versions of all Canadiens playoff games and all Sportsnet-produced series; Amazon may produce French versions only of playoff games not involving the Canadiens.

wikis.title: United States media rights
wikis.summary: The sixth season of the seven-year ESPN and TNT Sports deals, including ABC's schedule and the playoff split.
wikis.body:
- "This will be the sixth season of the league's seven-year U.S. national broadcast rights deals with the ESPN family of networks and TNT Sports."
- ESPN keeps the opening day tripleheader and airs games primarily on Tuesdays and Thursdays, plus Sunday night doubleheaders on four weekends between late February and April.
- ABC's Hockey Saturday has 16 regular season games on free-to-air television between January and April, including one doubleheader, three tripleheaders, a Saturday afternoon game on January 16 before the NFL Wild Card games, a Sunday afternoon edition on January 31 before the NFL Conference Championship games, and the Stadium Series - "the first time since 2024 that the outdoor game will be on ABC instead of ESPN". ESPN has the All-Star skills competition and ABC the All-Star Game.
- TNT primarily carries Wednesday night games, select Tuesday and Thursday games, the Thanksgiving Showdown, the Winter Classic and a Martin Luther King Jr. Day doubleheader, plus a Friday doubleheader in opening week and one Monday game on November 16. Its Sunday schedule includes the Heritage Classic in October, five consecutive weekends in February and March and the last Sunday of the regular season in April; the March 21 game is the first time under its contract that TNT will air the NHL instead of two Sunday night NCAA March Madness Round of 32 games (it still avoids the March 28 Regional Finals). Games may be simulcast on truTV, with TBS as overflow; not all TNT Sports regular season games are exclusive and some are subject to local blackout.
- NHL Network televises games when other national broadcasters do not and primarily simulcasts local coverage.
- Streaming: ESPN+ (the ESPN app's Select plan) has 47 exclusive games, primarily Tuesdays and Thursdays; Disney+ joins Hulu in simulcasting them; ESPN+ keeps the NHL Power Play out-of-market package and on-demand replays of every concluded game. HBO Max ad-free tiers stream all TNT Sports-produced games.
- Postseason: first- and second-round games split between ESPN-produced telecasts (ESPN, ABC or ESPN2) and TNT Sports-produced telecasts (TNT or TBS, with selected truTV simulcasts); each US team's regional broadcaster also televises local first-round coverage except games on ABC. ESPN has first choice of conference final, TNT Sports the other, and TNT airs the Stanley Cup Final "for the third and last time under its seven-year contract".
- Radio: fourth season of the league's six-year deal with SiriusXM and SiriusXM Canada simulcasting all 32 teams' local regular season and postseason broadcasts.

wikis.title: Local rights after FanDuel Sports Network, radio and personnel
wikis.summary: The collapse of FanDuel Sports Network and the new regional deals, plus radio and announcer changes and international coverage.
wikis.body:
- FanDuel Sports Network "wound down operations after the 2025-26 season, affecting seven teams", due to continued financial difficulties.
- Commissioner Gary Bettman initially said the league was not interested in a centralized production hub like MLB Local Media; on July 21, 2026 Sports Business Journal reported the league was developing a production hub within NHL Productions led by former MLB Network president Rob McGlarry, with teams covering only production costs. On September 2, 2026 it was confirmed six teams would use the hub as part of new regional rights with Amazon Prime Video.
- Detroit Red Wings move to Detroit SportsNet, a new part-time RSN operated with MLB Local Media and shared with the Detroit Tigers, plus a team-run direct-to-consumer service; MLB provides distribution support but not production, with a DTC option through the MLB app.
- Los Angeles Kings renewed with FanDuel Sports Network West after the channel was acquired by the Los Angeles Angels in March 2026 and renamed "Angels Broadcast Television"; in September 2026 the Angels announced a sale to Colorado Avalanche owner Stan Kroenke, and the Kings announced a direct-to-consumer service through DAZN.
- Nashville Predators signed a multi-year deal with Scripps Sports, with WNPX as flagship station and a DTC platform to be announced.
- On September 2, 2026 Amazon Prime Video announced regional rights to the Columbus Blue Jackets, St. Louis Blues, Carolina Hurricanes and Minnesota Wild, each with a standalone subscription on Prime Video not requiring Amazon Prime, while continuing cable/satellite and some over-the-air distribution; Amazon also acquired the rights to the Anaheim Ducks and Dallas Stars, whose games go to Prime subscribers in-market, with the Ducks keeping 65 games on KCOP-TV and the Stars a 17-game package after both declined to renew with Victory+.
- Montreal Canadiens renewed regional rights with Bell Media's RDS (French) and TSN2 (English) in a multi-year deal of unspecified length.
- DAZN becomes the DTC streaming platform for MSG Network (Sabres, Devils, Islanders, Rangers), replacing the Gotham Sports App; Monumental+ also becomes available on DAZN after DAZN acquired operator ViewLift Media from Capitals owner Ted Leonsis.
- Personnel: Eddie Olczyk stepped down from the Seattle Kraken after four seasons but stays as TNT's lead analyst; on July 29, 2026 the Columbus Blue Jackets parted with radio play-by-play announcer Bob McElligott after 17 years and will simulcast TV commentary; Todd Crocker replaces Joe Bowen on Toronto Maple Leafs radio; Aaron Cooney replaces Steve Carroll on Anaheim Ducks radio.
- Radio: on July 7, 2026 Rogers closed six news and sports stations including the Flames' CFAC and the Canucks' CISL; Canucks broadcasts move to 104.9/107.5/92.5 Kiss Throwbacks, and on August 12, 2026 the Flames announced a five-year deal with Corus Radio moving to 770 CHQR.
- International: NHL.TV will be available in around 200 countries on DAZN; for the ninth consecutive season the NHL Saturday and NHL Sunday packages air across selected European broadcasters; ESPN airs games in Latin America, Brazil, the Caribbean, sub-Saharan Africa, Oceania and the Netherlands, and via Disney+ in select Asian and European markets.

- Resolution is based on seats in "the State Duma of the Federal Assembly of the Russian Federation", by a consensus of credible reporting, and if ambiguous "solely by the official results reported by Russian government sources such as the Central Election Commission of the Russian Federation."
- Coalition note: a listed party contesting in a jointly listed coalition has its market represent the whole coalition and count all its seats; where two or more listed parties form one coalition, the market of the party that won most seats in the previous election represents it; if the coalition dissolves, each market again represents its own party.

## The market
