- Outcomes listed (with a "View resolved" link for others; the FAQ says the market has "4 possible outcomes"):
  - October 31 - $697,977 volume - 5% - "Buy Yes 5 cents / Buy No 96 cents".
  - December 31 - $906,538 volume - 15% - "Buy Yes 15 cents / Buy No 86 cents".
- The FAQ section instead states "The current leading outcome is 'December 31' at 14%, followed by 'October 31' at 5%", and repeatedly explains a price of 14 cents for "December 31"; the market cards above show 15% for December 31.
- US visitors see a notice: "Trading is blocked in the United States on polymarket.com. Switch to polymarket.us to trade prediction markets."
- 35 comments; related markets listed: "Saudi-Houthi ceasefire agreement announced by October 31?" 22%, "US x Iran ceasefire continues through September 20?" 97%, "Israel x Iran ceasefire continues through September 30?" 87%.

## Market context note (site's own)
- "Recent US-mediated diplomacy, including September 2026 visits by envoys to Moscow and Kyiv, has produced limited temporary halts on strikes against capitals and prisoner exchanges but no broader ceasefire. Russia continues rejecting proposals that fall short of its territorial objectives in Donbas and annexed regions, while Ukraine maintains it will not cede land or accept deals without durable security arrangements. Ongoing aerial campaigns against energy and infrastructure targets persist amid a stalemated frontline. Trilateral talks are scheduled for October, though prior rounds yielded minimal progress on core disputes."
- The page labels this an "Experimental AI-generated summary referencing Polymarket data. This is not trading advice and plays no role in how this market resolves." and stamps it "Updated Sep 20, 2026, 3:00 PM UTC".

## Resolution rules
- Resolves "Yes" if a ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine goes into effect by 11:59 PM Eastern European Time (EET) on the specified date "and remains continuously in effect for at least 10 calendar days"; otherwise "No".
- A ceasefire is "any mutually agreed suspension of direct military engagement between Russia and Ukraine", officially announced by both countries or confirmed by a consensus of credible reporting, constituting a general suspension of direct kinetic military engagement across the primary theater. A broader peace deal, normalization agreement, political framework, truce or humanitarian pause (including holiday ceasefires) counts if it otherwise qualifies.
- Not counted: informal understandings, backchannel communication, de-escalation without an announced agreement, unilateral pauses, or agreements applying only to specific conflict categories or locations.
- Every calendar day (EET) the ceasefire is in effect, including the first, counts toward the 10-day total, ending 11:59 PM EET on the 10th day inclusive. If a qualifying ceasefire starts before the market's end date, the market stays open until the ceasefire ends or the 10 days are reached.
- A ceasefire is "no longer in effect" when a consensus of credible reporting indicates the general suspension has substantively ended; temporary or technical lapses, isolated incidents, localized violations or accusations alone do not invalidate it. "Where official government statements conflict with a consensus of credible field reporting, the reporting will take precedence over the government statements."
- Resolution source: "a consensus of credible sources."

## Worked examples given in the rules
- Qualifying: the April 8, 2026 US-Iran ceasefire (framework kept functioning despite maritime confrontations and alleged violations); the November 27, 2024 Israel-Hezbollah ceasefire (mutually agreed per credible reporting even without a single joint declaration).
- Not qualifying: the November 24, 2023 Israel-Hamas humanitarian pause (lasted about 7 days, short of the 10-day requirement); the July 22, 2022 Black Sea Grain Initiative (not a general suspension across the primary theater); the May 2023 Sudan SAF-RSF ceasefires (never substantively took effect; reporting treated them as failed despite remaining in force on paper).

- Resolves "Yes" if either condition is met:
  1. "The seasonally adjusted annualized percent change in quarterly U.S. real GDP from the previous quarter is less than 0.0 for two consecutive quarters between Q2 2025 and Q4 2027 (inclusive), as reported by the Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA)."
  2. "The National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER) publicly announces that a recession has occurred in the United States, at any point during 2025, 2026, or 2027, with the announcement made by the time the BEA releases the advance estimate for Q4 2027."
- "Otherwise, this market will resolve to 'No'."
- "Note that advance estimates will be considered. For example, if upon release, the advance estimate for Q3 2026 was negative, and the Q2 2026's most recent, up-to-date estimate was also negative, this market would resolve to 'Yes'. If on December 31, 2027 the latest estimate for quarterly GDP in Q3 2026 was negative, this market will stay open until the Advance estimate of Q4 2027 is published, at which point it will resolve to 'Yes' if Q4 2027 was negative or if the NBER declares a recession by then."

If the GDP advance estimate for Q4 2026 has not been released by June 30, 2028, 11:59 PM ET, this market will resolve based on the available releases at that time." wikis.title: James Talarico interviewed on The Breakfast Club about the 2026 Texas Senate race
wikis.summary: A 1h 3m Breakfast Club episode from 29 August 2026 in which James Talarico, the Democratic nominee for the U.S. Senate in Texas, discusses his record, the primary with Jasmine Crockett, redistricting, the Texas THC ban, a Black agenda, Gaza, policing and his Christian faith.
wikis.body:
## The episode

- "INTERVIEW: James Talarico on Texas Senate Race, Ken Paxton, Jasmine Crockett, Black Voters & Businesses + More", **The Breakfast Club** on The Black Effect Network, published "August 29, 2026 at 7:10 PM UTC", length **1h 3m**, rating "Clean".
- Hosts listed as Charlamagne Tha God, DJ Envy and Jessica Moore; on air the hosts are "DJ Envy, Jess Hilarious, Charlamagne Tha Guy", with Angela Rye in the studio. Guest: James Talarico.

## The race

- Talarico is "the Democratic nominee in the 2026 U.S. Senate election in Texas", running for what he calls "LBJ's Senate seat" against Ken Paxton, whom he calls "the most corrupt politician in our state".
- Says polling shows the campaign outperforming recent Texas Democratic nominees with Black voters, and that "we're leading in every poll that's come out this month against Ken Paxton"; expects opponents to "drop $200 million to try to stop us".
- Campaign has 59,000 volunteers (a December video went to "our 50,000 volunteers"). Says that on winning he would "represent the most African Americans of any senator in the country".
- Calls Texas "a pink state": Republicans who won statewide by 25-30 points now win by single digits, and in 2018 "Beto got within two and a half points of beating Ted Cruz".
- On Texas voting rules: registration closes a month in advance, no online registration, re-registration on every move; "one of the hardest places to vote in the country" with "the second lowest voter turnout rate".

## Record and background

- Sixth grade language arts teacher at Rhodes Middle School, west San Antonio, from "the fall of 2011, right after the state legislature in Texas cut $5 billion from public schools"; 45 students in one classroom.
- Then an education nonprofit, then elected to the Texas House from Round Rock at 28 with 51% of the vote in a district party figures called a lost cause. Now in his fourth term, says he has passed 60 bipartisan bills.

## What he says he would do

- Pass the John Lewis Voting Rights Act and a national ban on gerrymandering; supports Kamala Harris's Urban League list (Electoral College, expanding the court to 13 justices, statehood for Puerto Rico and D.C.) and banning corporate PACs and super PACs.
- "I would not vote to send weapons to the Netanyahu government"; all military aid "conditioned on ending the death and the destruction in Gaza and the West Bank". On the word genocide: the term "is being litigated in the International Criminal Court" and "certainly there's evidence to bring those charges", but a senator's job is to act, not to litigate terms.
- Federal maternal-health plan (paid family leave, provider training, data, doula and midwife coverage) against a crisis "three times deadlier for black women", with Harris County "the deadliest place for a black woman to give birth in the entire country".
- HBCU funding "up to parity"; federal entrepreneurial grants for Black-owned businesses after Texas defunded the HUB programme.

## Texas fights he recounts

- Broke quorum "a year ago yesterday" with House colleagues, leaving for Illinois over the mid-decade map he calls racist; Texas Rangers were sent after them and they received bomb and death threats in Chicago.
- The new Texas THC ban: "Now it's a felony to have Delta 8", a law that "just went into effect"; he blames "big beer, big tobacco" and calls it "a gift to the drug cartels".
- Passed Javier Ambler's law banning reality TV policing contracts in Texas, after his constituent Javier Ambler was tased to death by the Williamson County Sheriff's Department while being filmed for Live PD; the George Floyd Act "didn't even get a hearing".

## Jasmine Crockett

- Friends and fellow "troublemakers" in the Texas House; he says he called her "my friend... a leader" in a video the day she entered the race and told online attackers at a town hall to keep her name out of their mouths, conceding "it's possible I could have showed more leadership". She endorsed him and the whole ticket the morning after the primary.

## Faith

- Champions separation of church and state but not "a separation of faith and politics"; "The only thing worse than a tyrant is a tyrant who thinks they're on a mission from God." In seminary, grandson of a Baptist preacher, and a critic of Texas bills mandating the Ten Commandments in classrooms.
- Closes on Matthew 25: "what would Jesus say if he walked onto the floor of the U.S. Senate? I think he would say, I was hungry and you kicked me off food stamps. I was sick and you kicked me off Medicaid. I was a stranger and you deported me and my family."
- Asked which party Jesus would make more uncomfortable: "both", because "Jesus is far more radical than any political party" - radical from the Latin for root.

## Call to action

- Volunteers can sign up at **jamestallarico.com** for door knocking, phone banks and texting; "action is the best antidote to that despair".

wikis.title: James Talarico on The Breakfast Club: Texas Senate race, redistricting, THC ban and Gaza
wikis.summary: First part of a Breakfast Club interview with James Talarico, Democratic nominee in the 2026 U.S. Senate election in Texas, covering his background, the primary against Jasmine Crockett, voting rights and redistricting, the Texas THC ban, a Black agenda, Gaza and criminal justice.
wikis.body:
## The episode

- Episode page headline: "INTERVIEW: James Talarico on Texas Senate Race, Ken Paxton, Jasmine Crockett, Black Voters & Businesses + More", show **The Breakfast Club**, channel **The Black Effect Network**, frequency "Updated Daily".
- Published "August 29, 2026 at 7:10 PM UTC"; length **1h 3m**; rating "Clean".
- Hosts listed: Charlamagne Tha God, DJ Envy, Jessica Moore. Guest: James Talarico. On air the hosts introduce themselves as "DJ Envy, Jess Hilarious, Charlamagne Tha Guy", with Angela Rye also in the studio.
- Episode blurb: "Today on The Breakfast Club, James Talarico on Texas Senate Race, Ken Paxton, Jasmine Crockett, Black Voters & Businesses. Listen For More!"; YouTube channel given as https://www.youtube.com/@BreakfastClubPower1051FM.

## Who Talarico says he is

- Introduced as "the Democratic nominee in the 2026 U.S. Senate election in Texas". Says the seat is "LBJ's Senate seat".
- Before politics he was a public school teacher, sixth grade language arts at Rhodes Middle School on the west side of San Antonio; entered the classroom "in the fall of 2011, right after the state legislature in Texas cut $5 billion from public schools"; at one point had 45 students in one classroom with students sitting on the air conditioning unit.
- Afterwards led an education nonprofit in Central Texas, then ran for a Texas House seat in his hometown of Round Rock at 28, in a Trump district in Williamson County that "hadn't voted for a Democrat for president since Jimmy Carter"; won with 51% of the vote. Now in his fourth term in the Texas House, says he has passed 60 bipartisan bills.
- Says he is in seminary studying to become a minister one day; his granddad was a Baptist preacher.

## Polling and the campaign

- Says private and public polling shows the campaign "outperforming recent Democratic nominees in Texas" with Black voters, and that "we're leading in every poll that's come out this month against Ken Paxton" - "the last three... it might've been the last four or five".
- Says the campaign has 59,000 volunteers (earlier in the interview he refers to sending a video to "our 50,000 volunteers" in December).
- Expects opponents to "drop $200 million to try to stop us".
- Says that when he wins in November he will "represent the most African Americans of any senator in the country".
- On Texas voting rules: registration closes "a whole month in advance", there is no online voter registration, registration must be changed on every move; he says Texas is "one of the hardest places to vote in the country" and has "the second lowest voter turnout rate".
- Compares 2026 to 2018, when "Beto got within two and a half points of beating Ted Cruz"; says the backlash in this, "the second Trump midterm", is bigger, and that Republicans who once won Texas statewide races by 25-30 points now win by single digits, making Texas "a pink state".

## Redistricting and the quorum break

- Calls the mid-decade Texas map "this racist redistricting map" and "the most aggressive attack on black political power since Jim Crow", saying it dilutes the voting power of Black and brown Texans.
- "A year ago yesterday" he and Texas House colleagues broke quorum and left the state for Illinois to deny the House a quorum; the Texas Rangers were called to find and arrest them and they received bomb threats and death threats in Chicago. He says the goal was to draw national attention, after which "California and Virginia and other states" joined the fight.
- Policy asks: pass the John Lewis Voting Rights Act, and a national ban to end gerrymandering "in red states and blue states". He backs the reforms Kamala Harris raised at the Urban League - revisiting the Electoral College, expanding the court to 13 justices, statehood for Puerto Rico and D.C. - plus banning corporate PACs and super PACs.

## Jasmine Crockett and the primary

- Says he and Crockett were friends and "troublemakers" together in the Texas House as two of the only young members.
- Says that on the first day she entered the race, in December, he put out a video to volunteers and staff saying "congresswoman Crockett is my friend. She is a leader and she deserves our utmost respect", and repeated it through the campaign; asked whether he should have defended her sooner after a town hall two weeks earlier where he told online attackers to keep her name out of their mouths, he says "it's possible I could have showed more leadership".
- Says he was asked on The View whether Crockett is electable and answered "absolutely".
- Says Crockett endorsed him and the entire ticket the morning after the primary - "If I'm being very honest, I don't know if I could have done that the morning after" - and has since campaigned for down-ballot candidates across Texas.

## The Texas THC ban

- "THC products are virtually banned in the state of Texas. Now it's a felony to have Delta 8", a law he says "just went into effect"; he contrasts it with needing three DUIs for a felony. He says he is for legalizing weed.
- Blames corruption - "big beer, big tobacco" pushing the ban - and says the ban is "a gift to the drug cartels", pushing buyers to the black market. Says Texas legalized hemp "I think it was six years ago" and it is now a booming industry of local small businesses.

## A Black agenda

- Maternal mortality: says the crisis in Texas is "three times deadlier for black women" and that Harris County, home to Houston, is "the deadliest place for a black woman to give birth in the entire country"; the campaign has a federal plan. Credits Representative Toni Rose of Dallas with a state bill extending postpartum Medicaid coverage to one year. Federal asks: universal paid family leave, better provider training and data collection, and insurance coverage of doula and midwife services to end maternal care deserts.
- HBCUs: he has toured HBCUs, held a town hall at Prairie View A&M and gave the commencement address at Paul Quinn College, "the oldest HBCU in Texas"; wants HBCU funding brought "up to parity" with institutions serving similar numbers of low-income students.
- Black businesses: says Texas has attacked and defunded the HUB (historically underutilized businesses) program, and proposes federal entrepreneurial grants, citing public investment in Tesla and in R&D behind the internet as precedents.

## Gaza and AIPAC

- "I would not vote to send weapons to the Netanyahu government"; says all military aid "needs to be conditioned on ending the death and the destruction in Gaza and the West Bank".
- On not using the word genocide: says "the legal term genocide is being litigated in the International Criminal Court" and "certainly there's evidence to bring those charges", that the U.S. should abide by the court's ruling, but that his job as a senator "would not be to litigate what terms are used".
- Quotes a theologian: "I screamed at God for the starving children until I realized the starving children was God screaming at me."
- Says AIPAC "has not spent against me in this race" but that its influence "has a chilling effect"; says an article called him anti-Semitic after he spoke out on Gaza. Says the same chilling effect applies to AI, with candidates wary of "these giant AI companies" and naming OpenAI alongside AIPAC.

## Criminal justice

- Calls the Carmelo Anthony verdict in Texas a tragedy, noting "there were no black members of the jury", and says he got backlash for saying so.
- Passed Javier Ambler's law after the death of his constituent Javier Ambler, "unarmed black man who was killed by the Williamson County Sheriff's Department", pulled over for not dimming his brights, who told officers he had a heart condition and was tased until he died while being filmed for the reality show Live PD. The law bans reality TV policing contracts with Texas law enforcement agencies. He worked on it with Ambler's sister Kimberly.
- Says the George Floyd Act that session "didn't even get a hearing".

## Competition, faith and attacks

- Says "the best color for Texas is purple": after 12 Democrats flipped Republican districts and Beto's near miss, the 2019 session saw Republicans funding public schools and dropping culture-war bills. Angela Rye pushes back that post-Shelby v. Holder Republican politics mirror "fascism and authoritarianism"; he answers that extremism is itself a result of a lack of competition.
- Cites a Texas bill "to go after furries in schools" over an untrue internet rumor about litter boxes as an example of primary-driven "red meat" politics.
- Responds to a quote calling him "a leftist lab experiment gone wrong" and to talk of a 2028 national run: "I'm going to be, God willing, the U.S. senator from Texas for the next six years... not going to be applying for any other jobs."
- Responds to Joe Rogan's warning that liberals would "ruin" Texas by turning it blue.
- On religion: champions "the separation of church and state" but not "a separation of faith and politics"; says Democrats ceded religion 50 years ago; says he fought Texas bills to force teachers to post the Ten Commandments and to teach Christian Bible stories as absolute truth; "The only thing worse than a tyrant is a tyrant who thinks they're on a mission from God."

wikis.title: Talarico's path from teaching to the Texas House
wikis.summary: Talarico's account of teaching in San Antonio, leading an education nonprofit and flipping a Williamson County seat.
wikis.body:
- Taught sixth grade language arts at Rhodes Middle School, west side of San Antonio, "one of the poor zip codes in the state of Texas".
- Entered the classroom "in the fall of 2011, right after the state legislature in Texas cut $5 billion from public schools"; had 45 students in one classroom, some sitting on the air conditioning unit.
- Then led an education nonprofit helping Central Texas schools.
- Ran for the Texas House in his hometown of Round Rock at age 28, having never run before, in a Trump district in a county that had not voted for a Democrat for president since Jimmy Carter; party figures called the race "a lost cause". Flipped it with 51% of the vote.
- Now in his fourth term; says he has passed 60 bipartisan bills, many on education, as a Democrat without either chamber, the governor's mansion or any agency.

wikis.title: Mid-decade redistricting and the 2025 quorum break
wikis.summary: Talarico on the Texas mid-decade map, leaving the state to break quorum, and the federal voting-rights package he would push.
wikis.body:
- Calls the new Texas map "racist" for "systematically... diluting the voting power of black and brown Texans", so that "a white Texan has a lot more political power".
- Calls the past 12 months "the most aggressive attack on black political power since Jim Crow", citing Supreme Court cases and the Texas map.
- "A year ago yesterday" he and House colleagues broke quorum by leaving Texas for Illinois so the chamber could not take up the maps. The Texas Rangers were called to find and arrest them; they got bomb threats and death threats in Chicago.
- Says the tactic is not sustainable for a part-time legislature, but succeeded in making "the whole national media" cover the map, after which California, Virginia and other states moved to "cancel out the stolen seats in Texas".
- Explains mid-decade redistricting as unprecedented - lines are meant to be redrawn after a census - "like changing the rules after halftime"; says the plain word is "cheating".
- Asks: pass the John Lewis Voting Rights Act, and a national ban on gerrymandering in red and blue states; supports Kamala Harris's Urban League list (Electoral College, expanding the court to 13 justices, statehood for Puerto Rico and D.C.).

wikis.title: The Senate primary with Jasmine Crockett
wikis.summary: Talarico on his friendship with Jasmine Crockett, the online attacks during the primary and her endorsement the next morning.
wikis.body:
- Says they bonded in the Texas House as two of the only young members and "tended to be the troublemakers".
- Says the primary was painful "because of that friendship" and that primaries turn on tactics and personalities rather than policy differences.
- Says he posted a video the first day she entered the race, in December, to 50,000 volunteers and all campaign staff, calling her "my friend... a leader and she deserves our utmost respect", and repeated it as vitriol spread online.
- Two weeks before the interview, at a town hall where Keith Edwards and Rogue DNC came up, he told those attacking Crockett online to keep her name out of their mouths. Asked if he should have said it sooner: "it's possible I could have showed more leadership".
- Rejects the "not electable" line: asked point blank on The View, he said "absolutely" and that he would be behind her "1,000%" had she won.
- Says she endorsed him and the whole ticket the morning after the primary and has campaigned statewide since; he argues attacks on her hurt his own coalition and chances in November.

wikis.title: Texas THC ban
wikis.summary: Talarico on the newly effective Texas ban on THC products, which he blames on industry lobbying.
wikis.body:
- "THC products are virtually banned in the state of Texas. Now it's a felony to have Delta 8." He says the law "just went into effect" and that people are not aware it is happening.
- Contrasts the penalty with DUIs: "you have to have three DUIs to get a felony. And now just having Delta eight can get you that felony."
- Says he is for legalizing weed.
- Blames "big beer, big tobacco" for pushing the ban because readily available THC hurts their bottom line, and cites "a lot of research" that THC and cannabis products "are safer and less addictive than beer or tobacco".
- Says Texas legalized hemp "I think it was six years ago", creating a booming industry of local small businesses, and that the ban is "a gift to the drug cartels" because buyers will move to the black market where "they don't know what they're getting".
- Says young Texans and veterans use THC products for PTSD, and seniors use them too.

wikis.title: Platform for Black Texans
wikis.summary: Talarico's answers on maternal mortality, HBCU funding and Black-owned business capital.
wikis.body:
- Maternal mortality in Texas is "three times deadlier for black women"; Harris County, home to Houston, is "the deadliest place for a black woman to give birth in the entire country". The campaign has "a comprehensive plan to combat that crisis at the federal level".
- Credits Representative Toni Rose of Dallas with a state bill extending postpartum Medicaid coverage to one year.
- Federal proposals: universal paid family leave, better provider training, better data collection, and requiring insurance companies to cover doula and midwife services to end maternal care deserts.
- HBCUs: town hall at Prairie View A&M; commencement address at Paul Quinn College, "the oldest HBCU in Texas"; wants to close the funding gap between HBCUs and institutions with similar numbers of low-income students, naming Prairie View, Texas Southern and Paul Quinn.
- Business: says the HUB (historically underutilized businesses) program has been attacked and defunded in Texas; proposes federal entrepreneurial grants for young Black entrepreneurs who lack generational wealth and networks, citing public investment in Tesla and in the R&D behind the internet.
- Pressed by a host on spending with Black outlets, staff and vendors, he answers "Definitely" without figures.

wikis.title: Gaza, military aid and AIPAC
wikis.summary: Talarico says he would not vote to send weapons to the Netanyahu government and describes AIPAC's chilling effect on candidates.
wikis.body:
- Asked how he would vote on military aid to Israel: "I would not vote to send weapons to the Netanyahu government", with all aid "conditioned on ending the death and the destruction in Gaza and the West Bank".
- Asked why he says "death and destruction" rather than genocide: says "the legal term genocide is being litigated in the International Criminal Court", that "certainly there's evidence to bring those charges", that the U.S. "should abide by whatever ruling the court comes to", but that a senator's job is to act rather than "to litigate what terms are used".
- Says he would use "every bit of our nation's diplomatic and financial leverage to protect the lives of Palestinians"; calls October 7th horrific and grieves both Israeli and Palestinian lives.
- Quotes a theologian: "I screamed at God for the starving children until I realized the starving children was God screaming at me."
- Says he has stood with the Jewish community in Central Texas against anti-Semitism and with Muslim neighbours against Islamophobia, and that an article calling him anti-Semitic after he spoke on Gaza was "very painful".
- Says AIPAC "has not spent against me in this race", but that big-PAC money creates a chilling effect on what candidates will say - naming AIPAC and OpenAI - and calls money in politics "the rot at the core of our broken system".

wikis.title: Policing and justice reform
wikis.summary: Talarico on the Carmelo Anthony verdict, Javier Ambler's law banning reality-TV policing, and the George Floyd Act.
wikis.body:
- On the Carmelo Anthony case in Texas, which he called a tragedy: says he is "not an expert on this particular case" but that "there were no black members of the jury", which to him is "the only evidence you need" that the system is not working for Black Texans. Says he got backlash for saying it.
- Javier Ambler, his constituent, "unarmed black man who was killed by the Williamson County Sheriff's Department": pulled over for not dimming his brights, told officers he had a heart condition, "they tased him so many times he died right in front of them", filmed for the reality show Live PD.
- Working with Ambler's sister Kimberly, he went office by office and passed Javier Ambler's law, banning reality TV policing - no show like Live PD or Cops can contract with a Texas law enforcement agency.
- Reason given: research shows such shows increase policing and violent interactions because aggression makes better ratings.
- Says the George Floyd Act, with far more significant policing reforms, "didn't even get a hearing" that same session.

wikis.title: Faith, Christian nationalism and a purple Texas
wikis.summary: Talarico on separating church and state without separating faith from politics, and his argument that political competition improves policy.
wikis.body:
- Separation of church and state is in the First Amendment and he calls himself its "fiercest champion" in the legislature; says Democrats confused it with "a separation of faith and politics" about 50 years ago and ceded religion to the other side.
- "I'm a Christian, and I know that the most dangerous form of government is theocracy. The only thing worse than a tyrant is a tyrant who thinks they're on a mission from God."
- Says he fought Texas bills that would have forced every teacher to post the Ten Commandments and taught Christian Bible stories exclusively as absolute truth; is in seminary; his granddad was a Baptist preacher.
- Names the civil rights, farm workers and labor movements as faith-rooted, and Dr. King, Dolores Huerta, Mr. Rogers and Jimmy Carter as examples; says "no party has a monopoly on faith".
- Asked about white Christian nationalism, says love "is not shrinking from a fight" and cites Jesus flipping the tables in the temple, the story he began the campaign with.
- Competition: "the best color for Texas is purple". Cites 12 Democrats flipping Republican districts and Beto's 2.5-point margin, after which the 2019 session saw Republicans funding schools, expanding healthcare and dropping culture-war bills. Says safe seats reward extremism - his example is a Texas bill "to go after furries in schools" based on an untrue litter-box rumour.
- Angela Rye pushes back, citing Shelby v. Holder and Republican politics "mirroring fascism and authoritarianism"; he answers that extremism follows from a lack of competition, and says Ken Paxton "has spent his career waging war against black Texans" but is now talking about affordability and healthcare because he is behind in the polls.

wikis.title: Talarico on the church-state line, Matthew 25 and the campaign's closing call to volunteer
wikis.summary: Closing part of the Breakfast Club interview, in which James Talarico sets out where he draws the line on faith in public life, reads Matthew 25 against federal policy, and asks listeners to volunteer at jamestallarico.com.
wikis.body:
## Where he draws the line on faith in public life

- "I am never going to force my religion, my faith down the throats of my neighbors, my Muslim and Jewish and Hindu and Buddhist and atheist neighbors, because that's not love."
- "the schoolhouse, the courthouse, the state house is not the place to do that" - but he will talk about how his faith influences his views and motivates his public service, "because I can only show up as me".
- Says he tries to be sensitive to "the religious trauma that a lot of people have" from organized religion.
- A host says he would not object to religion in politics if politicians "actually lived like that", citing denying kids food or money for disenfranchised areas. Talarico agrees and adds that Christians should be honest about falling short, citing "do not judge" as a common commandment and humility as necessary to the work.

## Matthew 25

- Asks listeners and viewers, "even those who aren't religious", to read Matthew 25, "the parable of the sheep and the goats".
- Argues the story gathers "all of us as people and all of us as nations, as communities", answering those who say the commandments are only for individuals and not grounds to "guarantee healthcare".
- Paraphrases the judgment - "I was hungry and you didn't give me something to eat. I was sick, and you didn't heal me. I was a stranger, and you didn't welcome me" - and "what you did for the least of these is what you did for me".
- Applies it to the present: "what would Jesus say if he walked onto the floor of the U.S. Senate? I think he would say, I was hungry and you kicked me off food stamps. I was sick and you kicked me off Medicaid. I was a stranger and you deported me and my family."

## Closing call to action

- Directs listeners to the campaign website **jamestallarico.com** to sign up to volunteer; says the campaign needs door knockers, phone bankers and text messagers, and will train people who have never volunteered.
- "if you're doom scrolling, action is the best antidote to that despair", quoting an organizer friend: "you can't wring your hands when you're rolling up your sleeves."

## Last question

- Asked which political party would be most uncomfortable if Jesus came back today: "I think both political parties would be deeply uncomfortable. I think Jesus is far more radical than any political party."
- Says by radical he does not mean extreme - "The word radical comes from the Latin word for root" - and that Jesus "goes to the root of our problems and he calls us to a deeper love, a deeper justice, a deeper peace".
- The hosts close with "Breakfast Club, good morning."

wikis.title: The Terminal List Season 2: Everything We Know So Far (podcast episode)
wikis.summary: A 37-minute episode of The Bookshelf Chronicles previewing The Terminal List season 2 on Prime Video - its October 21, 2026 premiere, the True Believer plot, Chris Pratt's physical state, the cast, the global shoot and the show's themes.
wikis.body:
## The episode
- Podcast: The Bookshelf Chronicles, updated weekly; tagline "Open a book. Discover a world." Length 37 minutes, rating Clean. Published "August 19, 2026 at 5:15 PM UTC". The page notes "This episode includes AI-generated content."
- Episode description: a preview of the second season of the Prime Video series The Terminal List, "scheduled for release on October 21, 2026", adapting Jack Carr's novel True Believer and moving "from a personal revenge story into a high-stakes international espionage thriller", covering Chris Pratt's return and physical transformation, military authenticity across global filming locations, and how the 2025 prequel Dark Wolf bridged the gap.
- In the transcript the hosts say the recording date is "August nineteenth, twenty twenty six" and tell listeners to "circle Wednesday, October twenty one" - "roughly two months away from the premiere", a "full eight episode drop".

## Season 1 recap as given
- Season one followed Navy SEAL Lieutenant Commander James Reece, whose troop is wiped out on a mission in Syria and who returns home to find his wife and daughter murdered, then hunts a corrupt conspiracy, writing names on the back of his daughter's drawing.
- The hosts describe an unreliable narrator "suffering from severe PTSD and a suspected brain tumor" and say the season "racked up over a billion viewing minutes almost immediately".
- Season one dropped in July 2022; season two drops October 2026 - "a nearly five year gap".

## What the episode covers
- Why the gap and how the 2025 prequel The Terminal List: Dark Wolf worked as a bridge.
- The season 2 plot drawn from True Believer: Reece adrift and "the most wanted man on the planet", holiday-season terror attacks, and a forced bargain with the intelligence community.
- Chris Pratt's weight loss and his illness during the Africa shoot.
- The returning and new cast, the international production footprint, the veteran military advisors turned executive producers, and the season's themes of moral injury and "violent redemption".

wikis.title: The five-year gap and the Dark Wolf prequel
wikis.summary: Why season 2 took until 2026 and how the 2025 prequel The Terminal List: Dark Wolf set up the espionage world.
wikis.body:
- Season one dropped in July 2022, season two in October 2026 - "a nearly five year gap"; the hosts cite Chris Pratt's packed theatrical schedule plus "the labor strikes and the massive production halts that completely paralyzed Hollywood".
- They argue Amazon was not passive: in 2025 it released The Terminal List: Dark Wolf, giving Taylor Kitsch's character Ben Edwards - "Reese's former seal teammate who transitions into a CIA operative" - his own series.
- One host challenges the strategy as a risk of "evaporating momentum" and of being perceived as filler; the other argues it was "structural load bearing", zooming the camera out from season one's myopic view into the CIA's Ground Branch.
- Ground Branch explained in the episode: the CIA Special Activity Center has the Political Action Group (psychological warfare, election interference) and the Special Operations Group (SOG); Ground Branch is SOG's tactical paramilitary arm, recruiting "almost exclusively from Tier one military units like Seal Team six or Delta Force". SEALs act under Title 10 of the US Code (military action); Ground Branch operators act under Title 50 governing covert intelligence operations - "They do not exist on paper. They wear no uniforms. If they are caught, the US government will legitimately deny they exist."
- Dark Wolf is said to have introduced "the institutional forces, the bureaucratic realities, and the gray area morality of covert operations" that matter for True Believer.

wikis.title: Season 2 plot: adapting True Believer
wikis.summary: The season's premise - Reece adrift and hunted, holiday-season terror attacks and a forced alliance with the agencies that betrayed him.
wikis.body:
- Season two adapts Jack Carr's second novel, True Believer; showrunner David DiGilio is named alongside Carr as engineering "a massive pivot in genre".
- Reece begins "in a state of profound isolation", "the most wanted man on the planet, completely off the grid, drifting across the ocean", in contrast to season one's constant tactical noise.
- The catalyst is "a series of highly coordinated, massive terrorist attacks striking Western targets", timed to the holiday season to "maximize psychological shatter" and to "violently destabilize global financial markets", exploiting fourth-quarter retail and supply chain reliance.
- Intelligence agencies, "caught completely flat footed", conclude the only person able to penetrate the terror cell is the man at the top of their most wanted list, so they "strike a bargain with the devil they know".
- The hosts contrast Reece with James Bond - "Bond is a scalpel. Reese in season one was a broadsword" - and say the season forces him into shifting geopolitical loyalties, old allies with hidden agendas and new partners he has no reason to trust.
- The conspiracy is described as "a web tying Russian dark money to Western state secrets" that "ultimately ties back into James Reese's own family history"; the hosts state explicitly that they are analysing a fictional narrative framework and "are absolutely not taking a stance on real world foreign policy".

wikis.title: Chris Pratt's physical transformation and illness on set
wikis.summary: The gaunt first-look images of August 2026 and the E. coli and tick bite fever Pratt is said to have contracted during the Africa shoot.
wikis.body:
- "The first look images that dropped in mid August twenty twenty six" are called "genuinely alarming": Pratt "looks gaunt ... weathered, emaciated, and completely hollowed out", "not the standard hyper muscular star lord action hero physique".
- He initially lost weight intentionally to convey Reece's time lost at sea; then, "while filming in incredibly demanding remote environments in Africa, Pratt contracted a severe dual front illness ... simultaneously hit with E. Coli and tick bite fever".
- The hosts describe tick bite fever as a rickettsial infection attacking the endothelium of blood vessels, causing widespread vasculitis, spiking fever, severe muscle aches, joint pain and debilitating fatigue, while E. coli attacks the gastrointestinal tract, causing dehydration and electrolyte depletion.
- They say Pratt "did not halt production", because halting an international shoot of that scale "costs millions of dollars a day", and describe him as "operating with a core temperature of one hundred and three degrees".
- The result, they argue, is exhaustion on screen that "is not a performance", grounding the character in human frailty and mirroring the real physical toll on special operations veterans - deteriorating joints, chronic injuries, "endocrine system disruption".
- A "dramatic physical recovery is a central emotional beat of the season" - not a training montage but "a desperate, painful clawing back to baseline capability".

wikis.title: Returning cast and shifting dynamics
wikis.summary: Tom Hopper, Constance Wu, Dar Salim and Luke Hemsworth, and how season one changed their characters' relationships with Reece.
wikis.body:
- Tom Hopper returns as Raife Hastings, "this massive, imposing former seal" whose family wealth and connections were instrumental in Reece's crusade. Showrunner David DiGilio is quoted describing Raife in season two as "drifting outside the teams", which the hosts read as a profound loss of identity for an operator.
- Constance Wu returns as Katie Buranek, the investigative journalist; her reporting elevated her career but "she has suffered personally for her unwavering belief" in Reece, having aided a man the FBI was hunting and whom "in the eyes of the government" is a domestic terrorist - a bind as the agencies she exposed now court Reece.
- Dar Salim returns as Mohammed "Mo" Farooq, whom Reece trained; the sources are said to hint at "severely tense confrontations" and to mention "themes of loyalty and radicalization" around Mo, a character straddling Western military training and understanding of the regions where radical ideologies take root.
- Luke Hemsworth returns as Jules Landry, "the incredibly abrasive, crass CIA contractor"; the creative team is said to have made Hemsworth keep a real-life mullet he was sporting in Australia because "That is exactly what Landry would look like" - framed as authentic to the private military contractor world, outside conventional grooming standards.

wikis.title: Gabriel Luna as Freddie Strain and the new cast
wikis.summary: The new season's key addition, how he was cast, and the wider international roster.
wikis.body:
- Gabriel Luna joins as Freddie Strain, described as "a former Seal Team six senior chief who has made the jump to becoming a CIA ground Branch officer", tying back to the organisational world of Dark Wolf.
- Strain is "a fascinating dual figure": an elite, stone-cold professional sniper and "a deeply dedicated family man" with a wife and children. His "absolute, unwavering conviction that Reese survived the events of season one" is the catalyst that pulls Reece out of the shadows.
- Casting story: "there wasn't some grueling, month long audition process" - Pratt and Luna "bonded years ago at a Christmas party hosted by Arnold Schwarzenegger", and Pratt knew Luna had "the right frequency for the role".
- The expanded international cast named includes Costa Ronin, Martin Sensmeier and Olga Kurylenko, "a roster built to reflect a massive geopolitical scope".
- Thematically the hosts call Strain "a thematic mirror held up directly to James Reece" - "the living proof of what a highly functional lethal operator looks like when they actually have a loving family to go home to".

wikis.title: Global production footprint
wikis.summary: Where season 2 was shot and why the production chose real locations over digital environments.
wikis.body:
- Principal photography started in South Africa, "capturing the Hastings families world and executing some brutal action sequences".
- From there the production moved through Toronto - "the ultimate architectural chameleon, capable of doubling for dozens of major Western cities" - and shot in Washington, D.C. for "the authentic, imposing halls of intelligence power".
- Then "the massive pivot to North Africa and Europe": Morocco is heavily cited, with Marrakesh, Casablanca and Tangier standing in for locations across the Middle East and Eastern Europe, plus European shoots in Croatia and Hungary.
- The hosts stress the logistics - moving hundreds of crew, specialised camera and lighting equipment and "an entire armory of prop weapons across international borders" - as "genuinely analogous to orchestrating an actual military deployment".
- The argument for real locations is "the physics of authenticity": light bouncing off stone in the Medina in Marrakesh, real dust, real heat and ambient noise creating "a subconscious reality for the viewer that CGI simply cannot replicate".

wikis.title: Military authenticity and the veteran executive producers
wikis.summary: How former operators Jared Shaw and Max Adams shape the show from inside the production.
wikis.body:
- The episode emphasises "the continued elevated involvement of real special operations veterans in the production hierarchy".
- Named: Jared Shaw, "a former Navy seal who also portrays a character on screen", and Max Adams, "a former Army ranger".
- Crucially, both are executive producers rather than day-rate consultants, which the hosts say shifts their influence "from reactive to proactive": in the writers' room ensuring operational logic, in the editing bay "dictating the rhythm of a firefight", vetting tactical maneuvers, jargon, room-clearing technique and "the dark highly specific gallows humor and culture of the operator community".
- They call this "an absolute firewall against the show slipping into absurd Hollywood caricature action tropes".

wikis.title: Themes: moral injury and 'violent redemption'
wikis.summary: The episode's closing argument about what happens to Reece after the list is finished.
wikis.body:
- Central question: "what happens to a human being who allowed himself to be completely hollowed out and consumed by violence when the violence is supposedly finished."
- The hosts call this "a profound exploration of moral injury", "a theme deeply embedded in Carr's novels", examining "the psychological toll of state sponsored violence": Reece was "forged into a weapon by the United States government", turned that programming back on the institution that betrayed him, and is now asked by those same institutions to work for them.
- "The official promotional [material] has described season two as a journey of violent redemption finding a new purpose"; one host explicitly pushes back on the word redemption, asking whether a character who crossed that moral line can find purpose in a quiet life "or is the tragic reality that he is fundamentally irreversibly a weapon" - and whether, for a man conditioned by war, "peace is actually a form of psychological hell".
- Strain "represents the fragile hope that peace is possible"; Reece "represents the terrifying fear that the damage is permanent".
- On franchise momentum: Carr's extensive library of source novels, the proven Dark Wolf expansion and Pratt's dedication mean "This eight episode Drop in October is not just a second season of television. It is positioned as a foundational event that could solidify a sprawling, interconnected, long running, tactical universe."
- Closing question: "if an elite operator must constantly return to the very masters who broke him in order to save the world. Does true freedom for a soldier ever actually exist?"

## How the saros works, as the page explains it

- "The periodicity and recurrence of solar eclipses is governed by the Saros cycle, a period of approximately 6,585.3 days (18 years 11 days 8 hours)."
- Two eclipses separated by one saros share a very similar geometry: they occur at the same node with the Moon at nearly the same distance from Earth and at the same time of year.
- "Each series typically lasts 12 to 13 centuries and contains 70 or more eclipses."
- Every saros series begins with a number of partial eclipses near one of Earth's polar regions, then produces several dozen central eclipses before ending with a group of partial eclipses near the opposite pole.
- Nodes: the Moon's orbit is inclined about 5 degrees to Earth's orbit around the Sun; the Moon moves from south to north of Earth's orbit at the ascending node, and from north to south at the descending node.
- Central solar eclipses are those in which the central axis of the Moon's shadow strikes Earth's surface. All partial (penumbral) eclipses are non-central; umbral eclipses (total, annular and hybrid) may be central (usually) or non-central (rarely).
- Hybrid eclipses, also known as annular/total eclipses, are both total and annular along different sections of the umbral path.
- Greatest eclipse is "the instant when the axis of the Moon's shadow passes closest to Earth's center". For total eclipses it is nearly equal to the instants of greatest magnitude and greatest duration; for annular eclipses greatest duration may occur at greatest eclipse or near the sunrise and sunset points of the path.

## Calendar

- The Gregorian calendar is used for all dates from 1582 Oct 15 onwards; before that date the Julian calendar is used.
- The Julian calendar has no year 0, so 1 BCE is followed by 1 CE. Years in this catalog are numbered astronomically and include the year 0: "the astronomical year 0 corresponds to 1 BCE, and astronomical year -1 corresponds to 2 BCE".

## Predictions

- Solar coordinates are from the VSOP87 theory (Bretagnon and Francou, 1988); the Moon's coordinates from the ELP-2000/82 theory (Chapront-Touze and Chapront, 1983).
- The revised value used for the Moon's secular acceleration is n-dot = -25.858 arc-sec/cy*cy, "as deduced from the Apollo lunar laser ranging experiment (Chapront, Chapront-Touze, and Francou, 2002)".
- The largest uncertainty comes from fluctuations in Earth's rotation, mainly tidal friction of the Moon, expressed as DeltaT: pre-1950s from empirical fits to historical records (Morrison and Stephenson, 2004); 1955-present from published observations; future extrapolated from current values weighted by the long-term trend from tidal effects.
- Polynomial expressions simplify evaluating DeltaT for any time from -1999 to +3000.

## Sources and credit the page gives

- Based on data published in *Five Millennium Canon of Solar Eclipses: -1999 to +3000* and *Five Millennium Catalog of Solar Eclipses: -1999 to +3000*. Global maps in the links were extracted from full-page plates in the Canon by Dan McGlaun; Besselian elements provided by Jean Meeus. "Fred Espenak assumes full responsibility for the accuracy of all eclipse calculations."
- Reuse is permitted with the acknowledgment "Eclipse Predictions by Fred Espenak (NASA's GSFC)".
- The page ends with the date 2009 Sep 26.

## How the saros works, as the page explains it

- "The periodicity and recurrence of solar eclipses is governed by the Saros cycle, a period of approximately 6,585.3 days (18 years 11 days 8 hours)."
- Two eclipses separated by one saros share a very similar geometry: they occur at the same node with the Moon at nearly the same distance from Earth and at the same time of year.
- "Each series typically lasts 12 to 13 centuries and contains 70 or more eclipses."
- Every saros series begins with a number of partial eclipses near one of Earth's polar regions, then produces several dozen central eclipses before ending with a group of partial eclipses near the opposite pole.
- Nodes: the Moon's orbit is inclined about 5 degrees to Earth's orbit around the Sun; the Moon moves from south to north of Earth's orbit at the ascending node, and from north to south at the descending node.
- Central solar eclipses are those in which the central axis of the Moon's shadow strikes Earth's surface. All partial (penumbral) eclipses are non-central; umbral eclipses (total, annular and hybrid) may be central (usually) or non-central (rarely).
- Hybrid eclipses, also known as annular/total eclipses, are both total and annular along different sections of the umbral path.
- Greatest eclipse is "the instant when the axis of the Moon's shadow passes closest to Earth's center". For total eclipses it is nearly equal to the instants of greatest magnitude and greatest duration; for annular eclipses greatest duration may occur at greatest eclipse or near the sunrise and sunset points of the path.

## Calendar

- The Gregorian calendar is used for all dates from 1582 Oct 15 onwards; before that date the Julian calendar is used.
- The Julian calendar has no year 0, so 1 BCE is followed by 1 CE. Years in this catalog are numbered astronomically and include the year 0: "the astronomical year 0 corresponds to 1 BCE, and astronomical year -1 corresponds to 2 BCE".

## Predictions

- Solar coordinates are from the VSOP87 theory (Bretagnon and Francou, 1988); the Moon's coordinates from the ELP-2000/82 theory (Chapront-Touze and Chapront, 1983).
- The revised value used for the Moon's secular acceleration is n-dot = -25.858 arc-sec/cy*cy, "as deduced from the Apollo lunar laser ranging experiment (Chapront, Chapront-Touze, and Francou, 2002)".
- The largest uncertainty comes from fluctuations in Earth's rotation, mainly tidal friction of the Moon, expressed as DeltaT: pre-1950s from empirical fits to historical records (Morrison and Stephenson, 2004); 1955-present from published observations; future extrapolated from current values weighted by the long-term trend from tidal effects.
- Polynomial expressions simplify evaluating DeltaT for any time from -1999 to +3000.

## Sources and credit the page gives

- Based on data published in *Five Millennium Canon of Solar Eclipses: -1999 to +3000* and *Five Millennium Catalog of Solar Eclipses: -1999 to +3000*. Global maps in the links were extracted from full-page plates in the Canon by Dan McGlaun; Besselian elements provided by Jean Meeus. "Fred Espenak assumes full responsibility for the accuracy of all eclipse calculations."
- Reuse is permitted with the acknowledgment "Eclipse Predictions by Fred Espenak (NASA's GSFC)".
- The page ends with the date 2009 Sep 26.

## How the saros works, as the page explains it

- "The periodicity and recurrence of solar eclipses is governed by the Saros cycle, a period of approximately 6,585.3 days (18 years 11 days 8 hours)."
- Two eclipses separated by one saros share a very similar geometry: they occur at the same node with the Moon at nearly the same distance from Earth and at the same time of year.
- "Each series typically lasts 12 to 13 centuries and contains 70 or more eclipses."
- Every saros series begins with a number of partial eclipses near one of Earth's polar regions, then produces several dozen central eclipses before ending with a group of partial eclipses near the opposite pole.
- Nodes: the Moon's orbit is inclined about 5 degrees to Earth's orbit around the Sun; the Moon moves from south to north of Earth's orbit at the ascending node, and from north to south at the descending node.
- Central solar eclipses are those in which the central axis of the Moon's shadow strikes Earth's surface. All partial (penumbral) eclipses are non-central; umbral eclipses (total, annular and hybrid) may be central (usually) or non-central (rarely).
- Hybrid eclipses, also known as annular/total eclipses, are both total and annular along different sections of the umbral path.
- Greatest eclipse is "the instant when the axis of the Moon's shadow passes closest to Earth's center". For total eclipses it is nearly equal to the instants of greatest magnitude and greatest duration; for annular eclipses greatest duration may occur at greatest eclipse or near the sunrise and sunset points of the path.

## Calendar

- The Gregorian calendar is used for all dates from 1582 Oct 15 onwards; before that date the Julian calendar is used.
- The Julian calendar has no year 0, so 1 BCE is followed by 1 CE. Years in this catalog are numbered astronomically and include the year 0: "the astronomical year 0 corresponds to 1 BCE, and astronomical year -1 corresponds to 2 BCE".

## Predictions

- Solar coordinates are from the VSOP87 theory (Bretagnon and Francou, 1988); the Moon's coordinates from the ELP-2000/82 theory (Chapront-Touze and Chapront, 1983).
- The revised value used for the Moon's secular acceleration is n-dot = -25.858 arc-sec/cy*cy, "as deduced from the Apollo lunar laser ranging experiment (Chapront, Chapront-Touze, and Francou, 2002)".
- The largest uncertainty comes from fluctuations in Earth's rotation, mainly tidal friction of the Moon, expressed as DeltaT: pre-1950s from empirical fits to historical records (Morrison and Stephenson, 2004); 1955-present from published observations; future extrapolated from current values weighted by the long-term trend from tidal effects.
- Polynomial expressions simplify evaluating DeltaT for any time from -1999 to +3000.

## Sources and credit the page gives

- Based on data published in *Five Millennium Canon of Solar Eclipses: -1999 to +3000* and *Five Millennium Catalog of Solar Eclipses: -1999 to +3000*. Global maps in the links were extracted from full-page plates in the Canon by Dan McGlaun; Besselian elements provided by Jean Meeus. "Fred Espenak assumes full responsibility for the accuracy of all eclipse calculations."
- Reuse is permitted with the acknowledgment "Eclipse Predictions by Fred Espenak (NASA's GSFC)".
- The page ends with the date 2009 Sep 26.

wikis.body:
## What the page gives

- A NASA Goddard (eclipse.gsfc.nasa.gov) page by **Fred Espenak**: "The following table delineates the path of the Moon's umbral shadow during the Hybrid Solar Eclipse of 2031 Nov 14."
- "The geographic coordinates (WGS 84) of the northern and southern limits and the central line are listed at 120-second intervals. This provides adequate detail for making plots of the path on larger scale maps."
- Local circumstances on the central line in each row: "the ratio of the apparent diameters of the Moon to the Sun, the Sun's altitude and azimuth (degrees), the path width (kilometers) and the duration on the central line (minutes and seconds)."
- The global visibility of the eclipse is shown on an Orthographic Map; the path "is displayed in greater detail on an Google Map". The map features are described in the Key to Solar Eclipse Path Tables.

## Greatest eclipse and greatest duration

- Instant of Greatest Eclipse (GE): Time = 21:06:12.3 UT Lat = 00°38.0'S Long = 137°37.8'W; Sun Altitude = 72.1° Path Width = 38.3 km; Sun Azimuth = 188.7° Central Duration = 01m08.3s
- Instant of Greatest Duration (GD): Time = 21:10:26 UT Lat = 00°58'S Long = 136°27'W; Sun Altitude = 71.9° Path Width = 38.4 km; Sun Azimuth = 195.6° Central Duration = 01m08.4s

## Path table

- 103 timed rows at 120-second intervals, from 19:24 UT to 22:48 UT, plus an opening and a closing row labelled "Limits".

## Predictions and stated caveats

- "ΔT = 77.9 seconds".
- "Predictions for the Hybrid Solar Eclipse of 2031 Nov 14 were generated using the VSOP87/ELP2000-85 solar and lunar ephemerides and a value of ΔT = 77.9 seconds."
- "The eclipse predictions presented here DO NOT include the effects of mountains and valleys along the edge of the Moon. Such corrections for the lunar limb profile may shift the limits of the eclipse path north or south by ~1-3 kilometers, and change the eclipse duration by ~1-3 seconds."
- "More detailed predictions including the effects of the lunar limb profile are normally posted 12-18 months before each eclipse".

## How the saros works, as the page explains it

- "The periodicity and recurrence of solar eclipses is governed by the Saros cycle, a period of approximately 6,585.3 days (18 years 11 days 8 hours)."
- Two eclipses separated by one saros share a very similar geometry: they occur at the same node with the Moon at nearly the same distance from Earth and at the same time of year.
- "Each series typically lasts 12 to 13 centuries and contains 70 or more eclipses."
- Every saros series begins with a number of partial eclipses near one of Earth's polar regions, then produces several dozen central eclipses before ending with a group of partial eclipses near the opposite pole.
- Nodes: the Moon's orbit is inclined about 5 degrees to Earth's orbit around the Sun; the Moon moves from south to north of Earth's orbit at the ascending node, and from north to south at the descending node.
- Central solar eclipses are those in which the central axis of the Moon's shadow strikes Earth's surface. All partial (penumbral) eclipses are non-central; umbral eclipses (total, annular and hybrid) may be central (usually) or non-central (rarely).
- Hybrid eclipses, also known as annular/total eclipses, are both total and annular along different sections of the umbral path.
- Greatest eclipse is "the instant when the axis of the Moon's shadow passes closest to Earth's center". For total eclipses it is nearly equal to the instants of greatest magnitude and greatest duration; for annular eclipses greatest duration may occur at greatest eclipse or near the sunrise and sunset points of the path.

## Calendar

- The Gregorian calendar is used for all dates from 1582 Oct 15 onwards; before that date the Julian calendar is used.
- The Julian calendar has no year 0, so 1 BCE is followed by 1 CE. Years in this catalog are numbered astronomically and include the year 0: "the astronomical year 0 corresponds to 1 BCE, and astronomical year -1 corresponds to 2 BCE".

## Predictions

- Solar coordinates are from the VSOP87 theory (Bretagnon and Francou, 1988); the Moon's coordinates from the ELP-2000/82 theory (Chapront-Touze and Chapront, 1983).
- The revised value used for the Moon's secular acceleration is n-dot = -25.858 arc-sec/cy*cy, "as deduced from the Apollo lunar laser ranging experiment (Chapront, Chapront-Touze, and Francou, 2002)".
- The largest uncertainty comes from fluctuations in Earth's rotation, mainly tidal friction of the Moon, expressed as DeltaT: pre-1950s from empirical fits to historical records (Morrison and Stephenson, 2004); 1955-present from published observations; future extrapolated from current values weighted by the long-term trend from tidal effects.
- Polynomial expressions simplify evaluating DeltaT for any time from -1999 to +3000.

## Sources and credit the page gives

- Based on data published in *Five Millennium Canon of Solar Eclipses: -1999 to +3000* and *Five Millennium Catalog of Solar Eclipses: -1999 to +3000*. Global maps in the links were extracted from full-page plates in the Canon by Dan McGlaun; Besselian elements provided by Jean Meeus. "Fred Espenak assumes full responsibility for the accuracy of all eclipse calculations."
- Reuse is permitted with the acknowledgment "Eclipse Predictions by Fred Espenak (NASA's GSFC)".
- The page ends with the date 2009 Sep 26.

## How the saros works, as the page explains it

- "The periodicity and recurrence of solar eclipses is governed by the Saros cycle, a period of approximately 6,585.3 days (18 years 11 days 8 hours)."
- Two eclipses separated by one saros share a very similar geometry: they occur at the same node with the Moon at nearly the same distance from Earth and at the same time of year.
- "Each series typically lasts 12 to 13 centuries and contains 70 or more eclipses."
- Every saros series begins with a number of partial eclipses near one of Earth's polar regions, then produces several dozen central eclipses before ending with a group of partial eclipses near the opposite pole.
- Nodes: the Moon's orbit is inclined about 5 degrees to Earth's orbit around the Sun; the Moon moves from south to north of Earth's orbit at the ascending node, and from north to south at the descending node.
- Central solar eclipses are those in which the central axis of the Moon's shadow strikes Earth's surface. All partial (penumbral) eclipses are non-central; umbral eclipses (total, annular and hybrid) may be central (usually) or non-central (rarely).
- Hybrid eclipses, also known as annular/total eclipses, are both total and annular along different sections of the umbral path.
- Greatest eclipse is "the instant when the axis of the Moon's shadow passes closest to Earth's center". For total eclipses it is nearly equal to the instants of greatest magnitude and greatest duration; for annular eclipses greatest duration may occur at greatest eclipse or near the sunrise and sunset points of the path.

## Calendar

- The Gregorian calendar is used for all dates from 1582 Oct 15 onwards; before that date the Julian calendar is used.
- The Julian calendar has no year 0, so 1 BCE is followed by 1 CE. Years in this catalog are numbered astronomically and include the year 0: "the astronomical year 0 corresponds to 1 BCE, and astronomical year -1 corresponds to 2 BCE".

## Predictions

- Solar coordinates are from the VSOP87 theory (Bretagnon and Francou, 1988); the Moon's coordinates from the ELP-2000/82 theory (Chapront-Touze and Chapront, 1983).

wikis.body:
## What the page gives

- A NASA Goddard (eclipse.gsfc.nasa.gov) page by **Fred Espenak**: "The following table delineates the path of the Moon's umbral shadow during the Total Solar Eclipse of 2034 Mar 20."
- "The geographic coordinates (WGS 84) of the northern and southern limits and the central line are listed at 120-second intervals. This provides adequate detail for making plots of the path on larger scale maps."
- Local circumstances on the central line in each row: "the ratio of the apparent diameters of the Moon to the Sun, the Sun's altitude and azimuth (degrees), the path width (kilometers) and the duration on the central line (minutes and seconds)."
- The global visibility of the eclipse is shown on an Orthographic Map; the path "is displayed in greater detail on an Google Map". The map features are described in the Key to Solar Eclipse Path Tables.

## Greatest eclipse and greatest duration

- Instant of Greatest Eclipse (GE): Time = 10:17:25.4 UT Lat = 16°03.6'N Long = 022°14.0'E; Sun Altitude = 73.1° Path Width = 159.1 km; Sun Azimuth = 161.6° Central Duration = 04m09.3s
- Instant of Greatest Duration (GD): Time = 10:18:22 UT Lat = 16°14'N Long = 022°31'E; Sun Altitude = 73.1° Path Width = 159.0 km; Sun Azimuth = 163.5° Central Duration = 04m09.3s

## Path table

- 100 timed rows at 120-second intervals, from 08:38 UT to 11:56 UT, plus an opening and a closing row labelled "Limits".

## Predictions and stated caveats

- "ΔT = 79.5 seconds".
- "Predictions for the Total Solar Eclipse of 2034 Mar 20 were generated using the VSOP87/ELP2000-85 solar and lunar ephemerides and a value of ΔT = 79.5 seconds."
- "The eclipse predictions presented here DO NOT include the effects of mountains and valleys along the edge of the Moon. Such corrections for the lunar limb profile may shift the limits of the eclipse path north or south by ~1-3 kilometers, and change the eclipse duration by ~1-3 seconds."
- "More detailed predictions including the effects of the lunar limb profile are normally posted 12-18 months before each eclipse".

## Acknowledgments

- "All eclipse calculations are by Fred Espenak, and he assumes full responsibility for their accuracy."
- Reproduction is freely permitted with the acknowledgment: "Eclipse Predictions by Fred Espenak, NASA's GSFC".

## How the saros works, as the page explains it

- "The periodicity and recurrence of solar eclipses is governed by the Saros cycle, a period of approximately 6,585.3 days (18 years 11 days 8 hours)."
- Two eclipses separated by one saros share a very similar geometry: they occur at the same node with the Moon at nearly the same distance from Earth and at the same time of year.
- "Each series typically lasts 12 to 13 centuries and contains 70 or more eclipses."
- Every saros series begins with a number of partial eclipses near one of Earth's polar regions, then produces several dozen central eclipses before ending with a group of partial eclipses near the opposite pole.
- Nodes: the Moon's orbit is inclined about 5 degrees to Earth's orbit around the Sun; the Moon moves from south to north of Earth's orbit at the ascending node, and from north to south at the descending node.
- Central solar eclipses are those in which the central axis of the Moon's shadow strikes Earth's surface. All partial (penumbral) eclipses are non-central; umbral eclipses (total, annular and hybrid) may be central (usually) or non-central (rarely).
- Hybrid eclipses, also known as annular/total eclipses, are both total and annular along different sections of the umbral path.
- Greatest eclipse is "the instant when the axis of the Moon's shadow passes closest to Earth's center". For total eclipses it is nearly equal to the instants of greatest magnitude and greatest duration; for annular eclipses greatest duration may occur at greatest eclipse or near the sunrise and sunset points of the path.

## Calendar

- The Gregorian calendar is used for all dates from 1582 Oct 15 onwards; before that date the Julian calendar is used.
- The Julian calendar has no year 0, so 1 BCE is followed by 1 CE. Years in this catalog are numbered astronomically and include the year 0: "the astronomical year 0 corresponds to 1 BCE, and astronomical year -1 corresponds to 2 BCE".

## Predictions

- Solar coordinates are from the VSOP87 theory (Bretagnon and Francou, 1988); the Moon's coordinates from the ELP-2000/82 theory (Chapront-Touze and Chapront, 1983).
- The revised value used for the Moon's secular acceleration is n-dot = -25.858 arc-sec/cy*cy, "as deduced from the Apollo lunar laser ranging experiment (Chapront, Chapront-Touze, and Francou, 2002)".
- The largest uncertainty comes from fluctuations in Earth's rotation, mainly tidal friction of the Moon, expressed as DeltaT: pre-1950s from empirical fits to historical records (Morrison and Stephenson, 2004); 1955-present from published observations; future extrapolated from current values weighted by the long-term trend from tidal effects.
- Polynomial expressions simplify evaluating DeltaT for any time from -1999 to +3000.

## Sources and credit the page gives

- Based on data published in *Five Millennium Canon of Solar Eclipses: -1999 to +3000* and *Five Millennium Catalog of Solar Eclipses: -1999 to +3000*. Global maps in the links were extracted from full-page plates in the Canon by Dan McGlaun; Besselian elements provided by Jean Meeus. "Fred Espenak assumes full responsibility for the accuracy of all eclipse calculations."
- Reuse is permitted with the acknowledgment "Eclipse Predictions by Fred Espenak (NASA's GSFC)".
- The page ends with the date 2009 Sep 26.

wikis.body:
## What the page gives

- A NASA Goddard (eclipse.gsfc.nasa.gov) page by **Fred Espenak**: "The following table delineates the path of the Moon's antumbral shadow during the Annular Solar Eclipse of 2034 Sep 12."
- "The geographic coordinates (WGS 84) of the northern and southern limits and the central line are listed at 120-second intervals. This provides adequate detail for making plots of the path on larger scale maps."
- Local circumstances on the central line in each row: "the ratio of the apparent diameters of the Moon to the Sun, the Sun's altitude and azimuth (degrees), the path width (kilometers) and the duration on the central line (minutes and seconds)."
- The global visibility of the eclipse is shown on an Orthographic Map; the path "is displayed in greater detail on an Google Map". The map features are described in the Key to Solar Eclipse Path Tables.

## Greatest eclipse and greatest duration

- Instant of Greatest Eclipse (GE): Time = 16:18:07.5 UT Lat = 18°14.5'S Long = 072°36.4'W; Sun Altitude = 66.7° Path Width = 102.1 km; Sun Azimuth = 18.2° Central Duration = 02m57.7s
- Instant of Greatest Duration (GD): Time = 16:29:24 UT Lat = 20°04'S Long = 069°44'W; Sun Altitude = 65.9° Path Width = 101.7 km; Sun Azimuth = 3.5° Central Duration = 02m57.8s

## Path table

- 105 timed rows at 120-second intervals, from 14:34 UT to 18:02 UT, plus an opening and a closing row labelled "Limits".
- Verbatim extremes and end rows (columns: Universal Time, northern limit lat/long, southern limit lat/long, central line lat/long, diameter ratio, Sun altitude, Sun azimuth, path width km, central-line duration):

## Predictions and stated caveats

- "ΔT = 79.9 seconds".
- "Predictions for the Annular Solar Eclipse of 2034 Sep 12 were generated using the VSOP87/ELP2000-85 solar and lunar ephemerides and a value of ΔT = 79.9 seconds."
- "The eclipse predictions presented here DO NOT include the effects of mountains and valleys along the edge of the Moon. Such corrections for the lunar limb profile may shift the limits of the eclipse path north or south by ~1-3 kilometers, and change the eclipse duration by ~1-3 seconds."
- "More detailed predictions including the effects of the lunar limb profile are normally posted 12-18 months before each eclipse".

## Acknowledgments

- "All eclipse calculations are by Fred Espenak, and he assumes full responsibility for their accuracy."
- Reproduction is freely permitted with the acknowledgment: "Eclipse Predictions by Fred Espenak, NASA's GSFC".

- Orthographic Map, Google Map, Animated Map, Path Table, Besselian Elements Table, Saros 135 Table.

## Page date

- The page carries no labelled publication or revision date; it ends with the bare date "2014 Feb 26".

- Two eclipses separated by one saros share a very similar geometry: they occur at the same node with the Moon at nearly the same distance from Earth and at the same time of year.
- "Each series typically lasts 12 to 13 centuries and contains 70 or more eclipses."
- Every saros series begins with a number of partial eclipses near one of Earth's polar regions, then produces several dozen central eclipses before ending with a group of partial eclipses near the opposite pole.
- Nodes: the Moon's orbit is inclined about 5 degrees to Earth's orbit around the Sun; the Moon moves from south to north of Earth's orbit at the ascending node, and from north to south at the descending node.
- Central solar eclipses are those in which the central axis of the Moon's shadow strikes Earth's surface. All partial (penumbral) eclipses are non-central; umbral eclipses (total, annular and hybrid) may be central (usually) or non-central (rarely).
- Hybrid eclipses, also known as annular/total eclipses, are both total and annular along different sections of the umbral path.
- Greatest eclipse is "the instant when the axis of the Moon's shadow passes closest to Earth's center". For total eclipses it is nearly equal to the instants of greatest magnitude and greatest duration; for annular eclipses greatest duration may occur at greatest eclipse or near the sunrise and sunset points of the path.

## Calendar

- The Gregorian calendar is used for all dates from 1582 Oct 15 onwards; before that date the Julian calendar is used.
- The Julian calendar has no year 0, so 1 BCE is followed by 1 CE. Years in this catalog are numbered astronomically and include the year 0: "the astronomical year 0 corresponds to 1 BCE, and astronomical year -1 corresponds to 2 BCE".

- Solar coordinates are from the VSOP87 theory (Bretagnon and Francou, 1988); the Moon's coordinates from the ELP-2000/82 theory (Chapront-Touze and Chapront, 1983).
- The revised value used for the Moon's secular acceleration is n-dot = -25.858 arc-sec/cy*cy, "as deduced from the Apollo lunar laser ranging experiment (Chapront, Chapront-Touze, and Francou, 2002)".

- Polynomial expressions simplify evaluating DeltaT for any time from -1999 to +3000.
