## How the saros works, as the page explains it

- "The periodicity and recurrence of solar eclipses is governed by the Saros cycle, a period of approximately 6,585.3 days (18 years 11 days 8 hours)."
- Two eclipses separated by one saros share a very similar geometry: they occur at the same node with the Moon at nearly the same distance from Earth and at the same time of year.
- "Each series typically lasts 12 to 13 centuries and contains 70 or more eclipses."
- Every saros series begins with a number of partial eclipses near one of Earth's polar regions, then produces several dozen central eclipses before ending with a group of partial eclipses near the opposite pole.
- Nodes: the Moon's orbit is inclined about 5 degrees to Earth's orbit around the Sun; the Moon moves from south to north of Earth's orbit at the ascending node, and from north to south at the descending node.
- Central solar eclipses are those in which the central axis of the Moon's shadow strikes Earth's surface. All partial (penumbral) eclipses are non-central; umbral eclipses (total, annular and hybrid) may be central (usually) or non-central (rarely).
- Hybrid eclipses, also known as annular/total eclipses, are both total and annular along different sections of the umbral path.
- Greatest eclipse is "the instant when the axis of the Moon's shadow passes closest to Earth's center". For total eclipses it is nearly equal to the instants of greatest magnitude and greatest duration; for annular eclipses greatest duration may occur at greatest eclipse or near the sunrise and sunset points of the path.

## Calendar

- The Gregorian calendar is used for all dates from 1582 Oct 15 onwards; before that date the Julian calendar is used.
- The Julian calendar has no year 0, so 1 BCE is followed by 1 CE. Years in this catalog are numbered astronomically and include the year 0: "the astronomical year 0 corresponds to 1 BCE, and astronomical year -1 corresponds to 2 BCE".

## Predictions

- Solar coordinates are from the VSOP87 theory (Bretagnon and Francou, 1988); the Moon's coordinates from the ELP-2000/82 theory (Chapront-Touze and Chapront, 1983).
- The revised value used for the Moon's secular acceleration is n-dot = -25.858 arc-sec/cy*cy, "as deduced from the Apollo lunar laser ranging experiment (Chapront, Chapront-Touze, and Francou, 2002)".
- The largest uncertainty comes from fluctuations in Earth's rotation, mainly tidal friction of the Moon, expressed as DeltaT: pre-1950s from empirical fits to historical records (Morrison and Stephenson, 2004); 1955-present from published observations; future extrapolated from current values weighted by the long-term trend from tidal effects.
- Polynomial expressions simplify evaluating DeltaT for any time from -1999 to +3000.

## Sources and credit the page gives

- Based on data published in *Five Millennium Canon of Solar Eclipses: -1999 to +3000* and *Five Millennium Catalog of Solar Eclipses: -1999 to +3000*. Global maps in the links were extracted from full-page plates in the Canon by Dan McGlaun; Besselian elements provided by Jean Meeus. "Fred Espenak assumes full responsibility for the accuracy of all eclipse calculations."
- Reuse is permitted with the acknowledgment "Eclipse Predictions by Fred Espenak (NASA's GSFC)".
- The page ends with the date 2009 Sep 26.

## What the page gives

- A NASA Goddard (eclipse.gsfc.nasa.gov) page by **Fred Espenak**: "The following table delineates the path of the Moon's antumbral shadow during the Annular Solar Eclipse of 2038 Jan 05."
- "The geographic coordinates (WGS 84) of the northern and southern limits and the central line are listed at 120-second intervals. This provides adequate detail for making plots of the path on larger scale maps."
- Local circumstances on the central line in each row: "the ratio of the apparent diameters of the Moon to the Sun, the Sun's altitude and azimuth (degrees), the path width (kilometers) and the duration on the central line (minutes and seconds)."
- The global visibility of the eclipse is shown on an Orthographic Map; the path "is displayed in greater detail on an Google Map". The map features are described in the Key to Solar Eclipse Path Tables.

## Greatest eclipse and greatest duration

- Instant of Greatest Eclipse (GE): Time = 13:45:47.9 UT Lat = 02°05.7'N Long = 025°26.7'W; Sun Altitude = 65.3° Path Width = 107.2 km; Sun Azimuth = 179.2° Central Duration = 03m18.5s
- Instant of Greatest Duration (GD): Time = 13:52:31 UT Lat = 02°11'N Long = 023°40'W; Sun Altitude = 65.1° Path Width = 107.4 km; Sun Azimuth = 186.8° Central Duration = 03m18.6s

## Predictions and stated caveats

- "ΔT = 82.3 seconds".
- "Predictions for the Annular Solar Eclipse of 2038 Jan 05 were generated using the VSOP87/ELP2000-85 solar and lunar ephemerides and a value of ΔT = 82.3 seconds."
- "The eclipse predictions presented here DO NOT include the effects of mountains and valleys along the edge of the Moon. Such corrections for the lunar limb profile may shift the limits of the eclipse path north or south by ~1-3 kilometers, and change the eclipse duration by ~1-3 seconds."
- "More detailed predictions including the effects of the lunar limb profile are normally posted 12-18 months before each eclipse".

## Acknowledgments

- "All eclipse calculations are by Fred Espenak, and he assumes full responsibility for their accuracy."
- Reproduction is freely permitted with the acknowledgment: "Eclipse Predictions by Fred Espenak, NASA's GSFC".

## How the saros works, as the page explains it

- "The periodicity and recurrence of solar eclipses is governed by the Saros cycle, a period of approximately 6,585.3 days (18 years 11 days 8 hours)."
- Two eclipses separated by one saros share a very similar geometry: they occur at the same node with the Moon at nearly the same distance from Earth and at the same time of year.
- "Each series typically lasts 12 to 13 centuries and contains 70 or more eclipses."
- Every saros series begins with a number of partial eclipses near one of Earth's polar regions, then produces several dozen central eclipses before ending with a group of partial eclipses near the opposite pole.
- Nodes: the Moon's orbit is inclined about 5 degrees to Earth's orbit around the Sun; the Moon moves from south to north of Earth's orbit at the ascending node, and from north to south at the descending node.
- Central solar eclipses are those in which the central axis of the Moon's shadow strikes Earth's surface. All partial (penumbral) eclipses are non-central; umbral eclipses (total, annular and hybrid) may be central (usually) or non-central (rarely).
- Hybrid eclipses, also known as annular/total eclipses, are both total and annular along different sections of the umbral path.
- Greatest eclipse is "the instant when the axis of the Moon's shadow passes closest to Earth's center". For total eclipses it is nearly equal to the instants of greatest magnitude and greatest duration; for annular eclipses greatest duration may occur at greatest eclipse or near the sunrise and sunset points of the path.

## Calendar

- The Gregorian calendar is used for all dates from 1582 Oct 15 onwards; before that date the Julian calendar is used.
- The Julian calendar has no year 0, so 1 BCE is followed by 1 CE. Years in this catalog are numbered astronomically and include the year 0: "the astronomical year 0 corresponds to 1 BCE, and astronomical year -1 corresponds to 2 BCE".

## Predictions

- Solar coordinates are from the VSOP87 theory (Bretagnon and Francou, 1988); the Moon's coordinates from the ELP-2000/82 theory (Chapront-Touze and Chapront, 1983).
- The revised value used for the Moon's secular acceleration is n-dot = -25.858 arc-sec/cy*cy, "as deduced from the Apollo lunar laser ranging experiment (Chapront, Chapront-Touze, and Francou, 2002)".
- The largest uncertainty comes from fluctuations in Earth's rotation, mainly tidal friction of the Moon, expressed as DeltaT: pre-1950s from empirical fits to historical records (Morrison and Stephenson, 2004); 1955-present from published observations; future extrapolated from current values weighted by the long-term trend from tidal effects.
- Polynomial expressions simplify evaluating DeltaT for any time from -1999 to +3000.

## Sources and credit the page gives

- Based on data published in *Five Millennium Canon of Solar Eclipses: -1999 to +3000* and *Five Millennium Catalog of Solar Eclipses: -1999 to +3000*. Global maps in the links were extracted from full-page plates in the Canon by Dan McGlaun; Besselian elements provided by Jean Meeus. "Fred Espenak assumes full responsibility for the accuracy of all eclipse calculations."
- Reuse is permitted with the acknowledgment "Eclipse Predictions by Fred Espenak (NASA's GSFC)".
- The page ends with the date 2009 Sep 26.

- Solar eclipses of Saros 142 all occur at the Moons descending node and the Moon moves northward with each eclipse. ## How the saros works, as the page explains it

- "The periodicity and recurrence of solar eclipses is governed by the Saros cycle, a period of approximately 6,585.3 days (18 years 11 days 8 hours)."
- Two eclipses separated by one saros share a very similar geometry: they occur at the same node with the Moon at nearly the same distance from Earth and at the same time of year.
- "Each series typically lasts 12 to 13 centuries and contains 70 or more eclipses."
- Every saros series begins with a number of partial eclipses near one of Earth's polar regions, then produces several dozen central eclipses before ending with a group of partial eclipses near the opposite pole.
- Nodes: the Moon's orbit is inclined about 5 degrees to Earth's orbit around the Sun; the Moon moves from south to north of Earth's orbit at the ascending node, and from north to south at the descending node.
- Central solar eclipses are those in which the central axis of the Moon's shadow strikes Earth's surface. All partial (penumbral) eclipses are non-central; umbral eclipses (total, annular and hybrid) may be central (usually) or non-central (rarely).
- Hybrid eclipses, also known as annular/total eclipses, are both total and annular along different sections of the umbral path.
- Greatest eclipse is "the instant when the axis of the Moon's shadow passes closest to Earth's center". For total eclipses it is nearly equal to the instants of greatest magnitude and greatest duration; for annular eclipses greatest duration may occur at greatest eclipse or near the sunrise and sunset points of the path.

## Calendar

- The Gregorian calendar is used for all dates from 1582 Oct 15 onwards; before that date the Julian calendar is used.
- The Julian calendar has no year 0, so 1 BCE is followed by 1 CE. Years in this catalog are numbered astronomically and include the year 0: "the astronomical year 0 corresponds to 1 BCE, and astronomical year -1 corresponds to 2 BCE".

## Predictions

- Solar coordinates are from the VSOP87 theory (Bretagnon and Francou, 1988); the Moon's coordinates from the ELP-2000/82 theory (Chapront-Touze and Chapront, 1983).
- The revised value used for the Moon's secular acceleration is n-dot = -25.858 arc-sec/cy*cy, "as deduced from the Apollo lunar laser ranging experiment (Chapront, Chapront-Touze, and Francou, 2002)".
- The largest uncertainty comes from fluctuations in Earth's rotation, mainly tidal friction of the Moon, expressed as DeltaT: pre-1950s from empirical fits to historical records (Morrison and Stephenson, 2004); 1955-present from published observations; future extrapolated from current values weighted by the long-term trend from tidal effects.
- Polynomial expressions simplify evaluating DeltaT for any time from -1999 to +3000.

## Sources and credit the page gives

- Based on data published in *Five Millennium Canon of Solar Eclipses: -1999 to +3000* and *Five Millennium Catalog of Solar Eclipses: -1999 to +3000*. Global maps in the links were extracted from full-page plates in the Canon by Dan McGlaun; Besselian elements provided by Jean Meeus. "Fred Espenak assumes full responsibility for the accuracy of all eclipse calculations."
- Reuse is permitted with the acknowledgment "Eclipse Predictions by Fred Espenak (NASA's GSFC)".
- The page ends with the date 2009 Sep 26.

## How the saros works, as the page explains it

- "The periodicity and recurrence of solar eclipses is governed by the Saros cycle, a period of approximately 6,585.3 days (18 years 11 days 8 hours)."
- Two eclipses separated by one saros share a very similar geometry: they occur at the same node with the Moon at nearly the same distance from Earth and at the same time of year.
- "Each series typically lasts 12 to 13 centuries and contains 70 or more eclipses."
- Every saros series begins with a number of partial eclipses near one of Earth's polar regions, then produces several dozen central eclipses before ending with a group of partial eclipses near the opposite pole.
- Nodes: the Moon's orbit is inclined about 5 degrees to Earth's orbit around the Sun; the Moon moves from south to north of Earth's orbit at the ascending node, and from north to south at the descending node.

- The Gregorian calendar is used for all dates from 1582 Oct 15 onwards; before that date the Julian calendar is used.

wikis.body:
## What the page gives

- A NASA Goddard (eclipse.gsfc.nasa.gov) page by **Fred Espenak**: "The following table delineates the path of the Moon's umbral shadow during the Total Solar Eclipse of 2041 Apr 30."
- "The geographic coordinates (WGS 84) of the northern and southern limits and the central line are listed at 120-second intervals. This provides adequate detail for making plots of the path on larger scale maps."
- Local circumstances on the central line in each row: "the ratio of the apparent diameters of the Moon to the Sun, the Sun's altitude and azimuth (degrees), the path width (kilometers) and the duration on the central line (minutes and seconds)."
- The global visibility of the eclipse is shown on an Orthographic Map; the path "is displayed in greater detail on an Google Map". The map features are described in the Key to Solar Eclipse Path Tables.

## Greatest eclipse and greatest duration

- Instant of Greatest Eclipse (GE): Time = 11:50:55.3 UT Lat = 09°37.3'S Long = 012°11.3'E; Sun Altitude = 63.2° Path Width = 71.7 km; Sun Azimuth = 336.7° Central Duration = 01m50.6s
- Instant of Greatest Duration (GD): Time = 11:52:03 UT Lat = 09°23'S Long = 012°28'E; Sun Altitude = 63.2° Path Width = 71.7 km; Sun Azimuth = 335.4° Central Duration = 01m50.6s

- 96 timed rows at 120-second intervals, from 10:16 UT to 13:26 UT, plus an opening and a closing row labelled "Limits".

## How the saros works, as the page explains it

- "The periodicity and recurrence of solar eclipses is governed by the Saros cycle, a period of approximately 6,585.3 days (18 years 11 days 8 hours)."
- Two eclipses separated by one saros share a very similar geometry: they occur at the same node with the Moon at nearly the same distance from Earth and at the same time of year.
- "Each series typically lasts 12 to 13 centuries and contains 70 or more eclipses."
- Every saros series begins with a number of partial eclipses near one of Earth's polar regions, then produces several dozen central eclipses before ending with a group of partial eclipses near the opposite pole.
- Nodes: the Moon's orbit is inclined about 5 degrees to Earth's orbit around the Sun; the Moon moves from south to north of Earth's orbit at the ascending node, and from north to south at the descending node.
- Central solar eclipses are those in which the central axis of the Moon's shadow strikes Earth's surface. All partial (penumbral) eclipses are non-central; umbral eclipses (total, annular and hybrid) may be central (usually) or non-central (rarely).
- Hybrid eclipses, also known as annular/total eclipses, are both total and annular along different sections of the umbral path.
- Greatest eclipse is "the instant when the axis of the Moon's shadow passes closest to Earth's center". For total eclipses it is nearly equal to the instants of greatest magnitude and greatest duration; for annular eclipses greatest duration may occur at greatest eclipse or near the sunrise and sunset points of the path.

## Calendar

- The Gregorian calendar is used for all dates from 1582 Oct 15 onwards; before that date the Julian calendar is used.
- The Julian calendar has no year 0, so 1 BCE is followed by 1 CE. Years in this catalog are numbered astronomically and include the year 0: "the astronomical year 0 corresponds to 1 BCE, and astronomical year -1 corresponds to 2 BCE".

## Predictions

- Solar coordinates are from the VSOP87 theory (Bretagnon and Francou, 1988); the Moon's coordinates from the ELP-2000/82 theory (Chapront-Touze and Chapront, 1983).
- The revised value used for the Moon's secular acceleration is n-dot = -25.858 arc-sec/cy*cy, "as deduced from the Apollo lunar laser ranging experiment (Chapront, Chapront-Touze, and Francou, 2002)".
- The largest uncertainty comes from fluctuations in Earth's rotation, mainly tidal friction of the Moon, expressed as DeltaT: pre-1950s from empirical fits to historical records (Morrison and Stephenson, 2004); 1955-present from published observations; future extrapolated from current values weighted by the long-term trend from tidal effects.
- Polynomial expressions simplify evaluating DeltaT for any time from -1999 to +3000.

## Sources and credit the page gives

- Based on data published in *Five Millennium Canon of Solar Eclipses: -1999 to +3000* and *Five Millennium Catalog of Solar Eclipses: -1999 to +3000*. Global maps in the links were extracted from full-page plates in the Canon by Dan McGlaun; Besselian elements provided by Jean Meeus. "Fred Espenak assumes full responsibility for the accuracy of all eclipse calculations."
- Reuse is permitted with the acknowledgment "Eclipse Predictions by Fred Espenak (NASA's GSFC)".
- The page ends with the date 2009 Sep 26.

## What the page gives

- A NASA Goddard (eclipse.gsfc.nasa.gov) page by **Fred Espenak**: "The following table delineates the path of the Moon's umbral shadow during the Total Solar Eclipse of 2042 Apr 20."
- "The geographic coordinates (WGS 84) of the northern and southern limits and the central line are listed at 120-second intervals. This provides adequate detail for making plots of the path on larger scale maps."
- Local circumstances on the central line in each row: "the ratio of the apparent diameters of the Moon to the Sun, the Sun's altitude and azimuth (degrees), the path width (kilometers) and the duration on the central line (minutes and seconds)."
- The global visibility of the eclipse is shown on an Orthographic Map; the path "is displayed in greater detail on an Google Map". The map features are described in the Key to Solar Eclipse Path Tables.

- "More detailed predictions including the effects of the lunar limb profile are normally posted 12-18 months before each eclipse".

## How the saros works, as the page explains it

- "The periodicity and recurrence of solar eclipses is governed by the Saros cycle, a period of approximately 6,585.3 days (18 years 11 days 8 hours)."
- Two eclipses separated by one saros share a very similar geometry: they occur at the same node with the Moon at nearly the same distance from Earth and at the same time of year.
- "Each series typically lasts 12 to 13 centuries and contains 70 or more eclipses."
- Every saros series begins with a number of partial eclipses near one of Earth's polar regions, then produces several dozen central eclipses before ending with a group of partial eclipses near the opposite pole.
- Nodes: the Moon's orbit is inclined about 5 degrees to Earth's orbit around the Sun; the Moon moves from south to north of Earth's orbit at the ascending node, and from north to south at the descending node.
- Central solar eclipses are those in which the central axis of the Moon's shadow strikes Earth's surface. All partial (penumbral) eclipses are non-central; umbral eclipses (total, annular and hybrid) may be central (usually) or non-central (rarely).
- Hybrid eclipses, also known as annular/total eclipses, are both total and annular along different sections of the umbral path.
- Greatest eclipse is "the instant when the axis of the Moon's shadow passes closest to Earth's center". For total eclipses it is nearly equal to the instants of greatest magnitude and greatest duration; for annular eclipses greatest duration may occur at greatest eclipse or near the sunrise and sunset points of the path.

## Calendar

- The Gregorian calendar is used for all dates from 1582 Oct 15 onwards; before that date the Julian calendar is used.
- The Julian calendar has no year 0, so 1 BCE is followed by 1 CE. Years in this catalog are numbered astronomically and include the year 0: "the astronomical year 0 corresponds to 1 BCE, and astronomical year -1 corresponds to 2 BCE".

## Predictions

- Solar coordinates are from the VSOP87 theory (Bretagnon and Francou, 1988); the Moon's coordinates from the ELP-2000/82 theory (Chapront-Touze and Chapront, 1983).
- The revised value used for the Moon's secular acceleration is n-dot = -25.858 arc-sec/cy*cy, "as deduced from the Apollo lunar laser ranging experiment (Chapront, Chapront-Touze, and Francou, 2002)".
- The largest uncertainty comes from fluctuations in Earth's rotation, mainly tidal friction of the Moon, expressed as DeltaT: pre-1950s from empirical fits to historical records (Morrison and Stephenson, 2004); 1955-present from published observations; future extrapolated from current values weighted by the long-term trend from tidal effects.
- Polynomial expressions simplify evaluating DeltaT for any time from -1999 to +3000.

## Sources and credit the page gives

- Based on data published in *Five Millennium Canon of Solar Eclipses: -1999 to +3000* and *Five Millennium Catalog of Solar Eclipses: -1999 to +3000*. Global maps in the links were extracted from full-page plates in the Canon by Dan McGlaun; Besselian elements provided by Jean Meeus. ## How the saros works, as the page explains it

- "The periodicity and recurrence of solar eclipses is governed by the Saros cycle, a period of approximately 6,585.3 days (18 years 11 days 8 hours)."
- Two eclipses separated by one saros share a very similar geometry: they occur at the same node with the Moon at nearly the same distance from Earth and at the same time of year.
- "Each series typically lasts 12 to 13 centuries and contains 70 or more eclipses."
- Every saros series begins with a number of partial eclipses near one of Earth's polar regions, then produces several dozen central eclipses before ending with a group of partial eclipses near the opposite pole.
- Nodes: the Moon's orbit is inclined about 5 degrees to Earth's orbit around the Sun; the Moon moves from south to north of Earth's orbit at the ascending node, and from north to south at the descending node.
- Central solar eclipses are those in which the central axis of the Moon's shadow strikes Earth's surface. All partial (penumbral) eclipses are non-central; umbral eclipses (total, annular and hybrid) may be central (usually) or non-central (rarely).
- Hybrid eclipses, also known as annular/total eclipses, are both total and annular along different sections of the umbral path.
- Greatest eclipse is "the instant when the axis of the Moon's shadow passes closest to Earth's center". For total eclipses it is nearly equal to the instants of greatest magnitude and greatest duration; for annular eclipses greatest duration may occur at greatest eclipse or near the sunrise and sunset points of the path.

## Calendar

- The Gregorian calendar is used for all dates from 1582 Oct 15 onwards; before that date the Julian calendar is used.
- The Julian calendar has no year 0, so 1 BCE is followed by 1 CE. Years in this catalog are numbered astronomically and include the year 0: "the astronomical year 0 corresponds to 1 BCE, and astronomical year -1 corresponds to 2 BCE".

## Predictions

- Solar coordinates are from the VSOP87 theory (Bretagnon and Francou, 1988); the Moon's coordinates from the ELP-2000/82 theory (Chapront-Touze and Chapront, 1983).
- The revised value used for the Moon's secular acceleration is n-dot = -25.858 arc-sec/cy*cy, "as deduced from the Apollo lunar laser ranging experiment (Chapront, Chapront-Touze, and Francou, 2002)".
- The largest uncertainty comes from fluctuations in Earth's rotation, mainly tidal friction of the Moon, expressed as DeltaT: pre-1950s from empirical fits to historical records (Morrison and Stephenson, 2004); 1955-present from published observations; future extrapolated from current values weighted by the long-term trend from tidal effects.
- Polynomial expressions simplify evaluating DeltaT for any time from -1999 to +3000.

## Sources and credit the page gives

- Based on data published in *Five Millennium Canon of Solar Eclipses: -1999 to +3000* and *Five Millennium Catalog of Solar Eclipses: -1999 to +3000*. Global maps in the links were extracted from full-page plates in the Canon by Dan McGlaun; Besselian elements provided by Jean Meeus. "Fred Espenak assumes full responsibility for the accuracy of all eclipse calculations."
- Reuse is permitted with the acknowledgment "Eclipse Predictions by Fred Espenak (NASA's GSFC)".
- The page ends with the date 2009 Sep 26.

## How the saros works, as the page explains it

- "The periodicity and recurrence of solar eclipses is governed by the Saros cycle, a period of approximately 6,585.3 days (18 years 11 days 8 hours)."
- Two eclipses separated by one saros share a very similar geometry: they occur at the same node with the Moon at nearly the same distance from Earth and at the same time of year.
- "Each series typically lasts 12 to 13 centuries and contains 70 or more eclipses."
- Every saros series begins with a number of partial eclipses near one of Earth's polar regions, then produces several dozen central eclipses before ending with a group of partial eclipses near the opposite pole.
- Nodes: the Moon's orbit is inclined about 5 degrees to Earth's orbit around the Sun; the Moon moves from south to north of Earth's orbit at the ascending node, and from north to south at the descending node.
- Central solar eclipses are those in which the central axis of the Moon's shadow strikes Earth's surface. All partial (penumbral) eclipses are non-central; umbral eclipses (total, annular and hybrid) may be central (usually) or non-central (rarely).
- Hybrid eclipses, also known as annular/total eclipses, are both total and annular along different sections of the umbral path.
- Greatest eclipse is "the instant when the axis of the Moon's shadow passes closest to Earth's center". For total eclipses it is nearly equal to the instants of greatest magnitude and greatest duration; for annular eclipses greatest duration may occur at greatest eclipse or near the sunrise and sunset points of the path.

## Calendar

- The Gregorian calendar is used for all dates from 1582 Oct 15 onwards; before that date the Julian calendar is used.
- The Julian calendar has no year 0, so 1 BCE is followed by 1 CE. Years in this catalog are numbered astronomically and include the year 0: "the astronomical year 0 corresponds to 1 BCE, and astronomical year -1 corresponds to 2 BCE".

## Predictions

- Solar coordinates are from the VSOP87 theory (Bretagnon and Francou, 1988); the Moon's coordinates from the ELP-2000/82 theory (Chapront-Touze and Chapront, 1983).
- The revised value used for the Moon's secular acceleration is n-dot = -25.858 arc-sec/cy*cy, "as deduced from the Apollo lunar laser ranging experiment (Chapront, Chapront-Touze, and Francou, 2002)".
- The largest uncertainty comes from fluctuations in Earth's rotation, mainly tidal friction of the Moon, expressed as DeltaT: pre-1950s from empirical fits to historical records (Morrison and Stephenson, 2004); 1955-present from published observations; future extrapolated from current values weighted by the long-term trend from tidal effects.
- Polynomial expressions simplify evaluating DeltaT for any time from -1999 to +3000.

## Sources and credit the page gives

- Based on data published in *Five Millennium Canon of Solar Eclipses: -1999 to +3000* and *Five Millennium Catalog of Solar Eclipses: -1999 to +3000*. Global maps in the links were extracted from full-page plates in the Canon by Dan McGlaun; Besselian elements provided by Jean Meeus. "Fred Espenak assumes full responsibility for the accuracy of all eclipse calculations."
- Reuse is permitted with the acknowledgment "Eclipse Predictions by Fred Espenak (NASA's GSFC)".
- The page ends with the date 2009 Sep 26.

## How the saros works, as the page explains it

- "The periodicity and recurrence of solar eclipses is governed by the Saros cycle, a period of approximately 6,585.3 days (18 years 11 days 8 hours)."
- Two eclipses separated by one saros share a very similar geometry: they occur at the same node with the Moon at nearly the same distance from Earth and at the same time of year.
- "Each series typically lasts 12 to 13 centuries and contains 70 or more eclipses."
- Every saros series begins with a number of partial eclipses near one of Earth's polar regions, then produces several dozen central eclipses before ending with a group of partial eclipses near the opposite pole.
- Nodes: the Moon's orbit is inclined about 5 degrees to Earth's orbit around the Sun; the Moon moves from south to north of Earth's orbit at the ascending node, and from north to south at the descending node.
- Central solar eclipses are those in which the central axis of the Moon's shadow strikes Earth's surface. All partial (penumbral) eclipses are non-central; umbral eclipses (total, annular and hybrid) may be central (usually) or non-central (rarely).
- Hybrid eclipses, also known as annular/total eclipses, are both total and annular along different sections of the umbral path.
- Greatest eclipse is "the instant when the axis of the Moon's shadow passes closest to Earth's center". For total eclipses it is nearly equal to the instants of greatest magnitude and greatest duration; for annular eclipses greatest duration may occur at greatest eclipse or near the sunrise and sunset points of the path.

## Calendar

- The Gregorian calendar is used for all dates from 1582 Oct 15 onwards; before that date the Julian calendar is used.
- The Julian calendar has no year 0, so 1 BCE is followed by 1 CE. Years in this catalog are numbered astronomically and include the year 0: "the astronomical year 0 corresponds to 1 BCE, and astronomical year -1 corresponds to 2 BCE".

## Predictions

- Solar coordinates are from the VSOP87 theory (Bretagnon and Francou, 1988); the Moon's coordinates from the ELP-2000/82 theory (Chapront-Touze and Chapront, 1983).
- The revised value used for the Moon's secular acceleration is n-dot = -25.858 arc-sec/cy*cy, "as deduced from the Apollo lunar laser ranging experiment (Chapront, Chapront-Touze, and Francou, 2002)".
- The largest uncertainty comes from fluctuations in Earth's rotation, mainly tidal friction of the Moon, expressed as DeltaT: pre-1950s from empirical fits to historical records (Morrison and Stephenson, 2004); 1955-present from published observations; future extrapolated from current values weighted by the long-term trend from tidal effects.
- Polynomial expressions simplify evaluating DeltaT for any time from -1999 to +3000.

## Sources and credit the page gives

- Based on data published in *Five Millennium Canon of Solar Eclipses: -1999 to +3000* and *Five Millennium Catalog of Solar Eclipses: -1999 to +3000*. Global maps in the links were extracted from full-page plates in the Canon by Dan McGlaun; Besselian elements provided by Jean Meeus. "Fred Espenak assumes full responsibility for the accuracy of all eclipse calculations."
- Reuse is permitted with the acknowledgment "Eclipse Predictions by Fred Espenak (NASA's GSFC)".
- The page ends with the date 2009 Sep 26.

wikis.body:
## What the page gives

- A NASA Goddard (eclipse.gsfc.nasa.gov) page by **Fred Espenak**: "The following table delineates the path of the Moon's antumbral shadow during the Annular Solar Eclipse of 2046 Feb 05."
- "The geographic coordinates (WGS 84) of the northern and southern limits and the central line are listed at 120-second intervals. This provides adequate detail for making plots of the path on larger scale maps."
- Local circumstances on the central line in each row: "the ratio of the apparent diameters of the Moon to the Sun, the Sun's altitude and azimuth (degrees), the path width (kilometers) and the duration on the central line (minutes and seconds)."
- The global visibility of the eclipse is shown on an Orthographic Map; the path "is displayed in greater detail on an Google Map". The map features are described in the Key to Solar Eclipse Path Tables.

## Greatest eclipse and greatest duration

- Instant of Greatest Eclipse (GE): Time = 23:04:57.2 UT Lat = 04°46.9'N Long = 171°23.8'W; Sun Altitude = 67.9° Path Width = 310.1 km; Sun Azimuth = 157.4° Central Duration = 09m42.4s
- Instant of Greatest Duration (GD): Time = 22:48:53 UT Lat = 01°56'N Long = 174°39'W; Sun Altitude = 66.4° Path Width = 316.7 km; Sun Azimuth = 138.7° Central Duration = 09m45.6s

## Path table

- 110 timed rows at 120-second intervals, from 21:16 UT to 00:54 UT, plus an opening and a closing row labelled "Limits".
- Verbatim extremes and end rows (columns: Universal Time, northern limit lat/long, southern limit lat/long, central line lat/long, diameter ratio, Sun altitude, Sun azimuth, path width km, central-line duration):


## Predictions and stated caveats

- "ΔT = 88.7 seconds".
- "Predictions for the Annular Solar Eclipse of 2046 Feb 05 were generated using the VSOP87/ELP2000-85 solar and lunar ephemerides and a value of ΔT = 88.7 seconds."
- "The eclipse predictions presented here DO NOT include the effects of mountains and valleys along the edge of the Moon. Such corrections for the lunar limb profile may shift the limits of the eclipse path north or south by ~1-3 kilometers, and change the eclipse duration by ~1-3 seconds."
- "More detailed predictions including the effects of the lunar limb profile are normally posted 12-18 months before each eclipse".

## Acknowledgments

- "All eclipse calculations are by Fred Espenak, and he assumes full responsibility for their accuracy."
- Reproduction is freely permitted with the acknowledgment: "Eclipse Predictions by Fred Espenak, NASA's GSFC".

## Links the page offers for this eclipse

- Orthographic Map, Google Map, Animated Map, Path Table, Besselian Elements Table, Saros 141 Table.

## Page date

- The page carries no labelled publication or revision date; it ends with the bare date "2014 Feb 26".

wikis.title: 2027 Pan American Games (Lima 2027)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the XX Pan American Games, to be held in Lima, Peru from 23 July to 8 August 2027, covering the host change from Barranquilla, the bidding, participants, sports programme and marketing.
wikis.body:
## Overview

- "The 2027 Pan American Games (Spanish: Juegos Panamericanos de 2027), officially the XX Pan American Games (Spanish: XX Juegos Panamericanos) and commonly known as Lima 2027, is an upcoming international multi-sport event governed by the Panam Sports Organization. It will be held from 23 July to 8 August in Lima, the capital of Peru, eight years after the city hosted the 2019 Pan American Games."
- Infobox: Host Lima, Peru; Motto "Together We Shine Brighter" (Spanish: "Juntos brillamos más"); Nations "41 (expected)"; Events "38 sports"; Opening 23 July 2027; Closing 8 August 2027; Main venue National Stadium of Peru; Website lima2027.org.pe. Navigation: ← 2023 Santiago, 2031 Asunción →.

## Host change

- "Barranquilla, Colombia was initially announced as the host in August 2021. However, the city was stripped of its hosting rights in January 2024 after the country's Ministry of Sports failed to meet contractual obligations, as well as financial reasons."
- The first bidding process was to begin in January 2021 but "in July 2021, the president of Panam Sports Neven Ilic confirmed that the bidding process would be postponed until January 2022. The deadline to submit bids for the event was 15 November 2021."
- "On 27 August 2021, at an event in Barranquilla, Colombia, it was announced, that after a round of direct negotiations, the city was signed as the host of the games." The bidding-results table records no votes: "As part of the Olympic Agenda 2020 process, no bidding process was held. Barranquilla was appointed as host city."
- "on 3 January 2024, Barranquilla was stripped of hosting rights by PanAm Sports", after failed negotiations over contractual obligations and financial guarantees. "PanAm Sports also considered legal action for damages of USD$8 million caused by no signature of the host city contract."
- Colombian Olympic Committee president Ciro Solano said there had been Paraguayan pressure; he told AFP: "Paraguay has been insisting on holding the [2027 PanAm] Games since August".

## Second selection

- "The new host city was confirmed at a virtual Extraordinary General Assembly on 12 March 2024." Vote: Lima (Peru) 28, Asunción (Paraguay) 24.
- Lima was "seen as a safe choice, given the little time available to organize the Games and the little need for additional works, in addition to the fact that only the new Pan-American Village would need to be built". Its project "will reuse almost all infrastructure from those Games, in line with Olympic Agenda 2020+5". Then-president of Peru Dina Boluarte "announced her support for the bid on 18 January 2024."
- Asunción hosted the 2025 Junior Pan American Games; as Paraguay is landlocked, "it was proposed that the surfing events be held in El Salvador".
- Earlier interested cities: Buenos Aires (Argentina), Santa Cruz de la Sierra (Bolivia), Barranquilla (Colombia); later, São Paulo (Brazil) and a joint Jalisco–Nuevo León bid (Mexico). "On 16 January 2024, the Mexican Olympic Committee announced they would withdraw their bid for the 2036 Summer Olympics to focus on bidding for the Pan American Games and the Youth Olympic Games."

## Participants

- "All 41 nations of the Pan American Sports Organization are expected to compete." The list runs from Antigua and Barbuda to the Virgin Islands, with Peru marked as host.

## Sports

- "In October 2024, during the Panam Sports General Assembly held in Asunción, Paraguay, the International Cricket Council (ICC) made the formal proposal for cricket to be added to this edition's program, as it will be one of the five optional sports during the 2028 Summer Olympics."
- "The final program of 36 sports was named on June 19, 2025." 33 sports were chosen by the National Olympic Committees and three by the Organizing Committee.
- Basketball, breaking, bowling and racquetball were dropped from the 2023 edition. "Basketball will not be held for the first time ever at the Pan American Games", after a dispute with FIBA and Panam Sports, "with the former wanting a youth tournament, and the latter not wanting to downgrade the prestige of the tournament."
- "during the Panam Sports General Assembly in August 2025, bowling and racquetball were reinstated due at the request of several National Olympic Committees, bringing the number of sports to 38." Cricket "will make its Pan American Games debut". (The infobox likewise gives 38 sports.)
- The programme listed includes aquatics (artistic swimming, diving, open water swimming, swimming, water polo), archery, athletics, badminton, baseball and softball, basque pelota, bowling, boxing, canoeing, cricket, cycling, equestrian, fencing, field hockey, football, golf, gymnastics, handball, judo, karate, modern pentathlon, racquetball, roller sports, rowing, rugby sevens, sailing, shooting, sport climbing, squash, surfing, table tennis, taekwondo, tennis, triathlon, volleyball and beach volleyball, water skiing, weightlifting and wrestling.

## Calendar

- "The preliminary sports schedule was released on May 14, 2026." The calendar table runs from Wed 21 July to Sun 8 August, with the opening ceremony and closing ceremony marked.

## Marketing

- "The emblem was first unveiled on 6 August 2025, during the Panam Sports General Assembly held before the start of the 2025 Junior Pan American Games in Asunción, Paraguay. However, on 12 June 2026, a new emblem was unveiled, as the previous one was scrapped due to criticism alleging it was created using generative AI." The new emblem "draws inspiration from the welcoming, vibrant, and intimate nature of Lima."
- Mascot: "On 1 July 2026, after over 2,700 submissions, the organising committee revealed the final three in the running to be the mascot of the Games. The final three designs were: Rimo, a leaf-toed gecko, Kusi, a Galápagos sea lion, and Sisa, an amancaes flower." "On 22 July, it was announced that Rimo was the winner of the contest, receiving roughly a third of the 30,123 votes cast in the contest."

## See also (as listed)

2019 Pan American Games; 2025 Bolivarian Games — "held in Lima, with Ayacucho as host cities".

wikis.title: National Stadium of Peru (Estadio Nacional del Perú)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on Lima's Estadio Nacional: its capacity and construction, history from the 1897 field through the 1964 disaster, the tournaments it has hosted, the 2010-11 renovation and the concerts held there.
wikis.body:
## Facts from the infobox

- Name: National Stadium of Perú / Estadio Nacional del Perú. Location: Lima District, Lima, Peru; coordinates 12°04′02″S 77°02′01″W; elevation 135 m (443 ft).
- Owner: Government of Peru. Operator: Peruvian Sports Institute. Capacity 40,272. Surface grass. Field size 104.9 x 67.86 m. Public transit at Estadio Nacional.
- Built 1951–1952; opened 27 October 1952; renovated 1992, 1996, 2004, 2011; expanded 2004, 2011. Architect: José Betín Diez Canseco (renovation). Project manager: Miguel Dasso. Tenant: Peru national football team (1952 – present).

## Capacity and status

- "Its current capacity is 40,272 seats as stated by the Peruvian Football Federation and Instituto Peruano del Deporte. An additional 3,509 spectators can be seated in the box suites that stand above the four main stands. However, government regulations limit ticket sales to 90% of the stadium's maximum capacity, reducing it in the stands to 36,244 and 3,158 in box suites."
- "The stadium was first inaugurated on 27 October 1952 for the 1953 South American Championship—replacing the old National Stadium—and is Peru's principal and national stadium. It has hosted three of the six South American Championship/Copa América football competitions held in Peru. It is referred to as the Coloso de José Díaz because of its proximity to a street of the same name."
- The Peruvian Sports Institute (IPD), a branch of the Ministry of Education, administers it. "The artificial turf was installed for the 2005 FIFA U-17 World Championship. The most recent renovation started in 2010 and concluded in 2011. The re-inauguration ceremony of the renovated stadium was held on 24 July 2011 with a match between the Peru national under-20 football team and the Spain national under-20 football team."

## Early history

- Unión Cricket obtained land in Santa Beatriz from the Municipality of Lima; "On July 18, 1897, the field was officially inaugurated and named Estadio Guadalupe."
- "In 1921, the English residents of Peru that owned the stadium renovated and renamed the stadium from Estadio Guadalupe to Stadium Nacional and donated it to the Peruvian government." Its wooden stands went to the Estadio Teodoro Lolo Fernández when it was demolished for the new stadium.
- "In the 1950s, Miguel Dasso and the Peruvian President General Manuel A. Odria funded the project for the construction of the new stadium. The new stadium was planned to have a capacity of 53,000 and have it entirely made out of cement. The northern and southern stands would have a capacity of 15,000 each while the eastern and western stands would have three levels."
- The 27 October 1952 inauguration had luxury boxes and elevators; the ceremony "started early at 10:00 AM and lasted through the night" and honoured athletes including Teodoro Fernández, Alejandro Villanueva, Jorge Alcalde, Olympic gold medalist Edwin Vásquez and Pan American gold medalists.

## 1964 disaster

- "On 24 May 1964, Peru hosted Argentina in the Estadio Nacional before a crowd of 47,157 for a qualifying match pertaining to the 1964 Olympic Games that were to be hosted in Tokyo." Argentina led 1–0; a late Peru equaliser was disallowed by Uruguayan referee Ángel Eduardo Pazos, provoking a pitch invasion.
- "The police used tear gas and brutal force to quell the disturbances. The stadium's exits were closed which trapped the spectators inside the stadium." President Fernando Belaúnde Terry declared a month-long state of emergency. "More than 300 people were killed and at least 4,000 were injured."

## Tournaments hosted

- The old Stadium Nacional was sole venue for the South American Championship in 1927, 1935 and 1939; the present stadium hosted the 1953 and 1957 editions.
- Copa Libertadores: the 1971 final playoff (Nacional of Uruguay beat Estudiantes de La Plata 2–0), a leg of the 1972 final for Universitario de Deportes, and a leg of the 1997 final for Sporting Cristal.
- "In 1992, modern lighting was installed in the stadium and in 1996, an electronic scoreboard was installed to replace the old manual one." The northern-stand tower "was abandoned for many years until in 2004, it was used again for the Copa America."
- A "five million dollar government investment program to remodel older Peruvian stadiums" prepared it for the 2004 Copa América, "the first time the Estadio Nacional was not the sole venue for the South American competition". Peru's biggest stadium, Estadio Monumental (capacity 80,093, Universitario de Deportes), was not used in 2004.
- The 2005 FIFA U-17 World Championship, including the final, was played there; the artificial turf installed for it drew criticism from Peruvian First Division clubs "because of the constant injuries it causes", and is given as the reason the national team did not play there in the 2010 World Cup qualifiers. "The artificial turf was removed following the 2010 renovations."
- "In 2008, the athletics track was temporarily covered with asphalt for the rally race Caminos del Inca... Shortly after, the 6-lane Olympic running track was restored."

## 2010 renovations

- Undertaken "in a bid to the 2015 Pan American Games", including "the construction of 371 luxury boxes, 703 underground parking spaces, a new tower with a panoramic gourmet restaurant among other improvements. The renovations concluded in 2011. However, Toronto won the bidding process."
- Re-inaugurated 24 July 2011 with a 0–0 U-20 draw between Peru and Spain; "Two months later on 5 September 2011, the senior national team played its first match in the renovated stadium against Bolivia. The match ended in a 2–2 draw with goals by Rinaldo Cruzado and Claudio Pizarro."
- It hosted the opening and closing ceremonies of the 2019 Pan American Games and 2019 Parapan American Games. "It will host the Pan American Games again in 2027, which will be hosted by Lima."
- "Sixteen Peruvian sporting federations are headquartered at the national stadium," including boxing, karate, bodybuilding, kung fu, taekwondo and volleyball.

## Matches listed

- 2004 Copa América: 6 July Venezuela 0–1 Colombia and Peru 2–2 Bolivia (Group A); 9 July Colombia 1–0 Bolivia and Peru 3–1 Venezuela; 20 July Argentina 3–0 Colombia (semi-final); 21 July Uruguay 1–1 (3–5 p) Brazil; 25 July final Argentina 2–2 (2–4 p).
- 2005 U-17 World Championship: 16 September Uruguay 0–2 Mexico, Turkey 1–0 Australia; 19 September Mexico 3–0 Australia, Uruguay 2–3 Turkey; 23 September United States 1–1 Ivory Coast, Gambia 0–2 Netherlands; 2 October Netherlands 2–0 Turkey (third place), Mexico 3–0 Brazil (final).

## Other events

Concerts listed include Phil Collins (1995), Santana (1995), Travis, R.E.M. (11 November 2008), Soda Stereo (8–9 December 2007), Deep Purple, Whitesnake and Cyndi Lauper (amphitheater), Canto Por El Sur, Voces Solidarias, Los Fabulosos Cadillacs (29 November 2008), Iron Maiden (26 March 2009), The B-52's and New York Dolls, KISS (14 April 2009), Marc Anthony, Oasis (30 April 2009), Boy George, RBD, Jonas Brothers and Demi Lovato (18–19 May 2009), Red Hot Chili Peppers (14 September 2011), WWE tours, Justin Bieber (17 October 2011), Elton John (1 February 2012), Jamiroquai (20 February 2013), Alejandro Sanz (26 February 2013), The Cure (18 April 2013), The Killers (4 April 2013), Metallica (20 March 2014), Paul McCartney (25 April 2014), One Direction (27 April 2014), Teen Top (20 August 2014), Romeo Santos (23 April 2015), Coldplay (5 April 2016), Slipknot (18 October 2016), Aerosmith (24 October 2016), Justin Bieber (5 April 2017), Linkin Park (11 May 2017), Ed Sheeran (13 May 2017), Incubus and Maroon 5 (19 September 2017), Bruno Mars (30 November 2017), Depeche Mode (18 March 2018), Radiohead (17 April 2018), Bon Jovi (2 October 2019), Coldplay (13–14 September 2022), Daddy Yankee (18–19 October 2022), Bad Bunny (13–14 November 2022), Harry Styles (29 November 2022), Romeo Santos (10, 11, 12, 14 February 2023), Roger Waters (29 October 2023), Luis Miguel (24–25 February 2024), Libido (6 July 2024), Niall Horan (6 October 2024), Paul McCartney (27 October 2024), Shakira (17 February and 15, 16, 18 November 2025), Tabernacle Choir and Orchestra at Temple Square (22 February 2025), System of a Down (27 April 2025), Guns N' Roses (5 November 2025), Bad Bunny (16–17 January 2026), Ed Sheeran (20 May 2026) and TINI (30 May 2026).

wikis.title: Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum - Wikipedia article
wikis.summary: Wikipedia's article on the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum, covering its construction and renovations, ownership and lease, Olympic history, sports tenants, concerts and civic events, attendance records and commemorations.
wikis.body:
## The stadium

- A multi-purpose stadium at 3911 South Figueroa Street in the Exposition Park neighborhood of Los Angeles, "commissioned in 1921 and completed in 1923 as a memorial to Los Angeles veterans of World War I" and rededicated in 1968 to all United States veterans of that war. Home of the USC Trojans football team.
- Owned jointly by the State of California, Los Angeles County and the City of Los Angeles, and operated by the University of Southern California under a 98-year master lease implemented in July 2013 that also covers BMO Stadium.
- Designed by John and Donald Parkinson; original construction cost US$954,872.98. Groundbreaking December 21, 1921; opened May 1, 1923, "in just over 16 months", with a capacity of 75,144. Renovations are listed for 1930, 1964, 1977-78, 1983, 1993, 1995, 2011 and 2017-2019.
- Capacity 77,500 today (93,607 before 2018), with 42 suites, 1,100 club seats, 24 loge boxes and a 500-person rooftop terrace. "For most of its history the Coliseum was among the largest stadiums in the United States, seating over 100,000 for several decades."
- Designated a National Historic Landmark and added to the National Register of Historic Places on July 27, 1984, "a day before the opening ceremony of the 1984 Summer Olympics"; NRHP reference 84003866, California Historical Landmark No. 960, 29.2 acres, Art Moderne.

## Olympics

Hosted the Summer Olympics in 1932 (field hockey, gymnastics, equestrian show jumping, athletics and the ceremonies) and 1984, becoming the first stadium to host them twice, and will host athletics and the closing ceremonies at the 2028 Summer Olympics, making it "the first stadium to have hosted the Summer Olympics three times". The Olympic cauldron, built in 1932 and reused in 1984, is lit for special occasions and, since May 1, 2023, on the first of each month for the venue's centennial.

## Renovation and naming

The 2018-2019 project began in January 2018 and finished for the 2019 football season, with the budget rising "from the initial estimate of $270 million to $315 million" and capacity cut by about 16,000 seats. United Airlines became the first naming-rights partner on January 29, 2018; after objections from veterans' groups the parties settled on "United Airlines Field at Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum" on June 7, 2019, and the signage was covered during Rams games in 2019.

## Tenants and notable events

- USC since 1923; the inaugural game on October 6, 1923 saw USC beat Pomona 23-7. UCLA played there 1928-1981.
- Los Angeles Rams 1946-1979 and 2016-2019, ending with a 31-24 win over Arizona on December 29, 2019; Los Angeles Raiders 1982-1994; Super Bowl I on January 15, 1967 (61,946) and Super Bowl VII in 1973 (90,182).
- Los Angeles Dodgers 1958-1961, including games three, four and five of the 1959 World Series, each over 92,000, with game five at 92,706.
- Los Angeles FC beat Inter Miami CF 3-0 before 75,673 on February 21, 2026 in the stadium's first regular-season MLS game.
- Civic and cultural events include John F. Kennedy's 1960 Democratic National Convention acceptance speech, a Billy Graham crusade on September 8, 1963 that drew 134,254 - the largest gathering in the stadium's history - and concerts from Wattstax in 1972 to Rammstein in 2022.
- A March 29, 2008 Dodgers-Red Sox exhibition drew an announced 115,300, a Guinness World Record for attendance at a baseball game.

## Figures the article gives more than one way

The 1977-78 east grandstand work is said to have left "the capacity was just 71,500", while the article's own seating table gives 92,604 for 1976-1982. The 2007 K-1 Dynamite!! USA crowd was claimed by promoters at 54,000 but estimated by other officials at 20,000 to 30,000. USC's and UCLA's media guides disagree over which record college football crowds to list. The succession box gives the Pro Bowl span as 1950-1972 while the text says 1951 to 1972.

## About this capture

One long Wikipedia page split into three parts: part 1 holds the infobox and the article through the attendance records, part 2 holds the sculpture, Court of Honor, cauldron, popular culture and reference sections, and part 3 holds Olympic venue navigation boxes and categories. The capture gives no publication or last-edited date, only the permanent link oldid=1374685845.

wikis.title: Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum: construction, renovations, operation, tenants and events
wikis.summary: The main text of the Wikipedia article on the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum, covering its infobox details, construction and renovations, lease and naming rights, Olympic and professional sports tenants, concerts, civic events and attendance records.
wikis.body:
## Infobox

- Also known as The Coliseum, L.A. Coliseum, The Grand Old Lady. Address 3911 South Figueroa Street, Los Angeles, California, United States; coordinates 34deg0'51"N 118deg17'16"W. Website lacoliseum.com.
- Owner: State of California, Los Angeles County and City of Los Angeles. Operator: University of Southern California.
- Capacity 77,500; 93,607 (pre-2018). Executive suites 42. Surface Bermuda grass. Public transit Expo Park/USC, Expo/Vermont.
- Groundbreaking December 21, 1921; opened May 1, 1923; renovated 1930, 1964, 1977-78, 1983, 1993, 1995, 2011, 2017-2019.
- Cost: "US$954,872.98 (original)" ($18 million in 2025 dollars); "$954,869 (renovations in 2010)" ($1.41 million in 2025 dollars); "$315 million (renovations in 2018)".
- Architects John and Donald Parkinson (original), DLR Group (renovations). General contractors Edwards, Widley & Dixon Company (original); Hunt & Hathaway Dinwiddie Construction Company (renovations).
- Tenant: USC Trojans (NCAA), 1923-present. Former tenants include LA Giltinis (MLR, 2021-2022), Los Angeles Rams (NFL, 1946-1979 and 2016-2019), Los Angeles Christmas Festival (NCAA, 1924), UCLA Bruins (NCAA, 1928-1981), Los Angeles Dons (AAFC, 1946-1949), Los Angeles Dodgers (MLB, 1958-1961), Los Angeles Chargers (AFL, 1960), Los Angeles Wolves (USA, 1967), Los Angeles Toros (NPSL, 1967), Los Angeles Aztecs (NASL, 1977, 1981), Los Angeles Raiders (NFL, 1982-1994), Los Angeles Express (USFL, 1983-1985), Los Angeles Dragons (SFL, 2000), Los Angeles Xtreme (XFL, 2001), Los Angeles Temptation (LFL, 2009-2011, 2015).
- Historic designations: area 29.2 acres (11.8 ha); architectural style Art Moderne; NRHP reference number 84003866; California Historical Landmark No. 960; added to NRHP and designated a National Historic Landmark on July 27, 1984.
- The logo has been used since 2022 and was first used for the stadium's 100th anniversary (2023). The article carries an "needs more citations" maintenance tag dated August 2026.

## Overview

A multi-purpose stadium in the Exposition Park neighborhood of Los Angeles, "commissioned in 1921 and completed in 1923 as a memorial to Los Angeles veterans of World War I" and rededicated in 1968 to all United States veterans of the war. It is home to the USC Trojans football team. "For most of its history the Coliseum was among the largest stadiums in the United States, seating over 100,000 for several decades." It was designated a National Historic Landmark on July 27, 1984, "a day before the opening ceremony of the 1984 Summer Olympics". It "will become the first stadium to have hosted the Summer Olympics three times when it hosts the 2028 Summer Olympics", having hosted in 1932 and 1984.

## Planning and construction

- William Miller Bowen, head of the Sixth District Agricultural Association, announced plans in January 1919 to build a football field for USC in Exposition Park. The Community Development Association's executive board decided in November 1919 that Los Angeles needed a municipal stadium seating about 75,000; CDA president William May Garland advocated building it as a potential host of the 1924 Summer Olympics. A municipal bond issue on the ballot of August 31, 1920 needed a two-thirds majority and "was narrowly defeated". In November 1921 the CDA leased part of Exposition Park, built the stadium itself and rented it back to the city and county until its debts were paid.
- Groundbreaking December 21, 1921; construction completed "in just over 16 months, on May 1, 1923". Initial construction costs $954,873. "The Coliseum opened in 1923 with a capacity of 75,144, the largest stadium in Los Angeles at the time." The field runs east to west with the press box on the south side.

## Later additions and renovations

- Ahead of the 1932 Olympics the stadium was extended to 79 rows with two tiers of tunnels, "expanding the seating capacity to 101,574". The Olympic cauldron was added and the stadium was briefly known as Olympic Stadium; the cauldron and rings remain above the peristyle at the east end.
- One of the first all-electric scoreboards in the nation was installed over the peristyle's center arch in 1937, replaced in 1972 and again in 1983. A 6,000-square-foot HD video scoreboard began construction in August 2011 and went into operation on September 3, 2011; the current jumbotrons flanking the peristyle were installed in 2017. The large clock and thermometer were installed in 1955.
- 1964: first major renovation in over three decades; bench seating replaced by individual chairs; "seating capacity was reduced to approximately 93,000".
- 1977-1978: a larger east grandstand was installed at the behest of Rams owner Carroll Rosenbloom and "the capacity was just 71,500" - a figure that does not match the article's own seating table, which gives 92,604 for 1976-1982.
- 1984 Olympics preparation: a new track, the field permanently placed inside it, Olympic rings and a 25-step hydraulic staircase on the peristyle.
- 1993: a $15 million renovation before the football season lowered the field by 11 feet and replaced the running track with 14 new rows of seats. A planned multi-stage HNTB split-bowl scheme was shelved after the 1994 Northridge earthquake, when $93 million was required from government agencies including FEMA for repairs. Bentley Management Group was hired as project manager in 2000.
- 2008: additional seating raised capacity to 93,607 in September 2008.
- 2018-2019: after taking the master lease in 2013, USC unveiled "an estimated $270 million project" in October 2015; construction began January 2018 and was completed for the 2019 football season using only university funds; "the project budget increased from the initial estimate of $270 million to $315 million mainly due to the tight construction schedule." Work included replacing every seat, a new press box with box suites and premium lounges, renaming the peristyle the Julia and George Argyros Plaza, a new sound system, stadium-wide Wi-Fi, two HD jumbotrons and new concessions. "Capacity was reduced by about 16,000 seats." Current official capacity 77,500, with 42 suites, 1,100 club seats, 24 loge boxes and a 500-person rooftop terrace.

## Seating capacity table (college football)

1930: 75,144; 1934: 101,574; 1939: 105,000; 1946: 103,000; 1947-1964: 101,671; 1965-1966: 97,500; 1967-1975: 94,500; 1976-1982: 92,604; 1983-1995: 92,516; 1996-2007: 92,000; 2008-2017: 93,607; 2018: 78,500; 2019-present: 77,500.

## Operation and lease

- The Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum Commission provides public oversight of the master lease with USC; it has six voting members appointed by the three ownership interests and meets quarterly. USC's Vice President of Auxiliary Services is the Coliseum's Chief Operating Officer and Coliseum staff are university employees.
- The Commission ran the stadium directly until 2013. In May 2008 the two sides signed a 25-year lease giving the Commission 8% of USC's ticket sales, "approximately $1.5 million annually", in exchange for a list of renovations that "failed to materialize". In July 2013 they implemented "a significantly more extensive 98-year master lease agreement" covering the Coliseum and the adjacent BMO Stadium property, requiring USC to make approximately $100 million in initial physical repairs and pay $1.3 million each year in rent to the State of California.

## Naming rights

Naming rights went on the market in June 2008 with a predicted value of $6 million to $8 million a year. On January 29, 2018 United Airlines became the first naming rights partner. After veterans' groups and the Commission's new president objected to "United Airlines Memorial Coliseum", and United considered withdrawing, the parties agreed on June 7, 2019 to "United Airlines Field at Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum". During Los Angeles Rams home games in the 2019 season the stadium reverted to its original name and "United Airlines Field" signage was covered because of the franchise's partnership with American Airlines.

## USC and UCLA

- USC agreed to play all home games at the Coliseum. "On October 6, 1923, Pomona and USC played in the inaugural game at the Coliseum, with the Trojans prevailing 23-7."
- In May 2021 USC held commencement ceremonies in the Coliseum for the classes of 2020 and 2021, twice a day for a week, awarding over 36,000 diplomas - "the first time in 70 years that USC had held its commencement in the stadium". In September 2024 the university said the main ceremony was attracting more than 60,000 guests and would move permanently to the Coliseum beginning with the May 2025 ceremony.
- UCLA played home games there from 1928 to 1981 and moved to the Rose Bowl in Pasadena in 1982.

## Olympic Games

- 1932: hosted field hockey, gymnastics, the show jumping part of the equestrian event and track and field, plus the opening and closing ceremonies. The 1932 games "marked the introduction of the Olympic Village, as well as the victory podium".
- 1984: the first stadium to host the Summer Olympics twice, again the primary track and field venue and the site of the ceremonies.
- 2028: will host athletics and the closing ceremonies of the Olympics and Paralympics, becoming the first stadium to host these Olympic events at three different editions.

## Professional football

- Rams: the Cleveland Rams moved in in 1946, left for Anaheim before the 1980 season, moved to St. Louis in 1995 and returned to Los Angeles in 2016 (the NFL gave permission on January 12, 2016). They played the San Francisco 49ers before "an NFL record attendance of 102,368 on November 10, 1957", a paid-attendance record that stood until September 2009 at Cowboys Stadium. In 1958 they averaged 83,680 over six home games, including 100,470 against the Chicago Bears and 100,202 against the Baltimore Colts. First NFL game back was a preseason game against Dallas on August 13, 2016 before 89,140; the first regular-season home game since 1979 came on September 18, 2016, a 9-3 win over Seattle before 91,046. January 6, 2018: first Rams playoff game there since the 1978 NFC Championship, a 26-13 wild card loss to Atlanta. November 19, 2018: first Monday Night Football game there since 1985, moved from Estadio Azteca over field conditions, a 54-51 Rams win, "the highest-scoring game in Monday Night Football history". January 12, 2019: 30-22 divisional playoff win over Dallas. December 29, 2019: final game, beating Arizona 31-24; the Rams went 16-14 at the Coliseum in their 2016-2019 stint. February 16, 2022: Super Bowl LVI victory celebration at the peristyle end.
- Raiders: moved in in 1982, began looking to leave as early as 1986, and "in 1995, the Raiders left Los Angeles and returned to Oakland" (the tenant list gives their span as 1982-1994). Their largest crowds were 91,505 on October 25, 1992 (Dallas), 91,494 on September 29, 1991 (San Francisco) and 90,380 on January 1, 1984 (a playoff game with Pittsburgh).
- Championship games: the Rams hosted the 1949, 1951 and 1955 NFL championship games; the Coliseum hosted the NFL Pro Bowl from 1951 to 1972 and again in 1979. The first AFL-NFL World Championship Game, on January 15, 1967, Green Bay against Kansas City, drew 61,946 - lower than anticipated, against 72,418 for a regular-season Packers-Rams game a month earlier. Super Bowl VII in 1973 (Miami against Washington) drew 90,182. The 1975 NFC Championship Game drew 88,919, "the highest for an NFC Championship Game"; the 1983 AFC Championship Game drew 91,445, "still the largest crowd for a conference championship game since the conference-title format began with the 1970 season".
- Other teams: Los Angeles Dons (AAFC) 1946-1949; the AFL's Los Angeles Chargers in 1960; the USFL's Los Angeles Express 1983-1985, including the longest professional American football game in history on June 30, 1984, a triple-overtime 27-21 Express win over the Michigan Panthers decided by a 24-yard Mel Gray touchdown; the Los Angeles Dragons (SFL) in 2000; Lingerie Bowl halftime events in 2004, 2005 and 2006; Los Angeles Temptation games 2009-2011 and from 2015.

## Major League Baseball

- The Brooklyn Dodgers moved west in 1958 and played at the Coliseum until Dodger Stadium was ready for the 1962 season. The football bowl was a poor fit: foul territory was almost nonexistent down the first base line, and some seats were as far as 710 feet from the plate. The left-field fence was only 251 feet from the plate; Commissioner Ford Frick ordered a 42-foot screen in left field. A second screen 333 feet from the plate was ordered but the Los Angeles building code's earthquake provisions forbade it.
- In the first week of the 1959 season 24 home runs were hit there, three by Lee Walls; Wally Moon hit 19 homers that season, "all but five of them in the Coliseum", giving rise to "Moon Shots". Sports Illustrated ran a critical editorial titled "Every Sixth Hit a Homer!", and Warren Spahn called for a 300-foot minimum for home runs.
- The majors added a note to Rule 1.04 requiring any stadium built after June 1, 1958 to have at least 325 feet down each foul line; Frick vetoed the expansion Los Angeles Angels' request to use the Coliseum in 1961.
- On September 15, 1959 a Joe Adcock drive that cleared the screen but stuck in the mesh was called a ground-rule double, then a homer, then a ground-rule double again.
- Each of the three 1959 World Series games there drew over 92,000, with game five drawing 92,706, "a major league record for a non-exhibition game". A May 1959 exhibition against the New York Yankees honoring Roy Campanella drew 93,103 (the Yankees won 6-2). The largest regular-season attendance was 78,672, the Dodgers' home debut against the San Francisco Giants on April 18, 1958. The Coliseum also hosted the second 1959 MLB All-Star Game.
- The March 29, 2008 exhibition against the Boston Red Sox drew an announced 115,300, "setting a new Guinness World Record for attendance at a baseball game", breaking a record set at a 1956 Summer Olympics demonstration game at the Melbourne Cricket Ground; Boston won 7-4. Dimensions compared: 2008 - LF 201 ft, LCF 280 ft, CF 380 ft, RCF 352 ft, RF 300 ft; 1959 - LF 251 ft, LCF 320 ft, CF 417 ft, RCF 375 ft, RF 300 ft. The article elsewhere gives the 1959 power alleys as 320 feet.

## Soccer

- First official match: United States against Mexico on March 7, 1965 in World Cup qualification, a 2-2 draw before 22,570.
- The U.S. men's team has played 22 matches there, most recently in 2000: 11 in official competition and 11 friendlies. The team won the 1991 CONCACAF Gold Cup there, beating Honduras on penalties. The Coliseum staged the Gold Cup final in 1996, 1998 and 2000, and the fifth-place, third-place and final matches of the 2014 Copa Centroamericana before 41,969.
- Mexico is the most active national team there, with 14 competitive and 72 friendly matches. Argentina played Mexico in a friendly on May 14, 1985.
- Club soccer: Los Angeles Wolves (United Soccer Association, 1967, including the final); Los Angeles Toros (NPSL, 1967); Los Angeles Aztecs (NASL, 1977 and 1981). "On February 21, 2026, Los Angeles FC opened their season against Inter Miami CF at the stadium, making it the first regular season Major League Soccer game at the stadium. Los Angeles FC won 3-0 in front of 75,673 fans, the second-largest in league history for a standalone regular season match."

## Other sporting events

NCAA Men's Division I Outdoor Track and Field Championships in 1934, 1939, 1949 and 1955; the first Senior Olympics in June 1970; the July 1972 "Super Bowl" of Motocross, "the first motocross race held inside a stadium", last hosted in 1998; Evel Knievel's 1973 jump over 50 stacked cars, broadcast on ABC's Wide World of Sports, alongside "The World's Richest Demolition Derby"; the first stadium short course off-road race in 1979, last held 1992; the 1982 Speedway World Final, the only one held in the United States, where Bruce Penhall retained his title before an estimated 40,000; X Games IX in 2003 and X Games XVI in 2010; the 2007 K-1 Dynamite!! USA event, whose promoters claimed 54,000 attended "which would have set a new attendance record for a mixed martial arts event in the United States; however, other officials estimated the crowd between 20,000 and 30,000"; a Stadium Super Trucks round on April 27, 2013; the opening and closing ceremonies of the 2015 Special Olympics World Summer Games in August 2015; a celebrity boxing press conference on June 16, 2018; and NASCAR's Busch Light Clash on February 6, 2022 on a temporary quarter-mile track won by Joey Logano, with Martin Truex Jr. winning in 2023 and Denny Hamlin in 2024 before the event moved to Bowman Gray Stadium in 2025.

## Civic events and concerts

- John F. Kennedy's acceptance speech at the 1960 Democratic National Convention, where he first used the term "the New Frontier".
- "The largest gathering in the Coliseum's history was a Billy Graham crusade on September 8, 1963, with 134,254 in attendance."
- The Los Angeles Lakers' 2009 NBA championship parade terminated there on June 17, 2009 before a crowd of over 90,000. The Los Angeles FIFA Fan Festival for the 2026 FIFA World Cup was held at the Coliseum.
- Concerts: Wattstax on August 20, 1972, attended by over 100,000; the California World Music Festival April 7-8, 1979; the Rolling Stones on October 9 and 11, 1981 (with Prince booed off on the first night), playing to 90,000 a night in 1981 and "a record 90,000 fans for four nights in 1989"; Bruce Springsteen and the E Street Band's four Born in the U.S.A. Tour shows on September 27, 29, 30 and October 2, 1985 before 82,000 each night; U2 on November 17-18, 1987 and June 21, 1997; Motley Crue with Guns N' Roses on December 13, 1987; Monsters of Rock on July 24, 1988; Amnesty International's Human Rights Now! concert on September 21, 1988; the Electric Daisy Carnival, last held there in 2010 before its organizer was blacklisted after a drug-related death; RBD before 70,000 in 2006; LA Rising on July 30, 2011; Roger Waters on May 19, 2012; Kanye West with Drake on December 9, 2021; Rammstein on September 23 and 24, 2022; and Kx5 (Deadmau5 and Kaskade) before 50,000 on December 10, 2022, "the largest ever one-day EDM headlining event in North America at the time".

## Attendance records

Largest recorded crowds as tabulated: 134,254 Billy Graham crusade (September 8, 1963); 115,300 Dodgers vs Boston Red Sox exhibition (March 29, 2008); 104,953 USC vs Notre Dame (1947); 103,303 USC vs UCLA (1939); 103,000 UCLA vs USC (1945); 102,548 UCLA vs USC (1954); 102,368 Rams vs 49ers (November 10, 1957); 102,050 USC vs UCLA (1947); 100,470 Rams vs Chicago Bears (1958); 100,333 USC vs UCLA, second meeting (1945).

The article records that the college football figures differ between sources: the 2006 USC media guide lists the 1939 USC-UCLA game (103,303) and the first 1945 meeting (103,000), while "the UCLA Media guide does not list the 1939 game against USC, and only lists attendance for the second game in 1945". The largest crowd for a USC game against an opponent other than UCLA or Notre Dame was 96,130 against Stanford on November 10, 1951; the largest for a UCLA game against a school other than USC was 92,962 against Saint Mary's College of California on November 1, 1946.

wikis.title: Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum: sculpture, Court of Honor, the cauldron and references
wikis.summary: The later sections of the Coliseum article, covering the 1984 Olympic Gateway statues, the Court of Honor plaques, the occasions the Olympic cauldron has been lit, appearances in popular culture, and the article's reference list and succession boxes.
wikis.body:
## Sculpture and commemorations

A pair of life-sized bronze nude statues of male and female athletes atop a 20,000-pound (9,100-kilogram) post-and-lintel frame formed the Olympic Gateway created by Robert Graham for the 1984 games; the statues were modeled on American water polo player Terry Schroeder and American-Guyanese long jumper Jennifer Innis and "were noted for their anatomical accuracy". A decorative facade bearing the Olympic rings stood in front of the peristyle for the 1984 games and remained through that year's football season. The stadium rim and tunnels were repainted in alternating pastel colors from architect Jon Jerde's graphic design for the games; these colors remained until 1987.

## Court of Honor plaques

Between the double peristyle arches at the east end are the "Court of Honor" plaques, "recognizing many of the memorable events and participants in its history, including a full list of 1932 and 1984 Olympic gold medalists." Honorees listed with their plaque years include the 1959 Dodgers World Series (1961), the 1963 Billy Graham Crusade (1965), the 50th Anniversary of Armistice (1969), Count Baillet-Latour (1964), Elgin Baylor (2009), Joan Benoit (2017), Thomas Bradley (2019), the Community Development Association (1932), Pierre de Coubertin (1958), Anita DeFrantz (2017), Mildred "Babe" Didrickson (1961), William May Garland (1949), Elroy "Crazy Legs" Hirsch (2005), Rafer Johnson (2009), Thomas LaBonge (2022), the Israeli Olympic Athletes (1984), Pope John Paul II (1987), President John F. Kennedy (1964), Nelson Mandela (2014), John McKay (2001), Jim Murray (1999), Walter F. O'Malley (2008), Jesse Owens (1984), Jackie Robinson (2005), Knute Rockne (1955), Pete Rozelle (1998), Vin Scully (2008), Bruce Springsteen and the E Street Band (2016), Amos Alonzo Stagg (1965), Peter V. Ueberroth (2022), Pop Warner (1956), Kenny Washington (1972), Jerry West (2009), John R. Wooden (2008) and Rosalind Wyman (2021), along with several Coliseum Commission and earthquake-restoration plaques.

## Coliseum Cauldron

Built for the 1932 Summer Olympics and reused in 1984, the cauldron "is lit during special events (such as the period when an edition of the Olympic Games are being held in another city or in mourning for some personality related to the city)." Listed lightings include: for the Israeli athletes killed at the 1972 Munich Olympics; for several days after the 1986 Space Shuttle Challenger disaster; for over a week after the September 11 attacks in 2001; during the mourning period after Ronald Reagan's death; in April 2005 after the death of Pope John Paul II, who had celebrated Mass at the Coliseum in 1987; at the Dodgers' 50th anniversary game on March 29, 2008; for the 2015 Special Olympics World Summer Games, lit by Rafer Johnson; for the Rams' first home game back on September 18, 2016; on the evening of September 13, 2017 while Los Angeles awaited confirmation as host of the 2028 Summer Olympics; for the Coliseum Gladiator MMA Championship Finals on September 23, 2017; for the Rams' January 6, 2018 playoff game; to honor victims of the 2018 California wildfires and the Thousand Oaks shooting; for Rams games on December 30, 2018, January 12, 2019 and December 29, 2019; to honor Kobe Bryant after his death on January 26, 2020; Rafer Johnson after his death on December 2, 2020; Tom LaBonge and Tommy Lasorda, both after deaths on January 14, 2021; for the Kanye West and Drake Larry Hoover benefit concert on December 9, 2021; for the 2022 NASCAR Busch Light Clash on February 6, 2022, lit by Jeff Gordon; after the death of Vicente Fernandez on February 17, 2022; for the 2023 Busch Light Clash, lit by Caleb Williams; "Since May 1, 2023 the Cauldron has been ceremoniously lit the first of each month to commemorate the centennial of the venue's lasting legacy"; and on November 1, 2024 during the Dodgers' victory parade for their eighth World Series championship. This section carries a "needs more citations" tag dated February 2026.

## In popular culture

- Television, 2024: the Coliseum features in the Paris-to-Los Angeles handoff video in the 2024 Olympics closing ceremony, with Kate Courtney pedaling the flag to the Coliseum and handing off to Michael Johnson and then skateboarder Jagger Eaton.
- Video games, 1996: Microsoft Flight Simulator for Windows 95 included a challenge to fly through the needle of the Coliseum and land on the field.

## See also and people

The "See also" section links BMO Stadium, lists of stadiums and the history of the NFL in Los Angeles, and names figures connected to the venue: A.J. Barnes (active in the fight against giving USC preferential rights in the Coliseum, 1932), Lloyd G. Davies, Harold A. Henry, Rosalind Wiener Wyman (first Los Angeles City Council representative on the Coliseum Commission, 1958) and Ransom M. Callicott (1962).

## References, external links and succession boxes

The rendered reference list follows, citing among others Michael Benson's Ballparks of North America (1989), the National Register nomination form by James H.
