Charleton (June 21, 1984), Los Angeles Times coverage of the naming-rights dispute and the 2013 lease, the Berkeley Daily Gazette report of the October 6, 1923 opening game, the 1932 and 1984 Olympics official reports, Alan Schwarz's New York Times piece "201 Feet to Left, 440 Feet to Right: Dodgers Play the Coliseum" (March 26, 2008), and a Los Angeles Times report on the LAFC-Inter Miami record crowd dated February 24, 2026.

External links point to Wikimedia Commons, the official website, the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum Commission, the Los Angeles Sports Council, USC Trojans.com and a 1954 Sanborn map.

Succession boxes record the venue as the Summer Olympics opening and closing ceremonies venue in 1932 (after Olympisch Stadion, Amsterdam; before Olympiastadion, Berlin), in 1984 (after Central Lenin Stadium, Moscow; before Seoul Olympic Stadium) and in 2028 (after the River Seine and Jardins du Trocadero, Paris; before Brisbane Olympic Stadium); CONCACAF Gold Cup final venue in 1991 and in 1996, 1998 and 2000; host of the NFC Championship Game in 1976 and 1979 and the AFC Championship Game in 1984; host of Super Bowls I (1967) and VII (1973); host of the 1959 second MLB All-Star Game; and host of the NFL Pro Bowl "1950-1972" and 1979 - a span that differs from the "1951 to 1972" given in the article's own text. Further boxes list it as home of the USC Trojans (1923-present), UCLA Bruins (1928-1981), Los Angeles Rams (1946-1979, 2016-2019), Los Angeles Dodgers (1958-1961), Los Angeles Chargers (1960) and Los Angeles Raiders (1982-1994).

wikis.title: Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum article - Olympic venue navigation boxes and categories
wikis.summary: The closing part of the Wikipedia capture: navigation templates listing Olympic and other venues, plus the article's category lists, with no article prose.
wikis.body:
This part is site chrome only. It holds navigation boxes for the venues of the 1932, 1984 and 2028 Summer Olympics in Los Angeles, and for Super Bowl venues.

The 1984 boxes list venues including Albert Gersten Pavilion, Cromwell Field and Loker Stadium, Dodger Stadium, the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum, the Los Angeles Memorial Sports Arena, Olympic Swim Stadium, Pauley Pavilion, the Rose Bowl, Santa Anita Park, The Forum, and out-of-area venues Harvard Stadium (Boston), Navy-Marine Corps Memorial Stadium (Annapolis) and Stanford Stadium.

The 2028 box groups venues by area: Downtown and Exposition Park/USC (Dodger Stadium, BMO Stadium, Galen Center, Memorial Coliseum, Crypto.com Arena, Peacock Theater), Westside (Riviera Country Club, Venice Beach), the San Fernando Valley, San Pedro, Griffith Park, Long Beach, Carson (Dignity Health Sports Park), Inglewood (Intuit Dome, SoFi Stadium), the San Gabriel Valley, Orange County, Oklahoma City, and football (soccer) preliminary venues including Etihad Park, ScottsMiracle-Gro Field, Geodis Park and Energizer Park.

The 1932 box lists the 160th Regiment State Armory, Los Angeles Harbor, Olympic Auditorium, Long Beach Marine Stadium, Olympic Stadium, the Rose Bowl in Pasadena, the Swimming Stadium and others.

The page then ends with its categories, including World War I memorials in the United States, Monuments and memorials in Los Angeles, NFL venues in Los Angeles, National Historic Landmarks in Los Angeles County, Sports venues completed in 1923, 1923 establishments in California, USC Trojans football venues, UCLA Bruins sports venues, Venues of the 1932, 1984 and 2028 Summer Olympics, Olympic stadiums, X Games venues, Major League Rugby stadiums, Stadium Super Trucks tracks and NASCAR tracks. Hidden categories include "Articles needing additional references from August 2026", "from August 2019" and "from February 2026". No publication or last-edited date is stated.

wikis.title: 2028 ICC Men's T20 World Cup
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the eleventh ICC Men's T20 World Cup, co-hosted by Australia and New Zealand from 21 October to 19 November 2028, covering its format, schedule, qualification and stage structure.
wikis.body:
## Overview

- "The 2028 ICC Men's T20 World Cup will be the eleventh edition of the ICC Men's T20 World Cup, co-hosted by Cricket Australia and New Zealand Cricket from 21 October to 19 November 2028."
- Infobox: Dates "21 October – 19 November 2028"; Administrator International Cricket Council; format Twenty20 International; tournament format(s) "Group stage, Super 10 and Knockout stage"; Hosts Australia and New Zealand; Participants 20; Matches 55. Navigation shows ← 2026 and 2030 →.
- "It will be the first time that New Zealand would host the event, while Australia had previously hosted the competition in 2022."
- "India are the defending champions." The tenth edition, "held in 2026 in India and Sri Lanka, was contested by 20 teams, and was won by India, who defeated New Zealand in the final."
- The competition "was first played in 2007 in South Africa".

## Host selection

- "In November 2021 as part of the 2024–2031 ICC men's hosts cycle, the ICC announced that the 2028 Men's T20 World Cup would be played in Australia and New Zealand."

## Format

- "In July 2026, the ICC announced a new format for the tournament." 20 teams in five groups of four, round robin; the top two in each group advance to the Super 10 stage, where 10 teams are split into two groups of five for a second round robin.
- The top three from each Super 10 group advance to the knockout stage: two eliminators, two semi-finals and the final. "For the first time in the tournament's history, the knockout stage was expanded to feature six teams." Super 10 group winners go straight to the semi-finals; second- and third-placed teams play the eliminators.
- Group stage: 30 matches in total; tournament total 55 matches.

## Schedule

- "In March 2026, the ICC announced that the 2028 tournament will be held from 21 October to 19 November 2028."
- "The tournament will be part of the 2027–2031 ICC Men's Future Tours Programme."
- Knockout dates given: eliminators "November 2028"; the final "19 November 2028".

## Qualification

- "In July 2026, the ICC confirmed the qualification process with the reintroduction of the Men's T20 World Cup Global Qualifier which served as the third stage of the qualification pathway until 2022."
- Direct qualifiers: hosts Australia and New Zealand (2), plus the teams that reached the Super 8 stage of the previous tournament (7): England, India, Pakistan, South Africa, Sri Lanka, the West Indies and Zimbabwe.
- Three further places went to "the next best-ranked teams in the ICC Men's T20I Team Rankings as on 9 March 2026, that had not finished in the top seven: Afghanistan, Bangladesh and Ireland."
- The remaining eight places come from a Global Qualifier contested by the bottom eight teams from the previous T20 World Cup (excluding Scotland) — Canada, Italy, Namibia, Nepal, the Netherlands, Oman, the United Arab Emirates and the United States — plus the eight teams advancing from the regional qualifiers. Global Qualifier teams are listed as "TBD"; total 20.

## Stage tables

- Group stage standings tables (Groups A–E) are placeholders: teams are shown as A1–A4, B1–B4 and so on, with "First match(es) will be played: unknown. Source: Cricinfo [citation needed]".
- Classification rules: "1) Points; 2) Wins; 3) Net run rate; 4) Results of games between tied teams; 5) T20I Rankings ahead of the tournament [citation needed]".
- Super 10 tables list placeholders X1–X5 and Y1–Y5; the knockout bracket is likewise placeholders (Group winners, eliminator winners, semi-final winners), all "To be determined".

wikis.title: Melbourne Cricket Ground
wikis.summary: Wikipedia's article on the Melbourne Cricket Ground, the 100,024-capacity stadium opened in 1853 that hosted the first Test match, the 1956 Olympics and the AFL Grand Final, with its development, sports, events and records.
wikis.body:
## Overview
- The source is the English Wikipedia article on the Melbourne Cricket Ground (MCG), the multi-purpose stadium in Yarra Park, East Melbourne, Victoria, Australia, established by the Melbourne Cricket Club in 1853. Part 1 runs from the infobox through the ground's history, stadium development, cricket, Australian rules football, the war years and the Olympic and Commonwealth Games; part 2 covers rugby, soccer, concerts, other uses, records and statues; part 3 is navigation boxes and categories.

## Key facts
- Opened 23 September 1853; owned by the Victoria State Government through the MCG Trust and operated by the Melbourne Cricket Club. Capacity 100,024 (95,000 seats plus 5,000 standing), 109 executive suites, grass surface, estimated cost A$725 million excluding the original 1853 construction.
- Called the largest stadium in Australia and the Southern Hemisphere, the eleventh-largest globally and the second-largest cricket stadium by capacity; on the Victorian Heritage Register (2001) and the Australian National Heritage List (2005); built "atop a Wurundjeri camping ground and site of numerous corroborees".
- Hosted the world's first Test match (Australia beating England by 45 runs, 15-19 March 1877, before a first-day crowd of about 1,000) and the first One Day International (5 January 1971); hosts the Boxing Day Test and the AFL Grand Final, contracted there every year until 2059.
- Major events: the 1956 Olympic opening and closing ceremonies, athletics and hockey and football finals (103,000 on the opening day, 22 November 1956); football at the 2000 Olympics; the 2006 Commonwealth Games ceremonies and athletics; the 1992 and 2015 Cricket World Cup finals; the 2020 Women's and 2022 Men's T20 World Cups; State of Origin matches; and, from 11 September 2026, NFL International Series games.
- Redevelopment history runs from the 1854 wooden members' stand through the 1936 Southern Stand, the 1956 Olympic (Northern) Stand, the 1968 Western/W.H. Ponsford Stand, the Great Southern Stand of 1992 (renamed the Shane Warne Stand in 2022) and the A$400 million-plus rebuild completed for the 2006 Commonwealth Games.
- Attendance records as the page gives them: 143,000 for the Billy Graham Crusade on 15 March 1959 in the table (with 143,750 quoted in the record list below it), 121,696 for the 1970 VFL Grand Final, 100,024 at the 2022 and 2023 AFL grand finals, 109,500 for Ed Sheeran in March 2023, 94,199 on day one of the 2025 Boxing Day Test, 93,013 at the 2015 World Cup final, 91,671 at the 2026 State of Origin Game II and 90,307 for the 2025 British & Irish Lions Test. The Australia v Greece soccer match of 25 May 2006 is given as 95,103 in the soccer section and 97,103 in the records list.
- A 150th anniversary Australia v England Test "is scheduled to be held from 11 to 15 March 2027 and is expected to be the first day-and-night men's Test at the ground"; some 2032 Olympic football matches, including a quarter-final, are planned there.

## Date wording
- The page gives no publication or last-updated date for itself; its dated statements are "as of" notes on statistics ("All records correct as of 11 January 2026", "Last updated 26 May 2025", cricket details "As of 2 February 2024") and its footer carries only an oldid.

wikis.title: Melbourne Cricket Ground - history, stadium development, cricket, football and the Games
wikis.summary: The first part of the Wikipedia article on the Melbourne Cricket Ground, covering the stadium's details, its 1853 founding and land history, stand-by-stand development, cricket and Australian rules football at the ground, its wartime use and the 1956 Olympics and 2006 Commonwealth Games.
wikis.body:
## Stadium
- The Melbourne Cricket Ground (MCG), "also known locally as the 'G'", is a multi-purpose stadium in Yarra Park, East Melbourne, Victoria, Australia, at 120 Barassi Way; coordinates 37 deg 49'12"S 144 deg 59'0"E.
- Established by the Melbourne Cricket Club (MCC) in 1853; opened 23 September 1853. Owned by the Victoria State Government through its appointed MCG Trust and operated by the MCC.
- Capacity 100,024 (95,000 seats plus 5,000 standing room); 109 executive suites; grass surface; field size 174 m x 149 m (general), 160 m x 141 m (AFL), 172.9 m x 147.8 m (cricket).
- Renovations listed: 1992 (Southern Stand), 2006 (Northern Stand), 2032 (proposed Shane Warne Stand). Cost "Estimated A$725 million (excluding original 1853 construction)".
- Record attendance in the infobox: 109,500 for Ed Sheeran's +-=/x Tour, and 143,000 for the Billy Graham Crusade (pre-configuration).
- Described as the largest stadium in Australia, eleventh-largest globally, second-largest cricket stadium by capacity and the largest in the Southern Hemisphere; listed on the Victorian Heritage Register (designated 19 April 2001, no. H1928) and the Australian National Heritage List (designated 26 December 2005, no. 105885); home of the Australian Sports Museum.
- Tenants: AFL clubs Melbourne (1858-present), Richmond (1965-present), Collingwood (1993-present), Essendon (1991-present), Hawthorn (2000-present), Carlton (2005-present), North Melbourne (1985-2005) and University (1911-1914); the Australian (1877-present) and Victorian (1851-present) cricket teams, Melbourne Stars (2011-present) and Melbourne Renegades (2026-present); Melbourne Storm (2000); Australian national soccer teams and Melbourne Victory friendlies.
- Cricket details: first men's Test 15-19 March 1877 (Australia v England), last 26-29 December 2025 (Australia v England); first men's ODI 5 January 1971 (Australia v England), last 4 November 2024 (Australia v Pakistan); first men's T20I 1 February 2008 (Australia v India), last 31 October 2025; first women's Test 18-20 January 1935, last 28-31 January 1949; first women's ODI 18 December 1988, last 23 January 2014; first women's T20I 1 February 2008, last 8 March 2020. "As of 2 February 2024. Source: Cricinfo."
- Host of the annual AFL Grand Final ("the world's second-highest attended league championship event") and the Boxing Day Test; two Cricket World Cup finals (1992 and 2015); 1956 Olympic opening and closing ceremonies, athletics and the hockey and football finals; 2006 Commonwealth Games opening and closing ceremonies and athletics; State of Origin matches; football at the 2000 Olympics; the Bledisloe Cup.

## Early history
- "The MCG is built atop a Wurundjeri camping ground and site of numerous corroborees."
- The MCC was founded in November 1838 and, after grounds at the Old Mint site, Burial Hill (now Flagstaff Gardens, from January 1839), the south bank of the Yarra (from October 1846) and South Melbourne, chose the current site in 1853 from three offered by Governor La Trobe - a ten-acre (about 4 ha) section of the Government Paddock at Richmond, now Yarra Park.
- The area was the Government or Police Paddock between European settlement in 1835 and the early 1860s, agisting horses of the Mounted, Border and Native Police, and in 1850 formed part of a 200-acre (81 ha) recreation reserve.
- A board of trustees was appointed in 1861, mostly MCC appointees for forty years; in 1906 the Lands ministry appointed five new trustees, giving the government a majority, "and the government has appointed and overseen the trust since".
- The land grant stipulated use "for cricket and cricket only" until the Melbourne Cricket Ground Act 1933 widened allowable uses; that act was replaced by acts in 1989 and 2009.

## Stadium development
- First grandstand: the wooden members' stand of 1854; the first public grandstand a 200-metre, 6,000-seat temporary structure in 1861; a 2,000-seat double-facing stand in 1876 for James Lillywhite's 1877 English tour, during which the MCG hosted the world's first Test match.
- In 1881 the original members' stand was sold to Richmond Cricket Club for £55 and replaced by a brick stand, its foundation stone laid by Prince George of Wales and Prince Albert Victor on 4 July, opening that December; a telephone was installed and the wickets and goal posts turned from east-west to north-south. A scoreboard showing batsmen's names and dismissals followed in 1882.
- The Lillywhite tour stand burned down in 1884 and was replaced by a stand seating 450 members and 4,500 public; second-storey wings in 1897 took "The Grandstand" to 9,000, and it was lit with electric light in 1900.
- Early 20th century: an open wooden stand (1904), the 2,084-seat Grey Smith Stand (1906), the 4,000-seat Harrison Stand (1908) and the 8,000-seat Wardill Stand (1912); grandstand capacity reached nearly 20,000 and full ground capacity almost 60,000.
- The second brick members' stand was replaced in 1927 for £60,000; the Southern Stand opened at the end of 1936, seating 18,200 under cover and 13,000 in the open, with a Health Department maximum of 84,000 seated and 94,000 standing.
- The Northern (Olympic) Stand was built for the 1956 Olympics, notionally lifting capacity to 120,000, revised down after the 1956 VFL Grand Final crowd of 115,802. The Western Stand (foundation stone laid by the Duke of Edinburgh on 3 March 1967, completed 1968, renamed the W.H. Ponsford Stand in 1986) gave the ground its highest-capacity configuration, in which the record sporting crowd of 121,696 was set at the 1970 VFL Grand Final.
- Australia's first full-colour video scoreboard replaced the old one in 1982 on Level 4 of the Western Stand; it caught fire in 1999 and was replaced in 2000, with a second screen added in 1994. Light towers were installed in 1985.
- Concrete cancer found in 1988 led to the Great Southern Stand, completed in 1992 for the Cricket World Cup at a final cost of $150 million by John Holland, part-funded by the VFL for a 30-year ground-sharing deal; it was renamed the Shane Warne Stand in 2022 shortly after Warne's death.
- The 1928 Members', 1956 Olympic and 1968 Ponsford stands were demolished between late 2003 and 2005 and replaced for the 2006 Commonwealth Games at a cost exceeding A$400 million, pushing capacity just above 100,000; the highest attendance since is 100,024 at the 2022 and 2023 AFL grand finals.
- A $55 million refurbishment of the Great Southern Stand ran from 2011 to 2013; new scoreboards more than twice the size were installed in late 2013; LED sports lighting replaced all playing-field lights between November 2019 and February 2020.

## Cricket
- First cricket match at the venue 30 September 1854; first inter-colonial match Victoria v New South Wales from 26 March 1856, arranged after the MCC challenged any colonial team for £1000, with New South Wales winning by three wickets.
- Spiers and Pond's agent W.B. Mallam recruited Heathfield Stephenson's English team, which arrived on Christmas Eve 1861 and played a Victorian XVIII at the MCG from New Year's Day 1862 before a crowd estimated at 25,000 on the first day and more than 45,000 over four days - "at that time it was the largest number of people to ever watch a cricket match anywhere in the world" - winning by an innings and 96 runs.
- On Boxing Day 1866 an Indigenous Australian cricket team played an MCC team before 11,000 spectators.
- First Test: Lillywhite's 1877 tour, with John Conway selecting the Australian side (only five Australian-born players) and Dave Gregory as first captain. Charles Bannerman made an unbeaten 165 before retiring hurt; Ned Gregory scored Test cricket's first duck; Australia 245 and 104 to England's 196 and 108, Australia winning by 45 runs with Tom Kendall taking 7 for 55. The first ever Test "began with a crowd of only 1000 watching". England won the return match by four wickets; two years later Fred Spofforth took Test cricket's first hat-trick at the ground.
- Test scheduling: one or two Tests a summer through most of the 20th century, one a summer since 1982; from 1980 mostly, and every year since 1995, starting on Boxing Day. "No other venue in Melbourne has hosted a Test."
- The Merri Creek black soil pitch was considered the worst in Australia by the 1980s; drop-in pitches have been used since 1996; the pitch received "the first official International Cricket Council 'poor' rating by an Australian pitch in 2017" and a Sheffield Shield match was abandoned in 2019.
- Highlights: the highest first-class team score in history, Victoria's 1107 in the 1926-27 Boxing Day match (Ponsford 352, Ryder 295); the 1954-55 watered-pitch scandal, with England winning by 128 runs after Frank Tyson's 7 for 27; Joe Solomon given out when his hat fell on the stumps in 1960-61; the first ODI on 5 January 1971, a 40-over match Australia won by 5 wickets after the Test was washed out; the 1977 Centenary Test, won by Australia by 45 runs, "exactly the same margin as the first Test in 1877"; the underarm delivery of 1 February 1981; the 1985 Benson & Hedges World Championship of Cricket; the 1992 World Cup final before more than 87,000, won by Pakistan; Darrell Hair's seven no-balls against Muttiah Muralitharan in the 1995 Boxing Day Test.
- The 2015 World Cup final on 29 March drew "an Australian record cricket crowd of 93,013"; the 2020 ICC Women's T20 World Cup final on International Women's Day drew "a record crowd for women's cricket of 86,174", Australia winning by 85 runs.
- "A 150th anniversary Test match between Australia and England, commemorating the first Test match in 1877, is scheduled to be held from 11 to 15 March 2027 and is expected to be the first day-and-night men's Test at the ground."
- Cricket attendance table (top entries): 94,199 Australia v England Test, 26 December 2025; 93,013 2015 World Cup final; 91,112 Test, 26 December 2013; 90,800 Australia v West Indies, 11 February 1961; 90,293 India v Pakistan, 2022 T20 World Cup, 23 October 2022.

## Australian rules football
- As of 2024 six AFL clubs have home-game deals: Melbourne and Richmond ten games each, Collingwood nine, Hawthorn six or seven, Carlton five, Essendon four; Geelong and St Kilda one each.
- The match now considered the first Australian rules football game, Melbourne Grammar v Scotch College from 7 August 1858, was played in the adjacent parkland; football was first played on the MCG proper in an 1869 trial game with a police team, and the first official match followed in 1879 after the Victorian Football Association formed, including two night matches under the newly invented electric light.
- The first of nearly 3,000 VFL/AFL games at the MCG was on 15 May 1897, Melbourne beating Geelong 64 to 19.
- The VFL/AFL grand final has been played at the MCG almost every season since 1902, except 1942-1945 (military occupation), 1991 (Great Southern Stand construction) and 2020-2021 (COVID-19 restrictions moved them to the Gabba and Perth Stadium). The MCG is contracted to host the grand final every year until 2059, and 10 non-grand-final finals must be played there over each five-year period.
- Grand final attendance record 121,696 in 1970; since full seating, 100,024 at the 2022 and 2023 grand finals, 100,022 in 2018 and 2025, and 100,021 in 2017.
- VFL/MCC relations: VFL president Allen Aylett sought in March 1983 to cut the MCC's revenue share from 15 to 10 per cent, threatening to move Collingwood v Melbourne; Premier John Cain Jr became involved; a VFL members' area in the Southern Stand was agreed in the mid-1980s. Richmond joined Melbourne at the ground from 1965, North Melbourne from 1985 (playing the first MCG night football match in almost 110 years on 29 March 1985), Essendon in 1992, Collingwood fully from 2000 and Hawthorn from 2000. The AFL moved its headquarters into the Southern Stand complex in 1992 under an agreement for at least 45 AFL games a year at the ground.
- Records noted: Matthew Richardson most goals at the ground (as of 2011), Scott Pendlebury most matches (as of 2021); 14 goals in a match by Gary Ablett Sr. (1989 and 1993) and John Longmire (1990). The city-end scoreboard caught fire from an electrical fault before a Richmond-Carlton match on 27 August 1999, delaying play half an hour.

## World War II
- The government requisitioned the ground from 1942 to 1945, occupied in turn by the United States Army Air Forces, the RAAF, the United States Marine Corps and again the RAAF; more than 200,000 personnel were barracked there.
- From April to October 1942 the US Fifth Air Force named it "Camp Murphy" after Colonel William Murphy, killed in Java; in 1943 the First Regiment of the First Marine Division rested there, hosting a "get together" of American and Australian troops on the arena on 14 March 1943. A commemorative plaque was unveiled in 1977 by MCC president Sir Albert Chadwick and Medal of Honor recipient Colonel Mitchell Paige.

## Olympic and Commonwealth Games
- The MCG was the main stadium of the 1956 Olympics, hosting the opening and closing ceremonies, track and field, and the hockey and soccer finals. It was one of seven possible venues; the impasse nearly caused the Games to be moved, prompting a three-day summit convened by Prime Minister Robert Menzies.
- On the opening day, 22 November, "103,000 people filled the stadium to capacity"; Ron Clarke carried the torch, John Landy took the Olympic oath and Merv Wood carried the flag.
- Betty Cuthbert won three golds (100 m in 11.5 seconds, 200 m and the 4 x 100 m relay); Marlene Matthews was third in both sprints and was controversially left out of the relay; Shirley Strickland defended her 80 m title with an Olympic record. Australian men won silvers in the 4 x 400 m relay and high jump (Charles Porter) and bronzes to Hec Hogan (100 m), John Landy (1500 m) and Allan Lawrence (10,000 m).
- An exhibition baseball game between the Australian national team and a US armed services team drew an estimated 114,000 - a Guinness World Record for baseball attendance until a 29 March 2008 exhibition at the Los Angeles Coliseum drew 115,300.
- A demonstration Australian rules match on 7 December 1956 saw the VAFA side beat a VFL/VFA amateur combination 81 to 55.
- The ground hosted soccer preliminaries at the 2000 Sydney Olympics, and the opening and closing ceremonies and athletics of the 2006 Commonwealth Games (15-26 March), with a seating capacity of 80,000 during the Games, 47 events, eleven Games records broken, and Australia topping the medal table with 16 golds and 41 medals.

wikis.title: Melbourne Cricket Ground - other sports, concerts, records and statues
wikis.summary: The second part of the MCG article: rugby union and league, soccer, concerts and other uses, the ground's attendance and cricket and AFL records, and its statues.
wikis.body:
## Rugby union
- First rugby union at the ground on 29 June 1878, Sydney's Waratah Club v Carlton Football Club, a draw before 6,000-7,000. Later fixtures: the Wanderers v a Royal Navy squadron team (29 June 1881); Victoria v the British Lions on 19 August 1899 (lost 30-0 before about 7,000); the First Wallabies beating Victoria 26-6 on 10 August 1908 before 1,500; Melbourne v East Melbourne on 6 July 1912; Victoria beaten 51-0 by the Springboks on 18 June 1921 before 11,214; the British Lions beating Victoria 41-36 on 13 September 1930; the NZ Maoris beating a Southern States side 35-8 on 21 May 1949; Queensland beating Victoria 31-12 on 29 July 1950; the All Blacks beating an Australian XV 56-11 on 30 June 1951.
- Tri Nations Tests: 26 July 1997, New Zealand 33-18 before 90,119; 11 July 1998, Australia 24-16 before 75,127; 30 June 2007, Australia 20-15 before 79,322. In the 2023 Rugby Championship New Zealand beat Australia 38-7 before 83,944.
- In 2025 the British & Irish Lions won the second Test 26-29 after trailing 23-5, before 90,307 - "the largest ever crowd for a British & Irish Lions match, and the MCG's largest ever rugby union crowd".

## Rugby league
- First played 15 August 1914, New South Wales losing to England 15-21.
- State of Origin: Game II 1994 drew 87,161, "a new record rugby league crowd in Australia"; Game II 1995 drew 52,994; the 1997 game, affected by the Super League war, drew 25,105; Game II 2015 drew "an all-time record State of Origin crowd of 91,513" (New South Wales 26-18); 6 June 2018 drew 87,122 (New South Wales 22-12); Game II 2024 on 26 June drew 90,084 (New South Wales 38-18); Game II 2026 on 17 June saw Queensland win 44-24 before 91,671, "a new all-time State of Origin attendance record".
- Melbourne Storm played two games at the ground in 2000: beating St George Illawarra 70-10 before 23,239 on 3 March and Cronulla 22-16 before 15,535 on 24 June.

## Soccer
- On 9 February 2006 Premier Steve Bracks and FFA chairman Frank Lowy announced an annual world-class soccer event at the MCG from 2006 to 2009; the first was Australia's 1-0 win over Greece on 25 May 2006 "in front of a sell-out crowd of 95,103".
- Other matches listed: the 1956 Olympic final, USSR v Yugoslavia, 8 December 1956; Australia v Juventus (1984); the 1998 World Cup qualifier v Iran on 29 November 1997 with 95,000 in attendance, drawn 2-2 with Iran progressing on away goals; Manchester United v Australia (1999, 60,000); Brazil B v Australia (1999, 70,795); Italy v the Olyroos at the 2000 Olympics (93,252); the 2002 qualifier v Uruguay (84,656), won 1-0 but lost on aggregate; Australia v Argentina (70,171); the 2009 qualifier v Japan (81,872, Australia winning 2-1 on two Tim Cahill headers); Melbourne Victory v Liverpool in July 2013 (95,446); the 2015 International Champions Cup final between Real Madrid and Manchester City, "a soccer MCG record crowd of 99,382"; Brasil Global Tour matches in June 2017; Melbourne Victory v Manchester United (15 July 2022); Newcastle United v Tottenham Hotspur (22 May 2024), the first meeting of two English teams at the ground.
- "Some of the 2032 Olympics games, including the quarter-final, are planned to be held at the venue."

## Concerts
- First rock concert: David Cassidy in 1974; David Bowie in 1978; in 1993 Paul McCartney, U2 and Madonna played three concerts selling 147,241 tickets; the Rolling Stones (1995), Michael Jackson (1996), the Three Tenors (1997), Elton John and Billy Joel (1998).
- The Police with Fergie and Fiction Plane on Australia Day 2008, the first MCG concert in 10 years; Sound Relief for the Red Cross Victorian Bushfire Appeal on 14 March 2009 with 80,518 in attendance; Guns N' Roses on 14 February 2017 (73,756) and 3 December 2022; a free Killers concert after the 2017 AFL Grand Final; Billy Joel on 10 December 2022.
- Eminem on 24 February 2019 sold 80,708 tickets, then the highest attendance for a single concert at the MCG and the highest attended show of his career; Ed Sheeran's two +-=/x Tour shows on 2 and 3 March 2023 drew 108,000 and 109,500; Taylor Swift's three Eras Tour shows on 16-18 February 2024 drew 96,000 each night for 288,000 in total, breaking the venue record for most tickets sold by one artist per promoter Frontier Touring; AC/DC played the PWR/UP Tour on 12 and 16 November 2025 with Amyl and the Sniffers.

## Other uses
- Tennis: an asphalt court was laid in 1878 for Victoria's first game of tennis, a grass court in 1879, the first Victorian Championship in 1880, the first inter-colonial championship in 1883 and the first NSW-Victoria interstate match in 1884; tennis moved to the Warehousemen's Cricket Ground in 1889.
- Cycling: one of Australia's first bicycle races, for velocipedes, was held in 1869; the 1898 Austral Wheel Race drew 30,000 for £400 in prize money (£240, £120 and £40 for the first three).
- American football: the NFL played its first game at the ground on 11 September 2026 under a multiple-season International Series deal, the San Francisco 49ers beating the Los Angeles Rams 27-7 before a sell-out 100,021, "the seventh-highest crowd for a regular-season game in NFL history".
- Miscellaneous: Queen Elizabeth II visited twice in 1954, attended a Richmond v Fitzroy match on 5 April 1970 and the Commonwealth Games opening ceremony on 15 March 2006; Billy Graham's 1959 event drew at least 143,000; Pope John Paul II held a service on 27 November 1986 and a Polish community celebration the next day; the ground hosted the start of *The Amazing Race Australia 1* (2011) and a repeat challenge in *The Amazing Race US 39* (2025); WWE Super Show-Down on 6 October 2018; the state memorial service for Shane Warne on 30 March 2022.

## Records
- Sporting firsts: first Test match (1877), first ODI (1971), highest first-class score (1107, Victoria v NSW, 1926), Australia's first international lacrosse match (1907, 30,000), and the fastest ball bowled in Australia, 160.7 km/h by Shaun Tait on 5 February 2010.
- All-time attendance table: 143,000 Billy Graham Crusade (15 March 1959); 121,696 VFL Grand Final Carlton v Collingwood (26 September 1970); 120,000 40th Eucharistic Congress (25 February 1973); 119,195 VFL Grand Final (27 September 1969); 118,192 VFL Grand Final (25 September 1971). The list beneath gives the Billy Graham crusade as 143,750, and the Australia v Greece 2006 soccer crowd as 97,103 where the soccer section says 95,103.
- Other records listed: highest VFL/AFL home-and-away crowd 99,256 (Melbourne v Collingwood, 1958); highest club soccer crowd 99,382 (2015 International Champions Cup); highest aggregate for a Test 373,691 (2024 Boxing Day Test v India); highest single-day Test attendance in history 94,199 (2025 Boxing Day Test, day 1); highest ODI crowd 93,013; highest T20I crowd 90,293; highest domestic T20 crowd 80,883 (Stars v Renegades, 2015-16 BBL); highest women's cricket crowd 86,174; highest State of Origin crowd 91,513; highest rugby union crowd 90,307.
- Stadium firsts claimed: world's first all-colour cricket scoreboard with instant replays, first electronic sight screens, first super sopper, first scrolling signage at an oval ground, first international cricket match on a one-piece portable pitch (Boxing Day Test, 2000) and the world's tallest floodlights.
- Test batting records: most career runs Don Bradman 1,671 in 17 innings (1928-1948), then Ricky Ponting 1,338, Steve Waugh 1,284, Steve Smith 1,279 and Allan Border 1,272; most by a non-Australian Jack Hobbs 1,178 in 18 innings. Highest individual score 307 by Bob Cowper v England (11 February 1966). Most centuries Bradman 9, Matthew Hayden 6. Highest average 128.53 (Bradman).
- Test bowling records: most wickets Dennis Lillee 82 in 26 innings (1972-1983), then Shane Warne 56, Nathan Lyon 50, Hugh Trumble 46 and Graham McKenzie 45; most by a non-Australian Sydney Barnes 35 in ten innings. Best innings figures 9/86 Sarfraz Nawaz (10 March 1979); best match figures 15/124 Wilfred Rhodes (1 January 1904).
- Team records: highest innings 8/624 declared, Australia v Pakistan, 26 December 2016; lowest completed innings 36, South Africa v Australia, 12 February 1932. Highest partnership 346 for the 6th wicket, Bradman (270) and Jack Fingleton (136), 1 January 1937. "All records correct as of 11 January 2026."
- ODI records: highest total 5/355 (Australia v England, 22 November 2022); highest score 180 off 151 by Jason Roy (14 January 2018); best figures 6/42 by Ajit Agarkar (2004) and Yuzvendra Chahal (2019); highest partnership 269 (Head and Warner, 2022). "Last updated 26 May 2025."
- T20I records: highest total 5/186 (India v Zimbabwe, 6 November 2022); highest score 89 off 43 by David Warner (11 January 2009); best figures 4/30 by Josh Hazlewood (31 January 2014); highest partnership 113 (Kohli and Pandya, 23 October 2022).
- VFL/AFL records: highest team score 32.24 (216) Hawthorn v Essendon, 1 August 1992; largest winning margin 165 points (Hawthorn 197 to Port Adelaide 32, 13 August 2011); lowest score 0.8 (8) Melbourne v South Melbourne, 13 July 1912; most goals in a game 14 (Ablett Sr. twice, Longmire once); most disposals 54 by Tom Mitchell (24 March 2018); most games 243 by Scott Pendlebury; most goals 464 by Matthew Richardson. "All records correct as of 16 April 2024."

## Statues
- A Tom Wills statue (2001) outside the ground commemorates the first game of Australian rules football.
- Tattersall's Parade of the Champions statues: Don Bradman (May 2003), Betty Cuthbert (August 2003), Ron Barassi (September 2003), Keith Miller (February 2004), Dick Reynolds (June 2004), Shirley Strickland (November 2004), Haydn Bunton Sr. (April 2005), Leigh Matthews (August 2005), Bill Ponsford (December 2005) and Dennis Lillee (December 2006).
- Australia Post Avenue of Legends, announced in 2010 for at least five statues in Yarra Park: Shane Warne (December 2011), Norm Smith (September 2012), John Coleman (September 2013), Neil Harvey (January 2014), Jim Stynes (September 2014) and Kevin Bartlett (March 2017, the most recent addition).

## End matter in this part
- See also links, the reference list, a Further reading list (including Richard Cashman, *Paradise of Sport*, 1995; Betty Cuthbert, *Golden Girl*, 1966; Harry Gordon, *Australia and the Olympic Games*, 1994; Garry Linnell, *Football Ltd*, 1995; Jack Pollard, *Australia Test Match Grounds*, 1990; *The Oxford Companion to Australian Sport*, 2nd ed., 1997) and External links (the MCG official website, a virtual tour, sportsvenue-technology.com, Austadiums and the "Around the Grounds" web documentary), followed by succession-box markup for the 1956 Olympics and the 1992 and 2015 Cricket World Cup finals. No publication or last-updated date is stated.

wikis.title: 2030 Commonwealth Games (Ahmedabad)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the XXIV Commonwealth Games, planned for Ahmedabad, India in October 2030, covering the host selection, rival and declined bids, preparations, venues and the sports programme.
wikis.body:
## Overview

- "The 2030 Commonwealth Games, officially known as the XXIV Commonwealth Games and commonly known as Amdavad 2030, is a planned multi-sport event scheduled to take place in Ahmedabad, Gujarat, India, in October 2030. This will be the second Commonwealth Games to be hosted in India, following the 2010 Games in Delhi, and the third in Asia. It will also be the centenary edition of the event."
- Infobox: Host city Ahmedabad, India; Nations "74 Commonwealth teams (expected)"; Opening "TBA"; Main venue Narendra Modi Stadium; navigation ← XXIII, XXV →. (The infobox gives the opening as TBA while the lead says October 2030.)
- The article carries a maintenance note: "It has been suggested that this section be split out into another article. (Discuss) (May 2026)".

## Host selection

- "Potential host cities began exploring bids as early as 2021. A deadline of 31 March 2025 was set for potential host cities to express interest in hosting, and a deadline of 31 August 2025 was set for bid dossiers. India and Nigeria submitted formal proposals to host the 2030 Commonwealth Games by the 31 August deadline, Commonwealth Sport announced on 1 September."
- "On 15 October 2025, Commonwealth Sport announced that the Indian bid had been recommended by its bid evaluation commission." The host city election was held at the Commonwealth Sport General Assembly in Glasgow on 26 November 2025, where Ahmedabad was declared host; the bidding table records the vote as "Unanimous".

### India's bid

- "On 30 January 2025, Bhupendrabhai Patel, and members of the Athletics Federation of India, met with Commonwealth Games Federation vice-president Chris Jenkins in Gandhinagar to discuss a bid". The venue plan uses two complexes built with Ahmedabad's 2036 Summer Olympics bid in mind: "Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel Sports Enclave would host aquatics, boxing, 3x3 basketball, cricket, gymnastics and kabaddi, and Naranpura Sports Complex for badminton, judo and table tennis." A new complex in Karai would feature "a 50,000 capacity athletics stadium, a 5,000 capacity indoor arena, and a shooting range". The city "will also host the 2029 World Police and Fire Games."
- CGF chief executive Katie Sadleir, 16 February 2025: "hosting the Olympics would be an incredible achievement, and having the 2030 Commonwealth Games in India would be the right step towards that goal. With the right leadership, infrastructure, and passion, it is on track to become one of the top 10 countries in the Olympics."
- An expression of interest was submitted on 21 March 2025. In June 2025 an Indian delegation met the CGF in London; a government press release said: "We are designing a model for hosting the Games that focuses on long-term impact rather than short-term spectacle, using existing venues wherever possible and ensuring that the Games leave behind a meaningful legacy for local communities."
- "On 13 August 2025, the Indian Olympic Association formally approved the bid during its Special General Meeting in New Delhi." Two weeks later the Government of India approved the bid "and agreed to all monetary guarantees required by the CGF".
- Domestically, "Ahmedabad and Bhubaneswar were reportedly the two main contenders; ultimately, victory was secured by the Western city on the strength of superior athletic venues and an established competency in hosting high-profile events."

### Eliminated bid: Abuja, Nigeria

- "On 28 March 2025, the Nigeria Olympic Committee submitted an expression of interest". Spokesperson Tony Nezianya said a bid by the capital would "provide a compelling narrative for the nation’s progress and readiness." Abuja had previously bid for the 2014 Games, losing to Glasgow. President Bola Tinubu backed the bid in July 2025; a Nigerian delegation met the CGF in London in August 2025.

### Proposed and declined bids

- South Africa: a bid was speculated ahead of the 2024 Commonwealth heads of government meeting in Samoa; Durban had been awarded the 2022 Games but was stripped of them and replaced by Birmingham in 2017. "In June 2025, South Africa had been invited to bid for the 2030 edition"; SASCOC intends to target the Commonwealth Games in 2030 "before mounting a serious campaign for the Olympics in 2040."
- Canada: in March 2025 Commonwealth Sport Canada proposed a "United Canada" bid across provinces; president Rick Powers said there would be no new construction and that the plan "would lower costs by 60% compared to a single city hosting". Director Claire Carver-Dias suggested including lacrosse if held in a First Nations territory. An expression of interest was submitted 31 March 2025 with support from the government, Indigenous peoples and Manitoba, Newfoundland and Labrador, Ontario and Prince Edward Island; "in June 2025, the government of Ontario withdrew the province from the bid."
- Alberta: a bid featuring Calgary and Edmonton drew "a potential for C$4 million in financial backing"; "On 3 August 2023, the Government of Alberta withdrew from Alberta's 2030 Commonwealth Games bid process thereby terminating the bid."
- Hamilton, Ontario: businessmen planned a bid marking 100 years since the city hosted the original Games; in April 2021 chair Lou Frapporti said Hamilton would drop a 2026 bid and refocus on 2030; "In February 2023, it was announced that Hamilton was no longer Canada's preferred candidate."
- Australia declined, its Commonwealth Games Association chief executive Craig Phillips citing proximity to the 2032 Brisbane Olympics and Victoria's withdrawal from the 2026 Games. In Western Australia, Basil Zempilas wanted Perth to bid but missed the expression-of-interest deadline; John Carey called it "a brain fart that would cost the state billions".

## Development and preparations

- Promised upgrades: "roads, beautification, housing facilities, the Ahmedabad Metro system, and the construction or renovation of sports facilities. To allow for construction projects, some surrounding slums will be vacated prior to the event."
- The expansion of Ahmedabad International Airport "will also be completed before the Games". "Almost all events are scheduled to be held in four cities in Gujarat: Ahmedabad, Gandhinagar, Vadodara, and Ekta Nagar."
- "In September 2025, the Veer Savarkar Sports Complex was opened, at a cost of ₹825 crores. It is 21 acres in size and has six zones, including an aquatics centre and tennis courts."
- "Venues are 85% complete as of May 2026, according to Indian officials."
- August 2026: the Commonwealth Games flag "was transferred to Gujarat from Glasgow as part of preparations". "India finished fourth at the previous Commonwealth Games with 39 medals, including 13 gold medals." The flag bears the message "Sport Unites Us All".

## Venues (as tabled)

- Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel Sports Enclave — ceremonies, capacity 132,000, existing.
- Indoor Arena — events TBA, capacity 18,000, new.
- Aquatics Centre — capacity 12,000.
- Veer Savarkar Sports Complex; Gandhinagar; Mahatma Mandir (existing with temporary stands); IIT Gandhinagar; Karai Police Academy Sports Hub (athletics).

## Participating associations

- "All 74 Commonwealth Games Associations are expected to participate in the 2030 Commonwealth Games." India is listed as host.

## Sports

- "In October 2021, the CGF announced a new Games roadmap that will, starting with the 2030 Commonwealth Games, change the requirements for competed sports." Between 15 and 17 sports per edition; a new "Compulsory Sports" category of athletics and swimming plus their para counterparts; "Core Sports" abolished; hosts free to choose from a pre-assembled list within the 15–17 limit.
- After the 26 November 2025 host announcement, the first eight sports were named: athletics and swimming (compulsory, with Paralympic counterparts); bowls and weightlifting (with Paralympic equivalents), artistic gymnastics, netball and boxing retained from Glasgow 2026; plus table tennis and its Paralympic equivalent, "a sport that was absent from Glasgow 2026".
- "In April 2026, cricket and field hockey were confirmed, and there were proposals made to include up to two Indian traditional sports, with competitive yoga, kabaddi, kho kho and mallakhamba being discussed."
- "In June 2026, Commonwealth Sport chief executive Katie Sadleir said the Ahmedabad Games would feature a full programme of 17 sports, up from the reduced schedule used in Glasgow. She said organisers were aiming for a 60 percent reduction in hosting costs compared with earlier editions."
- "A further five to seven disciplines or sports from the following list of fifteen optional sports will also be chosen at a later date: archery, badminton, 3x3 basketball, beach volleyball, cycling, diving, judo, rhythmic gymnastics, rugby sevens, shooting, squash, tennis, triathlon and wrestling." (The sentence says fifteen optional sports but lists fourteen.)
- Programme list shown: athletics, bowls, boxing, cricket, field hockey, gymnastics (artistic), netball, swimming, table tennis, weightlifting, para powerlifting.

## Broadcasting

- Australia – Seven Network.

wikis.title: Narendra Modi Stadium, Ahmedabad
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the 132,000-capacity Narendra Modi Stadium in Motera, Ahmedabad - the world's largest cricket stadium - covering its rebuild, naming, design and the World Cup, IPL, political and concert events it has hosted.
wikis.body:
## The stadium

- An international cricket stadium in Motera, Ahmedabad, Gujarat, India, with a total capacity of 132,000 - "the world's largest cricket stadium and the largest overall stadium in the world by capacity". Owned and operated by the Gujarat Cricket Association.
- Groundbreaking 2015, built 2015-2020, opened 24 February 2020, at a cost of ₹800 crore (US$83 million). Architect Populous; builder and main contractor Larsen and Toubro; structural engineer Walter P Moore. 63 acres, oval field 160 m x 140 m, Bermuda grass, 11 centre pitches, four dressing rooms, 76 corporate boxes.
- It replaced Sardar Patel Gujarat Stadium, demolished in 2015, and on completion replaced the Melbourne Cricket Ground as the world's largest cricket stadium.
- Named after prime minister Narendra Modi, who proposed the rebuild while Chief Minister of Gujarat (2001-2014) and President of the Gujarat Cricket Association (2009-2014). Originally called Motera Stadium, it was renamed at its official inauguration by president Ram Nath Kovind on 24 February 2021.
- Tenants: India's men's and women's national teams, Gujarat's men's and women's teams, Gujarat Titans (2022-) and Gujarat Giants (2023-). The stadium will also be used for the 2030 Commonwealth Games.

## Events

- Opened to the public on 24 February 2020 with the "Namaste Trump" event for US president Donald Trump's visit, with an approximate attendance of 125,000.
- First international cricket match: a day-night pink-ball Test between India and England beginning 24 February 2021.
- Hosted five matches of the 2023 Cricket World Cup including the opening game and the final, where Australia beat India by 6 wickets before 92,453 on 19 November 2023.
- Hosted seven matches of the 2026 ICC Men's T20 World Cup, including the final on 8 March 2026, where India beat New Zealand by 96 runs before 86,824 - India's record 255/5 being the highest total in a T20 World Cup final.
- Hosted the 2022, 2023, 2025 and 2026 IPL finals, the 2022 National Games of India opening ceremony (29 September 2022), the 75 Years of Friendship through Cricket event with Modi and Anthony Albanese (9 March 2023), and two Coldplay shows on 25 and 26 January 2025.

## Conflicting attendance and cost figures in the article

- Record attendance: the infobox gives 111,989 (Coldplay), while the Notable achievements section calls the 2022 IPL final's 104,859 "the highest attendance in the history of the stadium and cricket in general"; the Namaste Trump event is given as about 125,000.
- Cost: ₹800 crore (US$83 million) final, against a ₹700 crore estimate rendered as both "US$73 million" and "$93 million" in different sections.
- Parking: 13000 in the infobox (tagged failed verification) against "3,000 cars and 10,000 two-wheelers" in the design section.

wikis.title: Narendra Modi Stadium, Ahmedabad - construction, design, tournaments and records
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the world's largest cricket stadium in Motera, Ahmedabad - how it was rebuilt and named, its design and facilities, and the World Cup, IPL, political and concert events it has hosted.
wikis.body:
## The stadium

- "Narendra Modi Stadium is an international cricket stadium in Motera, Ahmedabad, Gujarat, India. With a total capacity of 132,000, it is the world's largest cricket stadium and the largest overall stadium in the world by capacity."
- Address: Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel Sports Enclave, Motera, Ahmedabad, Gujarat, India. Coordinates 23°05'29"N 72°35'50"E; elevation 84 m (276 ft).
- Owner and operator: Gujarat Cricket Association. 76 executive suites. Surface Bermuda grass. Field size 160 metres (180 yd) x 140 metres (150 yd); oval. Acreage 63 acres (25 ha).
- Record attendance in the infobox: 111,989 (Coldplay's Music of the Spheres World Tour).
- Construction: groundbreaking 2015, built 2015-2020, opened 24 February 2020. Cost ₹800 crore (US$83 million). Architect Populous; builder and main contractor Larsen and Toubro; structural engineer Walter P Moore Engineers and Consultants.
- Tenants: India men's and women's national teams (2020-present), Gujarat men's and women's teams (2020-present), Gujarat Titans (2022-present), Gujarat Giants (2023-present). End names: Adani Pavilion End and Jio End.
- Public transit: Narendra Modi Stadium; Ahmedabad Metro Red Line, Motera Stadium station. Parking given as 13000 in the infobox, tagged "[failed verification]".
- It is named after the prime minister of India, Narendra Modi, and sits near the Sabarmati River. It will also be used for the 2030 Commonwealth Games.

## International firsts and lasts (infobox)

- First men's Test 24-28 February 2021: India v England. Last men's Test 2-6 October 2025: India v West Indies.
- First men's ODI 6 February 2022: India v West Indies. Last men's ODI 12 February 2025: India v England.
- First men's T20I 12 March 2021: India v England. Last men's T20I 8 March 2026: India v New Zealand.
- First women's ODI 24 October 2024: India v New Zealand. Last women's ODI 29 October 2024: India v New Zealand.
- Source given as Cricinfo.

## Origins and naming

- It replaced Sardar Patel Gujarat Stadium, which hosted cricket in the city until its demolition in 2015, including the 1987, 1996 and 2011 Cricket World Cups. In 2014 it was decided a new stadium should be built on the same plot.
- Originally named Motera Stadium. "It took five years to build, at an estimated cost of ₹800 crore (US$83 million). After completion, the new arena replaced the Melbourne Cricket Ground as the world's largest cricket stadium." It has four dressing rooms, 11 centre pitches and two practice grounds, which can also host domestic matches.
- On 24 February 2020 it first opened to the public with the Namaste Trump event, "which saw an approximate attendance of 125,000 people".
- On 24 February 2021 it was officially inaugurated by Indian president Ram Nath Kovind and renamed "Narendra Modi Stadium" in honour of Modi, who had been Chief Minister of Gujarat (2001-2014) and President of the Gujarat Cricket Association (2009-2014); the ceremony was hours before the venue's first international cricket match, a day-night pink-ball Test between India and England.
- On 29 September 2022 the opening ceremony of the 2022 National Games of India was held there.

## Domestic cricket and media

- Home ground of the Gujarat cricket team, the Gujarat women's cricket team and the IPL franchise Gujarat Titans. Two further grounds, "Narendra Modi Stadium A Ground" and "Narendra Modi Stadium B Ground", sit on the eastern side and host Ranji Trophy and other domestic matches.
- The 2022 Vijay Hazare Trophy final was held there: Maharashtra scored 248/9 and Saurashtra chased it in 46.3 overs, with hundreds from Maharashtra's Ruturaj Gaikwad and Saurashtra's Sheldon Jackson.
- In 2021 the stadium featured in an episode of History TV18's documentary show Modern Marvels, depicting the entire construction.

## Records listed

- Test - best bowling in a match: Axar Patel 11/70, India v England, 13 February 2021. Most runs: Rahul Dravid (India) 771 runs (Mat 7, Inn 14, HS 222, Ave 59.30, SR 49.10, 100s-3, 50s-1), Sachin Tendulkar 642, VVS Laxman 574 - "including stats of Sardar Patel Stadium". Most wickets: Anil Kumble (India) 36 wickets (Mat 7, Runs 964, BBI 7/115, BBM 10/233, Ave 26.77, Econ 2.29, SR 70.1, 5W/I 3, 10W/M 1) - also including Sardar Patel Stadium stats.
- ODI - highest individual score: Devon Conway 152 (121), New Zealand v England, 2023. Best bowling: Prasidh Krishna 4/14 (9.0 overs), India v West Indies, 9 February 2022. Most runs: Rohit Sharma 355. Most wickets: Kapil Dev (India) 10 wickets (Mat 6, Runs 156, Best 3/26, Ave 15.60, Econ 3.04) - the last two including Sardar Patel Stadium stats.

## Contradictions inside the page

- Record attendance: the infobox gives 111,989 for Coldplay's Music of the Spheres World Tour, while the Notable achievements section says the 2022 IPL final "was attended by 104,859 people, the highest attendance in the history of the stadium and cricket in general". The Namaste Trump event is separately given "an approximate attendance of 125,000 people", and a cited reference is titled "1.25 lakh to attend 'Kem chho Trump' show in Ahmedabad". The design section also notes an IPL 2024 Royal Challengers Bangalore v Rajasthan Royals game with "a near houseful crowd of over 1 lakh".
- Parking: the infobox says 13000 (tagged failed verification), while the Design and facilities section says "The parking lot can accommodate 3,000 cars and 10,000 two-wheelers."
- Cost: the infobox and lead give ₹800 crore (US$83 million); the Conception section says reconstruction was estimated at "₹700 crores (₹7 billion (US$73 million))" and the Building work section gives "around ₹700 crore ($93 million)" for the same estimate.
- Rooms: the Design section says the stadium has "a 55-room clubhouse" and separately lists "50 rooms" among the premises' facilities.
- Completion: the Conception section says the redevelopment was "originally planned to be completed in 2019" and finished February 2020, while the Building work section says it "was planned to be finished in 2 years" from a January 2017 start.
- IPL finals hosted: the Service section says the stadium hosted the 2022, 2023 and 2025 IPL finals, the Domestic cricket section says it "hosted the 2022 and 2023 IPL finals", and the IPL Finals table also lists the 2026 final.
- The contractor is called "Larsen & Toubro" in the bid table and "Larsen & Turbo" in the sentence naming the winner.

wikis.title: Planning, bidding and construction of the Narendra Modi Stadium
wikis.summary: How Modi's proposal replaced a renovation, how the reconstruction contract was tendered and won by Larsen & Toubro, and how the build ran to February 2020.
wikis.body:
## Conception

- The idea to build a new stadium was proposed by Narendra Modi himself, who was president of the Gujarat Cricket Association and Chief Minister of Gujarat at the same time. Shortly before Modi moved to Delhi on becoming prime minister, minor upgrades and development at the pavilion end were discussed; "Modi asked officials to build a new, larger stadium instead of pursuing minor renovation work".
- In October 2015 the stadium was demolished for reconstruction, "though some media referred to it as a renovation". The total cost of reconstruction was estimated at ₹700 crores (₹7 billion, US$73 million); "However, the final cost was reported at ₹800 crore (US$83 million). The redevelopment, originally planned to be completed in 2019, finished in February 2020."

## Bids

- After demolition began at the end of 2015, the GCA issued a request for tender on 1 January 2016 in The Times of India and The Indian Express. Nine bidders bought tender documents; three submitted technical and financial bids on time: the Shapoorji Pallonji Group, Nagarjuna Construction Company and Larsen & Toubro.
- A Tender Commercial Committee of nine experts evaluated the tenders, with STUP Consultants, a Mumbai civil engineering consultancy, appointed project management consultant. Bidders were evaluated on efficiency, resources, project length and ease of implementation, among others.

| Bidder | Bid | Evaluation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Larsen & Toubro | ₹677.19 crore (US$70 million) | Lowest-1 (L1) - winning bid, financially lowest and technically ranked first |
| Shapoorji Pallonji & Co. Ltd. | ₹847.88 crore (US$88 million) | Lowest-2 (L2) |
| Nagarjuna Construction Co. Ltd. | ₹1,065 crore (US$110 million) | Highest (L3) |

## Building work

- L&T took over construction in December 2016. On 16 January 2017 the Gujarat Cricket Association oversaw the project, which formally began the same day. "The stadium was planned to be finished in 2 years, and the reconstruction project was estimated to cost around ₹700 crore ($93 million)."
- Final completion was in February 2020, and it hosted an England-India day-night test match in 2021.
- Mumbai-based commercial kitchen consultant "Span Asia" was hired to work with Populous and L&T on concession counters, main stadium kitchens, player kitchens, VIP/VVIP and corporate boxes, press and media boxes, pantries and the GCA Club.

wikis.title: Design and facilities
wikis.summary: The stadium's stands, roof, pitches, drainage and the sports and hospitality facilities on the 63-acre site.
wikis.body:
- Built on 63 acres with four entry points, one of which has a metro line. 76 corporate boxes holding 25 persons each, a 55-room clubhouse, an Olympic size swimming pool, and four dressing rooms. A food court and hospitality area in each spectator stand. An indoor cricket academy and practice pitches with dormitories for 40 athletes.
- Stands generally follow a two-tier structure with a three-tier main pavilion. The two-tier structure is supported from beneath by numerous Y-shaped columns, eliminating pillars so spectators have an unobstructed view of the field from all parts of the stadium.
- An LED light system lines the inside edge of the roof, eliminating the need for floodlights and reducing shadows on the pitch. The LEDs are installed on an antibacterial, fireproof PTFE-membrane canopy covering 30 metres (98 ft) of the 55 metres (180 ft) width of the seating area. The roof was installed by Walter P. Moore and "was specifically designed to be lightweight and separate from the seating bowls in order to improve earthquake resistance".
- 11 centre pitches. The playing field has sensors detecting when the grass needs water, which can automatically activate 67 fully automated underground pop-up sprinklers. Ground surface Bermuda grass, with an extensive drainage system.
- Premises facilities include an indoor cricket practice area, badminton, tennis and squash courts, a table tennis area, a 3D projector theatre, three practice grounds and 50 rooms.
- Parking for 3,000 cars and 10,000 two-wheelers. A ramp is designed to move around 60,000 people simultaneously. The upper stands can remain empty for smaller events while keeping a crowd atmosphere; an IPL 2024 Royal Challengers Bangalore v Rajasthan Royals game saw "a near houseful crowd of over 1 lakh".
- A skywalk bridge to the nearest metro station was planned, with construction to be completed after September 2020; "As of November 2023, the skywalk is yet to be constructed."
- The gallery includes images of the Namaste Trump event, an "Iron Bull at the stadium entrance", and the 2023 Border-Gavaskar Trophy fourth Test.

wikis.title: Political and non-cricket events at the stadium
wikis.summary: The Namaste Trump rally, the 75 Years of Friendship through Cricket event, the 2022 National Games opening and the Coldplay concerts.
wikis.body:
## Namaste Trump

- In 2020 the stadium hosted the "Namaste Trump" event, organised for the maiden visit of US president Donald Trump to India by prime minister Narendra Modi; 125,000 attendees were recorded. The event "mirrored the 'Howdy Modi' event held in Houston, Texas, US".
- "Before it became clear that the complex would continue to use the name 'Sardar Patel Sports Enclave' and that only the stadium would receive a new name, Congress first criticized the decision."

## 75 Years of Friendship through Cricket

- On 9 March 2023 the stadium hosted the 75 Years of Friendship through Cricket Event, attended by Narendra Modi and visiting Australian prime minister Anthony Albanese, held alongside the fourth Test of the Border-Gavaskar Trophy between India and Australia.
- The two prime ministers sang their national anthems and shook hands with the players, visited a gallery on 75 years of cricket friendship, took a lap of honour in a specially designed golf cart while the crowd waved Indian and Australian flags, and tossed the coin to start the Test.

## Other events

- On 29 September 2022 the opening ceremony of the 2022 National Games of India was held at the stadium, inaugurated by Prime Minister Modi.
- British rock band Coldplay played two shows at the stadium on 25 and 26 January 2025 as part of their Music of the Spheres World Tour; the infobox gives the stadium's record attendance as 111,989 for that tour.
