wikis.title: Lang Park (Suncorp Stadium), Brisbane
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on Lang Park in Milton, Brisbane - officially Brisbane Stadium (Lang Park) and known as Suncorp Stadium - covering its history, redevelopments, tenants, planned Olympic upgrade and the tournaments, internationals and concerts it has hosted.
wikis.body:
## The stadium

- Lang Park, "officially named Brisbane Stadium (Lang Park) and known under naming rights as Suncorp Stadium", is a multi-purpose stadium in Milton, Brisbane, Queensland, Australia, at 40 Castlemaine Street.
- Capacity 52,500; grass (Strathayr turf); field 136 x 82 m, rectangular. Owner Stadiums Queensland (2003-present); operator ASM Global.
- Groundbreaking 1911, opened 1914; the infobox gives cost as "A$280 million (2003 redevelopment)"; architects HOK Sport & PDT Architects in Association, structural engineer Ove Arup & Partners.
- Home ground of the Brisbane Broncos and the Dolphins (NRL), the Queensland Reds (Super Rugby) and Brisbane Roar FC (A-League Men); frequent host of the Australia national rugby union team and both Australian national soccer teams. Nicknamed "the Cauldron".
- The redevelopment was "the first major sporting facility in Australia with no car parking"; access is by foot from the CBD, the Milton CityCat stop (opened January 2015), buses, and Milton and Roma Street stations.

## History

- The site was the North Brisbane Cemetery, Brisbane's primary cemetery until 1875; the Paddington Cemeteries Act (1911) redeveloped it as a recreational site, and in 1914 it was fenced and named Lang Park after John Dunmore Lang.
- Athletics, soccer and then rugby league tenancies followed; the Brisbane Rugby League took over the lease in 1957 and the ground became a major home of rugby league in Queensland.
- The Lang Park Trust (1962) built the Frank Burke Stand (1962), Ron McAuliffe Stand (1975) and Western Grandstand (1994). Suncorp has held naming rights since 1994.
- The Brisbane Broncos played there 1988-1992 before moving to ANZ Stadium, returning in 2003 after the early-2000s redevelopment into a 52,500 all-seater rectangular stadium.
- It was damaged in the 2010-2011 Queensland floods, the whole playing field covered by flood water, with an electrical fire in a transformer room but "no major damage from the fire".
- It hosted the NRL's inaugural Magic Round in 2019 (agreement to host in Brisbane until the 2027 season) and the 2021 NRL Grand Final on 3 October 2021.

## Planned Olympic upgrade

- October 2025: Premier of Queensland David Crisafulli announced a "next generation" renovation in time for the 2032 Summer Olympics, with accessibility improvements and a capacity expansion.
- June 2026 plans: wraparound LED video screens, "supersized" scoreboards, media mesh screens at both ends, new terrace viewing platforms and entertainment zones, new external screens, and "an increase in capacity to 54,000 fans", with construction "set to begin by the end of 2026". A cited October 2025 Courier Mail headline instead reads "'Roofed 65,000-seat stadium': Suncorp expansion prayers answered".
- The stadium is set to host rugby sevens and the football final at the 2032 Summer Olympics.

## Events hosted

- Tournaments: 2003 Rugby World Cup (7 matches), 2008 Rugby League World Cup including the final, 2015 AFC Asian Cup (7 matches), 2017 Rugby League World Cup semi-final and final, 2023 FIFA Women's World Cup (8 matches including the third place play-off, capacity reduced to 49,461 for media requirements), two Super Rugby grand finals, and ten scheduled 2027 Men's Rugby World Cup fixtures from 2 October to 31 October 2027.
- 42 Australia rugby league internationals, 36 rugby union internationals, and men's and women's soccer internationals, including a scheduled Australia v Brazil friendly on 29 September 2026.
- Boxing: Manny Pacquiao vs. Jeff Horn for the WBO welterweight championship, "with 51,052 people in attendance".
- Concerts from Robbie Williams in December 2006 through Ed Sheeran (20-22 February 2026) and Robbie Williams (20 November 2026).

## Conflicting attendance records in the article

- Infobox: record attendance 59,185 (2022/23 Ed Sheeran); the concert table matches this to 18 February 2023 and says all three February 2023 Ed Sheeran shows "broke the record for attendance".
- "Facts" box: "Record crowd 52,540 - Rugby league, 12 July 2017, Queensland vs New South Wales, 2017 State of Origin series".
- Body: the 29 July 2006 Bledisloe Cup match "saw a new ground record set for crowd size, at 52,498".
- Test table: the 2008 World Cup final (23 November 2008, 50,599) is marked "Record Test attendance at Lang Park".

wikis.title: Lang Park (Suncorp Stadium), Brisbane: history, redevelopment, tenants and events hosted
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on Lang Park in Milton, Brisbane - its origins on a former cemetery, its redevelopments, tenants and capacity, and the tournaments, internationals and concerts it has hosted.
wikis.body:
## The stadium

- Lang Park, "officially named Brisbane Stadium (Lang Park) and known under naming rights as Suncorp Stadium", is a multi-purpose stadium in the Brisbane suburb of Milton, Queensland, Australia.
- Address given as 40 Castlemaine Street, Milton; coordinates 27°27'53"S 153°0'34"E.
- Former names listed in the infobox: Lang Park; Suncorp-Metway Stadium.
- Owner: Stadiums Queensland (2003-present). Operator: ASM Global. Website suncorpstadium.com.au.
- Capacity 52,500. Surface grass (Strathayr turf). Field size 136 x 82 m, rectangular. Video screens (x2) and lights.
- Construction: groundbreaking 1911, opened 1914. Cost given as "A$280 million (2003 redevelopment)". Architects HOK Sport & PDT Architects in Association; structural engineer Ove Arup & Partners.
- Record attendance in the infobox: 59,185 (2022/23 Ed Sheeran).
- Public transit: Milton and Roma Street stations; the Milton CityCat stop, which opened in January 2015; 375 City bus and 385 CityXpress "BUZ" bus (every 10-15 minutes, 6am to 11pm, 7 days a week); match-day shuttles from the CBD, Chermside, Carindale and Eight Mile Plains.
- "the redevelopment was the first major sporting facility in Australia with no car parking", with no public parking at the stadium; paid parking stations are within 10 minutes' walk in the CBD. Ticket holders get free transport on match days.
- Nicknamed "the Cauldron".

## Tenants (infobox)

- Rugby league: Brisbane Broncos (NRL) 1988-1992 and 2003-present; Dolphins (NRL) 2023-present; South Queensland Crushers (NRL) 1995-1997; Queensland rugby league team 1980-2000 and 2003-present; Brisbane Broncos Women (NRLW, selected matches); Australia national rugby league team (selected matches).
- Rugby union: Queensland Reds (Super Rugby) 2005-present; Australia national rugby union team (selected matches).
- Association football: Brisbane Roar (A-League Men) 2005-2020 and 2022-present; Brisbane Roar Women (A-League Women, selected matches); Australia men's and women's soccer teams (selected matches).

## Average attendance per team (table)

| Team | Sport | Average | Season |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Queensland Maroons | Rugby league | 52,433 (only one game) | 2023 |
| Brisbane Broncos (NRL) | Rugby league | 41,612 | 2023 |
| Dolphins (NRL) | Rugby league | 29,516 | 2023 |
| Brisbane Roar | Association football | 18,556 | 2007-08 |
| Queensland Reds | Rugby union | 14,516 | 2024 |

## Contradictions inside the page

- Record crowd: the infobox gives record attendance 59,185 (Ed Sheeran, 2022/23); the concert table gives Ed Sheeran 18 February 2023 as 59,185 and notes all three February 2023 shows "broke the record for attendance"; the "Facts" box gives "Record crowd 52,540 - Rugby league, 12 July 2017, Queensland vs New South Wales, 2017 State of Origin series"; the body says the 29 July 2006 Bledisloe Cup match "saw a new ground record set for crowd size, at 52,498".
- Great Britain's last rugby league test at the ground: the body says "On 8 November 2006, a crowd of 44,358 saw the Great Britain national rugby league team play against Australia for the last time"; the test-match table lists that fixture (Australia 33-10 Great Britain, 44,358, 2006 Tri-Nations) as 18 November 2006.
- 2017 Rugby League World Cup semi-final: the body says the venue "played host to the first semi-final on 24 November and the tournament final on 2 December"; the test table dates the semi-final (Australia 54-6 Fiji, 22,073) 23 November 2017.
- Queensland Reds arrival: the body says "In 2006, the stadium became the new home of the Queensland Reds Super Rugby team"; the infobox lists the Reds as tenants from 2005.
- Brisbane Roar arrival: the body says "In 2005, the newly established football team Queensland Roar of the A-League also elected to play their home games at Suncorp Stadium"; the infobox lists Brisbane Roar from 2005, and the 1996/1997 NSL grand final is dated 25 May 1997 in the body while a cited quote in the references also gives 25 May 1997.
- Rugby union table: rows 15 and 16 are both dated 27 August 2011, one as the 2011 Tri Nations Series / Bledisloe Cup (Australia 25-20 New Zealand, 51,858) and the other as the 2012 Bledisloe Cup (Australia 18-18 New Zealand, 51,888).
- First rugby league there: the body says Lang Park "hosted its first game of first grade rugby league during the 1930s, with regular BRL games commencing there in 1955", and separately that it hosted its first Brisbane rugby league grand final in 1958.
- 1961 BRL grand final: the body says "A record crowd of 19,824 saw Northern Suburbs defeat Fortitude Valley at Lang Park in the BRL grand final in September 1961", while the cited reference is titled "Norths thrash Valleys 29-5".
- Planned Olympic capacity: the body says the June 2026 plans include "an increase in capacity to 54,000 fans", while a cited October 2025 Courier Mail headline reads "'Roofed 65,000-seat stadium': Suncorp expansion prayers answered".

## Other events and records noted

- Boxing: hosted Manny Pacquiao vs. Jeff Horn for the WBO welterweight championship, "with 51,052 people in attendance".
- Men's soccer internationals listed include Australia 1-1 Paraguay on 7 October 2006 (47,609), Australia 1-0 Iraq on 1 June 2008 (48,678, 2010 FIFA World Cup qualifier), Australia 1-0 New Zealand on 22 September 2022 (25,392), and a scheduled friendly Australia v Brazil on 29 September 2026 with no result or attendance given.
- Women's soccer internationals listed: Argentina 0-2 New Zealand and Australia 4-1 South Korea both on 3 March 2019; Australia 0-1 Canada on 3 September 2022 (25,016); Australia 1-3 Brazil on 28 November 2024 (47,501).
- Forty-two Australia rugby league internationals hosted, the first on 30 July 1962 (Australia 10-17 Great Britain, 34,766) and the most recent listed 18 October 2024 (Australia 18-0 Tonga, 33,196, 2024 Pacific Championships); the 2008 World Cup final on 23 November 2008 (Australia 20-34, 50,599) is marked "Record Test attendance at Lang Park".
- Thirty-six rugby union internationals listed, from 27 July 1996 (Australia 25-32 New Zealand, 40,167) to 19 July 2025 (Australia 19-27 British & Irish Lions, 52,229, 2025 Tom Richards Trophy).
- Three non-Australia rugby league tests, all England matches: v Wales 10 June 1975 (6,000, England lost 12-7); v New Zealand 15 November 2008 (26,659, lost 32-22); v Samoa in the 2014 Four Nations (47,813, England won 32-26).
- Popular culture: Wally Lewis became known as "The Emperor of Lang Park"; a XXXX advertisement jingle is quoted. A Sports Media Hall of Fame was introduced in 2006 by Queensland Minister for Sport Tom Barton, with five inductees (George Lovejoy, Jack Reardon, Steve Ricketts, Gerry Collins, Frank O'Callaghan).
- Statues outside the stadium: Wally Lewis, Darren Lockyer, Mal Meninga, Arthur Beetson, John Eales, Allan Langer, and the Matildas 2023 World Cup team.
- Awards: in 2009, as part of the Q150 celebrations, named one of the Q150 Icons of Queensland for its role as a "structure and engineering feat".
- Controversies: on 16 June 2011 The Weekend Australian reported the stadium risked losing Queensland NRL finals to Sydney or having capacity limited to 25,000 because legislation allowed only 24 'special events' (attendance above 25,000) a year; on 6 September 2011 legislation lifted the limit to 35,000 for those 24 events. The pitch's grass quality was criticised by coaches and players during the 2015 AFC Asian Cup.
- In 2009 the stadium "was ranked 2nd to Cardiff's Millennium Stadium" and above Twickenham. New Zealand journalist Wynne Gray called it perhaps the best rugby stadium in the world: "It is so intimate you can hear the smack of bodies, the boot on leather, you feel the power and rhythm of the games."

wikis.title: Origins and early tenants of Lang Park (1875-1957)
wikis.summary: How the site moved from Brisbane's North Brisbane Cemetery to a fenced park named Lang Park and through athletics, soccer and rugby league tenancies.
wikis.body:
- The site was originally the North Brisbane Cemetery and until 1875 was Brisbane's primary cemetery.
- By 1911 the area was heavily populated, so the Paddington Cemeteries Act (1911) was introduced and the site was redeveloped as a recreational site.
- In 1914 it was fenced off and named Lang Park after John Dunmore Lang. It was used as a parade ground during World War I.
- In 1932 the ground was leased by the Queensland Amateur Athletics Association (QAAA). In 1935 the Queensland Soccer Council (QSC) became a sub-tenant of the QAAA, intending it as the home ground for Brisbane soccer fixtures, leaving the Brisbane Cricket Ground. The Latrobe Soccer Club became a sub-tenant of the QSC.
- By 1937 the QSC was considering sub-leasing Lang Park to "another code of football" (most likely Western Suburbs Rugby League) as it "was not satisfied with the financial returns ... under the sub-lease to the Latrobe-Milton club". Latrobe replied: "'If no action Is taken to introduce the Ipswich clubs into the Brisbane competition this' season ... the Latrobe-Milton Club cannot accept an increase in rental for Lang Park. Give us competition play with Ipswich and my club will hold the ground as headquarters for the code."
- On 11 February 1950 the Lang Park Police Citizens Youth Club officially opened, prompted by concern about rising juvenile delinquency; boxing, wrestling, basketball and gymnastics still take place there.
- "Contemporaneous records are scant", but it appears the QSC did not renew its lease after World War II.
- In 1953 the Brisbane Rugby League (BRL) amalgamated with the Queensland Rugby League (QRL); QRL secretary Ron McAullife negotiated a 21-year lease from the Brisbane City Council, and the QRL contributed GBP 17,000 to the ground's development.

wikis.title: Lang Park as the home of Queensland rugby league (1955-1994)
wikis.summary: The BRL and QRL years at Lang Park - grand finals, crowd records, the Lang Park Trust and its grandstands, and the arrival and departure of the Brisbane Broncos.
wikis.body:
- Regular BRL games began in 1955; the page also says the ground hosted its first first-grade rugby league game "during the 1930s".
- 1958: hosted its first Brisbane rugby league grand final, Brothers defeating Valleys 22 points to 7.
- September 1961: "a record crowd of 19,824 saw Northern Suburbs defeat Fortitude Valley at Lang Park in the BRL grand final" (the cited article is titled "Norths thrash Valleys 29-5").
- In the 1960s Fonda Metassa "famously burst from the back of an ambulance to return to the field after being carted off injured in a match for Norths against Redcliffe".
- Heavy QRL use made the ground no longer viable as a public recreation facility because of spoilage of the running track.
- 1962: the Lang Park Trust was created under an act of Parliament, enabling the Frank Burke Stand (1962), Ron McAuliffe Stand (1975) and Western Grandstand (1994). Its board held one Queensland Government member, one Brisbane City Council member, two Queensland Rugby League members and one Brisbane Rugby League member.
- From the 1960s it hosted interstate and international rugby league, including the inaugural State of Origin match. It was the home ground of the Western Suburbs Panthers until 1972, when they moved to Purtell Park in Bardon.
- 1988: the Brisbane Broncos entered the NSWRL premiership alongside the Gold Coast Chargers and Newcastle Knights, playing out of Lang Park until 1992, when they moved to the 60,000-capacity ANZ Stadium (the 1982 Commonwealth Games stadium). The move followed a dispute over the Broncos' sponsor Power's Brewery competing with QRL sponsor XXXX.
- 1994: Lang Park was renamed Suncorp Stadium after naming sponsorship from Queensland financial institution Suncorp; the Western Stand was built that year, replacing the Frank Burke Stand.
- 25 May 1997: the 1996/1997 National Soccer League Grand Final was played before "then a capacity crowd of 40,446", Brisbane Strikers FC beating Sydney United FC 2-0.

wikis.title: The 2000s redevelopment of Lang Park and the events that followed
wikis.summary: The early-2000s rebuild into a 52,500-seat rectangular stadium and the tenancies, records, floods and finals that followed.
wikis.body:
- Lang Park was heavily redeveloped in the early 2000s into a "52,500 all-seater state of the art rectangular stadium"; the infobox gives the cost as A$280 million for the 2003 redevelopment, and Stadiums Queensland assumed ownership in 2003.
- The redeveloped stadium first hosted rugby union at the 2003 Rugby World Cup.
- 2005: the newly established A-League team Queensland Roar elected to play home games at Suncorp Stadium.
- 2006: the Queensland Reds moved in from Ballymore Stadium; Queensland Rugby Union CEO Theo Psaros said "our hearts may be at Ballymore but our heads say it's time to move."
- 29 July 2006: the Bledisloe Cup clash between the Wallabies and All Blacks returned to Brisbane for the first time in over a decade for the 2006 Tri Nations Series; Australia narrowly lost and "the game saw a new ground record set for crowd size, at 52,498".
- 7 October 2006: Australia 1-1 Paraguay friendly, at which Tony Vidmar, Stan Lazaridis, Zeljko Kalac and goal scorer Tony Popovic retired from international soccer.
- 8 November 2006 (dated 18 November 2006 in the test table): a crowd of 44,358 saw Great Britain play Australia at the ground for the last time.
- 2010-2011 Queensland floods: the stadium suffered significant damage with the entire playing field covered by flood water; an electrical fire started in a transformer room due to water ingress, "however there was no major damage from the fire".
- 2011 A-League Grand Final: a crowd of over 50,000; Brisbane Roar scored twice in the last five minutes to level with the Central Coast Mariners and won 4-2 on penalties.
- September 2016: the video screens installed in 2003 were announced for replacement; construction started March 2017 and finished in early May 2017 in time for an NRL double header.
- 2019: hosted the NRL's inaugural Magic Round, all eight matches of a round at one venue. The NRL has an agreement to host Magic Round in Brisbane until the 2027 season. The 2025 Magic Round ran 1-4 May 2025 with a total attendance of 149,329.
- 2020: the Melbourne Storm played their "home" finals there because Victoria was locked down during its second wave of coronavirus infections.
- 26 June 2021: Queensland lost the State of Origin match to New South Wales 26-0 and with it the series.
- A COVID-19 lockdown in New South Wales that began 26 June 2021 and ran into October led the stadium to host twenty-one extra games, including the 2021 NRL Grand Final on 3 October 2021 - the second rugby league premiership grand final played outside Sydney, after the 1997 Super League Grand Final.

wikis.title: Planned 2032 Olympic redevelopment of Suncorp Stadium
wikis.summary: The announced 'next generation' renovation of the stadium ahead of the Brisbane 2032 Summer Olympics and what the June 2026 plans include.
wikis.body:
- In October 2025 the Premier of Queensland, David Crisafulli, announced the stadium would receive a "next generation" renovation in time for the 2032 Summer Olympics, "expected to receive accessibility improvements, and an expansion in capacity".
- Plans for the Olympic redevelopment were unveiled in June 2026 and include wraparound LED video screens, "supersized" scoreboards, media mesh screens fitted at both ends of the stadium, new terrace viewing platforms and entertainment zones with both seated and standing areas, new external screens, and "an increase in capacity to 54,000 fans", with construction "set to begin by the end of 2026".
- A cited October 2025 Courier Mail headline reads "'Roofed 65,000-seat stadium': Suncorp expansion prayers answered", which does not match the 54,000 figure in the body.
- The stadium "is set to host Rugby Sevens, and the final for Football in the 2032 Summer Olympics".
- The article is categorised under "Venues of the 2032 Summer Olympics", "Olympic rugby venues" and "Olympic stadiums".

wikis.title: 2034 Winter Olympics (Utah 2034)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the XXVII Olympic Winter Games, scheduled for Utah from February 10 to 26, 2034, covering host selection, the doping-clause dispute, preparations, venues, branding and broadcast rights.
wikis.body:
## Overview

- "The 2034 Winter Olympics, officially the XXVII Olympic Winter Games, and branded as Utah 2034, is a future international multi-sport event scheduled to take place in the U.S. state of Utah from February 10 to 26, 2034."
- Infobox: Location Utah, United States; Opening February 10, 2034; Closing February 26, 2034; Stadium Rice-Eccles Stadium.
- Sequence given: Winter, after "Alpes 2030", before "TBD 2038"; Summer, after Brisbane 2032, before "TBD 2036".
- "They will be the fifth Winter Olympics, and tenth overall, to be hosted by the United States"; having hosted the 2002 Winter Olympics, Salt Lake City "will join St. Moritz, Lake Placid, Innsbruck, and Cortina d'Ampezzo as the fifth city to have hosted or co-hosted multiple Winter Olympic Games."
- "This will also be the first Olympics held in the United States that will be branded under a host U.S. state instead of a city."
- Note on the branding in other languages: Arapaho *Niico'ooowu' 2034*; Gosiute Shoshoni *Tit'-so-pi 2034*; Navajo *Sooléí 2034*; Shoshoni *Soónkahni 2034*.

## Host selection

- Under Olympic Agenda 2020 the IOC Future Host Commission runs non-committal "continuous dialogue" with interested parties, then recommends preferred candidates for "targeted dialogue" with the IOC executive board, after which the bid goes to the delegates for final approval.
- November 29, 2023: the IOC Executive Board invited the United States Olympic & Paralympic Committee (USOPC) to targeted dialogue, "with Salt Lake City named the sole preferred candidate".
- July 24, 2024, at the 142nd IOC Session in Paris, France: Salt Lake City elected host "via a referendum to the 95 IOC delegates."
- Election result table: Salt Lake City, United States - Yes 83, No 6, Abstention 6.

## WADA vs USADA conflict

- "The IOC insisted that Utah agree that it may 'terminate Olympic host city contracts in cases where the supreme authority of the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) in the fight against doping is not fully respected or if the application of the world antidoping code is hindered or undermined.'"
- The page says this "was intended to undermine the United States Department of Justice's criminal investigation into the allegations that the World Anti-Doping Agency failed to sanction and covered up drug use by Chinese swimmers."
- "The Chinese have accused the western mainstream media, in particular The New York Times, of atrocity propaganda against the Chinese athletes."
- "IOC president Thomas Bach has attempted to alleviate concerns that the city could lose its second Olympics if organizers do not fulfill an agreement to play a peacemaker between anti-doping authorities. Bach downplayed the gravity of a termination clause that the IOC inserted into Utah's host contract in July."

## Development, preparations and cost

- The 2002 Games "left a strong legacy", with venues such as Utah Olympic Park continuing to host international events and world championships; "in the 2013-14 season, Utah hosted 16 winter sports events, contributing $27.3 million to the state economy."
- The USOPC said in 2022 it was "already in dialogue with the IOC, not yet for a specific year but as part of their evolving process", and had named Salt Lake City its preferred candidate for a future U.S. Winter Olympics in 2022, "citing its existing infrastructure."
- "A report by the Future Host Commission estimated that the privately-funded Games would cost $3.9 billion. By comparison, a record $51 billion was spent by Sochi for the Winter Games twenty years prior."

## Venues

- "The Games will utilize nearly all of the facilities originally constructed for the 2002 Winter Olympics", with these differences:
  - Alpine skiing at Snowbasin only, instead of being split between Snowbasin, Deer Valley and Park City.
  - Big air events "will provisionally take place at a temporary venue constructed in downtown Salt Lake City at the 'Block 85' parking lot across from Delta Center (South Temple and 300 West)", the 2002 medals plaza site.
  - "In a reversal from 2002, ice hockey will take place at Delta Center, while Maverik Center will host figure skating and short-track speed skating."
  - Curling on a temporary rink at the Salt Palace convention center instead of The Ice Sheet at Ogden; organizers cited "an unwillingness of Ogden managers to expand their venue with temporary seating, and a desire to host the event in Salt Lake City proper to capitalize on curling's growing American popularity."
- Early April 2024: Organizing Committee president Fraser Bullock "stated that he would not rule out the possibility" that facilities built for new or relocated professional teams (such as the proposed Power District Stadium for a possible MLB team) could be used, "noting that the exact venue plans may evolve as the Games draw closer."
- With the 2024 acquisition of the NHL's Arizona Coyotes by Ryan Smith and relocation to Salt Lake City, "the city earmarked US$900 million to renovate Delta Center and construct a sports and entertainment district around the arena by October 2027", including seating-bowl work "to increase its hockey capacity to 17,000 seats with unobstructed views." (The venue table separately lists Delta Center capacity as 16,070.)
- February 2026: the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints announced a "significant financial donation" to the Utah 2034 Organizing Committee and committed to allowing use of church-owned property, such as "Block 85", "which will return as the medal plaza and host big air events".

### Salt Lake City Zone (venue, events, capacity, status)

- Downtown Salt Lake City - snowboarding (big air), freestyle skiing (big air), Medals Plaza - 30,000 - Temporary
- Delta Center - ice hockey (finals) - 16,070 - Existing
- Maverik Center - figure skating, short track speed skating - 10,100
- Rice-Eccles Stadium - opening and closing ceremonies - 51,444
- Salt Palace - curling - 6,500
- International Broadcast Center - n/a; Main Press Center - n/a
- University of Utah student housing - Olympic Village - 5,000+ - Existing, renovated
- Utah Olympic Oval - speed skating - 7,500

### Wasatch Back Zone

- Deer Valley - freestyle skiing (aerials/moguls) - 12,000 - Existing
- Park City Mountain Resort - snowboarding and freestyle skiing (halfpipe/slopestyle) - 15,000
- Soldier Hollow - biathlon, cross-country skiing, Nordic combined - 15,000 - Existing, renovated
- Utah Olympic Park Track - bobsleigh, luge, skeleton - 12,000
- Utah Olympic Park Jumps - ski jumping, Nordic combined - 15,000

### Other venues

- Peaks Ice Arena, Provo - ice hockey - 10,000 - Existing, renovated
- Snowbasin Resort, Weber County - alpine skiing - 19,000 - Existing

## Marketing and branding

- "The Games were originally billed as Salt Lake City-Utah 2034 upon the approval of the bid, as the changes implemented by Olympic Agenda 2020 allow regions to be credited as Olympic hosts as opposed to only cities."
- "On November 24, 2025, a new provisional emblem was unveiled, shortening the branding of the Games to simply Utah 2034."
- Organizing Committee CEO Brad Wilson said the new branding was meant to be more inclusive of the surrounding regions, saying he "want[ed] everyone in Utah to feel like they're a part of Team 2034, whether they live in our amazing capital city or whether they live in Vernal or Layton."
- Salt Lake City mayor Erin Mendenhall "felt that it 'hurt' for the city to not be part of the branding, but that she wanted the Games to 'uplift the state', and that Salt Lake City 'always will be' an Olympic city."

## Broadcasting

- "On March 13, 2025, the IOC announced that Comcast would become a 'strategic partner' of the organization, which will include the renewal of NBCUniversal's long-running broadcast rights to the Olympic Games in the United States through 2036 under an agreement valued at US$3 billion", plus co-developing digital advertising and assisting Olympic Broadcasting Services with in-venue distribution and its Olympic Video Player service.

wikis.title: Yellow Line (Line 2), Mumbai Metro
wikis.summary: Wikipedia's article on the Mumbai Metro Yellow Line (Line 2) from Dahisar East to Mandale: its failed Reliance PPP, the rebuilt Metro 2A and 2B sections, opening dates through 2026-2027, costs and technical details.
wikis.body:
## What the line is

- The Yellow Line (**Line 2**) of the Mumbai Metro runs from **Dahisar** in the northwest to **Mandale** in Mankhurd via Andheri, BKC and Chembur, in Mumbai, Maharashtra, India. Owner **MMRDA**, operator **Maha Mumbai Metro Operation Corp. Ltd. (MMMOCL)**. Fully elevated and grade-separated, standard gauge, 25 kV 50 Hz AC overhead catenary, 2 tracks.
- Infobox status: "Fully Operational: Line 2A" and "Partly Operational: Line 2B"; 17 stations; line length 18.589 km (11.551 mi); work began November 2016; opened 2 April 2022; daily ridership 212,000 (July 2023).
- The line is built in two sections: **Metro 2A** (Dahisar East-DN Nagar, 18.589 km, 17 stations) and **Metro 2B** (DN Nagar-Mankhurd, 23.643 km, 20 stations).

## Openings

- **2 April 2022** - Dahisar East to Dahanukarwadi opened, with Line 7's Dahisar East-Aarey; CM Uddhav Thackeray flagged off the first train at 4pm, public service from 8pm.
- **19 January 2023** - Dahanukarwadi to Andheri (West), eight new stations, inaugurated by Prime Minister Narendra Modi; the article calls this section 9.5 km (5.903 mi).
- **2026 on Line 2B** - the lead says a 5.8 km (3.6 mi) Diamond Garden-Mandale section opened on **7 April 2026**, while the article's tables date those five stations **8 April 2026**; Chembur is dated **13 August 2026**. The 2B openings are listed as 6.411 km (3.984 mi), bringing the article's total to 25.011 km (15.541 mi).
- Remaining 2B stations are listed as **December 2026** (Juhu to Saraswat Nagar) and **December 2027** (Bandra to Eastern Express Highway).

## History in brief

- Planned from 2004, launched by then President Pratibha Patil in August 2009 and contracted in January 2010 to a Reliance Infrastructure consortium on a 35-year BOT concession (MMRDA estimate ₹8,250 crore, RInfra estimate ₹11,000 crore). It never started: Coastal Regulation Zone rules blocked the carsheds, and after years of public blame between MMRDA and RInfra, RInfra terminated the agreement on 13 November 2014.
- Rebuilt on an EPC model with the DMRC as implementing agency from 12 December 2015 (₹334 crore). A RITES study had found an all-underground 40.2 km line feasible at ₹28,900 crore, 134% above earlier estimates; MMRDA instead split the project and built elevated.
- Metro 2B's elevated design drew protests (Khar, Santacruz, Mahim; Javed Akhtar took part) and Bombay High Court petitions, which the Court dismissed after MMRDA argued an underground line would take 2 years longer and cost "over 5.5 times more per kilometer". Two 2B stations, MMRDA Station and Kurla Terminus, were cancelled.
- 2B's first contractors, Simplex Infrastructure and an RCC-MBZ joint venture, were sacked on 4 February 2020 having completed 5% and 4.46% of their work; J Kumar Infraprojects (₹1,307.88 crore) and Nagarjuna Construction Company (₹760 crore) took over.

## Cost

- Metro 2A cost **₹6,410 crore (US$670 million)** - 48% from the State Government, 52% from an ADB loan - with about a 7% escalation attributed to the delay from October 2019 to January 2023.
- Metro 2B is estimated at **₹10,986 crore**, including ₹1,274 crore of land acquisition, half from the Centre and State; the article names the ADB with the New Development Bank in one place and the World Bank in another.
- On 2 March 2019 India signed a **$926 million** ADB loan for Lines 2 and 7, "the single largest infrastructure loan ever extended by the ADB", covering 63 six-car trainsets and signalling.

## Technical

- **Trains**: BEML, ₹3,015 crore for 378 cars (63 trainsets) shared with Line 7, plus 126 more cars; built in Bangalore and "the first driverless metro trains to be made in India"; 6 coaches, 1,660 passengers (crush load 2,092), 3.2 m wide.
- **Depots**: Charkop (16.40 ha, 20 stabling lines) serves 2A and Line 7; Mandale (28 ha, double-decker, 76 stabling lines) is "the largest metro depot in Mumbai" and under construction.
- **Signalling**: Alstom Urbalis 400 CBTC, part of a EUR90 million contract. **Power**: Adani Electricity Mumbai Limited from 2 December 2022, about 120 million units for both lines. **Fares**: automated fare collection by a Datamatics and AEP Ticketing consortium, ₹160 crore.
- Stations have 185 m platforms for 8-car rakes and single-pier supports, built with pre-cast "pi-girders".

## Unresolved in the article

- The station count is given as 39, 37 and 36 in different places; Metro 2B is 23.643 km with 20 stations in one section and 23.5 km with 22 stations in another; the 2B opening is dated both 7 and 8 April 2026; and the navigation box still lists the stations opened in 2026 as "under construction".

wikis.title: Yellow Line (Mumbai Metro): planning, construction, stations, cost and infrastructure
wikis.summary: The body of the Wikipedia article on Mumbai Metro's Yellow Line (Line 2), covering the abandoned Reliance Infrastructure PPP, the EPC rebuild as Metro 2A and 2B, opposition to the elevated 2B corridor, construction milestones, the station list with opening dates, costs and the line's rolling stock, depots, signalling, power and fare collection.
wikis.body:
## Overview (infobox and lead)

- The Yellow Line (**Line 2**) is a rapid transit metro line of the Mumbai Metro in Mumbai, Maharashtra, India, connecting **Dahisar** in the northwest with **Mandale** in Mankhurd via Andheri, BKC and Chembur.
- Infobox status: "Fully Operational: Line 2A"; "Partly Operational: Line 2B". Owner **MMRDA**; operator **Maha Mumbai Metro Operation Corp. Ltd. (MMMOCL)**; locale Mumbai Suburban district; termini Dahisar (East) and Mandale; connecting lines Line 7 and Line 1.
- Infobox technical: **17 stations**; line length **18.589 km (11.551 mi)**; 2 tracks; grade-separated, elevated; 1,435 mm standard gauge; 25 kV 50 Hz AC overhead catenary; rolling stock BEML; depots Charkop (2A) and Mandale (2B).
- Infobox history: work began **November 2016**; opened **2 April 2022** ("4 years ago"). Daily ridership **212,000 (July 2023)**.
- Lead: Phase One of Line 2A partially opened 2 April 2022 from Dahisar (East) to Dahanukarwadi; Line 2A "was fully opened on 19 January 2023 from Dahanukarwadi to Andheri (West) and consisted of eight new stations".
- Lead: construction of "Metro 2A (between Dahisar and D.N. Road)" began November 2016 and was completed April 2022; the section "will be 18.589 km (11.551 mi) long, and comprise 17 of the 39 stations that form part of this route"; the new "9.5 km (5.903 mi) section from Dahanukarwadi to DN Nagar, was inaugurated on 19 January 2023, by PM Narendra Modi".
- Lead: "On 7 April 2026, a 5.8 km (3.6 mi) section of Line 2B from Diamond Garden to Mandale was made operational for passengers."

## Opening table (Planning section)

| Line | From | To | Opening | Distance |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 2A | Dahisar (East) | Dahanukarwadi | 2 April 2022 | 18.6 km (11.6 mi) |
| 2A | Dahanukarwadi | Andheri (West) | 19 January 2023 | (same 18.6 km entry) |
| 2B | Maharashtranagar Mandale | Deshbhakt N.G. Acharya Udyan-Diamond Garden, Chembur | 8 April 2026 | 6.411 km (3.984 mi) |
| 2B | Deshbhakt N.G. Acharya Udyan-Diamond Garden, Chembur | Chembur | 13 August 2026 | (same 6.411 km entry) |
| Total | | | | 25.011 km (15.541 mi) |

## Contradictions inside the article

- **Date of the 2B opening**: the lead says the Diamond Garden-Mandale section "was made operational for passengers" on **7 April 2026**, and cites a Hindu piece "Mumbai Metro lines 2B and 9 to be launched today" dated 7 April 2026; the Planning table and the station table give **8 April 2026** for those stations.
- **Number of stations**: the lead says Metro 2A comprises "17 of the 39 stations that form part of this route"; the Stations section says "There will be a total of 37 stations on Line 2", made up of 17 on 2A and 20 on 2B; the numbered station table runs to number 36.
- **Length of Metro 2B**: the Construction section says Metro 2B "is 23.643 km (14.691 mi) long and connects DN Nagar to Mankhurd with 20 stations"; the EPC section says the corridor approved in September 2016 "was proposed to be 23.5 km (14.6 mi) long and to have 22 stations"; the Current status table is headed "Work is in progress at some of the 22 stations".
- **Metro 2B lenders**: the EPC section says the non-government half would be "financed through loans from the Asian Development Bank and the New Development Bank"; the Cost section says "the Asian Development Bank and the World Bank".
- **Northern terminus naming**: the lead calls Metro 2A "between Dahisar and D.N. Road"; elsewhere the section is Dahisar East to DN Nagar.
- **Line 2B station status**: the station table gives 2026 opening dates for Chembur, Diamond Garden, Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Chowk, Deonar, Mankhurd and Maharashtranagar Mandale, while the article's navigation box (part 2) lists those same stations as "Under construction".

## Public private partnership with RInfra

- The 2004 MMRDA masterplan proposed a 38.24 km (23.76 mi) Colaba-Bandra-Charkop line as the Yellow Line, plus a 13.37 km (8.31 mi) Bandra-Kurla-Mankhurd line (Line 3) and a 7.5 km (4.66 mi) Charkop-Dahisar line (Line 4). The updated masterplan merged Charkop-Bandra-Mankhurd and Charkop-Dahisar into a single 32 km (19.88 mi) Dahisar-Bandra-Mankhurd line with 27 stations, to be built as a PPP.
- Then President Pratibha Patil launched the project in August 2009. MMRDA appointed Reliance Infrastructure (RInfra) with SNC Lavalin Inc. (Canada) and Reliance Communication through international competitive bidding; the concession agreement was signed in January 2010 on a build-operate-transfer basis for 35 years with a 10-year extension clause.
- Cost estimates differed: MMRDA estimated **₹8,250 crore (US$860 million)**, Reliance Infrastructure **₹11,000 crore**. Construction was to begin August 2010 and conclude mid-2013; by December 2012 work had not begun, leading to calls to cancel the line.
- Land for carsheds at Charkop and Mankhurd was blocked by Coastal Regulation Zone laws and the Union Ministry of Environment and Forests refused depot clearance; MMRDA planned to shift the rake depot to a 19 hectare plot at Malwani, near Malad, outside CRZ. MMRDA said an elevated-underground combination was deemed impossible because of land needed for ramps and slip roads.
- On 6 September 2012 MMRDA told RInfra to start work or face legal action; RInfra blamed the government for failing to provide land, right-of-way permits and clearances. On 8 February 2013 then RInfra CEO Sumit Banerjee said MMRDA had failed to meet its responsibilities. On 9 August 2013 DNA reported a 27-acre casting yard plot was being marked for Line 3, "a clear indication" the line "will not take off in the near future". Chief Minister Prithviraj Chavan said on 30 August 2013 that "it is now clear that Mumbai's Metro II project will now not happen."
- On 13 November 2014 Reliance Infrastructure terminated the agreement between MMTPL and the Maharashtra government, saying that "Due to non-fulfilment of various critical obligations by Maharashtra government and the Mumbai Metropolitan Region Development Authority (MMRDA), the project could not take off." MMRDA confirmed mutual-consent termination and said the project would be built by MMRCL under an EPC model.

## EPC model

- September 2013: MMRDA appointed RITES to study an underground 32 km line and a merger with the 7.5 km Charkop-Dahisar line. RITES reported in the last week of May 2014 that an underground line extended to Dahisar was feasible: 40.2 km (25.0 mi) with 37 underground stations, estimated at **₹28,900 crore**, "134% higher" than the original ₹7,660 crore (Charkop-Bandra-Mankhurd) plus ₹4,680 crore (Charkop-Dahisar). RITES proposed a major car depot at Oshiwara and a minor one at Mandale, Mankhurd.
- June 2015: MMRDA proposed an 18.6 km Dahisar East-Andheri East line and a 12 km BKC-Mankhurd line within a 6-line plan estimated at **₹64,000 crore (US$6.6 billion)**. The detailed project report, approved August 2015, estimated **₹12,000 crore (US$1.2 billion)**.
- 15 June 2015: MMRDA announced three parts - Dahisar East-DN Nagar (2A), DN Nagar-BKC (2B), BKC-Mankhurd (2C). On 1 July 2015 a disputed 22-acre plot in Mankhurd beside the Sion Panvel highway was allotted for the carshed.
- The plan was later cut to two sections, Dahisar-DN Nagar (2A) and DN Nagar-Mankhurd (2B). Metro 2A was approved by the Maharashtra Government on 6 October 2015; in November 2015 the Department of Economic Affairs cleared an Asian Development Bank loan request. The Maharashtra Cabinet approved 2B on 27 September 2016, estimated at **₹10,986 crore** including **₹1,274 crore** of land acquisition.
- February 2020: MMRDA metropolitan commissioner R.A. Rajeev said the line would be identified as the Yellow Line. A May 2021 WRI India study estimated Metro 2A and Line 7 had the potential to create 1.1 million jobs.

## Elevated Metro 2B and opposition

- Central Railway first permitted 2B at 22 metres over the Central Line to allow an elevated CST-Panvel high-speed line and elevated CST-Kalyan line; MMRDA objected over operations and emergency evacuation at that height, and CR then allowed 13 metres for 2B with the CST-Panvel line at 22 metres.
- Protests: SV Road residents at Sacred Heart Boys' School, Khar on 12 August 2017; protests at Santacruz and Mahim on 5 October 2017, with celebrities including Javed Akhtar. Petitions in the Bombay High Court from the Juhu Vile Parle Development Cooperative Housing Association, the Gulmohar Area Society Welfare Group and Balabhai Nanavati Hospital. The Indira Nagar-Nanavati Hospital section faced legal issues over the Juhu Aerodrome funnel area.
- June 2018 MMRDA affidavit: it had taken "a conscious decision to go for an elevated Metro", citing insufficient land for ramps, an underground line taking 2 years longer and costing "over 5.5 times more per kilometer", and calling the design "a highly technical issue". In August 2019 the Court asked petitioners to explain their reasoning after their advocate said he "had not come prepared". The Bombay High Court ruled for MMRDA and dismissed all petitions.

## Cancelled stations

- Two originally proposed 2B stations were cancelled: **MMRDA Station**, because it overlapped the Kalanagar flyover ramp, and **Kurla Terminus**, cancelled in September 2020 because it lay in the restricted funnel zone for Mumbai Airport, was only 474 metres from the proposed SG Barve Marg station, and would have sat between the SCLR rail overbridge and another permanent structure.

## Depot and the Line 7 link

- Line 7's depot was to be at Dahisar, but land acquisition was delayed by litigation filed in 2016. In 2020 MMRDA proposed using Charkop for both Line 2A and Line 7 via a ring metro link, using an empty plot after Ovaripada station on Line 7 for the connecting pillars. In November 2021 MMRDA cancelled the Dahisar depot and proposed a depot for Lines 7, 7A and 9 at Rai Murdhe in Bhayandar.
- Lines 2A and 7 were commissioned together on 2 April 2022 (Dahanukarwadi-Aarey via Dahisar East) and extended on 19 January 2023, giving circular service between Andheri West and Gundavali via Dahisar East.

## Construction

- MMRDA appointed the DMRC as implementing agency on 12 December 2015, paying **₹334 crore (US$35 million)**. DMRC had sole responsibility for civil and technical works and O&M on 2A; on 2B, MMRDA does civil works and DMRC technical work and O&M. In July 2018 the state granted MMRDA special planning authority status.

### Metro 2A

- 18.589 km, Dahisar East to DN Nagar, 17 stations. Prime Minister Narendra Modi laid the foundation stone on 11 October 2015.
- Two DMRC tenders (Dahisar East-Dahanukarwadi, 9 stations; Valnai-Andheri West, 8 stations) were both won by J Kumar Infra Projects Limited in June 2016 for **₹1,300 crore (US$130 million)**, bidding below the reserve price.
- Soil testing began July 2016; construction November 2016. Commissioning was scheduled for October 2019 but rolling-stock and civil-works problems pushed it to December 2020, and the COVID-19 pandemic delayed it further.
- Progress as of 13 September 2017: 77% of soil investigation for pier foundations, 76% barricading, 37% piles, 19% pile caps; 110 piers cast, 75 pier caps erected, 26 U girders erected.
- April 2019 rooftop solar PV tenders; track laying began June 2019.
- Platforms are **185 metres (607 ft)** long for 8-car rakes. Stations sit on a single pier (unlike Line 1's three) because of limited space on New Link Road, and used pre-cast "pi-girders" cast at a Bandra casting yard. Most spans are 25-28 metres; a 51-metre steel girder was installed on New Link Road in Kandivali for a 700-metre radius curve.
- September 2020: commissioner R.A. Rajeev said almost 80% of construction was done. Pre-trials at Charkop from February 2021; electrification complete 26 May and first trial runs from 31 May; dynamic trial on the 20 km Dhanukarwadi-Aarey stretch from 19 June. Final I-girder launched at Adarsh Nagar Junction, Andheri, on 6 October 2021. RDSO provisional approval January 2022; CMRS inspection from February 2022.
- **2 April 2022**: Dhanukarwadi-Dahisar East opened with Line 7's Dahisar East-Aarey. Chief Minister Uddhav Thackeray flagged off the first train at 4pm with Deputy CM Ajit Pawar, Urban Development Minister Eknath Shinde, NCP chief Sharad Pawar and Leader of Opposition in the Legislative Council Pravin Darekar; public service from 8pm.
- RDSO approval for Dhanukarwadi-DN Nagar came October 2022, CMRS inspection December 2022, and the final section (with Line 7's Goregaon East-Gundavali) was inaugurated on **19 January 2023** by Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

### Metro 2B

- 23.643 km, DN Nagar to Mankhurd, 20 stations. Foundation stone laid by Prime Minister Narendra Modi on 24 December 2016.
- MMRDA surveyed with drones carrying 360-degree cameras accurate to 3 mm. Bids invited 4 January 2017; four packages (ESIC Nagar-Khira Nagar, Saraswat Nagar-ILFS, MTNL Metro-Chembur, Diamond Garden-Mandale), tendered alongside Metro 4, drew 10 firms/consortia including L&T, Afcons, Tata, NCC and JMC, Reliance Infrastructure-RdE, JKumar, ITD Cementation, CHEC-TPL, Simplex and a GHEC-RCC-JV-China consortium. Eight bidders were shortlisted for the Mandale depot in November 2017.
- **13 November 2017**: Simplex Infrastructure won package one, **₹1,080 crore (US$110 million)**, for a 12 km viaduct and 11 elevated stations (ESIC Nagar, Prem Nagar, Indira Nagar, Old Airport, Khira Nagar, Saraswat Nagar, National College, Bandra (W), MMRDA Office, Income Tax Office, BKC).
- **3 March 2018**: an RCC Infra Ventures-MBZ-Ukraine joint venture won package two, **₹521 crore (US$54 million)**, for a 5.9 km viaduct, the Mandale car depot and 6 stations (MTNL Metro, SG Barve Marg, Kurla Terminus, Kurla East, Chembur). Construction began April 2018.
- March 2019: MMRDA altered the BKC Road alignment to avoid passing in front of Shiv Sena president Uddhav Thackeray's residence.
- **4 February 2020**: both contracts terminated for delay - Simplex had done 5% of the work in 30 months against a schedule of 65%, RCC-MBZ 4.46%. J Kumar Infraprojects took package one in June 2021 for **₹1,307.88 crore (US$140 million)**; Nagarjuna Construction Company took package two in March 2022 for **₹760 crore (US$79 million)**. Construction resumed March 2023; MMRDA said 70% of the Mandale depot was done by the end of May 2023.
- Current-status table (2B), latest column 25 September 2023: soil investigation 100.00%, utility works 94.31%, piling 80.88%, pile caps 79.18%, piers cast 63.48%, pier cap casting 68.09% and erection 59.47%, U girder casting 58.08% and erection 40.00%, Mandale depot 80.72%; station work described as foundation (pile and pile cap) work in progress at 5 stations.

## Stations

- "There will be a total of 37 stations on Line 2. Metro 2A, from Dahisar to Andheri (West), has 17 stations. Metro 2B, from Andheri (West) to Mankhurd, will have 20 stations." MMRDA partnered with bike-sharing app MBYK for bicycle sharing at stations.
- Line 2A, all elevated: Dahisar (East) (interchange Line 7), Anand Nagar, Kandarpada, Mandapeshwar, Eksar, Borivali (West), Shimpoli, Kandivli (West) and Dahanukarwadi opened **2 April 2022**; Valnai-Meeth Chowky, Malad (West), Lower Malad, Bangur Nagar, Goregaon (West), Oshiwara, Lower Oshiwara (Line 6 Adarsh Nagar, under construction) and Andheri (West) (Line 1 D N Nagar) opened **19 January 2023**.
- Line 2B, all elevated: Hare Ram Hare Krishna Mandir - Juhu, Prem Nagar, Indira Nagar (Vile Parle), Nanavati Hospital, Khira Nagar (Western) and Saraswat Nagar listed as **December 2026**; Bandra (Western), Income Tax Office (Line 3 BKC; BKC HSR under construction), ILFS, MTNL, SG Barve Marg (Line 8, proposed), Kurla (East) and Eastern Express Highway (Line 4 Siddharth Colony, under construction) listed as **December 2027**; Chembur (VNP and RC Marg Junction) **13 August 2026**; Deshbhakt N.G. Acharya Udyan-Diamond Garden, Chembur, Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Chowk (Chembur), Deonar, Mankhurd (Harbour; Line 8 proposed) and Maharashtranagar Mandale **8 April 2026**.
- The route-map diagram gives chainages from 0.0000 at Dahisar East to 41.5074 at Maharashtranagar Mandale, with Mandale Depot beyond, and shows Charkop Depot after Dahanukarwadi (8.2003).

## Cost

- Metro 2A was built for **₹6,410 crore (US$670 million)**. Originally due October 2019, it was completed January 2023, and MMRDA said the delay escalated cost by about 7%. The State Government bore 48% of the cost; MMRDA took an Asian Development Bank loan for 52%. On 26 November 2016 MMRDA allotted **₹340 crore (US$35 million)** to DMRC for rolling stock, signalling and telecommunications on Metro 2A and Line 7.
- Metro 2B is estimated at **₹10,986 crore**, including **₹1,274 crore** land acquisition; half from the Centre and State, the rest from loans.
- On 2 March 2019 the Union Ministry of Finance said it had signed a **$926 million** loan agreement with the ADB for Lines 2 and 7 - "the single largest infrastructure loan ever extended by the ADB" - to procure 63 six-car trainsets and signalling and safety systems.

## Infrastructure

- **Rolling stock**: BEML won a **₹3,015 crore (US$310 million)** contract in November 2018 for 378 metro cars (63 trainsets) for the Yellow Line and Line 7, beating Alstom, Bombardier (acquired by Alstom in 2021), CAF, CRRC, Titagarh Rail Systems and Hyundai Rotem; 126 more cars (21 trainsets) were ordered for extensions. Built at BEML's Rail Coach Factory in Bangalore, Karnataka, the rakes are capable of driverless operation - "the first driverless metro trains to be made in India". Manufacturing began 29 July 2019, the first coach was built in 75 days and unveiled in September 2019, and the first trainset arrived in Mumbai on 28 January 2021. Each 6-coach trainset carries 1,660 passengers with a dense crush load of 2,092, is 3.2 metres wide, stainless steel, 4 doors per side per coach, with regenerative braking.
- **Depots**: Charkop serves Line 2A and Line 7, on a 16.40 hectare site with 20 stabling lines and 305 employees, 30% of them women (as of October 2022). Mandale, on a 28 hectare site, is "the largest metro depot in Mumbai", double-decker with 76 stabling lines, under construction and to serve Lines 2A and 2B.
- **Signalling**: Alstom Urbalis 400 CBTC; Alstom won a **EUR90 million** contract for signalling and telecommunications on the Yellow Line and Line 7 plus Pune Metro Lines 1 and 7.
- **Power**: 25 kV 50 Hz AC overhead catenary; MMRDA signed with Adani Electricity Mumbai Limited on 2 December 2022 to supply Metro 2A and Metro 7, needing "around 120 million units" for both lines.
- **Fare collection**: a consortium of Datamatics (India) and AEP Ticketing solutions S.R.L (Italy) won a **₹160 crore (US$17 million)** automated fare collection contract for the Yellow Line and Line 7 in February 2019.

wikis.title: Reliance Infrastructure PPP and its collapse
wikis.summary: The 2009-2014 attempt to build the line as a Reliance-led public private partnership, blocked by depot land and ended by termination.
wikis.body:
- 2004 MMRDA masterplan: a 38.24 km Colaba-Bandra-Charkop line as the Yellow Line, a 13.37 km Bandra-Kurla-Mankhurd line (Line 3) and a 7.5 km Charkop-Dahisar line (Line 4). Later merged into a 32 km, 27-station Dahisar-Bandra-Mankhurd corridor, to be built PPP like Line 1.
- Launched by then President Pratibha Patil in August 2009. MMRDA selected a Reliance Infrastructure consortium with SNC Lavalin Inc. (Canada) and Reliance Communication; concession signed January 2010, build-operate-transfer, 35 years plus a 10-year extension clause.
- Cost estimates: MMRDA ₹8,250 crore (US$860 million); Reliance Infrastructure ₹11,000 crore.
- Schedule: construction from August 2010, completion mid-2013. Nothing had begun by December 2012.
- Blocker: no land for carsheds at Charkop and Mankhurd under Coastal Regulation Zone law; the Union Ministry of Environment and Forests refused depot clearance. MMRDA looked at a 19 hectare plot at Malwani near Malad, outside CRZ. It said a part-underground alignment was impossible because of land needed for ramps and slip roads.
- 6 September 2012: MMRDA threatened legal action; RInfra blamed the government for failing to supply land, right-of-way permits and clearances. 8 February 2013: RInfra CEO Sumit Banerjee said MMRDA had not met its responsibilities.
- 9 August 2013: DNA reported a 27-acre casting yard was being reassigned to Line 3, "a clear indication" the line "will not take off in the near future". 30 August 2013: CM Prithviraj Chavan said "it is now clear that Mumbai's Metro II project will now not happen."
- 13 November 2014: RInfra terminated the MMTPL agreement, citing "non-fulfilment of various critical obligations by Maharashtra government and the... MMRDA" after four years. MMRDA said the termination was by mutual consent and that the line would instead be built by MMRCL on an EPC model.

wikis.title: The EPC rebuild: RITES study, splitting into 2A and 2B
wikis.summary: How the line was re-planned after 2014 - an underground study, a three-way then two-way split, and cabinet approvals.
wikis.body:
- September 2013: MMRDA appointed RITES to study building the 32 km line underground and merging the separate 7.5 km Charkop-Dahisar line into it.
- RITES reported in the last week of May 2014 that an underground line extended to Dahisar was feasible: 40.2 km with 37 underground stations, at ₹28,900 crore - "134% higher" than ₹7,660 crore (Charkop-Bandra-Mankhurd) plus ₹4,680 crore (Charkop-Dahisar). It proposed a major depot at Oshiwara and a minor one at Mandale, Mankhurd; extending to Mankhurd was meant to solve depot land acquisition.
- June 2015: MMRDA proposed an 18.6 km Dahisar East-Andheri East line and a 12 km BKC-Mankhurd line inside a six-line plan costing ₹64,000 crore (US$6.6 billion). The detailed project report, approved August 2015, put the line at ₹12,000 crore (US$1.2 billion).
- 15 June 2015: three parts announced - Dahisar East-DN Nagar (2A), DN Nagar-BKC (2B), BKC-Mankhurd (2C). 1 July 2015: a 22-acre plot in Mankhurd beside the Sion Panvel highway, disputed with the State Home Ministry over a jail, was allotted for the carshed.
- Revised to two sections. Metro 2A approved by the Maharashtra Government on 6 October 2015; November 2015 the Department of Economic Affairs cleared an ADB loan request. Metro 2B approved by the Maharashtra Cabinet on 27 September 2016 - proposed as 23.5 km with 22 stations, at ₹10,986 crore including ₹1,274 crore land acquisition, half Centre and State, the rest loans from the Asian Development Bank and the New Development Bank.
- February 2020: MMRDA metropolitan commissioner R.A. Rajeev said the line would be identified as the Yellow Line. A WRI India study published May 2021 estimated Metro 2A and Line 7 could create 1.1 million jobs.

wikis.title: Opposition to the elevated Metro 2B corridor
wikis.summary: Protests, High Court petitions and MMRDA's defence of an elevated rather than underground 2B, plus the two cancelled stations.
wikis.body:
- Central Railway first required 22 metres of clearance over the Central Line for its own elevated CST-Panvel high-speed and CST-Kalyan plans; MMRDA objected over operations and emergency evacuation at that height and was then allowed 13 metres, with the CST-Panvel line at 22 metres.
- Protests: SV Road residents at Sacred Heart Boys' School, Khar, 12 August 2017; further protests at Santacruz and Mahim on 5 October 2017, joined by celebrities including Javed Akhtar.
- Bombay High Court petitions from the Juhu Vile Parle Development Cooperative Housing Association, the Gulmohar Area Society Welfare Group and Balabhai Nanavati Hospital; separate legal issues over the Indira Nagar-Nanavati Hospital section crossing the Juhu Aerodrome funnel area.
- June 2018 MMRDA affidavit: it had made "a conscious decision to go for an elevated Metro" after weighing both, citing insufficient land for ramps, an underground line taking 2 years longer and costing "over 5.5 times more per kilometer", and arguing petitioners lacked the scientific experience to evaluate a "highly technical issue".
- August 2019: the Court asked petitioners to explain their reasoning after their advocate said he "had not come prepared". The Court ultimately ruled for MMRDA and dismissed all petitions against Metro 2B.
- Cancelled stations: MMRDA Station (overlapped the Kalanagar flyover ramp) and Kurla Terminus (cancelled September 2020 - in the Mumbai Airport restricted funnel zone, only 474 metres from the proposed SG Barve Marg station, and squeezed between the SCLR rail overbridge and another permanent structure).

wikis.title: Building and opening Metro 2A
wikis.summary: Contracts, engineering and the two opening dates for the Dahisar East-Andheri West section.
wikis.body:
- 18.589 km, Dahisar East to DN Nagar, 17 stations. Foundation stone laid by Prime Minister Narendra Modi on 11 October 2015. DMRC appointed implementing agency 12 December 2015 for ₹334 crore (US$35 million), with sole responsibility for civil and technical works and O&M on 2A.
- J Kumar Infra Projects Limited won both DMRC packages in June 2016 for ₹1,300 crore (US$130 million), bidding below the reserve price: 9 stations Dahisar East-Dahanukarwadi, 8 stations Valnai-Andheri West.
- Soil testing July 2016; construction November 2016. Target October 2019 slipped to December 2020 over rolling stock and civil works, then further because of COVID-19.
- 13 September 2017 progress: 77% soil investigation for pier foundations, 76% barricading, 37% piles, 19% pile caps, 110 piers cast, 75 pier caps erected, 26 U girders erected.
- Engineering: 185 m platforms for 8-car rakes; single-pier stations (Line 1 used three) because of limited space on New Link Road; pre-cast "pi-girders" from a Bandra casting yard; spans mostly 25-28 m; a 51 m steel girder at Kandivali for a 700 m radius curve. Rooftop solar tenders April 2019; track laying from June 2019.
- Testing: pre-trials at Charkop February 2021; electrification complete 26 May 2021, first trial runs 31 May; dynamic trial on the 20 km Dhanukarwadi-Aarey stretch from 19 June; final I-girder at Adarsh Nagar Junction 6 October 2021; RDSO provisional approval January 2022; CMRS inspection from February 2022.
- 2 April 2022: Dhanukarwadi-Dahisar East opened with Line 7's Dahisar East-Aarey. CM Uddhav Thackeray flagged off the first train at 4pm with Ajit Pawar, Eknath Shinde, Sharad Pawar and Pravin Darekar; public service from 8pm.
- 19 January 2023: the final section (with Line 7 Goregaon East-Gundavali) inaugurated by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, after RDSO approval in October 2022 and CMRS inspection in December 2022.

wikis.title: Building Metro 2B
wikis.summary: The DN Nagar-Mankhurd section: packages, terminated contractors, replacements and progress percentages.
wikis.body:
- 23.643 km, DN Nagar to Mankhurd, 20 stations. Foundation stone laid by Prime Minister Narendra Modi on 24 December 2016. MMRDA does civil works; DMRC handles technical work and O&M.
- Surveying used drones with 360-degree cameras "up to 3-millimeter accuracy", faster and more accurate than a regular survey and a guard against false compensation claims.
- Bids invited 4 January 2017 in four packages - ESIC Nagar-Khira Nagar, Saraswat Nagar-ILFS, MTNL Metro-Chembur, Diamond Garden-Mandale - tendered with Metro 4; 10 firms or consortia bid in total. Eight bidders were shortlisted for the Mandale depot in November 2017.
- 13 November 2017: Simplex Infrastructure won package one, ₹1,080 crore (US$110 million) - 12 km viaduct and 11 elevated stations.
- 3 March 2018: RCC Infra Ventures with MBZ-Ukraine won package two, ₹521 crore (US$54 million) - 5.9 km viaduct, Mandale car depot and 6 stations. Construction began April 2018.
- March 2019: the BKC Road alignment was altered to avoid passing in front of Uddhav Thackeray's residence.
- 4 February 2020: both contracts terminated for delay - Simplex 5% complete in 30 months against 65% scheduled, RCC-MBZ 4.46%.
- June 2021: J Kumar Infraprojects awarded ₹1,307.88 crore (US$140 million) for package one. March 2022: Nagarjuna Construction Company awarded ₹760 crore (US$79 million) for package two. Work resumed March 2023; Mandale depot 70% complete by end of May 2023.
- Status table as of 25 September 2023: soil investigation 100.00%, utilities 94.31%, piling 80.88%, pile caps 79.18%, piers 63.48%, pier cap casting 68.09% / erection 59.47%, U girder casting 58.08% / erection 40.00%, Mandale depot 80.72%; station foundation work in progress at 5 stations.

wikis.title: Stations and opening dates
wikis.summary: The full station list for Lines 2A and 2B with interchanges and the dates the article gives for each opening.
wikis.body:
- Article totals: "There will be a total of 37 stations on Line 2" - 17 on 2A (Dahisar to Andheri West) and 20 on 2B (Andheri West to Mankhurd). The lead instead says 2A is "17 of the 39 stations that form part of this route", and the numbered table ends at 36.
- **Line 2A, 2 April 2022**: Dahisar (East) (Line 7), Anand Nagar, Kandarpada, Mandapeshwar, Eksar, Borivali (West), Shimpoli, Kandivli (West), Dahanukarwadi.
- **Line 2A, 19 January 2023**: Valnai-Meeth Chowky, Malad (West), Lower Malad, Bangur Nagar, Goregaon (West), Oshiwara, Lower Oshiwara (Line 6 Adarsh Nagar, under construction), Andheri (West) (Line 1 D N Nagar).
- **Line 2B, 8 April 2026**: Deshbhakt N.G. Acharya Udyan-Diamond Garden Chembur, Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Chowk (Chembur), Deonar, Mankhurd (Harbour; Line 8 proposed), Maharashtranagar Mandale. The lead dates this section's opening 7 April 2026 instead.
- **Line 2B, 13 August 2026**: Chembur (VNP and RC Marg Junction).
- **Line 2B, December 2026**: Hare Ram Hare Krishna Mandir - Juhu, Prem Nagar, Indira Nagar (Vile Parle), Nanavati Hospital, Khira Nagar (Western), Saraswat Nagar.
- **Line 2B, December 2027**: Bandra (Western), Income Tax Office (Line 3 Bandra Kurla Complex; BKC HSR under construction), ILFS, MTNL, SG Barve Marg (Line 8, proposed), Kurla (East), Eastern Express Highway (Line 4 Siddharth Colony, under construction).
- All stations are listed as elevated. MMRDA partnered with the bike-sharing app MBYK for bicycle sharing at stations on the line.
- Route map chainages run 0.0000 km at Dahisar East to 41.5074 km at Maharashtranagar Mandale, with Charkop Depot after Dahanukarwadi (8.2003 km) and Mandale Depot at the end.

wikis.title: Cost and funding
wikis.summary: What each section cost, who paid, and the record ADB loan for Lines 2 and 7.
wikis.body:
- Metro 2A cost **₹6,410 crore (US$670 million)**. Scheduled for October 2019 and completed January 2023, with MMRDA saying the delay escalated cost by about 7%.
- Metro 2A funding split: State Government 48%; an Asian Development Bank loan covering 52%.
- 26 November 2016: MMRDA allotted **₹340 crore (US$35 million)** to DMRC to implement and commission rolling stock, signalling and telecommunications for Metro 2A and Line 7.
- Metro 2B estimated at **₹10,986 crore**, including **₹1,274 crore** land acquisition; half from the Centre and State Government. The Cost section names the Asian Development Bank and the World Bank as the other lenders, while the earlier EPC section names the Asian Development Bank and the New Development Bank.
- 2 March 2019: the Union Ministry of Finance signed a **$926 million** loan with the ADB for Lines 2 and 7, "the single largest infrastructure loan ever extended by the ADB", funding 63 six-car trainsets plus signalling and safety systems.
- Earlier estimates in the article: ₹8,250 crore (MMRDA) and ₹11,000 crore (RInfra) for the PPP; ₹28,900 crore for the RITES all-underground option; ₹12,000 crore in the August 2015 detailed project report.

wikis.title: Rolling stock, depots, signalling, power and fares
wikis.summary: The line's BEML driverless trainsets, Charkop and Mandale depots, Alstom CBTC, Adani power supply and the Datamatics fare system.
wikis.body:
- **Rolling stock**: BEML won ₹3,015 crore (US$310 million) in November 2018 for 378 metro cars (63 trainsets) for the Yellow Line and Line 7, against Alstom, Bombardier (acquired by Alstom in 2021), CAF, CRRC, Titagarh Rail Systems and Hyundai Rotem; 126 more cars (21 trainsets) were ordered for extensions. Built at BEML's Rail Coach Factory in Bangalore, Karnataka, and capable of driverless operation - "the first driverless metro trains to be made in India". Manufacturing began 29 July 2019; the first coach took 75 days and was unveiled in September 2019; the first trainset reached Mumbai on 28 January 2021.
- **Trainset specification**: 6 coaches, passenger capacity 1,660, dense crush load 2,092, 3.2 metres wide, stainless steel, 4 doors per side per coach, regenerative braking.
- **Charkop depot**: serves Line 2A and Line 7; 16.40 hectare site, 20 stabling lines, 305 employees of whom 30% were women as of October 2022.
- **Mandale depot**: 28 hectare site, "the largest metro depot in Mumbai", double-decker with 76 stabling lines, under construction, to serve Lines 2A and 2B once complete.
- **Signalling**: Alstom Urbalis 400 CBTC. Alstom won a EUR90 million contract covering signalling and telecommunications for the Mumbai Yellow Line and Line 7 and for Pune Metro Lines 1 and 7.
- **Power**: 25 kV 50 Hz AC overhead catenary. MMRDA signed with Adani Electricity Mumbai Limited on 2 December 2022; "around 120 million units is required to power both lines".
- **Fare collection**: a Datamatics (India) and AEP Ticketing solutions S.R.L (Italy) consortium won a ₹160 crore (US$17 million) automated fare collection contract for the Yellow Line and Line 7 in February 2019.
