wikis.title: The Exorcist III
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on William Peter Blatty's 1990 film The Exorcist III: its plot and cast, the troubled development and studio-imposed exorcism reshoots, release, reviews, box office, awards, the 2016 director's cut and its legacy.
wikis.body:
## Overview
- 1990 American supernatural psychological horror film written and directed by William Peter Blatty, based on his 1983 novel Legion.
- "The third installment in The Exorcist film series and the final installment in Blatty's 'Trilogy of Faith' after The Ninth Configuration (1980), serving as a follow-up and direct sequel of The Exorcist (1973)."
- Stars George C. Scott, Ed Flanders, Jason Miller, Scott Wilson, Nicol Williamson and Brad Dourif. Produced by Carter DeHaven; production companies Morgan Creek Productions and Carter DeHaven Productions; distributed by 20th Century Fox. Cinematography Gerry Fisher; edited by Todd Ramsay and Peter Lee Thompson; music by Barry De Vorzon.
- Release date August 17, 1990; running time 110 minutes; budget $11 million; box office $44 million.
- Plot: Lieutenant William F. Kinderman investigates demonic murders in Georgetown bearing the hallmarks of the Gemini, a serial killer executed fifteen years earlier, and finds him possessing the body of Damien Karras. Blatty based aspects of the Gemini Killer on the real-life Zodiac Killer, "although there is no evidence of interest in this film by The Zodiac Killer".
- Karras's tombstone in the film lists "his death at the age of 40 on October 9, 1975".

## Cast (selected)
- George C. Scott (Lt. William F. Kinderman), Ed Flanders (Father Joseph Dyer), Brad Dourif (James Venamun / the Gemini Killer), Scott Wilson (Dr. Temple), Nicol Williamson (Father Paul Morning), Jason Miller (Patient X / Damien Karras), Grand L. Bush (Sgt. Mel Atkins), Harry Carey Jr. (Father Tom Kanavan), Zohra Lampert (Mary Kinderman), Lee Richardson (Father Riley), Mary Jackson (Mrs. Clelia), Viveca Lindfors (Nurse X).
- Cameos: C. Everett Koop and Larry King as themselves, Patrick Ewing as the Angel of Death, Fabio (uncredited), Samuel L. Jackson as the Blind Dream Man, Colleen Dewhurst as the uncredited voice of Pazuzu, Teresa Wright (uncredited).

## Development
- Blatty initially had no desire to write a sequel but developed a story titled Legion around Kinderman, conceived as a feature with William Friedkin attached; Warner Bros. was keen despite Exorcist II: The Heretic's failure. Blatty: "everybody wanted Exorcist III ... I hadn't written the script, but I had the story in my head... and Billy [Friedkin] loved it". Friedkin left over conflicting opinions.
- The project went into development hell and Blatty published Legion as a novel in 1983; it was a bestseller. Steve Jaffe packaged the project and served as associate producer. Morgan Creek and Carolco both wanted it; Blatty chose Morgan Creek "after Carolco suggested the idea of a grown-up Regan MacNeil giving birth to possessed twins".
- Blatty offered the director's chair to John Carpenter, who withdrew: "I was ambivalent about the script, primarily because it didn't have an exorcism... Blatty was resistant. He wanted to direct it and wanted to stay very close to his novel... I couldn't get what I needed. So I withdrew from The Exorcist III." Under the Morgan Creek deal Blatty directed, filming on location in Georgetown.
- Casting: Kinderman was recast because Lee J. Cobb had died in 1976; George C. Scott signed on, calling it "a horror film and much more... a real drama, intricately crafted, with offbeat interesting characters". Several cast members carried over from The Ninth Configuration.

## Filming and the imposed exorcism
- Shot on location in Georgetown for eight weeks in mid-1989 under the tentative title Exorcist: Legion, with additional interiors at DEG Studios in Wilmington, North Carolina. Principal photography finished on time and "only slightly over budget".
- Four months later Morgan Creek demanded a new ending. Blatty: "James Robinson, the owner of the company, [had a] secretary [who] had insisted to him that this has nothing to do with The Exorcist. There had to be an exorcism."
- 20th Century Fox put up an additional $4 million in post-production for an effects-laden exorcism sequence with Nicol Williamson as Father Paul Morning, a character created for the new climax.
- Brad Dourif, who had played both Karras and the Gemini Killer, was recast with Jason Miller; when Miller could not recite many of his scenes "due to his severe alcoholism", Blatty recalled Dourif, who agreed on condition of rehearsal time with an acting assistant. All Dourif scenes in the final cut were re-shot at Hollywood Center Studios in Los Angeles - a performance he thought weaker than his Wilmington work.
- Blatty on the climax: "It's all right, but it's utterly unnecessary and it changes the character of the piece." He also described the compromise: "The original story that I sold [Morgan Creek] (and that I shot) ended with Kinderman blowing away Patient X. There was no exorcism... I foolishly thought: I can do a good exorcism, I'll turn this pig's ear into a silk purse. So I did it."
- Dourif recalled George C. Scott saying "the folks would only be satisfied if Madonna came out and sang a song at the end", and judged that "the original version was a hell of a lot purer... As it stands now, it's a mediocre film."
- Blatty confirmed that the asexual voice saying "I must save my son, the Gemini" is Pazuzu returned or "Old Scratch himself"; the voice deliberately echoes Mercedes McCambridge's in The Exorcist and was performed uncredited by Colleen Dewhurst, twice married to and divorced from George C. Scott.
- The novel and Blatty's original screenplay end differently: the Gemini Killer summons Kinderman for a final speech and dies once his abusive evangelist father Karl dies of a heart attack (in the screenplay, forced supernaturally by Karl's death), with flashbacks giving the killer's motives.

## Release, reception and box office
- First shown in October 1989 at the European MIFED film market, then opened in 1,288 US theaters on August 17, 1990, distributed by 20th Century Fox rather than Warner Bros. Linda Blair claimed it was rush-released ahead of the parody Repossessed, "hijacking the latter's publicity".
- Rotten Tomatoes "As of April 2026": 60% of 47 critics positive; consensus: "The Exorcist III is a talky, literary sequel with some scary moments that rival anything from the original." CinemaScore grade "C".
- Mark Kermode called it "a restrained, haunting chiller"; Vincent Canby (The New York Times) said it "is a better and funnier (intentionally) movie than either of its predecessors"; Ralph Novak (People) called it "one of the shrewdest, wittiest, most intense and most satisfying horror movies ever made". Owen Gleiberman (Entertainment Weekly) called it "an ash-gray disaster"; Kim Newman (Empire) faulted "the house-of-cards plot"; Kevin Thomas (Los Angeles Times) called it "a handsome, classy art film".
- Box office: opened first with $9,312,219 in the United States and Canada; total $26,098,824 domestic and $18 million international for $44 million worldwide. Blatty blamed the imposed title: "I begged them when they were considering titles not to name it Exorcist anything -- because Exorcist II was a disaster beyond imagination... But they went and named it Exorcist III." Working titles included The Exorcist: 1990.
- The lead notes the film "gained a cult following over time and is now largely considered the best sequel of the franchise".

## Awards
- 1991: won a Saturn Award for Best Writing (William Peter Blatty) and was nominated for Best Supporting Actor (Brad Dourif) and Best Horror Film at the 17th Saturn Awards.
- George C. Scott was nominated for a Golden Raspberry Award for Worst Actor at the 11th Golden Raspberry Awards, losing to Andrew Dice Clay.

## Director's cut
- Blatty said of the release version: "It's still a superior film... for me... it's a more frightening film than The Exorcist", while hoping to recover deleted footage. In 2007 his wife Julie Witbrodt reported Morgan Creek's claim that all the footage was lost, including an alternative opening in the morgue; Mark Kermode said the search was "ongoing".
- Documented deleted scenes include the morgue opening (with Karras's heart monitor showing signs of life), the aftermath of Father Kanavan's death, a longer Father Riley conversation, the exhumation of Karras's body revealing Brother Fain, a different isolation cell, and a face-morphing shot cut from the new exorcism climax.
- March 2011: a fan edit called Legion by "Spicediver" removed the exorcism elements and recreated the director's cut arc without lost footage; Dourif presented a screening at Mad Monster Party in Charlotte on March 25, 2012.
- December 2015: Morgan Creek hinted the director's cut had been discovered. On October 25, 2016, Scream Factory released a two-disc Collector's Edition. Blu-ray producer Cliff MacMillan: "Unfortunately, that footage has been lost to time. To that end, we turned to VHS tapes of the film's dailies to assemble the director's cut... This director's cut is a composite of varying footage quality from the best available sources."

## Legacy and adaptation
- "The film became a focal point of the trial of serial killer Jeffrey Dahmer." Detectives testified he identified with the Gemini Killer and played the film for some victims; Tracy Edwards testified Dahmer rocked and chanted and especially enjoyed a sequence with a possessed Karras; Dahmer bought yellow contact lenses to resemble Miller and to emulate Emperor Palpatine from Return of the Jedi (1983).
- The Exorcist: Legion VR, an episodic VR game by Wolf & Wood, Ltd., published by Fun Train for Steam VR, Meta Quest and PlayStation VR in 2018, is loosely based on the film; the player is an unnamed detective, and after a first episode with a similar church crime scene the remaining episodes are standalone stories.

wikis.title: A Quiet Place (2018 film)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia's article on A Quiet Place, John Krasinski's 2018 horror film about a family surviving blind creatures that hunt by sound - its origins, production, sign-language work, $341 million box office and awards.
wikis.body:
## The film

- **A Quiet Place**, a 2018 American post-apocalyptic horror film directed by **John Krasinski**, from a screenplay he co-wrote with **Scott Beck and Bryan Woods**, based on their story.
- A mother (**Emily Blunt**) and father (Krasinski) survive and raise their children (**Millicent Simmonds**, **Noah Jupe**) on a farm in Millbrook, New York, in a world overrun by blind creatures with an acute sense of hearing.
- Cinematography Charlotte Bruus Christensen; editing Christopher Tellefsen; music Marco Beltrami. Produced by Michael Bay, Andrew Form and Brad Fuller for Paramount Pictures, Platinum Dunes and Sunday Night Productions.
- Running time **90 minutes**; United States; English and American Sign Language. Budget **$17 million**.

## Dates

- World premiere as the opening-night film at **South by Southwest, March 9, 2018**, selected from 2,458 submissions.
- US theatrical release **April 6, 2018** in 3,508 theaters; China **May 18, 2018**.
- Home media: Digital HD June 26, 2018; disc July 10, 2018; a 4K Steelbook edition February 25, 2020.
- Written January 2016 onward by Beck and Woods; Krasinski read it in July 2016 and was announced as director in March 2017; filming ran May to November 2017, 36 days, in Dutchess and Ulster counties in upstate New York.

## Money

- **$188 million** in the United States and Canada, **$152 million** elsewhere, **$341 million** worldwide (the lead says "more than $340 million"). Deadline Hollywood estimated net profit at **$93 million** against an estimated $86 million in prints and advertising.
- Opening weekend **$50.2 million** - Paramount's biggest opening since *Star Trek Beyond* in July 2016 - after $18.9 million on day one including $4.3 million in previews. Its 34% second-weekend drop was "the second-best-ever second weekend for a scary movie behind *It*".

## Reception

- Rotten Tomatoes **96%** (387 reviews, 8.2/10); Metacritic **82/100** (55 critics, "universal acclaim"); CinemaScore B+.
- **Emily Blunt won the Screen Actors Guild Award** for Outstanding Performance by a Female Actor in a Supporting Role. The film won Critics' Choice Best Sci-Fi/Horror Movie, Saturn Awards for Best Horror Film and Best Writing, and top-ten placings from the American Film Institute and the National Board of Review. It was nominated for the Academy Award for Best Sound Editing, the Golden Globe for Best Original Score and the WGA Award for Best Original Screenplay.
- Krasinski called the film "all about parenthood"; critics including Bishop Robert Barron read pro-life themes into it, while Richard Brody of The New Yorker attacked what he saw as pro-gun themes, which Krasinski rejected.

## Craft

- The crew kept quiet on set so diegetic sounds could be recorded and amplified; sound editors Erik Aadahl and Ethan Van der Ryn cut sound entirely for Regan's point of view and modelled the creatures' clicking on animal echolocation.
- Deaf mentor Douglas Ridloff coached the cast in ASL, Simmonds helped teach her co-stars, and the producers eventually subtitled all sign-language dialogue rather than relying on "context clues".
- Industrial Light & Magic built the creatures under Scott Farrar, referencing prehistoric fish, black snakes, bats and bog people; Krasinski performed their motion capture.

## The series

- *A Quiet Place Part II* premiered March 8, 2020 and was released theatrically May 28, 2021 (the lead says simply "released in 2020").
- *A Quiet Place Part III* is in production for **July 30, 2027**; the spin-off prequel *A Quiet Place: Day One*, directed by Michael Sarnoski and starring Lupita Nyong'o, was released **June 28, 2024**.

wikis.title: A Quiet Place (2018) - film article from plot to sequels
wikis.summary: The body of the Wikipedia article on John Krasinski's 2018 horror film A Quiet Place: credits, plot, cast, how Beck and Woods's script reached Krasinski, filming, sound and sign language, creature design, box office, reviews, awards and the themes critics found in it.
wikis.body:
## Infobox

- **A Quiet Place**, "2018 film by John Krasinski". Directed by **John Krasinski**; screenplay by **Bryan Woods, Scott Beck and John Krasinski**; story by **Bryan Woods and Scott Beck**.
- Produced by Michael Bay, Andrew Form and Brad Fuller. Starring Emily Blunt and John Krasinski. Cinematography **Charlotte Bruus Christensen**; edited by **Christopher Tellefsen**; music by **Marco Beltrami**.
- Production companies **Paramount Pictures**, **Platinum Dunes**, **Sunday Night Productions**; distributed by Paramount Pictures.
- Release dates: **March 9, 2018** (SXSW), **April 6, 2018** (United States). Running time **90 minutes**; country United States; languages English and American Sign Language.
- Budget **$17 million**; box office **$341 million**.

## Lead

- A 2018 American post-apocalyptic horror film about a mother (Emily Blunt) and father (Krasinski) surviving and raising their children (Millicent Simmonds and Noah Jupe) "in a post-apocalyptic world inhabited by blind extraterrestrial creatures with an acute sense of hearing".
- Beck and Woods developed the concept in college and began writing in January 2016; they told Platinum Dunes they wanted Blunt for the mother. Krasinski read the script for the father's role in July 2016 and was announced as director, co-writer and co-star with Blunt in March 2017. Filming took place in upstate New York from May to November 2017.
- Premiered at South by Southwest March 9, 2018; released in the United States April 6, 2018 by Paramount Pictures; "grossed more than $340 million worldwide and received critical acclaim".
- Chosen by the National Board of Review and the American Film Institute as one of the top ten films of 2018. Nominated for the Golden Globe for Best Original Score, the Academy Award for Best Sound Editing and the Writers Guild of America Award for Best Original Screenplay; Blunt won the Screen Actors Guild Award for Outstanding Performance by a Female Actor in a Supporting Role.
- "It is the first film in the A Quiet Place universe. Its sequel, A Quiet Place Part II, was released in 2020."

## Figures given more than one way

- **Gross**: the infobox says **$341 million**; the lead says "more than $340 million"; the Theatrical run section gives **$188 million** in the United States and Canada and **$152 million** elsewhere for **$341 million**.
- **Sequel release**: the lead says *A Quiet Place Part II* "was released in 2020"; the Sequels section says it premiered on March 8, 2020 and "was released theatrically on May 28, 2021".
- The article's date categories include both "Films set in 2020" and "Films set in 2021", and it carries a references-cleanup tag dated August 2026 for duplicated citations.

## Plot (as summarised in the article)

- Sightless aliens with sharp hearing and impenetrable armoured skin have killed most of humanity. The Abbott family - father Lee, mother Evelyn, deaf daughter Regan, sons Marcus and Beau - survive on an isolated farm in Millbrook, New York using sand paths and American Sign Language.
- On a supply trip, Beau takes batteries for a toy Space Shuttle without anyone noticing; when he switches it on he is killed by an alien. Regan carries the guilt.
- Over a year later Evelyn is pregnant. Lee's attempts at a hearing aid for Regan produce only a high-pitched noise. Alone and in labour, Evelyn steps on a nail, drops a picture frame and draws an alien into the house; she turns the outside lights red, distracts the creature with an egg timer and gives birth after Lee has Marcus set off fireworks as a lure.
- Lee moves Evelyn and the baby to a hiding spot under the barn floor; the alien breaks water pipes and Evelyn hides behind the falling water to mask the baby's noise.
- Marcus and Regan light a signal fire on a corn silo; Marcus falls in, Regan follows and is nearly swallowed by the corn before he pulls her out. The alien attacks and Regan's hearing aid emits the whine that drives it off, breaking a hole that frees them.
- Lee is wounded protecting the children, signs to Regan "I have always loved you" and shouts to draw the alien away. Back at the house Regan puts the hearing aid on a microphone, the amplified noise exposes the tissue under the creature's head armour, and Evelyn kills it with Lee's pump shotgun. The film ends with Evelyn racking the shotgun as a pack of aliens approaches.

## Cast

- Emily Blunt as Evelyn Abbott; John Krasinski as Lee Abbott, an engineer; Millicent Simmonds as Regan Abbott, the 15-year-old deaf daughter; Noah Jupe as Marcus Abbott, 12; Cade Woodward as Beau Abbott, 4; Leon Russom as a man in the woods.
- Krasinski also provided the motion capture for the creatures.
- Krasinski on casting Regan: he wanted a deaf actress "for many reasons; I didn't want a non-deaf actress pretending to be deaf... a deaf actress would help my knowledge and my understanding of the situations tenfold." He noticed Jupe in the 2016 miniseries *The Night Manager* and watched an early screening of *Suburbicon* (2017).

## Development and writing

- Beck and Woods began writing in **January 2016** from a college concept, and told Platinum Dunes they wanted Emily Blunt for the mother. Michael Bay's first-look deal took the script to Paramount; a Paramount executive suggested during writing that it could be a *Cloverfield* crossover, but the studio took the final script as a stand-alone. Paramount bought it.
- Producers Andrew Form and Brad Fuller sent it to Krasinski for the father; he read it in **July 2016**. The idea of parents protecting children appealed to him, his second child with Blunt having just been born. Beck and Woods cited Bong Joon-ho's *The Host* (2006) as a significant influence.
- Krasinski pitched his vision to Blunt, who suggested he direct, then asked the producers to let him co-write and direct. He wrote with Blunt in mind but did not ask her - "I just thought if she does this, she has to come to it on her own." Blunt initially did not want the part but read the script on a flight and felt she had to do it, as the story "represented some of my deepest fears - of not being able to protect my children."
- Beck and Woods said Krasinski's takeover "wasn't about reshaping it in any massive way" and that he "really protected our vision of the script"; Krasinski said the scripts differed "in a bunch of little ways, but the heart was all theirs".
- Krasinski's additions: sign language, the sand paths, the lights, and the walk to the forest and the pharmacy. He was anxious about so little dialogue before realising it was the film's "superpower"; the sign-language idea came when Simmonds showed him the ASL translation of a scene's dialogue and he found the gestures "so much more cinematic than saying the words would've been".
- Blunt contributed through pre-production; Krasinski said she "offered up the greatest ideas" and credited her with "raising the game" for him as a filmmaker.
- March 2017: Krasinski announced as director and co-writer - his third directing credit and first for a major studio. Budget **$17 million**.

## Filming

- Shot in **36 days**, May to November 2017, in Dutchess and Ulster counties in upstate New York. The production spent locally, including buying 20 tons of corn grown by local farmers it hired.
- Locations: a soundstage in the town of Pawling and the city of Beacon (Dutchess County); the Wallkill Valley Rail Trail in New Paltz, Ulster County, using the Springtown Truss Bridge; and Main Street in Little Falls, Herkimer County.

## Sound and music

- The crew stayed quiet during filming so diegetic synchronized sounds - "the sound of rolling dice on a game board" - could be recorded and amplified in post.
- Krasinski added a score so audiences would have a cinematic experience rather than feel part of a "silence experiment"; some music was cut, which he found more impactful.
- Supervising sound editors **Erik Aadahl** and **Ethan Van der Ryn** removed sound for scenes from the deaf daughter's perspective, and advised organising shots to show the creatures noticing a sound before revealing its source. Marco Beltrami supplied music that would not interfere with the sound design.
- The creatures communicate through clicking; Aadahl and Van der Ryn drew on animal echolocation such as bats, and wove in feedback - normally avoided by sound editors - at a bearable loudness.
- Simmonds worked with the sound designers on what the film's cochlear implants would sound like and what Regan could hear without them.

## Use of sign language

- Deaf mentor **Douglas Ridloff** taught ASL to the actors and made corrections; an ASL interpreter worked on set for Simmonds. Simmonds grew up with ASL and helped teach her fellow actors: "In the movie, we've been signing together for years and years. So it should look fluent."
- She observed the father's signs were "short and brief", showing a survival mentality, while the mother's were more expressive; Krasinski said Regan's signing was "very defiant, it's very teenage defiant".
- Simmonds suggested the daughter rebel rather than cower in the sign-language argument with her father, and that his closing "I love you" become "I've always loved you".
- Producers Form and Fuller had planned to use only "context clues" rather than subtitles, but decided subtitles were needed for the hearing-aid argument and then added them for all sign-language dialogue.

## Creature design

- Production designer **Jeffrey Beecroft** headed creature design; **Industrial Light & Magic** created the creatures under visual effects supervisor **Scott Farrar**.
- The director wanted creatures that looked evolved beyond needing eyes and "somewhat humanoid". An early design had rhinoceros-like horns, dropped as not scary enough. Designers referenced prehistoric fish, black snakes and bats, particularly movement, and bog people - "cadavers that have been mummified in peat, turning the skin black and giving it a sagging, leathery look". Krasinski provided the motion capture.

## Marketing

- First trailer November 2017; a 30-second Super Bowl LII commercial on **February 4, 2018**. Of seven playoff trailers, *A Quiet Place* and *Red Sparrow* ran in the pregame with the lowest views - 149,000 on YouTube, 275,000 on Facebook and 2,900 social conversations. Krasinski presented the full trailer on *The Ellen DeGeneres Show* on February 12, 2018.
- The studio spent an estimated **$86 million** on prints and advertising.

## Release and box office

- World premiere as the opening-night film at **South by Southwest, March 9, 2018**, selected from 2,458 submissions and earning "raves" per IndieWire. Social media views afterwards passed 52 million across platforms, outpacing *Get Out* (2017) at 46.9 million.
- Forecasts: The Tracking Board (March 14) credited "stellar reviews out of SXSW"; Deadline projected about $20 million opening (March 15); Variety reported tracking of $16-30 million (March 27), settling to a low-$20 million floor. BoxOffice estimated $17 million opening and $60 million domestic on February 9, raised by March 30 to $27.5 million and $85 million, drawing "very favorable" comparisons to *10 Cloverfield Lane* and *Don't Breathe*.
- Released in **3,508** US and Canadian theaters on April 6, 2018 alongside *Blockers*, *Chappaquiddick* and *The Miracle Season*. First day **$18.9 million** including **$4.3 million** in Thursday previews at 2,750 theaters; Saturday **$19.1 million**, unusual for a front-loaded horror release; opening weekend **$50.2 million**, number one and Paramount's biggest opening since *Star Trek Beyond* in July 2016.
- Second weekend $32.9 million, down 34% - "the second-best-ever second weekend for a scary movie behind *It*" - finishing behind *Rampage* ($35.7 million). Third weekend back at number one with $20.9 million (down 36%); fourth weekend $10.7 million, second to *Avengers: Infinity War*.
- International: $51.7 million in the first two weeks, led by the UK ($9.2 million), Mexico ($5.1 million), Australia ($4.6 million), Brazil ($3.9 million), Indonesia ($3.4 million), the Philippines ($2.7 million) and Taiwan ($1.9 million); Russia opened to $2.2 million, the biggest ever for a Paramount horror film there. Third overseas weekend $15 million from 57 markets (down 37%); fourth $6.6 million. As of May 20, 2018 the largest markets were the UK ($16.3 million), Australia ($9.3 million), Mexico ($7.5 million) and Brazil ($6.9 million). China opened May 18 with $17.7 million from 8,731 screens.
- Totals: **$188 million** US and Canada, **$152 million** elsewhere, **$341 million** worldwide. Deadline Hollywood estimates net profit at **$93 million**.

## Critical response

- Rotten Tomatoes **96%** from 387 reviews (average 8.2/10); consensus: "A Quiet Place artfully plays on elemental fears with a ruthlessly intelligent creature feature that's as original as it is scary - and establishes director John Krasinski as a rising talent." Metacritic **82 out of 100** from 55 critics, "universal acclaim". CinemaScore **B+**; PostTrak 81% positive and 63% "definite recommend".
- Peter Travers (Rolling Stone) 3.5/4: "This new horror classic will fry your nerves to a frazzle." Owen Gleiberman (Variety): "a tautly original genre-bending exercise, technically sleek and accomplished... though it's a little too in love with the stoned logic of its own premise." Michael Phillips (Chicago Tribune) 2.5/4: "I don't know if I'd call A Quiet Place enjoyable; it's more grueling than cathartic."
- Stephen King tweeted: "A QUIET PLACE is an extraordinary piece of work. Terrific acting, but the main thing is the SILENCE, and how it makes the camera's eye open wide in a way few movies manage." Nick Allen (RogerEbert.com) called it "Krasinski's breakthrough as a triple-threat entertainer". Peter Bradshaw (The Guardian) called it "a cracking back-to-basics thriller".
- Matthew Monagle (Film School Rejects) called it "the early frontrunner for the sparsely intellectual horror movie of the year", alongside *The Babadook* and *The Witch*. Tatiana Tenreyro (Bustle) wrote that while not a silent film "It is the first of its kind within the modern horror genre for how little spoken dialogue it actually has."
- In **July 2025** The Hollywood Reporter ranked it **number 23** on its "25 Best Horror Movies of the 21st Century".

## Accolades

- **Wins**: American Film Institute Top 10 Films of the Year (January 4, 2019); Critics' Choice Movie Award for Best Sci-Fi/Horror Movie (January 13, 2019); Hollywood Film Awards Hollywood Sound Award - Erik Aadahl, Ethan Van der Ryn, Brandon Proctor (November 4, 2018); Motion Picture Sound Editors, Feature Film - Effects/Foley (February 17, 2019); National Board of Review Top Ten Films (January 8, 2019); Satellite Award for Best Sound (Editing and Mixing) (February 17, 2019); Saturn Awards for Best Horror Film and Best Writing - Bryan Woods, Scott Beck, John Krasinski (September 13, 2019); Screen Actors Guild Award, Outstanding Performance by a Female Actor in a Supporting Role - **Emily Blunt** (January 27, 2019).
- **Nominations**: Academy Award for Best Sound Editing - Erik Aadahl and Ethan Van der Ryn (February 24, 2019); BAFTA Best Sound - Aadahl, Michael Barosky, Brandon Procter, Van der Ryn (February 10, 2019); Critics' Choice Best Original Screenplay and Best Young Performer (Millicent Simmonds); Golden Globe Best Original Score - Marco Beltrami (January 6, 2019); Hollywood Music in Media Award; MPSE Music Underscore and Dialogue/ADR; MTV Movie & TV Awards Most Frightened Performance (Emily Blunt); People's Choice Awards Movie of the Year, Drama Movie of the Year and Drama Movie Star (Blunt and Krasinski); Producers Guild Award for Best Theatrical Motion Picture; San Diego Film Critics Society Best Film, Director, Editing and Original Screenplay; Satellite Best Original Screenplay; Saturn nominations for Simmonds, editing and special effects; Teen Choice Choice Drama Movie; Writers Guild of America Best Original Screenplay.

## Commentary and themes

- Krasinski called the primary theme a dramatization of "fears associated with modern parenthood", saying he "was already in a state of terror about whether or not [he] was a good enough father", and told CBS News "the scares were secondary to how powerful this could be as an allegory or metaphor for parenthood. For me, this is all about parenthood."
- Travers (Rolling Stone) framed it around Evelyn's line "Who are we, if we can't protect our children?"; John DeFore (The Hollywood Reporter) called it "a terrifying thriller with a surprisingly warm heart", comparing it to Jeff Nichols' *Take Shelter* (2011).
- Krasinski said political readings were not his aim but welcomed the conversation; he researched *Don't Breathe* (2016) and *Get Out* (2017), compared the premise to US politics in 2018 - "You can close your eyes and stick your head in the sand, or you can try to participate" - and cited *Jaws* (1975) as an influence.
- Roman Catholic Bishop Robert Barron read the family's silent agrarian life as monastic and saw pro-life themes in the parents' choices; Sonny Bunch of The Washington Post expanded on the pro-life reading.
- Richard Brody (The New Yorker) criticised what he saw as conservative and pro-gun themes, calling the film "the antithesis of 'Get Out'" and "both apparently unconscious and conspicuously regressive". Krasinski replied in Esquire: "I never saw it that way... my whole metaphor was solely about parenthood."

## Home media and follow-ups

- Digital HD **June 26, 2018**; Ultra HD Blu-ray, Blu-ray and DVD **July 10, 2018**; a 4K Steelbook+Blu-Ray+Digital edition on **February 25, 2020**.
- *A Quiet Place Part II*, written and directed by Krasinski with Blunt, Simmonds, Jupe, Cillian Murphy and Djimon Hounsou, premiered March 8, 2020 and was released theatrically May 28, 2021.
- *A Quiet Place Part III* is "currently in production and is set to release on July 30, 2027".
- The spin-off prequel *A Quiet Place: Day One*, written and directed by Michael Sarnoski and starring Lupita Nyong'o "as a terminally ill woman attempting to escape New York City during the early stages of the alien invasion", was released **June 28, 2024**.

wikis.title: How the script reached Krasinski
wikis.summary: Beck and Woods's college concept, Platinum Dunes and Paramount, and how Krasinski came to co-write, direct and star.
wikis.body:
- Scott Beck and Bryan Woods began writing in **January 2016** from a concept conceived in college, and told Platinum Dunes they wanted Emily Blunt for the mother.
- Michael Bay's first-look deal with Paramount took the script to the studio. A Paramount executive suggested during writing that the film could be a crossover with the *Cloverfield* franchise; the studio accepted the final script as a distinct, stand-alone story and bought it.
- Producers Andrew Form and Brad Fuller sent the script to John Krasinski for the father's role; he read it in **July 2016**, drawn by parents protecting children as his second child with Blunt had just been born. Beck and Woods cited Bong Joon-ho's *The Host* (2006) as a significant influence.
- Krasinski pitched his vision to Blunt, who suggested he direct, and then asked the producers to let him co-write and direct. He wrote with her in mind but would not ask her: "I just thought if she does this, she has to come to it on her own." Blunt at first did not want the part, then read the script on a flight and felt she had to do it - the story "represented some of my deepest fears - of not being able to protect my children."
- Beck and Woods said Krasinski "really protected our vision of the script"; he said the heart of it "was all theirs". His own contributions: sign language, sand paths, the lights, the walk to the forest and the pharmacy.
- March 2017: announced as director and co-writer alongside Blunt - his third film as director and first for a major studio. Budget $17 million.

wikis.title: Sound design and the film's near-silence
wikis.summary: How the sound team, the score and the quiet set shaped the film.
wikis.body:
- The crew avoided noise during filming so diegetic synchronized sounds, such as dice rolling on a game board, could be recorded and then amplified in post-production.
- Krasinski added a musical score so audiences would have "a cinematic experience and some familiarity with a traditional film component, instead of feeling like they're part of a 'silence experiment'"; cutting some music proved more impactful than letting the score dominate.
- Supervising sound editors Erik Aadahl and Ethan Van der Ryn removed sound for scenes told from the deaf daughter's perspective, and advised organising shots to show the creatures noticing a sound before revealing its cause. Marco Beltrami supplied music written not to interfere with the sound design.
- The blind creatures communicate in clicks; the editors drew on animal echolocation such as bats, and worked in feedback - a sound editors normally avoid - at a loudness that would not bother audiences.
- Millicent Simmonds worked with the sound designers on what the film's cochlear implants would sound like and what Regan could hear without them.
- Krasinski was anxious about having almost no dialogue before realising minimal dialogue was the film's "superpower".

wikis.title: American Sign Language on set and on screen
wikis.summary: The ASL coaching, Simmonds's input into her character, and the decision to subtitle all signing.
wikis.body:
- Deaf mentor **Douglas Ridloff** was hired to teach ASL to the actors and correct them on set, alongside an ASL interpreter for Millicent Simmonds so spoken and signed language could be interpreted both ways.
- Simmonds grew up with ASL and helped teach her fellow actors: "In the movie, we've been signing together for years and years. So it should look fluent."
- She observed that signing reflected character: the father's signs were "short and brief", showing a survival mentality, while the mother's were more expressive, wanting her children to experience more than survival. Krasinski said Regan's signing was "very defiant, it's very teenage defiant".
- Simmonds suggested the daughter rebel rather than cower during the sign-language argument with her father, and that his closing "I love you" become "I've always loved you" to make up for the earlier argument.
- Producers Andrew Form and Bradley Fuller had planned to give only "context clues" rather than on-screen subtitles, but decided subtitles were necessary for the hearing-aid argument and then subtitled all sign-language dialogue.

wikis.title: Designing the creatures
wikis.summary: Who built the aliens and what they were modelled on.
wikis.body:
- Production designer **Jeffrey Beecroft** headed creature design; **Industrial Light & Magic** created the creatures, led by visual effects supervisor **Scott Farrar**.
- Krasinski wanted them to look like they had evolved to no longer need eyes, and to be "somewhat humanoid".
- An initial design gave them rhinoceros-like horns coming out of their faces; later redesigns dropped this "because it was not scary enough".
- References: prehistoric fish, black snakes and bats, particularly their movement patterns, plus bog people - "cadavers that have been mummified in peat, turning the skin black and giving it a sagging, leathery look".
- Krasinski himself provided the motion capture for the creatures.

wikis.title: Box office run
wikis.summary: Forecasts, the $50.2 million opening and the film's unusually strong holds.
wikis.body:
- Released in **3,508** US and Canadian theaters on April 6, 2018 alongside *Blockers*, *Chappaquiddick* and *The Miracle Season*, after an estimated **$86 million** in prints and advertising.
- Forecasts ranged from $16-30 million (Variety tracking) to $27.5 million (BoxOffice, March 30, with an $85 million domestic total); Deadline projected about $20 million.
- First day **$18.9 million** including **$4.3 million** in Thursday previews from 2,750 theaters; Saturday rose to **$19.1 million**, unlike front-loaded horror releases; opening weekend **$50.2 million**, number one and Paramount's biggest opening since *Star Trek Beyond* in July 2016.
- Second weekend $32.9 million, down only 34%, "the second-best-ever second weekend for a scary movie behind *It*"; third weekend back at number one with $20.9 million; fourth weekend $10.7 million behind *Avengers: Infinity War*.
- International: $51.7 million in two weeks, led by the UK, Mexico, Australia, Brazil, Indonesia, the Philippines and Taiwan; a $2.2 million Russian opening, Paramount's biggest ever for a horror film there; $17.7 million opening in China from 8,731 screens on May 18.
- Totals: **$188 million** US and Canada, **$152 million** elsewhere, **$341 million** worldwide. Deadline Hollywood estimated net profit at **$93 million**.

wikis.title: Reviews, awards and the arguments over its themes
wikis.summary: Acclaim and prizes, and the parenthood, pro-life and pro-gun readings critics brought to the film.
wikis.body:
- Rotten Tomatoes **96%** (387 reviews, 8.2/10); Metacritic **82/100** (55 critics, "universal acclaim"); CinemaScore B+; PostTrak 81% positive.
- Stephen King called it "an extraordinary piece of work... the main thing is the SILENCE". Peter Travers (Rolling Stone) 3.5/4 called it a "new horror classic"; Owen Gleiberman (Variety) found it "a little too in love with the stoned logic of its own premise"; Michael Phillips (Chicago Tribune) 2.5/4 found it "more grueling than cathartic". The Hollywood Reporter ranked it 23rd on its "25 Best Horror Movies of the 21st Century" in July 2025.
- Major awards: **Emily Blunt won the Screen Actors Guild Award** for Outstanding Performance by a Female Actor in a Supporting Role; the film won the Critics' Choice Best Sci-Fi/Horror Movie, Saturn Awards for Best Horror Film and Best Writing, a Satellite Award for Sound, an MPSE Effects/Foley award, and AFI and National Board of Review top-ten placings. It was nominated for the Academy Award for Best Sound Editing, the Golden Globe for Best Original Score, BAFTA Best Sound and the WGA Award for Best Original Screenplay.
- Themes: Krasinski called it a dramatization of "fears associated with modern parenthood" - "the scares were secondary to how powerful this could be as an allegory or metaphor for parenthood."
- Bishop Robert Barron saw monastic and pro-life themes in the family's silent agrarian life and the parents' sacrifices; Sonny Bunch (The Washington Post) expanded on the pro-life reading.
- Richard Brody (The New Yorker) called it "the antithesis of 'Get Out'" and "conspicuously regressive" for what he saw as pro-gun themes; Krasinski told Esquire "I never saw it that way... my whole metaphor was solely about parenthood."

wikis.title: The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring (2001 film)
wikis.summary: The English Wikipedia article on The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring, covering the 2001 Peter Jackson film's credits, plot, cast and near-misses in casting, its departures from Tolkien, the New Zealand locations, box office records and its four Academy Awards.
wikis.body:
## The film

- "*The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring* is a 2001 epic fantasy film directed by Peter Jackson from a screenplay by Fran Walsh, Philippa Boyens, and Jackson", the first instalment of the trilogy, based on Tolkien's 1954 first volume.
- Produced by Barrie M. Osborne, Peter Jackson, Fran Walsh and Tim Sanders; cinematography Andrew Lesnie; edited by John Gilbert; score by Howard Shore. WingNut Films and New Line Cinema; distributed by New Line Cinema.
- Premiered 10 December 2001 at the Odeon Leicester Square in London, released 19 December 2001 in the United States and 20 December 2001 in New Zealand, "internationally in most major territories on 10,000 screens". Running time 178 minutes; budget $93 million; infobox box office $897.5 million.
- "Financed and distributed by American studio New Line Cinema, but filmed and edited entirely in Jackson's native New Zealand, concurrently with the other two parts of the trilogy."

## Production and casting

Jackson began storyboarding with Christian Rivers in August 1997 and set Richard Taylor and Weta Workshop to designing Middle-earth; Alan Lee and John Howe joined as primary conceptual designers in November 1997. Ngila Dickson joined as costume designer on 1 April 1999 and, with 40 seamstresses, "created 19,000 costumes, 40 per version for the actor and their doubles". The principal actors trained for six weeks in sword fighting with Bob Anderson, riding and boating before filming began on 11 October 1999, and the nine Fellowship actors later got a tattoo of the Elvish symbol for nine. Elijah Wood was cast first, on 7 July 1999, from 150 auditions; Liv Tyler was among the last, on 25 August 1999. The article lists many actors approached or turned down, including Sean Connery, Patrick Stewart, Anthony Hopkins and David Bowie for Gandalf, Daniel Day-Lewis, Nicolas Cage, Russell Crowe and Stuart Townsend (cast and then replaced during filming) for Aragorn, and Lucy Lawless for Galadriel.

Locations across New Zealand stood in for Middle-earth: Matamata for Hobbiton, Kaitoke Regional Park for Rivendell, the Arrow River and Skippers Canyon for the Ford of Bruinen, Paradise near Glenorchy for Lothlórien and Parth Galen, and the Whakapapa skifield in Tongariro National Park for the Mordor prologue.

## Changes from the novel

The prologue compresses the Last Alliance's seven-year siege of Barad-dûr into a single battle and shows Sauron exploding, "though Tolkien only said his spirit flees". Tom Bombadil is omitted, the 17-year gap before Gandalf returns is compressed, and the Uruk-hai ambush and Boromir's death - the opening of *The Two Towers* in the book - are moved to the film's climax. In Moria, Gandalf resists the plan rather than advocating it, and the dead Dwarves are shown at once rather than at Balin's tomb.

## Reception

- Opening day $18.2 million in the United States and Canada from 3,359 cinemas plus $11.5 million in 13 countries; $47.2 million opening weekend and $75.1 million over five days, setting a December opening record ahead of *Ocean's Eleven*; number one in 29 international markets.
- Initial release: "$313.4 million in the United States and Canada and $555 million in the rest of the world for a worldwide total of $868.4 million", the second-highest-grossing film of 2001 and then the fifth-highest-grossing of all time. After reissues, $326 million domestic and $570 million overseas for $897 million.
- Rotten Tomatoes 91% from 269 reviews; Metacritic 92/100 from 34 critics ("universal acclaim"); CinemaScore "A−".
- Won four Academy Awards from thirteen nominations - Best Cinematography, Best Makeup, Best Original Score and Best Visual Effects - plus the 2002 Hugo Award for Best Dramatic Presentation, BAFTAs including Best Film and Best Direction, three Saturn Awards and a SAG award for Ian McKellen.
- Named by AFI in 2007 as one of the 100 greatest American films, "being both the most recent film and the only film released in the 21st century to make it to the list", and selected for the United States National Film Registry in 2021.

## Inconsistencies within the page

- The accolades prose credits "five BAFTAs, including Best Film, the David Lean Award for Best Direction, the Audience Award (voted for by the public), Best Special Effects, and Best Make-up", while the accolades table records four wins and does not list the Audience Award.
- The lead gives the original-run gross as "$868 million" and the total after reissues as "$897 million", where the box office section gives "$868.4 million" and the infobox "$897.5 million".

The second part of the capture is Middle-earth navigation boxes and the category list; no published or last-updated date is stated.

wikis.title: The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring (2001): plot, cast, production, release and reception
wikis.summary: Part 1 of the English Wikipedia article on The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring, covering the 2001 film's credits and infobox figures, plot, cast and the actors considered, changes from Tolkien's novel, design and New Zealand filming locations, score, release, box office, reviews and awards.
wikis.body:
## The film

- "*The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring* is a 2001 epic fantasy film directed by Peter Jackson from a screenplay by Fran Walsh, Philippa Boyens, and Jackson", based on Tolkien's 1954 *The Fellowship of the Ring*, the first instalment of the trilogy.
- Produced by Barrie M. Osborne, Peter Jackson, Fran Walsh and Tim Sanders. Cinematography Andrew Lesnie; edited by John Gilbert; music by Howard Shore. Production companies WingNut Films and New Line Cinema; distributed by New Line Cinema.
- Release dates: 10 December 2001 (Odeon Leicester Square), 19 December 2001 (United States), 20 December 2001 (New Zealand). Running time 178 minutes. Countries New Zealand and United States; language English. Budget $93 million; box office $897.5 million.
- Ensemble cast: Elijah Wood, Ian McKellen, Liv Tyler, Viggo Mortensen, Sean Astin, Cate Blanchett, John Rhys-Davies, Billy Boyd, Dominic Monaghan, Orlando Bloom, Christopher Lee, Hugo Weaving, Sean Bean, Ian Holm and Andy Serkis.
- "The Fellowship of the Ring was financed and distributed by American studio New Line Cinema, but filmed and edited entirely in Jackson's native New Zealand, concurrently with the other two parts of the trilogy."
- "It grossed $868 million worldwide during its original theatrical run, making it the second-highest-grossing film of 2001 and the fifth-highest-grossing film of all time at the time of its release. Following subsequent reissues, it has grossed $897 million."
- At the 74th Academy Awards it was nominated for thirteen awards including Best Picture, winning Best Cinematography, Best Makeup, Best Original Score and Best Visual Effects.
- "In 2007, the American Film Institute named it one of the 100 greatest American films in history, being both the most recent film and the only film released in the 21st century to make it to the list. In 2021, the film was selected for preservation in the United States National Film Registry by the Library of Congress for being 'culturally, historically, or aesthetically significant'."
- *The Two Towers* and *The Return of the King* followed in 2002 and 2003.

## Plot

The prologue sets out the forging of the Rings of Power, Sauron's One Ring, Isildur severing Sauron's finger, and the Ring's passage to Gollum and then Bilbo Baggins. Bilbo leaves the Shire at his 111th birthday, passing the Ring to Frodo. Gandalf learns its nature, is imprisoned by Saruman at Isengard and escapes on a Great Eagle. Frodo, Sam, Merry and Pippin flee the Nazgûl to Bree, are helped by Strider and reach Rivendell, where Elrond's council decides the Ring must be destroyed at Mount Doom and the Fellowship is formed. In Moria the Fellowship finds the Dwarves dead and Gandalf falls with the Balrog; in Lothlórien Galadriel warns Frodo that one of his companions will try to take the Ring. At Parth Galen Boromir tries to take it and is mortally wounded by Lurtz's Uruk-hai, who capture Merry and Pippin; Frodo leaves for Mordor with Sam while Aragorn, Legolas and Gimli set out to rescue the others.

## Score

- Composed by Howard Shore and "performed by the New Zealand Symphony Orchestra, the London Philharmonic Orchestra, the London Voices, The London Oratory School Schola, and the Maori Samoan Choir", with several vocal soloists.
- "Two original songs, 'Aníron' and the end title theme 'May It Be', were composed and sung by Enya, who allowed her label, Reprise Records, to release the soundtrack to The Fellowship of the Ring and its two sequels." Shore also composed "In Dreams", sung by Edward Ross of the London Oratory School Schola.

## Discrepancies within the page

- **BAFTA wins**: the accolades prose says the film won "five BAFTAs, including Best Film, the David Lean Award for Best Direction, the Audience Award (voted for by the public), Best Special Effects, and Best Make-up", while the accolades table records four wins - Best Film, Best Direction, Best Makeup and Hair, and Best Special Visual Effects - and does not list the Audience Award at all.
- **Original-run gross**: the lead gives "$868 million worldwide during its original theatrical run" and the box office section "$868.4 million"; the lead gives "$897 million" after reissues against the infobox's "$897.5 million".

wikis.title: Cast and the actors who were considered
wikis.summary: The ensemble cast, how each was chosen, and the long list of actors approached or turned down for the major roles.
wikis.body:
- "Before filming began on 11 October 1999, the principal actors trained for six weeks in sword fighting (with Bob Anderson), riding and boating", partly so they would bond and get used to life in Wellington, and were trained to pronounce Tolkien's verses properly. "After the shoot, the nine cast members playing the Fellowship got a tattoo, the Elvish symbol for the number nine, with the exception of John Rhys-Davies, whose stunt double got the tattoo instead."
- **Elijah Wood as Frodo Baggins**: "the first actor to be cast on 7 July 1999", selected from 150 actors who auditioned; he sent an audition dressed as Frodo. Jake Gyllenhaal auditioned unsuccessfully "after his agency miscommunicated his direction to an American accent".
- **Ian McKellen as Gandalf the Grey**: Sean Connery was approached "but did not understand the plot"; Patrick Stewart turned it down as he disliked the script; Patrick McGoohan declined for health reasons; Anthony Hopkins and Christopher Plummer also turned it down; Richard Harris expressed interest; John Astin and David Bowie auditioned; Sam Neill declined over a scheduling conflict with *Jurassic Park III*. McKellen had to sort out a two-month overlap with *X-Men* with 20th Century Fox. "In 2026, Jackson stated that he is glad that Connery declined." McKellen based his accent on a recording of Tolkien reading *The Hobbit*, and worked with the hobbit actors' scale doubles rather than the actors.
- **Viggo Mortensen as Aragorn**: Daniel Day-Lewis turned it down twice; Nicolas Cage declined over family obligations; Stuart Townsend was cast and replaced during filming "when Jackson realised he was too young"; Russell Crowe turned it down "because he believed Jackson was not interested in casting him"; Jason Patric was considered. Executive producer Mark Ordesky saw Mortensen in a play, and Mortensen's son persuaded him to take the role; he read the book on the plane, took a crash course in fencing from Bob Anderson and began with the Weathertop scenes.
- **Sean Astin as Samwise Gamgee**: Astin, a new father, bonded protectively with the 18-year-old Wood. James Corden, Graham Norton and Corey Feldman read for the part.
- **Sean Bean as Boromir**: initially considered for Aragorn; Bruce Willis expressed interest and Liam Neeson was sent the script but passed.
- **Dominic Monaghan as Merry**: cast after auditioning for Frodo. **Billy Boyd as Pippin.**
- **John Rhys-Davies as Gimli**: Billy Connolly was considered and later played Dáin II Ironfoot in *The Hobbit*. Rhys-Davies's heavy prosthetics limited his vision and he developed eczema around his eyes; he also played Gimli's father Glóin.
- **Orlando Bloom as Legolas**: initially auditioned for Faramir, a role that went to David Wenham.
- **Liv Tyler as Arwen**: approached after *Plunkett & Macleane*; Helena Bonham Carter had expressed interest. Tyler was "one of the last actors to be cast, on 25 August 1999".
- **Cate Blanchett as Galadriel**: Lucy Lawless was considered but turned it down as she was pregnant, and later regretted it.
- **Christopher Lee as Saruman the White**: a major fan who read the book once a year and had met Tolkien; he auditioned for Gandalf "but was judged too old".
- **Hugo Weaving as Elrond**: David Bowie expressed interest; Jackson said "To have a famous, beloved character and a famous star colliding is slightly uncomfortable."
- **Ian Holm as Bilbo Baggins**: had played Frodo in a 1981 radio adaptation. Sylvester McCoy was kept as a potential Bilbo for six months before Jackson chose Holm.
- **Andy Serkis as Gollum** (voice/motion-capture), appearing briefly: heard shouting in Mordor and seen only as eyes and nose in Moria. Serkis was working on the 1999 *Oliver Twist* miniseries when approached, and was initially doubtful about a role where his face would not appear.

wikis.title: Changes from Tolkien's novel
wikis.summary: The condensations and reworkings Jackson, Walsh and Boyens made, from the prologue to the Moria sequence.
wikis.body:
- "Jackson, Walsh and Boyens made numerous changes to the story, for purposes of pacing and character development. Jackson said his main desire was to make a film focused primarily on Frodo and the Ring, the 'backbone' of the story."
- "The prologue condenses Tolkien's backstory, in which The Last Alliance's seven-year siege of Barad-dûr is a single battle, where Sauron is shown to explode, though Tolkien only said his spirit flees."
- Events and characters are condensed or omitted, "as with Tom Bombadil". "The time between Gandalf leaving the Ring to Frodo and returning to reveal its inscription, which is 17 years in the book, is compressed for timing reasons."
- "The filmmakers also decided to move the opening scenes of *The Two Towers*, the Uruk-hai ambush and Boromir's death, to the film's linear climax."
- The Moria sequence's tone was altered: in the book Gandalf advocates the Moria road against the rest of the Company, suggesting "there is a hope that Moria is still free...there is even a chance that Dwarves are there", and the Dwarves' deaths are only discovered at Balin's tomb. In the film Gandalf resists the plan as foreshadowing, Saruman is shown aware of his hesitance with an illustration of the Balrog in one of his books, and "[t]he corpses of the dwarves are instantly shown as the Company enter Moria."
- "One detail that critics have commented upon is that, in the novel, Pippin tosses a mere pebble into the well in Moria ('They then hear what sounds like a hammer tapping in the distance'), whereas in the film, he knocks an entire skeleton in ('Next, the skeleton ... falls down the well, also dragging down a chain and bucket. The noise is incredible.')."

wikis.title: Development and design
wikis.summary: The 1997 start of storyboarding and design work, the conceptual designers and the costume department.
wikis.body:
- "Director Peter Jackson began working with Christian Rivers to storyboard the series in August 1997, as well as getting Richard Taylor and Weta Workshop to begin creating his interpretation of Middle-earth. Jackson told them to make Middle-earth as plausible and believable as possible, and to think of it in a historical manner."
- In November 1997, "Alan Lee and John Howe became the film trilogy's primary conceptual designers, having had previous experience as illustrators for the book and various other tie-ins."
- "Lee worked for the Art Department creating places such as Rivendell, Isengard, Moria, and Lothlórien, giving Art Nouveau and geometry influences to the Elves and Dwarves respectively." Howe contributed Bag End and the Argonath but "focused on the design of the characters' armour, having studied it his entire life."
- "Grant Major turn[ed] the Art Department's designs into architecture, and Dan Hennah scout[ed] locations."
- "On 1 April 1999, Ngila Dickson joined the crew as costume designer. She and 40 seamstresses created 19,000 costumes, 40 per version for the actor and their doubles, wearing them out for an impression of age."

wikis.title: New Zealand filming locations
wikis.summary: The table of Middle-earth locations and the real New Zealand places that stood in for them.
wikis.body:
"Filming took place at many places across New Zealand." The Arrow River in the Otago region of South Island stood in for the Ford of Bruinen, where Arwen confronts the nine Nazgûl.

Fictional location - specific New Zealand location - general area:

- Mordor (prologue) - Whakapapa skifield - Tongariro National Park
- Hobbiton - Matamata - Waikato
- Gardens of Isengard - Harcourt Park - Upper Hutt
- The Shire woods - Otaki Gorge Road - Kāpiti Coast District
- Bucklebury Ferry - Keeling Farm, Manakau - Horowhenua
- Forest near Bree - Tākaka Hill - Tasman District
- Trollshaws - Waitarere Forest - Horowhenua
- Flight to the Ford - Tarras - Central Otago
- Ford of Bruinen - Arrow River, Skippers Canyon - Queenstown and Arrowtown

wikis.title: Release, marketing and home media
wikis.summary: The London premiere, the record-breaking trailer, the DVD and Blu-ray editions and the extended version.
wikis.body:
- "The world premiere of The Fellowship of the Ring was held at the Odeon Leicester Square in London on 10 December 2001. It was released on Wednesday, 19 December 2001 internationally in most major territories on 10,000 screens."
- "A special featurette trailer was released in April 2000. This trailer was downloaded over 1.7 million times within its first 24 hours of release, breaking *Star Wars: Episode I – The Phantom Menace*'s for being the most downloaded trailer."
- The theatrical version was released on VHS and DVD on 6 August 2002 by New Line Home Entertainment. "It was the best-selling DVD release at the time with 14.5 million copies being sold. This record was dethroned by *Finding Nemo* the following year."
- "On 12 November 2002, an extended edition was released on VHS and DVD, with 30 minutes of new material, added special effects and music, plus 20 minutes of fan-club credits, totalling 228 minutes. The DVD set included four commentaries and over three hours of supplementary material."
- Theatrical Blu-ray of the trilogy released in the US on 6 April 2010 (two sets, with and without digital copies), with the individual *Fellowship* disc on 14 September 2010. Extended Blu-ray editions released in the US on 28 June 2011, runtime 228 minutes. Ultra HD Blu-ray released 30 November 2020 in the United Kingdom and 1 December 2020 in the United States, with both theatrical and extended cuts.

wikis.title: Box office
wikis.summary: The film's opening records at home and abroad and its original and post-reissue grosses.
wikis.body:
- Opening day: "$18.2 million in the United States and Canada from 3,359 cinemas and $11.5 million in 13 countries, including $3 million from 466 screens in the United Kingdom."
- "It grossed $75.1 million in its first five days in the United States and Canada, including $47.2 million on its opening weekend, placing it at number one at the US box office, setting a December opening record, beating *Ocean's Eleven*."
- It opened at number one in 29 international markets "and remained there for a second week in all but the Netherlands". Record opening day gross in Australia of $2.09 million from 405 screens, beating the $1.3 million record set by *The Phantom Menace*; record opening weekend in Germany with 1.5 million admissions and in Spain with $5.3 million from 395 screens; a record $2.5 million in 15 days in New Zealand, a record that "would last for less than a decade before being surpassed by *Avatar*". In Denmark it became the highest-grossing film, surpassing *Titanic*.
- In its first 15 days it had grossed $183.5 million internationally and $178.7 million in the United States and Canada, for $362.2 million worldwide.
- Initial release: "$313.4 million in the United States and Canada and $555 million in the rest of the world for a worldwide total of $868.4 million." Box Office Mojo estimates over 54 million tickets sold in the US and Canada in the initial run.
- "Following subsequent reissues, the film has grossed $326 million in the United States and Canada and $570 million in the rest of the world for a worldwide total of $897 million."

wikis.title: Critical response
wikis.summary: The aggregate scores and the named reviews, positive and mixed.
wikis.body:
- Rotten Tomatoes: 91% approval from 269 reviews, consensus "Full of eye-popping special effects, and featuring a pitch-perfect cast, The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring brings J.R.R. Tolkien's classic to vivid life." Metacritic: 92 out of 100 from 34 critics, "universal acclaim". CinemaScore: "A−".
- Colin Kennedy (*Empire*), five of five: "history should quickly regard Peter Jackson's The Fellowship of the Ring as the first instalment of the best fantasy epic in motion picture history... this is a labour of love that never feels laboured."
- Roger Ebert (*Chicago Sun-Times*), three of four: not "a true visualization of Tolkien's Middle-earth" but "a work for, and of, our times... an awesome production in its daring and breadth".
- *USA Today*, three of four: "this movie version of a beloved book should please devotees as well as the uninitiated".
- Elvis Mitchell (*The New York Times*): "The playful spookiness of Mr. Jackson's direction provides a lively, light touch".
- Lisa Schwarzbaum (*Entertainment Weekly*), grade A: "I may have never turned a page of Tolkien, but I know enchantment when I see it".
- Nev Pierce (BBC), four of five: "Funny, scary, and totally involving", saying Jackson turned "the book's least screen-worthy volume into a gripping and powerful adventure movie".
- Xan Brooks (*The Guardian*): "Rather than a stand-alone holiday blockbuster, The Fellowship of the Ring offers an epic act one", with an ending "closer in spirit to an art-house film than a popcorn holiday romp".
- Rita Kempley (*The Washington Post*), five of five, praised "Mortensen, as Strider" as "a revelation" and McKellen as "positively Merlinesque".
- Richard Corliss (*Time*): "His movie achieves what the best fairy tales do: the creation of an alternate world, plausible and persuasive".
- J. Hoberman (*The Village Voice*): "Peter Jackson's adaptation is certainly successful on its own terms." Peter Travers (*Rolling Stone*): "He's made a three-hour film that leaves you wanting more".
- Mixed: Peter Bradshaw (*The Guardian*) praised the art direction but found "a strange paucity of plot complication" and the tone too self-important: "It's a leap I didn't feel much like making". Jonathan Rosenbaum (*Chicago Reader*) granted it was "full of scenic splendors with a fine sense of scale" but found the narrative thrust "relatively pro forma" and the battle scenes boring.

wikis.title: Accolades
wikis.summary: The film's Academy Award, BAFTA, Saturn and guild wins and nominations, and the lists it has appeared on.
wikis.body:
## Summary given in the prose

"In 2002, the film won four Academy Awards from thirteen nominations. It won the 2002 Hugo Award for Best Dramatic Presentation. It won Empire readers' Best Film award, as well as five BAFTAs, including Best Film, the David Lean Award for Best Direction, the Audience Award (voted for by the public), Best Special Effects, and Best Make-up. The film was nominated for an MTV Movie Award for Best Fight between Gandalf and Saruman."

## Academy Awards

- Won: Best Cinematography (Andrew Lesnie); Best Makeup (Peter Owen and Richard Taylor); Best Original Score (Howard Shore); Best Visual Effects (Jim Rygiel, Randall William Cook, Richard Taylor, Mark Stetson).
- Nominated: Best Picture (Peter Jackson, Fran Walsh, Barrie M. Osborne), Best Director (Jackson), Best Supporting Actor (Ian McKellen), Best Adapted Screenplay (Walsh, Boyens, Jackson), Best Art Direction (Grant Major, Dan Hennah), Best Costume Design (Ngila Dickson, Richard Taylor), Best Film Editing (John Gilbert), Best Original Song (Enya, Nicky Ryan, Roma Ryan for "May It Be"), Best Sound (Christopher Boyes, Michael Semanick, Gethin Creagh, Hammond Peek).

## British Academy Film Awards (per the table)

- Won: Best Film (Jackson, Osborne, Walsh, Tim Sanders); Best Direction (Jackson); Best Makeup and Hair (Peter Owen, Peter King, Richard Taylor); Best Special Visual Effects (Rygiel, Taylor, Alex Funke, Cook, Stetson).
- Nominated: Best Actor in a Leading Role (McKellen), Best Adapted Screenplay, Best Cinematography, Best Costume Design, Best Editing, Best Original Music, Best Production Design, Best Sound.

## Other awards

- Saturn Awards: won Best Fantasy Film, Best Director (Jackson) and Best Supporting Actor (McKellen); nominated for Best Writing, Best Costume Design, Best Make-up, Best Music and Best Special Effects.
- Screen Actors Guild: McKellen won Outstanding Performance by a Male Actor in a Supporting Role; the cast was nominated.
- Nominated: Directors Guild of America (Jackson); four Golden Globes (Best Motion Picture - Drama, Best Director, Best Original Score, Best Original Song); Producers Guild of America; Writers Guild of America (Best Adapted Screenplay).

## Lists

- AFI's "10 Top 10" in June 2008 ranked it the second best fantasy film, after a poll of over 1,500 people from the creative community.
- In 2021 Writers Guild members voted its screenplay 76th in "101 Greatest Screenplays of the 21st Century (so far)".
- In June 2025 it ranked number 87 on *The New York Times*' "The 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century" and number 14 on the "Readers' Choice" edition.

wikis.title: The Fellowship of the Ring article: Middle-earth navigation boxes and categories
wikis.summary: Part 2 of the Wikipedia article on The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring, consisting of the Tolkien and Middle-earth navigation boxes and the page's category list, with no article prose.
wikis.body:
