- The navigation boxes list Middle-earth video games and adaptations, including *Game Two: Shadows of Mordor*, *War in Middle Earth*, *Riders of Rohan*, *Elendor*, the game adaptations of *The Fellowship of the Ring*, *The Two Towers* and *The Return of the King*, *War of the Ring* and *The Third Age*, alongside the wider *Lord of the Rings* franchise boxes.
- The page ends with its category list, which includes "Films whose director won the Best Direction BAFTA Award", "High fantasy films", "Hugo Award for Best Dramatic Presentation–winning works", "The Lord of the Rings (film series)", "Middle-earth (film franchise) films", "Nebula Award for Best Script–winning works", "New Line Cinema films", "New Zealand epic films", "New Zealand fantasy adventure films", "Saturn Award–winning films", "United States National Film Registry films inducted in 2021" and "WingNut Films films", plus hidden maintenance categories.
- No published or last-updated date is stated.

wikis.title: Avengers: Infinity War
wikis.summary: Wikipedia's article on the 2018 Marvel Studios film Avengers: Infinity War, covering its plot, cast, production, marketing, release, $2.052 billion box office, reception and accolades.
wikis.body:
## The film

- "Avengers: Infinity War is a 2018 American superhero film based on the Marvel Comics superhero team the Avengers ", produced by Marvel Studios and distributed by Walt Disney Studios Motion Pictures, "the sequel to The Avengers (2012) and Avengers: Age of Ultron (2015), and the 19th film in the Marvel Cinematic Universe (MCU)". Directed by Anthony and Joe Russo, written by Christopher Markus and Stephen McFeely, produced by Kevin Feige, shot by Trent Opaloch, edited by Jeffrey Ford and Matthew Schmidt, scored by Alan Silvestri.
- Running time 149 minutes; budget "$325-400 million"; box office "$2.052 billion". Premiered at the Dolby Theatre in Hollywood on April 23, 2018 and released in the United States on April 27, 2018, as part of Phase Three of the MCU.
- Story: "the Avengers and the Guardians of the Galaxy attempt to stop Thanos from collecting the six powerful Infinity Stones as part of his quest to kill half of all life in the universe" - ending with Thanos completing the Gauntlet, snapping his fingers, and half of all life disintegrating.
- Ensemble cast led by Robert Downey Jr., Chris Hemsworth, Mark Ruffalo, Chris Evans, Scarlett Johansson, Benedict Cumberbatch, Don Cheadle, Tom Holland, Chadwick Boseman, Paul Bettany, Elizabeth Olsen, Anthony Mackie, Sebastian Stan, Danai Gurira, Letitia Wright, Dave Bautista, Zoe Saldaña, Josh Brolin and Chris Pratt. Feige said of Thanos that "you could almost go so far as to say he is the main character of" the film.

## Making and marketing

Announced in October 2014 as Avengers: Infinity War - Part 1, drawing on Jim Starlin's The Infinity Gauntlet (1991) and Jonathan Hickman's Infinity (2013); the Russos joined in April 2015 and the writers a month later. "Principal photography began on January 23, 2017, under the working title Mary Lou , at Pinewood Atlanta Studios", with further shooting in Scotland, Downtown Atlanta and Queens, and wrapped July 14, 2017; it and Endgame were "the first time that a Hollywood feature film was shot entirely with IMAX digital cameras". Marketing cost an estimated $150 million in prints and advertising; the first teaser, debuted on Good Morning America on November 29, 2017, "was viewed 230 million times in its first 24 hours, becoming the most viewed trailer in that time period".

## Box office and reception

- "Avengers: Infinity War grossed $678.8 million in the United States and Canada, and $1.374 billion in other territories, for a worldwide total of $2.052 billion", with a then-record worldwide opening weekend of $640.5 million and a record North American opening weekend of $258.2 million. It was the fastest film to $1 billion (11 days) and the fourth to pass $2 billion.
- Rotten Tomatoes: "an approval rating of 85% , with an average score of 7.7/10 , based on 486 reviews"; Metacritic 68/100 from 54 critics; CinemaScore "A". Critics praised Josh Brolin's Thanos and the scale of the action, while A. O. Scott wrote that "[c]onsidered on its own ... Avengers: Infinity War makes very little sense" and Stephanie Zacharek said viewers need "every one of the previous 18 Marvel Cinematic Universe movies to fully get it".
- It received a Best Visual Effects nomination at the 91st Academy Awards, plus Annie, BAFTA and two Critics' Choice nominations, and ranked seventh in Empire's 2020 poll of the 100 greatest films of the 21st century.
- The ending drove memes and the largest ban in Reddit's history: "[t]he ban of over 300,000 accounts, which included Anthony Russo", on the /r/thanosdidnothingwrong subreddit on July 9, 2018, watched by over 60,000 people on a Twitch stream.
- "Avengers: Endgame was released on April 26, 2019, with the Russos returning to direct, and Markus and McFeely once again writing the screenplay."

## About the page

The article is listed in 78 languages. Most of this capture is citation apparatus: after the article's prose, three parts of stored `<ref name=...>{{Cite ...}}</ref>` markup are followed by the rendered numbered reference list, external links (Commons, Wikiquote, the official website, IMDb, Disney A to Z) and the Marvel Cinematic Universe navigation boxes. Citation retrieval dates run as late as June 2026 (the Rotten Tomatoes entry).

wikis.title: Avengers: Infinity War (2018 film)
wikis.summary: The main body of the Wikipedia article on Avengers: Infinity War - infobox, lead, plot, cast, production, music, marketing, release, box office and reception.
wikis.body:
## The film

- "Avengers: Infinity War is a 2018 American superhero film based on the Marvel Comics superhero team the Avengers ." Produced by Marvel Studios, distributed by Walt Disney Studios Motion Pictures, "it is the sequel to The Avengers (2012) and Avengers: Age of Ultron (2015), and the 19th film in the Marvel Cinematic Universe (MCU)", directed by Anthony and Joe Russo and written by Christopher Markus and Stephen McFeely.
- Infobox: based on Avengers by Stan Lee and Jack Kirby; produced by Kevin Feige; cinematography Trent Opaloch; edited by Jeffrey Ford and Matthew Schmidt; music by Alan Silvestri; release dates April 23, 2018 (Dolby Theatre) and April 27, 2018 (United States); running time 149 minutes; country United States; language English; budget "$325-400 million"; box office "$2.052 billion". A hidden editorial comment gives the theatrical runtime as 149:09, and the budget range is marked "PER TALK PAGE".
- Premise: "the Avengers and the Guardians of the Galaxy attempt to stop Thanos from collecting the six powerful Infinity Stones as part of his quest to kill half of all life in the universe."
- Lead history: announced in October 2014 as Avengers: Infinity War - Part 1; the Russos joined in April 2015 and Markus and McFeely a month later, drawing on "Jim Starlin 's 1991 comic book The Infinity Gauntlet and Jonathan Hickman 's 2013 comic book Infinity"; Marvel shortened the title in 2016. "Filming began in January 2017 at Pinewood Atlanta Studios in Fayette County, Georgia", running to July 2017 shooting back-to-back with Avengers: Endgame (2019), with additional filming in Scotland, Downtown Atlanta and New York City. "With an estimated budget of $325-400 million, the film is one of the most expensive films ever made."
- Lead reception: positive reviews praising Brolin's performance, the Russos' direction, visual effects, action, dark tone and score; "becoming the fourth film and the first superhero film to gross over $2 billion worldwide", the highest-grossing film of 2018 and "the fourth -highest-grossing film at the time of its release both worldwide and in the United States and Canada"; nominated for Best Visual Effects at the 91st Academy Awards. "The sequel, Avengers: Endgame , was released in April 2019."
- The page's hatnote: "'Infinity War' redirects here. For other uses, see Infinity War (disambiguation) ." It is listed in 78 languages.

wikis.title: Plot
wikis.summary: The article's plot summary, from Thanos's attack on the Asgardian ship to the snap that erases half of all life.
wikis.body:
- Having taken the Power Stone from Xandar, Thanos and his lieutenants - Ebony Maw, Cull Obsidian, Proxima Midnight and Corvus Glaive - intercept the ship carrying Asgard's survivors. Thanos subdues Thor, extracts the Space Stone from the Tesseract, overpowers the Hulk, kills Loki and fatally wounds Heimdall, who sends Hulk to Earth by the Bifröst before dying; the ship is destroyed.
- Hulk crash-lands in the Sanctum Sanctorum and reverts to Bruce Banner, warning Stephen Strange and Wong, who recruit Tony Stark. Maw and Obsidian arrive for the Time Stone and capture Strange; Stark and Peter Parker stow away on Maw's ship while Wong guards the Sanctum.
- The Guardians rescue Thor, who goes with Rocket and Groot to Nidavellir to have Eitri forge Stormbreaker, while Quill, Gamora, Drax and Mantis go to Knowhere, where Thanos already has the Reality Stone. Thanos kidnaps Gamora, who reveals the Soul Stone's location to stop Nebula's torture; on Vormir, Red Skull says the Stone requires sacrificing someone he loves, and "Thanos sacrifices Gamora, earning the Stone."
- Midnight and Glaive ambush Wanda Maximoff and Vision in Edinburgh for the Mind Stone; Rogers, Romanoff and Wilson rescue them, and the group goes to Wakanda, "which Rogers believes has the resources to remove the Stone without killing Vision".
- On Titan, Stark, Parker and Strange meet Quill, Drax and Mantis. "Using the Time Stone, Strange views millions of possible futures, seeing only one in which the Avengers win." Thanos justifies his plans "as necessary to guarantee the survival of an overpopulated universe"; Quill's rage at Gamora's death breaks the group's hold, and Strange trades the Time Stone for Stark's life.
- In Wakanda the Avengers, T'Challa and Wakandan forces hold off Thanos's army while Shuri works to extract the Mind Stone; Banner fights in the Hulkbuster armor, and Thor, Rocket and Groot arrive. Thanos reaches Vision, uses the Time Stone to reverse Wanda's destruction of the Stone, rips it out and completes the Gauntlet. "Thor severely wounds Thanos with Stormbreaker, but Thanos activates the completed Gauntlet by snapping his fingers before teleporting away."
- "Half of all life across the universe disintegrates", including Barnes, T'Challa, Groot, Wanda, Wilson, Mantis, Drax, Quill, Strange, Parker, Maria Hill and Nick Fury, who first sends an emergency signal on a modified pager. Stark and Nebula are stranded on Titan; Banner, M'Baku, Okoye, Rhodes, Rocket, Rogers, Romanoff and Thor remain in Wakanda; "Meanwhile, Thanos watches a sunrise on a remote planet."''

wikis.title: Cast and characters
wikis.summary: The billed cast with filmmakers' comments, the Children of Thanos, and the cameos including Stan Lee's.
wikis.body:
- **Robert Downey Jr. as Tony Stark / Iron Man** - Joe Russo: Stark "senses this greater threat approaching, so he is doing everything in his power to keep the Earth safe".
- **Chris Hemsworth as Thor** - his storyline picks up after Thor: Ragnarok (2017); at Hemsworth's recommendation the writers consulted Taika Waititi and Eric Pearson. Joe Russo said Thor has "the driving hero's arc of the movie which stands in direct opposition to Thanos' argument" and would have been the main protagonist had he killed Thanos.
- **Mark Ruffalo as Bruce Banner / Hulk** - Ruffalo described Hulk here "as having the mental capacity of a five-year-old"; Joe Russo said Hulk's refusal to appear reflects that "Banner only wants Hulk for fighting".
- **Chris Evans as Steve Rogers / Captain America** - embodies the "spirit" of Nomad and receives "new vibranium gauntlets from Shuri to replace his old shield". An early draft had Rogers first appear only at the end in Wakanda; the writers were called "insane" for it and conceded it was "not [a] satisfying" approach.
- **Scarlett Johansson as Natasha Romanoff / Black Widow** - Johansson: "a dark time ... she's hardened even more than she probably was before."
- **Benedict Cumberbatch as Dr. Stephen Strange** - "[ending] up being the reasonable adult in the room"; Julian "JayFunk" Daniels again assisted with finger-tutting.
- **Don Cheadle as James Rhodes / War Machine** - walks again via a Stark apparatus after his Civil War paralysis, reluctant to rejoin.
- **Tom Holland as Peter Parker / Spider-Man** - "Downey helped coach Holland through his death scene, which was not as drawn out in the script."
- **Chadwick Boseman as T'Challa / Black Panther** - the Wakandan actors improvised their war chants on set, unknown to the Russos, who found it "incredibly cool".
- **Paul Bettany as Vision** - Anthony Russo called him "a living MacGuffin". **Elizabeth Olsen as Wanda Maximoff**, **Anthony Mackie as Sam Wilson / Falcon**, **Sebastian Stan as Bucky Barnes** (named White Wolf by the Wakandans), **Tom Hiddleston as Loki** (Hiddleston learned of Loki's death before Ragnarok's production; it was "the first scene of the film that the Russos had conceptualized"), **Idris Elba as Heimdall**, **Peter Dinklage as Eitri**, **Benedict Wong as Wong**, **Pom Klementieff as Mantis**, **Karen Gillan as Nebula**, **Dave Bautista as Drax** (who sat in a sauna each day to remove his makeup), **Zoe Saldaña as Gamora** (Ariana Greenblatt as a young Gamora), **Vin Diesel as Groot** (Terry Notary providing motion capture), **Bradley Cooper as Rocket** (Sean Gunn again the stand-in), **Gwyneth Paltrow as Pepper Potts**, **Benicio del Toro as the Collector**, and **Chris Pratt as Peter Quill / Star-Lord**, who called it a "guest star" appearance.
- **Josh Brolin as Thanos** - seeking the Stones "for the sake of 're-balanc[ing] the universe'". Feige said "you could almost go so far as to say he is the main character of" the film; McFeely described it as Thanos's "hero journey". Brolin likened him to "the Quasimodo of this time" and the novel Perfume, while Joe Russo referenced The Godfather (1972) to him. "Thanos does not wear armor for most of the film, which is symbolic of his growing power as he collects the Infinity Stones." Brolin also performed the motion capture.
- Other returning MCU actors: Danai Gurira (Okoye), Letitia Wright (Shuri), William Hurt (Thaddeus Ross), Kerry Condon (F.R.I.D.A.Y.), Winston Duke (M'Baku), Florence Kasumba (Ayo), Jacob Batalon (Ned), Isabella Amara, Tiffany Espensen and Ethan Dizon; Samuel L. Jackson and Cobie Smulders make uncredited cameos in the post-credits scene.
- The "Children of Thanos": Terry Notary (Cull Obsidian), Tom Vaughan-Lawlor (Ebony Maw), Carrie Coon (Proxima Midnight) and Michael James Shaw (Corvus Glaive), all providing voice and motion capture; Coon, pregnant during filming, mainly did facial capture with stuntwoman Monique Ganderton standing in. "Ebony Maw's look was inspired by the Marvel Comics character Mephisto".
- Ross Marquand voices Red Skull, replacing Hugo Weaving; the character was created through CGI with stand-ins. "Avengers co-creator Stan Lee makes a cameo appearance in the film as Parker's school bus driver", screenwriter Stephen McFeely cameos as Ross's aide, and Kenneth Branagh voices an Asgardian distress caller. David Cross was invited to cameo as Tobias Fünke from Arrested Development but a scheduling conflict prevented it, "Fünke still appears in the film as a specimen in the Collector's collection, played by an uncredited extra". Jon Favreau's Happy Hogan and a Joe Russo paparazzi cameo did not make the theatrical cut.

wikis.title: Production
wikis.summary: From the 2014 two-part announcement to filming in Atlanta, Scotland and New York, the visual-effects vendors and the budget.
wikis.body:
- "In October 2014, Marvel Studios announced a two-part sequel to Avengers: Age of Ultron (2015) entitled Avengers: Infinity War ", Part 1 for May 4, 2018 and Part 2 for May 3, 2019, to be filmed back-to-back. The Russos were hired in April 2015; Markus and McFeely signed the next month, drawing on The Infinity Gauntlet (1991) and Infinity (2013). Anthony Russo said the film was inspired by 1990s heist films, with Thanos "on a smash-and-grab". Feige said the films were "two distinct" projects; the Russos renamed them in May 2016 and Marvel shortened the first title that July.
- "Principal photography began on January 23, 2017, under the working title Mary Lou , at Pinewood Atlanta Studios in Fayette County, Georgia , with Trent Opaloch as director of photography ." The film and Endgame "were shot using ARRI Alexa IMAX 2D cameras, thus marking the first time that a Hollywood feature film was shot entirely with IMAX digital cameras".
- Marvel confirmed Downey, Pratt and Holland in early February 2017. Additional filming began in Scotland in February 2017 - Edinburgh, Glasgow and the Scottish Highlands, with studio work at Wardpark Studios in Cumbernauld. Late June 2017 filming took place in Downtown Atlanta, early July in Atlanta's Central Park, and mid-month in Queens, New York. "Filming concluded on July 14, 2017." For the final scene, where Thanos settles in a nipa hut, the filmmakers worked with Thailand-based Indochina Productions "to acquire footage of the Banaue Rice Terraces at Ifugao, Philippines".
- Joe Russo said in July 2017 that a couple of unfinished scenes would be shot "in the next few months". In early March 2018 Disney moved the US release to April 27, 2018 to match international markets.
- Visual effects by Industrial Light & Magic, Framestore, Method Studios, Weta Digital, DNEG, Cinesite, Digital Domain, Rise, Lola VFX and Perception. "With an estimated budget in the range of $325-400 million, it is one of the most expensive films ever made . Evans and Hemsworth both earned $15 million for the film."

wikis.title: Music
wikis.summary: Alan Silvestri's score, the Black Panther theme and the soundtrack releases.
wikis.body:
- "In June 2016, Alan Silvestri , who composed the score for The Avengers (2012), was revealed to be returning to score both Infinity War and Endgame ." He recorded from January 2018 to late March, calling it "a really different experience than anything I'd done before, especially in regard to the approach and balancing quick shifts in tone".
- "Ludwig Göransson 's theme from Black Panther is used in the film."
- "Hollywood Records and Marvel Music released regular and deluxe soundtrack albums digitally on April 27, 2018, with physical releases on May 18. The deluxe edition featured some extended and additional tracks."

wikis.title: Marketing
wikis.summary: Convention footage, the record-setting trailers, tie-ins from Fortnite to a prequel comic, and the estimated $150 million campaign.
wikis.body:
- May 2017: Downey's Random Act Funding partnered with Omaze on a set-visit contest. At D23 Expo 2017 a life-sized Legacy Effects Thanos statue was displayed with the Black Order, and a large cast contingent presented a 10-years-of-MCU clip plus Infinity War footage that left fans "literally on their feet and jumping"; CinemaBlend's Eric Eisenberg was "literally shaking". The footage also screened at the 2017 San Diego Comic-Con, after which the film "generated over 90,000 new conversations on social media from July 17 to 23", third behind Thor: Ragnarok and Justice League; by the week of October 16 it had "over 679,000 total social media conversations".
- "The first teaser for Avengers: Infinity War debuted on Good Morning America on November 29, 2017." Gael Cooper of CNET noted nearly 500,000 views in its first 15 minutes with the counter apparently stuck at 467,331; "[t]he trailer was viewed 230 million times in its first 24 hours, becoming the most viewed trailer in that time period, surpassing the record of It ."
- January 2018: Marvel Comics published the two-issue prequel comic Avengers: Infinity War Prelude. A Super Bowl LII commercial "generated the most social media buzz of all the films advertised" and was "viewed 17.6 million times across YouTube and Facebook". The "Marvel: The Universe Unites" charity campaign ran from February 27, with a planned $250,000 Marvel donation to the Starlight Children's Foundation if posts reached 1 million likes, Disney donating 10% of US Marvel Disney Store sales (up to $50,000) to Make-A-Wish, and Hasbro and Funko each donating $1 million in cash and products.
- "A second trailer was released on March 16, which earned over 1 million views on YouTube in less than three hours"; it "was viewed 179 million times in the first 24 hours, the third-most viewed trailer in that time period", and the biggest second-trailer release, passing Beauty and the Beast (2017)'s 128 million.
- A week before release the Burj Khalifa was lit nightly counting down to the film; tie-in events ran across seven Marvel mobile games; in early May Marvel and Epic Games announced the Fortnite "Infinity Gauntlet Limited Time Mashup", which the Russos had proposed to Epic's Donald Mustard. On November 20 Little, Brown published Barry Lyga's novel Thanos - Titan Consumed, outside MCU canon.
- "All-in-all, the studio spent an estimated $150 million on prints and advertisements promoting the film." Partners included Coca-Cola, Quicken Loans/Rocket Mortgage, the Infiniti QX50 (which appears in the film), Ziploc, Go-Gurt, Yoplait, Synchrony Bank, American Airlines and Stand Up to Cancer, with Duracell, Unilever, Quaker Oats, Chevron and Samsung in smaller markets and a OnePlus Infinity War phone edition in the UK. "Deadline Hollywood estimated the media value was $150 million, the largest for any Marvel film, with Coca-Cola contributing an estimated $40 million."

wikis.title: Release and home media
wikis.summary: The Dolby Theatre premiere, the worldwide rollout and screen counts, the Chinese run extension, and the home-video editions.
wikis.body:
- "Avengers: Infinity War held its world premiere at the Dolby Theatre in Hollywood, Los Angeles , on April 23, 2018, screening also at the adjacent El Capitan Theatre and Grauman's Chinese Theatre ." It was released in most countries, including the US, on April 27, with a few debuts from April 25, in IMAX and 3D.
- In the US it opened in "4,474 theaters, 408 of which were IMAX; this was the widest release for a Disney title ever and the second-widest ever after Despicable Me 3 ' s (2017) 4,529 theaters". Three AMC locations screened it for 24 hours straight, and 53 had 2am or 3am showtimes. India had "the biggest release ever for a Hollywood film, opening on nearly 2,000 screens in four languages"; the film also played "in 515 4DX theaters in 59 countries". It had originally been scheduled for May 4 in the US. The Chinese release opened May 11 and was granted a "rare" 30-day extension, ending July 9 instead of June 10. The film is part of Phase Three of the MCU.
- Only limited footage was screened during the early-April press tour to reduce spoiler leaks - "highly unusual as most Marvel movies are screened in their entirety for press about a month before they hit theaters". AMC in New York City and Orlando ran an eleven-film MCU marathon from April 25 ending with Infinity War, as did the El Capitan.
- **Home media.** "Avengers: Infinity War was released on digital download by Walt Disney Studios Home Entertainment on July 31, 2018, and on Ultra HD Blu-ray , Blu-ray , and DVD on August 14", with featurettes, commentary, deleted scenes, a blooper reel and, digitally, a roundtable of MCU directors (the Russos, Favreau, Whedon, Gunn, Coogler, Reed and Waititi). The physical versions were "the top home media release of the week in which they were first released". The release used the cropped 2.39:1 ratio rather than the IMAX 1.90:1; Joe Russo said they "spent a long time trying to" include the IMAX version but IMAX "has agency over that format". "The IMAX Enhanced version of the film was made available on Disney+ beginning on November 12, 2021."

wikis.title: Box office
wikis.summary: Worldwide totals and records, pre-sale records, the North American opening weekend and international market records.
wikis.body:
- "Avengers: Infinity War grossed $678.8 million in the United States and Canada, and $1.374 billion in other territories, for a worldwide total of $2.052 billion", becoming the fourth-highest-grossing film of all time, the highest-grossing film of 2018, the highest-grossing MCU film and the highest-grossing superhero film.
- "Its worldwide opening weekend of $640.5 million was the biggest of all time , beating The Fate of the Furious ' s (2017) $541.9 million", later beaten by Endgame's $1.222 billion. It was "the fastest film to make $1 billion at the worldwide box office, doing so in 11 days", eclipsing The Force Awakens's 12. In its second weekend it passed "$13.5 million from 4DX screens", an all-time format record. It crossed $2 billion on June 12, 2018 - the fourth film to do so after Avatar, Titanic and The Force Awakens - in 48 days. IMAX contributed $140 million worldwide, third-largest in the format and the largest for a Marvel film. Deadline Hollywood calculated a net profit of $500 million, first on its list of 2018's "Most Valuable Blockbusters".
- **Pre-sales.** A December 2017 Fandango survey made it the most anticipated film of 2018; it took "just 6 hours to surpass the previous 24-hour record set by Black Panther", and Atom said it sold more tickets on its first pre-sale day than Black Panther sold in its first month. Within 72 hours it set AMC's superhero pre-sale record, "257.6% ahead of Black Panther ' s, 751.5% ahead of Captain America: Civil War , and 1,106.5% ahead of Avengers: Age of Ultron". A week before release the WSJ said it had sold "more than $50 million worth of advance tickets", behind only The Force Awakens and The Last Jedi, with more than 2,500 showtimes sold out.
- **United States and Canada.** "$106.7 million on its opening day ... (including $39 million from Thursday night previews), for an opening weekend total of $258.2 million" - the best MCU preview night and fourth-best ever; the second-best opening day ever; record Saturday ($83 million) and Sunday ($69.2 million) grosses; and the highest-grossing opening weekend ever, beating The Force Awakens's $248 million. IMAX added $22.5 million. It earned $25 million the following Monday (best April Monday) and $23.5 million Tuesday (best MCU Tuesday), tying The Force Awakens for fastest to $300 million in five days. Second weekend: $115.5 million, second-best ever, passing $400 million in nine days; third weekend still number one, passing $500 million in 15 days with a record MCU domestic IMAX total of $48.1 million; fourth weekend second behind Deadpool 2; fifth third behind Solo: A Star Wars Story and Deadpool 2; past $600 million by May 23 in 26 days; in the top ten through its ninth weekend. It became the fourth-highest-grossing film ever in the market and the second-highest-grossing superhero film, behind Black Panther.
- **Other territories.** It opened to "$382.7 million from 52 markets, opening number one in all", the number two international opening behind The Fate of the Furious, with a record $18.5 million from IMAX outside the US, Canada and China. All-time opening-weekend records were set in South Korea ($39.2 million), Mexico ($25.4 million), Brazil ($19.1 million), India ($18.6 million for a Western release), the Philippines ($12.5 million), Thailand ($10 million), Indonesia ($9.6 million) and many other markets; France had the biggest superhero opening at $17.7 million, Germany's $14.7 million was its best superhero opening, the UK took $8.9 million on its opening day and $41.4 million for the weekend, Japan had the second-biggest MCU opening at $9 million and Australia the second-highest opening weekend ever at $23.2 million.
- Russia: a $4.9 million opening day, the biggest of all time. "Originally, the Russian government ordered it to be released on May 11, but after a scandal the government made concessions and agreed to let it premiere on May 3 with a condition that on May 9, during the Victory Day , only Russian films would be played"; it was the first film in Russia to sell more than 1 million tickets in a day and grossed $17.6 million, an opening-weekend record.
- China opened to $200 million (RMB 1.266 billion), the second-highest opening weekend in local currency, with $20.5 million from IMAX, and it broke China's pre-sale record of 400 million yuan ($63 million). In India it became "the first Hollywood film to earn over ₹ 2 billion net ($29.7 million)"; it became the highest-grossing MCU film in the UK and, in its sixth weekend, in Japan with $33 million. "As of June 17, 2018 [ update ] , the film's top markets are China ($373.4 million), the United Kingdom ($95.7 million), and South Korea ($92.8 million)."

wikis.title: Critical and audience response
wikis.summary: Aggregator scores, praise for Brolin and the action, criticism of the film's dependence on the wider MCU, and audience grades and repeat viewers.
wikis.body:
- "The review aggregator Rotten Tomatoes reported an approval rating of 85% , with an average score of 7.7/10 , based on 486 reviews", with the consensus that the film "ably juggles a dizzying array of MCU heroes ... a thrilling, emotionally resonant blockbuster that (mostly) realizes its gargantuan ambitions." Metacritic "assigned the film a score of 68 out of 100 based on 54 critics", indicating "generally favorable" reviews.
- Praise: Todd McCarthy (The Hollywood Reporter) credited the filmmakers with acknowledging "the traffic jam of egos and play[ing] it for laughs", and said Brolin's "calm, considered reading of the character bestows this conquering beast with an unexpectedly resonant emotional dimension"; Owen Gleiberman (Variety) called it "a brashly entertaining jamboree" and Brolin's motion-capture performance "supremely effective"; Peter Travers (Rolling Stone) said it is "too much of a good thing" but "a fireworks explosion of action and laughs that won't quit"; Richard Roeper (Chicago Sun-Times) called it Marvel's "biggest and most ambitious movie yet", though "certainly not the best", praising Brolin as "the film's most interesting performance". Josh Spiegel likened the finale to "the ending of The Empire Strikes Back ... Han Solo frozen in the carbonite , on steroids".
- Criticism: A. O. Scott (The New York Times) wrote that "[c]onsidered on its own ... Avengers: Infinity War makes very little sense", though it "was never meant to be viewed or judged in isolation", and called the action "tedious and predictable"; Richard Brody (The New Yorker) blamed "the dispersion of its drama throughout the many cinematic installations"; Stephanie Zacharek (Time) said "[y]ou need to have seen and internalized every one of the previous 18 Marvel Cinematic Universe movies to fully get it" and "[t]here's no pacing ... It's all sensation and no pulse"; Justin Chang (Los Angeles Times) called its bid for catharsis "unsuccessful".
- **Audiences.** CinemaScore gave an average grade of "A"; PostTrak audiences gave "an 87% overall positive score and a 68% 'definite recommend'". YouTube personality Tony "Nem" Mitchell watched the film 103 times in theaters, "a world record"; around his 44th viewing IMAX gave him 50 free tickets and the Russos invited him to Endgame's premiere. Seventeen-year-old Kieran Harvey from Staffordshire also watched it 100 times, saying he "didn't plan on seeing it this many times it just sort of happened".

wikis.title: Avengers: Infinity War: internet reaction, accolades, the sequel, and the start of the citations
wikis.summary: The tail of the article's reception section - the film's memes and the mass Reddit ban - plus its accolades, sequel, notes, and the beginning of the stored citation markup.
wikis.body:
This part finishes the article's prose and then turns into the article's stored reference markup (`<ref name="...">{{Cite ...}}</ref>` templates, about 95 of them in this part). The first citation is Steve Watts, "Avengers: Infinity War Announced as 2-Part Film", IGN, October 29, 2014.

## See also and notes

The "See also" entry is "'What If... Zombies?!', an episode of the MCU television series What If...? that reimagines the events of this film". The notes identify the Asgardian ship attack as depicted in Thor: Ragnarok (2017) and Nick Fury's pager message as "[i]dentified off-screen as a message to Carol Danvers / Captain Marvel".

wikis.title: Internet reaction and the Thanos subreddit ban
wikis.summary: The memes the ending produced and the record Reddit ban that mimicked the snap.
wikis.body:
- "The ending of the film sparked various Internet meme reactions, including one referencing Spider-Man saying he does not feel good as he disintegrates, which was applied to other things. The website, DidThanosKill.Me was created for fans to see if they would have been spared by Thanos or not."
- The ending also spawned the subreddit /r/thanosdidnothingwrong. A user suggested banning half of its roughly 20,000 subscribers "in order to mimic the events of the film"; the community agreed, Reddit's administrators approved a random ban of half the subscribers, and it was set for July 9, 2018. Notice of the ban pushed subscribers to over 700,000, "including both of the Russos who subscribed". Brolin posted a video saying "Here we go, Reddit users," ending with a snap.
- "Over 60,000 people watched a live Twitch stream of the ban occurring, which lasted several hours. The ban of over 300,000 accounts, which included Anthony Russo, was the largest in Reddit's history." Those banned gathered in the new subreddit /r/inthesoulstone. A participant described it as embodying "the spirit of the Internet"; Andrew Tigani of Screen Rant said it showed "how impactful the film has already become to pop culture".

wikis.title: Accolades and sequel
wikis.summary: The film's award nominations and ranking, and the release of Avengers: Endgame.
wikis.body:
- "At the 91st Academy Awards , Avengers: Infinity War received a nomination for Best Visual Effects ." Other nominations include an Annie Award, a British Academy Film Award and two Critics' Choice Awards, among others. "In 2020, Infinity War was ranked seventh in an Empire magazine poll for the 100 greatest films of the 21st century."
- "Avengers: Endgame was released on April 26, 2019, with the Russos returning to direct, and Markus and McFeely once again writing the screenplay."

wikis.title: Citation definitions in this part
wikis.summary: What the stored reference markup in this part covers.
wikis.body: Roughly 95 named citation definitions follow the prose, beginning with the October 2014 IGN announcement of the two-part film and running through cast and production sources. Visible entries near the end of the part include an Inverse piece on Tom Vaughan-Lawlor as Ebony Maw (March 6, 2018) and Anthony Breznican's Entertainment Weekly article of March 8, 2018, "Behold Iron Man's new armor in Avengers: Infinity War - Robert Downey Jr. says he'll need it". Each entry carries the original URL, an archive URL, and archive and access dates.

wikis.title: Avengers: Infinity War: citation definitions
wikis.summary: A block of the article's stored reference markup - about 98 named citation templates, with no article prose.
wikis.body:
This part contains no prose from the article: it is a continuous block of the article's stored citation markup, roughly 98 `<ref name="...">{{Cite ...}}</ref>` definitions, each with author, title, outlet, original URL, archive URL, archive date and access date.

It opens mid-citation with the rest of Anthony Breznican's Entertainment Weekly piece of March 8, 2018 on Iron Man's new armor, continues through further Entertainment Weekly behind-the-scenes entries (named EWBTS and similar), and ends mid-entry with an Entertainment Weekly item of August 2, 2018 about a Jon Favreau deleted scene and the start of "HollandDeathScene", Ryan Parker's Hollywood Reporter piece of August 1, 2018 on Robert Downey Jr. and Tom Holland's death scene.

wikis.title: Avengers: Infinity War: last citation definitions and the rendered reference list
wikis.summary: The final block of stored citation markup followed by the article's rendered numbered reference entries.
wikis.body:
The part begins with the remainder of the Hollywood Reporter citation on how "Robert Downey Jr. Coached Tom Holland Through That Heartbreaking 'Infinity War' Scene" (August 1-2, 2018) and about 34 further citation definitions, then switches to the rendered reference list - roughly 164 numbered entries in this part.

The rendered entries are the article's formatted citations: author, title, publication, date, archive date and retrieval date. The part ends with the aggregator and review sources for the reception section: Rotten Tomatoes (Fandango Media, retrieved June 29, 2026), Metacritic (Fandom, Inc., retrieved April 20, 2020) and Todd McCarthy's Hollywood Reporter review of April 24, 2018.

wikis.title: Avengers: Infinity War: end of the reference list, external links and navigation boxes
wikis.summary: The closing citations of the article - reviews, the Reddit-ban coverage and awards lists - followed by its external links and the Marvel Cinematic Universe navigation boxes.
wikis.body:
**Final citations.** Reviews by Owen Gleiberman (Variety), Peter Travers (Rolling Stone), Richard Roeper (Chicago Sun-Times), Josh Spiegel ("Why 'Avengers: Infinity War' May Feel Unsatisfying", The Hollywood Reporter, April 28, 2018), A. O. Scott (The New York Times), Richard Brody (The New Yorker, April 27, 2018), Stephanie Zacharek (Time) and Justin Chang (Los Angeles Times), all from April 2018.

Then the repeat-viewing and meme coverage: Polygon on the YouTuber who watched the film 44 times (June 8, 2018), ComicBook.com on the fan crossing 100 viewings (July 18, 2018), CBR on the fan who reached 103 (June 10, 2019), UNILAD on the fan with 100 viewings and tickets to prove it, CBR's meme roundup (May 11, 2018), Time on "The 'I Don't Feel So Good' Meme" (May 2, 2018), CBR's "Infinity War: Find Out If You Were Killed By Thanos", and the Reddit-ban reporting from Polygon (July 3, 2018), io9 ("Thanos Has Snapped His Fingers and Killed Half of a Subreddit", July 9, 2018), ComicBook.com, Screen Rant and The Verge ("Thanos subreddit successfully bans half its community", July 10, 2018).

Awards and sequel sources close the list: The Hollywood Reporter's Oscars 2019, Annie Awards, BAFTA and Critics' Choice winners lists; Empire's "The 100 Greatest Movies Of The 21st Century" (March 18, 2020); and USA Today on the first trailer for "Marvel's newly titled 'Avengers: Endgame'" (December 7, 2018).

**External links.** Sister-project links (media from Commons, quotations from Wikiquote), the official website, the film at IMDb, and at Disney A to Z.

**Navigation boxes.** Marvel Cinematic Universe boxes listing franchise songs ("All the Stars", "King's Dead", "Pray for Me", "Agatha All Along", "Lift Me Up" and others), inspired media and docuseries (Marvel Studios: Legends, Marvel Studios: Assembled), shorts (The Good, the Bart, and the Loki; Deadpool and Korg React) and video games.

wikis.title: 2027 UEFA Champions League final
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the 2027 UEFA Champions League final, set for the Estadio Metropolitano in Madrid on 5 June 2027, and the two UEFA bidding processes that led to that venue.
wikis.body:
## The match

- The 2027 UEFA Champions League final "will be the final match of the 2026-27 UEFA Champions League, the 72nd season of Europe's premier club football tournament organised by UEFA, and the 35th season since it was renamed from the European Champion Clubs' Cup to the UEFA Champions League".
- "It will be played at the Estadio Metropolitano in Madrid, Spain, on 5 June 2027."
- Infobox: Event 2026-27 UEFA Champions League; Date 5 June 2027; Venue Estadio Metropolitano, Madrid; previous 2026, next 2028.
- Kick-off listed in the match details as 18:00 UTC+2, "Winner SF1 v Winner SF2". "The winner of semi-final 1 will be designated as the 'home' team for administrative purposes."
- Caption: "The Metropolitano Stadium in Madrid will host the final."

## What the winners get

- The right to play the winners of the 2026-27 UEFA Europa League in the 2027 UEFA Super Cup.
- A place in the final of the 2027 FIFA Intercontinental Cup.
- Qualification for the 2029 FIFA Club World Cup.
- Entry to the league phase of the 2027-28 UEFA Champions League, "unless they have already qualified for the Champions League through their league performance (in which case the access list will be rebalanced)".

## Match rules listed

- 90 minutes; 30 minutes of extra time if necessary; penalty shoot-out if scores still level.
- Maximum of twelve named substitutes; maximum of five substitutions, "with a sixth allowed in extra time"; maximum of three substitution opportunities, "with a fourth allowed in extra time".

## Host selection - first bidding process

- On 17 May 2023 UEFA opened the bidding process for the 2027 final, run in parallel with that of the 2026 final. Bidders could bid for one or both finals, and "bidding associations could only be appointed one UEFA final in a given year".
- Venue requirements: natural grass, UEFA category four stadium, "with a gross capacity of at least 70,000 preferred".
- Timeline: 17 May 2023 applications formally invited; 17 July 2023 closing date for registering intention to bid; 26 July 2023 bid requirements made available; 15 November 2023 preliminary bid dossier; 21 February 2024 final bid dossier; 22 May 2024 appointment of host.
- UEFA announced on 18 July 2023 that three associations had expressed interest in hosting the 2026 and 2027 finals in this process. The table lists two: Hungary, Puskas Arena, Budapest, capacity 67,215 (noted as "Stadium appointed as host of 2026 Champions League final"); Italy, San Siro, Milan, capacity 75,817.
- The UEFA Executive Committee suspended the host decision at its meeting in Dublin, Republic of Ireland, on 22 May 2024, which "allowed the Italian Football Federation to submit additional information on the refurbishment plans for the San Siro in Milan".
- At the following Executive Committee meeting in Prague, Czech Republic, on 24 September 2024, the San Siro was not selected, "because the municipality of Milan could not guarantee that refurbishment works would not affect the stadium and its surroundings during the final". UEFA then opened a new bidding process.

## Host selection - second bidding process

- Opened on 30 September 2024 with the same venue requirements, "though associations that already were appointed to host a final in 2027 could not bid".
- Timeline: 30 September 2024 applications formally invited; 21 October 2024 closing date for registering intention to bid; 24 October 2024 bid requirements made available; 15 January 2025 preliminary bid dossier; 19 March 2025 final bid dossier; 11 September 2025 appointment of host.
- UEFA announced on 23 October 2024 that two associations had expressed interest in hosting the 2027 final in this process: Azerbaijan, Olympic Stadium, Baku, capacity 69,870; Spain, Estadio Metropolitano, Madrid, capacity 70,692 (noted as also bidding for the 2027 Women's Champions League final, with a different venue).
- The Executive Committee was originally to appoint the host at its meeting in Bilbao, Spain, on 21 May 2025, but this was postponed "for operational reasons" until September 2025.
- The Estadio Metropolitano was selected by the UEFA Executive Committee at its meeting in Tirana, Albania, on 11 September 2025. "This will be the second time the Metropolitano will be hosting the final since having previously done so in 2019."

## Notes on the page's own numbers

- The article text says UEFA announced on 18 July 2023 that **three** associations had expressed interest in the first process, while the cited reference for that statement is titled "Nine national associations interested in hosting UEFA club competition finals in 2026 and 2027". The first-process table lists two associations.
- Likewise the second process is described in the text as **two** interested associations, while its cited reference is titled "Six national associations interested in hosting 2027 UEFA Champions League and UEFA Women's Champions League finals".

## Cited sources (titles and dates as given)

- UEFA Circular Letter No. 52/2024, "Invitation to bid to host the UEFA Champions League Final 2027 and the UEFA Women's Champions League Final 2027", 30 September 2024.
- UEFA Circular Letter No. 24/2023, invitation to bid for the 2026 and 2027 finals, 17 May 2023.
- UEFA, "Nine national associations interested in hosting UEFA club competition finals in 2026 and 2027", 18 July 2023.
- UEFA, "UEFA Executive Committee to meet in Dublin", 17 May 2024; "Budapest to host UEFA Champions League Final 2026", 22 May 2024; "UEFA women's football strategy 2024-30 approved", 24 September 2024.
- UEFA, "Six national associations interested in hosting 2027 UEFA Champions League and UEFA Women's Champions League finals", 23 October 2024.
- UEFA, "UEFA Executive Committee to meet in Bilbao", 15 May 2025; "Estadio Metropolitano to host 2027 UEFA Champions League final", 11 September 2025.

## Page metadata

- Short description: "Football match in Madrid, Spain". Categories include "Scheduled association football competitions", "June 2027 sports events in Europe", "2027 in Madrid".
- The capture gives no publication or last-modified date; it ends with a permanent link carrying oldid=1375793288.

wikis.title: NBER Business Cycle Dating
wikis.summary: NBER page explaining how its Business Cycle Dating Committee defines and dates US business cycle peaks and troughs, and which data it uses.
wikis.body:
## The chronology

- The NBER's Business Cycle Dating Committee "maintains a chronology of US business cycles" identifying "the months of peaks and troughs of economic activity."
- Expansions are the periods between a trough and a peak; recessions are the periods between a peak and a trough.
- "By convention, the NBER classifies the peak month as the last month of the expansion and the trough month as the last month of the recession."
- "Expansion is the normal state of the economy; most recessions are brief." The time for the economy to return to its previous peak level or trend path "may be quite extended."
- "According to the NBER chronology, the most recent peak occurred in February 2020. The most recent trough occurred in April 2020."

## Definition of a recession

- A recession "involves a significant decline in economic activity that is spread across the economy and lasts more than a few months."
- The three criteria — "depth, diffusion, and duration" — are treated "as somewhat interchangeable": each must be met individually to some degree, but "extreme conditions revealed by one criterion may partially offset weaker indications from another."
- Example given: for the February 2020 peak, the committee concluded the drop in activity "had been so great and so widely diffused throughout the economy that, even if it proved to be quite brief, the downturn should be classified as a recession."

## Measures used

- Because a recession "must influence the economy broadly and not be confined to one sector," the committee emphasises economy-wide measures.
- Monthly measures of aggregate real economic activity published by federal statistical agencies: real personal income less transfers, nonfarm payroll employment, employment as measured by the household survey, real personal consumption expenditures, manufacturing and trade sales adjusted for price changes, and industrial production.
- "There is no fixed rule about what measures contribute information to the process or how they are weighted." In recent decades the two measures given most weight are real personal income less transfers and nonfarm payroll employment.
- Quarterly peaks and troughs are determined separately, using expenditure-side and income-side estimates of real gross domestic product (GDP and GDI), which are not available monthly, plus quarterly averages of the monthly indicators, "particularly payroll employment."

## Timing of announcements

- The approach to dating turning points is "retrospective": the committee waits "until sufficient data are available to avoid the need for major revisions."
- For a peak it waits "until it is confident that a recession has occurred," so it "tends to wait to identify a peak until a number of months after it has actually occurred."
- If activity began to rise again immediately after a peak announcement, the committee would find a new expansion underway rather than a continuation of the previous expansion.
- For a trough it waits "until it is confident that an expansion is underway"; if activity declined again immediately, that would be a new recession, not a continuation.

## Other page elements

- The page offers registration "for future Business Cycle announcements" (account log-in or creation required).

The page states no publication or last-updated date.

wikis.body:
## Episode

- Show: The Times of Israel Daily Briefing, described as "your 20-minute audio update on what's happening in Israel, the Middle East and the Jewish world"; this episode runs 32 min.
- Host: Amanda Borschel-Dan. Guest: political correspondent Ariela Karmel. Produced by Ari Schlacht.
- Published September 15, 2026 at 11:05 AM UTC; the page also heads the episode "September 15".

## What the description says

- "Israel's upcoming election officially took shape last week, as the last of 38 parties submitted their candidate slates for the October 27 vote."
- "Yesterday" (relative to the episode), the left-wing Democrat Party petitioned the Central Elections Committee to bar National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir's far-right Otzma Yehudit slate from running.
- The Democrat Party is led by Yair Golan; it accused the right-wingers of undermining democracy, denying "the existence of the State of Israel as a democratic state," and inciting racism. Karmel calls this expected political theater used by both sides of the aisle.
- Karmel is quoted from a recent analysis: "Reflecting a broad rightward shift among the Israeli electorate, Yashar leader Gadi Eisenkot is winning voters on the right and leading in the polls by presenting a party that in many ways resembles the Likud of yesteryear."
- She also discusses Likud's attempts to brand the Yashar head as a "leftist".

- "Israel's election takes shape as 38 parties submit slates, in battle between pro- and anti-Netanyahu blocs"
- "Finalizing slate, Netanyahu fills reserved Likud slots with allies, ideologues"
- "Democrats seek to bar Otzma Yehudit from election as polls show continued deadlock"
- "As parties lock in, Eisenkot plots path to power through heart of old Likud"

wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the 21st World Athletics Championships, scheduled for 10-19 September 2027 at the Beijing National Stadium, covering host selection, the approved qualification system and entry standards, and media rights.
wikis.body:
## The championships

- "The 2027 World Athletics Championships (Chinese: 2027年世界田径锦标赛) will be the twenty-first edition of the World Athletics Championships and are scheduled to be held from 10 to 19 September 2027 in the National Stadium in Beijing, China." "It will be the second time Beijing has hosted the event following the 2015 edition."
- Infobox: host city Beijing; country China; motto "Every Step Counts"; organisers World Athletics and the Chinese Athletic Association; edition 21st; events 49; dates 10-19 September 2027; main venue Beijing National Stadium; previous Tokyo 2025; next Nairobi 2029.
- Short description: "Athletics competition in Beijing, China". The venue section: "The track and field events are scheduled to be in the Beijing National Stadium in China."

## Host selection

- Cities that expressed interest: Beijing; Istanbul, Turkey; Rome, Italy; London, United Kingdom; and Nairobi, Kenya - "the latter two both eventually declining to bid".
- "When the Italian Athletics Federation withdrew its candidacy after the government declined to fund the event on 28 February 2024, World Athletics president Sebastian Coe announced the decision to award the championships to Beijing."

## Qualification

- "World Athletics approved the timetable and qualification system for the 2027 World Athletics Championships on 26 May 2026."
- Qualifying windows: marathon 3 November 2025 to midnight on 2 May 2027; 10,000 m, race walks, combined events and relays 23 February 2026 to midnight on 22 August 2027; all other events 23 August 2026 to midnight on 22 August 2027.
- The system is "based on a combination of entry standards and world rankings"; the entry standards "were set with the aim of qualifying about 40% of the athletes".
- Area champions in individual events (except the marathons) count as qualified "provided there is no other qualified athlete entered from the same area in the same event".
- The top five finishers at Platinum Label marathons during the qualification period, and the winners of Gold Label marathons held in 2027 until 2 May, count as having achieved the requirements.
- The 2026 World Athletics Relays in Gaborone, Botswana were the relay qualifier: the top 12 teams in each event secured places, with the remaining four places per relay discipline "allocated to the best-ranked teams at the end of the qualification period, based on top lists".

### Entry standards and quotas (men / women)

### Wild cards

- Available to "the defending world champions from 2025, winners at the World Athletics Ultimate Championship 2026, winners of the 2026 World Race Walking Tour and World Combined Events Tour, the leading hammer performers on the 2026 Continental Tour, and the winners of the 2027 Wanda Diamond League".
- "If a member federation has four athletes in one event as a result of this criterion, all four will be permitted to compete." Where a federation has more than one wild-card athlete per event, it "will need to select one of those athletes to accept the spot".

## Event schedule and participants

- The schedule tables (men, women, mixed) carry date columns Sep 11 through Sep 19, with morning (M) and evening (E) sessions; the legend is P preliminary round, Q qualifiers, H heats, 1/2 semifinals, F final. No per-event rows survive in this capture.

## Media coverage

- "In the United States, television rights to the championships belong to NBC Sports."
- "China plans to rapidly expand its athletics scope in the coming years, with the country set to host the World Indoor Championships in 2025. With this, the hosting rights of the last four World Athletics Championships have been given to the four most powerful economies of the world, namely the US, the European Union, Japan, and now China."
- "Eurovision Sport and ESPN jointly hold and distribute World Athletics media rights in Europe and Africa." Warner Bros. Discovery has agreed a deal with them "to broadcast the nine-day event on its channels - Eurosport 1, Eurosport 2 and Eurosport App - including its platform discovery+ on a non-exclusive basis in more than 45 countries across Europe (excluding the Nordics region - Denmark, Finland, Norway, Sweden)". Streaming on discovery+ in Austria, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, the United Kingdom and Ireland. This paragraph is marked "[citation needed]".

wikis.title: Catalog of Solar Eclipses of Saros 141
wikis.summary: NASA/Fred Espenak catalog of Saros series 141: its statistics (41 annular and 29 partial eclipses over 1244.08 years from 1613 May 19 to 2857 Jun 13) and a table of all 70 eclipses at greatest eclipse.
wikis.body:
## What the page is

- NASA Goddard catalog page for **Saros series 141**, listing "concise details and local circumstances at greatest eclipse for every solar eclipse in Saros 141".
- Background it gives on the cycle: "The periodicity and recurrence of solar eclipses is governed by the Saros cycle, a period of approximately 6,585.3 days (18 years 11 days 8 hours)." Eclipses one saros apart "share a very similar geometry", occur at the same node, "with the Moon at nearly the same distance from Earth and at the same time of year".
- "Each series typically lasts 12 to 13 centuries and contains 70 or more eclipses." A series begins with partial eclipses near one pole, produces "several dozen central eclipses", then ends with partial eclipses near the opposite pole.

## Statistics for Saros 141

- Eclipses of Saros 141 "all occur at the Moons ascending node and the Moon moves southward with each eclipse".
- "The series began with a partial eclipse in the northern hemisphere on 1613 May 19."
- "The series will end with a partial eclipse in the southern hemisphere on 2857 Jun 13."
- First Eclipse = 1613 May 19 17:43:36 TD; Last Eclipse = 2857 Jun 13 09:35:05 TD.
- Duration of Saros 141 = 1244.08 Years ("The total duration of Saros series 141 is 1244.08 years").
- Composed of 70 solar eclipses: All Eclipses 70 (100.0%); Partial (P) 29 (41.4%); Annular (A) 41 (58.6%); Total (T) 0 (0.0%); Hybrid (H) 0 (0.0%).
- Umbral eclipses: All Umbral Eclipses 41 (100.0%), all Central (two limits) 41 (100.0%); Central (one limit) 0; Non-Central (one limit) 0.
- Sequence of the 70 eclipses: "7P 41A 22P".

## Extreme durations and magnitudes

- Longest Annular Solar Eclipse: 1955 Dec 14, 12m09s.
- Shortest Annular Solar Eclipse: 2442 Oct 04, 01m08s.
- Largest Partial Solar Eclipse: 2478 Oct 26, magnitude 0.96448.
- Smallest Partial Solar Eclipse: 2857 Jun 13, magnitude 0.06372.

## Catalog

- The catalog table lists all 70 eclipses with columns: Seq. Num., Rel. Num., Calendar Date, TD of Greatest Eclipse, ΔT (s), Luna Num., Ecl. Type, Gamma, Ecl. Mag., Sun Lat, Sun Long, Sun Alt (°), Path Width (km), Central Dur.
- First and last rows verbatim:

```
08570 -33 1613 May 19 17:43:36 103 -4782 Pb 1.5171 0.0712 63.3N 137.6E 0
11538 36 2857 Jun 13 09:35:05 3414 10605 Pe -1.4973 0.0637 65.5S 70.9E 0
```

- Rows for 2001-2100 verbatim:

```
09529 -11 2010 Jan 15 07:07:39 67 124 A 0.4002 0.9190 1.6N 69.3E 66 333 11m08s
09569 -10 2028 Jan 26 15:08:59 76 347 A 0.3901 0.9208 3.0N 51.5W 67 323 10m27s
09609 -09 2046 Feb 05 23:06:26 90 570 A 0.3765 0.9232 4.8N 171.4W 68 310 09m42s
09650 -08 2064 Feb 17 07:00:23 122 793 A 0.3597 0.9262 7.0N 69.7E 69 295 08m56s
09691 -07 2082 Feb 27 14:47:00 162 1016 A 0.3361 0.9298 9.4N 47.1W 70 277 08m12s
09733 -06 2100 Mar 10 22:28:11 203 1239 A 0.3077 0.9338 12.0N 162.4W 72 257 07m29s
```

- Catalog fields link out: catalog number to a small global visibility map; calendar date to the central path on Google maps; TD of greatest eclipse to a large global map (years 1901 through 2100); saros number to the saros catalog; gamma to a Besselian elements table; central duration to a path coordinates table (years 1901 through 2100). The page also offers an "Animation of Saros 141".
- Parameter definitions are in "Key to Catalog of Solar Eclipse Saros Series".

## Calendar and prediction notes

- "The Gregorian calendar is used for all dates from 1582 Oct 15 onwards. Before that date, the Julian calendar is used." Years "are numbered astronomically and include the year 0"; astronomical year 0 corresponds to 1 BCE.
- Solar coordinates from "the VSOP87 theory [Bretagnon and Francou, 1988]"; the Moon's from "the ELP-2000/82 theory [Chapront-Touze and Chapront, 1983]".
- "The revised value used for the Moon's secular acceleration is n-dot = -25.858 arc-sec/cy*cy, as deduced from the Apollo lunar laser ranging experiment (Chapront, Chapront-Touze, and Francou, 2002)."
- "The largest uncertainty in the eclipse predictions is caused by fluctuations in Earth's rotation due primarily to tidal friction of the Moon," expressed as ΔT: calculated from empirical fits (Morrison and Stephenson, 2004) pre-1950s, from published observations 1955-present, and extrapolated for the future "from current values weighted by the long term trend from tidal effects".

## Acknowledgments

- Based on data published in "Five Millennium Canon of Solar Eclipses: -1999 to +3000" and "Five Millennium Catalog of Solar Eclipses: -1999 to +3000". Global maps were extracted from the Canon's plates "by Dan McGlaun"; "The Besselian elements were provided by Jean Meeus".
- "Fred Espenak assumes full responsibility for the accuracy of all eclipse calculations." Required acknowledgment: "Eclipse Predictions by Fred Espenak (NASA's GSFC)".

## Page date

- The page carries no labelled publication or revision date; it ends with the bare date "2009 Sep 26".

wikis.title: Rice-Eccles Stadium
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on Rice-Eccles Stadium at the University of Utah: its construction and renovations, playing surface, Olympic role, tenants, concerts and other events, and attendance records.
wikis.body:
## Overview
- Outdoor college football stadium on the campus of the University of Utah in Salt Lake City, Utah; home field of the Utah Utes of the Big 12 Conference.
- Address 451 South 1400 East; coordinates 40 deg 45'36"N, 111 deg 50'56"W; elevation 4,637 feet (1,413 m) AMSL, "400 feet (120 m) above downtown Salt Lake City".
- Owner and operator: University of Utah. Website stadium.utah.edu. Public transit at Stadium station. 25 executive suites.
- Capacity 54,383 (2024-present); former capacities 45,807 (2014-2020), 45,017 (2003-2013), 45,634 (1998-2002). Record attendance 54,383 vs BYU, 2024.
- Surface: FieldTurf CoolPlay (2015-present); FieldTurf (2002-2015); natural grass (2000-2001); Sportgrass (1998-1999). The field runs "in the traditional north-south configuration".
- Construction: groundbreaking June 1997; opened September 12, 1998; cost US$50,000,000 (equivalent to $99,000,000 in 2025). Architect FFKR Architects; structural engineer Reaveley Engineers + Associates; services engineers Van Boerum & Frank Associates; general contractor Layton Construction.
- Tenants: Utah Utes (NCAA) 1998-present; Real Salt Lake (MLS) 2005-2008; Salt Lake Stallions (AAF) 2019.
- "It was built to serve as the stadium for the opening and closing ceremonies of 2002 Winter Olympics, a role it is expected to reprise for the 2034 Winter Olympics."

## History
- When Salt Lake City was awarded the 2002 Winter Olympics in June 1995, Robert Rice Stadium - the largest outdoor stadium in the city, built in 1927 of concrete, timber and earth-fill - was judged unsuitable. In 1996 athletic director Chris Hill announced plans to renovate it to Olympic standards, initially expected to take three years.
- In 1997 Spencer Eccles, a Utah alumnus and chairman of First Security Corporation (now part of Wells Fargo), announced the George S. and Dolores Dore Eccles Foundation would donate $10 million; in recognition the university added George Eccles's name alongside that of Robert L. Rice, who had funded the original Rice Stadium renovation in 1972. Before 1972 it was Ute Stadium, opened in 1927 with a Utah win over Colorado Mines.
- After the 1997 season's final home game on November 15 - "fittingly a 31-14 victory over Rice" - the stadium was almost completely demolished and rebuilt in steel, concrete and glass; only the 1982 south end zone stands remained. The project was timed not to disrupt the 1997 home schedule, and the new stadium was ready "less than 10 months later" for the 1998 home opener, a 45-22 win over Louisville on September 12. The article says it then seated 45,017, plus a new six-story press box, while the infobox lists the 1998-2002 capacity as 45,634.

## Renovations
- 2014: a row of bleachers was added in standing room areas on the east, west and north sections, plus forty ADA seats, "for a total of 790 new seats, increasing capacity to 45,807".
- June 2010: Utah accepted an invitation to the Pacific-10 Conference (renamed Pac-12 after Utah and Colorado joined), playing in it from 2011-2012. KSL.com and the Deseret News reported the university was "seriously considering expanding the stadium by at least 10,000 seats, which would bring the expected capacity to 51,444".
- 2019: a south end zone seating renovation was announced, "planned to add 6,000 more seats, high-end suites, locker rooms, offices, terrace seating, and a restaurant, all for $80 million". The Ken Garff Family donated $17.5 million and the section was named the "Ken Garff Red Zone". Construction completed August 12, 2021 and opened that season; the article states that after construction "the stadium's capacity had increased by 5,637 seats".
- The Ken Garff Red Zone has new home and visiting locker rooms, sports medicine and hospitality areas, the University Club restaurant, Diglisic Lounge, Layton Field Club and premium seating. "Utah's new locker room is 5,300 square feet with 90 lockers", with hidden storage, wireless charging and a locking box.

## Features
- Olympic Cauldron Park stood immediately south of the stadium with a 2002 Winter Olympic museum, the cauldron and memorabilia; only the cauldron remains, refurbished and relocated to a new Olympic plaza at the southwest corner. Hoberman Arch was located there until its removal in October 2014.
- Playing surface history: SportGrass on reopening in 1998 (Rice Stadium had been among the first facilities to use it), full natural grass installed in 2000 for two seasons, then covered by asphalt blacktop for the 2002 Olympic ceremonies, FieldTurf since 2002, last replaced in 2015.
- It was the second-highest field in the Pac-12, "about 700 feet (210 m) lower than Colorado's Folsom Field" and "over 2,000 feet (610 m) above the third-highest, Washington State's Martin Stadium"; after the 2024 move to the Big 12, Colorado and Utah again have the two highest fields in the conference.

## Events
- 2002 Winter Olympics: opening ceremony February 8, 2002 and closing ceremony February 24, 2002. The grass field was paved with asphalt, a stage built, scoreboards removed, temporary seating brought in "allowing more than 50,000 spectators", and the Olympic cauldron installed atop the southern bleachers. The venue was temporarily renamed Rice-Eccles Olympic Stadium; "an estimated 3.5 billion people worldwide watched the opening and closing ceremonies on television".
- 2002 Winter Paralympics: opening ceremony March 7, 2002; closing ceremony March 16, 2002.
- 2027 NHL Winter Classic: "On January 7, 2026, the National Hockey League and Smith Entertainment Group announced that the Utah Mammoth ice hockey team would host the 2027 NHL Winter Classic at the stadium", against the Colorado Avalanche. "The Mammoth will become the final active NHL team to host or be involved in an outdoor game."
- 2034 Winter Olympics and Paralympics: the stadium is expected to host the opening and closing ceremonies for a second time.
- Tenants: Real Salt Lake played there from 2005 until October 2008, when Rio Tinto Stadium opened in Sandy. The Salt Lake Stallions played there in the AAF's lone 2019 season. The first Utes game at the stadium was the 45-22 win over Louisville on September 12, 1998 "with 44,112 in attendance"; the Utes have a 120-41 (.745) record at the stadium through the 2024 season.
- Other events: an AMA Supercross Championship round from 2001 to 2004, 2009 to 2013 and 2017; in 2020 it hosted the final seven rounds in a "COVID-19 bubble" with no fans; since 2021 it has hosted the series' Championship round. First Monster Jam event in 2022, returning yearly the week before the Supercross championship; Monster Jam World Finals XXIV and XXV were held in July 2025 and 2026. Mexico played Switzerland in an international friendly on June 7, 2025, losing 4-2 "in front of 41,000 fans".

## Concerts (as tabled)
- June 17, 2000: NSYNC with Pink, No Strings Attached Tour.
- May 24, 2011: U2 with The Fray, 360 deg Tour - attendance 47,710, revenue $3,029,760; "Postponed from June 3, 2010, due to Bono's emergency back surgery."
- July 28, 2018: Imagine Dragons with Grace VanderWaal, Zedd, Mike Shinoda, Tyler Glenn, Vagabon, A.W. and Cameron Esposito - LoveLoud 2018 / Evolve World Tour.
- July 17, 2021 and June 17-18, 2022: Garth Brooks, The Garth Brooks Stadium Tour (2022 with Mitch Rossell).
- August 5, 2022: Imagine Dragons with Macklemore and Kings Elliot, Mercury World Tour - 36,071, $2,893,663.
- June 7, 2024: Luke Combs with Cody Jinks, Charles Wesley Godwin, Hailey Whitters and The Wilder Blue, Growin' Up and Gettin' Old Tour - 73,339, $7,500,000; June 8, 2024 with Colby Acuff, Drew Parker, Mitchell Tenpenny and Jordan Davis - $6,800,000.
- June 29, 2024: George Strait with Chris Stapleton and Little Big Town, Stadium Tour - 50,000+.
- April 29, 2025: Post Malone with Sierra Ferrell and Jelly Roll, Big Ass Stadium Tour - 40,551, $6,204,677.
- July 28, 2026: Post Malone with Carter Faith and Jelly Roll, Big Ass Stadium Tour II - about 40,500+.
- August 7, 2026: Zach Bryan with MJ Lenderman and Fey Fili, With Heaven on Tour.
- June 19, 2027: Metallica with Limp Bizkit and Avatar, M72 World Tour.

## Attendance records
- Top entries: 1. November 9, 2024, 7:30 pm vs #9 BYU, L 22-21, 54,383. 2. August 31, 2023 vs Florida, W 24-11, 53,644. 3. October 15, 2022 vs #7 USC, W 43-42, 53,609. 4. October 28, 2023 vs #7 Oregon, L 35-6, 53,586. 5. October 19, 2024 vs TCU, L 7-13, 53,299.
- Further entries run down to 51,511; the table as printed ranks November 25, 2023 vs Colorado (51,511) at 18 above November 26, 2021 vs Colorado (51,595) at 19, and September 16, 2023 vs Weber State (51,532) at 20, so the listed order does not match the listed figures.

wikis.title: Solo Leveling: Beyond the System anime film announced
wikis.summary: Anime News Network report that Crunchyroll announced a Solo Leveling anime film, Solo Leveling: Beyond the System, at its Anime Expo panel, with A-1 Pictures returning and Tao Tajima directing.
wikis.body:
## The announcement

- Anime News Network news article by Alex Mateo, "posted on 2026-07-03 17:44 EDT".
- Standfirst: "Promotional concept video, teaser visual unveiled for Solo Leveling: Beyond the System film".
- "Crunchyroll announced during its panel at Anime Expo on Friday that the Solo Leveling series is getting an anime film titled Solo Leveling: Beyond the System."
- "The film, which continues the story after the second season, is currently in production." No release date or window is given.
- Crunchyroll shared a promotional concept video and a teaser visual. Image courtesy of Crunchyroll; copyright line "© Solo Leveling Animation Partners".

## Staff and production companies

- "A-1 Pictures is returning to animate the film."
- Co-producers: Crunchyroll, Aniplex, Netmarble, D&C MEDIA and Kakao Piccoma.
- "Tao Tajima is directing the film, and is also serving as the director of photography, editor, and colorist."
- "Tomoko Sudo is returning as character designer and key animator."

## Background the article gives on the franchise

- The anime adapts the Solo Leveling webtoon by writer Chugong and "the late artist DUBU" (REDICE STUDIO). Its first season debuted in Japan in January 2024; Crunchyroll added the English dub the same month.
- Solo Leveling -ReAwakening-, "a compilation film for the Solo Leveling anime's first season and a preview of the first two episodes of the second season", screened in Japan from November to December 2024. Crunchyroll and Sony Pictures screened it in December 2024 "in select theaters in the U.S. and Canada".
- The second season debuted in January 2025; Crunchyroll streamed it and an English dub.
- The webtoon adaptation of Chugong's Solo Leveling novel series, illustrated by DUBU, "launched on WEBTOON in March 2018 and ended in December 2021". Yen Press publishes the manhwa and original novels in English in print; several services including Tapas release the web novel and webtoon digitally; Kadokawa publishes the webtoon in Japanese as Ore Dake Level-Up na Ken (I'm the Only One Who Has Leveled Up).
- "The webtoon is also inspiring a Korean live-action adaptation."
- Games: Solo Leveling: Arise launched for Android, iOS and Windows in May 2024; Netmarble's Solo Leveling: ARISE OVERDRIVE launched for Xbox Series X|S (and Xbox Cloud) and PC via Steam "last November".

## Source and disclosures

- Source given as "Crunchyroll's Anime Expo panel (Alex Mateo)".
- Disclosure printed with the article: "Kadokawa World Entertainment (KWE), a wholly owned subsidiary of Kadokawa Corporation, is the majority owner of Anime News Network, LLC. One or more of the companies mentioned in this article are part of the Kadokawa Group of Companies."
- The page notes: "this article has been modified since it was originally posted; see change history" - without giving the date of the modification.
