wikis.title: Godzilla x Kong: The New Empire (2024 film)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia's article on Godzilla x Kong: The New Empire, Adam Wingard's 2024 Monsterverse sequel - its credits and plot, Queensland shoot and visual effects, release dates, $572.5 million gross and mixed reviews.
wikis.body:
## The film

- **Godzilla x Kong: The New Empire**, a 2024 American monster film directed and co-written by **Adam Wingard**, produced by **Legendary Pictures** and distributed by **Warner Bros. Pictures** worldwide and **Toho** in Japan.
- Sequel to *Godzilla vs. Kong* (2021); the fifth Monsterverse film, the 38th Godzilla film and the 13th King Kong film. Screenplay by Terry Rossio, Simon Barrett and Jeremy Slater; story by Rossio, Wingard and Barrett.
- Stars **Rebecca Hall**, **Brian Tyree Henry**, **Dan Stevens**, **Kaylee Hottle**, **Alex Ferns** and **Fala Chen**; Hall, Henry and Hottle reprise their roles. The article notes this was Hottle's final film role before her death in 2026, citing a Newsweek report of July 21, 2026 that she died at 18.
- Cinematography Ben Seresin; editing Josh Schaeffer; music Tom Holkenborg and Antonio Di Iorio. Running time **115 minutes**; budget **$135-150 million**.
- Wingard says the "x" in the title is silent; Legendary meant it "to indicate more of a collaboration than a fight rematch".

## Dates

- Announced as a sequel **March 20, 2022**; Wingard and Dan Stevens confirmed **May 2022**; shot in Gold Coast, Queensland from **July 29, 2022**, finishing in Australia in **November 2022**.
- Premiere at Grauman's Chinese Theatre **March 25, 2024**; international release **March 27**; United States **March 29**; Japan **April 26** via Toho. It had previously been dated **March 15** and **April 12**.
- Home media: digital **May 14, 2024**; disc **June 11, 2024**; Max **July 4, 2024**.
- Sequel *Godzilla x Kong: Supernova*, announced two months after release with **Grant Sputore** directing, planned for **March 26, 2027**.

## Money

- **$196.8 million** United States and Canada, **$375.7 million** elsewhere, **$572.5 million** worldwide. The lead calls it the eighth-highest-grossing film of 2024 and the highest-grossing Monsterverse, Godzilla and King Kong film; the box office section says only that it "holds the record for the highest-grossing Godzilla film ever" as of 2024.
- Opened to **$80 million** after a **$37 million** first day including **$10 million** in previews, "the best-ever total for a Monsterverse film" - the fifth-best Easter weekend of all time.

## Reception

- Rotten Tomatoes **54%** (253 reviews, 5.6/10); Metacritic **47/100** (51 critics). Audiences gave it a CinemaScore of **A-** and 96% PostTrak approval.
- "Many comparing it unfavorably to *Godzilla Minus One*, which had been released four months prior" - reviewers at Variety, Deadline and elsewhere suggested Legendary hire that film's team.
- Awards: won Most Popular U.S. Film in China at the Chinese American Film Festival (November 8, 2024); nominated at the Family Film and TV Awards, the Indiana Film Journalists Association (visual effects), the Saturn Awards (Best Fantasy Film; Kaylee Hottle) and the Annie Awards (character animation). The accolades table is mis-captioned "Accolades received by Ghostbusters: Frozen Empire".

## Craft

- Effects supervised by Alessandro Ongaro, with Scanline VFX (opening chase, Egypt and Rio fights, Kong's glove), DNEG (surface scenes, Hollow World jungles, Iwi pyramid) and Wētā FX (Hollow Earth, 130 giant apes, Shimo).
- Mothra was always planned but Legendary lacked the rights at the start of post-production, so a placeholder named "Phosphera" stood in.
- Rendering was at 5K because of the wide anamorphic lenses; Wingard told the crew to relax scale and speed so the monsters could move fast.
- The Rome sequence pays tribute to a shot from *Godzilla Minus One*; the Egyptian fight was modelled on *They Live* (1988).

wikis.title: Godzilla x Kong: The New Empire - film article from plot to sequel
wikis.summary: The body of the Wikipedia article on Adam Wingard's 2024 monster film Godzilla x Kong: The New Empire: credits, plot, cast, development and filming in Queensland, visual effects, release dates, box office, mixed reviews and awards.
wikis.body:
## Infobox

- **Godzilla x Kong: The New Empire**, "2024 film by Adam Wingard". Directed by **Adam Wingard**; screenplay by **Terry Rossio, Simon Barrett and Jeremy Slater**; story by **Terry Rossio, Adam Wingard and Simon Barrett**; based on Godzilla and Mothra by Toho Co., Ltd.
- Produced by Thomas Tull, Jon Jashni, Brian Rogers, Mary Parent, Alex Garcia and Eric McLeod. Starring Rebecca Hall, Brian Tyree Henry, Dan Stevens, Kaylee Hottle, Alex Ferns and Fala Chen.
- Cinematography **Ben Seresin**; edited by **Josh Schaeffer**; music by **Tom Holkenborg** and **Antonio Di Iorio**.
- Production company **Legendary Pictures**; distributed by **Warner Bros. Pictures** worldwide and **Toho** in Japan.
- Release dates **March 25, 2024** (TCL Chinese Theatre) and **March 29, 2024** (United States). Running time **115 minutes**; country United States; language English.
- Budget **$135-150 million**; box office **$572.5 million**.

## Lead

- A 2024 American monster film, sequel to *Godzilla vs. Kong* (2021) and the fifth film in Legendary's **Monsterverse**, the **38th** film in the Godzilla franchise and the **13th** in the King Kong franchise.
- Hall, Henry and Hottle reprise their roles; "it is Hottle's final role before her death in 2026".
- Plot premise: "Kong encounters more of his species in the Hollow Earth and must unite again with Godzilla to stop the tyrannical Skar King and the powerful, frost-breathing Shimo from invading the Earth's surface."
- Legendary announced a sequel in **March 2022**; in **May 2022** Wingard was confirmed to return and Stevens cast. Filming began **July 2022** in Gold Coast, Australia and finished **November 2022**.
- Premiered at Grauman's Chinese Theatre **March 25, 2024**; released in the US **March 29**. "The film received mixed reviews from critics, with many comparing it unfavorably to *Godzilla Minus One*, which had been released four months prior."
- Grossed **$572.5 million** worldwide against a $135-150 million budget, "becoming the eighth-highest-grossing film of 2024 and the highest-grossing film of the Monsterverse, as well as in the Godzilla and King Kong franchises".
- A sequel, *Godzilla x Kong: Supernova*, is planned for **March 26, 2027**.
- A note says the "x" in the title is silent according to Wingard, though he pronounces it in the abbreviation *GxK*, and that Legendary meant it "to indicate more of a collaboration than a fight rematch".

## Things the page states inconsistently

- **Release dates**: the infobox and lead give the US release as March 29, 2024 after a March 25 premiere; the Release section adds that it "was released internationally on March 27 and in the United States on March 29", and in Japan on **April 26** via Toho, having previously been slated for **March 15** and **April 12**.
- **Highest-grossing claim**: the lead calls it the highest-grossing film of the Monsterverse and of both the Godzilla and King Kong franchises; the Box office section says only "As of 2024, it holds the record for the highest-grossing Godzilla film ever".
- The accolades table is captioned "**Accolades received by Ghostbusters: Frozen Empire**", a different film, while listing this film's nominations.

## Plot (as summarised in the article)

- Three years after defeating Mechagodzilla, Kong holds territory in Hollow Earth and searches for his own kind, while Godzilla keeps order on the surface - killing Titanus Scylla for attacking Rome and resting in the Colosseum.
- A Monarch outpost in Hollow Earth picks up an unidentified signal; it gives Jia, the last known Iwi survivor from Skull Island, hallucinations, worrying her adoptive mother Dr. Ilene Andrews. Godzilla absorbs radiation from a French nuclear plant and heads for the lair of the Titan Tiamat in the Arctic.
- Kong finds an uncharted realm holding a surviving tribe of his species, including the juvenile ape Suko. Andrews, Jia, Titan veterinarian Trapper and podcaster Bernie Hayes descend to find the outpost destroyed, and trace the signal to a subterranean Iwi tribe who communicate telepathically; the signal is their distress call.
- Hieroglyphics reveal that the Skar King, a tyrannical ape titan, once warred on Godzilla's species and triggered an ice age before being trapped in Hollow Earth, and that Jia is the key to reawakening Mothra.
- The Skar King summons his enslaved ice-breathing Titan Shimo with a crystal that causes her pain; Shimo frostbites Kong's arm and he escapes with Suko's help, losing his axe. Trapper fits Kong with a prototype exoskeletal glove; Jia awakens Mothra.
- Godzilla kills Tiamat and absorbs cosmic radiation, turning his dorsal plates magenta. Kong surfaces in Cairo to call him; they fight until Mothra intervenes. The three Titans fight the Skar King's forces, then chase him and Shimo to Rio de Janeiro, where Shimo starts a second ice age. Suko arrives with Kong's axe and destroys the control crystal; Shimo freezes the Skar King and Kong shatters him.
- Godzilla undoes the ice age with atomic breath and returns to the Colosseum; Jia chooses to stay with Andrews; Mothra restores the barrier; Kong returns to Hollow Earth with Shimo and Suko and becomes his tribe's leader.

## Cast

- **Rebecca Hall** as Dr. Ilene Andrews, a Monarch scientist and anthropological linguist; **Brian Tyree Henry** as Bernie Hayes, conspiracy theorist and former Apex employee; **Dan Stevens** as Trapper, a Monarch veterinarian; **Kaylee Hottle** as Jia - "This was Hottle's final film role before her death in 2026"; **Alex Ferns** as Mikael, a Monarch pilot; **Fala Chen** as the Iwi Queen.
- Also Rachel House (Hampton), Ron Smyck (Harris), Chantelle Jamieson (Jayne), Greg Hatton (Lewis), Kevin Copeland (Submarine Commander), Tess Dobré (Submarine Officer), Tim Carroll (Wilcox), Anthony Brandon Wong (Talk Show Announcer).
- **Allan Henry** performance-captured both Kong and the Skar King - "a Titan with chimpanzee, gibbon, and orangutan-like traits"; **Luke Hawker** did motion capture for Suko.
- A reference cites Newsweek, July 21, 2026: "Kaylee Hottle, 'Godzilla vs. Kong' Star, Dies at 18".

## Development

- March 2019: producer Alex Garcia said Legendary hoped to make more Monsterverse films if they succeeded. February 2021: Wingard said the Monsterverse was at a "crossroads" - "It's really at the point where audiences have to kind of step forward and vote for more of these things."
- *Godzilla vs. Kong* opened March 24, 2021 in theaters and on HBO Max simultaneously, grossing **$470 million** worldwide against a **$330 million** break-even point, becoming HBO Max's most successful launch title until *Mortal Kombat*, and the most pirated film of 2021.
- April 4, 2021: Legendary CEO Josh Grode said "we have a number of ideas for more movies"; the hashtag #ContinueTheMonsterverse trended, supported by *Kong: Skull Island* director Jordan Vogt-Roberts. April 27, 2021: The Hollywood Reporter said Legendary was "quietly taking steps to stretch the series", with *Son of Kong* among potential titles. August 2021: writer Max Borenstein said "there will be some new, interesting installments coming".
- **March 20, 2022**: the sequel announced to shoot later that year in Gold Coast, Queensland and elsewhere in South East Queensland. **May 2022**: Wingard returning to direct, Dan Stevens cast - the two had worked together on *The Guest* (2014); Production Weekly reported the working title **Origins**. **June 30, 2022**: Mary Parent, Alex Garcia, Eric McLeod, Brian Rogers, Thomas Tull and Jon Jashni confirmed as producers. **July 1, 2022**: Toho confirmed Godzilla would feature.

## Pre-production

- Wingard said pre-production began January 2022. In August 2022 Warner Bros. and Legendary announced a synopsis, that Hall, Henry and Hottle would reprise, and that Chen, Ferns and House would join, with production designer Tom Hammock, editor Josh Schaeffer and composer Tom Holkenborg returning, and Terry Rossio writing with Jeremy Slater and Simon Barrett.
- Final credits: "screenplay by" Rossio, Barrett and Slater; "story by" Rossio, Wingard and Barrett. Michael Dougherty and Zach Shields, co-writers of *Godzilla: King of the Monsters* and *Godzilla vs. Kong*, shared off-screen "additional literary material" credit with James Ashcroft, Eli Kent and Nicole Perlman.
- The Third Floor did extensive previsualization, including checking the Rio de Janeiro locations on Google Earth.

## Filming

- Principal photography began in the Gold Coast, Queensland on **July 29, 2022**; Ben Seresin confirmed as director of photography. Filming in Australia finished in **November 2022**, when crew gear suggested a working title of *Godzilla and Kong*.
- A mostly visual-effects unit went to Rio de Janeiro to shoot plates and gather data for a digital recreation of the city, including aerial photography and Lidar. Surfers Paradise stood in for the Rio beach where the climactic battle starts.

## Post-production and visual effects

- Visual effects supervised by **Alessandro Ongaro**. Wingard said Mothra was always planned but Legendary lacked the rights when post-production began, so a placeholder character named "**Phosphera**" was used until they were secured; he denied rumours that Phosphera was replaced due to poor testing, saying Mothra was in the first draft.
- **Scanline VFX**: the opening Kong chase by "Wart-Dogs" - likened to wolves and African wild dogs with "the twitchy, unpredictable energy of a hyena" - the climactic Egypt and Rio fights, and Kong's mechanical glove.
- **DNEG**: many surface scenes with Godzilla and Kong, the Hollow World jungles and the Iwi crystal pyramid.
- **Wētā FX**: the Hollow Earth, its giant apes - **130** of them in the Skar King's lair - and Shimo. The Skar King was designed as "a long and skinny orangutan" for contrast; supervisor Kevin Smith: "Kong is Mike Tyson, but Skar King is a little shifty and more graceful". His long arms needed extensions and prosthetics on the motion-capture performers, and his spine-built weapon featured "108 or 110 vertebrae, plus the jaw handle and the thing at the end". Shimo aimed at "a fine balance between creating something beautiful but also menacing", moving cat-like, "not super brutal like Godzilla would be"; her ice breath used up to **30 layers** of effects.
- Wingard told the crew not to worry about scale and relative speed so monsters could move fast, adapting the gravity and speed of water simulations. Rendering was in **5K resolution** because the film was shot with wide anamorphic lenses.

## Influences

- After seeing the *Godzilla Minus One* (2023) trailer, Wingard and Ongaro paid tribute by recreating a shot of the ground bursting beneath Godzilla's footfall in the Rome sequence.
- The Egyptian Godzilla-Kong battle was inspired by the Roddy Piper / Keith David fight in *They Live* (1988).

## Music

- Tom Holkenborg announced in August 2022 to return; Antonio Di Iorio announced as co-composer in December 2023. WaterTower Music released the single "Main Title Theme" on **March 13, 2024** and the full soundtrack on **March 22, 2024**.
- For the Japanese release, Ai, Yaffle and OZworld contributed the theme "**Rise Together**", released **April 17, 2024**.

## Release

- Red carpet premiere at Grauman's Chinese Theatre **March 25, 2024**; international release **March 27**; United States **March 29**; Japan **April 26** via Toho. Previously slated for **March 15** and **April 12**. "Incidentally, Toho's *Godzilla Minus One* was withdrawn from U.S. theaters eight weeks before the release".
- Home media: digital **May 14, 2024**; Blu-ray, DVD and Ultra HD Blu-ray **June 11, 2024**; streaming on Max **July 4, 2024**.

## Box office

- **$196.8 million** in the United States and Canada, **$375.7 million** elsewhere, **$572.5 million** worldwide. "As of 2024, it holds the record for the highest-grossing Godzilla film ever."
- Projections were $50-55 million domestic from 3,850 theaters plus $80-90 million from 63 international territories. It made **$37 million** on day one including **$10 million** in Thursday previews, "the best-ever total for a Monsterverse film", lifting estimates to $75 million; it opened to **$80 million**, topping the box office, the second-best opening of the series and the fifth-best Easter weekend ever behind *Batman v Superman: Dawn of Justice*, *Furious 7*, *The Super Mario Bros. Movie* and *The Fate of the Furious*.
- Second weekend **$31.2 million** (down 61%), still first; third weekend **$15.5 million**, second to *Civil War*. In Japan it debuted at number two behind *Detective Conan: The Million-dollar Pentagram*.

## Critical response

- Rotten Tomatoes: **54%** of 253 critics' reviews positive, average 5.6/10; consensus "Come to Godzilla x Kong: The New Empire for the sheer monster-mashing spectacle -- and stay for that too, because the movie doesn't have much else to offer." Metacritic **47 out of 100** from 51 critics, "mixed or average". CinemaScore **A-**; PostTrak reported 96% said the film "met or exceeded their expectations".
- Several critics compared it unfavourably to *Godzilla Minus One*, released in the US in December 2023. Owen Gleiberman (Variety) found it mediocre and more like a superhero film and a "product" against *Minus One*'s "lyrical majesty", but praised the Rome battle. Pete Hammond (Deadline) likened the ape tribe to *Planet of the Apes*, noted Godzilla mostly plays a supporting role despite top billing, called the humans "one dimensional caricatures" with "nice rapport", called *Minus One* "far more impressive" and suggested Legendary hire its team. James Berardinelli suggested *Minus One* writer-director Takashi Yamazaki make the next Monsterverse film. The Sioux City Journal called the visual effects inferior to *Minus One*'s.
- Michael Phillips (Chicago Tribune): "Wingard and the writers work like rogue chefs at an Olive Garden, tossing everything they can at any number of walls to see what sticks."
- Alissa Wilkinson (The New York Times), pull quote: "Beyond the main cast, the humans in this movie exist only to get squashed like ants by falling debris and mangled buildings. They are expendable, but it doesn't matter. The meaning of these films isn't in metaphor at all. It's in punching."
- The Guardian praised the choreography and called Rebecca Hall "ever luminous" but felt Stevens and Henry struggled with the comedy; Empire called the journey to the climax "a mixed bag" and the characters "shallow but fun"; IndieWire called the CGI dull, suggesting *Godzilla* (2014) as a reference point; the Los Angeles Times called the film "a roaring headache" while citing "two impressively goopy moments" and the director's "penchant for gleeful experimentation and over-the-top style".

## Accolades

- **Chinese American Film Festival** (November 8, 2024): Most Popular U.S. Film in China - **won**.
- Family Film and TV Awards (November 9, 2024): Best Feature Film - nominated.
- Indiana Film Journalists Association Awards (December 16, 2024): Best Visual Effects - Kevin Smith, Kevin Sherwood, Bruce Bright, Michael Meinardus - nominated.
- Saturn Awards (February 2, 2025): Best Fantasy Film - nominated; Best Performance by a Younger Actor in a Film - Kaylee Hottle - nominated.
- Annie Award (February 8, 2025): Outstanding Achievement for Character Animation in a Live Action Production - Ludovic Chailloleau, Jonathan Paquin, Craig Penn, Florian Fernandez, Marco Barbati - nominated.

## Sequel

- Two months after release, a sequel was announced with **Grant Sputore** directing, planned for **March 26, 2027** as *Godzilla x Kong: Supernova*.

## Notes in the article

- The film is described as the fifth Godzilla film completely produced by an American studio, with the earlier US releases of *Godzilla, King of the Monsters!*, *King Kong vs. Godzilla* and *Godzilla 1985* adding footage with Western actors to Japanese films; *Invasion of Astro-Monster* was the first Toho-American co-production (with UPA), and TriStar's 1998 *Godzilla* the first entirely American-produced one.
- The three-year gap in the plot follows *Godzilla vs. Kong* (2021).

wikis.title: Getting the sequel made
wikis.summary: How Godzilla vs. Kong's hybrid-release success led Legendary to greenlight another Monsterverse film.
wikis.body:
- March 2019: producer Alex Garcia said Legendary hoped to make more Monsterverse films - "It's one brick at a time". February 2021: Wingard said the franchise was at a "crossroads" and audiences would have to "vote for more of these things".
- *Godzilla vs. Kong* opened March 24, 2021 simultaneously in theaters and on HBO Max during pandemic theater shutdowns, grossing **$470 million** worldwide against a **$330 million** break-even point, becoming HBO Max's most successful launch title until *Mortal Kombat* and the most pirated film of 2021.
- April 4, 2021: Legendary CEO Josh Grode said "we have a number of ideas for more movies"; #ContinueTheMonsterverse trended on Twitter with support from *Kong: Skull Island* director Jordan Vogt-Roberts.
- April 27, 2021: The Hollywood Reporter reported Legendary "quietly taking steps to stretch the series into one or more installments" and negotiating with Wingard; *Son of Kong* was among potential titles. August 2021: Monsterverse writer Max Borenstein teased "some new, interesting installments".
- March 20, 2022: the sequel announced for filming in Gold Coast, Queensland. May 2022: Wingard confirmed to direct, Dan Stevens cast (they had worked on *The Guest*), and Production Weekly reported the working title *Origins*. June 30, 2022: the producing team confirmed. July 1, 2022: Toho confirmed Godzilla's involvement.

wikis.title: Filming in Queensland and recreating Rio
wikis.summary: Where the film shot and how the climactic Rio de Janeiro battle was built.
wikis.body:
- Principal photography began in the Gold Coast, Queensland on **July 29, 2022**, with Ben Seresin returning as director of photography, and finished in Australia in **November 2022** - when crew gear suggested a then-title of *Godzilla and Kong*.
- The Third Floor did extensive previsualization, including checking on Google Earth the Rio de Janeiro locations the production wanted for the climax.
- A unit made up mostly of visual effects staff travelled to Rio de Janeiro to shoot plates for compositing and to gather data for a digital recreation of the city, including aerial photography and Lidar.
- Surfers Paradise on the Gold Coast was turned into the Rio beach where the climactic battle begins.

wikis.title: Visual effects and creature design
wikis.summary: Which studios did what, and how the Skar King and Shimo were built.
wikis.body:
- Visual effects supervised by **Alessandro Ongaro**. Mothra was in the plan from the first draft, but Legendary did not hold the rights when post-production began, so a placeholder named "**Phosphera**" was used until they were secured; Wingard denied that poor testing caused the change.
- **Scanline VFX**: the opening scene of Kong chased by "Wart-Dogs" - likened to wolves and African wild dogs with "the twitchy, unpredictable energy of a hyena" - the climactic Egypt and Rio fights, and Kong's mechanical glove.
- **DNEG**: many surface scenes with Godzilla and Kong, the Hollow World jungles, and the Iwi crystal pyramid.
- **Wētā FX**: the Hollow Earth, its giant apes - **130** in the Skar King's lair scenes - and Shimo. The Skar King was designed as a long, skinny orangutan for contrast: "Kong is Mike Tyson, but Skar King is a little shifty and more graceful" (supervisor Kevin Smith). His long arms required extensions and prosthetics on the motion-capture performers; his spine weapon had "108 or 110 vertebrae, plus the jaw handle and the thing at the end". Shimo aimed for "a fine balance between creating something beautiful but also menacing", moving cat-like rather than "super brutal like Godzilla"; her ice breath used up to **30 layers** of effects including frozen vapor and ice shards.
- Wingard told the crew not to worry about scale and relative speed so the monsters could move quickly, changing the gravity and speed of the water simulations; rendering was at **5K resolution** because of the wide anamorphic lenses.
- Influences: a shot of the ground bursting beneath Godzilla's footfall in the Rome sequence pays tribute to *Godzilla Minus One*; the Egyptian battle was inspired by the Roddy Piper / Keith David fight in *They Live* (1988).

wikis.title: Shrek 2 (2004 film)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia's article on Shrek 2, the 2004 DreamWorks animated sequel - its credits and plot, production and casting, Cannes premiere and record-breaking release, $933.8 million box office, reviews, awards and spin-offs.
wikis.body:
## Infobox

- **Shrek 2**, "2004 DreamWorks Animation film". Directed by **Andrew Adamson, Kelly Asbury and Conrad Vernon**; screenplay by **Andrew Adamson, Joe Stillman, J. David Stem and David N. Weiss**; story by Andrew Adamson; based on *Shrek!* by William Steig.
- Produced by Aron Warner, David Lipman and John H. Williams. Starring Mike Myers, Eddie Murphy, Cameron Diaz, Julie Andrews, Antonio Banderas, John Cleese, Rupert Everett and Jennifer Saunders.
- Edited by Michael Andrews and Sim Evan-Jones; music by **Harry Gregson-Williams**. Production companies **DreamWorks Animation** and **PDI/DreamWorks**; distributed by **DreamWorks Pictures**.
- Release dates **May 15, 2004** (Cannes) and **May 19, 2004** (United States). Running time **92 minutes**; country United States; language English.
- Budget **$150 million**; box office **$933.8 million**.

## Contradiction inside the article

- **Budget**: the infobox and the box office section both say **$150 million**; the Production section says "The film was produced with a $70 million budget."

## Lead

- A 2004 American animated fantasy comedy, loosely based on the 1990 children's picture book *Shrek!* by William Steig, a direct sequel to *Shrek* (2001) and the second instalment in the *Shrek* film series.
- Myers, Murphy and Diaz reprise Shrek, Donkey and Princess Fiona; new characters are voiced by Antonio Banderas, Julie Andrews, John Cleese, Rupert Everett and Jennifer Saunders.
- Premise: Shrek and Donkey meet Fiona's parents while the Fairy Godmother, who wants Fiona to marry her son Prince Charming, plots to destroy the marriage; Shrek and Donkey team with Puss in Boots to foil her.
- Development began in **2001**; after disagreements with producers, first-film screenwriters Ted Elliott and Terry Rossio were replaced with Adamson. The story was inspired by *Guess Who's Coming to Dinner* (1967). The lead actors' salaries rose to **$10 million** each, "among the highest contracts in their respective careers".
- "The film is dedicated to the memory of *Shrek* creator William Steig, who died on October 3, 2003, seven months before the film was released."
- Premiered at the **2004 Cannes Film Festival** on May 15, competing for the Palme d'Or, and released in theaters May 19 by DreamWorks Pictures. A note records that the distribution rights were bought back from Paramount by DreamWorks Animation in July 2014, transferred to 20th Century Fox, and reverted to Universal Pictures in 2018.
- It "grossed $933.8 million worldwide, and scored the second-largest three-day opening weekend in United States history and the largest opening for an animated film at the time of its release"; became the **highest-grossing film of 2004** and the fifth-highest-grossing film overall at the time; remains "DreamWorks Animation's highest-grossing film to date and the highest-grossing film released by DreamWorks Pictures"; and held the worldwide animated record until Pixar's *Toy Story 3* passed it in 2010.
- Two Academy Award nominations, Best Animated Feature and Best Original Song; the soundtrack charted in the Top 10 of the US Billboard 200.
- Sequels *Shrek the Third* (2007) and *Shrek Forever After* (2010) followed, with *Shrek 5* scheduled for **June 30, 2027**. Puss in Boots got the film *Puss in Boots* (2011), the streaming series *The Adventures of Puss in Boots* (2015-2018) and *Puss in Boots: The Last Wish* (2022).

## Plot (as summarised in the article)

- Newlyweds Shrek and Fiona are invited by her parents to a royal ball in Far Far Away. King Harold and Queen Lillian are repulsed to find they are ogres; Shrek and Harold argue at dinner; Fiona meets the Fairy Godmother, "a celebrity potions saleswoman". Shrek reads Fiona's childhood diary and its infatuation with Prince Charming.
- The Fairy Godmother had arranged with Harold for Charming to rescue and marry Fiona so she could rule Far Far Away through him, and orders Harold to be rid of Shrek; Harold hires Puss in Boots to assassinate him. Puss fails, confesses, and joins Shrek.
- At her potions factory the Fairy Godmother refuses to help, "insisting ogres do not deserve happy endings"; Shrek's party steals a potion labelled "Happily Ever After" and wrecks the factory. Shrek, Fiona and Donkey become human, human and a white stallion; the change must be sealed with a kiss by midnight.
- The Fairy Godmother sends Charming to impersonate human Shrek, and gives Harold a love potion for Fiona's tea. Shrek, Donkey and Puss overhear, are arrested, and are rescued from the dungeon by the fairy tale creatures, who storm the castle with Mongo, "a monstrous living gingerbread man created by the Muffin Man".
- Fiona knocks Charming out rather than falling in love; Harold reveals he swapped the teacups. The Fairy Godmother's spell is blocked by Harold, reflects off his breastplate and disintegrates her into bubbles. Harold reverts to the Frog Prince, having used the same potion years earlier to win Lillian.
- At midnight Fiona declines to stay human; all revert. In a mid-credits scene Dragon, who has married Donkey, arrives with dragon-donkey hybrid babies.

## Voice cast

- Mike Myers (Shrek), Eddie Murphy (Donkey), Cameron Diaz (Princess Fiona), Julie Andrews (Queen Lillian), Antonio Banderas (Puss in Boots), John Cleese (King Harold), Rupert Everett (Prince Charming), Jennifer Saunders (Fairy Godmother).
- **Larry King** as Doris the Ugly Stepsister, with **Jonathan Ross** in the British version. Aron Warner (Big Bad Wolf); Cody Cameron (Pinocchio, the Three Little Pigs); Christopher Knights and Simon J. Smith (Three Blind Mice); Conrad Vernon (Gingy, Muffin Man, Mongo, Cedric, Announcer); Chris Miller (Magic Mirror); Mark Moseley (Dresser); Kelly Cooney Cilella (Fast Food Clerk); Kelly Asbury (Page, Elf, Nobleman, Nobleman's son); Andrew Adamson (Captain of the Guard).
- Cameos: **Joan Rivers** as herself - "the first time that a real person had been represented on screen by the Shrek animation team" - re-dubbed by Kate Thornton for the UK release. **Simon Cowell** appears on *Far Far Away Idol* on the DVD special features and before the credits on the American VHS.

## Production

- In 2001, soon after the first film's success, Myers, Murphy and Diaz negotiated **$10 million** each up front, against **$350,000** each for the first film. Executive producer Jeffrey Katzenberg, who led the negotiations, said the payments were probably the highest of the actors' careers; each was expected to work **15 to 18 hours** in total.
- Ted Elliott and Terry Rossio wanted a traditional fairytale sequel, disagreed with the producers and left; Adamson replaced them, inspired by *Guess Who's Coming to Dinner* (1967) and helped by Joe Stillman, J. David Stem and David N. Weiss. Co-directors Asbury and Vernon spent most of production in Northern California while Adamson worked with the voice actors in Glendale, California.
- Production began in **2001**, before the first film was completed. More human characters were added and appearance and movement improved with new animation and rendering systems; Puss in Boots "necessitated development of a whole new set of film production tools" for his fur, belt and hat plume, including an upgraded fur shader. All character setup was completed in the first three years.
- An early version had Shrek abdicate and call a fairy tale election, with Pinocchio running an "honesty" campaign and Gingy a "smear" campaign; Adamson dropped it as "too overtly satiric and political" and "more intellectual than emotional".
- The film is darker in lighting than the original; designers drew on the 19th-century French illustrator Gustav Doré. Production designer Guillaume Aretos: "There are a lot of medieval paintings and illustrations [and] my own influences, which are classical paintings from the 15th and 16th centuries."
- Casting Banderas: he took the role because he had enjoyed the first film and says he was chosen for his Spanish accent; Katzenberg approached him while he was on Broadway in *Nine*. The filmmakers showed him "a lot of paintings of the character" and he realised how "little" Puss was; he says he developed a strategy that determined Puss's personality.

## Soundtrack

- Composed solely by **Harry Gregson-Williams**, his fifth film with DreamWorks Animation. The soundtrack reached **No. 8** on the US Billboard 200 and **No. 1** on the US Soundtracks chart, and features two versions of Bonnie Tyler's "Holding Out for a Hero".

## Release

- Selected in April 2004 to compete for the **Palme d'Or** at the 2004 Cannes Film Festival.
- Originally scheduled for **June 18, 2004**, moved to **May 21**, then forward two days to **May 19** due to "fan demand". The first five minutes were shown on Nickelodeon's *U-Pick Live* the day before release.
- Opened in **4,163** theaters - "the first film with over 4,000 theaters in overall count", passing *X2* for the widest release, a record it held until *Spider-Man 3* in 2007. Over 3,700 theaters was its opening-day count.
- Re-released in US theaters for one week from **April 12, 2024** for its twentieth anniversary.

## Home media

- VHS and DVD **November 5, 2004**, the same day as Pixar's *The Incredibles*; Game Boy Advance Video **November 17, 2005**.
- "One of the best-selling DVD releases of all time with over **37 million copies** being sold grossing **$458 million**" - but 5 million more copies were printed than sold, causing DreamWorks to miss forecast first-quarter earnings that year by **25%**.
- Rights history: Paramount acquired DreamWorks' 1997-2005 live-action films in February 2006 after Viacom's **$1.6 billion** purchase, and signed a six-year distribution deal for DreamWorks Animation films; that deal ended **December 31, 2012**; DreamWorks Animation reacquired its films in July 2014 and moved them to 20th Century Fox; NBCUniversal bought DreamWorks Animation for **$3.8 billion** on April 28, 2016.
- Other editions: the "DreamWorks Animation Ultimate Box Set" (August 16, 2010); a 3D Blu-ray sold exclusively with select Samsung televisions (December 1, 2010); *Shrek: The Whole Story* box set (December 7, 2010); a stand-alone Blu-ray/DVD combo (August 30, 2011); stand-alone 3D Blu-ray (November 1, 2011); Ultra HD Blu-ray from Universal Pictures Home Entertainment (November 22, 2022). The DVD carries two commentary tracks - Vernon and Asbury, and Warner with editor Michael Andrews.
- **Far Far Away Idol**: a DVD and VHS feature parodying *American Idol* with Simon Cowell, set right after the film. On the DVD the viewer picks the winner; choosing anyone but Shrek, Fiona, Donkey or Puss triggers an ending where Cowell declares himself the victor and performs "My Way". DreamWorks announced on **November 8, 2004** that with **750,000 votes** cast the winner was Doris.

## Box office

- Opened at No. 1 with **$108 million** Friday-to-Sunday and **$129 million** since its Wednesday launch, from a then-record 4,163 theaters, averaging **$25,952** per theater. The three-day figure was then the second-highest opening weekend, behind *Spider-Man*'s $114.8 million; its **$44.8 million** Saturday was the highest single-day gross at the time, beating *Spider-Man*'s $43.6 million.
- Second weekend: No. 1 again from 4,223 theaters with **$95.6 million** over the four-day Memorial Day weekend, narrowly beating *The Day After Tomorrow*'s $85.8 million. Ten weeks in the weekly Top 10 until July 29; 149 days in theaters, closing November 25, 2004. Released in the UK on July 2, 2004 and topped the box office there for two weekends until *Spider-Man 2*.
- Totals: **$439.8 million** domestic and **$494 million** foreign for **$933.8 million** worldwide - the highest-grossing film of 2004 and of its franchise, 14th on the all-time domestic list and 42nd worldwide. An estimated **71,050,900** tickets sold in the US.
- It took the animated worldwide record from *Finding Nemo* (2003), though *Nemo* still had a higher overseas-only gross. With DVD sales and merchandise estimated at almost **$800 million**, it is DreamWorks' most profitable film.
- Records held and lost: highest-grossing animated film worldwide until *Toy Story 3* (2010); highest-grossing animated film at the North American box office until *Finding Dory* (2016); highest-grossing non-Disney animated film there until *The Super Mario Bros. Movie* (2023); highest-grossing non-Disney animated film worldwide until *Despicable Me 2* (2013); highest-grossing non-Disney-or-Universal animated film worldwide until China's *Ne Zha 2* in 2025, "after 21 years" - and it "remains to this day the highest-grossing non Disney or Universal animated film made in United States".

## Critical response

- Rotten Tomatoes **89%** from 239 reviews, average 7.7/10; consensus: "It may not be as fresh as the original, but topical humor and colorful secondary characters make Shrek 2 a winner in its own right." Metacritic **75 out of 100** from 40 critics, "generally favorable". CinemaScore **A**.
- Roger Ebert 3/4: "bright, lively, and entertaining". Robert Denerstein (Denver Rocky Mountain News): "sharply funny". James Kendrick (QNetwork) called the plot "familiar, but funny". J. R. Jones (Chicago Reader): "unassailable family entertainment". Michael O'Sullivan (The Washington Post): "better and funnier than the original". Kevin Lally (Film Journal International) called it "inventive and often very funny" though not as good as the first. Sean Naughton (Complex): "one of the best-animated sequels ever".
- Dissent: Peter Rainer (New York magazine) said the film "manages to undo much of what made its predecessor such a computer-generated joy ride."

## Accolades

- **Academy Awards**: nominated Best Animated Feature (Andrew Adamson), losing to *The Incredibles*, and Best Original Song ("Accidentally in Love"). "Accidentally in Love" was also nominated for the Golden Globe for Best Original Song and a Grammy for Best Song Written for Visual Media.
- **Cannes Film Festival**: nominated for the Palme d'Or (Adamson, Asbury, Vernon).
- **People's Choice Awards (31st)**: won Favorite Animated Movie, Favorite Animated Movie Star (Eddie Murphy for Donkey), Favorite Movie Comedy, Favorite Movie Villain (Jennifer Saunders as Fairy Godmother) and Favorite Sequel; nominated Favorite Motion Picture.
- Other wins: BMI Film Music Award and Most Performed Song from a Film; Hollywood Film Awards Animation of the Year; Italian Online Movie Awards Best Animated Feature Film; MTV Movie Awards Mexico Favorite Voice (Eugenio Derbez as Donkey in Latin America); Phoenix Film Critics Society Best Original Song; Russian National Movie Awards Best Blockbuster Movie; Teen Choice Awards for Choice Movie: Animated/Computer Generated and Choice Movie - Comedy.
- Nominations also from the Annie Awards (five, including Antonio Banderas for voice acting), the Broadcast Film Critics Association, Dallas-Fort Worth Film Critics, Gold Derby, Golden Schmoes (including "Most Overrated Movie of the Year"), Golden Trailer, the Grammys, the International Film Music Critics Association, International Online Cinema Awards, the Irish Film & Television Academy (Cameron Diaz), the Italian National Syndicate of Film Journalists, Motion Picture Sound Editors, MTV Movie & TV Awards (Banderas), Nickelodeon Kids' Choice Awards, the Online Film & Television Association, the Online Film Critics Society, the Satellite Awards, the **3rd Visual Effects Society Awards** (Outstanding Performance by an Animated Character - Antonio Banderas and Raman Hui), the World Soundtrack Awards and the Young Artist Awards.
- In 2008 the American Film Institute nominated the film for its Top 10 Animation Films list.

## Other media and follow-ups

- Video games: *Shrek 2* (2004), *Shrek 2 Activity Center: Twisted Fairy Tale Fun* (2004), *Shrek 2: Beg for Mercy* (2004), *Shrek SuperSlam* (2005), *Shrek Smash n' Crash Racing* (2006).
- Book: *Shrek 2: The Movie Storybook*, published by Scholastic in 2004, written by Tom Mason and Dan Danko, illustrated by Michael Koelsch.
- *Shrek the Third* (May 18, 2007) and *Shrek Forever After* (May 21, 2010) followed; *Shrek 5* is in development for **June 30, 2027**.
- Spin-offs: *Puss in Boots* (October 28, 2011); on November 6, 2018 Variety reported Chris Meledandri had been tasked to reboot both *Shrek* and *Puss in Boots* with the original cast potentially returning; *Puss in Boots: The Last Wish* (December 21, 2022) "is a sequel rather than a reboot".

wikis.title: Writing and animating the sequel
wikis.summary: The change of screenwriters, the abandoned election plot, and the new tools built for Puss in Boots.
wikis.body:
- Ted Elliott and Terry Rossio, the first film's screenwriters and co-producers, insisted the sequel be a traditional fairytale; after disagreements with the producers they left and were replaced by **Andrew Adamson**, whose writing was inspired by *Guess Who's Coming to Dinner* (1967) and completed with Joe Stillman, J. David Stem and David N. Weiss.
- Co-directors Kelly Asbury and Conrad Vernon spent most of production in Northern California while Adamson worked with the voice actors in Glendale, California.
- Production began in **2001**, before the first *Shrek* was finished. More human characters were added, and appearance and movement were improved with several new animation and rendering systems; all character setup was done in the first three years.
- Puss in Boots "necessitated development of a whole new set of film production tools to handle the appearance of his fur, belt, and hat plume", with his fur requiring an upgrade to the fur shader.
- An early version had Shrek abdicate the throne and call a fairy tale election, with an "honesty" campaign for Pinocchio and a "smear" campaign for Gingy; Adamson dropped it as "too overtly satiric and political" and "more intellectual than emotional".
- The film is darker in lighting than the original, with designers drawing on Gustave Doré; production designer Guillaume Aretos cited "medieval paintings and illustrations" and "classical paintings from the 15th and 16th centuries".

wikis.title: The $10 million voice deals and Banderas's casting
wikis.summary: What the returning stars were paid and how Antonio Banderas came to play Puss in Boots.
wikis.body:
- In 2001, soon after the first film's success, Mike Myers, Eddie Murphy and Cameron Diaz each negotiated **$10 million** up front for the sequel, against **$350,000** each for the first film.
- Executive producer Jeffrey Katzenberg, who led the negotiations, said the payments were probably the highest in the actors' entire careers. Each actor was expected to work **between 15 and 18 hours** in total.
- Antonio Banderas signed on as Puss in Boots. He said his initial motivation was that he had enjoyed the first film, and that he was chosen for his Spanish accent.
- Katzenberg approached him while he was on Broadway in the musical *Nine*. The filmmakers showed him "a lot of paintings of the character" and he realised how "little" Puss was; he says he developed a strategy for playing Puss after accepting that determined the character's personality.
- Other casting notes: Larry King voiced Doris the Ugly Stepsister, replaced by Jonathan Ross in the British version; Joan Rivers's cameo as herself was "the first time that a real person had been represented on screen by the Shrek animation team", re-dubbed by Kate Thornton in the UK.

wikis.title: Release and the theater-count record
wikis.summary: The shifting release date, the Cannes competition slot, and the widest release then on record.
wikis.body:
- Selected in April 2004 to compete for the **Palme d'Or** at the 2004 Cannes Film Festival, where it premiered on **May 15, 2004**.
- Originally scheduled for **June 18, 2004**, then moved to **May 21**, then forward two days to **May 19** "due to 'fan demand'". The first five minutes aired on Nickelodeon's *U-Pick Live* the day before release.
- It opened in **4,163** theaters, "the first film with over 4,000 theaters in overall count", surpassing *X2* for the widest release of any film; it held that record until *Spider-Man 3* in 2007. Its opening-day count was over 3,700 theaters.
- The film was re-released in US theaters for one week from **April 12, 2024** for its twentieth anniversary.

wikis.title: Home media and Far Far Away Idol
wikis.summary: The record DVD run, the over-printing that hit DreamWorks' earnings, and the American Idol parody short.
wikis.body:
- VHS and DVD on **November 5, 2004**, the same day as Pixar's *The Incredibles*; Game Boy Advance Video on November 17, 2005.
- "One of the best-selling DVD releases of all time with over **37 million copies** being sold grossing **$458 million**" - but 5 million more copies were printed than sold, causing DreamWorks to miss its forecast first-quarter earnings that year by **25%**.
- Later editions: the DreamWorks Animation Ultimate Box Set (August 16, 2010); a 3D Blu-ray sold only with select Samsung TVs (December 1, 2010); the *Shrek: The Whole Story* box set (December 7, 2010); a stand-alone Blu-ray/DVD combo (August 30, 2011); a stand-alone 3D Blu-ray (November 1, 2011); Ultra HD Blu-ray from Universal (November 22, 2022). The DVD has commentaries by Vernon and Asbury, and by Warner and editor Michael Andrews.
- **Far Far Away Idol**: a DVD and VHS feature parodying *American Idol*, set immediately after the film, with Shrek, Fiona and Simon Cowell judging. On the DVD the viewer picks the winner; picking anyone but Shrek, Fiona, Donkey or Puss triggers an alternate ending in which Cowell declares himself the winner and performs "My Way". The VHS pointed viewers to a voting website; DreamWorks announced on November 8, 2004 that, from **750,000 votes**, the winner was Doris.
- Rights: Paramount bought DreamWorks' 1997-2005 live-action catalogue in February 2006 after Viacom's $1.6 billion acquisition and took six years of DreamWorks Animation distribution, which ended December 31, 2012; DreamWorks Animation reacquired the films in July 2014 and moved to 20th Century Fox; NBCUniversal bought the studio for $3.8 billion on April 28, 2016, and the rights reverted to Universal in 2018.

wikis.title: Box office and the animated records
wikis.summary: The opening weekend figures, the worldwide total, and which records the film took and lost.
wikis.body:
- Opening: **$108 million** Friday-to-Sunday, **$129 million** from its Wednesday launch, from a then-record **4,163** theaters, averaging **$25,952** per theater. Second-highest opening weekend at the time behind *Spider-Man* ($114.8 million); its **$44.8 million** Saturday was then the highest single-day gross, beating *Spider-Man*'s $43.6 million.
- Second weekend: **$95.6 million** over the four-day Memorial Day frame from 4,223 theaters, still No. 1, ahead of *The Day After Tomorrow*'s $85.8 million. Ten weeks in the weekly Top 10 to July 29; 149 days in theaters, closing November 25, 2004. UK release July 2, 2004, topping that box office for two weekends until *Spider-Man 2*.
- Totals: **$439.8 million** domestic, **$494 million** foreign, **$933.8 million** worldwide; the highest-grossing film of 2004 and of the franchise; 14th all-time domestic and 42nd worldwide; an estimated **71,050,900** US tickets sold.
- With DVD sales and merchandise estimated at almost **$800 million**, it is called DreamWorks' most profitable film. The box office section gives its budget as $150 million, while the production section says $70 million.
- Records: took the worldwide animated record from *Finding Nemo* (2003), though *Nemo* kept a higher overseas-only gross; lost it to *Toy Story 3* (2010). Held the North American animated record until *Finding Dory* (2016), the non-Disney animated record there until *The Super Mario Bros. Movie* (2023) and worldwide until *Despicable Me 2* (2013), and the non-Disney-or-Universal worldwide record until *Ne Zha 2* in 2025.

wikis.title: Reviews and awards
wikis.summary: Aggregate scores, what critics wrote, and the film's Oscar nominations and People's Choice sweep.
wikis.body:
- Rotten Tomatoes **89%** from 239 reviews (7.7/10), consensus: "It may not be as fresh as the original, but topical humor and colorful secondary characters make Shrek 2 a winner in its own right." Metacritic **75/100** from 40 critics. CinemaScore **A**.
- Roger Ebert 3/4 called it "bright, lively, and entertaining"; Michael O'Sullivan (The Washington Post) called it "better and funnier than the original"; J. R. Jones (Chicago Reader) "unassailable family entertainment"; Kevin Lally (Film Journal International) "inventive and often very funny"; Sean Naughton (Complex) "one of the best-animated sequels ever". Peter Rainer (New York) dissented, saying it "manages to undo much of what made its predecessor such a computer-generated joy ride."
- Academy Awards: nominated for **Best Animated Feature** (losing to *The Incredibles*, alongside fellow nominee *Shark Tale*) and **Best Original Song** for "Accidentally in Love", which was also up for a Golden Globe and a Grammy.
- Nominated for the **Palme d'Or** at Cannes. Won five **People's Choice Awards**: Favorite Animated Movie, Favorite Animated Movie Star (Eddie Murphy), Favorite Movie Comedy, Favorite Movie Villain (Jennifer Saunders) and Favorite Sequel.
- Other wins: two BMI Film & TV Awards, Hollywood Film Awards Animation of the Year, Italian Online Movie Awards Best Animated Feature, MTV Movie Awards Mexico (Eugenio Derbez), Phoenix Film Critics Society Best Original Song, Russian National Movie Awards Best Blockbuster, and two Teen Choice Awards.
- Nominations included five Annie Awards, the Visual Effects Society (Antonio Banderas and Raman Hui), Motion Picture Sound Editors, the Satellite Awards and the Online Film Critics Society. In 2008 the American Film Institute nominated the film for its Top 10 Animation Films list.

wikis.title: Sequels, spin-offs and tie-ins
wikis.summary: The rest of the Shrek series, the Puss in Boots spin-offs, and the games and book tied to this film.
wikis.body:
- *Shrek the Third* released **May 18, 2007**; *Shrek Forever After* released **May 21, 2010**; *Shrek 5* is in development for **June 30, 2027**.
- Puss in Boots, introduced in this film, got the spin-off film *Puss in Boots* (**October 28, 2011**) and *Puss in Boots: The Last Wish* (**December 21, 2022**), described as "a sequel rather than a reboot", plus the streaming series *The Adventures of Puss in Boots* (2015-2018).
- On November 6, 2018 Variety reported that Chris Meledandri had been tasked to reboot both *Shrek* and *Puss in Boots*, with the original cast potentially returning.
- Video games: *Shrek 2* (2004), *Shrek 2 Activity Center: Twisted Fairy Tale Fun* (2004), *Shrek 2: Beg for Mercy* (2004), *Shrek SuperSlam* (2005), *Shrek Smash n' Crash Racing* (2006).
- Book: *Shrek 2: The Movie Storybook*, published by Scholastic in 2004, written by Tom Mason and Dan Danko and illustrated by Michael Koelsch.

wikis.title: Man of Tomorrow (2027 film)
wikis.summary: The English Wikipedia article on Man of Tomorrow, James Gunn's upcoming DC Universe follow-up to Superman in which Superman and Lex Luthor team up against Brainiac, covering its cast, development, 2026 shoot and July 9, 2027 release date.
wikis.body:
## The film

- "*Man of Tomorrow* is an upcoming American superhero film featuring the DC Comics characters Superman and Lex Luthor. Written and directed by James Gunn, it will be the fourth film in the DC Universe (DCU) and a follow-up to *Superman* (2025)." Produced by Gunn and Peter Safran of DC Studios for DC Studios, Troll Court Entertainment and The Safran Company, distributed by Warner Bros. Pictures.
- "Superman and Lex Luthor reluctantly team up to face a bigger threat, the superintelligent alien android Brainiac."
- David Corenswet and Nicholas Hoult reprise Superman and Luthor, with Rachel Brosnahan, Edi Gathegi, Nathan Fillion, Isabela Merced, Skyler Gisondo, Frank Grillo, María Gabriela de Faría, Sara Sampaio and Milly Alcock, and Lars Eidinger, Aaron Pierre and Xolo Maridueña joining. Cinematography Sam McCurdy; editor Fred Raskin; score by David Fleming; visual effects supervisor Stéphane Ceretti.
- Scheduled for release in the United States on July 9, 2027, as part of "the DCU's Chapter One: Gods and Monsters". No runtime, budget or gross is given.
- Gunn said the film is set in "real time" after *Superman*, "roughly occurring in mid-2027", and that *Peacemaker* season 2 is "a 'prequel' to *Man of Tomorrow* that directly sets-up the film's events", introducing Checkmate and the prison Salvation, "Salvation being a major aspect of *Man of Tomorrow*".

## How it came together

Gunn said in June 2025 he was writing a follow-up that "would not be a direct sequel" and would not be called *Superman 2*. In August 2025 David Zaslav announced Gunn would direct; Gunn had finished a detailed treatment. On social media in September 2025, Gunn, Corenswet and Hoult announced the title and the July 9, 2027 date with artwork by Jim Lee, Jorge Jiménez and Mitch Gerads. Lars Eidinger was cast as Brainiac in late December 2025 after a "worldwide search". Ohio awarded the production nearly $2 million in tax credits in February 2026 for filming in Cincinnati. Luthor's Warsuit - the first live-action use - was built by Judianna Makovsky and Legacy Effects. Adria Arjona was cast in April 2026 after screen tests with Eva De Dominici, Sydney Chandler and Grace Van Patten, reported by *Variety* and *Deadline* as Maxima, though *The Hollywood Reporter* and TheWrap said her role was unclear.

## Filming

Principal photography ran from April 20, 2026 under the working title *Exodus*, wrapping on August 26 "having lasted approximately 93 days over the course of four months". Locations included Trilith Studios, the Federal Correctional Institution in Atlanta, Terminal Station in Macon, Georgia standing in for the *Daily Planet* newsroom, Cincinnati and the United Kingdom. Paramount Skydance CEO David Ellison visited the set during filming "in anticipation of the proposed acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery by Paramount Skydance".

## Contradiction within the page

The lead places the shoot "primarily at Trilith Studios in Atlanta, Georgia", while the Filming section says "primarily at Trilith Studios in Fayetteville, Georgia".

The second part of the capture is the IMDb external link, the DC Studios and Superman franchise navigation boxes and the category list; no published or last-updated date is stated.

wikis.title: Man of Tomorrow (upcoming DC Studios film): cast, production and release
wikis.summary: Part 1 of the English Wikipedia article on Man of Tomorrow, the upcoming James Gunn Superman film, covering its credits, premise, full cast, development from June 2025, casting, the 2026 shoot and its scheduled July 9, 2027 release.
wikis.body:
## The film

- "*Man of Tomorrow* is an upcoming American superhero film featuring the DC Comics characters Superman and Lex Luthor. Written and directed by James Gunn, it will be the fourth film in the DC Universe (DCU) and a follow-up to *Superman* (2025)."
- Produced by Peter Safran and James Gunn of DC Studios. Cinematography Sam McCurdy; edited by Fred Raskin; music by David Fleming. Production companies DC Studios, Troll Court Entertainment and The Safran Company; distributed by Warner Bros. Pictures.
- Release date July 9, 2027. Country United States; language English. The infobox gives no runtime, budget or gross.
- Starring David Corenswet, Nicholas Hoult, Rachel Brosnahan, Edi Gathegi, Nathan Fillion, Isabela Merced, Skyler Gisondo, Frank Grillo, Sara Sampaio, María Gabriela de Faría, Lars Eidinger, Aaron Pierre, Milly Alcock and Xolo Maridueña.
- Premise: "Superman and Lex Luthor reluctantly team up to face a bigger threat, the superintelligent alien android Brainiac."
- "Gunn revealed in June 2025 that he was working on a follow-up to the first DCU film, *Superman*, ahead of its release the following month. The title and first details were revealed in September, and Eidinger was cast as Brainiac in December."
- "It will be part of the DCU's Chapter One: Gods and Monsters." The film "is expected to be released in IMAX", a statement the page tags as needing an update.
- Gunn said the film is set in "real time" after *Superman*, "roughly occurring in mid-2027".

## Contradiction within the page

The lead says filming took place "primarily at Trilith Studios in Atlanta, Georgia", while the Filming section says principal photography took place "primarily at Trilith Studios in Fayetteville, Georgia, under the working title *Exodus*."

## Dates given

- Principal photography began April 20, 2026; Gunn announced on August 26 that filming had wrapped, "having lasted approximately 93 days over the course of four months".
- Five days of filming in Cincinnati, Ohio were scheduled between June 15 and August 21. Grillo was set to shoot for ten weeks between the UK and Georgia; Eidinger filmed from May until the end of August.

wikis.title: Cast of Man of Tomorrow
wikis.summary: The announced cast and characters, including the returning DCU actors and the roles still undisclosed.
wikis.body:
- **David Corenswet as Kal-El / Clark Kent / Superman**: "A survivor from the destroyed planet Krypton who lives on Earth as a powerful superhero", working as a journalist for the *Daily Planet* in Metropolis.
- **Nicholas Hoult as Lex Luthor**: "The former CEO of LuthorCorp and Superman's arch-nemesis who is incarcerated in Van Kull Prison." After exploring "a lot about the evil part of Lex" in *Superman* (2025), Gunn was interested in "getting into the heart of Lex, and... getting to know Lex as more of a human being". "The film features Luthor's high-tech powered exoskeleton Warsuit, which he uses to match Superman's strength, for the first time in a live-action film."
- **Rachel Brosnahan as Lois Lane**, a *Daily Planet* reporter and Clark's girlfriend and colleague.
- **Edi Gathegi as Michael Holt / Mister Terrific**, a member of the Justice Gang sponsored by Maxwell Lord.
- **Nathan Fillion as Guy Gardner / Green Lantern**. Fillion said the character's hairstyle was updated for this film "after he wore the same bowl cut wig for both *Superman* and the television series *Lanterns* (2026–present)".
- **Isabela Merced as Kendra Saunders / Hawkgirl**, "reincarnated from an alien, retaining her memories and past trauma with a grumpy demeanor".
- **Skyler Gisondo as Jimmy Olsen**; **Frank Grillo as Rick Flag Sr.**, "the director of A.R.G.U.S."; **Sara Sampaio as Eve Teschmacher**, "Luthor's former assistant and girlfriend who is secretly involved with Jimmy"; **María Gabriela de Faría as Angela Spica / The Engineer**, "an ally of Luthor whose abilities come from nanotechnology in her body".
- **Lars Eidinger as Brainiac**, "a superintelligent alien android from the planet Colu". Eidinger characterized Brainiac as "the incarnation of Satan" and the Shakespearean fool, contrasting him with Superman as the Übermensch. Gunn contrasted Brainiac with Superman as "what happens when intelligence loses all connection to humanity", and said he drew on the original Otto Binder version from the 1950s, the "surprisingly scary" Marv Wolfman version, animated adaptations and the "truly creepy and wonderful" AI version from the Absolute Universe.
- **Aaron Pierre as John Stewart / Green Lantern**.
- **Milly Alcock as Kara Zor-El / Supergirl**, "raised on a chunk of the destroyed planet Krypton and watched everyone around her die, making her a more jaded person than her cousin". DC Studios executive Lars P. Winther said Supergirl "is now spending more time with her cousin on Earth following her 'wild ways' in her intergalactic-set film, *Supergirl* (2026)."
- **Xolo Maridueña as Jaime Reyes / Blue Beetle**, reprising his role from the DC Extended Universe film *Blue Beetle* (2023).
- Undisclosed roles: Adria Arjona, "reported to be Maxima, the warrior-queen of the planet Almerac who believes Superman is her suitable mate"; Andre Royo; Matthew Lillard; Sinqua Walls. Neva Howell reprises Martha Kent and Stephen Blackehart reprises LuthorCorp employee Sydney Happersen.

wikis.title: Development of Man of Tomorrow
wikis.summary: How the follow-up was announced between June 2025 and September 2025, and how Peacemaker season 2 sets it up.
wikis.body:
- In June 2025, ahead of *Superman*'s release, Gunn said he was working on the script for a follow-up "that would not be a direct sequel, but would feature Clark Kent / Superman in a major role". He said it would not be called *Superman 2*, and would not be a *World's Finest* or *Batman vs. Superman* film.
- Corenswet and Brosnahan "had options for a potential sequel in their contracts, but following the first film's release in July a direct sequel was not expected to be announced in the near future."
- In August 2025, Warner Bros. Discovery CEO David Zaslav announced Gunn would direct, describing it as the "next movie in the 'Super-Family'"; Gunn called it the "next story in what I'll call the 'Superman Saga'". He had finished a detailed treatment - "60-page treatments with dialogue and everything", as with his previous films - and had begun a full script, saying filming would begin "sooner rather than later".
- In September 2025, Gunn, Corenswet and Hoult each posted artwork announcing the title *Man of Tomorrow* and a July 9, 2027 release. The pieces, showing Superman and Luthor with Luthor in his armoured suit, were drawn by DC Comics artists Jim Lee, Jorge Jiménez and Mitch Gerads.
- Gunn said filming was scheduled to start around April 2026 and that they moved quickly because they "knew immediately where we were going". He said *Man of Tomorrow* was "as much a Lex movie as it is a Superman movie".
- In late September 2025 Gunn released a picture of the completed second script draft, its cover featuring an anatomical illustration of a brain, prompting Brainiac speculation; "Gunn previously considered using Brainiac in *Superman*."
- Gunn said the second season of *Peacemaker* (2025) was "a 'prequel' to *Man of Tomorrow* that directly sets-up the film's events"; Hoult cameos as Luthor in the episode "Ignorance Is Chris", in which Rick Flag Sr. offers Luthor "an opportunity for redemption". The season 2 finale "Full Nelson" introduces Checkmate and the inter-dimensional prison Salvation - "two important aspects of Gunn's overarching DCU story that he had planned out before being hired as co-head of DC Studios", with Salvation "being a major aspect of *Man of Tomorrow*".

wikis.title: Pre-production and casting
wikis.summary: Eidinger's casting as Brainiac, the Ohio tax credit, the Warsuit build and the long Maxima casting search.
wikis.body:
- November 2025: Grillo confirmed he was preparing to return as Flag "for a major role"; Brainiac was confirmed as the main antagonist; Gunn was storyboarding.
- "Lars Eidinger was cast as Brainiac in late December, after a 'worldwide search' from which Eidinger emerged as the frontrunner." Gunn approached him over Zoom about a self-tape, which they became "obsessed" with, before an in-person audition in Atlanta. "Eidinger underwent a 3D modeling scan of his body and spent two hours getting the character's makeup applied and mask designed. He also watched *Superman* to prepare for the audition."
- January 2026: Gunn said casting was underway for smaller roles and a prominent female character, but debunked Wonder Woman speculation, adding Eidinger's casting was the most important new addition and that other supporting roles were characters from earlier DCU projects.
- February 2026: "the Ohio Department of Development revealed that *Man of Tomorrow* would be partially filmed in Cincinnati, Ohio. The production was awarded nearly $2 million through the state's tax credit program, after *Superman* was also filmed there."
- "A practical, mobile version of Luthor's high-tech Warsuit was designed by Judianna Makovsky and Legacy Effects to be worn by Hoult during filming." Commentators noted its comics-accurate design, "which features more green than purple and is slightly bulkier."
- Returning *Superman* actors revealed before production: Merced, Brosnahan, Gisondo, Sampaio, de Faría, Gathegi and Fillion. In March, Aaron Pierre was revealed to be reprising John Stewart from *Lanterns*.
- Early April 2026: Adria Arjona, Eva De Dominici, Sydney Chandler and Grace Van Patten screen-tested in Atlanta for Maxima as finalists. Arjona had previously starred in *The Belko Experiment* (2016), which Gunn produced. *Deadline Hollywood* initially reported Arjona, Marisa Abela and Ella Purnell were testing, which Gunn refuted. Journalist Jeff Sneider reaffirmed the four finalists and reported Maxima would have a small role before a larger one in an eventual third Superman film, questioning whether some were testing for another role such as Wonder Woman.
- Arjona was cast later that month. *Variety*'s Angelique Jackson and *Deadline* reported she was cast as Maxima, while Borys Kit and Aaron Couch of *The Hollywood Reporter* and Umberto Gonzalez at TheWrap "reported that it was unclear whether she would portray Maxima." Gonzalez noted speculation the film adapts the 1992 storyline "Panic in the Sky"; "Gunn previously said he was not specifically inspired by that storyline."
- Later in April, Gunn announced Andre Royo - who starred in his film *Super* (2010) - was cast in an undisclosed role, prompting speculation he would play Martian Manhunter, "who was briefly referenced in *Superman*". Gunn also revealed Stephen Blackehart was reprising Sydney Happersen.

wikis.title: Filming, post-production, music and release
wikis.summary: The April to August 2026 shoot and its locations, the returning crew, and the scheduled release.
wikis.body:
## Filming

- "Principal photography began on April 20, 2026, taking place primarily at Trilith Studios in Fayetteville, Georgia, under the working title *Exodus*." Sam McCurdy is the cinematographer, "after previously working with Gunn on *Peacemaker*".
- "During the first week of filming, some scenes were shot in parts of the Federal Correctional Institution, Atlanta, which caused minimal disruption to the prison's operations."
- Early May 2026: Matthew Lillard and Sinqua Walls joined in undisclosed roles. Lillard had starred as Shaggy Rogers in *Scooby-Doo* (2002) and *Scooby-Doo 2: Monsters Unleashed* (2004), which Gunn wrote. Later that month Milly Alcock was revealed as Supergirl; in June Neva Howell announced her return as Martha Kent.
- Five days of filming were scheduled in Cincinnati, Ohio between June 15 and August 21, with filming also set for Terminal Station in Macon, Georgia "to stand-in for the *Daily Planet* newsroom", as well as Atlanta and the United Kingdom.
- "Filming was halfway completed by the end of June 2026", when DC Studios executive Lars P. Winther said Paramount Skydance CEO David Ellison had visited the set "in anticipation of the proposed acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery by Paramount Skydance", and was "interested in and supportive of the studio's DC plans."
- Mid-July 2026: Xolo Maridueña revealed as Blue Beetle, reintroducing the character into the DCU; "Gunn previously called Maridueña's Blue Beetle 'the first DCU character'."
- Gunn said his friend Rick Devens was slated for a background cameo but could not appear because of scheduling conflicts with the twenty-eighth season of *Big Brother*.
- "Gunn announced on August 26 that filming had wrapped, having lasted approximately 93 days over the course of four months."

## Post-production and music

- "Visual effects supervisor Stéphane Ceretti returns from *Superman* and some of Gunn's prior films, while Fred Raskin serves as the editor."
- In December 2025 Gunn said he had selected various licensed songs for the film. In April 2026 he confirmed David Fleming would return from *Superman* to compose the score.

## Release

- "*Man of Tomorrow* is scheduled to be released theatrically by Warner Bros. Pictures in the United States on July 9, 2027." It "is expected to be released in IMAX" (flagged as needing an update), and "will be part of the DCU's Chapter One: Gods and Monsters."

wikis.title: Man of Tomorrow article: external links, DC navigation boxes and categories

Gorilla Grodd*; DC Elseworlds titles including *The Penguin* (2024) and *The Batman: Part II* (2028); and other titles including *Super/Man: The Christopher Reeve Story* (2024).

wikis.title: Nobel Prize announcement dates 2026
wikis.summary: NobelPrize.org page giving the date, time and awarding institution for each 2026 Nobel Prize announcement and outlining the nomination timetable.
wikis.body:
## 2026 announcements

- "This year's Nobel Prize announcements will take place on 5–12 October."
- "All of the prize announcements will be broadcast live on the official digital channels of the Nobel Prize. In-depth information about the prizes will be published here at nobelprize.org."
- Each announcement has a YouTube live stream; the page links a "Playlist of all YouTube live streams".

| Day | Prize | Time | Institution |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Monday 5 October | Physiology or Medicine | 11:30 CEST at the earliest | Nobel Assembly at Karolinska Institutet |
| Tuesday 6 October | Physics | 11:45 CEST at the earliest | Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences |
| Wednesday 7 October | Chemistry | 11:45 CEST at the earliest | Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences |
| Thursday 8 October | Literature | 13:00 CEST at the earliest | Swedish Academy |
| Friday 9 October | Peace | 11:00 CEST | Norwegian Nobel Committee, at the Norwegian Nobel Institute |
| Monday 12 October | Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel | 11:45 CEST at the earliest | Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences |

- Only the peace prize time is given without the hedge "at the earliest".

## How laureates are selected

- "After a long selection process, the Nobel Prize-awarding institutions finally make their choice. In October, the world will learn about the discoveries and achievements honoured by this year's prizes."

## The nomination process

- September — Nomination starts: "From September, thousands of people from all over the world are invited to nominate for the following year's prizes. For the peace prize, an invitation letter is not required."
- 31 January — Deadline for nominations: "The deadline for submissions is midnight on 31 January."
- February–September — Evaluation process: "Submitted nominations are considered by a Nobel committee of 5 to 10 members. Committees review the candidates, consult with experts and narrow down their list with the help of evaluation reports."
- October — Final vote: "After months of evaluation and discussion of candidates, the prize-awarding institutions take a final vote to select their newest laureates."
- First Monday in October — Announcements: "The prizes are announced over a span of eight days."
- 10 December — Nobel Day: "The laureates receive their medals, prize money and diplomas in Stockholm and Oslo."

## Also on the page

- "Nobel Calling Stockholm is eight days filled with activities across the city in connection with the announcements of the Nobel Prizes."
- Links: "Information for the media", "Who can nominate?", "Laureates' first reactions" ("Read and watch recollections of the 'magic call.'"), "Why is there a Nobel Prize?".

The page states no publication or last-updated date.

## Rules

- "Narendra Modi" resolves Yes if he "becomes Prime Minister of India as a result of government formation following the next Indian general election and meets all constitutional requirements before Apr 30, 2030." Outcome verified from Lok Sabha.
- The market resolves to "the first person who, as a result of government formation following the election, is formally appointed, sworn in, or invested as Prime Minister according to the country's constitutional procedures, commands the confidence of the parliament/legislature, and exercises the full powers of the office (not serving in a caretaker/acting capacity from the previous government)."
- "If no government forms by Apr 30, 2030, the Contract resolves to 'No one' if that is an option and No for all other strikes. If new elections are called before government formation, the Contract resolves to 'No one' immediately and No for all other strikes."

## Timeline and payout

- Market open: Jul 20, 2026 · 5:00pm EDT. Closes after the outcome occurs; projected payout 30 minutes after closing.

wikis.title: Hellscape Defense Strategy Deters Taiwan Invasion (John Batchelor Show, 16 September 2026)
wikis.summary: John Batchelor Show segment in which Rebecca Grant and Gordon Chang describe Hellscape, Admiral Samuel Paparo's offensive drone-and-loitering-munition concept for countering a Chinese invasion of Taiwan.
wikis.body:
## The episode

- The John Batchelor Show, episode "4. Hellscape Defense Strategy Deters Taiwan Invasion - REBECCA GRANT & GORDON CHANG 091626". Length 9 min. Rating Clean. Show frequency "Updated Daily".
- Published September 16, 2026 at 10:43 PM UTC. The page also carries a "September 16" date label.
- Host: John Batchelor. Guests in the segment: Rebecca Grant of the Lexington Institute and Gordon Chang. Episode caption number "CAPTION 1954"; the description ends "(4)", marking it as the fourth segment.

## Apple's episode description

- "Rebecca Grant reports the United States Indo-Pacific Command developed an offensive tactical framework named Hellscape to counter potential Chinese invasions of Taiwan."
- "Designed by Admiral Samuel Paparo, Hellscape deploys swarms of cheap drones, loitering munitions like Damocles, and unmanned vehicles to confuse attacking Chinese forces."
- "This strategy draws upon lessons from Ukrainian drone warfare to disrupt enemy spectrum operations and clear pathways for heavy precision weapons."
- "Regional allies including Japan, Australia, and the Philippines are integrating into this defense architecture."
- "To ensure deterrence succeeds, Taiwan must receive delayed military shipments of advanced electronic warfare systems for its fighter jets without delay."

## What the transcript says

- The segment discusses an article whose headline Batchelor reads as: "China would face a hellscape in a war over Taiwan. New tech may give America an edge."
- Grant: Hellscape is "a new strategic concept", contrasted with "Taiwan's porcupine defense, where with artillery and reserve forces, they'd make it really tough if Chinese forces got ashore". "Hellscape is an offensive concept. It's the brainchild of Admiral Samuel Papi Paparo, who is the commander out in the Pacific."
- Its method: "putting so many drones, loitering munitions, unmanned vehicles, missiles, et cetera, into the air that it confuses a Chinese offensive operation and also forces China to defend itself against these low-cost munitions. And then the U.S. or Taiwan comes in with a more sophisticated heavy punch." It has "some roots in Ukraine, but really targeted towards China's massed forces in the Pacific".
- Chang asks whether drone warfare works across "a wide body of water". Grant: yes, "because so much of Hellscape is really about using the air dimension", and where Ukraine fights a war of attrition "in a pulsed fashion", "The Hellscape in the Pacific would be a massive counter to a Chinese invasion or onslaught."
- On Damocles: "There's a new munition called Damocles. It's a little vertical takeoff, small. It's not even really a drone. It's what they call a launched effect. But it's got an explosively formed penetrating warhead. It's got electromagnetic, kinetic and kinetic possibilities." Used against "a landing craft or an aircraft or a tank", with "an incredible ability to loiter and then hit a target when it moves"; "multiply that out by hundreds and thousands".
- Cost: "a lot of this is based on lower-cost munitions. things that Taiwan can easily do and that can be tailored for the defense of Taiwan or for another Pacific region ally, Philippines, Australia"; "a hellscape is affordable as well as effective".
- Allies: Japan, the Philippines and Australia are "really, really key allies" and Grant says "there's no question that those allies will participate in close discussions with Admiral Papparoa, with our Pacific Air Forces, with our Army units in the Pacific". Japan is "going through a big process of how they want to be able to carry out offensive, defensive operations"; she says "Prime Minister Takeuchi is doing a lot to lead in that direction", and cites Japan's air force, situational awareness, routine Chinese incursions and sea-based missile defence with "our Aegis system on their destroyers".
- China's counter: "China is putting a lot into developing their space-based kill web, getting enough reconnaissance satellites up over the Pacific"; the US has space control and "recently acknowledged by the airport secretary recently. that the Space Force does has those weapons on orbit" (transcript wording). China "is going to try to get inside the spectrum wage spectrum and electronic warfare as well", and "its mass is a big counter for them". Grant: "China has no recent combat experience. I want to keep it that way."
- Taiwan: Grant would "like to see more training exercises with Taiwan" and "the U.S. Marines there on a regular basis". Taiwan "have bought top of the line systems. Often they struggle to get deliveries from us or permissions" - their F-16s "are capable, but they also need some of our more sophisticated systems, like the IVEWS integrated electronic warfare system that is not a pod, but it goes in the jet". "We have a family of affordable, low-cost munitions that are being tested on the F-16. We need to see more of that reaching Taiwan."
- On the name: "Hellscape is the official name for it," Batchelor says; Grant replies "You're not going to find it in a military doctrine manual, but Admiral Papparo, commander out in the Pacific, is really good at talking about it."

## Notes on the transcript

- The automatic transcript spells the Indo-Pacific commander three ways in one segment - "Samuel Papi Paparo", "Papparoa" and "Papparo" - against "Admiral Samuel Paparo" in Apple's description.
- It also signs off "Rebecca Grant, Gordon Chang, I'm John Bessler", although the host is named John Batchelor elsewhere on the page.
