wikis.title: Nominations for the Nobel Peace Prize 2026
wikis.summary: Norwegian Nobel Committee press release giving the number of 2026 Nobel Peace Prize candidates and the dates of the nomination deadline, announcement and ceremony.
wikis.body:
## The numbers

- "There are 287 candidates nominated for the Nobel Peace Prize for 2026, of which 208 are individuals and 79 are organizations."
- Release dated 30 Apr 2026.

## Statement quoted on the page

"The number of nominations remains consistently high, reflecting the robust global interest in the Nobel Peace Prize. In an increasingly conflictual world, there is no lack of candidates whose principled commitment and innovative action points towards a brighter future. The values that underpin the prize - and its commitment to peaceful dialogue, conflict resolution and international cooperation - are more important than ever," - the capture carries the quotation without naming a speaker.

## Process

- "Nominations are submitted to the Norwegian Nobel Committee's secretariat by 31 January each year."
- Committee members may add further names during their first meeting after the deadline. "In 2026, the first meeting of the Committee was held on 26 February."
- Under Alfred Nobel's will the Committee awards the prize "to the person or organization that has conferred the greatest benefit on humankind in the field of peace"; after discussing qualified nominations it decides a short-list at its first meeting each year.
- For each candidate and topic the Committee seeks evaluations from leading experts and academics, and reviews scholarly articles and other background material.
- "Proposals received for the award of a prize, and investigations and opinions concerning the award of a prize, may not be divulged until 50 years have elapsed." Nominee names are not announced to media or to candidates; names appearing in media may come from people claiming to have nominated, or be speculation.

## Dates ahead

- "The Nobel Peace Prize laureate(s) of 2026 will be announced on Friday, 9 October, with the award ceremony taking place on 10 December in Oslo, Norway."

wikis.title: Delcy Rodríguez sworn in as Venezuela's interim president
wikis.summary: CBS News piece on Delcy Rodríguez taking office as Venezuela's interim president after Nicolás Maduro's capture, with her background and the U.S. reaction.
wikis.body:
## The swearing-in

- "Delcy Rodríguez was sworn in early Monday as Venezuela's new interim president while her predecessor Nicolás Maduro awaited arraignment in a federal U.S. court on drug smuggling charges, two days after he was captured in Caracas by American special forces."
- Rodríguez, 56, is described as "a powerful figure and longtime confidant of Maduro", "backed thus far as the nation's new leader by Venezuela's military".
- She "served as Venezuela's vice president from 2018 until Sunday", stepping in "as ordered by the country's supreme court following the dramatic events of the weekend."
- Her brother, Jorge Rodríguez, is president of the National Assembly, Venezuela's legislature.
- She "quickly denounced the U.S. operation as a violation of the United Nations founding charter and a unilateral attempt to force regime change on Saturday, but soon adopted a more conciliatory tone." In a social media post after a Sunday Cabinet meeting she called for "respectful international relations" between Caracas and Washington and invited "the U.S. government to collaborate with us on an agenda of cooperation."
- "Venezuela's roughly 30 million people face a deeply uncertain future"; it was "still unclear on Monday how much autonomy Washington will allow the country, given Mr. Trump's assertion that America will 'run' Venezuela, at least for some time."

## U.S. reaction

- Trump said Saturday the U.S. had been in contact with Rodríguez and "she's essentially willing to do what we think is necessary to make Venezuela great again."
- In an interview with The Atlantic published on Sunday, Trump added: "If she doesn't do what's right, she is going to pay a very big price, probably bigger than Maduro."
- Secretary of State Marco Rubio, on CBS News' "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Sunday: "We are going to make our assessments of people... We're going to make an assessment on the basis of what they do, not what they say publicly in the interim, not what, you know, some of what they've done in the past in many cases, but what they do moving forward."
- On ABC's "This Week" the same day Rubio said the administration does not consider Rodríguez or her cohorts to have a legitimate claim to power: "This is not about the legitimate president. We don't believe that this regime in place is legitimate via an election... Ultimately, legitimacy for their system of government will come about through a period of transition and real elections. It's the reason why Maduro is not just an indicted drug trafficker - he [was an] illegitimate president. He was not the head of state."

## Rodríguez's background

- Born in Caracas. Her father, Jorge Antonio Rodríguez, was a prominent leader of the country's socialist movement; he was arrested for involvement in the 1976 kidnapping of American businessman William Niehous and died in police custody, "reportedly as he was tortured by the previous Venezuelan regime's security forces."
- Studied law at the Central University of Venezuela in Caracas, with further education in Britain and France.
- Held positions under Hugo Chávez but rose to prominence under Maduro: Minister of Popular Power for Communication and Information 2013-2014; Minister of Foreign Affairs 2014-2017.
- Presided over an assembly created in response to mass street protests in 2017, "widely seen as an attempt to sideline the opposition-controlled National Assembly".
- Vice president from 2018; also appointed Minister of Economy and Finance in 2020, "credited with helping to achieve some progress toward stabilizing Venezuela's sanctions-wracked economy after years of soaring inflation"; Minister of Petroleum added in 2024.
- "Rodríguez has not been indicted on any criminal charges in the U.S., though she was hit with sanctions imposed during President Trump's first term, for her role in helping Maduro 'maintain power and solidify his authoritarian rule.'"

## Byline and photos

- By Duarte Dias, digital journalist in CBS News' London bureau. "January 5, 2026 / 10:17 AM EST".
- Photo captions: Rodríguez with her brother Jorge Rodríguez arriving for a meeting with diplomatic representatives in Caracas, Sept. 29, 2025 (JUAN BARRETO/AFP/Getty); Maduro with wife Cilia Flores and Vice-President Delcy Rodríguez at Venezuela's Supreme Court of Justice in Caracas, July 31, 2024 (FEDERICO PARRA/AFP/Getty).
- An accompanying video is listed: "Who is Delcy Rodriguez, Venezuela's interim president?" (04:23).

wikis.title: 2026 MLB postseason and World Series schedule
wikis.summary: MLB.com's announcement of the 2026 postseason schedule, round by round, with dates, formats and broadcasters.
wikis.body:
## The announcement

- "On Monday, Major League Baseball announced its 2026 postseason schedule."
- "All dates are subject to change." The full schedule is also at MLB.com/postseason.
- The postseason "won't wait for October this year": it begins Tuesday, Sept. 29 with Game 1 of each of the four best-of-three Wild Card Series, and ends with a possible World Series Game 7 on Saturday, Oct. 31 - "Halloween night".
- "Does the start date of the World Series depend on when the ALCS and NLCS end? No, not this year." Game 1 is fixed for Friday, Oct. 23.

## Rounds at a glance

- Wild Card Series (presented by AbbVie): Sept. 29 - Oct. 1, best-of-three.
- Division Series (presented by Booking.com): from Saturday, Oct. 3, best-of-five, 2-2-1.
- League Championship Series: NLCS Game 1 Sunday, Oct. 11; ALCS Game 1 Oct. 12; best-of-seven, 2-3-2.
- World Series (presented by Capital One): Game 1 Friday, Oct. 23; best-of-seven, 2-3-2.

## Broadcast

- All Wild Card Series games on NBC, Peacock and NBC Sports Network - "the first time NBC has hosted postseason baseball since the 2000 AL Championship Series between the Mariners and Yankees."
- ALDS and ALCS simulcast on TBS, truTV and HBO Max. NLDS and NLCS on FOX or FS1, with FOX Deportes and FOX One. All World Series games on FOX, with FOX Deportes and FOX One.
- MLB.TV: postseason games on TNT Sports platforms, FOX and FS1 are available to MLB.TV subscribers who are authenticated subscribers to the applicable network through a participating pay TV provider.
- Spanish-language: FOX Deportes coverage plus telecasts on Universo and Univision; radio on ESPN Radio, with Univision Radio in Spanish.

## Byline

- Credited to MLB.com, "August 10th, 2026".

wikis.title: 2026 Wild Card Series

wikis.body:

wikis.title: 2026 League Championship Series
wikis.summary: The best-of-seven ALCS and NLCS, beginning Oct. 11 and 12 with possible Game 7s on Oct. 19 and 20.
wikis.body:

wikis.title: 2026 World Series
wikis.summary: The best-of-seven World Series starting Friday, Oct. 23, with a possible Game 7 on Halloween night.
wikis.body:

- "The World Series is a best of seven, with a 2-3-2 format, and the team with the better 2026 record hosts Games 1-2 and 6-7 (if necessary)."
- "There are travel days on Oct. 25 and 29, with the latter dependent on the series lasting more than five games."
- "If a winner-take-all Game 7 is needed to decide the 2026 World Series champion, that game would be played on Halloween night (Saturday, Oct. 31)."

wikis.title: Samuel Charap on how a Ukraine ceasefire could set Europe up for a bigger war (80,000 Hours Podcast #240)
wikis.summary: 80,000 Hours Podcast episode #240, recorded 27 February 2026, in which RAND's Samuel Charap argues that a Ukraine ceasefire would not remove the risk of a NATO-Russia war and sets out the phased ceasefire and framework agreement he thinks is needed.
wikis.body:
## The episode

- "#240 - Samuel Charap on how a Ukraine ceasefire could accidentally set Europe up for a bigger war", 80,000 Hours Podcast, 1h 16m, published March 24, 2026 at 4:51 PM UTC and recorded on February 27, 2026. Interviewed by Rob Wiblin. Transcript and video at https://80k.info/sc26.
- Samuel Charap is "the Distinguished Chair in Russia and Eurasia Policy at the RAND Corporation", a long-time advocate of a negotiated settlement, author of Everyone Loses: The Ukraine Crisis and the Ruinous Contest for Post-Soviet Eurasia (2017) and coauthor with Jeremy Shapiro of the Foreign Affairs piece "Europe's next war: The rising risk of a NATO-Russia conflict".

## The argument

- A ceasefire will not make Europe safe: the war has remilitarised Europe, further militarised Russia, deepened Russian resentment and collapsed communication, leaving "an environment that's ripe for the kind of miscalculation, misunderstanding, miscommunication that can lead to conflict".
- He is not worried mainly about deliberate aggression on a NATO member, because "Russia itself sees itself as the weaker party vis-a-vis NATO". His scenarios are a broken ceasefire dragging in European neighbours, instability in Belarus prompting Russian intervention, hybrid sabotage escalating tit-for-tat, and no-notice Russian exercises on a NATO border being misread.
- Russia's motives were mixed - "both these sort of imperialist drivers and security-driven factors" - and the war has been "a strategic catastrophe for Russia".

## What he proposes

- A phased ceasefire moving domain by domain (energy infrastructure first, then deep strikes, then maritime, then the ground), paired with a framework agreement, followed by a long structured negotiation - not a peace treaty.
- A capable, defensively armed Ukrainian military as the first layer of deterrence, plus automatic "snapback" of sanctions, weapons and other benefits if Russia attacks again - a concept borrowed from the Iran nuclear deal (JCPOA) - with deep-strike missiles stockpiled in neighbouring countries.
- He is sceptical of the UK and French "multinational force in Ukraine": "The idea that Russia would be completely deterred by the presence of a small number of UK and French forces inside Ukraine, I think, is low probability. I think it is a higher probability that the promise of such a presence will deter Russia from accepting a ceasefire."
- Territory (Russia's demand for the part of Donetsk it does not hold, Ukraine's "fortress belt") he treats as secondary to the security issues; both sides have shown some flexibility.
- Obstacles: Russian optimism that time is on its side, and siloed negotiations in which "you don't have all the parties at the table at the same time".
- Russia has accepted Ukraine's EU membership since the Istanbul Communiqué of March 2022, though he says the US expectation of EU accession in 2027 "is just not going to happen".
- He wants a commitment to start a Russia-NATO negotiation embedded in any settlement, and favours a bilateral US-Russia successor to the expired New START rather than a trilateral deal with China.

## Broader views

- He rejects the Munich/Hitler analogy for dealing with autocracies and argues reputation is largely case-specific: "China's view of whether the US would respond to an attempt to take Taiwan is likely to be more shaped by US activities in Asia and the Asia-Pacific than it is by the US response to Russian aggression in Ukraine."
- He rejects conceding Russia a sphere of influence and holds that Article 5 still deters, backed by 80,000 US forces in Europe and a Baltic tripwire.
- Closing advice: "everyone needs to be in the room", and move "with some degree of haste towards a phased ceasefire, combined with some sort of framework agreement".

wikis.title: Samuel Charap on how a Ukraine ceasefire could set Europe up for a bigger war (80,000 Hours Podcast #240)
wikis.summary: Apple Podcasts page and transcript of 80,000 Hours Podcast episode #240, in which RAND's Samuel Charap argues a Ukraine ceasefire would not remove the risk of a NATO-Russia war and sets out what a workable negotiated settlement would contain.
wikis.body:
## The episode

- Title: "#240 - Samuel Charap on how a Ukraine ceasefire could accidentally set Europe up for a bigger war", on the 80,000 Hours Podcast (video podcast). Length 1h 16m. Rating: Clean. Frequency: Updated Weekly.
- "Published March 24, 2026 at 4:51 PM UTC". A date stamp on the page reads "March 24".
- "This episode was recorded on February 27, 2026."
- Links to learn more, video and full transcript: https://80k.info/sc26
- Hosts & Guests listed on the page: Rob Wiblin (Host), Luisa Rodriguez (Host), Zershaaneh Qureshi (Host). The transcript is conducted by Rob.
- Credits: video and audio editing by Dominic Armstrong, Milo McGuire, Luke Monsour and Simon Monsour; music by CORBIT; transcripts and web by Nick Stockton, Elizabeth Cox and Katy Moore.

## The guest

- "Samuel Charap is the Distinguished Chair in Russia and Eurasia Policy at the RAND Corporation, and one of the most influential voices in the US policy debate on how the war in Ukraine should end."
- "He's argued for a negotiated settlement since early in the war, sticking with that position even when it has been highly unfashionable in DC and attracted heated criticism. He's been specialising in Russia-Ukraine relations for decades, speaks both Russian and Ukrainian, and in 2017 wrote Everyone Loses: The Ukraine Crisis and the Ruinous Contest for Post-Soviet Eurasia."
- His recent piece, co-written with Jeremy Shapiro in Foreign Affairs, is "Europe's next war: The rising risk of a NATO-Russia conflict".
- He was previously a guest on the show in 2022.

## The episode's own summary

- "Many people believe a ceasefire in Ukraine will leave Europe safer. But today's guest lays out how a deal could potentially generate insidious new risks - leaving us in a situation that's equally dangerous, just in different ways."
- "He's not worried about a Russian blitzkrieg on Estonia. He forecasts instead a fragile peace that breaks down and drags in European neighbours; instability in Belarus prompting Russian intervention; hybrid sabotage operations that escalate through tit-for-tat responses."
- "Samuel's case isn't that peace is bad, but that the Ukraine conflict has remilitarised Europe, made Russia more resentful, and collapsed diplomatic relations between the two. That's a postwar environment primed for the kind of miscalculation that starts unintended wars."
- "What he prescribes isn't a full peace treaty; it's a negotiated settlement that stops the killing and begins a longer negotiation that gives neither side exactly what it wants, but just enough to deter renewed aggression."
- "None of this is clean or satisfying: Russia invaded, committed war crimes, and is being offered a path back to partial normalcy. But Samuel argues that the alternatives - indefinite war or unstructured ceasefire - are much worse for Ukraine, Europe, and global stability."

## Chapters listed

Cold open (00:00:00); Could peace in Ukraine lead to Europe's next war? (00:00:47); Do Russia's motives for war still matter? (00:11:58); What does a good ceasefire deal look like? (00:18:16); What's still holding back a ceasefire (00:40:15); Why Russia might accept Ukraine's EU membership (00:47:51); How to prevent a spiraling conflict with NATO (00:49:58); What's next for nuclear arms control (00:51:56); Finland and Sweden strengthened NATO - but also raised the stakes for conflict (00:55:36); Putin isn't Hitler: How to negotiate with autocrats (00:58:53); Why Russia still takes NATO seriously (01:04:33); Neither side wants to fight this war again (01:14:04).

## Negotiating with autocrats

- Charap on the objections to a pro-negotiation stance: "I think that there's this sort of Hitler analogy that does distort a lot of our views of nasty autocracies, right? Most autocracies historically have not thought the kind of world domination that Nazi Germany did."
- On reputation: "what we know from political science studies of this is that essentially states look to other states' behaviour in the particular case, not from somewhere else across the world" - so "China's view of whether the US would respond to an attempt to take Taiwan is likely to be more shaped by US activities in Asia and the Asia-Pacific than it is by the US response to Russian aggression in Ukraine." He adds this is "not an argument for not responding to Russian aggression in Ukraine ... we need to attach costs to norm violation".
- "since the advent of nuclear weapons, and given that Russia has more than any other country, there's not going to be an outcome in confronting Russia that looks like Nazi Germany's capitulation." He points to Cold War stability with the Soviet Union as the model, "viewing negotiation as a tool of statecraft, along with coercive elements, rather than some alternative to using coercive elements".
- On 1989-1991: "The geopolitical miracle of 1989-1991, where an empire largely peacefully - although it's sort of overrated because there was some violence - imploded ... that's unlikely to happen. Or at least betting on that is not a wise foreign policy move."

## Site chrome

- The page carries Apple Podcasts navigation: sign-in prompts ("To listen to explicit episodes, sign in", "Stay up to date with this show"), an "Episode Webpage" link and a long country/region selector listing territories across Africa/Middle East/India, Asia Pacific, Europe, Latin America and the Caribbean, and the United States and Canada.

wikis.title: How a post-ceasefire Europe could stumble into a NATO-Russia war
wikis.summary: Charap's account of why the postwar environment is primed for miscalculation and which accidental escalation scenarios he thinks are most likely.
wikis.body:
- Charap on the postwar security environment: "we can see a lot of the trends that have emerged during the war - that is, the remilitarisation of Europe; the further militarisation of Russia; a deep sense of resentment ... after so many Russians have died, as Russians see it, at the hands of a Western proxy; the fears that are quite pervasive in Europe about Russian aggression; and the lack of communication and the sort of breakdown in the entire infrastructure of interaction ... it's an environment that's ripe for the kind of miscalculation, misunderstanding, miscommunication that can lead to conflict."
- He cautions against focusing too much on "opportunistic aggression scenarios ... like Russia up and deciding that it, say, wants to take Lithuania or accomplish a sort of fait accompli in a Russian-speaking area in Estonia", rather than a breakdown "where one thing leads to another and you end up in a war, but not necessarily because one side had initial aggressive intent".

## The scenarios he names

- A ceasefire in Ukraine breaking down, "because often ceasefires do break down", with a future Russia-Ukraine war dragging in European neighbours: "a lot of European leaders have basically said, 'If this were to happen again, we're going to be much more deeply involved.'"
- Instability in Belarus: "Belarus is essentially Russia's most important ally. It provides Russia with this sort of strategic depth between itself and NATO. And if Moscow were to see itself as losing Belarus, it would not hesitate to act." He cites the large-scale protest movement in the summer of 2020 after a falsified presidential election, and Alexander Lukashenko as president "for now, going on 30 years".
- Hybrid incidents below the threshold of conventional war: "sabotage: these Russian paid agents apparently blowing up factories or attempting to subvert Western military aid for Ukraine - never involving uniformed Russian military personnel firing direct shots, but nonetheless are getting increasingly more assertive", with growing demand in central and eastern Europe to respond and the risk of "a snowball effect".
- Russian snap (no-notice) exercises, which "has been the cover for aggression against Ukraine in the past"; if held on a NATO ally's border, an ally "might see what Russia is doing as preparation for aggression and might respond in kind". He notes "NATO and Russia's border has expanded greatly since Finland's entry into the alliance in 2023".

## Why he doubts a deliberate attack

- "Russia itself sees itself as the weaker party vis-a-vis NATO, and it sees itself as likely to lose a war and therefore has been hesitant to engage." He says the fear of a united Western response "serves as an effective deterrent" and that "Russia is deterred precisely because it thinks it's not a war it could win. It entered Ukraine, I should note, thinking that that would be a war that it could win easily."
- He clarifies the article's claim: "the risks won't dramatically decrease with the ceasefire, that they won't disappear; not that they're necessarily going to be greater after a ceasefire than they were before", and rejects the idea "that essentially if there's a ceasefire in Ukraine, then Russia is going to be coming for us, NATO, next. That I don't buy."
- Risks of the ongoing war: "Russia is at war, full-scale conventional war involving a whole range of high end weapons systems - including long-range strike - in a country that borders four NATO allies", with Ukraine fighting with alliance-supplied weapons and Russia subverting that supply chain. He also cites the resource argument: "It's going to be an ongoing struggle for Europe to arm itself while it is emptying its caches of weapons to provide to Ukraine."
- Cold-open quote: "The idea that Russia would be completely deterred by the presence of a small number of UK and French forces inside Ukraine, I think, is low probability. I think it is a higher probability that the promise of such a presence will deter Russia from accepting a ceasefire."

wikis.title: Do Russia's motives for the war still matter?
wikis.summary: Charap on the mix of imperialist and security motives behind the invasion, why the war has been a strategic catastrophe for Russia, and why the question now is what Putin needs to stop.
wikis.body:
- Asked whether identity or nationalist motivation now seems more central: "I don't think I ever argued exclusively that it was one set of issues that drove this decision - in the way that some, like John Mearsheimer, have argued ... Usually decisions to go to war are motivated by a variety of factors. Monocausality is very rare in these contexts. But it's clear that, as Putin has articulated in his decision making, there were both these sort of imperialist drivers and security-driven factors."
- "there's enough evidence to suggest that Russia was initially seeking regime change in Ukraine, since it retreated from the capital in the spring of 2022 almost four years ago, it's hard to argue that they've been pursuing that same objective. They've been pursuing other objectives that are perhaps no less objectionable ... the question now is much more about what he'll need to stop, essentially."
- On Russia's position: "this is a strategic catastrophe for Russia. It has set itself back in terms of economic development by generations - demographically, strategically, in terms of its place in the world, and its reputation." He notes European military budgets have "almost doubled" since before the war and that the German military, "previously sort of something of a laughingstock, is now spending a lot of money, with the Chancellor saying, 'We want the Bundeswehr to be the most powerful military in Europe'".
- On Putin: "I don't think that Putin is going to be happy about the existence of an independent Ukraine, regardless. The question is what he can accept in order to end the fighting and the bombardment of Ukraine. So this is not going to be his ideal outcome. He's still going to be contemptuous of Ukraine and Ukrainians."
- He argues the proposition must be tested "that there might be some mutually acceptable accommodation that can be reached, and that the security motives ... can be compelling enough to overcome any of the sort of lingering imperialist drive".

wikis.title: What a good ceasefire deal would contain
wikis.summary: The elements Charap says must be on the table - Ukraine's status, postwar military postures, ceasefire modalities and territory - and his proposed phased ceasefire plus framework agreement.
wikis.body:
## Elements

- "the question about Ukraine's status ... is going to be a big piece of this, and how the reality of Ukraine's non-alignment would be codified." Russia is focused on Ukraine's postwar security relationship with the West - how much and what kind of weapons the West will supply, and the nature and posture of the postwar Ukrainian military. Ukraine has been insistent on security assurances "that if this were to happen again that they wouldn't be on their own".
- Secondary issues Russia might raise: "the section of the Orthodox Church that previously was part of the Moscow Patriarchate in Ukraine" and "the nature of the Russian language and its status in Ukraine".
- Ceasefire modalities: "This is a huge line of contact, by global standards: almost over 1,000 kilometres - and that is extremely difficult to monitor", with a need for thinned-out zones so that "major cities [are] not in artillery range".
- Territory: Russia's demand for the part of the Donetsk region it does not control, "which Ukraine refers to as its 'fortress belt.'" Charap considers territory "a secondary one that could be potentially more easily resolved if the bigger picture security issues were addressed", and notes flexibility on both sides - "the Russians have said that they don't have to have their military there, they could just have the National Guard. And the Ukrainians have said they could do this as a DMZ".
- He compares the scale of negotiation needed to "how the Good Friday accord was negotiated or Dayton in Bosnia".

## Snapback guarantees and the porcupine model

- The first and most important layer is a capable Ukrainian military: "I think the Ukrainians have come to terms with the reality that nobody is going to fight for them", so the aim is a defensively oriented military "capable of holding territory, and making any gains for Russia to be incredibly painful, too painful in fact, to initiate".
- The second layer is external commitments, structured as a "snapback arrangement": "any benefits that Russia gets out of a ceasefire - be it sanctions relief; be it Ukraine's non-alignment; be it limitations to Western assistance, say we wouldn't provide targeting data in peacetime, that we would in wartime - snap back ... if it chooses to have a major violation of the ceasefire and attack Ukraine again." The benefits would return automatically, requiring a vote to stop them.
- The snapback concept comes from the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action, the Iranian nuclear deal, "where there were sanctions that were relieved and that would be reimposed - that were in fact reimposed - in the event of Iranian violation". He compares the general form to NATO's Article 5. The article he cowrote with Jeremy Shapiro in Foreign Affairs argued that legislating it with a review mechanism "avoids the messy political debates problem and gets political buy-in in key countries", denying Russia "salami-slicing tactics".
- Weapons: during a ceasefire the West would supply defensive systems - air defence above all, plus landmines, obstructions to armoured assault, anti-tank and anti-aircraft systems and a surveillance network - while deep-strike missile systems would be held in "stockpiles in neighbouring countries ready to go if Russia were to attack again".
- On the defensive advantage: "with the pervasive use of UAVs [unmanned aerial vehicles], that has come to favour the defence, essentially - because both armoured assault and even small infantry group assault has become impossible. There's this sort of kill zone, and the battlefield has become essentially transparent."
- Caveat: "a determined aggressor will do what it wants, sometimes despite knowing that it will, in fact, lose ... this is not a guarantee in the sense like, you buy a webcam with a guarantee."

## Boots on the ground

- Charap is sceptical of a Western troop presence: the French president and UK Prime Minister "publicly committed to deploying this force to Ukraine after a ceasefire", called the "multinational force in Ukraine". If those forces came under attack the alliance would face "either retreating and essentially losing a lot of credibility that way, or of launching a Russia-NATO war, neither of which is a particularly good outcome."
- On NATO membership: when he "was last in Kyiv in December of last year", he consistently heard "no one is going to fight for us", and he thinks NATO membership "has essentially been taken off the table", though formulating that is challenging "because of the way it's been inserted into the Ukrainian constitution".

## Process

- He proposes a phased ceasefire "moving from one domain to another": starting with energy infrastructure, then no deep strikes beyond a certain distance from the front line, then the maritime domain, "eventually moving closer and closer towards a full-fledged ceasefire on the ground".
- Then a framework agreement alongside the ceasefire, followed by a longer detailed negotiation: "it's not going to be a peace treaty in the traditional sense, because Ukraine and Russia will have territorial disputes; there will be lots of unanswered issues." A withdrawal process on the ground would need a monitoring mission.
- Incentives for Ukraine: "keeping an accelerated path towards EU membership on the table, having significant financial incentives in the form of reconstruction and postwar military aid, a commitment to essentially build up the Ukrainian military into a very capable defensive force."
- The core dilemma: "the biggest one in negotiations to end war is fundamentally about how sides that are currently fighting each other can credibly commit to stop in the other's eyes."

wikis.title: What is still holding back a ceasefire
wikis.summary: Charap's two main obstacles - Russian optimism about the war's course and the siloed structure of the current negotiations - plus each side's incentives to stop.
wikis.body:
- "one major one, and I think we need to start here, is Russia's current optimism about the course of the war. I don't think they are in a rush to end this, because they think that time is on their side ... And they see their position improving in six months compared to where it is today. So why make major compromises if you don't have to?" He notes Russia has been "slowly but surely gaining territory essentially for the last three years, or even longer, since the Ukrainian successful counteroffensives in the fall of 2022".
- The second obstacle is the structure of the talks: "There are siloed arrangements between certain parties where the others are not privy to them. For example, there's a Ukraine-European security guarantees document. There's a Ukraine-US Security guarantees document. This has all been reported; none of it's been published yet ... There's an agreement about postwar Ukrainian reconstruction. There's some US-Russia document. And then there's this direct question about territorial compromise."
- "my concern is that you don't have all the parties at the table at the same time talking about all the issues that are central to their concerns." If Russia rejects the "coalition of the willing" force, "then it's not going to work".
- Ukraine's reluctance stems from expecting Russia not to stick to a deal; Charap says this fear "is common to belligerents who are trying to end a war", and "I think Russia is convinced that Ukraine might do the same".
- On the Trump factor: "while it is true that I think there's a plausible case to be made that Russia might have concluded that all they have to do is wait and Trump's impatience will lead to a full end to US support for Ukraine, I think on the flip side, they also recognise that Trump's interest in negotiating an end to the war represents a window of opportunity", and that talk of "some normalisation of US-Russia relations after a ceasefire ... is not something that's going to be on the table forever".
- He adds that "there are many in the Russian establishment that don't view the acquisition of a few more kilometres or the destruction of X more percentage of Ukrainian energy generation as worth the costs to Russia", citing war-economy distortions and mounting sanctions.
- On Ukraine: "the longer this goes on, the worse off they will end up being in the postwar context ... In fact, they would accept an unconditional ceasefire. It's Russia that is essentially pushing to attach its political conditions to ending the fighting."

wikis.title: Why Russia might accept Ukraine's EU membership
wikis.summary: Charap on Russia having conceded EU accession since 2022 and why that is an underappreciated concession.
wikis.body:
- Asked whether Russia could swallow Ukraine joining the EU while staying out of NATO: "Russia has accepted that since 2022. That was actually part of the Istanbul Communiqué in March of 2022, the deal that almost was in the early weeks of the war."
- "I think it's an underappreciated concession in a way. And a concession not necessarily to Ukraine, but to reality: to the reality that Russia is not going to be able to stop that process."
- He contrasts this with 2013, "before the annexation of Crimea", when Russia "put a lot of economic pressure and provided a lot of economic incentives for then-president Yanukovych to not sign an association agreement with the EU".
- "this is another element of the strategic catastrophe from a Russian perspective: that they've essentially politically and economically ceded the point that Ukraine, the government-controlled Ukraine, will be beyond Russia's sphere of influence".
- On timing: "EU membership is a long and winding road. The US side seems to think that the EU could commit to doing that in 2027, which is just not going to happen. It's a very bureaucratic process. But it can move relatively quickly, and I think Ukraine and the EU are both committed to making that happen."

wikis.title: The three rings of the conflict and preventing a spiral with NATO
wikis.summary: Charap's framing of the war as Russia-Ukraine, Russia-NATO and Russia-US strategic stability, and his call to commit to a Russia-NATO negotiation.
wikis.body:
- "this conflict, generally speaking, you can think of as having three rings, essentially: There's the Russia-Ukraine piece; There's the Russia-NATO piece - which I think is part of this dynamic, clearly, given both the assistance and the breakdown in relations; And then there's the broader strategic stability, mostly a Russia-US ring, which has been directly affected by the conflict with Russian suspension of implementation of New START and the lack of a treaty to replace it."
- "in attempts to resolve it, we need to think about addressing all three rings, even if not immediately."
- "What I could imagine being important to embed in a Russia-Ukraine ceasefire or framework agreement is a commitment to start a Russia-NATO negotiation process to ensure broader stability in the continent. That is going to be a long-term negotiation, not something that can be done in weeks or months, but nonetheless that the sides would commit to begin it. Because right now there just isn't any discussion of that."

wikis.title: What is next for nuclear arms control
wikis.summary: Charap on New START's expiry, why he favours a bilateral US-Russia arrangement rather than a trilateral deal with China, and what verification buys.
wikis.body:
- The host notes New START "expired a couple of weeks ago", that it had limited US and Russian active nuclear arsenals "for a couple of decades", and that "Russia, I believe, offered to extend it for a year, and the US just batted that away and said it wasn't very interested."
- Charap: "strategic stability is about avoiding, again, inadvertent conflict, making crises less potentially escalatory, avoiding first-use pressures in a crisis - so 'use them or lose them' concerns - and avoiding misinterpretation. Under New START, every test of an ICBM was notified, every movement of launchers in and out of service essentially was notified, there were opportunities for inspection and so on."
- On the Trump administration's sequencing: "We can talk about a lot of things after a ceasefire, but we need to see the war in Ukraine ended."
- On a trilateral deal including China - "that was the Trump administration position toward the end of his first term" - Charap says "there is grounds for having US-Russia arms control despite the buildup of the Chinese arsenal". He says China is "projected by 2035 to have as many warheads as the US has warheads deployed under New START, at least", that "the US will still have something like three times as many warheads overall", and that the Chinese buildup is "five times larger than it was in 2019".
- "the deterrence relationships between China and the US and Russia and the US are fundamentally different. And therefore, in my view, you would want two separate arrangements." He adds: "We still control over 85% of the world's nuclear weapons, and thus I think have a special responsibility to minimise the chances of their use."
- "I think there's a debate in the US now about how many we need in light of the Chinese buildup, and maybe it's going to be more than 1,550, which was the limit under New START. But I think having a limit - that is verifiable, particularly - avoids the kind of worst-case assumptions that often drive these things."

wikis.title: Finland and Sweden in NATO: a stronger alliance and a longer border
wikis.summary: Charap revisits his 2022 caution about Nordic accession and what the expanded NATO-Russia border means for managing the postwar period.
wikis.body:
- The host recalls that in 2022 Charap warned about Sweden and Finland joining NATO on escalation grounds, notes they joined "in 2023 and 2024", and asks whether the analysis was mistaken.
- Charap: "I'm not sure necessarily I argued against it. I just think I was pointing out the potential escalation risks. At the time, in mid-2022, of course we had no idea about this environment we were entering into. And if someone told anyone in my field that the US would be providing long-range strike to Ukraine that Ukraine would be using to hit cities inside of Russia in 2021, I would have looked for the nearest bomb shelter."
- "public opinion in Sweden and Finland shifted pretty dramatically, and they had always been in the position of being as integrated with NATO as possible without actually being members".
- "from Finland's perspective, the security environment in the immediate sense has somewhat improved, because a lot of the units that were previously stationed along its border have been chewed to pieces in Ukraine. But Russia has announced plans to dramatically increase its presence near Finland, in the Baltic, in the years to come."
- "logistically it makes defence of the Baltic states much easier, but it does create a potential more unstable security dynamic involving Russia." Finland-Russia relations "have been almost completely cut off, to the point of border crossings being closed", and "in the postwar context, we're going to have to, as an alliance, think about how to manage what is now a much longer border between NATO and Russia to avoid miscalculation and misunderstandings."
- Elsewhere in the episode he dates Finland's entry to the alliance to 2023.

wikis.title: Spheres of influence, extended deterrence and Charap's closing advice (80,000 Hours #240, part 2)
wikis.summary: The final stretch of the Samuel Charap interview - why he rejects conceding Russia a sphere of influence, why he thinks Article 5 still deters, and the two messages he would give ceasefire negotiators.
wikis.body:
## Not a sphere of influence

- Charap: "I think we need to accept these countries for what they are, not sugarcoat it, but also see that in the past, even with countries that are objectionable both in their domestic political regimes and their foreign policy behaviour, we have been able to find agreements that serve our interests."
- Asked how his position differs from Hugh White's argument (from an earlier episode of the show) that the US should accept Russian military power and resolve in its near abroad: "I don't think a Russian sphere of influence is a viable solution ... These countries don't want to be subjugated to particularly this Russia. But just generally speaking, they want their independence."
- "even with Ukraine, in the 80% of Ukraine that the Ukrainian government is likely to end up with, Russia's influence will be dramatically attenuated. So I hardly see the outcome that we're describing as one of ceding influence to them."
- He cites the United States "now, interestingly, under Trump" leading a reconciliation process between Armenia and Azerbaijan in Russia's near abroad: "That seems to make sense to me. If the US can get it done, great. That war has been going on essentially since before the Soviet collapse."
- "just saying this is Russia's sphere of influence and we must retreat is not really a viable policy option, nor is it a desirable one ... it's not a matter of just recognising Russia's interests and therefore retreating, but taking into account the reality that Russian influence is not going to go away."
- He disagrees with White's claim that the lack of a Western military response in Ukraine shows a broader lack of US commitment to NATO, pointing to "the distinction between NATO and non-NATO Europe, particularly under the Biden administration, but even going forward under Trump, where we have just heard the undersecretary of war make the case for returning NATO to its sort of factory settings - in other words, focusing on territorial defence and deterrence".

## Why Russia still takes NATO seriously

- "I am convinced that Article 5 is an effective deterrent, that Russia believes in it, and believes that it would be at war with the United States if it were to attack a NATO ally. And I think Russia sees that war as one that it could not win conventionally, and that would have therefore the potential for nuclear escalation."
- On extended deterrence: it "rests on something of a bluff, or something of a commitment that we don't know what will happen if called, an uncertainty. And that risk that leaves something to chance is precisely the kind of fear that deterrence is meant to create. After all, deterrence comes from the word 'terror.'"
- On whether Europe will cede whatever it cannot convince Russia it would fight a nuclear war over: the host revises it to "some meaningful probability", and Charap agrees, noting "the same problem existed in the Cold War ... there was always the question of, 'Would we trade Boston for Berlin?'"
- On US skin in the game: "It has 80,000 forces stationed in Europe. It has nuclear weapons reportedly stationed in Europe. And it maintains, including forces that are conventional forces, but nonetheless in the Baltic states themselves. So you would have what they call a tripwire, which is what existed in West Berlin ... a force that's not going to defeat an invading Russian army, but will make it harder for the US president to ignore a bunch of US soldiers being killed in the process."
- He allows the political-will question is real: "if I were living in Estonia, I would be concerned that the US public is not as taken with the Russian threat as they are", and acknowledges White's point about "the pervasive fear of communism, essentially, in the Cold War, being something that drove people to consider making unpalatable decisions".

## Closing advice

- Asked what he would tell US or NATO officials they are getting wrong: "I think everyone needs to be in the room. That despite the current focus on territory ... ultimately both countries' bottom lines relate to their future security and their desire to have whatever ending comes be the end. I don't think either side wants to have reason to fight this war again."
- "thinking through the sequencing and moving with some degree of haste towards a phased ceasefire, combined with some sort of framework agreement, that that can end the bloodshed and begin a longer term, structured negotiating process."
- The host closes: "My guest today has been Samuel Charap. Fingers crossed we'll finally see the end of this war in the next year or two or three." Charap: "I hope so. Thanks for having me. It's been a pleasure."

wikis.title: Announcement of the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine
wikis.summary: Nobel Prize channel live stream page for the announcement of the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

wikis.title: The 2026 Nobel Prize announcements
wikis.summary: Nobel Foundation press release setting the dates, times and venues of the six 2026 Nobel Prize announcements, 5-12 October.
wikis.body:
## Overview

- Press release from the Nobel Foundation, dated 2 February 2026.
- "This year's Nobel Prize announcements will take place from 5-12 October."
- "All prize announcements will be broadcast live on the official digital channels of the Nobel Prize"; in-depth information about the prizes will be published at www.nobelprize.org. A YouTube live stream is listed for each announcement.
- "Media wishing to attend the announcements should apply to the respective prize-awarding institution in the early fall."
- The page is also offered in Swedish. Photo of the Nobel Prize Medal credited to Alexander Mahmoud.

## Schedule as stated

| Prize | Time | Venue |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Physiology or Medicine | Monday, 5 October, 11:30 CEST at the earliest | Nobel Assembly at Karolinska Institutet, Wallenbergsalen, Nobel Forum, Nobels vag 1, Solna |
| Physics | Tuesday, 6 October, 11:45 CEST at the earliest | Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences, Session Hall, Lilla Frescativagen 4A, Stockholm |
| Chemistry | Wednesday, 7 October, 11:45 CEST at the earliest | Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences, Session Hall, Lilla Frescativagen 4A, Stockholm |
| Literature | Thursday, 8 October, 13:00 CEST at the earliest | The Swedish Academy, Borssalen, Kallargrand 4, Stockholm |
| Peace | Friday, 9 October, 11:00 CEST | Norwegian Nobel Committee, Norwegian Nobel Institute, Store Sal, Henrik Ibsens gate 51, Oslo |
| Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel | Monday, 12 October, 11:45 CEST at the earliest | Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences, Session Hall, Lilla Frescativagen 4A, Stockholm |

Only the Peace announcement time is given without the hedge "at the earliest".

## About the Nobel Foundation (as the page states)

- "a private foundation established in 1900 on the basis of the will of Alfred Nobel and the founding statutes promulgated in connection with the will", whose primary purpose is to ensure Alfred Nobel's will is fulfilled, which manages the assets behind the prize and the Nobel Prize trademarks.

wikis.title: 2027 FIFA Women's World Cup
wikis.summary: The English Wikipedia article on the 2027 FIFA Women's World Cup in Brazil, covering the 2024 host vote, the eight stadiums, qualification slots and qualified teams, the full group and knockout schedule, and the tournament's branding, broadcasters, sponsors and the UEFA boycott.
wikis.body:
## The tournament

- "The 2027 FIFA Women's World Cup is scheduled to be the 10th edition of the FIFA Women's World Cup", hosted by Brazil from 24 June to 25 July, with 32 teams from six confederations at 8 venues in 8 host cities. Spain are the defending champions.
- "This will be the second and last edition of the tournament to be contested by 32 teams, with FIFA expanding to 48 teams for the next edition in 2031."
- Awarded to Brazil on 17 May 2024, "making this the first FIFA Women's World Cup to be held in South America and Latin America". Brazil becomes "the sixth country—after Sweden, the United States, Germany, France, and Canada—to host both the men's and women's World Cup", and "the first country to host eight different FIFA competitions".
- Format: eight groups of four, top two advancing to a round of 16, 64 games in total. All times BRT (UTC−3).

## Host vote

Bidding opened 23 March 2023 with fourteen countries interested; Chile, Italy, South Africa and the Nordic bid dropped out, and the merged United States–Mexico bid withdrew in April 2024 "to focus on the 2031 Women's World Cup instead". At the 74th FIFA Congress in Bangkok on 17 May 2024, Brazil won 119 votes to the Belgium–Germany–Netherlands bid's 78, with 3 for neither and 7 abstentions.

## Venues

Announced 7 May 2025; all eight stadiums hosted 2014 FIFA World Cup matches, after Belém (Estádio Mangueirão) and Natal were also considered. Estádio do Maracanã, Rio de Janeiro (73,139); Arena BRB Mané Garrincha, Brasília (69,910); Estádio Mineirão, Belo Horizonte (66,658); Arena Castelão, Fortaleza (57,867); Estádio Beira-Rio, Porto Alegre (50,848); Neo Química Arena, São Paulo (48,905); Casa de Apostas Arena Fonte Nova, Salvador (47,915); Arena Pernambuco, Recife (45,440).

## Qualification

Slots approved by the FIFA Council on 10 December 2024: AFC 6, CAF 4, CONCACAF 4, CONMEBOL 3 (including hosts Brazil), OFC 1, UEFA 11, plus 3 from a ten-team inter-confederation play-off. Russia remains suspended and excluded from European qualification. Algeria and Malawi will debut - "Malawi became the lowest ranked team to ever qualify for a World Cup in either gender" - North Korea returns after 2011, Cameroon qualified after initially failing to when the 2026 Women's Africa Cup of Nations was expanded, and "Nigeria failed to qualify for the first time in Women's World Cup history." Teams listed as qualified at the time of the capture: Australia, China, Japan, North Korea, Philippines, South Korea; Algeria, Cameroon, Malawi, Morocco; Argentina, Brazil, Colombia; New Zealand; Denmark, France, Germany, Spain.

## Schedule

The final draw is set for 11 December 2026 at the Museum of Modern Art in Rio de Janeiro. Group play runs from 24 June 2027; the round of 16 is 10-13 July, quarter-finals 16-17 July, semi-finals 20 July (São Paulo) and 21 July (Rio de Janeiro), the third-place match 24 July in São Paulo, and the final on 25 July 2027 at the Estádio do Maracanã.

## Around the tournament

- The emblem was unveiled on 25 January 2026 at Copacabana, combining "W" (women, world) and "M" ("mulheres", "mundo"), with the slogan "Go Epic" ("Vai Ser Épico").
- Broadcasters include Netflix in the United States and Canada, Grupo Globo and CazéTV in Brazil, the BBC and ITV in the United Kingdom and the EBU across the European Union, with Saran Media Group holding rights across much of central Asia and eastern Europe. FIFA partners are Adidas, Aramco, Coca-Cola, Hyundai–Kia, Lenovo, Qatar Airways and Visa.
- Half-price tickets are expected "for students, elderly people and low-income youth registered in the CadÚnico".
- On 30 July 2026 "all 55 UEFA member associations agreed on an indefinite boycott of FIFA competitions" over the FIFA Forward Enterprise proposal to sell stakes in FIFA's tournament operations; the proposal was scrapped on 31 July and UEFA "provisionally suspended their boycott for the 2026–27 season, including for the 2027 FIFA Women's World Cup, on 27 August."

## Tension in the page's own figures

The article says the vote "was open to 207 eligible member associations" and the table gives "Total votes 207" (119 + 78 + 3 + 7 abstentions), while the same paragraph says "Norway and the Philippines were unable to vote due to technical difficulties". The infobox gives the dates as "24 June – 25 July" without stating a year.

The second part of the capture is the tail of the citation list, the external link, the stadium and Women's World Cup navigation boxes and the category list; no published or last-updated date is stated.

wikis.title: 2027 FIFA Women's World Cup: hosting, venues, qualification and match schedule
wikis.summary: Part 1 of the English Wikipedia article on the 2027 FIFA Women's World Cup in Brazil, covering the host vote, the eight stadiums, team base camps, qualification slots and qualified teams, the draw and full group and knockout schedule, and the tournament's branding, broadcasters, sponsors, ticketing and the UEFA boycott.
wikis.body:
## The tournament

- "The 2027 FIFA Women's World Cup is scheduled to be the 10th edition of the FIFA Women's World Cup", Portuguese title *Copa do Mundo Feminina da FIFA 2027*.
- Host country Brazil. Dates given in the infobox as "24 June – 25 July" (no year stated there); 32 teams from 6 confederations; 8 venues in 8 host cities. Preceded by 2023, followed by 2031.
- "The tournament will include 32 teams for the second time after FIFA announced the expansion of the tournament in July 2019. Spain are the defending champions, having won their first title in 2023. This will be the second and last edition of the tournament to be contested by 32 teams, with FIFA expanding to 48 teams for the next edition in 2031."
- "On 17 May 2024, FIFA announced that Brazil won the hosting rights, making this the first FIFA Women's World Cup to be held in South America and Latin America. Brazil will become the sixth country—after Sweden, the United States, Germany, France, and Canada—to host both the men's and women's World Cup, having hosted the men's tournament in 1950 and 2014. It is also the first country to host eight different FIFA competitions."
- A footnote lists those competitions: "Brazil hosted the 2016 Olympic football tournaments, the 2000 FIFA Club World Championship, the 2013 FIFA Confederations Cup, the 2019 FIFA U-17 World Cup, the 2008 FIFA Futsal World Cup, and the first three editions of the FIFA-organised Beach Soccer World Cup in 2005, 2006, and 2007."
- Format: "The Women's World Cup, since the 2023 edition, opens with a group stage consisting of eight groups of four teams, with the top two teams from each group advancing to knockout rounds, starting with a round of 16 teams. The number of games played overall is 64."
- All times are given as BRT (UTC−3), with kick-off times "subject to change".

## Tension in the vote figures

The article says voting "was open to 207 eligible member associations" and the vote table gives "Total votes 207" (Brazil 119, Belgium–Germany–Netherlands 78, none of the bids 3, abstentions 7, majority required 104), while the same paragraph states that "Norway and the Philippines were unable to vote due to technical difficulties".

wikis.title: Host selection and the 74th FIFA Congress vote
wikis.summary: The bidding process from March 2023, the withdrawals, and the 17 May 2024 vote in Bangkok.
wikis.body:
- "On 23 March 2023, FIFA announced that bidding had begun for the 2027 FIFA Women's World Cup. Member associations interested in hosting the tournament had to submit a declaration of interest by 21 April, and provide the completed bidding registration by 8 December."
- "Fourteen countries initially indicated interest in hosting the event. These were Brazil, Chile, Italy, Mexico, South Africa, and the United States, along with the two joint bids of Belgium–Germany–Netherlands and Denmark–Finland–Iceland–Norway–Sweden (the 'Nordic bid')."
- "Chile, Italy, South Africa and the Nordic countries would later drop out, while the U.S. Soccer Federation and the Mexican Football Federation merged their bids into a joint submission. The U.S. and Mexico withdrew their bid in April 2024—just weeks before the host selection—to focus on the 2031 Women's World Cup instead."
- "Voting for the host took place on 17 May 2024, during the 74th FIFA Congress in Bangkok, and it was open to 207 eligible member associations. The Brazilian bid won with 119 ballots, while the Belgium–Germany–Netherlands bid received 78 ballots. Costa Rica, Curaçao, Dominican Republic, Namibia, Nigeria, Sudan, and Togo abstained from the vote, Libya did not vote for either candidate, and Norway and the Philippines were unable to vote due to technical difficulties."
- Vote table: Brazil 119; Belgium, Germany and Netherlands 78; none of the bids 3; abstentions 7; total votes 207; majority required 104.

wikis.title: Qualification and slot allocation
wikis.summary: How the six confederations qualify, the slots approved in December 2024, and the ten-team inter-confederation play-off.
wikis.body:
- "Three of FIFA's confederations (AFC, CAF and CONCACAF) organise their qualifications through continental championships, while the other three (CONMEBOL, OFC and UEFA) organise their own qualifying competitions. The Brazil national team qualified automatically as a host."
- "Russia had been suspended from all FIFA and UEFA competitions since 28 February 2022 due to the Russian invasion of Ukraine, and were excluded from the European qualification process."
- "In July 2026, UEFA threatened to boycott all FIFA competitions if the FIFA Forward Enterprise proposal went ahead, which would have then placed UEFA's qualification spots in doubt."
- "The allocation of slots below was approved by the FIFA Council on 10 December 2024. The slot for the host nation will be taken directly from the quotas allocated to their confederation." AFC 6; CAF 4; CONCACAF 4; CONMEBOL 3 (including hosts Brazil); OFC 1; UEFA 11; inter-confederation play-off tournament 3.
- "A ten-team play-off tournament will decide the final three spots at the Women's World Cup." Play-off slots: AFC 2, CAF 2, CONCACAF 2, CONMEBOL 2, OFC 1, UEFA 1.
- "Algeria and Malawi will make their debut. Both countries will make their first appearance in a FIFA women's tournament, while Malawi became the lowest ranked team to ever qualify for a World Cup in either gender. North Korea returns after last appearing in 2011. Cameroon returns after not making the 2023 edition and became the first country to ever qualify for Women's World Cup after initially failing to, as a late expansion to the 2026 Women's Africa Cup of Nations gave them a reprieve. Vietnam and Zambia failed to qualify after debuting in 2023, and Nigeria failed to qualify for the first time in Women's World Cup history."

- **CONMEBOL (3)**: Argentina, Brazil (host), Colombia.

wikis.title: Branding, broadcasting, sponsors, ticketing and the UEFA boycott
wikis.summary: The emblem and slogan, the announced broadcasters and sponsors, the discounted-ticket plan, and the 2026 UEFA boycott of FIFA competitions.
wikis.body:
## Branding

"The official emblem was unveiled on 25 January 2026 during an event at Copacabana in Rio de Janeiro. The emblem's design was inspired by the Brazilian flag as well as football pitches, crafted from the union of 'W' (representing the words 'women' and 'world') and 'M' (from the equivalent Portuguese words 'mulheres' and 'mundo'). The slogan 'Go Epic' ('Vai Ser Épico' in Portuguese) was also unveiled the same day."

## Broadcasters

Australia - Paramount+ and Network 10; Belgium - RTBF, VRT; Brazil - Grupo Globo and CazéTV; Canada - Netflix; China - CCTV; Czech Republic - CRo, CT; Denmark - DR, TV 2; European Union - EBU; Finland - Yle; France - M6; Germany - Magenta Sport; Greenland, Liechtenstein and Luxembourg - EBU; Hungary - MTVA; Iceland - RÚV; India - Zee; Indonesia - TVRI; Malta - PBS; Mexico - Tudn Mexico; Netherlands - NOS; Norway - NRK, TV 2 Direkte; Poland - TVP; Singapore - Mediacorp; Slovakia - RTVS; South Africa - SABC; South Korea - JTBC and Naver; Spain - RTVE; Sub-Saharan Africa - New World TV; Sweden - SR, SVT, TV4; Switzerland - SRG SSR; Thailand - MONOMAX Sports; Türkiye - Saran Media Group and S Sport; Ukraine - Suspilne; United Kingdom - BBC, ITV; United States - Netflix. Saran Media Group holds rights in Albania, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bulgaria, Croatia, Estonia, Georgia, Ireland, Kazakhstan, Kosovo, Kyrgyzstan, Latvia, Lithuania, Moldova, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Romania, Serbia, Slovenia, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan.

## Sponsorships

- FIFA partners: Adidas, Aramco, Coca-Cola, Hyundai–Kia, Lenovo, Qatar Airways, Visa.
- FIFA Women's World Cup sponsors: AB InBev (Budweiser and others), Frito-Lay (Lay's), Mengniu Dairy, Unilever (Rexona).
- FIFA Women's World Cup supporters: Airbnb, DoorDash, Globant, Salesforce, Valvoline, Verizon.

## Ticketing

"It is expected that all matches of the 2027 FIFA Women's World Cup are going to have half price tickets for students, elderly people and low-income youth registered in the CadÚnico (a Brazilian government system used to identify low-income families and ensure access to social benefits)."

## UEFA boycott

"On 30 July 2026, following FIFA's announcement of FIFA Forward Enterprise (a proposal to sell stakes in FIFA's tournament operations, including for the Women's World Cup, to private investors), all 55 UEFA member associations agreed on an indefinite boycott of FIFA competitions until the proposal was shelved and assurances were made that such a proposal would not be tabulated again. FIFA Forward Enterprise was scrapped on 31 July, and following written assurances that a similar proposal wouldn't be brought up, UEFA provisionally suspended their boycott for the 2026–27 season, including for the 2027 FIFA Women's World Cup, on 27 August."

wikis.title: 2027 NCAA Division I men's basketball tournament
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the 2027 NCAA Division I men's basketball tournament, its expansion to 76 teams, schedule, venues and broadcasters.
wikis.body:
## Overview

- "The 2027 NCAA Division I men's basketball tournament will involve a total of 76 teams playing in a single-elimination tournament" to determine the Division I men's college basketball national champion for the 2026-27 season.
- "The 88th edition of the tournament is scheduled to begin on March 16, 2027, and it will conclude with the championship game on April 5, 2027, at Ford Field in Detroit."
- "This tournament will mark the introduction of the Opening Round and an expansion of the field of participants from 68 teams to 76."
- Infobox: Season 2026-27; Teams 76; Finals site Ford Field, Detroit, Michigan.

## Tournament procedure

- "On May 7, 2026, the NCAA announced that the men's and women's Division I tournaments will expand to 76 teams beginning in 2027."
- Field: 32 automatic bids to conference champions and 44 "at-large" bids (up from 36) from the selection committee, which seeds teams 1 to 76.
- "Twenty-four teams (the 12 lowest-seeded automatic qualifiers and the 12 lowest-seeded at-large teams) will compete in the 'March Madness Opening Round' (an expanded version of the First Four); the winners of these games will advance to the main 64-team bracket."

## Schedule and venues

- Opening Round, March 16 and 17: University of Dayton Arena, Dayton, Ohio (Host: University of Dayton); Intrust Bank Arena, Wichita, Kansas (Host: Wichita State University).
- First and second rounds, March 18 and 20: PPG Paints Arena, Pittsburgh (Host: Duquesne University); CHI Health Center Omaha (Host: Creighton University); Dickies Arena, Fort Worth (Host: University of North Texas); Numerica Veterans Arena, Spokane (Host: University of Idaho).
- First and second rounds, March 19 and 21: Spectrum Center, Charlotte (Hosts: UNC Charlotte / Atlantic Coast Conference); Target Center, Minneapolis (Host: University of Minnesota); KFC Yum! Center, Louisville (Host: University of Louisville); Golden 1 Center, Sacramento (Host: California State University, Sacramento).
- Regional semifinals and finals (Sweet Sixteen and Elite Eight), March 25 and 27: South Regional at Frost Bank Center, San Antonio (Host: University of Texas at San Antonio); West Regional at Crypto.com Arena, Los Angeles (Host: Pepperdine University).
- Regionals, March 26 and 28: Midwest Regional at T-Mobile Center, Kansas City (Host: Big 12 Conference); East Regional at Madison Square Garden, New York (Hosts: Big East Conference / St. John's University).
- National semifinals and championship game (Final Four), April 3 and 5: Ford Field, Detroit (Host: Michigan State University).
- "Detroit will host the Final Four for the second time, having previously hosted in 2009."

## Media coverage

wikis.title: Google map of the Annular Solar Eclipse of 2027 Feb 06
wikis.summary: NASA eclipse-site page with an interactive Google map of the path of the Annular Solar Eclipse of 2027 Feb 06, giving its Greatest Duration of 07m53.5s and how to read the map.
wikis.body:
## What the page is

- An interactive Google map on NASA's eclipse site (Goddard Space Flight Center) showing the path of the **Annular Solar Eclipse of 2027 Feb 06**: "This interactive Google map shows the path of the Annular Solar Eclipse of 2027 Feb 06."
- Page title: "NASA - Annular Solar Eclipse of 2027 Feb 06". The page requires Javascript and lists tested browsers (Firefox 3.5+, Chrome 4+, Safari 4+, Opera 10.5+, Explorer 8+, and mobile Safari/Chrome/Opera Mini/Android builds).

## What the map shows

- Northern and southern path limits are blue, the central line is red. "You MUST be somewhere within the central path (between the blue lines) to see the annular phase of the eclipse." The eclipse is longest on the central line.
- Yellow lines crossing the path "indicate the time and position of maximum eclipse at 10-minute intervals".
- A green marker labelled GE marks the point of Greatest Eclipse; a magenta marker labelled GD marks the point of Greatest Duration, "the location where the annular eclipse lasts the longest along the entire path".
- **"In this case, the Greatest Duration is 07m53.5s."**
- Clicking the map adds a red marker whose popup gives Latitude, Longitude, Eclipse Type (total, annular or partial), Duration of Totality (or Annularity), Eclipse Magnitude ("the fraction of the Sun's diameter eclipsed") and Eclipse Obscuration ("the fraction of the Sun's area eclipsed"), plus a table of event times in Universal Time with the Sun's altitude and azimuth (azimuth measured from due North eastward: North = 0°, East = 90°, South = 180°, West = 270°).
- Maximum zoom is limited to "~1 mile/inch (~0.7 kilometers/centimeter)" because the curved path is approximated in segments; a Maximum Zoom link disables the limit.

## Prediction basis and caveats

- "Predictions for the Annular Solar Eclipse of 2027 Feb 06 were generated using the VSOP87/ELP2000-85 solar and lunar ephemerides and a value of ΔT = 71.6 seconds."
- The predictions "DO NOT include the effects of mountains and valleys along the edge of the Moon". Lunar-limb corrections "may change the contact times and eclipse durations by ~1-3 seconds" and the exact location of Greatest Duration "by ~10-20 kilometers"; the page's other note says limb corrections "may shift the limits of the eclipse path north or south by ~1-3 kilometers, and change the eclipse duration by ~1-3 seconds".
- "More detailed predictions including the effects of the lunar limb profile are normally posted 12-18 months before each eclipse".
- Advice given: you can be hundreds of miles from the point of Greatest Duration and still enjoy annularity "lasting within a fraction of a second of the maximum possible (as long as you stay within several miles of the central line)", and "better to see a shorter eclipse from clear sky that a longer eclipse under clouds".

## Related pages and credit

- Links offered for this eclipse: Orthographic Map, Google Map, Animated Map, Path Table, Besselian Elements Table, Saros 131 Table.
- "All eclipse calculations are by Fred Espenak, and he assumes full responsibility for their accuracy." Reproduction is permitted with the acknowledgment "Eclipse Predictions by Fred Espenak, NASA's GSFC".
- Other interactive Google eclipse maps by Xavier Jubier are noted in a footnote.
- The page ends with the unlabelled date "2014 Mar 14".

wikis.title: RTS Link fares to be presented to Singapore and Johor governments; January 2027 opening unaffected by energy crisis
wikis.summary: AsiaOne report on Malaysian Transport Minister Anthony Loke's update on the Johor Bahru-Singapore RTS Link: opening still January 2027, proposed fares going to both governments in the third quarter.
wikis.body:
## What the minister said

- The Johor Bahru-Singapore Rapid Transit System Link (RTS Link) is "on track for opening in January 2027 despite the ongoing global energy crisis", said Malaysian Transport Minister Anthony Loke.
- Fares are "to be presented to both the Singapore and Malaysian governments in the third quarter of this year".
- Loke spoke during a site visit at the Bukit Chagar Customs, Immigration and Quarantine (CIQ) complex on Friday (April 3). Later in the same article the page calls it "the ICQ building".
- Quote: "So far, I am confident that costs remain within original estimates."
- The project "has remained on schedule, with no requests for cost revisions received from contractors involved".

## Construction status

- "Physical construction is nearly completed", with work presently focused on installation and integration testing.
- Installation of e-gates at the ICQ building is complete; works are now turning to installation of body and baggage scanners.
- The project "will next move into the final field readiness stage which involves system installation, acceptance testing, integration and dynamic testing".

## Fares

- Operator RTS Operations (RTSO) will present the proposed fare rates to both governments before they are announced, to obtain agreement from the Land Public Transport Agency of Malaysia and the Land Transport Authority of Singapore.
- "Earlier in February, Loke had suggested that fares could be priced around $5 to $7 per trip."
- On a season pass for frequent cross-border travellers, Loke said this is an issue of commercial viability to be discussed with RTSO.

## The service

- Once passenger service begins, the 4km shuttle runs from Woodlands North station to Bukit Chagar station.
- Maximum speed 80kmh; capacity up to 10,000 passengers per hour in each direction.

Published April 04, 2026 2:00 AM by Sean Ler.

wikis.title: Egypt's Toshka Project: a 310 km river into the Sahara
wikis.summary: Overengineered documentary on the Toshka (New Valley) Project, the canal taking Lake Nasser water 310 km west into the Sahara, and the debate over whether it has worked.
wikis.body:
## The project

- "How Egypt is digging a 310 km river into the Sahara Desert, and why it has taken almost thirty years."
- "Around 95% of Egyptians live on roughly 5% of Egypt's land", packed into the Nile valley and delta, "a green strip a few kilometres wide". "The population keeps growing. The green strip does not."
- "The Toshka Project, also known as the New Valley Project, pulls water from Lake Nasser behind the Aswan High Dam, lifts it with the Mubarak Pumping Station, and pushes it west into open Sahara Desert through the Sheikh Zayed Canal."
- Plan: "irrigate desert, create farmland where none has ever existed, and build a second inhabited valley parallel to the Nile".
- "Construction on this 310 km desert river began in the 1990s. It is still underway today."

## The debate the video sets out

- "Original targets for reclaimed desert farmland and resettled population were enormous. Actual delivery has come in far below those targets, over a much longer timeline, at very high cost."
- "Persuading private investors to farm remote Sahara Desert has proven difficult. Several reclaimed areas have struggled with soil quality and salinity."
- "Digging a river into the Sahara does not create new water. It relocates Nile water that was already allocated, into a desert where evaporation rates are extreme, in a country whose Nile share is fixed by agreement and increasingly contested as upstream nations build their own dams."
- "That argument about Egypt, the Nile and the Sahara is not settled, and this documentary presents both sides of it."

## Chapters

00:00 Introduction: A River in the Sahara; 01:40 Egypt's Farmland & Population Crisis; 03:27 The Toshka Project Plan; 05:24 Building the Lake Nasser Pumping Station; 08:50 Excavating 310 km of Desert Canal; 12:06 Blasting Through the Granite Ridge; 13:48 Blocking Saline Groundwater; 15:43 Concrete Lining in 50C Heat; 18:07 Desert Irrigation & Soil Preparation; 21:16 Water Reaches Toshka: The First Harvest; 23:03 Battling Soil Salinization & Drainage; 25:52 Transforming the Sahara (Satellite View); 26:52 Project Delays, Costs & Reality Check; 27:54 Conclusion & Next Megaproject.

Channel: Overengineered. Published 2026-09-11. The page gives no cost figure or hectare target in numbers.

wikis.title: Golden Gate Bridge vs Millau Viaduct (Legends vs Modern Icons)
wikis.summary: YouTube page for a Free Documentary - Engineering episode comparing San Francisco's Golden Gate Bridge with France's Millau Viaduct.
wikis.body:
## What the page is

- YouTube video "Golden Gate Bridge vs Millau Viaduct | Legends vs Modern Icons | FD Engineering", channel Free Documentary - Engineering, published 2023-05-26.
- Format: "A contest of superlatives! Two opponents. Three categories. And... lots of surprises." The questions posed are which bridge has the most groundbreaking design, how difficult the structures were to build, and how the bridges compete in practice.
- Other listed episodes: Ports, Towers, Stadiums, Planes, Skyscrapers.

## Figures given

- Golden Gate Bridge: span 1,280 m; 227 m tall; held the record as the world's longest suspension bridge for 27 years.
- Millau Viaduct: height 343 m; length 2,460 m.

wikis.title: Golden Gate Bridge
wikis.summary: The San Francisco suspension bridge presented as the 'legend' of the episode.
wikis.body:
- "THE landmark of San Francisco. An architectural masterpiece."
- Span of 1,280 metres; "it held the record being the longest suspension bridge of the world for an impressive twenty-seven years".
- "At two hundred and twenty-seven meters tall, it is more than huge."
- "Its construction was nothing less than a technical miracle. To build such a large bridge over the open sea, in the middle of an earthquake zone - that was an unimaginable risk."
- Called "the most famous bridge in the world - a genuine legend".

wikis.title: Millau Viaduct
wikis.summary: The French bridge set against the Golden Gate Bridge.
wikis.body:
- "A bridge of superlatives in the hearth of France."
- Height of 343 metres - "higher than the Eiffel Tower".
- Length of 2,460 metres - "longer than the Champs-Elysees".
- "It is the tallest bridge in the world and yet appears graceful and almost weightless."
- "Building this giant was only possible by state-of the-art technology and courageous engineers."
