wikis.title: Meta Connect 2026 date and teased smart glasses
wikis.summary: Tom's Guide news report that Meta Connect 2026 is set for September 23-24, 2026 in San Francisco, with Mark Zuckerberg's Instagram teaser slides hinting at new smart glasses.
wikis.body:
## The event

- Meta's annual consumer show for 2026 "is set to take place **September 23 and 24, 2026**".
- Announced by Meta CEO **Mark Zuckerberg** on his Instagram page, in several teaser slides.
- "Based on a map slide, it looks like Meta Connect 2026 will take place in the same building that last year's edition was held in, in **San Francisco**."
- "The final slide reveals that the Keynote should kick off at **4 pm Pacific on Wednesday, September 23**."

## The teaser slides

- One slide shows a sunglasses emoji above "demos, special guests, AI updates, better wifi", plus "a poorly blurred word, which appears to be 'performance.'"
- The next slide shows Zuckerberg holding "what are clearly glasses, colored over with a blue pen"; other devices on the table "appear to be more glasses, and maybe a puck of some kind".

## What the article expects (rumour)

- Something with smart glasses will debut; "One rumor from March hinted at Ray-Ban Meta glasses finally designed for prescription lenses that could launch this year."
- "Early rumors this year suggest that Meta is looking to challenge Apple with its own smartwatch this year" - possibly what "performance" refers to. The watch is "reportedly code-named **Malibu 2**" and would offer a Meta AI assistant.
- Meta "has insisted that the **Quest 4** headset is still coming"; Meta CTO **Andrew Bosworth** "confirmed the rumored headset will launch at some point in February".
- A render leaked earlier in the year appeared to show mock-ups of prototype lightweight VR HMDs, "though that device isn't supposed to launch until 2027".

wikis.title: Leaked Intel Core Ultra 400 'Nova Lake' launch schedule
wikis.summary: Tom's Hardware news report on a leaked slide setting Intel Nova Lake-S mass production in Q4 2026 and a staggered Core Ultra 400 desktop launch starting with a 28-core SKU in Q1 2027.
wikis.body:
## Schedule (all reported from a leaked slide)

- Intel is "reportedly on track to start mass production of its Nova Lake-S CPUs in the fourth quarter of 2026, according to a slide published by @wxnod".
- "only the 28-core version will launch in the first quarter of 2027, with the 52-core model arriving later in the year".
- "Some rumors pointing to a timeframe between late May and September, 2027" for the flagship 52-core model.
- Earlier leaks and roadmap disclosures across 2025 also placed mass production in Q4 2026, "so the new slide confirms that plan".
- Normally Intel launches flagship and unlocked models first; reports suggest the 52-core model "will fit in a different class above a typical flagship, primarily targeting the HEDT crowd".
- The slide "does not look like an official Intel roadmap or an Intel presentation slide"; the article's "more plausible explanation" is a motherboard maker's or OEM partner's presentation, "which means that while it is most likely accurate, it is not final".
- The embedded post is dated September 3, 2026.

## Reported Nova Lake-S specifications

- Up to **52 cores** on the range-topping part, using **two compute tiles**; Core Ultra 7 400-series projected up to **44 cores**, also two compute tiles. Exact configurations "currently unknown".
- Core mix: up to **16 Coyote Cove** high-performance cores with 16MB of L2 cache, up to **32 Arctic Wolf** energy-efficient cores, and up to **four low-power Arctic Wolf** cores.
- Each pair of Coyote Cove cores reportedly shares a **2 MB L2 cache** (a commenter disputes this, saying "It's 2MB per P-core, but they're clustered in pairs so each has access up to 4MB").
- **bLLC (big Last Level Cache)** scaling to **288 MB**, described as Intel's answer to AMD's X3D gaming CPUs.
- CPUs with two compute chiplets "will reportedly consume up to 474W of power and will require motherboards featuring three 12V EPS power plugs".
- I/O: dual-channel DDR5 supporting up to **DDR5-8000**, up to **24 PCIe 5.0 lanes** from the CPU (16 for graphics, splittable into two x8 or four x4, plus two x4 links for SSDs).

## Platform

- Requires Intel's new **900-series chipsets** and the **LGA1954** socket, according to leaks.
- Intel "reportedly intends to keep LGA1954 around for a longer time than it usually does with its sockets"; Z990 motherboards with LGA1954 have already been seen.

## Successors

- The slide lists **Razor Lake** and **Hammer Lake** processors succeeding Nova Lake-S "sometime after the fourth quarter of 2027", with no technical details given.

wikis.title: Nova Lake (microprocessor)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia stub article on Intel's upcoming Nova Lake / Core Ultra Series 4 desktop and mobile processors, covering socket, microarchitectures, instruction-set extensions and expected launch timing.
wikis.body:
## Overview

- "Nova Lake is a codename for **Core Ultra Series 4** desktop and mobile processors developed by **Intel**."
- "Nova Lake is expected to use a new **LGA 1954** socket."
- "The first Nova Lake processors are expected to launch in **late 2026**."
- "Nova Lake is expected to be the first consumer platform to support **AVX10.1, AVX10.2 and APX** extensions."
- "Nova Lake is expected to include SKUs with **bLLC (big Last Level Cache)**, to compete with AMD's 3D V-Cache after a long period of lagging behind in gaming benchmarks."
- Marked as a computer hardware stub.

## Infobox

- Marketed by / designed by / common manufacturer: Intel. CPUID code and product code: "Unknown".
- Application: Desktop and mobile. GPU: **Intel Arc**. Socket: LGA 1954.
- Technology node: **Intel 18A**.
- Microarchitecture: **Coyote Cove** (P-cores), **Arctic Wolf** (E-cores).
- Instruction set x86-64; instructions IA-32, x86-64. Extensions listed: MMX, SSE, SSE2, SSE3, SSSE3, SSE4.1, SSE4.2, AVX, AVX2, AVX10.2, APX, AES-NI, SHA-NI, RDRAND, SM3, SM4, VT-x, VT-d.
- Brand name: Core Ultra. Support status: Supported.
- Predecessors: **Panther Lake** (mobile) and **Arrow Lake** (desktop and mobile). Successor: **Razor Lake** (desktop and mobile).

## Disagreements within the page

- **Process node**: the infobox gives the technology node as "Intel 18A"; the "Intel CPU core roadmaps" navbox at the foot of the page instead lists Nova Lake under "**Intel 18A and/or TSMC N2P**".
- **Extensions**: the prose says Nova Lake is expected to be the first consumer platform to support "AVX10.1, AVX10.2 and APX", but the infobox extensions list includes AVX10.2 and APX and does not list AVX10.1.
- **GPU**: the infobox gives "Intel Arc"; a cited reference title (TechSpot, 2025-10-24) says "up to 52 cores, **Xe3 GPU**, and LGA 1954 socket". The article body itself gives no core count.

## Cited sources (reference list)

- TechSpot, Skye Jacobs, 2025-03-30: "Intel's comeback plan: Panther Lake in 2025, Nova Lake in 2026, says CEO Lip-Bu Tan".
- Tom's Hardware, Hassam Nasir, 2025-10-03: official confirmation of the Nova Lake and Diamond Rapids microarchitectures via an ISA reference document.
- TechSpot, Kishalaya Kundu, 2025-10-24: "Intel confirms Nova Lake CPU launch in 2026".
- Tom's Hardware, Jon Martindale, September 10, 2025: "Intel confirms Arrow Lake refresh set for 2026, Nova Lake later that year".
- Intel, "Intel Architecture Instruction Set Extensions and Future Features" (PDF), November 10, 2025.
- wccftech.com on Nova Lake Core Ultra Series 4 desktop CPU die SKUs.

wikis.title: Amazon Leo approaches its initial service launch
wikis.summary: Light Reading news report that Amazon Leo, after targeting a 'mid-2026' launch, now says its constellation and deployment pace put commercial service on a path to 'later this year'.
wikis.body:
## Timing

- Headline framing: "After saying it was targeting a 'mid-2026' initial service launch, Amazon Leo now says its current LEO satellite constellation and deployment pace puts it on a path to launch services 'later this year.'"
- Amazon CEO **Andy Jassy** declared in May that Amazon Leo was targeting a "mid-2026" service launch; a few weeks earlier another Amazon exec said the initial launch was "months away".
- "the exact timing remains somewhat squishy" but the debut is "evidently still on track to happen later in 2026".

## Satellites and launches

- Amazon Leo announced "last week" it had deployed **396 satellites**, after launch partner **United Launch Alliance (ULA)** deployed **29 more** on **July 2**. That was "the last mission for its launch campaign with ULA's Atlas V rocket".
- Melissa Wuerl, Amazon Leo's director of launch systems: "Atlas V has played a critical role in the early deployment phase for Amazon Leo, launching **224 satellites** with a 100% success rate across all eight missions, and we're excited to build on that foundation with ULA as we transition to Vulcan." She cites "hundreds of flight-ready satellites standing by at the Cape and a new, dedicated vertical integration facility ready to support **Leo Vulcan 1**".
- The next ULA mission uses the heavy-lift **Vulcan** rocket, "capable of delivering 40-plus satellites into low-Earth orbit".
- Chris Weber, lead exec for Amazon Leo's consumer, enterprise and government businesses, said on X that last week's launches provide enough satellites "to support continuous service across initial latitudes" and "we've completed enough launches for initial service this yr, and future missions just add coverage and capacity", with "lots of work ahead - including raising all these new satellites to their assigned altitude".
- Launch partners: ULA, **Arianespace** and Jeff Bezos's **Blue Origin**. Blue Origin's New Glenn "recently had a setback when one exploded during a prelaunch test".

## Regulatory and customers

- The **FCC** approved a **24-month extension** on the first half of the constellation, which "eventually will span **3,236 LEO satellites**"; the 100% deployment milestone of **July 30, 2029** is retained.
- In its original extension request, Amazon "expected to deploy about 700 satellites by the end of July 2026".
- Amazon Leo is serving beta customers and "has not announced pricing plans" or where services will first be available. It has contracts with **JetBlue** and **Delta Airlines** and "recently signed a deal with **AT&T**".

## Globalstar deal and direct-to-device

- "In April, Amazon cut a deal to acquire **Globalstar** for about **$11.6 billion**." A linked related headline on the same page instead says "Amazon nets Globalstar for **$11.5B**, signs new Apple pact".
- "The transaction is expected to close in **2027**"; petitions to deny were due at the FCC "today (July 6)".
- Once closed, the deal would accelerate Amazon Leo's expansion into direct-to-device (D2D), "gain a key client in Apple, and bring more competition to Starlink".
- Amazon Leo's D2D system is "currently slated for a **2028** launch", supported by existing Gen 1 satellites and future generations.

wikis.title: Leaker claims PS6 and Xbox “Project Helix” still set for 2027 launch
wikis.summary: Sportskeeda news report relaying leaker Kepler_L2's claim that the PlayStation 6 and the next Xbox, codenamed “Project Helix”, remain on track for Holiday 2027 despite reports of a delay.
wikis.body:
## What the page reports

- Byline: Suraj Bhowal. "Published Mar 14, 2026 23:08 IST". Edited by Sijo Samuel Paul.
- The article carries its own caveat: "Note : This article is based on a third-party report, so users are advised to take it with a grain of salt."

## Conflicting launch windows

- "In mid-February 2026, Bloomberg suggested that next-gen PS6 and Xbox “Project Helix” consoles would be delayed to 2028 or 2029 due to the current memory crisis."
- The page says that report "conflicted with previous claims from prominent leakers Kepler_L2 and Moore's Law Is Dead, who suggested a 2027 launch".
- "However, Kepler_L2 has reiterated that the PS6 and Xbox consoles will arrive in 2027."

## Kepler_L2's quotes

- Replying to a question about the launch window: "Both Xbox and PS6 are still in track for Holiday 2027."
- On the chance of slippage: "It's possible for things to be delayed but very unlikely at this point. The RAM/NAND situation is bad but has mostly stabilized and will likely be at least a little bit better by the end of 2027."
- The article's reading: the RAM/NAND situation is bad but has stabilised enough for a 2027 launch, and a delayed launch is "very unlikely".

## Hardware claims

- Moore's Law Is Dead "suggests both the next-gen Xbox “Project Helix” console and Sony PlayStation 6 will be based on the AMD RDNA 5-based graphics architecture".
- The same leaker "claims the Xbox “Project Helix” console’s GPU will have more Compute Cores, making it more powerful than the PS6".

## Illustrations

- Images credited to Sony: the DualSense controller buttons, and the PlayStation 5 Pro console.

wikis.title: The Chronicles of Narnia: The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe (2005 film)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia's article on the 2005 Disney and Walden Media film of The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe - its credits and plot, casting and New Zealand shoot, Harry Gregson-Williams's score, the Royal Film Performance premiere, $745 million box office, reviews, awards and home video.
wikis.body:
## Infobox

- **The Chronicles of Narnia: The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe**, "2005 film by Andrew Adamson". Directed by **Andrew Adamson**; screenplay by **Ann Peacock, Andrew Adamson, Christopher Markus and Stephen McFeely**; based on *The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe* by **C. S. Lewis**.
- Produced by Mark Johnson and Phillip Steuer. Cinematography **Donald McAlpine**; edited by **Sim Evan-Jones and Jim May**; music by **Harry Gregson-Williams**.
- Production companies **Walt Disney Pictures**, **Walden Media** and **Mark Johnson Productions**; distributed by **Buena Vista Pictures Distribution**.
- Release dates **7 December 2005** (Royal Film Performance), **8 December 2005** (United Kingdom), **9 December 2005** (United States). Running time **143 minutes**; countries United Kingdom and United States; language English.
- Budget **$180 million**; box office **$745 million**.
- Starring Georgie Henley, Skandar Keynes, William Moseley, Anna Popplewell, Tilda Swinton, James McAvoy, Jim Broadbent and Liam Neeson.

## Lead

- A 2005 high fantasy film based on the 1950 novel, "the first published and second chronological novel" in *The Chronicles of Narnia*, and the first instalment in the film series.
- The Pevensie children, evacuated during the Blitz, find a wardrobe leading to Narnia and ally with the lion **Aslan** (Liam Neeson) against **Jadis, the White Witch** (Tilda Swinton).
- Premiered 7 December 2005 as the Royal Film Performance; released 8 December in the UK and 9 December in the US. "The film was a critical and commercial success, grossing $745 million worldwide against a $180 million budget and becoming the third-highest-grossing film of 2005."
- An extended edition was released on DVD on **12 December 2006**. "Combining both releases of the film, in regular and extended edition, it was the third-best-selling and first-highest-grossing DVD in North America in 2006, taking in $332.7 million that year."
- Awards: won **Best Makeup** at the 78th Academy Awards, with nominations for Best Sound Mixing and Best Visual Effects; won **Best Makeup and Hair** at the 59th BAFTAs, with nominations for Best Costume Design and Best Special Visual Effects; Golden Globe nominations for Best Original Score and Best Original Song ("Wunderkind" by Alanis Morissette); Grammy nominations for the score and for "Can't Take It In" by Imogen Heap.
- Followed by *Prince Caspian* (2008) and *The Voyage of the Dawn Treader* (2010) "to diminishing critical and financial reception"; the three films grossed **$1.5 billion** worldwide.

## Where the article states things two ways

- **DVD ranking for 2006**: the lead says the two editions combined made it "the third-best-selling and first-highest-grossing DVD in North America in 2006, taking in $332.7 million that year"; the Home media section says the DVD "overtook Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire to become the top-selling DVD in North America for 2006" and that "As of December 2008, it has grossed $353.5 million in DVD sales, equivalent to 12,458,637 units sold".
- **Rank in 2005**: the lead calls it the third-highest-grossing film of 2005 (worldwide, as the box office section confirms), while the United States and Canada section says it was "the second-highest-grossing film of 2005 behind Star Wars: Episode III - Revenge of the Sith" on **$291.7 million** domestically.
- **Walden Media record**: the box office section says it is "the most successful film of Walden Media worldwide", and the US and Canada section repeats "it is the largest film of Walden Media worldwide".
- The accolades section carries an unsourced-material tag dated August 2019.

## Plot (as summarised in the article)

- September 1940: after the Blitz, the Pevensie children - Peter, Susan, Edmund and Lucy - are evacuated from London to Professor Kirke's country home.
- Lucy hides in a wardrobe during hide-and-seek and enters a magical winter world, meeting the faun **Mr. Tumnus**, who admits he meant to hand her to the White Witch, Jadis, who has cursed Narnia to "an eternal winter with no Christmas", and sends her home instead.
- Edmund follows Lucy back and meets Jadis, who claims to be Queen of Narnia and, with her servant Ginarrbrik, offers him Turkish delight and kingship for his siblings. He then denies Narnia to spite Lucy, though Professor Kirke suggests she is telling the truth.
- Fleeing the housekeeper after breaking a window, all four enter Narnia. Talking beavers tell them Aslan plans to return, and of the prophecy that when "two sons of Adam and two daughters of Eve sit on the thrones of Cair Paravel", Jadis's reign will end.
- Edmund is imprisoned by Jadis, who sends wolves led by Maugrim after the others and turns Tumnus to stone. **Father Christmas** gives Lucy a dagger and a healing cordial, Susan a horn and bow, and Peter a sword and shield. Peter kills Maugrim; Aslan's troops rescue Edmund.
- Jadis claims Edmund under "a blood contract law"; Aslan secretly offers himself and is killed at the Stone Table, then resurrected "citing magic beyond Jadis' understanding", and frees the petrified Narnians in her castle.
- In the battle, Edmund is mortally wounded breaking Jadis's wand; Aslan arrives with the restored Narnians and kills Jadis; Susan shoots Ginarrbrik and Lucy heals Edmund. The four are crowned Peter the Magnificent, Susan the Gentle, Edmund the Just and Lucy the Valiant.
- Fifteen years later, hunting a white stag, the adult siblings find the lamppost and return through the wardrobe as children. Asked why they were in it, Peter says Kirke would not believe them; he replies, "Try me." In a mid-credit scene Kirke tells Lucy they will probably return to Narnia when they least expect it.

## Cast

- **Georgie Henley** (Lucy), with Rachael Henley - her real-life sister - as adult Lucy; **Skandar Keynes** (Edmund), with Mark Wells as the adult; **William Moseley** (Peter), with Noah Huntley; **Anna Popplewell** (Susan), with Sophie Winkleman.
- **Liam Neeson** voices Aslan; **Tilda Swinton** is Jadis; **James McAvoy** is Mr. Tumnus; **Jim Broadbent** is Professor Digory Kirke; **Ray Winstone** and **Dawn French** voice Mr. and Mrs. Beaver; **Kiran Shah** is Ginarrbrik; Elizabeth Hawthorne is Mrs. Macready; **James Cosmo** is Father Christmas; **Michael Madsen** voices Maugrim (uncredited); Patrick Kake is General Oreius; Shane Rangi is General Otmin; Judy McIntosh is Helen Pevensie; **Rupert Everett** voices Mr. Fox; producer Philip Steuer voices Phillip, Edmund's talking horse.
- The radio announcer is **Douglas Gresham**, co-producer and C. S. Lewis's stepson. Keynes's voice broke during filming, so some of his track was re-looped by his sister Soumaya. The father glimpsed in a photo is editor Sim Evan-Jones's father.
- Casting: Tilda Swinton was the first choice for Jadis; otherwise, from 2002, Adamson "went through 2,500 audition tapes, met 1,800 children and workshopped 400" before choosing the Pevensies. Moseley and Popplewell were found at the very start, Henley and Keynes late. Moseley was remembered by casting director Pippa Hall from *Cider with Rosie* (1998), beat 3,000 boys and quit school to learn his lines.
- Aslan's voice: **Brian Cox** was cast on **9 December 2004** before Adamson changed his mind; **Liam Neeson** sought the role and was announced on **17 July 2005**.

## Pre-production

- In the early 1990s Frank Marshall and Kathleen Kennedy planned a film version; they could not find UK studio space in 1996, and their plan to set it in modern times drew Douglas Gresham's opposition, as did his feeling that technology had not caught up.
- Perry Moore began negotiations with the C. S. Lewis estate in 2000; **Walden Media announced on 7 December 2001** that it had the rights. Directors discussed included **Rob Minkoff, John Boorman and David Fincher**; **Guillermo del Toro** turned it down for *Pan's Labyrinth*. On **1 March 2004** Disney agreed with Walden Media to co-produce and finance this and all future Narnia films.
- *Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone*'s success let the producers keep the story British. Mark Johnson: "When The Lion, The Witch and the Wardrobe was being developed at Paramount, the imperative was to set it in the U.S., and it just doesn't hold. [...] It's not the book."
- After winning an Academy Award for *Shrek*, Adamson wrote a 20-page treatment from memory, which is why the film opens with the Luftwaffe bombing and ends with an enormous battle, neither of which take much space in the novel.
- Other changes: the battle is shown from the start rather than only on Aslan's arrival; an accident with a window sends all four children into the wardrobe; Tumnus meets Edmund, which he does not do until the novel's end; the mother is named Helen after Georgie Henley's own mother; Finchley was chosen because Anna Popplewell is from there; Lucy finds the wardrobe while looking for a hiding place; the carved wardrobe and Kirke's reactions hint at *The Magician's Nephew*; and the children's father is fighting in the war rather than in London.
- Design: Wētā Workshop head **Richard Taylor** cited Hieronymus Bosch's *The Garden of Earthly Delights*, and felt Narnia had to be less dark and gritty than their Middle-earth. Many creature designs were made for digital creation, so **Howard Berger** and KNB FX spent three months retooling them for animatronics; Berger's children suggested changing the White Witch's hair from black to blonde because Swinton's wig looked "too Gothic".

## Filming

- Principal photography began in New Zealand on **28 June 2004**, shot largely in chronological order so the young actors' development would mirror their characters'. Henley and Keynes were not shown the Narnia set beforehand, and Henley had not seen McAvoy in his Tumnus costume.
- The first scene shot was the railway scene at the former RNZAF Base Hobsonville, followed by the Blitz scene, which Adamson called their first formal day.
- New Zealand's Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry refused permission to import twelve reindeer, citing **Q fever** in the North American population, though ten wolves and wolf hybrids were allowed into Auckland. Mark Rappaport's Creature Effects, Inc. built four animatronic reindeer with replaceable skins - brown for Father Christmas, white for the White Witch.
- After Auckland the production moved to the South Island in November: **Flock Hill** in Canterbury, and **Elephant Rocks** near Duntroon in North Otago as Aslan's camp; the castle scene was shot at **Purakaunui Bay** in the Catlins.
- After the Christmas break they filmed in the **Czech Republic** (Prague and České Švýcarsko National Park), **Slovenia** and **Poland**, wrapping in February.
- A sequence of creatures set on fire was reportedly removed to secure a PG rating from the MPAA.

## Music

- Score composed and conducted by **Harry Gregson-Williams**, who had worked with Adamson on *Shrek* (2001) and *Shrek 2* (2004). Three original songs appear: "Can't Take It In" (**Imogen Heap**), "**Wunderkind**" (**Alanis Morissette**) and "Winter Light" (**Tim Finn**). Evanescence's Amy Lee also wrote a song that was not included.
- Recorded at Abbey Road Studios and in Los Angeles with the 75-piece Hollywood Studio Symphony Orchestra, a 140-member choir (mostly the Bach Choir), electric violinist Hugh Marsh and vocalist Lisbeth Scott. Gregson-Williams conducted from late September to early November 2005, used ancient folk instruments "for colour", added choral textures and solo voice at dramatic moments, and included electronic music.
- EMI released a separate compilation, *Music Inspired by The Chronicles of Narnia*, in September 2005, with contemporary Christian artists including Bethany Dillon, Kutless and Nichole Nordeman, the single "Waiting for the World to Fall" by Jars of Clay, and it won Special Event Album of the Year at the GMA Music Awards.
- "**Lazy Sunday**" ("The Narnia rap") by The Lonely Island and Chris Parnell, a 2005 *Saturday Night Live* sketch spoofing hardcore rap in which Parnell and Andy Samberg rap about seeing the film at a matinee, became "an overnight hit", is credited with helping revive SNL, and its bootleg uploads to the newly launched YouTube drew a combined five million views, bringing "widespread attention to YouTube".

## Release and box office

- World premiere in London on **7 December 2005** as the **59th Royal Film Performance**, in aid of The Film and Television Charity, at the Royal Albert Hall, attended by the then Prince of Wales and Duchess of Cornwall. Released 8 December in the UK and 9 December in North America and the rest of Europe.
- Worldwide **$745 million**, the 55th-highest-grossing film of all time worldwide, with a worldwide opening of **$107.1 million** - Disney's fifth-largest opening worldwide (the largest at the time). It is the third-largest 2005 release worldwide, the highest-grossing Narnia film worldwide and in both North America and overseas, and Walden Media's most successful film.
- United States and Canada: opened with **$23 million** on around 6,800 screens at 3,616 theatres on Friday 9 December 2005, averaging $6,363 per theatre. Opening weekend **$65.6 million**, then the 24th-best opening weekend (now 54th), Disney's third-largest at the time (now 34th), and the second-biggest December opening behind *The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King* - now fourth, behind *The Hobbit: An Unexpected Journey*, *I Am Legend* and *Avatar*.
- Domestic total **$291.7 million**, second for 2005 behind *Revenge of the Sith*, ahead of *Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire* "by only $1.7 million", though that film made $895.9 million worldwide. It is the highest-grossing film of the 2005 holiday period, the second-highest-grossing Christian film, the sixth-largest family-children's book adaptation, the ninth-highest-grossing fantasy live-action film and the 10th-highest-grossing film in Disney company history. Box Office Mojo estimates over **45 million** tickets sold in North America.
- First Lady Laura Bush hosted a screening at the White House Family Theater.

## Critical reception

- Rotten Tomatoes **76%** from 216 reviews, average 7.1/10; consensus: "With first-rate special effects and compelling storytelling, this adaptation stays faithful to its source material and will please moviegoers of all ages." Metacritic **75 out of 100** from 39 critics. CinemaScore reported "a rare 'A+' grade".
- Roger Ebert 3/4; Ebert and Roeper "Two Thumbs Up"; Leonard Maltin 3/4, "an impressive and worthwhile family film", though "it does go on a bit and the special effects are extremely variable"; Duane Dudak (Milwaukee Journal Sentinel) 3/4; Stuart Klawans (The Nation): "All ticket buyers will get their money's worth"; Elizabeth Weitzman (New York Daily News) 4/4, "A generation-spanning journey that feels both comfortingly familiar and excitingly original"; Mick LaSalle (San Francisco Chronicle) listed it as the second best film of the year; Kit Bowen 3/4.
- John Anderson (Newsday) was negative: "there's a deliberateness, a fastidiousness and a lack of daring and vision that marks the entire operation."

## Accolades

- **Wins**: Academy Award for **Best Makeup** (Howard Berger and Tami Lane); BAFTA **Best Makeup and Hair** (Howard Berger, Greg Nicotero, Nikki Gooley) and the Orange Rising Star award (James McAvoy); Satellite Award for Outstanding Motion Picture, Animated or Mixed Media; Broadcast Film Critics Association Best Family Film (Live Action); Costume Designers Guild Fantasy Film (Isis Mussenden); Saturn Awards for **Best Costume Design** (Mussenden) and **Best Make-up** (Berger, Gooley, Nicotero); Movieguide Best Film for Families and the Epiphany Prize; the CAMIE Award; the BeliefNet Film Award for Best Spiritual film; Phoenix Film Critics Society Best Performance by a Youth - Female (**Georgie Henley**); Young Artist Awards for Best Family Feature Film - Drama and Best Performance by a Young Actress Age Ten or Younger (Henley).
- **Nominations**: Academy Awards for Best Sound Mixing (Terry Porter, Dean A. Zupancic, Tony Johnson) and Best Visual Effects (Dean Wright, Bill Westenhofer, Jim Berney, Scott Farrar); BAFTAs for Special Visual Effects and Costume Design; Golden Globes for Best Original Score (Harry Gregson-Williams) and Best Original Song ("Wunderkind", Alanis Morissette); Grammys for Best Score Soundtrack Album (Gregson-Williams) and Best Song Written for Visual Media ("Can't Take It In", Imogen Heap); the Hugo Award for Best Dramatic Presentation; the Humanitas Prize; Annie Award for Best Character Animation (Matt Shumway); Australian Film Institute awards for production design (Roger Ford) and cinematography (Donald McAlpine); Empire Awards for Best Newcomer (Henley and McAvoy) and Best Sci-Fi/Fantasy; London Film Critics Circle for McAvoy and Tilda Swinton; MTV Movie Award for Best Villain; two Motion Picture Sound Editors categories; Online Film Critics Society Best Breakthrough Performance (Henley); Saturn nominations for Best Fantasy Film, Director, Writing, Actress (Swinton), Young Actor (William Moseley) and Visual Effects; two Visual Effects Society categories, including Outstanding Animated Character for "Aslan"; World Soundtrack Award for "Can't Take It In"; and a 2007 Best DVD Special Edition nomination for the Extended Edition.
- Georgie Henley "received critical acclaim for her performance as Lucy Pevensie", winning several awards for best young performance or leading actress.

## Home media

- DVD released **4 April 2006** in a one-disc set (separate full-screen and widescreen) and a deluxe two-disc widescreen boxed set. It "sold four million copies on its first day of release" and overtook *Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire* as the top-selling DVD in North America for 2006; as of December 2008 it had grossed **$353.5 million** in DVD sales, "equivalent to 12,458,637 units sold".
- A four-disc extended cut followed on **12 December 2006**, available until 31 January 2007 before Disney put it on moratorium. The extended cut "runs approximately 150 minutes" and adds "The Dreamer of Narnia", a previously unreleased feature-length film about C. S. Lewis, plus production featurettes; most of the extra footage beyond the extended battle is longer establishing shots and footage of the Pevensies walking in Narnia.
- Blu-ray released **13 May 2008** in the United States and **16 June 2008** in the United Kingdom.

wikis.title: Casting the Pevensies and Aslan
wikis.summary: The long search for four children, and the switch of Aslan's voice from Brian Cox to Liam Neeson.
wikis.body:
- Tilda Swinton was the first choice for Jadis, the White Witch; everything else took time.
- From 2002, Adamson "went through 2,500 audition tapes, met 1,800 children and workshopped 400 before coming down to the final four actors for the Pevensies". William Moseley and Anna Popplewell came from the very start of casting; Georgie Henley and Skandar Keynes were cast relatively late.
- Moseley was cast because casting director Pippa Hall remembered casting him as an extra in *Cider with Rosie* (1998); he beat 3,000 boys and quit school to learn his lines.
- **Brian Cox** was originally cast as Aslan's voice on **9 December 2004**, but Adamson changed his mind; **Liam Neeson** sought out the role and was announced on **17 July 2005**.
- Family details: Rachael Henley, Georgie's real-life sister, plays adult Lucy; Skandar Keynes's voice broke during filming, so his sister Soumaya re-looped some lines; the radio announcer is co-producer Douglas Gresham, C. S. Lewis's stepson; the photo of the children's father is of editor Sim Evan-Jones's father.

wikis.title: Getting the film made and what it changed from the book
wikis.summary: A decade of failed attempts, the Disney-Walden deal, and Adamson's departures from C. S. Lewis.
wikis.body:
- Frank Marshall and Kathleen Kennedy planned a version in the early 1990s but could not find British studio space in 1996, and their modern-day setting drew Douglas Gresham's opposition, along with his view that technology had not caught up.
- Perry Moore began talks with the C. S. Lewis estate in 2000; **Walden Media announced on 7 December 2001** that it had the rights, and considered Rob Minkoff, John Boorman and David Fincher to direct. Guillermo del Toro declined for *Pan's Labyrinth*. On **1 March 2004** Disney agreed to co-produce and finance this and all future Narnia films.
- *Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone* made a British setting possible. Mark Johnson: "When The Lion, The Witch and the Wardrobe was being developed at Paramount, the imperative was to set it in the U.S., and it just doesn't hold. [...] It's not the book."
- Adamson, fresh from an Academy Award for *Shrek*, wrote a 20-page treatment from memory - which is why the film opens on the Luftwaffe bombing and ends with a huge battle, neither prominent in the novel. He showed the battle from its start because he "could vividly remember a huge battle", an example of how Lewis left much to readers' imagination.
- Other changes: a broken window drives all four children into the wardrobe; Tumnus meets Edmund, which does not happen until the novel's end; the mother is named Helen after Georgie Henley's own mother; the Pevensies come from Finchley because Anna Popplewell does; Lucy finds the wardrobe while seeking a hiding place; the carved wardrobe and Kirke's reactions nod to *The Magician's Nephew*; and the father is fighting in the war rather than in London.

wikis.title: Filming in New Zealand and Europe
wikis.summary: The chronological shoot, the reindeer that were refused entry, and the locations used.
wikis.body:
- Principal photography began in New Zealand on **28 June 2004**, shot "in a primarily chronological order" so the young actors' maturing would mirror their characters'. Henley and Keynes were not shown the Narnia set before shooting their entrances, and Henley had not seen James McAvoy in costume as Mr. Tumnus.
- The first scene shot was the railway scene at the former RNZAF Base Hobsonville, then the Blitz scene - "their first formal day of shooting".
- New Zealand's Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry refused permission to bring in twelve reindeer for the White Witch's sledge, citing **Q fever** in the North American reindeer population; ten wolves and wolf hybrids were allowed in for filming in Auckland. Mark Rappaport's Creature Effects, Inc. built four animatronic reindeer with replaceable skins - brown for Father Christmas, white for the White Witch.
- After Auckland, the production moved to the South Island in November: **Flock Hill** in Canterbury, **Elephant Rocks** near Duntroon in North Otago as Aslan's camp, and **Purakaunui Bay** in the Catlins for the castle scene.
- After the Christmas break they shot in the **Czech Republic** (Prague and České Švýcarsko National Park), **Slovenia** and **Poland**, wrapping in February.
- Design was led by Wētā Workshop's Richard Taylor, citing Bosch's *The Garden of Earthly Delights* and deliberately keeping Narnia less dark than Middle-earth; Howard Berger's KNB FX spent three months retooling digital designs for animatronics, and Berger's children suggested making the White Witch blonde.
- In post-production a sequence of creatures set on fire was reportedly cut to secure an MPAA PG rating.

wikis.title: The score, the songs and 'Lazy Sunday'
wikis.summary: How Harry Gregson-Williams recorded the music, the three original songs, and the SNL rap that helped launch YouTube.
wikis.body:
- **Harry Gregson-Williams** composed and conducted, after *Shrek* (2001) and *Shrek 2* (2004) with Adamson.
- Three original songs feature: "Can't Take It In" (**Imogen Heap**), "**Wunderkind**" (**Alanis Morissette**) and "Winter Light" (**Tim Finn**). Evanescence's Amy Lee wrote a song that was not used.
- Recorded at Abbey Road Studios and in Los Angeles, using the 75-piece Hollywood Studio Symphony Orchestra, a 140-member choir (mostly the Bach Choir), electric violinist Hugh Marsh and vocalist Lisbeth Scott. Gregson-Williams conducted from late September to early November 2005, used ancient folk instruments "for colour", added choral textures and a solo voice at dramatic moments, and included electronic music.
- The soundtrack drew two Golden Globe nominations, Best Original Score and Best Original Song for "Wunderkind".
- EMI's separate compilation *Music Inspired by The Chronicles of Narnia*, released September 2005, featured contemporary Christian artists including Bethany Dillon, Kutless and Nichole Nordeman, with the single "Waiting for the World to Fall" by Jars of Clay; it won Special Event Album of the Year at the GMA Music Awards.
- "**Lazy Sunday**", the Lonely Island and Chris Parnell "Narnia rap" from a 2005 *Saturday Night Live* sketch, spoofs hardcore rap by having Parnell and Andy Samberg rap about a matinee of the film - Samberg calls it "two guys rapping about very lame, sensitive stuff". It became an overnight hit, is credited with helping revive SNL, and its bootleg uploads to the newly launched **YouTube** drew a combined five million views, bringing the site "widespread attention" and kick-starting its success.

wikis.title: Box office run
wikis.summary: The film's worldwide and domestic grosses and the records it set on release.
wikis.body:
- Worldwide **$745 million**, the 55th-highest-grossing film of all time worldwide, with a worldwide opening of **$107.1 million** - Disney's fifth-largest opening worldwide, the largest at the time. Third-largest worldwide among 2005 releases, the highest-grossing Narnia film worldwide and in both North America and overseas, and Walden Media's most successful film.
- United States and Canada: **$23 million** on opening day, Friday 9 December 2005, from around 6,800 screens at 3,616 theatres - $6,363 per theatre, $3,383 per screen. Opening weekend **$65.6 million**: the 24th-best at the time (now 54th), Disney's third-largest then (now 34th), the second-biggest December opening behind *The Return of the King* (now fourth, behind *The Hobbit: An Unexpected Journey*, *I Am Legend* and *Avatar*), and the third-largest opening weekend of 2005.
- Domestic total **$291.7 million**, second for 2005 behind *Star Wars: Episode III - Revenge of the Sith*, and ahead of *Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire* "by only $1.7 million" - though that film made $895.9 million worldwide.
- Further rankings claimed: highest-grossing film of the 2005 holiday period; second-highest-grossing Christian film; sixth-largest family-children's book adaptation; ninth-highest-grossing fantasy live-action film; 10th-highest-grossing film in Disney company history. Box Office Mojo estimates over **45 million** tickets sold in North America.

wikis.title: Reviews and awards
wikis.summary: Aggregate scores, what critics said, and the Oscar and BAFTA wins for makeup.
wikis.body:
- Rotten Tomatoes **76%** from 216 reviews (7.1/10); consensus: "With first-rate special effects and compelling storytelling, this adaptation stays faithful to its source material and will please moviegoers of all ages." Metacritic **75/100** from 39 critics. CinemaScore "a rare 'A+' grade".
- Roger Ebert 3/4; Ebert and Roeper "Two Thumbs Up"; Leonard Maltin 3/4 called it "an impressive and worthwhile family film" while noting "it does go on a bit and the special effects are extremely variable"; Elizabeth Weitzman (New York Daily News) 4/4; Mick LaSalle (San Francisco Chronicle) ranked it the second best film of the year. John Anderson (Newsday) objected to "a deliberateness, a fastidiousness and a lack of daring and vision".
- Won the **Academy Award for Best Makeup** (Howard Berger and Tami Lane) and the **BAFTA for Best Makeup and Hair** (Berger, Greg Nicotero, Nikki Gooley), with James McAvoy taking the BAFTA Orange Rising Star award.
- Oscar nominations for Best Sound Mixing and Best Visual Effects; BAFTA nominations for Special Visual Effects and Costume Design; Golden Globe nominations for the score and "Wunderkind"; Grammy nominations for the score and "Can't Take It In".
- Other wins include a Satellite Award, a Broadcast Film Critics Association award for Best Family Film, the Costume Designers Guild fantasy award (Isis Mussenden), Saturn Awards for costume and makeup, Movieguide's Best Film for Families and Epiphany Prize, the CAMIE Award and the BeliefNet Best Spiritual Film award.
- **Georgie Henley** "received critical acclaim" as Lucy, winning Phoenix Film Critics Society and Young Artist awards among others.

wikis.title: Home video and the extended edition
wikis.summary: The record-selling 2006 DVD, the four-disc extended cut and the Blu-ray.
wikis.body:
- DVD released **4 April 2006** as a one-disc set (separate full-screen and widescreen) and a deluxe two-disc widescreen box with extra artwork and materials from Disney and Walden Media.
- It "sold four million copies on its first day of release" and overtook *Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire* to become the top-selling DVD in North America for 2006. As of December 2008 it had grossed **$353.5 million** in DVD sales, "equivalent to 12,458,637 units sold". The article's lead instead calls the two editions combined "the third-best-selling and first-highest-grossing DVD in North America in 2006, taking in $332.7 million that year".
- A four-disc **extended cut** was released **12 December 2006** and sold until 31 January 2007, after which Disney put it on moratorium. It runs "approximately 150 minutes" against the theatrical 143, keeps the two-disc special edition features, and adds "The Dreamer of Narnia", a previously unreleased feature-length film about C. S. Lewis, plus production featurettes. Beyond the extended battle, most added footage is longer establishing shots of Narnia and the Pevensies walking.
- Blu-ray released **13 May 2008** in the United States and **16 June 2008** in the United Kingdom.

wikis.title: Kong: Skull Island (2017 film)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on Jordan Vogt-Roberts's 2017 King Kong reboot for Legendary and Warner Bros. - its 1973 Vietnam-era expedition story, cast, Apocalypse Now-inspired script, Vietnam and Hawaii shoot, $568.6 million gross and generally positive reviews.
wikis.body:
## The film

- A 2017 American monster film directed by Jordan Vogt-Roberts, produced by Legendary Pictures and distributed by Warner Bros. Pictures - "a reboot of the King Kong franchise, the second film in the Legendary's Monsterverse franchise, and the eighth film in the King Kong franchise". Screenplay by Dan Gilroy, Max Borenstein and Derek Connolly, story by John Gatins. 118 minutes; United States; English. Budget $185 million; box office $568.7 million in the infobox.
- In 1973 a team of scientists and Vietnam War soldiers travel to Skull Island and meet its monsters, including Kong. Stars Tom Hiddleston, Samuel L. Jackson, John Goodman, Brie Larson, Jing Tian, Toby Kebbell, John Ortiz, Corey Hawkins, Jason Mitchell, Shea Whigham, Thomas Mann, Terry Notary and John C. Reilly. Kong is given as "104 feet (31.7 m)-tall" and performed in motion capture by Terry Notary, with facial reference from Kebbell.

## Production

- Announced by Legendary at the 2014 San Diego Comic-Con with Universal as distributor, then moved to Warner Bros. to build a shared universe with Godzilla; Vogt-Roberts was announced as director in September 2014. Peter Jackson had earlier handpicked Adam Wingard for a sequel to his 2005 King Kong.
- Max Borenstein's script went through drafts set in the present day and in 1917 before Vogt-Roberts pitched the end of the Vietnam War; Borenstein's paradigm was Apocalypse Now. Dan Gilroy and Derek Connolly also wrote on it. In April 2016 artist Joe DeVito sued the producers over elements of his Skull Island universe.
- Kong's design, by Stephen Rosenbaum and Carlos Huante, was a throwback to the bipedal 1933 version; the Skullcrawlers drew on the 1933 pit lizard, Evangelion, Spirited Away and Pokémon's Cubone. Princess Mononoke influenced the monsters' approach.
- Principal photography ran October 19, 2015 to March 18, 2016 in northern Vietnam, on Oahu in Hawaii and on Australia's Gold Coast. Henry Jackman scored the film with 1970s psychedelic guitars.

## Release and reception

- Premiered at the Cineworld Empire Leicester Square in London on February 28, 2017 and released in the United States on March 10, 2017, having been moved from November 4, 2016; presented in 70mm in select cinemas.
- $168 million in the United States and Canada and $400.6 million elsewhere for $568.6 million worldwide (the infobox says $568.7 million and the lead "$569 million"). US opening weekend $61 million, 35% above projection. It set Vietnam's biggest opening ever with $2.5 million and took $71.6 million in China, its largest international market. "It is the second highest-grossing film in the Monsterverse to date."
- Rotten Tomatoes 76% from 392 reviews (average 6.5/10); Metacritic 62 from 49 critics; CinemaScore "B+"; PostTrak 80% positive. Peter Bradshaw gave it one of five stars, calling it "fantastically muddled and exasperatingly dull".
- Nominated for Best Visual Effects at the Academy Awards, four Visual Effects Society Awards, an Annie Award, three Teen Choice Awards and two Saturn Awards; won Best Teaser Poster at the Golden Trailer Awards.

## Franchise

- Godzilla vs. Kong was released on March 24, 2021; the animated series Skull Island on June 22, 2023; and John Goodman reprised Bill Randa in Monarch: Legacy of Monsters from November 2023.

wikis.title: Kong: Skull Island (2017 film) - plot, cast, production, release and reception
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on Jordan Vogt-Roberts's 2017 Monsterverse reboot of King Kong, covering its 1973 Vietnam-era story, cast, script and creature design, Vietnam and Hawaii shoot, $568.6 million gross and reviews.
wikis.body:
## The film

- "Kong: Skull Island is a 2017 American monster film directed by Jordan Vogt-Roberts. Produced by Legendary Pictures and distributed by Warner Bros. Pictures, it is a reboot of the King Kong franchise, the second film in the Legendary's Monsterverse franchise, and the eighth film in the King Kong franchise."
- Screenplay by Dan Gilroy, Max Borenstein and Derek Connolly; story by John Gatins; based on King Kong by Edgar Wallace and Merian C. Cooper. Produced by Thomas Tull, Mary Parent, Jon Jashni and Alex Garcia; cinematography Larry Fong; edited by Richard Pearson; music by Henry Jackman.
- Release dates: February 28, 2017 (Empire, Leicester Square) and March 10, 2017 (United States). Running time 118 minutes. Country United States; language English.
- Budget $185 million; box office $568.7 million in the infobox.
- "In the film, a team of scientists and Vietnam War soldiers in 1973 travel to an uncharted island in the Pacific Ocean named Skull Island and encounter many of the island's monsters, including the mighty Kong."
- "The film was announced in July 2014 at San Diego Comic-Con, and Vogt-Roberts was announced as the director in September 2014. The project began at Universal Pictures as an origin story but was moved to Warner Bros. to develop a shared cinematic universe featuring Godzilla and Kong. Principal photography began in October 2015 in Hawaii and various locations around Vietnam and ended in March 2016."
- It was "theatrically released on March 10, 2017 to generally positive reviews from critics", was "a box office success, grossing $569 million against a $185 million budget", and received a nomination for Best Visual Effects at the 90th Academy Awards.
- "A sequel, Godzilla vs. Kong, was released in 2021, and an animated series, Skull Island, was released in 2023."

## Sequel and franchise

- In September 2015 Legendary moved the film from Universal to Warner Bros., "which sparked media speculation that Godzilla and King Kong would appear in a film together"; in October 2015 Legendary confirmed Godzilla vs. Kong and plans for a shared franchise "centered around Monarch" that "brings together Godzilla and Legendary's King Kong in an ecosystem of other giant super-species, both classic and new".
- Vogt-Roberts said he was interested in a film about Marlow and Gunpei on the island: "I keep joking that personally I'm more interested in doing a $30 million version of young John C. Reilly on the island. Just some weird, the odd-ball monster comedy with him and Gunpei."
- Joe Morton appears as an older Dr. Houston Brooks in Godzilla: King of the Monsters (2019). Godzilla vs. Kong was released on March 24, 2021.
- In January 2021 Netflix and Legendary Television announced an anime-style Monsterverse series; Skull Island, a joint venture of Legendary Television, Tractor Pants Productions, Powerhouse Animation Studios and Netflix Animation, was released on June 22, 2023. In November 2023 John Goodman reprised Bill Randa in Monarch: Legacy of Monsters, alongside Anders Holm as a young Randa.

## External links and navboxes in this part

- The official website; the film at IMDb, the TCM Movie Database (archived), Rotten Tomatoes and Metacritic; an "Official Monarch Themed website" archived March 18, 2017 at the Wayback Machine.
- "Monsterverse" navbox: films Godzilla (2014), Kong: Skull Island (2017), Godzilla: King of the Monsters (2019), Godzilla vs. Kong (2021), Godzilla x Kong: The New Empire (2024) and Godzilla x Kong: Supernova (2027); television Skull Island (2023) and Monarch: Legacy of Monsters (2023-present).
- "King Kong" navbox: American live-action films from King Kong (1933) through Godzilla x Kong: Supernova (2027), characters and related entries.

## Inconsistencies inside the page

- Worldwide gross: the infobox gives $568.7 million, the lead says "grossing $569 million", and the Box office section gives "$168 million in the United States and Canada and $400.6 million in other territories for a worldwide gross of $568.6 million".
- Kong's height: the cast section gives "104 feet (31.7 m)-tall", while J.R. Jones's quoted review refers to "a 100-foot gorilla".
- Filming: the lead says photography "began in October 2015 in Hawaii and various locations around Vietnam and ended in March 2016", while the Filming section dates it October 19, 2015 to March 18, 2016 and adds Australia's Gold Coast.
- The lead lists Eugene Cordero and Marc Evan Jackson among the film's stars, while the infobox's starring list does not include them.

wikis.title: Plot of Kong: Skull Island
wikis.summary: The film's story as the article summarises it, from the 1944 dogfight to the post-credits Monarch scene.
wikis.body:
- In 1944 two World War II fighter pilots, American Hank Marlow and Japanese Gunpei Ikari, parachute onto an island in the South Pacific after a dogfight and fight until "the fight is interrupted by a giant ape".
- In 1973 Bill Randa, head of the organization Monarch, convinces the government to let him lead a research expedition to the recently discovered Skull Island. He recruits a U.S. Army unit under Lieutenant Colonel Preston Packard, tracker and former British SAS Captain James Conrad, and anti-war photographer Mason Weaver.
- Packard's men drop seismic explosives developed by Bill's seismologist Houston Brooks to map the island and prove Brooks's Hollow Earth theory. The giant ape attacks, scattering the survivors. Conrad, Weaver, Landsat official Nieves, Brooks, biologist San Lin and the soldier Slivko head north to an extraction point, while Packard, his men, Bill and another Landsat official search for Packard's right-hand man Chapman.
- Conrad's group meets the Iwi natives and an older Marlow, who explains that the ape, Kong, protects the island from subterranean reptilian "Skullcrawlers" awakened by the bombing, which killed Kong's entire species. "The Iwi believe when Kong dies, a larger Skullcrawler will awaken and ravage the island." Marlow and Ikari became friends on the island before Ikari was killed by a Skullcrawler.
- Chapman is ambushed and devoured by a Skullcrawler. The group builds a boat from parts of Marlow's and Ikari's downed planes, rides down the river - where Nieves is torn apart by carnivorous birds - and reaches Packard's group.
- Marlow leads them through a mass grave of dinosaurs and Kong's family. The Skullcrawler that killed Chapman kills Bill and other soldiers before Weaver triggers a flammable gas explosion that kills it. Packard reveals his plan to kill Kong; Marlow and Brooks warn this would let the Skullcrawlers run rampant, but he refuses to listen. Conrad and Weaver meet Kong up close, see "his true peaceful nature" and resolve to save him.
- Packard lures Kong with the remaining seismic charges and incapacitates him with ignited napalm. Conrad, Weaver and Marlow persuade the other soldiers to spare Kong, but Packard refuses to yield; the larger Skullcrawler emerges from the lake and Kong crushes Packard before he can detonate the charges. Kong kills the Skullcrawler with the humans' help and the survivors leave the island.
- Marlow reunites with his wife and meets his son for the first time. In a post-credits scene Monarch detains and recruits Conrad and Weaver, and Lin and Brooks show archive footage of cave paintings depicting Godzilla, Mothra, Rodan and King Ghidorah; "The final image shows Godzilla and Ghidorah in battle."

wikis.title: Cast of Kong: Skull Island
wikis.summary: The principal cast with the actors' own descriptions of their roles, plus the supporting and cameo players.
wikis.body:
- Tom Hiddleston as James Conrad, "an ex-British Special Air Service Captain who served in the Vietnam War with the Australian Special Air Service Regiment" hired as hunter-tracker. Hiddleston described him as holding "no political allegiance in the conflict" but who "understands conflict": "He's a former soldier who has been formed by an understanding of war, but his specific skill set is something that's attached to the power of nature."
- Samuel L. Jackson as Lieutenant Colonel Preston Packard, Sky Devils helicopter squadron leader. Jackson compared him to Captain Ahab: "He does have to exact some measure of revenge for the people he's lost. That's just the nature of how we operate—eye for an eye!"
- John Goodman as William "Bill" Randa, a senior Monarch official in charge of the expedition.
- Brie Larson as Mason Weaver, an anti-war photographer and investigative photojournalist. Larson: "It's a group of misfits that are all coming from different angles looking at the same thing", and Weaver has an "interest and respect for nature" and "a closer, more loving, and intimate relationship with Kong".
- Jing Tian as San Lin, a Monarch biologist. "According to Vogt-Roberts and Borenstein, her role was initially larger, but rewrites reduced it." Alison de Souza of the Straits Times wrote her role would be described in Chinese as a "hua ping" (花瓶), meaning a vase, "which refers to insignificant parts", and that she "hardly does or says a thing".
- Toby Kebbell as Major Jack Chapman, Sea Stallion pilot and Packard's right-hand man; John Ortiz as Landsat official Victor Nieves; Corey Hawkins as Houston Brooks, "a geologist and Yale University graduate" (an older version played by Joe Morton appears in Godzilla: King of the Monsters); Jason Mitchell as warrant officer Glenn Mills; Shea Whigham as Captain Earl Cole, "who wields an AK-47 instead of an M16"; Thomas Mann as Reg Slivko, "known for carrying a portable record player".
- Terry Notary and Toby Kebbell as Kong in motion capture: "A 104 feet (31.7 m)-tall ape who is the last of his kind and is worshiped as the king and god on Skull Island by the Iwi natives." Notary said this Kong is an adolescent, played like a "14-year-old that's trapped in the life of an adult", and that it took three days to film the motion capture scenes. Kebbell "provided some facial reference – certain subtleties, certain looks".
- John C. Reilly as Hank Marlow, "a U.S. Army Air Forces lieutenant of the 45th Pursuit Squadron stranded on Skull Island for nearly 29 years since World War II". Will Brittain plays young Marlow and Marlow's son.
- Also: Eugene Cordero as Reles; Marc Evan Jackson as Landsat employee Steve Woodward; Richard Jenkins as Senator Al Willis; Miyavi as Gunpei Ikari; Robert Taylor as the captain of the Athena; Thomas Middleditch voicing Jerry; Moisés Arias, Nick Robinson and Erin Moriarty as bar guests; Dat Phan as a bar thug.

wikis.title: Development and writing
wikis.summary: How the project moved from a Peter Jackson sequel at Universal to a Warner Bros. Monsterverse entry, and the many drafts that reshaped the story.
wikis.body:
## Development

- In 2013 Peter Jackson, director of the 2005 King Kong remake, "initially handpicked Adam Wingard to direct Skull Island, a sequel to Jackson's film", later suggesting Guillermo del Toro. When the film moved studios, Wingard and Jackson were dropped while producer Mary Parent remained.
- It was officially announced by Legendary Pictures at the 2014 San Diego Comic-Con with Universal Pictures as distributor; Legendary then moved it to Warner Bros. "to develop a crossover film featuring Kong and Godzilla". Legendary offered Joe Cornish the directing job; in September 2014 Jordan Vogt-Roberts was announced.
- In 2016 the then-newly launched Tencent Pictures provided financial support, "but the China-based studio did not produce the project".

## Writing

- Max Borenstein, writer of 2014's Godzilla, wrote the first draft seeking continuity between the King Kong and Godzilla worlds; John Gatins was hired for the second draft.
- Borenstein did not want to repeat the "Beauty and the Beast" plot and took into account "the outdated elements of the treatment of the island natives and the damsel in distress". His initial influence was Apocalypse Now: "What popped into my head for the paradigm of the movie was Apocalypse Now. That's obviously a war movie, but I liked the idea of people moving upriver to face a misunderstood force that they think of as a villain, but ultimately they come to realize is much more complicated."
- Before Vogt-Roberts signed on, Borenstein considered opening during the Vietnam War and jumping to the present; Legendary rejected it, so he set it in 1917 during World War I, with Hiddleston's character leading a rescue team to find his missing brother, stranded while searching for a "Titan Serum" believed to cure all illnesses. He then retooled it to the present day.
- Vogt-Roberts liked the Apocalypse Now concept and pitched it with the story at the end of the Vietnam War, which the studio accepted. Dan Gilroy had also collaborated on the Borenstein/Gatins draft; on August 18, 2015 Derek Connolly was confirmed as doing rewrites. Borenstein did a final pass and credited the script to all the writers: "It was definitely collaborative in terms of what's on the screen, though none of us worked together."
- Gilroy said backstories were dropped: "Brie's [character] was somebody who was really war-weary and had taken photographs for far too long. She didn't believe in anything – so the first time she saw Kong, it was like an awakening... Tom [Hiddleston]'s character was a guy whose unit had been attacked by a big monster out of Vietnam – so he was in search of this thing. Instead of them approaching him at the bar and giving him a job, I had him like, 'I want on board.' I like those characters a lot… but they didn't want to go with that." He still felt the film turned out to be a "good movie".
- "In April 2016, artist Joe DeVito sued producers of the movie for using elements of his Skull Island universe, which he claimed he created and the producers used without his permission."

wikis.title: Creature design and influences
wikis.summary: How Kong and the Skullcrawlers were designed, and the films, anime and games Vogt-Roberts cites as influences.
wikis.body:
## Creature design

- Vogt-Roberts asked Stephen Rosenbaum, who hired Carlos Huante, to help create Kong's design. The team combined "new-school and old-school techniques; using keyframe animation to give it the scale that it needed while developing motion-capture facial expressions that added to his character".
- "Vogt-Roberts wanted Kong to look iconic and straightforward enough that a third-grader could draw him, and the image would still be recognizable." He wanted Kong to feel like a "lonely god, he was a morose figure, lumbering around this island", taking the design back to the 1933 incarnation, "a bipedal creature that walks in an upright position".
- Vogt-Roberts: "If anything, our Kong is meant to be a throwback to the '33 version. [Kong] was a movie monster, so we worked really hard to take some of the elements of the '33 version, some of those exaggerated features, some of those cartoonish and iconic qualities, and then make them their own… I think there are very modern elements to him, yet hopefully, he feels very timeless at the same time."
- Hayao Miyazaki's Princess Mononoke influenced the monsters: "Miyazaki['s] Princess Mononoke was actually a big reference in the way that the spirit creatures sort of have their own domains and fit within that."
- The Skullcrawlers used the two-armed pit lizard from the 1933 King Kong as a reference: "That creature ... is also this crazy fusion of all of the influences throughout my life – like the first angel from Evangelion, and No-Face from Spirited Away, and Cubone from Pokémon."

## Influences

- Vogt-Roberts: "you obviously have Apocalypse Now and just the era of '70s filmmaking, with films like The Conversation, too. Also, Platoon was an inspiration, and the South Korean film The Host as well. The entire Neon Genesis Evangelion series was a big influence. There's a huge anime and video game influence in my DNA, and I think it very much bred itself into this film."
- Other inspirations: the South Korean films The Good, the Bad, the Weird and Oldboy, and video games including the Aliens series, The Legend of Zelda series and Shadow of the Colossus.
- The opening scene with an American and a Japanese pilot stranded on the same island was inspired by Hell in the Pacific (1968). The film references the Italian horror film Cannibal Holocaust "when a giant spider impales a soldier with its leg".

wikis.title: Casting, filming and music
wikis.summary: How the cast came together between 2014 and 2016, where the film was shot, and Henry Jackman's 1970s-flavoured score.
wikis.body:
## Casting

- Tom Hiddleston was announced as the lead at the same time as Vogt-Roberts. J. K. Simmons and Michael Keaton were attached for a time but left due to scheduling difficulties.
- Brie Larson was cast as the female lead in July 2015; Corey Hawkins joined on August 5, 2015. In August 2015 Deadline Hollywood reported early talks with Samuel L. Jackson to replace Simmons's role and that John C. Reilly was eyed for Keaton's; Tom Wilkinson was offered a role.
- Toby Kebbell joined in August 2015, with Jackson and Reilly confirmed; "Jackson's deal was worth five million dollars". Jason Mitchell joined in August 2015; John Goodman and Thomas Mann in September 2015; John Ortiz, Shea Whigham and Eugene Cordero in October 2015; Will Brittain in November 2015.
- In May 2016 Kebbell revealed Terry Notary would perform Kong through motion capture, with Kebbell providing guidance.

## Filming

- "Principal photography on the film began on October 19, 2015, and concluded on March 18, 2016."
- Filming took place in northern Vietnam - Tràng An, Vân Long and Tam Cốc (Ninh Bình Province), Hạ Long Bay (Quảng Ninh Province) and the entrance of the Tú Làn Caves System (Tân Hoá, Trung Hoá Village, Minh Hoá District, Quảng Bình Province) - with The Creatv Company in Vietnam and Nicholas Simon as line producer.
- It also shot on Oahu in Hawaii, with Renee Confair as production supervisor, including Honolulu's Chinatown, Kualoa Ranch and Waikane Valley (Ohulehule Forest Conservancy), and on Australia's Gold Coast from mid-January 2016, with Jennifer Cornwell as production manager.

## Music

- Henry Jackman composed the score, blending "'70s psychedelic guitars into the score to blend with the film's setting in the 1970s". Vogt-Roberts wanted Vietnam-era songs, which give a "striking dichotomy, sets the tone and gives us great moments of fun".
- The score was recorded at AIR Lyndhurst Studios with the London Voices, conducted by Gavin Greenaway, with additional music by Alex Belcher, Halli Cauthery and Stephen Hilton. The soundtrack was released digitally in March 2017 through WaterTower Music and on a double LP by Waxwork Records in 2018.

wikis.title: Release, merchandise and home media
wikis.summary: The date shift to March 2017, the London premiere, the Walmart toy line and tie-in comic, and the home video releases.
wikis.body:
- "Kong: Skull Island was originally scheduled to be released on November 4, 2016, but was pushed back to March 10, 2017. The new release date coincided with the franchise's 84th anniversary. It was presented in 70mm in select cinemas."
- The film premiered at the Cineworld Empire Leicester Square in London on February 28, 2017.
- Merchandise was a Walmart exclusive in 2017: "A large Kong figure was the main toy featuring a Jack Chapman with a missile launcher", also sold on Amazon.com, plus two Kong Halloween costumes - a standard one and an inflatable Kong suit.
- On April 7, 2017 Legendary announced a four-issue graphic novel series, Skull Island: The Birth of Kong, acting as both prequel and sequel: an adult Houston Brooks nearing retirement from Monarch in 2012 learns that his missing estranged son with San Lin, Aaron, led a team on a secret mission to Skull Island in the mid-1990s. Written by Arvid Nelson with art by Mohammad "Zid" Yazid (issue No. 4 cover by Drew Johnson), it ran between April 12 and November 21, 2017, with a paperback collection on December 12, 2017. A novelization by Tim Lebbon was released on March 14, 2017.
- Home media: HD Digital on June 20, 2017, and 4K Ultra HD, 3D Blu-ray, Blu-ray and DVD on July 18, 2017. It debuted at the top of the NPD VideoScan First Alert sales chart and the dedicated Blu-ray chart for the week ending July 23, 2017. In the United States and Canada the DVD earned $16.6 million and the Blu-ray $23.3 million, "totaling $39.9 million in domestic video sales".

wikis.title: Box office performance
wikis.summary: The film's opening, its worldwide gross and the markets where it performed best, including a Vietnam record.
wikis.body:
- "Kong: Skull Island grossed $168 million in the United States and Canada and $400.6 million in other territories for a worldwide gross of $568.6 million." With a $185 million production budget "and about $136 million more spent on international marketing costs, the film needed to make at least $450–500 million worldwide to break-even".
- It was projected to gross $40–50 million in its North American opening weekend and $110–135 million worldwide. It made $20.2 million on its first day from 3,846 theaters, including $3.7 million from Thursday night previews, and "a better-than-expected $61 million on its opening weekend, defying the film's initial projection by 35%". IMAX contributed $7.6 million from 382 theaters, 12.5% of the opening weekend.
- Second weekend: $27.8 million, a drop of 54.4%, finishing second behind Beauty and the Beast.
- Internationally it debuted with $85.1 million from 20,900 screens in 65 markets, opening everywhere except Japan and China, and scored "the fourth-biggest March release with $4.8 million from 672 theaters in IMAX (the second biggest without China in it)".
- Biggest openings: United Kingdom and Ireland ($7.6 million); South Korea ($7.4 million); Russia ($6.2 million); Mexico ($5.7 million); France ($4.1 million); Taiwan ($3.6 million); Australia ($3.6 million); Brazil ($3.4 million); Germany ($3.4 million); Malaysia ($2.65 million); India ($2.4 million); Spain ($1.6 million); Italy ($1.6 million).
- "In Vietnam (where the film was primarily shot and set), it scored the biggest opening of all time there with $2.5 million; this was the week after a huge model of the primate outside the theater caught on fire at the film's premiere."
- It later opened in China with $71.6 million, "its largest international market", and $3.5 million in Japan, where it was released as King Kong: Giant God of Skull Island (Kingu Kongu: Dokurotou no Kyoshin). "After its overseas run, the film would gross US$400 million internationally. It is the second highest-grossing film in the Monsterverse to date."

wikis.title: Critical response and accolades
wikis.summary: The film's aggregate scores, the split among reviewers and the awards it was nominated for, including an Oscar nod for visual effects.
wikis.body:
## Critical response

- Rotten Tomatoes: "76% of 392 critics' reviews are positive, with an average rating of 6.5/10." Consensus: "Offering exhilarating eye candy, solid acting, and a fast-paced story, Kong: Skull Island earns its spot in the movie monster's mythos without ever matching up to the classic original." Metacritic: 62 out of 100 from 49 critics, "generally favorable". CinemaScore "B+"; PostTrak 80% positive with 60% definitely recommending.
- Michael Phillips (Chicago Tribune), three and a half of four: "I saw little in [Vogt-Roberts'] first feature to indicate the deftness and buoyant spirit he brings to Skull Island. This time, the money's on the screen, but it bought a really good movie, too."
- Mike Ryan (Uproxx): "Kong: Skull Island is still a hoot ... I just wished it had embraced its craziness just a little bit more." Todd McCarthy (The Hollywood Reporter): "all the requisite elements are served up here in ideal proportion, and the time just flies by". Kyle Anderson (Nerdist News): "It's certainly not a perfect movie, and a lot of the characters feel like sketches more than fully-fledged people, but it roars along enjoyably from start to finish."
- Peter Bradshaw (The Guardian), one of five: a "fantastically muddled and exasperatingly dull quasi-update of the King Kong story". Matthew Lickona (San Diego Reader), one of five: "on the human side, the film is clumsily written, over-cast and underacted, with only frustrated soldier Samuel L. Jackson striking the right tone of crazy amid the chaos."
- Chris Klimek (NPR): "Kong is at its mediocre best when it pretends to be a nature documentary about Skull Island's bizarro flora and fauna", but "every time the movie threatens to get interesting, one of its hordes of ersatz, non-animated characters shows up and starts talking again."
- Anthony Lane (The New Yorker) said what the film "yearns to be, is a pop-culture Apocalypse Now, with the human foe removed, the political parable toned down, and the gonzo elements jacked up." J.R. Jones questioned the 1973 setting, noting a present-day story is impossible "when satellite photos would surely alert us to the existence of a 100-foot gorilla".
- On Larson: Ann Hornaday (The Washington Post) said she "serves as a cautionary poster girl for aspiring actresses everywhere: One year you're winning an Oscar ... the next, you're widening your eyes and gasping your way through a great big monkey movie." Michael Salfino (The Wall Street Journal): "a starring role in a popcorn movie on the heels of a passion project can open up an actor to ridicule."
