wikis.title: Angkor Wat and the Khmer empire
wikis.summary: Britannica's article on the Angkor Wat temple complex, together with the Khmer empire article carried on the same page, covering its founding, golden age and decline.
wikis.body:
## Angkor Wat

- "Angkor Wat, temple complex at Angkor, near Siem Reap, Cambodia, that was built in the 12th century by King Suryavarman II (reigned 1113-c. 1150) of the Khmer empire."
- "The vast religious complex of Angkor Wat comprises more than a thousand buildings"; it is "the world's largest religious structure, covering some 400 acres (160 hectares), and marks the high point of Khmer architecture."
- "Construction is believed to have spanned some three decades."
- Dated 802-1431 for the Khmer empire; related places listed: Cambodia, Laos, Thailand, Vietnam.

## Khmer empire

- "Khmer empire, ancient Cambodian state that ruled vast areas of mainland Southeast Asia from about 802 CE to 1431, reaching its peak between the 11th and 13th centuries. Also known as the kingdom of Angkor, it was the successor state of the earlier kingdoms of Funan and Chenla".
- "For most of the empire's history, its capital was Angkor, near modern Siem Reap."
- "Like other early Southeast Asian kingdoms, it was heavily influenced by Indian customs in political organization, culture, and religion."

## Credits

- Angkor Wat article: The Editors of Encyclopaedia Britannica; "This article was most recently revised and updated by Ethan Teekah." Dated Sep. 15, 2026.
- Khmer empire article: Ethan Teekah and Britannica Editors.

wikis.title: Angkor Wat: building, design and later history
wikis.summary: The temple's construction under Suryavarman II, its Hindu design and Buddhist conversion, and its restoration and World Heritage status.
wikis.body:
- "It was built by Suryavarman II as a vast funerary temple within which his remains were to be deposited. Construction is believed to have spanned some three decades."
- "From the end of the 9th century until early in the 13th century, numerous construction projects were undertaken, the most notable of which was Angkor Wat."
- "All of the original religious motifs derived from Hinduism, and the temple was dedicated to the god Vishnu. The five central towers of Angkor Wat symbolize the peaks of Mount Meru, which according to Hindu mythology is the dwelling place of the gods. The mountain is said to be surrounded by an ocean, and the complex's enormous moat suggests the oceans at the edge of the world."
- "A 617-foot (188-meter) bridge allows access to the site. The temple is reached by passing through three galleries, each separated by a paved walkway."
- "The temple walls are covered with bas-relief sculptures of very high quality representing Hindu gods and ancient Khmer scenes as well as scenes from the Mahabharata and the Ramayana."
- "After the Cham people of modern-day Vietnam sacked Angkor in 1177, King Jayavarman VII (reigned 1181-c. 1220) decided that the Hindu gods had failed him. When he built a new capital nearby, Angkor Thom, he dedicated it to Buddhism. Thereafter, Angkor Wat became a Buddhist shrine, and many of its carvings and statues of Hindu deities were replaced by Buddhist art."
- "In the early 15th century Angkor was abandoned. Still, Theravada Buddhist monks maintained Angkor Wat, which remained an important pilgrimage site".
- "Angkor Wat was 'rediscovered' by explorer Henri Mouhot after the French colonial regime was established in 1863."
- "In the 20th century various restoration programs were undertaken, but they were suspended amid the political unrest that engulfed Cambodia in the 1970s. When work resumed in the mid-1980s, the required repairs were extensive. Notably, sections had to be dismantled and rebuilt."
- "In 1992 the Angkor complex, which included Angkor Wat, was designated a World Heritage site by UNESCO and was immediately added to the list of World Heritage in Danger... Angkor was removed from the danger list in 2004."
- "The temple complex appears on the Cambodian flag."

wikis.title: Early kingdom: Jayavarman II
wikis.summary: The empire's first ruler, consecrated about 802, his three capitals and the founding of Kambuja-desa.
wikis.body:
- "While the earlier kingdoms of Funan (c. 1st-6th century CE) and Chenla (c. 6th-early 9th century) were both advanced polities with complex economies, the Khmer empire vastly surpassed them in power, splendor, and influence."
- "He was consecrated at Indrapura (east of modern Kampong Cham) under the royal name Jayavarman II about 802. He had been sent from 'Java,' where he had been held in captivity or exile, about 800 to rule as Java's vassal over disunited principalities that had been Chenla."
- "It is unclear whether the use of the term Java in this context refers to the modern island of Java or the ancient kingdom of Srivijaya, which was based on the modern island of Sumatra."
- "Jayavarman soon defied Java, asserted Khmer independence, and began to rule as devaraja ('God-King') and chakravartin ('World Ruler') in 802."
- Capitals: Indrapura; then Hariharalaya (modern Roluos), "9 miles (15 km) southeast of modern Siem Reap"; then Mahendraparvata on Phnom Kulen, "about 30 miles (48 km) north of modern Siem Reap"; he returned to Hariharalaya and died "near the middle of the 9th century."
- "Jayavarman seems to have left no inscriptions of his own, and the monuments that can be dated to his reign are small and were hastily built."
- "he appears to have established what came to be called Kambuja-desa... He was Cambodia's first nationally oriented king."

wikis.title: Foundations of Angkor and the 10th-11th century
wikis.summary: Indravarman I's Bakong, Yasovarman I's founding of Yasodharapura, and the reigns down to Suryavarman I.
wikis.body:
- "A king named Indravarman I (ruled 877-c. 890) constructed a large reservoir and several temples there, including a pyramidical structure called the Bakong - the first Cambodian temple to be built primarily of stone rather than brick."
- "The so-called 'temple mountain' became the model for the many larger royal temples at Angkor".
- "Indravarman's son and successor, Yasovarman I (ruled c. 890-c. 910), moved the capital 9 miles (15 km) to the northwest, closer to modern Siem Reap. This location subsequently became Angkor - a name derived from the Sanskrit word nagara, meaning 'city.'"
- "The city that Yasovarman founded, Yasodharapura, retained that name and remained Cambodia's capital until it was abandoned in the 16th century."
- "The city walls of the roughly square-shaped Yasodharapura measured about 2.5 miles (4 km) on each side."
- "a consistent feature of Angkorean civilization, unmatched in medieval Europe, was religious toleration."
- "After Yasovarman's death, there were several decades of warfare and disorder until Rajendravarman II began his rule in 944. He set in motion a period of peace and prosperity that lasted nearly a century. After his death in 968, he was succeeded by Jayavarman V, who ruled until about 1000." He had Banteay Srei built; in Angkor he began the temple mountain Ta Keo, "completed under his successor, Suryavarman I."
- "Suryavarman I ruled from about 1004 to about 1050. He extended the Khmer empire westward into present-day Thailand. There he constructed the large mountaintop temple known as Preah Vihear. During his reign, the number of cities under Angkor's rule grew from roughly 20 to almost 50."

wikis.title: The Khmer golden age under Suryavarman II
wikis.summary: Suryavarman II's accession about 1113, his conquests, religious reform and the building of Angkor Wat.
wikis.body:
- "After 50 years of unrest, Suryavarman II defeated rival claimants and established himself as sole ruler of the Khmer empire about 1113."
- "Warlike and ambitious, he expanded the empire to the frontiers of the Burmese Pagan kingdom in the west and to the Gulf of Thailand in the south, bringing most of modern Thailand and much of modern Laos under his rule."
- "He also avenged earlier attacks on Angkor by armies launched from the kingdom of Champa... A campaign against Dai Viet, which had recently declared its independence from China, was less successful."
- "Suryavarman was also a religious reformer, who blended the mystical sects of Vishnu and Shiva... and promulgated Vaishnavism as the official religion, rather than Buddhism".
- "His major accomplishment, from a modern perspective, was the Angkor Wat temple complex, still the largest religious structure in the world... The temple, which eventually became his tomb and probably was an astronomical observatory as well, was dedicated to the Hindu god Vishnu."
- "Its bas-reliefs, running for nearly a half mile inside its third enclosure, depict events in the well-known Indian epics Mahabharata and Ramayana... as well as Suryavarman himself holding court."
- "in the 12th century, when its towers were gilded and its moats properly maintained, it must have been even more breathtaking."

wikis.title: Jayavarman VII and the empire's zenith
wikis.summary: His defeat of the Chams, coronation in 1181, and his programme of temples, roads, rest houses and hospitals.
wikis.body:
- "Suryavarman II's successor, Yasovarman II (ruled 1160-66)... was overthrown by one of his officials after returning from a military campaign in Thailand."
- "In 1177, heading an army of his own, the prince attacked Angkor and defeated the Cham forces. The battles are vividly depicted in the bas-reliefs of his temple mountain, the Bayon."
- "In 1181, at the age of 61, he was crowned king of a reconstituted Khmer empire and began a brilliant reign of more than 30 years, during which he brought the empire to its zenith".
- "To forestall further Cham attacks, Jayavarman annexed the Cham capital, and Angkor controlled Champa until Jayavarman's death."
- "During his reign Jayavarman continued his military activities, bringing Champa, southern Laos, and portions of the Malay Peninsula and Burma under his control."
- He built "the Bayon, a distinctively Mahayana Buddhist central pyramid temple designed to serve as the primary locus of the royal cult and also as his own personal mausoleum"; funerary temples for his mother and father; and provincial temples housing "reduced replicas of the Royal Buddha".
- "He rebuilt the city of Angkor, now known as Angkor Thom, and rebuilt and extended the system of highways... In addition, he constructed more than 100 rest houses along these roads and built more than 100 hospitals, which he dispersed throughout his kingdom and placed under the protection of Baisajyaguru Vaiduryaprabha, the Great Buddha of Healing."
- "He was more than 90 years old when he died. The Khmer empire reached its peak under his rule, and Angkor Thom is estimated to have been home to approximately 1 million people in the beginning of the 13th century, making it one of the largest cities in the premodern world."
- Scholars note "the overwhelming demands that he placed on the material and human resources of his kingdom may have been a major factor in its subsequent loss of creativity and its eventual demise."

wikis.title: Decline of the Khmer empire
wikis.summary: The contraction after 1220, Zhou Daguan's 1296 account, and the Tai sack of Angkor in 1431.
wikis.body:
- "After the death of Jayavarman VII (about 1220), few stone monuments were erected at Angkor, and only a few inscriptions were incised. Little by little, the Khmer empire began to contract."
- "by the early 13th century, vigorous new kingdoms in what is now northern Thailand - centering on the city of Sukhothai - became powerful enough to throw off Angkorean domination... In the mid-13th century, Tai armies even raided Angkor."
- "For the next 200 years, however, Angkor remained a glittering, crowded, and wealthy city. It impressed a Chinese visitor, Zhou Daguan, who arrived there with a diplomatic mission in 1296. Zhou's account is the longest and most-detailed extant description of the Khmer capital".
- Explanations for decline offered: "a mass conversion of the populace to Theravada Buddhism undermined the existing social hierarchy"; "serious environmental degradation may have undermined the region's vital irrigation system. Likely, both influenced the empire's weakening."
- "However, the key factor in the fall of the Angkorean state was competition from the rising Tai power in Ayutthaya. In 1351 a Tai kingdom whose court modeled itself culturally on Angkor was founded at Ayutthaya (Ayodhya, or Siam), not far from present-day Bangkok."
- "After a series of attacks, a Tai army sacked Angkor in 1431, marking the end of the Khmer empire. At this point, the Khmer capital moved to Lovek, near the modern capital of Phnom Penh."

wikis.title: 50 years of the Opel test centre at Dudenhofen
wikis.summary: History of Opel's Dudenhofen proving ground on its 50th anniversary, listing the tracks added over the decades and the testing the Opel Astra undergoes there.
wikis.body:
## The proving ground

- The Opel "proving ground" in Dudenhofen "opened 50 years ago"; it "has become the largest and most important Opel test centre in Europe".
- "At the beginning, in 1966 April, the 2.6 sq km proving ground has a combination of various streets and roads with a total length of 33 kilometers."
- A 5km, 33-degree banked high-speed circuit encloses the proving ground.
- A "skid pad", a concreted area 100 metres in diameter, is "used to determine the steering behavior or to precisely measure the swerving of the vehicle in corners".

## Additions over time

- 1980s: a 4.4km "sound and comfort track" is added.
- 1992: "the entire high-speed circuit is renewed in 24 weeks due to the heavy use".
- 2004: an oval track with watering and drainage system for slingshot tests and slalom drives is added.
- 2006: an all-wheel-drive test bench, "along with a modern industrial gasoline station with 32 pumps for 16 different types of fuel".
- 2012 (second circuit renewal): "test drivers can take the steep curve at 250km/h without the influence of any lateral force - they can theoretically take their hands of the steering wheel".

## Instrumentation

- An internal weather station delivers data on humidity, wind speed and direction.
- Highly sensitive sensors embedded in the road surface "permanently deliver data on the temperature and dampness of the surface".

## Testing the Astra

- New vehicles such as the current Opel Astra face "around 40,000 kilometres of extreme stress on the proving ground", a distance "equivalent to over 200,000 kilometres or 15 years on 'real roads'".
- "The latest Astra underwent strains that are equivalent to those of an entire life cycle in only 24 weeks."
- The "endurance test" uses an endurance track with "various different road surfaces such as asphalt and cobblestone, bumps and numerous corners", where engineers check whether the performance and quality validated on prototypes "made it into regular production".

wikis.title: Spain's AV350 plan to raise Madrid - Barcelona high-speed line to 350km/h
wikis.summary: Report on the AV350 project unveiled by Spain's transport minister to lift the Madrid - Barcelona line from 300km/h to 350km/h, with the aerodynamic sleepers and access projects it involves.
wikis.body:
## The announcement

- "Transport minister Oscar Puente announced the AV350 plan on November 17."
- "SPAIN's minister of transport and sustainable mobility, Oscar Puente, has unveiled the AV350 project to raise the maximum speed on the Madrid - Barcelona high-speed line from 300km/h to 350km/h, describing it as a major qualitative leap that will enable Spain to operate the fastest high-speed services in Europe and be matched only by China."
- "The upgrade is expected to cut the journey time between Madrid and Barcelona to under 2 hours, saving nearly 1 hour on Spain's busiest high-speed line that carried 14.6 million passengers in 2024."
- "According to Puente, the aim is not only to reduce journey times but also to increase capacity."

## Aerodynamic sleepers

- "A central element of the plan is the phased installation of new aerodynamic sleepers developed by infrastructure manager Adif in collaboration with engineering consultancy Sener."
- "The sleepers are designed to reduce the downforce in the space immediately above the ballast bed by 21%, preventing ballast from coming loose and striking trains at very high speeds."
- "The new sleepers will enable the maximum operating speed to be increased by 12%, while further aerodynamic refinements, including to the design of the train, will help meet the new target of 350km/h."

## Madrid access projects

- New infrastructure "will enable high-speed services from Barcelona to access Chamartin station in the north of the city, without passing through the existing tunnel that connects Atocha station with Chamartin".
- "Also being studied is a new connection between the Madrid - Barcelona and Madrid - Valladolid high-speed lines that would enable services from Barcelona to reach destinations in the north of Spain without passing through Chamartin."
- Further options: an intermediate station on the new Chamartin connection to serve Barajas Airport, and a spur letting Madrid - Seville and Madrid - Valencia services reach Chamartin without using the Atocha - Chamartin tunnel.
- On the Madrid - Seville line, "a new high-speed station could be built at Parla, south of Madrid", enabling "direct services from Andalucia to Catalonia to serve a population of 6 million within a 1-hour journey time to the station".

## Catalonia projects

- "In Catalonia, the project includes a new line from Lleida to the under-construction La Sagrera station in Barcelona."
- This "would relieve the congested Camp de Tarragona - Barcelona Sants section", where traffic is expected to grow as the Mediterranean Corridor "that will eventually connect Barcelona with Algeciras" is completed.
- Releasing capacity between Camp de Tarragona and Barcelona Sants "would enable the construction of a new intermediate station to serve Barcelona's El Prat airport".
- That element "will be studied separately from other new infrastructure, with the Ministry of Transport and Sustainable Mobility launching tenders for two feasibility study contracts worth a total of EUR 2.3m".

wikis.title: Great Pyramid of Giza
wikis.summary: Britannica article on the Great Pyramid of Giza: its builder and date, dimensions, internal chambers, theories of construction and the archaeology of the site.
wikis.body:
## Overview

- "Great Pyramid of Giza, ancient Egyptian pyramid that is the largest of the three Pyramids of Giza, located on a rocky plateau on the west bank of the Nile River in northern Egypt."
- "It was built by Khufu (Cheops), the second king of Egypt's 4th dynasty (c. 2543-c. 2436 BCE), and was completed in the early 25th century BCE."
- "The Pyramids of Giza are often collectively considered one of the Seven Wonders of the World, and they are the last of the wonders still standing."
- Also called: Great Pyramid, Great Pyramid of Khufu, Great Pyramid of Cheops.

## Description

- "It originally stood about 482 feet (147 meters) tall, but erosion and the removal of most of the polished limestone casing stones ... have lowered the pyramid's height to 449 feet (137 meters)."
- "The base and three sides each measure 755 feet (230 meters) in length. The pyramid's sides rise at an angle of 51.87 degrees and are accurately oriented to the four cardinal points of the compass."
- Core of yellowish limestone blocks; inner passages of finer light-coloured limestone; the interior burial chamber "built of huge blocks of granite".
- "Approximately 2.3 million blocks of stone were cut, transported, and assembled to create the 5.75-million-ton structure".

## Interior

- "The entrance to the Great Pyramid is on the north side, about 59 feet (18 meters) above ground level."
- A sloping corridor descends through the masonry into the rock and "ends in an unfinished underground chamber".
- An ascending passageway leads to the Queen's Chamber and to the Grand Gallery, "a tall corbelled passageway ... 151 feet (46 meters) long".
- At the upper end of the Grand Gallery a narrow passage gives access to the King's Chamber, "entirely lined and roofed with granite".
- Two narrow shafts run obliquely to the exterior; "it is not known whether they were designed for a religious purpose or if they were meant for ventilation".
- "Above the King's Chamber are five compartments separated by massive horizontal granite slabs", whose likely purpose was to shield the burial chamber ceiling from the thrust of the overlying masonry. "The pyramid's subterranean chambers were never completed."

## Construction

- "Questions persist over how the pyramid was built. The most plausible theory is that the Egyptians employed a sloping and encircling embankment of brick, earth, and sand, which was increased in height and in length as the pyramid rose; stone blocks were hauled up the ramp by means of sledges, rollers, and levers."
- "According to the ancient Greek historian Herodotus, the Great Pyramid took 20 years to construct and required the labor of 100,000 men."
- "By the late 20th century, however, archaeologists found evidence that a more limited workforce may have occupied the site on a permanent rather than a seasonal basis. It was suggested that as few as 20,000 workers, with accompanying support personnel (bakers, physicians, priests, etc.), would have been adequate for the task."

## Archaeology

- "Formal excavations of the Great Pyramid of Giza began in the 19th century."
- "One of the first notable discoveries occurred in the 1830s, when a British Egyptologist found laborers' graffiti indicating that the pyramid belonged to Khufu."
- "Later excavations uncovered two boats buried near the Great Pyramid. The king's remains, however, have never been found."
- "Since the early 21st century, 3D scanners and other noninvasive technologies have been used to explore the pyramid, and in 2023 it was announced that a hidden corridor had been discovered."
- Credited to The Editors of Encyclopaedia Britannica; "This article was most recently revised and updated by Teagan Wolter." Dateline: Britannica Editors, Sep. 9, 2026.
- A news item on the page: "2,000-year-old Roman concrete may offer clues on how Pyramid of Giza was built - Sep. 4, 2026, 2:53 AM ET (South China Morning Post)".

## Also on the page

- The page continues into Britannica's "ancient Egypt" article (dated Aug. 10, 2026, by John R. Baines and others), covering the civilization "in northeastern Africa that dates from the 4th millennium BCE" from prehistory to the Islamic conquest in the 7th century CE: the Nile's annual inundation and floodplain, the First Cataract at Aswan as the country's only well-defined boundary, trade with Byblos for timber and imports of obsidian and lapis lazuli from Anatolia and Afghanistan, cereal agriculture (emmer wheat and barley), and a population estimated "as having risen from 1 to 1.5 million in the 3rd millennium BCE to perhaps twice that number in the late 2nd millennium and 1st millennium BCE". It notes that "The construction of the great pyramids of the 4th dynasty (c. 2543-c. 2436 BCE) has yet to be fully explained and would be a major challenge to this day."

wikis.title: Stages of Stonehenge, 3000-1520 BCE
wikis.summary: Britannica's account of Stonehenge's six construction stages, from the first circular enclosure of 3000-2935 BCE to the Y Holes of 1640-1520 BCE, plus the monument today and the Preseli bluestone quarries.
wikis.body:
## Overview

- Britannica article section "Stages of Stonehenge", credited to Mike Parker Pearson and the Editors of Encyclopaedia Britannica, dated Aug. 28, 2026.
- Construction stages given: first 3000-2935 BCE; second 2640-2480 BCE; third 2470-2280 BCE; fourth 2280-2030 BCE; fifth 2030-1750 BCE; sixth 1640-1520 BCE.
- "As with all radiocarbon dating, the precise dates of such events can only be estimated within many decades, if not centuries."
- A long foot is "an ancient unit of measurement equivalent to 1.056 statute feet or 0.32187 metre".

## Key figures

- First-stage enclosure: more than 330 feet (100 metres) in diameter, with 56 Aubrey Holes.
- Sarsen uprights: most about 25 tons and about 18 feet (5.5 metres) high; giant trilithon uprights 29 feet (9 metres) and 32 feet (10 metres) high, weighing more than 45 tons; lintels "weighing some 7 tons each".
- Bluestones: "weigh up to 4 tons each, and the taller ones are over 6 feet (2 metres) high."
- Avenue: almost 2 miles (3 km) long, 60 to 115 feet (18 to 35 metres) wide.

## Page also notes

- A news line on the page: "Ritual solstice structure 1,000 years older than Stonehenge unearthed in Czech Republic - Aug. 25, 2026, 10:00 AM ET (Live Science)".

wikis.title: First stage: 3000-2935 BCE
wikis.summary: The circular enclosure, the 56 Aubrey Holes, the cremation cemetery and Bluestonehenge on the River Avon.
wikis.body:
- "The oldest part of the Stonehenge monument was built during the period from 3000 to 2935 BCE. It consists of a circular enclosure that is more than 330 feet (100 metres) in diameter, enclosing 56 pits called the Aubrey Holes, named after John Aubrey, who identified them in 1666."
- "The ditch of the enclosure is flanked on the inside by a high bank and on the outside by a low bank, or counterscarp."
- "The diameters of the outer bank, the ditch, the inner bank, and the circle of Aubrey Holes are equivalent to 270, 300, 330, and 360 long feet... respectively."
- Ditch deposits included "antler picks, which were used to dig the ditch itself, as well as bones of cattle and deer that were already centuries old when they were placed there."
- "The circular enclosure had two entrances: the main access on the northeast and a narrower entrance on the south."
- "excavation and archival research by the Stonehenge Riverside Project revealed that they probably held Welsh bluestones."
- "Human cremation burials were found within and around most of the holes, as well as within the encircling ditch and bank. (Of an estimated 150-240 cremation burials at Stonehenge, 64 had been excavated by the first decade of the 21st century.)" The great majority were of adult males.
- "The area surrounding the Aubrey Holes was used as a place of burial from roughly 3000 to 2300 BCE. It is the largest known cemetery from the 3rd millennium BCE in Britain."
- Bluestonehenge: "A second, smaller bluestone circle, 30 feet (10 metres) in diameter... was built on the bank of the River Avon over 1 mile (1.6 km) from the Aubrey Holes. Found by the Stonehenge Riverside Project in 2009, it consisted of about 25 Welsh bluestones and may have been used for cremating and removing the flesh from the bodies whose remains were buried and scattered at Stonehenge." Its stones "were later dismantled and presumably brought to Stonehenge."
- Stone sources: "Most of the surviving 45 original bluestones of Stonehenge are of spotted dolerite (also called diabase) from southwest Wales, specifically the Preseli Mountains." "A source for one of the rhyolites, however, was identified in 2011 as Pont Saeson, north of the Preselis." The Altar Stone and two other sandstone monoliths "likely came from the Brecon Beacons, a cluster of mountains about 60 miles (100 km) east of the Preseli range."
- "Although most experts consider these Welsh stones to have been brought by human agency, some geologists argue that they might have been carried toward the Salisbury Plain thousands of years earlier by ice-age glaciers."
- "The Heelstone, a large unworked sarsen outside the northeastern entrance, also may have been erected during the first stage of Stonehenge, if not earlier."
- Rows of timber-post holes within the northeastern entrance are thought to date to this period; "the posts that they contained may have served to mark the movement of the moon toward its northern major limit."

wikis.title: Second stage: 2640-2480 BCE
wikis.summary: The sarsen circle and trilithons, the bluestone Q and R Holes, the Station Stones and the Durrington Walls builders' camp.
wikis.body:
- "Except for human burials, there is no evidence of activity between Stonehenge's first and second stages of construction."
- "About 2500 BCE the sarsen stones were brought from the Avebury area of the Marlborough Downs, about 20 miles (32 km) to the north." They were dressed smooth outside the northeastern entrance "by pounding with sarsen hammers."
- Arrangement: "a horseshoe-shaped setting of five tall trilithons (paired uprights with a lintel) - the central and largest of which is known as the giant trilithon - surrounded by 30 uprights linked by curved lintels to form a circle."
- "the circumference of the sarsen circle is 300 long feet."
- "The lintels, weighing some 7 tons each, are held on top of the uprights by mortise-and-tenon (dovetail) joints, and the ends of the curved lintels of the sarsen circle fit together with tongue-and-groove joints. All the joints were created using hammer stones, presumably in imitation of woodwork."
- "Most of the sarsen uprights weigh about 25 tons and are about 18 feet (5.5 metres) high. The uprights of the giant trilithon, however, were 29 feet (9 metres) and 32 feet (10 metres) high, weighing more than 45 tons."
- Survival: "Only one of the giant trilithon's uprights still stands, reaching a height above ground of about 23 feet (7 metres). Only six lintels (out of a total of 230) sit in place on the sarsen circle, with two more lying on the ground. Three of the five sarsen trilithon lintels are in place, with the other two on the ground. Four of the uprights from the sarsen circle are absent, and one is much shorter than the others." A hole for an absent sarsen "suggests that this stone and others were reused as construction materials for Roman buildings and medieval churches in the vicinity."
- Q and R Holes: Atkinson's records suggested they predated the sarsen circle and trilithons, "but Darvill and Wainwright's excavation in 2008 cast doubt on this stratigraphic relationship. It is more likely that the bluestone arc was indeed constructed as part of the sarsen circle and trilithon monument, with bluestones brought from the Aubrey Holes." Bluestones may also have come from Bluestonehenge, "where they had been removed by at least 2280 BCE."
- Station Stones: "Four upright stones... were erected near the Aubrey Hole ring, probably also during the second stage... Only two of the stones - both of sarsen - have survived." They were "placed in a rectangular formation, aligned along the same solstitial axis as the great trilithon and the bluestone arc." Two missing stones were partially covered by the South Barrow and North Barrow; the South Barrow "was raised on top of the floor of a 36-by-33-foot (11-by-10-metre) building in the shape of a D".
- "Three of them formed a facade across the entrance, of which the sarsen known as the Slaughter Stone is the sole survivor."
- Durrington: "two sets of concentric timber circles were built within a large settlement almost 2 miles (3 km) to the northeast" - the Southern Circle and the smaller Northern Circle. "Nine houses, up to about 18 feet (5.5 metres) square in plan, were excavated in 2004-07 and reckoned to form part of a 42-acre (17-hectare) settlement that may have supported up to 1,000 such dwellings. This seasonally occupied and short-lived community is thought to have been the builders' camp. By 2460 BCE its ruins were enclosed by the bank and ditch of Britain's largest henge enclosure, Durrington Walls. Outside its south entrance stood a third concentric timber circle - Woodhenge."

wikis.title: Third stage: 2470-2280 BCE
wikis.summary: The ceremonial avenue from Stonehenge to the River Avon and its solstitial alignment, alongside the Durrington avenue.
wikis.body:
- "Radiocarbon dating indicates that the side ditches and banks of a ceremonial avenue almost 2 miles (3 km) long were dug from Stonehenge to the River Avon at some time in the period between 2470 and 2280 BCE."
- "It is possible that the avenue traces the path of the bluestones that were moved from the Aubrey Holes and Bluestonehenge to the Q and R holes during Stonehenge's second stage of construction."
- "The avenue varies in width from about 60 to 115 feet (18 to 35 metres) and terminates at a small henge at the riverside. This henge, measuring 100 feet (30 metres) in diameter, was built after the bluestones at its centre were removed."
- "About the first 1,600 feet (500 metres) of the avenue from Stonehenge are aligned toward the summer solstice sunrise and the winter solstice sunset. Excavations in 2008 revealed that this stretch of the avenue's banks was built upon preexisting natural chalk ridges coincidentally sharing this same solstitial alignment."
- "At Durrington Walls a similar avenue about 560 feet (170 metres) long and 100 feet (30 metres) wide had been built about 2500 BCE between the Southern Circle and the River Avon and remained in use for several centuries. The Durrington avenue was aligned toward the summer solstice sunset, while the Southern Circle faced the winter solstice sunrise."
- "This solstitial alignment raises the possibility that Stonehenge and Durrington were built as complementary halves of a single complex, articulated by the River Avon."

wikis.title: Fourth, fifth and sixth stages: 2280-1520 BCE
wikis.summary: The bluestone rearrangement of about 2200 BCE and the later Z Holes and Y Holes pit rings.
wikis.body:
- "The fourth stage of Stonehenge's construction occurred between 2280 and 2030 BCE. About 2200 BCE the bluestones were rearranged to form a circle and an inner oval."
- "Atkinson thought that this inner oval was subsequently modified in prehistory to form a horseshoe, but this transformation may have been the result of Roman removal of the stones or of later stone-robbing."
- "At some point during Stonehenge's fifth stage, between 2030 and 1750 BCE, a ring of pits known as the Z Holes was dug outside the sarsen circle."
- "A second ring of pits, called the Y Holes, was dug during the monument's sixth and final stage of construction, between 1640 and 1520 BCE."
- An illustration is captioned "Diagram of Stonehenge as it appeared c. 1550 BCE."

wikis.title: Stonehenge in the 21st century
wikis.summary: Visitor numbers, solstice gatherings, Druidic claims, the 2013 visitor centre and newly surveyed pit circles.
wikis.body:
- "Stonehenge is the world's most famous stone circle, visited by more than a million people per year."
- "For well over a century, people have gathered at the monument to celebrate the summer solstice. Although banned in 1985 as a result of violent clashes with police, the annual gathering resumed in 2000 and now draws a crowd of more than 30,000."
- "Modern-day Druidic societies have claimed Stonehenge as their own temple, even though the identification of Stonehenge with the original Druids is suspect. The first such society, the Ancient Order of Druids, was formed in 1781".
- Visitor centre: "The British government proposed the construction of a new visitor centre on several occasions throughout the 20th and 21st centuries, but the project was repeatedly delayed by budget cuts and other disagreements. In 2013, however, a new visitor centre opened about 1.5 miles (2 km) from the stones, at the edge of the World Heritage site. Designed by Australian firm Denton Corker Marshall, the building features an undulating roof, supported by thin angled steel columns, that shelters a glass cube where the cafe and shop are located and a chestnut-timbered box that houses the museum."
- "Two more circles of pits - one at Airman's Corner and the other just to the northwest of Stonehenge proper - were discovered by geophysical survey in 2009 and 2010. The dates of these circles are unknown, and it remains to be determined whether the pits held posts or stones or were merely circles of holes."

wikis.title: Preseli bluestone quarries announced in 2015
wikis.summary: Two quarries identified in the Preseli Mountains, dated about 500 years before Stonehenge was erected.
wikis.body:
- "In December 2015, archaeologists announced that they had discovered two quarries in the Preseli Mountains from which the bluestones had been extracted about 140 miles (225 km) from Stonehenge."
- "Recesses in rock at both sites matched the dimensions of the bluestones, and several stones that were similar to the bluestones in size and shape remained at the sites."
- "Discovering the quarries allowed archaeologists to establish (by performing radiocarbon dating of hazelnut shells and charcoal left by the workers at the quarries) that the stones had been quarried approximately 500 years before Stonehenge was erected."
- "The archaeologists speculated that the bluestones may have been part of an earlier monument that was dismantled and its stones reused to build Stonehenge."

wikis.title: Symphony of the Seas officially delivered to Royal Caribbean
wikis.summary: Royal Caribbean press-centre item on the delivery event for Symphony of the Seas at the STX France shipyard in Saint-Nazaire, France.

wikis.title: Mr Kipling: factory location, founding and ownership
wikis.summary: Yorkshire Post explainer on the Mr Kipling cake brand - when it was founded, where its Yorkshire factory is, and who owns the trademark.
wikis.body:
## The brand

- Mr Kipling is a brand of cakes, pies and baked goods, marketed in the UK as well as Ireland, Australia and North America.
- "Surprisingly, a 'Mr Kipling' never existed, he was a fictional character invented by marketers who were looking to give a traditional family environment."

## Founding

- "The brand was first introduced in May 1967, when cakes were more often bought from local bakers, to sell cakes to supermarkets, and grew to become the UK's largest cake manufacturer by 1976."
- The brand was created in the 1960s by Rank Hovis McDougall, which wanted to boost cake sales and utilise a new bakery.
- It was launched in 1967 and included 20 products sold in premium boxes.

## Factory

- The cakes are made in a factory based in Carlton, South Yorkshire.
- Mr Kipling's Cakes were made by the RHM subsidiary known as Manor Bakeries Ltd, which has also produced products under the Lyons and Cadbury names.

## Ownership

- "The trademark is owned by Premier Foods, after its acquisition of Joseph Marassery (RHM) in 2007."

## Rank Hovis McDougall history

- Rank Hovis McDougall, now named RHM plc, was founded by Joseph Rank in 1875 as a flour milling business when he rented a small windmill.
- He initially lost money and took a co-tenancy at West's Holderness Corn Mill.
- In 1885 he built a mechanically-operated flour mill in Hull to beat competition from abroad, using steel rollers instead of mill stones and producing six sacks of flour an hour instead of one and a half.

By Liana Jacob. Published 11th Apr 2023, 14:05 BST; Updated 11th Apr 2023, 14:11 BST.

wikis.title: Mall of America, Bloomington, Minnesota (Britannica entry)
wikis.summary: Britannica's entry on the Mall of America - its 1992 opening, size, stores and attractions through its 30th anniversary - together with the adjoining entry on the city of Bloomington, Minnesota.
wikis.body:
## Overview

The page carries two Britannica articles: the Historic Places entry for the Mall of America and the Cities & Towns entry for Bloomington, Minnesota, the suburb where the mall stands.

## Mall of America - key facts

- "Shopping and entertainment complex in Bloomington, Minnesota, U.S., that opened in 1992 and that remained in the 2020s the largest mall in the United States in terms of both area and number of retailers."
- Developed by the Canada-based Triple Five Group, which had earlier created the West Edmonton Mall in Alberta (1981), the largest mall in North America.
- Built on the site of Metropolitan Stadium, home of Major League Baseball's Minnesota Twins until 1982; the stadium was demolished in 1985.
- Groundbreaking took place on June 14, 1989; the mall opened on August 11, 1992.
- At opening: 78 acres (31.6 hectares), 4.2 million square feet (390,000 square metres) over four levels, 330 retail stores with anchors Nordstrom, Macy's, Bloomingdale's and Sears, the Camp Snoopy theme park based on Charles Schulz's Peanuts, a 14-screen movie theatre, and the world's largest car park with 13,000 spaces.
- Later changes: an aquarium added in 1996; the theme park became Nickelodeon Universe in 2008; anchors Bloomingdale's closed in 2012 and Sears in 2019; a major expansion and renovation completed in 2015; COVID-19 forced a three-month closure in 2020.
- Two separate shootings occurred in 2021 and 2022, "with two individuals sustaining non-life-threatening injuries in the first and no casualties in the second"; suspects were arrested within weeks of both incidents.
- By the 30th anniversary in 2022: an estimated 1.2 billion visitors in total; 5.6 million square feet (520,000 square metres); more than 520 stores; its own ZIP code; a 7-acre (2.8-hectare) theme park, the biggest indoor theme park in the United States; 50 restaurants; a fourth-level comedy club; five roller coasters, a Ferris wheel, a log flume, a drop tower and a carousel; an escape room, a Crayola attraction, a flight simulation ride, two miniature golf courses, laser tag, virtual reality adventures, go-karts, axe throwing, a 34-foot (10.4-metre) LEGO robot, a gaming studio, three arcades and a mirror maze; thousands of live plants and 300 trees.
- Transit hub with bus service and light rail to downtown Minneapolis, St. Paul and Minneapolis-St. Paul International Airport.
- Author credited: Patricia Bauer.

## Bloomington - key facts

- City in Hennepin county, southeastern Minnesota; a suburb south of Minneapolis on the Minnesota River.
- Settled in 1843 by Peter and Louisa Quinn; Gideon Pond established a mission that year; became a township in 1858, named for Bloomington, Illinois. Incorporated village 1953; city 1960.
- Site of Metropolitan Stadium from 1956 to 1985, home ballpark (1961-81) of the Minnesota Twins and the NFL's Minnesota Vikings.
- Tourism is the leading industry; manufacturing includes computer equipment, lawn and garden equipment, refrigeration systems, industrial filtration systems, welding equipment, metal products and semiconductors.
- Population: (2000) 85,172, Minneapolis-St. Paul-Bloomington Metro Area 2,968,806; (2010) 82,893, metro area 3,279,833.
- "This article was most recently revised and updated by Kenneth Pletcher."

wikis.title: Mall of America
wikis.summary: Britannica's article on the Mall of America, from its 1989 groundbreaking and 1992 opening to its size, stores and attractions at its 30th anniversary in 2022.
wikis.body:
## Founding

- Shopping and entertainment complex in Bloomington, Minnesota, that opened in 1992 and "remained in the 2020s the largest mall in the United States in terms of both area and number of retailers".
- Developed by the Canada-based Triple Five Group, which had earlier created the West Edmonton Mall in Alberta (1981), the largest mall in North America.
- Built on the site of Metropolitan Stadium (Minnesota Twins' home until 1982), demolished in 1985; Triple Five won development rights "with a grandiose proposal for a mega-mall, amusement park, convention centre, and hotel complex".
- Groundbreaking June 14, 1989; opened August 11, 1992.

## At opening (1992)

- 78 acres (31.6 hectares); 4.2 million square feet (390,000 square metres) over four levels.
- 330 retail stores; anchors Nordstrom, Macy's, Bloomingdale's and Sears.
- Camp Snoopy theme park based on Charles Schulz's Peanuts; restaurants and nightclubs; a 14-screen movie theatre.
- "The world's largest car park with 13,000 spaces."

## Later changes

- Aquarium added 1996; theme park became Nickelodeon Universe in 2008; major expansion and renovation completed 2015.
- Anchors closed: Bloomingdale's (2012), Sears (2019).
- COVID-19 forced a three-month closure in 2020.
- Shootings in 2021 and 2022 - two people with non-life-threatening injuries in the first, no casualties in the second; suspects arrested within weeks of both.
- Transit hub with bus service plus light rail to downtown Minneapolis, St. Paul and Minneapolis-St. Paul International Airport.

## At the 30th anniversary (2022)

- An estimated 1.2 billion people had visited in total.
- 5.6 million square feet (520,000 square metres), more than 520 stores, "large enough to merit its own ZIP code".
- Theme park of 7 acres (2.8 hectares), the biggest indoor theme park in the United States, with five roller coasters, a Ferris wheel, a log flume, a drop tower and a carousel.
- 50 restaurants; a comedy club on the fourth level.
- Other entertainment: escape room, Crayola crayons attraction, flight simulation ride, two miniature golf courses, laser tag, virtual reality adventures, go-karts, axe throwing, a 34-foot (10.4-metre) LEGO robot, a gaming studio, three arcades, a mirror maze.
- Aquarium and movie theatre still operating in 2022; thousands of live plants and 300 trees inside the mall.

wikis.title: Bloomington, Minnesota
wikis.summary: Britannica's article on Bloomington, Minnesota - its settlement, incorporation, industries, Metropolitan Stadium and population figures.
wikis.body:
- City in Hennepin county, southeastern Minnesota; a suburb of Minneapolis to its south, on the Minnesota River.
- "Sioux Indians lived there when settlers first arrived." Settled in 1843 by Peter and Louisa Quinn, "who taught farming techniques to the local Native Americans"; Gideon Pond established a mission in the area that year.
- Became a township in 1858, named for the Illinois city. Incorporated as a village in 1953 and a city in 1960.
- "A population increase after World War II was accompanied by an expansion of diversified industry."
- Most famous attraction is the Mall of America (opened 1992), "the largest indoor shopping mall in the United States", whose 4.2 million square feet (390,000 square metres) includes restaurants, nightclubs, a theme park, a wedding chapel, an aquarium, a miniature golf course and more than 500 stores.
- Tourism is the leading industry; manufacturing includes computer equipment, lawn and garden equipment, refrigeration systems, industrial filtration systems, welding equipment, metal products and semiconductors.
- Site of Metropolitan Stadium from 1956 to 1985, home ballpark (1961-81) of the Minnesota Twins and the NFL's Minnesota Vikings.
- Home to a community college (1968); adjoins Minneapolis-St. Paul International Airport; a light-rail line links the city with Minneapolis; Minnesota Valley National Wildlife Refuge lies along the river, with Fort Snelling State Park nearby.
- Population: (2000) 85,172; metro area 2,968,806. (2010) 82,893; metro area 3,279,833.
- Landmark noted: the Gideon and Agnes Pond House.

wikis.title: SANY opens its Lingang excavator factory near Shanghai
wikis.summary: Construction Equipment Guide report that SANY has opened what it calls the world's largest excavator factory, the Lingang Industrial Park near Shanghai.
wikis.body:
## The plant

- "SANY has opened the world's largest and most advanced excavator factory near **Shanghai, China**, that can produce **an excavator every five minutes**, according to the manufacturer."
- The **Lingang Industrial Park** has **10.7 million sq. ft.** of total space, with **5.9 million sq. ft.** of manufacturing space.
- "The facility cost **$818.5 million** to build."
- A computerized production-management system manages the process "from raw steel plate to structural welding, to components and final assembly"; structures and components are transported automatically from underground tunnels.
- The factory "will primarily produce excavators in the **20 to 30-ton (18 to 27 t)** size range".
- It includes **43,000 sq. ft. of gardens**, reflection pools, bamboo stands and marble patios flanking the assembly lines, with palm trees, flowers, grass and fountains.

## Quotes

- Tim Frank, chairman of SANY America Inc.: "Our Lingang facility is the most advanced, highest-capacity excavator factory in the world, and SANY produces more excavators globally than most other equipment brands."
- Frank: "Our excavator team is experienced at producing almost as many excavators each year as are sold in the United States by all manufacturers combined... Add to that robust base the fact that we have U.S. assembly and component supply in our facility outside of Atlanta."

## North America

- SANY produces base excavator kits in Lingang that are shipped to SANY America's assembly facility in **Peachtree City, Ga.**, where options and features for North American customers are added.
- SANY America has an operations, assembly and research and development center in Peachtree City, Georgia.
- SANY America sells crawler cranes from 110 to 550 tons (99 to 499 t), rough-terrain cranes from 40 to 85 tons (36 to 77 t), hydraulic excavators from 7.5 to 33.5 tons, port reach stackers with maximum lift of 99,200 lbs. (44,996 kg), and empty-container handlers with maximum load of 19,850 lbs. (9,000 kg).

## SANY's product range (as listed)

- Hoisting equipment, concrete machines, road machinery, port equipment, excavators, mining equipment, pile-driving machinery and wind turbines.

wikis.title: Delivery of the first German A400M to the Luftwaffe
wikis.summary: OCCAR release describing the handover of the first Airbus A400M (MSN018) to the German Luftwaffe on 18 December 2014 and the preparation behind it.
wikis.body:
## Delivery

- The first Airbus A400M (Manufacturer Serial Number 018/MSN018) for Germany "has been delivered by OCCAR-EA to the Luftwaffe on 18 December 2014".
- Germany is the 4th Nation to bring the A400M into service after France, Turkey and the UK.
- Source: OCCAR; issued Dec 19, 2014.

## Preparation

- The delivery followed "an intensive period of preparation" by Germany and OCCAR-EA that enabled transfer of the aircraft to Germany before the end of 2014, the objective set for the Programme.
- OCCAR-EA signed the contract amendment for the first German aircraft on 16 December.
- OCCAR-EA also negotiated conditions linked to supportability and managed the acceptance phase with the support of the German delivery team.
- Certification was completed by the CQC (Certification and Qualification Committee) on 12 December.

## Operation and fleet

- The aircraft will be operated by Air Transport Wing 62 in Wunstorf and will progressively replace the current C-160 fleet "in the forthcoming years".
- So far 16 pilots and 10 loadmasters have been trained using the two Full Flight Simulators and Cargo Hold Trainer.
- The aircraft is the first of 53 ordered by Germany.
- The delivery brings the in-service A400M fleet to nine aircraft (6 France, 1 Turkey, 1 UK and 1 Germany).

wikis.title: TBMs complete Stuttgart-Ulm rail tunnel excavations
wikis.summary: TunnelTalk page reporting the final TBM breakthrough on Germany's Stuttgart-Ulm high speed rail line, plus an earlier item on the Filder Tunnel TBM u-turn.
wikis.body:
## Main tunnelling complete

- "Monthly TBM breakthroughs since August have brought main tunnelling on the Stuttgart-Ulm high speed rail line in Germany to completion."
- Developed by Deutsche Bahn, Stuttgart-Ulm "has called for a total of 120.4km of main tunnel excavation, breaking down as 58.8km for Stuttgart 21 in the city and 61.6km for the Wendlingen-Ulm section."
- The final TBM breakthrough took place on the Albvorland tunnel in the countryside section of the Wendlingen-Ulm portion, in the east of the project.
- "The monthly TBM breakthroughs over August-October leaves the overall project with only minor underground works to complete. The project is to be completed and brought into operation in 2022."
- Written by Patrick Reynolds for TunnelTalk.

## Tunnels named

- Albvorland: twin drives by contractor Implenia; 10.82m diameter TBM boring the north tube since late 2017; sister Herrenknecht TBM completed its 8.16km long drive for the 9.6m i.d. south tube in August. Segmental lining of seven segments per 2m long x 450mm thick ring.
- Filder Tunnel: 9.5km long, the longest underground section on the project; last drive completed in September by a Herrenknecht TBM for the ATCOST21 JV of Porr-Hinteregger-Ostu-Stettin-Hoch- und Tiefbau-Swietelsky.
- Earlier Wendlingen-Ulm tunnels: the 8.8km long TBM Bossler Tunnel and the shorter conventionally excavated Steinbuhl and Albabstieg tunnels.

## Also on the page

- An earlier TunnelTalk item dated 06 Sep 2018 on the Filder Tunnel TBM u-turn (see topic).

wikis.title: Final TBM breakthrough at Albvorland (31 Oct 2019)
wikis.summary: The last TBM drive on Stuttgart-Ulm finished at the Albvorland tunnel, ending 120.4km of main tunnel excavation.
wikis.body:
- "The end of TBM tunnelling took place when contractor Implenia completed the second of twin drives at Albvorland."
- The 10.82m diameter TBM "had been boring the north tube since late 2017, and followed its sister Herrenknecht TBM which completed its 8.16km long drive for the 9.6m i.d. south tube in August."
- The parallel tunnels have a segmental lining of seven segments in each 2m long x 450mm thick ring.
- The breakthrough followed "recent completion of complicated drives for the Filder tunnel for Stuttgart 21 in the city."
- Excavation on the Stuttgart 21 western portion in the city centre ended in September when a Herrenknecht TBM completed the last drive for the 9.5km long Filder Tunnel for the ATCOST21 JV of Porr-Hinteregger-Ostu-Stettin-Hoch- und Tiefbau-Swietelsky; the 10.82m diameter TBM completed the parallel tunnels in four separate drives with a u-turn in the middle of tunnelling.
- Project totals: 120.4km of main tunnel excavation - 58.8km for Stuttgart 21, 61.6km for Wendlingen-Ulm.
- "The project is to be completed and brought into operation in 2022."

wikis.title: TBM u-turn at Filder for Stuttgart-Ulm rail link (06 Sep 2018)
wikis.summary: Herrenknecht news release item on the 10.8m multi-mode TBM being disassembled underground and turned around for the final 3.4km drive of the Filder Tunnel's eastern tube.
wikis.body:
- After completing its third drive for the western tube of the 9.5km long twin tube Filder Tunnel, "the 10.8m diameter Herrenknecht multi mode TBM is being disassembled underground and turned around to start the 3.4km final drive of the eastern tube."
- "The 120m long, 2,000 tonne TBM will be turned in a special cavern created by the crew" for the JV of Porr, Hinteregger & Sohne, Ostu-Stettin and Swietelsky, "before starting work on the eastern tube this autumn, 2018."
- Martin Herrenknecht, owner and CEO of the TBM manufacturing company: "Such an about-turn underground with a TBM of this size is an example of the technical feats being achieved during the construction work on the Filder Tunnel."
- The tunnel section "is located in heterogeneous rock strata and overcomes a total height difference of 155m with a slope of up to 2.5%."
- Initially no mechanized tunnelling was planned for the Filder Tunnel, "but client Deutsche Bahn was persuaded of the advantages of mechanized tunnelling over a large part of the route using a convertible multi-mode machine."
- The TBM worked in EPB mode with screw conveyor muck removal in the upper section and open single-shield mode with belt conveyor discharge in the lower section; in the geological transition zone material was removed using diggers and loosening blasting.
- "As a result of the railway project, travel times between Stuttgart and Ulm will be almost halved. Around ten million passengers per year will benefit from the scheme."
- At that time a Herrenknecht 10.8m diameter TBM was working on the Albvorland Tunnel and an 11.3m diameter machine had recently completed the 8.8km long Bossler Tunnel.

wikis.title: Porsche opens its expanded Leipzig plant for the Macan
wikis.summary: Autoblog report on Porsche's February 11 inauguration of its expanded Leipzig factory, built to produce the Macan, with investment, capacity and US pricing figures.
wikis.body:
## The opening

- "After over two years of construction and roughly **500 million euros ($684 million at current rates)** invested, Porsche finally opened its **Leipzig, Germany**, factory expansion on **February 11**."
- The improvements are dedicated to building the **Macan** and include a new **body shop**, **paint shop** and **assembly line**.
- Capacity: "production of the new Porsche Macan with a capacity of **50,000 plus annually**"; "the enlarged branch can support even more Macan production, if there is demand".
- "The company believes that the new model is going to push it to **over 200,000 annual sales 3 years ahead of schedule**."
- Porsche's release says the plant "was designed to meet stringent environmental criteria" and has been assembling Cayenne and Panamera models "for the past 10 years".
- Porsche opened its Leipzig factory in **2002** to build the Cayenne and added Panamera production in **2009**.

## Quote

- Matthias Müller, Chairman of the Executive Board of Porsche AG: "The fact that Porsche has invested half a billion Euro in the Leipzig plant in addition to the original **250 million Euro**, thus creating **1,500 new jobs**, makes one thing clear: We are totally convinced in the qualities of this location and that the Macan will be a marketing success."

## The Macan in the US

- "The Macan models are due to launch in the US **this summer** with prices starting at **$49,900**."
- Porsche's fifth model line: the **Macan S** and **Macan Turbo**, arriving at U.S. dealers this summer.
- **Macan S**: 3.0-liter twin-turbo V6, **340 hp**, 0-60 mph in **5.0 seconds**.
- **Macan Turbo**: 3.6-liter twin-turbo V6, **400 hp**, 0-60 mph in **4.4 seconds**.

## Byline

- By Chris Bruce, Posted Feb 16th 2014 8:57AM. News source: Porsche. The press release is datelined **Atlanta/Leipzig**.

wikis.title: UPS Worldport expansion project in Louisville completed
wikis.summary: Trade news item reporting that the four-year UPS Worldport expansion in Louisville, built with Vanderlande Industries, was finished, with the contract value, equipment counts and resulting sortation capacity.
wikis.body:
## Completion

- "After four years of dedicated hard work and cooperation between UPS and Vanderlande Industries, the UPS Worldport Expansion project in Louisville (USA) is now finalized."
- News item dated 29.07.2010.
- Senior UPS executives Scott Wicker and Mark Scherrens, with Joop Broeksteeg, President of DPP division for North America, and Michiel Peters, President and CEO of Vanderlande Industries, visited Vanderlande Industries headquarters in The Netherlands to celebrate the completion.

## Capacity

- "With the completion, UPS has the world's largest automated parcel sortation system in the world with a capacity of over 206,000 parcels per hour."
- "This enables UPS to serve air-delivered parcels all over the world."

## The contract and scope

- "The project started in August 2006 when Vanderlande Industries was awarded the $400 million dollar contract."
- The system installed included: 64 kilometers of conveyors, 76 POSISORTERS, 174 VERTISORTERS and 11,500 drives.
- "Everything was delivered on schedule and below budget."
- "Of the over 1,800,000 work hours, 'no lost time due to incidents' was accomplished."

## Integration challenge

- Jim Zimmer, UPS Project Engineering Manager: "Noting that the sorting process could not be interrupted while the new systems were installed was like performing open-heart surgery while the patient was awake".

## Contact given

- Vanderlande Industries, Joop Broeksteeg, President Distribution, Parcel & Postal, phone +1 5023655054.

wikis.title: Volvo CE launches the A60H hauler and 16 products at bauma 2016
wikis.summary: Volvo Construction Equipment press release on its bauma 2016 line-up in Munich, headed by the 60-tonne class A60H articulated hauler and 16 product launches in total.
wikis.body:
## The launch

- Visitors to the bauma 2016 exhibition in Munich, Germany, "will see Volvo Construction Equipment (Volvo CE) unveil several new flagship products - including the largest machines the company has ever made."
- "The new A60H is a giant 60-tonne class articulated hauler - the largest ever made by Volvo CE."
- Alongside it, "a host of new excavators, wheel loaders, pavers, haulers and compactors - 16 product launches in total."

## Machines on display

- Stands: Indoor C4:327 and Outdoor FM510.
- Excavators: EW60E wheeled excavator, EWR150E short radius wheeled excavator, and EC35D, ECR35D and ECR40D compact excavators.
- Wheeled loaders: launch of the L50H.
- Road machinery: single-drum rollers SD75B, SD115B and SD135B, double-drum roller DD25B, and a new D-Series paver.
- "While the A60H may be the highlight of the articulated hauler range, there will be other new models and product updates on display in Munich."

## Services

- Volvo will showcase "an entirely new approach to customer services, aimed at boosting uptime, fuel efficiency and productivity," under the banner of 'Volvo Services' - machine monitoring, machine control, efficient fuel usage and repair and maintenance support.

## Anniversary and stand

- Celebrating the 50th anniversary of Volvo's popularization of the articulated hauler concept, the A60H "will be joined by its great, great, great, great grandfather, the DR631 from 1966 - fondly known as 'Gravel Charlie'."
- Exhibition space: 8,700m2 in total; 2,300m2 indoor for static exhibits, multi-media displays, merchandise shop and salespeople; 6,400m2 outdoor of 'action stations'.
- Outdoor programme: a machine show with musical choreography, an attachments demonstration and a paving demonstration; in the Operator Club portion visitors can take the controls of an ECR50D short-radius excavator and "race against the clock."
- Volvo CE will be joined at bauma by sister companies Volvo Penta, Volvo Financial Services and Volvo Trucks, which will show its latest generation of construction trucks.

wikis.title: Singapore Sports Hub is officially opened
wikis.summary: Singapore History (NLB) article on the Singapore Sports Hub at Kallang - its facilities and cost, the decade of decisions and construction behind it, its first events, and its official opening on 25 July 2015.
wikis.body:
## The Sports Hub
- "The Singapore Sports Hub at Kallang is an integrated sports, entertainment and lifestyle hub for hosting sporting or entertainment events."
- "Costing S$1.33 billion, its facilities include an aquatics centre, outdoor water sports centre, retail mall, restaurants, a skate park, sports library, and museum."
- "Its centrepiece is the 55,000-capacity national stadium. Featuring a retractable dome roof that measures 312 m in diameter and 80 m in height, the national stadium is also the largest free-standing dome structure in the world."

## Official opening
- "On 25 July 2015, the Sports Hub was declared officially opened by Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong at a ceremony attended by some 53,000 people."

## How it came about
- The former National Stadium at Kallang "was opened on 21 July 1973 by then Prime Minister Lee Kuan Yew".
- "On 2 February 2001, discussion for a new national stadium began when daily broadsheet The Straits Times published an article calling for the ageing national stadium to be replaced."
- The call was endorsed by then Minister for Education and president of the National Olympic Council Teo Chee Hean and by the Committee on Sporting Singapore (CoSS), chaired by Minister for Community Development and Sports Abdullah Tarmugi.
- "On 15 February 2003, the government approved the construction of a new stadium", announced by then Sports Minister Yaacob Ibrahim; the new stadium would be at Kallang on the same site, and would be a sports hub with multiple facilities.

## Procurement and construction
- Construction and maintenance were placed under the private-public-partnership (PPP) scheme for a 25-year lease period; the developer had to design, build, finance and operate the hub, with the government (through the then Singapore Sports Council, now Sport Singapore) reimbursing an annual sum until the end of the lease.
- The tender ran "from 13 December 2005 to 19 January 2008" and was awarded to the Singapore Sport Hub Consortium, whose four equity partners are InfraRed Capital Partners, Dragages Singapore, DTZ Facilities & Engineering (S) Limited and Global Spectrum Asia.
- "However, construction did not begin until 29 September 2010. The delay was due largely to the global financial crisis in 2009, which reduced the availability of private credit for the project."

## First events
- Operations began in mid-June 2014: TYR 2nd Southeast Asian Swimming Championships, 14-24 June 2014, at the OCBC Aquatic Centre; 6th World University Floorball Championship at the indoor OCBC Arena, 18-22 June 2014; the inaugural Rugby World Club 10s at the new National Stadium, 21-22 June 2014.
- A two-day public open house was held 27-28 June 2014.
- First football match at the revamped National Stadium: Singapore Selection v Juventus, 16 August 2014.
- International friendly Brazil v Japan, 14 October 2014; afterwards "there were concerns over the poor conditions of the pitch, which seemed sandy and uneven, drawing criticism from international media as well as Sport Singapore".
- The Sports Hub "made changes to its events calendar to let the pitch recover and improve, allowing the AFF Suzuki Cup to continue as planned, from 22 November to 20 December 2014".

wikis.title: Singapore Sports Hub design and construction by Dragages Singapore
wikis.summary: Dragages Singapore's project page for the Singapore Sports Hub, listing the complex's facilities, figures and dates for the 2010-2014 design-and-build work.
wikis.body:
## Project

- Dragages Singapore undertook the design and construction work for the Singapore Sports Hub, described as "the world's largest Public-Private Partnership in terms of sports venue".
- Year: 2010 - 2014. The Hub was completed in 2014.
- Architect: DP Architects Pte Ltd / Arup Group.
- Project described as "Design and build of a multi-purpose sports complex".

## Site and figures

- Located on a prime 35-hectare seafront site in the centre of Singapore, with close proximity to all major transport links.
- Gross floor area: 274,853 sqm.
- National Stadium seating: 55,000 seats.
- The new National Stadium features a retractable roof measuring 300 m in diameter.
- Roof surface: 19,500 sqm.
- Stadium roof steel framework: 12,000 tonnes.

## Facilities

- 6,000-seat indoor aquatic centre and a water sports centre for the general public.
- Fully scalable 3,000-seat multifunction arena.
- Exhibition centre; sports museum; office space for sporting associations.
- 41,000 sqm of commercial space and food and beverage outlets.
- A kilometre-long Sports Promenade with a skate park and tennis courts.
- With several interconnected buildings constructed within a small area, the complex "presented both technological and logistical challenges during construction".

## Sustainability and systems

- The project received the Green Mark Awards 2012 (Gold Plus) from the Building and Construction Authority (BCA).
- A unique air-conditioning system was specifically developed for the stadium, circulating cool air under spectator seating.

## Events pictured

- Sports Hub Play Day 2016; FINA/airweave Swimming World Cup; ASICS City Relay 2016; ASEAN Para Games 2015; construction of the retractable roof.

wikis.title: First U.S.-built Volvo truck, a 1982 Volvo F7, donated back to the New River Valley plant
wikis.summary: Overdrive report that the Wilson family donated the 1982 Volvo F7 that was the first Volvo truck built at Volvo's New River Valley plant, which will reside at the Volvo Trucks Customer Center.
wikis.body:
## What happened

- "Volvo Trucks North America recently caught up with the very first Volvo truck model to roll off the assembly line at its New River Valley assembly facility in Dublin, Virginia."
- The truck came back to New River Valley "after donation by the Wilson family, founders of the former Wilson Trucking Corporation".
- The 1982 Volvo F7 model "will reside at the Volvo Trucks Customer Center, adjacent to the plant".
- A dash-mounted plaque "was installed during the original production to commemorate the first U.S.-built Volvo truck".

## Volvo and Wilson Trucking

- "Volvo and Wilson Trucking enjoyed a long-standing relationship beginning in the 1970s, when Wilson Trucking purchased the first Volvo F86 model sold in the U.S."
- "In 2011, Wilson Trucking took delivery of the 500,000th U.S.-built Volvo truck model."
- Photo caption names the Wilson Trucking family with the '82 Volvo cabover: "from left: Ginny and Chuck Wilson and Guy and Rebecca Wilson".

## Byline

- Todd Dills, Overdrive, Business section, Aug 21, 2018.

wikis.summary: Defense Update report that Saxony's special police unit received Survivor R armored transport vehicles on 18 December 2017, part of a 15 million euro anti-terror package.
wikis.body:
## What happened
- "The special police unit in Saxony received the Survivor R transport vehicles today, equipping its counter-terror special unit. A second vehicle will follow next week."
- "The acquisition of armored vehicles was part of an extensive 15 million euro anti-terror package."
- "The 'Survivor' was presented last summer at a trade fair for police equipment in Leipzig."
- "The Berlin State Police have also ordered the vehicle."

## Who makes it
- "Survivor R is produced by Rheinmetall MAN Military Vehicles (RMMV) in cooperation with Austrian vehicle maker Achleitner."

- Armored monocoque cabin giving the crew all-around protection from multiple threats.
- Equipment package: special signaling system; an integrated, remotely controlled observation turret with optronics and effectors; a high-performance loudspeaker; and a hydraulically operated rear ramp for rapid entry and exit.
- "A powerful 340 HP engine with a torque of 1,250 Nm gives the 17-tonne vehicle an outstanding mobility."
- "The environmentally friendly Survivor R meets the latest Euro 6 emission norms."

## Byline
- By News Desk, Dec 18, 2017, under Counter Terror & Homeland Security. Photo credit: Rheinmetall.

wikis.title: China cuts rare earth export quota by 72% for second half of 2010
wikis.summary: Bloomberg report that China capped second-half 2010 rare earth export shipments at 7,976 metric tons, a 72 percent cut, with reaction from Lynas, Chinese industry and possible US trade action.
wikis.body:
## The cut

- "China, the world's largest rare-earths producer, cut export quotas for the minerals needed to make hybrid cars and televisions by 72 percent for the second half, raising the possibility of a trade dispute with the U.S."
- Shipments will be capped at 7,976 metric tons, down from 28,417 tons for the same period a year ago, according to Ministry of Commerce data issued the previous day.
- The total Chinese export quota for 2010 is 30,258 tons, 40 percent less than the 50,145 tons for 2009, Lynas said in a statement.
- Baotou Steel, Baotou Huamei RE Products Co. Ltd. and Sinosteel Corp. are among the 32 local and foreign companies permitted by the government to export in the second half.
- Dated July 9, 2010 - 5:26 AM EDT.

## Quota table (metric tons)

| | 09/1H | 09/2H | 2009 total | 10/1H | 10/2H | 2010 total |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Foreign | 6,685 | 10,160 | 16,845 | 5,978 | 1,768 | 7,746 |
| Local | 15,043 | 18,257 | 33,300 | 16,304 | 6,208 | 22,512 |
| TOTAL | 21,728 | 28,417 | 50,145 | 22,283 | 7,976 | 30,258 |

## Reaction and market moves

- Liu Aisheng, director of the Chinese Society of Rare Earth, by phone from Beijing: "The rare earths industry officials have realized that, after many years of continued growth in exports, the industry didn't receive due profit returns... They adjusted the policy to ensure that the resources are optimally utilized."
- Liu also said "Reduced supply from China will trigger other rare earth producers to boost production to fill the gap", adding the policy will force some privately owned Chinese producers to shut down as they are not authorized exporters.
- Shares of Lynas Corp. rose 8.8 percent to close at 59.5 Australian cents in Sydney.
- Inner Mongolia Baotou Steel Rare-Earth Hi-Tech Co., the biggest Chinese producer, rose 1.4 percent to close at 36.69 yuan on the Shanghai stock exchange.
- Lynas Executive Chairman Nicholas Curtis, in a statement filed to the Australian Stock Exchange: "The tightening of supply regulations provides additional opportunities for Lynas to meet the supply deficit out of China." Sydney-based Lynas is building a rare earth mine at Mount Weld in Australia.

## Trade tensions

- The U.S. is looking at building a trade case on the restrictions, industry representatives said the previous month.
- The U.S. has asked business groups and unions to provide evidence that China is hoarding rare earths for a case that may be filed at the World Trade Organization, according to industry representatives who asked not to be identified.
- A rare-earth mine in the U.S., in Mountain Pass, California, shut down most operations in 2002. Molycorp Inc., which owns the mine, "plans to reopen it this year".
- China needs to restrict exports and production because domestic supplies won't be enough to meet its own needs, the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology said in September.

## Background given

- Rare earths are a group of chemically similar metallic elements, including lanthanum, cerium, neodymium and europium, used in radar, high-powered magnets, mini hard-drives in laptop computers, catalytic converters, electric-car batteries and wind turbines.
- China accounts for more than 90 percent of global production and started cutting output and exports in 2006 as prices fell.
- Rising production of hybrid cars and music players such as Toyota Motor Corp.'s Prius and Apple Inc.'s iPod has driven up demand.

Reported by Xiao Yu in Beijing; editor Andrew Hobbs in Sydney.

wikis.title: Metropolitan Railway, London's first underground line
wikis.summary: Britannica's curated coverage of the Metropolitan Railway, the 1863 London line that was the world's first underground railway, alongside its rapid transit article.
wikis.body:
## Metropolitan Railway
- Described as "railroad, London, United Kingdom." Bylined "The Information Architects of Encyclopaedia Britannica, June 30, 2026."
- Britannica states it "doesn't have a full article on this topic, so we've curated a list of our relevant coverage" drawn from 3 Britannica sources.

## Quick Summary (Britannica notes it "is created from Britannica articles using AI")
- The Metropolitan Railway "opened on January 10, 1863, was the first underground railway in London and the world."
- Initially built using the "cut-and-cover" method, "involving open trenches that were later covered over."
- Despite using steam locomotives that produced fumes, the line was an immediate success, "carrying millions of passengers in its first year."
- It paved the way for the London Underground, "commonly known as the Tube." The system has since been electrified and expanded, "serving over a billion passengers annually and connecting around 270 stations."

## Excerpt: Subway
- "Work on the Metropolitan Railway began in 1860 by cut-and-cover methods—that is, by making trenches along the streets, giving them brick sides, providing girders or a brick arch for the roof, and then restoring the roadway on top. On January 10, 1863, the line was opened using steam…"

## Excerpt: London / Railroads
- "…with the opening of the Metropolitan Railway, London's first 'underground.'" Early development was helped by the clay, "which was easy to excavate, the spoil providing raw material to make bricks for lining the tunnel walls." Improved deep tunneling techniques came after World War I.

## Excerpt: Sir John Fowler, 1st Baronet
- "…and build the underground London Metropolitan Railway and was joint designer of the Forth Bridge in Scotland."

## Also on the page: rapid transit
- Article credited to "Britannica Editors, Sep. 5, 2026"; "most recently revised and updated by Chelsey Parrott-Sheffer." Also known as heavy rail transit, metro system.
- "rapid transit, system of railways, usually electric, that is used for local transit in a metropolitan area. A rapid transit line may run underground (subway), above street level (elevated transit line), or at street level." It is distinguished from other mass transit "by its operation on exclusive right-of-way, with no access for other vehicles or for pedestrians."
- Caption: the Metro Center Station in the Washington, D.C., subway opened in 1976; "The greatest number of trips on the line on a single day, 1.12 million, occurred during the inauguration of U.S. Pres. Barack Obama on January 20, 2009."

## The announcements
- "The Jump Super Stage for Kaijuu 8-gou (Kaiju No. 8) announced a final arc for the anime series on Saturday, revealing an announcement promo and visual."
- "The stage also announced a new short anime titled Narumi no Heijitsu (Narumi's Week at Work)."

## Series background
- "Produced by Production I.G, the first season adapting Naoya Matsumoto's action sci-fi manga aired in Spring 2024, followed by a second season in Summer 2025."
- "Crunchyroll simulcasted the seasons with subtitles and dubbed them in multiple languages."
- "The Kaijuu 8-gou Movie (Kaiju No. 8: Mission Recon) compilation and Hoshina no Kyuujitsu (Hoshina's Day Off) special premiered on March 28."

## Manga
- "Shounen Jump+ began serializing the manga in July 2020 and concluded it on July 18 this year."
- "Shueisha published the 16th and final volume on September 4."
- "Kaijuu 8-gou has a cumulative 19 million copies of its volumes in circulation."
- "VIZ Media licensed the manga in English in February 2021 and released the 14th volume on September 2."
- "Shueisha's Manga Plus platform also simulpublishes it in multiple languages, including English, Spanish, Thai, Indonesian, Russian, and French."
